cards.question: Kandinsky, Mondrian and Hilma af Klint each turned to abstraction within about a decade. What linked them?
options: They had studied one another's work
cards.answer: A shared interest in theosophy. Mondrian joined the Dutch Theosophical Society in 1909; Kandinsky's On the Spiritual in Art of 1911 names Blavatsky's movement; af Klint painted from séances and later followed Rudolf Steiner. None needed the others. A common belief that colour and form could show unseen forces pushed each the same way.
cards.move: When separate people arrive at the same place, look for the road they shared.
cards.trap: Similar results suggest copying, the most direct link one can picture.
cards.reference: Sixten Ringbom, The Sounding Cosmos: A Study in the Spiritualism of Kandinsky and the Genesis of Abstract Painting, Åbo Akademi, 1970

cards.question: Which of these painters was making abstract paintings first?
cards.answer: Hilma af Klint, from 1906, about five years before Kandinsky. She showed the work to almost no one and asked that it stay unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944. Histories of abstraction were written from what hung in Paris, Munich and Moscow; she entered them after a Los Angeles exhibition in 1986.
cards.move: A history can only include what its historians were able to see.
cards.trap: Kandinsky is the name standard histories put first, so it comes first.
cards.reference: Tracey Bashkoff (ed.), Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 2018

cards.question: True or false: Kandinsky's so-called first abstract watercolour, inscribed 1910, is securely dated to that year.
cards.answer: False. Many scholars read it as a study for Composition VII of 1913 and suspect the earlier date was written on later, once being first had begun to matter. Apart from the inscription, little supports 1910. A key date in the story of abstract art rests on the artist's own pencil.
cards.move: A date written by someone who gains from it is a claim, not a record.
cards.trap: Trusting the date on the sheet because the artist himself wrote it.
cards.reference: Vivian Endicott Barnett, Kandinsky Watercolours: Catalogue Raisonné, Volume One 1900-1921, Sotheby's Publications, 1992

cards.question: What did researchers find beneath the paint of Malevich's Black Square in 2015?
cards.answer: Earlier pictures in colour. Tretyakov Gallery researchers using X-rays found traces of two earlier compositions under the black. They also read a faint pencil note on the border echoing a 19th-century Paris joke: an all-black picture titled as a night-time fight in a cellar. Pure abstraction's founding image covers colour and a gag.
cards.move: Before calling a work a pure beginning, look at what lies beneath it.
cards.reference: State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow, technical study of Malevich's Black Square, announced November 2015

cards.question: What revealed that Mondrian's New York City I had been hanging upside down for decades?
cards.answer: The tape, and a photograph. Its strips of coloured tape crowd together at the edge hung as the bottom; a curator argued they belong at the top, like a dense sky. A 1944 photograph of his studio showed it that way round. It still hangs upside down: turning it could loosen the old tape.
cards.move: Something can look right for decades simply because nobody checked the other way.
cards.reference: Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, Düsseldorf, announcement on Mondrian's New York City I, October 2022

cards.question: How did Harvard bring back the lost colour of Rothko's faded murals in 2014 without touching the paint?
cards.answer: With light. The crimson in the five panels, mixed partly with Lithol Red, a fugitive synthetic pigment, had turned pale blue and brown in a sunlit dining room. Conservators photographed the canvases, calculated the missing colour point by point, and projected it back onto them. Switch off the projectors, and it fades again.
cards.move: The gentlest repair is one that can be switched off.
cards.reference: Mary Schneider Enriquez (ed.), Mark Rothko's Harvard Murals, Harvard Art Museums, 2014

cards.question: After several minutes in front of one of Ad Reinhardt's late black paintings, what do attentive viewers begin to see?
options: A cross of slightly different blacks
Their own reflection in the gloss
cards.answer: A cross of slightly different blacks. Each canvas, about 1.5 m square, is divided into nine squares of near-black reds, blues and greens, arranged so that a cross emerges as the eye adapts. He drained oil from his paint to keep the surface matte and free of glare. Photographs almost never show the cross.
cards.move: Some differences appear only to someone willing to keep looking.
cards.trap: Taking black paintings to be plain black, as a glance confirms.
cards.reference: Barbara Rose (ed.), Art as Art: The Selected Writings of Ad Reinhardt, Viking, 1975

cards.question: True or false: Mondrian left the De Stijl group partly because a fellow member started painting diagonal lines?
cards.answer: True. Mondrian held that only horizontals and verticals could express balance. When Theo van Doesburg tilted his lines in the mid-1920s, calling the change Elementarism, Mondrian withdrew from De Stijl around 1925. Yet Mondrian had painted diamond-shaped canvases himself, keeping every line upright inside a tilted frame.
cards.move: The smallest rule in a system is often the one defended hardest.
cards.trap: Doubting that a partnership could break over the angle of a line.
cards.source: Blotkamp, Mondrian: The Art of Destruction, 1994
cards.reference: Carel Blotkamp, Mondrian: The Art of Destruction, Reaktion Books, 1994

cards.question: Kandinsky painted ten large canvases he called Compositions between 1910 and 1939. How many can be seen today?
cards.answer: Seven. Compositions I, II and III were destroyed in the Second World War and survive only in black-and-white photographs, so their colours are known from studies. The early Kandinsky in the books is partly a reconstruction. A painter obsessed with colour left three of his largest statements as grey photographs.
cards.move: A body of work you can see today may be missing its beginning.
cards.trap: Assuming a famous painter's major works all reached museums.
cards.reference: Hans K. Roethel and Jean K. Benjamin, Kandinsky: Catalogue Raisonné of the Oil Paintings, Volume One 1900-1915, Sotheby Publications, 1982

cards.question: Did the CIA's covert cultural funding make Abstract Expressionism a world-famous style?
cards.answer: Through the Congress for Cultural Freedom, the CIA quietly funded magazines, festivals and exhibitions that set American freedom against Soviet realism. Abstract Expressionism, apolitical and unmistakably American, suited that message, and touring shows of the 1950s carried Pollock and Rothko across Europe. Frances Stonor Saunders documented the money; the timing fits the style's rise abroad.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, what had happened before the money arrived decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The style was famous before any secret money: Life magazine asked in 1949 whether Pollock was the greatest living painter in the United States. The touring shows came from the Museum of Modern Art's own programme, and congressmen openly attacked modern art as communist. Covert help, where it existed, joined a success already made by dealers, critics and collectors.
cards.reference: Frances Stonor Saunders, Who Paid the Piper? The CIA and the Cultural Cold War, Granta, 1999

cards.question: Why does one of the Riace warriors have copper lips and silver teeth?
cards.answer: To stand out against bright metal. The two Greek bronzes of the 400s BC have lips and nipples inlaid in reddish copper and eyes of calcite; one shows a row of silver teeth. Such contrasts suit bronze polished to a warm brown, the finish most specialists think intended. Today's dark patina is largely corrosion.
cards.move: Judge an old object by its first surface, not by what time added.
cards.reference: Carol C. Mattusch, Classical Bronzes: The Art and Craft of Greek and Roman Statuary, Cornell University Press, 1996

cards.question: Many of the finest surviving ancient Greek bronze statues were found where?
cards.answer: In the sea. On land, a bronze statue was a store of metal, and over the centuries almost all were melted into coins, tools and weapons. Only what sank out of reach escaped: the Riace warriors, the god from Cape Artemision, the Antikythera youth and the Marathon boy all came up from the seabed.
cards.move: Ask what protected the survivors, not only what destroyed the rest.
cards.trap: Picturing tombs, where so many other ancient treasures were kept safe.
cards.reference: Jens M. Daehner & Kenneth Lapatin (eds), Power and Pathos: Bronze Sculpture of the Hellenistic World, J. Paul Getty Museum, 2015

cards.question: What metal did Benin's royal casters mostly use for the works called the Benin Bronzes?
options: Bronze alloyed from local copper and tin
Copper traded from central African mines
cards.answer: Brass from European trade rings. Portuguese and later traders paid for goods with manillas, horseshoe-shaped brass rings, and Benin's casters melted them down. A 2023 study of manillas from shipwrecks found their lead isotopes and trace elements matched analyses of the plaques and heads: the brass came from ores in the Rhineland, in western Germany.
cards.move: A name given by collectors describes the collectors, not the thing.
cards.trap: Trusting the name bronze, which collectors used for any cast copper alloy.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0283415

cards.question: True or false: a bronze cast from Rodin's plaster long after his death can legally be an original Rodin?
cards.answer: True. Rodin gave his works and his reproduction rights to the French state in 1916, and French law counts the first twelve casts of a sculpture, eight numbered and four artist's proofs, as originals. The Musée Rodin kept casting from his plasters for decades after he died in 1917, and sold them as originals.
cards.move: Check who defines original before arguing about whether something is one.
cards.trap: Assuming an original must be made in the artist's lifetime.
cards.reference: https://www.musee-rodin.fr/en/museum/institution/original-bronze-casts

cards.question: What did the Vichy regime do to France's bronze public statues from 1941?
cards.answer: It melted them down for their metal. A law of 11 October 1941 ordered public bronzes removed so their copper and tin could be recovered, much of it for the German war economy. Estimates run from about 1,500 to 1,750 statues, over a hundred in Paris alone. Many plinths stood empty for decades.
cards.move: In a shortage, anything made of a scarce material becomes a reserve.
cards.reference: Kirrily Freeman, Bronzes to Bullets: Vichy and the Destruction of French Public Statuary, 1941–1944, Stanford University Press, 2009

cards.question: How were life-size Greek bronzes such as the Riace warriors usually cast?
options: In a single pour of metal
In pieces, then joined in bronze
cards.answer: In pieces, then joined in bronze. Founders cast head, arms, legs and torso separately in hollow lost-wax moulds, then fused the joints by pouring molten bronze into them. Small pours fill thin walls; one huge pour risks a half-filled figure. Cellini's heroic one-pour Perseus of 1549 was the exception, and some toes failed to fill.
cards.move: The famous way of doing something is often the rare way.
cards.trap: Picturing the one dramatic pour that Renaissance founders made famous.
cards.reference: Carol C. Mattusch, Greek Bronze Statuary: From the Beginnings through the Fifth Century B.C., Cornell University Press, 1988

cards.question: Why do conservators keep some excavated bronzes in cases of deliberately dry air?
cards.answer: To halt bronze disease. Chloride from the soil lies in pits as cuprous chloride; with moisture and oxygen it turns into a pale green powder and releases acid, which attacks fresh metal and makes more chloride. Below about 40% relative humidity the reaction stalls and the powder stops spreading.
cards.move: When damage feeds itself, cut off the one ingredient it cannot do without.
cards.source: Scott, Copper and Bronze in Art, 2002
cards.reference: David A. Scott, Copper and Bronze in Art: Corrosion, Colorants, Conservation, Getty Conservation Institute, 2002

cards.question: True or false: the great bronze ritual vessels of Shang China were cast by the lost-wax method?
cards.answer: False. Shang founders cast in piece moulds: clay was pressed around a model, cut off in sections, carved with decoration and reassembled round a core. The joins left thin ridges of metal. Lost wax appears in China centuries later, and even its early cases are debated. The Shang masterpieces needed no wax at all.
cards.move: A method that seems universal may just be the one you learned first.
cards.trap: Assuming lost wax, the textbook casting method, was used everywhere.
cards.reference: Robert W. Bagley, Shang Ritual Bronzes in the Arthur M. Sackler Collections, Harvard University Press, 1987

cards.question: Organic residue in the casting core of the Capitoline Wolf, long called Etruscan, dates it to when?
options: The eleventh or twelfth century AD
cards.answer: The eleventh or twelfth century AD. A restorer, Anna Maria Carruba, argued the wolf was cast in one pour, a medieval habit, not in ancient sections. Radiocarbon from organic matter trapped in its clay core then gave a range of about 1021 to 1153. Only the twins are Renaissance; the wolf is Romanesque.
cards.move: An old label is a claim to test, not a starting point to adjust.
cards.trap: Holding to the fifth-century date the wolf carried for centuries.
cards.source: Calcagnile et al., Nucl. Instrum. Methods B, 2019
cards.reference: Calcagnile, Quarta, D'Elia et al., Solving an historical puzzle: Radiocarbon dating the Capitoline she wolf, Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B, 2019

cards.question: Are the bronzes cast from Degas's wax figures after his death truly works by Degas?
cards.answer: Yes. Every form in them is his: the Hébrard foundry cast them in editions from moulds of his own waxes and clays soon after he died in 1917. Bronze preserves shapes the fragile originals were already losing. Without the casts, few would ever see his sculpture, and many figures would be crumbled wax.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether choosing the material is part of art.
cards.counterpoint: No. Degas modelled in wax and clay, exhibited only one sculpture, and never had any cast in bronze. Choosing a material, a surface and an edition size are artistic decisions, and he made none of them. Surviving waxes show colour, fabric and texture that bronze flattens. A cast he never approved records his forms, not his finished work.
cards.source: National Gallery of Art, Degas sculpture catalogue
cards.reference: Suzanne Glover Lindsay, Daphne S. Barbour & Shelley G. Sturman, Edgar Degas Sculpture, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 2010

cards.question: What happened to the Paris dealer who held much of Picasso's and Braque's Cubist work when war broke out in 1914?
cards.answer: He lost the lot. Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler was German, so France seized his stock as enemy property. After the war the state sold it in four auctions from 1921 to 1923, hundreds of Cubist works dumped at once onto a small market. The movement's core archive was scattered by a wartime property law.
cards.move: A market can be flooded by a rule that has nothing to do with it.
cards.reference: Pierre Assouline, An Artful Life: A Biography of D. H. Kahnweiler, Grove Weidenfeld, 1990

cards.question: Which army put painters with an eye for Cubism to work during the First World War, and on what?
cards.answer: The French army, on camouflage. In 1915 it set up a camouflage section under the painter Lucien-Victor Guirand de Scévola, who later credited Cubist ways of breaking up forms. Artists painted guns and lorries in broken patches and built fake trees to hide lookouts. Fragmenting an object on canvas became a way of hiding one.
cards.move: A technique invented for one purpose often finds its real use elsewhere.
cards.reference: Roy R. Behrens, False Colors: Art, Design and Modern Camouflage, Bobolink Books, 2002

cards.question: What was odd about the real-world material Picasso glued into his first collage in 1912?
cards.answer: It was itself a fake. Still Life with Chair Caning includes a piece of oilcloth printed to look like woven cane, on an oval canvas ringed with rope. The one scrap of everyday life he let into a painting was already a machine-printed imitation. Reality entered art as wipe-clean table covering.
cards.move: Ask whether the real thing in front of you is itself a copy.
cards.source: Richardson, A Life of Picasso II, 1996
cards.reference: John Richardson, A Life of Picasso, Volume II: 1907-1917, Random House, 1996

cards.question: True or false: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon went on public show roughly nine years after Picasso painted it.
cards.answer: True. Painted in 1907, it stayed in the studio, seen by friends, dealers and a few painters, until an exhibition organised by the writer André Salmon in Paris in 1916, who gave it its title. It was not reproduced widely until the 1920s. The founding picture of Cubism spent its first decade as studio talk.
cards.move: Influence can travel by word of mouth long before the public sees anything.
cards.trap: A picture this famous seems as if it must have been famous at once.
cards.reference: William Rubin, Hélène Seckel and Judith Cousins, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Studies in Modern Art 3, Museum of Modern Art, 1994

cards.question: Which earlier trade taught Braque the wood-grain effects he brought into Cubist pictures?
cards.answer: House painting and decorating. Braque trained in his father's decorating firm in Le Havre, where craftsmen faked wood and marble with combs and glazes. In 1912 he dragged a decorator's comb through paint and glued printed wood-grain wallpaper into his first papier collé. Cubism borrowed textures from the trade of making cheap rooms look costly.
cards.move: Look at someone's first trade to understand their later tricks.
cards.trap: Wood grain suggests a woodworker rather than a painter of imitations.
cards.reference: John Golding, Cubism: A History and an Analysis 1907-1914, Faber and Faber, 1959

cards.question: Where did the two ancient Iberian stone heads Picasso kept while painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon come from?
cards.answer: From the Louvre, stolen. Géry Pieret, a Belgian adventurer who acted as Apollinaire's secretary, took them and sold them to Picasso in 1907. When the Mona Lisa vanished in 1911, the heads became dangerous: they were handed back, and Apollinaire spent days in jail. Faces behind the Demoiselles had walked out of the Louvre.
cards.move: Ask how the objects on a studio shelf got there.
cards.reference: Peter Read, Picasso and Apollinaire: The Persistence of Memory, University of California Press, 2008

cards.question: True or false: neither Picasso nor Braque showed in the 1911 Paris Salon room that introduced Cubism to the public?
cards.answer: True. Room 41 of the Salon des Indépendants hung Metzinger, Gleizes, Le Fauconnier, Léger and Delaunay, and the press uproar made them the Cubists. Picasso and Braque sold privately through Kahnweiler, shunning the Salons. The first book on Cubism, in 1912, was by Gleizes and Metzinger. The public met the style through other painters.
cards.move: Who reached the audience first shapes what a name comes to mean.
cards.trap: Assuming the inventors of a style were the ones who showed it.
cards.reference: David Cottington, Cubism and Its Histories, Manchester University Press, 2004

cards.question: True or false: Einstein's relativity gave the Cubists their talk of a fourth dimension?
cards.answer: False. Their fourth dimension came from geometry, not physics: Esprit Jouffret's 1903 treatise on four-dimensional figures, explained in cafés by the actuary Maurice Princet, and Henri Poincaré's popular books. Relativity barely reached the public before the eclipse of 1919. Both drew on the century's new geometries; neither borrowed from the other.
cards.move: Two changes arriving together may share a source rather than cause each other.
cards.trap: Linking two revolutions of the same decade as cause and effect.
cards.reference: Linda Dalrymple Henderson, The Fourth Dimension and Non-Euclidean Geometry in Modern Art, Princeton University Press, 1983

cards.question: Who first spoke of little cubes in Braque's 1908 landscapes, according to the critic who put the word in print?
cards.answer: Henri Matisse. He sat on the 1908 Salon d'Automne jury that turned down Braque's L'Estaque landscapes, and Louis Vauxcelles, who printed the word cubes that November, credited him with the jibe. Apollinaire, meanwhile, wrote the preface for Braque's show. The movement's name began as a rival's sneer relayed by a hostile critic.
cards.move: Many labels begin as insults from rivals and stick anyway.
cards.trap: Crediting Picasso, the name everyone attaches to the movement.
cards.reference: Alex Danchev, Georges Braque: A Life, Hamish Hamilton, 2005

cards.question: Cézanne's 1904 letter, later read as a recipe for Cubism, told a young painter to treat nature by which three forms?
cards.answer: Cylinder, sphere and cone. Writing to Émile Bernard in April 1904, Cézanne named no cube; he was talking about modelling volume in light, not breaking objects into facets. The letter appeared in print in 1907, just as Picasso and Braque began their experiments. A movement named after cubes adopted a recipe without one.
cards.move: Check the original wording before trusting the version everyone cites.
cards.trap: Letting the movement's name slip a cube into the list.
cards.reference: Michael Doran (ed.), Conversations with Cézanne, University of California Press, 2001

cards.question: True or false: modern black-and-white camera film can be developed under the red safelight used for printing?
cards.answer: False. Black-and-white printing paper is made sensitive mainly to blue and green, so dim red or amber light cannot fog it. Most black-and-white film since the mid-twentieth century is panchromatic, sensitive to red as well, and must go into its developing tank in total darkness. The red-lit room of films is the printing stage.
cards.move: Before copying a routine, check it was built for your material.
cards.trap: Picturing the red darkroom glow of films as the whole process.
cards.reference: Michael Langford, Anna Fox & Richard Sawdon Smith, Langford's Basic Photography, 9th edition, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: How did Gustave Le Gray get both detailed clouds and a lit sea into his 1850s seascapes?
cards.answer: By printing two negatives on one sheet. Collodion plates were far more sensitive to blue than to other colours, so a sky exposed long enough for the darker sea burned out white. Le Gray exposed one plate for the sky and one for the water, sometimes on different days, and joined them along the horizon.
cards.move: When one setting cannot hold everything, capture the parts separately and join them.
cards.source: Metropolitan Museum, Le Gray, The Great Wave
cards.reference: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/261941

cards.question: In the zone system, neighbouring zones differ by one stop. How many times more light does Zone VIII send than Zone V?
cards.answer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times the light.
cards.move: On a scale where each step doubles, multiply the steps, never add them.
cards.trap: Counting three zones and answering three times, as on a ruler.
cards.hint: Count the stops between the zones, then ask what one stop does to the light.
steps: One stop is a doubling of light.
Zone V to Zone VIII is 3 stops.
2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times the light.
cards.reference: Ansel Adams, The Negative, New York Graphic Society, 1981

cards.question: Why can a black-and-white print sit in daylight for a century without darkening?
cards.answer: Because the unexposed silver salts were washed out. In 1819 the astronomer John Herschel found that hyposulphite of soda, now sodium thiosulphate, dissolves them, and in 1839 he saw it could fix a camera image. Talbot's first prints were only soaked in strong salt, which slowed the darkening. Darkroom workers still call fixer hypo.
cards.move: Making something is half the job; stopping it from changing is the other.
cards.reference: Larry J. Schaaf, Out of the Shadows: Herschel, Talbot and the Invention of Photography, Yale University Press, 1992

cards.question: How much did Ansel Adams's prints of Moonrise, Hernandez change over his lifetime?
cards.answer: A great deal. The 1941 negative was thin and flat, and early prints show a grey sky with streaky clouds. In 1948 Adams chemically intensified the negative up to the horizon, and later prints darken the sky almost to black around a bright moon. A 1941 print and a 1975 one show different nights.
cards.move: Ask which print you are looking at before saying what a photograph shows.
cards.reference: Ansel Adams, Examples: The Making of 40 Photographs, Little, Brown and Company, 1983

cards.question: What did two chemists in Widnes publish in 1890 that turned darkroom craft into measurement?
cards.answer: The characteristic curve. Ferdinand Hurter and Vero Charles Driffield exposed plates in measured steps, measured how dark each developed patch became, and plotted density against the logarithm of exposure. The S-shaped curve made a plate's speed, contrast and latitude into numbers. Their H&D speed ratings were printed on plate boxes for decades.
cards.move: A craft becomes a science the day someone plots its results.
cards.reference: W. B. Ferguson (ed), The Photographic Researches of Ferdinand Hurter & Vero C. Driffield, Royal Photographic Society, 1920

cards.question: One patch of a negative has density 2.3, another 0.3. How many times more light passes the thinner patch?
cards.answer: 10 to the power 2.0 = 100 times.
cards.move: On a logarithmic scale, subtract the readings, then raise ten to the difference.
cards.trap: Dividing 2.3 by 0.3 and answering about eight.
cards.hint: Each whole unit of density cuts the light passing through by a factor of ten.
steps: Density is the base-10 logarithm of incident over transmitted light.
The difference is 2.3 − 0.3 = 2.0.
10 to the power 2.0 = 100 times.
cards.reference: ISO 5-2:2009, Photography and graphic technology — Density measurements — Part 2: Geometric conditions for transmittance density, International Organization for Standardization, 2009

cards.question: True or false: portrait photographers were retouching negatives to smooth sitters' skin before 1860?
cards.answer: True. At the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1855 the Munich photographer Franz Hanfstaengl showed the same portrait negative before and after retouching. Retouchers worked on the glass with pencil and etching knife, softening wrinkles and freckles. Flattering the face is as old as the studio.
cards.move: A new tool for altering pictures rarely brings the first altered pictures.
cards.trap: Assuming smoothing skin began with software, where the complaints are loudest.
cards.reference: Helmut Gernsheim & Alison Gernsheim, The History of Photography, Oxford University Press, 1955

cards.question: Why can a black-and-white print that was properly fixed still turn yellow years later?
cards.answer: Because the fixer was not washed out. Fibre-based paper soaks up thiosulphate, the fixing agent, and holds it in its fibres. Left there, it slowly breaks down and attacks the silver image, forming yellow-brown silver sulphide, first in the highlights. Hence long washes. Stains can surface decades after a print looked perfect.
cards.move: Cleaning up after a process is part of the process.
cards.source: Stroebel et al., Basic Photographic Materials, 2000
cards.reference: Leslie Stroebel, John Compton, Ira Current & Richard Zakia, Basic Photographic Materials and Processes, 2nd edition, Focal Press, 2000

cards.question: A light meter reading at night calls for a 30-second exposure on black-and-white film. What does the film need?
options: Less, since light keeps adding up
cards.answer: Much longer, often several times as long. Film obeys the rule that half the light for twice the time gives the same result only over short exposures. In dim light each silver grain collects photons too slowly to hold a stable latent image, and some effect is lost. Night photographers carry correction tables.
cards.move: A rule that holds in the usual range may fail at the extremes.
cards.trap: Trusting the meter, which assumes light and time trade evenly.
cards.reference: Karl Schwarzschild, On the deviations from the law of reciprocity for bromide of silver gelatine, Astrophysical Journal, 1900

cards.question: What exposed Wolfgang Beltracchi, the forger of early twentieth-century masters, in 2008?
cards.answer: A white pigment. A painting sold as Heinrich Campendonk's Red Picture with Horses, dated 1914, contained titanium white, which was not made commercially as a pigment until years later. Beltracchi had used a tube of zinc white whose maker did not list its titanium. The canvas had fetched a record €2.88 million at auction.
cards.move: A careful liar is often undone by a detail he never thought to check.
cards.source: Koldehoff & Timm, Falsche Bilder, echtes Geld, 2012
cards.reference: Stefan Koldehoff & Tobias Timm, Falsche Bilder, echtes Geld: Der Fälschungscoup des Jahrhunderts, Galiani Berlin, 2012

cards.question: Fresh lead white carries excess lead-210, which halves every 22 years. After 220 years, by what factor has that excess shrunk?
cards.answer: 2 multiplied by itself 10 times = 1,024 times smaller.
cards.move: Count the halvings first; the size of the fall follows from the count.
cards.trap: Answering ten, counting the halvings instead of multiplying them together.
cards.hint: Count the half-lives first, then ask what each one does.
steps: 220 ÷ 22 = 10 half-lives.
Each half-life divides the excess by 2.
2 multiplied by itself 10 times = 1,024 times smaller.

cards.question: Infrared shows that beneath the paint, the artist moved a figure's arm. What does that usually suggest?
options: The painting is the first version
The painting is a later copy
cards.answer: The painting is the first version. A copyist sees the finished picture and reproduces it; only an artist still working out the composition changes course midway. Infrared reflectography sees through many paints to the carbon underdrawing, and such changes, called pentimenti, turn up far more often in first versions than in replicas.
cards.move: Weigh a clue by how much likelier it is under one story than another.
cards.trap: Reading a correction as a mistake, and a mistake as a lesser hand.
cards.source: van Asperen de Boer, Applied Optics, 1968
cards.reference: J. R. J. van Asperen de Boer, Infrared Reflectography: A Method for the Examination of Paintings, Applied Optics, 1968

cards.question: True or false: a painting whose canvas, ground and pigments all test as seventeenth-century can still be modern?
cards.answer: True. Materials can prove a painting too young, never old enough. Old canvases, old panels and period pigments can all be bought: Han van Meegeren acquired minor seventeenth-century paintings, scraped them down and painted his Vermeers on the genuine canvas. A clean result from a materials test only means the forger made no mistake there.
cards.move: A test that can only say no cannot say yes.
cards.trap: Treating a passed test as proof, not as the absence of disproof.
cards.source: Lopez, The Man Who Made Vermeers, 2008
cards.reference: Jonathan Lopez, The Man Who Made Vermeers: Unvarnishing the Legend of Master Forger Han van Meegeren, Harcourt, 2008

cards.question: If the last tree ring in an oak panel dates to 1500, when was the picture painted?
cards.answer: Not before about 1511, and probably not before 1517. Panel makers cut away the sapwood, the pale outer rings, so the last ring left is years short of felling: for Baltic oak, add at least 9 sapwood rings, typically about 15. Then add at least two years of seasoning.
cards.move: Some evidence can only tell you the earliest a thing could be.
cards.source: Klein, Structural Conservation of Panel Paintings, 1998
cards.reference: Peter Klein, Dendrochronological Analyses of Panel Paintings, in Dardes & Rothe (eds), The Structural Conservation of Panel Paintings, Getty Conservation Institute, 1998

cards.question: True or false: radiocarbon dating can tell a canvas woven around 1700 from one woven around 1900?
cards.answer: False. From about 1650 to 1950 the carbon-14 in the air wobbled, with solar changes and then coal smoke diluting it, so the calibration curve that turns a measurement into a date runs nearly flat. One result fits dates across centuries. A canvas for a Watteau and one for a Monet can read the same.
cards.move: A precise measurement can still point to many different answers.
cards.trap: Trusting the lab's quoted error of a few decades as the date's.
cards.reference: https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2026/ay/d6ay90027e

cards.question: Why did the Warhol Foundation's authentication board, which ruled on disputed Warhols, shut itself down in 2012?
cards.answer: Because saying no had become ruinously expensive. A collector, Joe Simon-Whelan, sued after the board rejected his 1964 self-portrait, alleging a conspiracy to control the Warhol market. Defending the case cost the foundation millions in legal fees. Other artists' foundations also stopped giving opinions, leaving owners with nobody entitled to say yes.
cards.move: An expert who can be sued for an opinion soon stops giving one.
cards.reference: https://philanthropynewsdigest.org/news/warhol-foundation-dissolves-authentication-board

cards.question: In 2014 a Geneva lab reported that over half the works it examined were fakes or misattributed. What follows?
options: Little about the market as a whole
About half the art on sale is fake
Its methods must be badly flawed
cards.answer: Little about the market as a whole. Owners pay for a lab's costly opinion when they already doubt an attribution; confident owners send nothing. The lab's cases were suspects by selection. Its director still extrapolated to half the art in circulation, and the figure spread through the press as a market statistic.
cards.move: Ask what made each case land on the desk before counting it.
cards.trap: Reading the lab's hit rate as a rate for all art.
cards.reference: https://news.artnet.com/market/over-50-percent-of-art-is-fake-130821

cards.question: A test flags 95% of fakes and 5% of genuine paintings. If 2% of lots are fake, what percentage of flagged lots are fake?
cards.answer: 19 fakes / 68 flagged ≈ 28 percent.
cards.move: When the thing sought is rare, most alarms are false.
cards.trap: Answering 95%, the share of fakes the test catches.
cards.hint: Picture 1,000 lots and count the flagged fakes and flagged genuine works separately.
steps: Take 1,000 lots: 20 are fake, and 95% of them, 19, are flagged.
980 are genuine, and 5% of them, 49, are flagged too.
Flagged lots: 19 + 49 = 68.
19 fakes / 68 flagged ≈ 28 percent.

diagram.label: lots at auction
diagram.caption: Of 68 lots flagged, only 19 are fake: about 28 per cent.

cards.reference: Gerd Gigerenzer & Ulrich Hoffrage, How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats, Psychological Review, 1995

cards.question: What lets radiocarbon date the linseed oil in a modern forgery to within a few years?
cards.answer: Fallout from nuclear tests. Bomb tests of the 1950s and early 1960s nearly doubled the carbon-14 in northern air, and it has fallen year by year since, so plants grown after 1955 carry a datable signature. In 2019 a speck of oil from a painting dated 1866 proved to come from flax harvested after 1958.
cards.move: A disturbance that ruins one kind of record can become a clock for another.
cards.reference: Laura Hendriks, Irka Hajdas et al., Uncovering modern paint forgeries by radiocarbon dating, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2019

cards.question: Why was the first photograph scanned into a computer, in 1957, so small and coarse?
cards.answer: Because the machine could hold no more. At the US National Bureau of Standards, Russell Kirsch fed a photograph of his three-month-old son into a drum scanner linked to SEAC, an early stored-program computer. The image it could store was 176 pixels on a side, about 31,000 dots in all: enough for one small face.
cards.move: Early versions of a technology are shaped by what the machine could hold.
cards.reference: https://www.nist.gov/mathematics-statistics/first-digital-image

cards.question: A phone camera goes from 12 to 48 megapixels. How much finer can detail along one edge become?
cards.answer: Up to twice as fine. Pixels fill an area, so four times as many means twice as many along each edge: 4,000 across becomes 8,000. Many 48-megapixel phone sensors also group pixels in fours under one colour filter and, in dim light, merge each group, handing back 12 megapixels anyway.
cards.move: When a count covers an area, the gain along a line is its square root.
cards.trap: Reading four times the pixels as four times the detail.
cards.reference: https://www.forbes.com/sites/paulmonckton/2022/02/28/what-is-pixel-binning-quad-bayer-nonacell/

cards.question: How can a phone take a colour photograph of a scene too dark for its owner to see colour?
cards.answer: By merging a burst. Google's Night Sight, described in 2019, captures a series of frames, aligns them to cancel hand shake, and averages away the noise, lengthening each exposure when the scene holds still. It produced clean colour pictures at about 0.3 lux, a light level at which human vision has turned grey and indistinct.
cards.move: Many weak measurements, carefully combined, can beat one strong one.
cards.source: Liba et al., ACM Transactions on Graphics, 2019

cards.question: True or false: in 2005 Kodak sold more digital cameras in the United States than any other company?
cards.answer: True. IDC counted about 7 million Kodak digital cameras shipped to US retailers in 2005, ahead of Canon and Sony. Kodak's trouble was not ignoring digital: cameras earned thin margins where film and processing had earned fat ones, and phones then swallowed the camera market. Kodak filed for bankruptcy in January 2012.
cards.move: A company can win the new market and still lose the old profits.
cards.trap: Recalling the story of Kodak shelving its own 1975 digital camera.
cards.reference: https://www.reviewed.com/cameras/news/kodak-leads-in-digital-camera-sales-in-the-us

cards.question: Should news outlets publish only photographs that carry a signed record of every edit since capture?
cards.answer: Yes. Generated and altered images are now cheap and convincing, and a reader cannot tell them apart by eye. The C2PA standard lets a camera sign an image at capture and log each later change. A newsroom that insists on it can show its work, and anything unsigned invites the question it should.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what an unsigned picture comes to mean.
cards.counterpoint: No. Most of the world's cameras and phones do not sign images, and platforms often strip the data. Photographers in dangerous places may need to hide time and location. A rule would drop authentic witness pictures while a signed record proves only that nothing changed after capture, not that the scene was staged honestly.
cards.reference: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, C2PA Technical Specification, version 1.0, 2022

cards.question: What was the charge-coupled device, the sensor in early digital cameras, first invented to do?
cards.answer: To store data. In 1969 Willard Boyle and George Smith at Bell Labs designed it as a memory that passed packets of charge along a chip like buckets in a line. Light frees charge in silicon, so the chip could also read an image. The memory failed; the sensor won them a 2009 Nobel Prize.
cards.move: An invention often succeeds at a job it was never designed for.
cards.reference: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/press-release/

cards.question: A 24-megapixel camera records 14 bits per pixel in its raw file. Uncompressed, how many megabytes is one picture?
cards.answer: 336 million bits / 8 bits per byte = 42 megabytes.
cards.move: Before multiplying, check how many numbers each item really stores.
cards.trap: Multiplying by three colours per pixel and reaching about 126 megabytes.
cards.hint: A raw file keeps each pixel's single filtered reading; colour is computed later.
steps: Each pixel holds one colour reading, not three: 24 million readings.
24 million × 14 bits = 336 million bits.
336 million bits / 8 bits per byte = 42 megabytes.
cards.source: Fraser & Schewe, Real World Camera Raw, 2005
cards.reference: Bruce Fraser & Jeff Schewe, Real World Camera Raw with Adobe Photoshop CS2, Peachpit Press, 2005

cards.question: Light is scarce and noise dominates. Quadruple the light reaching each pixel: how much cleaner does the image get?
cards.answer: Twice as clean. Photons arrive at random, so a pixel expecting 100 varies by about the square root, 10: one part in ten. At 400 photons the variation is 20, one part in twenty. Signal grows four times, noise twice. This shot noise is physics, not a sensor flaw, and no engineer can remove it.
cards.move: Averages sharpen with the square root of the count, not the count.
cards.trap: Assuming the image cleans up in step with the light collected.
cards.reference: James R. Janesick, Photon Transfer: DN to λ, SPIE Press, 2007

cards.question: Why is one of image compression's most-used test pictures cropped from a 1972 magazine centrefold?
cards.answer: Because it was to hand in 1973. Engineers at the University of Southern California needed a glossy image to scan for a paper and tore the top off a Playboy page. The 512-pixel square of a face and shoulder became standard because everyone could compare results on it. IEEE journals began refusing it in 2024.
cards.move: Whatever becomes the benchmark stays long after anyone would choose it again.
cards.source: Munson, IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 1996
cards.reference: David C. Munson Jr., A note on Lena, IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 1996

cards.question: If a phone adds lunar detail learned from other photographs, is its moon shot still a photograph?
cards.answer: Yes. Every digital image is already computed: colours are interpolated, noise removed, frames merged. Recognising the moon and restoring texture that optics and shake destroyed is one more step on that line. The moon shows Earth the same face every night, so the added detail is what was really there, faithfully rendered.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a photograph must come from the light.
cards.counterpoint: No. In 2023 a user photographed a deliberately blurred picture of the moon on a monitor, and a Samsung phone returned craters the blurred source did not contain. A photograph records light from the scene; this one supplied detail from a trained model's memory. Accurate or not, it shows what the moon usually looks like, not what the lens saw.
cards.reference: Samsung Newsroom, How Samsung Galaxy Cameras Combine Super Resolution Technologies With AI Technologies to Produce High-Quality Images of the Moon, March 2023

cards.question: Why did Dutch experts accept van Meegeren's Supper at Emmaus as a Vermeer in 1937?
options: Its style matched Vermeer's famous interiors
It filled a gap a leading scholar predicted
It came with a documented noble provenance
cards.answer: It filled a gap a leading scholar predicted. Abraham Bredius, the doyen of Dutch art history, believed the young Vermeer had painted religious scenes under Italian influence, and none was known. Van Meegeren painted one to order. Bredius hailed it as a masterpiece and Museum Boijmans bought it. Its heavy-lidded faces now look plainly 1930s.
cards.move: Be most suspicious of the evidence you were hoping to find.
cards.trap: Assuming a fake must look just like the famous Vermeers to fool anyone.
cards.reference: https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/101464/the-men-at-emmaus

cards.question: How did a sculptor prove in 1961 that the Metropolitan Museum's Etruscan warriors were modern?
cards.answer: He produced a missing thumb. Alfredo Fioravanti, one of the forgers, confessed at the US consulate in Rome and brought out a thumb he had kept for decades. It fitted a cast of the Old Warrior's hand. The Met announced the forgery that February.
cards.move: The one who made a thing can often prove it with a single leftover piece.
cards.source: Archaeology magazine, Tracking the Etruscan Warriors
cards.reference: https://archive.archaeology.org/online/features/hoaxes/warriors.html

cards.question: What date did the Getty Museum's label give for the marble kouros it bought in 1985?
cards.answer: Two dates: Greek, about 530 BC, or modern forgery. The statue's paperwork, meant to trace it to a Swiss collection in the 1930s, proved fake, while studies of its weathered marble surface never settled the matter. It stayed on show under both dates until the museum removed it in 2018.
cards.move: An honest label can say what is unknown instead of choosing a side.
cards.reference: The Getty Kouros Colloquium, Athens, 25–27 May 1992, Kapon Editions, 1993

cards.question: True or false: the Louvre's gold tiara of the Scythian king Saitaphernes, bought in 1896, was exposed by laboratory analysis?
cards.answer: False. Its maker exposed it. Israel Rouchomovsky, a goldsmith in Odessa, had made it in 1894 for dealers who called it a gift for an archaeologist. In 1903 he came to Paris to claim it, and experts believed him only after he remade part of it from memory. The Louvre had paid 200,000 francs.
cards.move: Many deceptions end with a confession, not with a clever test.
cards.trap: Picturing the laboratory unmasking that modern forgery stories feature.
cards.source: Artnet News, the tiara of Saitaphernes
cards.reference: https://news.artnet.com/art-world/the-hunt-the-tiara-of-saitaphernes-2558944

cards.question: Who painted the fake Rothkos and Pollocks that closed Knoedler, a New York gallery founded in 1846?
cards.answer: A Chinese immigrant painting at his home in Queens. Pei-Shen Qian made the canvases for the dealer Glafira Rosales, who spoke of an anonymous collector. From 1994 Knoedler sold about 40 of them for over $60 million; the whole scheme came to about $80 million. Qian was reportedly paid a few thousand dollars a picture.
cards.move: Follow the money to see who in a chain was really fooled.
cards.reference: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2017/01/31/no-further-jail-time-for-glafira-rosales-for-her-role-in-dollar80m-knoedler-forgery-scandal

cards.question: Besides the paintings, what did John Drewe forge in the Myatt–Drewe fraud, and where did he put it?
cards.answer: Their history, placed inside the archives. Drewe won access to the Tate Gallery archive and the Victoria and Albert Museum's library, then slipped in doctored exhibition catalogues and gallery records listing John Myatt's fakes as long-known works. A researcher checking a picture's provenance found the fraud's own paperwork waiting on the shelf.
cards.move: Check who put the record there before trusting what it confirms.
cards.reference: Laney Salisbury & Aly Sujo, Provenance: How a Con Man and a Forger Rewrote the History of Modern Art, Penguin Press, 2009

cards.question: In 1983 handwriting experts compared a Hitler diary page with known samples of his hand. Why did they wrongly confirm it?
options: Their reference samples were forged too
The forger had traced genuine letters
Hitler's hand varied too much to judge
cards.answer: Their reference samples were forged too. Among the documents supplied as genuine Hitler writing was material from the same forger, Konrad Kujau. A match between two fakes by one hand proved only that one man wrote both. Stern had paid 9.3 million marks; within two weeks of publication, chemists found post-war whitener in the paper.
cards.move: Two checks that drink from the same well are one check.
cards.trap: Tracing, the forger's familiar trick for copying a signature.
cards.reference: Robert Harris, Selling Hitler: The Story of the Hitler Diaries, Faber and Faber, 1986

cards.question: True or false: the turkeys in Schleswig Cathedral's supposedly medieval murals are what exposed their forger?
cards.answer: False. Birds unknown in Europe before Columbus were read instead as evidence that Norsemen had reached America and brought turkeys home. The painter Lothar Malskat, who repainted the murals from 1937, exposed himself: in 1952 he confessed to faking Gothic murals in Lübeck as well. Only then were the turkeys seen for what they were.
cards.move: An oddity tends to be read as support for what the reader already believes.
cards.trap: Assuming so glaring an anachronism must have given the fake away.
cards.reference: Jonathon Keats, Forged: Why Fakes Are the Great Art of Our Age, Oxford University Press, 2013

cards.question: Why is a prolific forger of medieval miniatures, active around 1900, known only as the Spanish Forger?
cards.answer: Because of one panel. In 1930 Belle da Costa Greene, the Morgan Library's director, judged a Betrothal of Saint Ursula, then given to the fifteenth-century Spanish master Jorge Inglés, to be modern. The name stuck to its unknown maker, probably French. Hundreds of his pictures are now known, many on genuine old vellum.
cards.move: A name given in error can stick long after the error is known.
cards.reference: William Voelkle, The Spanish Forger, Pierpont Morgan Library, New York, 1978

cards.question: What showed that the British Museum's crystal skull, long sold as Aztec, was not carved before Columbus?
options: A confession by the dealer who sold it
Marks left by a rotating cutting wheel
cards.answer: Marks left by a rotating cutting wheel. Scanning electron microscopes showed regular, parallel grooves cut by abrasive on a turning wheel, a lapidary tool unknown in the Americas before Europeans arrived. Pre-Columbian carvers ground stone by hand. Quartz holds no carbon to date, so the tool marks had to speak instead.
cards.move: When the material cannot be dated, date the tool that shaped it.
cards.trap: Carbon dating, the test that famously unmasks old fakes.
cards.source: Sax et al., J. Archaeological Science, 2008
cards.reference: Margaret Sax, Jane M. Walsh, Ian C. Freestone, Andrew H. Rankin & Nigel D. Meeks, The origins of two purportedly pre-Columbian Mexican crystal skulls, Journal of Archaeological Science, 2008

cards.question: Why do the buildings in Niépce's view from his window at Le Gras catch sunlight on both sides?
cards.answer: Because the plate stayed open while the sun crossed the sky. Around 1827 Niépce coated pewter with bitumen of Judea, an asphalt that hardens in light, and it is extremely slow. The textbook figure is eight hours; Jean-Louis Marignier, who re-created the process, concluded it took several days. The picture averages many mornings and afternoons.
cards.move: A long exposure records an average, and averages show things no moment contained.
cards.reference: Jean-Louis Marignier, Niépce: l'invention de la photographie, Belin, 1999

cards.question: True or false: when France gave the daguerreotype free to the world in August 1839, Britain shared the gift?
cards.answer: False. On 14 August 1839, days before the French announcement, Daguerre's agent Miles Berry took out an English patent on the process. Anyone making daguerreotypes in England and Wales needed a licence from the patent holders, who sold them for a fee. In England and Wales, the invention given free to the world cost money.
cards.move: Read the date on the fine print before trusting the headline.
cards.trap: Taking free to the world, the famous phrase, at its word.
cards.reference: Helmut & Alison Gernsheim, L.J.M. Daguerre: The History of the Diorama and the Daguerreotype, Secker & Warburg, 1956

cards.question: Daguerre's 1839 camera lens worked at about f/15, Petzval's 1840 portrait lens at f/3.6. How many times more light did Petzval's admit?
cards.answer: 4.17 × 4.17 ≈ 17.4 times the light.
cards.move: When a width changes, ask whether what matters is an area.
cards.trap: Dividing the f-numbers and answering four, forgetting the opening is an area.
cards.hint: The f-number measures the width of the opening; light passes through an area.
steps: Light admitted goes with the square of the ratio of f-numbers.
4.17 × 4.17 ≈ 17.4 times the light.

diagram.caption: An opening 4.17 times wider lets in 17.4 times the light.

cards.source: Kingslake, A History of the Photographic Lens, 1989
cards.reference: Rudolf Kingslake, A History of the Photographic Lens, Academic Press, 1989

cards.question: Why did Hippolyte Bayard photograph himself as a drowned man in 1840?
cards.answer: In protest. Bayard had made direct positive prints on paper and shown them in Paris by mid-1839, but the state's reward went to Daguerre. His self-portrait slumped as a corpse carries a note on the back saying he drowned himself in despair at the neglect. The first staged photographs include a complaint about credit.
cards.move: Staging a picture to make a point is as old as the picture itself.
cards.reference: Geoffrey Batchen, Burning with Desire: The Conception of Photography, MIT Press, 1997

cards.question: Maxwell's 1861 colour photograph of a tartan ribbon shows red, yet its plates were blind to red light. How?
options: The plate was faintly red-sensitive after all
The red plate was coloured by hand
The red dye also reflected ultraviolet
cards.answer: The red dye also reflected ultraviolet. The collodion plates responded mainly to blue and ultraviolet, and the red filter let some ultraviolet through. Many red dyes reflect it, so the ribbon's red stripes registered on the red plate anyway. Ralph Evans worked this out in 1961. The demonstration worked for a reason Maxwell never intended.
cards.move: A result that comes out right has not yet shown the method worked.
cards.trap: Assuming the right colour came through the channel built for it.
cards.reference: doi:10.3390/heritage6020054

cards.question: Who wrote the word photographie in his notes years before 1839, and where?
cards.answer: Hercule Florence, a French-born artist living in Campinas, Brazil. In the early 1830s, far from Paris, he fixed images with silver salts, printed labels and diplomas by light, and called the method photographie in his notebooks. They lay unread until the historian Boris Kossoy studied them in the 1970s.
cards.move: A claim to be first usually means first among those who were noticed.
cards.reference: Boris Kossoy, Hercule Florence: a descoberta isolada da fotografia no Brasil, Duas Cidades, 1980

cards.question: Why do shop signs in many daguerreotypes read backwards, though negatives made later photographs read true?
options: The lens flipped the picture left to right
The plate was viewed from its lens side
The mercury fumes reversed the silver image
cards.answer: The plate was viewed from its lens side. A lens turns the image upside down, which is only a rotation: turn the plate round and it reads upright. A negative is printed face to face onto paper, which flips it back; a daguerreotype never had that second step.
cards.move: Check whether a fault comes from the tool or from a missing step.
cards.trap: Blaming the lens, the part known to invert the picture.
cards.reference: M. Susan Barger & William B. White, The Daguerreotype: Nineteenth-Century Technology and Modern Science, Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991

cards.question: True or false: by the 1860s a typical studio portrait needed only seconds of exposure?
cards.answer: True. Faster lenses and, from 1851, wet collodion plates cut exposure from the minutes of 1839 to a few seconds in a bright studio. Head rests were still used. The solemn expressions of Victorian portraits owe more to manners, which treated a broad grin as foolish, than to chemistry.
cards.move: A number from the start of a story rarely holds by its middle.
cards.trap: Carrying the famous exposure times of 1839 forward by twenty years.
cards.reference: Beaumont Newhall, The History of Photography: From 1839 to the Present, Museum of Modern Art, 1982

cards.question: Which was the first book to be illustrated with photographs?
cards.answer: Anna Atkins's British Algae. From October 1843 she issued Photographs of British Algae in parts, each page a cyanotype: seaweed laid directly on paper coated with iron salts and printed blue by sunlight. Talbot's followed in June 1844; Daguerre's manual had engraved plates only. The first photographic book needed no camera.
cards.move: The version everyone cites is the famous one, not always the first.
cards.trap: Talbot's book, because histories of the medium name it first.
cards.reference: Larry J. Schaaf, Sun Gardens: Victorian Photograms by Anna Atkins, Aperture, 1985

cards.question: What change in 1840 let Talbot cut camera exposures from most of an hour to a minute or two?
cards.answer: He stopped waiting for the picture to appear. His earlier paper had to darken visibly. With the calotype, a brief exposure left an invisible latent image, which gallic acid and silver nitrate then developed into a full negative. Chemistry took over most of the work of light, as in every film camera since.
cards.move: When one stage is slow, find a later stage that can amplify its output.
cards.reference: Larry J. Schaaf, The Photographic Art of William Henry Fox Talbot, Princeton University Press, 2000

cards.question: How did restorers choose to handle the paint Cimabue's Santa Croce crucifix lost in the 1966 flood?
cards.answer: They left the losses visible. Soaked for hours in muddy, oily water, the panel swelled and shrank, and over half its paint flaked away. Umberto Baldini's team filled the gaps with fine hatched strokes of colour that read as tone from a distance and as repair up close. The Christ is honestly part erased.
cards.move: A good repair lets you see where the original stops.
cards.reference: Umberto Baldini, Teoria del restauro e unità di metodologia, Nardini Editore, 1978

cards.question: Roughly how many people lived in Florence in 1427, when Masaccio and Donatello were at work?
cards.answer: About 40,000. The city's tax census of 1427, the Catasto, counted fewer than 40,000 people, well under half the population before the Black Death of 1348. The artists who defined an age worked in a place the size of a modern market town, where most of them could know each other by sight.
cards.move: A place's fame is no guide to its size.
cards.trap: Scaling from today's Florence, a city of well over 300,000.
cards.source: Herlihy and Klapisch-Zuber, Tuscans and Their Families, 1985
cards.reference: David Herlihy and Christiane Klapisch-Zuber, Tuscans and Their Families: A Study of the Florentine Catasto of 1427, Yale University Press, 1985

cards.question: Which guild did a painter working in 15th-century Florence have to join?
cards.answer: The physicians' and apothecaries' guild, the Arte dei Medici e Speziali. Apothecaries sold pigments alongside drugs and spices, so painters were enrolled with the trade that supplied them. Stone carvers joined the masons and woodworkers instead. A painter's name sat in the same register as a spice dealer's.
cards.move: Institutions are often sorted by supply chain, not by what people think they do.
cards.trap: Filing painters with sculptors, as artists working with their hands.
cards.source: Wackernagel, The World of the Florentine Renaissance Artist
cards.reference: Martin Wackernagel, The World of the Florentine Renaissance Artist, trans. Alison Luchs, Princeton University Press, 1981

cards.question: Did the Black Death help bring about the art of Renaissance Florence?
cards.answer: The plague of 1348 killed perhaps half the city. Survivors inherited concentrated wealth, and scarce labour pushed up wages. Fear of death drove bequests for chapels, altarpieces and confraternities, the very commissions that fed painters. Millard Meiss argued in 1951 that the shock even changed how Florentine and Sienese painters pictured the sacred.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the fifty-year gap between cause and effect decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The great burst came two generations later, after 1400, and cities hit just as hard produced nothing comparable. What Florence had was banking money, rival guilds and public competitions for civic works. Later historians also challenged Meiss's stylistic shift, finding the changes he described already under way before the plague.
cards.source: Meiss, Painting in Florence and Siena, 1951
cards.reference: Millard Meiss, Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death, Princeton University Press, 1951

cards.question: Why did the oxen lifting stone for Florence's cathedral dome never need turning round?
cards.answer: Because the hoist could reverse. Brunelleschi's hoist of about 1420 had gearing that could be shifted to wind the rope the other way, so animals walking the same circle could raise or lower a load. Turning a team between lifts would have cost time on every load. The dome rose at a steady walk.
cards.move: Before speeding up the work, look at the time lost between jobs.
cards.reference: Ross King, Brunelleschi's Dome: The Story of the Great Cathedral in Florence, Chatto & Windus, 2000

cards.question: How did Masaccio's Trinity, a showpiece of early perspective, get through the late sixteenth century unharmed?
cards.answer: Hidden behind an altar. Around 1570 Giorgio Vasari, who praised Masaccio in print, set a new stone altar and altarpiece in front of it in Santa Maria Novella. The fresco was uncovered about 1860, cut from the wall and moved, then returned in 1952 to its painted skeleton below. Being covered up preserved it.
cards.move: Sometimes what saves a thing is being put out of sight.
cards.reference: Rona Goffen (ed.), Masaccio's Trinity, Cambridge University Press, 1998

cards.question: Why did Florence's guilds fill the empty niches of Orsanmichele with statues in the early 1400s?
options: A city deadline, or lose the niche
A vow after an outbreak of plague
Rivalry kindled by the 1401 door contest
cards.answer: A city deadline. The niches on the guilds' grain-hall church had been assigned in 1339, and most stood empty for decades. In 1406 the commune gave the guilds ten years to fill theirs or forfeit them. Ghiberti's bronze Baptist and Donatello's St Mark followed. A clause in a decree bought early masterpieces.
cards.move: Before crediting a mood for a change, look for the deadline behind it.
cards.trap: Crediting civic rivalry, which had left the niches empty for decades.
cards.reference: Diane Finiello Zervas (ed.), Orsanmichele a Firenze, Franco Cosimo Panini, 1996

cards.question: Ghiberti's two Baptistery doors took 1403 to 1424 and 1425 to 1452. What share of his 77 years, to the nearest 10 per cent?
cards.answer: 48 / 77 = about 0.62, so 60 per cent to the nearest 10.
cards.move: Measure a great work in the years of life it consumed.
cards.hint: Add the two spans of years, then compare the total with his lifespan.
steps: 48 / 77 = about 0.62, so 60 per cent to the nearest 10.
cards.reference: Richard Krautheimer, Lorenzo Ghiberti, Princeton University Press, 1956

cards.question: True or false: the patterned marble front of Florence Cathedral was finished before Michelangelo was born?
cards.answer: False. It was finished in 1887. The medieval front, left half-built, was pulled down in 1587, and the cathedral faced its square with rough bare masonry for nearly three centuries. Emilio De Fabris's design, chosen by competition, went up from 1876. The Gothic face in every photograph is younger than the Statue of Liberty.
cards.move: A building's style tells you what it imitates, not when it was built.
cards.trap: Trusting Gothic-looking marble to be as old as its style.
cards.reference: Ross King, Brunelleschi's Dome: The Story of the Great Cathedral in Florence, Chatto & Windus, 2000

cards.question: What worried the committee that met in January 1504 to decide where Michelangelo's David should stand?
cards.answer: Weather and omens. Giuliano da Sangallo urged the covered Loggia so rain and frost would not ruin the soft marble. The city's herald wanted David to replace Donatello's Judith, a woman killing a man, as a bad sign for the state. David took Judith's place by the town-hall door and stood outdoors until 1873.
cards.move: Where a work is placed can decide what it is taken to mean.
cards.reference: Charles Seymour Jr., Michelangelo's David: A Search for Identity, University of Pittsburgh Press, 1967

cards.question: How can conservators map grains of Egyptian blue too small to see on an ancient statue?
options: The grains glow in infrared under visible light
The grains fluoresce under an ultraviolet lamp
The grains show up dark on an X-ray
cards.answer: The grains glow in infrared under visible light. Egyptian blue, the oldest synthetic pigment, re-emits absorbed light as strong near-infrared luminescence. A modified camera photographs a statue under ordinary light, and grains under a millimetre across shine white against dark stone. Faces and hems that look bare turn out to be dotted with blue.
cards.move: What looks blank to the eye may be loud to a different sensor.
cards.trap: Reaching for ultraviolet, the lamp museums use to spot later retouching.
cards.reference: Verri, The spatially resolved characterisation of Egyptian blue, Han blue and Han purple by photo-induced luminescence digital imaging, Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry, 2009

cards.question: Why were some of the Parthenon sculptures in London scraped with copper tools in 1937?
cards.answer: To make them whiter. Joseph Duveen, the dealer paying for their new gallery, wanted white marble, so workmen used copper tools and carborundum, a hard abrasive, to strip a brownish surface layer that may have held traces of ancient finish. The museum played the damage down; its extent was aired only in the late 1990s.
cards.move: A patron paying for the display can end up deciding what the object is.
cards.reference: Ian Jenkins, Cleaning and Controversy: The Parthenon Sculptures 1811–1939, British Museum Occasional Paper 146, 2001

cards.question: True or false: paint on ancient Greek marble statues was already documented in the nineteenth century?
cards.answer: True. In 1834 the architect Gottfried Semper argued that Greek buildings and statues had been painted, and in 1886 excavators on the Athenian Acropolis dug up the Peplos Kore with colour on her dress. She and other korai had been dumped in pits after the Persian sack of 480 BC, which sheltered the paint.
cards.move: When a finding sounds new, look up when it was first reported.
cards.trap: Taking today's exhibitions of painted statues as a recent discovery.
cards.reference: https://www.theacropolismuseum.gr/en/statue-kore-peplos-kore

cards.question: What did laser cleaning of the portals of Amiens Cathedral reveal in the 1990s?
cards.answer: That the stone saints had been painted. Laser cleaning, begun in 1992, exposed thirteenth-century blues, reds, ochres and gilding under the grime, best kept in the sheltered recesses and tympanums. Since 1999 summer evenings have projected those colours back onto the west front with light. The grey Gothic façade is a weathered one.
cards.move: The plain version of an old thing is often just the worn version.
cards.source: Amiens Métropole, La polychromie de la Cathédrale
cards.reference: https://www.amiens.fr/Vivre-a-Amiens/Culture-Patrimoine/Les-Archives-municipales-et-communautaires/Tresors-d-Archives/Tresors-d-archives/La-polychromie-de-la-Cathedrale

cards.question: Do the brightly painted modern reconstructions of Greek statues show roughly what ancient viewers saw?
cards.answer: Near enough. Each colour is placed where analysis found pigment, and the pigments themselves, from Egyptian blue to cinnabar, are identified. Pliny records that Praxiteles valued most the marbles the painter Nikias had finished. Showing the colour that survives is more honest than showing a white marble no Greek ever saw.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how much of the top layer is lost.
cards.counterpoint: Too crude. What survives is mostly the base layer; the shading, glazes, gilding and wax that finished a surface are the first to go. Reconstructions therefore show something like underpaint, and they resemble each other more than originals by different workshops would have. The evidence says colour, but not these flat colours.
cards.reference: Vinzenz Brinkmann & Raimund Wünsche (eds), Gods in Color: Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, Arthur M. Sackler Museum, Harvard, 2007

cards.question: Why did the painted faces of the Terracotta Army often flake away within minutes of being uncovered?
cards.answer: Because the paint sat on lacquer. Qin craftsmen coated each clay soldier in east Asian lacquer, then painted over it. After two thousand years in damp earth, the lacquer shrinks and curls as soon as it meets dry air, taking the colour with it. Excavators now keep fresh surfaces moist as they dig.
cards.move: Something preserved by its surroundings can be destroyed by being rescued from them.
cards.reference: Catharina Blänsdorf, Erwin Emmerling & Michael Petzet (eds), Die Terrakottaarmee des Ersten Chinesischen Kaisers Qin Shihuang, Bayerisches Landesamt für Denkmalpflege, 2001

cards.question: True or false: some late-Gothic German wooden altarpieces were delivered deliberately unpainted?
cards.answer: True. From about 1490 carvers such as Tilman Riemenschneider delivered limewood altarpieces with only a thin, tinted glaze, letting the carving carry the image. His Münnerstadt altarpiece was finished bare in 1492; a dozen years later the parish had Veit Stoss paint it. The later colour, not the bare wood, was the alteration.
cards.move: Correct an old mistake without overcorrecting into a new one.
cards.trap: Having learned old sculpture was painted, assuming all of it was.
cards.reference: Michael Baxandall, The Limewood Sculptors of Renaissance Germany, Yale University Press, 1980

cards.question: Which colours on ancient marble statues are most likely to have vanished leaving no trace for analysis?
options: Plant and insect dyes like madder
Earth reds and yellows like ochre
cards.answer: Plant and insect dyes like madder. Mineral pigments are stable crystals and leave grains to detect; dyes are organic molecules that light breaks down and damp and microbes consume. So the colours found lean towards the durable ones, and a reconstruction built only from finds is harsher and flatter than the original.
cards.move: What your instrument can detect decides the picture it gives you.
cards.trap: Picking blue, because blue is the famous lost colour of antiquity.
cards.reference: Jan Stubbe Østergaard (ed), Tracking Colour: The Polychromy of Greek and Roman Sculpture in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Preliminary Report 1, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, 2009

cards.question: Paint vanished from a marble relief centuries ago. How can low, raking light still show its patterns?
options: Pigment left a stain that catches light
Oil in the paint polished the marble
Painted areas weathered less and stand proud
cards.answer: Painted areas weathered less and stand proud. While it lasted, paint shielded the stone beneath from rain and wind; bare marble around it wore away faster. The difference is a fraction of a millimetre, but light skimming the surface throws tiny shadows along each border. Meanders and hems reappear as faint relief.
cards.move: Something that is gone can leave its outline in what it protected.
cards.trap: Looking for a trace of the colour itself rather than its shield.
cards.reference: Vinzenz Brinkmann, Die Polychromie der archaischen und frühklassischen Skulptur, Biering & Brinkmann, 2003

cards.question: Why do most Roman marble portraits carved before about AD 130 stare with smooth, blank eyeballs?
options: Blank eyes signalled calm or divinity
Irises and pupils were painted on
Glass eyes were set in and fell out
cards.answer: Irises and pupils were painted on. The paint wore away, leaving smooth stone. Under Hadrian, sculptors began carving the iris as a ring and drilling the pupil. That shift is precise enough to help date a portrait: a carved pupil points to the second century or later.
cards.move: A missing detail is not proof it was never there.
cards.trap: Reading the blankness as a style chosen by the sculptor.
cards.reference: Diana E. E. Kleiner, Roman Sculpture, Yale University Press, 1992

cards.question: Why do so many Roman marble statues lean against a carved tree stump?
cards.answer: Because the originals were bronze. Greek sculptors cast many famous figures in hollow bronze, strong in tension, which could balance on slim ankles. Marble cracks under that load, so Roman copyists added stumps and struts. The Doryphoros, the spear-bearer, survives mainly in marble copies, whose full-length versions lean on a trunk the original never had.
cards.move: When a copy adds a part, ask what the original managed without it.
cards.source: Metropolitan Museum, Roman Copies of Greek Statues
cards.reference: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/roman-copies-of-greek-statues

cards.question: What makes polished white marble look more like skin than other white stones do?
options: Its surface takes a glossier polish
Light enters the stone before scattering back
It reflects more light than other stones
cards.answer: Light enters the stone before scattering back. Calcite crystals are slightly translucent, so light travels a short way inside before it re-emerges, softening shadows as skin does. Plaster and opaque stones return it from the surface and look chalky. Computer graphics had to model the same effect before rendered faces stopped looking like plastic.
cards.move: A surface often looks the way it does because of what lies just beneath.
cards.trap: Crediting the polish, the part of the finish the eye notices first.
cards.reference: Jensen, Marschner, Levoy & Hanrahan, A Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport, Proceedings of SIGGRAPH, 2001

cards.question: Michelangelo's David stands 5.17 metres tall. Roughly how many tonnes of marble is it?
cards.answer: Marble weighs about 2.7 tonnes per m³: 1.9 × 2.7 ≈ 5 tonnes, close to the usual 5.6.
cards.move: Triple every dimension of a thing and its weight rises twenty-seven times.
cards.trap: Scaling the weight by three, as the height is, instead of by twenty-seven.
cards.hint: Start from the weight of a man, then scale him up in all three directions.
steps: A 1.75 m man weighs about 70 kg: about 0.07 m³ of water.
David is about 3 times taller, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 times the volume.
Marble weighs about 2.7 tonnes per m³: 1.9 × 2.7 ≈ 5 tonnes, close to the usual 5.6.
cards.reference: https://www.galleriaaccademiafirenze.it/en/artworks/david-michelangelo/

cards.question: True or false: Hiram Powers carved each of the six full-size marble versions of his Greek Slave himself?
cards.answer: False. Between 1844 and 1869 professional carvers in his Florence studio copied his plaster model into marble, transferring measured points with a pointing machine. That was ordinary practice: the sculptor modelled in clay, assistants cut the stone, and the master might only finish the surface. The fame went to the man who shaped the clay.
cards.move: A signature names who was responsible, not whose hands did the work.
cards.trap: Picturing the lone sculptor with a chisel, the image museums sell.
cards.source: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Greek Slave model
cards.reference: https://americanart.si.edu/artwork/model-of-the-greek-slave-20060

cards.question: What kept Michelangelo from carving for most of 1518 to 1520?
cards.answer: Building a road. Pope Leo X wanted the marble for the façade of San Lorenzo in Florence to come from Seravezza, on Florentine territory, rather than from Carrara. So Michelangelo opened quarries and drove a road through the mountains to the sea. In March 1520 the contract was cancelled. The façade is still bare brick.
cards.move: Behind every material is a supply route that someone had to build.
cards.reference: William E. Wallace, Michelangelo at San Lorenzo: The Genius as Entrepreneur, Cambridge University Press, 1994

cards.question: Why is Michelangelo's David so slender when seen from the side?
cards.answer: Because the block had been cut into before him. Quarried at Carrara in the 1460s for a figure on Florence cathedral, the tall, narrow block was begun by Agostino di Duccio, then taken up and dropped by Antonio Rossellino. It lay unused until 1501. Michelangelo fitted David into a slab others had spoiled.
cards.move: Before praising a design, ask what it was forced to fit inside.
cards.reference: John T. Paoletti, Michelangelo's David: Florentine History and Civic Identity, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: A marble figure is copied at exactly twice the height. By what factor does the pressure on its ankles rise?
cards.answer: Pressure is weight over area: 8 / 4 = 2 times.
cards.move: Scale a thing up and it grows heavier faster than it grows stronger.
cards.trap: Answering eight, the weight, and forgetting the ankles thicken too.
cards.hint: Compare how the weight and the area carrying it each grow with size.
steps: Weight grows with volume: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times heavier.
The ankles' cross-section grows with area: 2 × 2 = 4 times larger.
Pressure is weight over area: 8 / 4 = 2 times.
cards.reference: Galileo Galilei, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, trans. Henry Crew & Alfonso de Salvio, Macmillan, 1914

cards.question: True or false: a marble statue in clean, dry air can crumble into grains from daily sunshine alone?
cards.answer: True. Calcite, the crystal marble is made of, expands along one axis when warmed and shrinks slightly across it. Repeated heating and cooling pries neighbouring grains apart, and the surface loosens into a powder, a decay called sugaring. Thin marble cladding panels on sunny façades have bowed out of shape for the same reason.
cards.move: A small daily push, repeated for centuries, breaks what no single blow could.
cards.trap: Blaming city smoke and acid rain, the familiar enemies of stone.
cards.source: Siegesmund et al., Int. J. Earth Sciences, 2000
cards.reference: Siegesmund, Ullemeyer, Weiss & Tschegg, Physical weathering of marbles caused by anisotropic thermal expansion, International Journal of Earth Sciences, 2000

cards.question: By weight, what becomes of most of the stone cut from Carrara's marble quarries today?
options: Sawn slabs for floors and walls
cards.answer: Ground calcium carbonate powder. Only sound, fault-free blocks can be sawn, and freeing them from a mountain shatters far more rock than it frees. Estimates range, but around three quarters of what leaves the quarries goes to crushing plants, ending up in paper, paint, plastics and toothpaste. Michelangelo's mountain is mostly sold by the sack.
cards.move: Ask where the bulk goes, not where the showpiece goes.
cards.trap: Picturing statues and worktops, the uses of marble everyone has seen.
