cards.source: The Dial, The Curse of Carrara Marble
cards.reference: https://www.thedial.world/articles/news/issue-30/carrara-marble-mining

cards.question: Judging from his unfinished Prisoners, how did Michelangelo bring a figure out of a block?
options: From the front face, cutting backwards
Evenly from all sides at once
From a full-size model, point by point
cards.answer: From the front face, cutting backwards. The Prisoners in Florence have knees and chests carved free while their backs are still raw block. Vasari likened the method to raising a wax figure slowly out of water: the highest parts surface first. A cut too deep at the front could not be made good further back.
cards.move: Unfinished work shows the method that finished work hides.
cards.trap: Projecting the later studio habit of copying a plaster model point by point.
cards.reference: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Painters, Sculptors and Architects, trans. Gaston du C. de Vere, Everyman's Library, 1996

cards.question: Why did the forger Tom Keating write words in lead white on canvases before painting over them?
cards.answer: To plant evidence against himself. Lead white blocks X-rays, so the words would show on any X-ray. Keating, a restorer who claimed some 2,000 fakes of Samuel Palmer and others, said he acted against dealers who grew rich on artists. Some canvases also hid a glycerine layer that would lift the paint in cleaning.
cards.move: Some people break the rules chiefly to show the rule-keepers up.
cards.source: Keating, Norman & Norman, The Fake's Progress, 1977
cards.reference: Tom Keating, Geraldine Norman & Frank Norman, The Fake's Progress, Hutchinson, 1977

cards.question: Attributed to a follower of Leonardo, what did today's Salvator Mundi fetch at a London sale in 1958?
cards.answer: About £45. Cleaned, restored and attributed to Leonardo himself, the same walnut panel sold at Christie's in New York in 2017 for $450 million. The panel was the same at both sales; the name on the label was not. That gap is the space every forger works in.
cards.move: Ask how much of a price is the thing and how much the name.
cards.trap: Letting the $450 million pull the guess into the thousands or millions.
cards.reference: https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/homes-and-property/fine-art-antiques/leonardo-da-vinci-s-saviour-of-the-world-sold-for-45-in-1958-now-for-sale-at-100m-1.3265906

cards.question: If no expert can tell a forgery from the original, is the forgery worth less as art?
cards.answer: Yes. A painting is not only a surface but an achievement: someone found that composition, that light, for the first time. A forger who copies a style solves no problem the original artist had not already solved. Admiring the fake means admiring an invention its maker never made, so exposure rightly changes its worth.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether art is an object or a deed.
cards.counterpoint: No. The pleasure a picture gives lives in what the eye meets, and that has not changed. Van Meegeren's Emmaus drew crowds in Rotterdam in 1938; nothing on the canvas altered when his name replaced Vermeer's. Prices fell because the market pays for names and scarcity, and that is snobbery, not aesthetics.
cards.reference: Denis Dutton (ed), The Forger's Art: Forgery and the Philosophy of Art, University of California Press, 1983

cards.question: True or false: the young Michelangelo carved a Cupid that was then aged and sold as an ancient Roman statue?
cards.answer: True. In 1496 he carved a sleeping Cupid; it was treated to look excavated, and the dealer Baldassarre del Milanese sold it to Cardinal Raffaele Riario as an antique. The cardinal found out and demanded his money back, but the affair brought Michelangelo to Rome, where his first great commissions followed. The Cupid is lost.
cards.move: Talent and fraud are not opposites; skill is what makes a fraud possible.
cards.trap: Assuming a genius would never need to pass work off as another's.
cards.reference: Giorgio Vasari, The Lives of the Artists, trans. Julia Conaway Bondanella & Peter Bondanella, Oxford University Press, 1991

cards.question: Why did Eric Hebborn insist that his drawings in the manner of old masters were not forgeries?
cards.answer: Because he never signed them. Hebborn drew in the manner of masters from Mantegna to Van Dyck on old paper and let experts supply the names; a wrong attribution, he argued, was their error. Suspicion began in 1978, when a curator found two supposed old drawings on the same paper. He later claimed 1,000 fakes.
cards.move: A claim can mislead even when nobody wrote a false word.
cards.reference: Eric Hebborn, Drawn to Trouble: The Forging of an Artist, Mainstream Publishing, 1991

cards.question: True or false: Giorgio de Chirico denounced some of his own genuine early paintings as forgeries?
cards.answer: True. In later life he disowned genuine canvases from his celebrated metaphysical years, sometimes out of spite towards their owners, while painting new versions of the same works and dating them to the 1910s. The market paid for early dates, and he could assign them. Scholars now accept many of the disowned pictures as genuine.
cards.move: The person with most to gain from a record is its least safe keeper.
cards.trap: Assuming the artist is the one witness who cannot be wrong.
cards.reference: https://brooklynrail.org/2017/05/criticspage/The-Trouble-with-De-Chirico-/

cards.question: What did a novelist and a rock star set out to show about the art world by inventing a painter in 1998?
cards.answer: That people would claim to remember him. William Boyd wrote a biography of Nat Tate, an abstract painter said to have destroyed nearly all his work before killing himself in 1960, and drew the surviving pictures himself. At the New York launch, where David Bowie read from the book, guests said they knew the work.
cards.move: Nobody likes to admit ignorance in a room where everyone seems to know.
cards.reference: William Boyd, Nat Tate: An American Artist 1928–1960, 21 Publishing, 1998

cards.question: Why was Mark Landis never prosecuted, after fooling some 46 American museums with forgeries over three decades?
options: The statute of limitations had run
He was judged unfit to stand trial
He never took money for them
cards.answer: He never took money for them. Landis gave his copies away, sometimes posing as a priest, and claimed no tax deduction. Fraud needs a victim who lost something, and a free gift left the museums poorer only in pride. A museum registrar, Matthew Leininger, exposed him in 2008; Landis went on donating.
cards.move: Before asking why nobody punished it, ask who was harmed and how.
cards.trap: The statute of limitations, the usual technicality that frees old crimes.
cards.reference: https://www.uc.edu/news/articles/legacy/enews/2012/03/uc-exhibit-focus--museums-vulnerability-to-an-artful-dodger-who-donates-forgeries.html

cards.question: Keating, Hebborn and van Meegeren each blamed resentment of the art world. What does that reveal about forgers' motives?
options: Little: the silent ones left no reasons
Resentment of experts drives most forgers
Most forgers are artists who failed first
cards.answer: Little: the silent ones left no reasons. A forger's motive enters the record only if he is caught and then chooses to explain, and memoirs favour grievance over greed. Forgers never caught, or caught and silent, are missing from the count. The famous confessions are a sample chosen by the wish to be heard.
cards.move: Stated reasons come mostly from people who wanted to state them.
cards.trap: Taking the famous confessions as a portrait of all forgers.
cards.reference: Noah Charney, The Art of Forgery: The Minds, Motives and Methods of Master Forgers, Phaidon, 2015

cards.question: Should a convicted forger be free to sell openly signed pastiches of the masters he once faked?
cards.answer: Yes. The crime was the lie about who painted a picture, not the skill. A pastiche signed by its maker and sold as his tells the truth, and the sentence has been served. John Myatt, jailed in 1999, has sold such genuine fakes openly for years, and buyers know what they get.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a label can travel with the object.
cards.counterpoint: No. Notoriety is the selling point, so the fraud keeps paying. A signature on the front can be painted out or hidden under a frame, and a skilled pastiche is a fake waiting for its next owner. Paintings outlive paperwork: once the bill of sale is lost, only the forger's skill remains, and that skill was the weapon.
cards.reference: Laney Salisbury & Aly Sujo, Provenance: How a Con Man and a Forger Rewrote the History of Modern Art, Penguin Press, 2009

cards.question: What finally stopped a London colourman selling mummy brown in the 1960s?
cards.answer: Supply, not scruples. C. Roberson & Co., artists' colourmen since the early 1800s, told Time magazine in 1964 that it had no mummy left to grind. The paint mixed ground Egyptian remains with white pitch and myrrh. A colour made from human bodies outlived the Victorians and ended only when the stock room was empty.
cards.move: Ask whether a practice was abandoned or simply ran out.
cards.reference: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/ground-mummies-were-once-ingredient-paint-180950350/

cards.question: True or false: Europeans swallowed ground Egyptian mummies as medicine before painters ever used them.
cards.answer: True. From the Middle Ages apothecaries sold mumia, powdered embalmed remains, taken for bruises, wounds and bleeding; demand peaked in the 16th and 17th centuries. The paint came out of that drug trade, supplied by the same merchants. The pigment was a side line of a pharmacy shelf.
cards.move: The famous use of a thing is rarely its first use.
cards.trap: The paint is the story everyone tells, so it seems to come first.
cards.reference: Richard Sugg, Mummies, Cannibals and Vampires: The History of Corpse Medicine from the Renaissance to the Victorians, Routledge, 2011

cards.question: Why is an embalmed Egyptian body called a mummy in the first place?
cards.answer: Because of a drug that was not in it. The Persian mum meant wax, and mumiya was a natural bitumen prized as medicine. Seeing black resin on embalmed bodies, medieval writers took them for a source of that drug, and the name slid from the tar to the corpse. The paint called mummy inherited both.
cards.move: A name can record a mistake long after the mistake is forgotten.
cards.reference: Karl H. Dannenfeldt, Egyptian Mumia: The Sixteenth Century Experience and Debate, The Sixteenth Century Journal, 1985

cards.question: What did Edward Burne-Jones do with his tube of mummy brown once he learned what it was made of?
options: Sent it back to his colourman
Used it up on one last canvas
cards.answer: Buried it in his garden. Assured by Alma-Tadema that the paint was ground from real Egyptian mummies, he fetched the tube from his studio and buried it there and then, as his wife Georgiana later recalled. A Victorian painter answered a paint label with a funeral: a tube laid in the earth like a body.
cards.move: Knowing where a material comes from can end a habit overnight.
cards.trap: Returning a product that disappoints is what a customer usually does.
cards.reference: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, 2 vols, Macmillan, 1904

cards.question: Should museums treat paintings thought to contain mummy brown as holding human remains?
cards.answer: If a pigment contains ground human bodies, the painting holds human remains, whatever the frame. Museums already limit how they show Egyptian mummies and return ancestral remains on request; consistency means at least labelling such works and consulting Egypt. The dead never agreed to become a brown on a Victorian palette.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how sure the evidence must be decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Almost no painting can be shown to contain mummy. Tubes sold under the name were often bitumen or earth, and analysis rarely tells them apart in a paint layer. Treating works as remains on suspicion would pull canvases from walls on a label, not on evidence. Respect is better spent where remains are certain.
cards.source: McCouat, Journal of Art in Society, 2013
cards.reference: Philip McCouat, The Life and Death of Mummy Brown, Journal of Art in Society, 2013

cards.question: Why did Victorian art manuals warn against mummy brown even when the mummy in it was genuine?
cards.answer: Because it made poor paint. Jules Adeline's art dictionary of 1891 granted a rich colour but said it dried with difficulty, was not permanent, and might contain ammonia and particles of fat. Embalming resins and bitumen stay soft in oil. Buyers of the real thing paid for a glaze that might never set.
cards.move: Judge a material by how it behaves, not by the story attached.
cards.reference: Jules Adeline, Adeline's Art Dictionary, Appleton, 1891; reprinted Frederick Ungar, New York, 1966

cards.question: A lab finds calcium phosphate, the mineral of bone, in a Victorian brown paint. What does that say about mummy?
cards.answer: Very little on its own. Ground mummy would contain bone, but so does bone black, charred animal bone, one of the century's commonest dark pigments and often mixed into browns. The finding is likely with mummy and just as likely without it. Only embalming markers, such as bitumen and resins, begin to narrow it.
cards.move: Evidence that is common without the cause cannot prove the cause.
cards.trap: Reading bone in the paint as proof of a human body.
cards.reference: Nicholas Eastaugh, Valentine Walsh, Tracey Chaplin and Ruth Siddall, Pigment Compendium: A Dictionary of Historical Pigments, Elsevier Butterworth-Heinemann, 2004

cards.question: A Victorian London colourman told a chemist how long one Egyptian mummy met his customers' demand. How long?
cards.answer: About twenty years. He told the chemist Arthur Church so, and Church printed it in his handbook on paint. Mummy was a glazing brown, brushed thinly into shadows, and one dried body grinds to kilograms of powder. For a single shop, that is five bodies a century.
cards.move: Before picturing an industry, ask how much each customer actually used.
cards.trap: Picturing warehouses of mummies ground by the tonne for artists.
cards.source: Church, The Chemistry of Paints and Painting, 1901
cards.reference: A. H. Church, The Chemistry of Paints and Painting, 3rd edition, Seeley and Co., London, 1901

cards.question: True or false: some of the mummy sold in sixteenth-century Europe was made from people dead only a few years?
cards.answer: True. In 1564 Guy de la Fontaine, a royal physician, visited a mummy dealer in Alexandria who admitted his stock was recent corpses, of slaves and the unclaimed, filled with bitumen and dried. Demand had outrun the old tombs. The ancient Egyptian in the jar was sometimes a stranger dead a few seasons.
cards.move: When demand outgrows a genuine source, suspect the supply of counterfeits.
cards.trap: Assuming Egypt's ancient tombs could meet all of Europe's demand.
cards.reference: Heather Pringle, The Mummy Congress: Science, Obsession, and the Everlasting Dead, Hyperion, 2001

cards.question: Mummy brown owed much of its darkness to bitumen in the bodies. Which Egyptian mummies contain the most?
cards.answer: Late and Graeco-Roman burials. Chemical analysis found petroleum bitumen absent or rare in early mummies, appearing in the New Kingdom and commonest in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, when far more people were embalmed. Those plentiful late bodies were what dealers could buy. The brown on a Victorian palette came from ordinary townspeople, not pharaohs.
cards.move: The famous examples of a thing are rarely the ones in circulation.
cards.trap: Picturing the pharaohs of the pyramid age, the mummies everyone knows.
cards.reference: Katherine A. Clark, Salima Ikram and Richard P. Evershed, The significance of petroleum bitumen in ancient Egyptian mummies, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, vol. 374, 2016

cards.question: As the 1400s went on, what did Florentine patrons start writing into contracts instead of gold and blue?
cards.answer: The master's own hand. Early contracts itemised materials: gold leaf, and ultramarine at a stated price by weight. Michael Baxandall traced a shift across the century toward clauses requiring the master himself to paint the figures, above all the faces, rather than his assistants. Paying for skill became the new way to show off.
cards.move: When the costly thing becomes common, status moves to what cannot be bought in bulk.
cards.reference: Michael Baxandall, Painting and Experience in Fifteenth-Century Italy, Oxford University Press, 1972

cards.question: Lorenzo de' Medici noted his family spent 663,755 florins from 1434 to 1471. At 3.5 g of gold per florin, how many tonnes of gold?
cards.answer: 2,323 kg / 1,000 = about 2.3 tonnes.
cards.move: Turn a sum of money into a physical pile before judging its size.
cards.trap: Stopping at kilograms and reading 2,323 as the answer.
cards.hint: Multiply florins by grams, then divide by a thousand twice.
steps: 663,755 florins x 3.5 g = about 2,323,000 g.
2,323 kg / 1,000 = about 2.3 tonnes.
cards.source: Gombrich, The Early Medici as Patrons
cards.reference: E. H. Gombrich, The Early Medici as Patrons of Art, in Norm and Form, Phaidon, 1966

cards.question: Where was Botticelli's Primavera hanging when a Medici inventory recorded it in 1499?
options: Over the altar of a family chapel
Above a daybed in a town house
cards.answer: Above a daybed in a town house. The inventory of Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici's house on Via Larga places it over a lettuccio, a built-in bench bed. Much Florentine painting was domestic: chests, bed-heads, birth trays. Most of it was used, worn out and thrown away, which is why museum walls look so churchy.
cards.move: Where things ended up tells you little about where they began.
cards.trap: Surviving Renaissance painting is mostly religious, so a chapel seems likely.
cards.reference: John Shearman, The Collections of the Younger Branch of the Medici, The Burlington Magazine, 1975

cards.question: How much freedom did Isabella d'Este give Perugino when she ordered a painting from him in 1503?
cards.answer: Almost none. Her written programme fixed the subject, a battle of Love and Chastity, named the figures, their actions and their places, and allowed him to leave things out but not to add anything of his own. Perugino's finished picture, now in the Louvre, is a patron's plan executed by a star.
cards.move: Ask who wrote the brief before crediting the author with the idea.
cards.reference: D. S. Chambers, Patrons and Artists in the Italian Renaissance, Macmillan, 1970

cards.question: True or false: Piero de' Medici objected to angels in his palace chapel frescoes while they were being painted.
cards.answer: True. In a letter of 1459, Benozzo Gozzoli answers Piero's objections to some seraphim in the Magi chapel of the Medici palace and offers to hide them behind small clouds. The patron checked the work on the wall, and the painter offered to rearrange heaven to suit him.
cards.move: A finished work often hides the arguments that shaped it.
cards.trap: Picturing frescoes as fixed at the design stage, then painted untouched.
cards.reference: D. S. Chambers, Patrons and Artists in the Italian Renaissance, Macmillan, 1970

cards.question: Florence voted the mercenary John Hawkwood a marble tomb in 1393. What honours him in its cathedral today?
options: A marble tomb with his effigy
cards.answer: A painted horse and rider. The tomb was never built; a painted substitute went up in the 1390s, and in 1436 Paolo Uccello replaced it with a fictive bronze statue frescoed in greenish earth. The works made him repaint his first horse. The commune honoured its general for the price of a wall.
cards.move: An honour can be kept cheaply by imitating the expensive version.
cards.trap: Picturing a bronze like the equestrian statues Italy soon raised.
cards.reference: John Pope-Hennessy, The Complete Work of Paolo Uccello, Phaidon, 1950

cards.question: Julius II's tomb was planned in 1505 with some 40 statues. How many by Michelangelo's own hand stand in the version finished in 1545?
cards.answer: Three: Moses, with Leah and Rachel beside him. After Julius died in 1513, his heirs forced new contracts in 1513, 1516, 1532 and 1542, each smaller. Assistants carved the rest, and the tomb went to San Pietro in Vincoli rather than St Peter's. Julius himself lies in St Peter's, not under his monument.
cards.move: A plan's scale says little about what survives the renegotiations.
cards.trap: Letting the planned forty set the guess for the finished tomb.
cards.reference: Howard Hibbard, Michelangelo, Harper & Row, 1974

cards.question: According to his bookseller, what did Cosimo de' Medici do to settle his conscience over money made in banking?
cards.answer: He spent it on a friary. Vespasiano da Bisticci says Cosimo, uneasy that some of his wealth was ill-gotten, asked Pope Eugenius IV for a remedy and was told to spend 10,000 florins on building. He rebuilt San Marco, spending far more. Fra Angelico's frescoes in its cells were part of the penance.
cards.move: Behind a generous gift, look for the debt the giver wanted cleared.
cards.reference: Vespasiano da Bisticci, The Vespasiano Memoirs, trans. William George and Emily Waters, Routledge, 1926

cards.question: What did Julius II first ask Michelangelo to paint on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in 1508?
cards.answer: Twelve apostles, with ornament filling the rest. In a letter of 1523 Michelangelo recalled telling the Pope it would be a poor thing, since the apostles too were poor, and Julius let him paint as he liked. The Creation scenes grew from the painter's objection, not the patron's plan.
cards.move: The first brief and the finished work can belong to different people.
cards.trap: Assuming the famous Genesis scenes were what the Pope ordered.
cards.reference: E. H. Ramsden (trans. and ed.), The Letters of Michelangelo, 2 vols, Peter Owen, 1963

cards.question: Who paid for Botticelli's Adoration of the Magi of about 1475, in which Medici faces play the kings?
cards.answer: Not the Medici. The patron was Guasparre del Lama, a money-changer of modest standing, for his altar in Santa Maria Novella. Casting Cosimo and his sons as the Magi advertised his loyalty to the city's real rulers. His own face is thought to be in the crowd: a broker painted into the Medici circle.
cards.move: When the powerful appear in a picture, ask who wanted to flatter them.
cards.reference: Ronald Lightbown, Sandro Botticelli: Life and Work, 2 vols, Paul Elek, 1978

cards.question: A 3 m column 10 m from the viewer is drawn 15 cm tall. In cm, how tall is an identical column 25 m away?
cards.move: Check which numbers in a problem matter before using all of them.
cards.trap: Taking off a fixed amount for each extra metre of distance.
cards.hint: Twice as far away means half as tall on the picture.
steps: In perspective, drawn size falls as 1 / distance.
25 m is 2.5 times as far as 10 m.
cards.reference: Leon Battista Alberti, On Painting, trans. John R. Spencer, Yale University Press, 1956

cards.question: How did Brunelleschi test whether his painting of Florence's Baptistery matched the building itself?
cards.answer: With a peephole and a mirror. He drilled a hole through the panel at the vanishing point; a viewer stood where he had painted from and looked through the back, at a mirror reflecting the picture. Painted and real Baptistery lined up. The sky was burnished silver, so real clouds drifted across it.
cards.move: A claim about how things look should come with a way to check it.
cards.reference: Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, The Life of Brunelleschi, ed. Howard Saalman, Pennsylvania State University Press, 1970

cards.question: True or false: the perspective of Leonardo's Last Supper is built for a monk standing on the refectory floor.
cards.answer: False. The vanishing point sits at Christ's right temple, where a nail hole left by the construction lines still shows, well above any standing monk's eye. The ideal viewpoint lies high up and several metres back. Diners on the floor saw a room they could never stand in, and accepted it.
cards.move: A rule's inventors often bent it the moment it got in the way.
cards.trap: Assuming perspective always matches a real viewer's position in the room.
cards.reference: Martin Kemp, Leonardo da Vinci: The Marvellous Works of Nature and Man, J. M. Dent, 1981

cards.question: How did Piero della Francesca get a human head into exact perspective?
cards.answer: Point by point. In his treatise on perspective for painters, from the 1470s, he draws a head in plan and in side view, marks numbered points on horizontal slices through it, and projects each point onto the picture separately. A painter of altarpieces was plotting a face the way software renders one.
cards.move: Anything can be drawn exactly if you are willing to go point by point.
cards.reference: J. V. Field, Piero della Francesca: A Mathematician's Art, Yale University Press, 2005

cards.question: Why are the feet of Mantegna's foreshortened dead Christ smaller than strict perspective allows?
cards.answer: Because strict perspective would have hidden him. Seen from the soles at that range, correct projection makes the feet huge and lets them block the chest and face. Mantegna shrank them and kept the head large, putting meaning ahead of geometry. The wounded feet stay readable without eclipsing the body.
cards.move: An exact method still needs someone to decide what matters most.
cards.reference: Martin Kemp, The Science of Art: Optical Themes in Western Art from Brunelleschi to Seurat, Yale University Press, 1990

cards.question: In a strict perspective drawing of a colonnade running parallel to the picture, which identical round columns come out widest?
cards.answer: Those towards the edges. Sight lines to a column far to one side meet the flat picture at a slant, so its outline is stretched sideways, like a torch beam striking a wall at an angle. Leonardo noticed the paradox: the columns farthest from the eye are drawn fattest. Painters quietly corrected them by eye.
cards.move: An exact rule can still produce a result nobody would accept.
cards.trap: Reasoning that columns at one depth must be drawn one width.
cards.reference: M. H. Pirenne, Optics, Painting and Photography, Cambridge University Press, 1970

cards.question: Eye 1.5 m up, picture 1 m ahead. Floor lines appear 50 cm and 10 cm below the horizon. How many metres apart are they?
cards.answer: 15 - 3 = 12 m of floor.
cards.move: On a flat picture, the far distance is packed into a thin strip.
cards.trap: Assuming equal drops in the picture mean equal stretches of floor.
cards.hint: By similar triangles, the drop below the horizon shrinks in proportion to distance.
steps: A floor line d metres away sits 1.5 x 1 / d metres below the horizon.
15 - 3 = 12 m of floor.

diagram.caption: 40 cm of picture holds 12 m of floor; the last 10 cm hold everything past 15 m.

cards.reference: J. V. Field, The Invention of Infinity: Mathematics and Art in the Renaissance, Oxford University Press, 1997

cards.question: Where do the receding lines meet in the painted architecture on Roman villa walls?
cards.answer: Mostly not at one point. At Boscoreale and Pompeii, receding beams and cornices converge in pairs towards a vertical axis down the middle, like a fishbone, so each zone looks deep but no single eye position fits the whole wall. Erwin Panofsky called this the vanishing axis. The single vanishing point waited for Florence.
cards.move: Looking right in each part does not make the whole consistent.
cards.reference: Erwin Panofsky, Perspective as Symbolic Form, trans. Christopher S. Wood, Zone Books, 1991

cards.question: Is linear perspective mainly a cultural convention rather than a faithful record of how people see?
cards.answer: Perspective assumes one unmoving eye, a flat picture and lines that stay straight, none of which matches two moving eyes and a curved retina. Many traditions showed space convincingly without it. Panofsky called it a symbolic form, and Nelson Goodman argued that pictures depict by learned rules. Its authority is five centuries of training.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether one fixed eye fairly models seeing decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Perspective is geometry: light travels in straight lines, so a correct picture sends the eye the same bundle of rays the scene would send from one point. A camera, which no culture trained, produces the very same construction. Gombrich and Pirenne argued that what is conventional is the fixed viewing position, not the rules themselves.
cards.reference: E. H. Gombrich, Art and Illusion: A Study in the Psychology of Pictorial Representation, Pantheon Books, 1960

cards.question: A painted square-tiled floor's diagonals meet the horizon 60 cm each side of the vanishing point. From how many cm should it be viewed?
cards.answer: Viewing distance = 60 cm.
cards.move: A picture built by rule tells you where to stand, if you read it.
cards.hint: Work out where a line at 45 degrees to the picture vanishes.
steps: Diagonals of square tiles run at 45 degrees to the picture.
Such lines vanish where a 45-degree sight line from the eye meets the picture.
That point lies as far from the central vanishing point as the eye is from the picture.
Viewing distance = 60 cm.
cards.reference: Martin Kemp, The Science of Art: Optical Themes in Western Art from Brunelleschi to Seurat, Yale University Press, 1990

cards.question: At Warhol's first solo show, in Los Angeles in 1962, what did one soup-can canvas cost?
cards.answer: $100. The Ferus Gallery lined up 32 canvases, one per Campbell's variety, on a narrow ledge like a supermarket shelf. Few sold, and the dealer Irving Blum kept the set together by buying all 32 from Warhol for $1,000, paid in instalments. The whole run now belongs to the Museum of Modern Art.
cards.move: Price a thing at the moment it was made, not the moment it became famous.
cards.trap: Today's huge Warhol prices pull the guess up to $10,000.
cards.source: Frei and Printz, Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, 2002
cards.reference: Georg Frei and Neil Printz (eds.), The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Volume 1, Phaidon, 2002

cards.question: Who designed the Brillo carton that Warhol reproduced as sculpture in 1964?
cards.answer: An abstract painter. James Harvey, a second-generation Abstract Expressionist, earned his living as a commercial designer and drew the Brillo box. When Warhol's painted plywood copies went on show at the Stable Gallery in 1964, Harvey's day job was exhibited in Manhattan as art. He died the following year.
cards.move: Behind most anonymous design is a named person with ambitions of their own.
cards.source: Frei and Printz, Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, 2004
cards.reference: Georg Frei and Neil Printz (eds.), The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Volume 2, Phaidon, 2004

cards.question: Where did the images in Roy Lichtenstein's comic-strip paintings come from?
cards.answer: Mostly from real comic books, panel by panel. His 1963 fighter-plane diptych reworks a drawing by Irv Novick from a 1962 DC war comic. Lichtenstein cropped, simplified and enlarged, but the original artists were neither credited nor paid. Novick's dogfight hangs in the Tate, four metres wide, under another man's name.
cards.move: Ask who drew the thing before admiring who enlarged it.
cards.reference: Diane Waldman, Roy Lichtenstein, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1993

cards.question: True or false: the term Pop art was first used by an American critic.
cards.answer: False. It came out of the Independent Group at London's Institute of Contemporary Arts in the mid-1950s and is usually credited to the British critic Lawrence Alloway. Richard Hamilton's 1956 collage for the show This Is Tomorrow already has a bodybuilder holding a giant lollipop marked POP. The label was British before the soup cans.
cards.move: The most famous practitioner is rarely the one who named the thing.
cards.trap: Warhol and New York dominate the story, so the name seems American.
cards.reference: Anne Massey, The Independent Group: Modernism and Mass Culture in Britain, 1945-59, Manchester University Press, 1995

cards.question: Should artists be free to build new works on other people's photographs without permission or payment?
cards.answer: Art has always fed on existing images, and Pop was built on them: labels, comics, press photos. Requiring licences hands owners a veto over commentary and lets only rich artists borrow. Transformation, not payment, should be the test; a silkscreened Prince says something a studio portrait never did.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether the new work competes with the original decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Photographers live by licensing exactly this use. In 2023 the US Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that licensing Warhol's Orange Prince to a magazine was not fair use of Lynn Goldsmith's 1981 photograph: both were portraits sold to illustrate stories about Prince. Adding a style is not a licence to compete with the source.
cards.reference: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508 (2023)

cards.question: How did Roy Lichtenstein get his machine-looking printers' dots onto canvas in the early 1960s?
cards.answer: By hand, through holes. In 1961 he pushed paint through a perforated metal screen with a dog-grooming brush; later came perforated paper stencils, and assistants did much of the dabbing. The dots imitated cheap printing but were applied by hand, each visible from across a room. The mechanical look was a craftsman's illusion.
cards.move: A machine look can take more handwork than the machine ever did.
cards.reference: Michael Lobel, Image Duplicator: Roy Lichtenstein and the Emergence of Pop Art, Yale University Press, 2002

cards.question: What did James Rosenquist's years painting billboards above Times Square teach him about big pictures?
cards.answer: That big images dissolve close up. Up against a giant face or plate of spaghetti, he saw only shapes of colour. His canvases crop fragments at that scale and jam them together. F-111, of 1964 to 1965, runs 26 metres round a room: a fighter plane cut by cake, a tyre, a hairdryer.
cards.move: Stand where the maker stood, and familiar images turn into shapes.
cards.reference: James Rosenquist with David Dalton, Painting Below Zero: Notes on a Life in Art, Alfred A. Knopf, 2009

cards.question: True or false: the line about everyone being world-famous for fifteen minutes first appeared in a Swedish museum's catalogue?
cards.answer: True. It was printed, credited to Warhol, in the catalogue of his 1968 retrospective at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm. Whether he ever said it is doubted: the curator Pontus Hultén is among those proposed as its real author, and Warhol later played with the line. His most quoted sentence may be exhibition copy.
cards.move: Trace a famous saying to its first printing before assigning it.
cards.trap: Picturing Warhol saying it to a camera, as he so often spoke.
cards.reference: Blake Gopnik, Warhol, Ecco, 2020

cards.question: Which of these showed the word POP first, years before Pop art had a name?
cards.answer: A Paolozzi pin-up collage, of 1947. Eduardo Paolozzi's I was a Rich Man's Plaything glues a pulp-magazine cover girl beside a revolver whose smoke reads POP, nine years before Hamilton's bodybuilder. He projected it among his scrapbook collages at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in 1952. The famous lollipop was the word's second outing.
cards.move: The famous first is often just the first that got noticed.
cards.trap: Choosing Hamilton's lollipop, the image credited with naming the movement.
cards.source: Spencer, Eduardo Paolozzi: Writings and Interviews, 2000
cards.reference: Robin Spencer (ed.), Eduardo Paolozzi: Writings and Interviews, Oxford University Press, 2000

cards.question: In 1965 Warhol's Brillo boxes were shipped to a gallery in Toronto. How did Canadian customs treat them?
cards.answer: Taxed as ordinary merchandise. Asked for an opinion, the director of the National Gallery of Canada said they were not sculpture, so duty was charged as on goods for sale, about 20 per cent. Copies of a grocery carton crossed a border and were treated as exactly that.
cards.move: Where money is at stake, someone must decide what counts as art.
cards.trap: Assuming officials would defer to the art world's label.
cards.reference: David Bourdon, Warhol, Harry N. Abrams, 1989

cards.question: Why are some bright yellows in Van Gogh's paintings slowly turning brown?
options: Light altering the chromium in the paint
Yellowed varnish lying over the paint
Soot and grime from years of display
cards.answer: Light altering the chromium. His chrome yellow, a synthetic lead chromate, darkens where light reduces its chromium to a greenish-brown form. Synchrotron studies in 2011 found the change in a thin skin at the paint surface, worst in the paler, sulfur-rich grades. Cleaning cannot fix it: the brown is the paint itself.
cards.move: Before blaming the dirt on top, check the thing underneath.
cards.trap: Varnish yellows and can be removed, so it seems the natural culprit.
cards.reference: Monico et al., Degradation Process of Lead Chromate in Paintings by Vincent van Gogh Studied by Means of Synchrotron X-ray Spectromicroscopy, Analytical Chemistry, 2011

cards.question: How could green wallpaper poison a Victorian room without anyone touching it?
cards.answer: Through the air, with help from mould. Scheele's green and emerald green were cheap copper-arsenic pigments. In damp rooms, moulds feeding on the paste turn arsenic into a volatile gas, later identified as trimethylarsine, which smells of garlic. How many it sickened is still argued; the garlic smell in damp bedrooms is not.
cards.move: A stable substance can still move if something living digests it.
cards.reference: Lucinda Hawksley, Bitten by Witch Fever: Wallpaper and Arsenic in the Victorian Home, Thames & Hudson, 2016

cards.question: True or false: the first published recipe for Prussian blue, printed in 1724, called for dried animal blood?
cards.answer: True. The published recipe of 1724 heated dried ox blood with potash, then added iron salts and alum. The blood supplied the nitrogen and carbon that become the cyanide groups binding the iron. Later makers used horn, hoof and leather scraps. The first modern synthetic blue came out of the slaughterhouse.
cards.move: Synthetic describes the process, not where the raw materials came from.
cards.trap: A synthetic pigment sounds like pure laboratory chemistry, not animal waste.
cards.source: Kraft, Bulletin for the History of Chemistry, 2008
cards.reference: Alexander Kraft, On the Discovery and History of Prussian Blue, Bulletin for the History of Chemistry, 2008

cards.question: How did an iron factory vessel in Scotland give painters one of their strongest modern blues?
cards.answer: By contaminating a batch. In 1928 chemists at Scottish Dyes in Grangemouth found a stable blue-green impurity in phthalimide made in an iron vessel. The iron had joined the reaction. The compound, named phthalocyanine, was launched by ICI in 1935 as Monastral Blue. A reject batch became a staple of every artists' paint range.
cards.move: Before throwing out a contaminated batch, ask what the contamination made.
cards.reference: Frank H. Moser and Arthur L. Thomas, Phthalocyanine Compounds, Reinhold, 1963

cards.question: True or false: synthetic alizarin, first made from coal tar in 1868, is a different molecule from the red in madder root.
cards.answer: False. It is the same molecule. In 1868 Carl Graebe and Carl Liebermann made alizarin from anthracene, a coal-tar product, so factories could replace the plant rather than imitate it. Within a few decades most of the madder fields around Avignon, once a major crop, had gone.
cards.move: A perfect chemical copy leaves the original nothing to compete on but price.
cards.trap: Synthetic sounds like imitation, so a different compound seems likely.
cards.reference: Simon Garfield, Mauve: How One Man Invented a Colour That Changed the World, Faber and Faber, 2000

cards.question: Why did Japanese woodblock prints turn suddenly and intensely blue around 1830?
cards.answer: Because Prussian blue became cheap. Made in Europe since the early 1700s, it had reached Japan only in small, costly amounts; from about 1829 Chinese makers supplied it in bulk through Canton. Printers seized a blue that stayed bright where dayflower blue faded. Hokusai's Great Wave, of about 1831, rides that glut.
cards.move: A style can begin with a drop in the price of one material.
cards.reference: Henry D. Smith II, Hokusai and the Blue Revolution in Edo Prints, in John T. Carpenter (ed.), Hokusai and His Age, Hotei Publishing, 2005

cards.question: True or false: zinc white, sold as a non-toxic substitute for lead white, gives a tougher, more flexible oil film?
cards.answer: False. Zinc oxide reacts with the fatty acids of drying oil to form zinc soaps, and the film turns brittle within decades. Zinc-rich grounds and layers, common from the late 19th century, crack and flake apart. Lead white also forms soaps but ages into a tough skin. The safer white proved the weaker one.
cards.move: A safer replacement can fail in ways the old material never did.
cards.trap: Assuming the newer, safer product must also be the sturdier one.
cards.reference: Gillian Osmond, Zinc white: a review of zinc oxide pigment properties and implications for conservation, AICCM Bulletin, 2012

cards.question: How did a yellow used by Titian and Vermeer drop out of art history for two centuries?
cards.answer: It fell out of use, then out of the books. Lead-tin yellow, made by roasting lead and tin oxides, left palettes in the 18th century, and later writers mistook its traces for Naples yellow. Richard Jacobi identified it in 1941; Hermann Kühn mapped it across old masters. The Milkmaid's bodice spent two centuries unnamed.
cards.move: A thing can be in plain sight and still be missing from the record.
cards.reference: Hermann Kühn, Lead-Tin Yellow, in Artists' Pigments vol. 2, ed. Ashok Roy, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1993

cards.question: Should the European Union ban cadmium pigments from artists' paints?
cards.answer: Cadmium is a toxic metal that builds up in soil and in the kidneys of people who eat what grows there. Painters rinse brushes into sinks, and the cadmium passes through sewage works into sludge spread on farmland. Safer yellows and reds exist. A persistent poison should not go down the drain for a shade.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the size of this source against all the others decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The cadmium in paint is locked in a sulphide or selenide that barely dissolves, and artists' paint is a tiny share of the cadmium reaching farmland, far below what phosphate fertiliser brings. In 2014 the EU chemicals agency's risk committee found no risk that justified a ban. Substitutes still fall short on opacity and lightfastness.
cards.reference: European Chemicals Agency, Committee for Risk Assessment opinion on the Swedish proposal to restrict cadmium and its compounds in artists' paints, 2014

cards.question: Van Gogh's Roses of 1890, now in New York, shows pale white blooms against green. What colour did he paint them?
cards.answer: Pink. He used a red lake made from eosin, a synthetic dye of the 1870s that fades fast in light, and the petals have lost nearly all of it. He wrote to Theo that such colours were unstable, so he laid them on raw. The roses paled on the wall, not on the easel.
cards.move: What survives on the surface may not be what was put there.
cards.trap: Trusting the colours on the wall as the colours he chose.
cards.source: Vellekoop et al., Van Gogh's Studio Practice, 2013
cards.reference: Marije Vellekoop, Muriel Geldof, Ella Hendriks, Leo Jansen and Alberto de Tagle (eds.), Van Gogh's Studio Practice, Mercatorfonds and Yale University Press, 2013

cards.question: Why could grinding lapis lazuli very finely still fail to give a painter ultramarine?
cards.answer: Because most of the stone is not blue. Ground lapis gives a dull grey-blue: the blue mineral, lazurite, is mixed with white calcite and pyrite. Cennini's recipe kneads the powder into a dough of wax, resin and oil, then works it under lye. The blue grains sink out; the grey stays in the dough.
cards.move: Often the cost of a thing is the waste that must be removed.
cards.reference: Cennino Cennini, The Craftsman's Handbook (Il Libro dell'Arte), trans. Daniel V. Thompson, Yale University Press, 1933

cards.question: How did France come to have a cheap artificial ultramarine by 1828?
options: A chemist's accident in a dye works
A public prize with a price ceiling
A painter's experiments with kitchen clay
cards.answer: A public prize with a price ceiling. In 1824 the Société d'Encouragement pour l'Industrie Nationale offered 6,000 francs for an artificial ultramarine as good as the natural one and costing no more than 300 francs a kilogram. Jean-Baptiste Guimet, an engineer at the Toulouse gunpowder works, won in 1828 and kept his process secret.
cards.move: Name the price you need, and inventors will aim at it.
cards.trap: Picturing a lucky accident, the way other famous colours were found.
cards.reference: Philip Ball, Bright Earth: The Invention of Colour, Viking, 2001

cards.question: True or false: ultramarine, ground from a gemstone, withstands dilute acid better than most pigments?
cards.answer: False. Dilute acid bleaches it quickly, with a smell of rotten eggs. The blue comes from sulfur ions held in a cage of aluminium silicate; acid breaks the cage, hydrogen sulfide escapes and the colour goes. Conservators use this as a test: a drop of acid under the microscope, and the blue vanishes.
cards.move: Hard to scratch and hard to dissolve are different kinds of tough.
cards.trap: Assuming a gemstone's hardness means it resists chemical attack too.
cards.reference: Joyce Plesters, Ultramarine Blue, Natural and Artificial, in Artists' Pigments vol. 2, ed. Ashok Roy, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1993

cards.question: What put grains of ultramarine into the dental tartar of a woman buried at a German convent?
cards.answer: Most likely, painting books. Researchers found lazurite grains in the hardened plaque of a woman buried at Dalheim around 1000 to 1200. The likeliest route is licking a brush to a point while painting with ultramarine, kept for the finest manuscripts. A craft usually credited to monks left its blue in a woman's teeth.
cards.move: A name missing from the records is not a worker missing from the work.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/sciadv.aau7126

cards.question: What household job did cheap synthetic ultramarine take on in Victorian Britain?
cards.answer: Making the washing look white. Laundry blue, such as Reckitt's from the 1850s, put synthetic ultramarine in the final rinse. Blue cancels the yellow that old cotton and soap leave, so the eye reads the cloth as whiter, though it reflects slightly less light. The painters' costliest blue ended in a cloth bag.
cards.move: A colour cast is often cured by adding its opposite, not removing it.
cards.reference: https://cameo.mfa.org/wiki/Reckitt's_Blue

cards.question: Why is a corner of Michelangelo's unfinished Entombment in London still bare panel?
cards.answer: Probably because the blue never arrived. The blank at lower right was most likely meant for the kneeling Virgin, whose mantle needed ultramarine, the costliest pigment, which painters often added last. Michelangelo left for Florence and the marble block that became David. His Manchester Madonna, in the same gallery, lacks the same blue.
cards.move: An unfinished work often shows which material was hardest to get.
cards.reference: https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/michelangelo-the-entombment-or-christ-being-carried-to-his-tomb

cards.question: Ghirlandaio's 1485 contract priced ultramarine at 4 florins per 28 g ounce. At 3.5 g of gold a florin, grams of gold per gram?
cards.answer: 14 g / 28 g = 0.5 g of gold per gram of blue.
cards.move: Test a proverbial comparison by putting both sides in one unit.
cards.trap: Taking the saying worth its weight in gold literally.
cards.hint: Turn the price of one ounce into grams of gold first.
steps: 4 florins x 3.5 g = 14 g of gold per ounce.
An ounce of ultramarine weighs about 28 g.
14 g / 28 g = 0.5 g of gold per gram of blue.
cards.reference: Michael Baxandall, Painting and Experience in Fifteenth-Century Italy, Oxford University Press, 1972

cards.question: Ground in egg, ultramarine glows; ground in linseed oil, the same powder looks dark and dull. Why?
options: The oil yellows over the blue
The oil bends light like the grains
The oil dissolves some of the blue
cards.answer: The oil bends light like the grains. Lazurite, the blue mineral, and linseed oil share a refractive index near 1.5, so light crosses each grain's edge without scattering. Lean egg tempera leaves air around the grains, and every edge shines. Thick ultramarine in oil reads almost black, so painters often laid it over white.
cards.move: What surrounds a particle can matter as much as the particle.
cards.trap: Blaming yellowed oil, the usual suspect when old paint looks wrong.
cards.reference: Rutherford J. Gettens and George L. Stout, Painting Materials: A Short Encyclopaedia, Van Nostrand, 1942

cards.question: True or false: Yves Klein patented the blue named after him, International Klein Blue?
cards.answer: False. In 1960 Klein lodged a sealed description with France's patent office in a Soleau envelope, which proves a date but grants no monopoly. What it described was a binder, a synthetic resin in solvents, not a new pigment. The blue was ordinary synthetic ultramarine, held so lightly it kept the velvet of dry powder.
cards.move: Ask what exactly a registration protects before calling it ownership.
cards.trap: Repeating the famous story that an artist once patented a colour.
cards.reference: Hannah Weitemeier, Yves Klein 1928-1962: International Klein Blue, Taschen, 1994

cards.question: True or false: Guimet was the only chemist to make artificial ultramarine in 1828, the year the French prize was won?
cards.answer: False. Christian Gmelin, a chemistry professor in Tübingen, made it independently that year and published his method, while Guimet kept his secret. Chemists had already noticed blue deposits in soda furnaces in the 1810s and matched them to ultramarine. The prize fixed the price, but the recipe was ripe for anyone to find.
cards.move: Before crediting a reward, ask who was about to succeed without it.
cards.trap: Crediting the prize alone, as if nobody else was close.
cards.reference: Joyce Plesters, Ultramarine Blue, Natural and Artificial, in Artists' Pigments vol. 2, ed. Ashok Roy, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1993

cards.question: Is a photo a record of what was there?
cards.answer: Partly a reconstruction. Each pixel on a camera sensor measures only one colour, behind a red, green or blue filter. The other two values are interpolated from the neighbours. Every ordinary digital photograph is roughly two-thirds informed guesswork, done well enough that nobody notices.
cards.move: Two of every three colour values in your photos were guessed.
cards.source: Bayer filter demosaicing, standard in digital sensors
cards.reference: Bayer, Color imaging array, US Patent 3,971,065, 1976

cards.question: Who can take a film away from its director when the shoot runs far over budget?
cards.answer: The completion guarantor. Banks lending against an independent film demand a bond promising delivery on budget, and the bond company reads the daily cost reports in return. In the last resort it can take over, replace the director and finish the film. Usually the threat suffices: a visit from the guarantor rewrites the schedule.
cards.move: Whoever pays when a plan fails ends up holding the real power over it.
cards.reference: Vogel, Entertainment Industry Economics: A Guide for Financial Analysis, 9th edn, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: Why did Fox owe Shirley MacLaine her full fee for a musical it never made?
cards.answer: Her contract guaranteed $750,000 whether or not the film was shot. Fox cancelled Bloomer Girl and offered her a western in Australia; she refused. In 1970 the California Supreme Court held she need not take a different, lesser job to cut the studio's loss. Pay-or-play clauses still pay stars for films that never roll.
cards.move: A guarantee is worth what it costs the other side to cancel it.
cards.reference: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp., 3 Cal.3d 176, Supreme Court of California, 1970

cards.question: Why does a Georgia peach logo appear in the end credits of so many blockbusters?
cards.answer: It is worth 10% of the budget spent there. Since 2008 Georgia has given productions a tax credit of 20% of qualifying local spending, plus 10% for showing the state's logo, and a production owing no Georgia tax can sell the credit to one that does. Studios built soundstages outside Atlanta to collect it.
cards.move: Follow a location decision back to the tax code before the scenery.
cards.reference: Georgia Entertainment Industry Investment Act, O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.26, 2008

cards.question: True or false: El Mariachi reached cinemas in 1993 having cost about $7,000 in total?
cards.answer: False. About $7,000 paid for Robert Rodriguez's shoot on 16 mm film, some of it earned as a paid volunteer in a drug trial. Columbia then spent many times that sum on sound, a blow-up to 35 mm and prints before release. The legendary figure bought the raw footage, not the film audiences saw.
cards.move: Ask which stage a famous price tag covers before comparing it with others.
cards.trap: True, because the $7,000 figure is quoted as the film's cost.
cards.reference: Rodriguez, Rebel Without a Crew, Dutton, 1995

cards.question: A shoot needs 30 outdoor days, each with an independent 95% chance of good weather. What is the chance none is lost?
cards.answer: About 20%. The days must all go well, so the chances multiply: 0.95 multiplied by itself 30 times is about 0.21. That is why budgets carry a contingency, often around a tenth of the total, and why outdoor schedules keep cover sets ready for a wet morning. A safe-looking day is a risky month.
cards.move: Many small risks in a row add up to a likely failure.
cards.trap: About 95%, since every single day is very likely fine.

diagram.caption: Each day is 95% safe; thirty in a row come off only about one time in five.

cards.source: Honthaner, The Complete Film Production Handbook
cards.reference: Honthaner, The Complete Film Production Handbook, 4th edn, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: What did New Zealand's Parliament rewrite within days in 2010 to keep The Hobbit films from leaving?
cards.answer: Its employment law. After an actors' union dispute, Warner Bros. executives flew to Wellington amid talk of moving the shoot abroad. Parliament then passed, under urgency, an amendment making film workers contractors rather than employees unless their contracts said otherwise, and the government raised its subsidy. A national labour law was reshaped around one production.
cards.move: When one buyer can walk away, the rules tend to bend towards it.
cards.reference: Employment Relations (Film Production Work) Amendment Act 2010, New Zealand Parliament, 2010

cards.question: Coming to America brought in about $288 million. Under Paramount's contract definition, how much net profit did it make?
cards.answer: None at all. Before any net profit, Paramount's formula deducted distribution fees, overheads, interest and the stars' shares of the gross, so costs grew with the takings. The columnist whose idea it used sued for his share; in 1990 a Los Angeles judge called the formula unconscionable. Paramount later settled for $900,000.
cards.move: Before accepting a share of the profit, read who gets to define it.
cards.trap: Subtracting the budget from the takings and calling the rest profit.
cards.reference: O'Donnell & McDougal, Fatal Subtraction: The Inside Story of Buchwald v. Paramount, Doubleday, 1992

cards.question: Should governments pay film productions to shoot within their borders through tax credits?
cards.answer: Productions are mobile and nearly every rival offers incentives, so a place that refuses simply loses the work. Credits bring crews, studios and suppliers that stay: rebates helped fill soundstages in Budapest and London year after year, and the skilled jobs they sustain grew from the first subsidised shoots. Screen tourism adds more on top.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether the jobs stay once the subsidy stops.
cards.counterpoint: Independent audits keep finding that a state recovers well under half of each credit dollar in new tax, so the rest is taken from schools and roads. Many jobs are short and filled by crews flown in, and when a neighbour bids higher the productions move. Tannenwald's 2010 review found little lasting return for the money.
cards.reference: Tannenwald, State Film Subsidies: Not Much Bang for Too Many Bucks, Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, 2010

cards.question: Jack Nicholson took a reduced $6 million fee to play the Joker in 1989's Batman. Roughly what did the role earn him?
cards.answer: Over $50 million, by most estimates; some reach $90 million. Nicholson swapped a higher fee for a share of the gross takings and of merchandise bearing the Joker, and the film took over $400 million worldwide. The small figure was only the floor of the deal. Every Joker T-shirt sold paid him a little more.
cards.move: Price a deal by its share of the upside, not by its headline sum.
cards.trap: Letting the $6 million fee set the scale for the whole payday.
cards.reference: https://www.slashfilm.com/1155076/box-office-smash-batman-likely-never-made-a-profit-and-it-was-the-jokers-fault/

cards.question: A studio feature has a 110-page script. Roughly how many shooting days will it need?
cards.answer: 110 / 2.5 = about 44 shooting days.
cards.move: Break a schedule into the unit the planners themselves count in.
cards.trap: Guessing a week or two, forgetting each minute needs many setups.
cards.hint: Start from how many script pages a crew gets through in a day.
steps: A script page runs about one minute on screen.
A studio unit typically shoots 2 to 3 pages a day; take 2.5.
110 / 2.5 = about 44 shooting days.
cards.reference: Singleton, Film Scheduling: Or, How Long Will It Take to Shoot Your Movie?, 2nd edn, Lone Eagle, 1991

cards.question: Of roughly 15 minutes of dinosaurs on screen in Jurassic Park, how many are computer-generated?
cards.answer: About 6 minutes, by most counts; some say nearer 4. Most dinosaur shots are Stan Winston's full-size animatronics and puppets; Industrial Light & Magic's computer animation took the wide, running shots no machine could do. Its test was so convincing that Phil Tippett's planned stop-motion was dropped, and his team directed the digital dinosaurs instead.
cards.move: A landmark is remembered for its novelty, not for what it mostly was.
cards.trap: About 14 minutes, remembering it as the great computer-graphics film.
cards.source: Shay & Duncan, The Making of Jurassic Park
cards.reference: Shay & Duncan, The Making of Jurassic Park, Ballantine Books, 1993

cards.question: What missing ingredient made early computer animation look stuttering and fake beside live action?
cards.answer: Motion blur. A film camera's shutter is open for about half of each frame, so anything moving smears slightly; early renderers drew every frame as a frozen, perfectly sharp instant. In 1984 Cook, Porter and Carpenter at Lucasfilm showed how to render blur by sampling across the exposure. The eye reads the smear as speed.
cards.move: A copy looks false when it is more perfect than the original.
cards.reference: Cook, Porter & Carpenter, Distributed Ray Tracing, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH) 18(3), 1984

cards.question: Why did computer-generated skin look like wax or plastic until about 2001?
cards.answer: Renderers treated light as bouncing off the surface. In real skin much of it goes in, scatters among the layers and comes out nearby, softening shadows and glowing red at thin edges like ears. Henrik Wann Jensen and colleagues published a practical model of this subsurface scattering in 2001, and Gollum's skin soon used it.
cards.move: When something looks lifeless, check what happens beneath its surface.
cards.reference: Jensen, Marschner, Levoy & Hanrahan, A Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport, SIGGRAPH, 2001

cards.question: True or false: a three-dimensional computer-animated hand appeared in a feature film six years before Tron?
cards.answer: True. Futureworld, in 1976, showed a computer-animated hand and face made years earlier at the University of Utah by Ed Catmull, later a Pixar founder, and Fred Parke. Tron, in 1982, was the first to build long sequences this way. A few seconds of shaded polygons came before the famous light cycles.
cards.move: The first famous example is rarely the first example.
cards.trap: False, because Tron is the film everyone links with early computer graphics.
cards.reference: Price, The Pixar Touch: The Making of a Company, Knopf, 2008

cards.question: Should performances captured on set and finished by animators be eligible for acting awards?
cards.answer: The actor chooses every beat: the timing, the eyes, the voice, the weight of the body. Andy Serkis played Gollum and Caesar on set, opposite the other actors, and the animation follows his recorded face and movement. Heavy make-up has never disqualified a performance; pixels laid over the same performance should not either.
cards.move: The question turns on how much of the final image the actor controlled.
cards.counterpoint: The final image is built by animators who adjust, exaggerate and sometimes replace what the actor did, frame by frame. Voters cannot see where the capture ends and the animators' choices begin. An acting award to one name would erase dozens of artists whose decisions are the ones on screen.
cards.reference: Menache, Understanding Motion Capture for Computer Animation and Video Games, Morgan Kaufmann, 2000

cards.question: Why was every frame of O Brother, Where Art Thou?, from 2000, scanned into a computer before release?
cards.answer: To turn summer green into dusty gold. Shot in lush Mississippi, the film needed the look of a Depression-era drought, and no filter could drain the greens alone. Roger Deakins and Cinesite scanned the negative and regraded it digitally, widely cited as the first Hollywood feature finished that way throughout.
cards.move: When no tool can change one part alone, change the medium itself.
cards.reference: Fisher, Escaping from Chains, American Cinematographer, October 2000

cards.question: Pixar's computers grew vastly faster between Toy Story, 1995, and Monsters University, 2013. What happened to render time per frame?
cards.answer: It stayed at hours. Monsters University took about 29 hours to render each frame, on a farm of some 24,000 cores, because artists spent every gain on more hair, light bounces and detail. Graphics people call this Blinn's law: render time holds steady as machines speed up. The picture improves; the wait does not shrink.
cards.move: Faster tools save time only if the ambitions stay where they were.
cards.trap: Expecting faster machines to shorten the wait, as if the job stayed fixed.
cards.reference: https://gamesbeat.com/the-making-of-pixars-latest-technological-marvel-monsters-university/

cards.question: True or false: Masahiro Mori drew his 1970 uncanny valley curve from measurements of how people reacted to robots?
cards.answer: False. Mori's essay in the Japanese magazine Energy was a thought experiment: the curve dipping into a valley where near-human figures turn eerie was sketched, not measured. Computer-animated films such as The Polar Express, in 2004, made it famous. Experiments since have found the dip in some setups and not others.
cards.move: Ask whether a famous curve was measured or simply drawn.
cards.trap: Taking a curve that vivid examples seem to confirm for measured data.
cards.reference: Mori, The Uncanny Valley, trans. MacDorman & Kageki, IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine 19(2), 2012

cards.question: Mad Max: Fury Road, praised for real vehicles and stunts, has about 2,700 shots. How many carry digital visual effects?
cards.answer: About three quarters: more than 2,000 shots. The stunts were real, but digital work erased safety rigs, replaced skies, added the sandstorm, extended landscapes and removed Charlize Theron's left forearm for Furiosa. The effects in it are the kind nobody notices, which is why the film reads as practical.
cards.move: The work that goes unnoticed is often the work that went best.
cards.trap: Letting the famous real stunts stand for the whole film.
cards.source: fxguide on Fury Road's visual effects
cards.reference: https://www.fxguide.com/fxfeatured/a-graphic-tale-the-visual-effects-of-mad-max-fury-road/

cards.question: Should studios be allowed to recreate dead actors digitally for new roles, with their estates' consent?
cards.answer: An estate already licenses a performer's name, voice and likeness, and consent keeps control with those who knew the actor's wishes. Rogue One brought back Peter Cushing's Grand Moff Tarkin in 2016 with his estate's approval. Since 2024 California law has required exactly this consent, so the practice is regulated, not wild.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether heirs can consent to a performance.
cards.counterpoint: A performance is choices made by a living person, and a replica makes new choices the actor never made, for a fee the actor never set. Heirs may have money motives the performer would have rejected, and every recreated role is one no living actor gets. Consent from heirs is not consent from the face doing the work.
cards.reference: California Assembly Bill 1836, Use of Likeness: Digital Replica, 2024

cards.question: Why did one studio lose almost its entire silent-era library in a single day?
cards.answer: Because it was kept in one place. In July 1937 the nitrate film in Fox's storage vaults at Little Ferry, New Jersey, caught fire and destroyed most of the studio's negatives from before 1935. Whole careers went with them: nearly all of Theda Bara's films, Fox's biggest star of the 1910s, are lost.
cards.move: Keep what cannot be replaced in more than one place.
cards.reference: Slide, Nitrate Won't Wait: A History of Film Preservation in the United States, McFarland, 1992

cards.question: Of the American silent features made from 1912 to 1929, what share survives complete in its original 35mm form?
cards.answer: About 14%. A Library of Congress survey of nearly 11,000 features found about 70% entirely lost; most of the rest survive incomplete, in foreign versions or on smaller-gauge copies. The silent era that film histories describe is reconstructed from a small, lucky fraction of what audiences actually saw.
cards.move: Before judging a whole era, ask how much of it is left to judge.
cards.trap: About 45%: the silent films one hears of all seem to exist.
cards.reference: Pierce, The Survival of American Silent Feature Films: 1912–1929, Council on Library and Information Resources and Library of Congress, 2013

cards.question: Who destroyed most of the silent films that are now lost?
cards.answer: Largely their owners. Once talkies took over around 1929, silent films had almost no resale value, while nitrate was costly to store, dangerous, and held recoverable silver. Studios let negatives rot, melted prints down or dumped them. The last known print of MGM's London After Midnight went in a studio vault fire in 1965.
cards.move: Things are lost less through disaster than through no longer seeming worth keeping.
cards.reference: Cherchi Usai, Silent Cinema: An Introduction, BFI Publishing, 2000

cards.question: True or false: a burning roll of nitrate film can keep burning under water?
cards.answer: True. Cellulose nitrate releases oxygen as it decomposes, so smothering does not stop it; once alight, a roll can burn even submerged, giving off toxic nitrous gases. That is why archives keep nitrate in small, fire-rated vault cells, so a fire in one cannot reach the others.
cards.move: Before choosing how to put out a fire, ask what it is feeding on.
cards.trap: Fire needs air, so water should always put it out.
cards.reference: National Film Preservation Foundation, The Film Preservation Guide: The Basics for Archives, Libraries, and Museums, 2004

cards.question: Once a nitrate film has been fully copied, should an archive keep the flammable original?
cards.answer: The original is the best evidence there will ever be. Every copy loses sharpness, tone and colour. In past decades archives copied nitrate onto safety film and then destroyed it, and modern scanners have since shown how much those copies missed. Kept cold and dry, nitrate can last well over a century.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what the same money would otherwise save.
cards.counterpoint: Nitrate is a fire hazard that needs costly, specialised vaults for as long as it exists. Budgets are fixed, and every year spent guarding a film that is already safely copied is a year not spent copying one that exists only once and is decaying now. Saving the unsaved film preserves more cinema.
cards.reference: Frick, Saving Cinema: The Politics of Preservation, Oxford University Press, 2011

cards.question: True or false: colour films from the 1940s often survive in truer colour than films from the 1970s?
cards.answer: True. Three-strip Technicolor recorded each scene on three black-and-white negatives, one per primary colour, and silver images barely fade. From the 1950s most films used single-strip Eastmancolor, whose dyes decay; many 1970s prints and negatives have faded towards pink. A 1939 film can be reprinted from its separations with its colour intact.
cards.move: Newer is not sturdier; ask what the thing is made of.
cards.trap: Assuming newer film stock must have kept its colour better.
cards.source: Read and Meyer, Restoration of Motion Picture Film
cards.reference: Read and Meyer, Restoration of Motion Picture Film, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2000

cards.question: A reel of acetate film starts to smell of vinegar. Left in the same store, how does its decay proceed?
options: It slows as the acid escapes
cards.answer: It speeds up. The acetate base breaks down into acetic acid, and that acid catalyses further breakdown, so once decay passes a threshold it feeds itself. The film shrinks, curls and turns brittle, and its fumes spread to cans nearby. Cold, dry storage is the only brake: it slows the chemistry that cannot be reversed.
cards.move: A process that makes its own fuel only moves one way.
cards.trap: Expecting decay to run at a steady pace, like slow fading.
cards.source: Image Permanence Institute, acetate storage guide
cards.reference: Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, Image Permanence Institute, Rochester Institute of Technology, 1993

cards.question: A nitrate reel never meets a flame. Left for decades in a warm, damp can, what does it become?
cards.answer: A brown, acrid powder. Nitrate decays in stages with no fire at all: the image fades and yellows, the emulsion turns sticky and blisters, the reel welds into one solid block, and at last it crumbles to dust. Warmth and damp speed every stage. Many lost films ended as powder in their cans.
cards.move: The dramatic danger is rarely the one that does most of the damage.
cards.trap: Treating fire as nitrate’s only danger, so an unburnt reel must be safe.
cards.reference: National Film Preservation Foundation, The Film Preservation Guide: The Basics for Archives, Libraries, and Museums, 2004

cards.question: Why did Charlie Chaplin burn the negative of a feature he had paid to make?
cards.answer: To settle a tax question. A Woman of the Sea, directed by Josef von Sternberg in 1926, was shelved after a single preview. In 1933, with the tax authorities examining his finances, Chaplin had the negatives burned on 21 June before witnesses, so its cost could be written off as a total loss.
cards.move: When a thing is worth more destroyed than kept, expect it to go.
cards.source: Robinson, Chaplin: His Life and Art
cards.reference: Robinson, Chaplin: His Life and Art, McGraw-Hill, 1985

cards.question: Keeping a film master costs $1,059 a year; a 4K digital master, $12,514. Extra for 100 titles over 10 years, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: 1,145,500 × 10 years = 11,455,000, about 11.5 million dollars.
cards.move: Count what it costs to keep a thing, not only to make it.
cards.trap: Assuming digital storage is cheap because disks keep getting cheaper.
cards.hint: Find the extra cost of one title for one year first.
steps: 12,514 − 1,059 = 11,455 dollars extra per title per year.
11,455 × 100 titles = 1,145,500 dollars a year.
1,145,500 × 10 years = 11,455,000, about 11.5 million dollars.
cards.reference: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Science and Technology Council, The Digital Dilemma: Strategic Issues in Archiving and Accessing Digital Motion Picture Materials, 2007

cards.question: In Walter Murch's weighting of what a cut must serve, how much does continuity of space count?
cards.answer: Four per cent. Murch's Rule of Six ranks emotion at 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, where the eye is looking 7%, the flat screen 5%, and three-dimensional space 4%. Emotion outweighs the other five combined, so an editor sacrifices from the bottom: a glass that jumps hands is forgiven when the moment lands.
cards.move: When something must give, decide in advance which things are allowed to break.
cards.source: Murch, In the Blink of an Eye
cards.reference: Murch, In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing, 2nd edn, Silman-James Press, 2001

cards.question: In a typical Hollywood feature made between 1930 and 1960, how long did the average shot last?
cards.answer: About 10 seconds. David Bordwell's counts put most studio-era features between 8 and 11 seconds a shot. The celebrated long takes were exceptions; the slowness people remember lies in the staging, not the cutting. By 2000 many features averaged 3 to 6 seconds a shot, and action films often cut every 2 or 3.
cards.move: The famous exception is the one you remember, not the one that was typical.
cards.trap: Picturing the famous unbroken takes and taking them for the norm.
cards.reference: Bordwell, Intensified Continuity: Visual Style in Contemporary American Film, Film Quarterly 55(3), 2002

cards.question: True or false: the Kuleshov effect was established by measuring audience reactions in the 1920s?
cards.answer: False. The original footage is lost, and the evidence is Kuleshov's and Pudovkin's own later accounts, which even disagree on the shots used. The first controlled recreation, in 1992, found viewers mostly read the face as neutral whatever it was cut with. A 2016 study with a better design found only a modest effect.
cards.move: Before citing a classic demonstration, ask who counted the results, and how.
cards.trap: Assuming a textbook effect rests on a textbook experiment.

cards.question: Which kind of cut do viewers fail to notice most often, even when told to look for cuts?
cards.answer: A cut on movement. Eye-tracking studies by Tim Smith and John Henderson found viewers miss a large share of edits, and miss most often those that match an action across the join: a hand reaching in one shot, closing in the next. Attention rides the motion, and the camera change slips past like a blink.
cards.move: Hide a change inside something that is already moving.
cards.reference: Smith & Henderson, Edit Blindness: The Relationship Between Attention and Global Change Blindness in Dynamic Scenes, Journal of Eye Movement Research 2(2), 2008

cards.question: Is a director's cut the truer version of a film than the one first released?
cards.answer: Release versions are often shaped by committee: cut to a running time, bent by test screenings, patched with scenes the director never wanted. Blade Runner opened in 1982 with a studio-imposed voice-over and a happy ending assembled from aerial footage left over from The Shining. The 2007 Final Cut, now the standard, drops both.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, ask whether limits damaged the work or formed it.
cards.counterpoint: A deadline and a running time are part of how films get made well, not just obstacles. Coppola's Apocalypse Now Redux put back almost fifty minutes in 2001; in 2019 he released a Final Cut about twenty minutes shorter than Redux. When the director himself trims his own restoration, the first cut was not simply mutilation.
cards.reference: Sammon, Future Noir: The Making of Blade Runner, HarperPrism, 1996

cards.question: What pattern did a 2010 study find growing, decade by decade, in the lengths of Hollywood shots?
cards.answer: A 1/f rhythm, the statistical pattern also found in how human attention drifts. James Cutting's team measured the shots of 150 films from 1935 to 2005: runs of long and short shots clustered at every scale, more strongly in later films. Nobody planned it; editors converged on it by feel, one cut at a time.
cards.move: A pattern nobody designed can still emerge from many small choices made by feel.
cards.reference: Cutting, DeLong & Nothelfer, Attention and the Evolution of Hollywood Film, Psychological Science 21(3), 2010

cards.question: A film's shots average 6 seconds each. How long is its median shot, the one in the middle?
cards.answer: Shorter than 6 seconds. Shot lengths are lopsided: most shots are brief, and a few long takes drag the average up. Barry Salt's counts, begun in the 1970s, show this long tail film after film. One two-minute take adds as much running time as twenty 6-second shots.
cards.move: When a few giants sit in the data, the average describes almost nobody.
cards.trap: Treating the average shot as the typical one, as if lengths were symmetrical.
cards.reference: Salt, Statistical Style Analysis of Motion Pictures, Film Quarterly 28(1), 1974

cards.question: True or false: Hollywood features edited on Avid computers in the 1990s no longer had their camera negative cut by hand?
cards.answer: False. The computer edited video copies of the rushes, then printed a cut list of key numbers, codes exposed along the film's edge at the factory. A negative cutter found those frames and spliced the original negative, in gloves, with cement. Most features were finished this way until digital grading took over in the 2000s.
cards.move: A new tool at one stage can leave the old craft untouched at the next.
cards.trap: Assuming the computer's cut became the film, as it did later.
cards.reference: Ohanian, Digital Nonlinear Editing: Editing Film and Video on the Desktop, 2nd edn, Focal Press, 1998

cards.question: Apocalypse Now exposed 1,250,000 feet of film, at 90 feet a minute, for a 147-minute cut. Minutes shot per minute used?
cards.answer: 13,900 / 147 = about 94.5 minutes shot per minute used.
cards.move: Count what was thrown away to learn what the finished thing really cost.
