cards.trap: Guessing about 10 to 1, as if most footage made the cut.
cards.hint: Turn the footage into minutes first, then set it against the running time.
steps: 1,250,000 / 90 = about 13,900 minutes of film, some 230 hours.
The released cut keeps 147 of those minutes.
13,900 / 147 = about 94.5 minutes shot per minute used.
cards.source: Murch, In the Blink of an Eye
cards.reference: Murch, In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing, 2nd edn, Silman-James Press, 2001

cards.question: With almost no raw film stock after 1917, what did Lev Kuleshov's students cut to learn editing?
cards.answer: Existing prints, above all D. W. Griffith's Intolerance. New stock was scarce and precious, so Kuleshov's workshop took imported films apart and reassembled them in different orders to see how the meaning shifted. The editing theory later called Soviet montage was first rehearsed by rearranging an American epic on the bench.
cards.move: Take a master's finished work apart to learn what each piece does.
cards.reference: Leyda, Kino: A History of the Russian and Soviet Film, Allen & Unwin, 1960

cards.question: How did one 1980 western lead to the sale of the studio Chaplin and Pickford founded?
cards.answer: By being paid for long after it should have been stopped. United Artists' new managers kept funding Michael Cimino's Heaven's Gate as it ran months over schedule and several times over budget. It opened to savage reviews and earned a few million dollars in America. In 1981 its owner, Transamerica, sold United Artists to MGM.
cards.move: Never let a single bet grow big enough to sink the house.
cards.reference: Bach, Final Cut: Dreams and Disaster in the Making of Heaven's Gate, William Morrow, 1985

cards.question: A flop opens to $30 million; each later weekend takes 40% of the previous one. All weekends together, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: 30 / 0.6 = 50 million dollars.
cards.move: When each step keeps a fixed share, the first step is most of the total.
cards.trap: Expecting a long tail that keeps adding, when each weekend shrinks.
cards.hint: A total that keeps a fixed fraction each time adds up to the first term divided by what is lost.
steps: The weekends run 30, 12, 4.8, 1.9 and so on.
Each keeps 0.4 of the last, so the total is 30 / (1 - 0.4).
30 / 0.6 = 50 million dollars.

diagram.caption: The opening weekend alone brings in 30 of the 50 million the film will ever take.

cards.reference: Vogel, Entertainment Industry Economics: A Guide for Financial Analysis, 9th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: True or false: Citizen Kane made money for RKO on its first release in 1941?
cards.answer: False. RKO booked a loss. William Randolph Hearst, the press baron the film was taken to portray, had his newspapers refuse to review or advertise it; many cinema chains stayed away. Its reputation came later, through revivals, television and critics, until it topped five Sight and Sound critics' polls in a row, 1962 to 2002.
cards.move: Today's canon tells you what lasted, not what sold.
cards.trap: A film now ranked the greatest seems bound to have succeeded.
cards.source: Carringer, The Making of Citizen Kane
cards.reference: Carringer, The Making of Citizen Kane, University of California Press, 1985

cards.question: Waterworld cost about $175 million in 1995. Roughly what did it gross in cinemas worldwide?
cards.answer: About $260 million, most of it outside North America, where it took under $90 million. After the cinemas' cut that still left a loss on its theatrical run, but not the wipeout of legend. The verdict had been set by a year of stories about its runaway budget, written before anyone had seen it.
cards.move: A reputation formed before the results came in may never check them.
cards.trap: About $50 million: the word flop suggests nobody went at all.
cards.reference: https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0114898/

cards.question: How soon after its opening can a studio book a film as a flop?
cards.answer: Within days. A wide release's weekly takings fall in a fairly predictable pattern, so the opening weekend lets studios project the whole run. John Carter opened on 9 March 2012; about ten days later Disney told investors to expect an operating loss of roughly $200 million on it, while it was still in cinemas.
cards.move: When the pattern is known, the first data point settles the ending.
cards.reference: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2012-03-19/disney-sees-200-million-john-carter-loss-for-film-studio

cards.question: True or false: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, which grossed about $940 million, officially lost money?
cards.answer: True, on paper. A 2010 profit statement for the 2007 film showed it about $167 million in the red. Distribution fees, advertising and interest, much of it paid to Warner Bros. and its own affiliates, were deducted before any net profit. Anyone paid a share of net profits got nothing from a near-billion-dollar hit.
cards.move: Ask who writes the costs before trusting the bottom line.
cards.trap: Reading a near-billion-dollar gross as proof the books show a profit.
cards.reference: https://deadline.com/2010/07/studio-shame-even-harry-potter-pic-loses-money-because-of-warner-bros-phony-baloney-accounting-51886/

cards.question: A film costs $200 million to make and $100 million to market. Cinemas keep half of ticket sales. Break-even worldwide gross, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: 300 / 0.5 = 600 million dollars.
cards.move: Before comparing sales with costs, find out how much of each sale is yours.
cards.trap: Stopping at 300, as if the studio kept the whole ticket price.
cards.hint: Work out what the studio must receive, then how much must be sold to hand it that.
steps: Costs to recover: 200 + 100 = 300 million dollars.
The studio receives half of every ticket sold.
300 / 0.5 = 600 million dollars.
cards.reference: Epstein, The Hollywood Economist: The Hidden Financial Reality Behind the Movies, Melville House, 2010

cards.question: True or false: Carolco Pictures filed for bankruptcy only after its pirate epic Cutthroat Island flopped?
cards.answer: False. Carolco filed for Chapter 11 protection on 10 November 1995, six weeks before Cutthroat Island opened on 22 December. Years of costly films and heavy debts had already broken it. The flop finished the company off, and the story later shrank to one film sinking a studio. The bankruptcy papers came first.
cards.move: Check the dates before blaming the last event for the collapse.
cards.trap: Assuming the famous flop caused the collapse it is remembered for.
cards.reference: https://variety.com/2024/film/global/cutthroat-island-lost-fortune-renny-harlin-geena-davis-box-office-poison-book-excerpt-1236193554/

cards.question: Why might a studio spend millions releasing a film it already expects to flop?
cards.answer: Because the cinema run sets the price of what follows. Pay-television and other later deals have often paid for each film partly according to its box office, and a film that skipped cinemas sells for far less. Prints and adverts buy a track record. The cinema release works as an advertisement for the television sale.
cards.move: Judge a step by what it unlocks later, not only by its own return.
cards.reference: Epstein, The Big Picture: The New Logic of Money and Power in Hollywood, Random House, 2005

cards.question: It's a Wonderful Life lost money in 1946. What made it a Christmas television fixture decades later?
options: A 1970s cinema reissue found a new audience
Critics voted it among the best American films
Its copyright lapsed, so showing it cost nothing
cards.answer: Its copyright lapsed. It was not renewed in 1974, so for years any station could broadcast the film free, and many did, over and over each December. By the 1980s it was playing on many stations at once every December. Repetition, not rediscovery by critics, turned a money-loser into the season's default film.
cards.move: What people see most often is often what costs least to show.
cards.trap: Crediting its fame to merit finally recognised, not to a price of zero.
cards.source: Basinger, The It's a Wonderful Life Book
cards.reference: Basinger, The It's a Wonderful Life Book, Alfred A. Knopf, 1986

cards.question: Why did Jack Foley's craft begin with a film that had already been shot?
cards.answer: Because the film was shot silent. Universal made Show Boat in 1928 as a silent, then had to give it sound once talkies took over. Jack Foley's small crew projected it on a wall and performed the footsteps, doors and rustles live, into one microphone, while the picture ran.
cards.move: Many lasting methods began as a patch for someone else's deadline.
cards.reference: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation, Focal Press, 2009

cards.question: True or false: the footsteps heard in most feature films were recorded on set, with the actors?
cards.answer: False. The boom microphone hangs above the actors, aimed at their mouths, so footfalls come out faint and muddy. Sets also lie: a marble palace floor is often painted plywood, and its real footsteps would sound hollow. A Foley artist re-walks each character later, in sync, on a matching surface.
cards.move: Ask what the microphone was pointed at before trusting what it caught.
cards.trap: Assuming a sound was captured together with the picture it accompanies.
cards.source: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
cards.reference: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound, 4th edition, Focal Press, 2012

cards.question: Two actors talk, seated, never walking or touching a prop. Which Foley pass will the scene still get?
cards.answer: Clothing movement. Foley artists call it the cloth or moves pass: they rustle fabric matched to each costume in front of a microphone, following every shrug and breath. Once production noise is cleaned away, a scene without it sounds dead, like two mannequins talking. Leather jackets are performed with leather.
cards.move: Stillness on screen is never silence; something small is always moving.
cards.trap: Nothing visibly moves, so it seems nothing needs a sound.
cards.reference: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation, Focal Press, 2009

cards.question: Why does a film need Foley even for scenes whose production sound was perfect?
cards.answer: For the foreign versions. Dubbing replaces the dialogue track, and every footstep, rustle and clinking cup caught by the same microphone goes out with it. Distributors therefore demand a music-and-effects track with no voices at all, and Foley rebuilds those small noises so an Italian or Japanese dub still sounds inhabited.
cards.move: When one part must be swapped out, check what else it carries.
cards.source: Holman, Sound for Film and Television
cards.reference: Holman, Sound for Film and Television, 3rd edition, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: What sound did the cameras on 1960s Italian western sets record?
cards.answer: None. Italian studios usually shot without sound, and casts mixed Italian, Spanish, German and American actors each speaking their own language. Everything was made afterwards: every line dubbed, every hoof, spur and creaking door performed in a studio. Directors could call out instructions in the middle of a take, as in the silent era.
cards.move: Seamless is often a sign of reconstruction rather than capture.
cards.reference: Frayling, Sergio Leone: Something to Do with Death, Faber and Faber, 2000

cards.question: Why is a Foley stage built to sound like no room at all?
cards.answer: So the mixer can choose the room later. Foley stages are heavily damped and the microphone sits close, so each sound comes out dry, with almost no echo of its own. The mixer then adds the reverberation of the scene's space: a cathedral, a car, a corridor. One pair of shoes can be placed anywhere.
cards.move: Record things plain when you do not yet know where they will be used.
cards.reference: Viers, The Sound Effects Bible: How to Create and Record Hollywood Style Sound Effects, Michael Wiese Productions, 2008

cards.question: A Foley footstep slips two frames off the picture, at 24 frames a second. Which error do viewers spot more easily?
cards.answer: Sound two frames early. Two frames last about 83 milliseconds. Broadcast tests behind ITU-R BT.1359 found viewers detect sound leading the picture from about 45 ms, but sound lagging only from about 125 ms. In the world light outruns sound, so late sound looks natural; early sound never happens.
cards.move: The errors the world never makes are the ones people notice first.
cards.trap: Assuming the ear judges timing the same way in both directions.
cards.reference: International Telecommunication Union, Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1, Relative Timing of Sound and Vision for Broadcasting, 1998

cards.question: Why does a knife driven into a cabbage pass for a stabbing on screen?
cards.answer: Because timing, not likeness, does the work. Michel Chion called it synchresis: the mind welds any sound that lands exactly on a visible impact to that impact, provided its weight is roughly right. A wet crunch on the frame of the blow becomes flesh. Heard with no picture, it is plainly a vegetable.
cards.move: What arrives at the same instant gets read as one event.
cards.reference: Chion, Audio-Vision: Sound on Screen, trans. Gorbman, Columbia University Press, 1994

cards.question: In a car chase, which of these sounds is most likely performed by a Foley artist?
cards.answer: The seat. Foley covers what bodies touch and move at human scale: hands on a wheel, a seatbelt, a jacket, a creaking seat. Engines, tyres and crashes are too big to perform, so they come from recordings of real cars and from effects libraries. The roar is borrowed; the creak is acted.
cards.move: The work hardest to notice is often the work done by hand.
cards.trap: Assuming the loudest, most dramatic sounds must be the handmade ones.
cards.source: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
cards.reference: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound, 4th edition, Focal Press, 2012

cards.question: True or false: in most wildlife documentaries, the animals' footsteps and chewing were recorded on location?
cards.answer: False. Wildlife is filmed with long lenses from far away, and no microphone zooms like a lens; close sound would also carry wind, engines and crew. So footsteps, chewing and panting are usually performed later by Foley artists in a studio. An elephant's tread might be rocks pressed into a tub of straw and earth.
cards.move: Check which parts of a record were captured and which were added.
cards.trap: Trusting that a documentary records its sound the way it records pictures.
cards.reference: https://theconversation.com/the-animal-sounds-in-most-nature-documentaries-are-made-by-humans-heres-how-they-do-it-and-why-it-matters-220713

cards.question: In Hitchcock's Blackmail of 1929, one of Britain's first talkies, how did a Czech star speak flawless London English?
cards.answer: Another actress said her lines live. Anny Ondra's accent did not suit a London shopkeeper's daughter, and there was not yet a way to replace a voice afterwards. So Joan Barry stood out of frame at a microphone and spoke the dialogue while Ondra mouthed it. The dubbing happened during the take.
cards.move: When a tool is missing, look for the person quietly doing its job.
cards.reference: Truffaut, Hitchcock, Simon & Schuster, 1967

cards.question: Hitchcock's Rope was shot in takes capped by a 1,000-foot film magazine. At 24 frames a second and 16 frames per foot, how many minutes?
cards.move: Before blaming the artist's choice, find the length of the roll.
cards.trap: Dividing 1,000 by 24 and mixing feet with frames.
cards.hint: First find how many feet of film pass the lens each second.
steps: 24 frames a second / 16 frames per foot = 1.5 feet a second.
1.5 x 60 = 90 feet a minute.
cards.source: Spoto, The Dark Side of Genius
cards.reference: Spoto, The Dark Side of Genius: The Life of Alfred Hitchcock, Little, Brown, 1983

cards.question: How was the dizzying shot down the bell-tower stairwell in Vertigo filmed?
cards.answer: On a model lying on its side. The camera pulled back from a miniature stairwell while zooming in, so the frame held its size as the perspective stretched. Laid flat, the shaft let the camera run on a dolly instead of hanging from a crane. The famous drop ran along the studio floor.
cards.move: Turn an impossible direction into an easy one, then rotate the result.
cards.source: Auiler, Vertigo: The Making of a Hitchcock Classic
cards.reference: Auiler, Vertigo: The Making of a Hitchcock Classic, St. Martin's Press, 1998

cards.question: True or false: Hitchcock shot his films strictly to storyboard, leaving nothing to decide in the cutting room?
cards.answer: False. Bill Krohn's study of the studio production files found Hitchcock changing plans on set, shooting extra coverage to choose from later, and reshaping scenes in the edit. The legend of a film finished on paper came mostly from Hitchcock's own interviews, where it made him sound in total command.
cards.move: When the only witness is the hero, look for the paperwork.
cards.trap: True, because Hitchcock said so himself, often and persuasively.
cards.reference: Krohn, Hitchcock at Work, Phaidon, 2000

cards.question: Which Hitchcock film won the Academy Award for Best Picture?
cards.answer: Rebecca, in 1940, his first American film, and the statuette went to its producer, David O. Selznick. Hitchcock was nominated for best director five times and never won a competitive Oscar. Vertigo, a modest earner on release, topped the Sight and Sound critics' poll of the greatest films in 2012.
cards.move: A reputation today tells little about the verdict when the work was new.
cards.trap: Vertigo, the one now ranked among the greatest films.
cards.reference: Wiley & Bona, Inside Oscar: The Unofficial History of the Academy Awards, Ballantine Books, 1996

cards.question: In which country did Hitchcock direct his first completed feature, The Pleasure Garden of 1925?
cards.answer: Germany. Gainsborough Pictures co-produced it with the Munich studio Emelka, so the young Englishman shot in Munich and on location in Italy. Earlier, as an art director at UFA near Berlin, he had watched F. W. Murnau making The Last Laugh, told almost without intertitles. His first lessons in pure visual storytelling were German.
cards.move: Look for where a style was learned before calling it a native one.
cards.reference: Taylor, Hitch: The Life and Times of Alfred Hitchcock, Pantheon, 1978

cards.question: Paramount's logo opens Psycho, 1960. Who paid for the film to be made?
cards.answer: Hitchcock himself. Paramount disliked the gruesome novel, so he financed it through his own company, Shamley Productions, for about $800,000, with the fast, cheap crew of his television series, taking 60% of the film instead of a fee. Paramount only distributed it. He later traded the rights for a large stake in Universal's parent company.
cards.move: The name at the front is not always the name that paid.
cards.trap: Assuming the studio whose logo opens the film paid for it.
cards.reference: Rebello, Alfred Hitchcock and the Making of Psycho, Dembner Books, 1990

cards.question: True or false: Hitchcock shot Dial M for Murder, a thriller set almost entirely in one flat, in 3-D?
cards.answer: True. Warner Bros. ordered it in 3-D in 1953, at the height of the craze, and Hitchcock worked around a bulky 3-D camera, sinking it in a pit for low angles and filling the foreground with lamps and furniture. By the 1954 release the fad had faded, and most audiences saw it flat.
cards.move: The best-remembered uses of a technology are rarely a full list of them.
cards.trap: Picturing 3-D only as monsters and spears flying at the audience.
cards.reference: Zone, 3-D Revolution: The History of Modern Stereoscopic Cinema, University Press of Kentucky, 2012

cards.question: Why could audiences almost never see Vertigo or Rear Window in cinemas through the 1970s?
options: Hitchcock owned them and held them back
cards.answer: Hitchcock owned them and held them back. His Paramount deal returned four films to him eight years after release, and Rope was his own company's. He kept all five off screens, The Trouble with Harry and The Man Who Knew Too Much among them. Universal bought them after his death and re-released them from 1983.
cards.move: Scarcity can be an owner's strategy rather than an accident of time.
cards.trap: Blaming faded colour, the story told by Vertigo's famous 1996 restoration.
cards.reference: The Times, Return of the missing Hitchcocks, 15 November 1983

cards.question: Refused permission to film at the United Nations, how did North by Northwest show Cary Grant arriving there?
cards.answer: With a hidden camera. Hitchcock's crew filmed from hiding across the street as Grant walked up to the real building, and passers-by had no idea a film was being made. The lobby and the delegates' lounge inside were rebuilt on a soundstage at MGM. Only the walk to the door is real.
cards.move: When the front door is closed, see what can be filmed from the street.
cards.reference: McGilligan, Alfred Hitchcock: A Life in Darkness and Light, ReganBooks, 2003

cards.question: Why does a 1939 film still top the inflation-adjusted North American box-office chart?
cards.answer: Because it kept coming back. Before television and home video, a cinema was the only place to see a film, so Gone with the Wind was re-released again and again: 1947, 1954, 1961, 1967 and later. Its adjusted total adds up the audiences of several decades, not the crowds of one run.
cards.move: Before comparing totals, ask how many chances each one had to add up.
cards.source: Harmetz, On the Road to Tara, 1996
cards.reference: Harmetz, On the Road to Tara: The Making of Gone with the Wind, Harry N. Abrams, 1996

cards.question: Big releases now usually take about three times their opening weekend. What multiple did Titanic reach in its first North American run?
cards.answer: About 21 times. It opened to $28.6 million in December 1997 and then barely fell, holding first place for 15 weekends in a row and taking about $600 million by the end of its run. Repeat viewing and word of mouth turned a normal opening into a months-long climb.
cards.move: A typical ratio describes the usual case, not the one you are asked about.
cards.trap: About 3 times: the ratio just given pulls every guess towards it.
cards.reference: https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Titanic-(1997)

cards.question: True or false: My Big Fat Greek Wedding, 2002, never topped the North American weekend chart?
cards.answer: True. Made for about $5 million, it opened in a small number of cinemas and climbed for months on word of mouth, peaking at number two. It finished with about $240 million in North America, one of the largest totals ever for a film that never led a single weekend.
cards.move: The loudest week and the biggest total are different contests.
cards.trap: A hit that big seems bound to have had a week on top.
cards.reference: https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0259446/

cards.question: True or false: the biggest box-office total ever recorded in a single market belongs to a Hollywood film in North America?
cards.answer: False. In 2025 the Chinese animated film Ne Zha 2 took over 15 billion yuan in China alone, about $2 billion. The best North American total, Star Wars: The Force Awakens, is under $950 million. The largest single audience for a film is no longer where most English-language box-office news is written.
cards.move: Check where the reporting comes from before trusting what it calls the biggest.
cards.trap: Box-office records in the news are mostly North American ones.
cards.reference: Xinhua, "Ne Zha 2" ends record-breaking China run with 2.13-bln-USD haul, 30 June 2025, https://english.news.cn/20250630/74574b4e9823406fb2da565b750fa4a7/c.html

cards.question: Where did the Indian wrestling drama Dangal take most of its box office?
cards.answer: In China. Released there in May 2017, months after its Indian opening, Aamir Khan's film about a father who trains his daughters to wrestle took around $190 million, more than it earned at home. For a while a Hindi film's biggest crowds were queuing in Chinese multiplexes.
cards.move: A product's home market is not always its biggest one.
cards.reference: Variety, Why 'Dangal's' Triumph in China Could Be a Game-Changer for India, 2017, https://variety.com/2017/film/asia/why-dangal-china-triumph-changes-could-be-game-changer-1202439053/

cards.question: A film opens in four big-city cinemas at $100,000 a screen. Widened to 2,000 screens, what happens to that average?
cards.answer: It falls far below that. A platform release starts in the few cinemas best suited to the film, in cities full of its likeliest fans, and sells out their shows. Each wider ring adds screens where fewer people want it. A record per-screen average in week one describes those four rooms, not the country.
cards.move: The first places anything is tried were chosen, not drawn at random.
cards.trap: Treating the first four cinemas as a fair sample of the country.
cards.reference: Vogel, Entertainment Industry Economics: A Guide for Financial Analysis, 9th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: True or false: the highest-grossing film worldwide in 2020 was a Hollywood production?
cards.answer: False. Depending on how the year is counted, first place went to Demon Slayer: Mugen Train, a Japanese anime, or The Eight Hundred, a Chinese war film; each took over $450 million. Cinemas in Japan and China reopened early in the pandemic while Hollywood held back its big releases. Neither contender was in English.
cards.move: A long record can end quietly when the conditions behind it change.
cards.trap: Recalling the Hollywood hits that dominate the film news one reads.
cards.reference: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/72369-highest-grossing-japanese-animated-film

cards.question: A Hollywood film grosses $300 million in China and $200 million in North America. Which market pays the studio more?
options: North America, by about a third
cards.answer: North America, by about a third. Under the 2012 US–China film deal, a foreign studio receives 25% of Chinese ticket sales: $75 million here. At home it keeps roughly half: about $100 million. Three fifths of the gross came from China; most of the studio's money did not.
cards.move: Rank sources by what reaches you, not by what passes through.
cards.trap: Ranking markets by ticket sales rather than by the studio's share of them.
cards.reference: Kokas, Hollywood Made in China, University of California Press, 2017

cards.question: What did a study of some 2,000 films find stars do to a film's box-office risk?
cards.answer: Almost nothing reliable. Arthur De Vany and David Walls found film revenues have such extreme tails that a few titles take most of the money and averages mislead. Star vehicles earned somewhat more on average, but flopped too; no name made a hit likely. Studios pay millions for odds that barely move.
cards.move: When outcomes swing wildly, a good average can still hide ruin.
cards.reference: De Vany and Walls, Uncertainty in the Movie Industry: Does Star Power Reduce the Terror of the Box Office?, Journal of Cultural Economics, 1999

cards.question: Roughly how many cinema tickets did Avengers: Endgame sell in North America, in millions?
cards.answer: 858 / 9.16 ≈ 94 million tickets.
cards.move: Divide money by price before comparing crowds across years.
cards.hint: Divide the takings by what an average ticket cost that year.
steps: Its North American gross was about $858 million.
An average ticket in 2019 cost about $9.16.
858 / 9.16 ≈ 94 million tickets.
cards.reference: National Association of Theatre Owners, Annual Average U.S. Ticket Price, 2020

cards.question: In the opening of 2001: A Space Odyssey, why do the leopard's eyes glow?
cards.answer: Front projection. The African landscapes were large photographs projected onto a screen of Scotchlite, a material that bounces light straight back towards its source. A half-silvered mirror put the projector on the camera's axis, so the actors hid their own shadows. The leopard's eyes, reflective like the screen, caught the projector beam and shone back.
cards.move: A flaw in the picture is often the clearest view of how it was made.
cards.reference: Bizony, 2001: Filming the Future, Aurum Press, 1994

cards.question: How did 2001: A Space Odyssey fill its spaceship screens with moving computer readouts in 1968?
cards.answer: Without computers. The readouts were drawings, animated and shot on film, then back-projected onto the screens from projectors hidden behind the set, each loop timed to the action. No machine of the day could draw such images live. The film's vision of computing was painted by hand, one frame at a time.
cards.move: Check whether a picture of the future was made with the tools of the past.
cards.reference: Agel (ed.), The Making of Kubrick's 2001, Signet, 1970

cards.question: Why could British cinemas not show A Clockwork Orange for over 25 years after 1973?
cards.answer: Kubrick withdrew it himself. The British censor had passed it uncut with an X certificate in 1971. After newspapers tied crimes to the film and his family received threats, Kubrick had Warner Bros. pull it from British distribution. It returned to British cinemas in 2000, the year after he died.
cards.move: When something vanishes, ask who had the power and the reason to remove it.
cards.trap: The censor banned it, because that is how films usually disappear.
cards.reference: LoBrutto, Stanley Kubrick: A Biography, Donald I. Fine, 1997

cards.question: True or false: Arthur C. Clarke said HAL's name was a deliberate one-letter shift from IBM?
cards.answer: False. Clarke repeatedly called it a coincidence: HAL stood for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer, a name built from what the machine did. There are only 17,576 three-letter strings and a great many acronyms in the world, so some name was bound to sit one letter from a famous one.
cards.move: Before calling a match designed, count how many matches were possible.
cards.trap: True, because a pattern that neat looks deliberate.
cards.reference: Clarke, The Lost Worlds of 2001, Signet, 1972

cards.question: Barry Lyndon's candlelit scenes used an f/0.7 lens. How much more light does it admit than an f/1.4 lens?
cards.answer: About four times. Light through a lens scales with the area of its opening, so with the square of the ratio of f-numbers: (1.4 / 0.7)² = 4. The Zeiss lenses, built for NASA, let candles alone light a room, at the price of focus so shallow that actors could barely lean forward.
cards.move: When a width changes, the area changes by its square.
cards.trap: About twice, because the f-number was halved.

diagram.caption: Halve the f-number and the opening doubles in width but lets in four times the light.

cards.reference: Alcott, Photographing Stanley Kubrick's Barry Lyndon, American Cinematographer, March 1976

cards.question: Where did Kubrick film the ruined Vietnamese city of Hue for Full Metal Jacket?
cards.answer: In East London. Beckton Gas Works, a derelict industrial site due for demolition, had concrete buildings that resembled the colonial blocks of Hue. The crew knocked holes in them with explosives and a wrecking ball, and brought in palm trees from Spain. Kubrick, who avoided flying, staged the battle within driving distance of his home.
cards.move: Before building what is needed, look for what is about to be torn down.
cards.reference: Baxter, Stanley Kubrick: A Biography, HarperCollins, 1997

cards.question: True or false: the old 4:3 television version of The Shining shows more picture than audiences saw in cinemas?
cards.answer: True. Kubrick shot on the full, nearly square frame and had cinemas mask the top and bottom to a widescreen shape. For video he approved the unmasked frame, so viewers at home saw extra ceiling and floor. The usual cropping for television ran the other way here.
cards.move: Before assuming something was cut away, ask how it was first captured.
cards.trap: Assuming the full-screen version cropped a wide picture, as usual.
cards.reference: Castle (ed.), The Stanley Kubrick Archives, Taschen, 2005

cards.question: Danny's Apollo 11 sweater in The Shining is cited as proof of a hidden Moon-landing confession. How strong is that evidence?
options: Strong, since Kubrick controlled every detail
Weak, since some detail fits any theory
Suggestive, given his NASA lens deal
cards.answer: Weak. The Shining holds hundreds of props, patterns and posters, and readers hunting for the Moon landings, for genocide or for the Minotaur have each found their clues, as the 2012 documentary Room 237 shows. Every theory finds its sweater; the misses are never counted.
cards.move: The more places a theory may look, the less its finds are worth.
cards.trap: Taking Kubrick's control of detail as proof each detail is a message.
cards.reference: Ascher (dir.), Room 237, IFC Midnight, 2012

cards.question: Days after 2001: A Space Odyssey opened in 1968, Kubrick cut 19 minutes. How did prints already in cinemas lose them?
cards.answer: By instructions sent to the cinemas. Kubrick and his editor Ray Lovejoy settled the trims in a few days in April, and detailed lists of what to remove went to the cinemas already screening the 70 mm prints, so the cuts could be made there. The version audiences know is the recut, not the premiere.
cards.move: Ask which version is meant before quoting what a work contains.
cards.reference: http://www.visual-memory.co.uk/amk/doc/brown3.html

cards.question: To earn an R rating in America, how was the orgy scene in Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut, 1999, altered?
options: Digital figures were added in front
About a minute of it was cut
Its shots were darkened and blurred
cards.answer: Digital figures were added in front. Rather than cut shots, Warner Bros. placed computer-generated cloaked onlookers between the camera and the most explicit action, so the scene kept its length and rhythm. Kubrick had died that March. Europe saw the scene unaltered; American viewers saw it only on a later unrated home release.
cards.move: Something can be hidden by adding to it as well as by cutting.
cards.trap: Assuming a censor's demand is met by cutting, as it usually is.
cards.reference: Kolker & Abrams, Eyes Wide Shut: Stanley Kubrick and the Making of His Final Film, Oxford University Press, 2019

cards.question: Before fast film stock, how were most night exteriors in Westerns really shot?
cards.answer: In broad daylight. Day for night meant filming in sun, underexposing by a stop or two, often through a blue filter, and keeping the glowing sky out of frame. Hard sun gave moonlight its sharp shadows. The French call it la nuit américaine, the title Truffaut gave his 1973 film about film-making.
cards.move: Look at what a place can do, not what the story says it is.
cards.reference: Brown, Cinematography: Theory and Practice, Focal Press, 2002

cards.question: Why did the same film lamps flicker on a 24-frame shoot in Europe but not in America?
cards.answer: Mains frequency. On magnetic ballasts, discharge lamps such as HMIs pulse twice per cycle: 120 times a second on America's 60 Hz supply, 100 on Europe's 50 Hz. At 24 frames a second, 120 gives exactly 5 pulses a frame; 100 gives 4.17, so brightness drifts from frame to frame. Crews shot at 25 instead.
cards.move: When two rhythms meet, check whether one divides the other.
cards.reference: Box, Set Lighting Technician's Handbook, 4th edn, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: True or false: on early silent-era film stock, red lips photographed almost black?
cards.answer: True. Orthochromatic stock responded to blue and green light but hardly at all to red, so red came out dark and blue skies bleached to white. Make-up was designed around it, with pale bases and lip colours chosen for how they read in grey. Panchromatic stock, sensitive to red, took over in the later 1920s.
cards.move: A recording shows what the instrument could sense, not what was there.
cards.trap: Assuming film sees each colour as bright as the eye does.
cards.reference: Salt, Film Style and Technology: History and Analysis, 2nd edn, Starword, 1992

cards.question: On film balanced for tungsten studio lamps, how does daylight through a window come out?
cards.answer: Too blue. Studio tungsten lamps burn at about 3,200 kelvin and daylight averages about 5,600, so daylight carries far more blue than the film expects. Crews tape orange gel over whole windows, or blue gel on the lamps, to make the sources match. Left alone, the faces look right and the windows glow blue.
cards.move: A colour looks right or wrong only against what the eye was set for.
cards.trap: Too orange, because sunlight feels warm on the skin.
cards.reference: Malkiewicz, Film Lighting: Talks with Hollywood's Cinematographers and Gaffers, Prentice Hall, 1986

cards.question: A key light is set three stops brighter than the fill. How many times more light is that?
cards.answer: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the light.
cards.move: Steps that each double do not add up; they multiply.
cards.trap: Answering 3 or 6 by adding the stops instead of doubling.
cards.hint: Ask what a single stop does to the amount of light.
steps: One stop doubles the light.
Three stops is three doublings in a row.
2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the light.
cards.reference: Ray (ed.), The Manual of Photography, 9th edn, Focal Press, 2000

cards.question: What was klieg eyes, the complaint that sent film actors of the 1920s to eye doctors?
cards.answer: Inflamed, burning eyes caused by ultraviolet light from carbon-arc studio lamps, the Kliegl brothers' klieg lights among them. An arc between carbon rods throws out ultraviolet along with its white glare, and actors worked close under banks of them for hours. Glass screens over the arcs, and later tungsten lamps, ended most cases.
cards.move: When a whole group shares one symptom, look at what they all stood under.
cards.reference: Bordwell, Staiger & Thompson, The Classical Hollywood Cinema: Film Style and Mode of Production to 1960, Columbia University Press, 1985

cards.question: A softbox 1 m from an actor's face is moved back to 4 m. What happens to the shadows?
cards.answer: They get harder-edged. Softness depends on how large the source looks from the face, not on its fabric. At four times the distance the box spans a quarter of the angle, so it acts more like a point. The sun, enormous but tiny in the sky, casts some of the hardest shadows there are.
cards.move: Judge a source by how big it looks from where the subject stands.
cards.trap: Thinking distance spreads and diffuses light, the way fog does.
cards.source: Hunter, Biver & Fuqua, Light: Science and Magic
cards.reference: Hunter, Biver & Fuqua, Light: Science and Magic, 3rd edn, Focal Press, 2007

cards.question: Films light moonlit scenes blue. Measured with an instrument, how does moonlight's colour compare with sunlight's?
cards.answer: Slightly redder. Moonlight is sunlight bounced off grey-brown lunar rock, which reflects red a little better than blue. The blue is added by the eye: in dim light the rod cells take over, and they are most sensitive to blue-green, so night looks cool. Cinema copies the perception, not the physics.
cards.move: Ask whether a colour belongs to the thing or to the eye that sees it.
cards.trap: Picturing cool moonlight because cinema has always painted night blue.
cards.reference: Jensen, Durand, Stark, Premože, Dorsey & Shirley, A Physically-Based Night Sky Model, SIGGRAPH, 2001

cards.question: True or false: a lamp scoring 95 out of 100 on the colour rendering index can still turn skin wrong on camera?
cards.answer: True. The standard index averages how eight pale, pastel test colours look under the lamp, judged by a model of the human eye. Saturated reds are left out of that average, and camera sensors respond differently from eyes. In 2016 the film Academy presented a Spectral Similarity Index built for cameras instead.
cards.move: Before trusting a score, ask which cases were averaged to make it.
cards.trap: Trusting a high score without asking what the test sampled.
cards.reference: https://www.oscars.org/science-technology/projects/spectral-similarity-index-ssi

cards.question: An actor stands 1 m from a bare lamp; the wall behind is 3 m from it. How many stops darker is the wall?
cards.answer: One stop halves the light and 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, so 9 times less is about 3.2 stops.
cards.move: When something spreads out in two directions, distance cuts it by the square.
cards.trap: Answering about 1.6 stops, as if light fell in step with distance.
cards.hint: Light spreads over an area, so ask how the area grows with distance.
steps: The wall is 3 times farther from the lamp than the face.
Light falls with the square of distance: 3 x 3 = 9 times less.
One stop halves the light and 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, so 9 times less is about 3.2 stops.
cards.source: Brown, Motion Picture and Video Lighting
cards.reference: Brown, Motion Picture and Video Lighting, 2nd edn, Focal Press, 2008

cards.question: What did Jaws change about the way a big film was launched?
cards.answer: It opened everywhere at once, pushed by television. Prestige films usually opened in a few big-city cinemas and spread slowly as prints and reviews travelled. In June 1975 Universal put Jaws into more than 400 cinemas together and bought national prime-time TV advertising the week before. The opening weekend itself became the event.
cards.move: When everyone can hear the news at once, the first day decides the rest.
cards.reference: Cook, Lost Illusions: American Cinema in the Shadow of Watergate and Vietnam, 1970–1979, Scribner, 2000

cards.question: What makes a film four-quadrant, and why do studios chase that label?
cards.answer: It sells to all four quarters of the audience, split by sex and by age under or over 25. Most films reach one or two. Only a film that reaches all four justifies the largest release and advertising budget, which is why blockbusters pack in action, romance, adult jokes and a rating that admits children.
cards.move: When one product must please everyone, look for the parts added for each group.
cards.reference: Epstein, The Big Picture: The New Logic of Money and Power in Hollywood, Random House, 2005

cards.question: True or false: under US law, a trailer showing an actor later cut from the film can be false advertising?
cards.answer: True. In 2022 two viewers sued Universal after renting Yesterday for Ana de Armas, who appears in its trailer but was cut from the film. A federal judge in California ruled that a trailer is commercial speech, an advertisement, so false-advertising law can apply to it. The trailer is a promise.
cards.move: Once something is used to sell, it is judged as a sales pitch.
cards.trap: A trailer looks like part of the creative work, so free speech.
cards.reference: Woulfe v. Universal City Studios LLC, US District Court for the Central District of California, order of December 2022

cards.question: Snakes on a Plane was 2006's most joked-about film online before release. What did its opening weekend take?
cards.answer: About $15 million in North America, below modest forecasts. Fans had even shaped the film: New Line reshot scenes for an adult rating and added a line fans had already made famous online. But the people posting jokes were a small, loud sample, and enjoying the joke required no ticket.
cards.move: The people talking loudest are rarely a fair count of the people paying.
cards.trap: About $50 million: that much noise seemed to promise a crowd.
cards.source: Box Office Mojo, Snakes on a Plane
cards.reference: https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0417148/

cards.question: Should reactions at test screenings be allowed to change a film's ending?
cards.answer: A film is made to be watched, and a test screening is the only evidence of how it plays before millions have paid. Fatal Attraction's first ending tested badly; the reshot climax helped make it one of 1987's biggest hits. Refusing that evidence gambles other people's money on one person's hunch.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on when success is measured.
cards.counterpoint: Test audiences judge a film in one sitting, on scorecards, and reward the familiar. After a disastrous preview in 1942, RKO cut about 40 minutes from Welles's The Magnificent Ambersons and shot a softer ending; the removed footage was later destroyed. A preview score measures first-night comfort, not what a film will mean in decades.
cards.reference: Carringer, The Magnificent Ambersons: A Reconstruction, University of California Press, 1993

cards.question: A big franchise film earns a B from CinemaScore's opening-night audience poll. How should its studio read that grade?
cards.answer: As a warning sign. CinemaScore surveys people leaving on opening night, the keenest fans, who chose to go first. Most wide releases score in the A range. For a franchise film, a B means even the most willing crowd was let down. Among its own fans, a B is a failing grade.
cards.move: Grade a verdict by how friendly the jury was to begin with.
cards.trap: Calling it a solid pass, forgetting that only eager fans were polled.
cards.reference: https://www.cinemascore.com/

cards.question: True or false: most films that critics pan were kept from critics until opening day?
cards.answer: False. Studios do hide some weak films, and a hidden film is very likely weak. But among 1,303 wide releases studied, cold openings were a small minority, while panned films were common; most were screened as usual. The chance a hidden film is bad is high; the chance a bad film was hidden is low.
cards.move: A rule that holds one way round rarely holds the other.
cards.trap: Flipping the true rule that hidden films are usually bad into its reverse.

cards.question: How did The Blair Witch Project get audiences to half-believe its footage was real?
cards.answer: By marketing the fiction as fact for months before release. Its website posted police reports and missing-person details for the three student film-makers, and in July 1999 the Sci-Fi Channel aired Curse of the Blair Witch, a mock documentary about their disappearance. Some viewers walked in expecting the last tapes of three missing students.
cards.move: The frame around a story decides how far the story is believed.
cards.reference: Telotte, The Blair Witch Project Project: Film and the Internet, Film Quarterly, 2001

cards.question: Should studio spending on Oscar campaigns be capped?
cards.answer: Awards campaigns turn a vote on artistic merit into a contest of budgets. Studios spend millions on screenings, dinners, advertising and consultants to reach a few thousand voters, and small films cannot match that. The Academy already limits parties and mailings, which admits the problem. A cap would let the films, not the chequebooks, compete.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether exposure or money is deciding votes.
cards.counterpoint: Campaigns are how small films get seen at all. Voters cannot watch everything, and screenings and advertising put a modest independent film in front of them. A cap would be hard to police, since publicity, press tours and festival screenings blur together, and it would favour films already famous before the season began.
cards.reference: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Awards Campaign Promotional Regulations, 2024

cards.question: Why are the weekend box-office figures announced on Sunday partly a forecast?
cards.answer: Because Sunday is not over. Studios report the weekend on Sunday, projecting that evening's shows from the pattern of earlier weekends, and publish actual takings on Monday. The gap is usually small but runs both ways, and a close race for first place can flip. The Sunday estimate is the figure the headlines keep.
cards.move: The first figure published is the one remembered, so look for the correction.
cards.reference: Vogel, Entertainment Industry Economics: A Guide for Financial Analysis, 9th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: How tall were the Kong models animated for most of King Kong's shots in 1933?
cards.answer: About 45 centimetres. Marcel Delgado built them on jointed metal skeletons covered in rubber and rabbit fur, and Willis O'Brien's animators moved them a fraction between frames. A giant head and hand were built for close-ups. The fur that seems to ripple in the wind is fingerprints, pressed flat and springing back between frames.
cards.move: The size something plays is no guide to the size it is.
cards.trap: About 6 metres, with the giant on the screen in mind.
cards.source: Goldner & Turner, The Making of King Kong
cards.reference: Goldner & Turner, The Making of King Kong, A. S. Barnes, 1975

cards.question: A 1:16 model ship must move like a real one. By the square-root rule, how many frames a second should a 24-frame camera run?
cards.answer: 24 x 4 = 96 frames a second.
cards.move: When size shrinks, time shrinks by less; check the rule before scaling.
cards.trap: Running 16 times faster, as if time shrank with size.
cards.hint: Gravity sets the pace: a fall takes time in proportion to the square root of its height.
steps: Motion under gravity speeds up by the square root of the scale.
The square root of 16 is 4.
24 x 4 = 96 frames a second.
cards.reference: Fielding, The Technique of Special Effects Cinematography, 4th edn, Focal Press, 1985

cards.question: Why did James Cameron's Titanic build most of a ship at nearly full size instead of relying on models?
cards.answer: Water does not scale. Drops and spray keep their real size whatever the model's, so a model liner throws splashes as big as its lifeboats. For the 1997 film, the ship's starboard side was built at about 90% scale in a vast seafront tank at Rosarito, Mexico. Models were still used, filmed slowed down.
cards.move: Find the one ingredient that refuses to shrink with everything else.
cards.reference: Marsh, James Cameron's Titanic, HarperPerennial, 1997

cards.question: What were the surface details on the original Star Wars spaceship models made from?
cards.answer: Pieces of shop-bought plastic model kits. Industrial Light & Magic's model makers cut up kits of tanks, cars, ships and aircraft and glued the parts onto the hulls, a practice called kitbashing, so every surface read as dense machinery at a glance. Enthusiasts still identify the donor kits, piece by piece, from photographs.
cards.move: Complexity that reads at a glance can be borrowed rather than designed.
cards.reference: Smith, Industrial Light & Magic: The Art of Special Effects, Del Rey, 1986

cards.question: True or false: Blade Runner 2049, winner of the 2018 visual effects Oscar, relied partly on physical miniatures?
cards.answer: True. Weta Workshop built large, detailed miniatures of the film's city, which were shot with real light and haze and then extended digitally. Miniatures never disappeared from big productions; they stopped being noticed once audiences assumed every effect was digital. A good model now passes for computer graphics.
cards.move: What gets talked about is the loud part of a practice, not all of it.
cards.trap: False, because a recent effects film must be all digital.
cards.reference: Lapointe, The Art and Soul of Blade Runner 2049, Titan Books, 2017

cards.question: How can a camera pan across a miniature hung close to the lens without the illusion breaking?
cards.answer: By turning around the lens's nodal point, the spot inside it where the light rays cross. Pivoted there, near and far objects keep their alignment, so a model castle hung a metre from the camera stays perched on a real hill kilometres away. Pivot anywhere else and the model slides across the landscape.
cards.move: Find the one point from which near and far never shift against each other.
cards.reference: Vaz & Barron, The Invisible Art: The Legends of Movie Matte Painting, Chronicle Books, 2002

cards.question: True or false: in Star Wars, 1977, the model spaceships mostly stood still while the camera flew past them?
cards.answer: True. ILM's Dykstraflex, a computer-controlled camera rig, tracked, panned and tilted past models fixed on poles before a blue screen, and could repeat the same move exactly for each separate element. That let many ships, engine glows and lasers be layered into one shot. The dogfights were flown by the camera.
cards.move: Motion on a screen does not say which of two things moved.
cards.trap: Picturing models flown on wires past a fixed camera, as in older films.
cards.source: Rinzler, The Making of Star Wars, 2007
cards.reference: Rinzler, The Making of Star Wars: The Definitive Story Behind the Original Film, Del Rey, 2007

cards.question: A 1:25 model train, filmed by the square-root rule, must pass for a real one at 100 km/h. Model speed in km/h?
cards.answer: The model must move 5 times faster to make up for it: 4 x 5 = 20 km/h.
cards.move: When two things are rescaled at once, apply both before trusting the result.
cards.trap: Answering 4 km/h, dividing by the scale and forgetting the camera.
cards.hint: Scale the distance first, then ask what the fast camera does to time.
steps: Model distances are 25 times smaller: 100 / 25 = 4 km/h if time were unchanged.
The camera runs √25 = 5 times fast, so each real second lasts 5 on screen.
The model must move 5 times faster to make up for it: 4 x 5 = 20 km/h.
cards.reference: Brosnan, Movie Magic: The Story of Special Effects in the Cinema, Little, Brown, 1974

cards.question: How were the rolling, glowing storm clouds of Close Encounters of the Third Kind, 1977, made?
options: Cotton wool animated frame by frame
Paint injected into a tank of water
cards.answer: Paint injected into a tank of water. Douglas Trumbull's team filled a large tank with a layer of fresh water over salt water, and white paint squirted in spread along the boundary between them like cloud under a warm layer of air. Lit and filmed slowly, the swirls became a sky of weather.
cards.move: To fake something huge, find a small system that behaves the same way.
cards.trap: Picking high-speed smoke, the usual way to make small effects look huge.
cards.reference: American Cinematographer, special issue on Close Encounters of the Third Kind, January 1978

cards.question: Why was Toho's 1954 Godzilla a man in a heavy rubber suit rather than a stop-motion puppet like King Kong?
cards.answer: Time. Effects director Eiji Tsuburaya admired King Kong's stop-motion, but animating a monster frame by frame would have taken far longer than Toho's schedule allowed. So the actor Haruo Nakajima wore a suit of roughly 100 kg and trampled a 1:25 miniature Tokyo, shot at high speed so everything he broke fell heavily.
cards.move: The schedule often chooses the technique before the artist does.
cards.reference: Ryfle, Japan's Favorite Mon-Star: The Unauthorized Biography of the Big G, ECW Press, 1998

cards.question: What does a film music cue labelled 4M2 tell the people scoring it?
cards.answer: It is the second music cue in reel 4. Cues are numbered reel by reel at the spotting session, where composer, director and music editor watch the cut and fix where each piece starts and stops. Films are no longer cut on reels, but a two-hour score still runs from 1M1 into 6M or 7M.
cards.move: Old labels outlive the machines that made them; read them as history.
cards.source: Davis, Complete Guide to Film Scoring
cards.reference: Davis, Complete Guide to Film Scoring: The Art and Business of Writing Music for Movies and TV, 2nd edition, Berklee Press, 2010

cards.question: Why does every finished film keep a second-by-second log of the music in it?
cards.answer: Because royalties are paid from it. The cue sheet lists every cue, its composers and publishers, how it is used, as background, theme or song performed on screen, and its exact duration. Collecting societies read it to pay writers whenever the film is broadcast. Twelve seconds of a radio in the background earns its share.
cards.move: Money follows the paperwork, so whoever keeps the log decides who gets paid.
cards.reference: Kohn and Kohn, Kohn on Music Licensing, 4th edition, Wolters Kluwer, 2010

cards.question: Before sound films, how did a small-town pianist know what to play under a chase?
cards.answer: From books sorted by mood. Studios sent cue sheets suggesting pieces scene by scene, and publishers sold anthologies such as Erno Rapée's Motion Picture Moods for Pianists and Organists, 1924, with ready music indexed under headings like chase, storm, love or mystery. The same few hurries and agitatos served thousands of films.
cards.move: A shared vocabulary is what lets strangers improvise the same thing.
cards.reference: Rapée, Motion Picture Moods for Pianists and Organists, G. Schirmer, 1924

cards.question: Film runs at 24 frames per second. A cue's click track runs at 96 beats per minute. How many frames per beat?
cards.answer: 24 / 1.6 = 15 frames per beat.
cards.move: Put both rates in the same unit of time before dividing them.
cards.trap: Dividing 96 by 24 and getting 4, mixing minutes with seconds.
cards.hint: Turn the tempo into beats per second first.
steps: 96 beats per minute / 60 seconds = 1.6 beats per second.
Each second holds 24 frames.
24 / 1.6 = 15 frames per beat.
cards.source: Karlin and Wright, On the Track
cards.reference: Karlin and Wright, On the Track: A Guide to Contemporary Film Scoring, 2nd edition, Routledge, 2004

cards.question: A film uses a 1970s hit record in one scene. Whose permission must it get?
cards.answer: The publisher's and the label's. The song and the recording are separate copyrights: a synchronisation licence from the publisher covers the composition, a master-use licence from the label covers that particular recording. A new soundalike recording avoids the label but never the publisher, which is one reason films use cover versions.
cards.move: A single object can carry two owners; ask who owns each layer.
cards.trap: The record seems to be the thing used, so the label alone.
cards.source: Passman, All You Need to Know
cards.reference: Passman, All You Need to Know About the Music Business, 10th edition, Simon & Schuster, 2019

cards.question: How does an orchestra recording to picture know exactly when a hit is coming?
cards.answer: It watches a line cross the screen. A streamer is a vertical stripe that sweeps across the projected picture over a few seconds and ends in a punch, a brief flash on the exact frame of the hit. The conductor sees it coming and lands the downbeat on the flash.
cards.move: A countdown people can see beats one they have to count.
cards.source: Karlin and Wright, On the Track, 2004
cards.reference: Karlin and Wright, On the Track: A Guide to Contemporary Film Scoring, 2nd edition, Routledge, 2004

cards.question: From the cue's first beat, the hit must fall on bar 16's first beat, in 4/4, 30 seconds later. Tempo, in beats per minute?
cards.answer: 2 × 60 = 120 beats per minute.
cards.move: Count the gaps between the posts, not the posts.
cards.trap: Counting 16 full bars, 64 beats, and landing on 128.
cards.hint: Count the beats already gone by when bar 16 begins, not the bars named.
steps: Bar 16 begins after 15 full bars: 15 × 4 = 60 beats.
60 beats in 30 seconds = 2 beats a second.
2 × 60 = 120 beats per minute.
cards.reference: Hagen, Scoring for Films: A Complete Text, Criterion Music, 1971

cards.question: Should directors cut their films to temporary music borrowed from other scores?
cards.answer: A temp track is the clearest brief a composer can get. Directors rarely have words for music; a borrowed cue shows the tone, pace and weight a scene needs. Editors cut rhythm to it, and test audiences need music to judge a film. Without it, everyone guesses until the score arrives, too late.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a reference can stay only a reference.
cards.counterpoint: Temp music becomes a cage. After weeks of hearing a borrowed cue, directors fall for it and ask composers for near-copies, which flattens scores into soundalikes of whatever was borrowed. The cut itself is shaped around someone else's phrasing. The composer is hired to be original, then paid to imitate.
cards.reference: Kalinak, Film Music: A Very Short Introduction, Oxford University Press, 2010

cards.question: Les Misérables, 2012, had its cast sing live on set. How was the orchestra matched to them?
options: Played live, just off the set
Recorded first, fed into their ears
cards.answer: Recorded afterwards, following the singers. Each actor heard a live pianist through a hidden earpiece, and was free to slow down, break or hold a note. The orchestra was recorded later to fit the voices, reversing the usual order in which singers mime to a track laid down first. The conductor followed the actors.
cards.move: When one performance matters most, make everything else follow it.
cards.trap: Assuming the usual playback method, with singers keeping time to a recording.
cards.reference: Hooper (director), Les Misérables, Working Title Films and Universal Pictures, 2012

cards.question: Why was the score of Arrival, 2016, ruled out of the Oscar race?
cards.answer: Because another composer's piece carries its key moments. Max Richter's On the Nature of Daylight, released in 2004, opens and closes the film, and the Academy's rules exclude scores diluted by pre-existing music. Jóhann Jóhannsson's original work was judged to fail that test. The film's emotional frame belonged to a track brought in from outside.
cards.move: Where the key moments come from says who authored the whole.
cards.reference: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Special Rules for the Music Awards, 89th Academy Awards, 2016

cards.question: Whose money helped pay for The 400 Blows, the debut of French cinema's fiercest young critic?
cards.answer: His father-in-law's. Truffaut had married Madeleine Morgenstern, whose father Ignace ran the distribution company Cocinor, and his backing helped finance the film. The critic who had savaged the French film establishment made his debut with money from inside it. The film won Truffaut the directing prize at Cannes in 1959.
cards.move: Ask who paid for a rebellion before judging how rebellious it was.
cards.reference: de Baecque & Toubiana, Truffaut: A Biography, Knopf, 1999

cards.question: Which feature, made five years before Breathless by a photographer with no film training, already worked like the New Wave?
cards.answer: La Pointe Courte, shot by Agnès Varda in 1954 in a fishing quarter of Sète, on a tiny budget, through a company she founded for it. Alain Resnais edited it. It set documentary scenes of fishermen beside a couple's stylised conversations. The woman later called the grandmother of the New Wave was 26.
cards.move: Look for the movement's work done before the movement had a name.
cards.reference: Varda, Varda par Agnès, Cahiers du cinéma, 1994

cards.question: True or false: the label New Wave began in a magazine survey of young people, not in film criticism?
cards.answer: True. The journalist Françoise Giroud used la nouvelle vague in L'Express in 1957, for a survey of young French people, before the Cahiers critics had made a feature. The press then pinned it on the young directors around Cannes in 1959. A tag for a generation's attitudes became a school of film.
cards.move: A label often belongs to whoever needed a headline, not to the people labelled.
cards.trap: False, because movements usually seem to name themselves.
cards.reference: Marie, The French New Wave: An Artistic School, Blackwell, 2003

cards.question: Why is Godard's Breathless full of jump cuts inside single shots?
options: To imitate the rhythm of jazz
cards.answer: To cut the running time. Godard's first assembly ran far longer than his producer, Georges de Beauregard, would release. Rather than drop whole scenes, Godard cut inside shots, snipping pauses out of conversations. In the drive with Jean Seberg, the street jumps behind her head while her face barely changes.
cards.move: A style admired later may have started as a way out of a problem.
cards.trap: To imitate jazz, because the cutting looks like a chosen style.
cards.reference: Brody, Everything Is Cinema: The Working Life of Jean-Luc Godard, Metropolitan Books, 2008

cards.question: Should the director be treated as the author of a film?
cards.answer: The Cahiers critics showed that studio directors such as Hitchcock and Hawks carried the same obsessions and style across films written by different people. Someone decides where the camera stands, what the actors do and which take survives. The film carries that person's way of seeing, whoever typed the script.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, ask who could have been replaced without changing the film.
cards.counterpoint: Films are made by writers, cinematographers, editors and producers whose work the theory erased. Pauline Kael argued in 1971 that Herman Mankiewicz wrote much of Citizen Kane, and its look owes a great deal to Gregg Toland's camera. End credits run to hundreds of names because hundreds of people made the film.
cards.reference: Truffaut, Une certaine tendance du cinéma français, Cahiers du cinéma 31, January 1954

cards.question: How could Breathless shoot at night on Paris streets in 1959 with almost no film lights?
cards.answer: On film made for still cameras. Raoul Coutard loaded Ilford HPS, a fast stock sold to photographers in short lengths, spliced it into rolls long enough for a movie camera, and had the laboratory push the development to gain more speed. Street lamps and shop windows did the lighting.
cards.move: When the proper supply is missing, look at what a neighbouring trade sells.
cards.reference: Andrew (ed.), Breathless: Jean-Luc Godard, Director, Rutgers University Press, 1987

cards.question: Why does Godard's Contempt, 1963, open with Brigitte Bardot lying naked, asking which parts of her body are loved?
options: Godard's riposte to the French censor
A scene taken from Moravia's novel
cards.answer: The producers demanded more nudity. Joseph E. Levine and Carlo Ponti, paying for a Bardot film, found the first cut too chaste, and Godard shot a new opening in response. He filmed it through red and blue filters as a flat inventory of her body, which critics read as a dry reply to the order.
cards.move: Before reading intent into a scene, ask who asked for it.
cards.trap: Reading every scene of an auteur's film as his free choice.
cards.reference: MacCabe, Godard: A Portrait of the Artist at Seventy, Bloomsbury, 2003

cards.question: How was the dialogue of Godard's Breathless, shot on Paris streets in 1959, recorded?
options: Live, on a portable Nagra recorder
Live, with microphones hidden on set
cards.answer: Afterwards, dubbed in a studio. Coutard's Cameflex camera was light enough to hold by hand but far too noisy for sound, so the film was shot silent, with Godard often calling out lines during takes. The actors re-recorded every word later. The street talk that sounds so spontaneous was all post-synchronised.
cards.move: What looks improvised on screen may have been rebuilt piece by piece.
cards.trap: Linking the handheld street look to the era's portable sound recorders.
cards.reference: Neupert, A History of the French New Wave Cinema, University of Wisconsin Press, 2002

cards.question: True or false: Agnès Varda's Cléo from 5 to 7 follows its heroine from five o'clock until seven?
cards.answer: False. The film runs about 90 minutes in close to real time, from 5 until about 6:30 in the evening, with chapter titles on screen keeping the clock. The half-hour the title promises never arrives: the story ends at a hospital, where Cléo finally hears the result of her cancer test.
cards.move: A title is a promise made before the work, not a description of it.
cards.trap: Taking the times in the title as the span of the film.
cards.reference: Flitterman-Lewis, To Desire Differently: Feminism and the French Cinema, University of Illinois Press, 1990

cards.question: Cahiers du cinéma's December 1962 New Wave issue listed French directors with a first feature since 1959. About how many?
cards.answer: About 160: its dictionary ran to 162 entries, a few of them older mentors. The names still taught, Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rohmer, Rivette, Varda, Resnais, are a small fraction of that list. Most debutants made one or two films and faded, and the wave is remembered through the handful who kept working.
cards.move: Count the ones who started, not only the ones still standing.
cards.trap: Counting the dozen names that survived into the film histories.
cards.reference: Cahiers du cinéma, no. 138, special issue Nouvelle Vague, December 1962

cards.question: How did Metropolis put real actors inside skyscrapers that were only table-top models?
cards.answer: With a mirror. In the Schüfftan process a mirror at 45 degrees before the lens reflected the model, and the silvering was scraped off wherever the actors should appear, so the camera saw the full-size set through clear glass there. Model and actors met inside the camera, in one exposure, with nothing added afterwards.
cards.move: Before combining two things later, ask whether they can be combined at once.
cards.reference: Minden & Bachmann (eds), Fritz Lang's Metropolis: Cinematic Visions of Technology and Fear, Camden House, 2000

cards.question: How did Mary Poppins set live actors among cartoons without coloured fringes around their hair?
cards.answer: Sodium light. Actors stood before a screen lit by sodium-vapour lamps, which glow in one narrow band of yellow. A prism in the camera sent that yellow to a second film, making a perfect matte, and all other light to the colour negative. Fine hair and transparent veils kept edges that blue screens lost.
cards.move: Separate things by a property only one of them has.
cards.source: Iwerks & Kenworthy, The Hand Behind the Mouse
cards.reference: Iwerks & Kenworthy, The Hand Behind the Mouse, Disney Editions, 2001

cards.question: True or false: the house front that falls around Buster Keaton in Steamboat Bill, Jr. was a lightweight prop?
cards.answer: False. The facade was a real timber frame weighing around two tonnes by most accounts, and an open attic window was placed to pass around Keaton with only a few centimetres to spare. A light prop would have flexed and floated as it fell. Keaton stood on a marked spot and did not move.
cards.move: When something looks too dangerous to be real, ask what faking it would cost.
cards.trap: True, because no studio would drop a real wall on its star.
cards.source: Meade, Buster Keaton: Cut to the Chase
cards.reference: Meade, Buster Keaton: Cut to the Chase, HarperCollins, 1995

cards.question: What makes the big orange fireball in most film explosions?
cards.answer: Petrol and a small charge. Crews scatter petrol or naphtha into the air with a little explosive, and it burns as a slow, bright fireball with little blast. Military explosives do the opposite: a violent shock, a brief flash, a cloud of grey dust. The explosion most people picture was built for cameras.
cards.move: Ask where a picture in your head came from before trusting it.
cards.trap: Military high explosive, because real bombs look that way in films.
cards.reference: Rickitt, Special Effects: The History and Technique, Billboard Books, 2007

cards.question: Why do crews making artificial rain light it from behind rather than from the camera side?
cards.answer: Lit from the front, falling water nearly vanishes. Each drop is a tiny lens that shines only when light passes through it towards the lens, so rain towers are backlit against dark backgrounds, often with drops larger than real rain. A real downpour on location often barely registers on film, and crews add their own.
cards.move: Something that is obvious to the eye can still be invisible to the camera.
cards.reference: Box, Set Lighting Technician's Handbook, 4th edn, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: How did Fred Astaire dance up the walls and across the ceiling in Royal Wedding, 1951?
cards.answer: The room turned, not Astaire. The set was built inside a huge rotating drum, with the furniture bolted down and the camera fixed to the room, turning with it. On screen the room stays level, so as it rolled, Astaire, simply dancing on whatever surface was beneath him, seemed to climb the walls.
cards.move: When everything in the frame moves together, the frame itself may be moving.
cards.reference: Mueller, Astaire Dancing: The Musical Films, Knopf, 1985

cards.question: True or false: the windows and bottles that shatter in today's films are mostly made of sugar glass?
cards.answer: False. Boiled sugar was the classic breakaway glass, but it is fragile to handle, softens under hot lamps and turns sticky in damp air. Modern breakaway windows and bottles are mostly cast from brittle plastic resins, which keep their shape for weeks and break into blunt, safer shards. Sugar survives mainly in the retold story.
cards.move: The famous method is often one the trade has quietly retired.
cards.trap: Repeating the sugar-glass story told in countless behind-the-scenes clips.
cards.reference: Rickitt, Special Effects: The History and Technique, 2nd edn, Billboard Books, 2007

cards.question: Why did The Mandalorian film its chrome-armoured hero among giant LED screens rather than in front of green?
cards.answer: For the reflections. Green screen would have mirrored green in every curve of the polished armour. ILM's LED stage, first used on the 2019 series, displayed the digital landscape around the actors, so it lit their faces and shone in the metal. Rear projection returned, driven by a game engine.
cards.move: Choose a method by what the shiniest thing in the scene will reflect.
cards.reference: Kadner, The Virtual Production Field Guide, Epic Games, 2019

cards.question: Forced perspective, which makes the nearer actor look bigger, normally forbids camera moves. How did The Fellowship of the Ring move anyway?
options: Part of the set moved with the camera
Wide lenses hid the distance change
cards.answer: Part of the set moved with the camera. When a camera moves, near and far things shift at different rates and the trick shows. Weta put one actor's section of the set on a motorised platform that moved with the camera, keeping the distances in proportion. Gandalf and Frodo could share moving shots.
cards.move: When a trick breaks under movement, move part of the trick too.
cards.trap: Assuming an epic released in 2001 did its moving shots digitally.
cards.source: Sibley, The Making of the Movie Trilogy
cards.reference: Sibley, The Lord of the Rings: The Making of the Movie Trilogy, Houghton Mifflin, 2002

cards.question: Should film-makers replace dangerous practical stunts and live gunfire with digital effects wherever possible?
cards.answer: Real danger buys a few seconds of screen time and can cost a life. A helicopter downed by special-effects explosions killed Vic Morrow and two children filming Twilight Zone: The Movie in 1982, and a prop gun killed the cinematographer Halyna Hutchins on Rust in 2021. Digital doubles and added muzzle flashes now look convincing.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how much real risk an image may justify.
cards.counterpoint: Deaths are rare set against the vast number of stunts performed under coordinators, safety officers and firearms rules, and each disaster tightened those rules. Performers and audiences respond to real weight, speed and fire: films like Mad Max: Fury Road are praised for exactly that. Digital work has costs too, in long crunch hours for effects artists.
cards.reference: Farber & Green, Outrageous Conduct: Art, Ego, and the Twilight Zone Case, Arbor House, 1988

cards.question: Why did hundreds of lost silent films turn up under a hockey rink in the Yukon?
cards.answer: Because Dawson City was the end of the line. Prints arrived years after release and were not worth the freight back, so they piled up. Around 1929 many were dumped into a disused swimming pool as fill, later covered by a rink. In 1978 a bulldozer found more than 500 reels, preserved by permafrost.
cards.move: What is too costly to move is sometimes the thing that lasts.
cards.reference: Morrison (director), Dawson City: Frozen Time, Hypnotic Pictures, 2016

cards.question: How did thousands of the earliest American films survive on paper instead of film?
cards.answer: Through a gap in copyright law. Until 1912 US law did not protect motion pictures, so producers registered them as photographs, depositing rolls of paper contact prints of every frame at the Library of Congress. Paper outlasted the nitrate. In the 1950s and 1960s Kemp Niver copied about 3,000 of them back onto film.
cards.move: Paperwork filed for one purpose often preserves what nothing else kept.
cards.reference: Niver, Motion Pictures from the Library of Congress Paper Print Collection 1894–1912, University of California Press, 1967

cards.question: In 1981 a print of Dreyer's own cut of The Passion of Joan of Arc turned up. Where?
cards.answer: In a Norwegian psychiatric hospital. Dreyer's cut was thought lost to fire soon after its 1928 release, and the versions shown for decades were patched together from alternate takes. Then a cupboard at Dikemark Hospital, near Oslo, yielded a print with Danish intertitles, shipped there around 1928 and never returned.
cards.move: Look for the lost thing where it was last sent, not where it belongs.
cards.trap: A film archive is where a missing film ought to be.
cards.source: Danish Film Institute, Carl Th. Dreyer
cards.reference: https://www.carlthdreyer.dk/en/carlthdreyer/films/features/different-versions-jeanne-darc

cards.question: True or false: since the 2008 Buenos Aires find, Metropolis can be seen exactly as it premiered in 1927?
cards.answer: False. A worn 16mm duplicate in Buenos Aires restored about 25 minutes cut after the Berlin premiere, and the 2010 restoration put them back. But a few short scenes are still missing and are bridged by explanatory titles, and the recovered footage stays scratched and slightly cropped, easy to spot beside the rest.
cards.move: Recovered is not the same claim as complete; check which one is made.
cards.trap: The headlines said the complete film had been found.
cards.reference: Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung, Metropolis: the 2010 reconstruction, restoration notes, 2010

cards.question: Some silent features survive only as shortened 16mm or 9.5mm prints made for home viewing. Why did those last?
options: They were printed on non-flammable film
Studios made far more of them
cards.answer: They were printed on non-flammable film. Kodak sold 16mm from 1923 only on acetate safety base, and Pathé's 9.5mm was also non-nitrate, so home copies neither burned nor decomposed like 35mm cinema prints. Features cut down for rental libraries such as Kodascope sometimes became the only copy left.
cards.move: What lasts is often decided by the material, not by anyone's care.
cards.trap: Survival seems to reward the prints someone cherished most.
cards.reference: Cherchi Usai, Silent Cinema: An Introduction, BFI Publishing, 2000

cards.question: Should a rediscovered silent film be cleaned digitally beyond how it looked when new?
