cards.answer: Scratches, dust and flicker were never part of the film; they are damage done since. Removing them lets audiences see what the camera recorded, often more clearly than viewers of a worn print ever did. A restoration that leaves the damage in treats accidents as art and keeps these films looking quaint to new audiences.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what counts as the original.
cards.counterpoint: Digital cleaning also strips grain, softens faces and smooths the texture audiences actually saw. Once the tools can invent detail, the restorer starts making a new film. An archive's duty is to show the film as it was projected in its day, and to keep the untouched scan so later restorers can choose differently.
cards.reference: Fossati, From Grain to Pixel: The Archival Life of Film in Transition, Amsterdam University Press, 2009

cards.question: Why did a found print of Orson Welles's Too Much Johnson sit unrecognised for four years?
cards.answer: Because nobody knew what it was. Welles shot the untitled comic footage in 1938 to be projected during a stage play; it was never shown then, and his own copy was said to have burned in 1970. Reels found in 2008 in a shipping firm's warehouse in Pordenone, Italy, were only identified in December 2012.
cards.move: A find only counts once someone knows what they are holding.
cards.source: Wood, New York Review of Books, 2013
cards.reference: https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2013/12/19/discovering-orson-welles/

cards.question: True or false: the long-lost 1916 Sherlock Holmes film starring William Gillette turned up in 2014 inside a major film archive?
cards.answer: True. The only filmed record of Gillette's famous stage Holmes was found at the Cinémathèque française in Paris, which had held it without knowing: the reels carried French titles and had been wrongly labelled. It was restored and shown again in 2015. The film had spent decades hidden on an archive's own shelves.
cards.move: Search what is already catalogued before searching the attics.
cards.trap: Picturing the usual rescue from an attic, a barn or a closed cinema.
cards.reference: https://www.bfi.org.uk/news/cinematheque-francaise-discovers-1916-sherlock-holmes-film

cards.question: Kodak's edge date symbols repeat every 20 years. A nitrate reel carries the symbol also used in 1921. When could it date from?
cards.answer: 1921 or 1941. The same edge symbol was printed in 1921, 1941, 1961 and 1981, but Kodak stopped making nitrate base in 1951, so a nitrate reel cannot be from 1961. Archivists then weigh the rest: style, titles, laboratory marks. Twenty years apart, a silent comedy and a wartime newsreel can share a code.
cards.move: Use every clue at once; each rules out part of the rest.
cards.trap: Applying the 20-year cycle but forgetting that the base is nitrate.
cards.reference: https://www.kodak.com/content/products-brochures/Film/Guide-to-Identifying-Year-of-Manufacture-for-KODAK-Motion-Picture-Films.pdf

cards.question: Of the American silent features that survive in any form, what share were found in other countries?
cards.answer: About a quarter. David Pierce's 2013 survey for the Library of Congress counted more than 3,300 surviving features; 26% were found abroad, and many have since been copied and sent home. Prints shipped overseas were rarely sent back to be melted down. For many films, the best chance was to have been exported.
cards.move: What travelled far from home often outlived what stayed there.
cards.trap: Assuming American films survived mainly in American vaults.
cards.source: Pierce, Library of Congress and CLIR, 2013
cards.reference: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-film-preservation-board/documents/pub158.final_version_sept_2013.pdf

cards.question: Why do sound crews record a minute of an empty, quiet room on every set?
cards.answer: To have silence that matches. Every room hums with its own air, lights and distant traffic, and the dialogue carries that bed. Cut out a cough and leave digital zero, and the gap sounds as if the sound has failed. Editors patch it with that room's tone, recorded while the whole crew stood still.
cards.move: Real quiet always has a texture; pure nothing sounds like a fault.
cards.source: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures
cards.reference: Purcell, Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures: A Guide to the Invisible Art, Focal Press, 2007

cards.question: In a cinema, what sets how quiet the quietest moment of a film can be?
options: The bit depth of the file
cards.answer: The auditorium's own background noise. A 24-bit file can span about 144 decibels, far more than a cinema can use. The limit is the room: air handling, projector fans, the audience breathing and rustling. Mixers keep quiet passages above that floor, which is why a whisper on screen is louder than a real one.
cards.move: The weakest link is often the room, not the machine.
cards.trap: Digital sound seems limited by its format, as tape once was.
cards.reference: Kerins, Beyond Dolby (Stereo): Cinema in the Digital Sound Age, Indiana University Press, 2011

cards.question: Why did film cameras stop moving freely for a few years around 1929?
cards.answer: Because they were too loud. Early sound microphones picked up the camera's mechanical whirr, so cameras and their operators were shut inside soundproofed booths with a glass front. Shots turned static until padded covers, called blimps, let cameras out again. Actors, meanwhile, had to play to microphones hidden in flower vases.
cards.move: Every new tool quietly imposes a cost on the tools around it.
cards.reference: Crafton, The Talkies: American Cinema's Transition to Sound, 1926–1931, Scribner, 1997

cards.question: True or false: most of the dialogue in The Jazz Singer, the 1927 talkie, appears on intertitles?
cards.answer: True. Its Vitaphone discs carried a full orchestral score and Al Jolson's songs, but synchronised speech lasts only a couple of minutes, much of it Jolson improvising between numbers. The plot's conversations are still printed on cards, in the silent manner. The talking picture arrived as a silent film with islands of speech.
cards.move: A famous first is usually a small part of the thing it names.
cards.trap: Taking the label first talkie to mean a film full of talk.
cards.reference: Eyman, The Speed of Sound: Hollywood and the Talkie Revolution, 1926–1930, Simon & Schuster, 1997

cards.question: How does a sound mix make an audience hear a soldier's hearing fail?
cards.answer: By taking the world away. In Saving Private Ryan's Omaha Beach landing, after a blast near Captain Miller, the battle sinks to a muffled, underwater bed with a thin ringing, while the picture stays chaotic. The audience hears through his stunned ears. The gunfire rushes back only when his hearing does.
cards.move: Taking a sense away can say more than turning another one up.
cards.reference: Spielberg (director), Rydstrom (sound design), Saving Private Ryan, DreamWorks and Paramount, 1998

cards.question: When does a modern film mix dare to use true digital silence?
cards.answer: Almost never, but A Quiet Place, 2018, did it about three times. In shots heard through Regan, a deaf girl played by the deaf actress Millicent Simmonds, with her hearing implant out, the mixers cut to digital zero, no room tone at all. The cinema's own hush becomes the soundtrack: the audience hears itself breathe.
cards.move: An absence only registers against a presence people have learnt to expect.
cards.source: Slate, A Quiet Place sound editors, 2018
cards.reference: https://slate.com/culture/2018/07/a-quiet-place-on-dvd-sound-editors-ethan-van-der-ryn-and-erik-aadahl-give-advice-for-optimal-silence.html

cards.question: A horror mixer adds a faint click a tenth of a second before the jump-scare crash. What happens to the audience's jolt?
cards.answer: It gets weaker. A faint sound roughly 30 to 500 milliseconds before a startling one damps the startle reflex; the effect, prepulse inhibition, has been replicated in countless laboratories. The nervous system uses the warning to brace. A mixer after the full jolt clears the track to near silence before the bang.
cards.move: A small warning takes the edge off a large surprise.
cards.trap: Expecting a warning sound to wind the audience tighter before the blow.
cards.reference: Braff, Geyer & Swerdlow, Human studies of prepulse inhibition of startle: normal subjects, patient groups, and pharmacological studies, Psychopharmacology, 2001

cards.question: True or false: audiences first heard Charlie Chaplin's voice on film in 1936, singing in nonsense words?
cards.answer: True. Modern Times, 1936, has a recorded score and sound effects but no spoken lines from the Tramp until he performs a café song. The lyrics, written on his cuff, fly off, and he improvises gibberish mixing French and Italian. Chaplin's first real talking picture came four years later, with The Great Dictator.
cards.move: Before crediting the famous occasion, look for a smaller one before it.
cards.trap: Remembering The Great Dictator's famous speech as the first time he spoke.
cards.source: Robinson, Chaplin: His Life and Art
cards.reference: Robinson, Chaplin: His Life and Art, McGraw-Hill, 1985

cards.question: How much music does No Country for Old Men contain, and why do viewers miss it?
cards.answer: About 16 minutes, by Carter Burwell, and most of it barely sounds like music. He wrote long sustained tones that blend into wind, engine hum and the drone of motel rooms, so the score passes for ambience. Many viewers leave sure the film has none. Part of the dread they felt was scored.
cards.move: What was made to go unnoticed cannot be measured by who noticed it.
cards.source: Coen brothers, No Country for Old Men, 2007
cards.reference: Coen and Coen (directors), Burwell (music), No Country for Old Men, Miramax and Paramount Vantage, 2007

cards.question: Cinemas play a test signal 20 dB below full scale at 85 dB. Room noise is 35 dB. Usable range, in dB?
cards.move: A range runs from the floor to the ceiling, not from the middle.
cards.trap: Counting from 85 dB, as if the calibration level were the ceiling.
cards.hint: Find the loudest level the system allows first, then subtract the floor.
steps: Full scale is 20 dB above the test signal: 85 + 20 = 105 dB.
The quietest usable sound must sit above the room's 35 dB.
cards.reference: SMPTE RP 200:2012, Relative and Absolute Sound Pressure Levels for Motion-Picture Multichannel Sound Systems

cards.question: What did the 2021 buyers of Jodorowsky's Dune storyboard book fail to get for their €2.66 million?
cards.answer: The right to make anything from it. A crypto collective, Spice DAO, bought a copy of the pitch book for Alejandro Jodorowsky's abandoned 1970s Dune at Christie's in Paris, then announced plans for an animated series. Copyright stayed with its authors. They owned the book the way a buyer of a novel owns paper.
cards.move: Owning the object and owning the right to copy it are separate purchases.
cards.reference: Christie's Paris, sale of a copy of the Jodorowsky Dune storyboard book, November 2021

cards.question: True or false: Orson Welles's last feature, shot in the 1970s, premiered more than 30 years after he died?
cards.answer: True. The Other Side of the Wind was shot between 1970 and 1976, but the money ran out and its negative sat in a Paris vault, frozen by disputes among its backers, including an Iranian company caught up in the 1979 revolution. Netflix paid for the edit, guided by Welles's notes. It premiered in 2018.
cards.move: Unfinished work has a second life once the lawyers stop arguing.
cards.trap: A director dead since 1985 seems unable to release anything later.
cards.reference: Karp, Orson Welles's Last Movie: The Making of The Other Side of the Wind, St. Martin's Press, 2015

cards.question: True or false: once about $90 million had been spent on Batgirl, releasing it was bound to beat shelving it?
cards.answer: False. The $90 million was gone either way; only what came next could be weighed. Release meant more spending on effects and marketing against uncertain returns, while shelving let Warner Bros. Discovery take a tax write-down in 2022. A nearly finished superhero film was locked away unseen by arithmetic, not by quality.
cards.move: Decide on what is still to be spent, not on what already went.
cards.trap: Abandoning it feels like throwing away all the money already spent.
cards.reference: The Hollywood Reporter, report on Warner Bros. Discovery shelving Batgirl, August 2022

cards.question: How long did Terry Gilliam's Don Quixote film take from its first shooting day to its premiere?
cards.answer: Eighteen years. Shooting began in Spain in 2000 and collapsed within a week: military jets roared over the location, a flash flood swept away equipment, and the lead, Jean Rochefort, could not ride. The insurers took the script rights. Gilliam won them back and premiered The Man Who Killed Don Quixote at Cannes in 2018.
cards.move: A project abandoned is often only paused until the rights come home.
cards.source: Fulton and Pepe, Lost in La Mancha
cards.reference: Fulton and Pepe (directors), Lost in La Mancha, IFC Films, 2002

cards.question: Should a dead director's unfinished film be completed by other people?
cards.answer: An unfinished film is seen by almost no one. Eisenstein shot Que Viva Mexico in 1930–32 and never cut it; the version Grigori Aleksandrov assembled in 1979 at least let audiences see the footage as a film. A careful completion, labelled as such, serves the work better than cans in a vault.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whose choices viewers believe they see.
cards.counterpoint: Editing is where a film is authored. Whoever cuts the footage makes the thousand choices the director never made, then sells them under a famous name. Better to show the material openly as fragments, rushes and notes, clearly unfinished, than to present a guess as the work itself.
cards.reference: Geduld and Gottesman (eds), Sergei Eisenstein and Upton Sinclair: The Making and Unmaking of Que Viva Mexico, Indiana University Press, 1970

cards.question: What stopped Henri-Georges Clouzot's L'Enfer in 1964, despite a budget with no ceiling?
cards.answer: Partly the missing ceiling itself. Columbia, impressed by his tests, gave Clouzot unlimited money, and he shot experiment after experiment with light, colour and distortion while the schedule slid. His lead actor left, ill; then Clouzot had a heart attack, and the shoot stopped for good. The footage lay in cans until a 2009 documentary.
cards.move: Remove every limit and a piece of work may lose its reason to end.
cards.source: Bromberg and Medrea, L'Enfer d'Henri-Georges Clouzot
cards.reference: Bromberg and Medrea (directors), L'Enfer d'Henri-Georges Clouzot, Lobster Films, 2009

cards.question: True or false: an animated feature begun in the 1960s was taken from its director in 1992 and finished cheaply by others?
cards.answer: True. Richard Williams worked on The Thief and the Cobbler for almost three decades. When he missed a deadline in 1992, Warner Bros. withdrew and the completion bond company, which had guaranteed delivery, fired him and his team. Its hired crew finished the film fast and cheap; Miramax later released it as Arabian Knight.
cards.move: Whoever pays next weighs what is left to do, not what was done.
cards.trap: Assuming nearly thirty years already invested would buy him time to finish.
cards.reference: https://www.rogerebert.com/features/the-story-of-richard-williams-and-his-unfinished-fairy-tale-the-thief-and-the-cobbler

cards.question: The negative of Eisenstein's banned Bezhin Meadow was lost in the war. What is the 1967 version made from?
options: A rough-cut print found in Berlin
Single frames saved from each shot
cards.answer: Single frames saved from each shot. Soviet authorities halted the film in 1937, and the negative was reportedly destroyed in wartime bombing. In 1967 Sergei Yutkevich and Naum Kleiman arranged frame clippings kept from the cut into a silent film of stills, about half an hour long, with titles and music by Prokofiev.
cards.move: When the whole is gone, the fragments someone kept become the work.
cards.trap: Expecting the usual rescue story, a forgotten print turning up somewhere.
cards.reference: Bordwell, The Cinema of Eisenstein, Harvard University Press, 1993

cards.question: Where did a complete workprint of Jerry Lewis's shelved The Day the Clown Cried surface in 2025?
options: With a Swedish actor who kept it
cards.answer: With a Swedish actor. Lewis gave his footage to the Library of Congress in 2015, sealed until 2024; opened, it proved to be hours of fragments with no finished cut. Then in May 2025 Hans Crispin revealed that he had held a complete workprint for decades. The famous donation was never the whole film.
cards.move: The most publicised copy is not always the most complete one.
cards.trap: Recalling the widely reported donation to the Library of Congress.
cards.reference: https://newsroom.loc.gov/news/footage-from-jerry-lewis--film--the-day-the-clown-cried--opens-for-research-at-library-of-congress/s/73d6a4a2-2e21-4b63-aa03-aa8f0a778e64

cards.question: What survives of Something's Got to Give, the film Marilyn Monroe left unfinished in 1962?
cards.answer: Far more than legend suggests. Shooting stopped after Monroe was fired in June 1962, and she died that August, but Fox kept the footage. In 2001 about 37 minutes were assembled from it for a documentary, Marilyn: The Final Days, putting her last completed scenes, including a night-time swim, in order for the first time.
cards.move: Unfinished work often survives in pieces long after the plan has died.
cards.reference: Marilyn: The Final Days, documentary, Prometheus Entertainment for AMC, 2001

cards.question: Why are blockbusters orange and teal?
cards.answer: Skin tones sit in the orange range, and teal is directly opposite on the colour wheel — so pushing shadows teal makes faces jump forward. Digital grading made the move cheap and instant in the 2000s, and a look that once took effort became the default.
cards.move: Faces are orange, so the shadows went teal. That is the whole reason.
cards.reference: Misek, Chromatic Cinema: A History of Screen Color, Wiley-Blackwell, 2010

cards.question: What does GDP actually count?
cards.answer: Activity, not wellbeing. A car crash raises it: the ambulance, the repairs, the legal fees all count. Cleaning up after a hurricane counts. Raising your own children does not. Simon Kuznets, who built the measure in 1934, warned in the same report that it should never be read as welfare.
cards.move: GDP counts the crash and ignores the childcare. That was known from day one.

cards.question: How do the world's flowers get priced?
cards.answer: Mostly through a few enormous clocks in the Netherlands. At the Aalsmeer auction the price starts high and counts down until a buyer stops it — so hesitating costs you the lot. A large share of the cut flowers sold worldwide passes through that building within hours of being cut.
cards.move: Most of the world's flowers are priced by a clock running backwards.
cards.reference: Royal FloraHolland, Annual Report, 2022

cards.question: What made global manufacturing possible?
cards.answer: A steel box. Before standard containers, cargo was loaded piece by piece and moving goods across an ocean could cost a substantial fraction of their value. Standardising the box — not the ship — collapsed that cost until where something is made stopped depending much on where it is sold.
cards.move: The container, not the ship, is what moved the factories.

cards.question: Can average pay rise while everyone earns less?
cards.answer: Yes. If well-paid jobs grow as a share of the workforce, the average can climb even when pay falls within every single group. The overall number and the group-by-group numbers can point in opposite directions, and both are correct — which is why the headline needs the breakdown.
cards.move: An average can rise while every part of it falls.
cards.reference: Wagner, Simpson's Paradox in Real Life, The American Statistician, 1982

cards.question: How much can an insurance loss cost one person?
cards.answer: Everything they own. Until the 1990s, the individuals backing Lloyd's of London — the "Names" — carried unlimited personal liability. Asbestos claims written decades earlier surfaced at once and ruined thousands of them, over policies most had never read for risks nobody had priced.
cards.move: They had unlimited liability. The word unlimited was meant literally.
cards.source: Lloyd's of London, asbestos and the Names, 1988-1996
cards.reference: Duguid, On the Brink: How a Crisis Transformed Lloyd's of London, Palgrave Macmillan, 2014

cards.question: Why did paying off debts after 1929 leave many American borrowers worse off in real terms?
cards.answer: Because selling to raise cash pushed prices down, and debts were fixed in dollars. Consumer prices fell about a quarter between 1929 and 1933, so each dollar owed cost about a third more in goods and labour. Irving Fisher named it debt deflation in 1933: a farmer paid the same mortgage with ever more bushels.
cards.move: A debt fixed in money grows whenever the prices around it fall.
cards.reference: Fisher, The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions, Econometrica, 1933

cards.question: How did America's money supply shrink by about a third after 1929 while the Federal Reserve's own money grew?
cards.answer: Through the banks. About 9,000 failed or suspended from 1930 to 1933, and their deposits, the bulk of all money, froze or vanished. Savers kept cash at home and surviving banks hoarded reserves, so each Fed dollar supported fewer dollars of deposits. The Fed's notes kept circulating while the money built on them collapsed.
cards.move: Money is mostly promises between banks, and fear cancels promises.
cards.source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History, 1963
cards.reference: Friedman & Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960, Princeton University Press, 1963

cards.question: True or false: most American families owned shares when the stock market crashed in 1929?
cards.answer: False. By Galbraith's count, only about 1.5 million Americans had accounts with brokers, out of 120 million. The crash ruined a small, visible class of investors; the Depression reached everyone else through failed banks, lost jobs and collapsing farm prices. Far more families lost savings in failed banks than on shares.
cards.move: The most photographed victims are rarely the most numerous ones.
cards.trap: Picturing the crowds on Wall Street as the whole country.
cards.reference: Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929, Houghton Mifflin, 1955

cards.question: In the 1930s, which best predicted how soon a country's economy began to recover?
options: When it left the gold standard
How far its stock market fell
How high it raised its tariffs
cards.answer: When it left gold. Eichengreen and Sachs found that countries which cut the link early, like Britain in 1931, could lower interest rates and let prices rise, and recovered sooner. France and the rest of the gold bloc held on until 1936 and were still sliding. The exit date sorted the league table.
cards.move: Look for the constraint a country chose to keep, not the shock it suffered.
cards.trap: Picking the market crash, the most vivid image of the Depression.
cards.source: Eichengreen and Sachs, J. Economic History, 1985
cards.reference: Eichengreen & Sachs, Exchange Rates and Economic Recovery in the 1930s, Journal of Economic History, 1985

cards.question: US duties on taxed imports averaged about 59% in 1932. Besides the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Act, what pushed that rate up?
options: Falling prices, as many duties were fixed
cards.answer: Falling prices. Many duties were set in cents per pound or per item; as import prices collapsed, the same cents became a bigger share of the price. Douglas Irwin estimates deflation explains a large part of the rise. A duty of 5 cents on a 20-cent item is 25%; at 10 cents it is 50%.
cards.move: Before crediting a law, ask what would have happened without it.
cards.trap: Crediting the whole rise to the famous act, since it made headlines.
cards.reference: Irwin, Peddling Protectionism: Smoot-Hawley and the Great Depression, Princeton University Press, 2011

cards.question: Why do two standard series disagree by about seven points on American unemployment in 1936?
cards.answer: Because of how relief workers are counted. Stanley Lebergott's series treats people on federal work programmes such as the WPA as unemployed and gives about 17%; Michael Darby counted them as employed and got about 10%. Private jobs are identical in both. Whether the New Deal recovery looks fast or slow turns on one column.
cards.move: Before comparing two figures, check who each one counts as what.

cards.question: How much of a share's price did American buyers on credit typically have to put down by late 1929?
cards.answer: About 40 to 50%, not the 10% of legend. Rappoport and White found that brokers raised margin requirements from late 1928 and charged steep rates on loans to speculators, as if pricing in a fall. Ten or twenty per cent had been common earlier. The lenders saw the danger before October did.
cards.move: Watch what lenders demand; it shows what they privately expect.
cards.reference: Rappoport & White, Was the Crash of 1929 Expected?, American Economic Review, 1994

cards.question: True or false: an investor who bought American shares at the 1929 peak waited about 25 years to break even?
cards.answer: False, once dividends and falling prices are counted. The Dow's price regained its 1929 high only in 1954, but by Mark Hulbert's reckoning a Dow portfolio bought at the peak, dividends reinvested, was back to even in real terms by late 1936. Deflation made every dividend cheque buy more.
cards.move: An index of prices is not a record of what owners earned.
cards.trap: Reading the Dow's price chart as an investor's wealth.
cards.reference: Hulbert, 25 Years to Break Even? Not Really, The New York Times, April 2009

cards.question: In 1937 the American recovery broke, and industrial output fell by about a third within a year. What set it off?
options: Tighter money and a smaller deficit
A new wave of bank failures
cards.answer: Tighter money and a smaller deficit. The Fed doubled banks' reserve requirements in 1936 and 1937, the Treasury stopped letting gold inflows expand the money supply, and new social security taxes shrank the federal deficit. Bank failures, the villain of 1930 to 1933, stayed rare. Output turned up after both policies were reversed in 1938.
cards.move: A relapse often comes from the cure being withdrawn too early.
cards.trap: Blaming the banks, because they were the villains last time.
cards.reference: Irwin, Gold sterilization and the recession of 1937-1938, Financial History Review, 2012

cards.question: Was the Federal Reserve's failure to stop banks collapsing the main cause of the Great Depression?
cards.answer: The Fed was created as lender of last resort, yet watched thousands of banks fail and deposits vanish without flooding the system with cash. Friedman and Schwartz traced the depth of the slump to that passivity in 1963, and in 2002 Ben Bernanke, then a Fed governor, publicly accepted the charge on the Fed's behalf.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is what fell first, money or spending.
cards.counterpoint: Spending fell before the money did. Peter Temin showed that in 1929 and 1930 consumption and building dropped while interest rates fell, which a squeeze on money would not produce. The Fed's mistakes deepened a slump that began elsewhere: in a housing bust, a farm crisis and a world economy chained to gold.
cards.source: Temin, Did Monetary Forces Cause the Great Depression?
cards.reference: Temin, Did Monetary Forces Cause the Great Depression?, W. W. Norton, 1976

cards.question: Why did Northern Rock's savers queue for their money in 2007 when their deposits were insured?
cards.answer: Because the insurance left them holding part of the loss. Britain's scheme then covered all of the first £2,000 but only 90% of the next £33,000, and payouts could take months. For anyone with savings, running was rational. The queues stopped only when the Chancellor promised to guarantee every deposit, whole.
cards.move: A guarantee with a gap in it invites people to race for the gap.
cards.reference: House of Commons Treasury Committee, The Run on the Rock, Fifth Report of Session 2007-08, HC 56, 2008

cards.question: How did Lehman Brothers make its borrowing look smaller each time its quarterly accounts closed in 2008?
cards.answer: By booking borrowing as sales. In deals called Repo 105, it handed over bonds for cash before the books closed, recorded them as sold, and paid down debt with the cash; days later it bought them back. About $50 billion left the balance sheet in mid-2008. The debts came back once the photograph was taken.
cards.move: Ask what the numbers looked like the week after the report.
cards.reference: Valukas, Report of Examiner, In re Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., US Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York, 2010

cards.question: Of the mortgage securities Moody's rated AAA in 2006, how many were later downgraded?
cards.answer: More than four in five. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission found 83% were downgraded. The models treated mortgage defaults in different places as largely unconnected, so a pool of shaky loans looked safe. When house prices fell across the country at once, the loans failed together, and the top slices failed with them.
cards.move: Spreading risk works only if the pieces cannot all fall at once.
cards.trap: Guessing few, as if loans in different states failed independently.

diagram.caption: Of every 100 mortgage securities Moody's rated AAA in 2006, 83 were later downgraded.

cards.reference: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, US Government Printing Office, 2011

cards.question: True or false: the US Treasury lost money on the capital it put into banks during the 2008 crisis?
cards.answer: False. Under the Capital Purchase Programme the Treasury bought about $205 billion of shares in over 700 banks, and repayments, dividends and the sale of warrants brought back more than that. The losses in the bailouts fell elsewhere, on the car makers and on some small banks that never repaid.
cards.move: A headline sum authorised is not a sum spent, still less one lost.
cards.trap: Recalling the $700 billion bailout headline as money spent and gone.
cards.source: US Treasury, TARP reports to Congress
cards.reference: US Department of the Treasury, Troubled Asset Relief Program: Monthly Report to Congress, 2023

cards.question: Should the Federal Reserve have lent to rescue Lehman Brothers in September 2008?
sides: No, it was right not to
cards.answer: Lehman's collapse turned a banking loss into a world panic: a big money market fund broke the buck, and short-term lending froze. The next day the Fed lent $85 billion to AIG anyway. Laurence Ball's study of Lehman's balance sheet argues it had enough collateral for a legal loan. The choice was made, not forced.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether the law or the will was missing.
cards.counterpoint: The Fed may lend only against sound collateral, and officials judged Lehman insolvent, with no buyer willing to take it whole. Saving a second investment bank after Bear Stearns in March would have told every lender that none could fail, and rewarded the firms that borrowed most. Moral hazard is paid for in the next crisis.
cards.source: Ball, The Fed and Lehman Brothers, 2018
cards.reference: Ball, The Fed and Lehman Brothers: Setting the Record Straight on a Financial Disaster, Cambridge University Press, 2018

cards.question: Where did the bank run of 2008 mostly happen, given that few depositors queued at bank counters?
cards.answer: In the repo market, where banks borrowed overnight against bonds and lenders kept a margin, the haircut, by lending less than the collateral was worth. Gorton and Metrick found the average haircut on collateral other than Treasury bonds rose from about zero in early 2007 to nearly 50% in late 2008. Nobody queued.
cards.move: A run can happen wherever short-term lenders can quietly lend less.
cards.source: Gorton & Metrick, Journal of Financial Economics, 2012
cards.reference: Gorton & Metrick, Securitized banking and the run on repo, Journal of Financial Economics, 2012

cards.question: True or false: the rise in American mortgage defaults after 2007 was confined to subprime and low-income borrowers?
cards.answer: False. Adelino, Schoar and Severino found defaults rose across all incomes and credit scores, and the share owed by middle-income and prime borrowers grew. Subprime loans failed at higher rates, but prime loans were far more numerous. How much each group supplied is disputed: Mian and Sufi reply that many incomes were overstated on applications.
cards.move: A modest rate across many can outweigh a high rate among few.
cards.trap: Equating the group with the worst default rate with most defaults.
cards.reference: https://www.nber.org/papers/w20848

cards.question: At the end of 2007 Lehman Brothers held assets about 31 times its equity. What percentage fall in asset values erases the equity?
cards.move: The more a firm borrows, the smaller the loss that ends it.
cards.trap: Assuming a bank can only fail after a fall of a third or more.
cards.hint: Equity is the slice of assets the owners would lose first.
steps: Equity is 1 part in every 31 of assets.
1 / 31 = 0.032 of assets.
cards.reference: Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended 30 November 2007, 2008

cards.question: After the US government rescued the insurer AIG in 2008, where did much of the rescue money go?
options: To banks that had bought its protection
cards.answer: To banks that had bought its protection. AIG had sold credit default swaps, insurance-like contracts on mortgage bonds, and owed collateral it lacked. The rescue let those banks be paid in full, 100 cents on the dollar: Goldman Sachs, Société Générale and Deutsche Bank each received more than $11 billion. Saving AIG saved its creditors.
cards.move: When a rescue is announced, ask whose debts it pays.
cards.trap: Assuming an insurer's rescue mainly protects its policyholders.
cards.reference: Office of the Special Inspector General for the Troubled Asset Relief Program, Factors Affecting Efforts to Limit Payments to AIG Counterparties, 2009

cards.question: In September 2008 Ireland guaranteed its banks' debts. How large were the liabilities covered, compared with a year's national output?
cards.answer: More than twice it. The guarantee covered about €400 billion of six banks' liabilities, deposits and most bonds alike, in an economy producing under €190 billion a year. Meant to stop a run, it turned bank losses into state debts: rescuing the banks cost about €64 billion, and in 2010 Ireland needed an EU-IMF bailout.
cards.move: Measure a promise against the income of whoever has to keep it.
cards.trap: Expecting a bailout to be a few per cent of output, as usual.

items.label: Ireland's output a year, at most

diagram.caption: About €400 billion guaranteed by an economy making under €190 billion a year.

cards.reference: https://inquiries.oireachtas.ie/banking/volume-1-report/chapter-7/

cards.question: Which earlier share price do takeover bids for a listed company tend to cluster at?
cards.answer: The target's highest share price of the previous 52 weeks. Baker, Pan and Wurgler found that offers bunch at precisely that peak, and that targets become sharply likelier to accept once a bid clears it. A window drawn by the calendar helps price deals worth billions.
cards.move: A price someone once paid is a memory, not a valuation.
cards.source: Baker, Pan and Wurgler, J. Financial Economics, 2012
cards.reference: Baker, Pan & Wurgler, The effect of reference point prices on mergers and acquisitions, Journal of Financial Economics, 2012

cards.question: What happened when J.C. Penney swapped its endless sales for steady everyday prices in 2012?
cards.answer: Its shoppers walked away. The plan scrapped most coupons and sale events in favour of steady everyday prices; sales fell by about a quarter within the year and the company lost $985 million. The chief executive was out by April 2013, and the old sale tags came back.
cards.move: People buy the saving they can see, not the price they pay.
cards.reference: J.C. Penney Company, Inc., Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended 2 February 2013, 2013

cards.question: Besides income and local prices, what shapes how much rent a newcomer to a city chooses to pay?
cards.answer: The rents of the city they left. Simonsohn and Loewenstein found that movers arriving from pricier cities rent more expensive homes than equally paid movers from cheaper ones. The gap fades when they move again within their new city: the old price list stays in the head until the next lease.
cards.move: The last prices you lived with are still shopping for you.
cards.reference: Simonsohn & Loewenstein, Mistake #37: The Effect of Previously Encountered Prices on Current Housing Demand, The Economic Journal, 2006

cards.question: When New York taxi card screens suggested higher tip percentages, what happened?
options: Tips barely moved; riders kept their habits
Tips rose, but more left no card tip
Tips fell, as riders resented the pressure
cards.answer: Tips rose, but more left no card tip. Across 13 million New York rides, Haggag and Paci found that higher suggested percentages lifted the amounts people tipped. The same suggestions pushed more riders to skip the card tip entirely. A 30% button pulled the average up and pushed some riders off the screen.
cards.move: A preset amount is the seller's hope, printed as your option.
cards.trap: Believing the tip is set by the ride, not by the screen.
cards.reference: Haggag & Paci, Default Tips, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 2014

cards.question: True or false: printing a minimum payment on a credit-card bill lowers what people choose to repay?
cards.answer: True. In Neil Stewart's experiment, people shown a minimum repaid less than people shown no minimum at all, and later studies in Britain and the United States found the same pull. A floor meant to guarantee some repayment becomes the number people start from. Real card accounts show payments bunched at the printed minimum.
cards.move: Written minimums turn into targets; pick your number before reading theirs.
cards.trap: Assuming a minimum can only push payments upward.

cards.question: A shop raises an €80 jacket to €100 for two weeks, then advertises a sale. Under 2022 EU rules, what earlier price must it show?
options: €100, the price just before the sale
Any price it once genuinely charged
cards.answer: €80, its lowest price in 30 days. Since May 2022 EU law has required any announced price cut to cite the lowest price charged in the previous 30 days, and in 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled the percentage must be counted from it. A '30% off' tag of €70 is 12.5% off.
cards.move: Before trusting a discount, ask what the price was a month ago.
cards.trap: Taking the price just before the sale as the natural reference.
cards.reference: Directive (EU) 2019/2161 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Article 2, inserting Article 6a into Directive 98/6/EC, 2019

cards.question: When estate agents valued a house after seeing its list price, what set them apart from amateurs?
cards.answer: Not their accuracy but their denial. In Northcraft and Neale's study, agents who toured the same house valued it higher when handed a higher list price, much as students did. The students admitted the list price had swayed them; most agents said they had ignored it. The anchor worked on people sure it had not.
cards.move: Feeling unmoved by a number is no evidence that it did not move you.
cards.reference: Northcraft & Neale, Experts, Amateurs, and Real Estate: An Anchoring-and-Adjustment Perspective on Property Pricing Decisions, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1987

cards.question: True or false: the 2003 finding that the last digits of a social security number sway what people bid replicated at full size?
cards.answer: False. In Ariely, Loewenstein and Prelec's study, people with high final digits bid far more for wine and computer accessories. Maniadis, Tufano and List re-ran the design in 2014 and found a much weaker pull. Anchoring itself is well replicated; the first, striking measurement of this version sat at the high end.
cards.move: Expect the next measurement of a dramatic effect to be smaller.
cards.trap: Assuming a famous result's first measured size is its true size.
cards.reference: Maniadis, Tufano & List, One Swallow Doesn't Make a Summer: New Evidence on Anchoring Effects, American Economic Review, 2014

cards.question: Warning people about anchors barely weakens them. What did weaken a seller's price's hold on car experts?
cards.answer: Arguing against it. Mussweiler, Strack and Pfeiffer gave car mechanics and dealers a seller's price for a used car; those first asked to list reasons it might be wrong were anchored far less. Earlier studies found forewarning did little. Knowing about the bias is not the cure; building the case for another number is.
cards.move: Before accepting a figure, argue for a different one out loud.
cards.reference: Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer, Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect: Considering the Opposite Compensates for Selective Accessibility, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2000

cards.question: Should employers be barred from asking job candidates what they earned before?
cards.answer: A past salary anchors every offer after it, so one badly paid job or a career break follows a worker from employer to employer, and pay gaps compound. Since Massachusetts's ban took effect in 2018 many US states have followed, and several studies of job-changers there find pay rose, most for women and Black workers.
cards.move: It turns on whether a banned question removes the anchor or only hides it.
cards.counterpoint: Silence does not stop employers guessing; it changes what they guess from. Well-paid candidates volunteer their salary anyway, so those who stay quiet are read as cheap and the anchor returns by inference. Without the figure, employers lean harder on age, career gaps and old job titles, signals that can carry the same biases less visibly.
cards.reference: Agan, Cowgill & Gee, Do Workers Comply with Salary History Bans? A Survey on Voluntary Disclosure, Adverse Selection, and Unraveling, AEA Papers and Proceedings, 2020

cards.question: True or false: in a mail-order catalogue test, raising an item's price from $34 to $39 sold more of it?
cards.answer: True. Anderson and Simester mailed versions of a clothing catalogue in which the same items cost $34, $39 or $44. The $39 versions sold more than the cheaper $34 ones. A price ending in 9 reads as a keen price, and here that signal outweighed a real saving. Five dollars lost to a single digit.
cards.move: A price is read as a message before it is paid as a cost.
cards.trap: Assuming a higher price can only mean fewer buyers.
cards.source: Anderson and Simester, Quantitative Marketing and Economics, 2003
cards.reference: Anderson & Simester, Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments, Quantitative Marketing and Economics, 2003

cards.question: What happens to a used car's auction price as its odometer rolls past a round ten thousand?
cards.answer: It drops in a step, not a slope. In over 22 million wholesale used-car sales, Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor found prices fall abruptly at each 10,000 mark on the clock, with smaller steps at each 1,000. The pattern traces to final buyers, who read the first digit and skim the rest: charm pricing in reverse.
cards.move: When a number matters, read all of it, not just the front.
cards.source: Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor, American Economic Review, 2012

cards.question: On eBay, what happens to items listed at a round $100 rather than at nearby precise prices?
options: No difference in offers or speed
cards.answer: Lower offers, which arrive sooner. In millions of eBay bargaining exchanges, Backus, Blake and Tadelis found that items listed at multiples of $100 drew offers 5–8% lower but 6–11 days sooner, and were 3–5% likelier to sell. A round number reads as a seller in a hurry; house sales show the same pattern.
cards.move: A round number invites haggling; a precise one says the sums are done.
cards.trap: Assuming a few dollars either way cannot change how buyers bid.
cards.source: Backus, Blake & Tadelis, J. Political Economy, 2019

cards.question: What do prices ending in 99 cents do to how often a shop changes its prices?
cards.answer: They make prices stickier. In years of scanner data from Dominick's, a Chicago supermarket chain, Levy and colleagues found prices ending in 9 were both the most common and the least likely to change. A tag at $2.99 skips the small moves and waits for a cost rise big enough to justify $3.49.
cards.move: A price that is convenient to keep will be kept longer than it should.
cards.reference: Levy, Lee, Chen, Kauffman & Bergen, Price Points and Price Rigidity, Review of Economics and Statistics, 2011

cards.question: Scanner data from US grocery chains: a one-cent rise from a price ending in 99 hits sales like a rise of how much?
cards.answer: About twenty cents. Studying supermarket scanner data, Strulov-Shlain estimated that shoppers react to the step from $4.99 to $5.00 roughly as if it were twenty times bigger. Retailers do use 99 endings, yet price as if the effect were far smaller, forgoing an estimated 1–4% of gross profits.
cards.move: The first digit you read sets the size you feel.
cards.trap: Assuming shoppers weigh a cent as a cent.

diagram.caption: Shoppers treat the one-cent step from $4.99 to $5.00 like a twenty-cent rise.

cards.reference: doi:10.1093/restud/rdac082

cards.question: With new US pennies no longer minted, cash totals get rounded to the nearest five cents. Since most prices end in 99, who gains?
options: Shops, by about a cent a sale
Neither side, to a fraction of a cent
Shoppers, by about a cent a sale
cards.answer: Neither side, to a fraction of a cent. Only the total is rounded, and sales tax and mixed baskets scatter its last digit almost evenly. In nearly 200,000 real convenience-store sales, Whaples found shoppers gained about a cent per 40 transactions; a 2025 Richmond Fed estimate put the national cost near $6 million a year.
cards.move: Check which number actually gets rounded before counting who loses.
cards.trap: Rounding each 99-cent tag up, as if items were paid one by one.
cards.reference: https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief/2025/eb_25-27

cards.question: Can ignoring the cents on price tags be rational for shoppers, and who pays for it?
cards.answer: Yes, and sellers can end up paying. In Kaushik Basu's 1997 model, shoppers who skim the cents make 99 every seller's best ending, since unread cents cost no sales. Once all prices end in 99 the cents carry no news, so skimming is sensible. Sellers then earn less than if everyone read every digit.
cards.move: When every seller plays the same trick, it stops carrying information.
cards.reference: Basu, Why are so many goods priced to end in nine? And why this practice hurts the producers, Economics Letters, 1997

cards.question: True or false: US heart-attack patients just past their 80th birthday got bypass surgery less often than those just short of it?
cards.answer: True. Olenski and colleagues compared patients admitted within two weeks either side of turning 80, alike at baseline. About 7% of those still 79 had bypass surgery, against 5.3% of the new 80-year-olds. A few weeks of age changed nothing in their hearts; it changed the first digit on the chart.
cards.move: A threshold in the head is not a threshold in the body.
cards.trap: Assuming doctors weigh the patient's health, not the digit in front.

cards.question: In 2002 a German café converted its DM 4.50 cake at 1.95583 marks to the euro, then priced it at €2.49. Percentage rise?
cards.move: Convert both prices into one currency before judging a change.
cards.trap: Seeing 2.49 below 4.50 and feeling the price has fallen.
cards.hint: First turn the mark price into euros; 1.95583 is just under 2.
steps: 4.50 / 1.95583 = about €2.30, the exact euro price.
2.49 - 2.30 = €0.19 added by the new charm price.
cards.reference: Council Regulation (EC) No 2866/98 of 31 December 1998 on the conversion rates between the euro and the currencies of the Member States adopting the euro, 1998

cards.question: A US supermarket began printing prices with sales tax included on its shelf tags. What happened to sales of those items?
options: They rose, as shoppers trusted them
cards.answer: They fell by about 8%. Chetty, Looney and Kroft posted tax-inclusive tags on hundreds of products in one grocery store for three weeks. The same tax was already charged at the till, and shoppers knew the rates when asked. Sales still dropped against comparison aisles and stores: a $4.99 tag sells on the number printed.
cards.move: What a buyer sees at the shelf outweighs what they know at the till.
cards.trap: Expecting no change, since the tax was charged either way.
cards.reference: Chetty, Looney & Kroft, Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence, American Economic Review, 2009

cards.question: If the Strait of Hormuz closed, how much Gulf oil could go round it by pipeline?
cards.answer: Only a few million barrels a day, out of about 20 million that pass through. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea and the UAE's line to Fujairah are the only big bypasses, and much of their capacity is already in use. Kuwait, Qatar and southern Iraq have no way out but the strait.
cards.move: Check the size of the backup before calling a risk diversified.
cards.reference: US Energy Information Administration, World Oil Transit Chokepoints, 2024

cards.question: How did Denmark stop ship captains understating their cargo's value to cut the toll at the Sound?
cards.answer: It kept the right to buy the cargo at the declared price. From the 1560s the Sound toll was levied on the value each master declared, and the crown could take the goods at that figure. Declare low and risk selling your cargo cheap; declare high and overpay. Honesty became the cheapest option.
cards.move: Let people name their own price, then make them stand by it.
cards.source: Haan et al., European Economic Review, 2012
cards.reference: Haan, Heijnen, Schoonbeek & Toolsema, Sound taxation? On the use of self-declared value, European Economic Review 56(2), 2012

cards.question: True or false: every ship through the Panama Canal's locks is raised and lowered using fresh water?
cards.answer: True. The locks are filled by gravity from Gatun Lake, a rain-fed reservoir, and each crossing lets roughly 200 million litres run out to the sea. In the 2023 drought the canal authority cut daily crossings and the depth ships could load to. One of the world's busiest trade routes depends on the rainy season.
cards.move: Find out what a system spends each time it runs.
cards.trap: Assuming a canal between two oceans simply uses the sea.
cards.reference: Panama Canal Authority, Annual Report, fiscal year 2023, 2023

cards.question: Diverting from Suez round the Cape adds about 3,600 nautical miles. At 15 knots, how many extra days at sea?
cards.move: Turn a distance into days before judging what a detour costs.
cards.hint: A knot is one nautical mile per hour; start with a day's run.
steps: 15 knots x 24 hours = 360 nautical miles a day.
cards.reference: UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport 2024, United Nations, 2024

cards.question: True or false: Turkey may charge merchant ships a toll for passing through the Bosphorus?
cards.answer: False. The Montreux Convention of 1936 gives merchant ships free passage in peacetime; Turkey may charge only fixed fees for lighthouses, sanitary control and rescue services. So one of the busiest straits on earth earns its owner little, while Egypt took about $10 billion from the Suez Canal in 2023.
cards.move: Owning the gate is worth only what the treaties let you charge.
cards.trap: Carrying over the Suez and Panama model of paying to pass.
cards.reference: Convention Regarding the Regime of the Straits, signed at Montreux, 20 July 1936

cards.question: How does crude on a fully loaded supertanker cross Egypt when the Suez Canal is too shallow for it?
cards.answer: Partly by pipe. The SUMED pipeline runs about 320 km from Ain Sukhna on the Gulf of Suez to Sidi Kerir near Alexandria. A supertanker pumps part of its oil ashore, sails through the canal lighter, and takes the oil back on the Mediterranean side. Canal and pipeline sell one crossing in two pieces.
cards.move: When the channel is too narrow, split the load, not the journey.
cards.reference: US Energy Information Administration, World Oil Transit Chokepoints, 2017

cards.question: The 2021 Suez blockage held up about $9.6 billion of goods a day. Roughly what is one day's delay to those goods worth?
cards.answer: About $100 million. Hummels and Schaur, from what firms pay to fly goods rather than ship them, value each day in transit at 0.6% to 2.1% of the goods' value: $60 million to $200 million on $9.6 billion. Interest alone would be nearer $1 million. The headline measured the flow, not the damage.
cards.move: Separate what a delay touches from what it destroys.
cards.trap: Treating the value of goods delayed as the value lost.

cards.question: Red Sea war cover rose from 0.05% to 0.7% of hull value per transit. Extra cost for a $150 million ship, in thousands of dollars?
cards.answer: 150,000 x 0.0065 = 975 thousand dollars.
cards.move: Price a small percentage against the full value it is charged on.
cards.trap: Counting the whole 0.7% as new and forgetting the old premium.
cards.hint: Work out the rise in percentage points before touching the ship's value.
steps: The premium rose by 0.7% - 0.05% = 0.65% of the ship's value.
$150 million is 150,000 thousand dollars.
150,000 x 0.0065 = 975 thousand dollars.
cards.reference: https://www.policyholderpulse.com/red-sea-transit-insurance-premiums-coverage-exclusions/

cards.question: True or false: during Panama's 2023 drought, a gas carrier paid close to $4 million just to jump the queue?
cards.answer: True. With Gatun Lake low, the canal cut daily crossings, and ships without bookings bid at auction for the few spare slots. On 8 November 2023 Japan's Eneos paid $3.975 million for its gas carrier to pass, on top of the ordinary toll. Waiting weeks, or sailing round South America, would have cost more.
cards.move: A queue has a price, and scarcity reveals it.
cards.trap: Measuring the claim against ordinary tolls of a few hundred thousand.
cards.reference: https://maritime-executive.com/article/panama-canal-auction-sets-record-4m-for-slot-as-congestion-grows

cards.question: Somali pirates collected roughly $120 million a year in ransoms in the late 2000s. What did piracy cost the world yearly?
cards.answer: About $2 billion. Besley, Fetzer and Mueller found that attacks in 2008 raised charter rates on exposed routes by 8% to 12%, as owners paid for guards, insurance, speed and detours. That put the yearly loss at $0.9 billion to $3.3 billion, against about $120 million taken. Theft destroyed far more than it took.
cards.move: The damage a thief does is rarely the size of the haul.
cards.trap: Equating the harm with the ransoms because that number is given.
cards.reference: Besley, Fetzer & Mueller, The Welfare Cost of Lawlessness: Evidence from Somali Piracy, Journal of the European Economic Association, 2015

cards.question: Why are shipping containers 20 and 40 feet long, when the two pioneering lines used neither size?
cards.answer: Because a committee chose round numbers and the government paid for them. Sea-Land ran 35-foot boxes and Matson 24-foot ones, but American standards panels around 1960 chose 10, 20, 30 and 40 feet, and federal shipbuilding subsidies went only to ships built for those sizes. The pioneers rebuilt their fleets around a committee's measurements.
cards.move: A standard is a political settlement long before it is an engineering one.
cards.reference: Levinson, The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger, Princeton University Press, 2006

cards.question: How did Felixstowe, a small Suffolk harbour, overtake London and Liverpool as Britain's container port?
cards.answer: By being too small to be regulated. The National Dock Labour Scheme of 1947 reserved work at major ports for registered dockers, but Felixstowe fell outside it. Containers need a fraction of the old gangs, so Felixstowe adopted them in 1967 without a fight. London's upstream docks closed; the ships went to the seaside.
cards.move: Look for where the rules stop before asking where the growth starts.
cards.source: Hansard, Felixstowe Dock and Railway Bill, 1985
cards.reference: https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1985/may/13/felixstowe-dock-and-railway-bill

cards.question: Roughly what share of the containers handled at the world's ports have nothing in them?
cards.answer: About one in five. Trade is lopsided: East Asia ships out far more boxes of goods than it takes back, so lines must haul empties home to be filled again. Since the 1990s empties have made up around 20% of port handling. A box of shoes to Europe often returns carrying air.
cards.move: Every one-way flow hides a return trip somebody pays for.
cards.source: Notteboom, Pallis and Rodrigue, Port Economics, 2022
cards.reference: https://porteconomicsmanagement.org/pemp/contents/part1/maritime-shipping-and-international-trade/world-container-throughput/

cards.question: Between 1962 and 1990, which did most to raise trade between rich countries?
cards.answer: The container. Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller dated when each country got container ports or rail terminals and tracked its trade. Among rich countries, containers raised trade by several hundred per cent over 20 years, several times the effect of GATT membership or trade deals. Tariff cuts and boxes arrived together.
cards.move: When two causes arrive together, ask which one you can date separately.
cards.trap: Crediting the treaties, because trade policy is what gets reported.
cards.source: Bernhofen et al., J. International Economics, 2016
cards.reference: Bernhofen, El-Sahli & Kneller, Estimating the effects of the container revolution on world trade, Journal of International Economics, 2016

cards.question: True or false: more than 10,000 shipping containers fall overboard in an average year?
cards.answer: False. The World Shipping Council's surveys put average losses since 2008 under 1,500 a year, with 221 lost in 2023 and 576 in 2024, when ships rerouted round the stormy Cape. Over 250 million boxes are carried each year. A single ship spilling hundreds in a storm makes most of a bad year.
cards.move: Count the whole traffic before judging the size of the spill.
cards.trap: Recalling the rubber ducks and trainers washed up after famous spills.
cards.source: World Shipping Council, Containers Lost at Sea
cards.reference: https://www.worldshipping.org/containers-lost-at-sea

cards.question: Why can a cargo owner whose goods arrive undamaged still get a bill after a container ship's accident?
cards.answer: Because of general average, a maritime rule older than insurance: when a ship spends or sacrifices something to save the voyage, every cargo owner aboard shares the cost in proportion to value. Ever Given's owner declared it after the 2021 Suez grounding. Intact goods are released only once their owners post security.
cards.move: Sharing a risk means paying for other people's bad luck too.
cards.reference: Comité Maritime International, York-Antwerp Rules 2016, adopted at the CMI Conference in New York, 2016

cards.question: Why did container freight rates rise about sevenfold in 2021 while the volume of trade grew only modestly?
cards.answer: Because ships take years to build and port queues trapped the ones afloat. With part of the fleet idle at anchor, extra demand met no extra ships, so price adjusted instead: Drewry's index rose from about $1,420 in 2019 to $10,377 in September 2021. The ships ordered then arrived from 2023, into a slump.
cards.move: When supply cannot move, a small shift in demand moves the price enormously.
cards.reference: Drewry Supply Chain Advisors, World Container Index, weekly composite assessments 2019-2023, 2023

cards.question: Fuel burned per hour rises with the cube of speed. Slow a ship from 20 to 16 knots: what happens to fuel per voyage?
cards.answer: Falls to about 64%. Per hour, 0.8 cubed is 0.51, but the slower ship spends 1.25 times as long at sea, so per voyage the saving follows the square: 0.8 squared is 0.64. A line keeping a weekly service must also add ships to the loop, which eats part of the gain.
cards.move: When a rate falls, check whether the time it runs for grows.
cards.trap: Applying the cube to the whole voyage and forgetting the extra hours.

diagram.caption: At 16 knots each hour burns 51% of the fuel, but the longer voyage needs 64%.

cards.source: Notteboom & Vernimmen, Journal of Transport Geography, 2009
cards.reference: Notteboom & Vernimmen, The effect of high fuel costs on liner service configuration in container shipping, Journal of Transport Geography, 2009

cards.question: Before 2020, shipping a 40-foot container from Shanghai to northern Europe cost about $1,500. Roughly how many US cents per pair of boxed shoes?
cards.answer: $1,500 / 6,900 = about 22 cents a pair.
cards.move: Divide a big bill by everything it carries before calling it big.
cards.trap: Guessing dollars per pair because ocean freight sounds expensive.
cards.hint: Start with how many shoeboxes fit in the box's usable space.
steps: A 40-foot box holds about 67 cubic metres; real packing fills perhaps 55.
A shoebox of about 33 x 20 x 12 cm takes roughly 0.008 cubic metres.
55 / 0.008 = about 6,900 pairs per container.
$1,500 / 6,900 = about 22 cents a pair.
cards.reference: ISO 668:2020, Series 1 freight containers: Classification, dimensions and ratings, International Organization for Standardization, 2020

cards.question: True or false: a shipping line that loses a container of phones must, by default, repay what the phones were worth?
cards.answer: False. Under the Hague-Visby Rules, used for much of the world's sea cargo, liability is capped at 666.67 special drawing rights, an IMF unit worth roughly $1.35, per package, or 2 per kilogram if higher, unless a value was declared. A container whose cartons are not listed counts as one package.
cards.move: Read the cap before counting on the compensation.
cards.trap: Assuming whoever loses the goods must pay their full value.
cards.reference: Protocol amending the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law relating to Bills of Lading (SDR Protocol), Brussels, 1979

cards.question: What did the first study of decoy options, in 1982, show that choice theory had ruled out?
cards.answer: An added option raising the share of an existing one. Standard models held that a newcomer can only take buyers away, a property called regularity. Huber, Payne and Puto added options clearly worse than one of the existing choices, and that choice gained share. An option almost nobody picked sold its neighbour.
cards.move: More choice can change the winner, not just split the vote.
cards.source: Huber, Payne & Puto, J. Consumer Research, 1982

cards.question: Shoppers split evenly between a $170 and a $240 camera. When a $470 model was added, what happened to the $170 camera's share?
options: It fell to about a fifth
cards.answer: It fell to about a fifth. In Simonson and Tversky's study the cheap Minolta dropped from 50% to 22% once a pricier model appeared; the middle camera rose from 50% to 57% and the newcomer took 21%. Once $170 became the extreme, it lost more than half its buyers.
cards.move: Extremes make the middle look safe; ask who added the extreme.
cards.trap: Judging the cheap camera on its own, not against the new top price.
cards.reference: Simonson & Tversky, Choice in Context: Tradeoff Contrast and Extremeness Aversion, Journal of Marketing Research, 1992

cards.question: True or false: decoys that reliably sway choices among options described by numbers work as well on realistic product displays?
cards.answer: False. Shown as pictures or realistic descriptions instead of tables of attributes, decoys mostly stopped working in Frederick, Lee and Baskin's studies; Yang and Lynn found the same with real products. The effect's discoverers now say it needs the dominance to be plain at a glance. It lives most comfortably in a table of numbers.
cards.move: A result is only as wide as the materials it was tested on.
cards.trap: Assuming an effect found on number tables holds on real shelves.
cards.source: Frederick, Lee & Baskin, J. Marketing Research, 2014

cards.question: Do decoys only work on creatures that can explain their choices?
cards.answer: No. Female túngara frogs offered two recorded male calls preferred caller B over caller A; when Lea and Ryan added a third, inferior call, the females switched to A. Mate-choice theory had assumed stable rankings, just as rational-choice economics does. The decoy works on a brain that has never heard of a price.
cards.move: When a frog shares your mistake, look for wiring, not motives.
cards.reference: Lea & Ryan, Irrationality in mate choice revealed by túngara frogs, Science, 2015

cards.question: Does having to explain a choice to others make people more or less swayed by a decoy?
options: Less swayed, since they think harder
No change, since the options are the same
More swayed, since the decoy supplies a reason
cards.answer: More swayed, since the decoy supplies a reason. In Simonson's experiments, decoy and compromise effects were stronger among people who expected to justify their decision to others. A clearly dominated option hands the chooser an easy argument: this one beats that one. Picking the decoy's target went with more elaborate, harder deliberation, not less.
cards.move: A choice you can defend is not always the choice you should make.
cards.trap: Expecting accountability to make people more careful and less biased.

cards.question: Can switching to the middle option after a shop adds an expensive top model ever be rational?
cards.answer: Yes, for a buyer who does not know what suits them. In Emir Kamenica's 2008 model, such shoppers read the product line itself: sellers stock what typical customers want, so a new top model signals that the middle one is the ordinary choice. The added option can carry information, not only exploit a bias.
cards.move: What a seller chooses to offer is itself a piece of evidence.
cards.reference: Kamenica, Contextual Inference in Markets: On the Informational Content of Product Lines, American Economic Review, 2008

cards.question: A newcomer almost identical to brand A, and just as good, goes on sale beside brands A and B. Whose share falls most?
options: B's, as A now looks better
A's, as the newcomer splits its buyers
cards.answer: A's. Tversky called it the similarity effect: a near-copy competes for the same buyers, so it draws mostly from its twin, not evenly from all. A decoy helps its target only by being plainly worse. Put a red bus beside the blue one, and the buses split their riders while the car keeps its share.
cards.move: A newcomer takes first from whatever it most resembles.
cards.trap: Treating any similar newcomer as a decoy that makes A shine.
cards.reference: Tversky, Elimination by Aspects: A Theory of Choice, Psychological Review, 1972

cards.question: True or false: when a strong option is shown as sold out, choices shift towards the remaining option most like it?
cards.answer: True. Researchers call it a phantom decoy: an attractive option that turns out to be unavailable. In Highhouse's hiring experiments, a strong phantom candidate pushed choices towards the remaining candidate most like it. The best option on display sets the standard even when nobody can take it: a sold-out label still works the shelf.
cards.move: The option you cannot have still sets the standard for those you can.
cards.trap: Assuming an option nobody can pick cannot sway the choice.
cards.reference: Highhouse, Context-Dependent Selection: The Effects of Decoy and Phantom Job Candidates, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1996

cards.question: Pooling decades of decoy experiments, which kind of brand gains share when a decoy is aimed at it?
cards.answer: Premium brands, rarely budget ones. Heath and Chatterjee's 1995 meta-analysis found decoys raised a target's share mainly when the target was the higher-quality brand. Aimed at a lower-quality brand, they seldom helped it, and they took more share from budget rivals than from premium ones. The trick flatters quality far more easily than cheapness.
cards.move: A tactic that lifts the strong may do nothing for the weak.
cards.trap: Assuming a trick that works one way must work both ways.
cards.reference: https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/22/3/268/1791719

cards.question: Where has the decoy effect shown up in real purchases worth thousands of dollars?
cards.answer: In online diamond sales. A diamond is sold as a table: carat, cut, colour, clarity, price. Wu and Cosguner found that a stone beaten on every count by another raised sales of the stone that beat it, and estimated a retailer could profit by placing such decoys on purpose. The lab's format, real money.
cards.move: Expect a lab effect to survive where the real choice looks like the lab.
cards.reference: Wu & Cosguner, Profiting from the Decoy Effect: A Case Study of an Online Diamond Retailer, Marketing Science, 2020

cards.question: What problem was Kenya's M-Pesa originally built to solve?
cards.answer: Repaying microloans. A Vodafone project begun in 2003 let borrowers of Faulu, a Kenyan microfinance lender, repay loans through Safaricom's airtime sellers. In the 2005 pilot, users found other uses, from settling each other's loans to sending money to relatives. Safaricom relaunched it in 2007 for person-to-person transfers: the side use became the product.
cards.move: Watch what people do with a tool before deciding what it is for.
cards.reference: Hughes & Lonie, M-PESA: Mobile Money for the Unbanked: Turning Cellphones into 24-Hour Tellers in Kenya, Innovations: Technology, Governance, Globalization, 2007

cards.question: How long before Bitcoin could customers of a real bank spend anonymous digital cash?
cards.answer: More than a decade. From 1995, Mark Twain Bank in Missouri issued eCash built on David Chaum's 1982 idea of blind signatures: a bank signs a digital coin without seeing its serial number, so spending leaves no trail to the customer. Too few shops joined, and Chaum's company DigiCash filed for bankruptcy in November 1998.
cards.move: A payment method works only when both sides already use it.
cards.source: Brunton, Digital Cash, Princeton University Press, 2019
cards.reference: Brunton, Digital Cash: The Unknown History of the Anarchists, Utopians, and Technologists Who Created Cryptocurrency, Princeton University Press, 2019

cards.question: True or false: under America's 2025 stablecoin law, a dollar stablecoin's issuer may pay holders interest on it?
cards.answer: False. The GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, bars licensed issuers from paying holders any interest or yield merely for holding the coin, largely to stop stablecoins draining deposits from banks. The issuer still earns interest on the Treasury bills in reserve. A dollar parked in a stablecoin works for the issuer, not the holder.
cards.move: When your money sits idle somewhere, ask who is earning on it.
cards.trap: Assuming a digital dollar must pay interest like a savings account.
cards.reference: Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, signed 18 July 2025

cards.question: True or false: El Salvador still requires its shops to accept bitcoin as payment?
cards.answer: False. The 2021 law that obliged every business to accept bitcoin was amended in January 2025, as a condition of a $1.4 billion IMF loan: accepting it became voluntary, and taxes can no longer be paid in it. The US dollar, El Salvador's official currency since 2001, stayed the money people spend.
cards.move: A famous law may have been quietly amended; look up its current text.
cards.trap: Remembering the 2021 headline and missing the quieter 2025 amendment.
cards.source: IMF, El Salvador Extended Fund Facility, 2025
cards.reference: International Monetary Fund, El Salvador: Request for an Extended Arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility, Country Report, 2025

cards.question: Bitcoin halves its new-coin reward every 210,000 blocks, and its code targets one block every ten minutes. How many years between halvings?
cards.answer: 1,458 / 365 = about 4.0 years.
cards.move: When a rhythm looks scheduled, find which quantity was really fixed.
cards.trap: Thinking the code sets a date rather than a block count.
cards.hint: Turn the blocks into minutes first, then the minutes into days.
steps: 210,000 blocks x 10 minutes = 2,100,000 minutes.
2,100,000 / 1,440 minutes a day = about 1,458 days.
1,458 / 365 = about 4.0 years.
cards.reference: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/kernel/chainparams.cpp

cards.question: Where does the money sitting in a Chinese Alipay or WeChat Pay balance actually live?
cards.answer: At the central bank. Since January 2019 China has required payment firms to hold 100% of customer balances at the People's Bank of China, in accounts that pay no interest. Before, the platforms parked this float at commercial banks and kept the interest. A phone balance became, in effect, a claim on the central bank.
cards.move: Ask who holds the money behind the number on your screen.
cards.reference: People's Bank of China, Notice on Matters Concerning the Full Centralised Deposit of Customer Reserve Funds of Payment Institutions, 2018

cards.question: How did US agents get back most of the bitcoin ransom paid after the 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack?
cards.answer: By following it. Every bitcoin transfer is on a public ledger; investigators traced the 75 coins Colonial paid through a chain of addresses to one whose key the FBI held, and seized 63.7 of them. Bitcoin hides names, not movements. The price had fallen: those coins were worth $2.3 million of the $4.4 million paid.
cards.move: A record anyone can read stays private only until one entry is linked.
cards.reference: US Department of Justice, Department of Justice Seizes $2.3 Million in Cryptocurrency Paid to the Ransomware Extortionists Darkside, press release, 7 June 2021

cards.question: By one leading estimate, what share of Kenyan households did mobile money lift out of extreme poverty by 2014?
cards.answer: About 2%, roughly 194,000 households. Suri and Jack compared households whose nearest M-Pesa agents multiplied fastest with others, and found the largest gains among women who moved from farming into business. Critics dispute the design and the size; even at face value, the figure is modest. A celebrated success, counted in thousands rather than millions.
cards.move: A famous success still needs its size checked.
cards.trap: Picking a fifth, because M-Pesa is development's best-known success story.
cards.reference: Suri & Jack, The long-run poverty and gender impacts of mobile money, Science, 2016

cards.question: What fee does a shop in India pay to receive a customer's payment through UPI, the national phone payment system?
cards.answer: Nothing, by government rule. Since January 2020 banks and apps may not charge merchants for ordinary UPI payments; the government pays them a small subsidy instead. With no cost at either end, UPI passed ten billion payments a month in 2023. A street vendor's printed code takes payments as free as a department store's.
cards.move: When a service is free at both ends, look for who pays in between.
cards.trap: Expecting card-like fees, since someone must pay to run the system.
cards.source: India, Payment and Settlement Systems Act
cards.reference: Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, section 10A, inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, Government of India

cards.question: Should central banks issue digital cash that anyone can hold directly?
cards.answer: As notes fall out of use, the public loses its only direct claim on the central bank, and payments run entirely through private firms that can fail, charge or exclude. A digital pound or euro keeps a public option, sets a floor under fees, and gives people money whose safety depends on no bank's solvency.
cards.move: It turns on whether holding limits can stop a digital bank run.
cards.counterpoint: A safe digital account one tap away turns every banking scare into a run at the speed of a phone; the Bank of England floated a holding limit of £10,000 to £20,000, which concedes the risk. Deposits fund lending, so moving them to the central bank shrinks credit, and a state ledger of purchases invites surveillance.
cards.source: Bank of England and HM Treasury, 2023
cards.reference: Bank of England and HM Treasury, The digital pound: a new form of money for households and businesses?, Consultation Paper, February 2023

cards.question: What did British munitions factories of the First World War reveal about long working weeks?
cards.answer: That extra hours stop paying. Re-analysing the records of the wartime Health of Munition Workers Committee, John Pencavel found output rose in step with hours up to about 49 a week, then ever more slowly. Output at 70 hours differed little from output at 56: fourteen extra hours bought almost nothing.
cards.move: Find the point where extra hours stop adding output, then stop.

cards.question: What did Iceland's much-reported 'four-day week' trials of 2015 to 2019 really change?
cards.answer: Hours, not days. About 2,500 workers, over 1% of the workforce, went from 40 hours to 35 or 36 on the same pay, mostly by shortening days: shorter meetings, staggered shifts, earlier closing. Unions then won shorter hours, or the right to them, for most workers. Headlines said four days; timesheets said 35 hours.
cards.move: Check what a policy changed before repeating what it was called.
cards.reference: Haraldsson & Kellam, Going Public: Iceland's Journey to a Shorter Working Week, Alda and Autonomy, 2021

cards.question: In Britain's 2022 trial, 56 of 61 firms kept a four-day week afterwards. What does that show about firms in general?
options: Most firms would gain from it
Only small firms can manage it
Little: the firms chose to take part
cards.answer: Little: the firms chose to take part. They volunteered, were coached through the switch, designed their own schedules, and there was no comparison group. Revenue figures came from only some of the firms, and were self-reported. Fifty-six of sixty-one is a result about volunteers, not about employers in general.
