cards.move: Ask who chose to be measured before generalising from the result.
cards.trap: Treating a trial's volunteers as a fair sample of all employers.
cards.reference: https://autonomy.work/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/The-results-are-in-The-UKs-four-day-week-pilot.pdf

cards.question: In 1930 Keynes forecast that by 2030 living standards would be four to eight times higher and working weeks fifteen hours. How has it gone?
options: Incomes on track; hours far off
Hours on track; incomes far off
cards.answer: Incomes on track; hours far off. Real income per head in Britain and the United States has risen roughly five- to eightfold since 1930, inside Keynes's range: growth of 2% a year compounds to about sevenfold in a century. Weekly hours fell only modestly. The riches arrived; the leisure mostly did not.
cards.move: Before calling a century forecast wild, compound the growth rate yourself.
cards.trap: Assuming an eightfold rise in a century must be fantasy.
cards.source: Pecchi and Piga, Revisiting Keynes, MIT Press, 2008
cards.reference: Pecchi & Piga (eds.), Revisiting Keynes: Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren, MIT Press, 2008

cards.question: Should the law give every worker a four-day week on full pay?
cards.answer: The best evidence now has a comparison group: across 141 organisations and about 2,900 workers, burnout, job satisfaction and health improved after the switch, and not in control firms. Few employers dare cut hours alone, fearing they will look less committed, so a legal default spreads the gain, as the forty-hour week once did.
cards.move: It turns on whether firms that never volunteered would gain as much.
cards.counterpoint: That study's control group was just 12 companies, every firm chose to take part, and hours fell by about five a week, not eight. Nurses, drivers and care workers cannot squeeze a week of shifts into four days: covering the same hours needs 25% more staff. A law would send that bill to hospitals and councils.
cards.source: Fan et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2025

cards.question: True or false: Microsoft Japan's reported 40% productivity jump from its 2019 four-day week was measured against a comparison group?
cards.answer: False. The figure compared sales per employee in August 2019, the trial month, with August 2018. No group stayed on five days, so a whole year of other changes sits inside the comparison. One month against the same month a year earlier measures a year, not a policy.
cards.move: Ask what a change was compared with before believing its size.
cards.trap: Assuming a headline productivity figure came from a controlled comparison.
cards.source: Microsoft Japan, Work Life Choice Challenge
cards.reference: Microsoft Japan, Work Life Choice Challenge 2019 Summer: results announcement, October 2019

cards.question: In 1982 France cut the legal week from 40 to 39 hours, monthly pay unchanged. What happened to workers who had been on 40?
options: More of them lost their jobs
More were hired to share the work
cards.answer: More of them lost their jobs. Crépon and Kramarz compared them with similar workers already on 36 to 39 hours, whom the law left alone. Same monthly pay for fewer hours raised their hourly cost, above all near the minimum wage, and their job losses rose. The freed hour went to nobody.
cards.move: Before sharing out work, check what each share now costs.
cards.trap: Assuming fewer hours per worker spreads the same work over more people.
cards.reference: Crépon & Kramarz, Employed 40 Hours or Not Employed 39: Lessons from the 1982 Mandatory Reduction of the Workweek, Journal of Political Economy, 2002

cards.question: Kellogg's ran six-hour shifts at its Battle Creek cereal plant from 1930. Why did the six-hour day end?
cards.answer: Partly because workers voted it out. W.K. Kellogg moved to four six-hour shifts in 1930 to spread jobs through the Depression. After the Second World War, department after department chose eight hours and the extra pay, men leading the switch, with management pressing too. The last six-hour holdouts, mostly women, lost it in 1985.
cards.move: Shorter hours last only while people keep choosing them over pay.
cards.reference: Hunnicutt, Kellogg's Six-Hour Day, Temple University Press, 1996

cards.question: Countries with shorter working hours tend to produce more per hour worked. What mainly explains the link?
options: Short hours make each hour more productive
Long hours in poor countries are miscounted
Capital and technology raise both pay and leisure
cards.answer: Capital and technology, which raise pay and let people buy leisure. Bick, Fuchs-Schündeln and Lagakos found adults in poor countries work substantially more hours than those in rich ones. Tired workers do lose some output per hour, but machines, skills and methods drive the gap. Short weeks are how prosperity is spent, not made.
cards.move: When two good things travel together, look for what feeds both.
cards.trap: Reading the link as short hours causing high output per hour.
cards.reference: Bick, Fuchs-Schündeln & Lagakos, How Do Hours Worked Vary with Income? Cross-Country Evidence and Implications, American Economic Review, 2018

cards.question: Belgian workers won a legal right to request a four-day week in 2022. How many fewer hours does it give them?
cards.answer: None. The 2022 law lets a full-time employee ask to fit the same 38 hours into four longer days of up to 9.5 hours, and the employer may refuse with written reasons. It changes the shape of the week, not its length. The long weekend is paid for with four long days.
cards.move: Ask whether a reform shortens the work or only rearranges it.
cards.reference: Loi portant des dispositions diverses relatives au travail (Labour Deal), 3 October 2022, Moniteur belge, 2022

cards.question: Why did Britain's Supreme Court rule Uber drivers were workers but Deliveroo riders were not?
cards.answer: Because Deliveroo riders could send someone else. In 2021 the court found Uber controlled drivers' fares, terms and ratings, making them workers owed the minimum wage and holiday pay. In 2023 it found riders had a genuine right to pass a delivery to a substitute, so owed no personal service. One clause changed the category.
cards.move: Read the clause that decides the category, not the job it describes.
cards.source: UK Supreme Court, Uber and Deliveroo judgments
cards.reference: Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5; Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain v Central Arbitration Committee [2023] UKSC 43

cards.question: How were London's dockers hired in the 1880s?
cards.answer: At the dock gates, a few hours at a time. Foremen picked men from the crowd at each call-on, and a job could end after an hour. The great strike of 1889 won sixpence an hour, the docker's tanner, and a minimum engagement of four hours. Daily hiring at the call stands lasted until 1967.
cards.move: Most new ways of working have an old name; look it up.
cards.reference: Lovell, Stevedores and Dockers: A Study of Trade Unionism in the Port of London, 1870-1914, Macmillan, 1969

cards.question: Uber's pay formula ignores the driver's sex. Do male drivers in the United States still earn more per hour?
options: No, pay per hour is equal
cards.answer: Yes, about 7% more. Studying over a million US Uber drivers, Cook and colleagues traced the whole gap to three things: men had more experience on the app, drove in more lucrative places, and drove faster, fitting more trips into an hour. No discrimination was needed. A formula blind to sex still paid by speed.
cards.move: A rule that ignores a trait can still pay by what travels with it.
cards.trap: Assuming a formula that ignores sex must pay the sexes equally.
cards.source: Cook et al., Review of Economic Studies, 2021
cards.reference: doi:10.1093/restud/rdaa081

cards.question: True or false: in a typical week of 2017, about one US worker in ten did short jobs found through apps?
cards.answer: False. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted 1.6 million such workers in May 2017, about 1% of everyone employed. Counts over a whole year run several times higher, because many people do app work only now and then. Couriers are highly visible on city streets and small in the national payroll.
cards.move: Count the workers, not the adverts, before sizing a trend.
cards.trap: Judging the gig economy's size by how often its couriers pass by.
cards.reference: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Electronically mediated work: new questions in the Contingent Worker Supplement, Monthly Labor Review, September 2018

cards.question: Why is Amazon's platform for small online tasks named after an eighteenth-century chess machine?
cards.answer: Because that machine, the Mechanical Turk, hid a human chess player inside, and the platform does much the same: people do tasks sold as computation. Hara and colleagues tracked 2,676 of its workers and found median pay of about $2 an hour; only 4% earned over $7.25, partly because searching for tasks went unpaid.
cards.move: When software seems to think, ask whose hands are inside it.

cards.question: Prop 22 pays California drivers 120% of the $16.50 minimum for engaged time only. Excluding mileage, what is that per logged-in hour at 60% engagement?
cards.answer: $19.80 x 0.6 = $11.88 per logged-in hour.
cards.move: Before comparing a pay floor, ask which hours it counts.
cards.trap: Reading 120% of the minimum wage as pay for every hour online.
cards.hint: Waiting for a request counts as logged in but not as engaged.
steps: 120% of $16.50 = $19.80 per engaged hour.
Only 60% of logged-in time is engaged.
$19.80 x 0.6 = $11.88 per logged-in hour.
cards.reference: California Proposition 22, Protect App-Based Drivers and Services Act, Business and Professions Code sections 7448-7467, 2020

cards.question: Uber raised fares in some US cities, lifting drivers' pay per trip. Within a few months, what had happened to their hourly earnings?
options: Up roughly in line with fares
Down, as riders took fewer trips
cards.answer: Back near where they started. Hall, Horton and Knoepfle found that after fare rises drivers worked more hours while riders took fewer trips, so each driver waited longer. Within about two months hourly earnings were back at their old level. The better rate per trip went on idle time: emptier cars, not richer drivers.
cards.move: Where anyone can join, a better rate draws more people to share it.
cards.trap: Assuming a higher rate per trip means more pay per hour.
cards.reference: Hall, Horton & Knoepfle, Ride-Sharing Markets Re-Equilibrate, NBER Working Paper 30883, 2023

cards.question: True or false: most people in the US who start earning through online platforms are still doing so a year later?
cards.answer: False. Following millions of bank accounts, the JPMorgan Chase Institute found that more than half of those who began earning on platforms had stopped within twelve months. Surveys of current drivers or couriers hear only from those who stayed, often the ones for whom the work paid. The quitters give their verdict by being absent.
cards.move: Ask who left before trusting what those who stayed report.
cards.trap: Judging platform work by the people still on it, who liked it.
cards.reference: Farrell & Greig, Paychecks, Paydays, and the Online Platform Economy, JPMorgan Chase Institute, 2016

cards.question: Gig apps sell the freedom to choose your hours. In an experiment, how much pay would job seekers give up for it?
cards.answer: Almost nothing, on average. Mas and Pallais offered call-centre job applicants schedules at different wages. Most would pay little to set their own hours, yet the average applicant would forgo 20% of pay to avoid a schedule the employer could change at short notice. People pay to escape someone else's calendar, not to own one.
cards.move: Ask what people pay to avoid something, not only to get it.
cards.reference: Mas & Pallais, Valuing Alternative Work Arrangements, American Economic Review, 2017

cards.question: Should app couriers and drivers be classed as employees unless the platform proves otherwise?
cards.answer: The app sets the price, assigns the work, rates the worker and can switch them off: control in all but name. A presumption puts the burden of proof on the side holding the data. Spain's 2021 rider law did this for riders, and the EU's 2024 platform work directive requires every member state to follow.
cards.move: It turns on whether flexibility can survive inside an employment contract.
cards.counterpoint: Most platform workers log on for a few hours around other jobs and value choosing when; Chen and colleagues estimated Uber drivers gain more than twice the surplus they would on fixed schedules. Employment brings shifts and headcount caps. After Spain's rider law, Deliveroo left the country and other platforms moved riders to subcontracting fleets.
cards.source: Chen et al., Journal of Political Economy, 2019
cards.reference: Chen, Chevalier, Rossi & Oehlsen, The Value of Flexible Work: Evidence from Uber Drivers, Journal of Political Economy, 2019

cards.question: What does the share of its income a household spends on food reveal?
cards.answer: How poor it is. Ernst Engel found in 1857, from Belgian workers' budgets, that the share spent on food falls as income rises, though richer families spend more in money. In the United States today the poorest fifth of households spend around a third of their income on food, the richest under a tenth.
cards.move: Measure a burden as a share of what each person has.
cards.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Food Expenditure Series
cards.reference: USDA Economic Research Service, Food Expenditure Series: food spending as a share of income by quintile, 2024

cards.question: Of each dollar Americans spend on food, roughly how much reaches the farm?
cards.answer: About 15 cents. The US Department of Agriculture's food dollar series finds that the biggest slice goes to restaurants and food service, and most of the rest to processing, packaging, transport and retailing. So farm prices move shop prices less than expected: the wheat in a supermarket loaf is a small part of its price.
cards.move: Before blaming the raw material, price everything done to it afterwards.
cards.reference: Canning, A Revised and Expanded Food Dollar Series, USDA Economic Research Service, ERR-114, 2011

cards.question: True or false: Britain's official inflation figures treat a chocolate bar that shrinks but keeps its price as a price rise?
cards.answer: True. The Office for National Statistics tracks price per gram or millilitre, so a smaller pack at the same price registers as a rise. In 2017 it reported 2,529 products shrinking over five years, and 614 growing. A bar cut by a tenth at an unchanged price enters the index as an 11% rise.
cards.move: Before calling a change hidden, find out how it is counted.
cards.trap: Assuming statisticians record only the shelf price, so shrinking hides.
cards.reference: Office for National Statistics, Shrinkflation: how many of our products are getting smaller?, 2017

cards.question: Priced per portion rather than per calorie, how do vegetables compare with sweets and salty snacks?
cards.answer: Usually cheaper. Carlson and Frazão of the US Department of Agriculture priced foods three ways. Per calorie, vegetables and fruit look expensive, since they carry few calories. Per gram or per portion, they cost less than most meats and foods high in fat, sugar or salt. A carrot is cheap filling, dear fuel.
cards.move: Ask what a price is divided by before comparing two of them.
cards.trap: Recalling studies that ranked foods by price per calorie.
cards.reference: Carlson & Frazão, Are Healthy Foods Really More Expensive? It Depends on How You Measure the Price, USDA Economic Research Service, EIB-96, 2012

cards.question: Did company profits, more than rising costs, drive the food price surge of 2022 and 2023?
cards.answer: When every customer expects prices to rise, firms can raise theirs beyond their costs and blame the war. The European Central Bank found profits contributed more than wages to euro-area price growth in 2022, and grain traders, fertiliser makers and some manufacturers posted record earnings. The margin moved upstream, away from the checkout.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the answer depends on which link in the chain is measured.
cards.counterpoint: Britain's competition authority examined grocers in 2023 and found their margins had fallen, not risen, as energy, wages and wholesale prices climbed. UK food inflation peaked above 19% in March 2023 and eased as those costs fell back. Retail grocery margins are a few pence in the pound; there was little room to gouge.
cards.reference: Competition and Markets Authority, Competition and cost of living: the UK grocery sector, 2023

cards.question: When new supermarkets opened in America's food deserts, how much did local diets change?
cards.answer: Barely at all. Allcott, Diamond and Dubé tracked what households bought as supermarkets arrived: locals switched stores but bought much the same food. Families who moved to neighbourhoods with healthier shops kept their old habits too. Their model put only about 9% of the nutrition gap between rich and poor down to what shops offer.
cards.move: Before blaming the supply, check what people choose when it arrives.
cards.reference: Allcott, Diamond & Dubé, Food Deserts and the Causes of Nutritional Inequality, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019

cards.question: What did France do in 2019 to stop supermarkets using famous brands as loss leaders?
cards.answer: It banned selling food below cost plus 10%. Under the Egalim law, from February 2019 a retailer paying €1 for a product must charge at least €1.10, and promotions were capped at 34% off. Nutella and Coca-Cola, long sold near cost as bait, went up. Whether farmers, the intended winners, gained is disputed.
cards.move: A floor under one price shows up in someone else's basket.
cards.reference: https://agriculture.gouv.fr/egalim-comprendre-le-seuil-de-revente-perte-et-lencadrement-des-promotions

cards.question: Toilet paper is cheapest per roll in big packs and on promotion. Which American households use those savings least?
cards.answer: Low-income households. Orhun and Palazzolo followed the toilet paper bought by tens of thousands of American families over several years. The poorest bought small packs and missed sales, paying a few per cent more per sheet than bulk and sale buying would cost, even with cheaper brands. Bulk takes spare cash and cupboard space.
cards.move: A discount you need money to reach is not open to everyone.
cards.trap: Assuming the rich skip bargains because they can afford to.
cards.source: Orhun & Palazzolo, Journal of Marketing Research, 2019
cards.reference: Orhun & Palazzolo, Frugality Is Hard to Afford, Journal of Marketing Research, 2019

cards.question: True or false: big American supermarket chains mostly charge the same prices in rich and poor neighbourhoods?
cards.answer: True. DellaVigna and Gentzkow found chains set nearly identical prices across their stores, even where local incomes and competition differ widely, and that tailoring prices would raise profits by about 7%. Because poorer shoppers are more sensitive to price, one price leaves them paying more than local pricing would, and richer shoppers less.
cards.move: Check whether a price is set for the place or for the whole chain.
cards.trap: Picturing chains charging more wherever shoppers have fewer options.
cards.reference: DellaVigna & Gentzkow, Uniform Pricing in U.S. Retail Chains, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019

cards.question: Roughly how many pounds a year does a UK family of four spend on food and drink it then throws away?
cards.move: A small share of a weekly habit is a large sum over a year.
cards.trap: Picturing the odd mouldy leftover, not a fifth of the shopping.
cards.hint: Start from the weekly food shop, then ask what fraction goes in the bin.
steps: A family of four spends roughly £100 a week on food and drink at home.
Surveys suggest about a fifth of food bought is wasted.
cards.reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/media-centre/press-releases/urgent-action-needed-scale-tackle-food-waste-our-homes

cards.question: Why does very high inflation widen a government's budget deficit all by itself?
cards.answer: Because taxes arrive late. A tax assessed in March and paid in June loses value meanwhile: at 50% a month, prices more than triple in three months, so the payment buys under a third of what was due. Julio Olivera and Vito Tanzi described it. The state prints to fill the gap.
cards.move: When money is melting, whoever pays last pays least.
cards.reference: Tanzi, Inflation, Lags in Collection, and the Real Value of Tax Revenue, IMF Staff Papers, 1977

cards.question: What did German mortgage lenders get back after the 1923 hyperinflation had let borrowers repay in worthless marks?
cards.answer: Some of it, years later. After court battles and angry savers' campaigns, a revaluation law of 1925 restored many private mortgages to 25% of their gold value, reopening debts borrowers thought were settled. Holders of the government's war bonds were treated far worse. The state, the biggest debtor of all, largely kept its gain.
cards.move: After inflation, ask who writes the rules for settling old debts.
cards.reference: Feldman, The Great Disorder: Politics, Economics, and Society in the German Inflation, 1914-1924, Oxford University Press, 1993

cards.question: True or false: prices rose faster in Hungary in 1946 than in Zimbabwe in 2008?
cards.answer: True. At its peak in July 1946, Hungarian prices doubled about every 15 hours; Zimbabwe's worst month, November 2008, doubled them about every 25 hours. Hungary's pengő needed notes of 100 quintillion, the largest face value ever issued. It was replaced by the forint in August 1946 and is little remembered outside Hungary.
cards.move: The disaster you remember best is rarely the worst of its kind.
cards.trap: Picking Zimbabwe, whose trillion-dollar notes are recent and widely shown.
cards.reference: Hanke & Krus, World Hyperinflations, in Routledge Handbook of Major Events in Economic History, Routledge, 2013

cards.question: True or false: after Germany halted its hyperinflation in late 1923, the money in circulation kept growing fast?
cards.answer: True. Thomas Sargent showed that the central bank's money kept rising steeply for months after prices steadied. What changed was belief: the Reichsbank stopped lending to the government and the budget was cut, so people trusted the new money and wanted to hold it again. Cash that had been spent instantly now sat in wallets.
cards.move: A promise about tomorrow can matter more than the quantity today.
cards.trap: Assuming inflation stops only when the presses stop.
cards.source: Sargent, The Ends of Four Big Inflations, 1982
cards.reference: Sargent, The Ends of Four Big Inflations, in Hall (ed.), Inflation: Causes and Effects, University of Chicago Press, 1982

cards.question: Economists call it hyperinflation when prices rise 50% a month. How many times over do prices multiply in a year?
cards.answer: 25.63 x 5.06 = about 129.7 times.
cards.move: Growth rates multiply; adding them is the mistake that comes first.
cards.trap: Adding twelve 50% rises to get 600%, about seven times.
cards.hint: Each month multiplies prices by 1.5; square your way up.
steps: Two months: 1.5 x 1.5 = 2.25.
Four months: 2.25 x 2.25 = 5.06.
Eight months: 5.06 x 5.06 = 25.63.
25.63 x 5.06 = about 129.7 times.

diagram.caption: Adding twelve 50% rises gives ×7; compounding them gives ×130.

cards.reference: Cagan, The Monetary Dynamics of Hyperinflation, in Friedman (ed.), Studies in the Quantity Theory of Money, University of Chicago Press, 1956

cards.question: Why were there almost no hyperinflations before the twentieth century, despite centuries of clipped and debased coins?
cards.answer: Because metal cannot be diluted fast enough. Debasing coins pushed prices up over years, not weeks; prices doubling within a month needs paper that costs almost nothing to print. Peter Bernholz's catalogue finds one clear case before 1900, revolutionary France's assignats in 1795 and 1796. The rest arrived with paper money, total war and defeat.
cards.move: Ask how fast a thing can be made before fearing a flood of it.
cards.reference: Bernholz, Monetary Regimes and Inflation: History, Economic and Political Relationships, Edward Elgar, 2003

cards.question: What backed the Rentenmark, the currency that ended Germany's hyperinflation in November 1923?
cards.answer: Officially, a mortgage on German farmland and business property, which no noteholder could ever claim. The notes could not be exchanged for gold or for land. What held them up was a fixed ceiling on how many could be issued. One Rentenmark replaced a trillion paper marks, on a mortgage nobody could foreclose.
cards.move: A promise works when its limits are believed, whatever stands behind it.
cards.reference: Fergusson, When Money Dies: The Nightmare of the Weimar Collapse, William Kimber, 1975

cards.question: True or false: in a hyperinflation, prices rise faster than the quantity of money being printed?
cards.answer: True. As money loses value faster, people spend it the moment they receive it, so each note changes hands faster and the real value of all cash in circulation shrinks. Costantino Bresciani-Turroni documented it in Germany: by late 1923 people complained of a shortage of cash while the presses ran day and night.
cards.move: When people stop wanting to hold something, its price falls faster than its supply grows.
cards.trap: Assuming prices can only rise as fast as money is printed.
cards.reference: Bresciani-Turroni, The Economics of Inflation: A Study of Currency Depreciation in Post-War Germany, Allen & Unwin, 1937

cards.question: As a government prints money ever faster, what happens to the real resources it gains from printing?
options: They keep rising with the printing
cards.answer: They rise, peak, then fall. Printing taxes money holders: the take is inflation times the real cash people hold. Faster inflation makes people hold less, so past some rate the base shrinks faster than the rate rises. Cagan found governments in hyperinflation printing well beyond that peak, getting less for more.
cards.move: A tax that shrinks what it taxes has a ceiling on what it raises.
cards.trap: Assuming more printing always buys the state more.
cards.reference: Bailey, The Welfare Cost of Inflationary Finance, Journal of Political Economy, 1956

cards.question: Should a country stuck in hyperinflation give up its own currency and adopt the US dollar?
cards.answer: A government that has destroyed its money has no credibility left to rebuild it. Adopting the dollar ends inflation because no one can print it locally. Ecuador switched in 2000, as inflation headed towards 100%, and was in single digits within three years. Zimbabwe's price explosion stopped within weeks of dollars being allowed in 2009.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether credibility can be rebuilt at home.
cards.counterpoint: A dollarised country gives up the power to lend in a panic, cut rates or let its currency fall in a slump. Ecuador could not devalue when oil prices crashed in 2015. Zimbabwe ran short of dollars and relaunched its own currency in 2019, which then inflated again. Stability that cannot bend breaks in the next shock.
cards.reference: Edwards & Magendzo, Dollarization and Economic Performance: What Do We Really Know?, International Journal of Finance and Economics, 2003

cards.question: Why was the customary interest on Babylonian silver loans exactly 20% a year?
cards.answer: Because of the arithmetic of their units. The standard charge was one shekel per mina per month, and a mina held 60 shekels: 1/60 a month, 12/60 a year. Barley loans ran at a third. The same 20% recurs in law codes and contracts for centuries: money priced by a counting system.
cards.move: Before explaining a number, check whether the counting system chose it.
cards.source: Homer and Sylla, A History of Interest Rates
cards.reference: Homer & Sylla, A History of Interest Rates, 4th edition, Wiley, 2005

cards.question: Why are so many American credit cards issued by banks based in South Dakota or Delaware?
cards.answer: Because of a 1978 Supreme Court ruling. In Marquette v. First of Omaha, the Court let a nationally chartered bank charge customers anywhere the interest its home state allowed. South Dakota scrapped its rate cap in 1980, Citibank moved its card business to Sioux Falls, and Delaware followed. The loosest state's rules became the country's.
cards.move: When a rule can be exported, the loosest version wins.
cards.source: US Supreme Court, Marquette v. First of Omaha
cards.reference: Marquette National Bank of Minneapolis v. First of Omaha Service Corp., 439 U.S. 299 (1978)

cards.question: How could a Danish bank offer home loans at a negative interest rate in 2019?
cards.answer: Because each Danish mortgage is funded by a matching bond sold to investors, a system running since 1797. In 2019 investors were paying to hold safe Danish bonds, so Jyske Bank could offer a ten-year fixed loan at minus 0.5%. Before fees, the debt shrank each month by more than the homeowner paid.
cards.move: Every loan rate is someone's return; ask who is accepting it.
cards.reference: The Guardian, Danish bank launches world's first negative interest rate mortgage, 13 August 2019

cards.question: A car loan charges a 'flat' 5% a year on the full sum for three years, repaid monthly. Roughly what is the true annual rate?
cards.answer: Nearly 10%. A flat rate charges interest on the full sum all term, but repayments shrink the debt; on average only about half is owed. Interest of 15% of the loan over three years is about 9.3% a year on the real balance, 9.7% as an APR. An APR exists to show that gap.
cards.move: Ask what balance a rate is charged on, not just the rate.
cards.trap: Taking the quoted 5% at face value, as if the debt never shrank.
cards.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1974, section 20: total charge for credit

cards.question: Britain caps payday charges at 0.8% of the loan a day and 100% in total. After how many days does the total cap bite?
cards.move: Divide the limit by the rate to find when the limit arrives.
cards.trap: Assuming a daily charge this small could never double a debt.
cards.hint: Ask how many daily slices of 0.8% fit into 100%.
steps: The total cap is 100% of the sum borrowed.
Each day adds at most 0.8% of that sum.
cards.source: FCA, high-cost short-term credit price cap, 2015
cards.reference: Financial Conduct Authority, PS14/16: Detailed rules for the price cap on high-cost short-term credit, 2014

cards.question: A 40-year bond paying 0.5% a year was bought at par. If market rates rise to 4.5%, roughly how much of its price is lost?
cards.answer: About three-quarters. Money compounding at 4.5% grows almost sixfold in 40 years, so £100 due then is worth about £17 today. The tiny coupons add about £9. The price falls from £100 to roughly £26. Britain's 0.5% gilt due 2061, sold near £97 in 2020, traded near £22 in 2026.
cards.move: The longer the wait for money, the harder a rate change reprices it.
cards.trap: Guessing a tenth, as if four points of rate cost four percent.

diagram.caption: Market rates rise from 0.5% to 4.5%, and the £100 bond falls to about £26.

cards.source: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
cards.reference: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 10th edition, Pearson, 2018

cards.question: True or false: on one long reconstruction, real interest rates have been drifting down for about 700 years, not just since the 1980s?
cards.answer: True. Paul Schmelzing's Bank of England working paper rebuilt real rates back to 1311 and found a yearly decline of roughly 0.6 to 1.6 basis points, hundredths of a percentage point, through wars and plagues. The fall since the 1980s sits near that old trend line: the latest stretch of a very long slope.
cards.move: Before calling a trend new, look further back than your own lifetime.
cards.trap: Treating the fall since the 1980s as new because it is recent.
cards.reference: Schmelzing, Eight centuries of global real interest rates, R-G, and the 'suprasecular' decline, 1311-2018, Bank of England Staff Working Paper No. 845, 2020

cards.question: How do sharia-compliant home finance plans charge for the time value of money without charging interest?
cards.answer: Largely by copying interest. In one common British form, the bank buys the home and the customer pays rent while buying out the bank's share, and that rent usually follows market interest rates. Mahmoud El-Gamal calls this sharia arbitrage: the economics of a loan in a permitted legal form, often at extra cost.
cards.move: When a rule bans a price, look for it under another name.
cards.reference: El-Gamal, Islamic Finance: Law, Economics, and Practice, Cambridge University Press, 2006

cards.question: A $200,000 30-year mortgage at 6% costs $1,199 a month. What percentage of the first payment is interest?
cards.move: Early payments on a long loan mostly pay rent on the money.
cards.trap: Assuming each payment splits roughly evenly between interest and debt.
cards.hint: Each month's interest is charged on the whole balance still owed.
steps: Monthly rate: 6% / 12 = 0.5%.
First month's interest: $200,000 x 0.005 = $1,000.
cards.reference: Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, 13th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2020

cards.question: In the 2010s, how far below zero did any major central bank push its main policy rate?
cards.answer: About −0.75%. Switzerland's central bank held that rate from 2015 to 2022 and Denmark's matched it for a year; nobody went deeper. What stops them is cash: notes pay zero, so beyond some point storing paper beats paying to keep a deposit. The floor under interest rates is a vault full of banknotes.
cards.move: Find the cheapest way out before believing a price can go anywhere.
cards.trap: Picking −0.1%, as if negative rates were only a gesture.
cards.reference: Swiss National Bank, Monetary policy assessment and press release of 15 January 2015, 2015

cards.question: Germany brought in its first national minimum wage, €8.50 an hour, in 2015. What happened to the low-paid?
options: Pay rose; many moved to bigger firms
Pay barely rose; firms found loopholes
cards.answer: Pay rose; many moved to bigger firms. Dustmann and colleagues found the minimum raised low wages without cutting overall employment, as low-paid workers shifted from small firms to larger, more productive ones, which explains part of their wage gain. Other studies found losses in mini-jobs, part-time posts paying a few hundred euros a month.
cards.move: Count where people move, not just who loses the old place.
cards.trap: Expecting a wage floor to price the low-paid out of work.
cards.source: Dustmann et al., Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2022
cards.reference: doi:10.1093/qje/qjab028

cards.question: True or false: Sweden has no minimum wage set by law?
cards.answer: True. Sweden, like Denmark, leaves wage floors to collective agreements between unions and employers, and around nine workers in ten are covered by one. The floors differ by trade and are high by European standards. A Swedish shop assistant's lowest rate of pay is written in a union contract, not in a statute.
cards.move: A missing law is not a missing rule; look for who else sets it.
cards.trap: Assuming a high-wage welfare state must fix its minimum by law.
cards.reference: Eurofound, Minimum wages in 2024: Annual review, 2024

cards.question: How did Australia's 1907 Harvester judgment decide what a fair wage for a labourer was?
cards.answer: From a household budget, not from what the employer could afford. Justice Higgins asked what an unskilled worker needed to live as a human being in a civilised community, costing rent, food and fuel for a family of about five, and set seven shillings a day. That became Australia's basic wage, which lasted until 1967.
cards.move: A fair price is always someone's budget; ask whose.
cards.source: Ex parte H.V. McKay, Commonwealth Arbitration Court, 1907
cards.reference: Ex parte H.V. McKay (1907) 2 CAR 1, the Harvester judgment, Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration

cards.question: Under US federal law, what is the lowest hourly cash wage an employer may pay a waiter?
cards.answer: $2.13, as long as tips make up the rest. Congress created this tipped minimum in 1966, and it has not risen since 1991, longer than the $7.25 frozen since 2009. The employer tops up only when tips fall short. In most states, part of a diner's tip pays the legal minimum.
cards.move: Ask who really pays a wage before crediting who signs the cheque.
cards.reference: Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, section 3(m)(2)(A), as amended in 1966 and 1996

cards.question: Should young workers be allowed a lower minimum wage than adults?
cards.answer: Young workers bring the least experience and need the most training, so pricing them like adults shuts them out. When Denmark's agreed youth rates end at 18, hourly pay jumps 40% and employment falls by a third. A first job is worth more than its wage: it buys experience that raises every later one.
cards.move: It turns on whether a first job's experience is worth more than its pay.
cards.counterpoint: Paying someone less for the same work because of a birthday is age discrimination with a policy label. On the Danish study's own figures, 40% more pay for two-thirds as many workers leaves young people's total earnings only slightly lower. Youth rates also build a cliff where cheap workers become expensive overnight.

cards.question: After 138 US state minimum wage rises, jobs paying below each new minimum vanished. What happened to the total number of low-wage jobs?
options: It fell by about as many
cards.answer: It stayed roughly the same. Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer counted jobs by wage band against states without rises: over five years, the jobs lost below each new minimum were matched by extra jobs at or just above it. Most of the missing jobs had not gone; their pay had crossed the line.
cards.move: Before counting what vanished below a line, count what appeared above it.
cards.trap: Counting the vanished low-paid jobs as losses without looking just above.
cards.reference: Cengiz, Dube, Lindner & Zipperer, The Effect of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Jobs, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019

cards.question: How is Britain's National Living Wage now pinned down, and what makes it unusual among rich countries?
cards.answer: By a target tied to typical pay. The government told the Low Pay Commission to raise it to two-thirds of median hourly earnings by 2024, and it got there, one of the OECD's highest ratios. The remit since has been to hold that ratio, so the floor moves with ordinary pay.
cards.move: A floor measured against the middle rises whenever the middle does.
cards.reference: Low Pay Commission, National Minimum Wage: Low Pay Commission Report 2024, 2025

cards.question: What happened after Congress set American Samoa on a path to the US federal minimum wage in 2007?
cards.answer: Congress had to back off. The law raised Samoa's minimum 50 cents a year towards the mainland rate, in an economy where typical pay was far lower. Tuna canneries, the main private employers, cut jobs; one closed in 2009 with about 2,000 lost, and later laws delayed the rises. Same wage, different median, different bite.
cards.move: Judge a wage floor against local pay, not against another place's.
cards.source: US GAO, American Samoa minimum wage
cards.reference: US Government Accountability Office, American Samoa and Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands: Employment, Earnings, and Status of Key Industries Since Minimum Wage Increases Began, GAO-11-427, 2011

cards.question: The US federal minimum of $7.25 took effect in July 2009; prices have since risen about 50%. Its worth in 2009 dollars?
cards.answer: $7.25 / 1.50 = about $4.83 in 2009 dollars.
cards.move: Deflate by dividing, never by subtracting the percentage.
cards.trap: Taking 50% off $7.25 and getting $3.63.
cards.hint: Ask what $1.50 today buys in 2009 goods.
steps: Prices up about 50%: what cost $1.00 in 2009 now costs $1.50.
Real value = today's wage divided by 1.50.
$7.25 / 1.50 = about $4.83 in 2009 dollars.
cards.reference: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), 2025

cards.question: True or false: more than one US hourly worker in ten is paid the federal minimum of $7.25 or less?
cards.answer: False. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 1% of hourly-paid workers at or below $7.25 in 2023, fewer than a million people, many of them in tipped jobs. Thirty states and Washington DC set higher minimums, and employers elsewhere often pay above it. The federal figure is a headline more than a wage.
cards.move: A number often quoted is not necessarily a number often paid.
cards.trap: Assuming the famous federal figure is what many people earn.
cards.source: BLS, Characteristics of Minimum Wage Workers
cards.reference: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Characteristics of minimum wage workers, 2023, BLS Reports, 2024

cards.question: True or false: more $100 notes than $1 notes are in circulation in the United States?
cards.answer: True. By Federal Reserve counts, $100 notes overtook $1 notes in 2017, and by the end of 2022 about 18.5 billion hundreds were out. Small notes change hands; hundreds sit still, as savings at home and dollars held abroad. The $1 is the note people see; the $100 is the note they keep.
cards.move: What passes through your hands is a sample of what moves, not what exists.
cards.trap: Judging the stock of notes by the ones that pass through hands.
cards.source: Federal Reserve Board, currency in circulation data
cards.reference: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Currency in Circulation: Volume, 2024

cards.question: What is the largest-value banknote the Bank of England prints, and what is it for?
cards.answer: The £100 million 'titan', alongside the £1 million 'giant'. Neither circulates. Banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland may issue their own notes, but each must be fully backed by assets held at the Bank of England, and these notes let that backing sit compactly in its vaults. One titan stands behind ten million Scottish tenners.
cards.move: When anyone may print money, ask what they must lock away first.
cards.source: Bank of England, Scottish and Northern Ireland banknotes
cards.reference: Bank of England, Scottish and Northern Ireland banknotes: backing assets, giants and titans, 2024

cards.question: Of the money households and firms hold in Britain, roughly what share is notes and coins?
cards.answer: About 3%. The rest is bank deposits, and most deposits are created when banks lend: a new loan credits the borrower's account with money that did not exist before. The Bank of England set this out plainly in 2014. The notes in a wallet are the small change of a system kept in ledgers.
cards.move: The money you can touch is the smallest part of the money there is.
cards.trap: A third feels right because cash is the money people can see.
cards.source: McLeay, Radia & Thomas, Bank of England, 2014
cards.reference: McLeay, Radia & Thomas, Money creation in the modern economy, Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 2014 Q1

cards.question: When the Bank of England's quantitative easing loses money, who pays?
cards.answer: The Treasury, meaning taxpayers. QE paid for £875 billion of gilts with newly created reserves, on which the Bank pays Bank Rate. A 2009 indemnity gives the Treasury both profits and losses. Near-zero rates made QE a money-spinner for years; in 2022 Bank Rate overtook the gilts' interest and the payments reversed.
cards.move: Borrowing that floats with rates is cheap only until rates move.
cards.source: OBR, Economic and fiscal outlook, November 2022
cards.reference: Office for Budget Responsibility, Economic and fiscal outlook, November 2022

cards.question: In fiscal 2024 the US Mint shipped about 3.17 billion one-cent coins at 3.69 cents each. What was the loss, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: 8.5273 billion cents = $85.27 million.
cards.move: A tiny loss per unit is only tiny until you multiply by volume.
cards.trap: Counting the whole 3.69 cents as the loss, not the 2.69.
cards.hint: Work out the loss on a single coin first, then multiply by the number made.
steps: Each coin costs 3.69 - 1 = 2.69 cents more than it is worth.
3.17 billion x 2.69 cents = 8.5273 billion cents.
8.5273 billion cents = $85.27 million.
cards.reference: United States Mint, Annual Report 2024

cards.question: When the US Federal Reserve began losing money in 2022, where did the losses go?
cards.answer: Into a 'deferred asset', in effect an IOU to itself. The Fed pays interest on banks' reserves; once that bill exceeded its bond income, it stopped sending profits to the Treasury and booked the shortfall against future profits. The balance passed $200 billion by 2025. The Treasury is paid again only after it is cleared.
cards.move: Ask where a loss is recorded before deciding who bears it.
cards.reference: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Factors Affecting Reserve Balances (H.4.1), weekly statistical release, 2025

cards.question: True or false: US law lets the Treasury mint a platinum coin of any face value, even a trillion dollars?
cards.answer: True. A 1996 provision meant for collectors' bullion coins lets the Treasury Secretary set the denomination of platinum coins, and it names no limit. In the 2013 debt-ceiling fight it was proposed as a way round Congress; the Treasury and the Fed declined. A law written for collectors set no ceiling.
cards.move: Read what a law says, not only what it was meant for.
cards.trap: Assuming only the central bank, never the Treasury, can create money.
cards.reference: United States Code, Title 31, section 5112(k), as added by Public Law 104-208, 1996

cards.question: About £80 billion of Bank of England notes circulate, backed by interest-earning assets. At 5%, what does the Bank earn yearly, in £ billion?
cards.answer: £80 billion x 0.05 = £4 billion a year.
cards.move: Money that pays its holder nothing pays its issuer something.
cards.trap: Counting only face value minus printing cost as the issuer's gain.
cards.hint: A banknote is a loan to the Bank that pays its lender no interest.
steps: Notes in circulation pay their holders nothing.
The assets bought with them earn about 5% a year.
£80 billion x 0.05 = £4 billion a year.
cards.reference: Bank of England, Annual Report and Accounts, 1 March 2023 to 29 February 2024, Issue Department accounts, 2024

cards.question: From 2008 to 2014 the Federal Reserve roughly quadrupled base money, the reserves and cash it issues. How much did broad money grow?
cards.answer: By about half. Base money went from under $1 trillion to about $4 trillion, but the new reserves mostly sat at the Fed, earning interest there. Broad money, mainly bank deposits, rose from about $7.7 trillion to $11.5 trillion, near its usual pace. Four times the base, half as much again in money.
cards.move: Money created is not money spent until someone borrows it.
cards.trap: Applying the textbook multiplier, so money grows in step with reserves.
cards.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
cards.reference: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, FRED series BOGMBASE and M2SL, 2025

cards.question: Should central banks be allowed to pay for transfers straight to households when a slump is deep?
cards.answer: With rates at zero, bond buying mostly lifts asset prices, which helps people who own assets. A one-off transfer paid with newly created money reaches spending directly and adds no public debt. Adair Turner argues that, used rarely and under strict rules, it is less dangerous than letting demand and prices sink for years.
cards.move: It turns on whether a rule can hold once the first exception is made.
cards.counterpoint: The danger is not the first transfer but the second. Once governments learn the central bank will pay for handouts, every downturn and every election brings pressure for more, and independence ends quietly. The transfers of 2020 and 2021, largely matched by central bank bond buying, were followed by the fastest inflation in forty years.
cards.source: Turner, Between Debt and the Devil, 2015
cards.reference: Turner, Between Debt and the Devil: Money, Credit, and Fixing Global Finance, Princeton University Press, 2015

cards.question: Where does the rule that rent should take no more than 30% of income come from?
cards.answer: From American public housing law. The Brooke Amendment of 1969 capped public tenants' rent at 25% of income, and Congress raised it to 30% in 1981 to save money. A subsidy formula for the poorest became a yardstick for everyone. But 30% of a high income leaves plenty; of a low one, little.
cards.move: Before obeying a rule of thumb, find out whom it was written for.
cards.source: Housing and Urban Development Act of 1969
cards.reference: Housing and Urban Development Act of 1969, Public Law 91-152, section 213 (Brooke Amendment), 1969

cards.question: What happened to Berlin tenants who paid less under the city's 2020 rent freeze?
cards.answer: Many had to pay the difference back. Berlin froze most rents at their 2019 level and ordered cuts to the highest. In 2021 the Federal Constitutional Court struck the law down: rent was already regulated by federal law, so a state could not legislate on it. The savings became debts, owed to the landlords.
cards.move: A rule that may not survive court is a loan, not a gift.
cards.reference: Bundesverfassungsgericht, Beschluss des Zweiten Senats, 2 BvF 1/20, 25 March 2021

cards.question: Is rent high because landlords' costs are high, or are their costs high because rent is?
cards.answer: Mostly the second. David Ricardo argued in 1817 that corn is not dear because landlords take rent; rent is paid because corn is dear. Rents follow what tenants can pay for a scarce place, and property prices rise to match. A landlord with no mortgage charges the same as one with a huge one.
cards.move: Ask what the buyer can pay before blaming the seller's costs.
cards.reference: Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ed. Sraffa, Cambridge University Press, 1951

cards.question: In 1994 San Francisco extended rent control to small older blocks. What happened to the rental housing in them?
options: It grew by about a tenth
cards.answer: It shrank by about 15%. Comparing covered buildings with similar ones built just after the 1980 cut-off, Diamond, McQuade and Qian found landlords sold flats off as condominiums or rebuilt. Covered tenants stayed longer, but the lost supply raised rents citywide by about 5%, paid by the next arrivals.
cards.move: Judge a protection by the people who arrive after it, too.
cards.trap: Assuming buildings cannot leave the rental market, so supply stays put.
cards.reference: Diamond, McQuade & Qian, The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco, American Economic Review, 2019

cards.question: In 2014, which started building the most new homes: Tokyo, all of England, or California?
cards.answer: Tokyo, with about 142,000 housing starts, against about 137,000 in England and 84,000 in California. Japan's zoning is set nationally, and most building that fits the zone needs no local approval. Tokyo's rents stayed broadly flat for years while London's and San Francisco's climbed. A city a quarter England's size outbuilt it.
cards.move: Where prices rise, ask first who is allowed to build.
cards.trap: Picking England, which has about four times Tokyo's population.
cards.reference: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (Japan), Housing Starts Statistics, 2014

cards.question: What pushed Britain into controlling rents in 1915, in the middle of a world war?
cards.answer: A rent strike in Glasgow. As munitions workers crowded in, landlords raised rents; by late 1915 around 20,000 tenants refused to pay the increases, led largely by women such as Mary Barbour. With shipyard output at stake, Parliament froze rents at pre-war levels within weeks. Some form of rent control lasted over seventy years.
cards.move: Emergency rules outlive emergencies when enough people come to depend on them.
cards.reference: Increase of Rent and Mortgage Interest (War Restrictions) Act 1915, 5 & 6 Geo. 5, UK Parliament, 1915

cards.question: True or false: large new market-rate apartment blocks in poor neighbourhoods tend to push up rents in nearby buildings?
cards.answer: False. Asquith, Mast and Reed studied large new buildings in low-income areas of American cities and found nearby rents fell by about 6% against those slightly farther away. The new flats absorbed demand that would have bid up the old. Developers build where rents are already climbing, which is why the two look linked.
cards.move: Check whether the thing blamed simply goes where the trouble already is.
cards.trap: Seeing cranes arrive where rents rise and reading it as cause.
cards.reference: Asquith, Mast & Reed, Local Effects of Large New Apartment Buildings in Low-Income Areas, Review of Economics and Statistics, 2023

cards.question: In the 1990s France extended housing benefit to many more renters. Of each extra euro of benefit, how much went into higher rents?
cards.answer: Most of it. Gabrielle Fack estimated that between 50 and 80 cents of each extra euro ended up as higher rent for low-income tenants. Flats barely grew in number while the reform drew students into renting alone. A subsidy to buyers in a market that cannot expand ends up with the sellers.
cards.move: Before subsidising buyers, ask whether sellers can make any more.
cards.trap: Assuming the benefit stays with the tenant it is paid to.
cards.reference: Fack, Are housing benefit an effective way to redistribute income? Evidence from a natural experiment in France, Labour Economics, 2006

cards.question: In 2023 American rents on new leases had stopped rising, yet official rent inflation stayed high. Why?
options: The official index covers all sitting tenants
Rent controls were lifted in big cities
Owners' housing costs were counted twice
cards.answer: The official index covers all sitting tenants. Most leases run a year, so the average rent paid moves only as leases come up for renewal. Adams and colleagues, government and Federal Reserve economists, found new-tenant rent inflation leads the official measure by about four quarters. The official figure was reporting last year's market.
cards.move: Ask when the people in a statistic last had a chance to change.
cards.trap: Suspecting a flaw in the arithmetic rather than in the timing.
cards.reference: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faeri.20220685

cards.question: Should landlords be allowed to end a tenancy without giving any reason?
cards.answer: A landlord who cannot recover a home without proving a legal ground in court will screen tenants harder, price the risk into rents, or sell up. Court backlogs make eviction slow even for unpaid rent. Fewer landlords means fewer homes to let, and the tenants turned away are the ones with thin references.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is how fast courts handle the fair cases.
cards.counterpoint: Without a reason required, a tenant who asks for repairs can simply be removed, so many never ask. In England the end of a private tenancy has long been one of the commonest triggers of homelessness. Scotland ended no-fault eviction in 2017 and England followed from 1 May 2026, keeping grounds for arrears, sale and moving in.
cards.reference: Renters' Rights Act 2025, Acts of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, 2025

cards.question: Who named the Silk Road, and what was that person looking for in China?
cards.answer: A German geologist, Ferdinand von Richthofen, in 1877, and he was looking for coal. His travels from 1868 began as a survey of coal reserves for the Bank of California. His volumes pointed Germany to Shandong's coalfields, and in 1897 it seized the harbour at Qingdao. The romantic name came wrapped in a mining report.
cards.move: Ask what the person who named a thing wanted from it.
cards.reference: Wu, Empires of Coal: Fueling China's Entry into the Modern World Order, 1860-1920, Stanford University Press, 2015

cards.question: Under the Tang dynasty, what kept the oasis towns of the Silk Road busy?
cards.answer: The army's payroll. The Tang state shipped huge quantities of silk bolts to its garrisons in the northwest, because cloth was lighter than coin, and soldiers spent it locally. When rebellion in 755 pulled the troops back east, the money stopped and the oasis economies shrank. The trade followed the paymaster.
cards.move: Before crediting the merchants, find out who was paying the customers.
cards.reference: https://etc.worldhistory.org/interviews/trading-cultures-along-the-ancient-silk-road-an-interview-with-professor-valerie-hansen/

cards.question: True or false: most Silk Road goods were carried by merchants travelling the whole way between China and the Mediterranean?
cards.answer: False. Goods moved in relays: most traders worked a stretch of a few hundred kilometres between oases, and wares changed hands many times. Documents from Niya and Turfan show mostly small, local exchanges, often by barter. A bolt of silk reaching Syria had crossed Asia without any one trader carrying it all the way.
cards.move: A route on a map says nothing about who walked all of it.
cards.trap: Picturing a single caravan, the image every map and travel tale gives.
cards.reference: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History, Oxford University Press, 2012

cards.question: Why have so many ordinary Tang-era contracts and official papers from the Turfan oasis survived?
options: They were archived in Buddhist monasteries
They were copied onto stone tablets
They were cut into clothes for the dead
cards.answer: Scrap paper was cut into clothes for the dead. Discarded government documents and contracts were sold on and made into paper shoes, belts and hats for burials, and the dry desert kept them. Archaeologists piece the texts back together from the garments. A seventh-century town's paperwork survives because someone needed cheap funeral clothes.
cards.move: Ask why a record survived before trusting what it seems to show.
cards.trap: Assuming what survives was kept on purpose because it mattered.
cards.source: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History
cards.reference: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History, Oxford University Press, 2012

cards.question: Is China's Belt and Road lending, sold as a new Silk Road, a debt trap for poorer countries?
cards.answer: The loans come with hidden strings. AidData's study of 13,427 Chinese-financed projects found about $385 billion of debt kept off governments' books, often secured on export revenues, with confidentiality clauses. A borrower that cannot see its own obligations cannot bargain. Sri Lanka's port at Hambantota ended on a 99-year Chinese lease.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, what happens when a loan goes bad decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Hambantota was a Sri Lankan project, and the lease raised cash that shored up reserves and paid other debts. Researchers such as Deborah Brautigam report no case of China seizing an asset over a default; it has usually rescheduled or written loans down. Bad lending is not a plot.
cards.source: AidData, Banking on the Belt and Road, 2021
cards.reference: https://www.aiddata.org/publications/banking-on-the-belt-and-road

cards.question: What do undelivered letters found in a watchtower near Dunhuang reveal about who ran early Silk Road trade?
cards.answer: A diaspora of Sogdians, merchants from the region of Samarkand, with agents settled in Chinese cities. Their mailbag, written around 313 and found by Aurel Stein in 1907, reports the sack of Luoyang in 311 and the death of the Sogdians living there. Another letter is from a wife stranded in Dunhuang by her husband.
cards.move: Look for the network behind a trade, not the travellers on it.
cards.reference: de la Vaissière, Sogdian Traders: A History, trans. Ward, Brill, 2005

cards.question: What did a Florentine merchant's handbook of about 1340 warn would happen to silver taken to China?
cards.answer: That the ruler's officials would take it and hand over paper money instead, which merchants then used to buy silk and everything else. Francesco Pegolotti's Pratica della mercatura also costed the route from Tana, on the Sea of Azov, stage by stage. Europe printed its own first banknotes in Stockholm in 1661.
cards.move: A trade route also carries ideas about what money can be.
cards.source: Pegolotti, La Pratica della Mercatura, c. 1340
cards.reference: Pegolotti, La Pratica della Mercatura, ed. Allan Evans, Medieval Academy of America, 1936

cards.question: By weight, what was the main Chinese export on ships sailing to the Persian Gulf in the ninth century?
cards.answer: Ceramics. Silk was valuable but light; bowls and jars were cheap, heavy and could be packed by the thousand. The Belitung wreck, a sewn-plank ship from the Arabian Sea lost off Indonesia around 830, held about 60,000 ceramic pieces, mostly Changsha bowls, some painted with Arabic-style script. The sea road ran on pottery.
cards.move: A famous name tells you what was prized, not what was carried.
cards.trap: The route's name makes silk seem the bulk of it.
cards.reference: Krahl, Guy, Wilson & Raby (eds.), Shipwrecked: Tang Treasures and Monsoon Winds, Smithsonian Institution, 2010

cards.question: Pliny wrote that Indian goods sold in Rome at a hundred times their cost. If each middleman doubled the price, at least how many middlemen?
cards.answer: A seventh: 64 x 2 = 128, so 7 middlemen are enough.
cards.move: A few ordinary markups in a row multiply into an extraordinary one.
cards.trap: Dividing 100 by 2 and picturing about fifty middlemen.
cards.hint: Keep doubling from 1 until you pass 100.
steps: Each middleman multiplies the price by 2.
Six in a row: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64, short of 100.
A seventh: 64 x 2 = 128, so 7 middlemen are enough.
cards.source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 6
cards.reference: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 6, trans. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1942

cards.question: Under the early Han dynasty, much of the silk that reached Central Asian markets first left China how?
options: As state gifts to nomad rulers
cards.answer: As state gifts to nomad rulers. Under the heqin treaties from 198 BC, the Han court paid the Xiongnu, the steppe confederation to its north, yearly silk, grain and wine for peace, and the payments grew. Nomad elites traded the surplus westward. Money paid to keep raiders out stocked markets far beyond the frontier.
cards.move: Follow a good back to whoever handed it out, not whoever sold it.
cards.trap: Picturing the trade as Chinese merchants carrying silk out themselves.
cards.source: Yü Ying-shih, Trade and Expansion in Han China
cards.reference: Yü Ying-shih, Trade and Expansion in Han China: A Study in the Structure of Sino-Barbarian Economic Relations, University of California Press, 1967

cards.question: What became of America's 2024 federal rule that cancelling a subscription must be as easy as signing up?
cards.answer: A court threw it out days before it took full effect. In July 2025 the Eighth Circuit vacated the Federal Trade Commission's click-to-cancel rule, because the agency had skipped a preliminary economic analysis the law requires for rules costing over $100 million a year. The court never ruled on whether hard cancelling is fair.
cards.move: A rule can fall on its procedure without anyone judging its purpose.
cards.reference: Custom Communications, Inc. v. Federal Trade Commission, US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, 2025

cards.question: Why can one subscription to thousands of titles earn more than selling each title separately?
cards.answer: Because tastes average out. A buyer values single songs or articles very unevenly, so any price per item loses buyers or leaves money unclaimed. Summed over thousands of items, what each buyer will pay becomes predictable, and one price captures most of it. Bakos and Brynjolfsson showed this in 1999 for goods free to copy.
cards.move: Sell the average when individual tastes are too scattered to price.
cards.reference: Bakos & Brynjolfsson, Bundling Information Goods: Pricing, Profits, and Efficiency, Management Science, 1999

cards.question: A subscription service loses 5% of its remaining subscribers every month. What percentage of a January cohort is left after twelve months?
cards.move: Losses taken from what remains shrink as it shrinks, so never add them.
cards.trap: Subtracting twelve 5% losses from the start to get 40%.
cards.hint: Each month keeps 0.95 of the month before; square your way up.
steps: Eight months: 0.815 x 0.815 = 0.664.
cards.source: Fader and Hardie, J. Interactive Marketing, 2007
cards.reference: Fader & Hardie, How to Project Customer Retention, Journal of Interactive Marketing, 2007

cards.question: Gym members who chose a monthly fee of over $70 instead of $10-a-visit passes paid how much per visit?
cards.answer: About $17. DellaVigna and Malmendier followed thousands of members of three American gyms: those on monthly contracts came about four times a month and would have saved by paying per visit. Many kept paying for months after their last visit. People buy the member they plan to be, then pay for the one they are.
cards.move: Price a plan on your record, not on your intentions.
cards.trap: Assuming people who chose the flat fee must use it enough to gain.
cards.reference: DellaVigna & Malmendier, Paying Not to Go to the Gym, American Economic Review, 2006

cards.question: True or false: in Germany, consumer contracts signed since 2022 cannot roll over automatically for another full year?
cards.answer: True. Under the Fair Consumer Contracts Act, contracts made from March 2022 may still bind for two years at first, but then renew only open-ended, cancellable at a month's notice. Since July 2022, contracts sold online must also carry a cancellation button. A forgotten gym contract now costs one month, not twelve.
cards.move: When a cost comes from forgetting, the default decides who pays.
cards.trap: Assuming yearly rollovers are standard everywhere, as in many other countries.
cards.reference: Gesetz für faire Verbraucherverträge, Bundesgesetzblatt, 2021

cards.question: After America's click-to-cancel rule was struck down, how did regulators still make Amazon pay over Prime cancellations?
cards.answer: Under an older law. The Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act of 2010 already required clear terms and a simple way to stop recurring charges. The Federal Trade Commission sued in 2023; in September 2025, days into trial, Amazon settled for $2.5 billion, including $1.5 billion in refunds. Internally, the cancellation maze was nicknamed the Iliad.
cards.move: When a new rule falls, look for the old one that already covered it.
cards.reference: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/09/ftc-secures-historic-25-billion-settlement-against-amazon

cards.question: Each month, 4 in every 100 members cancel, however long they have belonged. What is the average length of a membership, in months?
cards.move: Halfway gone and gone on average are different moments; ask which is meant.
cards.trap: Giving the 17 months after which half have gone, not the average.
cards.hint: If the chance of leaving never changes, think of how long an average wait for a 1-in-25 event lasts.
steps: Each month a member has a 4 in 100, or 1 in 25, chance of leaving.
With a fixed chance each month, the average wait is 1 divided by that chance.
cards.reference: Gupta, Lehmann & Stuart, Valuing Customers, Journal of Marketing Research, 2004

cards.question: A newspaper offered 2.1 million readers a trial that renewed automatically or one that simply ended. Which left more subscribers two years later?
cards.answer: The trial that simply ended. Miller, Sahni and Strulov-Shlain found far more of those on auto-renewal kept paying straight after the trial than on the other offer. But readers wary of forgetting shunned it: sign-ups fell 24%, and two years on the paper had about 10% fewer subscribers. Readers saw the trap coming.
cards.move: Judge a tactic by everyone it reached, not only by those who said yes.
cards.trap: Judging auto-renewal only by the readers who accepted it.
cards.reference: Miller, Sahni & Strulov-Shlain, Sophisticated Consumers with Inertia: Long-Term Implications from a Large-Scale Field Experiment, Stanford GSB Working Paper, 2022

cards.question: True or false: since 2022, British insurers may not quote renewing home and car customers more than new ones?
cards.answer: True. From January 2022 the Financial Conduct Authority banned price walking, raising premiums year after year for customers who renew without shopping around. It had found about 6 million policyholders overpaying for their risk, by some £1.2 billion in 2018. A renewal quote may no longer exceed the price offered to an identical newcomer.
cards.move: Where a contract renews itself, check who is paying for staying.
cards.trap: Assuming firms may always charge loyal customers whatever they accept.
cards.reference: Financial Conduct Authority, General Insurance Pricing Practices: Policy Statement PS21/5, 2021

cards.question: Should carmakers be allowed to sell features already fitted to a car, such as heated seats, as monthly subscriptions?
cards.answer: One version of a car for everyone is cheaper than wiring dozens of variants, and charging only those who switch a feature on lets others pay less. A buyer who needs heated seats for one winter pays for one winter. Economists have shown that deliberately limited versions can leave every buyer better off.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether the car's base price really fell.
cards.counterpoint: The hardware is in the car, and its cost is already in the price every buyer pays. Charging monthly to switch it on charges twice for one part, and the second buyer of the car pays again. After a backlash, BMW stopped offering heated seats by subscription in 2023. Customers read locked hardware as confiscation.
cards.reference: Deneckere & McAfee, Damaged Goods, Journal of Economics and Management Strategy, 1996

cards.question: Should cities scrap rules requiring new buildings to include parking spaces?
cards.answer: A mandated parking space adds serious cost to every flat built, whether or not the resident owns a car — so renters without cars subsidise those with them. The requirement also forces buildings apart, which is what makes a district need a car in the first place.
cards.move: Both sides agree the cost is real. They disagree about who is currently paying it.
cards.counterpoint: Remove the minimum and the cars do not vanish; they park on streets that were not built for them, and the cost lands on everyone who lives there rather than on the developer. In places with weak public transport, a building with no parking is a building only car-free households can use.
cards.reference: Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking, Planners Press, 2005

cards.question: Should people be allowed to bet real money on election results?
cards.answer: A market makes people pay for being wrong, which is why prediction markets have often beaten polls. Money in the market is information nobody else is collecting, and banning it does not stop forecasting — it just leaves it to pundits who face no cost for a bad call.
cards.move: The forecasting argument and the manipulation argument are both correct, which is what makes this hard.
cards.counterpoint: A market on an outcome that people can influence is a market with an incentive to influence it. Enough money on a result gives someone a reason to suppress turnout, seed a story, or worse, and the sums that would move a contract are small next to the sums already in politics.
cards.reference: Wolfers & Zitzewitz, Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2004

cards.question: Should anyone be able to sit a degree's final exams without attending the university?
cards.answer: If the exam certifies the knowledge, then the knowledge is what should be certified, however it was acquired. Locking the assessment behind three years of fees turns a measure of competence into a measure of who could afford to be measured.
cards.move: What is on the exam and what the degree is for may be two different things.
cards.counterpoint: Most of what a degree gives is not on the exam: the supervision, the arguing, the lab where you learn what an experiment feels like when it fails. Certify only the testable part and universities will drift towards teaching only the testable part.
cards.reference: Kenyon Jones, The People's University: 150 Years of the University of London and its External Students, University of London, 2008

cards.question: Why did container ships get slower?
cards.answer: Deliberately, after 2008. Fuel use rises steeply with speed, so cutting speed by around a tenth saves a disproportionate share of the fuel. When freight rates collapsed and fuel stayed dear, slowing down beat sailing fast — and much of the fleet never sped back up.
cards.move: The world's cargo slowed down on purpose and mostly stayed slow.
cards.source: Slow steaming, adopted across container shipping post-2008
cards.reference: Cariou, Is slow steaming a sustainable means of reducing CO2 emissions from container shipping?, Transportation Research Part D, 2011

cards.question: What do most clauses of Bavaria's 1516 beer decree, the famous purity law, actually regulate?
cards.answer: The price. Most of the Ingolstadt decree sets what may be charged for beer: at most one pfennig a Mass in winter, two in summer. A single line allows only barley, hops and water; yeast, not yet understood, goes unmentioned. Historians often read the barley rule as keeping wheat and rye for bakers.
cards.move: Read a famous law in full before quoting its most famous line.
cards.source: Hornsey, A History of Beer and Brewing
cards.reference: Hornsey, A History of Beer and Brewing, Royal Society of Chemistry, 2003

cards.question: Why does canned stout need a rattling plastic capsule inside to pour with a thick, creamy head?
cards.answer: Because its foam relies on nitrogen, which barely dissolves in beer. The capsule fills with gas and beer under pressure at canning; when the can opens, pressure drops and it squirts a jet through a tiny hole, releasing bubbles at once. A pub tap does the same, forcing stout through a plate of fine holes.
cards.move: When something will not start on its own, give it a place to begin.
cards.source: Bamforth, Beer: Tap into the Art and Science
cards.reference: Bamforth, Beer: Tap into the Art and Science of Brewing, 3rd edition, Oxford University Press, 2009

cards.question: Wort reads 1.052 on a hydrometer; the finished beer reads 1.012. Brewers multiply the drop by 131.25. What strength, in % ABV?
cards.move: A reading that falls can hide two changes pulling the same way.
cards.trap: Reading the drop of 0.040 as 4% alcohol.
cards.hint: The hydrometer tracks density: sugar makes the wort heavier, alcohol makes beer lighter.
steps: Density drop as yeast turns sugar into alcohol: 1.052 - 1.012 = 0.040.
cards.reference: Palmer, How to Brew, 4th edition, Brewers Publications, 2017

cards.question: A clear-bottled lager left in sunshine can smell of skunk within minutes. Which ingredient is the light breaking down?
options: The yeast left in the bottle
cards.answer: The hops' bitter compounds. Riboflavin in beer absorbs blue light and passes the energy to iso-alpha acids, the bitter compounds. One splits, and a fragment joins sulphur to form 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol, kin to skunk-spray thiols and smelt at a few billionths of a gram per litre. Brown glass blocks that light; green and clear barely do.
cards.move: Ask what the damage needs, not only what looks fragile.
cards.trap: Blaming the yeast, since living things seem likeliest to spoil.
cards.source: Burns et al., Chem. Eur. J., 2001
cards.reference: Burns, Heyerick, De Keukeleire & Forbes, Mechanism for formation of the lightstruck flavor in beer revealed by time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance, Chemistry – A European Journal, 2001

cards.question: Should beer be required to list its ingredients and calories on the label, as fruit juice must?
cards.answer: European law has exempted drinks above 1.2% alcohol from ingredient and nutrition labels since 2011; orange juice must show both. Beer may contain sugar syrups, colourings or foam stabilisers, and a pint of ordinary lager carries roughly 200 kcal, mostly from alcohol. Drinkers counting calories or wary of additives deserve the facts juice buyers get.
cards.move: The question turns on whether alcohol is sold as a food or as a drug.
cards.counterpoint: Brewers already publish ingredients and energy voluntarily, on labels or behind QR codes, and small craft breweries changing recipes weekly would bear the heaviest cost of reprinting. A mandatory panel risks making beer look like a food, with a calorie count that frames it as healthy, when the real concern is alcohol, which warnings address more directly.
cards.reference: Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the provision of food information to consumers, Article 16(4), 2011

cards.question: In fifteenth-century England, what separated a drink called ale from one called beer?
cards.answer: Hops. Ale was the native malt drink, brewed without them and drunk fresh. Beer, hopped, arrived with brewers from the Low Countries; hops kept it longer and let brewers make it from less malt. Writers attacked it as foreign for generations, yet by the late 1600s most English ale was lightly hopped too.
cards.move: When two names cover one product, look for the ingredient that divides them.
cards.source: Unger, Beer in the Middle Ages, 2004
cards.reference: Unger, Beer in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, University of Pennsylvania Press, 2004

cards.question: What did Carlsberg do with the pure lager yeast its laboratory isolated in 1883?
cards.answer: Gave it away. Emil Christian Hansen grew a brewing yeast from a single cell, ending the spoiled batches that wild yeasts, hidden in brewers' mixed cultures, kept causing. Jacobsen, Carlsberg's founder, declined to patent the method and sent the strain to breweries abroad. Within decades, pure-culture yeast was standard practice in breweries worldwide.
cards.move: A method given away can shape an industry more than a patent.
cards.reference: Glamann, Jacobsen of Carlsberg: Brewer and Philanthropist, Gyldendal, 1991

cards.question: Lager yeast is a hybrid, and one parent loves the cold. Where was that parent first found in the wild, in 2011?
cards.answer: Patagonian beech forests. Saccharomyces eubayanus turned up on southern beech trees and the fungal galls they carry in Argentina, far from any medieval brewery. No search in Europe had turned it up. Later surveys found close relatives in Tibet and China, and how it reached Bavaria is still argued over.
cards.move: Where you choose to look decides what you are able to find.
