cards.trap: Assuming the ancestor lived where the product was perfected.
cards.reference: Libkind, Hittinger, Valério et al., Microbe domestication and the identification of the wild genetic stock of lager-brewing yeast, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2011

cards.question: After wet harvests, some beers foam out of the bottle the moment it opens, though carbonation is normal. What is to blame?
options: Yeast still fermenting in the bottle
Wild bacteria in the brewery pipes
cards.answer: Fungal proteins from mouldy barley. Fusarium fungi thrive on damp grain and make hydrophobins, small proteins that coat microscopic gas bubbles and stop them dissolving. They survive malting and brewing, then seed countless bubbles at once when the cap comes off. Checking the yeast, the obvious suspect, finds nothing wrong.
cards.move: When the amount is normal, look at what sets it free.
cards.trap: Blaming extra gas from yeast, the usual cause of bursting bottles.
cards.source: Sarlin et al., J. Inst. Brew., 2005
cards.reference: Sarlin, Nakari-Setälä, Linder, Penttilä & Haikara, Fungal hydrophobins as predictors of the gushing activity of malt, Journal of the Institute of Brewing, 2005

cards.question: True or false: India pale ale was invented as a new, extra-strong, extra-hoppy style so beer could survive the voyage to India?
cards.answer: False. Strong, heavily hopped October beers brewed for keeping existed in England long before, and George Hodgson's pale ale, shipped to India from the late 1700s, was one of them, not an invention. Brewing historians find India ales no stronger than many sold at home. The name India pale ale appears only around 1830.
cards.move: Each added detail in a story is one more thing that must be true.
cards.trap: Accepting the whole story because each detail makes it more vivid.
cards.reference: Cornell, Amber, Gold and Black: The History of Britain's Great Beers, History Press, 2010

cards.question: Where does the enzyme that curdles most American cheese come from today?
cards.answer: From microbes carrying a calf's gene. Chymosin, the milk-clotting enzyme in rennet, came from slaughtered calves' stomachs. In 1990 the FDA cleared chymosin made by bacteria given the cow's gene, the first recombinant DNA ingredient approved for US food. Most US cheese now uses it: a calf's stomach, replaced by a steel tank.
cards.move: Ask how an old ingredient is made now, not how it began.
cards.reference: US Food and Drug Administration, Chymosin enzyme preparation, affirmation of GRAS status, Federal Register, 23 March 1990

cards.question: True or false: the crunchy white specks inside a long-aged Parmesan are grains of salt?
cards.answer: False. They are mostly crystals of tyrosine, an amino acid freed as enzymes cut milk proteins apart over many months. Tyrosine dissolves poorly, so once enough builds up it comes out of solution as hard white clusters. X-ray analysis finds similar crystals in aged Gouda. Each crunch records months of protein breakdown.
cards.move: The first substance that comes to mind is not the only one that can crystallise.
cards.trap: Salt is the crystal everyone knows, and hard cheese tastes salty.
cards.source: Tansman et al., Dairy Science & Technology, 2015
cards.reference: Tansman, Kindstedt & Hughes, Crystal fingerprinting: elucidating the crystals of Cheddar, Parmigiano-Reggiano, Gouda, and soft washed-rind cheeses using powder x-ray diffractometry, Dairy Science & Technology, 2015

cards.question: Why did Swiss Emmental develop fewer and fewer holes over recent decades?
cards.answer: Because milk got cleaner. Holes form where carbon dioxide from propionic bacteria gathers around tiny particles, and a 2015 Agroscope study found microscopic hay dust in the milk doing that job. Closed modern milking systems keep hay out, so the gas had fewer places to start. Adding measured hay powder brought the holes back.
cards.move: When a result fades after a clean-up, suspect the dirt was doing something.
cards.reference: https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/sci-tech/mystery-solved_hay-particles-responsible-for-holes-in-swiss-cheese/41457054

cards.question: When milk becomes a hard aged cheese, where does most of its lactose go?
cards.answer: Out with the drained whey. Lactose dissolves in water, so when the curd is cut and drained, the whey carries most of it away. Starter bacteria ferment the small remainder into lactic acid within days or weeks, not months. Whey powder, sold by the tonne, is largely the milk sugar that cheese left behind.
cards.move: Before crediting the slow process, check what the first quick step removed.
cards.trap: Crediting months of ageing and its bacteria with eating the milk sugar.
cards.source: Fox et al., Fundamentals of Cheese Science, 2017
cards.reference: Fox, Guinee, Cogan & McSweeney, Fundamentals of Cheese Science, 2nd edition, Springer, 2017

cards.question: Should the United States drop its rule that raw-milk cheese must age at least 60 days before sale?
cards.answer: The rule dates from 1949 and rests on 1940s evidence, chiefly typhoid bacteria dying out in aged cheddar. A 2010 study found E. coli O157 still detectable in raw-milk Gouda and cheddar after 270 days, so ageing gives false comfort while banning young raw-milk cheeses outright. Safety should come from testing milk and inspecting dairies.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether ageing or testing better controls the risk decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The 60-day rule keeps off the shelf exactly the cheeses that carry most risk. A 2015 FDA and Health Canada assessment put the listeriosis risk from raw-milk soft-ripened cheese at 50 to 160 times that of pasteurised versions. Listeria strikes pregnant women and the elderly hardest. An imperfect barrier still blocks the worst category.
cards.source: FDA and Health Canada risk assessment, 2015
cards.reference: https://www.fda.gov/food/risk-and-safety-assessments-food/joint-fda-health-canada-quantitative-assessment-risk-listeriosis-soft-ripened-cheese-consumption

cards.question: Why did French researchers warn in 2020 that the white mould on Camembert could be in trouble?
cards.answer: It is a single clone. Since the early 1900s makers have used one white strain of Penicillium camemberti, chosen for its clean look. It multiplies only by copying itself and now makes few spores, so it is hard to propagate and cannot adapt. Before that choice, Camembert rinds were grey-green or bluish, even spotted brown.
cards.move: A choice made for looks can quietly remove the capacity to adapt.
cards.reference: Ropars, Didiot, Rodríguez de la Vega et al., Domestication of the emblematic white cheese-making fungus Penicillium camemberti and its diversification into cheese-specific lineages, Current Biology, 2020

cards.question: Why do the rules for Comté forbid feeding the cows silage, the fermented grass many dairies rely on?
cards.answer: To keep out spores that burst cheeses. Silage carries Clostridium bacteria whose spores survive the cow's gut, reach the milk on specks of dung and outlast cheesemaking. Months later, in the ripening cellar, they wake, turn lactate into butyric acid and gas, and split wheels with rancid cracks. The ban protects the long ageing.
cards.move: A rule that looks like it is about taste may be about hidden risk.
cards.reference: McSweeney (ed.), Cheese Problems Solved, Woodhead Publishing, 2007

cards.question: Roughly how many litres of milk go into one 40 kg wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano?
cards.answer: 12 × 40 kg = about 480 litres.
cards.move: Size the output by the scarce part of the input, not its bulk.
cards.trap: Guessing near 40 litres, as if milk became cheese almost whole.
cards.hint: Ask how much of each litre of milk can end up as cheese solids.
steps: Partly skimmed milk holds about 2.6% casein and 2.4% fat: some 50 g a litre that the curd can keep.
Aged Parmigiano is about 60% protein and fat: 600 g in every kilo.
600 ÷ 50 = 12 litres of milk per kilo of cheese.
12 × 40 kg = about 480 litres.
cards.reference: Walstra, Wouters & Geurts, Dairy Science and Technology, 2nd edition, CRC Press, 2006

cards.question: True or false: in the European Union, a German-made hard cheese may not be sold under the name parmesan?
cards.answer: True. In 2008 the European Court of Justice held that parmesan evokes Parmigiano Reggiano, a protected designation of origin, so within the EU the word belongs to cheese made to its rules in a zone around Parma and Reggio Emilia. Outside Europe it is widely treated as generic: an American supermarket shelf holds dozens.
cards.move: A name that is common in one market can be property in another.
cards.trap: Treating the English word as generic because it is everywhere.
cards.reference: Case C-132/05, Commission v Germany, Court of Justice of the European Communities, judgment of 26 February 2008

cards.question: Which of these three is the oldest evidence of cheesemaking found so far?
options: Milk fats in pottery sieves in Poland
A cheese lump in an Egyptian tomb
Curds buried with mummies in China
cards.answer: Milk fats in pottery sieves in Poland. Chemists found dairy fat in perforated pots from Kuyavia, about 7,000 years old, strainers for draining curds from whey; similar finds in Croatia are as old. The famous lumps from an Egyptian tomb and Chinese desert graves are only 3,200 to 3,600 years old; dry sand preserved them.
cards.move: The oldest thing that survived is not the oldest thing that existed.
cards.trap: Picking the preserved lumps, the finds that made the headlines.
cards.reference: Salque, Bogucki, Pyzel et al., Earliest evidence for cheese making in the sixth millennium BC in northern Europe, Nature, 2013

cards.question: In wild Bolivian chillies, what enemy does the burning capsaicin mainly protect the seeds from?
cards.answer: A fungus. Tewksbury's team found that Fusarium, entering through punctures made by sap-sucking bugs, killed more seeds than any animal, and that capsaicin slowed it. Where bugs were common, most plants in a population were pungent; where rare, many wild plants made no capsaicin at all. The heat may have begun as a fungicide.
cards.move: Before naming a defence's target, count what actually kills the thing defended.

cards.question: Why can birds swallow the hottest chillies whole without flinching?
cards.answer: Their version of the capsaicin receptor does not respond to it. Mammals crush chilli seeds; birds swallow them whole and pass them intact, far away. In trials, cactus mice shunned hot fruit that thrashers ate freely. The burn sorts diners, turning away the ones that grind seeds and inviting the ones that plant them.
cards.move: A deterrent that stops some visitors may be selecting the ones it wants.
cards.reference: Tewksbury & Nabhan, Directed deterrence by capsaicin in chillies, Nature, 2001

cards.question: True or false: the seeds of a chilli make almost none of its capsaicin?
cards.answer: True. Capsaicin is made in glands on the placenta, the pale ribs that hold the seeds, and the seeds taste hot mainly because they sit pressed against it. Scraping out seeds and ribs together tames a chilli; scraping out seeds alone and leaving the ribs keeps most of the fire in the pan.
cards.move: The thing that sits next to the cause often takes the blame.
cards.trap: Seeds come out with the heat, so they seem to be its source.
cards.reference: Bosland & Votava, Peppers: Vegetable and Spice Capsicums, 2nd edition, CABI, 2012

cards.question: Scoville units count dilutions until no heat is tasted. Pure capsaicin rates 16 million: how many litres of water would 1 mg need?
cards.answer: 16 kg of water = 16 litres.
cards.move: Turn a rating into a volume and the scale becomes something you can picture.
cards.trap: Treating the rating as an abstract score rather than a dilution.
cards.hint: Multiply the milligram by the rating, then turn milligrams into kilograms.
steps: 1 mg must be diluted 16,000,000 times its own weight.
16,000,000 mg = 16 kg of water.
16 kg of water = 16 litres.
cards.reference: Scoville, Note on Capsicums, Journal of the American Pharmaceutical Association, 1912

cards.question: What is the tongue's nerve reporting when a chilli burns?
cards.answer: A scald. The receptor capsaicin binds, TRPV1, is a heat sensor that normally opens at about 43 °C, where hot water starts to hurt. Capsaicin opens it at mouth temperature, so the nerve fires as for a burn. David Julius's lab found the receptor in 1997. The tongue is reporting a scald that never happened.
cards.move: A signal names the sensor that fired, not the thing that fired it.
cards.reference: Caterina, Schumacher, Tominaga, Rosen, Levine & Julius, The capsaicin receptor: a heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway, Nature, 1997

cards.question: A lab rates a dried chilli at 100,000 Scoville units. The fresh pod was 80% water. Its rating by fresh weight, in thousands?
cards.answer: 100,000 / 5 = 20,000 Scoville units, or 20 thousand.
cards.move: Before comparing two concentrations, check that both divide by the same thing.
cards.trap: Assuming drying changes nothing, since no capsaicin is lost.
cards.hint: Drying removes water, not capsaicin: ask how much fresh pod holds one gram of dry matter.
steps: 100 g of fresh pod at 80% water holds 20 g of dry matter.
The same capsaicin is spread over 100 g fresh instead of 20 g dry: 5 times the mass.
100,000 / 5 = 20,000 Scoville units, or 20 thousand.
cards.reference: Collins, Mayer Wasmund & Bosland, Improved method for quantifying capsaicinoids in Capsicum using high-performance liquid chromatography, HortScience, 1995

cards.question: True or false: in a blind test, whole milk cooled a capsaicin burn better than skimmed milk?
cards.answer: False. Penn State researchers in 2019 gave volunteers capsaicin-spiked tomato juice, then one of seven drinks: whole and skimmed milk did equally well, and both beat water and seltzer. Fat dissolves capsaicin, which made it the obvious hero. The result points instead to milk's proteins, such as casein, pulling capsaicin off the tongue.
cards.move: A mechanism that sounds right still has to beat its control.
cards.trap: True, because capsaicin dissolves in fat and whole milk has more.
cards.reference: https://www.psu.edu/news/research/story/milk-best-drink-reduce-burn-chili-peppers

cards.question: Why did the Nobel-winning chemistry of vitamin C depend on the paprika fields of Szeged?
cards.answer: Because paprika, a mild Capsicum, turned out to be one of the richest sources known. In the early 1930s Albert Szent-Györgyi had only small amounts of his hexuronic acid, extracted laboriously from adrenal glands. Testing local peppers in Szeged, he soon purified enough to send Haworth, who worked out its structure in 1933.
cards.move: The limit on a discovery is often the supply of raw material.
cards.source: American Chemical Society, National Historic Landmark
cards.reference: https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/szentgyorgyi.html

cards.question: A one-hour patch holding 8% capsaicin can ease nerve pain for about three months. How?
options: It releases endorphins that dull pain
It blocks nerves like a local anaesthetic
Pain-fibre endings retreat from the skin
cards.answer: Pain-fibre endings retreat from the skin. A massive dose overloads the TRPV1 nerve endings, and their terminals in the outer skin withdraw; biopsies show fewer fibres there for weeks. The endings regrow, so relief fades after roughly 12 weeks. The patch first burns, then leaves the skin with fewer wires to carry pain.
cards.move: A relief that lasts months points to a structure changed, not a signal blocked.
cards.trap: Endorphins, the popular explanation for the chilli-eater's high.
cards.source: Anand & Bley, British Journal of Anaesthesia, 2011
cards.reference: https://www.bjanaesthesia.org/article/S0007-0912(17)33029-5/fulltext

cards.question: Should extreme-heat novelty snacks be banned from sale to under-18s?
cards.answer: These products exist to be dared on video, and children are the audience. In 2023 a 14-year-old in Massachusetts died after a one-chip challenge; the autopsy named the capsaicin dose alongside an undetected heart defect. Children cannot know they have such a defect. Alcohol and tobacco carry age limits for the same reason.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, decide whether the risk lies in the product or the dare.
cards.counterpoint: Deaths are vanishingly rare against millions of chips sold, and that one involved a hidden heart condition. Hot sauces as strong sit on every supermarket shelf; banning one packet format fixes the headline, not the risk. The maker withdrew it within days. Clear dose labels and school warnings reach the same children without a law that shops cannot enforce.
cards.reference: https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/16/business/one-chip-challenge-autopsy/index.html

cards.question: A loaf bakes for 40 minutes in a 230 °C oven. How hot does the centre of the crumb get?
cards.answer: About 98 °C. While the crumb holds water, heat goes into making steam, so a boiling front near 100 °C creeps inward. Only the dried outer layer climbs well past 100 °C, and only there can a brown crust form. A loaf is a pot of boiling water wrapped in toast.
cards.move: Wherever water is boiling off, the temperature is capped near 100 °C.
cards.trap: Letting the 230 °C oven setting pull the guess far upward.
cards.source: Vanin et al., Trends Food Sci. Technol., 2009
cards.reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0924224409001307

cards.question: Why do bakers flood the oven with steam during the first minutes of a bake?
cards.answer: To keep the crust from forming too soon. Steam condenses on the cool dough, keeping its skin wet and stretchy so the loaf can expand fully. The wet surface starch also swells into a thin film that bakes glassy. Without steam, a loaf comes out dull, thick-skinned and torn at the sides.
cards.move: Delay the step that locks everything in until the growth is done.
cards.reference: Suas, Advanced Bread and Pastry: A Professional Approach, Delmar Cengage Learning, 2009

cards.question: Why does a crackling crust turn leathery within hours, even when the kitchen air is dry?
cards.answer: Water moves out from the crumb. Fresh from the oven, the crust is nearly dry while the crumb is around 40% water, and moisture diffuses outward. Damp crust starch turns rubbery instead of glassy. A few minutes in a hot oven drive the water back out, and the crunch returns for a while.
cards.move: When something spoils on its own, look for the source inside it.
cards.reference: Figoni, How Baking Works: Exploring the Fundamentals of Baking Science, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2011

cards.question: True or false: German bakers give pretzels their dark glossy crust by dipping them in caustic soda?
cards.answer: True. Laugenbrezeln are dipped briefly in cold sodium hydroxide solution of about 3 to 4%, the chemical in drain cleaner. The alkali speeds browning and sets a shiny skin. In the oven the film reacts with carbon dioxide and becomes sodium carbonate, the mild soda that gives the crust its faint soapy bite.
cards.move: How dangerous a substance sounds matters less than the dose and what it becomes.
cards.trap: Picturing drain cleaner and assuming no bakery could use it on food.
cards.reference: McGee, On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen, Scribner, 2004

cards.question: What is the main job of the slash a baker cuts across a loaf just before baking?
options: To let steam escape from inside
To help heat reach the centre
To choose where the loaf bursts
cards.answer: To choose where the loaf bursts. The surface sets while the dough is still expanding, so the loaf must split somewhere. A cut gives it a planned weak line, so it opens there instead of tearing along its side. The raised flap on a baguette, called the ear, is that controlled rupture.
cards.move: If something is bound to break, decide in advance where.
cards.trap: Assuming a vent is needed so trapped steam can get out.
cards.reference: Hamelman, Bread: A Baker's Book of Techniques and Recipes, Wiley, 2004

cards.question: Why does a crusty loaf crackle audibly for minutes after it comes out of the oven?
cards.answer: Its crust is cracking. Out of the oven, the thin, dry, glassy crust cools and contracts faster than the hot, moist crumb beneath, which stays swollen. The stiff shell cannot stretch to fit, so it splits into a web of fine cracks. Bakers call it singing; a pale, underbaked crust stays soft and silent.
cards.move: Bond a stiff layer to one that moves differently, and expect cracks.
cards.reference: Gisslen, Professional Baking, 7th edition, Wiley, 2017

cards.question: The cracker-like smell of fresh bread crust comes mainly from one molecule. What else is scented by it?
cards.answer: Basmati rice. The molecule, 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, forms in the hot crust when the amino acid proline meets fragments of sugar, so sugar alone cannot make it. The nose detects it at about a tenth of a millionth of a gram per litre of water. Pandan leaves and fresh popcorn owe their scent to it too.
cards.move: A smell is a molecule, and one molecule can turn up in many foods.
cards.trap: Crediting browned sugar, the flavour everyone links with browning.
cards.source: Schieberle & Grosch, Z. Lebensm. Unters. Forsch., 1987
cards.reference: Schieberle & Grosch, Evaluation of the flavour of wheat and rye bread crusts by aroma extract dilution analysis, Zeitschrift für Lebensmittel-Untersuchung und -Forschung, 1987

cards.question: One loaf bakes 25 minutes at 250 °C, its twin 40 minutes at 210 °C, both fully baked. Which has the thicker crust?
cards.answer: The cooler, longer bake. Crust is the layer that has dried out, and the drying front creeps inward with time. A hot oven browns the surface quickly, but the bake ends before much depth has dried. Long, moderate bakes give the thick, chewy crust of country loaves; hot, short ones a thin, crackling shell.
cards.move: Colour records how hot it got; depth records how long it lasted.
cards.trap: Equating a darker, hotter surface with a deeper crust.
cards.reference: Cauvain, Baking Problems Solved, 2nd edition, Woodhead Publishing, 2017

cards.question: A baguette is a cylinder 6 cm across with a 3 mm crust. Ignoring the ends, what percentage of its volume is crust?
cards.move: When a thin skin wraps something round, its share is bigger than it looks.
cards.trap: Taking 3 mm of a 30 mm radius as a tenth.
cards.hint: Compare the cross-section of the whole loaf with that of the crumb inside it.
steps: The radius is 30 mm; the crumb inside the crust has a radius of 27 mm.
Volume goes with the square of the radius: (27 ÷ 30)² = 0.81.
So the crumb is 81% of the volume.
cards.reference: Calvel, The Taste of Bread, trans. Wirtz, Aspen Publishers, 2001

cards.question: The rules for certified Neapolitan pizza set the oven at about 485 °C. How long does the pizza bake?
cards.answer: 60 to 90 seconds. At that heat the dome radiates so strongly that the rim puffs and blisters with dark spots before any crust can dry thick. The EU-registered rules ask for a soft, elastic pizza that folds easily, not a crisp one. A home oven at 250 °C needs about ten minutes.
cards.move: A number from your own kitchen is a poor guide to someone else's.
cards.trap: Carrying over a home oven's ten minutes to every pizza.
cards.reference: Commission Regulation (EU) No 97/2010 entering a name in the register of traditional specialities guaranteed (Pizza Napoletana (TSG)), 2010

cards.question: Why does clear ouzo turn milky the moment water is poured in, with no emulsifier present?
cards.answer: Because its anise oil, anethole, dissolves in strong alcohol but not in water. Diluting the spirit forces the oil out everywhere at once, as droplets about a micrometre across that scatter light. They hang there for hours with no stabiliser, a behaviour physicists named the ouzo effect in 2003. Pastis clouds the same way.
cards.move: Change the solvent and something dissolved can reappear all at once.
cards.reference: Vitale & Katz, Liquid droplet dispersions formed by homogeneous liquid-liquid nucleation: the ouzo effect, Langmuir, 2003

cards.question: How does homogenisation stop cream from rising to the top of a bottle of milk?
cards.answer: By shrinking the fat droplets. Forcing milk through a narrow gap at high pressure breaks globules of about 4 micrometres into ones under 1. Rising speed goes with the square of the radius, so a quarter of the size rises sixteen times slower: too slow to reach the top before the milk is drunk.
cards.move: When speed scales with a square, a modest shrink is a huge slowdown.
cards.source: Walstra et al., Dairy Science and Technology, 2006
cards.reference: Walstra, Wouters & Geurts, Dairy Science and Technology, 2nd edition, CRC Press, 2006

cards.question: True or false: butter, like the cream it is churned from, is fat droplets dispersed in water?
cards.answer: False. Cream is fat in water; butter is the reverse, water in fat. Churning tears the membranes round the fat globules, the freed fat runs together into one mass, and the leftover water, about 16% of butter, is trapped in it as droplets. So butter feels greasy on the fingers and cream feels wet.
cards.move: The same two ingredients can make opposite things depending on which one surrounds.
cards.trap: Butter comes from cream, so it seems to keep cream's structure.
cards.reference: McGee, On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen, Scribner, 2004

cards.question: Mayonnaise is mostly oil, plus vinegar and yolk, all runny liquids. What mainly lets it hold a peak?
options: The egg yolk setting like custard
The mustard's starch thickening the water
The oil droplets crammed against each other
cards.answer: The oil droplets crammed against each other. Round droplets can fill at most about 74% of a space; beyond that they flatten into many-sided cells, and any flow must deform them. At 75 to 80% oil, mayonnaise is packed oil cells in thin films of water. Whisk in more oil and it stiffens further.
cards.move: Crowding alone can turn a crowd of liquids into a solid.
cards.trap: Egg is the famous ingredient, so it seems to do the thickening.
cards.reference: McClements, Food Emulsions: Principles, Practices, and Techniques, 2nd edition, CRC Press, 2005

cards.question: Should a spread made without egg be allowed to call itself mayonnaise?
cards.answer: A name describes what food does on the plate, not a recipe frozen in law. Plant proteins can emulsify oil as egg yolk does, and buyers see the ingredients list. Rules written to stop cheating on oil content should not shield incumbents from a product that is better for people with egg allergies.
cards.move: Decide first whether a food name protects buyers or protects a recipe.
cards.counterpoint: A standard name is a promise that saves every shopper reading every label. United States rules define mayonnaise as at least 65% oil with egg yolk; that is what the word guarantees. Let any spread borrow it and the word stops meaning anything, and the cheapest imitation sets the price for honest makers.
cards.source: US Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 169.140
cards.reference: Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Section 169.140, Mayonnaise, US Food and Drug Administration, 2023

cards.question: A mayonnaise turns so stiff and greasy that more oil will not go in. What lets it take more?
cards.answer: A spoonful of water. The limit is room, not emulsifier: every droplet needs a film of water round it, and packed tighter the films thin until droplets merge. One yolk carries emulsifier for far more oil than recipes use. Add water or lemon juice little by little and the same yolk keeps swallowing oil.
cards.move: Find which ingredient has run out before adding more of the famous one.
cards.trap: Another yolk, because the yolk is the emulsifier everyone names.
cards.reference: This, Molecular Gastronomy: Exploring the Science of Flavor, Columbia University Press, 2006

cards.question: Why do the smallest droplets in an orange-oil drink emulsion shrink while the big ones grow?
cards.answer: Because curvature squeezes them. The tighter a droplet's curve, the higher the pressure inside, so oil in a small droplet dissolves more readily and drifts to larger ones. Citrus oils dissolve slightly in water, so such drinks coarsen on the shelf. Makers blend in an insoluble oil, which a shrinking droplet cannot shed.
cards.move: Where small units pay a higher cost to exist, the big ones absorb them.
cards.source: Journal of Food Science, 2012, on ripening

cards.question: True or false: brominated vegetable oil was put in citrus sodas to stop their flavour oil floating up?
cards.answer: True. Citrus oil is lighter than sugary water, so its droplets rise. Bromine atoms are heavy; bonded to vegetable oil, they made a weighting agent that brought the droplets up to the drink's density, at up to 15 parts per million. The US revoked its approval in 2024 after thyroid effects in animal studies.
cards.move: Ask what job an odd ingredient does before guessing why it is there.
cards.trap: False, as a bromine compound sounds like a preservative or flame retardant.
cards.source: US FDA, revocation of BVO authorisation, 2024
cards.reference: https://www.fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/brominated-vegetable-oil-bvo

cards.question: A tablespoon of mayonnaise holds 12 ml of oil as droplets 10 micrometres across. Their total surface, in square metres?
cards.move: Chop anything finely enough and its surface outgrows its volume.
cards.trap: Guessing a few square centimetres, the size of the spoon.
cards.hint: A sphere's surface divided by its volume is 6 over its diameter.
steps: Surface per volume of a sphere = 6 / diameter = 6 / 0.00001 m = 600,000 per metre.
12 ml = 0.000012 cubic metres of oil.

diagram.caption: As one drop, 12 ml of oil has 25 cm² of surface; as 10 µm droplets, 7.2 m².

cards.reference: McClements, Food Emulsions: Principles, Practices, and Techniques, 3rd edition, CRC Press, 2015

cards.question: True or false: lecithin is the molecule doing most of the emulsifying in an egg-yolk mayonnaise?
cards.answer: False. The main workers are low-density lipoproteins, tiny balls of protein and phospholipid in the yolk. At the oil surface they burst open and spread their proteins and phospholipids together into a film tougher than either alone. Lecithin, the textbook molecule, is one member of the team.
cards.move: A single named cause is often a team with one famous member.
cards.trap: True, because lecithin is the emulsifier every label and textbook names.
cards.reference: Anton, Egg yolk: structures, functionalities and processes, Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture, 2013

cards.question: When did espresso bars start serving coffee topped with a layer of fine foam?
cards.answer: After the Second World War. Earlier bar machines pushed water through with steam at 1.5 to 2 bar, giving a thin, often scorched cup. Achille Gaggia's spring-lever machines, sold from 1948, reached 8 to 10 bar, forcing coffee oils and carbon dioxide into a fine foam. Gaggia sold it as crema naturale: natural coffee cream.
cards.move: A new side effect sells better once someone gives it a flattering name.
cards.reference: https://www.gaggia.com/85-years-of-heritage-1938-1947/

cards.question: True or false: grinding espresso finer always extracts more of the coffee into the cup?
cards.answer: False. Past a point, very fine grounds pack so tightly that water forces a few fast channels through the puck and bypasses the rest. A 2020 study combining modelling with brewing found finer grinds lowered extraction and made shots erratic; less coffee, ground coarser, gave far more reproducible shots. Water takes the easy road.
cards.move: Past a certain point, more of the right thing starts to block itself.
cards.trap: Reasoning that smaller particles expose more surface, so they must extract more.
cards.reference: https://www.cell.com/matter/fulltext/S2590-2385(19)30410-2

cards.question: An 18 g coffee dose gives a 36 g espresso that is 10% dissolved coffee by weight. What percentage of the dose was extracted?
cards.answer: That is 20%.
cards.move: Check what a percentage is a percentage of before comparing two of them.
cards.trap: Answering 10%, which is the drink's strength, not the yield.
cards.hint: Find how many grams of coffee ended up dissolved in the cup, then compare with the dose.
steps: Dissolved coffee in the cup: 36 g x 10% = 3.6 g.
Share of the dose: 3.6 g / 18 g = 0.2.
That is 20%.
cards.reference: Illy & Viani (eds.), Espresso Coffee: The Science of Quality, 2nd edition, Elsevier Academic Press, 2005

cards.question: Italy's certified espresso standard sets how much ground coffee for a single shot?
cards.answer: About 7 g. The Istituto Nazionale Espresso Italiano specifies 7 g, give or take half a gram, brewed at 88 °C and 9 bar for about 25 seconds into roughly 25 ml. Specialty cafés elsewhere often pack 18 to 20 g into a double basket. An Italian bar shot is a small, quick thing.
cards.move: The examples closest to hand are rarely the ones that define the norm.
cards.trap: Picturing the 18 to 20 g doses used by specialty cafés abroad.
cards.reference: https://iei.coffee/en/espresso-italiano-certificato/

cards.question: Why does an espresso pulled too short and fast taste sour rather than weak?
cards.answer: Because coffee does not dissolve evenly. Acids wash out first, sugars and heavier browned compounds later, the most bitter ones last. A shot stopped early captures mostly the acids, with too little sweetness to balance them. Running longer adds sweetness, then bitterness, so baristas adjust the grind until the cup lands between sour and harsh.
cards.move: When parts arrive in order, the moment of stopping decides the mix.
cards.reference: Rao, The Professional Barista's Handbook, self-published, 2008

cards.question: What did the machine patented in Turin in 1884, often called the first espresso machine, make?
cards.answer: Coffee in bulk. Angelo Moriondo's machine used steam and hot water under pressure to brew large batches for his hotel and bar, not single cups. The cup made quickly to order came with Luigi Bezzera's patent of 1901 and the machines Desiderio Pavoni built from it, shown at the 1906 Milan fair as caffè espresso.
cards.move: Credit an invention to whoever made it do the job it is known for.
cards.reference: Morris, Coffee: A Global History, Reaktion Books, 2019

cards.question: Brewing water at 9 bar presses on a 58 mm espresso puck. What force is that, in kilograms-weight?
cards.move: Before straining at a small push, check the force the system already applies.
cards.trap: Picturing a few kilos, since the barista tamps it by hand.
cards.hint: Work out the puck's area in square centimetres first.
steps: The puck's radius is 2.9 cm.
Its area is 3.14 × 2.9 × 2.9 ≈ 26.4 cm².
1 bar is about 1 kg-weight on each cm², so 9 bar is about 9 kg per cm².
cards.reference: Hoffmann, The World Atlas of Coffee, 2nd edition, Mitchell Beazley, 2018

cards.question: True or false: a stovetop moka pot brews at a pressure close to an espresso machine's?
cards.answer: False. Steam in the lower chamber pushes water up through the coffee at under 2 bar, against about 9 in an espresso machine. That is too little to push through espresso-fine grounds or to whip oils and gas into lasting foam. Moka coffee is strong and heavy, but the cup carries no true crema.
cards.move: A product's nickname tells what it imitates, not how it works.
cards.trap: Trusting the nickname stovetop espresso to describe the physics.
cards.source: Navarini et al., Applied Thermal Engineering, 2009
cards.reference: Navarini, Nobile, Pinto, Scheri & Suggi-Liverani, Experimental investigation of steam pressure coffee extraction in a stove-top coffee maker, Applied Thermal Engineering, 2009

cards.question: Roughly how many roasted coffee beans go into one 18 g double espresso?
cards.answer: 18 ÷ 0.135 = about 130 beans.
cards.move: Turn a dose into a count, and a small portion looks very different.
cards.trap: Guessing a dozen or two, because the shot looks so small.
cards.hint: Start from the weight of one green bean and what roasting takes away.
steps: A green arabica bean weighs about 0.16 g.
Roasting removes about 15% of its weight: 0.16 × 0.85 ≈ 0.135 g.
18 ÷ 0.135 = about 130 beans.
cards.reference: Wintgens (ed.), Coffee: Growing, Processing, Sustainable Production, Wiley-VCH, 2004

cards.question: From the same 18 g dose, a barista pulls a short ristretto and a long lungo. Which extracts more of the coffee?
cards.answer: The lungo. Strength is how concentrated the cup is; extraction is how much of the dose dissolved. The ristretto tastes stronger because little water carries what it took. The lungo keeps flowing through the puck and dissolves more in total, spread through two or three times the liquid: weaker in the cup, yet more extracted.
cards.move: How concentrated something is says little about how much of it there is.
cards.trap: Reading the stronger taste as more coffee pulled from the grounds.
cards.reference: Lingle, The Coffee Brewing Handbook, Specialty Coffee Association of America, 1996

cards.question: What did the first Korean book to mention chilli, in 1614, say about the plant?
cards.answer: That it was highly poisonous. The encyclopedia Jibong yuseol called it Japanese mustard, since it had arrived from Japan, and warned of its toxicity. For centuries before, kimchi was pale, salted vegetables flavoured with garlic, ginger or brine. Chilli appears in kimchi recipes only in the 1700s, and red kimchi spread through the 1800s.
cards.move: Date a tradition by its ingredients, not by how old it feels.
cards.reference: https://journalofethnicfoods.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s42779-025-00271-9

cards.question: What were engineers copying when they designed the first mass-market kimchi refrigerator, launched in Korea in 1995?
cards.answer: A clay crock buried in winter ground. Soil cools a jar directly and holds it at a steady temperature and humidity, while an ordinary fridge blows dry air that pulls moisture from food. Dimchae was a chest opened from the top, like reaching into a jar. By 2011 about 81% of households owned one.
cards.move: Before building a machine, measure what the old method got right.
cards.reference: https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/tech-science/20111121/kimchi-refrigerator-maintains-taste-of-fermented-food

cards.question: A jar of young kimchi fizzes on the tongue and pushes up its lid. What is making the gas?
cards.answer: Lactic acid bacteria. The first to take over, Leuconostoc mesenteroides, is heterofermentative: from each sugar it makes lactic acid plus carbon dioxide. It thrives in the cold early days, when kimchi is most sparkling. Later and warmer, acid-tolerant Lactobacillus plantarum takes over, making acid without gas, and the fizz fades as sourness rises.
cards.move: Before naming the usual suspect, check who else can do the same job.
cards.trap: Crediting yeast, because bubbles in bread and beer come from yeast.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41538-025-00415-w

cards.question: True or false: in 2024 South Korea spent more buying kimchi from abroad than it earned selling kimchi abroad?
cards.answer: True. Exports hit a record $163.6 million, but imports, almost all from China, reached $189.9 million, and Korea has run a kimchi deficit most years since 2010. Chinese factory kimchi costs far less, so it fills the free, endlessly refilled side dishes of Korean restaurants.
cards.move: Where a thing is famous from and where it is made are separate questions.
cards.trap: Assuming the dish's homeland must sell more of it than it buys.
cards.reference: https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10622311

cards.question: What set off Korea's campaign in the 1990s for an international definition of kimchi?
cards.answer: Japanese kimuchi. Japanese makers sold cabbage in chilli seasoning, often soured with added acid instead of fermented, and in 1996 Japan pressed its version at Codex, the international food-standards body. The standard adopted in 2001 calls kimchi ripened by lactic acid made at low temperature, yet still permits added citric and acetic acid.
cards.move: A definition written to settle a dispute usually carries a compromise inside it.
cards.reference: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s42779-023-00171-w

cards.question: What had to be done to kimchi before a Korean astronaut could take it to the space station in 2008?
cards.answer: Its bacteria had to be stopped. Live lactic bacteria keep fermenting, and gas swelling a sealed pouch in orbit could burst it inside the cabin. Korea's atomic energy research institute spent years on a version sterilised by radiation that kept its taste and crunch. Yi So-yeon, the first Korean in space, flew with it.
cards.move: Before moving something alive, ask what it will keep doing on the way.
cards.reference: Choe Sang-Hun, Starship Kimchi: A Bold Taste Goes Where It Has Never Gone Before, The New York Times, 24 February 2008

cards.question: What does ISO 24220, the 2020 pickle standard some Chinese media hailed as a kimchi standard, say about kimchi?
cards.answer: That it does not apply to kimchi. The standard covers pao cai, Sichuan's salted fermented vegetables, and says so in its scope. Headlines calling it a global benchmark for kimchi set off an online row between the two countries, and in 2021 Seoul issued guidance to write kimchi as xinqi in Chinese, not paocai.
cards.move: A headline about a document is not the document.
cards.reference: ISO 24220:2020, Pao cai (salted fermented vegetables) — Specification and test methods, International Organization for Standardization, 2020

cards.question: Cabbage for kimchi soaks for hours in brine of around 10% salt. How salty is the finished kimchi?
cards.answer: About 2 to 3%. Brining is short: salt draws water out and wilts the leaves, but little gets in before the cabbage is rinsed and drained. At that level lactic bacteria thrive while most spoilage microbes are held back. Salted harder, it turns harsh and ferments sluggishly; too little, it softens and spoils.
cards.move: The strength of a treatment is not the strength of what it leaves behind.
cards.trap: Assuming the cabbage ends as salty as the brine it soaked in.
cards.source: Cheigh & Park, Crit. Rev. Food Sci., 1994
cards.reference: Cheigh & Park, Biochemical, microbiological, and nutritional aspects of kimchi (Korean fermented vegetable products), Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition, 1994

cards.question: True or false: the WHO's cancer research agency lists traditional Asian pickled vegetables as possibly carcinogenic?
cards.answer: True. In 1993 the International Agency for Research on Cancer put traditional Asian pickled vegetables in Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, chiefly on studies of stomach and oesophageal cancer in China, Japan and Korea. Heavy salt, nitrosamines and moulds are the suspects. The probiotic halo and the cancer list describe the same jars.
cards.move: Test a food's good name against the evidence that could sink it.
cards.trap: Trusting the health halo that fermented foods carry.
cards.reference: IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Volume 56: Some Naturally Occurring Substances, International Agency for Research on Cancer, 1993

cards.question: True or false: sour, over-ripe kimchi holds more live lactic bacteria than kimchi at its best?
cards.answer: False. Lactic bacteria multiply to hundreds of millions per gram as kimchi reaches its best, then the acid they have made starts to kill them. By the time it is sharply sour, their counts are falling. The acid records past growth, not the present population: the sourest jar is partly a graveyard.
cards.move: A trace left behind measures past activity, not present numbers.
cards.trap: Reading sourness as a count of how many bacteria are alive.
cards.reference: Hutkins, Microbiology and Technology of Fermented Foods, 2nd edition, Wiley-Blackwell, 2019

cards.question: Why are German pretzels dipped in a bath of lye before they are baked?
cards.answer: To make the Maillard reaction run fast. Browning speeds up in alkaline conditions, because the amino groups that react with sugars stay free instead of being tied up by acid. A dip in 3 to 4% sodium hydroxide gives a mahogany crust in minutes; baking turns the lye into milder sodium carbonate.
cards.move: Change the conditions and the same reaction can run many times faster.
cards.source: Martins et al., Trends Food Sci. Technol., 2000
cards.reference: Martins, Jongen & van Boekel, A review of Maillard reaction in food and implications to kinetic modelling, Trends in Food Science & Technology, 2000

cards.question: Swedish chemists announced acrylamide, a probable carcinogen, in fried and baked foods in 2002. What first put them on its trail?
options: A cancer cluster among chip-shop cooks
Blood of people never exposed to it
cards.answer: Blood of people never exposed to it. Studying tunnel workers poisoned by an acrylamide sealant in 1997, Margareta Törnqvist's group found its haemoglobin marker in unexposed controls too. Only a common source could explain it, which proved to be asparagine reacting with sugars in hot starchy food. The comparison group was the finding.
cards.move: When the people meant to show nothing show something, follow that thread.
cards.trap: Picturing hazards found the dramatic way, through a cluster of victims.
cards.source: Tareke et al., J. Agric. Food Chem., 2002
cards.reference: Tareke, Rydberg, Karlsson, Eriksson & Törnqvist, Analysis of acrylamide, a carcinogen formed in heated foodstuffs, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2002

cards.question: True or false: searing a steak over high heat first seals its juices inside?
cards.answer: False. The idea comes from the chemist Justus von Liebig in the 1840s, and it went untested for nearly a century. Seared steaks lose as much moisture as others, often more, since the hot surface drives water out. The loud sizzle in the pan is juice escaping as steam.
cards.move: A step that looks protective still needs a comparison without it.
cards.trap: A crisp brown crust looks like a barrier, so it feels like one.
cards.reference: McGee, On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen, Scribner, 2004

cards.question: A steak put in a hot pan straight from its wet packet turns grey before it browns. Why?
options: Water washes off the browning sugars
Wet meat lacks the proteins that brown
cards.answer: Surface water pins it near 100 °C. While water remains, the heat goes into boiling it off and the surface cannot climb higher. The Maillard reaction only becomes fast above about 140 °C, so the meat steams. Patting it dry, or salting it hours ahead, brings the crust minutes sooner.
cards.move: Find what is soaking up the energy before adding more of it.
cards.trap: Assuming the water removes an ingredient rather than capping the heat.
cards.reference: López-Alt, The Food Lab: Better Home Cooking Through Science, W. W. Norton, 2015

cards.question: What turns a white garlic bulb into soft, sweet black garlic over several weeks?
cards.answer: The Maillard reaction, run slowly. Whole bulbs sit at about 60 to 80 °C in humid heat for weeks; the garlic's stored fructans break into sugars, which react with amino acids and brown the cloves through. No microbes take part, though it is often sold as fermented. The cloves end up like liquorice jelly.
cards.move: A product's label can name a process that never happened to it.
cards.source: Kimura et al., J. Food Drug Anal., 2017
cards.reference: Kimura et al., Black garlic: a critical review of its production, bioactivity, and application, Journal of Food and Drug Analysis, 2017

cards.question: True or false: ordinary table sugar can join the Maillard reaction just as it is, without first breaking apart?
cards.answer: False. The reaction needs a reducing sugar, one whose reactive end is free to grab an amino acid. Sucrose locks both halves' reactive ends in the bond joining them; only once heat or acid splits it can they brown. A dough sweetened with honey darkens sooner than one with the same weight of sucrose.
cards.move: Before blaming an ingredient, check that it can take part in its current form.
cards.trap: True, since the Maillard reaction is simply sugar browning with protein.
cards.reference: Belitz, Grosch & Schieberle, Food Chemistry, 4th edition, Springer, 2009

cards.question: What links the crust on a seared steak to the slow yellowing of the eye's lens with age?
cards.answer: The same chemistry, at body heat for decades. Sugars bond to proteins' amino groups, as in the Maillard reaction, and slowly form brown, cross-linked products. Proteins at the lens's core are never replaced, so they collect them for life. Monnier and Cerami proposed in 1981 that this browning is part of ageing.
cards.move: Whatever is never replaced keeps a record of every slow reaction.
cards.reference: Monnier & Cerami, Nonenzymatic browning in vivo: possible process for aging of long-lived proteins, Science, 1981

cards.question: Dried milk, fruit and pasta slowly brown in storage. At what moisture does that browning run fastest?
options: Bone dry, with the reactants concentrated
Fully wet, as in a solution
Moderately moist, like soft dried fruit
cards.answer: Moderately moist. On the water-activity scale, 0 to 1, browning peaks around 0.6 to 0.8. Drier, the molecules cannot move to meet; wetter, they are diluted, and water, a product of the reaction, holds it back. Milk powder kept dry stays white for years; kept damp, it turns beige and loses usable lysine.
cards.move: When two forces pull opposite ways, look for the peak in between.
cards.trap: Fully wet, because chemical reactions are assumed to need a solution.
cards.reference: Labuza, The effect of water activity on reaction kinetics of food deterioration, Food Technology, 1980

cards.question: EU acrylamide rules name one ingredient that biscuit makers, baby biscuits included, should add where they can. Which?
options: An enzyme that breaks down asparagine
An antioxidant such as rosemary extract
Ammonium bicarbonate as the raising agent
cards.answer: An enzyme, asparaginase. It turns asparagine, the amino acid that becomes acrylamide during browning, into aspartic acid, which cannot. In dough it often cuts acrylamide by half or more without changing the bake. Regulation 2017/2158 lists it for biscuit makers where it works: one ingredient of the reaction is gone before the oven is lit.
cards.move: To stop an unwanted product, starve the reaction of its raw material.
cards.trap: An antioxidant, the usual remedy for anything linked to cancer.
cards.reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/2158/oj/eng

cards.question: Louis-Camille Maillard described sugars browning with amino acids in 1912. Who drew the map of it chemists still use?
cards.answer: John Hodge, a chemist at the US Department of Agriculture, in 1953. For forty years the reaction had a name and only pieces of a mechanism. Hodge, studying browning in dried foods, laid out its stages in one diagram: early bonding, a middle of fragments, late brown polymers. Chemists still teach from it.
cards.move: A name on a discovery says who noticed it, not who explained it.
cards.reference: Hodge, Dehydrated foods: chemistry of browning reactions in model systems, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 1953

cards.question: How did the arabica coffee plant come to exist as a species?
cards.answer: By an accidental cross. Coffea canephora, the robusta plant, and Coffea eugenioides mated in Ethiopian forests, and the offspring kept both parents' full sets of chromosomes, making a new species that pollinates itself. A 2024 genome study dates it to roughly 610,000 years ago. Self-pollination has kept arabica's genetic diversity narrow ever since.
cards.move: A thing that looks like one original may be two others fused.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-024-01695-w

cards.question: After Brazil, which country grows the most coffee?
cards.answer: Vietnam. It grows mostly robusta, the hardier, more bitter species used in instant coffee and blends, on the central highlands, where planting boomed from the 1990s. Its harvest is more than twice Colombia's. Robusta rarely carries a country's name on the bag, so the second-largest origin is one few drinkers could point to.
cards.move: The name printed on the label is not a measure of the volume behind it.
cards.trap: Colombia, whose name is advertised on bags and in cafés everywhere.
cards.source: USDA FAS, Coffee: World Markets and Trade
cards.reference: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, Coffee: World Markets and Trade, June 2024

cards.question: True or false: the tale of a goatherd whose goats found coffee appears in writing soon after coffee spread?
cards.answer: False. Coffee drinking is documented among Sufi communities in Yemen by the mid-1400s, but the goatherd story first appears in print in 1671, in a Latin treatise on coffee by Antoine Faustus Nairon, a Maronite scholar teaching in Rome. Two centuries separate the drink from its origin story.
cards.move: Date a story by its first telling, not by the events it describes.
cards.trap: Assuming a legend repeated everywhere must be as old as its subject.
cards.reference: Ukers, All About Coffee, The Tea and Coffee Trade Journal Company, 1922

cards.question: Why did Ceylon, once one of the world's great coffee exporters, stop growing coffee?
cards.answer: A fungus. Coffee leaf rust, Hemileia vastatrix, was recorded on the island in 1869 and stripped plantations of their leaves year after year; within about two decades exports had collapsed. Planters uprooted the bushes and put tea on the same hillsides. The island's famous tea gardens stand on ground first cleared for coffee.
cards.move: Behind a famous product, look for the crop it replaced and why.
cards.reference: McCook, Coffee Is Not Forever: A Global History of the Coffee Leaf Rust, Ohio University Press, 2019

cards.question: True or false: more than half of the world's known wild coffee species are threatened with extinction?
cards.answer: True. A 2019 assessment of all 124 known coffee species found 75 threatened, about 60%, including arabica in the wild. Nearly all coffee drunk is arabica or robusta, but wild relatives hold the genes for resisting disease and heat that breeders will need. Many survive only in shrinking patches of African and Madagascan forest.
cards.move: Judge a family by all its members, not the two that everyone meets.
cards.trap: Judging all coffee by the two species grown on every continent.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/sciadv.aav3473

cards.question: From how many coffee trees does most of the arabica grown in Latin America descend?
cards.answer: A handful, chiefly one. Dutch traders took coffee from Yemen to Java; in 1706 a Javan plant reached Amsterdam's botanical garden. A descendant given to Louis XIV in 1714 stocked the Paris hothouse; seedlings from these two founded plantations in Suriname and Martinique. That Typica line, with Bourbon from Réunion, underlies most Latin American coffee.
cards.move: When a whole region grows one plant, ask how few it started from.
cards.source: Anthony et al., Theor. Appl. Genet., 2002
cards.reference: Anthony, Combes, Astorga, Bertrand, Graziosi & Lashermes, The origin of cultivated Coffea arabica L. varieties revealed by AFLP and SSR markers, Theoretical and Applied Genetics, 2002

cards.question: Kona coffee in Hawaii grows below 1,000 m, yet rivals high-mountain coffees. What does altitude mostly stand in for?
cards.answer: Cooler temperatures that slow ripening. Arabica does best at mean temperatures of about 18 to 21 °C, and slow ripening lets beans build more sugars and acids. Near the equator that climate begins around 1,200 to 2,000 m. Kona, at about 19° north, finds it far lower: height was standing in for temperature.
cards.move: Before crediting a factor, ask what else changes along with it.
cards.trap: Crediting the height itself, as if thin air made the flavour.
cards.source: DaMatta & Ramalho, Braz. J. Plant Physiol., 2006
cards.reference: DaMatta & Ramalho, Impacts of drought and temperature stress on coffee physiology and production: a review, Brazilian Journal of Plant Physiology, 2006

cards.question: True or false: robusta, now around two-fifths of the world's coffee, was barely farmed before 1900?
cards.answer: True. Botanists described Coffea canephora, the robusta plant, from Central Africa only in the 1890s. Planters took it up after leaf rust wrecked arabica in the lowlands of Java, where the Dutch replanted with the tougher species in the early 1900s. The crop that now fills most instant coffee is younger than the motor car.
cards.move: A thing's present size says nothing about its age.
cards.trap: Assuming a crop this widespread must have an ancient history.
cards.reference: Wrigley, Coffee, Tropical Agriculture Series, Longman Scientific & Technical, 1988

cards.question: Roughly how many cups of coffee does one arabica tree yield in a year?
cards.answer: 340 g ÷ 10 g per cup = about 35 cups.
cards.move: Follow the losses step by step from the harvest to the table.
cards.trap: Picturing a whole tree as a year's supply of coffee.
cards.hint: Follow the weight from fresh cherry to roasted bean, then divide by one cup's dose.
steps: A tree gives about 2 kg of ripe cherries a year.
About a fifth of the cherry's weight ends up as green bean: 0.4 kg.
Roasting removes about 15%: roughly 0.34 kg of roasted coffee.
340 g ÷ 10 g per cup = about 35 cups.
cards.reference: Clifford & Willson (eds), Coffee: Botany, Biochemistry and Production of Beans and Beverage, Croom Helm, 1985

cards.question: Is buying Fairtrade-certified coffee an effective way to raise the incomes of the people who grow it?
cards.answer: Certified cooperatives get a guaranteed minimum price when markets crash, plus a premium for community projects. A 2014 review by Dragusanu, Giovannucci and Nunn found certified farmers often received higher prices, better access to credit and steadier incomes. Where prices can halve within a couple of years, a floor matters more than an average.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, who counts as the grower decides the answer.
cards.counterpoint: Cooperatives often sell only part of their certified coffee on Fairtrade terms, and certification costs fall on farmers. A 2014 study in Ethiopia and Uganda led by Christopher Cramer found wage workers in Fairtrade-producing areas often earned less than comparable workers elsewhere. The poorest people in coffee are hired pickers, and the label pays the landholders.
cards.reference: Dragusanu, Giovannucci & Nunn, The Economics of Fair Trade, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2014

cards.question: Where did the story that Marco Polo brought pasta home from China come from?
cards.answer: From an American trade magazine. In 1929 the Macaroni Journal, voice of the US pasta makers, ran a tale in which a sailor on Polo's voyage learns noodle-making in China. The sailor was named Spaghetti. Yet a Genoese inventory of 1279 already lists a basket of macaroni, sixteen years before Polo came home.
cards.move: Trace a charming origin story to its first printing before repeating it.
cards.source: Dickie, The Epic History of the Italians, 2007
cards.reference: Dickie, Delizia! The Epic History of the Italians and Their Food, Hodder & Stoughton, 2007

cards.question: Where does the earliest record of dried pasta made in bulk for export, from 1154, place its production?
cards.answer: Near Palermo, in Sicily. The geographer al-Idrisi, writing for the Norman king Roger II, described Trabia, where itriyya, dried strands of dough, were made in such quantity that ships carried them across the Mediterranean. Naples became the capital of macaroni only in the 1600s, when its poor switched from greens to pasta.
cards.move: The place most famous for a thing is often where it arrived later.
cards.trap: Naples owns the modern image of pasta, so it seems to own the start.
cards.reference: Serventi & Sabban, Pasta: The Story of a Universal Food, Columbia University Press, 2002

cards.question: True or false: the first printed recipe for spaghetti carbonara appeared in the United States?
cards.answer: True. The dish is first named in print in La Stampa in 1950, as a Roman favourite of American officers after the liberation. Its first known recipe came in 1952 in Vittles and Vice, a guide to Chicago restaurants, with bacon and Parmesan. Italy's La Cucina Italiana printed one in 1954, with Gruyère and garlic.
cards.move: The older a dish looks, the more worth checking its paper trail.
cards.trap: Carbonara feels Roman and ancient, so its recipe must be Italian first.
cards.reference: Cesari, Storia della pasta in dieci piatti, Il Saggiatore, 2021

cards.question: What happened when Italy's law requiring durum-wheat pasta collided with the European single market?
cards.answer: Italy lost at the border and kept the rule at home. A 1967 law let Italian dried pasta be made only from durum semolina. In 1988 the European Court of Justice ruled it could not bar soft-wheat pasta from other member states. Italian factories stayed bound; foreign packets beside theirs did not.
cards.move: A rule that stops at a border can end up binding only the home side.
cards.reference: Case 407/85, Drei Glocken GmbH and Kritzinger v USL Centro-Sud, European Court of Justice, judgment of 14 July 1988

cards.question: Roughly how many kilograms of pasta does the average Italian eat in a year?
cards.answer: 400 g x 52 weeks = about 21 kg a year.
cards.move: Build a yearly figure from one ordinary week, then multiply.
cards.trap: Picturing pasta at every meal and guessing a hundred kilos.
cards.hint: Start from the dry weight of one plate and how many plates a week.
steps: A standard portion of dry pasta is about 80 g.
Assume about 5 portions a week: 5 x 80 g = 400 g.
400 g x 52 weeks = about 21 kg a year.
cards.reference: https://internationalpasta.org/news/world-pasta-day-2024-a-billion-plates-of-pasta-in-10-years-to-feed-the-planet/

cards.question: In 1930 the Futurist Marinetti called on Italians to give up pasta. What did he urge instead, and why?
options: Rice, grown at home, not imported wheat
cards.answer: Rice, grown in the north instead of wheat bought abroad. His Manifesto of Futurist Cooking called pasta heavy, a cause of lethargy and pessimism, and promised that dropping it would free Italy from costly foreign grain. That chimed with the regime's drive for self-sufficiency in wheat. Italians went on eating pasta; the manifesto sold newspapers.
cards.move: Behind an aesthetic crusade, look for the balance of trade.
cards.trap: Meat, since Futurism worshipped war, speed and the virile body.
cards.reference: Marinetti, The Futurist Cookbook, trans. Suzanne Brill, Penguin Modern Classics, 2014

cards.question: How did Renaissance Italian recipe books usually dress a dish of macaroni?
cards.answer: With grated cheese, butter, sugar and cinnamon. Cookbooks such as Bartolomeo Scappi's of 1570 seasoned pasta as they seasoned meat, sweet and spiced, a rich man's dish. Tomatoes had barely reached Italy; the first printed pasta with tomato came from Naples in the 1830s. A Pope's cook sprinkled his macaroni like a dessert.
cards.move: Today's pairing of two foods is usually younger than either food.
cards.reference: Serventi & Sabban, Pasta: The Story of a Universal Food, Columbia University Press, 2002

cards.question: True or false: Italy's leading durum wheat for pasta in the 1980s was bred from a radiation-induced mutant?
cards.answer: True. Creso, released in 1974 by Italian state nuclear researchers, came from crossing a line that descended from irradiated Cappelli wheat, which gave it shorter, sturdier stalks. It became for years Italy's most sown durum. Mutation breeding needs no labelling, unlike genetic engineering, so much pasta sold as traditional grew from irradiated lines.
cards.move: Check how a traditional product was bred before calling it untouched.
cards.trap: False, as radiation breeding sounds like the modern tampering Italy resists.
cards.reference: Scarascia-Mugnozza, Bagnara, Bozzini et al., Mutation breeding for durum wheat improvement in Italy, Mutation Breeding Review No. 10, IAEA, 1993

cards.question: Should pasta labels have to say where the wheat in it was grown?
cards.answer: A packet with an Italian flag leads buyers to assume Italian wheat, when much of it is imported, often from Canada. Since 2018 Italy has required packets to say where the wheat was grown, if only as EU or non-EU. Farmers get a shot at a premium, and buyers who care about pesticides can choose.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether origin predicts anything measurable in the packet.
cards.counterpoint: Pasta quality comes from protein-rich wheat and the maker's skill, not a passport, and Italy grows too little durum of the needed quality to meet its own demand. Canadian durum is often among the best. Origin labels mostly work as disguised protectionism, inviting buyers to punish imported grain on a feeling rather than on any measured difference.
cards.source: Italian decree on wheat origin labelling, 2017
cards.reference: Decreto interministeriale 26 luglio 2017, indicazione dell'origine del grano duro per paste di semola di grano duro, Gazzetta Ufficiale, 2017

cards.question: Why do villages in Emilia serve free pasta every 25 July?
cards.answer: To repeat the Cervi family's feast. On 25 July 1943, when Mussolini fell, the Cervi farmers of Campegine cooked vats of pasta for their whole village. That December the seven Cervi brothers, active in the Resistance, were shot by Fascists. The pastasciutta antifascista returns each summer: a plate of noodles as a political act.
cards.move: A shared meal can carry a memory longer than any monument.
cards.source: Alcide Cervi, I miei sette figli, 1955
cards.reference: Alcide Cervi, I miei sette figli, ed. Renato Nicolai, 1955

cards.question: Which molecule gives both black pepper and some Syrah wines their peppery smell?
cards.answer: Rotundone, a sesquiterpene that Australian wine researchers identified as a potent aroma in 2008. Peppercorns hold about 10,000 times more of it than a peppery Shiraz. One taster in five on their panel could not smell it even at the highest dose: the same glass is spiced for some and plain for others.
cards.move: Before arguing about a smell, check that both noses can detect it.
cards.source: Wood et al., J. Agric. Food Chem., 2008

cards.question: True or false: medieval cooks used pepper chiefly to hide the taste of meat going off?
cards.answer: False. Pepper was dearer than meat, so anyone who could buy it could buy fresh meat, and bad meat was a hazard that town authorities policed. Recipes spiced fresh fish and game alike. Pepper was prized as flavour, medicine and display, and rents were sometimes paid in it.
cards.move: Price out a story before accepting the thrifty motive it assumes.
cards.trap: No fridges, strong spice: the explanation seems to fit itself.
cards.reference: Freedman, Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination, Yale University Press, 2008

cards.question: Which country ships more black pepper abroad than any other?
cards.answer: Vietnam. It grew about a third of the world's pepper in 2022 and supplied nearly three-fifths of all exports from producing countries. Planting took off in the 1990s on the red basalt soils of the Central Highlands. India, pepper's home, now eats most of what it grows.
cards.move: A place famous for a product may no longer be where it comes from.
cards.trap: The Malabar coast owns the history, so it seems to own the trade.
cards.reference: https://www.ipcnet.org/country/vietnam/

cards.question: Where does the oldest known peppercorn found outside India come from?
cards.answer: From the nose of Ramesses II. When the pharaoh was embalmed after his death in 1213 BC, black peppercorns were packed into his nostrils, probably to keep the nose in shape. Pepper then grew only in southern India, so the seeds had crossed thousands of kilometres of sea and desert to reach a royal corpse.
cards.move: A single seed in the wrong place can map a whole trade route.
cards.reference: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pepper/

cards.question: What does the tingle of Sichuan pepper feel like to the nerves it triggers?
cards.answer: A vibration of about 50 taps a second. London researchers put the ground husks on volunteers' lips in 2013 and had them match the tingle to a vibrating finger pad: they chose around 50 hertz, the range of light-touch nerve fibres. The spice fools the sense of touch, not of taste or heat.
cards.move: A sensation can be measured by matching it to one you can dial.
cards.source: Hagura et al., Proc. R. Soc. B, 2013
cards.reference: Hagura, Barber & Haggard, Food vibrations: Asian spice sets lips trembling, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2013

cards.question: True or false: a green peppercorn turns black mainly through its own enzymes, not through scorching by the sun?
cards.answer: True. Drying breaks the berry's cells, and an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, then oxidises a phenolic compound in the skin into dark pigments, much as a cut apple browns. Growers dip berries in hot water for a minute to crack the cells and speed it. Green peppercorns are made by killing that enzyme first.
cards.move: What happens during a process is not always what the process does.
cards.trap: The berries blacken while lying in the sun, so the sun gets credit.
cards.reference: doi:10.3390/molecules23020370

cards.question: What gives some white pepper its faint smell of a cowshed?
cards.answer: Skatole and p-cresol, the compounds that scent manure. White pepper is made by soaking ripe berries for days until the skins rot off, and bacteria in that soak make both. German chemists found them topping the odour list of faulty powders in 2005. The seed is washed white; the smell stays.
cards.move: A cleaning step can leave its own mark on what it cleans.
cards.source: Steinhaus & Schieberle, J Agric Food Chem, 2005
cards.reference: Steinhaus & Schieberle, Characterization of odorants causing an atypical aroma in white pepper powder (Piper nigrum L.) based on quantitative measurements and orthonasal breakthrough thresholds, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2005

cards.question: In Pliny's Rome, around AD 77, which pepper cost the most per pound?
cards.answer: Long pepper, at 15 denarii a pound, against 7 for white and 4 for black. It came from a different plant, Piper longum, whose catkin-like fruit Romans valued most. It later faded from European kitchens and is now a specialist's curiosity, while black pepper, the cheap one, conquered the table.
cards.move: Today's staple may have been yesterday's budget option.
cards.trap: White pepper, since it costs more than black in shops today.
cards.reference: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Books 12–16, trans. H. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1945

cards.question: Why can an English contract still be made binding by a single peppercorn?
cards.answer: Because English courts ask whether something was given in exchange, not whether it was worth enough. In 1959, in Chappell v Nestlé, the House of Lords held that chocolate wrappers binned on receipt counted, and remarked that a peppercorn stays good payment to someone who dislikes pepper. Leases still charge one peppercorn a year.
cards.move: A court that refuses to weigh a price leaves the bargain to the bargainers.
cards.source: Chappell v Nestlé, House of Lords, 1960
cards.reference: Chappell & Co Ltd v Nestlé Co Ltd, House of Lords, [1960] AC 87, 1959

cards.question: Two airtight jars of the same ground black pepper: one in a cupboard, one on a sunny sill. After months, the sill jar is…?
options: Just as hot as the other
cards.answer: Noticeably less pungent. Piperine, the molecule that bites, has double bonds that light can twist into other shapes, isomers such as chavicine and isochavicine, which bite far less. A lid keeps out air and moisture, not light. Chemists tracked the twist in ground pepper in 2007: clear glass on a bright shelf slowly blunts it.
cards.move: Before trusting a seal, ask which enemy it actually shuts out.
cards.trap: Just as hot, because airtight storage is what keeps spices fresh.
cards.source: J Agric Food Chem, 2007, piperine isomers
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17661483/

cards.question: True or false: the blight strain that ruined Ireland's potatoes in the 1840s is the one farmers still fight today?
cards.answer: False. In 2013 researchers sequenced blight DNA from potato leaves pressed in herbaria during the famine years. The famine strain, which they named HERB-1, differs from US-1, the lineage long blamed, and from modern strains; it was displaced during the 20th century. Its last traces sat for over a century in museum drawers.
cards.move: The culprit still at large may not be the one that did the damage.
cards.trap: Assuming the strain around today is the one that struck then.

cards.question: How did Prussia's king push reluctant peasants to grow potatoes in the 1750s?
cards.answer: By decree, again and again. Frederick II's circular of 24 March 1756 told Silesian officials to have potatoes planted on spare ground and to teach people to eat them, and similar orders followed for years. The tale of guards posted to tempt thieves is later legend. The famine of 1770 to 1772 finished the job.
cards.move: Where a crop spreads by order, look for the hunger that made it stick.
cards.reference: Earle, Feeding the People: The Politics of the Potato, Cambridge University Press, 2020

cards.question: How did Andean farmers make potatoes keep for years, centuries before refrigeration?
cards.answer: By freeze-drying them outdoors. Above 3,500 metres, potatoes are left to freeze on clear nights and thaw in the sun by day; people then tread on them to squeeze out the water. After a few cycles the result, chuño, is light, hard and keeps for years, which let Inca storehouses feed armies.
cards.move: Where the climate is harsh, look for the process that uses the harshness.
cards.reference: Reader, Potato: A History of the Propitious Esculent, Yale University Press, 2009

cards.question: Roughly how many kilograms of potatoes did an adult Irish labourer eat each day before the famine?
cards.answer: 4,000 / 0.7 = about 5,700 g, near 6 kg a day.
cards.move: Divide a day's energy by what one gram supplies to size any diet.
cards.trap: Picturing a plateful or two, about 1 kg.
cards.hint: Start from the energy a day of heavy field work burns.
steps: Heavy field work by hand burns about 4,000 kcal a day.
Almost all of it came from potatoes, with a little buttermilk.
Boiled potatoes give about 0.7 kcal per gram.
4,000 / 0.7 = about 5,700 g, near 6 kg a day.
cards.reference: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory, Princeton University Press, 1999

cards.question: By one careful estimate, what share of Old World population growth between 1700 and 1900 did the potato explain?
cards.answer: About a quarter. Nunn and Qian compared regions whose soil and climate suited potatoes with regions that did not, before and after the crop arrived. Suitable regions grew faster once it spread, enough to explain roughly a quarter of the growth in population and cities across Europe, Asia and Africa over two centuries.
cards.move: Compare the places a change could reach with those it could not.
cards.trap: Letting Ireland's vivid potato-fed boom stand for the whole Old World.
cards.source: Nunn & Qian, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2011
cards.reference: Nunn & Qian, The Potato's Contribution to Population and Urbanization: Evidence from a Historical Experiment, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2011

cards.question: Europe's first potatoes, brought from the Andes, cropped poorly for generations. What chiefly held them back?
options: Peasants' suspicion of the new crop
They formed tubers only as days shortened
cards.answer: Day length. Andean potatoes evolved near the equator, where days stay near 12 hours, and set tubers only when nights grow long. Under Europe's 16-hour summer days they made leaves until autumn, when frost cut the crop short. Herbarium DNA shows Chilean types, already suited to long days, spreading through Europe in the 1800s.
cards.move: Before blaming people for rejecting a tool, check whether the tool worked.
cards.trap: Peasant suspicion, the story every history of the potato tells.
cards.source: Ames & Spooner, American Journal of Botany, 2008
cards.reference: Ames & Spooner, DNA from herbarium specimens settles a controversy about origins of the European potato, American Journal of Botany, 2008

cards.question: How did Andean people eat wild potatoes too bitter and toxic to eat plain?
cards.answer: With a dip of clay. Wild potatoes carry far more glycoalkaloids, the bitter toxins of green potato skins, than modern ones. Aymara cooks served them with a slurry of edible clay, and Timothy Johns showed in the lab that such clays bind the toxins. Dinner came with its own antidote.
cards.move: An odd custom that has lasted for centuries may be doing a hidden job.
cards.reference: Johns, Detoxification function of geophagy and domestication of the potato, Journal of Chemical Ecology, 1986

cards.question: An Irish family in 1846 planted potatoes in ten plots scattered across their townland. How much did scattering protect them?
options: About half the plots, by chance
cards.answer: Almost not at all. Blight spores ride wind and rain for kilometres, so every plot in a townland met the same attack, and no potato grown in Europe then resisted it; the Lumper, the poor's main variety, rotted readily. Scattering guards against hail or flood, which strike one spot. Against blight, ten fields are one.
cards.move: Spreading a bet helps only if the risks do not travel together.
cards.trap: About half, as if each plot were a separate throw of the dice.
cards.reference: Bourke, The Visitation of God? The Potato and the Great Irish Famine, Lilliput Press, 1993

cards.question: Ireland counted 7.8 million people in 1831, 8.2 million in 1841, 6.6 million in 1851. Had 1830s growth continued, how many millions were missing?
cards.answer: 8.6 - 6.6 = 2.0 million missing.
cards.move: Measure a loss against the path things were on, not the starting point.
cards.trap: Answering 1.6 million, the plain drop between two censuses.
cards.hint: First find the growth over the 1830s as a ratio, then carry it one decade further.
steps: Growth in the 1830s: 8.2 / 7.8 = about 1.05 per decade.
Expected in 1851: 8.2 x 1.05 = about 8.6 million.
8.6 - 6.6 = 2.0 million missing.

diagram.caption: The 1830s trend pointed to 8.6 million in 1851; the census found 6.6. Two million missing.

cards.reference: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory, Princeton University Press, 1999

cards.question: True or false: an Irish famine a century before the Great Famine may have killed a larger share of the people?
cards.answer: True. In the Great Frost of 1739–40 potatoes froze in the ground and in storage pits, and a cold, wet year followed.
