Estimates put deaths in 1740–41 at 13% to 20% of about 2.4 million people, against roughly 12% in 1845–52. Irish speakers called it Bliain an Áir, the year of slaughter.
cards.move: The disaster everyone remembers is not always the worst of its kind.
cards.trap: False, since the 1840s famine is the one every history names.
cards.reference: Dickson, Arctic Ireland: The Extraordinary Story of the Great Frost and Forgotten Famine of 1740-41, White Row Press, 1997

cards.question: Midway through a roast, coffee beans begin to pop audibly. What causes this first crack?
options: Steam and gas splitting the bean
cards.answer: Steam and gas splitting the bean. Thick cell walls hold in water vapour and the carbon dioxide made by browning reactions, so pressure inside builds to several atmospheres. At around 200 °C in the bean, the structure fractures with a crack and the bean swells. Roasters time the rest of the roast from that sound.
cards.move: Two changes that arrive together may share a cause rather than cause each other.
cards.trap: Browning and cracking arrive together, so the browning seems to cause the crack.
cards.reference: Clarke & Vitzthum (eds.), Coffee: Recent Developments, Blackwell Science, 2001

cards.question: Why do bags of freshly roasted coffee beans carry a small one-way valve?
cards.answer: Because the beans keep exhaling. Roasting traps carbon dioxide in the bean, which seeps out for days and would swell a sealed bag. Leaving beans open to degas lets in the oxygen that stales them. The valve, introduced by the Italian packager Goglio in the 1960s, lets gas out and no air in.
cards.move: When a product must breathe out, stop it breathing in.
cards.reference: https://www.gcrmag.com/goglio-leads-the-pack-a-history-of-innovation-in-coffee-packaging/

cards.question: Green coffee costs €8 a kilo, and a dark roast loses 20% of the weight. What does a roasted kilo cost, in euros?
cards.move: A loss taken off the end must be divided back, not added on.
cards.trap: Adding 20% to the price and landing on €9.60.
cards.hint: Work out how much green coffee has to go into the roaster to get one roasted kilo out.
steps: 1 kg of green beans roasts down to 0.8 kg.
One roasted kilo needs 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 kg of green beans.
cards.reference: https://library.sweetmarias.com/how-to-calculate-weight-loss-in-coffee-roasting/

cards.question: Should coffee sold in California carry a cancer warning because roasting creates acrylamide?
cards.answer: Roasting creates acrylamide, which causes cancer in animals and is classed as a probable human carcinogen. California's law puts the burden on sellers to show a listed chemical poses no significant risk, and in 2018 a court ruled the coffee industry had not shown it. Buyers are entitled to know.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, judging the chemical or the whole drink decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The drink matters, not one molecule in it. In 2016 the WHO's cancer agency moved coffee out of its possible carcinogen group after reviewing over 1,000 studies, several of which linked it to lower liver and womb cancer risk. California agreed in 2019 and exempted coffee. A warning on everything teaches people to ignore warnings.

cards.question: Before the 1860s, who did the roasting for most American coffee drinkers?
cards.answer: They did, at home. Roasted beans went stale fast, so grocers sold coffee green and households roasted it in skillets. In 1868 John Arbuckle patented a glaze of egg and sugar that sealed roasted beans against air, and sold them in one-pound paper packages called Ariosa. The kitchen roaster retired with the frontier.
cards.move: Ask what had to be solved before a chore could leave the house.
cards.reference: Pendergrast, Uncommon Grounds: The History of Coffee and How It Transformed Our World, Basic Books, 1999

cards.question: Which vitamin is nearly absent from green coffee beans but made in quantity by roasting them?
cards.answer: Niacin, vitamin B3. Green beans hold about 1% trigonelline, a bitter alkaloid; roasting heat strips a methyl group from it, leaving nicotinic acid, which is niacin. Light roasts carry about 10 mg per 100 g, very dark Italian roasts about 40 mg. A cup from 10 g of dark beans holds a few milligrams.
cards.move: Processing can create a nutrient as well as destroy one.
cards.source: Adrian & Frangne, Adv. Exp. Med. Biol., 1991
cards.reference: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4899-2626-5_4

cards.question: Why can two coffees roasted to the same outside colour taste completely different?
cards.answer: Because colour is skin-deep. A fast, hot roast darkens the surface while the core lags, leaving a bean browned outside and underdeveloped inside, grassy and sour. A slower roast lets heat reach the centre. Roasters grind a sample and compare its colour with the whole bean's; a wide gap means the inside never caught up.
cards.move: When the outside changes fastest, judge a thing by its inside.
cards.reference: Rao, The Coffee Roaster's Companion, self-published, 2014

cards.question: A medium roast leaves beans about 15% lighter than they went in. What is most of the missing weight?
options: Water already in the green bean
Oils and chaff lost as smoke
cards.answer: Water already in the green bean. Green coffee is dried to about 11% moisture before shipping, and roasting drives nearly all of it off. Carbon dioxide, water made by browning reactions and other volatiles make up the few per cent left. The smoke pouring from a roaster is dramatic but light.
cards.move: The loss you can see is rarely the loss that weighs most.
cards.trap: Picturing the smoke and chaff as where the weight goes.
cards.reference: Clarke & Macrae (eds), Coffee, Volume 1: Chemistry, Elsevier Applied Science, 1985

cards.question: What gives a very dark roast most of its harsh, lingering bitterness?
cards.answer: Breakdown products of chlorogenic acids. Green beans are rich in these acids; roasting turns them first into lactones with a sharp bitterness, then, in dark roasts, into phenylindanes with a harsher, lingering one. Caffeine supplies only a small share of coffee's bitterness, which is why a decaffeinated dark roast still tastes bitter.
cards.move: The best-known suspect is not always the one doing most of the work.
cards.trap: Blaming caffeine, the one bitter molecule everyone has heard of.
cards.reference: Blumberg, Frank & Hofmann, Quantitative studies on the influence of the bean roasting parameters and hot water percolation on the concentrations of bitter compounds in coffee brew, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2010

cards.question: True or false: a very dark roast coffee usually holds less acrylamide than a light roast?
cards.answer: True. Acrylamide forms early in roasting, from the amino acid asparagine and sugars, and peaks within the first minutes. As the roast goes on, it is destroyed faster than it forms, so dark roasts end with less. Stored coffee keeps losing it slowly. The blackest beans are not the ones carrying the most.
cards.move: What forms along the way can also be used up along the way.
cards.trap: Assuming a darker, more burnt bean must carry more of a toxin.
cards.reference: Bagdonaite, Derler & Murkovic, Determination of acrylamide during roasting of coffee, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2008

cards.question: Why has no saffron crocus ever been grown from its own seed?
cards.answer: Because it is a sterile triploid, with three sets of chromosomes, and sets no viable seed. Every plant is a clone, multiplied from underground corms. A 2019 genetic study traced the crop to wild Crocus cartwrightianus near Athens: fields from Kashmir to La Mancha grow copies of one ancient plant.
cards.move: Where every plant is a copy, one disease can meet no resistance.
cards.source: Nemati et al., Mol. Phylogenet. Evol., 2019
cards.reference: Nemati et al., Saffron (Crocus sativus) is an autotriploid that evolved in Attica (Greece) from wild Crocus cartwrightianus, Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution, 2019

cards.question: Roughly how many crocus flowers must be picked by hand to make one gram of dried saffron?
cards.answer: 1,000 mg / 6.6 mg = about 150 flowers.
cards.move: Price a luxury by counting the hands that touch each gram.
cards.trap: Picturing a gram as a pinch from a handful of flowers.
cards.hint: Count the threads in one flower, then ask what a single dried thread weighs.
steps: Each flower carries 3 red stigmas, the only part kept.
3 stigmas x about 2.2 mg dried = about 6.6 mg per flower.
1,000 mg / 6.6 mg = about 150 flowers.
cards.reference: Kafi, Koocheki, Rashed & Nassiri (eds), Saffron (Crocus sativus): Production and Processing, Science Publishers, 2006

cards.question: True or false: saffron's colour dissolves far more readily in water than in oil?
cards.answer: True. Its pigment, crocin, comes from a carotenoid, the fat-soluble family of carrots and paprika, but it carries sugar groups at both ends that make it dissolve in water. That is why saffron is steeped in warm water or stock: a risotto turns gold, while oil stirred with saffron stays nearly clear.
cards.move: Check how a colour dissolves before choosing the liquid to carry it.
cards.trap: Assuming saffron behaves like paprika, whose red runs into fat.
cards.reference: Rubio Moraga, Nohales, Fernández Pérez & Gómez-Gómez, Glucosylation of the saffron apocarotenoid crocetin by a glucosyltransferase isolated from Crocus sativus stigmas, Planta, 2004

cards.question: Which country grows the great majority of the world's saffron?
cards.answer: Iran. Estimates of its share run from about 80% to over 90% of a world harvest of a few hundred tonnes, much of it from Khorasan, where some fields are still watered by qanats, underground channels centuries old. Spain, whose name sells saffron at a premium, exports far more than it grows.
cards.move: Ask where a product is grown, not where it was last packed.
cards.trap: La Mancha labels are the famous ones, so Spain seems the source.
cards.reference: https://www.fao.org/giahs/giahs-around-the-world/iran-qanat-based-saffron-system/en

cards.question: How does the international standard for saffron decide which grade a jar deserves?
cards.answer: By shining light through an extract. ISO 3632 measures how strongly a solution absorbs at three wavelengths: 440 nanometres for crocin, the colour; about 257 for picrocrocin, the bitterness; about 330 for safranal, the aroma. Top grade needs a colouring reading of at least 200. The thread's look counts far less than a spectrometer's needle.
cards.move: A grade is only as honest as the measurement that sets it.
cards.reference: ISO 3632-2:2010, Spices — Saffron (Crocus sativus L.) — Part 2: Test methods, 2010

cards.question: True or false: a saffron thread picked this morning smells far weaker than the same thread dried?
cards.answer: True. The famous smell, safranal, barely exists in the living flower. The stigma's own enzymes split it off a bitter molecule, picrocrocin, once drying heat reaches them, and the change goes on for weeks in the jar. Toasting threads over embers or in ovens makes the aroma as much as it keeps it.
cards.move: Some qualities are made by the processing, not saved from the harvest.
cards.trap: False, since drying always drives off the volatile oils that carry aroma.

cards.question: What did the famous Minoan fresco of a saffron gatherer at Knossos turn out to show?
cards.answer: A blue monkey. Arthur Evans's restorers pieced the fragments together soon after 1900 as a boy picking crocuses, giving him a human head. Later scholars noticed that Minoan painters coloured monkeys blue, never people, and that the fragments held a tail. The figure is now read as a monkey gathering flowers in a crocus field.
cards.move: A reconstruction shows what the restorer expected as much as what was found.
cards.reference: Immerwahr, Aegean Painting in the Bronze Age, Pennsylvania State University Press, 1990

cards.question: Saffron is graded by how strongly an extract absorbs blue light at 440 nm. Which cheap additive fools that test best?
cards.answer: Gardenia fruit extract. The fruit of Gardenia jasminoides makes many of the same crocin pigments as saffron, so the reading rises exactly as real saffron would make it rise. Synthetic dyes have their own check in the standard. Catching gardenia needs chromatography hunting for geniposide, a compound saffron never makes.
cards.move: A test that confirms the right ingredient cannot say whose it is.
cards.trap: Tartrazine, since a laboratory dye seems the most sophisticated forgery.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29622218/

cards.question: Pooled trials suggest saffron eases mild depression. What chiefly keeps psychiatrists cautious?
options: The effects found were too small
The trials were small, from one country
It was never tested against placebo
cards.answer: The trials were small and nearly all run in Iran, many by one research network. Pooled, they show effects close to standard antidepressants, larger than a herb usually earns. Reviews rate the certainty low because a few dozen patients per arm, from one setting, cannot show whether the result travels to other clinics.
cards.move: A strong result from one place is a lead, not yet a finding.
cards.trap: Too small an effect, the usual failing of herbal remedies.

cards.question: What has traditionally dyed the brownish-orange robes of Thai forest monks?
cards.answer: Jackfruit heartwood. Monks chip the wood, boil it into a dye and soak the cloth again and again, so each robe's shade drifts with the tree. Saffron, dearer per gram than silver, was never a dye for men living on alms. The robes are called saffron for their colour, as oranges name a shade.
cards.move: A colour's name is a comparison, not a list of ingredients.
cards.trap: Saffron threads, because the robes are known by that name.
cards.reference: https://www.abhayagiri.org/tales/2-two-making-robes

cards.question: Pasta water salted at 10 g per litre: by how many °C does its boiling point rise?
cards.move: Before crediting an ingredient with an effect, size the effect.
cards.trap: Believing salted water boils hotter enough to cook pasta faster.
cards.hint: Salt weighs 58.4 g per mole and splits in two; count particles, then use water's boiling constant, 0.512 °C per mole per kg.
steps: 10 g / 58.4 g per mole = 0.171 mol of salt in 1 kg of water.
Each unit splits into 2 ions: 0.171 x 2 = 0.342 mol of particles.
Each mole of particles per kg lifts water's boiling point 0.512 °C.
cards.reference: Atkins & de Paula, Atkins' Physical Chemistry, 8th edition, Oxford University Press, 2006

cards.question: A pinch of salt makes bitter grapefruit taste sweeter. What is the salt doing?
options: Silencing the bitterness that hid the sweetness
Drawing sugar out of the fruit's cells
Switching on the tongue's sweet receptors
cards.answer: Silencing the bitterness that hid the sweetness. Sodium ions suppress bitterness, and since bitter and sweet mask each other, removing one frees the other. Breslin and Beauchamp showed in 1997 that salt raised the sweetness of a bitter-sweet mixture without any added sugar. A pinch in bitter coffee works the same way.
cards.move: An improvement can come from removing a mask, not adding anything.
cards.trap: Salt draws out water, so it seems to draw out sugar too.
cards.reference: Breslin & Beauchamp, Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness, Nature, 1997

cards.question: How does soaking meat in salt water make it juicier after cooking, rather than drier?
cards.answer: Salt loosens the meat's protein scaffolding. Chloride ions bind to the filaments inside muscle fibres and push them apart, so the lattice swells and holds more water. Offer and Trinick watched single fibrils swell in brine under a microscope in 1983. A brined chicken breast enters the oven heavier than it left the butcher.
cards.move: Look for what the treatment does to structure, not only to water.
cards.reference: Offer & Trinick, On the mechanism of water holding in meat: the swelling and shrinking of myofibrils, Meat Science, 1983

cards.question: Why can almost no bacteria grow in saturated brine, though it is mostly water?
cards.answer: Because its water is held, not free. Microbes need water they can take up, measured as water activity, 0 to 1. Most bacteria stop below about 0.91, Staphylococcus aureus near 0.86; saturated brine sits near 0.75, so cells lose water instead of gaining it. Only salt-loving microbes thrive, and they turn salt ponds pink.
cards.move: Ask how much of a resource is usable, not how much is present.
cards.reference: Jay, Loessner & Golden, Modern Food Microbiology, 7th edition, Springer, 2005

cards.question: Should governments push the whole population's salt intake down, rather than only that of people at risk?
cards.answer: Blood pressure rises with salt across the whole population, and many strokes strike people whose readings count as normal. Small cuts for millions prevent more deaths than big cuts for a few. England cut average intake from about 9.5 g to 8.1 g a day in 2003–2011, largely by reformulating bread and processed food.
cards.move: The fight turns on whether a low-intake danger zone really exists.
cards.counterpoint: The benefit is proven in people with high blood pressure and high intake; for the rest it is inferred. A study of over 100,000 people in 17 countries found risk lowest between about 3 and 6 g of sodium a day, where most people already sit, and rising below it. Push everyone down and some will overshoot.
cards.reference: He, Pombo-Rodrigues & MacGregor, Salt reduction in England from 2003 to 2011: its relationship to blood pressure, stroke and ischaemic heart disease mortality, BMJ Open, 2014

cards.question: In a five-year trial across 600 Chinese villages, salt with a quarter swapped for potassium chloride changed deaths how?
cards.answer: About an eighth fewer. The 2021 trial followed about 21,000 older villagers with past strokes or high blood pressure. Those given the 75:25 blend had 14% fewer strokes and 12% fewer deaths than those on ordinary salt, with no rise in dangerous potassium levels. Villagers kept cooking as before; the shaker did the work.
cards.move: Change the default ingredient and a whole population's habit changes with it.
cards.trap: More deaths, since extra potassium can stop a weak heart.
cards.reference: Neal et al., Effect of salt substitution on cardiovascular events and death, New England Journal of Medicine, 2021

cards.question: Some large cohorts find people who eat the least salt die sooner. What do critics chiefly suspect?
options: Low-salt diets run short of iodine
Sick people eat less, salt included
Low salt harms the heart directly
cards.answer: Sick people eat less, salt included. Frail, ill and dieting people eat less of everything, so a low salt reading can mark illness rather than cause it. Many cohorts also judged intake from one urine sample, which swings day to day. The low end of the curve fills with the unwell.
cards.move: When the sick do less of something, doing less of it looks deadly.
cards.trap: Harm to the heart directly, the reading the curve seems to show.
cards.source: Cobb et al., Circulation, AHA advisory, 2014
cards.reference: Cobb et al., Methodological issues in cohort studies that relate sodium intake to cardiovascular disease outcomes: a science advisory from the American Heart Association, Circulation, 2014

cards.question: Why can two boxes both labelled kosher salt differ almost twofold in saltiness per spoonful?
cards.answer: Crystal shape. Diamond Crystal grows hollow, flaky pyramids in open pans; Morton rolls dense cubes into flat flakes. A teaspoon of the first weighs about 3 g, of the second about 5, and both are nearly pure sodium chloride. A recipe tested with one and cooked with the other comes out oversalted or bland.
cards.move: Measure by weight whenever the shape of the thing varies.
cards.reference: Nosrat, Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat: Mastering the Elements of Good Cooking, Simon & Schuster, 2017

cards.question: Why was salt, rather than bread or milk, chosen to carry iodine into diets?
cards.answer: Because nearly everyone eats a steady few grams a day in every season and class, and it comes from a handful of producers. Dosing a few salt works beats policing thousands of bakers. Switzerland began in 1922; WHO advises 20 to 40 mg of iodine per kilogram of salt. The shaker became a medicine.
cards.move: To reach everyone, pick the thing everyone already uses in the same amount.
cards.reference: WHO, UNICEF & ICCIDD, Assessment of iodine deficiency disorders and monitoring their elimination, 3rd edition, World Health Organization, 2007

cards.question: A ready meal's label lists 1.2 g of sodium. What percentage of WHO's 5 g daily salt limit is that?
cards.move: Check what a label counts before comparing it with a limit.
cards.trap: Reading 1.2 g as salt and answering 24%.
cards.hint: Salt is sodium chloride: sodium is only part of its weight.
steps: Sodium is 23 of the 58.5 units of weight in salt, so salt = sodium x 2.5.
1.2 g sodium x 2.5 = 3 g of salt.

diagram.caption: 1.2 g of sodium is 3 g of salt: 60% of the day's limit, not 24%.

cards.reference: World Health Organization, Guideline: Sodium intake for adults and children, WHO, 2012

cards.question: What best predicts which microbes end up living in a sourdough starter?
cards.answer: Not the city it lives in. A 2021 study of 500 starters, most from the United States, found little geographic pattern in their bacteria and yeasts: starters from one town differed as much as starters from different continents. Rise speed and aroma tracked instead with acetic acid bacteria, a group bakers had largely overlooked.
cards.move: Test a local legend by sampling widely before crediting the place.

cards.question: In a mature sourdough starter, which are more numerous: the yeasts or the bacteria?
cards.answer: The bacteria, by far. Lactic acid bacteria typically outnumber the yeasts 10 to 100 to one, at hundreds of millions of cells per gram. The bigger yeasts make most of the gas that lifts the loaf; the bacteria make its acids. Under a microscope, each scattered yeast cell sits in a crowd of tiny rods.
cards.move: The loudest worker in a team is rarely the most numerous one.
cards.source: Minervini et al., Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 2012
cards.reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3273004/

cards.question: True or false: French law lets a loaf sold as pain au levain contain some baker's yeast?
cards.answer: True. A 1993 decree allows baker's yeast up to 0.2% of the flour's weight, added only at the final mixing. The bread must instead prove its sourness chemically: a pH no higher than 4.3 and at least 900 parts per million of acetic acid in the crumb. The label is a laboratory test.
cards.move: Read how a label is defined in law before assuming what it excludes.
cards.trap: Assuming a protected sourdough label must forbid added yeast entirely.
cards.reference: https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000000727617/

cards.question: In wholemeal sourdough, what does most of the work of breaking down phytate, the bran compound that locks up minerals?
cards.answer: The wheat's own enzymes. Bran carries phytase, an enzyme that dismantles phytate best in mildly acid dough. In a 2005 trial, dough brought to about pH 5.5 lost roughly 70% of its phytate whether soured by a starter or by plain lactic acid; unsoured dough lost about 40%. The microbes supply acid; the grain cuts.
cards.move: Before crediting the newcomer, see what the old ingredients do under the same conditions.
cards.trap: Crediting the bacteria because they are the celebrated part of sourdough.
cards.source: Leenhardt et al., J. Agric. Food Chem., 2005

cards.question: Each day a starter, begun at 100 g, is fed its weight in flour and its weight in water, never discarded. Tonnes after 10 days?
cards.answer: That is about 5.9 tonnes.
cards.move: When something is multiplied each round, count the rounds before trusting a guess.
cards.trap: Adding 200 g a day and getting 2.1 kg instead of multiplying.
cards.hint: Each feed adds twice the starter's weight, so work out what it is multiplied by each day.
steps: Each day the starter triples: 100 g becomes 300 g.
Ten days: 3 to the power 10 = 59,049.
That is about 5.9 tonnes.

diagram.caption: Tripling from 100 g: 219 kg after a week, then 5.9 tonnes three days later.

cards.reference: Hamelman, Bread: A Baker's Book of Techniques and Recipes, Wiley, 2004

cards.question: Why do the yeast and the bacteria in a San Francisco-style sourdough starter not fight over its sugar?
cards.answer: They eat different sugars. The bacterium named after the city, Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis, feeds on maltose, the sugar flour enzymes cut from starch, and releases part of it as glucose. Its usual partner, the yeast Kazachstania humilis, cannot use maltose at all, so it lives on that spilt glucose. One diner's leftovers are the other's meal.
cards.move: Two rivals sharing one place may simply be eating different things.
cards.reference: Gänzle, Vermeulen & Vogel, Carbohydrate, peptide and lipid metabolism of lactic acid bacteria in sourdough, Food Microbiology, 2007

cards.question: A baker wants a sharper, more vinegary sourdough. Which change tilts its acids towards acetic acid?
cards.answer: A stiffer starter kept cool. Warm, wet dough speeds lactic acid most, so heat and water mainly add mild, yogurt-like sourness. Cool, firm dough slows lactic acid more than acetic acid, the sharp acid of vinegar, and the balance shifts towards it. Bakers set a loaf's tang with the starter's water and the thermostat.
cards.move: When one source makes two products, ask which one each condition favours.
cards.trap: Assuming warmth and moisture make every kind of sourness stronger.
cards.source: Gobbetti & Gänzle, Handbook on Sourdough Biotechnology
cards.reference: Gobbetti & Gänzle (eds), Handbook on Sourdough Biotechnology, Springer, 2013

cards.question: True or false: a well-fermented sourdough made from ordinary wheat flour is safe for people with coeliac disease?
cards.answer: False. Ordinary sourdough fermentation breaks down only a little of the gluten. The hopeful headlines trace to Italian trials in which selected bacteria plus fungal enzymes digested wheat for hours, bringing gluten below 10 parts per million, and patients tolerated it. A bakery loaf stays thousands of times above the 20 ppm gluten-free limit.
cards.move: Before trusting a result, check that the thing tested is the thing sold.
cards.trap: Stretching a specially processed trial loaf to every sourdough on sale.
cards.source: Greco et al., Clin. Gastroenterol. Hepatol., 2011
cards.reference: Greco, Gobbetti, Auricchio et al., Safety for patients with celiac disease of baked goods made of wheat flour hydrolyzed during food processing, Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, 2011

cards.question: Fresh dough sits near pH 6.0 and a ripe sourdough near 4.0. How many times more hydrogen ions does the sourdough hold?
cards.answer: 10 × 10 = 100 times more.
cards.move: On a scale of powers, a small step in the number is a giant change.
cards.trap: Reading a fall from 6 to 4 as a third more acidic.
cards.hint: Each whole step on the pH scale is a multiplication, not an addition.
steps: pH counts hydrogen ions on a scale of powers of ten.
6.0 − 4.0 = 2 steps on that scale.
10 × 10 = 100 times more.

diagram.caption: pH 6 to pH 4 feels like a small step; it is a hundred times the hydrogen ions.

cards.source: De Vuyst & Neysens, Trends in Food Science
cards.reference: De Vuyst & Neysens, The sourdough microflora: biodiversity and metabolic interactions, Trends in Food Science & Technology, 2005

cards.question: Should only bread raised by a live starter be allowed to call itself sourdough?
cards.answer: Supermarket loaves sold as sourdough can be ordinary yeasted bread soured with vinegar, acid powders or dried sourdough flavouring, made in hours. Buyers pay extra for a long fermentation that changes flavour, texture and keeping, and cannot see it on the shelf. Two days of honest fermentation compete on price with three hours.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether a process can be policed on the shelf decides it.
cards.counterpoint: A legal definition must fix numbers for acidity, hours and permitted yeast, and every number shuts out honest bakers whose methods differ while large firms engineer loaves to the letter. Enforcing it means laboratory tests whose cost lands on small bakeries. Ingredient lists already show added yeast and acids to anyone who cares to read them.
cards.reference: Whitley, Bread Matters: The State of Modern Bread and a Definitive Guide to Baking Your Own, Fourth Estate, 2006

cards.question: Around 1704 the average Briton ate under 2 kg of sugar a year. By 1900, roughly how much?
cards.answer: About 40 kg. Sidney Mintz's figures run from under 2 kg a head in 1704 to about 8 kg in 1800 and 40 kg in 1900, a twentyfold rise. Cheap Caribbean sugar, then beet, turned a luxury of the rich into calories for the poor: sweetened tea and jam on bread fuelled factory hands.
cards.move: When a starting figure is tiny, expect guesses about the end to stay tiny too.
cards.trap: Starting from 2 kg, a doubling or two feels like plenty.
cards.reference: Mintz, Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History, Viking, 1985

cards.question: Of the Africans carried across the Atlantic as slaves, roughly what share landed in what became the United States?
cards.answer: About 4%, some 390,000 of more than 10 million who survived the crossing. Most went to the sugar colonies of Brazil and the Caribbean, where cane work killed people faster than they had children, so planters kept buying more. Jamaica alone received far more Africans than all of mainland North America.
cards.move: The history told most often is not always the largest share of it.
cards.trap: American slavery is the story most told, so it seems the biggest.

diagram.caption: Of every hundred who survived the crossing, about four reached the future United States.

cards.reference: Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade, Yale University Press, 2010

cards.question: How did Europe start making sugar without tropical cane?
cards.answer: From a root chemists had studied for decades. Andreas Marggraf found in 1747 that beet held the same sugar as cane; his pupil Franz Achard opened the first beet-sugar factory in Silesia in 1801. When Britain cut France off from Caribbean sugar, Napoleon ordered beet planted in 1811. Blockade turned a curiosity into northern fields.
cards.move: A dormant invention often waits for a shortage to become an industry.
cards.reference: Abbott, Sugar: A Bittersweet History, Duckworth, 2008

cards.question: What did internal sugar-industry papers from the 1960s reveal about a landmark review on diet and heart disease?
cards.answer: That the industry paid for it. In 1965 the Sugar Research Foundation paid two Harvard nutritionists about $6,500 to review the evidence; their 1967 review, in a leading medical journal, played down sugar and blamed dietary fat. The funding went undisclosed. Researchers published the letters in 2016, half a century after the debate was framed.
cards.move: Before weighing a review, find out who asked for it and paid.
cards.source: Kearns, Schmidt & Glantz, JAMA Intern. Med., 2016
cards.reference: Kearns, Schmidt & Glantz, Sugar industry and coronary heart disease research: a historical analysis of internal industry documents, JAMA Internal Medicine, 2016

cards.question: Should governments tax sugary drinks to cut how much sugar people consume?
cards.answer: Britain's levy, announced in 2016 and charged from 2018, taxed drinks by sugar content, and makers cut the sugar before it began: sugar in taxed drinks fell by a third or more. Researchers later linked it to fewer obese girls aged 10 and 11. A tax that changes recipes reaches people who never read labels.
cards.move: Ask whether the gain came from the price or from the recipe change.
cards.counterpoint: Such taxes take a larger share of poorer households' budgets, and the evidence on body weight is thin: studies find small, uneven effects, and sugar can come back through sweets and food. Britain's gains came from reformulation, which a direct limit on sugar per litre could have required without taxing anyone.
cards.reference: Rogers et al., Associations between trajectories of obesity prevalence in English primary school children and the UK soft drinks industry levy, PLOS Medicine, 2023

cards.question: True or false: the Sugar Act of 1764, which angered American colonists, raised the duty on foreign molasses?
cards.answer: False. It halved it, from sixpence a gallon under the 1733 Molasses Act to threepence. But the old duty had been dodged for thirty years through smuggling and bribed customs men, so almost nobody paid it. The new act came with inspectors and courts. New England's rum distillers faced a real bill at last.
cards.move: Compare a new rule with what people actually paid, not with the old paper.
cards.trap: True, since a tax that caused protest must have gone up.
cards.source: Morgan & Morgan, The Stamp Act Crisis, 1953
cards.reference: Morgan & Morgan, The Stamp Act Crisis: Prologue to Revolution, University of North Carolina Press, 1953

cards.question: The US tariff of 1890 let all foreign raw sugar in duty-free. What did that do to Hawaii's sugar planters?
options: Barred their sugar from US ports
cards.answer: It erased their special advantage. Since an 1875 treaty, Hawaiian sugar alone had entered the US free; now everyone's did, and American growers got a bounty of two cents a pound besides. Hawaiian prices slumped. Annexation would make the islands domestic, bounty and all. In 1893 planters' allies overthrew the queen.
cards.move: A privilege given to everyone is a privilege taken from someone.
cards.trap: Enriched them, since duty-free entry sounds like a gift to exporters.
cards.source: Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom, Volume III, 1967
cards.reference: Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom, Volume III: 1874-1893, The Kalakaua Dynasty, University of Hawaii Press, 1967

cards.question: A German visitor saw Elizabeth I's black teeth in 1598. What did he blame, and whose habit did he think it was?
cards.answer: Sugar, and he thought it an English failing, not only hers. Paul Hentzner saw the ageing queen at Greenwich and called black teeth a defect the English seemed prone to from too much sugar. Sugar was then a costly import for the rich, eaten as sweetmeats and moulded table sculptures. Decay began at court.
cards.move: A disease of plenty begins at the top of the table.
cards.reference: Mintz, Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History, Viking, 1985

cards.question: Roughly how many tonnes of sugar cane must be cut and crushed to make one tonne of sugar?
cards.answer: 1 / 0.11 = about 9 tonnes of cane per tonne of sugar.
cards.move: The heavier the raw material, the closer the factory must sit to it.
cards.trap: Guessing two or three tonnes, as if cane were mostly sugar.
cards.hint: Start from how much of a cane stalk is sucrose, then allow for what the mill loses.
steps: Cane is roughly 13% sucrose by weight.
Mills recover about 85% of it: 0.13 x 0.85 = about 0.11 t of sugar per tonne of cane.
1 / 0.11 = about 9 tonnes of cane per tonne of sugar.
cards.source: Hugot, Handbook of Cane Sugar Engineering
cards.reference: Hugot, Handbook of Cane Sugar Engineering, 3rd edition, Elsevier, 1986

cards.question: What did it cost a British family in 1791 to stop eating slave-grown sugar?
cards.answer: Money as well as pleasure. Abolitionists reckoned some 300,000 people gave up West Indian sugar after William Fox's pamphlet urged it. The alternative, East Indian sugar grown without slaves, paid a higher import duty, because Parliament shielded its Caribbean colonies. Grocers advertised the dearer sugar as free-grown. Conscience came with a surcharge set by law.
cards.move: Find who set the price of the ethical choice.
cards.reference: Hochschild, Bury the Chains: Prophets and Rebels in the Fight to Free an Empire's Slaves, Houghton Mifflin, 2005

cards.question: Why do baker's yeast factories drip molasses into their aerated tanks bit by bit instead of all at once?
options: Too much sugar would kill the yeast
Rich sugar makes yeast brew alcohol
Molasses would foam over the tanks
cards.answer: Rich sugar makes yeast brew alcohol. Even with plenty of air, baker's yeast switches to fermenting when sugar is abundant, spending it on ethanol instead of new cells. Factories therefore feed molasses gradually, keeping sugar so scarce that the yeast burns it with oxygen and multiplies. The product is cells, not beer.
cards.move: If a machine wastes fuel when rich, feed it lean on purpose.
cards.trap: Picturing sugar as a poison at high doses, as in jam.
cards.source: Van Hoek et al., Appl. Environ. Microbiol., 1998
cards.reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC106631/

cards.question: What keeps a loaf rising in a hot oven after its yeast has died?
cards.answer: Physics. Yeast speeds up as the dough warms, then dies at around 60 °C, minutes into the bake. The rest of the oven spring comes from dissolved carbon dioxide leaving solution, trapped gas expanding, and water and alcohol turning to vapour. It stops when the crust sets hard enough to fix the loaf's size.
cards.move: When the engine stops, look for momentum still doing the work.
cards.reference: Cauvain (ed.), Technology of Breadmaking, 3rd edition, Springer, 2015

cards.question: What does the yeast eat in a dough of only flour, water, salt and yeast?
cards.answer: Sugar cut from starch by the flour's own enzymes. Milling cracks some starch granules, and amylases already in the grain snip them into maltose, which yeast then takes up. Millers measure this enzyme activity and often add malted flour to top it up. With too little, the dough rises sluggishly and the crust bakes pale.
cards.move: Ask who prepares the food before crediting whoever eats it.
cards.source: Delcour & Hoseney, Principles of Cereal Science, 2010
cards.reference: Delcour & Hoseney, Principles of Cereal Science and Technology, 3rd edition, AACC International, 2010

cards.question: True or false: sugar can be fermented into alcohol with no living yeast cell present?
cards.answer: True. In 1897 Eduard Buchner ground yeast with sand, pressed out its juice, and found that the cell-free liquid still turned sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Fermentation was the work of molecules the cell makes, later called enzymes. It earned him the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and opened the field of biochemistry.
cards.move: Always seeing two things together does not show that one needs the other.
cards.trap: Every fermentation ever seen had living yeast in it, so life seemed required.
cards.reference: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1907/summary/

cards.question: Where did the yeast species behind bread, beer and wine first come from?
cards.answer: Probably China. A 2018 study sequencing 1,011 strains found the most varied wild lineages of the species on trees in Chinese forests, and traced the domesticated ones to a single migration out of that region. The strains in a baker's packet are branches of a family whose roots grow in East Asian woodland.
cards.move: Look for where a family is most varied to find where it began.

cards.question: Why can dough made with old or badly stored dried yeast turn slack and sticky, not merely slow?
cards.answer: Dead yeast cells leak glutathione, a small sulphur-bearing molecule that cuts the sulphur bridges linking gluten proteins into a stretchy network, so the dough loosens and tears. Drying always kills some cells, and warmth, air and damp kill more in storage. Inactive yeast is sold on purpose to relax stiff pizza doughs.
cards.move: A dead ingredient is not an absent one: it can still act.
cards.source: Pyler & Gorton, Baking Science and Technology
cards.reference: Pyler & Gorton, Baking Science and Technology, 4th edition, Sosland Publishing, 2008

cards.question: Why does a brioche dough rich in sugar rise more slowly than a plain one made with the same yeast?
cards.answer: Sugar pulls water out of the yeast. A concentrated sugar solution draws water across the cell's membrane, so the cells shrink and slow down. Past about 5 to 10% sugar on flour weight, ordinary yeast lags. Suppliers sell osmotolerant strains for sweet doughs: cells that pile up glycerol inside to hold on to their water.
cards.move: Past a point, more of the food can starve the eater of something else.
cards.reference: Cauvain & Young, Baked Products: Science, Technology and Practice, Blackwell Publishing, 2006

cards.question: Yeast makes the gas that raises bread. Where do the loaf's bubbles themselves begin?
cards.answer: In air pockets from mixing. Carbon dioxide dissolves in the dough's water and cannot easily start a new bubble; it diffuses into the tiny air cells folded in during kneading. Yeast only inflates them. Baker and Mize showed in 1941 that dough mixed under a vacuum gives a dense, poorly risen loaf.
cards.move: Where something grows depends on where it can start, not on who feeds it.
cards.trap: Picturing each yeast cell blowing a little bubble of its own.
cards.reference: Baker & Mize, The origin of the gas cell in bread dough, Cereal Chemistry, 1941

cards.question: True or false: by weight, a rising bread dough makes more alcohol than carbon dioxide?
cards.answer: True. Yeast splits each glucose molecule into two of ethanol and two of carbon dioxide. Ethanol weighs 46 units a molecule, carbon dioxide 44, so 180 g of glucose yields about 92 g of alcohol and 88 g of gas. The gas shows; the alcohol mostly boils off in the oven.
cards.move: The product nobody sees may outweigh the one everybody watches.
cards.trap: Counting only the product that visibly lifts the dough.
cards.source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry
cards.reference: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 7th edition, W. H. Freeman, 2017

cards.question: Roughly how many yeast cells are in a 7 g sachet of dried baker's yeast, in billions?
cards.answer: 7 g ÷ 35 trillionths of a gram = about 200 billion cells.
cards.move: When the parts are too small to see, count them by weight.
cards.trap: Guessing millions, because a sachet holds only a spoonful.
cards.hint: Start from the size of one cell, then what it weighs once dried.
steps: A baker's yeast cell is about 6 µm across: roughly 110 cubic micrometres.
At about the density of water, one living cell weighs some 110 trillionths of a gram.
Drying leaves about a third of that: roughly 35 trillionths of a gram.
7 g ÷ 35 trillionths of a gram = about 200 billion cells.
cards.source: Milo & Phillips, Cell Biology by the Numbers
cards.reference: Milo & Phillips, Cell Biology by the Numbers, Garland Science, 2015

cards.question: Is there a human fingerprint on the ice cores before industry?
cards.answer: There is a dip. Atmospheric CO2 fell in the early 1600s, and the timing matches the collapse of the Americas' population after 1492. Tens of millions of hectares of farmland reverted to forest, and the regrowth pulled down enough carbon to show up in ice.
cards.move: A population collapse is visible in the ice, two centuries before the factories.
cards.source: Koch et al., Quaternary Science Reviews, 2019
cards.reference: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis, Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews, 2019

cards.question: How do you date something from the last seventy years?
cards.answer: By the bomb. Atmospheric nuclear testing from 1955 to 1963 nearly doubled carbon-14 in the air, then it declined on a known curve. Anything alive during that window carries a datable signature, accurate to a year or two — used on forged paintings, wine and human remains.
cards.move: Nuclear testing accidentally left the world a precise clock.
cards.reference: Levin & Kromer, The tropospheric 14CO2 level in mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (1959-2003), Radiocarbon, 2004

cards.question: What killed soldiers in the nineteenth century?
cards.answer: Disease, not the enemy — by a wide margin in most campaigns. Florence Nightingale's real achievement was statistical: she invented diagrams that made the ratio impossible to argue with, because the officials who could change things would not read a table.
cards.move: She is remembered for the lamp. The argument was won with a chart.
cards.source: Nightingale, Notes on Matters Affecting the Health of the British Army, 1858

cards.question: When was aluminium a luxury metal?
cards.answer: In the 1850s. It is one of the commonest elements in the crust but was brutally hard to separate, so it cost more than gold — Napoleon III is said to have reserved aluminium cutlery for his most important guests. A new electrolytic process collapsed the price within about a decade.
cards.move: Aluminium went from imperial cutlery to disposable foil in one lifetime.

cards.question: Where did modern finance and science actually meet?
cards.answer: In coffee houses. Seventeenth-century London called them "penny universities": the price of entry bought conversation. Lloyd's insurance market began in one, newspapers grew out of them, and scientific societies used them as informal meeting rooms before they had buildings.
cards.move: Lloyd's of London started as a coffee shop with good shipping gossip.
cards.source: Ellis, The Coffee House: A Cultural History, 2004

cards.question: How did the Palermo rising of January 1848, the first of that year's revolutions, begin?
cards.answer: By appointment. Posters went up three days early announcing a rising for 12 January, the birthday of King Ferdinand II, himself born in Palermo. The rising came on the day, drove Bourbon troops from most of Sicily and won 16 months of self-rule, six weeks before Paris rose.
cards.move: A date announced in public turns private discontent into common knowledge.
cards.reference: Rapport, 1848: Year of Revolution, Little, Brown, 2008

cards.question: In March 1848, France's electorate of about 250,000 men was widened overnight. To roughly how many?
cards.answer: About 9 million. The provisional government gave the vote to every man aged 21 or over, and in April over three-quarters of them voted. In December the new electorate gave Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte about 74% of the presidential vote; in 1851 he overthrew the Republic by coup.
cards.move: Estimate from the new rule, not from the old number.
cards.trap: Stretching the known 250,000 by a few times, not thirty-fold.
cards.reference: Agulhon, The Republican Experiment, 1848–1852, Cambridge University Press, 1983

cards.question: What did the supposedly failed revolutions of 1848 permanently win in the Austrian Empire?
cards.answer: The end of serfdom. Most people there were peasants, and their revolts drew more people than the national uprisings. In September 1848 the Vienna parliament, on Hans Kudlich's motion, abolished compulsory labour dues, and the restored monarchy kept the reform. Freed peasants then had little reason to fight on.
cards.move: Grant a group its main demand and it may leave the coalition.
cards.reference: Sperber, The European Revolutions, 1848–1851, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2005

cards.question: How did slavery end in the Danish West Indies in 1848?
cards.answer: In an afternoon, by revolt. On 3 July 1848, with thousands of enslaved people massed at Frederiksted, St Croix, under a leader called General Buddhoe, Governor-General Peter von Scholten proclaimed immediate emancipation, overriding Denmark's plan to phase slavery out by 1859. It followed France's abolition in its Caribbean colonies that spring.
cards.move: Gradual timetables are set by those who can afford to wait.
cards.source: Hall, Slave Society, Danish West Indies, 1992
cards.reference: Hall, Slave Society in the Danish West Indies: St Thomas, St John and St Croix, ed. Higman, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1992

cards.question: True or false: the Communist Manifesto, published in February 1848, helped inspire that month's revolution in Paris?
cards.answer: False. It was printed in German in London in the same week the Paris crowds rose, in a small run for a small émigré league, and few in Paris could have read it. It reached a mass readership only from the 1870s. Both it and the revolution sprang from the same hungry, restless decade.
cards.move: Two events at the same time may share a cause rather than cause each other.
cards.trap: Same month, famous text: it is natural to assume one caused the other.
cards.source: Sperber, Karl Marx: A Nineteenth-Century Life, 2013
cards.reference: Sperber, Karl Marx: A Nineteenth-Century Life, Liveright, 2013

cards.question: Where in Europe did 1848 produce a new federal state that still stands, and what war came first?
cards.answer: Switzerland. After a civil war of under four weeks in November 1847, which killed about a hundred men, the winning liberal cantons turned a loose league into a federal state with a two-chamber parliament partly modelled on the American Congress. Totally revised in 1874 and 1999, that federal state of 1848 still governs Switzerland.
cards.move: Judge a revolution by what was built afterwards, not only by what fell.
cards.source: Church & Head, A Concise History of Switzerland
cards.reference: Church & Head, A Concise History of Switzerland, Cambridge University Press, 2013

cards.question: Why did the Czech historian František Palacký refuse, in April 1848, to help prepare the German national parliament at Frankfurt?
cards.answer: Because he was no German, and feared a German nation-state. Palacký replied that he was a Czech of Slav descent, and argued that a reformed, federal Austria was the best shield for the small peoples of central Europe against Russia and a united Germany. In June he presided over a Slav Congress in Prague instead.
cards.move: One people's national unity can look like annexation to its neighbours.
cards.source: Sked, Decline and Fall of the Habsburg Empire
cards.reference: Sked, The Decline and Fall of the Habsburg Empire, 1815–1918, Longman, 1989

cards.question: True or false: the National Workshops of Paris in 1848 put Louis Blanc's plan for workers' cooperatives into practice?
cards.answer: False. Blanc wanted self-governing social workshops; the National Workshops were public relief under the minister of public works, Marie, no friend of Blanc's, paying men to dig and level ground. Enrolment passed 100,000 by June. Their closure that month set off the June Days, and Blanc took blame for a scheme he had disowned.
cards.move: A borrowed name can hide a very different design.
cards.trap: Matching the name to Blanc's famous call to organise labour.
cards.reference: Price, The French Second Republic: A Social History, Batsford, 1972

cards.question: The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 is nicknamed the parliament of professors. What was its largest occupational group?
cards.answer: Civil servants, judges and officials. They formed the biggest block of its roughly 800 members, with lawyers next; university professors numbered a few dozen, prominent in debate and in memoirs. Businessmen were few, and artisans and peasants almost absent. It was first of all a parliament of the German states' own employees.
cards.move: The loudest members of a group are rarely a fair sample of it.
cards.trap: Trusting a nickname built on the members who made the speeches.
cards.reference: Siemann, The German Revolution of 1848–49, Macmillan, 1998

cards.question: The Chartists said their petition of April 1848 carried 5.7 million signatures. Roughly how many did Commons clerks count?
cards.answer: About 2 million. The clerks counted 1,975,496 names and found many invented or joking entries, such as Victoria Rex and Punch, which the press mocked for years. Yet nearly 2 million names was still a vast petition. The ridicule of the padding buried the size of the real support.
cards.move: When a claim is exposed as padded, measure what remains before dismissing it.
cards.trap: Staying near the claimed 5.7 million because it was the only figure given.
cards.reference: Chase, Chartism: A New History, Manchester University Press, 2007

cards.question: Were the railways Britain built in India, on balance, good for Indians?
cards.answer: Railways cut the cost of moving goods across a subcontinent. Studies of district records find that places joined to the network traded more and saw real farm incomes rise. Before the lines, a drought meant local famine; afterwards grain could come in, and droughts killed fewer people. Whoever paid, the tracks outlasted the Raj.
cards.move: The hinge is what India would have built, and at what cost, without Britain.
cards.counterpoint: The lines were built for British purposes and billed to Indians. Private companies were guaranteed a 5% return, paid from Indian taxes when profits fell short, and routes ran to ports and garrisons, carrying raw cotton out and British goods in. Millions still died in the famines of 1876–78 and 1896–1900, with trains moving grain towards whoever could pay.
cards.reference: Donaldson, Railroads of the Raj: Estimating the Impact of Transportation Infrastructure, American Economic Review 108, 2018

cards.question: Around 1900, India under British rule held nearly 300 million people. Roughly how many men made up its elite Indian Civil Service?
cards.answer: About 1,000. In 1901 the service had only about a thousand members, some of them always on leave. It could govern nearly 300 million people only through Indian clerks, police, soldiers and landholders, and through princes who ran their own states: roughly one covenanted officer for every 300,000 subjects.
cards.move: Divide the governed by the governors before imagining an empire's machinery.
cards.trap: About 300,000, scaling a vast bureaucracy to 300 million people.

diagram.caption: About 1,000 officers for nearly 300 million people: one for every 300,000.

cards.reference: Gilmour, The Ruling Caste: Imperial Lives in the Victorian Raj, John Murray, 2005

cards.question: True or false: Britain's 99-year lease of 1898 covered Hong Kong Island?
cards.answer: False. Hong Kong Island was ceded outright in 1842, and the tip of the Kowloon peninsula in 1860, both in perpetuity. The 1898 lease covered only the New Territories, but they held most of the colony's land. Britain saw no way to run the ceded parts alone, so in 1997 all of it went back.
cards.move: A famous deadline can apply to only part of what it seems to govern.
cards.trap: True, because the famous lease is why Hong Kong was returned.
cards.source: Welsh, A History of Hong Kong, 1993
cards.reference: Welsh, A History of Hong Kong, HarperCollins, 1993

cards.question: What did enslaved people in the British Caribbean get when slavery was abolished in 1834?
cards.answer: More unpaid work. Under the 1833 Act, most freed people over six became apprentices, bound to work up to 45 hours a week for their former owners, without wages, for four to six more years. The owners received £20 million, about 40% of the Treasury's yearly income. Protest ended apprenticeship early, in 1838.
cards.move: Read the transition clauses before celebrating the date a law took effect.
cards.reference: Draper, The Price of Emancipation: Slave-Ownership, Compensation and British Slave Society at the End of Slavery, Cambridge University Press, 2010

cards.question: What did Britain use to replace enslaved labour on its sugar colonies after 1834?
cards.answer: Indentured Indians. In 1834 Britain chose Mauritius for what it called the great experiment: workers bound by contract for years instead of owned. Between 1834 and 1920 almost half a million landed at one depot in Port Louis, the Aapravasi Ghat; others were shipped on to the Caribbean and Africa.
cards.move: When one system of labour is abolished, look at what replaced it.
cards.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Aapravasi Ghat
cards.reference: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1227/

cards.question: What did the Indian census of 1901 provoke by ranking castes in order of social precedence?
cards.answer: A flood of petitions. Herbert Risley, the census commissioner, had castes listed by precedence, and caste associations wrote in to claim higher places, often as Brahmins or Kshatriyas, the priestly and warrior orders. A count meant to describe society gave people reasons to organise around its categories. The census taker became a judge of status.
cards.move: Rank people on a list and they will compete for the list.
cards.reference: Dirks, Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India, Princeton University Press, 2001

cards.question: In the 1870s and 1880s, roughly what share of British India's government revenue came from opium?
cards.answer: About a sixth, varying by year. After land tax, opium was the Raj's biggest revenue: the state held a monopoly on the poppy in Bengal and taxed opium from the princely states of western India, mostly for China. A drug China had fought two wars to keep out helped pay for governing India.
cards.move: To judge what a government depends on, read its revenue table.
cards.trap: Treating opium as a side trade beside land, cotton and tea.
cards.reference: Richards, The Indian Empire and Peasant Production of Opium in the Nineteenth Century, Modern Asian Studies 15, 1981, 59-82

cards.question: True or false: the British Empire reached its greatest extent after the First World War?
cards.answer: True. The peace settlement gave Britain League of Nations mandates over former German and Ottoman lands, among them Tanganyika, Palestine, Transjordan and Iraq, so it was largest in the early 1920s, covering about a quarter of the world's land. Southern Ireland left at the same moment. The widest map was drawn as the edges frayed.
cards.move: The peak of a thing's size is rarely the peak of its strength.
cards.trap: Picturing the Victorian heyday as the moment of greatest size.
cards.reference: Darwin, The Empire Project: The Rise and Fall of the British World-System, 1830-1970, Cambridge University Press, 2009

cards.question: True or false: as independence approached, British colonial officials were told to destroy or ship home embarrassing files?
cards.answer: True. From the late 1950s, officials in colony after colony were ordered to burn or remove papers that might embarrass Britain. Thousands of removed files, including records of the Kenya Emergency, sat unlisted at Hanslope Park until 2011, when a High Court case brought by Kenyan claimants forced them into view.
cards.move: An archive is what someone decided to keep, not what happened.
cards.trap: Assuming the archives left behind are a complete record.
cards.reference: Anderson, Guilty Secrets: Deceit, Denial, and the Discovery of Kenya's Migrated Archive, History Workshop Journal 80, 2015

cards.question: Estimate the population of the British Empire around 1921, Britain and Ireland included, in millions.
cards.answer: 320 + 47 + 90 = about 457 million.
cards.move: Estimate a whole by finding its biggest part first.
cards.trap: Picturing an empire of settlers and leaving India till last.
cards.hint: Start with the largest single part, then add everything else.
steps: India, by its 1921 census: about 320 million.
Britain and Ireland: about 47 million.
Dominions, African and other colonies: roughly 90 million.
320 + 47 + 90 = about 457 million.
cards.reference: Marten, Census of India, 1921, Volume I: India, Part I, Report, Government of India, 1924

cards.question: Building sandstone crushes under 40,000 kilonewtons per square metre and weighs 20 per cubic metre. How tall, in km, could a column rise?
cards.answer: 40,000 / 20 = 2,000 metres, which is 2 km.
cards.move: When a strong structure fails, suspect its shape before its material.
cards.trap: Guessing a few hundred metres, as if cathedrals strained their stone.
cards.hint: Each metre of height adds 20 kilonewtons on every square metre of the base.
steps: Each metre of column adds 20 kN on each square metre of its base.
40,000 / 20 = 2,000 metres, which is 2 km.
cards.simply: Stack 2,000 one-metre cubes of sandstone: only then does the bottom cube begin to crush. The highest Gothic vault, at Beauvais, is 48 m.
cards.source: Heyman, Ingenia, Royal Academy of Engineering
cards.reference: https://www.ingenia.org.uk/articles/why-ancient-cathedrals-stand-up-the-structural-design-of-masonry/

cards.question: How did the builders who finished Cologne Cathedral in 1880 know the medieval design?
cards.answer: From a drawing found in an attic. Work stopped around 1473, leaving a wooden crane on the half-built south tower until 1868. In 1814 half of the medieval façade plan, a parchment about 4 m tall, turned up in a Darmstadt inn; the other half surfaced in Paris in 1816.
cards.move: Unfinished work can wait centuries if the plan survives.
cards.reference: https://www.guide.freies-deutsches-hochstift.de/en/mediaguide/romantik-ausstellung/3-obergeschoss/im-bilde-vollendet/wand-reproduktion/

cards.question: Why does Beauvais Cathedral, with the highest Gothic vault ever built, have no nave?
cards.answer: Its builders kept overreaching. The 48 m choir vault fell in 1284 and was rebuilt with extra piers. Then, instead of a nave, they raised a 153 m crossing tower, finished in 1569; it fell in 1573. The money never recovered, and a 10th-century church still stands where the nave should be.
cards.move: Look at what was never built to see what the ambition cost.
cards.reference: https://cathedrale-beauvais.fr/en/historical-overview-of-beauvais-cathedral/

cards.question: True or false: the iron staples inside Notre-Dame de Paris can be dated by radiocarbon?
cards.answer: True. Medieval iron was smelted with charcoal, and a little of the charcoal's carbon stays in the metal, carrying its radiocarbon age. After the 2019 fire, six of twelve sampled staples were dated this way; the oldest were set in the 1160s, in the first building phase. Several thousand bind Notre-Dame's stones.
cards.move: Ask where a material's ingredients came from before ruling out a test.
cards.trap: False, since radiocarbon only dates things that were once alive.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0280945

cards.question: Fire destroyed most of Chartres Cathedral in 1194. Roughly how long did rebuilding its main body take?
cards.answer: About 25 years. The fire of 1194 left the west towers, the façade between them and the crypt; the new cathedral was largely complete by about 1220, a 26-year campaign. Money poured in from across France, and the builders kept one design throughout, which is why Chartres looks all of a piece.
cards.move: The famous slow cases are remembered because they were slow.
cards.trap: About 300 years, since famous cathedrals took centuries to finish.
cards.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Chartres Cathedral
cards.reference: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/81/

cards.question: What job do the heavy stone pinnacles on top of Gothic buttresses do?
cards.answer: They add weight. A stone vault pushes outwards as well as down, and that thrust runs through the flying buttress into the pier. A heavy pinnacle loading the pier's top bends the path of the thrust downwards, keeping it inside the masonry, where stone works squeezed rather than pulled apart. The ornament is ballast.
cards.move: Sometimes the answer to a sideways push is more weight on top.
cards.reference: Heyman, The Stone Skeleton: Structural Engineering of Masonry Architecture, Cambridge University Press, 1995

cards.question: A masonry arch stands firmly. Rebuilt at twice the size, in the same stone and proportions, does it still stand?
options: No, it crushes under its own weight
Yes, if its proportions are kept
cards.answer: Yes, if its proportions are kept. Doubling the size doubles the stress, but in a cathedral stress is a small fraction of what stone can bear, so crushing never decides. What decides is whether the line of thrust stays inside the masonry, which depends on shape alone. That is why medieval rules of proportion worked.
cards.move: Ask whether size or shape decides failure before scaling anything up.
cards.trap: Reasoning that bigger structures always fail under their own weight.
cards.reference: Heyman, The stone skeleton, International Journal of Solids and Structures 2, 1966, 249-279

cards.question: In 1339 Siena began a vast new nave that would have turned its cathedral into a transept. What became of it?
options: Completed in the 1500s after long pauses
Finished on a smaller scale by 1400
Abandoned in 1357, its walls left standing
cards.answer: Abandoned in 1357, its walls left standing. The plague of 1348 had taken much of Siena's workforce and wealth, and the new work had shown structural faults. The city stopped, pulled down unsafe parts and kept its old cathedral. The unfinished façade wall, the facciatone, still stands beside it, open to the sky.
cards.move: What is already built is not a reason to build the rest.
cards.trap: Assuming a city that had spent so much would finish the job.
cards.reference: Norman, Siena and the Virgin: Art and Politics in a Late Medieval City State, Yale University Press, 1999

cards.question: Who did most of the building work on the Gothic cathedrals of England and France?
options: Serfs owed labour to the bishop
cards.answer: Paid masons, carpenters and labourers. Fabric accounts, such as Exeter's rolls from 1279, list the wages paid each week beside stone, lime and timber. Crowds did haul carts of stone at Chartres in the 1140s, and letters hailed it as a wonder. The everyday work ran on a payroll.
cards.move: Account books describe the ordinary; chronicles describe the unusual.
cards.trap: Recalling chronicles of crowds dragging carts to the building site.
cards.reference: Erskine (ed.), The Accounts of the Fabric of Exeter Cathedral, 1279-1353, Devon and Cornwall Record Society, 1981

cards.question: Why do giant inverted arches stand in the crossing of Wells Cathedral?
cards.answer: They are a fourteenth-century emergency repair. After the central tower was raised in the early 1300s, the added weight made the crossing piers settle and crack. From 1338 the master mason William Joy inserted scissor arches, braces shaped like an X, on three sides of the crossing. They look like design; they are a splint.
cards.move: What looks like style is sometimes a repair everyone got used to.
cards.reference: Colchester (ed.), Wells Cathedral: A History, Open Books, 1982

cards.question: Few clothes worn by 18th-century English labouring women survive in museums. What is the likeliest reason?
options: Their clothes were worn to rags
Laws kept them in flimsy cloth
cards.answer: Their clothes were worn to rags. A gown was a poor family's capital: altered, handed down, pawned, then sold to the rag trade for paper. What survives was too fine to wear out. Ordinary dress lives on in some 5,000 fabric scraps pinned to the admission papers of babies left at London's Foundling Hospital.
cards.move: What was used up leaves no trace; absence is not proof of lack.
cards.trap: Reading the empty museum shelf as proof the poor had nothing.
cards.reference: Styles, Threads of Feeling: The London Foundling Hospital's Textile Tokens, 1740–1770, Foundling Museum, 2010

cards.question: True or false: from 1722 it was illegal in Britain to wear clothes of printed cotton calico?
cards.answer: True. To protect wool and silk weavers, who had torn calico gowns off women in the streets, the Calico Act banned wearing any printed, painted, stained or dyed calico from Christmas 1722. It stood until 1774. Behind it, Manchester learned to print its own cotton-and-linen cloth, which was exempted in 1736.
cards.move: Protection for an old trade can become the nursery of its rival.
cards.trap: Britain's cotton fame makes a ban on wearing cotton seem absurd.
cards.reference: Lemire, Fashion's Favourite: The Cotton Trade and the Consumer in Britain, 1660–1800, Oxford University Press, 1991

cards.question: Why were men's shirt collars once sold separately from the shirt?
cards.answer: To save washing. The collar soiled first, so in the 1820s Hannah Montague of Troy, New York, cut her husband's off to wash and starch it alone. Troy built an industry on detachable collars, and in 1864 its collar laundresses formed one of America's first all-women unions, winning a 25% rise.
cards.move: Where cleaning is costly, things get designed to be cleaned in parts.
cards.source: Turbin, Working Women of Collar City, 1992
cards.reference: Turbin, Working Women of Collar City: Gender, Class, and Community in Troy, New York, 1864–86, University of Illinois Press, 1992

cards.question: What did Edo Japan's rich merchants do when the law barred them from showy silks?
cards.answer: They made restraint the luxury. Sumptuary edicts barred townsmen from the most splendid fabrics, so merchants and kabuki actors set a new taste, iki, prizing subtlety. The display moved inward: sober colours and fine stripes outside, lavish silk linings within.
cards.move: Ban a display and the display moves somewhere the ban cannot reach.
cards.source: Shively, Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies, 1964
cards.reference: Shively, Sumptuary Regulation and Status in Early Tokugawa Japan, Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies, vol. 25, 1964–65

cards.question: What made the British textile firm Courtaulds rich before it turned to artificial silk?
cards.answer: Grief. Its fortune was black silk crape, the dull crinkled cloth of Victorian mourning, which etiquette kept widows in for a year or more. By 1850 its Essex mills employed over 2,000 people. As mourning dress went out of fashion, the firm needed a new product, and in 1904 bought the viscose patents.
cards.move: Every social rule is also somebody's order book.
cards.reference: Coleman, Courtaulds: An Economic and Social History, vol. 1: The Nineteenth Century: Silk and Crape, Clarendon Press, 1969

cards.question: Where did a Victorian labourer's Sunday suit usually spend Monday to Saturday?
cards.answer: At the pawnbroker's. Families pledged their best clothes on Monday for a few shillings to see out the week, and redeemed them on Saturday, after payday, to wear on Sunday. Clothing made up a large share of all pledges, and the weekly interest was the price of looking respectable one day in seven.
cards.move: Where credit is scarce, anything that holds its value becomes a bank.
cards.reference: Tebbutt, Making Ends Meet: Pawnbroking and Working-Class Credit, Leicester University Press, 1983

cards.question: True or false: the red coats of ordinary British soldiers in the 1700s were dyed with cochineal, the costly insect red?
cards.answer: False. Private soldiers' coats were mostly dyed with madder, a cheaper plant red that came out brick-coloured and faded towards brown or pink on campaign. Cochineal gave the bright scarlet of officers' coats, which they bought from their own tailors. The vivid red of battle paintings is usually an officer's.
cards.move: Ask whose clothes were painted and kept before picturing everyone's.
cards.trap: Picturing the scarlet of officers' portraits, the coats that were painted and kept.
cards.reference: Greenfield, A Perfect Red: Empire, Espionage, and the Quest for the Color of Desire, HarperCollins, 2005

cards.question: Florence's sumptuary law of 1343 banned many luxurious gowns. How could a woman keep one she already owned?
options: By wearing it only at home
By cutting it to a legal style
By paying to have it sealed
cards.answer: By paying to have it sealed. Officials inspected forbidden garments, entered each in a register and marked it with an official seal once the owner paid a fee; unsealed gowns drew fines. The law raised money as well as restraining display, and its register survives as an inventory of Florentine wardrobes, gown by gown.
cards.move: A ban you can pay your way out of is a tax.
cards.trap: Assuming a ban must mean altering the gown, not paying for it.
cards.reference: Killerby, Sumptuary Law in Italy 1200–1500, Clarendon Press, 2002

cards.question: When the sewing machine cut the time to stitch a shirt several-fold after 1850, what happened to home seamstresses' pay per shirt?
options: It fell, as piece rates were cut
It rose, as each woman made more
It held steady, fixed by custom
cards.answer: It fell, as piece rates were cut. More shirts per hour meant more shirts on the market and more women able to make them, so merchants lowered the rate for each. Outworkers often bought their machines on instalments, carrying the debt themselves. By the 1880s London's clothing outwork was Parliament's model case of sweated labour.
cards.move: A faster tool pays whoever controls the price of the work.
cards.trap: Assuming the gain from a faster tool goes to its user.
cards.source: Schmiechen, Sweated Industries and Sweated Labor, 1984
cards.reference: Schmiechen, Sweated Industries and Sweated Labor: The London Clothing Trades, 1860–1914, University of Illinois Press, 1984

cards.question: Did corsets seriously harm the health of most Victorian women who wore them?
cards.answer: Worn daily from girlhood, while bones still grow, corsets pressed on the lower ribs and organs for decades. Doctors of the period linked them to breathlessness, fainting and displaced organs, and skeletons of women from the era show ribs bent inward. A garment worn that long needed no extreme lacing to leave its mark.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how tightly the ordinary wearer laced decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Most women laced moderately: the waist sizes corsetmakers sold ran mostly from about 50 to 75 cm, and the tiny waists of fashion plates were drawings. Steele argues the medical campaign mixed real cases with moral panic about vanity. Many women found a corset supportive, much like a modern bra, and worked in one all day.
cards.source: Steele, The Corset: A Cultural History, 2001
cards.reference: Steele, The Corset: A Cultural History, Yale University Press, 2001

cards.question: When were the streets of ancient Rome at their noisiest?
cards.answer: At night. A law of Julius Caesar's time barred wagons from the city's streets from sunrise until the tenth hour of daylight, except for temple building, public works and hauling away rubble. So carts rolled in after dark, and Juvenal complained that their rumble in the narrow streets made sleep in Rome impossible.
cards.move: Push a nuisance out of one hour and it lands in another.
cards.reference: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/ancient/law_of_caesar.asp

cards.question: What was wrong with Rome's first public sundial?
cards.answer: It was made for another city. Taken from Catania, Sicily, in 263 BC and set in the Forum, it was drawn for a latitude four degrees further south, so its lines disagreed with Rome's hours. Romans followed it anyway for 99 years, until the censor Quintus Marcius Philippus put a corrected dial beside it.
cards.move: Borrowed tools carry the assumptions of the place they were made.
cards.reference: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, vol. 2, trans. H. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1942

cards.question: In 2 BC just over 200,000 men drew Rome's public grain. Estimate the city's whole population, in millions.
cards.answer: Add perhaps 400,000 slaves, foreigners and soldiers: about 1 million.
cards.move: A partial list becomes a census once you know who it leaves out.
cards.trap: Stopping at 200,000, as if the grain list counted everyone.
cards.hint: Start from the men on the grain list, then add their households and everyone left off it.
steps: About 200,000 citizen men were on the grain list in 2 BC.
With wives and children, about 3 people per man: 600,000 citizens.
Add perhaps 400,000 slaves, foreigners and soldiers: about 1 million.
cards.source: Res Gestae 15; Morley, Metropolis and Hinterland
cards.reference: Morley, Metropolis and Hinterland: The City of Rome and the Italian Economy, 200 B.C.-A.D. 200, Cambridge University Press, 1996

cards.question: True or false: most people in imperial Rome's epitaphs whose legal status is stated were former slaves?
cards.answer: True. In Lily Ross Taylor's 1961 study of epitaphs from Rome, freed slaves far outnumbered the freeborn among those whose status is given. That says more about who paid for stones than about Rome: freed people had reasons to record their citizenship, marriages and children in stone. The freeborn poor mostly left no epitaph.
cards.move: Ask who paid to be remembered before treating the remembered as typical.
cards.trap: False, since former slaves must have been a small minority.
cards.reference: Taylor, Freedmen and Freeborn in the Epitaphs of Imperial Rome, American Journal of Philology 82, 1961, 113-132

cards.question: True or false: Rome's cheap public grain was reserved for citizens who were poor?
cards.answer: False. Cheap grain was a citizen's right, rich or poor. When Gaius Gracchus's grain law passed in 123 BC, Piso Frugi, an ex-consul who had fought it, turned up to collect his ration. Cicero reports his reply: if Gracchus meant to share out Piso's goods among everyone, Piso would claim his share.
cards.move: Check who is on the list before calling a benefit charity.
cards.trap: True, because a food handout must have targeted the needy.
cards.reference: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, trans. J. E. King, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1927

cards.question: When Rome granted a household the right to draw aqueduct water, what exactly did the grant fix?
cards.answer: The bore of a bronze nozzle, not the flow. Frontinus, water commissioner from AD 97, calls each grant a calix: a stamped bronze pipe of set size, fitted where the private pipe left the tank. Flow depends on depth too; he warns that one set lower draws more. Rome sold water by the hole.
cards.move: Ask whether the thing measured is the thing being paid for.
cards.reference: Frontinus, De Aquaeductu Urbis Romae, ed. R. H. Rodgers, Cambridge University Press, 2004

cards.question: Rome gets about 15 hours of daylight at midsummer and 9 at midwinter. How many minutes longer was a Roman daytime hour in June?
cards.answer: 75 - 45 = 30 minutes longer.
cards.move: Check whether a unit is fixed or a share of something that changes.
cards.trap: Taking an hour to be sixty minutes, so the answer is zero.
cards.hint: Romans cut the daylight, however long it was, into the same number of hours.
steps: Sunrise to sunset was always divided into 12 hours.
Midsummer: 15 x 60 / 12 = 75 minutes.
Midwinter: 9 x 60 / 12 = 45 minutes.
75 - 45 = 30 minutes longer.
cards.reference: Hannah, Time in Antiquity, Routledge, 2009

cards.question: Rome's Monte Testaccio, a hill over 30 m high, is built of broken jars. What had most of them held?
cards.answer: Olive oil from southern Spain. Most sherds come from one kind of oil jar made in Baetica, with more from North Africa. Oil soaked into the unglazed clay and turned rancid, so these jars could not be reused, while wine jars could. The hill records which containers were thrown away, not what Rome used most.
cards.move: A rubbish heap shows what could not be reused, not what was used most.
cards.trap: Guessing wine, Rome's everyday drink, because it was consumed in bulk.
cards.source: Peña, Roman Pottery in the Archaeological Record, 2007
