cards.reference: Peña, Roman Pottery in the Archaeological Record, Cambridge University Press, 2007

cards.question: True or false: the firefighters Augustus created for Rome were recruited mainly from freed slaves?
cards.answer: True. In AD 6 Augustus formed seven cohorts of vigiles, each covering two of the city's fourteen regions, fighting fires and patrolling at night. Early recruits were mostly freedmen, and a law of AD 24 gave informally freed slaves full citizenship after six years' service. Rome's night watch was a ladder out of second-class freedom.
cards.move: Look at who was given a dangerous job, and what they were paid in.
cards.trap: Assuming the capital's guards would be citizen soldiers.
cards.reference: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles, Collection de l'École française de Rome 224, 1996

cards.question: Augustus capped the height of new buildings along Rome's streets. At roughly what height?
cards.answer: About 20 metres. Strabo gives the limit as 70 Roman feet, about 21 m, room for six or seven storeys of brick and timber; Trajan later lowered it to 60. Such blocks rarely survived fire and rebuilding. Juvenal's poorest tenant lives at the top, under the roof tiles, where the pigeons nest.
cards.move: What lasts was built to last, and homes rarely were.
cards.trap: Picturing Rome from its temples and low, one-storey ruins.
cards.reference: Strabo, Geography, vol. 2, trans. H. L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1923

cards.question: Why was Britain's 1800 law banning white flour repealed so quickly?
cards.answer: Because the poor would not eat what it made. After the failed harvest of 1799, it forbade millers to produce anything but wholemeal flour, to stretch the wheat. Labourers, who could spend over half their wages on bread, held white wheaten bread as their standard and called the law the Poison Act.
cards.move: A sensible downgrade to the planner is a demotion to the person living it.
cards.reference: Wells, Wretched Faces: Famine in Wartime England 1793–1801, Alan Sutton, 1988

cards.question: Around 1500, roughly how many calories did a monk of Westminster Abbey take in on an ordinary day?
cards.answer: About 6,000 on an ordinary day, just under 5,000 in Lent. Westminster was one of England's richest monasteries, and Barbara Harvey's reconstruction of its allowances gives each monk roughly a kilo of bread a day, 900 g of meat or fish, five eggs and 4.5 litres of ale.
cards.move: Drop the numbers from your own life before guessing at someone else's.
cards.trap: Reaching for today's 2,500-calorie guideline as if it were a medieval norm.
cards.source: Harvey, Living and Dying in England, 1993
cards.reference: Harvey, Living and Dying in England 1100–1540: The Monastic Experience, Clarendon Press, 1993

cards.question: True or false: a 1936 survey found that half of Britain could not afford a diet adequate for health?
cards.answer: True. John Boyd Orr's Food, Health and Income found that a diet fully adequate for health was reached only at incomes above those of half the population. The poorest tenth, about 4.5 million people, fell short on every count he measured. What they lacked was less bread than milk, eggs, fruit and vegetables.
cards.move: Before arguing over how many went without, agree on what enough means.
cards.trap: Picturing 1930s hunger as a small unemployed minority, not half the country.
cards.source: Boyd Orr, Food, Health and Income, 1936
cards.reference: Boyd Orr, Food, Health and Income: Report on a Survey of Adequacy of Diet in Relation to Income, Macmillan, 1936

cards.question: Why did the poorest English farm labourers of the 1790s drink tea?
cards.answer: Because it was the cheapest warm drink left. David Davies, a Berkshire rector who published labourers' budgets in 1795, called tea-drinking 'not the cause, but the consequence' of their poverty: malt was too dear to brew beer, and milk hard to get. Without weak tea and the brownest sugar, they had bread and water.
cards.move: Before blaming a habit for hardship, ask whether the hardship made the habit.
cards.source: Davies, The Case of Labourers in Husbandry, 1795
cards.reference: Davies, The Case of Labourers in Husbandry Stated and Considered, 1795; discussed in Burnett, Liquid Pleasures: A Social History of Drinks in Modern Britain, Routledge, 1999

cards.question: In 1858, peppermint humbugs from Bradford market killed about 20 people with arsenic. What was meant to be in them instead?
options: A cheap filler to replace sugar
A green dye to brighten them
cards.answer: A cheap filler to replace sugar. Sugar was dear, so confectioners bulked sweets with 'daff', a white powder such as plaster of Paris. A chemist's assistant sold arsenic trioxide in its place by mistake; about 200 people fell ill. Even a safe humbug was meant to be part chalk or plaster.
cards.move: Behind a one-off disaster, look for the routine that made it possible.
cards.trap: Arsenic and Victorian sweets call up the famous poisonous green colourings.
cards.reference: Whorton, The Arsenic Century: How Victorian Britain Was Poisoned at Home, Work, and Play, Oxford University Press, 2010

cards.question: True or false: under England's medieval Assize of Bread, a farthing loaf kept its price while its weight followed wheat?
cards.answer: True. Local officials read the market price of wheat and set loaf weights from fixed tables: when wheat grew dear, the farthing and halfpenny loaves shrank; when it was cheap, they grew. Buyers paid in small fixed coins, so the loaf absorbed every harvest. Bakers caught selling light bread went to the pillory.
cards.move: When a price cannot move, look for what quietly shrinks instead.
cards.trap: Assuming bread prices rose and fell, as shop prices do today.
cards.reference: Davis, Baking for the Common Good: A Reassessment of the Assize of Bread in Medieval England, Economic History Review, 2004

cards.question: In December 1918 Germany's health office blamed 763,000 civilian deaths on the Allied food blockade. How was that figure reached?
options: Counting death certificates that named starvation
Counting all deaths above the pre-war level
Modelling deaths from the calorie shortfall
cards.answer: Counting all deaths above the pre-war level. The memorandum compared each war year's civilian deaths with peacetime and credited the whole excess to the blockade, including extra deaths from tuberculosis and the influenza of 1918. Hunger made both deadlier, yet influenza also killed the well fed.
cards.move: An excess over a baseline counts everything that changed, not only the cause named.
cards.trap: Taking an official death toll as a count of named cases.
cards.reference: Cox, Hunger Games: or How the Allied Blockade in the First World War Deprived German Children of Nutrition, and Allied Food Aid Subsequently Saved Them, Economic History Review, 2015

cards.question: Estimate the calories in a Royal Navy sailor's full daily ration around 1800, in thousands of kcal.
cards.answer: 1,600 + 1,350 + 2,000 = about 4,950 kcal, roughly 5 thousand.
cards.move: Size a ration by the work it was meant to fuel.
cards.trap: Picturing sailors half-starved on a few weevilly biscuits.
cards.hint: Split it three ways: the daily biscuit, the daily beer, and the weekly meat and dry stores spread over seven days.
steps: Biscuit: about 450 g a day at roughly 3.5 kcal per gram is about 1,600 kcal.
Beer: about 4.5 litres of weak beer at roughly 0.3 kcal per ml is about 1,350 kcal.
Salt beef and pork, peas, oatmeal, butter and cheese, shared over the week, add about 2,000 kcal a day.
1,600 + 1,350 + 2,000 = about 4,950 kcal, roughly 5 thousand.
cards.reference: Macdonald, Feeding Nelson's Navy: The True Story of Food at Sea in the Georgian Era, Chatham Publishing, 2004

cards.question: In medieval English towns, who relied most on ready-cooked food from cookshops, and why?
cards.answer: The poor, not the rich. A family in one rented room often had no oven, little fuel and nowhere to store food, so a hot pie cost less than cooking. The rich kept kitchens and cooks. By the 1170s London already had a public cookshop on the riverbank, open day and night.
cards.move: Ask who lacks a kitchen before calling ready-made food a luxury.
cards.source: Carlin, Food and Eating in Medieval Europe
cards.reference: Carlin, Fast Food and Urban Living Standards in Medieval England, in Carlin & Rosenthal (eds), Food and Eating in Medieval Europe, Hambledon Press, 1998

cards.question: Would stopping Ireland's food exports in 1846–47 have prevented most deaths in the Great Famine?
sides: No, the gap was too big
cards.answer: Food kept leaving while people starved: grain, cattle, pigs and butter went to Britain through the worst months of 1846 and 1847. Irish ports had been closed to food exports in the dearth of 1782–83, so the remedy was known. Kept at home and handed out early, that food could have fed the hungriest districts.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the size of the lost crop against the exports decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The potato failure was vast: the lost crop held several times the food in all the grain Ireland exported. By 1847 Ireland imported far more grain than it sent out, and people still died, because the starving had no money and relief came late. Keeping the exports could have closed only part of the gap.
cards.reference: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory, Princeton University Press, 1999

cards.question: Why did revolutionary France keep the metre but give up the ten-hour day?
cards.answer: Because the metre solved a problem and decimal time created one. Towns across France had their own pounds and grain measures, so trade gained from one standard; a ten-hour day solved nothing and needed new clocks. Compulsory from September 1794, it was suspended in April 1795 by the law that named the metre and gram.
cards.move: A reform survives when it removes a cost people already feel.
cards.source: Alder, The Measure of All Things, 2002
cards.reference: Alder, The Measure of All Things: The Seven-Year Odyssey and Hidden Error That Transformed the World, Free Press, 2002

cards.question: Nobles were about 8% of the 16,594 people sentenced to death in the Terror. Roughly what share of France's nobles died this way?
cards.answer: About 1%. 8% of 16,594 is about 1,300 people, and France had well over 100,000 nobles, though estimates range. Most of the condemned were commoners, peasants and workers above all, many of them sentenced for armed revolt, desertion or hoarding grain.
cards.move: Always ask which total a percentage is taken from.
cards.trap: Reading the nobles' share of the victims as the victims' share of nobles.
cards.source: Greer, The Incidence of the Terror, 1935
cards.reference: Greer, The Incidence of the Terror during the French Revolution: A Statistical Interpretation, Harvard University Press, 1935

cards.question: True or false: the French Revolution gave workers the right to form trade unions?
cards.answer: False. The Le Chapelier law of June 1791 banned associations of workers or employers, and strikes, as threats to individual liberty, three months after the guilds were abolished. Strikes stayed a crime in France until 1864 and trade unions until 1884, nearly a century after the Bastille fell.
cards.move: Ask whose freedom a liberty law was written to protect.
cards.trap: Assuming a revolution made in the people's name gave workers that right.
cards.source: Sewell, Work and Revolution in France, 1980
cards.reference: Sewell, Work and Revolution in France: The Language of Labor from the Old Regime to 1848, Cambridge University Press, 1980

cards.question: How many of the 1789 grievance lists that opened the Revolution demanded a republic?
cards.answer: Almost none. The cahiers de doléances, written by tens of thousands of parishes, guilds and assemblies, asked for fairer taxes, regular meetings of the Estates-General and an end to seigneurial dues, addressed loyally to the king. France became a republic only in September 1792, after war and the king's flight.
cards.move: Do not read the ending of a story back into its first demands.
cards.reference: Shapiro & Markoff, Revolutionary Demands: A Content Analysis of the Cahiers de Doléances of 1789, Stanford University Press, 1998

cards.question: Was the Terror of 1793–94 driven mainly by war and rebellion rather than by revolutionary ideology?
cards.answer: The Terror followed the danger. It began with foreign armies on French soil and revolts in the Vendée, Lyon and Toulon, and most death sentences were passed in those rebel regions; Paris accounted for 2,639 of 16,594. Remove the civil war and the invasion, and most of the killing has no occasion.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the timing of the killing against the danger decides it.
cards.counterpoint: In Paris the killing peaked after the danger passed. The Law of 22 Prairial, in June 1794, denied defendants counsel, and executions there rose from about 3 a day to about 29, just as victories in Belgium lifted the threat of invasion. A politics that sorted citizens into the virtuous and enemies needed no war to keep killing.
cards.reference: Furet, Interpreting the French Revolution, Cambridge University Press, 1981; Greer, The Incidence of the Terror during the French Revolution, Harvard University Press, 1935

cards.question: When French peasants attacked châteaux in the summer of 1789, what did they most often go looking for?
cards.answer: The paperwork. Rioters demanded the terriers, the registers of what each household owed its lord in rents, dues and labour, and burned them in the courtyard, often sparing the house and the family. Without the record, a claim was hard to prove. Some lords were made to sign away their rights on the spot.
cards.move: Where a debt exists only on paper, the paper becomes the target.
cards.reference: Lefebvre, The Great Fear of 1789: Rural Panic in Revolutionary France, trans. White, New Left Books, 1973

cards.question: What does the map of French priests who refused the revolutionary oath of 1791 still predict, generations later?
cards.answer: Where people go to Mass and how they vote. About half the parish clergy refused to swear to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, clustered in the west, the north-east and the southern Massif Central. Timothy Tackett found the same regions standing out for churchgoing and conservative voting well into the twentieth century.
cards.move: A choice made under pressure can set a region's habits for generations.
cards.source: Tackett, Religion, Revolution, and Regional Culture, 1986
cards.reference: Tackett, Religion, Revolution, and Regional Culture in Eighteenth-Century France: The Ecclesiastical Oath of 1791, Princeton University Press, 1986

cards.question: From 1790 a French peasant could end a money due by paying 20 years' worth at once. At 5% interest, how costly was that?
options: A bargain against paying for ever
The same as paying for ever
Far dearer than paying for ever
cards.answer: The same as paying for ever. A lump sum lent at 5% earns a twentieth of itself each year, exactly the due it replaces. Few peasants had that capital, so most dues went on being paid, or refused, until the Convention abolished the rest without compensation in July 1793.
cards.move: Price any endless payment by dividing it by the interest rate.
cards.trap: Twenty years of payments looks smaller than payments without end.

y.label: worth now, in years of dues

diagram.caption: Twenty years of dues are worth only 12.5 now; even a century of them never reaches 20.

cards.source: Jones, The Peasantry in the French Revolution
cards.reference: Jones, The Peasantry in the French Revolution, Cambridge University Press, 1988

cards.question: Who were most of the men officially honoured afterwards as conquerors of the Bastille?
cards.answer: Craftsmen, journeymen and shopkeepers. George Rudé traced the trades of several hundred men on the official list: most were settled working people of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, joiners, cabinet-makers, locksmiths and wine-sellers, beside a few dozen soldiers. Vagrants and the destitute barely appear. The crowd had addresses and trades.
cards.move: Before believing a description of a crowd, ask who wrote it.
cards.trap: Imagining the crowd as a rabble of the destitute, as its enemies described it.
cards.source: Rudé, The Crowd in the French Revolution, 1959
cards.reference: Rudé, The Crowd in the French Revolution, Clarendon Press, 1959

cards.question: True or false: after revolutionary France legalised divorce in 1792, most divorces in its cities were sought by wives?
cards.answer: True. The law of September 1792 let either spouse divorce, on grounds from cruelty and desertion to simple incompatibility. In Rouen, Roderick Phillips found women behind most petitions brought by one spouse, many escaping violent or absent husbands. The restored monarchy abolished divorce in 1816; it returned only in 1884.
cards.move: Ask who most needed an exit before guessing who used it.
cards.trap: Assuming a revolution led by men wrote its new liberties for men.
cards.source: Phillips, Family Breakdown in Late Eighteenth-Century France
cards.reference: Phillips, Family Breakdown in Late Eighteenth-Century France: Divorces in Rouen, 1792–1803, Clarendon Press, 1980

cards.question: Were Europe's craft guilds, on balance, good for the economies they governed?
cards.answer: Guilds solved problems markets could not. By binding apprentices to masters for years, they made it worth a master's while to teach, and their travelling journeymen carried techniques from town to town. Hallmarks and inspections let buyers trust goods they could not test. An institution that lasted five centuries across Europe was doing something useful.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, ask whether the training needed the monopoly.
cards.counterpoint: Guilds mainly protected their members' incomes. They kept out almost all women and Jews, most migrants and anyone who could not pay the fees, and lobbied rulers for monopolies that raised prices. They fought labour-saving machines: the ribbon loom, which wove several ribbons at once, was banned across the Holy Roman Empire in 1685.
cards.reference: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Fjep.28.4.169

cards.question: True or false: some medieval craft guilds admitted only women?
cards.answer: True. The Book of Trades drawn up for Paris around 1268 records trades held as female monopolies, among them two kinds of silk spinning, silk ribbon-making and the making of silk head-coverings. Cologne later had guilds made up mainly of women. Where the thread was silk, the masters were often women.
cards.move: Check the exceptions before accepting a rule about who was shut out.
cards.trap: False, because guilds were brotherhoods of male masters.
cards.source: Farmer, The Silk Industries of Medieval Paris, 2017
cards.reference: Farmer, The Silk Industries of Medieval Paris: Artisanal Migration, Technological Innovation, and Gendered Experience, University of Pennsylvania Press, 2017

cards.question: Who still tests the coins of the Royal Mint in a court of law each year?
cards.answer: A medieval guild. At the Trial of the Pyx, a jury from the Goldsmiths' Company, sitting as a formal court, counts, weighs and tests the metal of coins set aside from every batch the Mint struck. Coins have been judged like this since at least 1282; since 1871 the trial sits in Goldsmiths' Hall.
cards.move: An institution outlives its era when it keeps a job everyone needs done.
cards.source: The Goldsmiths' Company, Trial of the Pyx
cards.reference: https://www.thegoldsmiths.co.uk/the-trial-of-the-pyx

cards.question: How were the scenes of York's medieval mystery plays shared out?
cards.answer: By trade. Each craft guild staged one pageant on a wagon, often a scene that suited its work: the shipwrights built Noah's Ark, the fishers and mariners staged the Flood, the goldsmiths brought the Magi's gifts and the bakers served the Last Supper. The cycle ran on Corpus Christi from the 1370s until 1569.
cards.move: Give each group the piece of the job it already knows.
cards.source: Beadle and King, York Mystery Plays, 1984
cards.reference: Beadle and King (eds.), York Mystery Plays: A Selection in Modern Spelling, Oxford University Press, 1984

cards.question: In 1378 the wool carders of Florence, the Ciompi, rose in revolt. What was their central demand?
cards.answer: A guild of their own. The carders worked under the wool guild, the Arte della Lana, subject to its courts but barred from joining or organising. In July they seized power, and three new guilds, one of them theirs, joined Florence's 21. By the end of August they were crushed and their guild abolished.
cards.move: People shut out of a system usually want a seat in it.
cards.trap: The abolition of all guilds, since guilds were the bosses' tool.
cards.reference: https://www.britannica.com/event/Revolt-of-the-Ciompi

cards.question: Which candidates could become guild masters on easier terms than everyone else?
cards.answer: Insiders. Across Europe, guild rules often let masters' sons, and men who married a master's widow or daughter, pay lower fees, serve shorter terms or make a cheaper masterpiece, the test piece. Outsiders paid in full. Sheilagh Ogilvie's survey finds such discounts widespread. A widow's hand could come with a workshop.
cards.move: When a test has exemptions, look at who gets them.
cards.reference: Ogilvie, The European Guilds: An Economic Analysis, Princeton University Press, 2019

cards.question: True or false: the phrase at sixes and sevens comes from a 1484 ruling between two London guilds?
cards.answer: False. The ruling was real: in 1484 the mayor, Robert Billesden, settled a precedence feud by making the Skinners and the Merchant Taylors swap sixth and seventh place yearly. But Chaucer had written of setting the world on six and seven a century earlier, in a phrase from dice. The guilds walked into an idiom.
cards.move: Before trusting an origin story, check which came first.
cards.trap: Finding a perfect match and not checking whether the phrase came first.
cards.reference: Benson (ed.), The Riverside Chaucer, Houghton Mifflin, 1987

cards.question: Of the apprentices bound to London's livery companies in the 1500s, what share went on to become freemen?
cards.answer: About 40%. Steve Rappaport's study of company records from 1490 to 1599 found only about 41% took up the freedom of the City. Others died, ran away, went home or finished without paying to join. The masters in company records are the minority who came through a filter of seven years or more.
cards.move: Count the ones who started, not only the ones who finished.
cards.trap: Judging apprenticeship by the masters, the ones the records remember.
cards.reference: Rappaport, Worlds within Worlds: Structures of Life in Sixteenth-Century London, Cambridge University Press, 1989

cards.question: A medieval guild statute forbids members to work by candlelight. What does the rule most safely show?
options: That some did, or might, work at night
That candles were too costly to use
cards.answer: That some did, or might. Rules are written against things people do. The Paris Book of Trades of about 1268 bans night work in craft after craft, often because poor light spoiled work and hid shoddy goods. A ban shows a temptation existed; how often it won needs other records, such as the fines.
cards.move: A ban is evidence that someone was tempted.
cards.trap: Reading a rule as a description of how people behaved.
cards.reference: Epstein, Wage Labor and Guilds in Medieval Europe, University of North Carolina Press, 1991

cards.question: What did the Holy Roman Emperor do about the ribbon loom in 1685?
cards.answer: He banned it. The engine loom wove many ribbons at once, and ribbon-weavers' guilds pressed for its suppression; an imperial edict of 1685 forbade it across the Empire and was renewed in 1719. Saxony allowed it openly only in 1765. Basel, outside the Empire, allowed it, and its ribbon trade flourished.
cards.move: Banning a machine at home rarely stops it working next door.
cards.reference: Epstein and Prak (eds.), Guilds, Innovation and the European Economy, 1400-1800, Cambridge University Press, 2008

cards.question: How did fashionable Parisians of the 1600s keep clean while avoiding baths?
cards.answer: By changing their linen. Doctors taught that hot water opened the pores and let disease, plague above all, into the body, and the public bathhouses of medieval Paris had closed. A clean white shirt was thought to draw off sweat and dirt, so the visible collar and cuffs stood for a clean body.
cards.move: What counts as clean depends on what people believe dirt does.
cards.reference: Vigarello, Concepts of Cleanliness: Changing Attitudes in France since the Middle Ages, Cambridge University Press, 1988

cards.question: Estimate how many tonnes of water a rural North Carolina housewife carried by hand in a year around 1885.
cards.answer: 90 kg x 365 days = ~33,000 kg, about 33 tonnes.
cards.move: Before judging how often people washed, weigh the water they had to carry.
cards.trap: Guessing a few tonnes because one bucket feels light.
cards.hint: Count her trips to the well each day, then the weight of a full bucket.
steps: About 9 trips a day x a 10-litre bucket weighing 10 kg = 90 kg a day.
90 kg x 365 days = ~33,000 kg, about 33 tonnes.
cards.source: Gordon, Rise and Fall of American Growth, 2016
cards.reference: Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth, Princeton University Press, 2016

cards.question: Why did 18th-century Japanese cities escape the sewage crisis of European ones?
cards.answer: Because excrement had a price. Farmers bought city waste as fertiliser, paying in cash or vegetables, so collectors carted it out instead of dumping it. In Osaka the right to sell a building's faeces belonged to the landlord, while the tenants sold their own urine.
cards.move: Give a waste a price and someone will come to collect it.
cards.reference: Hanley, Urban Sanitation in Preindustrial Japan, Journal of Interdisciplinary History, 1987

cards.question: Did clean water and sewers do more than better food to cut deaths in industrial cities?
cards.answer: Clean water was the sharpest single blow to death. In major US cities from 1900 to 1936, filtration and chlorination explain nearly half the fall in total mortality, three-quarters of the fall in infant deaths and nearly two-thirds of the fall in child deaths. Cities that cleaned their water saw typhoid collapse within years.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the order in which deaths fell is what decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Deaths were falling before the pipes arrived. In England and Wales, tuberculosis, spread through the air, killed fewer people decade after decade from the mid-1800s, long before any drug or sewer could touch it; better-fed bodies resisted it. And a re-analysis of the same US cities found filtration explained much less of the decline.
cards.reference: Cutler & Miller, The Role of Public Health Improvements in Health Advances: The Twentieth-Century United States, Demography, 2005

cards.question: What was the scholar who wrote the first known mention of toilet paper, in 589, worried about?
cards.answer: Sacrilege. Yan Zhitui wrote that paper bearing quotations from the Five Classics or the names of sages he dared not use 'for toilet purposes', so plain paper already was. By 1393 the Ming court at Nanjing was supplied with 720,000 sheets a year, each about 60 by 90 cm.
cards.move: A habit often enters the written record as a rule about its exceptions.
cards.reference: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Paper and Printing, in Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1, Cambridge University Press, 1985

cards.question: Why did wealthy English households of the 1600s and 1700s do their big laundry only every few weeks or months?
cards.answer: Because they owned enough linen to wait. The great wash was a hired job of several days: soaking in lye, boiling, beating, rinsing and drying on hedges. A house stocked with dozens of shirts, shifts and sheets could hold out for a month or a quarter. The poor, with one or two shirts, washed constantly.
cards.move: How rarely a chore is done can measure wealth rather than neglect.
cards.source: Davidson, A Woman's Work Is Never Done, 1982
cards.reference: Davidson, A Woman's Work Is Never Done: A History of Housework in the British Isles 1650–1950, Chatto & Windus, 1982

cards.question: From 1848 London ordered its cesspools abolished and houses drained into sewers. What did that do to the city's drinking water?
options: Cleaned it: cesspools stopped leaking into wells
Little change: supplies came from outside town
Fouled it: sewers emptied into the Thames
cards.answer: Fouled it: sewers emptied into the Thames. They had been built for rainwater and ran straight to the river, and several water companies still drew their supply from the tidal Thames in town. Flushing toilets and the end of cesspools moved the city's excrement from under its houses into its water pipes.
cards.move: Ask where the waste goes after it leaves the house.
cards.trap: Assuming a sanitary reform must have made the water cleaner.
cards.source: Halliday, The Great Stink of London, 1999
cards.reference: Halliday, The Great Stink of London: Sir Joseph Bazalgette and the Cleansing of the Victorian Metropolis, Sutton Publishing, 1999

cards.question: Chadwick's 1842 report said Liverpool labourers died at an average age of 15. What does that figure mostly reflect?
options: Most labourers dying in their teens
Huge numbers of deaths in infancy
Labourers leaving town before old age
cards.answer: Huge numbers of deaths in infancy. An average age at death pools every death, and in poor districts a large share of children died before five, dragging the mean down. A fast-growing town full of young migrants also produces young deaths. Those who survived childhood lived far beyond 15. Many of those coffins were small.
cards.move: Before trusting an average, ask what the extremes are doing to it.
cards.trap: Reading an average age at death as a typical lifespan.
cards.source: Chadwick, Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population, 1842
cards.reference: Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain, 1842; ed. Flinn, Edinburgh University Press, 1965

cards.question: True or false: in 1951, more than a third of households in England and Wales had no fixed bath?
cards.answer: True. The 1951 census found more than a third of households without a fixed bath, and many shared an outside lavatory. For millions the weekly bath was a tin tub by the fire, filled from the kettle. Most gained a bathroom only through the slum clearances and improvement grants of the next two decades.
cards.move: Judge how a decade lived from its census, not its advertisements.
cards.trap: Picturing post-war Britain from its new towns and advertisements.
cards.source: General Register Office, Census 1951 Housing Report
cards.reference: General Register Office, Census 1951 England and Wales: Housing Report, HMSO, 1956

cards.question: Estimate how many thousand tonnes of dung London's horses dropped on the city each day around 1900.
cards.answer: 3,000,000 kg = 3,000 tonnes, about 3 thousand tonnes a day.
cards.move: Every old technology had a waste stream; ask who shovelled it.
cards.trap: Picturing a few carriages rather than a city's whole freight engine.
cards.hint: Start from how many horses a city of six million needed for buses, cabs and carts, then weigh one horse's daily output.
steps: London had roughly 300,000 working horses around 1900.
A working horse drops roughly 10 kg of dung a day.
3,000,000 kg = 3,000 tonnes, about 3 thousand tonnes a day.
cards.source: Thompson, Victorian England: The Horse-Drawn Society, 1970
cards.reference: Thompson, Victorian England: The Horse-Drawn Society, inaugural lecture, Bedford College, University of London, 1970

cards.question: How can historians measure how long English people worked before anyone kept time sheets?
cards.answer: From criminal trials. Witnesses at the Old Bailey often said what they had been doing, and when, as a crime happened. Hans-Joachim Voth pooled such remarks to rebuild the working year: by 1800 Londoners worked well over 3,000 hours a year, as holy days and the habit of skipping Monday faded away.
cards.move: When no one recorded something, look for records made for another purpose.
cards.source: Voth, Time and Work in England, 2000
cards.reference: Voth, Time and Work in England 1750–1830, Clarendon Press, 2000

cards.question: True or false: in 1800, British industry got more of its power from water wheels than from steam engines?
cards.answer: True. Estimates of installed power give water wheels roughly three times the horsepower of steam engines in 1800, and the two were level only around 1830. Early cotton mills clustered on Pennine streams; steam's great advantage came later, when it freed factories to move into towns beside their workers and coal.
cards.move: The famous machine of an age is rarely the one doing most of the work.
cards.trap: The steam engine is the icon, so it must have powered the mills.
cards.reference: Crafts, Steam as a General Purpose Technology: A Growth Accounting Perspective, Economic Journal, 2004

cards.question: Income per head in Britain grew about 0.5% a year in the early 1800s. At that rate, how many years to double?
cards.answer: About 140 years. A doubling takes roughly 70 divided by the growth rate in per cent: 70 / 0.5 = 140, five generations. Total output grew nearer 2% a year and doubled in about 35 years, but most of it fed a growing population, not richer lives.
cards.move: Divide 70 by any growth rate before calling it a revolution.
cards.trap: Dividing 100% by 0.5% gives 200, forgetting that growth compounds.
cards.reference: Crafts & Harley, Output Growth and the British Industrial Revolution: A Restatement of the Crafts-Harley View, Economic History Review, 1992

cards.question: What were the Luddites of 1811–12 trying to achieve by smashing machines?
cards.answer: Better terms, not a world without machines. Hobsbawm called it collective bargaining by riot: knitters broke the frames of hosiers who cut what they paid per stocking or made shoddy goods, and spared those who paid the agreed rate. Parliament made frame-breaking a capital crime in 1812 and sent 12,000 troops.
cards.move: Before calling a protest irrational, ask what the protesters were bargaining for.
cards.reference: Hobsbawm, The Machine Breakers, Past & Present, 1952

cards.question: Did British workers' living standards rise during the Industrial Revolution, before 1850?
cards.answer: They rose, and faster after 1820. Lindert and Williamson's wage series show real earnings of blue-collar workers nearly doubling between 1820 and 1850. Cotton cloth, once a luxury, became cheap enough for everyone. Families who moved from farm to factory did so for higher pay, and kept moving.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the price index used to deflate wages decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Output raced ahead of pay. Robert Allen estimates that between 1780 and 1840 output per worker rose about 46% but real wages only about 12%, a lag he calls Engels' pause. Feinstein's cost-of-living index cut the optimists' gains sharply, and in the new industrial towns crowding and dirty water pushed death rates up in the 1830s.
cards.reference: Allen, Engels' Pause: Technical Change, Capital Accumulation, and Inequality in the British Industrial Revolution, Explorations in Economic History, 2009; Lindert & Williamson, English Workers' Living Standards during the Industrial Revolution: A New Look, Economic History Review, 1983

cards.question: Why were many of England's first water-powered cotton mills staffed by pauper children sent from distant parishes?
cards.answer: Because the mills stood where nobody lived. Water power meant remote Pennine and Derbyshire valleys with no labour force, so owners took apprentices from workhouses in London and the south, housed on site. Parishes were glad to shed their keep. At Styal, Quarry Bank Mill built an apprentice house beside the stream.
cards.move: A factory's site decides its workforce before any wage is offered.
cards.reference: Honeyman, Child Workers in England, 1780–1820: Parish Apprentices and the Making of the Early Industrial Labour Force, Ashgate, 2007

cards.question: True or false: Americans born around 1860 grew up shorter on average than those born around 1830, though incomes had risen?
cards.answer: True. Military records show average height of native-born American men falling by a couple of centimetres across those cohorts, while income per head grew. John Komlos points to what income leaves out: dearer food as farm goods went to distant markets, and crowded towns full of infection. City children paid in stature.
cards.move: When two measures of welfare part ways, ask what each one leaves out.
cards.trap: Taking rising income per head as a measure of how well people lived.
cards.reference: Komlos, Shrinking in a Growing Economy? The Mystery of Physical Stature during the Industrial Revolution, Journal of Economic History, 1998

cards.question: Robert Fogel asked how much poorer the United States would have been in 1890 with no railways at all. His answer?
options: A few per cent of national income
About a quarter of national income
More than half of national income
cards.answer: A few per cent of national income. Fogel measured railways against the next best option, canals, rivers and wagons, not against nothing, and put the saving on moving farm goods below 5% of 1890 output. The exact figure is still argued over, but the method stuck: an invention is worth its lead over the alternative.
cards.move: Value any invention by its lead over the next best option.
cards.trap: Comparing railways with no transport at all rather than with canals.
cards.source: Fogel, Railroads and American Economic Growth, 1964
cards.reference: Fogel, Railroads and American Economic Growth: Essays in Econometric History, Johns Hopkins Press, 1964

cards.question: By hand, spinning 45 kg of fine cotton yarn took about 50,000 hours. Working 12-hour days, 300 days a year, how many years?
cards.answer: About 14 years, against about 135 hours on a self-acting mule by 1825.
cards.move: Turn a pile of hours into a working life before judging it.
cards.trap: Dividing by 24 hours and 365 days, as if spinners never slept.
cards.hint: Turn the hours into working days first, then the days into years.
steps: 50,000 hours / 12 hours a day = about 4,170 working days.
4,170 days / 300 days a year = about 13.9 years.
About 14 years, against about 135 hours on a self-acting mule by 1825.

diagram.caption: The same 45 kg of yarn: about 14 working years by hand, under two weeks by machine.

cards.reference: Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective, Cambridge University Press, 2009, after Catling, The Spinning Mule, 1970

cards.question: Did Britain industrialise first mainly because of cheap coal and high wages, rather than a culture of useful knowledge?
cards.answer: The evidence is in prices. Around 1750 wages in London were far higher, relative to the cost of energy and capital, than in Paris, Vienna or Beijing, and coal was cheap on British coalfields. Only there did it pay to invent machines that swapped labour for coal. The same machines lost money elsewhere for decades.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, why the high-wage Dutch did not industrialise decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The Dutch Republic paid wages as high as Britain's and burned cheap peat, yet built no steam engines. Joel Mokyr points to what was rare in Britain: a large body of skilled mechanics and a culture that published, tested and shared useful knowledge. Prices explain which machines paid; they do not explain who could build them.
cards.reference: Allen, The Industrial Revolution in Miniature: The Spinning Jenny in Britain, France, and India, Journal of Economic History, 2009; Mokyr, The Enlightened Economy: An Economic History of Britain 1700–1850, Yale University Press, 2009

cards.question: True or false: Prussia was formally abolished only in 1947, by the Allies occupying Germany?
cards.answer: True. In 1871 Prussia became the largest state of the German Empire, with nearly two-thirds of its land and most of its people, and stayed a state under Weimar. The Nazis hollowed it out, but the Allied Control Council's Law No. 46 dissolved it on 25 February 1947, calling it a bearer of militarism.
cards.move: Absorbed is not the same as abolished; check when the law ended it.
cards.trap: Picturing Prussia dissolving into Germany at unification in 1871.
cards.reference: Clark, Iron Kingdom: The Rise and Downfall of Prussia, 1600–1947, Allen Lane, 2006

cards.question: How did the Ryukyu Kingdom serve two masters, China and Japan, for over 250 years?
cards.answer: By hiding one from the other. After the Japanese domain of Satsuma invaded in 1609, the islands kept paying tribute to China as a loyal kingdom while answering to Satsuma. When Chinese envoys came, Satsuma's officials kept out of sight and Ryukyuans avoided Japanese names and dress. Japan annexed the kingdom in 1879.
cards.move: A small state between giants may survive by keeping each one's story intact.
cards.reference: Smits, Visions of Ryukyu: Identity and Ideology in Early-Modern Thought and Politics, University of Hawai'i Press, 1999

cards.question: In 1898 the United States annexed Hawaii, five years after its queen was overthrown. By what legal route?
options: A treaty ratified by the Senate
cards.answer: A joint resolution of Congress. An annexation treaty had failed to reach the two-thirds Senate vote a treaty needs, after Native Hawaiian petitions with more than 20,000 signatures opposed it. A joint resolution needed only simple majorities in both houses. The Hawaiian flag came down at Iolani Palace in August 1898.
cards.move: When the front door needs a supermajority, watch for a side door.
cards.trap: Territory like Alaska came by treaty, so this must have too.
cards.reference: Silva, Aloha Betrayed: Native Hawaiian Resistance to American Colonialism, Duke University Press, 2004

cards.question: Charles Tilly counted about 25 independent states in Europe in 1900. About how many political units were there in 1500?
cards.answer: About 500. Tilly's count for 1500 is some 500 more or less independent units, against about 25 in 1900: 1 in 20 survived. Duchies, prince-bishoprics, city republics and free cities were swallowed by larger neighbours, and the states on today's map are the survivors.
cards.move: Before judging how stable something is, count what disappeared.
cards.trap: Imagining 1500 as today's map with a few extra kingdoms.
cards.source: Tilly, The Formation of National States, 1975
cards.reference: Tilly (ed.), The Formation of National States in Western Europe, Princeton University Press, 1975

cards.question: Why was the first king of united Italy called Victor Emmanuel the Second?
cards.answer: Because he kept his number as king of Sardinia: in law, Italy was the Kingdom of Sardinia enlarged and renamed in 1861. Sardinia's constitution, the Statuto granted in 1848, became Italy's and lasted until 1948. The first capital, the laws and the ruling house all came from Turin.
cards.move: When a union keeps one partner's names and numbers, ask who absorbed whom.
cards.reference: Riall, Risorgimento: The History of Italy from Napoleon to Nation-State, Palgrave Macmillan, 2009

cards.question: What did the new Austrian republic declare itself to be on the day it was founded, in November 1918?
cards.answer: A part of Germany. On 12 November 1918 its provisional assembly declared German-Austria a democratic republic and a component of the German Republic. The Allies forbade it: the Treaty of Saint-Germain bound Austria to independence and made it drop German from its name. In 1921 unofficial votes in Tyrol and Salzburg still backed union massively.
cards.move: An independence imposed from outside is not the same as one chosen.
cards.reference: Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Austria, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, 1919, Article 88

cards.question: How did Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania keep a legal existence through fifty years of Soviet rule?
cards.answer: Through missions that refused to close. The United States and most Western states never recognised the 1940 annexation, so pre-war Baltic diplomats kept offices running in Washington and elsewhere, handing their posts on for decades. In 1991 the three claimed to be restored, not newly created, and Estonia and Latvia rebuilt citizenship from pre-1940 citizens.
cards.move: A state can outlive its territory as long as someone keeps recognising it.
cards.source: Hiden & Salmon, The Baltic Nations and Europe
cards.reference: Hiden & Salmon, The Baltic Nations and Europe: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in the Twentieth Century, Longman, 1991

cards.question: True or false: Egypt went on calling itself the United Arab Republic for a decade after Syria walked out in 1961?
cards.answer: True. Syria left the union after an army coup in September 1961, but Nasser kept the name and the flag as a standing offer of wider Arab unity. Egypt became the Arab Republic of Egypt only in September 1971, a year after his death. For ten years a union of one sat on the map.
cards.move: Ask what a name still claims before assuming it describes anything.
cards.trap: Assuming a state's name changes as soon as its union ends.
cards.source: Podeh, The Decline of Arab Unity, 1999
cards.reference: Podeh, The Decline of Arab Unity: The Rise and Fall of the United Arab Republic, Sussex Academic Press, 1999

cards.question: Studying every state since 1816, Tanisha Fazal asked which were likeliest to be conquered or absorbed. Which were?
options: States far from any great power
cards.answer: Buffer states between two rivals. Fazal found that states lying between competing powers died far more often, because each rival preferred to seize the buffer before the other could. Position mattered more than size: Korea, contested by China, Russia and Japan, fell to Japan in 1910. Since 1945, conquest of recognised states has become rare.
cards.move: Where something stands can matter more than how big it is.
cards.trap: Assuming small states died because they were small.
cards.reference: Fazal, State Death: The Politics and Geography of Conquest, Occupation, and Annexation, Princeton University Press, 2007

cards.question: In Newfoundland's first 1948 referendum, self-government won 44.6%, union with Canada 41.1%, rule by commission 14.3%. Who won the runoff?
cards.answer: Union with Canada, narrowly: 52.3% to 47.7%. The commission option was gone, and its voters had already chosen not to restore the self-government that had gone bankrupt in 1934; most of them moved to Canada. Newfoundland, a dominion like Canada itself, became its tenth province on 31 March 1949.
cards.move: In a runoff, ask where the eliminated voters' second choices lie.
cards.trap: Expecting the first-round leader to win because it led.
cards.source: Neary, Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1988
cards.reference: Neary, Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1929–1949, McGill-Queen's University Press, 1988

cards.question: What did Möngke Khan organise between rival religions at Karakorum in 1254?
cards.answer: A formal debate. The Great Khan had Latin and Nestorian Christians, Muslims and Buddhists argue before his umpires. William of Rubruck, a Franciscan friar who spoke for the Latins, reports it ended with everyone drinking heavily. He records Möngke telling him that God gave men different ways, as he gave the hand different fingers.
cards.move: Tolerance can be policy as much as belief.
cards.reference: The Mission of Friar William of Rubruck, trans. Peter Jackson, Hakluyt Society, 1990

cards.question: Who first counted the households of north-eastern Russia for tax?
cards.answer: Their Mongol overlords. In 1257, the chronicles record, census-takers sent by the Golden Horde, the Mongol state on the Volga, counted the people of Suzdal, Riazan and Murom to fix tribute and military levies. Novgorod rioted and held out until 1259, when the count went ahead under the eye of Grand Prince Alexander Nevsky.
cards.move: Counting people is usually the first step in taxing them.
cards.source: Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde, 1985
cards.reference: Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde: The Mongol Impact on Medieval Russian History, Indiana University Press, 1985

cards.question: What else, besides a Great Khan's death, may have pushed the Mongols out of Hungary in 1242?
cards.answer: Possibly mud. A 2016 study of tree rings and written records found warm, dry summers from 1238 to 1241, then a cold, wet start to 1242 that likely turned the Hungarian plain into marsh. For an army of horsemen, a flooded plain meant lost pasture and stalled columns. Historians still weigh it against Ögedei's death.
cards.move: Before crediting a decision to politics, check what the ground was like.
cards.source: Büntgen and Di Cosmo, Scientific Reports, 2016
cards.reference: Büntgen and Di Cosmo, Climatic and environmental aspects of the Mongol withdrawal from Hungary in 1242 CE, Scientific Reports 6, 2016

cards.question: About 16 million men share a male-line ancestor who lived in Mongolia about 1,000 years ago. How many doublings turn one man into 16 million?
cards.answer: Four more: 1 million x 16 = 16 million, so 24 doublings in all.
cards.move: Doubling needs far fewer steps than intuition expects.
cards.trap: Guessing hundreds of generations, far more than 1,000 years allow.
cards.hint: The lineage is linked to Genghis Khan's family. Count the doublings to a thousand, then to a million.
steps: Ten doublings turn 1 into 1,024, roughly a thousand.
Ten more turn a thousand into roughly a million.
Four more: 1 million x 16 = 16 million, so 24 doublings in all.
cards.source: Zerjal et al., Am. J. Human Genetics, 2003
cards.reference: Zerjal et al., The Genetic Legacy of the Mongols, American Journal of Human Genetics 72, 2003

cards.question: Which is likelier: plague reached Italy by ship from the Black Sea, or Mongols hurled corpses into Caffa and fleeing ships brought it?
cards.answer: Plague arriving by ship. Every way the Caffa story can be true is also a way plague came by ship from the Black Sea, so it cannot be likelier. The catapult tale rests largely on one writer, the notary Gabriele de' Mussis of Piacenza, who was probably never there; plague had many routes west.
cards.move: Each added detail makes a story more vivid and less likely.
cards.trap: The Caffa catapult story, because its detail makes it convincing.
cards.simply: Picture every ship that sailed west from the Black Sea in 1347. The ones fleeing Caffa after a catapult attack are some of them, never more.
cards.reference: Wheelis, Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(9), 2002, 971-975, doi:10.3201/eid0809.010536

cards.question: What happened when the Mongol ruler of Persia issued paper money in Tabriz in 1294?
cards.answer: Trade stopped. Gaykhatu, short of silver, copied the paper notes of Mongol China, printed with Chinese characters and the Muslim profession of faith, and forbade dealing in metal coin. Merchants shut their shops rather than take the notes, and food ran short. Within about two months the notes were withdrawn.
cards.move: A decree can print money, but only its users make it worth anything.
cards.source: Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia
cards.reference: Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia, Cambridge University Press, 2001

cards.question: In 1206 Chinggis Khan organised every Mongol fighting man into units of a thousand. Roughly how many men?
cards.answer: About 100,000. The Secret History, the Mongols' own chronicle, names 95 commanders of a thousand in 1206: at most some 95,000 men, if every unit was full. Behind them stood a people of perhaps a million. Conquered nomads swelled later armies, but the force that broke the Jin of northern China began as this core.
cards.move: Fear inflates numbers; count the units, not the rumours.
cards.trap: Trusting enemy chroniclers' pictures of endless hordes.
cards.source: The Secret History, trans. de Rachewiltz
cards.reference: de Rachewiltz (trans.), The Secret History of the Mongols: A Mongolian Epic Chronicle of the Thirteenth Century, Brill, 2004

cards.question: True or false: the Mongol Empire had split into rival khanates before it reached its greatest extent?
cards.answer: True. After Möngke died in 1259, his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke fought a civil war, and by 1262 the Golden Horde and Persia's Ilkhanate were at war in the Caucasus. The greatest extent came with Kublai's conquest of Song China, completed in 1279. Maps of one vast empire colour four quarrelling states alike.
cards.move: A single colour on a map can hide a quarrel.
cards.trap: Assuming the largest map shows the empire at its most united.

diagram.caption: The khanates were at war seventeen years before the empire reached its greatest extent.

cards.reference: Morgan, The Mongols, 2nd edition, Blackwell, 2007

cards.question: Did the Mongol conquests, on balance, leave Eurasia richer than they found it?
cards.answer: The Mongols joined China, Persia and Russia under one family, protected merchants and moved craftsmen, doctors and scholars across Asia. Persian astronomers worked in Kublai's China, and Chinese physicians served in Tabriz. Friars and merchants crossed the continent and came back to write about it. For a century Eurasia was more connected than ever before.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whose ledger you read decides the answer.
cards.counterpoint: The conquests killed on a scale that took centuries to repair. Northern China's registered population collapsed, cities such as Merv, Nishapur and Baghdad were sacked, and Iran's irrigation decayed in many districts. The same roads that carried merchants carried plague west in the 1340s. A good century for long-distance traders was a ruinous one for farmers.
cards.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World, 2017
cards.reference: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion, Yale University Press, 2017

cards.question: Under Ögedei, loans at lamb interest doubled every year. How many ingots would 1 ingot owe after 10 unpaid years?
cards.answer: After 10 years: 32 x 32 = 1,024 ingots.
cards.move: Ask whether a debt adds or multiplies before agreeing to its terms.
cards.trap: Adding one ingot a year and answering about 11.
cards.hint: Work out five years first; ten years is five years done twice.
steps: Each year the debt doubles.
After 5 years: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32 ingots.
After 10 years: 32 x 32 = 1,024 ingots.

diagram.caption: After five years the debt is 32 ingots; the next five add almost a thousand.

cards.reference: Allsen, Mongolian Princes and Their Merchant Partners, 1200-1260, Asia Major, third series, 2, 1989, 83-126

cards.question: Mercator published his navigators' projection in 1569. Who first explained the mathematics that let others draw it?
cards.answer: An English mathematician, Edward Wright, in 1599. Mercator never said how he spaced his parallels, so nobody could copy the method exactly. Wright showed the spacing must grow as the running sum of the secant of latitude, and printed a table of it minute by minute: an integral, done by patient addition, before calculus existed.
cards.move: Whoever makes a method copyable often matters more than whoever invented it.
cards.source: Monmonier, Rhumb Lines and Map Wars, 2004
cards.reference: Monmonier, Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection, University of Chicago Press, 2004

cards.question: On Mercator's 1569 projection, how many times larger does a patch of land at 60° latitude look than at the equator?
cards.answer: Area is stretched 2 × 2 = 4 times.
cards.move: A stretch applied in two directions multiplies, so square it before judging.
cards.trap: Answering 2, as if only the east–west stretch counted.
cards.hint: Mercator stretches north–south exactly as much as east–west, and the east–west stretch is set by how short a parallel is.
steps: At latitude φ a parallel is cos φ times the equator's length, but is drawn full width: stretched 1 / cos φ.
cos 60° = 0.5, so east–west is stretched 1 / 0.5 = 2 times, and north–south by the same.
Area is stretched 2 × 2 = 4 times.
cards.source: Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual, 1987
cards.reference: Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual, US Geological Survey Professional Paper 1395, 1987

cards.question: True or false: early maps showed California as an island because Spanish sailors had not yet explored its gulf?
cards.answer: False. Francisco de Ulloa sailed to the head of the Gulf of California in 1539, and for some 80 years most maps drew Baja California as a peninsula. The island appeared in the 1620s and was copied from map to map for over a century; Ferdinand VI decreed in 1747 that California was no island.
cards.move: Knowledge can go backwards; ask whether an error came before the truth or after.
cards.trap: Assuming maps only ever improve, so an error means nobody had looked.
cards.reference: McLaughlin & Mayo, The Mapping of California as an Island: An Illustrated Checklist, California Map Society Occasional Paper No. 5, 1995

cards.question: In what form did Ptolemy's Geography, written about 150 AD, hand his picture of the world down to later centuries?
options: Sailing directions from port to port
cards.answer: Coordinates for about 8,000 places. The Geography is a set of instructions: how to draw a projection, then tables of latitude and longitude from Ireland to China. No map from Ptolemy's own hand survives. The oldest maps in its manuscripts were redrawn from the tables in Constantinople around 1300, over a thousand years later.
cards.move: Before trusting an old picture, ask who drew the copy you are holding.
cards.trap: Taking the maps in the surviving manuscripts for Ptolemy's own originals.
cards.reference: Berggren & Jones, Ptolemy's Geography: An Annotated Translation of the Theoretical Chapters, Princeton University Press, 2000

cards.question: What happened to the map of France when astronomers timed the moons of Jupiter from its coasts in the 1670s?
cards.answer: It shrank. Picard and La Hire timed eclipses of Io, Jupiter's nearest large moon, at coastal ports and compared them with the same eclipses in Paris: the difference in local time gave the longitude. Brest moved well east of where maps had put it, and the Atlantic coast pulled in towards Paris.
cards.move: Every longitude is a time difference; a map is only as good as its clocks.
cards.reference: Konvitz, Cartography in France, 1660–1848: Science, Engineering, and Statecraft, University of Chicago Press, 1987

cards.question: Why was the first map published by Britain's Ordnance Survey, in 1801, a map of Kent?
cards.answer: Because Kent was where a French invasion was expected. The Survey was a military body, set up under the Board of Ordnance in 1791, and its first map covered the coast facing France, so commanders could plan roads, batteries and lines of retreat. Britain's walking maps began as a defence plan for one county.
cards.move: Much civilian infrastructure began as a military worry about one place.
cards.source: Seymour, A History of the Ordnance Survey, 1980
cards.reference: Seymour (ed.), A History of the Ordnance Survey, Dawson, 1980

cards.question: Why is the Mediterranean on medieval sea charts turned several degrees anticlockwise from its true position?
cards.answer: Most likely because it was drawn with a compass. Chart makers built coasts from sailors' magnetic bearings and distances, and the needle then pointed some degrees east of true north. Putting magnetic north at the top rotated the whole sea to match. The leading explanation, though disputed: the chart fossilised a magnetic field.
cards.move: A steady error in an old record may be the fingerprint of its instrument.
cards.reference: Campbell, Portolan Charts from the Late Thirteenth Century to 1500, in Harley & Woodward (eds), The History of Cartography, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1987

cards.question: The Ottoman admiral Piri Reis's world map of 1513 bends its southern coast sharply east. What best explains the bend?
options: South America bent to fit the skin
An ice-free Antarctica from ancient sources
A secret Portuguese voyage far south
cards.answer: South America bent to fit the skin. The surviving fragment is drawn on gazelle-skin parchment, and its coast turns east where the parchment ran out. Antarctica's coast had lain under ice for millions of years. Compare enough wandering coastlines with enough real shores and some pair will look alike.
cards.move: Among thousands of shapes, some match by chance; count the misses too.
cards.trap: Treating a close match of shapes as evidence of a hidden source.
cards.source: McIntosh, The Piri Reis Map of 1513, 2000
cards.reference: McIntosh, The Piri Reis Map of 1513, University of Georgia Press, 2000

cards.question: True or false: explorers eventually found the Mountains of Kong, the West African range on maps for most of the 1800s, roughly where drawn?
cards.answer: False. The range first appeared on James Rennell's map of 1798, drawn from hearsay to fit his theory of the Niger, and map after map copied it for nearly a century. In 1888 the French officer Louis-Gustave Binger reached Kong and found no mountains. Dozens of agreeing maps were one guess, repeated.
cards.move: Ten copies of one source are still one source.
cards.trap: Taking many maps that agree as many separate confirmations.
cards.source: Bassett & Porter, Journal of African History, 1991
cards.reference: Bassett & Porter, From the Best Authorities: The Mountains of Kong in the Cartography of West Africa, Journal of African History, 1991

cards.question: Britain's 1714 Longitude Act paid its top prize for longitude within half a degree. Over a six-week voyage, allowed clock drift in seconds a day?
cards.answer: 120 / 42 = about 2.9 seconds a day.
cards.move: Convert a tolerance into the units of the instrument before judging it.
cards.trap: Treating half a degree as generous before converting it into time.
cards.hint: The Earth turns 360 degrees a day: turn the half degree into minutes of clock time first.
steps: 360° in 24 hours means 1° of longitude is 4 minutes of time.
Half a degree = 2 minutes = 120 seconds.
Six weeks = 42 days.
120 / 42 = about 2.9 seconds a day.
cards.reference: An Act for Providing a Publick Reward for such Person or Persons as shall Discover the Longitude at Sea, 1714; text in Andrewes (ed.), The Quest for Longitude, Harvard University, 1996

cards.question: Who collected the Ottoman Empire's salt and tobacco revenues after 1881?
cards.answer: Its foreign creditors. After defaulting in 1875, the empire accepted, in the 1881 Decree of Muharrem, a cut in its debt from about £191 million to £106 million. A council representing the bondholders took over the salt and tobacco monopolies and the taxes on stamps, spirits, fish and silk, collecting them with its own staff.
cards.move: Default can cost a state its tax offices as well as its credit.
cards.reference: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Decree-of-Muharrem

cards.question: When did the Ottoman Empire first convene an elected parliament?
cards.answer: In March 1877, thirteen years before Japan's first parliament. The constitution of December 1876 created a chamber of deputies, chosen through provincial councils, with Muslim, Christian and Jewish members. It lasted less than a year: in February 1878 Sultan Abdülhamid II sent it home, and it did not meet again until 1908.
cards.move: Early reforms are easy to miss when they are quickly reversed.
cards.source: Devereux, The First Ottoman Constitutional Period, 1963
cards.reference: Devereux, The First Ottoman Constitutional Period: A Study of the Midhat Constitution and Parliament, Johns Hopkins Press, 1963

cards.question: Why did an Ottoman sultan's brother, not his son, inherit the throne in 1617?
cards.answer: Because a brother had been left alive. New sultans often killed their brothers; Mehmed III had nineteen executed in 1595. Ahmed I, enthroned at 13 in 1603 without an heir, spared his brother Mustafa. When Ahmed died in 1617, Mustafa succeeded instead of a son, and the throne began passing to the dynasty's eldest male.
cards.move: One exception kept alive can quietly become the new rule.
cards.reference: Peirce, The Imperial Harem: Women and Sovereignty in the Ottoman Empire, Oxford University Press, 1993

cards.question: Under Süleyman the Magnificent, in the mid-1500s, how were most of the empire's viziers born?
options: Muslim, in Arab or Persian families
cards.answer: Christian, in Balkan villages. Most had been taken as boys through the devshirme, a levy of Christian children, or as captives on the frontier, then converted and trained in the palace school. Owing everything to the sultan and nothing to a family, they could be promoted, or executed, at will.
cards.move: A ruler who fears rivals may staff the top with outsiders.
cards.trap: Muslim Turks, since a Muslim Turkish dynasty ruled the empire.
cards.source: İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age, 1973
cards.reference: İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age 1300-1600, Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1973

cards.question: True or false: books were printed in Istanbul more than two centuries before any Ottoman Turkish book in Arabic script?
cards.answer: True. In 1493, by the date in its colophon, though some argue for 1504, the brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias, Jews exiled from Iberia, printed a Hebrew code of law in Istanbul. Armenian and Greek presses followed. İbrahim Müteferrika's press printed its first Ottoman Turkish book in 1729.
cards.move: Ask whose output was counted before accepting that something came late.
cards.trap: False, because the Ottomans shunned printing until the 1720s.
cards.reference: Sabev, Waiting for Müteferrika: Glimpses of Early Modern Ottoman Printing (1726-1746), Academic Studies Press, 2018

cards.question: How did the Ottoman treasury borrow from its own subjects before it ever borrowed abroad?
cards.answer: By selling slices of tax revenue. From 1775 the state sold esham: shares in the income of a tax source, such as a customs house, bought for a lump sum and paying a fixed annual amount for life. Holders could resell them. The first foreign loan came only in 1854, during the Crimean War.
cards.move: A state that cannot borrow openly will find another name for debt.
cards.source: Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire
cards.reference: Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire, Cambridge University Press, 2000

cards.question: Was the Ottoman Empire in decline from the late sixteenth century onwards?
cards.answer: Measure it on the battlefield and the answer is plain. After Vienna in 1683 the Ottomans lost Hungary at Karlowitz in 1699, then the Crimea to Russia by 1783. Janissaries became a rebellious hereditary caste; provincial magnates ruled in the sultan's name. An empire that keeps losing land to its rivals is declining.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, what you chose to measure decided the verdict.
cards.counterpoint: Decline was a story Ottoman advice writers told to demand reform, and later historians took it at face value. Baki Tezcan and others argue the empire remade itself: sultans checked by janissaries, jurists and markets, tax farms that bound in local elites, and a state that lasted two more centuries. Few declining empires last that long.
cards.reference: Tezcan, The Second Ottoman Empire: Political and Social Transformation in the Early Modern World, Cambridge University Press, 2010

cards.question: Süleyman's first siege of Vienna, in 1529, lasted barely three weeks. What mainly ended it?
options: Distance, rain and the approach of winter
cards.answer: Distance, rain and the approach of winter. The army left Istanbul in May and, slowed by rains that forced it to leave much of its heavy artillery behind, reached Vienna only in late September. With winter near and supplies thin, it withdrew in mid-October. The campaign season, more than the enemy, set the empire's reach.
cards.move: Before crediting the enemy, check the calendar and the supply line.
cards.trap: Recalling 1683, when a relieving army did break the siege.
cards.reference: Imber, The Ottoman Empire, 1300-1650: The Structure of Power, Palgrave Macmillan, 2002

cards.question: True or false: the Ottoman capitulations, privileges for French merchants, were first forced on a weakened empire?
cards.answer: False. Selim II granted them in 1569, at the height of Ottoman power, as a favour to a useful ally against the Habsburgs, and they were renewed at each accession. Only after 1740, when they were made permanent and Europe grew stronger, did they become a lever for foreigners to escape Ottoman courts and taxes.
cards.move: Ask what a rule meant when it was made, not what it later became.
cards.trap: Reading their later role back into how they began.
cards.reference: İnalcık, Imtiyāzāt, in The Encyclopaedia of Islam, new edition, vol. 3, Brill, 1971

cards.question: The Ottoman census of 1831, the empire's first modern count of people, recorded whom?
cards.answer: Only males, Muslim and non-Muslim. It was taken to find conscripts for the new army and payers of the poll tax levied on non-Muslims, so women were left out entirely. Historians turning it into a population must multiply by an assumed ratio of women to men. Half the empire is a guess in that count.
cards.move: Ask why a count was taken; the purpose decides who was left out.
cards.trap: Assuming a census counts everyone, as modern ones try to.
cards.reference: Karpat, Ottoman Population, 1830-1914: Demographic and Social Characteristics, University of Wisconsin Press, 1985

cards.question: How was the likely starting point of the Black Death pinned down?
cards.answer: By gravestones in Kyrgyzstan. Headstones near Lake Issyk-Kul, dated 1338 and 1339, give 'pestilence' as the cause of death. In 2022, ancient DNA from people buried there yielded a plague strain sitting at the root of the pandemic's family tree, some eight years before plague reached the Black Sea.
cards.move: Trust a finding more when two unrelated kinds of evidence point to it.

cards.question: True or false: the first known quarantine law, passed by Ragusa in 1377, imposed forty days of isolation?
cards.answer: False. It imposed thirty days. On 27 July 1377 the Great Council of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, voted that anyone arriving from a plague-struck place must first spend a month on the islet of Mrkan or in the town of Cavtat. The forty days, and the word quarantine, came later.
cards.move: A word's origin records the version that stuck, not the first one.
cards.trap: True, because quarantine means forty days in Venetian.
cards.source: Blažina Tomić and Blažina, Expelling the Plague
cards.reference: Blažina Tomić and Blažina, Expelling the Plague: The Health Office and the Implementation of Quarantine in Dubrovnik, 1377-1533, McGill-Queen's University Press, 2015

cards.question: Pollen from 261 lake and bog cores tracks European farming across the Black Death. What does it show?
options: Hardly any change in any region
Losses in some regions, growth elsewhere
cards.answer: Losses in some regions, growth elsewhere. Cereal pollen fell sharply in Scandinavia, France, south-west Germany, Greece and central Italy, but farming held up or grew in much of central and eastern Europe, Ireland and Iberia. The reading is contested, but the famous toll of about half fits only part of the map.
cards.move: A figure from the best-recorded places may not describe the rest.
cards.trap: Half of farming lost everywhere, like the famous death toll.
cards.source: Izdebski et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2022

cards.question: In Strasbourg in February 1349, what drove the killing of the city's Jews?
cards.answer: Fear and debt, not plague deaths. Plague had not yet reached Strasbourg when a coup removed the council that protected the Jews. On 14 February they were killed, about 2,000 by one count; debts owed to them were cancelled and their cash shared out. The chronicler Königshofen wrote that money killed them.
cards.move: When blame lands on a creditor, ask who gains if the debts vanish.
cards.source: Königshofen, via Fordham Internet History Sourcebook
cards.reference: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/jewish/1348-jewsblackdeath.asp

cards.question: What did England do with the fines it took from workers demanding post-plague wages?
cards.answer: It paid village taxes with them. Under the labour laws that capped pay after the Black Death, fines went to lighten each village's share of a parliamentary tax. In Essex in 1352 they came to £710, and £675 went to poorer villages: more than half the county's £1,234 assessment was paid from workers' fines.
cards.move: Follow a fine to see whose bill it quietly pays.
cards.source: Victoria County History of Essex, vol. 4
cards.reference: https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/essex/vol4/pp296-302

cards.question: What trace of the Black Death can still be found in the genes of living Europeans?
cards.answer: A defence with a price. In 2022 Klunk and colleagues compared DNA from Londoners and Danes who died before, during and after it. Variants of an immune gene, ERAP2, rose fast: two copies of the favoured version raised the odds of surviving by roughly 40%. That version now brings a higher risk of Crohn's disease.
cards.move: A defence chosen by one crisis can become a weakness in the next.
cards.reference: Klunk et al., Evolution of immune genes is associated with the Black Death, Nature 611, 2022, 312-319

cards.question: True or false: the Black Death killed people in poor health and in good health at about the same rate?
cards.answer: False. Sharon DeWitte and James Wood studied skeletons from East Smithfield, a London plague cemetery of 1348 to 1349. Compared with burials from ordinary times, people whose bones showed earlier stress, such as lesions or stunting, were likelier to be among the plague dead. Old hardship left marks that predicted who fell.
cards.move: Even a disaster that looks blind usually has a pattern in whom it takes.
cards.trap: Trusting chronicles that describe the healthy dying overnight.
cards.reference: DeWitte and Wood, Selectivity of Black Death mortality with respect to preexisting health, PNAS 105, 2008, 1436-1441

cards.question: England lost perhaps half its people in 1348 and 1349. When did its population regain the level it had before?
cards.answer: In the early 1600s, on most estimates. Plague kept returning every decade or so, and deaths outran births: England fell further, to around 2 million in the mid-1400s. Only under the early Stuarts did it pass its pre-plague level of roughly 4.5 to 5 million. Some villages never returned, surviving as bumps in fields.
cards.move: One blow heals; a blow that keeps repeating sets a new normal.
cards.trap: Expecting a rebound within a few generations, as after one blow.
cards.source: Broadberry et al., British Economic Growth, 2015
cards.reference: Broadberry, Campbell, Klein, Overton and van Leeuwen, British Economic Growth, 1270-1870, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: Were rats and their fleas the main spreaders of the Black Death in Europe's towns?
cards.answer: Plague is a disease of rodents, and the bacterium's biology suits fleas that feed on them. Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis as the cause, and rats thronged medieval towns and ships. Outbreaks followed trade routes and peaked in warm months, as flea-borne plague does. Nothing more exotic is needed to explain the pattern.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the speed of spread inside a town decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The Black Death moved faster than rat outbreaks usually do, and chroniclers seldom mention dead rats. In 2018 Katharine Dean and colleagues modelled nine European outbreaks: in seven, human fleas and body lice fitted the death curves better than rats. Passing from person to person in crowded homes, plague needed no rats at all.
cards.reference: Dean et al., Human ectoparasites and the spread of plague in Europe during the Second Pandemic, PNAS 115, 2018, 1304-1309

cards.question: Why did chroniclers call the plague's return in 1361 the mortality of children?
cards.answer: Because it fell hardest on the young. Chroniclers in England and France recorded that the second outbreak took children and youths above all. One explanation: most adults alive in 1361 had come through 1348, while those born since had never met it. The dead of 1361 were the generation meant to refill the villages.
cards.move: Ask what the survivors of the last disaster share before predicting the next.
cards.reference: Horrox (ed. and trans.), The Black Death, Manchester Medieval Sources, Manchester University Press, 1994

cards.question: A 2025 atlas traced 299,171 km of Roman roads. For what share of that length is the exact route known for certain?
cards.answer: About 3%. The Itiner-e dataset, published in 2025, nearly doubled the previous count of 188,555 km, but only 2.7% of its length follows a precisely known course. Almost 90% is placed from texts, old maps and remote sensing, and 7.4% is hypothetical. Most of the network is an informed line on a modern map.
cards.move: What survives in plain sight is rarely a fair sample of what existed.
cards.trap: About 90%, because the famous stretches still show on the ground.

diagram.caption: Of every 1,000 km of mapped Roman road, only 27 follow a course known for certain.

cards.source: de Soto et al., Scientific Data, 2025
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-06140-z

cards.question: Where does the textbook four-layer cross-section of a Roman road come from?
cards.answer: From a recipe for floors. In 1622 Nicolas Bergier took Vitruvius's instructions for laying house pavements, layer names and all, and applied them to roads. Later writers hardened his sections near Reims into a fixed four-layer rule, though excavated Roman roads vary with the ground and the local stone. The diagram outlived the evidence.
cards.move: A diagram repeated for centuries can rest on a single borrowed source.
cards.reference: Codrington, Roman Roads in Britain, SPCK, 1903

cards.question: In Diocletian's price edict of 301, how much dearer was moving cargo a given distance by wagon than by sea?
cards.answer: About fifty times. Estimates from the edict's maximum prices vary, but land haulage always comes out dozens of times dearer than sea; Stanford's model of Roman travel costs uses 52, with river barges at 5 to 10. Rome's grain came by ship from Egypt and Africa; roads carried soldiers, officials and letters.
cards.move: Follow the bulk freight, not the monuments, to see how an economy moved.
cards.trap: About twice as dear, since paved roads suggest easy haulage.
cards.reference: https://orbis.stanford.edu/assets/Scheidel_59.pdf

cards.question: Why do Roman roads still predict prosperity in Europe but not in North Africa?
