cards.answer: Because the wheel left North Africa and the Middle East. In late antiquity camel caravans replaced carts there, so the roads fell out of use and were not rebuilt. In Europe carts kept them busy, and denser Roman roads still line up with brighter night-time lights seen from satellites.
cards.move: Infrastructure lasts only as long as something keeps using it.
cards.source: Dalgaard et al., Journal of Comparative Economics, 2022
cards.reference: Dalgaard, Kaarsen, Olsson and Selaya, Roman roads to prosperity: Persistence and non-persistence of public infrastructure, Journal of Comparative Economics 50, 2022

cards.question: Who supplied the carts and mules for Roman officials travelling on state business?
cards.answer: The towns along the road. Under Tiberius, an edict at Sagalassos, in modern Turkey, made the town keep up to ten carts and ten mules for officials, at fixed fees in bronze coin: 10 asses a cart and 4 a mule per schoenus, a local measure of distance. Many had simply taken them unpaid.
cards.move: When a service looks free, find out who was made to provide it.
cards.reference: Mitchell, Requisitioned Transport in the Roman Empire: A New Inscription from Pisidia, Journal of Roman Studies 66, 1976, 106-131

cards.question: How can archaeologists tell which way carts moved through the streets of Pompeii?
cards.answer: From scrapes on the kerbstones. A cart turning a corner grinds its wheel against the kerb on one side, so the wear shows which way it turned. Mapping such marks and the ruts in stepping stones, Eric Poehler reconstructed a system in which many streets were one-way. The pavement kept the traffic log.
cards.move: Wear marks record what nobody thought worth writing down.
cards.source: Poehler, The Traffic Systems of Pompeii, 2017
cards.reference: Poehler, The Traffic Systems of Pompeii, Oxford University Press, 2017

cards.question: True or false: when the Via Appia opened in 312 BC, it was paved with fitted stone blocks?
cards.answer: False. Appius Claudius's road began as a levelled, drained track without a stone pavement. Livy records the paving arriving piece by piece: in 293 BC blocks of hard volcanic stone were laid from the temple of Mars, just outside Rome, to Bovillae. The polished blocks visitors walk on today belong to the road's later life.
cards.move: The version that survives is rarely the version that was first built.
cards.trap: Picturing the paved road that survives today as the original.
cards.reference: Livy, History of Rome, Books 8-10, trans. B. O. Foster, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1926

cards.question: An early Roman law made a right of way 8 Roman feet wide where it ran straight. How wide on a bend?
cards.answer: 16 feet. The Twelve Tables, Rome's first written code, fixed a way across private land at 8 feet on the straight and double that where it turned, as the jurist Gaius later quoted. A cart, or a pair of yoked oxen, swings wide on a turn. The law wrote the turning circle into property.
cards.move: Measure the room a thing needs when it turns, not when it runs straight.
cards.trap: Assuming a road's legal width is the same along its length.
cards.reference: The Digest of Justinian, vol. 1, ed. Mommsen, Krueger and Watson, University of Pennsylvania Press, 1985

cards.question: A Roman milestone bears the name and titles of an emperor who reigned 275 to 276. What does it date securely?
options: When the road was last repaired
cards.answer: When its inscription was cut. In the third century towns often raised milestones to greet each new emperor, with no roadwork behind them, and some stones were recut for a successor. One road can carry stones naming emperors across three centuries. The inscription is a loyalty card, not a building record.
cards.move: A name on a monument tells you who was honoured, not who worked.
cards.trap: Reading an emperor's name on a road as proof he built it.
cards.source: Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy, 1999
cards.reference: Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy: Mobility and Cultural Change, Routledge, 1999

cards.question: Pliny records Tiberius covering 200 Roman miles, of about 1.48 km each, in a day and a night. Average speed in km/h?
cards.move: Speed over a whole day is set by the stops, not the pace.
cards.trap: Picturing a gallop, when the feat was never stopping for a day.
cards.hint: Turn the Roman miles into kilometres first, then share them over the hours.
steps: 200 Roman miles x 1.48 km = 296 km.
A day and a night is 24 hours.
cards.reference: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, vol. 2, trans. H. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1942

cards.question: True or false: the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 drew the borders of Africa's colonies?
cards.answer: False. Its General Act of 1885 set rules for future claims on the coast, notification and effective occupation, and free trade and navigation in the Congo basin; it drew no map of Africa. Most lines came from dozens of bilateral treaties over the next 30 years, many straight because negotiators knew little of the interior.
cards.move: The meeting everyone remembers is rarely where the details were decided.
cards.trap: School history pictures diplomats in Berlin carving Africa on a map.
cards.source: Förster et al., Bismarck, Europe, and Africa, 1988
cards.reference: Förster, Mommsen & Robinson (eds), Bismarck, Europe, and Africa: The Berlin Africa Conference 1884–1885 and the Onset of Partition, Oxford University Press, 1988

cards.question: In 1529, how did Spain and Portugal settle where their 1494 dividing line fell on the far side of the world?
options: Astronomers timed an eclipse at both ends
Spain sold its claim to Portugal
The Pope marked it on a globe
cards.answer: Spain sold its claim to Portugal. The 1494 treaty put the line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands without saying which island or which league, and nobody could measure longitude at sea. After experts at Badajoz failed to agree in 1524, Spain took 350,000 ducats for the Moluccas in 1529.
cards.move: When a thing cannot be measured, expect it to be bought.
cards.trap: Remembering the papal line of 1493 and giving the Pope the job.
cards.reference: Davenport (ed.), European Treaties bearing on the History of the United States and its Dependencies to 1648, Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1917

cards.question: Why do the ruler-straight country roads of the American Midwest suddenly jog sideways every so often?
cards.answer: Because the Earth is round. The public land survey laid out square townships 9.7 km on a side along meridians, but meridians converge towards the pole, so the squares would have shrunk northwards. Surveyors reset the grid along correction lines, usually every 39 km, and roads that follow the grid step sideways there.
cards.move: Any grid laid on a curved surface must break somewhere; look for the seams.
cards.reference: Bureau of Land Management, Manual of Surveying Instructions for the Survey of the Public Lands of the United States, 2009

cards.question: True or false: the border between North and South Korea today follows the 38th parallel?
cards.answer: False. The 38th parallel was the line two US officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, picked in August 1945 to split the Soviet and American zones. Today's border is the 1953 armistice line, drawn where the fighting stopped. It crosses the parallel on a slant: Kaesong, once in the South, now lies in the North.
cards.move: A name can stay fixed long after the thing it names has moved.
cards.trap: The phrase 38th parallel still stands for the Korean border in the news.
cards.source: Cumings, The Korean War: A History, 2010
cards.reference: Cumings, The Korean War: A History, Modern Library, 2010

cards.question: What dispute were Mason and Dixon hired to settle when they surveyed their line in the 1760s?
cards.answer: A property quarrel between two families. The Penns of Pennsylvania and the Calverts of Maryland had long disputed where their grants met; an English astronomer and a surveyor ran the line by the stars from 1763 to 1767, setting stones carved with each family's arms. Only later did it divide free states from slave.
cards.move: A line drawn for one purpose can come to mean something else entirely.
cards.reference: Danson, Drawing the Line: How Mason and Dixon Surveyed the Most Famous Border in America, John Wiley & Sons, 2001

cards.question: Colorado's western border runs near 109°03′ west of Greenwich. Why such an untidy number for a ruler-straight line?
cards.answer: Because Congress measured it from Washington, not Greenwich. The 1861 act creating Colorado Territory set its sides at 37° and 41° north and at 25° and 32° west of the Washington meridian, which runs about 77° west of Greenwich. 32 plus 77 is 109. Greenwich became the world's zero only in 1884.
cards.move: When a number looks untidy, ask what zero it was measured from.
cards.source: Van Zandt, Boundaries of the United States, 1966
cards.reference: Van Zandt, Boundaries of the United States and the Several States, US Geological Survey Bulletin 1212, 1966

cards.question: True or false: the Four Corners monument stands hundreds of metres from the point where four US states legally meet?
cards.answer: False. Surveyors of the 1860s and 1870s set the corner with the instruments they had; once the states accepted it, the surveyed mark became the border. In 1925 the Supreme Court upheld a flawed Colorado–New Mexico survey line on that principle. The monument may miss its intended meridian; the law follows the stone.
cards.move: Once a boundary is marked and accepted, the marker outranks the map.
cards.trap: Recalling news stories that the monument had been put in the wrong place.
cards.source: US Supreme Court, New Mexico v. Colorado, 1925
cards.reference: New Mexico v. Colorado, 267 U.S. 30, 1925

cards.question: Why does a piece of Minnesota lie north of the 49th parallel, reachable by road only through Canada?
options: A swap to keep a fur-trading post
An undivided reserve of a Native nation
A treaty drafted on a faulty map
cards.answer: A treaty drafted on a faulty map. The 1783 peace ran the border to the north-western point of the Lake of the Woods and due west to the Mississippi, which their map showed further north; its source lies far south. An 1818 treaty dropped a line from there to the 49th parallel, stranding the Angle.
cards.move: Old boundary wording outlives the map it was written against.
cards.trap: Assuming an odd border must record a local deal, not a paper error.
cards.reference: Treaty of Paris, 1783, Article 2, and Convention of 1818, Article 2, in Miller (ed.), Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States of America, vol. 2, Government Printing Office, 1931

cards.question: Under the Sykes–Picot agreement of 1916, in which power's zone was Mosul, now in northern Iraq?
cards.answer: France's. The 1916 map drew zones of influence, not borders, and put Mosul in the French area reaching out from Syria. In December 1918 Clemenceau agreed to let Britain have it, and in 1925 the League of Nations kept Mosul in British-run Iraq against Turkey's claim. Today's Syria–Iraq border came from those later bargains.
cards.move: Before crediting a famous plan, check it against what was finally built.
cards.trap: Reading today's Iraqi Mosul back into the 1916 plan.
cards.source: Barr, A Line in the Sand, 2011
cards.reference: Barr, A Line in the Sand: Britain, France and the Struggle that Shaped the Middle East, Simon & Schuster, 2011

cards.question: Did the borders drawn by colonial powers cause much of Africa's conflict after independence?
sides: Yes, they caused much of it
cards.answer: Colonial negotiators, often knowing little of the ground, split many peoples' homelands between states. Michalopoulos and Papaioannou find that partitioned groups have suffered more political violence and discrimination since independence than groups left whole. Lines drawn for European bargaining handed new states rivals and grievances they had not chosen.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, comparing split peoples with whole ones decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Africa's borders have proved remarkably stable: since the Organisation of African Unity pledged in 1964 to keep them, wars between states over territory have been rare. Jeffrey Herbst argues the deeper problem was states too weak to govern their hinterlands, whatever the lines. Any redrawing would have split other peoples and invited new claims.
cards.reference: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa, American Economic Review, 2016; Herbst, States and Power in Africa, Princeton University Press, 2000

cards.question: Who first dated the end of the Western Roman Empire to 476?
cards.answer: A chronicler in Constantinople, four decades later. Marcellinus Comes, writing around 518, is the earliest surviving source to enter under 476 that the western empire perished with Romulus Augustulus. In Italy the change looked smaller: Odoacer kept the Senate and ruled nominally under the eastern emperor. The date later served Justinian's case for reconquering Italy.
cards.move: A turning point is often named later, by someone who needed one.
cards.reference: Croke, A.D. 476: The Manufacture of a Turning Point, Chiron 13, 1983, 81-119

cards.question: Lead from Roman silver smelting settled on Greenland's ice. When did those emissions collapse?
options: Around 410, with the sack of Rome
cards.answer: Around 165, with the Antonine Plague. Lead in Greenland ice tracks European smelting of lead-silver ores. It rose through the early empire, plunged with the plague of 165 and another in the third century, and stayed low for over 500 years. By this measure the Roman economy peaked three centuries before 476.
cards.move: The date everyone remembers is rarely when the change began.
cards.trap: Around 476, the date every textbook gives for the fall.

cards.question: Did the Western Roman Empire truly fall, rather than slowly transform into medieval Europe?
cards.answer: It fell, and people paid for it. In Britain, coins, wheel-thrown pottery and tiled roofs vanished within a few generations; across the West, trade goods thinned out and buildings shrank. By the comfort archaeology can measure, living standards fell for centuries. Calling that a transformation turns a catastrophe into a change of costume.
cards.move: The verdict turns on whether you count institutions or living standards.
cards.counterpoint: Much of Rome carried on under new management. Gothic and Burgundian kings issued codes of Roman law, kept Latin in government and relied on bishops who ran the cities; Theoderic's Italy still had a Senate and consuls. The richer eastern half lasted another thousand years. Britain's collapse was the extreme, not the rule.
cards.reference: Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization, Oxford University Press, 2005

cards.question: What did Alaric ask for in his last offer before sacking Rome in 410?
cards.answer: Very little. After earlier demands for gold, grain, land and a Roman generalship were refused, Alaric asked only for Noricum, a poor, raided frontier province on the Danube, and a yearly grant of grain, with no gold and no office. The emperor's ministers still said no. Months later, in August 410, his Goths entered Rome.
cards.move: Refusing a small demand can cost more than granting it.
cards.reference: Zosimus, New History, trans. R. T. Ridley, Australian Association for Byzantine Studies, 1982

cards.question: What happened to the last western emperor after he was deposed in 476?
cards.answer: He was pensioned off. Odoacer, who had just killed his father Orestes, spared the teenage Romulus Augustulus for his youth and, a chronicler adds, his good looks, gave him 6,000 gold solidi a year and sent him to live freely with relatives in Campania. The western empire ended in a retirement settlement.
cards.move: Grand endings often look, up close, like paperwork.
cards.reference: Excerpta Valesiana, in Ammianus Marcellinus, vol. 3, trans. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1939

cards.question: True or false: Romulus Augustulus, deposed in 476, was the last western emperor Constantinople recognised?
cards.answer: False. Constantinople never recognised him. Its western colleague was Julius Nepos, driven out of Italy in 475 by Romulus's father Orestes, who went on ruling from Salona in Dalmatia. Odoacer even struck coins in Nepos's name until Nepos was murdered in 480. For four years the West's lawful emperor lived across the Adriatic.
cards.move: Ask who recognised a ruler before calling him the last one.
cards.trap: Taking the textbook's last emperor to be the lawful one.
cards.reference: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire, vol. 2, Francis Cairns, 1983

cards.question: Victor of Vita says 80,000 Vandals and Alans, of every age and both sexes, crossed to Africa in 429. Estimate their fighting men, in thousands.
cards.answer: Perhaps half of those were of fighting age: about 20,000.
cards.move: Split a headcount into the people who can actually do the job.
cards.trap: Treating all 80,000 as warriors, as if it were an army roll.
cards.hint: Take out the women first, then the children and the old.
steps: Start from 80,000 people of all ages.
About half were male: 40,000.
Perhaps half of those were of fighting age: about 20,000.
cards.source: Victor of Vita, History of the Vandal Persecution
cards.reference: Victor of Vita, History of the Vandal Persecution, trans. John Moorhead, Liverpool University Press, 1992

cards.question: In 445, after Vandal wars, Rome cut the taxes due from the African provinces it had kept. To what share of before?
cards.answer: One-eighth. Novel 13 of Valentinian III set the tax of Numidia and Mauretania Sitifensis at an eighth of its old level, so ruined were they. Carthage and the richest estates had been Vandal since 439. The western court paid its soldiers from taxes, and its best-paying provinces now paid almost nothing.
cards.move: Judge a loss by what can still be collected, not by what is still held.
cards.trap: Choosing half, the size of an ordinary emergency relief.
cards.source: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire, 2005
cards.reference: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire: A New History, Macmillan, 2005

cards.question: How long did the Roman Senate go on meeting after the last western emperor was deposed?
cards.answer: More than a century. Under Odoacer and the Gothic kings the Senate still sat, and its leading men still held the consulship. Its last known collective act came in 603, when it acclaimed portraits of the eastern emperor Phocas in Rome. Around 630 its meeting house, the Curia, was turned into the church of Sant'Adriano.
cards.move: Institutions often outlive the power that once gave them meaning.
cards.reference: Humphries, Italy, A.D. 425-605, in Cameron, Ward-Perkins and Whitby (eds.), The Cambridge Ancient History, vol. 14, Cambridge University Press, 2000

cards.question: When Odoacer's soldiers were given a third of Italy in 476, a third of what?
cards.answer: Historians disagree. Procopius says the soldiers demanded a third of the land. In 1980 Walter Goffart argued that such settlements handed over a third of the tax due from estates, not the fields, which would explain why Italy's Roman landowners stayed rich. Critics reply that the texts speak of land. The ledger is still open.
cards.move: When a source gives a share, ask what it is a share of.
cards.reference: Goffart, Barbarians and Romans, A.D. 418-584: The Techniques of Accommodation, Princeton University Press, 1980

cards.question: How big is your blind spot?
cards.answer: Each eye has a hole in its field of view where the optic nerve leaves — large enough to swallow several full moons at arm's length. You never see it, because the brain fills the gap with a guess based on the surrounding pattern. The guess is usually right, which is the unsettling part.
cards.move: Your brain is painting over a hole in your vision. Continuously.
cards.source: Ramachandran, Nature, filling-in of the blind spot

cards.question: How old is your skeleton?
cards.answer: Younger than you. Bone is torn down and rebuilt continuously by two kinds of cell, and the adult skeleton turns over roughly every ten years. The shape persists; the material does not. What you feel as the most permanent part of the body is among the most rebuilt.
cards.move: Your skeleton is about ten years old, whatever your birthday says.

cards.question: Does your gut have a brain?
cards.answer: It has a nervous system of its own — hundreds of millions of neurons in the wall of the intestine — and it keeps coordinating digestion when the connection to the brain is severed. It is the only organ system that can run its reflexes without asking.
cards.move: The gut keeps working with the line to head office cut.

cards.question: Why does that shirt match indoors and clash outside?
cards.answer: Because colour vision takes only three samples of a continuous spectrum. Two objects reflecting quite different light can produce identical signals — a metameric match — under one light and separate under another. The colours did not change. The sampling did.
cards.move: Two colours can be the same colour, until you carry them to a window.
cards.reference: Wyszecki & Stiles, Color Science: Concepts and Methods, Quantitative Data and Formulae, Wiley, 1982

cards.question: What makes a heart beat?
cards.answer: The heart does. A cluster of pacemaker cells generates its own rhythm, and the brain only speeds it up or slows it down. A heart removed from the body and supplied with oxygen keeps beating on its own — which is precisely why transplantation is possible.
cards.move: The brain does not start the heartbeat. It only argues about the tempo.

cards.question: What makes the room spin when someone with the commonest kind of vertigo rolls over in bed?
cards.answer: Loose crystals. Grains of calcium carbonate, the otoconia, normally rest on the inner ear's gravity sensors. When some break free and drift into a semicircular canal, the part that senses rotation, they slosh with each tilt and fake a spin. A sequence of head turns from John Epley, 1992, rolls them back out.
cards.move: A sensor fed the wrong input will report it faithfully.
cards.reference: Epley, The canalith repositioning procedure: for treatment of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, 1992

cards.question: Why does the room spin when a drunk person lies down, and again the next morning?
cards.answer: Because alcohol changes the density of the balance sensors. It seeps into the cupula, the gel flap inside each semicircular canal, before it reaches the surrounding fluid, so the flap turns lighter and drifts with every tilt. Hours later it leaves the cupula first, the imbalance reverses, and the eyes flick the other way.
cards.move: Two things out of step can matter more than the level of either.
cards.reference: Money & Myles, Heavy water nystagmus and effects of alcohol, Nature, 1974

cards.question: In the dark, a jet accelerates forward at 1 g. By how many degrees nose-up does the pilot feel tilted?
cards.answer: The sensors read that as leaning back: 45 degrees nose-up.
cards.move: A sensor that measures force cannot tell a push from a lean.
cards.trap: Assuming the body can feel acceleration as something separate from tilt.
cards.hint: The inner ear's gravity sensors feel only the total pull; add the two pulls as arrows.
steps: Gravity pulls down on the inner ear's gravity sensors at 1 g.
Accelerating forward at 1 g presses them backward with another 1 g.
Two equal pulls at right angles combine along the diagonal between them.
The sensors read that as leaning back: 45 degrees nose-up.
cards.source: Previc & Ercoline, Spatial Disorientation in Aviation
cards.reference: Previc & Ercoline (eds), Spatial Disorientation in Aviation, AIAA, 2004

cards.question: A doctor loses both inner-ear balance organs to an antibiotic. What troubles him most in daylight?
options: The world jiggling as he walks
cards.answer: The world jiggling as he walks. Without the reflex that turns the eyes against each head movement, every footstep shakes the image. A physician who lost both organs to streptomycin wrote in 1952 that he could read in bed only with his head held still between the bars of the bedstead.
cards.move: A failure spread evenly is harder to feel than a lopsided one.
cards.trap: Equating a lost balance organ with spinning dizziness.
cards.source: J.C., New England Journal of Medicine, 1952
cards.reference: J.C., Living without a balancing mechanism, New England Journal of Medicine, 1952

cards.question: True or false: people whose inner-ear balance organs no longer work cannot get motion sick?
cards.answer: True. Motion sickness needs the inner ear: it arises when balance signals disagree with what the eyes and body expect. At sea in storms and in rotating rooms, people without working labyrinths stayed well while others vomited. Blind people, by contrast, still get seasick, so the eyes are not required.
cards.move: To find what a symptom needs, study the people who never get it.
cards.trap: Blaming motion sickness on the stomach or on what the eyes see.
cards.reference: Money, Motion sickness, Physiological Reviews, 1970

cards.question: Flying in cloud, a pilot holds a steady turn for half a minute, then rolls level. What do the inner ears report?
cards.answer: A turn the opposite way. The canals sense changes in rotation, not rotation itself; after 20 seconds or so of steady turning the turn feels level. Stopping it is a change in rotation, read as a new turn. A pilot who leans back into the old turn can enter a descending spiral.
cards.move: A sensor that reports change calls the return to normal a change too.
cards.trap: Assuming the wings being level is what the body feels.
cards.source: FAA, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge
cards.reference: Federal Aviation Administration, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25B, 2016

cards.question: What can cold water run into one ear briefly restore to some stroke patients?
cards.answer: Awareness of their own paralysis. After right-brain strokes some patients ignore the left side of space and deny that their left limbs are weak. Cold water in the left ear stirs the balance canals, and in a 1987 study the neglect and the denial faded for a while, returning as the stimulation wore off.
cards.move: A belief that no argument shifts may still yield to a change of input.
cards.reference: Cappa, Sterzi, Vallar & Bisiach, Remission of hemineglect and anosognosia during vestibular stimulation, Neuropsychologia, 1987

cards.question: Footprints show australopiths walked upright 3.7 million years ago. What did scans of their inner-ear canals suggest?
options: Balance organs still like a great ape's
Balance organs unlike any living primate
cards.answer: Balance organs still like a great ape's. Measuring the canals in fossil skulls in 1994, Spoor and colleagues found ape-sized vertical canals in australopiths, while Homo erectus already had the enlarged human ones. Upright walking came first; the equipment for running and balancing on two legs arrived later. The inner ear dates what footprints cannot.
cards.move: One piece of evidence that agrees does not settle the whole question.
cards.trap: Taking upright footprints as proof of a fully human body.
cards.reference: Spoor, Wood & Zonneveld, Implications of early hominid labyrinthine morphology for evolution of human bipedal locomotion, Nature, 1994

cards.question: Why do some people who feel the ground rocking for weeks after a cruise feel better while driving?
cards.answer: Because the brain is still running the model of motion it built at sea. In mal de débarquement syndrome the rocking persists after landing, sometimes for months, mostly in middle-aged women. Passive motion in a car or train matches that model and quiets the illusion; standing still exposes it again.
cards.move: An illusion learned from motion can be soothed by motion.
cards.reference: Cha, Mal de debarquement, Seminars in Neurology, 2009

cards.question: Ballet dancers spin for years without growing dizzy. What changed in them, according to eye and brain tests?
options: Their inner ears became less sensitive
Their eyes stopped reacting to rotation
Their brains discount the spinning signal
cards.answer: Their brains discount the spinning signal. After spins, dancers' eyes still flicked, if less, but the feeling of turning faded far sooner than in rowers of similar fitness, and the two measures no longer tracked each other. Scans linked this to less grey matter in a part of the cerebellum that handles balance signals.
cards.move: Training can change what reaches awareness, not only the sensor itself.
cards.trap: Picturing the sense organ toughening, as skin hardens into a callus.
cards.reference: Nigmatullina, Hellyer, Nachev, Sharp & Seemungal, The neuroanatomical correlates of training-related perceptuo-reflex uncoupling in dancers, Cerebral Cortex, 2015

cards.question: Which rare blood looks like group O on a routine test, yet cannot safely receive O blood?
cards.answer: The Bombay type, found in 1952. Carriers lack the H antigen, the base on which A and B are built, so their cells test as O. Their plasma carries anti-H, which destroys ordinary O cells. About 1 in 10,000 Indians have it, and 1 in a million Europeans; only Bombay blood is safe for them.
cards.move: A test that sorts by what is present can miss what is absent.
cards.source: Dean, Blood Groups and Red Cell Antigens, 2005
cards.reference: Dean, Blood Groups and Red Cell Antigens, National Center for Biotechnology Information, Bethesda, 2005

cards.question: How old is the difference between blood groups A and B?
cards.answer: Tens of millions of years, older than our species. The same two amino-acid changes separate A from B in humans, gibbons and Old World monkeys, and a 2012 study found the variants were inherited from a shared ancestor, not reinvented. Someone can share a blood group with a gibbon yet differ from a sibling.
cards.move: Ask how old a difference is before explaining it by recent history.

cards.question: An Rh-negative mother is injected with anti-D antibodies. Why does that stop her making her own?
cards.answer: Nobody is entirely sure. Untreated, an Rh-negative woman can be immunised by her Rh-positive baby's blood and attack the next baby's red cells; since the late 1960s anti-D has prevented most such cases. The usual story: injected antibody clears fetal cells before her immune system notices. It fails to explain all the evidence.
cards.move: A treatment can work reliably long before anyone knows why.
cards.reference: doi:10.1182/asheducation-2009.1.185

cards.question: Blood type was tested against 68 personality items; 3 came out significant. At a 5% threshold, how many would chance alone give?
cards.answer: About 3.4 items, close to the 3 found.
cards.move: Before counting hits, count how many times the net was cast.
cards.trap: Three hits look like a pattern rather than expected noise.
cards.hint: Treat each item as a separate lottery ticket with a 1 in 20 chance.
steps: With no real link, each item still has a 5% chance of passing.
About 3.4 items, close to the 3 found.

cards.question: True or false: for plasma transfusions, group AB is the universal donor?
cards.answer: True. Red cells carry the A and B antigens, so group O cells suit anyone; plasma carries the antibodies, and only AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B. So AB plasma can go to any patient, while O plasma, full of both, suits only group O. Just 3 to 4% of people are AB.
cards.move: When the thing being given changes, check whether the rule flips.
cards.trap: Carrying over the red-cell rule that makes O the universal donor.
cards.reference: Klein & Anstee, Mollison's Blood Transfusion in Clinical Medicine, 12th edition, Wiley-Blackwell, 2014

cards.question: Why does a person with group O blood carry antibodies against A and B cells they have never met?
cards.answer: Because they have met look-alikes. Gut bacteria carry sugars shaped much like the A and B antigens, and the immune system answers them: newborns have almost none of these antibodies, which build up over the first months. In 1969 Springer and Horton had people swallow a bacterium bearing B-like sugars, and their anti-B rose.
cards.move: When a defence exists before the threat, look for a rehearsal somewhere else.
cards.reference: Springer & Horton, Blood group isoantibody stimulation in man by feeding blood group-active bacteria, Journal of Clinical Investigation, 1969

cards.question: Why is one of the commonest human malaria parasites nearly absent from West and Central Africa?
cards.answer: Because most people there lack the door it uses. Plasmodium vivax enters red cells through a surface protein, the Duffy blood-group antigen, and in 1976 Miller and colleagues showed that Duffy-negative people resisted it; most West and Central Africans are Duffy-negative. The shield leaks: vivax has since been found infecting Duffy-negative people in Madagascar.
cards.move: Resistance can rest on a missing part rather than an added defence.
cards.reference: Miller, Mason, Clyde & McGinniss, The resistance factor to Plasmodium vivax in blacks: the Duffy-blood-group genotype, FyFy, New England Journal of Medicine, 1976

cards.question: About 15% of Europeans are Rh-negative. Roughly what share of Han Chinese people are?
cards.answer: Under 1%, around 0.3 to 0.5%. The gene loss behind Rh-negative blood is common in Europe, commonest among Basques, and rare in East Asia. Chinese blood services treat Rh-negative donors as a rare group, nicknamed panda blood for its scarcity.
cards.move: A figure learned in one population is only a guess in another.
cards.trap: Carrying the familiar European figure over to another population.
cards.reference: Daniels, Human Blood Groups, 3rd edition, Wiley-Blackwell, 2013

cards.question: If 16% of people are Rh-negative and couples pair at random, what % of pregnancies pair an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive baby?
cards.move: A parent showing a trait is not the same as passing it on.
cards.trap: Multiplying 16% by 84% Rh-positive fathers, as if each passes it on.
cards.hint: Not every Rh-positive father passes the gene on; start from how common the gene is.
steps: Rh-negative means two copies of the d gene, so d's share is the square root of 0.16 = 0.4.
A random father passes on the Rh-positive gene with chance 1 - 0.4 = 0.6.
cards.source: Hartl & Clark, Principles of Population Genetics
cards.reference: Hartl & Clark, Principles of Population Genetics, 4th edition, Sinauer Associates, 2007

cards.question: Early 2020 studies tied blood group A to severe COVID-19 and group O to protection. What did a study of 107,796 people find?
options: No link to infection or severity
The same link, about as strong
Group O at the higher risk
cards.answer: No link to infection or severity. Anderson and colleagues followed everyone tested in a Utah health system: blood group made no difference to testing positive, hospital admission or intensive care. Early, smaller studies are the likeliest to report striking effects, which shrink as numbers grow; genetic studies still find at most a small effect.
cards.move: Expect a striking first result to shrink when a bigger study checks it.
cards.trap: Expecting an effect reported by several early studies to hold at full strength.
cards.source: Anderson et al., JAMA Network Open, 2021
cards.reference: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2778155

cards.question: What inside a bone senses how hard it is being used?
cards.answer: Cells buried in it. About 42 billion osteocytes sit walled into the mineral, linked by channels far finer than a hair. Bending a bone squeezes fluid through those channels, and the osteocytes are thought to read that flow and signal the cells that add or remove bone. In orbit, with little load, astronauts' bones thin.
cards.move: The part that feels the strain is often hidden inside the structure.
cards.reference: Buenzli & Sims, Quantifying the osteocyte network in the human skeleton, Bone, 2015

cards.question: What happened when a drug made fragile spines about 35% denser?
cards.answer: Bones broke more, not less. In a four-year trial of 202 women, reported in 1990, sodium fluoride raised spine density by 35% yet did not significantly reduce spinal fractures, while fractures elsewhere roughly tripled. The new bone was dense but fragile, and the cortical shell of the forearm thinned by 4%.
cards.move: Adding more material does not make a structure stronger if it is badly built.

cards.question: Scale a person up to twice the height, keeping every proportion. How many times more stress does each thigh bone bear?
cards.answer: Stress is load per area: 8 / 4 = 2 times.
cards.move: When size grows, check whether the load or the support grows faster.
cards.trap: Answering 8, the growth in weight, and forgetting the thicker bones.
cards.hint: Weight follows volume, but a bone's strength follows the area of its cross-section.
steps: Weight grows with volume: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times.
A bone's cross-section grows with area: 2 x 2 = 4 times.
Stress is load per area: 8 / 4 = 2 times.
cards.source: Haldane, On Being the Right Size, 1927
cards.reference: Haldane, On Being the Right Size, in Possible Worlds and Other Essays, Chatto & Windus, 1927

cards.question: True or false: most older women who break a bone have bone density in the osteoporosis range?
cards.answer: False. Studies put the share of fractures in women whose scans fall short of the osteoporosis threshold at between about half and four in five. Far more women have moderately low density than very low, so even at lower individual risk the larger group produces most breaks: the many with modest risk outnumber the few.
cards.move: Count how many people are in each group before blaming the riskiest.
cards.trap: Assuming the highest-risk group must supply most of the cases.
cards.source: Siris et al., Archives of Internal Medicine, 2004
cards.reference: Siris et al., Bone mineral density thresholds for pharmacological intervention to prevent fractures, Archives of Internal Medicine, 2004

cards.question: People with low vitamin D levels break more bones. In a trial of 25,871 adults, what did daily vitamin D do to fractures?
options: Cut them by about a third
Cut hip fractures but not others
cards.answer: Made no clear difference. Over about five years, 769 of 12,927 people taking 2,000 units a day had fractures, against 782 of 12,944 on placebo, and hip fractures did not fall either. Low vitamin D often travels with frailty, illness and days spent indoors, which break bones on their own.
cards.move: A marker of trouble is not always a lever to pull.
cards.trap: If low levels go with fractures, adding vitamin D should prevent them.

cards.question: Tennis and squash players carry extra bone in the hitting arm. When does starting the sport roughly double that gain?
cards.answer: Before or around puberty. Kannus and colleagues compared the two arms of female national-level players: those who began before or around their first period had two to three times the side-to-side difference of those who began later. Growing bone can widen as well as densify, and a wider tube resists bending far better.
cards.move: The same effort buys most while the thing is still being built.
cards.trap: Assuming bone answers exercise about equally well at any age.
cards.source: Kannus et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 1995
cards.reference: Kannus et al., Effect of starting age of physical activity on bone mass in the dominant arm of tennis and squash players, Annals of Internal Medicine, 1995

cards.question: An astronaut's hip loses about 1.5% of its bone a month. A six-month mission equals how many years of 1%-a-year ageing?
cards.answer: 9% / 1% a year = 9 years.
cards.move: Check the time unit on a rate before calling it small.
cards.trap: Hearing 1.5% as small without noticing it is per month.
cards.hint: Work out the total lost in orbit, then divide by the yearly rate.
steps: 1.5% a month x 6 months = 9% lost in orbit.
Ageing on Earth takes about 1% a year.
9% / 1% a year = 9 years.

cards.question: In ageing spongy bone, losing a cross-strut doubles the free length of an upright strut. How much of its buckling strength remains?
cards.answer: About a quarter. A slender strut buckles at a load that falls with the square of its free length, Euler's rule, so doubling the length leaves a quarter. So losing a few horizontal struts cuts strength far more than the small drop in density suggests. Vertebrae, mostly spongy bone, crumble under loads they once carried.
cards.move: When a length enters squared, doubling it quarters the result.
cards.trap: Assuming strength falls in step with length, so half remains.
cards.reference: Gibson, The mechanical behaviour of cancellous bone, Journal of Biomechanics, 1985

cards.question: True or false: the commonest fracture caused by fragile bones is a broken hip?
cards.answer: False. Fractures of the spine's vertebrae are commoner, and only about a third of them come to medical attention: a vertebra slowly crushes, and the sign is a stooped back or lost height rather than a fall and an ambulance. Hip fractures are rarer, but vivid, costly and often deadly, so they dominate the story.
cards.move: The injury that makes the news is rarely the commonest one.
cards.trap: Picturing the dramatic fall and ambulance that a hip fracture brings.
cards.reference: Cummings & Melton, Epidemiology and outcomes of osteoporotic fractures, The Lancet, 2002

cards.question: Why does a crack running across a bone struggle more the further it grows?
cards.answer: Because bone's structure keeps turning it aside. Dense bone is built from osteons, cylinders around blood channels, bound by weak cement lines that deflect and twist a crossing crack. Koester, Ager and Ritchie found that after just half a millimetre, breaking across bone took over five times the driving force of splitting along it.
cards.move: Weak joints in the right places can make a whole harder to break.

cards.question: How did William Harvey show that blood circulates, before anyone had seen a capillary?
cards.answer: With arithmetic. In 1628 he took deliberately low estimates for the blood each beat expels, multiplied by the beats in half an hour, and got more blood than the whole body holds. Food could not replace that; the same blood had to come round. Malpighi first saw capillaries in 1661, four years after Harvey died.
cards.move: A rough sum done honestly can settle what no one can yet see.
cards.reference: Harvey, An Anatomical Disputation Concerning the Movement of the Heart and Blood in Living Creatures, trans. Whitteridge, Blackwell, 1976

cards.question: Where along its circuit does blood move most slowly?
cards.answer: In the capillaries, the narrowest vessels. There are billions side by side, so their combined cross-section is roughly a thousand times the aorta's. The same flow, spread that wide, slows from about 30 cm a second in the aorta to under 1 mm a second: just long enough to trade oxygen for waste.
cards.move: Split one stream into many channels and each one slows down.
cards.reference: Levick, An Introduction to Cardiovascular Physiology, 5th edition, Hodder Arnold, 2010

cards.question: When does heart muscle receive most of its own blood supply?
cards.answer: Between beats. When the left ventricle contracts, its wall squeezes its own coronary vessels almost shut, so most of its blood arrives as it relaxes. As the heart speeds up, relaxation shortens more than contraction, so a racing heart has less time to feed itself when it needs more: one reason exertion brings chest pain.
cards.move: Check when a supply can flow, not just how much is sent.
cards.source: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Physiology, 2021
cards.reference: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition, Elsevier, 2021

cards.question: An arteriole relaxes and its radius grows by 19%. At the same pressure, how much more blood flows through it?
cards.answer: About twice as much. For smooth flow through a tube, Poiseuille's law makes flow rise with the fourth power of the radius: 1.19 x 1.19 x 1.19 x 1.19 ≈ 2. So the body steers blood with its smallest arteries: narrowing them by a sixth halves an organ's supply.
cards.move: When a size is multiplied by itself four times, small changes stop being small.
cards.trap: Assuming flow grows in step with the width.

diagram.caption: Flow goes with the radius to the fourth power: 19% wider doubles it, a sixth narrower halves it.

cards.reference: Klabunde, Cardiovascular Physiology Concepts, 2nd edition, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2011

cards.question: In its roughly 120-day life, about how many laps of the body does a red blood cell make, in thousands?
cards.answer: About 170 thousand laps.
cards.move: Divide the stock by the flow and you get the time for one turn.
cards.trap: Picturing a slow journey, when a lap takes about a minute.
cards.hint: Compare the body's blood volume with what the heart pumps each minute.
steps: About 5 litres of blood; the resting heart pumps about 5 litres a minute.
So a typical cell completes about one lap a minute.
120 days x 1,440 minutes a day = 172,800 minutes.
About 170 thousand laps.

cards.question: What happens to the fluid that seeps out of the capillaries all day long?
cards.answer: Lymph vessels carry most of it back, a few litres a day. Textbooks long had capillaries soaking it up again at their venous end; Levick and Michel's revised account shows that in most tissues outward seepage continues almost the whole way along. The surplus drains into the great veins at the base of the neck.
cards.move: Find where the overflow goes before believing a system balances itself.
cards.reference: Levick & Michel, Microvascular fluid exchange and the revised Starling principle, Cardiovascular Research, 2010

cards.question: At rest, which part of the circulation holds the most blood?
cards.answer: The veins, about two thirds of it. Their walls are thin and stretchy, so they fill like soft bags at low pressure and serve as a reservoir; the arteries hold under a fifth and the capillaries under a tenth. When blood is lost, the veins tighten and push their reserve back towards the heart.
cards.move: The part that stores a thing is often not the part that uses it.
cards.trap: Picturing the vast capillary network as the body's main store.
cards.reference: Mohrman & Heller, Cardiovascular Physiology, 9th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2018

cards.question: Blood in the aorta moves at well under a metre a second. How fast does the pulse travel along the arteries?
options: About as fast as the blood
cards.answer: About 5 to 10 metres a second. The pulse is a pressure wave running along elastic walls, not blood arriving, so it reaches the wrist a fraction of a second after the beat, well ahead of the blood. Stiffer walls carry it faster: above about 10 to 12 m/s marks aged arteries.
cards.move: A signal travelling through a medium can outrun the medium itself.
cards.trap: Letting the blood's own slow speed set the speed of the pulse.
cards.source: Laurent et al., European Heart Journal, 2006
cards.reference: Laurent et al., Expert consensus document on arterial stiffness: methodological issues and clinical applications, European Heart Journal, 2006

cards.question: With 1 mmHg equal to 13.6 mm of water, how much higher is arterial pressure at ankles 1.2 m below the heart, in mmHg?
cards.answer: About 88 mmHg higher than at the heart.
cards.move: In any column of fluid, ask how high it stands before comparing pressures.
cards.trap: Assuming the heart sets one pressure for the whole body.
cards.hint: Turn the height of the column into millimetres of water first.
steps: Treat blood as water: 1.2 m is a column of 1,200 mm.
Each mmHg is 13.6 mm of water: 1,200 / 13.6 = 88.2.
About 88 mmHg higher than at the heart.
cards.simply: At the heart, mean arterial pressure is about 90 to 100 mmHg; at the ankles of someone standing it is nearly double. The veins there gain the same extra pressure, so the push driving blood through the ankles barely changes.
cards.reference: Rowell, Human Cardiovascular Control, Oxford University Press, 1993

cards.question: The lungs weigh about a kilogram. True or false: they receive as much blood each minute as the rest of the body combined?
cards.answer: True. The circulation is two loops in series: every drop the right ventricle pumps must cross the lungs before the left ventricle can send it anywhere else. So the lungs take the heart's whole output, about 5 litres a minute, while brain, gut, kidneys and muscles share the equal flow on the other side.
cards.move: In a chain, every link carries the full load.
cards.trap: Sizing an organ's blood supply by its weight, as for other organs.
cards.reference: West & Luks, West's Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials, 10th edition, Wolters Kluwer, 2016

cards.question: Did northern Europeans and East African herders inherit their adult milk digestion from shared ancestors?
cards.answer: No. Each population carries its own mutation, arisen separately within the last several thousand years, yet they sit in the same short stretch of DNA: a switch that normally turns the lactase gene off after weaning. Evolution flipped that one switch several separate times, wherever people kept animals for milk.
cards.move: The same solution twice can mean the same problem twice, not shared descent.
cards.reference: Tishkoff, Reed, Ranciaro et al., Convergent adaptation of human lactase persistence in Africa and Europe, Nature Genetics, 2007

cards.question: Why does the pancreas not digest itself with the protein-cutting enzymes it makes?
cards.answer: It makes them switched off. Trypsin leaves as inactive trypsinogen; its normal key, an enzyme called enteropeptidase, sits on the lining of the small intestine; freed trypsin then activates the rest in a cascade. A single mutation that stops trypsin being shut down causes a hereditary pancreatitis, in which the gland digests itself.
cards.move: Ship the dangerous tool unarmed, and keep the trigger somewhere else.
cards.reference: Whitcomb, Gorry, Preston et al., Hereditary pancreatitis is caused by a mutation in the cationic trypsinogen gene, Nature Genetics, 1996

cards.question: What is the gut doing when an empty stomach growls a couple of hours after a meal?
cards.answer: Housekeeping. Between meals a wave of strong contractions, the migrating motor complex, sweeps from the stomach to the end of the small intestine roughly every 90 to 120 minutes, clearing leftover food and bacteria. Pushing gas and fluid ahead of it makes the noise; eating stops it at once.
cards.move: A noisy system at rest may simply be cleaning itself.
cards.source: Deloose et al., Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol, 2012
cards.reference: Deloose, Janssen, Depoortere & Tack, The migrating motor complex: control mechanisms and its role in health and disease, Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology, 2012

cards.question: Counting every fold and villus, how large is the inner surface of the adult gut?
cards.answer: About 30 square metres. Measuring tissue under the microscope, researchers in Gothenburg put the whole tract at about 32 square metres in 2014, nearly all of it small intestine, with the large intestine adding only about 2. That is the floor of a small studio flat, not the often-quoted tennis court.
cards.move: A dramatic comparison deserves one look at how it was measured.
cards.trap: Recalling the textbook claim that the gut lining equals a tennis court.

diagram.caption: The measured gut lining, 32 m², is about an eighth of the tennis court often quoted.

cards.reference: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.3109/00365521.2014.898326

cards.question: About how many litres of fluid pour into the gut each day, counting drinks and the body's own secretions?
cards.answer: 2 + 1.5 + 2 + 2 + 1 = about 8.5 litres a day.
cards.move: Measure the flow through a system, not only what enters from outside.
cards.trap: Counting only what is drunk and forgetting the body's own secretions.
cards.hint: List what the mouth, stomach, liver, pancreas and intestine each pour in.
steps: Food and drink bring in about 2 litres.
Saliva adds about 1.5 litres and the stomach about 2.
Bile and pancreatic juice add about 2, the intestinal wall about 1.
2 + 1.5 + 2 + 2 + 1 = about 8.5 litres a day.
cards.reference: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, 3rd edition, Elsevier, 2017

cards.question: Why does fat absorbed from a meal bypass the liver, when sugars and amino acids go straight there?
cards.answer: Because it is packaged too large for blood capillaries. Gut cells wrap digested fat into chylomicrons, droplets too big to pass into the capillaries of the villi, so they enter lymph vessels instead. The lymph drains into a vein near the left collarbone, and muscles and fat tissue get first pick.
cards.move: The route a delivery takes decides who gets first pick of it.
cards.source: Trevaskis et al., Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews, 2008
cards.reference: Trevaskis, Charman & Porter, Lipid-based delivery systems and intestinal lymphatic drug transport: a mechanistic update, Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews, 2008

cards.question: The body's 3 grams of bile acid cycle between gut and liver 6 times a day, 97% reabsorbed each pass. Grams lost daily?
cards.answer: 18 x 0.03 = 0.54 grams a day.
cards.move: A small leak on a busy loop is charged again on every lap.
cards.trap: Taking 3% of the 3-gram pool and forgetting the six passes.
cards.hint: Count how many grams pass through the gut in a day, not how many the body holds.
steps: Grams passing through the gut each day: 3 x 6 = 18.
Share lost on each pass: 100% - 97% = 3%.
18 x 0.03 = 0.54 grams a day.
cards.source: Dawson & Karpen, Journal of Lipid Research, 2015
cards.reference: Dawson & Karpen, Intestinal transport and metabolism of bile acids, Journal of Lipid Research, 2015

cards.question: Before the stomach lets solid food into the intestine, how small must the pieces be ground?
options: Under a tenth of a millimetre
cards.answer: About 1 to 2 millimetres. The lower stomach grinds food against the nearly closed pylorus, its muscular outlet, which lets liquid and fine particles through and pushes larger pieces back for more churning. That is why solids leave the stomach only after a lag, while a drink starts leaving almost at once.
cards.move: A gate that sets a size limit also sets the pace.
cards.trap: Assuming chewed, swallowed lumps pass on much as they are.
cards.source: Kong & Singh, Journal of Food Science, 2008
cards.reference: Kong & Singh, Disintegration of solid foods in human stomach, Journal of Food Science, 2008

cards.question: True or false: most of the protein in a meal is digested in the stomach, by its acid and pepsin?
cards.answer: False. Pepsin starts the job but usually handles only about 10 to 20% of protein digestion. Most is done in the small intestine by pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin, and finished by enzymes on the gut lining. People whose whole stomach has been removed still digest most of their protein.
cards.move: The most dramatic stage of a process is rarely where most work happens.
cards.trap: The acid bath is the vivid picture of digestion, so it gets the credit.
cards.reference: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition, Elsevier, 2020

cards.question: What differs in the saliva of people whose ancestors lived on rice, wheat or tubers?
cards.answer: It carries more starch-cutting enzyme. The gene for salivary amylase, AMY1, comes in anything from about 2 to 15 copies per person, and enzyme levels track the copies. In 2007, populations with starch-rich diets averaged more copies than rainforest hunters, herders and Arctic peoples who eat little starch. Chewed bread is already being digested.
cards.move: What a people eat for long enough can be counted in their genes.
cards.reference: Perry, Dominy, Claw et al., Diet and the evolution of human amylase gene copy number variation, Nature Genetics, 2007

cards.question: What decides whether a fingertip grows a whorl, a loop or an arch?
cards.answer: Timing, largely. In the fourth month of pregnancy, ridges start at three spots on each fingertip, the pad's centre, near the nail and at the crease, and spread as waves, a Turing-type chemical pattern. Where the waves meet, and which set off first, fixes the type; chance fills in the details, even for identical twins.
cards.move: Where two spreading fronts meet can decide the whole shape.

cards.question: Can burning off the skin of the fingertips erase a person's fingerprints?
cards.answer: Only if the damage goes deep. The ridge pattern is anchored where the outer skin meets the dermis beneath, so shallow burns or scrapes regrow the same pattern. The gangster John Dillinger had acid put on his fingertips in 1934; when he was shot that summer, his scarred prints still matched FBI records.
cards.move: Damage to the surface rarely erases what is written underneath.
cards.reference: Burrough, Public Enemies: America's Greatest Crime Wave and the Birth of the FBI, 1933-34, Penguin Press, 2004

cards.question: Where was a murder first solved with the help of a fingerprint?
cards.answer: Argentina, in 1892. In Necochea, Francisca Rojas blamed a neighbour for the killing of her two children. Police found a bloody thumbprint on a door; it matched her right thumb, and she confessed. The method came from Juan Vucetich of the La Plata police. London's police opened their fingerprint bureau only in 1901.
cards.move: The famous version of a story is rarely the first version.
cards.trap: London and its famous detectives come to mind first.
cards.reference: Cole, Suspect Identities: A History of Fingerprinting and Criminal Identification, Harvard University Press, 2001

cards.question: True or false: fingerprint experts have declared a certain match between a crime-scene print and an innocent person?
cards.answer: True. After the 2004 Madrid train bombings, an FBI database search put an Oregon lawyer, Brandon Mayfield, among its closest candidates; three FBI examiners and a court-appointed expert called the match certain. Spanish police traced the print to an Algerian man. Searching tens of millions of prints makes a convincing look-alike far more likely.
cards.move: Search a big enough haystack and something will look like a needle.
cards.trap: Fingerprints are unique, so a careful expert cannot confuse two.
cards.reference: US Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General, A Review of the FBI's Handling of the Brandon Mayfield Case, 2006

cards.question: Should courts accept a fingerprint examiner's match without being told an error rate?
cards.answer: Fingerprint comparison has been tested at scale: in the FBI's 2011 black-box study, 169 examiners wrongly matched prints from different people in about 0.1% of comparisons, and a second examiner working blind caught those errors. Error rates vary with print quality, so a single quoted number would mislead jurors more than it informs them.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a match means certainty or probability.
cards.counterpoint: Jurors hear certainty, not probability. When five experts were shown prints they had matched years earlier, with a hint that they did not match, four changed their verdicts. A 2016 White House science review found false-match rates in one study could be as high as 1 in 306, in another 1 in 18, and said juries should hear them.

cards.question: What single change in the genes can leave a person with no fingerprints at all?
cards.answer: A mutation in SMARCAD1, traced in 2011 in a Swiss family. It hits a short version of the gene used only in skin, so carriers are otherwise healthy apart from fewer sweat glands on the hands; their fingertips are simply smooth. Border checks that demand prints gave the condition its nickname: immigration delay disease.
cards.move: One small switch can remove a feature that seems built from countless parts.
cards.reference: Nousbeck et al., A mutation in a skin-specific isoform of SMARCAD1 causes autosomal-dominant adermatoglyphia, American Journal of Human Genetics, 2011

cards.question: Why do a child's fingerprints fade from a surface sooner than an adult's?
cards.answer: Their residue lacks grease. Oak Ridge chemists led by Michelle Buchanan found children's prints rich in small fatty acids that evaporate, while adults' carry heavier waxy esters from the oil glands of the face, which switch on at puberty and reach the fingers by touch. A missing child's prints can vanish from a suspect's car.
cards.move: Ask what makes a trace last, not only who could have left it.
cards.source: Buchanan et al., Oak Ridge National Laboratory
cards.reference: https://impact.ornl.gov/en/publications/chemical-characterization-of-fingerprints-from-adults-and-childre/

cards.question: True or false: on a smooth, dry surface, the ridges of a fingertip increase its grip?
cards.answer: False. In 2009 Warman and Ennos pulled a fingertip across a smooth sheet of Perspex and found the ridges lowered friction: skin grips roughly in proportion to the area in contact, and ridges touch only with their crests. Their job may lie in wet or rough grip, or in touch, instead.
cards.move: An explanation repeated for a century can still be untested.
cards.trap: Treating ridges like tyre treads, a story assumed rather than tested.
cards.reference: Warman & Ennos, Fingerprints are unlikely to increase the friction of primate fingerpads, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2009

cards.question: Galton put the odds of two fingerprints matching by chance at 1 in 64 billion. What made his figure so small?
options: His sample of prints was small
He treated each region as independent
cards.answer: He treated each region as independent. Galton cut a print into 24 squares, gave each a one-in-two chance of being guessed, and multiplied, adding factors for pattern and ridge count. But neighbouring ridges share their flow, so one square predicts the next. Multiplying odds that lean on each other makes a coincidence look impossibly rare.
cards.move: Multiply chances only when one tells you nothing about the other.
cards.trap: Blaming a small sample, the usual weak point of old statistics.
cards.reference: Stigler, Galton and identification by fingerprints, Genetics, 1995

cards.question: True or false: the number of ridges on a person's fingertips is almost entirely set by their genes?
cards.answer: True. Total ridge count, summed over ten fingers, is among the most heritable human traits measured: Holt found correlations of about 0.95 between identical twins and about 0.5 between siblings, close to what genes alone would predict. The count is inherited; the exact print is not.
cards.move: A trait can be inherited in its totals while its details are not.
cards.trap: Knowing twins' prints differ and concluding ridges are not inherited.
cards.source: Holt, The Genetics of Dermal Ridges, 1968
cards.reference: Holt, The Genetics of Dermal Ridges, Charles C Thomas, 1968

cards.question: What makes a stressed mouse's new fur grow in grey, and why does it stay grey?
cards.answer: Its own nerves. Pain or stress fires the sympathetic nerves, which release noradrenaline beside the pigment stem cells in each follicle. Within days the stem cells all switch on at once, turn into pigment cells and leave, so nothing remains to colour future hairs. Blocking those nerves prevented the greying; removing stress hormones did not.
cards.move: A sudden alarm can burn through a store that never refills.
cards.reference: Zhang et al., Hyperactivation of sympathetic nerves drives depletion of melanocyte stem cells, Nature, 2020

cards.question: Can a single hair that has already turned grey regain its colour?
cards.answer: Sometimes. Hair grows about a centimetre a month, so pigment along a strand is a timeline. Scanning single hairs this way, a 2021 study found greyed hairs in several people that had darkened again from the root. In one person, a cluster of hairs regained colour around a holiday that coincided with lower reported stress.
cards.move: A change that looks final may just be slow to reverse.
cards.reference: Rosenberg, Rausser, Ren et al., Quantitative mapping of human hair greying and reversal in relation to life stress, eLife, 2021

cards.question: What goes wrong with the pigment stem cells in a follicle as hair greys?
cards.answer: They get stranded. In mice, these stem cells normally shuttle between two compartments of the follicle, maturing in one and reverting in the other. Over many cycles of shedding and regrowth, more lodge in the compartment where they cannot receive the signal to make pigment cells. They are still there, in the wrong room.
cards.move: Before concluding something has run out, check whether it has only moved.
cards.reference: Sun et al., Dedifferentiation maintains melanocyte stem cells in a dynamic niche, Nature, 2023

cards.question: When a person's hair seems to turn white in a few days, what is the likeliest explanation?
options: Stress bleaching pigment inside the hairs
Dark hairs falling out, sparing grey ones
Air bubbles forming inside the hair shafts
cards.answer: Dark hairs falling out. A hair shaft is dead, so pigment already in it cannot be withdrawn. In a sudden bout of alopecia areata, an immune attack on follicles, pigmented hairs are mostly shed and white ones spared. A partly grey head then turns white in days, because only the grey hairs are left.
cards.move: When a crowd changes colour overnight, ask who left.
cards.trap: Picturing fright draining the colour from hairs already grown.
cards.source: Nahm, Navarini & Kelly, Int J Trichology, 2013
cards.reference: Nahm, Navarini & Kelly, Canities subita: a reappraisal of evidence based on 196 case reports published in the medical literature, International Journal of Trichology, 2013

cards.question: True or false: by the age of 50, about half of all people have hair at least half grey?
cards.answer: False. Surveying 4,192 people across several continents, researchers in 2012 found the share of 50-year-olds with at least half their hair grey ranged from 6% to 23%, depending on ancestry and natural hair colour. People of Asian and African descent greyed later than those of European descent.
cards.move: A rule of thumb with suspiciously round numbers deserves a recount.
cards.trap: Trusting the neat dermatology rule of thumb known as 50-50-50.
cards.source: Panhard, Lozano & Loussouarn, Br J Dermatol, 2012
cards.reference: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2133.2012.11095.x

cards.question: Why does scalp hair lose its colour with age while the skin of the same scalp keeps its own?
cards.answer: Because the hair's pigment cells are rebuilt every cycle. Pigment cells in the skin are long-lived and work continuously; those in a hair bulb die off each time the follicle stops growing, and every new growth phase must be restocked from stem cells. Greying is a failure of that restocking, not of pigment itself.
cards.move: What is rebuilt from scratch on a cycle fails before what runs continuously.
cards.reference: Tobin & Paus, Graying: gerontobiology of the hair follicle pigmentary unit, Experimental Gerontology, 2001

cards.question: True or false: grey hair has darkened again in lung cancer patients treated with immune-boosting drugs?
cards.answer: True. In a Spanish series in 2017, 14 of 52 patients on drugs that release the immune system's brakes, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1, saw grey hair darken, mostly all over. Thirteen of the 14 had cancer that was stable or shrinking. In melanoma the same drugs can do the reverse, bleaching patches of skin.
cards.move: The same lever can darken one body and bleach another.
cards.trap: Expecting immune-boosting drugs to attack pigment cells, not restore them.
cards.reference: Rivera, Boada, Bielsa et al., Hair repigmentation during immunotherapy treatment with an anti-programmed cell death 1 and anti-programmed cell death ligand 1 agent for lung cancer, JAMA Dermatology, 2017

cards.question: About how many growth cycles does a single scalp hair follicle go through in an 80-year life?
cards.answer: 80 / 3.25 = about 25 cycles.
cards.move: Count how many times a store is drawn on before judging its size.
cards.trap: Picturing hair renewed every year, or growing without pause.
cards.hint: Start from how long one scalp hair keeps growing before it falls out.
steps: A scalp hair grows for about 3 years before it stops.
Rest and shedding add about 3 months: about 3.25 years a cycle.
80 / 3.25 = about 25 cycles.
cards.simply: Each cycle, the follicle must restock its pigment cells from its stem cells, so a lifetime of colour depends on a couple of dozen restockings.
cards.reference: Paus & Cotsarelis, The biology of hair follicles, New England Journal of Medicine, 1999

cards.question: Two vitiligo patches on one forearm, one with dark hairs and one with white hairs, get ultraviolet treatment. Which regains colour better?
cards.answer: The patch with dark hairs. New colour in treated vitiligo mostly spreads outward as dots around hair follicles, from pigment stem cells that survived in the follicle. White hairs signal that this reservoir is gone too, so the patch has little to draw on. Hairless skin, such as fingertips, responds poorly for the same reason.
cards.move: Ask where the repairs will come from before predicting a recovery.
cards.trap: Assuming the colour of the hair says nothing about the skin.
cards.reference: Birlea, Goldstein & Norris, Repigmentation through melanocyte regeneration in vitiligo, Dermatologic Clinics, 2017

cards.question: Hair with no pigment is made of translucent keratin, so why does it look white rather than clear?
cards.answer: Because it scatters light. A hair is full of internal boundaries, between cells and fibres and around air pockets in its core, and each reflects a little light of every colour. Many small reflections of all colours add up to white, as in snow. Grey is white hairs among dark ones.
cards.move: Many clear surfaces together can make something opaque.
cards.source: Robbins, Chemical and Physical Behavior of Human Hair
cards.reference: Robbins, Chemical and Physical Behavior of Human Hair, 5th edition, Springer, 2012

cards.question: True or false: serotonin made in the gut travels to the brain and helps set mood?
cards.answer: False. About 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut lining, but it cannot cross the barrier that screens the brain from the blood. Much of it is stored in platelets, which release it at wounds to help vessels narrow. The brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan, behind that barrier.
cards.move: The same molecule in two places can be two separate stories.
cards.trap: Linking the gut's huge store of serotonin directly to mood.
cards.reference: Gershon & Tack, The serotonin signaling system: from basic understanding to drug development for functional GI disorders, Gastroenterology, 2007

cards.question: Why do the commonest antidepressants so often cause nausea in the first weeks?
cards.answer: Because they act on the gut long before they lift mood. SSRIs block the recycling of serotonin everywhere, and the gut holds most of the body's serotonin. The extra serotonin stimulates 5-HT3 receptors on gut nerves that signal nausea to the brainstem: the same receptors the anti-sickness drug ondansetron blocks.
cards.move: A drug goes everywhere its target is, not only where it is wanted.
cards.reference: Stahl, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology, 5th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2021

cards.question: A gut bacterium calmed stressed mice through the vagus nerve. What did it do in healthy men?
cards.answer: No measurable effect. In 2011, Lactobacillus rhamnosus JB-1 reduced anxious behaviour and stress hormones in mice, and cutting the vagus nerve abolished the effect. In 2017 the same strain, given to 29 healthy men for eight weeks against a placebo, changed neither their stress response nor their scores on mood and thinking tests.
cards.move: A finding travels only as far as the subjects it was tested on.
cards.trap: Expecting a clean result in mice to carry over to people.
cards.source: Kelly et al., Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, 2017
cards.reference: Kelly, Allen, Temko et al., Lost in translation? The potential psychobiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus (JB-1) fails to modulate stress or cognitive performance in healthy male subjects, Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, 2017

cards.question: Does anxiety bring on an irritable gut, or does an irritable gut bring on anxiety?
cards.answer: Both. Following about a thousand Australian adults for 12 years, researchers found that anxiety at the start predicted new gut disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome, and that gut disorders at the start predicted new anxiety and depression. Some patients' troubles begin in the head, others' in the bowel, and the traffic runs both ways.
cards.move: Before deciding which came first, check whether each can start the other.
cards.reference: Koloski, Jones, Kalantar, Weltman, Zaguirre & Talley, The brain–gut pathway in functional gastrointestinal disorders is bidirectional: a 12-year prospective population-based study, Gut, 2012

cards.question: Do gut microbes help cause depression, rather than merely reflect it?
cards.answer: Faeces from depressed patients, transplanted into germ-free rodents, have produced depression-like behaviour. In a Belgian population study of about a thousand people, two bacterial groups, Coprococcus and Dialister, were depleted in depression even after allowing for antidepressants, and the pattern recurred in a Dutch cohort. Microbes make compounds that reach nerves and immune cells.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, a trial that changes the microbes is what decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Depression changes almost everything that shapes gut microbes: diet, sleep, exercise, bowel transit, alcohol and medication. Snapshot studies cannot tell which came first, and rodent tests of despair, such as how long a mouse keeps swimming, are weak stand-ins for human illness. No trial has yet shown that changing the microbes reliably treats depression in people.
cards.reference: Valles-Colomer, Falony, Darzi et al., The neuroactive potential of the human gut microbiota in quality of life and depression, Nature Microbiology, 2019

cards.question: How quickly can the gut tell the brain that sugar has arrived, and by what route?
cards.answer: Within a fraction of a second, by a synapse. Some sensory cells in the gut lining, called neuropod cells, touch vagus nerve fibres directly and signal with glutamate, a fast nerve messenger. In 2018 they were shown to pass on sugar's arrival within milliseconds, while gut hormones need minutes to travel through the blood.
cards.move: Before assuming a message is slow, check for a direct line.
cards.reference: Kaelberer, Buchanan, Klein et al., A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction, Science, 2018

cards.question: The vagus nerve links the brain and the gut. What share of its fibres carry signals up to the brain?
cards.answer: About 80%. Most vagal fibres are sensory, reporting stretch, nutrients, inflammation and toxins from the gut and other organs to the brainstem; a minority carry commands outward. That is why electrical stimulation of the vagus is used for epilepsy and hard-to-treat depression: the nerve is chiefly a channel of news from the body.
cards.move: Before calling a cable a command line, count which way the traffic runs.
cards.trap: Picturing the vagus as the brain's command line to the organs.
cards.reference: Berthoud & Neuhuber, Functional and chemical anatomy of the afferent vagal system, Autonomic Neuroscience, 2000

cards.question: After a water outbreak, irritable bowel syndrome struck 36% of those who fell ill and 10% who did not. Extra cases per 1,000 ill?
cards.answer: 360 - 100 = 260 extra cases.
cards.move: Subtract what would have happened anyway before crediting a cause.
cards.trap: Blaming the outbreak for all 360 cases, ignoring the background rate.
cards.hint: Some of those who fell ill would have developed the condition without any outbreak.
steps: Cases among 1,000 who fell ill: 36% of 1,000 = 360.
Cases expected anyway, at the rate in those who stayed well: 10% of 1,000 = 100.
360 - 100 = 260 extra cases.

diagram.caption: Of 100 who fell ill, 36 got IBS; 10 would have anyway, so 26 are extra.

cards.reference: Marshall, Thabane, Garg et al., Incidence and epidemiology of irritable bowel syndrome after a large waterborne outbreak of bacterial dysentery, Gastroenterology, 2006

cards.question: Mice bred unable to taste sweetness are offered sugar water and sweetener water for days. Which do they come to prefer?
options: Neither; they cannot tell them apart
cards.answer: The sugar water. In 2008, mice lacking a channel essential for sweet taste drank both alike at first, then shifted to sugar, which carries calories, over the calorie-free sweetener. Sugar also raised dopamine in their brains' reward centre with no taste involved. The gut and metabolism report calories to the brain, and liking follows.
cards.move: Liking can be taught by consequences the senses never notice.
cards.trap: Assuming the preference for sugar is built on its sweet taste.
cards.reference: de Araujo, Oliveira-Maia, Sotnikova et al., Food reward in the absence of taste receptor signaling, Neuron, 2008

cards.question: Which treatment for irritable bowel syndrome has beaten its comparison in trials with no drug, diet or procedure reaching the gut?
cards.answer: Gut-directed hypnotherapy. Hypnotised patients are guided to imagine calming the bowel, such as a warm hand on the abdomen. It beat psychotherapy with placebo pills in a small Manchester trial in 1984. In a Dutch trial of 354 adults in 2019, 41% treated singly and 33% in groups got adequate relief, against 17% given education.
cards.move: A symptom felt in one organ may be treated through another.
cards.source: Flik et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol, 2019

cards.question: Can a child regrow a fingertip that has been cut off?
cards.answer: Often, yes, if the cut lies beyond the last joint and the wound heals under a dressing rather than being stitched shut. In 1974 Illingworth reported children in Sheffield regrowing tips, nail included, within about three months. Regrowth seems to depend on the surviving nail bed, and the ability fades after about age 11.
cards.move: Closing a wound neatly can stop it rebuilding what was lost.

cards.question: Why can a skeleton full of healed lesions belong to the healthier of two people?
cards.answer: Because a lesion needs time to form. Bone reacts to infection, hunger or injury only over weeks, so marks appear only on people who survived the insult. Someone killed quickly by the same illness leaves a clean skeleton. Anthropologists call this the osteological paradox: the unmarked dead of a cemetery may be its frailest.
cards.move: A scar is evidence of survival before it is evidence of harm.
