cards.reference: Wood, Milner, Harpending & Weiss, The osteological paradox: problems of inferring prehistoric health from skeletal samples, Current Anthropology, 1992

cards.question: How strong is healed skin compared with the skin it replaced?
cards.answer: Weaker, for good. A cut has about a tenth of normal strength after a week, and by three months levels off at roughly 70 to 80% of unwounded skin, rarely improving much after. Scar collagen lies in dense parallel bundles, without the woven pattern, hair follicles or sweat glands of the surrounding skin.
cards.move: Something repaired is not the same as something restored.
cards.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 2021
cards.reference: Kumar, Abbas & Aster, Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Elsevier, 2021

cards.question: True or false: a graze resurfaces faster kept moist under a film than left open to form a scab?
cards.answer: True. In 1962 George Winter gave young pigs shallow wounds and covered some with polythene film: those kept moist grew new skin across about twice as fast as those left open. A scab is dried, dead tissue, and new skin cells must tunnel beneath it instead of gliding over a moist bed.
cards.move: What looks like protection can be the obstacle.
cards.trap: Treating the scab as the body's own bandage.

cards.question: Dementia caregivers healed a small standard wound 24% slower than matched peers. Which follow-up best tests whether stress caused it?
options: Repeat with many more caregivers and peers
Ask caregivers to rate their own stress
Wound the same people when calm, then stressed
cards.answer: Wound the same people when calm, then stressed. Caregivers may differ from peers in sleep, diet or health, and a bigger sample keeps all that. In 1998 the same team gave dental students identical mouth wounds in the summer holidays and three days before exams: exam-time wounds took 40% longer, about three days, to heal.
cards.move: More of the same comparison cannot remove what the comparison itself hides.
cards.trap: More people feels like stronger proof, but repeats the same comparison.

cards.question: Why does a wound in the skin of a foetus, early in pregnancy, heal without a scar?
cards.answer: The skin itself heals differently, not the womb around it. Until roughly 24 weeks of pregnancy, foetal wounds refill with collagen in its normal woven pattern, with hair follicles and glands, and little of the inflammation that drives adult scarring. When adult sheep skin was grafted onto foetal lambs and then wounded, it scarred anyway.
cards.move: To tell the tissue from its setting, swap one and keep the other.
cards.reference: Larson, Longaker & Lorenz, Scarless fetal wound healing: a basic science review, Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 2010

cards.question: Why might a burn suffered at night heal more slowly than one suffered by day?
cards.answer: Skin cells keep time. Hoyle and colleagues found the body clock in fibroblasts, the cells that rebuild skin, sets how readily they enter a wound, through daily swings in actin, the protein that powers crawling. In a burns database, night injuries took about 60% longer to heal. Cells in a dish kept the rhythm.
cards.move: When the hour changes an outcome, ask what inside is keeping time.
cards.source: Hoyle et al., Science Translational Medicine, 2017
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aal2774

cards.question: True or false: a well-healed broken bone ends up permanently stronger at the break than elsewhere?
cards.answer: False. The callus, a collar of new bone around the break, briefly makes the site thicker, but over months and years remodelling carves it back to the original shape and strength. Unlike skin, bone heals by making true bone again rather than scar. A child's healed fracture can become hard to find on later X-rays.
cards.move: A patch that looks bulky while healing is not the finished repair.
cards.trap: Mistaking the temporary thick collar of callus for lasting reinforcement.
cards.reference: Einhorn & Gerstenfeld, Fracture healing: mechanisms and interventions, Nature Reviews Rheumatology, 2015

cards.question: Three broken bones: one held rigid, one allowed to flex a little, one flexing a lot. Which grows a big bony callus?
cards.answer: The one flexing a little. Callus, a bridging collar of new bone, forms when the gap flexes by roughly 2 to 10% of its width. Held rigid, a break knits directly with little callus; flexing much more, it fills with fibrous tissue and may never unite. Surgeons choose their fixings partly by this rule.
cards.move: Some strain is the signal to build; none, or too much, stops it.
cards.trap: Assuming stiller is always better, so the rigid one grows most bone.
cards.reference: Perren, Physical and biological aspects of fracture healing with special reference to internal fixation, Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research, 1979

cards.question: Should people recovering from a broken bone avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen?
cards.answer: Inflammation is the first stage of bone repair: it recruits the cells that build the callus, and drugs like ibuprofen block the prostaglandins that signal it. Animal studies show slower healing, and a 2019 meta-analysis of 16 studies found NSAID users about twice as likely to suffer delayed healing or none. Other painkillers exist.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on dose, duration and who takes them.
cards.counterpoint: The same meta-analysis found no effect in children or with low doses, which is how most people use them, and much of the adult signal comes from observational studies in which worse fractures bring both more pain relief and slower healing. The usual alternative, opioids, carries dangers of its own.
cards.reference: Wheatley et al., Effect of NSAIDs on Bone Healing Rates: A Meta-analysis, Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2019

cards.question: A resting heart typically beats about 70 times a minute. A transplanted heart, cut off from its nerves, beats at rest how often?
cards.answer: About 100 a minute. The heart's own pacemaker runs faster than a normal resting pulse: roughly 118 minus 0.57 times age, about 95 at 40. At rest the vagus nerve holds it back. Transplant recipients typically live with a quick resting pulse that rises only slowly in exercise, waiting for adrenaline in the blood.
cards.move: Take away a brake and the true speed shows.
cards.trap: Assuming the heart's own pacemaker simply keeps the usual 70.
cards.reference: Jose & Collison, The normal range and determinants of the intrinsic heart rate in man, Cardiovascular Research, 1970

cards.question: Where did the rule that maximum heart rate is 220 minus age come from?
cards.answer: A line drawn through scattered points. In 1971 Fox, Naughton and Haskell plotted maximum heart rates from about 11 earlier sources and drew a straight line through them, without a formal fit. A 2001 meta-analysis of 351 studies put the line at 208 minus 0.7 times age, and individuals scatter about 10 beats either side.
cards.move: Before trusting a formula, ask whose data drew the line.
cards.reference: Robergs & Landwehr, The surprising history of the HRmax=220-age equation, Journal of Exercise Physiology online, 2002

cards.question: How can a ball striking the chest stop a healthy heart without damaging it?
cards.answer: Timing. In animal experiments a blow set off fibrillation only if it landed in a 15-millisecond window on the upstroke of the T wave, while heart muscle recovers unevenly from the last beat. The same blow a moment earlier or later did nothing. Victims are mostly young, with springy chests; the heart is sound.
cards.move: The same push can do nothing or everything, depending on when it lands.

cards.question: Slower resting pulses go with longer lives. In a trial of 19,102 heart patients, what did a pulse-slowing drug do?
cards.answer: Cut neither. In the 2014 SIGNIFY trial, ivabradine lowered resting pulses as intended, yet cardiovascular deaths and heart attacks were no fewer than on placebo, and patients with severe angina fared slightly worse. A slow pulse partly marks what produces it: fitness and a healthy heart. Slowing the needle did not change the engine.
cards.move: Pushing a gauge to a good reading does not fix what it measures.
cards.trap: If slow pulses mark long lives, slowing the pulse should help.

cards.question: Why can a leg muscle be held in one long contraction, but heart muscle cannot?
cards.answer: Its impulse is too long. A heart cell's impulse lasts about 250 milliseconds, nearly as long as the squeeze it triggers, and it cannot fire again until that ends, so each beat must ease off before the next. A skeletal muscle's impulse lasts about 2 milliseconds, so rapid impulses fuse into one sustained pull.
cards.move: A built-in pause can be what keeps a system working.
cards.source: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Physiology, 2021
cards.reference: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition, Elsevier, 2021

cards.question: About how many times does a human heart beat in an 80-year life, in millions?
cards.answer: 36.5 million x 80 = about 2,900 million beats.
cards.move: Carry a small rate through every unit of time before judging its total.
cards.trap: Recalling the billion heartbeats said to be every mammal's allowance.
cards.hint: Start from beats a minute and scale up to a year.
steps: About 70 beats a minute x 60 = 4,200 an hour.
100,000 x 365 = about 36.5 million a year.
36.5 million x 80 = about 2,900 million beats.
cards.simply: Across mammals from mouse to whale, Levine found lifetimes averaging under a billion beats: fast hearts, short lives. A human heart runs about three times past that pattern.
cards.reference: Levine, Rest heart rate and life expectancy, Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 1997

cards.question: True or false: in a healthy person at rest, the heart speeds up with each breath in?
cards.answer: True. Breathing in briefly quietens the vagus nerve, the heart's brake, so the pulse quickens; breathing out restores the brake and it slows. The swing, called respiratory sinus arrhythmia, is largest in the young and fit and shrinks with age and heart disease. A pulse as steady as a metronome is the worse sign.
cards.move: Some wobble in a signal can be the sign that it is working.
cards.trap: Picturing a healthy heart as a metronome, so any wobble means trouble.
cards.source: ESC and NASPE Task Force, Circulation, 1996
cards.reference: Task Force of the European Society of Cardiology and the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology, Heart rate variability: standards of measurement, physiological interpretation and clinical use, Circulation, 1996

cards.question: In atrial fibrillation the upper chambers quiver 400 or more times a minute. How fast do the ventricles typically beat, untreated?
cards.answer: Typically 100 to 180 a minute, and irregularly. The AV node, the one electrical gate between upper and lower chambers, needs time to recover after each impulse, so most chaotic impulses arrive while it is still shut. The ventricles beat only when a signal slips through: quickly, and never in rhythm.
cards.move: A gate that needs time to reset sets the pace behind it.
cards.trap: Assuming the lower chambers simply follow the upper ones beat for beat.
cards.reference: Opie, Heart Physiology: From Cell to Circulation, 4th edition, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2004

cards.question: Endurance athletes' pulses stay slow even when drugs block every nerve signal to the heart. What mainly explains it?
options: Their pacemaker cells fire more slowly
A larger heart pumping more per beat
Less adrenaline circulating in the blood
cards.answer: Their pacemaker cells fire more slowly. With nerves blocked, the heart runs at its own rate, and in athletes that rate is lower. D'Souza and colleagues found training cut rodents' HCN4 channels, which carry the current setting the pacemaker's tick. The big heart comes from the same training; it does not set the tempo.
cards.move: Two changes caused by one habit need not cause each other.
cards.trap: Crediting the athlete's big heart, which training built alongside the slow rate.
cards.reference: D'Souza et al., Exercise training reduces resting heart rate via downregulation of the funny channel HCN4, Nature Communications, 2014

cards.question: If the heart's natural pacemaker fails, what keeps the heart beating?
cards.answer: Backups lower down, each slower than the last. Cells around the AV node, the gate to the lower chambers, fire on their own at about 40 to 60 a minute; the ventricles' fibres at about 20 to 40. Normally the fastest site sets every beat. A slower drummer takes over when the lead stops.
cards.move: The fastest voice in a system can hide the backups waiting behind it.
cards.reference: Katz, Physiology of the Heart, 5th edition, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2011

cards.question: Before brain scans, how could surgeons tell which half of a patient's brain controlled speech?
cards.answer: By putting one half to sleep. In the test Juhn Wada devised in 1949, a barbiturate injected into one carotid artery anaesthetises one hemisphere for minutes. The patient counts aloud, arms raised; the opposite arm drops, and if the counting stops too, speech lives on that side. Then the count resumes.
cards.move: To learn what a part does, switch it off for a moment.

cards.question: Why does each half of the brain control the opposite side of the body?
cards.answer: Nobody knows for certain. In 1898 Cajal argued that crossing the optic nerves joined the two eyes' inverted images into one continuous map, and that touch and movement crossed to match. A newer idea: an early ancestor's head rotated half a turn against its body. Every vertebrate, down to the lamprey, is wired crossed.
cards.move: Ask whether a design solves a problem or inherits one.

cards.question: Where do most left-handed people have their main language areas?
cards.answer: In the left hemisphere, as in almost all right-handers. Handedness shifts the odds only modestly: among 326 healthy adults tested by Knecht and colleagues, right-hemisphere language rose from 4% of strong right-handers to 27% of strong left-handers. About three strong left-handers in four still speak from the hemisphere that runs their weaker hand.
cards.move: A visible trait is a weak guide to the hidden one it seems to mirror.
cards.trap: Mirroring the hand: left hand, so language on the right.

cards.question: A 1991 study of death certificates found left-handers died nine years younger. What mostly explains the gap?
options: Birth stress that also shortens life
cards.answer: Fewer left-handers among the old. Children born early in the century were often made to write with the right hand, so few elderly people called themselves left-handed, and the left-handers who died were mostly younger. Mean age at death compared generations, not risks; studies following living people forward found little or no gap.
cards.move: Compare the dead only after asking when each group was born.
cards.trap: Right-handed tools and cars make an accident story feel obvious.
cards.source: Galobardes et al., Am J Public Health, 1999

cards.question: True or false: everything the left eye sees is handled by the right half of the brain?
cards.answer: False. The split follows the field of view, not the eye: everything left of centre, seen by either eye, goes to the right hemisphere. At the optic chiasm only fibres from the inner half of each retina cross, so each optic nerve divides roughly in two. Close one eye and both hemispheres still see.
cards.move: Know what is being sorted before guessing where it will go.
cards.trap: Assuming the eyes cross over just as the limbs do.
cards.reference: Purves et al., Neuroscience, 5th edition, Sinauer Associates, 2012

cards.question: Does cutting the corpus callosum, the main bridge between the brain's halves, split a person into two minds?
cards.answer: In Sperry and Gazzaniga's tests from the 1960s, each hemisphere of such patients answered questions the other could not, and one hand could work against the other. A mind is what knows and acts; when two halves know different things and act at cross purposes, the single person seen at dinner is a united front.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what counts as one mind.
cards.counterpoint: Patients live, talk and plan as one person. In 2017 Pinto and colleagues found two such patients could report a stimulus anywhere in view, with either hand or in words; what failed was comparing the two sides. Perception was split, the self was not, and structures below the cut still link the halves.
cards.reference: Pinto et al., Split brain: divided perception but undivided consciousness, Brain, 2017

cards.question: Identical twin pairs share handedness about 80% of the time. If 1 in 10 people is left-handed, what % of random stranger pairs would?
cards.move: Before admiring how often two things agree, work out how often strangers would.
cards.trap: Reading 80% agreement between twins as strong evidence for genes.
cards.hint: Add the chance both are right-handed to the chance both are left-handed.
steps: Both right-handed: 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81.
Both left-handed: 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.01.
cards.simply: Line up 100 pairs of strangers: about 81 are both right-handed and 1 both left-handed. A 2022 pooling of twin studies found identical twins agreeing 80.5% of the time and non-identical twins 79.3%. Genes explain about a quarter of handedness.

diagram.label: pairs of strangers
diagram.caption: 81 + 1 = 82 in 100 stranger pairs share handedness, more than identical twins' 80.

cards.question: What happens to a deaf person's sign language after a stroke in the left hemisphere?
cards.answer: It breaks down much as speech does in hearing people, though signing is a language of space and movement. Hickok, Bellugi and Klima found left-hemisphere damage caused sign aphasia, while right-hemisphere damage spared signing grammar yet disturbed drawing and spatial judgement. The hands still moved; the grammar was gone.
cards.move: Sort abilities by what they compute, not by which sense carries them.
cards.reference: Hickok, Bellugi & Klima, The neurobiology of sign language and its implications for the neural basis of language, Nature, 1996

cards.question: Left-handers are about one person in ten but a far larger share of top fencers. What best explains the excess?
options: A right-hemisphere edge in spatial skill
Left-handers are born with faster reflexes
cards.answer: Opponents rarely practise against them. Most players spend their careers facing right-handers, so a left-hander's angles arrive unfamiliar. Raymond and colleagues found the excess in sports played against a direct opponent, such as fencing, but not in sports without one. A talent built into the brain would show up everywhere.
cards.move: An advantage that rests on being rare fades once it is common.
cards.trap: Reaching for a brain-based talent instead of the opponent's unfamiliarity.
cards.reference: Raymond, Pontier, Dufour & Møller, Frequency-dependent maintenance of left handedness in humans, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 1996

cards.question: Over 90% of people have language mainly on the left. In what share of brains is the left planum temporale, a language area, larger?
cards.answer: About two thirds. Geschwind and Levitsky measured the planum temporale, a patch of cortex behind the hearing area, in 100 brains: it was larger on the left in 65, on the right in 11 and equal in 24. Anatomy leans the way language does, but loosely: in one brain in nine, the right was bigger.
cards.move: A strong lean in function can sit on a weak lean in form.
cards.trap: Letting the near-universal left bias for language set the anatomical figure.
cards.reference: Geschwind & Levitsky, Human brain: left-right asymmetries in temporal speech region, Science, 1968

cards.question: An adult's yearly risk of dying roughly doubles every 8 years. How many times higher is it at 70 than at 30?
cards.answer: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32 times higher.
cards.move: When something doubles on a schedule, count the doublings before you guess.
cards.trap: Adding a fixed amount of risk per year instead of multiplying.
cards.hint: Count how many doublings fit between the two ages, then multiply.
steps: From 30 to 70 is 40 years.
40 / 8 = 5 doublings.
2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32 times higher.

diagram.caption: Five doublings between 30 and 70 multiply the risk by 32; the last two do most.

cards.source: Kirkwood, Phil Trans R Soc B, 2015
cards.reference: Kirkwood, Deciphering death: a commentary on Gompertz (1825), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2015

cards.question: True or false: in large family trees, a person's lifespan correlates with the lifespans of their siblings' spouses?
cards.answer: True. Mining family trees covering over 400 million people, a 2018 study found lifespans correlated between spouses and between siblings-in-law, who share no genes, because people marry partners like themselves in habits, wealth and place. Allowing for that pushed the heritability of lifespan below 7%, far under older estimates of 20% to 30%.
cards.move: Resemblance within families is not all in the genes.
cards.trap: Assuming only shared genes or a shared home can make lifespans alike.
cards.reference: Ruby, Wright, Rand et al., Estimates of the heritability of human longevity are substantially inflated due to assortative mating, Genetics, 2018

cards.question: What did Japanese officials discover in 2010 when they went looking for registered centenarians?
cards.answer: That many were long dead. The man listed as Tokyo's oldest, Sogen Kato, supposedly 111, was found mummified in his bedroom; he had probably died in 1978, and relatives had kept drawing his pension. A nationwide check of family registers then found about 230,000 people aged 100 or more whose whereabouts nobody could confirm.
cards.move: The oldest ages in any record are where record errors pile up.
cards.reference: Newman, Supercentenarians and the oldest-old are concentrated into regions with no birth certificates and short lifespans, bioRxiv, 2019

cards.question: Why did two decades-long studies of calorie-restricted monkeys reach opposite conclusions about lifespan?
cards.answer: Their control monkeys ate differently. At Wisconsin the controls ate freely from a diet high in sugar, so restricted animals looked healthier and lived longer. At the US National Institute on Aging the controls got measured portions of a more natural diet and were already fairly lean. The restricted monkeys there did not outlive them.
cards.move: Every effect is measured against a baseline; ask what the baseline was doing.
cards.reference: Mattison, Colman, Beasley et al., Caloric restriction improves health and survival of rhesus monkeys, Nature Communications, 2017

cards.question: Is there a fixed upper limit to the human lifespan?
cards.answer: Survival to 100 has soared, yet the highest reported age at death rose until the 1990s and then stalled. Jeanne Calment's 122 years, reached in 1997, is still unbeaten almost three decades later. Gains at extreme ages have shrunk, which suggests that bodies, not medicine, set a ceiling around 115, with rare outliers.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether death rates flatten at extreme ages is the hinge.
cards.counterpoint: Studies of verified Italians aged 105 and over found the yearly risk of death stops rising and levels off at about 50%. With a flat risk there is no hard ceiling, only ever-thinner odds, and a new record needs only enough people reaching extreme age. Statisticians also criticised how the 2016 analysis of a plateau split its data.
cards.reference: Barbi, Lagona, Marsili, Vaupel & Wachter, The plateau of human mortality: demography of longevity pioneers, Science, 2018

cards.question: Adult death rates double about every 8 years of age. If a treatment halved them at every age, how much longer would people live?
cards.answer: About 8 years. With risk doubling every 8 years, halving it at every age gives each person the risk of someone 8 years younger, which shifts the whole adult curve 8 years later. Because the risk keeps doubling, the gain is soon used up: the treated die of the same rising risk, only later.
cards.move: Against a risk that doubles, halving it buys one doubling time.
cards.trap: Reading half the risk of dying as roughly double the remaining life.
cards.source: Finch, Longevity, Senescence, and the Genome
cards.reference: Finch, Longevity, Senescence, and the Genome, University of Chicago Press, 1990

cards.question: True or false: wiping out every death from cancer would lengthen US life expectancy at birth by only about 3 years?
cards.answer: True. Olshansky, Carnes and Cassel calculated in 1990 that eliminating all cancer would add about 3 years to life expectancy at birth. Most cancer deaths come late in life, and the people spared still face a steeply rising risk of dying of something else within a few years.
cards.move: Removing one cause of an outcome leaves the others waiting.
cards.trap: Counting the lives saved without asking what those people die of next.
cards.reference: Olshansky, Carnes & Cassel, In search of Methuselah: estimating the upper limits to human longevity, Science, 1990

cards.question: Mix frail and robust people, each group's death risk doubling every 8 years. How does the whole population's risk rise at extreme ages?
options: Doubling more slowly than every 8 years
cards.answer: More slowly. The frail die first, so each year the survivors are a more robust crowd, and the average risk climbs less steeply than anyone's own risk does. Vaupel and colleagues showed in 1979 that this sorting alone can bend the curve towards a plateau, even if no individual's risk ever stops doubling.
cards.move: A group can change because of who leaves, while no member changes.
cards.trap: Assuming a mix behaves like the groups it is made of.
cards.reference: Vaupel, Manton & Stallard, The impact of heterogeneity in individual frailty on the dynamics of mortality, Demography, 1979

cards.question: Should ageing itself be classified as a disease?
cards.answer: Ageing is the main risk factor for cancer, heart disease and dementia, and its mechanisms can be slowed in animals. Regulators approve drugs for diseases, so a medicine that delays ageing itself has no clear route to approval. Naming it a disease would open trials of drugs aimed at the cause, not its consequences.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, what the label would change in practice is the hinge.
cards.counterpoint: A condition every person develops is the baseline against which disease is defined. Labelling old age a disease invites doctors to write it on death certificates instead of finding treatable causes, and hands marketers a licence. After objections, the WHO withdrew old age as a diagnosis from its new classification in 2022. Trials can target specific age-related conditions.
cards.source: Bulterijs et al., Frontiers in Genetics, 2015
cards.reference: Bulterijs, Hull, Björk & Roy, It is time to classify biological aging as a disease, Frontiers in Genetics, 2015

cards.question: Do people who reach 110 spend more years ill than those who die younger?
cards.answer: Less, on the evidence so far. Studying centenarians and supercentenarians in 2012, Andersen and colleagues found that the older the age at death, the later major diseases such as heart disease, stroke and cancer began. Among those reaching 110, illness was squeezed into the final years: a long life, mostly healthy, then a short decline.
cards.move: Those who go furthest may be those who break down latest, not slowest.
cards.source: Andersen et al., J Gerontol A, 2012
cards.reference: Andersen, Sebastiani, Dworkis, Feldman & Perls, Health span approximates life span among many supercentenarians: compression of morbidity at the approximate limit of life span, Journals of Gerontology Series A, 2012

cards.question: Breast milk carries large amounts of complex sugars that the baby cannot digest. What are they for?
options: Feeding bacteria in the baby's gut
Thickening the milk so it clings
Carrying surplus sugar out of the mother
cards.answer: Feeding bacteria in the baby's gut. These oligosaccharides are the third-largest solid ingredient of human milk, after lactose and fat, yet reach the colon undigested. There Bifidobacterium infantis, which carries a cluster of genes for breaking them down, thrives and crowds out rivals. In breastfed infants, bifidobacteria often make up most of the gut's bacteria.
cards.move: When a system makes something it cannot use, find who does.
cards.trap: Assuming whatever a body cannot use must be surplus it sheds.
cards.reference: Bode, Human milk oligosaccharides: every baby needs a sugar mama, Glycobiology, 2012

cards.question: Why does the heart drug digoxin lose its effect in some patients but not in others?
cards.answer: A gut bacterium disables it. Strains of Eggerthella lenta carrying a particular pair of genes convert digoxin to an inactive form before it can be absorbed. In 2013 researchers identified those genes and showed that the amino acid arginine, plentiful in dietary protein, suppressed them in mice and raised the drug's level in the blood.
cards.move: A dose is only what reaches its target after others take their share.
cards.reference: Haiser, Gootenberg, Chatman, Sirasani, Balskus & Turnbaugh, Predicting and manipulating cardiac drug inactivation by the human gut bacterium Eggerthella lenta, Science, 2013

cards.question: True or false: mice raised with no gut microbes eat more than normal mice yet carry less fat?
cards.answer: True. Conventionally raised mice carried about 42% more body fat than germ-free ones while eating less. Given gut microbes from normal mice, germ-free mice grew markedly fatter within two weeks without eating more. Bacteria ferment fibre the mouse cannot digest into fatty acids it can absorb, and they nudge the host towards storing fat.
cards.move: Count what is absorbed, not what is served.
cards.trap: Assuming the calories a body gets equal the calories it eats.
cards.reference: Bäckhed, Ding, Wang et al., The gut microbiota as an environmental factor that regulates fat storage, PNAS, 2004

cards.question: How did the first randomised trial of faecal transplants against recurrent gut infection end?
cards.answer: Early, because the comparison had become lopsided. In the Dutch trial published in 2013, one infusion of donor faeces cured 13 of 16 patients with recurrent Clostridioides difficile, against 4 of 13 on the antibiotic vancomycin. An interim analysis halted the trial, and relapsing patients from the antibiotic arms got donor faeces too.
cards.move: A test can end early because the answer arrived early.

cards.question: Should a healthy adult take probiotics after a course of antibiotics?
cards.answer: Antibiotics strip the gut and open the door to diarrhoea and to Clostridioides difficile. Pooled trials find probiotics taken alongside antibiotics cut antibiotic-associated diarrhoea by roughly 40%, and a Cochrane review found fewer C. difficile infections. The capsules are cheap and serious harm in healthy adults is rare, so the odds favour taking them.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the person's baseline risk is what decides it.
cards.counterpoint: In a small 2018 study, people given a probiotic mix after antibiotics took months to rebuild their native gut microbes, while those given back their own stored stool recovered within days. Most of the benefit in trials comes from hospital patients at high risk, not healthy adults, and products differ strain by strain.
cards.reference: Suez, Zmora, Zilberman-Schapira et al., Post-antibiotic gut mucosal microbiome reconstitution is impaired by probiotics and improved by autologous FMT, Cell, 2018

cards.question: How much do all the bacteria living in an adult's body weigh together?
cards.answer: About 200 grams. A 2016 recount put the bacteria in a 70 kg man at about 38 trillion, nearly all in the colon, close to his 30 trillion human cells. Being tiny, they weigh about 0.2 kg, near 0.3% of the body. One bowel movement empties a quarter to a third of them.
cards.move: Before repeating a striking figure, ask when someone last measured it.
cards.trap: The figure of one to two kilograms, repeated for decades.
cards.reference: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.1002533

cards.question: Why do colon bacteria that make vitamin B12 not spare vegans from needing supplements?
cards.answer: Because they make it downstream of the exit. B12 is absorbed at the far end of the small intestine, bound to intrinsic factor, a carrier protein made by the stomach. The colon comes after that point, so vitamin made there leaves in the faeces, much of it in forms human cells cannot use.
cards.move: A supply is useless if it arrives past the point of collection.
cards.reference: Degnan, Taga & Goodman, Vitamin B12 as a modulator of gut microbial ecology, Cell Metabolism, 2014

cards.question: Early studies tied obesity to a higher ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes bacteria. What did later pooled analyses find?
options: A weak link, inconsistent across studies
The reverse: lean people carry more Firmicutes
cards.answer: A weak link, inconsistent across studies. The ratio came from mice and from a dozen dieting volunteers in 2006. When Walters and colleagues in 2014, and Sze and Schloss in 2016, pooled larger human data sets, the ratio did not reliably separate lean from obese people. Microbial diversity gave a small, steadier signal.
cards.move: The first measurement of an effect tends to be its biggest.
cards.trap: Trusting the first vivid result, from small studies, as the settled size.
cards.reference: Sze & Schloss, Looking for a signal in the noise: revisiting obesity and the microbiome, mBio, 2016

cards.question: Of 38 published studies giving germ-free rodents a patient's gut microbes, 36 passed on the disease. What does that mostly show?
options: Gut microbes drive most of these diseases
Rodents are more fragile than people
Mouse studies are biased towards positive results
cards.answer: A bias towards positive results. Reviewing them in 2020, Walter and colleagues judged a 95% transfer rate implausible for diseases with many causes. Most studies used faeces from few donors, then counted each mouse, often caged with others, as independent evidence, inflating certainty. The rodents received microbes; the causal claims were extrapolated.
cards.move: Count the independent sources, not the number of measurements taken from them.
cards.trap: Counting every sick mouse as a separate proof, though few donors were tested.
cards.reference: Walter, Armet, Finlay & Shanahan, Establishing or exaggerating causality for the gut microbiome: lessons from human microbiota-associated rodents, Cell, 2020

cards.question: Should babies born by caesarean section be swabbed with their mother's vaginal fluid at birth?
cards.answer: Caesarean babies start life colonised by skin and hospital microbes instead of their mother's vaginal and gut bacteria, and caesarean birth is linked to higher rates of asthma and obesity. A 2016 pilot found swabbed babies' microbes shifted partway towards those of vaginally born infants. The swab is cheap and uses the mother's own bacteria.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether the early difference lasts is the hinge.
cards.counterpoint: The largest study, of about 600 British babies in 2019, found most birth-mode differences had faded by six to nine months, and the missing bacteria came mainly from the mother's gut, not her vagina. Vaginal fluid can carry group B streptococcus or herpes, which can kill a newborn. Obstetric bodies advise against it outside research.
cards.reference: Shao, Forster, Tsaliki et al., Stunted microbiota and opportunistic pathogen colonization in caesarean-section birth, Nature, 2019

cards.question: What made Golgi's 1873 silver stain able to show a single neuron whole?
cards.answer: Its unreliability. His black reaction darkens only a few cells in every hundred, seemingly at random, but each one entirely; stain every cell and the slice would be solid black. Why it picks those cells is still unknown. Cajal used it to show neurons are separate cells; Golgi denied it in his 1906 Nobel lecture.
cards.move: Show everything at once and nothing can be seen.
cards.source: Shepherd, Foundations of the Neuron Doctrine, 1991
cards.reference: Shepherd, Foundations of the Neuron Doctrine, Oxford University Press, 1991

cards.question: The cerebral cortex makes up about 82% of the brain's mass. What share of the brain's neurons does it hold?
cards.answer: About 20%. Of the brain's 86 billion or so neurons, only about 16 billion are in the cerebral cortex. Some 69 billion, four in five, are packed into the cerebellum, which weighs about 150 g, most of them tiny granule cells. The cortex's bulk is long wiring and support cells; the cerebellum's is sheer headcount.
cards.move: Where the weight is and where the numbers are can be different places.
cards.trap: Carrying the cortex's 82% share of weight over to its neurons.
cards.source: Azevedo et al., Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2009

cards.question: What limits how many neurons in the cortex can fire at the same moment?
cards.answer: Energy. Each spike is paid for by pumping back the ions that crossed the membrane. Dividing the cortex's power supply by the cost of a spike, Lennie estimated that possibly fewer than 1% of cortical neurons can be strongly active at once. Blood is steered to the busiest areas, and brain scanners watch that surge.
cards.move: Before asking why a system does so little, ask what it can afford.
cards.reference: Lennie, The cost of cortical computation, Current Biology, 2003

cards.question: True or false: the brain has about ten glial cells, its support cells, for every neuron?
cards.answer: False. The two are roughly equal, with fewer than 100 billion of each. The ten-to-one ratio filled textbooks for decades, but a 2016 review of 150 years of cell counting found that no count had ever supported it; direct counts pointed to about 1:1. The trillion glia so often quoted were never counted.
cards.move: Ask who counted before repeating a number everyone knows.
cards.trap: Trusting a ratio that textbooks repeated for fifty years.
cards.source: von Bartheld et al., J Comp Neurol, 2016

cards.question: How long do supplies take to travel down a nerve cell that runs from spine to toe?
cards.answer: Years, for some cargo. Its fibre, the axon, is about a metre long, and most of its supplies are made in the cell body by the spine. Vesicles ride fast transport, up to 400 mm a day: under three days. Scaffold proteins creep at 0.2 to 1 mm a day: about three to fourteen years.
cards.move: The far end of a long supply line lives on old stock.
cards.reference: Roy, Seeing the unseen: the hidden world of slow axonal transport, The Neuroscientist, 2014

cards.question: Bare axon speed rises with the square root of width. A 0.5 mm squid axon manages 25 m/s. What width gives 100 m/s, in mm?
cards.move: When returns grow as a square root, doubling the output costs four times the input.
cards.trap: Scaling width in step with speed and answering 2 mm.
cards.hint: Undo a square root by squaring the ratio of the speeds.
steps: Target speed over current speed: 100 / 25 = 4.
Speed goes with the square root of width, so width must rise 4 x 4 = 16 times.
cards.simply: A human motor fibre about 0.02 mm across, wrapped in fatty myelin, already carries signals at roughly 100 m/s. Insulation does with one four-hundredth of the width what bare girth would need a pencil-thick cable for.

series.label: speed goes as root of width

diagram.caption: From 25 to 100 m/s, four times the speed, the axon must grow sixteen times wider.

cards.reference: Hartline & Colman, Rapid conduction and the evolution of giant axons and myelinated fibers, Current Biology, 2007

cards.question: Why does a nerve fibre whose sodium pumps are poisoned keep firing for hours?
cards.answer: Because each impulse spends almost none of the stored charge. A spike lets in only enough sodium to shift the inside concentration by a tiny fraction, so the pump recharges a battery rather than paying for each shot. In 1955 Hodgkin and Keynes stopped squid axons' pumps with dinitrophenol, and the impulses kept running.
cards.move: Ask whether a cost is paid on each use or out of savings.
cards.reference: Hodgkin & Keynes, Active transport of cations in giant axons from Sepia and Loligo, Journal of Physiology, 1955

cards.question: True or false: the rods and cones of the eye pass on their light signals without firing nerve impulses?
cards.answer: True. Rods and cones signal with graded shifts in voltage, and light makes them release less transmitter, not more: they release it most steadily in the dark. The first all-or-nothing spikes on the way to the brain appear two cells later, in the ganglion cells whose fibres bundle into the optic nerve.
cards.move: The textbook case of a thing is rarely the only way it works.
cards.trap: Assuming every nerve cell talks in spikes, as textbook neurons do.
cards.source: Rodieck, The First Steps in Seeing, 1998
cards.reference: Rodieck, The First Steps in Seeing, Sinauer Associates, 1998

cards.question: True or false: each neuron releases just one kind of chemical messenger from its endings?
cards.answer: False. Many neurons release two or more: a fast transmitter such as glutamate or GABA alongside slower signalling peptides, and some dopamine neurons release glutamate. The one-transmitter idea misreads Dale's principle, which claimed only that a neuron releases the same messengers at every ending. One ending can hold small and large vesicles side by side.
cards.move: Check what a famous rule literally says before quoting its nickname.
cards.trap: Recalling the neat rule of one neuron, one transmitter.
cards.source: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science
cards.reference: Kandel, Schwartz, Jessell, Siegelbaum & Hudspeth, Principles of Neural Science, 5th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2013

cards.question: Microelectrode recordings suggested cortical neurons fire briskly. Why did later methods find many of them nearly silent?
options: Electrodes find cells by their firing
Early electrodes counted noise as spikes
cards.answer: Electrodes find cells by their firing. An experimenter lowers an electrode until a cell crackles on the loudspeaker, so quiet neurons are passed by unrecorded. Methods that sample blind, such as patching onto cells or imaging hundreds at once, found many cortical neurons firing less than once a second, and some hardly at all.
cards.move: If the net only catches what moves, the still ones go uncounted.
cards.trap: Blaming the animal's state rather than how the cells were found.
cards.reference: Shoham, O'Connor & Segev, How silent is the brain: is there a dark matter problem in neuroscience?, Journal of Comparative Physiology A, 2006

cards.question: What did a stroke in the visual cortex take from a woman blind since birth?
cards.answer: Her Braille. A fluent reader before, she found the dots no longer made words, though her sense of touch seemed otherwise unchanged. In people blind from early life, the occipital cortex, the sighted brain's visual area, is taken over for reading by touch. Magnetic pulses aimed there scramble Braille for other blind readers too.
cards.move: What a part was built for is no guide to what it now does.

cards.question: Children born blind, given sight by surgery at 8 to 17, could identify a shape by touch. Could they then recognise it by sight?
cards.answer: Only after some days. Held and colleagues tested five such children in India soon after surgery: matching shapes touch-to-touch was near perfect and sight-to-sight good, but touch-to-sight was barely better than a coin toss. Within days the matching improved. Molyneux had put this question to Locke in 1693; it took three centuries to test.
cards.move: Knowing a thing one way does not mean knowing it every way.
cards.trap: A shape is a shape, whichever sense first learned it.
cards.reference: Held et al., The newly sighted fail to match seen with felt, Nature Neuroscience, 2011

cards.question: True or false: a toddler's frontal cortex packs more synapses into each cubic millimetre than an adult's?
cards.answer: True. Counting synapses under the electron microscope, Huttenlocher found their density in the frontal cortex peaking at one to two years, about 50% above the adult average, then falling through childhood and adolescence. Development sculpts as much as it builds: surplus connections are pruned, and in the prefrontal cortex the pruning continues into the twenties.
cards.move: Getting better at something often means keeping less of what you had.
cards.trap: Learning adds connections, so the adult must have more.

cards.question: Does the adult human hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, keep making new neurons?
cards.answer: Contested, and tissue handling may decide it. Radiocarbon in neuron DNA suggested about 700 new neurons a day in each hippocampus (2013). A 2018 study found them fading to undetectable levels after childhood; a 2019 study of quickly preserved brains found thousands in people up to 87. Slow preservation can hide the marker both counted.
cards.move: When careful studies disagree, look at how the samples were kept.

cards.question: Should brain-training apps be allowed to advertise that they keep the mind sharp?
cards.answer: Practice changes brains, and one large trial found a lasting signal: in ACTIVE, 2,832 older Americans were randomised, and those given speed-of-processing training had about 29% lower dementia risk ten years later than controls. The games are cheap and harmless. Adults weigh modest evidence for crosswords, diets and exercise; they can weigh it here too.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether gains travel beyond the game.
cards.counterpoint: Players get better at the games and little else. In a six-week study of 11,430 people, gains on every trained task failed to transfer to untrained ones, even closely related tasks. The dementia signal came from a secondary analysis whose confidence interval brushed 1.0. In 2016 Lumosity's maker paid US regulators $2 million over such claims.

cards.question: After an arm is amputated, does the brain's map of the missing hand get taken over?
cards.answer: Apparently not. Schone, Makin and colleagues scanned three adults before and up to five years after planned arm amputations. Moving their phantom fingers lit up the same hand map as moving real ones had before surgery, and the lip area had not spread into it. The map stayed ready for a hand that was gone.
cards.move: Compare the same people before and after before announcing that something moved.
cards.reference: Schone et al., Stable cortical body maps before and after arm amputation, Nature Neuroscience, 2025

cards.question: A lazy eye can often be treated well into the school years. By when should a baby's dense one-sided cataract come out?
options: Within about six weeks of birth
cards.answer: Within about six weeks of birth. A cloudy lens starves one eye of sharp images while the other claims the visual cortex. Birch and Stager studied 45 such children: acuity was best when treated in the first six weeks and fell with each week of delay after. The window shuts in weeks, not years.
cards.move: Before borrowing a deadline from a similar case, ask which clock applies.
cards.trap: Letting the school-age window for a lazy eye set the deadline.
cards.reference: Birch & Stager, The critical period for surgical treatment of dense congenital unilateral cataract, Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science, 1996

cards.question: Stroke patients seemed to regain about 70% of their lost arm function within months, whatever the damage. Why did critics doubt the rule?
options: Therapy, not the brain, produced the gains
Recovery tracks loss partly by arithmetic
cards.answer: Recovery tracks loss partly by arithmetic. Recovery is the final score minus the first, so correlating it with the first builds in a link, and a scale's ceiling squeezes mild cases into looking proportional. Reanalyses found the rule explained far less of the variation than first reported; defenders dispute how much less.
cards.move: Correlate a change with its own starting point and a link appears for free.
cards.trap: Suspecting rehabilitation took the credit, the usual worry about recovery data.
cards.reference: Hope et al., Recovery after stroke: not so proportional after all?, Brain, 2019

cards.question: True or false: London bus drivers, who drive all day on fixed routes, show the same enlarged hippocampus as taxi drivers?
cards.answer: False. Maguire's team compared the two because both drive all day in city traffic; only taxi drivers must hold the street plan in mind. Taxi drivers had more grey matter at the back of the hippocampus, less at the front, and were worse at recalling a new complex figure. Bus drivers showed neither.
cards.move: Find a group that shares everything except the thing you suspect.
cards.trap: Crediting the change to long hours of driving rather than navigating.
cards.reference: Maguire, Woollett & Spiers, London taxi drivers and bus drivers: a structural MRI and neuropsychological analysis, Hippocampus, 2006

cards.question: What happened to the extra grey matter of new adult jugglers once they stopped practising?
cards.answer: It partly shrank back. In 2004 Draganski's team scanned volunteers before and after three months learning a three-ball cascade: a region that tracks visual motion gained grey matter. Three months without juggling later, the gain had faded, though it stayed above where it began. The tissue followed the practice, down as well as up.
cards.move: Ask what happens after the practice stops before calling a change permanent.
cards.reference: Draganski et al., Neuroplasticity: changes in grey matter induced by training, Nature, 2004

cards.question: How many different smells can a human nose tell apart?
cards.answer: Nobody knows. A 2014 paper in Science put the figure above a trillion, extrapolating from 26 people sniffing mixtures drawn from 128 odorants. In 2015 two reanalyses showed the method was so sensitive to its assumptions that the same data could support estimates many orders of magnitude apart.
cards.move: An extrapolation is only as solid as the model stretched across the gap.
cards.reference: https://elifesciences.org/articles/08127

cards.question: Which cells did the COVID-19 virus attack to take away people's sense of smell?
cards.answer: The neurons' neighbours. Smell neurons lack ACE2, the protein the virus uses to enter cells, but the support cells wrapped around them in the nasal lining carry it. When those sustentacular cells die, the neurons lose their upkeep and fall silent. Because that layer regrows, most people's smell came back within weeks or months.
cards.move: When something fails, check what keeps it running, not only the part itself.
cards.reference: Brann, Tsukahara, Weinreb et al., Non-neuronal expression of SARS-CoV-2 entry genes in the olfactory system suggests mechanisms underlying COVID-19-associated anosmia, Science Advances, 2020

cards.question: Where did the idea that humans have a feeble sense of smell come from?
cards.answer: From brain anatomy, not smell tests. In 1879 the anatomist Paul Broca classed humans as non-smellers because their olfactory bulbs are small beside large frontal lobes. Yet the bulbs hold similar numbers of neurons across mammals, and blindfolded volunteers crawling on all fours have tracked a chocolate scent trail through grass.
cards.move: Ask whether a famous weakness was ever measured, or only assumed.
cards.reference: McGann, Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth, Science, 2017

cards.question: Colour vision relies on three kinds of cone. How many kinds of odour receptor does the human nose use?
cards.answer: About 400: counts of working genes run from roughly 340 to 400, each coding one receptor, and hundreds more have decayed into broken copies. A smell is a pattern across many receptors at once, so a few hundred sensors can encode vastly more than a few hundred smells.
cards.move: A count you know from one system says little about the next one.
cards.trap: Carrying over the handful of channels that vision and taste use.
cards.reference: Malnic, Godfrey & Buck, The human olfactory receptor gene family, PNAS, 2004

cards.question: True or false: in a US national survey, about one in eight adults over 40 failed a simple smell test?
cards.answer: True. In the 2011–2012 national health survey, 12.4% of adults aged 40 and over had measurable smell loss, and it climbed steeply with age, to more than a third of those aged 80 and over. The test was eight scratch-and-sniff odours, from chocolate to natural gas.
cards.move: A loss that nobody can see is easy to count too low.
cards.trap: Assuming smell loss is rare because it is so seldom discussed.
cards.source: Hoffman et al., Rev Endocr Metab Disord, 2016
cards.reference: Hoffman, Rawal, Li & Duffy, New chemosensory component in the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES): first-year results for measured olfactory dysfunction, Reviews in Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders, 2016

cards.question: Why can the same smell register more strongly through one nostril than through the other?
cards.answer: Because the nostrils take turns. Swelling of the nasal tissue shifts every few hours, so one nostril carries fast airflow and the other slow. Odours that dissolve quickly into the nasal lining are caught best in fast air; slow-dissolving ones need slow air. Each nostril samples a slightly different chemical world.
cards.move: Two sensors running at different speeds can catch what one would miss.
cards.reference: Sobel, Khan, Saltman, Sullivan & Gabrieli, The world smells different to each nostril, Nature, 1999

cards.question: True or false: some women with no visible olfactory bulbs, the brain's first relay for smell, smell as well as anyone?
cards.answer: True. Israeli researchers found two left-handed women whose scans showed no bulbs, yet who scored normally on every smell test; a public brain-scan database held more, about 4% of its left-handed women. Missing bulbs had seemed to mean anosmia because the people whose bulbs get scanned are those who cannot smell.
cards.move: If you only look where things go wrong, everything you find looks broken.
cards.trap: Every known case without bulbs had lost the sense of smell.
cards.reference: Weiss, Soroka, Gorodisky et al., Human olfaction without apparent olfactory bulbs, Neuron, 2020

cards.question: Androstenone, a steroid in boar saliva, is sniffed by a room of volunteers. How do they describe it?
options: Nearly all call it sweaty and foul
Nearly all call it faintly musky
Some foul, some sweet, some smell nothing
cards.answer: Some foul, some sweet, some smell nothing. Variants of one receptor gene, OR7D4, predict much of the split: people with two copies of the common version tend to find it strong and offensive, while carriers of certain variants find it weaker and less unpleasant. One molecule reaches different noses as different smells.
cards.move: Before arguing over a sensation, check that both people receive it.
cards.trap: Assuming one molecule gives one smell, since its chemistry is fixed.
cards.reference: Keller, Zhuang, Chi, Vosshall & Matsunami, Genetic variation in a human odorant receptor alters odour perception, Nature, 2007

cards.question: Older adults who failed a five-smell test died more often within five years. What remained after allowing for age, illness and dementia?
options: About three times the odds of death
cards.answer: About three times the odds of death. Among 3,005 US adults aged 57 to 85, those who could not smell had 3.37 times the odds of dying, after allowing for age, health, cognition, mental health, smoking, alcohol and nutrition. The authors suggest the nose shows how well the body still renews itself.
cards.move: Adjust for the obvious causes first, then look at what is left.
cards.trap: Assuming smell loss is only a stand-in for being old and ill.
cards.reference: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0107541

cards.question: Is the difficulty of naming smells a limit of the human nose, or of the English language?
cards.answer: Of the language, at least in part. English speakers asked to name familiar odours often fumble and fall back on sources: it smells like lemon. Jahai foragers of the Malay Peninsula, whose language has about a dozen abstract smell words, named odours as concisely and consistently as colours, much as English uses red.
cards.move: Before blaming the instrument, check whether the vocabulary exists.
cards.reference: Majid & Burenhult, Odors are expressible in language, as long as you speak the right language, Cognition, 2014

cards.question: Why does a pinch of salt taste pleasant while a mouthful of brine tastes repellent?
cards.answer: Because two different sets of cells answer. Low salt enters dedicated taste cells through a sodium channel, ENaC, and reads as pleasant. At high concentrations salt also fires the cells that sense bitter and sour, which drive rejection. Mice lacking those two cell types stopped avoiding strongly salted water.
cards.move: When a little pleases and a lot repels, look for a second sensor.
cards.reference: Oka, Butnaru, von Buchholtz, Ryba & Zuker, High salt recruits aversive taste pathways, Nature, 2013

cards.question: What does a bitter-taste receptor do in the lining of the nose and sinuses?
cards.answer: It guards against bacteria. The receptor T2R38 sits on the hair-like cilia of the sinuses and detects signalling molecules that bacteria such as Pseudomonas release to coordinate. It triggers nitric oxide and faster sweeping of mucus. People carrying the gene version that cannot taste the bitter chemical PTC had more sinus infections.
cards.move: A sensor named for one job may have been built for another.
cards.source: Lee et al., Journal of Clinical Investigation, 2012
cards.reference: Lee, Xiong, Kofonow et al., T2R38 taste receptor polymorphisms underlie susceptibility to upper respiratory infection, Journal of Clinical Investigation, 2012

cards.question: How does a West African berry make lemon juice taste sweet for a while?
cards.answer: Through a protein that switches the sweet receptor on only in acid. Miraculin, from Synsepalum dulcificum, binds the tongue's sweet receptor and does not activate it at neutral pH. When acid arrives, the protein changes shape and turns the receptor on. Each sour mouthful then registers as sweet until the protein washes off.
cards.move: The same key can lock or unlock, depending on the conditions around it.
cards.reference: Koizumi, Tsuchiya, Nakajima et al., Human sweet taste receptor mediates acid-induced sweetness of miraculin, PNAS, 2011

cards.question: Add a little inosinate, from dried bonito, to a glutamate broth. What happens to the savoury taste?
options: It grows far beyond the two added
It grows by about the two added
It shrinks as they compete for receptors
cards.answer: It grows far beyond the two added. Glutamate binds a pocket in the umami receptor, T1R1–T1R3; inosinate binds beside it and holds the pocket closed around the glutamate, so the receptor stays switched on. That is why Japanese dashi pairs kombu, rich in glutamate, with shavings of dried bonito.
cards.move: Two causes acting on one mechanism rarely just add up.
cards.trap: Assuming two savoury ingredients simply add their strengths together.
cards.reference: Zhang, Klebansky, Fine et al., Molecular mechanism for the umami taste synergism, PNAS, 2008

cards.question: True or false: the sting of sparkling water comes only from bubbles bursting against the tongue?
cards.answer: False. Taste cells built to sense sourness detect the dissolved gas itself. An enzyme on their surface, carbonic anhydrase 4, turns carbon dioxide into acid they can register, and mice lacking those cells barely responded to fizzy water. Climbers taking acetazolamide, an altitude drug that blocks such enzymes, find beer and fizzy drinks taste flat.
cards.move: A sensation that feels mechanical may be chemistry in disguise.
cards.trap: Picturing fizz as pure touch, bubbles popping against the tongue.
cards.reference: Chandrashekar, Yarmolinsky, von Buchholtz, Oka, Sly, Ryba & Zuker, The taste of carbonation, Science, 2009

cards.question: What does the sensor that lets the tongue taste sour share with the inner ear's balance organs?
cards.answer: A gene. Sour-sensing cells detect acid through otopetrin-1, a channel that lets protons, the core of every acid, flow straight into the cell. The gene was named years earlier from mutant mice that walked with tilted heads, because their inner ears grew no ear stones. Mice lacking it respond far less to sour.
cards.move: A name records where something was found first, not what it mainly does.
cards.reference: Tu, Cooper, Teng et al., An evolutionarily conserved gene family encodes proton-selective ion channels, Science, 2018

cards.question: Rinse the mouth with a harmless compound that blocks the sweet receptor, then sip plain water. How does the water taste?
cards.answer: Sweet. The blocker, lactisole, holds the sweet receptor below its normal resting activity. Water rinses the blocker away, the receptor rebounds above that resting level, and the brain reads the rebound as sweetness. The same kind of release may explain why water tastes sweet after a mouthful of artichoke.
cards.move: A signal that swings back past zero can feel like a new cause.
cards.trap: Water carries nothing sweet, so nothing sweet can be tasted.
cards.reference: Galindo-Cuspinera, Winnig, Bufe, Meyerhof & Breslin, A TAS1R receptor-based explanation of sweet 'water-taste', Nature, 2006

cards.question: Quinine can be tasted at about 0.008 millimolar, table sugar only from about 10 millimolar. How many times more sensitive is bitter taste?
cards.move: Compare how little of each thing it takes, not how strong each feels.
cards.trap: Reading the tiny decimal as a gap of tens, not thousands.
cards.hint: Clear the decimal first: multiply both thresholds by 1,000.
steps: Divide the sugar threshold by the quinine threshold: 10 / 0.008.
cards.simply: Bitter is an alarm for poisons, which harm in tiny doses; sweet is a fuel gauge that only needs to notice a meal.
cards.reference: Hall & Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition, Elsevier, 2020

cards.question: Human sweet taste relies on a single receptor, built from two proteins. How many kinds of bitter receptor does the tongue carry?
cards.answer: About 25. Sweet has one job, spotting a few sugars, so one receptor, T1R2 joined to T1R3, suffices. Bitter guards against thousands of plant and microbial toxins of unrelated shapes, so it needs many receptors, several broadly tuned. They report through the same cells, which is why every poison tastes alike: bitter.
cards.move: A detector for many unlike threats needs many parts but one alarm.
cards.trap: Assuming each basic taste gets one receptor, as sweet does.
cards.reference: Meyerhof, Batram, Kuhn et al., The molecular receptive ranges of human TAS2R bitter taste receptors, Chemical Senses, 2010

cards.question: True or false: pure fatty acids, tasted with the nose blocked, taste rich and creamy?
cards.answer: False. Tasted alone, free fatty acids have a taste of their own, which volunteers sorted apart from sweet, sour, salty and savoury, and which is unpleasant, closest to bitter. The creaminess credited to fat comes mostly from texture and smell. At strength, the taste of fat is the taste of oil gone rancid.
cards.move: When several signals always arrive together, test each one alone.
cards.trap: Crediting the taste of fat with pleasures that belong to texture and smell.
cards.reference: Running, Craig & Mattes, Oleogustus: the unique taste of fat, Chemical Senses, 2015

cards.question: Why does a chromosome lose a little of its tip each time a cell divides?
cards.answer: The copying machinery cannot reach the end. DNA polymerase extends a strand only from a short primer laid ahead of it, and at a linear chromosome's tip there is no room for the last one. Alexei Olovnikov in 1971 and James Watson in 1972 each saw this. Bacteria, with circular chromosomes, have no tips.
cards.move: A process that cannot reach its own edge will wear that edge down.
cards.reference: Olovnikov, A theory of marginotomy, Journal of Theoretical Biology, 1973

cards.question: Why was the enzyme that rebuilds chromosome tips first found in a pond-dwelling single cell?
cards.answer: Because that cell is mostly tips. Tetrahymena keeps its working genes in thousands of tiny chromosomes, giving it tens of thousands of ends, so its extracts are rich in the enzyme that caps them. Carol Greider and Elizabeth Blackburn detected that enzyme, telomerase, on Christmas Day 1984; the work shared a Nobel prize in 2009.
cards.move: To find something rare, look where nature has made it common.
cards.reference: Greider & Blackburn, Identification of a specific telomere terminal transferase activity in Tetrahymena extracts, Cell, 1985

cards.question: Mice bred to lack telomerase entirely: when do signs of worn-out chromosome tips appear?
options: Late in life, in the first generation
cards.answer: After several generations of breeding. Lab mice are born with telomeres several times longer than a human's, so the first knockout mice lived normally. Each generation inherited shorter tips; by about the fourth to sixth, mice showed fused chromosomes, infertility and failing blood-forming tissue. The reserve ran down across lifetimes, not within one.
cards.move: A large reserve can hide a missing supply for a long time.
cards.trap: Assuming an enzyme that maintains chromosomes must be needed at once.
cards.reference: Blasco, Lee, Hande et al., Telomere shortening and tumor formation by mouse cells lacking telomerase RNA, Cell, 1997

cards.question: Hayflick's human cells stopped dividing after about 50 doublings. What did he grow with them to prove the limit was theirs?
options: Young cells of the opposite sex
cards.answer: Young cells of the opposite sex. In 1961 Hayflick and Moorhead mixed old male cells with young female ones in one flask, told apart by their sex chromosomes. The male cells reached their limit and died out while the female cells kept dividing. Same broth, same handling: the limit travelled with the cells.
cards.move: Put the suspect and a control in the same conditions, then compare.
cards.trap: Reaching for fresh broth, which leaves the rest of the handling untested.
cards.reference: Hayflick & Moorhead, The serial cultivation of human diploid cell strains, Experimental Cell Research, 1961

cards.question: True or false: people who inherit longer telomeres are less likely to develop cancer?
cards.answer: False. Using gene variants that fix telomere length at conception, which lifestyle cannot confound, a 2017 analysis found longer telomeres raised the risk of several cancers, including melanoma, glioma and lung adenocarcinoma. Longer tips let a cell divide more times before it halts, including a cell on its way to a tumour.
cards.move: What travels with good health is not always what produces it.
cards.trap: Treating long telomeres as youth, and youth as protection from cancer.
cards.reference: Telomeres Mendelian Randomization Collaboration (Haycock et al.), Association between telomere length and risk of cancer and non-neoplastic diseases: a Mendelian randomization study, JAMA Oncology, 2017

cards.question: Two newborns' telomeres differ by 3,000 base pairs, a normal gap. Adults lose about 30 a year. How many years of loss is the gap?
cards.move: Where someone starts can matter more than how fast they travel.
cards.trap: Assuming decades of lifestyle must outweigh a difference present at birth.
cards.hint: Divide the gap between the babies by what an adult loses in a year.
steps: The gap at birth is 3,000 base pairs; an adult loses about 30 a year.
cards.reference: Benetos, Kark, Susser et al., Tracking and fixed ranking of leukocyte telomere length across the adult life course, Aging Cell, 2013

cards.question: True or false: every cancer must switch on telomerase to stop its chromosome tips wearing away?
cards.answer: False. Most do, but roughly 10 to 15% of cancers use a second route, alternative lengthening of telomeres, copying tip sequences from one chromosome to another by recombination. It is commoner in tumours of bone and soft tissue and in some brain cancers. A drug that blocked telomerase alone would leave these cells dividing.
cards.move: A barrier with two doors is not closed by shutting one.
cards.trap: Treating telomerase as the one lock every tumour must pick.
cards.reference: Cesare & Reddel, Alternative lengthening of telomeres: models, mechanisms and implications, Nature Reviews Genetics, 2010

cards.question: How can a child who did not inherit a parent's faulty telomerase gene still show its effects?
cards.answer: By inheriting the parent's short telomeres. Chromosomes arrive with the tips they already have, so a parent with a telomerase defect passes on shortened ones even when the child gets the healthy copy of the gene. In families with such mutations, lung scarring and bone-marrow failure tend to strike earlier with each generation.
cards.move: An inheritance can include the state of things, not only the instructions.
cards.reference: Armanios & Blackburn, The telomere syndromes, Nature Reviews Genetics, 2012

cards.question: True or false: children of older fathers tend to be born with longer telomeres?
cards.answer: True. Unlike most cells, the stem cells that make sperm keep telomerase active, and sperm telomeres lengthen as men age. Each extra year of a father's age adds measurably to his child's telomere length, in several populations. The effect carries on: grandchildren whose paternal grandfathers were older fathers show it too.
cards.move: Ageing wears most things down; check which parts it builds up.
cards.trap: Old father, old cells: assuming age only shortens what is passed on.
cards.reference: Eisenberg, Hayes & Kuzawa, Delayed paternal age of reproduction in humans is associated with longer telomeres across two generations of descendants, PNAS, 2012

cards.question: Should telomere-length tests be sold to the public as a measure of biological age?
cards.answer: Short telomeres in blood are linked, across large studies, to heart disease and earlier death, and the test needs only a blood or saliva sample. People are already told their cholesterol and blood pressure, which also predict risk imperfectly. A number that falls with age can motivate change, and adults can judge it for themselves.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how precisely one person can be measured decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The common laboratory method, qPCR, is noisy enough that a retest can move a person far up or down the ranking. A single reading cannot show how fast someone is ageing, only where they stand, and nothing proven lengthens telomeres safely. The number sells worry, not a plan.
cards.source: Mather et al., J Gerontol A, 2011
cards.reference: Mather, Jorm, Parslow & Christensen, Is telomere length a biomarker of aging? A review, Journals of Gerontology Series A, 2011

cards.question: Is there a word every language shares?
cards.answer: Possibly one. "Huh?" — the sound for signalling you did not catch something — appears in essentially every language studied, with a strikingly similar form. It looks less like a word inherited from a common ancestor and more like one every language independently converges on, because conversation needs it.
cards.move: Every language on record has its own version of "huh?", and they all sound alike.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0078273

cards.question: What was writing invented for?
cards.answer: Accounting. The oldest substantial writing is Mesopotamian bookkeeping: receipts for grain, beer and livestock, and records of who owed what. Literature comes many centuries later. Writing began as an administrative technology and was only afterwards turned to anything anyone would read for pleasure.
cards.move: The first thing anyone wrote down was a receipt.

cards.question: How many colours does a language need?
cards.answer: No — and the ones that gain colour terms do so in a remarkably consistent order. Dark and light come first, then red, then green or yellow, and blue late. Languages carve the same continuous spectrum into different numbers of words, in more or less the same sequence.
cards.move: Blue is one of the last colours a language gets a word for.

cards.question: Are sign languages signed versions of speech?
cards.answer: Not at all — they have their own grammar, unrelated to the surrounding spoken language. The clearest proof arrived in 1980s Nicaragua, where deaf children brought together for the first time built a full language from scratch within a couple of school generations.
cards.move: Deaf children in Nicaragua invented a complete language in about a decade.
cards.reference: Senghas & Coppola, Children creating language: How Nicaraguan Sign Language acquired a spatial grammar, Psychological Science, 2001

cards.question: Why was silent reading once remarkable?
cards.answer: Because text was written to be spoken. Early manuscripts ran words together with little punctuation, and reading aloud was how you parsed them. Augustine noted with some surprise that Ambrose read without moving his lips. Spacing and punctuation are technologies for reading quietly.
cards.move: The space between words is an invention, and a fairly late one.
cards.reference: Saenger, Space Between Words: The Origins of Silent Reading, Stanford University Press, 1997

cards.question: Where did the Greek alphabet find vowels, when its Phoenician model wrote none?
cards.answer: In Phoenician consonants Greek had no use for. Aleph was a glottal stop, a catch in the throat; Greek speakers kept the letter for the vowel that followed it, and it became alpha. He became epsilon, yod became iota, ayin became omicron. Every European vowel letter descends from consonants recycled around 800 BC.
cards.move: The parts that do not fit a borrower often become its invention.
cards.source: Powell, Homer and the Greek Alphabet, 1991
cards.reference: Powell, Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet, Cambridge University Press, 1991

cards.question: True or false: Saint Cyril created the alphabet now called Cyrillic?
cards.answer: False. Cyril and his brother Methodius devised Glagolitic, a script of new, looped letters, for their mission to the Slavs in the 860s. Cyrillic was assembled later, probably by their disciples in Bulgaria around 900, largely from Greek capitals, and named in Cyril's honour. Croatian priests went on writing Glagolitic for centuries.
cards.move: A name on a thing honours someone; it does not prove who made it.
cards.trap: The alphabet carries his name, so he must have made it.
cards.source: Daniels & Bright, The World's Writing Systems, 1996
cards.reference: Daniels & Bright (eds), The World's Writing Systems, Oxford University Press, 1996

cards.question: Could the people who invented the alphabet read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
cards.answer: Probably not, argues the Egyptologist Orly Goldwasser. The earliest alphabetic texts were cut by Semitic-speaking workers at Egyptian turquoise mines in Sinai, early in the second millennium BC, though dates are disputed. They took hieroglyph pictures for the first sound of each word in their own language, so an ox head, alp, wrote a.
cards.move: A tool used by outsiders can be simpler than any expert would design.
cards.reference: Goldwasser, How the Alphabet Was Born from Hieroglyphs, Biblical Archaeology Review 36(2), 2010

cards.question: How far back can alphabetical order, with A before B before G, be traced?
cards.answer: More than 3,000 years. Clay tablets from Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, list the letters of a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet in an order that opens much like the Phoenician and Hebrew one. The order outlived the scripts that carried it: a child reciting A, B, C follows a list pressed into Bronze Age clay.
cards.move: An arbitrary order, once shared, can outlast everything it was for.
cards.reference: Healey, The Early Alphabet, British Museum Publications, 1990

cards.question: A Hangul syllable joins one of 19 initial consonants, one of 21 vowels, and one of 27 finals or none. How many syllables, in thousands?
cards.answer: 11,172 syllables is about 11.2 thousand.
cards.move: When counting combinations, count leaving a slot empty as one more choice.
cards.trap: Forgetting that having no final consonant is also an option.
cards.hint: Multiply the choices at each position, and count no final as a choice.
steps: 19 initial consonants x 21 vowels = 399 open syllables.
27 final consonants plus the option of none = 28 endings.
399 x 28 = 11,172 possible syllables.
11,172 syllables is about 11.2 thousand.
cards.reference: The Unicode Standard, Version 15.0, section 3.12 Conjoining Jamo Behavior, Unicode Consortium, 2022

cards.question: Why does G stand seventh in the Latin alphabet, when its Greek ancestor gamma stood third?
cards.answer: Because C already held third place. Etruscan had no g sound, so gamma reached Rome as C, writing k. In the 3rd century BC Rome added a stroke to C to make G and slotted it into seventh place, left empty when Z was dropped. Z came back later, tacked on at the very end.
cards.move: An odd position in a list often marks where something was taken out.
cards.reference: Gordon, Illustrated Introduction to Latin Epigraphy, University of California Press, 1983

cards.question: Mongolian script descends from right-to-left Aramaic and was turned to run vertically. Which way do its columns go?
options: Top to bottom, left to right
Top to bottom, right to left
Bottom to top, left to right
cards.answer: Top to bottom, left to right. The Mongols took the script from the Uyghurs around 1204, and its lines had been turned a quarter turn anticlockwise. The start of each right-to-left line swung to the top, and the first line swung to the left. Chinese columns, set beside it, run the other way.
cards.move: Work out how a thing was made before assuming it copies its neighbour.
cards.trap: Copying the Chinese layout, the best-known vertical script in the region.
cards.source: Kara, Books of the Mongolian Nomads, 2005
cards.reference: Kara, Books of the Mongolian Nomads: More than Eight Centuries of Writing Mongolian, Indiana University, 2005

cards.question: Should Kazakhstan finish replacing Cyrillic with the Latin alphabet for writing the Kazakh language?
cards.answer: The Cyrillic set was built for Russian and carries letters native Kazakh words hardly need. Latin letters match the keyboards, phones and Turkic languages, from Turkish to Azerbaijani, that already use them. The switch was decreed in 2017; every year of delay adds signs, forms and textbooks that will one day be reprinted anyway.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, who pays for the years of two scripts decides it.
