cards.move: A rule that names who may not act invites someone else to.
cards.reference: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Saishūshoku-tō mondai ni kakaru chōsa hōkoku (saishū matome), Tokyo, 30 March 2017

cards.question: Latin and French supply more of the English dictionary than Old English does. Why does ordinary speech hide it?
cards.answer: Because a dictionary counts each word once and speech counts every use. A 1973 dictionary survey put Latin and French at over a quarter each, Germanic at about a quarter. But the words on every line, the, of, and, to, is, are Old English. A sentence about photosynthesis borrows its nouns and keeps its glue.
cards.move: Count how often a thing is used, not how many kinds exist.
cards.reference: Finkenstaedt & Wolff, Ordered Profusion: Studies in Dictionaries and the English Lexicon, Carl Winter, Heidelberg, 1973

cards.question: Why does English have both frail and fragile, from the same Latin word?
cards.answer: Because Latin fragilis arrived twice. First by mouth, through Old French, where speech had worn it down to frail; English had it by the fourteenth century. Later, scholars borrowed it again straight from written Latin as fragile. Royal and regal, sure and secure match: one route through the street, one through the library.
cards.move: When two words look like cousins, ask which door each came in by.
cards.reference: Durkin, Borrowed Words: A History of Loanwords in English, Oxford University Press, 2014

cards.question: Were Roman soldiers really paid in salt, as the story behind salary goes?
cards.answer: No ancient source says so. Salarium, an allowance, does come from sal, salt, but no ancient text says soldiers received salt, and soldiers were paid in coin, mostly silver. The salt-wage story is modern: an Italian Latin dictionary of 1771 is among the first to state it.
cards.move: A true origin can still be carrying a made-up explanation.
cards.source: The Conversation, on salary and salt
cards.reference: https://theconversation.com/our-pay-is-called-a-salary-but-were-roman-soldiers-really-paid-in-salt-290057

cards.question: Why does the English word debt carry a b that nobody pronounces?
cards.answer: Scholars respelled it after Latin. English took the word from French as dette and first wrote it that way. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, writers who knew Latin debitum inserted the b to show its pedigree. Doubt, from dubitare, got the same treatment. The letter records a scholar's reading, not English speech.
cards.move: A spelling can record someone's taste rather than anyone's speech.
cards.trap: Assuming every silent letter is a sound that later fell away.
cards.reference: Crystal, Spell It Out: The Singular Story of English Spelling, Profile Books, 2012

cards.question: True or false: sincere comes from Latin sine cera, without wax, the mark of honest sculptors?
cards.answer: False. The tale: dishonest sculptors filled cracks in marble with wax, so honest work was sold without it. No Latin text supports it. Sincerus meant clean, pure or unmixed, and its origin is uncertain; the wax story is a later folk etymology. It survives on detail: the crack, the wax softening in the sun.
cards.move: Each vivid detail in a story is one more thing that must be true.
cards.trap: The sculptor story is too specific to feel invented.
cards.reference: https://www.etymonline.com/word/sincere

cards.question: Before it meant blowing up, what did the Latin-born verb explode mean in English?
cards.answer: To drive off with scornful noise, as an audience did a bad actor. Latin explodere joined ex, out, and plaudere, to clap, the root of applause: Roman crowds clapped performers off. English used it for rejecting ideas scornfully, hence an exploded theory. Bursting with a bang arrived only in the late 1700s.
cards.move: A word's older sense often hides inside one fixed phrase.
cards.source: Onions, Oxford Dictionary of English Etymology, 1966
cards.reference: Onions (ed.), The Oxford Dictionary of English Etymology, Clarendon Press, 1966

cards.question: In classical Latin, what was the plural of virus, the word for poison or slime?
cards.answer: None that survives. Virus was a rare neuter noun ending in -us, like vulgus, crowd, and it named a substance, as water does, so Roman authors never needed a plural. A regular neuter plural would have been vira. Virii fits no Latin pattern at all: it is a modern invention dressed as Latin.
cards.move: A rule learned from a few examples may not cover the rest.
cards.trap: Applying the cactus and cacti rule to every Latin word in -us.
cards.reference: Allen & Greenough, New Latin Grammar for Schools and Colleges, Ginn & Company, 1903

cards.question: French tête, head, descends from a Latin word. What did that Latin word first mean?
cards.answer: Pot or shell. Testa meant an earthenware pot or a shell, and everyday Latin used it jokingly for the skull, as English says nut. Classical authors wrote caput. French grew from spoken Latin, not from books, which is why its horse, cheval, comes from caballus, a nag, not from equus.
cards.move: Ask what people said at home, not what they wrote for posterity.
cards.trap: Assuming French inherited the Latin that literature preserved.
cards.source: Pope, From Latin to Modern French, 1934
cards.reference: Pope, From Latin to Modern French with Especial Consideration of Anglo-Norman, Manchester University Press, 1934

cards.question: True or false: the s in island is there because the word comes from Latin insula?
cards.answer: False. Island is native English: Old English īegland, from īeg, island, and land, and it was written iland for centuries. The s was added in the 1500s by writers who linked it to isle, which really does come from Latin insula through French. The resemblance was put there with a pen.
cards.move: A resemblance can be manufactured by whoever did the copying.
cards.trap: Seeing isle inside island and assuming a shared Latin root.
cards.source: Upward & Davidson, History of English Spelling, 2011
cards.reference: Upward & Davidson, The History of English Spelling, Wiley-Blackwell, 2011

cards.question: Which Latin words did the Anglo-Saxons already have before they ever reached Britain?
cards.answer: Words for Roman goods and building: street from strata, wine from vinum, cheese from caseus, kitchen from coquina. Germanic tribes picked them up trading with the Empire on the continent, which is why German has Straße, Wein, Käse and Küche. Four centuries of Roman Britain left Old English very few words of its own.
cards.move: Trace a word's route before assuming it came by the obvious road.
cards.source: Kastovsky, Cambridge History of the English Language
cards.reference: Kastovsky, Semantics and vocabulary, in Hogg (ed.), The Cambridge History of the English Language, vol. 1, Cambridge University Press, 1992

cards.question: What kept Egyptian hieroglyphs unread for some 1,400 years after the last one was carved?
cards.answer: A wrong theory of what they were. Late antique writers such as Horapollo explained the signs as symbols of ideas, and scholars up to Athanasius Kircher, in the 1600s, built mystical readings on it. In 1822 Champollion showed that many signs wrote sounds. The last dated one, at Philae in AD 394, spelled words.
cards.move: A wrong idea of what the problem is can outlast every clue.
cards.reference: Parkinson, Cracking Codes: The Rosetta Stone and Decipherment, British Museum Press, 1999

cards.question: Which misunderstood Spanish document helped unlock Maya writing four centuries after it was written?
cards.answer: Bishop Diego de Landa's account of Yucatán, from around 1566. He asked Maya informants for the sign for each Spanish letter, and they wrote the syllable of the letter's name, so b, said be, got the glyph for be. Long dismissed as nonsense, it let Yuri Knorozov show in 1952 that Maya glyphs spell syllables.
cards.move: A failed translation can still record the answer to another question.
cards.reference: Coe, Breaking the Maya Code, Thames & Hudson, 1992

cards.question: Why have thousands of Linear B clay tablets from Mycenaean palaces lasted more than 3,000 years?
options: Dry tombs sealed them from damp
cards.answer: Palace fires baked them hard. The tablets were unfired clay, working records meant to last a season before being softened and reused. When the palaces at Knossos and Pylos burned, the heat turned that year's paperwork into pottery. What survives is the administration of a palace's final months, not an archive anyone chose to keep.
cards.move: Ask what preserved your evidence before asking what it represents.
cards.trap: Assuming that what lasted was made to last.
cards.source: Chadwick, The Decipherment of Linear B, 1958
cards.reference: Chadwick, The Decipherment of Linear B, Cambridge University Press, 1958

cards.question: True or false: Etruscan can be sounded out with confidence, yet the meanings of many of its words remain unknown?
cards.answer: True. Etruscan was written in an alphabet adapted from Greek, so its sounds are known. But the language is unrelated to Latin, Greek or any living tongue, and most of its roughly 13,000 inscriptions are short epitaphs and dedications. The longest text survived as linen strips wrapped round an Egyptian mummy, now in Zagreb.
cards.move: Sounding out a message and understanding it are separate problems.
cards.trap: Being able to read a script feels like understanding it.
cards.reference: Bonfante & Bonfante, The Etruscan Language: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Manchester University Press, 2002

cards.question: Is the Indus script a writing system that recorded a spoken language?
sides: No, it is a symbol system
cards.answer: The signs behave like writing: they run in one direction, recur in fixed positions and combine by rules. A 2009 statistical study by Rao and colleagues found their sequences more ordered than random symbols and within the range of known scripts. One standard sign set across a vast area implies something taught and read.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, what you count as writing decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The texts are too short to be writing: the average inscription has about five signs, and no long text has turned up in several thousand finds. Farmer, Sproat and Witzel noted how many signs occur only once. Heraldic and religious emblem systems show the same statistical order, so the Rao measure cannot tell writing from symbols.
cards.reference: Rao, Yadav, Vahia et al., Entropic Evidence for Linguistic Structure in the Indus Script, Science 324, 2009

cards.question: The Linear A corpus holds about 1,400 inscriptions with about 7,400 signs in all. How many signs per inscription, on average?
cards.answer: 7,400 / 1,400 = about 5.3 signs per inscription.
cards.move: Count the words in the pile, not just the number of pages.
cards.trap: Hearing 1,400 inscriptions and picturing a large body of text.
cards.hint: Divide the signs by the objects that carry them.
steps: Total signs: about 7,400.
Inscriptions: about 1,400.
7,400 / 1,400 = about 5.3 signs per inscription.
cards.reference: https://sigla.phis.me/paper.html

cards.question: What did Alice Kober prove about the Linear B language without giving a single sound to its signs?
cards.answer: That it was inflected, changing word endings for grammar. In the 1940s she found sets of words sharing a stem but ending differently, later called Kober's triplets, and showed which signs must share a consonant or a vowel. She died in 1950; Michael Ventris, building such grids, read the tablets as Greek in 1952.
cards.move: Structure can be mapped long before anyone knows what it means.
cards.source: Fox, The Riddle of the Labyrinth, 2013
cards.reference: Fox, The Riddle of the Labyrinth: The Quest to Crack an Ancient Code, Ecco, 2013

cards.question: Dozens of rival decipherments of the Phaistos Disc each produce readable words. What does that tell a sceptic?
options: Short texts fit almost any reading
One of them is probably right
The disc was made as a hoax
cards.answer: Short texts fit almost any reading. The disc holds 242 stamped signs of 45 kinds, and no second text in its script has been found. Each decipherer chooses sounds for 45 signs, and that freedom lets one short text spell words in Greek, Luwian or almost anything. Rival readings cancel each other.
cards.move: When every guess can be made to fit, fitting proves nothing.
cards.trap: Assuming so many workable readings must include the true one.
cards.reference: Robinson, Lost Languages: The Enigma of the World's Undeciphered Scripts, McGraw-Hill, 2002

cards.question: In 2024 wood from a rongorongo tablet was radiocarbon-dated to about 1493 to 1509. What does that date establish?
options: The wood grew before Europeans came
The script existed before Europeans came
cards.answer: The wood grew before Europeans came. Radiocarbon dates when the wood grew, not when it was carved, and on an island short of trees wood was kept and reused: another tablet is cut into a European oar. Europeans arrived in 1722; the authors think the script older, but the wood cannot prove it.
cards.move: Date the act you care about, not the material it was done on.
cards.trap: Letting the striking 1400s date stand for the date of the writing.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-53063-7

cards.question: By 1915 Hittite cuneiform could be sounded out but not understood. Which sentence showed the language was Indo-European?
cards.answer: One about bread and water. Bedřich Hrozný read nu NINDA-an ezzateni watar-ma ekuteni. NINDA was a known Sumerian sign for bread, ezza- recalled German essen, eat, and watar looked like water: now you will eat bread and drink water. Thousands of tablets from the Hittite capital became readable.
cards.move: One secure word can unlock the grammar around it.
cards.reference: Hrozný, Die Sprache der Hethiter: ihr Bau und ihre Zugehörigkeit zum indogermanischen Sprachstamm, J. C. Hinrichs, 1917

cards.question: True or false: Swedish lagom comes from Vikings passing a mead horn laget om, around the team?
cards.answer: False. The drinking-horn tale is modern folklore. Lagom comes from lag, law or custom, in an old dative plural: roughly by the rules, as is fitting. Etymologists trace it through ordinary legal and everyday usage, with no feast in sight. The horn was added to the word later, not found underneath it.
cards.move: A story that explains every detail still needs a document behind it.
cards.trap: The Viking scene accounts for every syllable, so it feels documented.
cards.reference: Hellquist, Svensk etymologisk ordbok, Gleerup, Lund, 1922

cards.question: Where does the Scandinavian Law of Jante, the rule against thinking yourself special, come from?
cards.answer: A 1933 novel. In A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, Aksel Sandemose invented Jante, a small town modelled on his birthplace, Nykøbing Mors, and gave it ten commandments, the first being that you are not to think you are anything. A satirist's list became the region's shorthand for its own conformity.
cards.move: A saying that sounds like ancient law may be a novelist's joke.
cards.trap: The word law suggests a statute, so a medieval code sounds right.
cards.source: Sandemose, En flyktning krysser sitt spor, 1933
cards.reference: Sandemose, En flyktning krysser sitt spor, Oslo, 1933

cards.question: What does the Finnish word sisu, usually glossed as grit, literally refer to?
cards.answer: The insides. Sisu comes from sisä, inside, and its older sense is the innards, much as English says someone has guts. It became Finland's word for itself during the Winter War of 1939–40, when foreign reporters used it to explain how a small army held out for 105 days against the Soviet Union.
cards.move: Many words for courage began as words for body parts.
cards.reference: Häkkinen, Nykysuomen etymologinen sanakirja, WSOY, 2004

cards.question: Who first put the Norwegian word friluftsliv, open-air life, into print?
cards.answer: Henrik Ibsen, in On the Heights, a long poem written around 1860. Its young narrator leaves the valley and his bride for the high mountain plateau and chooses its solitude over the life below. A word now printed on school timetables and outdoor charity leaflets began in a playwright's verse about walking away from people.
cards.move: A cheerful word's first use may carry a much bleaker sense.
cards.source: Gelter, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education, 2000
cards.reference: Gelter, Friluftsliv: The Scandinavian Philosophy of Outdoor Life, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education, 2000

cards.question: Which language did Danish borrow its best-known export word, hygge, from?
cards.answer: Norwegian. Hygge meant wellbeing in Norwegian and appears in Danish writing around 1800; it goes back to Old Norse, and English hug may share the root. The word sold across Europe in 2016 as the essence of Danishness is a loan from the neighbours to the north.
cards.move: The word a country is famous for may be borrowed from next door.
cards.source: Wiking, The Little Book of Hygge, 2016
cards.reference: Wiking, The Little Book of Hygge, Penguin Life, 2016

cards.question: True or false: Sweden's right to roam, allemansrätten, is spelled out rule by rule in a written statute?
cards.answer: False. The constitution says only that everyone shall have access to nature under the right of public access; it never lists what that right contains. The content is custom, fenced in by other laws on trespass, damage and nature protection. A tent pitched for one night is allowed because nothing forbids it.
cards.move: Some rules live in what is forbidden, not in what is granted.
cards.trap: Assuming a right everyone knows must be written down somewhere.
cards.reference: Regeringsformen (SFS 1974:152), chapter 2, article 15, Sveriges riksdag

cards.question: A Swedish sambo, an unmarried live-in partner, dies without a will. What can the survivor claim?
options: An heir's share, as a spouse would
A share of the jointly used home
Nothing, since the law ignores sambos
cards.answer: A share of the jointly used home. Sweden's Cohabitees Act lets the survivor ask for the shared home and household goods bought for joint use to be divided between them. Beyond that there is no right to inherit. A partner of thirty years can leave with half the sofa and none of the savings.
cards.move: An everyday word for a relationship is not a legal status.
cards.trap: Reading a word everyone uses for partner as equal to spouse.
cards.reference: Sambolag (SFS 2003:376), sections 3, 8 and 18, Sveriges riksdag, 2003

cards.question: True or false: löyly, the Finnish word for sauna steam, shares an ancestor with the Hungarian word for soul?
cards.answer: True. Löyly and Hungarian lélek, soul, descend from a reconstructed Uralic word for breath or spirit, with relatives in Mansi and Khanty, spoken in western Siberia. Finnish kept the breath rising off the stones; Hungarian kept the soul. Linguists accept the link because the same sound changes recur across many other shared words.
cards.move: A resemblance counts as evidence only when it repeats in a pattern.
cards.trap: Dismissing a match between distant languages as chance resemblance.
cards.reference: Itkonen & Kulonen (eds.), Suomen sanojen alkuperä: Etymologinen sanakirja, vol. 2, Suomalaisen Kirjallisuuden Seura and Kotimaisten kielten tutkimuskeskus, Helsinki, 1995

cards.question: Why did Norway's 2020 call for a national dugnad, communal volunteer work, land unevenly with its residents?
cards.answer: Because the word carries a duty only insiders hear. Dugnad is unpaid work for the community, voluntary in name and expected in fact; NRK viewers voted it Norway's national word in 2004. A 2024 interview study found many immigrants unsure what the appeals asked. Where neighbours hear a summons, a newcomer hears a noun.
cards.move: An appeal that runs on shared expectation fails where the expectation is missing.
cards.source: Herrero-Arias et al., Archives of Public Health, 2024

cards.question: Do national words like hygge and lagom reveal something real about the people who use them?
cards.answer: A language grows everyday words for what its speakers keep talking about. Anna Wierzbicka's studies of cultural key words show such terms bundle expectations outsiders miss, and hygge carries unspoken rules about warmth, equality and not dominating the talk that Danes recognise at once. A word used every day is a record of priorities.
cards.move: The hinge is whether a common word proves a common behaviour.
cards.counterpoint: The hygge boom of 2016 was a publishing trend aimed at foreign buyers, selling candles and blankets as a national trait. When Terracciano and colleagues compared national stereotypes with measured personality across 49 cultures in 2005, the two did not match. English has cosy, and no one reads a national soul into it.
cards.source: Wierzbicka, Understanding Cultures through Their Key Words
cards.reference: Wierzbicka, Understanding Cultures through Their Key Words, Oxford University Press, 1997

cards.question: Why did an Elizabethan magistrate compile one of the first glossaries of English slang?
cards.answer: To expose vagrants. Thomas Harman's Caveat for Common Cursitors, first printed in 1566, set out the tricks of wandering beggars and listed their secret cant, such as bouse for drink and ken for a house. Later pamphleteers copied his list for decades, so much supposed Elizabethan underworld speech traces back to one Kent landowner's notes.
cards.move: When every source agrees, check whether they all copied one.
cards.source: Kinney, Rogues, Vagabonds and Sturdy Beggars, 1990
cards.reference: Kinney (ed.), Rogues, Vagabonds and Sturdy Beggars, University of Massachusetts Press, 1990

cards.question: Which ordinary English word did Jonathan Swift attack in 1710 as a vulgar new clipping?
cards.answer: Mob. Short for mobile vulgus, the fickle crowd, it was only a few decades old when Swift, writing in The Tatler, listed it with rep, pozz and phizz among the abbreviations spoiling the language. Mob became plain English; pozz, for positive, vanished. The complaint is remembered mostly because one of its targets survived.
cards.move: Today's sloppy shortcut is often tomorrow's dictionary word.
cards.reference: Swift, The Tatler No. 230 (1710), in Davis (ed.), The Prose Works of Jonathan Swift, vol. 2, Blackwell, 1939

cards.question: True or false: the British word yob began as boy spelled backwards?
cards.answer: True. Yob comes from back slang, a code of London costermongers, the street traders who reversed words so customers could not follow: yob for boy, esclop for police. John Camden Hotten recorded it in his slang dictionary of 1859. The code faded, and a word for a boy became a word for a lout.
cards.move: Not every neat origin story is a myth; check before scoffing.
cards.trap: A reversal that neat sounds like a later joke about the word.
cards.reference: Green, Green's Dictionary of Slang, Chambers, 2010

cards.question: When OK first appeared in a Boston newspaper in 1839, what was it?
cards.answer: A jokey misspelt abbreviation, for oll korrect. It surfaced in the Boston Morning Post amid a fad for comic initials such as O.W., oll wright. The 1840 campaign of President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed Old Kinderhook, gave OK a second meaning and a national stage, and it outlived every other joke in the fad.
cards.move: A close match between two sources can still be chance.
cards.trap: Choctaw okeh, it is so, matches OK too well to be chance.
cards.reference: Metcalf, OK: The Improbable Story of America's Greatest Word, Oxford University Press, 2010

cards.question: How did a secret slang of gay men reach millions of BBC radio listeners in the 1960s?
cards.answer: Through a comedy show. In Round the Horne, from 1965, two camp characters, Julian and Sandy, spoke Polari, a slang built from Italian, Romani, back slang and theatre talk: bona for good, omi for man. Audiences laughed at words many did not know were code, and the exposure hastened the code's decline.
cards.move: A secret language stops working the moment outsiders learn it.
cards.reference: Baker, Polari: The Lost Language of Gay Men, Routledge, 2002

cards.question: Before 1971, a quid was a pound and a tanner a sixpence. How many tanners made a quid?
cards.answer: 240 ÷ 6 = 40 tanners.
cards.move: Before converting, check which system the old number was counted in.
cards.trap: Using today's 100 pence and getting about 17 tanners.
cards.hint: Go through the shilling: the old pound was not split into 100.
steps: A quid was 20 shillings, known as bob.
A bob was 12 pence.
20 × 12 = 240 pence in a quid.
240 ÷ 6 = 40 tanners.
cards.reference: Green, Green's Dictionary of Slang, 3 volumes, Chambers, 2010

cards.question: In 17th-century thieves' cant, rum meant fine or excellent. What did rum mean to most Victorian readers?
cards.answer: Odd or strange. In cant a rum cove was a fine fellow and rum booze was good wine; by the late 18th century the word had flipped, by a path nobody has traced for certain. A rum go was a puzzling turn of events. The fine fellow had become a suspicious one.
cards.move: Praise can sour into suspicion without a single letter changing.
cards.trap: Linking the adjective to the drink and guessing it meant drunk.
cards.source: Coleman, A History of Cant and Slang Dictionaries
cards.reference: Coleman, A History of Cant and Slang Dictionaries, Volume 1: 1567–1784, Oxford University Press, 2004

cards.question: True or false: the whole nine yards first appears in print during the Second World War?
cards.answer: False. Digitised newspapers show the whole nine yards in an Indiana paper in 1908, and a variant, the whole six yards, in Kentucky in 1912. That rules out wartime origins, such as a fighter's 8-metre ammunition belt. With six and nine both in use, no fixed length fits. Nobody knows which yards were meant.
cards.move: A story with more details is not a story with more evidence.
cards.trap: The wartime tale of ammunition belts feels too specific to be invented.
cards.reference: https://www.wordorigins.org/big-list-entries/whole-nine-yards

cards.question: What kind of book was the first dictionary compiled in Australia?
cards.answer: A glossary of thieves' slang, written by a convict. James Hardy Vaux, transported for theft, compiled his Vocabulary of the Flash Language in 1812 at the Newcastle penal settlement and dedicated it to the commandant. It was printed in London in 1819 with his memoirs. Australia's first lexicographer was defining the words for picking pockets.
cards.move: The people being policed often leave the best record of how they spoke.
cards.reference: Vaux, The Memoirs of James Hardy Vaux, Including His Vocabulary of the Flash Language, ed. McLachlan, Heinemann, 1964

cards.question: Hooligan burst into London newspapers in the summer of 1898. Where did the word come from?
cards.answer: Nobody is sure. It appeared suddenly in police-court reports, and the likeliest source is a comic Irish family called the Hooligans in music-hall songs of the 1890s; Clarence Rook's 1899 tale of a Patrick Hooligan came after. Geoffrey Pearson showed that fear of rowdy youth was generations old. Only the word was new.
cards.move: A new word for a problem can make an old problem look new.
cards.source: Pearson, Hooligan: A History of Respectable Fears, 1983
cards.reference: Pearson, Hooligan: A History of Respectable Fears, Macmillan, 1983

cards.question: Where did Received Pronunciation, the accent of the early BBC, really come from?
cards.answer: From the Victorian public schools, not the court or any region. Boarders from across the country shed local accents together, so the result marked a class, not a place. The phonetician Daniel Jones called it Public School Pronunciation in his 1917 dictionary. Its native speakers are put at a few per cent of Britons.
cards.move: An accent from nowhere in particular is usually from somewhere exclusive.
cards.reference: Mugglestone, Talking Proper: The Rise and Fall of the English Accent as a Social Symbol, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press, 2003

cards.question: Before the Second World War, which way of saying car sounded upper-class in New York?
cards.answer: Dropping the r. Well-to-do New Yorkers followed the r-less British model, as Franklin Roosevelt's speeches show. After the war prestige flipped. In 1962 William Labov asked staff in three department stores for the fourth floor: at upmarket Saks about six in ten sounded an r, at bargain S. Klein about two in ten.
cards.move: Yesterday's polish can become today's accent to lose.
cards.source: Labov, English in New York City, 1966
cards.reference: Labov, The Social Stratification of English in New York City, Center for Applied Linguistics, 1966

cards.question: True or false: Elizabeth II's vowels stayed essentially unchanged across decades of her Christmas broadcasts?
cards.answer: False. Harrington, Palethorpe and Watson measured her vowels in Christmas broadcasts from the 1950s to the 1980s and found them drifting towards the standard southern accent of younger speakers. The vowel in had, for one, became more open. Even the most insulated speaker in the country moved with the community.
cards.move: Even the steadiest voice drifts with the voices around it.
cards.trap: An adult's accent, especially an elite one, seems fixed after youth.
cards.reference: Harrington, Palethorpe & Watson, Does the Queen speak the Queen's English?, Nature 408, 2000

cards.question: Norwich men were recorded, then asked how they pronounced words like tune and ear. Which way did their claims err?
cards.answer: They claimed more local forms. Peter Trudgill found many men claimed broad Norwich pronunciations they did not use on tape, while women more often claimed standard forms they did not use. For these men the local accent carried covert prestige, a value held but unspoken: toughness, being one of the lads.
cards.move: Ask whose approval a person is seeking before predicting how they will exaggerate.
cards.trap: Expecting everyone to polish their speech when describing it.
cards.reference: Trudgill, Sex, covert prestige and linguistic change in the urban British English of Norwich, Language in Society 1, 1972

cards.question: Should accent be a protected characteristic under British equality law?
cards.answer: Accent bias is measurable and it bites. In a survey of more than 5,000 Britons analysed by Coupland and Bishop, Birmingham and other urban accents ranked lowest for prestige, and later experiments found identical interview answers judged less competent in some regional voices. Accent tracks class and region, which the law leaves exposed.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether bias can be proved case by case decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Where accent stands in for race or national origin, discrimination is already unlawful. A new category would be hard to prove, since an employer can always cite clarity, and it would bring ordinary judgements about communication into court in jobs where being understood is the work. Training and anonymised early hiring stages reduce bias without new law.
cards.reference: Coupland & Bishop, Ideologised values for British accents, Journal of Sociolinguistics 11, 2007

cards.question: When Meiji Japan set out to build a standard spoken language, whose speech became its model?
cards.answer: Educated uptown Tokyo households. Kyoto had been the imperial seat for over a thousand years, but power moved to Tokyo in 1868, and reformers such as Ueda Kazutoshi, writing in 1895, proposed the speech of educated Tokyo people. That meant the Yamanote, the hillside districts of officials and professionals, not the working downtown.
cards.move: A standard follows where power sits now, not where it sat longest.
cards.trap: Assuming centuries of court prestige made Kyoto speech the national model.
cards.reference: Shibatani, The Languages of Japan, Cambridge University Press, 1990

cards.question: True or false: Hanover's name for the purest spoken German comes from Standard German having grown out of its local dialect?
cards.answer: False. Hanover's people once spoke Low German, and High German reached them as a written language learned at school. Northerners therefore pronounced the standard as it was spelled, with no central or southern dialect bending it. Theodor Siebs's stage pronunciation of 1898 leaned north, and Hanover kept the name.
cards.move: Those who learn a standard from books may end up its best speakers.
cards.trap: Assuming the purest standard must be spoken where it was born.
cards.reference: Barbour & Stevenson, Variation in German: A Critical Approach to German Sociolinguistics, Cambridge University Press, 1990

cards.question: How did the throaty r spread from Paris to Berlin, Copenhagen and Bergen while skipping the countryside between?
cards.answer: By hopping from city to city. The uvular r, made at the back of the throat, gained prestige among Parisians, probably by the 1700s, though its origin is contested. Educated townspeople elsewhere copied it, and only later did it seep from each city into the villages around. Early maps show it as islands.
cards.move: Status travels between hubs first and reaches the ground between them last.
cards.reference: Chambers & Trudgill, Dialectology, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 1998

cards.question: In a 1960 Montreal study, one bilingual voice read in English and in French. How did French-Canadian listeners rate the French version?
options: About the same as the English
cards.answer: Lower than the English one. Each speaker recorded both versions, so any gap had to come from the language, not the voice. French-Canadian listeners rated the English guises better-looking, more intelligent and more dependable, and on some traits marked the French guises down further than English-Canadian listeners did.
cards.move: A group can absorb the very ranking that places it lower.
cards.trap: Expecting listeners to favour speakers of their own language.
cards.source: Lambert et al., J. Abnormal Social Psychology, 1960
cards.reference: Lambert, Hodgson, Gardner & Fillenbaum, Evaluational reactions to spoken languages, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 60(1), 1960

cards.question: Reading word lists aloud, which New Yorkers pronounced the prestige r in car more than even the upper middle class?
cards.answer: The lower middle class. In Labov's 1966 survey they used less r than the upper middle class in casual talk, but as the task grew more careful they climbed past them. Labov read it as linguistic insecurity: a class close enough to the top to aim at its speech, and anxious enough to overshoot.
cards.move: Those just below a line often follow its rules hardest.
cards.source: Labov, Social Stratification in New York, 1966
cards.reference: Labov, The Social Stratification of English in New York City, Center for Applied Linguistics, 1966

cards.question: Strine, the jokey name for broad Australian speech, was popularised by what?
cards.answer: A 1965 comic phrasebook. Let Stalk Strine, by Afferbeck Lauder, alphabetical order said the Australian way, was written by Alastair Morrison. It spelled local speech as heard: Strine for Australian, Emma Chisit for how much is it. A joke about the accent became the accent's everyday name.
cards.move: The famous story about a place need not explain each of its words.
cards.trap: Convict roots are the best-known story about Australian speech.
cards.reference: Lauder (Alastair Morrison), Let Stalk Strine, Ure Smith, Sydney, 1965

cards.question: Australian fair dinkum, meaning genuine or honest, most likely came from where?
options: An English dialect word for work
cards.answer: An English dialect word for work. Dinkum meant work, or a fair share of it, in the dialects of the English Midlands, and fair dinkum first meant fair play in a day's labour. Dictionary editors find no evidence for the goldfields story; a Cantonese phrase sounding a little like it is chance.
cards.move: Sounding alike is where an etymology starts, never its proof.
cards.trap: A Cantonese phrase said to mean true gold sounds close enough.
cards.reference: Ramson (ed.), The Australian National Dictionary, Oxford University Press, 1988

cards.question: True or false: the British insult chav began life as an acronym?
cards.answer: False. Chav comes from Romani chavvi, child, a word used for generations in the south-east of England. The acronym explanations, council housed and violent and its variants, were invented after the word spread in the early 2000s. Every letter fits the story because every letter was chosen afterwards.
cards.move: An explanation built to fit every detail is proved by none of them.
cards.trap: An acronym that accounts for each letter feels too exact to be invented.
cards.reference: Jones, Chavs: The Demonization of the Working Class, Verso, 2011

cards.question: Why did Singapore's government start a campaign against its own local slang in 2000?
cards.answer: To protect standard English as the language of trade and schooling. The Speak Good English Movement urged people off Singlish, the local English that mixes in Hokkien, Malay and Tamil words such as kiasu, afraid to lose. Singlish outlasted the posters and became a badge of local identity.
cards.move: Official disapproval can turn a habit into a badge.
cards.reference: Rubdy, Creative destruction: Singapore's Speak Good English movement, World Englishes, 2001

cards.question: Why are people from Liverpool called Scousers?
cards.answer: After a stew. Lobscouse, a sailors' dish of meat, potato and ship's biscuit, was cheap food in a port city; scouse became the name for the stew, then for the people who ate it, then for their accent. Norway's lapskaus and Hamburg's Labskaus are the same pot on other North Sea quays.
cards.move: Nicknames for a people often start at their dinner table.
cards.reference: Crowley, Scouse: A Social and Cultural History, Liverpool University Press, 2012

cards.question: Why does aris mean backside in Cockney rhyming slang, when it rhymes with nothing rude?
cards.answer: Because it rhymes twice. Aris is short for Aristotle, which rhymes with bottle; bottle is short for bottle and glass, which rhymes with arse. Each step drops the rhyming word, so the meaning sits two rhymes out of sight. A Londoner who says someone fell on his aris has hidden the word behind a philosopher.
cards.move: A code gets safer each time the clue itself is encoded.
cards.source: Ayto, Oxford Dictionary of Rhyming Slang, 2002
cards.reference: Ayto, The Oxford Dictionary of Rhyming Slang, Oxford University Press, 2002

cards.question: Why do y'all, yinz and youse keep springing up in different English-speaking regions?
cards.answer: Because standard English has no plural you. Thou was the singular and you the plural, until you displaced thou and left one word doing both jobs. Speakers keep rebuilding the lost plural: y'all in the American South, yinz, from you ones, around Pittsburgh, youse in Ireland, Liverpool and Australia. The same hole gets patched locally.
cards.move: Where a language drops a distinction speakers need, they rebuild it locally.
cards.source: Wales, Personal Pronouns in Present-Day English, 1996
cards.reference: Wales, Personal Pronouns in Present-Day English, Cambridge University Press, 1996

cards.question: A 2010 petition asked for hella, Northern Californian slang for very, to name the SI prefix for 10^27. What happened?
options: The official prefix became ronna instead
Hella was adopted into the SI
No prefix was ever set for 10^27
cards.answer: The official prefix became ronna instead. Google's calculator and Wolfram Alpha played along and converted hella units, which made it look settled. But only the General Conference on Weights and Measures sets SI prefixes, and in 2022 it chose ronna for 10^27 and quetta for 10^30. Hella stayed where it started, on Bay Area streets.
cards.move: Before treating something as approved, find out who has the power to approve it.
cards.trap: Remembering hella working in Google's calculator and taking that as official.
cards.reference: https://www.bipm.org/en/cgpm-2022/resolution-3

cards.question: True or false: Scots wee, meaning small, began as a piece of baby talk, like teeny?
cards.answer: False. Wee began as a noun meaning a small amount, from Old English wǣg, a weight. A little wee meant a little bit, and in Scots and northern English the noun hardened into an adjective. The small-sounding vowel is a lucky fit. In a wee dram, a Scot is still weighing out the whisky.
cards.move: A word that sounds like its meaning may have fallen into it by chance.
cards.trap: The ee sound feels small, so the word seems made to fit.
cards.source: Hoad, Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Etymology
cards.reference: Hoad (ed.), The Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Etymology, Oxford University Press, 1986

cards.question: Craic, the Irish word for fun and lively talk, is spelled like Gaelic. Where did it come from?
options: Irish Gaelic, then borrowed into English
English crack, respelled the Irish way
Old Norse, by way of Viking Dublin
cards.answer: English crack, respelled the Irish way. In Scots and northern English, crack meant news or lively talk, as in what's the crack. Irish speakers borrowed it in the 20th century and wrote it craic, a spelling first found in a dictionary in 1977. English then took its own word back, in Gaelic dress.
cards.move: A spelling tells you where a word settled, not where it started.
cards.trap: The Gaelic spelling makes an ancient Irish origin look certain.
cards.reference: Dolan, A Dictionary of Hiberno-English, 2nd edition, Gill & Macmillan, 2004

cards.question: What happened to people who let a coin toss decide a real decision, such as quitting a job?
cards.answer: Those the coin told to make the change were happier six months later than those told to stay. Levitt asked more than 20,000 volunteers on a website to toss a coin over a real dilemma. His reading: when a choice is close, people lean towards the status quo more than they should.
cards.move: When two options feel equal, suspect that fear of change is tipping them.
cards.reference: Levitt, Heads or Tails: The Impact of a Coin Toss on Major Life Decisions and Subsequent Happiness, Review of Economic Studies, 2021

cards.question: A jam experiment found shoppers bought less from 24 jams than from 6. Across 50 later experiments, what was the average effect of more choice?
cards.answer: Near zero on average. Scheibehenne's meta-analysis found a mean effect of about zero, with wide variation: more choice hurt in some studies and helped in others. In the original study, 3% of shoppers bought from the 24-jar table and 30% from the six-jar table.
cards.move: Before trusting a famous experiment, ask what the pile of later ones says.
cards.trap: The retold jam story agrees with how choosing feels.
cards.reference: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd, Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload, Journal of Consumer Research, 2010

cards.question: Strangers asked to talk about deep topics expected it to be awkward. How did it actually turn out?
cards.answer: It was less awkward and more connecting than they expected. In Kardas, Kumar and Epley's studies, strangers forecast that deep questions would feel awkward and that partners would care little; afterwards they felt closer and more at ease than predicted, and partners were more interested than they thought.
cards.move: Ask the deeper question; the awkwardness is mostly rehearsed, not received.
cards.reference: Kardas, Kumar and Epley, Overly shallow? Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2022

cards.question: True or false: after a first conversation, strangers usually like you less than you think they do?
cards.answer: False. Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after conversations in the laboratory, at workshops and among new housemates, people underestimated how much their partners liked them. The gap appeared in the first minutes and lasted for months among housemates.
cards.move: Assume the conversation went better than it felt to you.
cards.trap: Dwelling on our own slips, we assume the other person noticed them.
cards.reference: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark, The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think? Psychological Science, 2018

cards.question: Why can a task you have just left unfinished keep hurting your work on the next one?
cards.answer: Attention residue. In Leroy's experiments, people pulled off a task before finishing it kept thinking about it, and did worse on the next task than people who had finished the first. The residue was strongest when the earlier task was unfinished and time was short.
cards.move: Finish something small before switching, or write down where you stopped.
cards.source: Leroy, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 2009
cards.reference: Leroy, Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 2009

cards.question: In an experiment, people interrupted mid-task were compared with uninterrupted people doing the same work. How did the interrupted ones finish?
options: At the same pace and stress
cards.answer: Faster, but under more stress. In Mark's experiments, interrupted people compensated by working faster, with no loss of quality, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. The speed was bought with strain, so an interruption's cost shows up in the person, not on the clock.
cards.move: Count the cost of an interruption in strain, not only minutes.
cards.trap: Assuming an interruption must show up as lost time.
cards.reference: Mark, Gudith and Klocke, The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress, Proceedings of CHI, 2008

cards.question: Scientists who narrowly missed a first major NIH grant: how did their next ten years compare with narrow winners?
cards.answer: Those who stayed in science did better. Wang, Jones and Wang compared applicants who narrowly missed an NIH R01 grant with narrow winners; over ten years the near-misses who kept going produced more highly cited work. But more of them dropped out, so part of the gain is a filter on survivors.
cards.move: Ask what happened to those who quit before praising those who continued.
cards.source: Wang, Jones and Wang, Nature Communications, 2019
cards.reference: Wang, Jones and Wang, Early-career setback and future career impact, Nature Communications, 2019

cards.question: Venture-backed founders whose first company failed started another. Compared with first-time founders, how likely was the new one to succeed?
cards.answer: About the same. Gompers and colleagues found first-time founders succeeded about 22% of the time and founders with an earlier success about 30%, while founders who had failed did no better than first-timers. Failure carried no measurable edge; success did.
cards.move: Learning from failure is a claim to test, not a given.
cards.trap: Assuming what a failure teaches must show in the next attempt.
cards.source: Gompers and colleagues, Journal of Financial Economics, 2010
cards.reference: Gompers, Kovner, Lerner and Scharfstein, Performance persistence in entrepreneurship, Journal of Financial Economics, 2010

cards.question: How much did strong social relationships raise the odds of survival, in a pooling of 148 studies?
cards.answer: By about 50%. Holt-Lunstad's meta-analysis of 148 studies with 308,849 participants found people with stronger social relationships had 50% greater odds of survival over an average of 7.5 years, comparable with quitting smoking. The studies are observational, so the link is not proof of cause.
cards.move: Schedule the people you would miss before the work you would not.
cards.source: Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, PLoS Medicine, 2010
cards.reference: Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review, PLoS Medicine, 2010

cards.question: About how many hours together does it take for an acquaintance to become a friend?
cards.answer: About 50 hours to become a casual friend, about 90 to become a friend, and over 200 for a close friend. Hall surveyed adults who had recently moved and tracked students. Time together predicted closeness, and the time counted most when spent joking, catching up and talking about things that mattered.
cards.move: Count friendship in hours spent, and spend them on purpose.
cards.source: Hall, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019
cards.reference: Hall, How many hours does it take to make a friend? Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019

cards.question: People who write a gratitude letter and deliver it: do they overestimate or underestimate how the recipient will feel?
cards.answer: They underestimate it. In Kumar and Epley's experiments, writers expected recipients to be modestly pleased and themselves to feel awkward. Recipients were more surprised and happier than writers guessed, and writers overestimated the awkwardness. The unsent thank-you is a small gain left undelivered.
cards.move: Say the thanks you have been holding; it lands better than you guess.
cards.reference: Kumar and Epley, Undervaluing Gratitude: Expressers Misunderstand the Consequences of Showing Appreciation, Psychological Science, 2018

cards.question: Is keeping a gratitude journal worth recommending to someone who feels low?
cards.answer: It costs nothing, takes minutes and trials suggest a small lift in well-being. Davis and colleagues' meta-analysis of gratitude interventions found better outcomes than in control groups, and unlike many remedies there is no bill, no waiting list and no side effect. Cheap, harmless and sometimes helpful is a fair standard for a first step.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the comparison group is the question that decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Small is not treatment. Effects in these trials are modest and often measured against groups that did nothing, so the gain may owe as much to attention and expectation as to gratitude. Told to be thankful, someone in real distress can add guilt to low mood, and a cheap habit can delay the help that would change it.
cards.source: Davis and colleagues, Journal of Counseling Psychology, 2016
cards.reference: Davis and colleagues, Thankful for the Little Things: A Meta-Analysis of Gratitude Interventions, Journal of Counseling Psychology, 2016

cards.question: What do 18-month-olds do when an adult they have just met visibly struggles to reach or open something?
cards.answer: They usually help, unasked and unrewarded. In Warneken and Tomasello's 2006 experiments, toddlers handed back dropped objects and opened cupboard doors for adults. Rewards later dulled it: in a 2008 follow-up, 20-month-olds given toys for helping helped less afterwards.
cards.move: A reward can turn a kindness into a transaction.
cards.reference: Warneken and Tomasello, Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees, Science, 2006

cards.question: Does a kind act done partly for the good feeling deserve less credit?
cards.answer: Motive is what separates kindness from self-service. Andreoni's warm-glow model treats giving as partly buying the donor a good feeling, and brain scans show giving activates reward regions. If a gift is partly a purchase of pleasure, credit should shrink with the share taken.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, motive or outcome is the question that decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The recipient cannot taste the motive: a meal feeds the same whoever is warmed by giving it. Givers who enjoy giving keep giving, while those asked to feel nothing quit first. Aknin and colleagues found that happiness and giving reinforce each other, so the pleasure is how charity sustains itself, and a kindness that costs nothing is not thereby smaller.
cards.reference: Andreoni, Impure Altruism and Donations to Public Goods: A Theory of Warm-Glow Giving, Economic Journal, 1990

cards.question: Students read a passage, then either re-read it or were tested on it. A week later, who recalled more?
cards.answer: The tested students. In Roediger and Karpicke's experiment, students who took recall tests remembered more a week later than those who re-read the passage several times, though re-readers did better after five minutes and felt more confident about their learning.
cards.move: Trust what you can recall unaided over what merely looks familiar.
cards.trap: Re-reading feels like progress because the text looks familiar.
cards.reference: Roediger and Karpicke, Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention, Psychological Science, 2006

cards.question: How did practising maths problems shuffled together compare, a week later, with practising them grouped by type?
cards.answer: Shuffled practice roughly tripled the score. In Rohrer and Taylor's experiment on volume-of-solid problems, students who did mixed practice scored 63% on a test a week later, against 20% for those who did the same problems grouped by type. Grouped practice looked better while practising, since the method was obvious.
cards.move: Practise choosing the method, not only carrying it out.
cards.reference: Rohrer and Taylor, The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning, Instructional Science, 2007

cards.question: In sport, about what share of differences in performance did deliberate practice account for in one meta-analysis?
cards.answer: About 18%. Macnamara and colleagues' meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 26% of differences in performance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and under 1% in professions. Practice matters a great deal; it leaves most of the difference unexplained.
cards.move: Treat effort as necessary, not sufficient, and keep looking for the rest.
cards.trap: Retold tales of champions make practice seem nearly the whole story.
cards.source: Macnamara, Hambrick and colleagues, Psychological Science, 2014
cards.reference: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald, Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis, Psychological Science, 2014

cards.question: How closely does grit, as the popular scale measures it, track the older trait of conscientiousness?
cards.answer: Very closely. Credé, Tynan and Harms's meta-analysis found grit and conscientiousness correlated at about 0.8, while grit's link with performance was only moderate. The overlap is why critics call grit an old trait with a new name; its defenders dispute that.
cards.move: Before adopting a new name for a virtue, ask what it adds.
cards.reference: Credé, Tynan and Harms, Much ado about grit: A meta-analytic synthesis of the grit literature, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2017

cards.question: In a study of 233 bereaved adults, which of the five stages of grief was already the most common at one month?
cards.answer: Acceptance. Maciejewski's team measured five grief responses for two years. Their peaks came in the predicted order, but acceptance was the most frequently endorsed from the first month and yearning was the strongest negative feeling. The stages overlapped rather than replaced each other.
cards.move: Doubt any model of feeling that tells you what comes next.
cards.reference: Maciejewski, Zhang, Block and Prigerson, An Empirical Examination of the Stage Theory of Grief, JAMA, 2007

cards.question: When time feels short, whom do people of any age prefer to spend an afternoon with?
cards.answer: Familiar people, such as family. In Fung, Carstensen and Lutz's experiments, older adults chose family over new acquaintances, and young adults chose the same when told to imagine moving far away soon. Older adults asked to imagine twenty more years chose like the young. What changes is the time left, not the age.
cards.move: Ask whom you would choose if the time left were short.
cards.source: Fung, Carstensen and Lutz, Psychology and Aging, 1999
cards.reference: Fung, Carstensen and Lutz, Influence of Time on Social Preferences: Implications for Life-Span Development, Psychology and Aging, 1999

cards.question: What did a fourteen-year follow-up of about 6,000 American adults find about purpose in life and dying?
cards.answer: Lower mortality, at every age. In Hill and Turiano's study, adults with a stronger sense of purpose were less likely to die during the follow-up, and the link held for young, middle-aged and older adults alike. It is an association: illness may also dull purpose.
cards.move: Ask what today is for, even if the answer is small.
cards.reference: Hill and Turiano, Purpose in Life as a Predictor of Mortality Across Adulthood, Psychological Science, 2014

cards.question: Among more than 40,000 Japanese adults followed for seven years, what happened to those who reported no ikigai?
cards.answer: They died at about one and a half times the rate. In the Ohsaki cohort of adults aged 40 to 79, those who said they had no ikigai, a sense of life worth living, had higher mortality over seven years. Reports of purpose and health may partly feed each other.
cards.move: Name one thing you would be sorry to lose, and tend it.
cards.reference: Sone and colleagues, Sense of life worth living (ikigai) and mortality in Japan: Ohsaki Study, Psychosomatic Medicine, 2008

cards.question: Over a lifetime, do people come to regret the things they did, or the things they did not do?
cards.answer: Mostly what they did not do. Gilovich and Medvec found that in the short run people regret actions more, but over the long run regrets of inaction grow. Actions can be explained away or repaired, while a missed chance leaves imagined outcomes open, and imagined outcomes are never disappointing.
cards.move: Ask which choice you would still be explaining in twenty years.
cards.reference: Gilovich and Medvec, The Experience of Regret: What, When, and Why, Psychological Review, 1995

cards.question: Photography students chose one of two prints to keep. Who liked it more later: those who could swap it, or those who could not?
cards.answer: Those who could not swap. In Gilbert and Ebert's studies, students whose choice was final grew fonder of their print than students who could change their minds within days, yet people expect the option to swap to leave them happier. A final choice lets the mind stop comparing.
cards.move: Keep an open door only where you will actually use it.
cards.reference: Gilbert and Ebert, Decisions and Revisions: The Affective Forecasting of Changeable Outcomes, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002

cards.question: After September 2001 Americans flew less and drove more. About how many extra road deaths did that avoidance cause in the following year?
cards.answer: About 1,500. Gigerenzer estimated that the fall in flying and rise in driving after September 2001 caused roughly 1,500 extra road deaths in the next twelve months, about half the 2,977 people killed in the attacks. Avoiding a vivid risk moved people onto a larger one.
cards.move: Count the risk of the alternative, not only the one that frightens.
cards.trap: A vivid catastrophe makes flying seem riskier than the road.
cards.reference: Gigerenzer, Out of the Frying Pan into the Fire: Behavioral Reactions to Terrorist Attacks, Risk Analysis, 2006

cards.question: How large must the possible win in an even coin toss be before most people accept a possible loss?
cards.answer: About twice as large. In Tversky and Kahneman's median estimate, losses weigh about 2.25 times as much as equal gains, so someone risking 100 on a coin toss typically wants a possible win near 225. Later estimates vary by person and setting.
cards.move: Check whether fear of losing is pricing a bet, not its odds.
cards.source: Tversky and Kahneman, J. Risk and Uncertainty, 1992
cards.reference: Tversky and Kahneman, Advances in Prospect Theory: Cumulative Representation of Uncertainty, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 1992

cards.question: What share of everyday actions did a diary study find people performed as habits, often while thinking of something else?
cards.answer: About 43%. Wood, Quinn and Kashy prompted students at intervals to record what they were doing. Close to half of the actions were habits: repeated almost daily, in the same place, and often carried out while the mind was on something else. Most of a day is run by what was decided long ago.
cards.move: Ask which of today's actions you chose, and which merely happened again.
cards.reference: Wood, Quinn and Kashy, Habits in Everyday Life: Thought, Emotion, and Action, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002

cards.question: Volunteers chose one daily action and logged it until it felt automatic. What was the median number of days that took?
cards.answer: About 66 days. In Lally's study, 96 volunteers were tracked for 12 weeks. The median time to reach a plateau of automaticity was 66 days, and individuals ranged from 18 to 254 days, depending on the person and the habit. Missing a single day did not derail the process.
cards.move: Plan for the slow version of change, and for missing a day.
cards.trap: The figure of 21 days is repeated so widely it feels established.
cards.source: Lally and colleagues, Eur. J. Social Psychology, 2010
cards.reference: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts and Wardle, How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world, European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010

cards.question: What happened to retirement-plan sign-ups at one large firm when joining became the default rather than a choice?
cards.answer: Participation among new hires rose from 37% to 86%. Madrian and Shea studied a US company that switched to automatic enrolment. But a large share of joiners stayed at the default contribution rate and default fund, so participation rose much faster than the amount saved.
cards.move: Set the default first, since most choices never move from it.
cards.source: Madrian and Shea, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2001
cards.reference: Madrian and Shea, The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2001

cards.question: Workers pledged to raise saving with each pay rise. Those who stayed in the plan for 40 months saved about what share of pay?
cards.answer: About 14%. In Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow plan, employees who stayed went from saving 3.5% to 13.6% of pay in 40 months. Each increase came out of a pay rise, so take-home pay never fell and no one felt a loss.
cards.move: Tie a new commitment to a future gain, before it is spent.
cards.trap: Small increments seem to add up to a small total.
cards.source: Thaler and Benartzi, Journal of Political Economy, 2004
cards.reference: Thaler and Benartzi, Save More Tomorrow: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving, Journal of Political Economy, 2004

cards.question: In datasets covering hundreds of thousands of teenagers, digital technology use explains at most what share of variation in well-being?
cards.answer: About 0.4%. Orben and Przybylski analysed three large datasets and found the link between technology use and adolescent well-being was tiny, about the size of the link between eating potatoes and well-being in the same data. Small on average does not mean nothing for any one teenager.
cards.move: Ask how big an effect is, not only whether one exists.
cards.trap: Loud public worry makes a large share feel likely.
cards.source: Orben and Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019
cards.reference: Orben and Przybylski, The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019

cards.question: What happened to well-being when people were paid to leave Facebook for four weeks before the 2018 US midterm elections?
cards.answer: It rose slightly. In Allcott and colleagues' experiment, those who deactivated reported modestly higher well-being, spent more time with friends and family offline, and knew less about the news. Afterwards their Facebook use stayed below its earlier level. The gain was small and the price was information.
cards.move: Stop a habit for a month before judging what it gives you.
cards.source: Allcott and colleagues, American Economic Review, 2020
cards.reference: Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow, The Welfare Effects of Social Media, American Economic Review, 2020

cards.question: Given $5 or $20 to spend by evening, who ended the day happier: those who spent it on themselves, or on others?
cards.answer: Those who spent it on others. In Dunn, Aknin and Norton's field experiment, participants handed $5 or $20 in the morning were happier that evening if they spent it on someone else. The amount made no difference; the recipient did.
cards.move: Try giving a small sum away and notice what it does to you.
cards.reference: Dunn, Aknin and Norton, Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness, Science, 2008

cards.question: In a study, adults spent $40 on either a time-saving purchase or a material one. Which lifted their mood more?
cards.answer: The time-saving purchase. In Whillans and colleagues' field experiment, spending $40 on saving time left people less pressed and in a better mood than spending it on a thing. In a survey of about 6,000 people in four countries, those who paid to save time reported more life satisfaction.
cards.move: Price a purchase in hours returned, not only in what it holds.
cards.reference: Whillans, Dunn, Smeets, Bekkers and Norton, Buying time promotes happiness, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2017

cards.question: Students predicted when they would finish their thesis. About what share finished by their own best-guess date?
cards.answer: About 30%. In Buehler, Griffin and Ross's study, the average prediction was 33.9 days and the average actual time 55.5 days. Even when asked for a worst case, students guessed 48.6 days on average, still short of what the work took.
cards.move: Estimate from how long similar tasks took, not from the plan.
cards.trap: A plan that pictures every step going right feels reliable.
cards.reference: Buehler, Griffin and Ross, Exploring the Planning Fallacy: Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994

cards.question: Do people with long commutes gain enough elsewhere, in pay or housing, to make up for the journey?
cards.answer: No. Stutzer and Frey, using German panel data, found that people with longer commutes reported lower satisfaction with life, and their extra pay or better housing did not make up for it. They called it the commuting paradox, since standard theory says people would be compensated.
cards.move: A cheaper home further out has a price paid daily in minutes.
cards.source: Stutzer and Frey, Scandinavian Journal of Economics, 2008
cards.reference: Stutzer and Frey, Stress that Doesn't Pay: The Commuting Paradox, Scandinavian Journal of Economics, 2008

cards.question: What did scientists around 1900 find predicted how powerfully a gas would anaesthetise?
cards.answer: How well it dissolves in olive oil. Hans Meyer and Charles Overton, working separately, found that potency tracked fat solubility across chemicals of very different shapes, which pointed to the fatty membranes of cells. In 1984 Nicholas Franks and William Lieb showed anaesthetics could block a fat-free protein, firefly luciferase. Proteins are now the suspects.
cards.move: A pattern that holds across everything can still point to the wrong place.
cards.reference: Franks, General anaesthesia: from molecular targets to neuronal pathways of sleep and arousal, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2008

cards.question: Why is Boston in 1846 remembered as the birth of anaesthesia when ether was used in Georgia in 1842?
cards.answer: Because Boston was public and Georgia went unpublished. Crawford Long removed a neck tumour from James Venable under ether in March 1842 but did not report it until 1849. William Morton's demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital in October 1846 was watched, written up and copied in Europe within months.
cards.move: Credit goes to whoever makes a discovery public, not whoever makes it first.
cards.reference: Fenster, Ether Day: The Strange Tale of America's Greatest Medical Discovery and the Haunted Men Who Made It, HarperCollins, 2001

cards.question: True or false: most reported cases of waking during general anaesthesia involve a drug that paralyses the muscles?
cards.answer: True. An audit across the UK and Ireland found awareness in about 1 in 19,600 general anaesthetics overall: about 1 in 8,200 when muscle-paralysing drugs were used, and about 1 in 136,000 without them. An unparalysed patient who starts to surface moves, and the anaesthetist deepens the dose. A paralysed one cannot signal anything.
cards.move: An alarm that has been switched off cannot warn anyone.
cards.trap: Picturing awareness as random bad luck, equally likely in any anaesthetic.
cards.source: Pandit et al., British Journal of Anaesthesia, 2014
cards.reference: Pandit et al., 5th National Audit Project (NAP5) on accidental awareness during general anaesthesia: summary of main findings and risk factors, British Journal of Anaesthesia, 2014

cards.question: True or false: a large randomised trial found that under an hour of general anaesthesia in infancy lowered IQ at age five?
cards.answer: False. The GAS trial randomised over 700 infants having hernia repairs to under an hour of general anaesthesia or to awake regional anaesthesia, and found equivalent IQ at five. Earlier alarm came from observational studies, in which children who need surgery differ from those who do not. Long or repeated exposures are less studied.
cards.move: Before blaming a treatment, ask what sent people to receive it.
cards.trap: Trusting studies that linked childhood surgery to later learning problems.
cards.reference: McCann et al., Neurodevelopmental outcome at 5 years of age after general anaesthesia or awake-regional anaesthesia in infancy (GAS): an equivalence, randomised, controlled trial, The Lancet, 2019

cards.question: In malignant hyperthermia, a rare inherited reaction to some anaesthetics, what is usually the earliest warning in theatre?
options: A sudden fall in blood pressure
Rising carbon dioxide in exhaled breath
cards.answer: Rising carbon dioxide in exhaled breath. A faulty calcium channel, usually from the RYR1 gene, lets calcium flood the muscles, which burn fuel furiously and pour out carbon dioxide. Temperature often climbs later, sometimes 1 °C every five minutes. Dantrolene, which stops the calcium leak, turned a usually fatal crisis into a rarely fatal one.
cards.move: A thing's name describes its most dramatic sign, not its first one.
cards.trap: Choosing temperature, because the condition is named after heat.
cards.source: Rosenberg et al., Orphanet J Rare Diseases, 2015
cards.reference: Rosenberg, Pollock, Schiemann, Bulger & Stowell, Malignant hyperthermia: a review, Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 2015

cards.question: How can xenon, a noble gas that forms almost no chemical bonds, put a patient to sleep?
cards.answer: By fitting into a pocket, not by reacting. Xenon atoms settle in the NMDA receptor, a switch for glutamate, the brain's main excitatory signal, and block the site its partner glycine must fill. Anaesthesia needs more than 60% xenon in the breath, and the gas is so costly that closed breathing circuits recycle it.
cards.move: A thing can act on the world through its shape alone.
cards.reference: Dickinson et al., Competitive inhibition at the glycine site of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor by the anesthetics xenon and isoflurane: evidence from molecular modeling and electrophysiology, Anesthesiology, 2007

cards.question: Why must an opened vial of propofol, the milky anaesthetic, be used within hours and never shared between patients?
cards.answer: Because it is food for bacteria. Propofol will not dissolve in water, so it is carried in an emulsion of soybean oil and egg lecithin, hence the milky look. Stray germs multiply in it. In 1990, infections after surgery at seven US hospitals were traced to syringes drawn up ahead and reused.
cards.move: What makes a medicine easy to deliver can also make it easy to spoil.
cards.reference: Bennett et al., Postoperative infections traced to contamination of an intravenous anesthetic, propofol, New England Journal of Medicine, 1995

cards.question: Core temperature often drops about 1 °C in the first hour of general anaesthesia. Where does most of that heat go?
options: Into the patient's own arms and legs
Into the cold air of the theatre
cards.answer: Into the patient's own arms and legs. Awake, the body keeps warm blood in its core by narrowing vessels in the limbs. Anaesthetics switch that reflex off, so core heat floods outwards, a redistribution behind most of the first hour's fall. Loss to the room dominates later. Warming patients before induction blunts the drop.
cards.move: Before blaming a loss on leakage, check whether it simply moved inside.
cards.trap: Blaming the open wound, the obvious place for heat to escape.
cards.reference: Sessler, Perioperative heat balance, Anesthesiology, 2000

cards.question: True or false: the largest randomised trial of pulse oximeters during anaesthesia showed that they cut complications and deaths?
cards.answer: False. A Danish trial of 20,802 patients, published in 1993, found oximeters caught far more episodes of low blood oxygen and changed what anaesthetists did, yet complications and deaths did not differ between the groups. The clip was already standard and stayed so; no one would now run a trial that withholds it.
cards.move: Count outcomes, not alarms, before deciding a safeguard works.
cards.trap: Taking every low reading caught as proof the monitor saved someone.
cards.reference: Moller et al., Randomized evaluation of pulse oximetry in 20,802 patients: II. Perioperative events and postoperative complications, Anesthesiology, 1993

cards.question: Half of patients stop moving at incision with 2% sevoflurane, or 104% nitrous oxide. With 60% nitrous oxide, what sevoflurane percentage gives that effect?
cards.answer: 0.42 x 2% = about 0.85% sevoflurane.
cards.move: When two things share a job, count each as a fraction of its full dose.
cards.trap: Keeping the full 2%, since 60% nitrous oxide is below its own dose.
cards.hint: The two gases' effects add, each counted as a fraction of its own full dose.
steps: 60 / 104 = about 0.58 of the nitrous oxide dose.
1 - 0.58 = 0.42 of the sevoflurane dose still needed.
0.42 x 2% = about 0.85% sevoflurane.
cards.reference: Gropper (ed.), Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition, Elsevier, 2020

cards.question: How long were London's surgeons legally in the same company as its barbers?
cards.answer: Just over two centuries. An Act of 1540 merged the Barbers' Company and the Guild of Surgeons, barring each trade from the other's work. The surgeons broke away only in 1745 as the Company of Surgeons, which became the Royal College of Surgeons in 1800. The barbers kept the hall.
cards.move: Old partnerships often outlast the reasons they were formed.
cards.source: Cope, Royal College of Surgeons history, 1959
cards.reference: Cope, The Royal College of Surgeons of England: A History, Anthony Blond, 1959

cards.question: In 1537, army surgeon Ambroise Paré ran out of boiling oil and dressed gunshot wounds with a mild salve. Who fared better?
cards.answer: The soldiers given the salve. Doctrine held that gunpowder poisoned wounds, so they were scalded with oil. Paré, a barber-surgeon's apprentice turned army surgeon, found the salve group resting next morning while the oil group lay feverish and swollen. Running out of supplies had handed him two groups to compare.
cards.move: A shortage can be the first fair comparison anyone gets to see.
cards.trap: Trusting the oil, because gunshot wounds were thought to be poisoned.
cards.source: Paré, Apologie and Treatise, ed. Keynes
cards.reference: Paré, The Apologie and Treatise of Ambroise Paré, ed. Geoffrey Keynes, Falcon Educational Books, 1951

cards.question: What did Henry VIII's 1540 Act give London's barber-surgeons each year for teaching anatomy?
cards.answer: The bodies of four executed criminals. The Act that created the Company of Barber-Surgeons let it take four hanged felons a year for public dissection. Supply never met demand, and the gallows became a scene of tussles between the company's men and the dead man's friends. Anatomy was taught on whoever the hangman provided.
cards.move: When a supply is fixed by law, look at who fights over it.
cards.reference: Tarlow & Battell Lowman, Harnessing the Power of the Criminal Corpse, Palgrave Macmillan, 2018

cards.question: True or false: a London barber-surgeon recommended lemon juice against scurvy more than a century before James Lind's 1747 trial?
cards.answer: True. John Woodall, surgeon-general to the East India Company, urged lemon juice for scurvy in The Surgions Mate, his 1617 manual for ship surgeons. The advice was known and then diluted by rival cures such as vinegar and malt. The Royal Navy made lemon juice standard issue only in 1795, 178 years later.
cards.move: The famous test of an idea is rarely where the idea began.
cards.trap: Assuming the famous 1747 trial was where the citrus idea began.
cards.source: Royal Museums Greenwich, The Surgeon's Mate
cards.reference: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/library-archive/surgeons-mate-john-woodall

cards.question: Which royal operation in 1686 helped raise French surgeons above their barber origins?
cards.answer: The removal of Louis XIV's anal fistula. Charles-François Félix, the king's first surgeon, from a trade still joined to barbers, rehearsed on other patients for months before operating in November 1686. The king recovered and rewarded him with land and nobility. Surgeons gained a Royal Academy in 1731 and left the barbers in 1743.
cards.move: One visible success can move a whole trade's standing.
cards.reference: https://tidsskriftet.no/en/2016/08/medical-history/sun-kings-anal-fistula

cards.question: True or false: the Church council held at Tours in 1163 declared that the Church abhors blood, barring clergy from surgery?
cards.answer: False. The phrase Ecclesia abhorret a sanguine appears in none of its canons; 18th-century French writers, notably the surgeon François Quesnay, spread it. The real restriction came at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, barring only priests, deacons and subdeacons from surgery that cut or burned. The famous line was written six centuries late.
cards.move: A quotation that fits the story perfectly is the first one to check.
cards.trap: True, since it fits the story of a Church hostile to cutting bodies.
cards.source: Amundsen, Bulletin of the History of Medicine, 1978
cards.reference: Amundsen, Medieval canon law on medical and surgical practice by the clergy, Bulletin of the History of Medicine, 1978

cards.question: True or false: Pierre Louis's famous 1835 count of pneumonia patients led him to reject bloodletting as useless?
cards.answer: False. Among 77 patients, those bled in the first four days died more often than those bled later, yet Louis concluded bleeding helped a little: early-bled survivors recovered a few days sooner.
