He shrank its reputation, not its use. The count remembered as ending the lancet recommended it.
cards.move: Read what a pioneer concluded, not only what later readers made of it.
cards.trap: True, since his count is remembered as the end of bloodletting.
cards.reference: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/pierre-charles-alexandre-louis-and-the-evaluation-of-bloodletting/

cards.question: Edinburgh's barbers and surgeons were incorporated as one craft in 1505. Which monopoly in the burgh came with it?
options: Distilling aqua vitae, an early whisky
cards.answer: Distilling aqua vitae. Spirit was then a medicine, and the new craft's freemen gained the sole right to make it in Edinburgh; James IV ratified their charter in 1506. The same charter required every member to know anatomy and all the veins, for bloodletting. For a time, Edinburgh's spirit came from its surgeons.
cards.move: Ask what a product was for when a trade first claimed it.
cards.trap: Soap and candles, since barbers used soap every working day.
cards.source: Dingwall, A Famous and Flourishing Society, 2005
cards.reference: Dingwall, A Famous and Flourishing Society: The History of the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh, 1505-2005, Edinburgh University Press, 2005

cards.question: How did a late medieval barber decide on which day to bleed a patient, and from which part of the body?
cards.answer: By the Moon's place in the zodiac. Almanacs showed a zodiac man, each body part ruled by a sign, and the rule was never to bleed a part while the Moon stood in its sign. A bloodletting calendar for 1457 was among the first things printed at Mainz. The sky booked the appointment.
cards.move: A rule followed precisely can still rest on nothing at all.
cards.source: Siraisi, Medieval and Early Renaissance Medicine, 1990
cards.reference: Siraisi, Medieval and Early Renaissance Medicine: An Introduction to Knowledge and Practice, University of Chicago Press, 1990

cards.question: What did divers find in the barber-surgeon's cabin of Henry VIII's warship Mary Rose, sunk in 1545?
cards.answer: Both trades in one cabin. Beside a mallet, instrument handles and syringes for flushing wounds and the urethra lay several cut-throat razors, a shaving bowl, a pewter bleeding bowl and a mortar for grinding drugs. His silk velvet coif, the cap of his craft, survived too. Shaving and surgery shared a shelf.
cards.move: Look at what sits on the same shelf to learn what a job was.
cards.reference: Gardiner with Allen (eds), Before the Mast: Life and Death Aboard the Mary Rose, Archaeology of the Mary Rose vol. 4, Mary Rose Trust, 2005

cards.question: How much can two successive drops from the same finger prick disagree on haemoglobin?
cards.answer: By more than 2 grams per decilitre in some people, enough to swing a verdict on anaemia. Rice University researchers drew six drops in a row from each of 11 donors; haemoglobin, platelets and white cells all varied significantly between drops. A single drop is a sample of a sample.
cards.move: Before trusting one small sample, see how much the next one differs.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26572995/

cards.question: Each normal range spans the middle 95% of healthy people. Across 20 independent tests, what percentage of healthy people get an abnormal flag?
cards.answer: About 64%.
cards.move: Run enough checks on anything and something will look wrong.
cards.trap: Guessing 5%, the rate for one test, for the whole panel.
cards.hint: Work out the chance that every result lands inside its range, then subtract.
steps: Chance one test comes back normal: 0.95.
Chance all 20 are normal: 0.95^20 = 0.358.
Chance at least one is flagged: 1 - 0.358 = 0.642.
About 64%.

diagram.caption: One test flags 5% of healthy people; twenty tests flag 64%.

cards.reference: Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, EP28-A3c: Defining, Establishing, and Verifying Reference Intervals in the Clinical Laboratory, 2008

cards.question: Which of these can push a healthy person's potassium result high enough to look dangerous?
options: A banana eaten before the test
A clenched fist during the draw
cards.answer: A clenched fist during the draw. Working forearm muscles release potassium into the local vein; a 1990 study found clenching could raise the reading by 1 to 2 mmol per litre, on a normal range of about 3.5 to 5. The alarm comes from the arm, not the heart.
cards.move: Ask what the act of measuring did to the thing measured.
cards.trap: Picking the banana, the food everyone links with potassium.
cards.reference: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199005033221806

cards.question: What can make HbA1c, the standard long-term blood sugar test, read falsely reassuring?
cards.answer: Red blood cells that die young. HbA1c measures how much haemoglobin has picked up sugar; a red cell lives about 120 days, so it averages two to three months. When cells are lost early, through haemolysis, bleeding or transfusion, they have less time to collect sugar. The number drops while the glucose does not.
cards.move: Know how long a measure takes to fill before reading its level.
cards.source: American Diabetes Association, Standards of Care, 2024
cards.reference: American Diabetes Association, Standards of Care in Diabetes, section 6: Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, Diabetes Care, 2024

cards.question: True or false: a high-dose hair-and-nail supplement can make a heart-attack blood test read falsely normal?
cards.answer: True. Many lab tests, including some for the heart-damage marker troponin, use biotin as a molecular hook, which excess biotin jams. Daily need is about 0.03 mg; hair and nail pills often hold 5 or 10 mg. In 2017 the FDA warned after a patient on high-dose biotin died following a falsely low troponin result.
cards.move: A harmless ingredient can still fool the instrument that reads you.
cards.trap: Assuming a vitamin cannot interfere with how a test works.
cards.reference: https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/in-vitro-diagnostics/biotin-interference-troponin-lab-tests-assays-subject-biotin-interference

cards.question: A D-dimer blood test for clots comes back normal. For which patient does that reliably rule out a clot in the lung?
options: One judged unlikely to have one
One judged very likely to have one
cards.answer: One judged unlikely to have one. D-dimer, a fragment released as clots break down, rises with nearly every clot, and with infection, cancer, pregnancy and age. In a low-suspicion patient a normal result settles it. In a high-suspicion patient its rare misses become too likely, so NICE sends them straight to a scan.
cards.move: A clean result is only as reassuring as the doubt you started with.
cards.trap: Any patient, since the test catches almost every clot.
cards.reference: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng158

cards.question: Why did the same blood creatinine result start reading as worse kidney function for Black Americans from 2021?
cards.answer: Because a race multiplier was dropped. The standard equation turned blood creatinine into an estimate of kidney function and multiplied it by 1.159 for Black patients, assuming more muscle. The same blood looked healthier on paper, delaying specialist referral and transplant listing. A 2021 equation from the same research group removed race altogether.
cards.move: Ask what assumption sits inside a formula before trusting the number it prints.
cards.reference: Inker et al., New Creatinine- and Cystatin C-Based Equations to Estimate GFR without Race, New England Journal of Medicine, 2021

cards.question: About how many millilitres of blood are drawn for tests from a patient during a 10-day stay in intensive care?
cards.answer: 41 x 10 days = about 410 ml.
cards.move: A little taken every day becomes a lot by the end of the month.
cards.trap: Guessing a few spoonfuls, picturing one small tube at a time.
cards.hint: Count the draws in a day and the millilitres each one takes.
steps: An intensive care patient has about 4.6 blood draws a day.
4.6 x 9 ml = about 41 ml a day.
41 x 10 days = about 410 ml.
cards.reference: Vincent et al., Anemia and blood transfusion in critically ill patients, JAMA, 2002

cards.question: Patients chosen because one cholesterol reading was high are retested a week later, untreated. What will their average be?
cards.answer: Lower. Any single reading is a person's usual level plus day-to-day variation and lab error. Choosing people for one high reading picks many caught on a high day, and their next result drifts back. Barnett and colleagues show that drift can pass for a treatment effect in any study that recruits on one measurement.
cards.move: Anyone picked for an extreme will look more ordinary the next time.
cards.trap: About the same, since nothing was done to change it.
cards.source: Barnett et al., Int J Epidemiology, 2005
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: Should patients see their test results online the moment they are ready, before a doctor has reviewed them?
cards.answer: The results describe the patient's own body, and delay is a harm of its own: days of waiting, chasing calls, results lost between clinics. In a 2023 survey of 8,139 US patients, 96% wanted immediate release even before a clinician had looked. Patients who see results early arrive with sharper questions.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether speed or explanation serves more.
cards.counterpoint: A number without context can terrify. A raised marker or a phrase like possible malignancy, read alone at midnight, is not the same news as one delivered by someone who can explain it and say what happens next. Some patients with abnormal results did report more worry, and the doctor who calls later meets panic.
cards.source: Steitz et al., JAMA Network Open, 2023
cards.reference: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2802672

cards.question: What did the WHO's ICD-11 change in 2019 about how chronic pain is classified?
cards.answer: It made some chronic pain a disease in its own right. Before, chronic pain was coded mostly as a symptom of something else. ICD-11 added chronic primary pain: pain lasting over three months with distress or disability that no other condition explains, such as fibromyalgia. A patient with no lesion now leaves with a diagnosis.
cards.move: A problem without a name gets counted as nothing.
cards.reference: Treede et al., Chronic pain as a symptom or a disease: the IASP Classification of Chronic Pain for the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), Pain, 2019

cards.question: In a 2016 US national survey, what share of adults reported pain on most days for six months?
cards.answer: About 1 in 5. The National Health Interview Survey put chronic pain at 20.4% of adults, around 50 million people. For 8%, the pain limited work or life activities most days. A condition that common rarely shows: no cast, no scar, and most sufferers are not held back on most days.
cards.move: What leaves no visible mark is counted too low by the eye.
cards.trap: Guessing low, because chronic pain is rarely seen or talked about.
cards.reference: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/pdfs/mm6736a2-H.pdf

cards.question: True or false: about one person in ten still has pain months after a routine groin hernia repair?
cards.answer: True. Persistent pain follows roughly 10% of groin hernia repairs, and 30% to 50% of leg amputations. The cut nerve, not a failed repair, is usually blamed. Severe, disabling pain after hernia repair is rarer, about 2% to 4%. Of millions of hernia operations a year, that leaves a large quiet population.
cards.move: Count what a routine fix leaves behind, not only what it removes.
cards.trap: Assuming a successful, routine operation ends the pain it causes.
cards.reference: Kehlet, Jensen & Woolf, Persistent postsurgical pain: risk factors and prevention, The Lancet, 2006

cards.question: What third kind of pain did pain scientists add in 2017, alongside tissue damage and nerve damage?
cards.answer: Nociplastic pain. The International Association for the Study of Pain adopted the term for pain that arises from altered processing in the nervous system, with no clear tissue injury and no nerve lesion. Fibromyalgia is the usual example. The label names the alarm system itself as the fault, not the site that hurts.
cards.move: When the parts all test healthy, suspect how they are wired together.
cards.reference: Kosek et al., Do we need a third mechanistic descriptor for chronic pain states?, Pain, 2016

cards.question: For what share of people with low back pain can a doctor name a specific cause?
cards.answer: Only about one in ten. The remaining 90% or so is labelled non-specific: no fracture, infection, tumour or trapped nerve explains it. This is the condition that causes more years lived with disability worldwide than any other. Most of that burden rests on a diagnosis that says what the pain is not.
cards.move: A common label can mean nobody knows yet.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27745712/

cards.question: On an ordinary day in 2020, roughly how many people worldwide were living with low back pain, in millions?
cards.answer: 7,800 x 0.08 = about 620 million people.
cards.move: A small daily share of a huge population is never a small number.
cards.trap: Picturing only the bedridden cases and guessing a few tens of millions.
cards.hint: Start from the world's population and the share in pain on any one day.
steps: World population in 2020: about 7,800 million people.
On any given day about 1 person in 13 has low back pain, roughly 8%.
7,800 x 0.08 = about 620 million people.
cards.reference: GBD 2021 Low Back Pain Collaborators, Global, regional, and national burden of low back pain, 1990-2020, and projections to 2050, The Lancet Rheumatology, 2023

cards.question: True or false: in a US trial, two-thirds of people with chronic back pain became nearly pain-free after four weeks of psychological treatment?
cards.answer: True. Pain reprocessing therapy teaches patients to treat their pain as a false alarm from the brain, not damage. 33 of 50 reached 0 or 1 out of 10, against 10 of 51 given a saline injection and 5 of 50 on usual care. Critics note the controls got far less attention.
cards.move: An alarm that keeps ringing may be faulty rather than warning of fire.
cards.trap: Assuming pain that lasts years must come from damaged tissue.
cards.reference: Ashar et al., Effect of Pain Reprocessing Therapy vs Placebo and Usual Care for Patients With Chronic Back Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial, JAMA Psychiatry, 2022

cards.question: Diagnosed by pressing tender points, fibromyalgia patients were about 90% women. Once symptom questionnaires replaced the pressure test, what did the ratio become?
cards.answer: Under 2 women to 1 man. The 1990 criteria required pain at 11 of 18 pressed points, and women on average feel pressure as pain at lower force, so many men with the same pain fell short. Symptom scoring narrowed the gap sharply. The diagnosis had partly sorted patients by the pressure of a thumb.
cards.move: Ask whether the test used to find a group decided who was found.
cards.trap: Still about 9 to 1, taking the sex ratio as fixed biology.
cards.reference: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0203755

cards.question: Chronic pain patients show less grey matter in pain-processing brain regions. What happened to it once a hip replacement ended the pain?
cards.answer: It came back. A 2009 German study scanned people with painful hip osteoarthritis, who showed the usual losses, then rescanned some after surgery had left them pain-free. Within months grey matter in those regions had partly returned. The shrinkage followed the pain rather than causing it: a brain reshaped by use, then reshaped by rest.
cards.move: Before calling a change a cause, see whether it undoes itself when the cause stops.
cards.source: Rodriguez-Raecke et al., Journal of Neuroscience, 2009
cards.reference: Rodriguez-Raecke et al., Brain gray matter decrease in chronic pain is the consequence and not the cause of pain, Journal of Neuroscience, 2009

cards.question: When British GPs sort new back pain patients by their risk of lasting disability, what do most of the questions ask about?
cards.answer: Fear, worry and mood, not the spine. Keele University's nine-item STarT Back tool gives five questions to how bothersome the pain is, fear of movement, catastrophising, anxiety and low mood. High scorers get intensive physiotherapy, low scorers reassurance. In a 2011 trial of 851 patients, this sorting cut disability more and cost less.
cards.move: How a person reads the first weeks may predict a long illness best.
cards.reference: Hill et al., Comparison of stratified primary care management for low back pain with current best practice (STarT Back): a randomised controlled trial, The Lancet, 2011

cards.question: How can a nurse with no thermometer tell whether a vial of vaccine has been spoiled by heat?
cards.answer: From a sticker that keeps a running total of heat. A vaccine vial monitor is a square inside a circle; the square darkens faster the warmer it gets, and never lightens. Once it matches the circle, the vial is discarded. First used on oral polio vaccine in 1996, billions have been printed since.
cards.move: Measure the total dose, not the reading at the moment you look.
cards.source: WHO, Getting started with vaccine vial monitors, 2002
cards.reference: World Health Organization, Getting started with vaccine vial monitors: questions and answers on field operations, WHO/V&B/02.35, 2002

cards.question: For vaccines such as hepatitis B and tetanus, which cold-chain accident is the bigger threat?
options: A day or two of summer heat
Freezing in a fridge or cool box
cards.answer: Freezing. Their aluminium adjuvant clumps when ice forms, the damage is permanent, and the vials look normal. A 2007 review found that 14% to 35% of fridges or shipments exposed vaccine to freezing temperatures. The cold chain's commonest fault is being too cold.
cards.move: Guard against the failure your precautions create, not only the one they prevent.
cards.trap: Picturing heat as the enemy, since the whole system is called cold.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17382434/

cards.question: How did the Pfizer Covid vaccine's permitted fridge life grow from five days to a month in 2021?
cards.answer: With data, not a new formula. The five-day limit for thawed vials at 2 to 8 °C was simply as far as stability testing had reached at authorisation. In May 2021, on further stability data from Pfizer, regulators extended it to a month. Ordinary clinic fridges could now hold the vaccine.
cards.move: A limit on a label may mark where testing stopped, not where things fail.
cards.reference: https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2021-05-20-fda-authorizes-storing-thawed-pfizer-covid-19-vaccine-refrigerator-30-days

cards.question: What made smallpox vaccine usable in tropical villages with no refrigerators?
cards.answer: A freeze-drying recipe from the 1950s. At London's Lister Institute, Leslie Collier dried vaccinia virus from the frozen state with peptone added, and the powder kept its potency for months at 37 °C. From 1967 the WHO eradication campaign used freeze-dried vaccine tested to its standards, which could cross a hot season in a bag.
cards.move: The cheapest cold chain is a product that no longer needs one.
cards.reference: Collier, The development of a stable smallpox vaccine, Journal of Hygiene, 1955

cards.question: True or false: many solar vaccine fridges in off-grid clinics stay cold through the night with no battery at all?
cards.answer: True. Solar direct-drive fridges, prequalified by the WHO from the early 2010s, run their compressor only while the sun shines and freeze a bank of ice. That frozen store keeps the vaccine cold overnight and through cloudy days. Batteries were dropped because in hot clinics they wore out quickly and were costly to replace.
cards.move: Store the thing you need, not the energy to make it later.
cards.trap: Assuming solar power must be kept as electricity for the night.
cards.reference: McCarney, Robertson, Arnaud, Lorenson & Lloyd, Using solar-powered refrigeration for vaccine storage where other sources of reliable electricity are inadequate, Vaccine, 2013

cards.question: Why does a vaccine carried outside the cold chain need a second heat sticker besides the vial monitor?
cards.answer: Because the vial monitor sums heat over days and barely registers a short spike. The controlled temperature chain, first licensed in 2012 for a meningitis A vaccine at up to 40 °C for four days, adds a peak threshold indicator that changes once 40 °C is passed. Benin's first such campaign reached about 150,000 people.
cards.move: A running total and a hard ceiling guard against different failures.
cards.reference: World Health Organization, Controlled Temperature Chain: Strategic Roadmap for Priority Vaccines 2017–2020, 2017

cards.question: How can a health worker tell whether a normal-looking vial of tetanus vaccine was once frozen?
cards.answer: By freezing another vial on purpose. In the shake test, a vial from the same batch is frozen solid, thawed and shaken beside the suspect one. Ice clumps the aluminium particles into heavy flakes that sink fast, leaving clear liquid above. A suspect vial that clears as fast as the control is thrown away.
cards.move: When damage is invisible, make a known-damaged sample to compare against.
cards.source: Kartoglu et al., Bulletin of the WHO, 2010
cards.reference: Kartoglu, Özgüler, Wolfson & Kurzatkowski, Validation of the shake test for detecting freeze damage to adsorbed vaccines, Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 2010

cards.question: Dried measles vaccine must survive a week at 37 °C. Mixed with its diluent at room temperature, how soon does it lose half its potency?
cards.answer: In about an hour. Freeze-drying holds the live virus in a dry cake; water lets it fall apart. At 20 to 25 °C the mixed vaccine loses half its potency, so it sits on ice and is discarded hours after mixing. Powder that passed a week-long heat test can spoil in one morning clinic.
cards.move: Ask what state a thing is in before trusting its tested limits.
cards.trap: Letting the powder's week of heat tolerance set the guess.
cards.reference: World Health Organization, Temperature sensitivity of vaccines, WHO/IVB/06.10, 2006

cards.question: True or false: a clinic fridge that read 2 to 8 °C at every twice-daily check has probably kept its vaccines in range?
cards.answer: False. Two readings a day sample two moments; a swing out of range between them leaves no trace. When US federal inspectors put their own monitors in the vaccine fridges of 45 providers for two weeks, vaccine at about three quarters spent at least 5 hours outside 2 to 8 °C.
cards.move: A check made at fixed times sees nothing that happens between them.
cards.trap: Treating a clean logbook as proof the fridge stayed in range.
cards.source: US HHS Office of Inspector General, 2012
cards.reference: Office of Inspector General, US Department of Health and Human Services, Vaccines for Children Program: Vulnerabilities in Vaccine Management, OEI-04-10-00430, 2012

cards.question: BCG comes in 20-dose vials, discarded six hours after opening. A clinic vaccinates 5 newborns per session. How many doses per child?
cards.answer: 20 / 5 = 4 doses per child.
cards.move: Count what is opened, not only what is used.
cards.trap: Thinking wastage means spoiled stock, not opened vials.
cards.hint: Each session opens one vial, and whatever is left at the end is thrown away.
steps: Each session opens one 20-dose vial.
Five doses are given; the other 15 are discarded.
20 / 5 = 4 doses per child.
cards.reference: World Health Organization, Monitoring vaccine wastage at country level: guidelines for programme managers, WHO/V&B/03.18 Rev.1, 2005

cards.question: What happened in Britain after a 1974 report linked the whooping cough vaccine to brain damage?
cards.answer: Uptake fell from about 80% to about 30% by 1978, and the disease came back. Between 1977 and 1979 more than 100,000 cases and 36 deaths were reported in large epidemics. Parliament answered with the Vaccine Damage Payments Act of 1979, a no-fault compensation scheme that still pays out today.
cards.move: When a protection is dropped, count what it was quietly holding back.
cards.reference: Baker, The pertussis vaccine controversy in Great Britain, 1974-1986, Vaccine, 2003

cards.question: In a 2018 survey across 140 countries, where did the largest share of people disagree that vaccines are safe?
cards.answer: France. One person in three there disagreed that vaccines are safe, the highest share of any country in the Wellcome Global Monitor, which polled about 140,000 people. Doubt ran generally higher in rich regions than in poorer ones. The country of Louis Pasteur made eleven infant vaccines compulsory that same year.
cards.move: The loudest controversy in the news says little about where doubt runs deepest.
cards.trap: Picking the United States, whose vaccine fights make the most headlines.
cards.reference: https://wellcome.org/reports/wellcome-global-monitor/2018/chapter-5-attitudes-vaccines

cards.question: True or false: a US infant vaccine was withdrawn about a year after licensing over a rare complication confirmed only after launch?
cards.answer: True. RotaShield, a rotavirus vaccine licensed in 1998, was pulled in 1999 after reports of intussusception, a telescoping of the bowel, reached a national reporting system. The excess risk was on the order of 1 in 10,000 infants. Trials of about 10,000 children could not reliably see so rare an event; mass use could.
cards.move: A study cannot see an event much rarer than one in its sample size.
cards.trap: Assuming a licensed vaccine's trials would have caught any serious harm.
cards.reference: Murphy et al., Intussusception among infants given an oral rotavirus vaccine, New England Journal of Medicine, 2001

cards.question: Which 1955 vaccine disaster shaped the legal rules that still govern American vaccine makers?
cards.answer: The Cutter incident. A company's polio vaccine held live virus its process failed to kill; about 40,000 children got mild polio, some 200 people were paralysed and 10 died. A jury later found Cutter liable though not negligent. That principle fed lawsuits that thinned the industry, until a 1986 law created a no-fault compensation fund.
cards.move: A disaster's longest effect is often the rule written in response.
cards.reference: Offit, The Cutter Incident: How America's First Polio Vaccine Led to the Growing Vaccine Crisis, Yale University Press, 2005

cards.question: Should schools turn away children whose parents refuse vaccines on grounds of personal belief?
cards.answer: A child in the next seat cannot opt out of an outbreak. After California ended belief exemptions in 2015, such exemptions among new kindergarteners fell from over 2% to about 0.5%. Exemptions cluster in the same schools, so a healthy state average hides pockets where measles, which needs about 95% vaccinated, finds its opening.
cards.move: The decider is whether a ban vaccinates the refusers or only moves them elsewhere.
cards.counterpoint: Coercion turns a hesitant parent into a hostile one, and it leaks. In California, medical exemptions rose after the ban and offset much of the gain, and some families moved to home schooling. Many hesitant parents come round when a trusted doctor takes time with them; a mandate spends that trust on the few who never will.

cards.question: What were the first conscientious objectors recognised by British law refusing, years before anyone was conscripted to fight?
cards.answer: Smallpox vaccination. Under the Vaccination Act of 1898, parents who convinced two magistrates that they conscientiously believed the jab would harm their child were exempted from it. Magistrates often refused, so a 1907 act let parents simply sign a declaration. Conscience was first written into law against a lancet, not a rifle.
cards.move: An exemption written for one fight becomes the template for the next.
cards.reference: Durbach, Bodily Matters: The Anti-Vaccination Movement in England, 1853–1907, Duke University Press, 2005

cards.question: Japan dropped the combined MMR vaccine in 1993. In one Yokohama ward, what happened to autism diagnoses among children born afterwards?
options: They fell back towards earlier levels
cards.answer: They kept rising, as before. Japan stopped MMR over meningitis from its mumps strain, which made its removal a test. A study of every child born in Kohoku ward from 1988 to 1996 found cumulative autism incidence climbed across the cohorts with no dip. Cohorts never given MMR had the highest rates.
cards.move: Take away the suspect and watch whether the trend even notices.
cards.trap: Expecting removal of a suspected cause to at least slow the rise.
cards.source: Honda et al., J Child Psychol Psychiatry, 2005
cards.reference: Honda, Shimizu & Rutter, No effect of MMR withdrawal on the incidence of autism: a total population study, Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 2005

cards.question: True or false: Japan's HPV vaccination rate fell from about 70% to under 1% without the vaccine ever being withdrawn?
cards.answer: True. In June 2013, after televised reports of girls with pain and abnormal movements, the health ministry suspended only its active recommendation; the vaccine stayed free and on the schedule. Uptake collapsed anyway. A Nagoya survey later found no excess of 24 reported symptoms in vaccinated women. The recommendation returned in April 2022.
cards.move: A quiet step back by an authority can move people as much as a ban.
cards.trap: Assuming a collapse that steep needs a ban or a proven harm.
cards.reference: Hanley, Yoshioka, Ito & Kishi, HPV vaccination crisis in Japan, The Lancet, 2015

cards.question: Of 3 million people over 80, 1 in 10 die yearly. If all are vaccinated, how many die within a week anyway, in thousands?
cards.answer: About 5,800 deaths within a week of the jab, about 5.8 thousand.
cards.move: Before reading meaning into timing, count how often it happens anyway.
cards.trap: Treating each death soon after a jab as needing a vaccine explanation.
cards.hint: Work out the yearly deaths first, then take one week's share of them.
steps: Deaths in a week: 300,000 / 52 = about 5,800.
About 5,800 deaths within a week of the jab, about 5.8 thousand.
cards.source: ONS, Deaths registered in England and Wales
cards.reference: Office for National Statistics, Deaths registered in England and Wales: 2019, 2020

cards.question: Should a family doctor be allowed to remove patients from the practice list because they refuse childhood vaccines?
cards.answer: An unvaccinated child in the waiting room exposes newborns and chemotherapy patients to measles. A doctor who has tried repeatedly and failed should be free to end a relationship built on distrust. The American Academy of Pediatrics said in 2016 that dismissal can be acceptable, after repeated counselling, as a last resort.
cards.move: What decides it is whether a doctor's leverage lies in the threat or the relationship.
cards.counterpoint: Dismissed families do not get vaccinated; they gather in the few practices that will take them, or drift away from medicine, and outbreaks follow such clusters. Many hesitant parents do vaccinate after continued conversations, sometimes years later, and only a doctor they still see can hold them. Dismissal also cuts siblings off from check-ups and ordinary care.
cards.reference: Edwards & Hackell, Countering Vaccine Hesitancy, Pediatrics, 2016

cards.question: True or false: in 1840s Vienna, mothers who gave birth in the street died of childbed fever less often than hospital mothers?
cards.answer: True. Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women who delivered on the way in rarely caught it. In the doctors' ward, 1841 to 1846, about 99 mothers in 1,000 died; in the midwives' ward, 39. Doctors came from dissecting corpses. After chlorine handwashing began in 1847, the doctors' ward fell to about 13 in 1,000.
cards.move: When the untreated do better, look at what the treatment carries in.
cards.trap: Assuming a hospital birth with doctors must be the safer one.

diagram.caption: The doctors' ward was the deadliest until chlorine handwashing cut it from 99 to 13.

cards.reference: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/ignaz-phillip-semmelweis-studies-of-death-in-childbirth/

cards.question: Which part of John Snow's work on London's 1854 cholera gave the strongest evidence that water spread it?
options: Removing the Broad Street pump handle
Seeing the germ under a microscope
cards.answer: Comparing two water companies' customers. Their pipes ran down the same streets, but one drew sewage-laden Thames water and the other cleaner water upstream. Early in the epidemic Snow counted 315 deaths per 10,000 houses for the first and 37 for the second. The famous pump handle came off when Soho's outbreak was already fading.
cards.move: An outbreak that has peaked will fall whatever is done next.
cards.trap: Crediting the pump handle, removed after the outbreak had already peaked.
cards.reference: Snow on Cholera: Being a Reprint of Two Papers by John Snow, M.D., The Commonwealth Fund, 1936

cards.question: What happened when Max von Pettenkofer drank a culture of cholera bacteria in 1892?
cards.answer: He got mild diarrhoea and declared Robert Koch refuted. The Munich hygienist, 73, held that the germ alone could not cause cholera without local soil conditions, and drank it during Hamburg's epidemic. Stomach acid, a weakened culture or partial immunity may explain his luck. Healthy carriers later showed a germ can infect without sickening.
cards.move: One person who got away with it proves nothing about the rest.
cards.reference: Evans, Death in Hamburg: Society and Politics in the Cholera Years 1830-1910, Oxford University Press, 1987

cards.question: Why did boiled hay broth keep growing microbes long after Pasteur's flask experiments?
cards.answer: Hay carries bacterial spores that survive boiling. In 1876 Ferdinand Cohn described these heat-proof resting forms; in 1877 John Tyndall showed that even hours of boiling could fail to sterilise such broths. His fix was to boil, wait for spores to sprout, and boil again. Life that seemed to arise from nothing had simply waited.
cards.move: When a result contradicts a rule, look for a hardier version of the usual suspect.
cards.reference: https://academic.oup.com/femsre/article/24/3/225/561657

cards.question: True or false: the engineers who built London's great sewers in the 1860s knew cholera spread through water?
cards.answer: False. Joseph Bazalgette and his board acted on the theory that disease rose from foul air; the Great Stink of 1858 pushed the plan through Parliament. By carrying sewage away from the river by the city, they also kept it further from drinking water. Its success could be read as proof of the bad-air theory.
cards.move: A plan that works is not proof its reasoning was right.
cards.trap: Assuming a measure that stopped cholera was built on the right theory.
cards.source: Halliday, The Great Stink of London, 1999
cards.reference: Halliday, The Great Stink of London: Sir Joseph Bazalgette and the Cleansing of the Victorian Metropolis, Sutton Publishing, 1999

cards.question: Which of these was the first animal disease shown by experiment to be caused by a microbe passing between hosts?
cards.answer: A disease of silkworms. In 1835 Agostino Bassi, an Italian trained in law, showed that muscardine, which was ruining silk farms, was caused by a fungus that spread from sick worms to healthy ones by contact. That was over 40 years before Koch's work on anthrax. The fungus now carries his name: Beauveria bassiana.
cards.move: The famous founder of an idea usually had a forgotten predecessor.
cards.trap: Anthrax, the disease Koch used to launch bacteriology in 1876.
cards.source: Ainsworth, Introduction to the History of Mycology, 1976
cards.reference: Ainsworth, Introduction to the History of Mycology, Cambridge University Press, 1976

cards.question: Koch's rules demand that a disease's germ be grown pure in the laboratory. Which of these has never been grown on lab media?
cards.answer: The leprosy bacillus. Gerhard Armauer Hansen saw it in 1873, one of the first bacteria linked to a human disease, but it has never grown on artificial media. It survives only in living tissue, and laboratories raise it in mouse footpads and armadillos. By the letter of Koch's rules, its guilt was never formally proved.
cards.move: A rule for proving guilt can fail on the most obvious culprit.
cards.trap: The tuberculosis bacillus, notorious for taking weeks to grow.
cards.source: Scollard et al., Clinical Microbiology Reviews, 2006
cards.reference: Scollard et al., The continuing challenges of leprosy, Clinical Microbiology Reviews, 2006

cards.question: Before antisepsis, 16 of Lister's 35 amputation patients died; afterwards, 6 of 40. At the old rate, how many fewer deaths is that?
cards.answer: 18 - 6 = 12 fewer deaths.
cards.move: Compare rates, not counts, whenever the two groups differ in size.
cards.trap: Answering 10, by subtracting the raw death counts 16 and 6.
cards.hint: Scale the old death rate up to 40 patients first.
steps: Old death rate: 16 / 35 = about 46%.
At that rate, 40 patients: 40 x 0.46 = about 18 deaths.
18 - 6 = 12 fewer deaths.
cards.reference: Tröhler, Statistics and the British controversy about the effects of Joseph Lister's system of antisepsis for surgery, 1867-1890, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 2015

cards.question: Why did the stomach bacterium behind most ulcers refuse to grow in the lab until Easter 1982?
cards.answer: Because the plates were thrown away too soon. Robin Warren had seen curved bacteria in stomach biopsies, but Barry Marshall's cultures in Perth were discarded after two days, the routine for throat swabs. Over the long Easter weekend one batch sat for five days, and colonies of Helicobacter pylori appeared. It simply grew slowly.
cards.move: A search that stops too early reports that nothing is there.
cards.reference: Marshall, Helicobacter connections, Nobel Lecture, Nobel Foundation, 2005

cards.question: Was the rejection of Semmelweis's handwashing mainly the fault of doctors who refused evidence, rather than of a weak case?
cards.answer: The numbers were stark: after chlorine washing began, deaths on the doctors' ward fell to the midwives' level within months. Colleagues who saw them still let his post in Vienna lapse in 1849. Accepting the finding meant accepting that doctors' own hands had killed mothers, and that, not the data, was the obstacle.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what counts as proof without a mechanism.
cards.counterpoint: Semmelweis did not publish his own full account until 1861, fourteen years on, and left others to report it second-hand. His cause, decaying organic matter, had no mechanism anyone could see, and he answered critics by calling them murderers. Without germs to point to, a doctor seeing mixed results elsewhere could reasonably doubt him.
cards.source: Loudon, The Tragedy of Childbed Fever, 2000
cards.reference: Loudon, The Tragedy of Childbed Fever, Oxford University Press, 2000

cards.question: What paid for Guy's Hospital in London, whose building began in 1721?
cards.answer: A timely exit from a financial bubble. Thomas Guy, a bookseller grown rich printing Bibles, held South Sea Company shares and sold them in 1720, before the crash. He spent much of the fortune on a hospital for patients St Thomas's turned away as incurable. It opened in 1726, over a year after his death.
cards.move: Ask where a gift's money came from, and when it was taken out.
cards.reference: Cameron, Mr Guy's Hospital 1726-1948, Longmans, Green, 1954

cards.question: In James Simpson's 1869 survey, what share of major amputations in large British hospitals ended in death?
cards.answer: About 40%. Simpson counted 855 deaths in 2,089 hospital amputations, against 226 in 2,098 done in country practice, about 11%. He called the difference hospitalism, blaming crowded, badly aired wards. Critics answered that city hospitals got the worst injuries. Either way, the operating table was safer in a farmhouse kitchen.
cards.move: Check where the danger sat before crediting the place that treated it.
cards.trap: Guessing low, from a modern sense that amputation is survivable.
cards.reference: Fitzharris, The Butchering Art: Joseph Lister's Quest to Transform the Grisly World of Victorian Medicine, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2017

cards.question: Should hospitals staff senior doctors seven days a week to cut higher death rates after weekend admission?
cards.answer: Patients admitted on Saturdays and Sundays are more likely to die within 30 days, a pattern found across England's millions of admissions. Illness does not keep office hours, yet scans, specialists and senior decisions thin out at weekends. Equal care every day of the week is a basic promise a hospital should keep.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how sick weekend patients were on arrival decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Weekend admissions are fewer and sicker: with clinics and surgeries shut, only the urgent come in, and records capture severity poorly. Studies that adjust better find much of the gap shrinks. Consultants are scarce, so weekend rotas pull them from weekday work, and no study has shown extra weekend staffing saves the lives claimed.
cards.reference: Freemantle et al., Increased mortality associated with weekend hospital admission: a case for expanded seven day services?, BMJ, 2015

cards.question: What did most to cut deaths at Britain's Scutari army hospital during the Crimean War, in 1855?
cards.answer: Engineers clearing drains and sewers. Deaths at the Scutari barrack hospital peaked in the winter after Florence Nightingale's nurses arrived in November 1854. In March 1855 a Sanitary Commission sent from London flushed blocked sewers and opened up ventilation, and the death rate fell steeply within months. Her own later statistics blamed the building.
cards.move: The famous figure on the scene is not always what changed the outcome.
cards.trap: Crediting the nurses, since the lady with the lamp gets the fame.
cards.reference: Small, Florence Nightingale: Avenging Angel, Constable, 1998

cards.question: How were patients bedded in Paris's great hospital, the Hôtel-Dieu, in the 18th century?
cards.answer: Several to a bed. Most of its roughly 1,200 beds were large ones shared by four or more, and patients far outnumbered beds. The surgeon Jacques Tenon's 1788 survey put its death rate above one in five, higher than the city's smaller hospitals. The fevered, the dying and the recovering shared one mattress.
cards.move: Before blaming a place's patients, count how many share each bed.
cards.source: The Curious History of L'Hôtel-Dieu de Paris
cards.reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5212799/

cards.question: Reviewers read the notes of thousands of patients who died in English hospitals. What share of deaths did they judge more likely than not avoidable?
cards.answer: About 1 in 30. Hogan and colleagues found 3.6% across 34 hospital trusts, mostly among frail, elderly patients with little life left. With so few, a hospital's overall death rate mainly reflects who arrives how sick: its standardised mortality ratio showed no significant link to the avoidable deaths found in its own notes.
cards.move: Before ranking places by deaths, ask how many of them anyone could prevent.
cards.trap: About 1 in 3, recalling scandals where hospitals killed through neglect.
cards.reference: Hogan et al., Avoidability of hospital deaths and association with hospital-wide mortality ratios: retrospective case record review and regression analysis, BMJ, 2015

cards.question: True or false: England's NHS had fewer than half as many hospital beds in 2019-20 as in 1987-88?
cards.answer: True. Beds fell from about 299,000 to about 141,000 while admissions rose. Stays became much shorter, much surgery became day surgery, and long-stay wards for mental illness and learning disability closed as care moved into the community. Many patients who once spent a week on a ward now go home the same evening.
cards.move: Count what a place does, not only how big it is.
cards.trap: False, since halving the beds sounds like a collapsed service.
cards.source: The King's Fund, NHS bed numbers, 2020
cards.reference: The King's Fund, NHS hospital bed numbers: past, present, future, 2020

cards.question: Why did Nightingale-style wards have tall windows facing each other along both long walls?
cards.answer: To sweep out foul air, because Nightingale held that disease rose from miasma, not germs. Her Notes on Hospitals demanded long, narrow pavilions with windows on opposite walls and open space between buildings. The theory was wrong, but the cross-draught diluted real airborne germs, and one nurse at the end could see every bed.
cards.move: A wrong theory can still build the right room.
cards.reference: McDonald (ed.), Florence Nightingale and Hospital Reform, Collected Works of Florence Nightingale vol. 16, Wilfrid Laurier University Press, 2012

cards.question: In 18th-century London, what did a sick poor person usually need before a voluntary hospital would take them in?
cards.answer: A letter from a subscriber. Hospitals like the Westminster and the London ran on donations, and each subscription bought the right to recommend patients. Many turned away fevers, the incurable, pregnant women and young children, partly because deaths looked bad to donors. Admission day meant queuing with a patron's letter in hand.
cards.move: Ask who holds the ticket before asking who needs the seat.
cards.source: Woodward, To Do the Sick No Harm, 1974
cards.reference: Woodward, To Do the Sick No Harm: A Study of the British Voluntary Hospital System to 1875, Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1974

cards.question: Should emergency stroke care be concentrated in a few large specialist hospitals rather than offered at every local one?
cards.answer: Outcomes follow expertise and volume. When London moved all acute stroke care into eight hyperacute units in 2010, with specialists and scanners round the clock, deaths fell further than in the rest of England; Manchester's partial version showed no such gain. A longer ambulance ride matters less than arriving where the team is waiting.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the travel time to the nearest unit decides it.
cards.counterpoint: London is dense and distances short. In rural areas a central unit can be an hour or more away, and an untreated stroke destroys roughly 1.9 million nerve cells a minute. Closing local services also drains smaller hospitals of the staff and skills that every other emergency needs.
cards.reference: Morris et al., Impact of centralising acute stroke services in English metropolitan areas on mortality and length of hospital stay: difference-in-differences analysis, BMJ, 2014

cards.question: How long were aluminium salts used to boost vaccines before anyone could say how they worked?
cards.answer: About eight decades, and it is still argued over. In 1926 Alexander Glenny found that diphtheria toxoid precipitated with alum raised far more antibody in guinea pigs. A 2008 paper tied it to an inflammation sensor in immune cells; other labs found alum worked without it. Billions of doses rested on an empirical result.
cards.move: A remedy can be trusted for decades before anyone can explain it.
cards.source: Marrack, McKee & Munks, Nature Reviews Immunology, 2009
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/nri2510

cards.question: Why does someone who survives tetanus still need the tetanus vaccine afterwards?
cards.answer: Because the disease leaves no immunity. Tetanus toxin is so potent that the amount which locks the muscles is far too small to provoke an antibody response. The vaccine delivers a larger dose of toxin made harmless, a toxoid, which the immune system can see. Survivors leave hospital with a course of injections.
cards.move: Surviving a threat and learning to recognise it are two different events.
cards.reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Epidemiology and Prevention of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases, 14th edition, Tetanus chapter, 2021

cards.question: True or false: the mRNA in the Pfizer and Moderna Covid vaccines uses the same four letters as a cell's own mRNA?
cards.answer: False. Every uridine, one of the four letters, is replaced by N1-methylpseudouridine, a close chemical cousin. Unmodified mRNA trips the cell's virus alarms and is shut down before much protein is made. Karikó and Weissman's 2005 work on the swap won a Nobel Prize in 2023. Ribosomes still read the altered letter as the original.
cards.move: A copy that works often had to differ from the original to get through.
cards.trap: Assuming a vaccine copies the virus's message letter for letter.
cards.reference: Karikó, Buckstein, Ni & Weissman, Suppression of RNA recognition by Toll-like receptors: the impact of nucleoside modification, Immunity, 2005

cards.question: Why did the first vaccines made from a bacterium's sugar coat fail to protect children under two?
options: Maternal antibodies mopped up the vaccine
Infant immune systems ignore bare sugars
Infant doses were cut too small
cards.answer: Infant immune systems ignore bare sugars. Polysaccharides, long sugar chains, stimulate B cells without help from T cells, a route that barely works before about age two and leaves little memory. Bolting the sugar to a protein, often tetanus toxoid, recruits T-cell help. That conjugate design made Hib meningitis rare in vaccinated countries.
cards.move: When a message is ignored, change the messenger rather than shouting louder.
cards.trap: Blaming mothers' antibodies, which do blunt the measles vaccine in infancy.
cards.source: Pollard, Perrett & Beverley, Nature Reviews Immunology, 2009
cards.reference: Pollard, Perrett & Beverley, Maintaining protection against invasive bacteria with protein-polysaccharide conjugate vaccines, Nature Reviews Immunology, 2009

cards.question: Each measles case infects about 15 people, and two vaccine doses protect 97% of children. What percentage must be vaccinated to stop outbreaks?
cards.move: A target for the protected must be divided by how often protection takes.
cards.trap: Stopping at 93%, forgetting that some vaccinated children stay unprotected.
cards.hint: Ask what share can stay unprotected if each case must infect fewer than one.
steps: Spread stops when each case infects fewer than one person on average.
So at most 1 in 15 can be susceptible: 1 - 1/15 = 93.3% must be immune.
Only 97% of the vaccinated are immune, so coverage = 93.3 / 0.97.
cards.source: Fine, Eames & Heymann, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2011
cards.reference: Fine, Eames & Heymann, Herd immunity: a rough guide, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2011

cards.question: Pfizer's 2020 trial reported 95% efficacy against Covid. Roughly what share of its vaccinated volunteers fell ill with it?
cards.answer: About 0.04%. Of about 18,200 vaccinated volunteers, 8 caught symptomatic Covid in the trial's first months, against 162 of about 18,300 on placebo. Efficacy compares the two groups: 8 against 162 is a 95% cut. It says nothing about how many would have fallen ill anyway, and under 1% of the placebo group did.
cards.move: A percentage cut means little until you know what it was cut from.
cards.trap: Reading 95% efficacy as 5% of vaccinated people still falling ill.

diagram.label: volunteers
diagram.caption: 95% efficacy means 8 ill against 162, not 5% of the vaccinated falling ill.

cards.question: Flu vaccines are reformulated every year. Why has measles vaccine, grown from a 1954 virus sample, never needed updating?
options: Its RNA copies itself with few errors
Its surface proteins cannot change and still work
It targets proteins hidden inside the virus
cards.answer: Its surface proteins cannot change and still work. Measles mutates like other RNA viruses, but a 2015 study found that changes to the sites antibodies bind on its H protein mostly broke its grip on the receptors it needs to enter cells. A strain from a Boston schoolboy still covers every genotype.
cards.move: When something never changes, ask whether it can afford to.
cards.trap: Assuming a vaccine that never ages means a virus that never mutates.
cards.reference: Fulton et al., Mutational analysis of measles virus suggests constraints on antigenic variation of the glycoproteins, Cell Reports, 2015

cards.question: True or false: in most years since 2017, the vaccine's own virus has paralysed more children than wild polio?
cards.answer: True. Oral polio vaccine is a live, weakened virus that passes between children. Where too few are immunised it circulates for months and can regain the power to paralyse. In 2021 there were 6 wild cases and about 700 vaccine-derived ones, mostly type 2, a strain whose wild form was declared eradicated in 2015.
cards.move: A fix that spreads by itself also spreads where nobody is watching.
cards.trap: Wild polio makes the news, so it seems the main cause.
cards.reference: Global Polio Eradication Initiative, Polio Eradication Strategy 2022–2026: Delivering on a Promise, World Health Organization, 2021

cards.question: How does a shingles vaccine made of a single viral protein beat the live-virus vaccine in people over 70?
cards.answer: Through its adjuvant. Shingrix pairs one protein, glycoprotein E, with AS01, which combines a detoxified fragment of bacterial membrane and QS-21, a saponin from the bark of a Chilean soapbark tree. It rouses ageing T cells. In trials it cut shingles by about 90% in people over 70; the live vaccine had managed about 38%.
cards.move: The helper added to a message can matter more than the message.
cards.reference: Cunningham et al., Efficacy of the herpes zoster subunit vaccine in adults 70 years of age or older, New England Journal of Medicine, 2016

cards.question: Why can a single dose of HPV vaccine give protection that most protein vaccines need several doses for?
cards.answer: Because of its shape. Its protein, L1, assembles itself into empty virus shells, each carrying 360 copies in a tight, repeating lattice. That pattern cross-links the receptors on antibody-making B cells and recruits long-lived ones. In 2022 the WHO endorsed one-dose schedules; a Kenyan trial had found about 97% efficacy 18 months after one dose.
cards.move: How a signal is arranged can matter as much as how strong it is.
cards.reference: Schiller & Lowy, Explanations for the high potency of HPV prophylactic vaccines, Vaccine, 2018

cards.question: How was teixobactin, an antibiotic announced in 2015, found in soil that had been searched for decades?
cards.answer: By growing bacteria that refuse to grow in a laboratory. Most soil microbes never form colonies on a dish, so earlier hunts had sampled only a small minority. A team led by Kim Lewis sealed soil bacteria in a device buried back in the soil, the iChip. A newly cultured species, Eleftheria terrae, made teixobactin.
cards.move: When a well-searched place runs dry, question the method of searching.
cards.reference: Ling et al., A new antibiotic kills pathogens without detectable resistance, Nature, 2015

cards.question: Where had halicin, the antibiotic picked out by a neural network in 2020, been before?
cards.answer: On the shelf as an abandoned diabetes candidate. An MIT team trained a model on about 2,300 molecules tested against E. coli, then had it score some 6,000 compounds already studied as drugs. It flagged halicin, which killed many resistant bacteria in lab and mouse tests. The name comes from HAL 9000.
cards.move: Old stock read with new eyes can be cheaper than a fresh search.
cards.reference: Stokes et al., A Deep Learning Approach to Antibiotic Discovery, Cell, 2020

cards.question: Achaogen won FDA approval for its new antibiotic plazomicin in June 2018. Where was the company ten months later?
options: Taken over by a large drug firm
cards.answer: In bankruptcy court. Achaogen filed for Chapter 11 in April 2019, and its drug was auctioned to Cipla. A good new antibiotic is held in reserve, so it sells little at first, while development and launch cost hundreds of millions of dollars. The approval arrived with a sales force it could not afford.
cards.move: A product meant to be used sparingly cannot live on payment per use.
cards.trap: Assuming approval, the hard part, means commercial success will follow.
cards.reference: Jacobs, Crisis Looms in Antibiotics as Drug Makers Go Bankrupt, The New York Times, 25 December 2019

cards.question: Linezolid reached patients in 2000 and daptomycin in 2003, each the first of a new class. When were their families first found?
cards.answer: In the 1980s, then set aside. DuPont announced the oxazolidinones in 1987 before dropping them; Upjohn chemists later refined the family into linezolid. Eli Lilly found daptomycin in the early 1980s and halted trials in 1991 over muscle toxicity; Cubist licensed it in 1997. The new classes of the 2000s were old shelf stock.
cards.move: A launch date says when a thing arrived, not when it began.
cards.trap: Assuming a drug was discovered shortly before the year it was approved.
cards.source: Eisenstein, Oleson & Baltz, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2010
cards.reference: Eisenstein, Oleson & Baltz, Daptomycin: from the mountain to the clinic, with essential help from Francis Tally, MD, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2010

cards.question: Should health systems pay for new antibiotics by yearly subscription instead of by the dose sold?
cards.answer: A good new antibiotic should sit unused until the old ones fail, so paying per dose rewards the opposite of care. From 2022 England paid up to £10 million a year per drug, whatever the volume. Only predictable income will bring investors back to a field where approval can still mean bankruptcy.
cards.move: What decides it is whether guaranteed fees change what firms start to research.
cards.counterpoint: Subscriptions pay for drugs that already exist; the shortage is in discovery, which a £10 million fee barely touches when one drug costs hundreds of millions to develop. One country's scheme is too small to steer global investment, and rewarding any approval invites tweaks of old classes rather than the genuinely new ones resistance demands.
cards.source: The Pharmaceutical Journal, subscription model explainer
cards.reference: https://pharmaceutical-journal.com/article/feature/everything-you-need-to-know-about-the-nhs-antimicrobial-resistance-subscription-model

cards.question: What did GlaxoSmithKline get from screening its chemical libraries against bacterial genes found by genome sequencing, 1995 to 2001?
cards.answer: No antibiotic. The company ran 67 screening campaigns against proteins bacteria cannot live without, finding 16 hits and 5 leads, none of which became a drug. The targets were sound; the chemicals were wrong. Libraries built for human medicines held few molecules able to cross a bacterial wall and escape its pumps.
cards.move: A good list of targets is worthless without something that can reach them.
cards.source: Payne et al., Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2007
cards.reference: Payne, Gwynn, Holmes & Pompliano, Drugs for bad bugs: confronting the challenges of antibacterial discovery, Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2007

cards.question: How does cefiderocol, approved in 2019, get inside bacteria whose outer membrane keeps most antibiotics out?
cards.answer: By posing as an iron carrier. One end of the molecule grips iron as the bacteria's own iron-scavenging molecules do, and bacteria starved of iron in the body pull it in through their iron-import channels. Soil bacteria got there first with albomycin. Mutations in those channels already let some strains resist it.
cards.move: The easiest way through a guarded door is to look like a delivery.
cards.reference: Zhanel et al., Cefiderocol: a siderophore cephalosporin with activity against carbapenem-resistant and multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacilli, Drugs, 2019

cards.question: Zosurabalpin, a new antibiotic class reported in 2024, jams the machinery that builds bacteria's outer coat. Which bacteria does it kill?
options: Most bacteria that have an outer coat
Mainly gut bacteria such as E. coli
cards.answer: Essentially only Acinetobacter baumannii. It blocks the transporter that carries lipopolysaccharide, the fat-and-sugar molecule of the outer coat, to the surface, and fits only Acinetobacter's version, a drug-resistant hospital killer. The narrowness spares gut bacteria. It also means doctors must identify the culprit before they can prescribe it.
cards.move: A shared part is not a shared weakness if every version is shaped differently.
cards.trap: Expecting a drug aimed at a common structure to hit every owner.
cards.reference: Zampaloni et al., A novel antibiotic class targeting the lipopolysaccharide transporter, Nature, 2024

cards.question: True or false: new antibiotics are usually approved after trials showing they cure more patients than the older drugs they rival?
cards.answer: False. Most pass non-inferiority trials, showing only that the new drug is no worse than an old one beyond a set margin, often 10 percentage points. They mostly enrol patients whose bacteria the old drug still kills, as resistant cases are too scattered to recruit. Drugs meant for superbugs are proven on ordinary infections.
cards.move: Ask who a trial enrolled before trusting what it says about others.
cards.trap: Assuming the trial proved it better on the resistant infections it targets.
cards.source: FDA guidance on complicated urinary infections
cards.reference: US Food and Drug Administration, Complicated Urinary Tract Infections: Developing Drugs for Treatment, Guidance for Industry, 2018

cards.question: True or false: in the first randomised trial of phage therapy for infected burns, the viruses did worse than the standard cream?
cards.answer: True. PhagoBurn, in French and Belgian burn units, assigned 27 patients to a cocktail of 12 viruses that kill Pseudomonas or to silver sulfadiazine cream. Bacteria fell more slowly under phages; the trial stopped early. The cocktail had lost most of its strength before use, so patients got a far weaker dose than planned.
cards.move: Rescues get published; quiet failures of the same method rarely do.
cards.trap: Trusting the steady stream of case reports of patients rescued by phages.
cards.source: Jault et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2019
cards.reference: Jault et al., Efficacy and tolerability of a cocktail of bacteriophages to treat burn wounds infected by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PhagoBurn): a randomised, controlled, double-blind phase 1/2 trial, The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2019

cards.question: What did the US approve in January 2025 that no pain drug had offered for over twenty years?
cards.answer: A new mechanism. Suzetrigine blocks NaV1.8, a sodium channel found mainly in peripheral pain-sensing nerves, so the signal is stopped before it reaches the spinal cord. It works outside the brain, gives no high, and is not a controlled substance. Its approval covers acute pain only, tested after bunion surgery and tummy tucks.
cards.move: Stopping a message at its source spares everything downstream.
cards.reference: https://news.vrtx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/vertex-announces-fda-approval-journavxtm-suzetrigine-first-class

cards.question: True or false: in a trial of 1,652 patients, regular paracetamol sped recovery from acute low back pain no more than placebo?
cards.answer: True. In the Australian PACE trial, median recovery took 17 days on regular paracetamol and 16 on dummy tablets. Most acute back pain settles within weeks whatever is taken, so the pill gets the credit for time. Guidelines that had recommended it first were revised within a few years.
cards.move: Before crediting a remedy, ask how the untreated ones did.
cards.trap: Reading recovery after the tablets as recovery because of them.
cards.reference: Williams et al., Efficacy of paracetamol for acute low-back pain: a double-blind, randomised controlled trial, The Lancet, 2014

cards.question: People born without the Nav1.7 sodium channel feel no pain. What gave one such woman pain in 2015?
cards.answer: Naloxone, the drug that reverses opioid overdoses. Losing Nav1.7 also makes sensory nerves produce more of the body's own opioids, enkephalins. When London researchers blocked them with naloxone, she felt pain for the first time. It helps explain why pure Nav1.7 blockers, long a hoped-for painkiller, disappointed in trials.
cards.move: A missing part can work through what the body builds to cope.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms9967

cards.question: True or false: codeine relieves pain on its own, without the body first turning any of it into morphine?
cards.answer: False. Most of its effect comes from the small share, around a tenth, that the liver enzyme CYP2D6 converts to morphine. Gene variants make some people poor converters, who get little relief, and others ultra-rapid, who can overdose on a normal dose. After child deaths, the FDA barred codeine for under-12s in 2017.
cards.move: The same dose is not the same drug in two different bodies.
cards.trap: Taking codeine for a weaker opioid that acts by itself.
cards.reference: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Safety Communication: FDA restricts use of prescription codeine pain and cough medicines and tramadol pain medicines in children, 2017

cards.question: After surgery, ibuprofen 400 mg has an NNT of 2.5; codeine 60 mg, 12. Per 120 patients, how many more does ibuprofen relieve?
cards.answer: 48 - 10 = 38 more patients.
cards.move: Turn a treatment ratio into people before comparing two options.
cards.trap: Assuming the prescription opioid must beat an over-the-counter pill.
cards.hint: Divide the patients by each NNT, then compare the two results.
steps: NNT is how many must be treated for one extra success beyond placebo.
Ibuprofen: 120 / 2.5 = 48 extra successes.
Codeine: 120 / 12 = 10 extra successes.
48 - 10 = 38 more patients.
cards.reference: https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD008659.pub3/full

cards.question: For a year, patients with chronic back or arthritis pain were given either opioids or non-opioid painkillers. Which group ended with less pain?
cards.answer: The non-opioid group. The SPACE trial randomised 240 US veterans to opioids or to non-opioid drugs, mostly paracetamol and anti-inflammatories, raising doses as needed. After 12 months, function was no different and pain intensity was slightly lower without opioids, 3.5 against 4.0 out of 10. The opioid group reported more side effects.
cards.move: The strongest drug for an afternoon is not the strongest over a year.
cards.trap: The opioid group, since a stronger drug should leave less pain.
cards.reference: Krebs et al., Effect of Opioid vs Nonopioid Medications on Pain-Related Function in Patients With Chronic Back Pain or Hip or Knee Osteoarthritis Pain: The SPACE Randomized Clinical Trial, JAMA, 2018

cards.question: Aspirin disables a platelet for its whole life. Platelets live about 10 days, replaced steadily. How many days until half are new?
cards.move: Ask whether a drug's effect lives in the blood or in what it touched.
cards.trap: Answering in hours, since aspirin itself leaves the blood within an hour.
cards.hint: Platelets have no nucleus, so a blocked one is never repaired; count replacements.
steps: Platelets live about 10 days, so about 10% are replaced each day, the oldest first.
Half the platelets is 50%.
cards.source: Patrono, New England Journal of Medicine, 1994
cards.reference: Patrono, Aspirin as an antiplatelet drug, New England Journal of Medicine, 1994

cards.question: True or false: after Britain limited the size of paracetamol packs in 1998, deaths from paracetamol overdose fell by about 40%?
cards.answer: True. Shops were limited to 16 tablets a pack and pharmacies to 32. Measured against the trend before the law, Hawton and colleagues estimated 43% fewer paracetamol poisoning deaths in England and Wales over the following 11 years, about 765 lives. Many overdoses are impulsive and use whatever is in the cupboard.
cards.move: Small frictions matter most for decisions made within a single hour.
cards.trap: Assuming anyone set on an overdose would simply buy several packs.
cards.reference: Hawton et al., Long term effect of reduced pack sizes of paracetamol on poisoning deaths and liver transplant activity in England and Wales: interrupted time series analyses, BMJ, 2013

cards.question: Why can a heart patient's daily low-dose aspirin stop protecting them if they take ibuprofen first?
cards.answer: Because ibuprofen reaches the target first. Aspirin protects by permanently plugging an enzyme in platelets, COX-1; ibuprofen sits loosely in the same channel and blocks aspirin's way in. When ibuprofen lets go, the aspirin has left the blood. The FDA advised in 2006: ibuprofen at least 30 minutes after aspirin, or 8 hours before.
cards.move: Two harmless habits can cancel each other when they compete for one door.
cards.reference: US Food and Drug Administration, Information for Healthcare Professionals: Concomitant Use of Ibuprofen and Aspirin, 2006

cards.question: Should doctors taper patients off long-term opioids when their pain has been stable on the same dose?
cards.answer: Long-term opioids have never been shown to keep relieving chronic pain beyond a few months, while overdose risk climbs with dose and tolerance builds. A patient stable on a high dose still carries that risk every day. Slow, agreed tapers let some patients discover their pain is no worse without the drug.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, weigh the risk of stopping against the risk of staying.
cards.counterpoint: Tapering is not neutral. In a 2021 study of over 100,000 US patients on stable long-term opioids, those tapered had about 68% more overdoses and more than twice the mental-health crises of those kept on their dose. A patient pushed off a drug they depend on may turn to street supply, which is far deadlier.
cards.reference: Agnoli et al., Association of Dose Tapering With Overdose or Mental Health Crisis Among Patients Prescribed Long-term Opioids, JAMA, 2021

cards.question: What went wrong for the first person treated for an infection with purified penicillin, in Oxford in 1941?
cards.answer: The drug worked and the supply ran out. Albert Alexander, a 43-year-old policeman, improved within a day of his first dose in February 1941. So little penicillin existed that it was extracted from his urine and injected again. When the supply was exhausted after five days the infection returned, and he died in March.
cards.move: A cure that cannot be made in quantity is still only an experiment.
cards.source: Abraham, Chain, Florey et al., The Lancet, 1941
cards.reference: Abraham, Chain, Fletcher, Florey, Gardner, Heatley & Jennings, Further observations on penicillin, The Lancet, 1941

cards.question: What made penicillin cheap enough to mass-produce during the Second World War?
cards.answer: A farm by-product and a rotten melon. At the US Department of Agriculture's laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, Andrew Moyer found in 1941 that corn steep liquor, a waste from starch milling, raised yields about tenfold. A mould from a cantaloupe bought in a Peoria market outproduced strains gathered worldwide. Both went into deep fermentation tanks.
cards.move: The breakthrough that matters is often in the making, not the discovery.
cards.source: American Chemical Society, National Historic Chemical Landmark
cards.reference: American Chemical Society, The Discovery and Development of Penicillin 1928-1945, National Historic Chemical Landmark brochure, 1999

cards.question: About one American in ten reports a penicillin allergy. What share of the whole population is truly allergic?
cards.answer: Under 1%. Many labels date from a childhood rash blamed on the drug but caused by the infection it was treating. True allergy also fades: about 80% of people who have it lose the sensitivity within ten years. The label steers doctors to broader, costlier antibiotics that breed more resistance.
cards.move: Something that happened after a pill was not necessarily caused by it.
cards.trap: Taking the reported figure at face value, since the rash followed the drug.
cards.reference: Shenoy, Macy, Rowe & Blumenthal, Evaluation and management of penicillin allergy: a review, JAMA, 2019

cards.question: True or false: penicillin kills bacteria just as well after they have stopped growing and dividing?
cards.answer: False. Penicillin blocks the enzymes that stitch cross-links into the bacterial cell wall. A growing cell keeps cutting its wall open to expand, and without fresh stitching it bursts. A dormant cell is not building, so it survives. Joseph Bigger called them persisters in 1944: a few can restart an infection after the course ends.
cards.move: A tool that attacks change can do nothing to what stays still.
cards.trap: Picturing an antibiotic as a poison that kills whatever it touches.
cards.reference: Bigger, Treatment of staphylococcal infections with penicillin by intermittent sterilisation, The Lancet, 1944

cards.question: Penicillin G leaves the blood with a half-life of about 30 minutes. What percentage of a dose remains after 3 hours?
cards.answer: 1/64 = 0.0156, so about 1.6% remains.
cards.move: When something halves on a schedule, count the halvings before guessing what is left.
cards.trap: Guessing a quarter or more, underestimating how fast six halvings shrink a dose.
cards.hint: Count how many half-lives fit into three hours.
steps: 3 hours is 180 minutes, and 180 / 30 = 6 half-lives.
After 6 halvings the fraction left is 1 / 2^6 = 1/64.
1/64 = 0.0156, so about 1.6% remains.
cards.source: Goodman & Gilman's Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics
cards.reference: Brunton, Hilal-Dandan & Knollmann (eds), Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2018

cards.question: Why was probenecid, a drug now taken for gout, first developed around 1950?
cards.answer: To make scarce penicillin last longer. The kidneys pump penicillin actively into the urine, clearing it within hours. Karl Beyer's team at Sharp & Dohme designed a molecule that competes for the same pump, so penicillin stays in the blood longer and at higher levels. It also stops the kidneys reclaiming uric acid, hence gout.
cards.move: When supply is short, slow the leak before building more.
cards.source: Beyer et al., American Journal of Physiology, 1951
cards.reference: Beyer, Russo, Tillson, Miller, Verwey & Gass, 'Benemid', p-(di-n-propylsulfamyl)-benzoic acid: its renal affinity and its elimination, American Journal of Physiology, 1951

cards.question: Why did attempts to repeat Fleming's 1928 plate, by dropping mould spores onto bacteria, keep failing?
cards.answer: Because penicillin kills only bacteria that are growing; established colonies shrug it off. Decades later Ronald Hare showed the mould had to get going first. A cool spell in London that summer let it spread while the staphylococci barely grew; warmer days then brought the bacteria up around a mould already making its drug.
cards.move: When a lucky result will not repeat, ask what the conditions were that day.
cards.reference: Hare, The Birth of Penicillin and the Disarming of Microbes, George Allen & Unwin, 1970

cards.question: After more than 80 years of use, which of these bacteria does plain penicillin still almost always kill?
cards.answer: Streptococcus pyogenes. Most Staphylococcus aureus now makes an enzyme that cuts penicillin, and gonorrhoea outgrew it by the end of the 1980s. The strep behind sore throats and scarlet fever has produced no strain resistant by standard tests, though some needing more drug were reported in 2020. Its first-choice drug is still penicillin.
cards.move: The famous early case is rarely the best guide to the present.
cards.trap: Picking staph, the bacterium penicillin is famous for killing first.
cards.source: Horn et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases, 1998
cards.reference: Horn, Zabriskie et al., Why have group A streptococci remained susceptible to penicillin? Report on a symposium, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 1998

cards.question: US penicillin output rose from 21 billion units in 1943 to 6.8 trillion in 1945. Roughly how many months did output take to double?
cards.answer: 24 months / 8.3 doublings = about 2.9 months per doubling.
cards.move: Turn a startling growth factor into doublings before judging its pace.
cards.trap: Guessing about a year per doubling, the pace of ordinary factories.
cards.hint: Find the overall growth factor, then ask how many doublings make it.
steps: 6,800 billion / 21 billion = about 324.
2^8 = 256 and 2^9 = 512, so 324 is about 8.3 doublings.
24 months / 8.3 doublings = about 2.9 months per doubling.
cards.reference: https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1556

cards.question: True or false: despite a vast wartime effort, chemists first built a penicillin entirely from scratch only in 1957?
cards.answer: True. During the war about 1,000 chemists in 39 Allied laboratories tried to synthesise it and failed: its four-atom beta-lactam ring was too strained for the methods of the day. John Sheehan at MIT completed penicillin V in 1957. Penicillin is still grown by mould in fermentation tanks, with chemists reshaping its side chain afterwards.
cards.move: What a living cell makes easily can still defeat a whole laboratory.
cards.trap: Assuming a drug this vital was soon made by chemists instead.
cards.reference: Sheehan, The Enchanted Ring: The Untold Story of Penicillin, MIT Press, 1982

cards.question: Does a placebo still work when the patient is told plainly that it is a sugar pill?
cards.answer: In some trials, yes. In a 2010 Harvard study, 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome got nothing, or pills from a bottle labelled placebo. After three weeks, 59% of pill-takers reported adequate relief against 35% of the others. The twice-daily ritual did work once credited to deception.
cards.move: Test whether the secret part of a ritual is the part that works.
cards.reference: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0015591

cards.question: True or false: the improvement in a drug trial's placebo group measures the placebo effect?
cards.answer: False. Patients enrol at their worst, and many drift back towards their usual level whatever they take. Only a third group given nothing separates these. When a 2001 review pooled 130 trials with such a group, placebo effects were small, mostly on pain and other self-reported outcomes.
cards.move: People seek help at their worst, so almost anything looks like it helped.
cards.trap: Crediting the dummy pill with every gain seen in its group.
cards.reference: Hróbjartsson & Gøtzsche, Is the placebo powerless? An analysis of clinical trials comparing placebo with no treatment, New England Journal of Medicine, 2001
