cards.question: In 1978, what cancelled the pain relief that dummy injections gave patients after wisdom-tooth surgery?
cards.answer: Naloxone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors. In a San Francisco trial, patients whose pain eased after a placebo felt it return when given naloxone, while non-responders did not get worse. So the relief ran partly on the brain's own opioids, endorphins. A saline injection had a chemistry that a drug could switch off.
cards.move: Something that can be blocked by a drug is not imaginary.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/80579/

cards.question: Patients who quit statins over side effects took statin, dummy and no pills in rotating months. How much statin-month symptom burden appeared on dummy pills?
cards.answer: About 90%. The 2020 SAMSON trial gave 60 people twelve monthly bottles, four each of atorvastatin, placebo and nothing, and they scored symptoms daily. Empty months were easy; dummy months hurt almost as much as statin months. Shown their own charts, about half went back on statins.
cards.move: Compare the bad months with the months you took nothing at all.
cards.trap: Believing aches that began with the drug must come from the drug.
cards.reference: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2031173

cards.question: Should doctors prescribe placebos openly, telling patients they are inert pills, for conditions like chronic pain?
cards.answer: Honest placebos remove the old objection, deception. Trials in irritable bowel syndrome and chronic back pain found real relief, and the pills carry no drug risks, no addiction and almost no cost. For pain that nothing else touches, withholding a harmless option that helps some patients is harder to defend than offering it.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether self-reported relief counts as cure decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The trials are small, short and unblinded: patients know they got a pill and report on their own symptoms, so expectation inflates exactly the outcome measured. Effects on objective measures are weak. Prescribing sugar pills also spends scarce consultation time and risks signalling that the complaint is imaginary, or delaying a treatment that works.
cards.reference: Carvalho et al., Open-label placebo treatment in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial, Pain, 2016

cards.question: A 2014 review gathered 53 trials comparing a real operation with a sham one. In about how many was the real operation no better?
cards.answer: About half. In 27 of the 53 trials the sham, often an incision or a scope with nothing done inside, worked as well as the procedure; patients improved after the sham in 39 of them. Where surgery did win, the margin was usually small. Several of the operations tested had been routine for years.
cards.move: A procedure's record of success means little until someone has faked it.
cards.trap: About 1 in 10, since cutting and repairing seems too physical to fake.

cards.question: True or false: in nerve-pain drug trials from 1990 to 2013, placebo responses grew in European and Asian trials as in American ones?
cards.answer: False. Tuttle and colleagues found the rise only in US trials, where placebo groups improved steadily while drug groups stayed flat, shrinking the drugs' advantage. Trials elsewhere showed no such rise. US trials had grown larger and longer over those years, which points to how trials were run, not to more suggestible patients.
cards.move: When a result drifts over time, check what changed in how it was measured.
cards.trap: True, treating the placebo response as a fixed property of a pill.
cards.reference: https://journals.lww.com/pain/abstract/2015/12000/increasing_placebo_responses_over_time_in_u_s_.27.aspx

cards.question: Why does the same painkiller dose relieve less pain when a hidden machine delivers it than when a doctor gives it openly?
cards.answer: Because part of any drug's effect is knowing it has arrived. In studies by Fabrizio Benedetti's group in Turin, surgical patients whose painkiller came by a hidden, pre-programmed infusion needed larger doses for the same relief as those who watched it given. Every open dose carries a placebo inside it; hidden dosing strips it out.
cards.move: Every visible treatment is two treatments: the substance and the scene around it.
cards.reference: Colloca, Lopiano, Lanotte & Benedetti, Overt versus covert treatment for pain, anxiety, and Parkinson's disease, The Lancet Neurology, 2004

cards.question: In a pain trial, 40% on the drug and 30% on placebo got relief. What percentage of the drug's responders owe it to the drug?
cards.move: Subtract what the dummy achieved before praising what the real thing did.
cards.trap: Answering 100%, crediting the drug with every patient who got better.
cards.hint: Ask how many of the drug group would have responded to a dummy pill.
steps: Of 100 patients on the drug, 40 get the relief.
About 30 of them would have got it from placebo, as the other arm did.

diagram.label: patients on the drug
diagram.caption: Of 40 relieved, 30 would have eased on a dummy anyway: only 10 owe it to the drug.

cards.reference: Laupacis, Sackett & Roberts, An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment, New England Journal of Medicine, 1988

cards.question: Volunteers took the painkiller ketorolac for two days, then a dummy pill that still eased their pain. Which drug switched that relief off?
cards.answer: Rimonabant. In Benedetti's tourniquet-pain experiments, naloxone blocked a placebo that followed morphine but not one that followed ketorolac, which is not an opioid. In 2011 the cannabinoid blocker switched that one off instead. The brain had learnt to echo the drug it had been given, by a different chemical route each time.
cards.move: A learnt response can copy the path of whatever taught it.
cards.trap: Naloxone, because placebo pain relief is known to run on opioids.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/nm.2435

cards.question: When was an enzyme that destroys penicillin first described in print?
cards.answer: In 1940, before any patient had been treated. Edward Abraham and Ernst Chain, from the same Oxford group that purified the drug, reported in Nature that extracts of E. coli broke penicillin down. The first patient with an infection was treated weeks later, in February 1941. The counter-move was in print before the first cure.
cards.move: Look for the counter-move before celebrating the move.
cards.reference: Abraham & Chain, An enzyme from bacteria able to destroy penicillin, Nature, 1940

cards.question: In 2019, roughly how many deaths worldwide were directly caused by drug-resistant bacterial infections?
cards.answer: About 1.3 million. The Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance study estimated 1.27 million deaths directly attributable to resistance in 2019, and 4.95 million in which a resistant infection played a part. The much-quoted 10 million is a 2014 projection for 2050, not a count. Even so, resistance already killed more people than HIV or malaria.
cards.move: Before repeating a big number, check whether it is a count or a forecast.
cards.trap: Recalling the famous 10 million, a forecast for 2050, as today's toll.
cards.reference: Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators (Murray et al.), Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019: a systematic analysis, The Lancet, 2022

cards.question: True or false: most antimicrobials sold worldwide go into farm animals rather than people?
cards.answer: True. A 2017 estimate put about 73% of global antimicrobial sales into animals raised for food, often in low daily doses to speed growth or to prevent disease in crowded herds. Low, steady doses favour resistant bacteria. Much of it is mixed into feed or drinking water, dosing a whole barn at once.
cards.move: Find the biggest user before blaming the most visible one.
cards.trap: Picturing prescriptions for people, the use everyone has seen.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aao1495

cards.question: Why did sulphonamide resistance in British E. coli fail to fall when prescriptions dropped by 97%?
cards.answer: Because the resistance gene was not travelling alone. UK prescribing fell through the 1990s, yet resistant E. coli from London patients rose from about 40% in 1991 to 46% in 1999. The gene sits on plasmids, mobile loops of DNA, beside genes for drugs still in use, which kept selecting the whole package.
cards.move: Stopping one cause changes little if the result is bundled with another.
cards.reference: Enne, Livermore, Stephens & Hall, Persistence of sulphonamide resistance in Escherichia coli in the UK despite national prescribing restriction, The Lancet, 2001

cards.question: Why did a gene reported in Chinese pigs in 2015 alarm doctors worldwide?
cards.answer: It beat colistin, a last-resort drug, and sat on a plasmid that bacteria swap. Colistin, an old drug sidelined for harming kidneys, had been revived against superbugs, while farms fed it to pigs by the tonne. The gene, mcr-1, soon turned up on several continents; China banned colistin in animal feed in 2017.
cards.move: A reserve kept for emergencies is only reserved if every user agrees.
cards.source: Liu et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2016
cards.reference: Liu et al., Emergence of plasmid-mediated colistin resistance mechanism MCR-1 in animals and human beings in China, The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2016

cards.question: How can a hospital sink pass resistant bacteria to patients who never use it?
cards.answer: Through its drain. Bacteria settle in the slime lining the U-bend and grow up the pipe, about 2.5 cm a day in a 2017 Virginia study. Once the film reaches the strainer, a running tap splashes it up to 76 cm onto whatever sits beside the basin. Some outbreaks ended only when pipes were replaced.
cards.move: Look for the reservoir that cleaning never reaches.
cards.source: Kotay et al., Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 2017
cards.reference: Kotay, Chai, Guilford, Barry & Mathers, Spread from the sink to the patient: in situ study using green fluorescent protein (GFP)-expressing Escherichia coli to model bacterial dissemination from hand-washing sink-trap reservoirs, Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 2017

cards.question: A TB cavity holds 10^8 bacteria; 1 in 10^6 resist drug A, 1 in 10^8 B. One bacterium resisting both per how many million cavities?
cards.answer: So one cavity in 10^6, that is 1 million.
cards.move: Two independent locks multiply the difficulty only if both are used together.
cards.trap: Seeing 100 resisters to drug A per cavity and expecting double ones.
cards.hint: Resistance to each drug arises separately, so the chances multiply.
steps: Chance one bacterium resists both: 10^-6 x 10^-8 = 10^-14.
Expected per cavity: 10^8 x 10^-14 = 10^-6.
So one cavity in 10^6, that is 1 million.
cards.source: Iseman, A Clinician's Guide to Tuberculosis, 2000
cards.reference: Iseman, A Clinician's Guide to Tuberculosis, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2000

cards.question: Should doctors stop telling patients to finish the whole antibiotic course even after they feel better?
cards.answer: The rule has little evidence behind it. Resistance is bred mostly in the harmless bacteria living on and in the body, which meet the drug every extra day, not in the infection itself. Trials keep finding shorter courses as good as long ones for pneumonia and urinary infections. Every needless day is more exposure.
cards.move: The decider is whether patients can be trusted with a rule that needs judgement.
cards.counterpoint: Patients judge feeling better poorly, and stopping early is not the same as a shorter course tested in a trial. For some infections, such as tuberculosis and streptococcal sore throat, stopping early does bring relapse or complications. A simple, universal message gets followed; a message to stop when better may become stop whenever.
cards.reference: Llewelyn et al., The antibiotic course has had its day, BMJ, 2017

cards.question: In a Dutch study, what share of travellers returning from southern Asia newly carried gut bacteria resistant to most penicillins and cephalosporins?
cards.answer: About 3 in 4. Of Dutch travellers who tested clear before leaving, 34% came home carrying ESBL bacteria, whose enzymes destroy most penicillins and cephalosporins; of those back from southern Asia, 75%. These were healthy tourists, not patients. Most carriers had lost the bacteria within a few months.
cards.move: Where a problem is most visible is not where most of it lives.
cards.trap: Picturing resistant bacteria as caught in hospitals, not on holiday.
cards.source: Arcilla et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2017
cards.reference: Arcilla et al., Import and spread of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae by international travellers (COMBAT study): a prospective, multicentre cohort study, The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2017

cards.question: Across Europe, about 1 in 6 Staphylococcus aureus blood infections resist methicillin. In the Netherlands, roughly what share do?
cards.answer: About 1 in 100. Since the late 1980s Dutch hospitals have practised search and destroy: patients at risk, including anyone treated in a foreign hospital, are swabbed on arrival and isolated until cleared, and carrier staff stay off wards until treated. Parts of southern and eastern Europe run at 1 in 3 or more.
cards.move: An average across many places says little about any one of them.
cards.trap: Assuming a rich, crowded European country sits near the European average.
cards.reference: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, Antimicrobial resistance in the EU/EEA (EARS-Net), Annual Epidemiological Report for 2019, 2020

cards.question: What was the surgical robot now found in thousands of hospitals first designed to do?
cards.answer: Let a surgeon operate on a wounded soldier from a safe distance. SRI International developed telepresence surgery in the 1980s and 1990s with US Army and DARPA funding, picturing a surgeon at a field hospital's controls and the robot beside the casualty. Intuitive Surgical took it commercial in 1995; hospitals, not battlefields, bought it.
cards.move: A tool built for one problem often earns its living solving another.
cards.reference: https://www.sri.com/hoi/telerobotic-surgery/

cards.question: What did it take for a surgeon in New York to remove a gallbladder in Strasbourg in 2001?
cards.answer: A private line under the Atlantic. Delay is the enemy of remote surgery, so France Telecom provided a dedicated fibre-optic connection that held the lag steady at about 155 milliseconds; ordinary internet delays jump about unpredictably. Jacques Marescaux worked a ZEUS robot's controls, and the 68-year-old patient went home 48 hours later.
cards.move: When acting at a distance, the delay matters more than the kilometres.
cards.reference: Marescaux et al., Transatlantic robot-assisted telesurgery, Nature, 2001

cards.question: True or false: a robot has stitched two ends of intestine together inside living pigs without a surgeon guiding its movements?
cards.answer: True. In 2022 a Johns Hopkins team reported that STAR, the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot, sewed keyhole bowel joins in four pigs, tracking tissue that shifted as the animals breathed. In comparison tests its stitches were more evenly spaced than surgeons'. Surgeons set up each operation and supervised, but did not steer the needle.
cards.move: What a familiar machine does is not the limit of what machines can do.
cards.trap: Assuming surgical robots only ever copy a surgeon's hand movements.
cards.reference: Saeidi et al., Autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis, Science Robotics, 2022

cards.question: In the first large randomised trial of robotic versus standard keyhole surgery for rectal cancer, published in 2017, what did the robot improve?
cards.answer: No outcome significantly. The ROLARR trial randomised 471 patients: conversion to open surgery was 8.1% with the robot and 12.2% without, a gap within chance, and no complication or function measure differed. Robots shine against open surgery, but the fair control is ordinary keyhole surgery. A larger Chinese trial in 2022 did report some gains.
cards.move: Compare a new tool with the best old one, not the worst.
cards.trap: Crediting the robot with gains that keyhole surgery alone already delivers.
cards.reference: Jayne et al., Effect of robotic-assisted vs conventional laparoscopic surgery on risk of conversion to open laparotomy among patients undergoing resection for rectal cancer: the ROLARR randomized clinical trial, JAMA, 2017

cards.question: Should public hospitals buy surgical robots while trials show little gain over standard keyhole surgery?
cards.answer: Trials capture the early part of a learning curve, not the mature technique. Robots give a steady, magnified 3D view and wristed instruments, and spare surgeons' necks and backs over long careers. Hospitals without them lose trainees and staff to those with them, and later designs are refined only by centres using today's.
cards.move: The decider is whether surgeon comfort and training count as outcomes worth paying for.
cards.counterpoint: A robot costs more than a million pounds, plus instruments and servicing for every operation, and in randomised trials against ordinary keyhole surgery patients often did no better. In a budget that also pays for nurses and scanners, money spent on appeal is money taken from care with proven benefit. Buy when the evidence arrives.
cards.source: Sheetz, Claflin & Dimick, JAMA Network Open, 2020
cards.reference: Sheetz, Claflin & Dimick, Trends in the adoption of robotic surgery for common surgical procedures, JAMA Network Open, 2020

cards.question: What could surgeons at the controls of the market-leading surgical robot not feel until 2024?
cards.answer: How hard they were pushing or pulling. For over two decades the console sent motion but no force back, so surgeons judged tension by eye, watching tissue blanch and stretch and sutures bite. The da Vinci 5, cleared in the US in 2024, finally sent force back to the hands through some instruments.
cards.move: When a sense is missing, people quietly rebuild it from another.
cards.reference: Okamura, Haptic feedback in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery, Current Opinion in Urology, 2009

cards.question: A da Vinci robot's wristed instruments carry a chip that counts their uses. Roughly how many operations before one stops working?
cards.answer: About 10 to 20. The maker programs each instrument with a fixed number of lives, long about 10 and later raised for some, after which the robot refuses it. Firms that reset the counters for hospitals have fought the maker in US antitrust courts. A clamp can retire with nothing wrong with it.
cards.move: Ask whether a tool wears out or is simply told to stop.
cards.trap: Picturing robotic tools lasting like ordinary steel instruments, resterilised for years.
cards.reference: Intuitive Surgical, Inc., Annual Report on Form 10-K for fiscal year 2023, US Securities and Exchange Commission, 2024

cards.question: US reports of injuries and deaths linked to surgical robots rose steeply from 2007 to 2013. Per operation, what happened to them?
options: They fell to about a tenth
cards.answer: They stayed roughly flat. Searching the FDA's adverse-event database, Alemzadeh and colleagues counted over 10,000 reports from 2000 to 2013, including 144 deaths, while robotic operations multiplied. Divided by procedures, injuries and deaths per operation held steady from 2007. Reporting is voluntary, so true counts are higher.
cards.move: A rising count means nothing until it is divided by how often.
cards.trap: Reading more reports of harm as more danger in each operation.
cards.reference: Alemzadeh, Raman, Leveson, Kalbarczyk & Iyer, Adverse events in robotic surgery: a retrospective study of 14 years of FDA data, PLoS ONE, 2016

cards.question: A $1.5 million robot lasts 7 years, needs $150,000 of servicing yearly and does 300 operations a year. Fixed cost per operation, in dollars?
cards.answer: Per operation: 364,000 / 300 = about 1,200 dollars.
cards.move: Spread a big purchase over every use before calling it cheap or dear.
cards.trap: Forgetting the servicing, which adds about 70% to each year's cost.
cards.hint: Turn the price into a yearly cost first, then share the year's cost out.
steps: Purchase spread over 7 years: 1,500,000 / 7 = about 214,000 a year.
Add servicing: 214,000 + 150,000 = about 364,000 a year.
Per operation: 364,000 / 300 = about 1,200 dollars.
cards.reference: Barbash & Glied, New technology and health care costs: the case of robot-assisted surgery, New England Journal of Medicine, 2010

cards.question: True or false: in a 2018 trial for early cervical cancer, women given keyhole or robotic surgery died more often than after open surgery?
cards.answer: True. The LACC trial randomised 631 women to open or minimally invasive radical hysterectomy, one in six of the latter by robot. At three years 99.0% of the open group were alive, against 93.8%, and cancer returned more often. In 2019 the FDA warned that robots were unproven for such cancer operations.
cards.move: A gentler way in can still be worse at the job itself.
cards.trap: Assuming smaller cuts can only mean smaller harm.

diagram.caption: 99.0% against 93.8% alive looks close; the deaths differ sixfold.

cards.reference: Ramirez et al., Minimally invasive versus abdominal radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer, New England Journal of Medicine, 2018

cards.question: Among 20-year-olds with no back pain at all, what share show disc degeneration on a spine scan?
cards.answer: About 1 in 3. A 2015 review of over 3,000 pain-free people put disc degeneration at 37% at age 20, rising to 96% at 80; disc bulges ran from 30% to 84%. Such findings are often normal ageing. A report listing them can describe almost any spine, sore or not.
cards.move: Before blaming a finding, ask how often it turns up in the healthy.
cards.trap: Assuming anything a scan reports as abnormal must be rare in healthy people.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25430861/

cards.question: Why is an MRI scanner's magnet left on even when nobody is being scanned?
cards.answer: Because turning it off is slow and costly. Its superconducting coils sit in liquid helium, where current circulates for years unpowered. Shutting down in a hurry means a quench: the helium boils off through a vent. In 2001 a steel oxygen cylinder, pulled into a live scanner in New York, killed a 6-year-old boy.
cards.move: A machine that is always on needs rules for when it looks off.
cards.reference: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/boy-killed-in-freak-mri-accident/

cards.question: True or false: after thyroid ultrasound spread through South Korean health check-ups, deaths from thyroid cancer fell sharply?
cards.answer: False. Between 1993 and 2011 diagnoses rose about fifteenfold, making it the country's most common cancer, yet the death rate from it stayed flat. Most tumours found were small papillary cancers that would never have harmed anyone. Nearly all were treated anyway, most by removing the thyroid, which means hormone pills for life.
cards.move: Finding more of a disease is not the same as preventing its harm.
cards.trap: Assuming that finding more cancers early must save more lives.
cards.reference: Ahn, Kim & Welch, Korea's thyroid-cancer epidemic: screening and overdiagnosis, New England Journal of Medicine, 2014

cards.question: Why does an ultrasound probe need a layer of gel against the skin?
cards.answer: Because a thin film of air would reflect almost all the sound back. Sound crosses a boundary well only when both sides resist it similarly, and air is thousands of times less resistant than tissue: about 99.9% bounces at a tissue-air boundary. The same law keeps ultrasound from seeing through air-filled lungs or gassy bowel.
cards.move: A gap of almost nothing can block what a wall of flesh lets through.
cards.reference: Szabo, Diagnostic Ultrasound Imaging: Inside Out, Elsevier Academic Press, 2004

cards.question: Years after MRI scans with gadolinium contrast dye, where has some of the metal been found?
cards.answer: In the brain. In 2014 Japanese radiologists saw deep brain regions brighten on plain scans in step with the number of past contrast doses; autopsies later confirmed gadolinium there. No harm has been shown, but the FDA added warnings in 2017, and Europe suspended several linear agents, the kind that release it more easily.
cards.move: Cleared from the blood is not the same as gone from the body.
cards.trap: Trusting the textbook line that the kidneys flush it out within hours.
cards.reference: https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/ucm589213.htm

cards.question: Enough childhood head CT scans can triple later brain tumour risk. Per 10,000 head scans in under-10s, how many extra tumours within ten years?
cards.answer: About 1. Pearce and colleagues followed about 180,000 young people scanned in Britain from 1985 to 2002. A brain dose of about 60 mGy, two or three scans, roughly tripled the risk; but brain tumours in children are so rare that this adds about one case per 10,000 head scans within ten years.
cards.move: A tripled risk means little until you know how small it started.
cards.trap: About 300, because a tripled risk sounds like a large share.
cards.reference: Pearce et al., Radiation exposure from CT scans in childhood and subsequent risk of leukaemia and brain tumours: a retrospective cohort study, The Lancet, 2012

cards.question: About how many standard chest X-rays deliver the same radiation dose as one CT scan of the abdomen?
cards.answer: 8 / 0.02 = 400 chest X-rays.
cards.move: Put two risks in the same unit before calling them similar.
cards.trap: Guessing a handful, picturing both as one quick picture.
cards.hint: Put both doses in millisieverts, the unit of radiation dose, then divide.
steps: A single chest X-ray taken from behind: about 0.02 mSv.
A CT scan of the abdomen: about 8 mSv.
8 / 0.02 = 400 chest X-rays.
cards.reference: Mettler, Huda, Yoshizumi & Mahesh, Effective doses in radiology and diagnostic nuclear medicine: a catalog, Radiology, 2008

cards.question: Kidney injury often follows a CT scan with contrast dye. Compared with matched patients scanned without dye, how often does it happen?
cards.answer: About equally often. McDonald and colleagues at the Mayo Clinic matched thousands of patients on illness and kidney function and found no difference in kidney injury; a follow-up found none in dialysis or death. Very ill people need urgent CTs, and ill kidneys falter anyway. Caution now centres on kidneys already badly failing.
cards.move: Before blaming what came first, ask what brought the person there.
cards.trap: About twice as often, blaming the dye for injuries that merely followed it.
cards.reference: McDonald et al., Intravenous contrast material-induced nephropathy: causal or coincident phenomenon?, Radiology, 2013

cards.question: Why is a radiologist who has just spotted one abnormality on a scan more likely to miss a second?
cards.answer: Because finding something tends to end the search. Called satisfaction of search, it was shown in experiments where adding an obvious abnormality to a film lowered radiologists' detection of a subtler one elsewhere on the same image. Checklists and a deliberate second sweep are the usual defences. The broken rib hides the lung nodule.
cards.move: After the first find, search again as if nothing had been found.
cards.reference: Berbaum et al., Satisfaction of search in diagnostic radiology, Investigative Radiology, 1990

cards.question: What mainly limits how fast an MRI scanner may switch its gradient magnetic fields on and off?
cards.answer: Twitching the patient's nerves. A magnetic field that changes quickly induces electric currents in the body, and past a threshold they fire peripheral nerves, felt as tingling or twitches. The IEC safety standard caps the rate of change well below levels that could stimulate the heart. Heating limits the scanner's radio pulses, not its gradients.
cards.move: The limit on a machine is often the body it is pointed at.
cards.trap: Heating the tissue, the best-known safety limit of MRI.
cards.reference: International Electrotechnical Commission, IEC 60601-2-33: Particular requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of magnetic resonance equipment for medical diagnosis, 2010

cards.question: Among women admitted to US hospitals with a confirmed heart attack, how many had no chest pain?
cards.answer: About 2 in 5. In over 1.1 million heart-attack patients from 1994 to 2006, 42% of women and 31% of men arrived without chest pain, reporting breathlessness, nausea, sweating or fatigue instead. Those without chest pain waited longer for care and died more often in hospital, especially younger women.
cards.move: The famous version of a warning is not the usual version.
cards.trap: Picturing the film heart attack, a man clutching his chest.
cards.reference: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1355992

cards.question: In a 1975 study of new hospital outpatients, what pointed doctors to the correct diagnosis most often?
cards.answer: The patient's own account. In a British clinic, the referral letter and history alone gave the diagnosis finally accepted in 66 of 80 patients, about 83%. Physical examination added it in 7 more, laboratory tests in a further 7. The most powerful instrument in the clinic was a doctor asking questions and listening.
cards.move: Ask the person who lived it before measuring anything.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1148666/

cards.question: Why does appendicitis pain usually start around the navel before settling low on the right?
cards.answer: Because two nerve systems report it in turn. Early swelling stretches the appendix, whose gut nerves enter the spinal cord at the same level as the skin around the navel, so the brain places the pain vaguely there. Later it irritates the lining of the abdominal wall, which has precise nerves, and the pain moves.
cards.move: Where it hurts and where the trouble is are two separate questions.
cards.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
cards.reference: Williams, O'Connell & McCaskie (eds), Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th edition, CRC Press, 2018

cards.question: When 23 online symptom checkers were tested on standard patient cases, how often did they name the right diagnosis first?
cards.answer: About a third of the time. A 2015 Harvard audit fed them 45 written cases; the correct diagnosis came first in 34% and in the top 20 in 58%. Triage advice leaned cautious, sending people to doctors for problems safe to treat at home. A list of twenty guesses reads like an answer.
cards.move: A long list of possibilities is not a diagnosis.
cards.reference: Semigran, Linder, Gidengil & Mehrotra, Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study, BMJ, 2015

cards.question: True or false: a fever happens because infection makes the body produce more heat than it can shed?
cards.answer: False. Signals from the immune system make the brain raise its thermostat, via a messenger called prostaglandin E2, and the body then shivers and narrows skin vessels to reach the new setting. That is why a rising fever feels cold. Ibuprofen and paracetamol reset the thermostat, which is why they do little for heatstroke.
cards.move: A body heading somewhere on purpose looks broken to an outsider.
cards.trap: Picturing fever as overheating, like an engine that runs too hot.
cards.reference: Dinarello & Porat, Fever, in Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 20th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2018

cards.question: A famous 1965 study found a third of patients diagnosed with hysteria later proved to have physical disease. What did later studies find?
cards.answer: Far fewer: about 4%. A 2005 review of 27 studies by Jon Stone and colleagues found that misdiagnosis of such functional symptoms, real but without structural damage, fell from 29% in the 1950s to about 4% from the 1970s on. That is no worse than for other neurological and psychiatric diagnoses.
cards.move: An old error rate can outlive the conditions that produced it.
cards.reference: Stone et al., Systematic review of misdiagnosis of conversion symptoms and hysteria, BMJ, 2005

cards.question: True or false: when a patient consults a GP about a headache, the chance it comes from a brain tumour is about 1 in 100?
cards.answer: False. It is about ten times smaller. Using UK GP records of 3,505 brain tumour patients and 17,173 controls, Hamilton and Kernick put it at 0.09%, about 1 in 1,100. Headache is common and brain tumours rare, so tumour headaches sit among thousands of ordinary ones. New neurological signs shift the odds far more.
cards.move: A sign common in a rare disease can still say almost nothing alone.
cards.trap: True, because headache is the textbook first sign of a tumour.
cards.source: Hamilton & Kernick, Br J Gen Pract, 2007
cards.reference: https://bjgp.org/content/57/542/695.short

cards.question: True or false: in Britain's spring 2020 Covid wave, losing smell or taste predicted a positive test better than fever did?
cards.answer: True. Among symptom-app users who were tested, 65% of positives reported loss of smell and taste, against 22% of negatives; it was the strongest single predictor, ahead of fever and persistent cough. Britain added it to the official symptom list only in May 2020, after weeks of telling people to watch for fever and cough.
cards.move: The symptom everyone watches for is not always the one that sorts cases.
cards.trap: False, because fever and cough were the famous signs of Covid.
cards.reference: Menni et al., Real-time tracking of self-reported symptoms to predict potential COVID-19, Nature Medicine, 2020

cards.question: Kidney cancer's textbook triad is blood in the urine, pain in the side and a lump you can feel. How many patients have all three?
cards.answer: Under 1 in 10. Each sign appears in only a minority of patients, and all three together mostly in advanced disease. Most kidney cancers are now found by chance, on scans done for something else, before any symptom at all. The textbook triad describes the late case that doctors of an earlier era saw most.
cards.move: Every extra detail in a classic picture makes fewer real cases fit it.
cards.trap: About half, since each of the three is the classic sign.
cards.source: Holland-Frei Cancer Medicine, renal cancer chapter
cards.reference: Kufe et al. (eds), Holland-Frei Cancer Medicine, 6th edition, BC Decker, 2003

cards.question: In a Belgian study of 3,890 children seen by family doctors, which clue to serious infection stood out as unusually powerful?
cards.answer: The doctor's gut feeling that something was wrong, even when the clinical assessment said the illness was not severe. That feeling was about 25 times as common in seriously ill children as in the rest, though the margin of error was wide. It was often set off by parents saying this illness felt different.
cards.move: An unease you cannot yet explain is still evidence worth writing down.
cards.source: Van den Bruel et al., BMJ, 2012

cards.question: Where did the drug that made organ transplants routine in the 1980s come from?
cards.answer: A bag of Norwegian soil. In 1969 a Sandoz biologist, Hans Peter Frey, collected soil samples on holiday on the Hardangervidda plateau. A fungus from one, Tolypocladium inflatum, made a compound that disappointed as an antifungal; in 1972 Jean-François Borel found it damped the immune system. It became ciclosporin.
cards.move: A compound that fails one test deserves to meet a different one.
cards.source: Svarstad et al., Biodiversity and Conservation, 2000
cards.reference: Svarstad, Bugge & Dhillion, From Norway to Novartis: cyclosporin from Tolypocladium inflatum in an open access bioprospecting regime, Biodiversity and Conservation, 2000

cards.question: True or false: in a kidney transplant, the failed kidneys are taken out and the new one goes in their place?
cards.answer: False. The donor kidney is usually placed low in the front of the abdomen, just above the groin, and joined to blood vessels running to the leg and to the bladder. The patient's own kidneys are normally left where they are. Someone who has had three transplants can be carrying five kidneys.
cards.move: Replacing a part need not mean putting the new one in the same place.
cards.trap: Assuming a transplant is a straight swap, like replacing a car part.
cards.reference: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-transplant/what-happens/

cards.question: How often does a healthy person die as a result of the operation to donate a kidney?
cards.answer: About 3 in 10,000. A study of more than 80,000 US living donors from 1994 to 2009 found surgical death within 90 days at 3.1 per 10,000, a rate steady over 15 years. Risk was higher in men and in donors with high blood pressure. Long-term survival matched similar healthy non-donors.
cards.move: Judge a risk by its measured rate, not by how drastic the act sounds.
cards.trap: Guessing 1 in 100, since giving away an organ sounds gravely dangerous.
cards.reference: Segev et al., Perioperative mortality and long-term survival following live kidney donation, JAMA, 2010

cards.question: Why did the pig that gave the first pig heart transplanted into a living person, in 2022, need ten gene edits?
cards.answer: Because human blood attacks pig tissue within minutes. Three pig genes for surface sugars, alpha-gal chief among them, were knocked out, since humans carry antibodies to them. Six human genes were added to calm clotting and inflammation, and a growth gene was disabled so the heart would not keep growing. David Bennett lived two months.
cards.move: To move something into hostile ground, first strip off what gets it noticed.
cards.reference: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2201422

cards.question: A donated heart must be transplanted within about four to six hours. How long can a donated kidney wait on ice?
cards.answer: A day or more. Kidneys tolerate cold storage far better than hearts, commonly up to 24 to 36 hours, though each extra hour worsens results. A patient whose new kidney starts slowly can stay on dialysis meanwhile, a safety net no heart recipient has. The spare hours let kidneys be matched carefully and flown far.
cards.move: Before applying one deadline to everything, ask what each item can tolerate.
cards.trap: Carrying the heart's few hours over to every organ.
cards.source: Jing et al., Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/aps2017182

cards.question: How did Boston surgeons check that two brothers were truly identical before the first lasting kidney transplant, in 1954?
cards.answer: Among other tests, by grafting a patch of skin from one brother onto the other. Skin from anyone else was rejected within weeks, so a graft that took meant neither immune system saw a stranger. Blood groups were matched and police compared fingerprints. Joseph Murray's patient, Richard Herrick, lived eight more years.
cards.move: Check compatibility on something small before risking something vital.
cards.reference: Merrill, Murray, Harrison & Guild, Successful homotransplantation of the human kidney between identical twins, Journal of the American Medical Association, 1956

cards.question: Of blood groups O, A and AB, which waits longest on average for a kidney from a deceased donor?
options: Group AB, the rarest of the three
Group O, the commonest of the three
cards.answer: Group O. An O kidney is compatible with patients of every group, but an O patient can accept only an O kidney. Left alone, other groups drain the O supply, so allocation schemes now reserve O kidneys mostly for O patients. AB patients can take any group and wait least.
cards.move: Whoever can give to everyone may be the one left waiting.
cards.trap: Picking AB, reasoning that the rarest group is hardest to match.
cards.source: NHS Blood and Transplant, kidney transplantation report
cards.reference: NHS Blood and Transplant, Annual Report on Kidney Transplantation 2022/23, 2023

cards.question: Each sibling has a 1 in 4 chance of matching a patient's tissue type exactly. With three siblings, what percentage chance of any match?
cards.move: Chances of at least one success never simply add; multiply the failures instead.
cards.trap: Adding 25% three times and arriving at 75%.
cards.hint: Work out the chance that every one of the siblings fails to match.
steps: Chance one sibling does not match: 3/4.
Chance none of the three match: 3/4 x 3/4 x 3/4 = 27/64.
cards.reference: Murphy & Weaver, Janeway's Immunobiology, 9th edition, Garland Science, 2016

cards.question: Should living kidney donors be paid a fixed, state-regulated sum to shorten transplant waiting lists?
cards.answer: Patients die on waiting lists while donation barely rises. Surgeons, hospitals and drug makers are all paid; only the donor is not. Iran has paid living unrelated donors through a regulated scheme since 1988 and reported clearing its kidney waiting list by 1999. A fixed state price shuts out brokers and bidding.
cards.move: The decider is whether a regulated price can protect the sellers it recruits.
cards.counterpoint: Payment recruits the poor. In a study of kidney sellers in Chennai, 96% sold to pay debts, most reported worse health afterwards and few would recommend it. A price turns a gift into a job for those with fewest choices, and once a sale is legal, families and lenders can press for it.
cards.reference: Ghods & Savaj, Iranian model of paid and regulated living-unrelated kidney donation, Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2006

cards.question: Surgeons once hesitated over organs from people who died of drug overdoses. How did US kidney recipients fare with them?
options: Worse at first, then catching up
About as well as other recipients
cards.answer: About as well as other recipients. A study of US transplants from 2000 to 2017 found graft and patient survival with overdose donors no worse than with trauma deaths. Such donors are often young and healthy; their frequent hepatitis C is now curable. By 2017 overdoses supplied more than one US donor in eight.
cards.move: How something came to you says less than how it performs.
cards.trap: Picturing drug use as damaging every organ it passes through.
cards.source: Durand et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2018
cards.reference: Durand et al., The drug overdose epidemic and deceased-donor transplantation in the United States: a national registry study, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2018

cards.question: Did we create antibiotic resistance?
cards.answer: We selected it; we did not invent it. Genes conferring resistance to several antibiotic classes have been recovered from 30,000-year-old permafrost, long before any human made a drug. Resistance is an ancient feature of microbial life that our use of antibiotics turned into an emergency.
cards.move: Resistance genes are older than agriculture.
cards.reference: D'Costa et al., Antibiotic resistance is ancient, Nature, 2011

cards.question: Should organ donation be opt-out by default, so everyone is a donor unless they register otherwise?
cards.answer: Defaults decide outcomes for anything people do not get round to. Most people say they support donation and never register, so opt-in measures paperwork rather than willingness. Countries that switched report more organs available, and objecting stays a single form away.
cards.move: The default changed the register. Whether it changed the operating theatre is a separate question.
cards.counterpoint: The jump in donations in opt-out countries mostly tracks transplant infrastructure and how families are approached, not the default itself — Spain's results came years after its law. And consent that was never given is not consent: families asked at the worst hour of their lives may refuse harder when the state has already assumed an answer.
cards.reference: Arshad, Anderson & Sharif, Comparison of organ donation and transplantation rates between opt-out and opt-in systems, Kidney International, 2019

cards.question: Should volunteers be deliberately infected with a disease to test a vaccine faster?
cards.answer: A challenge trial can answer in weeks what a field trial answers in a year, and during an epidemic that gap is counted in deaths. Healthy adult volunteers already accept comparable risks in kidney donation and firefighting, and the risk here is bounded, monitored and reversible.
cards.move: Notice the argument is not about the numbers. It is about who is allowed to accept a risk on behalf of everyone.
cards.counterpoint: You cannot fully consent to a disease nobody has yet characterised, and the volunteers most willing to sign up are often those with the least to fall back on. A single death in a trial where the researchers caused the infection would be a very different event, both morally and for every trial that came after it.
cards.reference: Eyal, Lipsitch & Smith, Human Challenge Studies to Accelerate Coronavirus Vaccine Licensure, Journal of Infectious Diseases, 2020

cards.question: Should we screen healthy people for cancer earlier and more often?
cards.answer: Screening moves a diagnosis from late to early, and early is where treatment works. Someone whose tumour is caught at stage one gets a different life from someone caught at stage three, and the cost of a scan is trivial against the cost of chemotherapy.
cards.move: Survival going up and deaths going down are not the same measurement, and only one of them is the point.
cards.counterpoint: In a population where the disease is rare, most positives are false, and each one buys biopsies, anxiety and sometimes surgery. Screening also finds tumours that would never have caused harm, and treating those is pure loss. Five-year survival rises whenever you diagnose earlier, even when the date of death does not move at all.
cards.reference: Welch & Black, Overdiagnosis in Cancer, Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 2010

cards.question: Should drug patents be shorter than twenty years?
cards.answer: The monopoly is paid for in lives: people who cannot afford a drug that costs cents to manufacture. A shorter term still rewards invention while moving the moment of cheap generics closer, and much of the underlying science was publicly funded anyway.
cards.move: Both sides are arguing about the same number from different ends of the development timeline.
cards.counterpoint: The patent clock starts at discovery, not at approval, so a drug that spends a decade in trials may see only a few protected years already. Cut it further and the projects that die first are the slow ones — antibiotics, rare diseases — where the payback was marginal to begin with.
cards.reference: Kesselheim, Avorn & Sarpatwari, The High Cost of Prescription Drugs in the United States: Origins and Prospects for Reform, JAMA, 2016

cards.question: When a treatment that works already exists, should new drugs still be tested against a sugar pill?
sides: No, test against the best existing drug
cards.answer: A placebo arm is the cleanest measurement there is, needs fewer patients, and answers the question that regulators actually ask. Against an existing drug you can only show something is not much worse, which is how a slow drift towards weaker medicines begins.
cards.move: The cleanest experiment and the useful question are pulling in opposite directions here.
cards.counterpoint: It means deliberately giving a patient nothing when something known to help exists. And the answer it produces is not the one anybody needs: no doctor is choosing between this drug and nothing, they are choosing between this drug and the one already on the shelf.
cards.reference: World Medical Association, Declaration of Helsinki, 2013 revision

cards.question: What problem at Harvard in 1895 turned the acoustics of rooms into a science?
cards.answer: A lecture hall in the new Fogg Art Museum where speech blurred into echoes. The physicist Wallace Sabine carried seat cushions between rooms at night, timing how long a sound took to die. The time rose with the room's volume and fell with its absorption; Boston's Symphony Hall of 1900 was built to his formula.
cards.move: A nuisance measured patiently can become a law.
cards.reference: Sabine, Collected Papers on Acoustics, Harvard University Press, 1922

cards.question: Sabine: seconds = 0.161 × volume ÷ absorption. A 20,000 m³ hall has 1,610 m² of absorption; an audience adds 690 more. Seconds when full?
cards.move: Count the people as part of the room they fill.
cards.trap: Working out the empty hall and forgetting the audience soaks up sound.
cards.hint: Add the audience to the absorption before dividing.
steps: Full absorption: 1,610 + 690 = 2,300 m².
cards.source: Beranek, Concert Halls and Opera Houses, 2004
cards.reference: Beranek, Concert Halls and Opera Houses: Music, Acoustics, and Architecture, 2nd edition, Springer, 2004

cards.question: What makes old shoebox halls like Vienna's Musikverein, opened in 1870, sound better than most modern halls?
options: Their curved ceilings focus the sound
Near side walls send sound in sideways
cards.answer: Near side walls send sound in sideways. Research from the late 1960s, by Harold Marshall and later Michael Barron, found that early reflections reaching the ears from the sides make listeners feel wrapped in sound. A narrow hall does it by shape. Thin wood panelling tends to soak up bass rather than sing along.
cards.move: When the best examples share two features, test each one alone.
cards.trap: Great old halls are full of wood, so the wood gets the credit.
cards.reference: Barron, Auditorium Acoustics and Architectural Design, E & FN Spon, 1993

cards.question: Why was the inside of New York's Philharmonic Hall, opened in 1962, torn out and rebuilt twice?
cards.answer: Because it sounded dry and thin from the opening night, with weak bass. Its acoustician, Leo Beranek, blamed design changes made during construction, and years of adjustments failed. Renamed Avery Fisher Hall, it was gutted and rebuilt inside in 1976, then rebuilt again as David Geffen Hall, which reopened in 2022.
cards.move: A room is an instrument, and a committee can detune it.
cards.reference: Beranek, Riding the Waves: A Life in Sound, Science, and Industry, MIT Press, 2008

cards.question: True or false: in St Paul's whispering gallery, the dome focuses a whisper across to the opposite side?
cards.answer: False. Lord Rayleigh showed that the sound creeps round the curved wall, reflected again and again at a grazing angle so it hugs the surface and spreads little. A whisper aimed along the wall carries about 30 metres across the gallery; one aimed at the middle of the dome is lost.
cards.move: Before crediting the obvious shape, check which surface the signal travels along.
cards.trap: Picturing the dome as a mirror focusing sound onto one point.
cards.reference: Rayleigh, The problem of the whispering gallery, Philosophical Magazine, 1910

cards.question: Why does bass coming straight from the stage weaken as it skims low over rows of seated listeners?
cards.answer: Because the rows act as a filter. Sound grazing over seats and heads sets up resonances in the gaps between rows, and the direct sound loses a band of low frequencies, roughly 100 to 200 Hz, often by over 10 decibels. The seat dip was measured in 1964. Reflections from the ceiling restore the bass.
cards.move: Before blaming the source, look at what the signal crossed.
cards.reference: Schultz and Watters, Propagation of Sound across Audience Seating, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1964

cards.question: A listener in a concert hall moves from row 10 to row 20, doubling the distance to the orchestra. How much quieter?
cards.answer: Only a couple of decibels. Outdoors, sound falls about 6 dB per doubling of distance, but in a hall most of what reaches a seat is reverberation, sound bounced round the room, filling it evenly. A few metres from the stage, reflected sound already outweighs direct sound, so the level barely changes. Clarity does.
cards.move: A rule measured in the open may not survive four walls.
cards.trap: The textbook rule of 6 dB per doubling, made for open air.
cards.reference: Kuttruff, Room Acoustics, 5th edition, Spon Press, 2009

cards.question: A studio is 3.43 m long; sound travels 343 m/s. At what lowest frequency, in Hz, does a standing wave fit between its end walls?
cards.answer: Frequency: 343 ÷ 6.86 = 50 Hz.
cards.move: Measure the room before blaming the speaker for a boomy note.
cards.trap: Fitting a whole wavelength in the room and answering 100 Hz.
cards.hint: Ask how much of one wave fits between two hard walls at the lowest resonance.
steps: The lowest standing wave fits half a wavelength between the walls.
Wavelength: 2 × 3.43 = 6.86 m.
Frequency: 343 ÷ 6.86 = 50 Hz.
cards.source: Everest and Pohlmann, Master Handbook of Acoustics
cards.reference: Everest and Pohlmann, Master Handbook of Acoustics, 5th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2009

cards.question: True or false: at the ancient theatre of Epidaurus, a whisper on stage is clearly understood in the top rows?
cards.answer: False. In 2017 acousticians from Eindhoven University of Technology measured the theatre at many seats: a whisper stopped being intelligible about halfway up, while a normally projected voice carried to the top. Guides' demonstrations take place in an empty, silent theatre, before visitors told exactly what to listen for.
cards.move: A demonstration staged to succeed is not a test.
cards.trap: Guides' demonstrations seem to prove it to visitors every day.
cards.reference: Eindhoven University of Technology, news release on the acoustics of ancient Greek theatres, 2017

cards.question: A violinist and a timpanist sit 17 metres apart on a big stage. How late does each hear the other?
options: Too little to matter, under 5 ms
cards.answer: About 50 milliseconds. Sound covers about 343 metres a second, so 17 metres takes a twentieth of a second. Played strictly by ear, the back of the orchestra would drag behind the front. So players watch the conductor's beat, and those at the back play slightly ahead of what they hear.
cards.move: Over distance, trust the shared signal you see, not the one you hear.
cards.trap: Sound feels instant across a room, so the lag seems negligible.
cards.source: Meyer, Acoustics and the Performance of Music
cards.reference: Meyer, Acoustics and the Performance of Music, 5th edition, Springer, 2009

cards.question: What was the inventor of Auto-Tune doing before he turned his maths on singers?
cards.answer: Hunting for oil. Andy Hildebrand spent years at Exxon interpreting seismic data, the echoes of sound pulses fired into rock. The same tool, autocorrelation, which finds a repeating pattern by comparing a signal with a delayed copy of itself, lets software find a voice's pitch fast. Auto-Tune shipped in 1997, a grandchild of oil prospecting.
cards.move: Methods travel further than the problems they were built for.

cards.question: What does a vocoder need, besides a voice, to produce its robot sound?
cards.answer: A second sound to shape. Homer Dudley's vocoder, built at Bell Labs in the 1930s to compress speech, splits the voice into frequency bands and uses their loudness to sculpt a carrier, often a keyboard chord. The notes come from the keyboard, not the singer. Auto-Tune needs only the voice, snapped to the nearest note.
cards.move: Two things that sound alike can be built on opposite ideas.
cards.source: Tompkins, How to Wreck a Nice Beach, 2010
cards.reference: Tompkins, How to Wreck a Nice Beach: The Vocoder from World War II to Hip-Hop, Melville House, 2010

cards.question: True or false: the producers of Cher's Believe first said its robotic vocal effect came from Auto-Tune?
cards.answer: False. In a 1999 Sound On Sound interview, producer Mark Taylor credited a DigiTech Talker vocoder pedal, apparently to guard a trade secret. The truth, admitted later, was Auto-Tune set to its fastest correction, so the voice jumped between notes instead of gliding. A tool built to hide tuning had been set to flaunt it.
cards.move: A secret method is often described as a better-known one.
cards.trap: True, since the effect is now simply called the Auto-Tune sound.
cards.source: Sound On Sound, Recording Cher's Believe
cards.reference: https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/recording-cher-believe

cards.question: What could Celemony's Melodyne do from 2009 that earlier pitch-correction software could not?
options: Correct a singer live, in real time
Retune one note inside a recorded chord
cards.answer: Retune one note inside a recorded chord. Earlier tools, Auto-Tune included, followed a single melodic line. Peter Neubäcker's Direct Note Access, shown in 2008 and released in 2009, separates overlapping notes in polyphonic audio, so an engineer can fix the one sour string of a strummed guitar chord long after the take.
cards.move: The most famous feature of a field is rarely its newest one.
cards.trap: Correcting live, because real-time sounds like the hardest trick.
cards.reference: Celemony, Melodyne editor with Direct Note Access, product release, 2009

cards.question: Should commercial recordings disclose when a singer's vocal has been pitch-corrected?
cards.answer: Listeners judge singers partly on singing in tune, and buy tickets on it. Silent correction sells a skill the performer may lack, much as undisclosed retouching sells a body that does not exist; France has required labels on retouched commercial photos of models since 2017. A plain credit would tell audiences what they are praising.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether records document performances or build them.
cards.counterpoint: Records have always been assembled: tape splices, retakes, the best syllables comped from twenty takes, reverb from rooms that never existed. Pitch correction is one more edit, routine in commercial pop, so a label would sit on nearly everything and tell nobody anything. The concert stage already exists as the test of raw skill.
cards.reference: Décret n° 2017-738 du 4 mai 2017 relatif aux photographies à usage commercial, Journal officiel de la République française, 2017

cards.question: Why does correcting a vocal by a semitone not make the singer sound like a sped-up tape?
cards.answer: Because the software moves the note and leaves the vowels alone. A voice is a buzz at the sung pitch, shaped by resonances of the throat and mouth, called formants, that make each vowel. Speeding up tape raises both, shrinking the singer's throat. Correction shifts the buzz and keeps the formants: same singer, new note.
cards.move: Before changing one quality of a thing, check what else is tied to it.
cards.reference: Zölzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, 2nd edn, Wiley, 2011

cards.question: Why does Auto-Tune ask whether it is hearing a soprano, an alto or tenor, or a low male voice?
cards.answer: To narrow where it looks for the pitch. It compares the voice with delayed copies of itself; the delay that matches is one cycle. A two-cycle delay matches too, and a strong overtone can pass for the note, so a wide search slips an octave. A named voice type fences it in.
cards.move: A tool that knows roughly where to look makes fewer wild mistakes.
cards.reference: https://media.uaudio.com/support/manuals/dd/Auto-Tune%20Realtime%20Advanced%20Manual.pdf

cards.question: A band tunes to A = 432 Hz, but Auto-Tune stays at its default A = 440. What happens to the singer's in-tune notes?
options: Left alone, since the key matches
Pulled about a third of a semitone sharp
cards.answer: Pulled about a third of a semitone sharp. 440 is about 1.9% above 432, a semitone about 6%, so each note true to the band sits some 32 cents, hundredths of a semitone, below the software's grid. That is under half a semitone, so each snaps up. The voice floats sharp over the band.
cards.move: A default left untouched is still a choice made about every result.
cards.trap: Assuming the software only needs the key, not the reference pitch.
cards.reference: https://images.equipboard.com/uploads/item/manual/81444/antares-auto-tune-artist-manual.pdf

cards.question: A detector is 95% right on corrected and natural vocals alike. If 1 vocal in 20 is natural, how often is a natural verdict right?
cards.answer: About half the time. Among 1,000 vocals, 50 are natural and the detector calls 47 or 48 of them natural. It also wrongly calls 5% of the 950 corrected ones natural: another 47 or 48. Half its natural verdicts are false: each real find stands beside an impostor.
cards.move: The rarer the thing you hunt, the more your alarms point at impostors.
cards.trap: Reading 95% accuracy as a 95% chance that each verdict is right.

diagram.label: vocals tested
diagram.caption: Of 950 vocals called natural, only 475 are: each real find stands beside an impostor.

cards.reference: Gigerenzer, Calculated Risks: How to Know When Numbers Deceive You, Simon & Schuster, 2002

cards.question: A singer's headphones play their voice back slightly sharp, as live pitch correction can. What does the voice do within a fraction of a second?
options: Holds steady until the singer notices
cards.answer: Drops, against the shift. Burnett and colleagues shifted singers' feedback by small amounts: most responses opposed the shift, beginning roughly a tenth to a fifth of a second later, before any deliberate choice. The voice steers by what it hears. A singer's monitor mix is part of the steering wheel.
cards.move: A system that corrects itself by feedback will fight any change to what it senses.
cards.trap: Voices follow what they hear, as when singing along with a band.
cards.reference: Burnett, Freedland, Larson & Hain, Voice F0 responses to manipulations in pitch feedback, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1998

cards.question: Whom did Leipzig's town council want as its cantor in 1723 before it settled for Bach?
cards.answer: Georg Philipp Telemann, then Christoph Graupner. Telemann used the offer to win a pay rise in Hamburg, and Graupner's employer in Darmstadt would not release him. Bach was the third choice, and one councillor noted that since the best could not be had, a middling one would have to do. He stayed 27 years.
cards.move: A ranking made at hiring time says more about the committee than the candidate.
cards.reference: David and Mendel, rev. Wolff, The New Bach Reader, W. W. Norton, 1998

cards.question: Why did Bach spend almost four weeks under arrest in Weimar in 1717?
cards.answer: For insisting on leaving. He had taken a post at Köthen, and the Duke of Weimar refused to let him go. The court secretary recorded him held from 6 November to 2 December for too stubbornly forcing his dismissal, then released in disgrace. A court musician was a servant, and servants did not resign.
cards.move: Look at the contract before admiring the career.
cards.reference: Wolff, Johann Sebastian Bach: The Learned Musician, W. W. Norton, 2000

cards.question: How much evidence is there that Bach wrote the Goldberg Variations for a count who could not sleep?
cards.answer: Very little. The story comes from Forkel's biography of 1802, sixty years later. The 1741 print carries no dedication to Count Keyserlingk, and Johann Gottlieb Goldberg, the harpsichordist said to have played them at night, was about 14. Bach issued them as the fourth part of his Clavier-Übung, a published keyboard series.
cards.move: Date the anecdote, then date the thing it explains.
cards.reference: Williams, Bach: The Goldberg Variations, Cambridge Music Handbooks, Cambridge University Press, 2001

cards.question: True or false: the well-tempered of Bach's title means the equal temperament pianos use today?
cards.answer: False. In Bach's day well-tempered meant any tuning in which all 24 keys were usable, and most such tunings left the keys unequal, so C major and F sharp major had different colours. Equal temperament, every semitone the same size, was one option and became the norm on pianos only in the 19th century.
cards.move: Read an old word in its own century before reading it in ours.
cards.trap: Reading the modern meaning of a tuning word back into 1722.
cards.source: Duffin, How Equal Temperament Ruined Harmony, 2007
cards.reference: Duffin, How Equal Temperament Ruined Harmony (and Why You Should Care), W. W. Norton, 2007

cards.question: Bach's obituary credits him with five yearly cycles of church cantatas. Roughly how much of that survives?
cards.answer: About two-thirds. A yearly cycle meant a cantata for every Sunday and feast day, about 60, so five cycles come to about 300, and around 200 sacred cantatas survive. His manuscripts were split among his heirs, and Wilhelm Friedemann sold much of his share. Whether all five cycles were ever complete is debated.
cards.move: Before praising a body of work, ask how much of it was lost.
cards.trap: Taking the roughly 200 cantatas on record for everything he wrote.
cards.source: Dürr, The Cantatas of J. S. Bach, 2005
cards.reference: Dürr, The Cantatas of J. S. Bach, trans. Jones, Oxford University Press, 2005

cards.question: Why did Bach, in a 1730 letter to an old school friend, count a healthy year in Leipzig as a loss?
cards.answer: Because part of his pay came from funerals. Writing to Georg Erdmann, he valued his post at about 700 thalers a year, part of it fees for burials and weddings, and complained that when a healthy wind blew, deaths fell and his income with them. He was asking Erdmann for a post elsewhere.
cards.move: Look at how a job is paid before judging what the worker hopes for.
cards.reference: Neumann and Schulze (eds), Bach-Dokumente, vol. 1, Bärenreiter, 1963, letter of 28 October 1730

cards.question: Why could Bach's Mass in B minor not be heard complete in any church service of his time?
cards.answer: It was too long for any liturgy. Lutheran Leipzig used only a short Latin Mass, Kyrie and Gloria; Bach wrote those two parts in 1733 for the Catholic court at Dresden, seeking a court title. He added the rest in 1748 and 1749, largely from older music. The first recorded complete performance came in 1859.
cards.move: A work can be finished long before any occasion exists for it.
cards.source: Stauffer, Bach: The Mass in B Minor
cards.reference: Stauffer, Bach: The Mass in B Minor: The Great Catholic Mass, Yale University Press, 2003

cards.question: Number the letters A=1, B=2 and so on: BACH sums to 14. Hunters then found 14 all over Bach's music. What does that show?
options: That Bach signed his music in numbers
That his engravers added the numbers
Little; count enough and 14 turns up
cards.answer: Little on its own. A piece offers thousands of countable things, notes, bars, entries, rests, and any small number will match some of them. Ruth Tatlow showed that such number alphabets were known in Bach's circle, yet a claim needs a count fixed before looking. Found after the fact, a 14 is what searching produces.
cards.move: Decide what you will count before you start counting.
cards.trap: The pattern keeps turning up, so it must have been put there.
cards.reference: Tatlow, Bach and the Riddle of the Number Alphabet, Cambridge University Press, 1991

cards.question: True or false: Bach's music was largely forgotten until Mendelssohn revived the St Matthew Passion in 1829?
cards.answer: False. The choral works went quiet, but the keyboard music never did. Mozart arranged Bach fugues for Baron van Swieten's Sunday gatherings in 1782, the boy Beethoven was playing the Well-Tempered Clavier in Bonn by 1783, and the collection was printed in 1801. The 1829 concert revived a public, not a composer.
cards.move: Before crediting the revival, check who never stopped using the thing.
cards.trap: A famous revival concert implies something had been lost before it.
cards.reference: Applegate, Bach in Berlin: Nation and Culture in Mendelssohn's Revival of the St. Matthew Passion, Cornell University Press, 2005

cards.question: In the 30 Goldberg Variations, every third from the 3rd is a canon, except the last, a medley of folk songs. How many canons?
cards.answer: So there are 9 canons.
cards.move: When counting a pattern, check what happens at its last step.
cards.trap: Stopping at 30 ÷ 3 = 10 and forgetting the exception.
cards.hint: List the variation numbers that are multiples of three.
steps: Multiples of 3 up to 30: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 variations.
The 30th is the medley, not a canon: 10 − 1.
So there are 9 canons.
cards.source: Schulenberg, The Keyboard Music of J. S. Bach
cards.reference: Schulenberg, The Keyboard Music of J. S. Bach, 2nd edition, Routledge, 2006

cards.question: How can the same four chords sound hopeful in Let It Be and bleak in Zombie?
cards.answer: By starting the loop on a different chord. Let It Be cycles C, G, A minor, F; Zombie cycles roughly E minor, C, G, D, which is the same circle entered at its minor chord. A loop has no fixed beginning, so wherever the ear lands first becomes home. Same circle, different front door.
cards.move: Where a cycle begins can decide what it seems to mean.
cards.reference: Everett, The Foundations of Rock: From Blue Suede Shoes to Suite: Judy Blue Eyes, Oxford University Press, 2009

cards.question: For how long has Pachelbel's Canon been a staple at weddings?
cards.answer: Only about fifty years. Written over a two-bar bass loop around three centuries ago, it survived in a single manuscript copy and was first printed in 1919. A lush, slowed-down 1968 recording by Jean-François Paillard's orchestra turned it into a hit. The music of countless aisles spent two centuries on an archive shelf.
cards.move: A tradition that feels ancient may be younger than the people keeping it.
cards.reference: Perreault, The Thematic Catalogue of the Musical Works of Johann Pachelbel, Scarecrow Press, 2004

cards.question: From a major key's seven chords, how many distinct four-chord loops exist, with no repeats and rotations counted once?
cards.move: Before counting, decide which differences are real and which are only a starting point.
cards.trap: Stopping at 840 and counting each rotation as a new song.
cards.hint: Count the ordered runs first, then ask how many of them are the same circle.
steps: Ordered runs of four different chords: 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 = 840.
A loop can start on any of its 4 chords, so each loop appears 4 times.
cards.reference: Brualdi, Introductory Combinatorics, Pearson, 2010

cards.question: Should a chord progression paired with a particular rhythm be protected by copyright?
cards.answer: A song's identity often lives in its groove: which chords, and exactly where they land. Chords alone are common, but a specific progression welded to a specific syncopation is a creative choice, and juries can hear it. Leaving it unprotected lets a famous artist lift the feel of an obscure song and keep every penny.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how much of the pairing is commonplace.
cards.counterpoint: In 2023 a New York jury found Ed Sheeran's Thinking Out Loud did not copy Let's Get It On, though both set a similar loop to a similar lilt; the defence played older songs built on the same pairing. Owning pairings would fence off a small commons that every songwriter draws on, and reward whoever sued first.
cards.reference: Griffin v. Sheeran, jury verdict, United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 2023

cards.question: In a sample of 100 classic rock songs, which chord most often moves straight to the home chord?
options: The chord on the scale's fifth note
The chord on the scale's fourth note
The chord on the scale's sixth note
cards.answer: The chord on the fourth note, IV. Trevor de Clercq and David Temperley analysed 20 songs per decade, 1950s to 1990s, from Rolling Stone's greatest list: IV appeared more often than V, and IV to I outnumbered the textbook V to I. Rock goes home through the hymnbook's amen, not the classroom's cadence.
cards.move: A rule taught from one repertoire may not describe another.
cards.trap: The fifth, because every harmony textbook ends its cadences there.
cards.reference: de Clercq & Temperley, A corpus analysis of rock harmony, Popular Music, 2011

cards.question: In a 2019 study of chord sequences from 745 US hits, which moment gave listeners the most pleasure?
options: A predictable chord after a predictable run
A surprising chord after an unpredictable run
A surprising chord after a predictable run
cards.answer: A surprising chord after a predictable run. Vincent Cheung and colleagues modelled 80,000 chords, played without melody or lyrics, and had listeners rate them. Surprise pleased when expectation was confident; a safe chord pleased after uncertainty; a shock inside confusion did little. A loop earns its twist by being predictable first.
cards.move: A surprise only lands where there was a confident expectation to break.
cards.trap: Assuming more surprise always means more pleasure, whatever came before.
cards.reference: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(19)31258-8

cards.question: True or false: in much rock, the sung melody stresses notes that are not in the chord playing beneath it?
cards.answer: True. David Temperley called it the melodic-harmonic divorce: the voice moves in its own pentatonic scale while the band turns a chord loop, and stressed melody notes are often not chord tones. Classical harmony teaches that strong-beat notes belong to the chord. In rock, the singer and the band share a key, not a chord.
cards.move: A rule learned from one tradition can be broken daily by another.
cards.trap: Harmony textbooks teach that important melody notes belong to the chord.
cards.reference: Temperley, The melodic-harmonic 'divorce' in rock, Popular Music, 2007

cards.question: What does the chord loop at the end of Hey Jude do that a classical cadence never does?
cards.answer: It runs the pull of fifths backwards. It cycles F, E flat, B flat, F: from E flat each chord climbs a fifth, where a classical cadence falls a fifth to reach home. Theorists call it a double plagal cadence: the hymn's amen twice over. About four of the single's seven minutes ride on it.
cards.move: A pattern can keep its parts and reverse the direction that gave them force.
cards.reference: Everett, The Beatles as Musicians: Revolver through the Anthology, Oxford University Press, 1999

cards.question: A loop of five chords, two beats each, runs in 4/4 under four-bar phrases. After how many bars do they realign?
cards.move: When two cycles differ, count both in the smallest shared unit first.
cards.trap: Multiplying the cycles, 10 x 16 beats, and landing on 40 bars.
cards.hint: Measure both cycles in beats before looking for where they meet.
steps: Loop: 5 chords x 2 beats = 10 beats.
Phrase: 4 bars x 4 beats = 16 beats.
They meet at the lowest common multiple of 10 and 16: 80 beats.
cards.reference: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Oxford University Press, 2008

cards.question: In 17th-century Venetian opera, a bass repeating four notes stepping down from the home note usually signalled what?
cards.answer: A lament. Ellen Rosand traced how the descending tetrachord, four notes stepping down a fourth from the home note, became Venetian opera's emblem of grief; Purcell's Dido sings her lament over a chromatic version. Repeating basses carried dances too. Pop's slow loops sliding down a scale inherit the mourning.
cards.move: A pattern that repeats in many settings can still carry one fixed meaning.
cards.trap: Ground basses underpinned dances, so a repeating bass sounds like dancing.
cards.reference: Rosand, The Descending Tetrachord: An Emblem of Lament, The Musical Quarterly, 1979

cards.question: Why was Nino Rota's score for The Godfather pulled from the 1973 Oscar race?
cards.answer: Because its love theme reused a melody Rota had written for Fortunella, a 1958 Italian comedy, and original-score rules shut out recycled music. The nomination was withdrawn. Two years later The Godfather Part II, built on the same theme, won the Oscar for original dramatic score for Rota and Carmine Coppola.
cards.move: A rule applied case by case can reward what it once banned.
cards.reference: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Official Academy Awards Database, 45th (1973) and 47th (1975) Awards

cards.question: True or false: Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey reached cinemas with none of the score he commissioned for it?
cards.answer: True. Alex North wrote and recorded music for the film early in 1968, and Kubrick dropped all of it, keeping the concert pieces he had edited to: Richard Strauss, Johann Strauss, Ligeti, Khachaturian. North reportedly found out at the premiere. His unused score was finally recorded and released in 1993.
cards.move: What has already been paid for is no argument for keeping it.
cards.trap: Assuming music already paid for and recorded had to be used.
cards.reference: LoBrutto, Stanley Kubrick: A Biography, Donald I. Fine Books, 1997

cards.question: When was Ennio Morricone's main music for Once Upon a Time in the West, 1968, recorded?
options: Alongside the shooting, week by week
cards.answer: Before the cameras started rolling. Sergio Leone had Morricone write and record the main themes first, then played the recordings on set, so actors timed their movements, and the camera its moves, to the music. Most films work the other way: the composer starts once the picture is cut, timing each cue to the frame.
cards.move: Ask what was fixed first; everything after it had to fit.
cards.trap: Assuming the score always comes last, fitted to a finished cut.
cards.reference: Frayling, Sergio Leone: Something to Do with Death, Faber and Faber, 2000

cards.question: A cue must hit 45 feet into a 35 mm reel; film runs 16 frames a foot, 24 a second. How many seconds in?
cards.answer: 720 / 24 = 30 seconds.
cards.move: Convert to the unit the machine counts in, then convert back.
cards.trap: Treating feet of film as if they mapped to seconds one to one.
cards.hint: Turn the length of film into frames first.
steps: 45 feet x 16 frames = 720 frames.
720 / 24 = 30 seconds.
cards.reference: Karlin and Wright, On the Track: A Guide to Contemporary Film Scoring, 2nd edition, Routledge, 2004

cards.question: Should directors stop editing films to borrowed temp music before the composer has started?
cards.answer: A temp track sets the target before the composer has seen a frame. After weeks of cutting to it, a director hears anything different as wrong, and the commissioned score becomes an imitation of the borrowed one. Composers get handed the same few favourite pieces, one reason so many big films sound alike.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the question is whether a sketch can stay a sketch.
cards.counterpoint: Directors are rarely musicians, and a temp track is the clearest way they have to say what a scene needs: this pace, this weight, quiet here. Without it composers guess and rewrite. Editors also need rhythm to cut to, and a good composer can take the brief and still write something of their own.
cards.reference: Sadoff, The role of the music editor and the 'temp track' as blueprint for the score, source music, and scource music of films, Popular Music, 2006
