cards.question: Why did Bernard Herrmann write his score for Psycho, 1960, for a string orchestra alone?
cards.answer: To give a black-and-white film a black-and-white sound, he said, and to fit a tight budget. Dropping brass, woodwind and percussion left one colour, which he could push from lush to shrieking. The stabbing violins of the shower cue were written for a scene Hitchcock had wanted played with no music.
cards.move: A narrower palette forces every remaining colour to work harder.
cards.source: Smith, A Heart at Fire's Center, 1991
cards.reference: Smith, A Heart at Fire's Center: The Life and Music of Bernard Herrmann, University of California Press, 1991

cards.question: True or false: cinemas in the United States pay no performance royalties for the music in the films they show?
cards.answer: True. In 1948, in Alden-Rochelle v. ASCAP, a federal court barred the songwriters' society from collecting licence fees from American cinemas, finding its system an illegal restraint of trade. Since then producers buy the performing rights up front along with the music. Composers still collect when the film plays on television or in cinemas abroad.
cards.move: Check where a rule stops before assuming it applies everywhere.
cards.trap: Radio, television and bars all pay, so cinemas surely do.
cards.reference: Alden-Rochelle, Inc. v. American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, 80 F. Supp. 888, S.D.N.Y., 1948

cards.question: John Williams has more Oscar nominations than any living person, over fifty. How many has he won?
cards.answer: Five: Fiddler on the Roof, for adapting its score, then Jaws, Star Wars, E.T. and Schindler's List. His nominations, 54 by 2024, are second only to Walt Disney's, yet in most of those years someone else won. His last win came at the ceremony of March 1994, more than thirty years ago.
cards.move: A long list of entries tells little about the number of wins.
cards.trap: Anchoring on 50-plus nominations and assuming a good share became wins.
cards.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, 2024
cards.reference: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, nominations for the 96th Academy Awards, 2024

cards.question: Why did the Oscar for the score of the 1936 film Anthony Adverse not go to its composer, Erich Korngold?
cards.answer: Because in the award's first years the scoring Oscar went to the studio's music department, and its head collected it. Leo Forbstein of Warner Bros took the statuette, though Korngold wrote the music. The Academy soon changed the rule, and composers began to receive the award in their own names.
cards.move: Check whose name is on a prize before crediting the work.
cards.reference: Carroll, The Last Prodigy: A Biography of Erich Wolfgang Korngold, Amadeus Press, 1997

cards.question: A cue starts on a click, one every 18 frames of 24-frame film. A door slams 9 seconds in. Which beat lands on it?
cards.answer: The first click is beat 1, so the slam falls on beat 13.
cards.move: When counting along a line, decide whether you count posts or gaps.
cards.trap: Answering 12 by counting the gaps instead of the clicks.
cards.hint: Turn the frame count into seconds per beat first.
steps: One beat lasts 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75 seconds.
9 ÷ 0.75 = 12 beats after the first click.
The first click is beat 1, so the slam falls on beat 13.
cards.source: Davis, Complete Guide to Film Scoring
cards.reference: Davis, Complete Guide to Film Scoring, Berklee Press, 1999

cards.question: Where did the recordings on Harry Smith's 1952 Anthology of American Folk Music come from?
cards.answer: From commercial 78s. Smith, a record collector, chose 84 tracks that companies had issued between 1927 and 1932 and sold as hillbilly and race records. The revival treated them as documents of a vanished America, yet several of the singers were alive, and Mississippi John Hurt was found and recording again in 1963.
cards.move: Before calling something a document, ask who made it to sell.
cards.reference: Smith (ed.), Anthology of American Folk Music, reissue with notes, Smithsonian Folkways Recordings, 1997

cards.question: What was Woody Guthrie's This Land Is Your Land first written to answer?
cards.answer: Irving Berlin's God Bless America, a radio hit for Kate Smith. Guthrie wrote his reply in February 1940 with the refrain God blessed America for me. Its verses about a No Trespassing sign and hungry people queuing by the relief office were left out of the versions later sung in schools.
cards.move: When a song becomes an anthem, check which verses were dropped.
cards.reference: Cray, Ramblin' Man: The Life and Times of Woody Guthrie, W. W. Norton, 2004

cards.question: True or false: Lead Belly won his 1934 release from Louisiana's Angola prison by singing a plea to the governor?
cards.answer: False. He did record a sung plea to Governor O. K. Allen for the Lomaxes in 1934, and the legend grew from it. He was freed that August under a law cutting sentences for good behaviour. The story had been true once before: in 1925 Texas governor Pat Neff pardoned him after he sang.
cards.move: Before crediting the plea, ask whether the door was opening anyway.
cards.trap: The plea came first and the release followed, so it looks causal.
cards.source: Wolfe & Lornell, Life and Legend of Leadbelly
cards.reference: Wolfe and Lornell, The Life and Legend of Leadbelly, HarperCollins, 1992

cards.question: Why does Cecil Sharp's 1916 to 1918 Appalachian collection make mountain music look almost purely English?
options: He noted down what fitted his idea
Isolation had kept other music out
Other musicians refused to sing for him
cards.answer: He noted down what fitted his idea. Sharp came looking for survivals of old English ballads and wrote those down, largely passing over Black musicians, instrumental dance tunes and newer songs learned from records and hymnbooks. The mountains he printed were the ones his notebook had room for.
cards.move: A collection shows the collector's question before it shows the place.
cards.trap: Believing the old story of mountain people sealed off from the world.
cards.source: Whisnant, All That Is Native and Fine, 1983
cards.reference: Whisnant, All That Is Native and Fine: The Politics of Culture in an American Region, University of North Carolina Press, 1983

cards.question: Should a singer's arrangement of a traditional song be protected by copyright?
cards.answer: Arranging a ballad is real work: choosing verses, shaping the tune, finding the guitar part. Martin Carthy taught Paul Simon his Scarborough Fair in 1965, and the hit version credited Simon and Garfunkel as arrangers, not him. Protecting the arrangement, never the song itself, pays for that craft and leaves the tradition free for everyone.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the question is where arranging ends and inheriting begins.
cards.counterpoint: Folk songs live because every singer changes them and nobody owns the change. Carthy had learned the ballad from others and shaped it as they had. Once arrangements carry rights, singers must fear that a verse order or a chord heard on a record brings a lawyer's letter, and the songs stop moving between people.
cards.reference: Frith and Marshall (eds), Music and Copyright, 2nd edition, Edinburgh University Press, 2004

cards.question: Where did Francis James Child find most of the 305 ballads in his English and Scottish Popular Ballads?
cards.answer: In libraries and manuscripts, not from singers. Child, a Harvard professor, published the collection in parts from 1882 to 1898, working mainly from printed books, broadsides and old manuscripts such as the Percy Folio, plus texts sent by correspondents. His oldest item, Judas, comes from a manuscript of the 13th century.
cards.move: Ask whether a collection was gathered in the field or at a desk.
cards.source: Child, English and Scottish Popular Ballads
cards.reference: Child (ed.), The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, 5 volumes, Dover reprint, 1965

cards.question: True or false: We Shall Overcome, which grew out of a church hymn, was never under copyright?
cards.answer: False. An arrangement credited to Zilphia Horton, Frank Hamilton, Guy Carawan and Pete Seeger was registered in the early 1960s, and a publisher licensed the song for decades, the writers' share funding Black cultural work in the South. A lawsuit ended in a 2018 settlement leaving the song in the public domain.
cards.move: A song everyone sings can still have an owner on paper.
cards.trap: An old hymn sung at marches sounds like it belongs to everyone.
cards.reference: We Shall Overcome Foundation v. The Richmond Organization, Inc., US District Court for the Southern District of New York, 2018

cards.question: Barbara Allen was a favourite of Appalachian singers. Where is the ballad first recorded?
options: In a Scottish songbook of the 1790s
cards.answer: In a London diary of 1666. On 2 January that year Samuel Pepys wrote of hearing the actress Mrs Knipp sing her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen. Allan Ramsay printed a text in Edinburgh in 1740. It went on to become one of the most widely collected ballads in North America.
cards.move: Where a thing was found last says little about where it began.
cards.trap: The Appalachian field notes, because that is where the song lived.
cards.reference: Latham and Matthews (eds), The Diary of Samuel Pepys, vol. 7, G. Bell and Sons, 1972

cards.question: Should archives hand control of old field recordings back to the communities that were recorded?
cards.answer: The singers were often poor, rural or imprisoned, and rarely had any say in where their voices went or who profited. A recording of a family's ballad or a village ritual belongs to the people it came from before it belongs to scholars. Returning copies, and a say over use, repairs a lopsided bargain.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is who can speak for a community.
cards.counterpoint: Many of those communities are now scattered, and nobody can speak for all of them; a veto held by one descendant can silence a whole tradition. Open archives are how grandchildren find their grandparents' songs at all. Copies can be sent back to the places recorded while the recordings stay free for anyone to hear.
cards.reference: Szwed, Alan Lomax: The Man Who Recorded the World, Viking, 2010

cards.question: Danny Boy is sung to an old Irish tune, the Londonderry Air. Who wrote its words?
options: Thomas Moore, for his Irish Melodies
cards.answer: An English barrister. Fred Weatherly, a lawyer and prolific songwriter, wrote the words in 1910 for another tune, then fitted them to the Londonderry Air in 1913, after his sister-in-law sent it from America. The tune itself had been noted down in County Londonderry and printed in 1855 without a name.
cards.move: Date the words and the tune separately; they rarely share a birthday.
cards.trap: Moore wrote the best-known Irish song lyrics, so his name comes first.
cards.reference: Weatherly, Piano and Gown, London, 1926

cards.question: Why do baroque orchestras usually tune their A to 415 Hz rather than 440?
cards.answer: As a convention, not a rediscovery. Pitch in the 17th and 18th centuries varied from town to town and organ to organ, from well below 415 to over 440. Period players settled on 415 because it sits almost exactly a semitone below 440, so a harpsichord can switch by sliding its keyboard one key.
cards.move: A historical standard can be a modern convenience wearing old clothes.
cards.source: Haynes, A History of Performing Pitch, 2002
cards.reference: Haynes, A History of Performing Pitch: The Story of A, Scarecrow Press, 2002

cards.question: Why does a clarinet jump a twelfth, not an octave, when the player opens its register key?
cards.answer: Because its bore is a cylinder closed at the reed end, and such a pipe resonates mainly at odd multiples of its lowest frequency: 1, 3, 5 times. The next resonance up is three times the fundamental, an octave plus a fifth. The same physics leaves its low notes hollow, weak in the even harmonics.
cards.move: The shape of the container picks which notes it can hold.
cards.source: Fletcher & Rossing, Physics of Musical Instruments, 1998
cards.reference: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd edition, Springer, 1998

cards.question: A piano's lowest A vibrates at 27.5 Hz and its highest A at 3,520 Hz. How many octaves apart are they?
cards.answer: 128 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, so 7 octaves.
cards.move: When each step multiplies, count the doublings, not the differences.
cards.trap: Treating octaves as equal gaps in hertz rather than equal ratios.
cards.hint: Ask how many times 27.5 must be doubled to reach 3,520.
steps: Each octave up doubles the frequency.
128 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, so 7 octaves.
cards.reference: ISO 16:1975, Acoustics: Standard tuning frequency (standard musical pitch)

cards.question: Tune twelve pure fifths upward from a C, each exactly 3 to 2. Where do you land against seven octaves up?
options: About a quarter of a semitone sharp
cards.answer: About a quarter of a semitone sharp. Twelve fifths multiply the frequency by 1.5 to the 12th power, about 129.7; seven octaves multiply it by 2 to the 7th, 128. The gap, about 1.4%, is the Pythagorean comma. Every keyboard tuning is a decision about where to hide it.
cards.move: Small errors repeated down a chain do not stay small.
cards.trap: Assuming a mismatch too small to hear per step stays that small.
cards.reference: Barbour, Tuning and Temperament: A Historical Survey, Michigan State College Press, 1951

cards.question: True or false: a 100 Hz tone needs more sound energy than a 3,000 Hz tone to seem equally loud?
cards.answer: True. Hearing is keenest between about 2,000 and 5,000 Hz, where the ear canal resonates like a short pipe, and far duller in the bass. At quiet levels a 100 Hz tone needs at least 20 dB more, a hundredfold the power, to match. So bass thins out when music is turned down.
cards.move: An instrument and an ear can disagree; decide which one you serve.
cards.trap: Assuming equal energy sounds equally loud at every pitch.
cards.reference: ISO 226:2003, Acoustics: Normal equal-loudness-level contours

cards.question: How can a sequence of tones seem to climb forever without its frequencies ever getting higher?
cards.answer: By stacking octaves under a fixed loudness curve. Roger Shepard built each tone from components an octave apart, loudest mid-range and fading at both ends. As the set steps up, top components fade out while new ones fade in at the bottom, so after twelve steps the sound is back where it began.
cards.move: A staircase that returns to its start was built as a circle.
cards.reference: Shepard, Circularity in Judgments of Relative Pitch, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1964

cards.question: A phone line passes nothing below about 300 Hz. A man speaks with a fundamental of 120 Hz. What pitch do listeners hear?
cards.answer: His usual pitch, about 120 Hz. The line strips the fundamental but keeps the harmonics at 360, 480, 600 Hz and up, spaced 120 Hz apart, and the brain reads pitch from that spacing: the missing fundamental. The same trick lets a laptop speaker that cannot play 100 Hz still carry a bass line.
cards.move: A pattern can reveal a missing piece that no single part contains.
cards.trap: Pitch seems to be the lowest frequency present, and that was cut.
cards.reference: Plack, The Sense of Hearing, 2nd edition, Psychology Press, 2014

cards.question: A string beats 3 times a second with a 440 Hz fork. Tightened slightly, it beats 4 times. What was its frequency in Hz?
cards.answer: So the string was at 443 Hz.
cards.move: A difference tells you how far, not which way; find a second clue.
cards.trap: Guessing 437 Hz, as if the beats alone said which side.
cards.hint: Beats give the size of the gap; the tightening gives its direction.
steps: Beats count the gap: the string is 437 or 443 Hz.
Tightening a string raises its pitch.
The gap widened as the pitch rose, so it started above 440.
So the string was at 443 Hz.
cards.reference: Hall, Musical Acoustics, 3rd edition, Brooks/Cole, 2002

cards.question: How does an unamplified opera tenor get heard over a full orchestra playing at the same time?
options: More power than the whole orchestra
cards.answer: A strong peak near 3,000 Hz. Trained singers lower the larynx and widen the throat so several resonances of the vocal tract cluster, the singer's formant, boosting the voice between about 2,500 and 3,500 Hz. An orchestra is loudest far lower, around 500 Hz, so the voice slips through a gap.
cards.move: To be heard in a crowd, be different rather than louder.
cards.trap: Opera voices are famously loud, so power seems the obvious answer.
cards.source: Sundberg, The Science of the Singing Voice
cards.reference: Sundberg, The Science of the Singing Voice, Northern Illinois University Press, 1987

cards.question: True or false: the international agreement fixing A at 440 Hz was reached at a 1939 conference in London?
cards.answer: True. In May 1939 a conference in London called by the International Standards Association adopted 440 Hz for the A above middle C, and ISO confirmed it in 1955. A story circulating online says Nazi Germany imposed the figure; the decision was a multinational one, taken in London, months before the war began.
cards.move: The more sinister the origin story, the more its paperwork deserves a look.
cards.trap: A vivid tale of the pitch as a wartime plot crowds out the record.
cards.source: Haynes, A History of Performing Pitch
cards.reference: Haynes, A History of Performing Pitch: The Story of A, Scarecrow Press, 2002

cards.question: Why is the saddle on a guitar set at a slant instead of square to the strings?
cards.answer: Because pressing a string onto a fret stretches it, and stretching raises its pitch. Thicker, stiffer strings go sharper, so their saddle point is set back a few millimetres to lengthen them. Without it, notes high on the neck drift sharp of the open strings. The slant corrects for the player's own fingers.
cards.move: Correct for the error the user brings along, not only the tool's.
cards.reference: French, Engineering the Guitar: Theory and Practice, Springer, 2009

cards.question: Why do heavily distorted rock guitars favour two-note power chords over full major chords?
cards.answer: Because distortion invents notes: clipping adds tones at the sums and differences of the frequencies going in. A tempered fifth is almost exactly 3:2, so those new tones line up with the root's family. The tempered major third sits about 14 cents off a pure 5:4, so its products land off and beat: mud.
cards.move: An ingredient that works alone can spoil once the heat is turned up.
cards.reference: Esa Lilja, Dealing with the 3rd: Anatomy of distorted chords and subsequent compositional features in classic heavy metal, in Karjalainen & Kärki (eds), Modern Heavy Metal: Markets, Practices and Cultures, Aalto University, 2015, pp. 393–403

cards.question: True or false: the first electric guitar sold commercially was a solid-body held upright like a Spanish guitar?
cards.answer: False. The first to sell in numbers was a lap steel, played flat on the knees: the Rickenbacker Frying Pan, cast aluminium with a horseshoe-magnet pickup, sold from 1932. Hawaiian music was the craze; steel players needed volume first. The electric guitar's first customers played sitting down, sliding a steel bar along the strings.
cards.move: The best-known form of an invention is rarely its first form.
cards.trap: True, since the Stratocaster and Les Paul fill every picture of one.
cards.reference: Millard (ed.), The Electric Guitar: A History of an American Icon, Johns Hopkins University Press, 2004

cards.question: Touching an open guitar string lightly above its 7th fret gives a harmonic. How many times the open string's frequency?
cards.answer: Each segment is a third as long and vibrates 3 times as fast: 3 times.
cards.move: Ask what a light touch forbids, not what a firm press chooses.
cards.trap: One and a half, because pressing down there plays a fifth.
cards.hint: Work out what fraction of the string the 7th fret marks off.
steps: The 7th fret raises a note a fifth, ratio 3:2, so it sits a third of the way along the string.
A light touch there forces a still point at one third, so the string vibrates in 3 equal segments.
Each segment is a third as long and vibrates 3 times as fast: 3 times.
cards.reference: Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976

cards.question: On a Fender Stratocaster, what does the bar Fender named the tremolo arm actually vary?
cards.answer: The pitch. Properly, tremolo is a wobble in volume and vibrato a wobble in pitch, and Leo Fender swapped them: the 1954 Stratocaster's synchronized tremolo bends pitch, while Fender amplifiers labelled vibrato pulse the volume. Guitarists inherited both errors. The whammy bar is a vibrato arm still wearing the wrong name tag.
cards.move: Check what a control does before trusting what it is called.
cards.trap: The volume, because that is what the word tremolo means.
cards.reference: Duchossoir, The Fender Stratocaster, Hal Leonard, 1994

cards.question: If each fret takes 1/18 of the string left, where does fret 2 sit on a 648 mm scale, in mm from the nut?
cards.move: When each step takes a share of what is left, the steps shrink.
cards.trap: Doubling the first gap to 72 mm, as if frets were evenly spaced.
cards.hint: Find the first fret, then apply the same rule to what remains.
steps: Fret 1: 648 / 18 = 36 mm from the nut.
String left: 648 - 36 = 612 mm.
Next gap: 612 / 18 = 34 mm.
cards.reference: Cumpiano & Natelson, Guitarmaking: Tradition and Technology, Chronicle Books, 1994

cards.question: A humbucker wires its two coils in opposite senses so mains hum cancels. Why doesn't the string's signal cancel too?
options: The coils' magnets face opposite ways
String notes are too high to cancel
The strings sit nearer one coil
cards.answer: The coils' magnets face opposite ways. Outside hum induces the same voltage in both coils, and the reversed wiring subtracts it. A moving string changes the field through each coil in opposite directions, because of the flipped magnets, so the reversed wiring flips it back and the two add. Seth Lover's 1959 patent reverses twice.
cards.move: When one reversal cancels noise, a second reversal can rescue the signal.
cards.trap: Assuming cancellation picks out pitches, the way a tone filter does.
cards.reference: Lover, Magnetic pickup for stringed musical instrument, US Patent 2,896,491, 1959

cards.question: True or false: swapping a short lead for a long one can audibly dull a passive electric guitar?
cards.answer: True. A passive pickup is a coil with high inductance, and a cable adds capacitance, roughly 100 picofarads a metre. Together they make a filter with a bright peak; more capacitance pulls it lower, by well over a thousand hertz from a short lead to a long one. Tone lives partly in the lead.
cards.move: Check whether the connection is part of the circuit before calling it neutral.
cards.trap: A cable is just a wire, so its length cannot change the sound.
cards.reference: Zollner, Physik der Elektrogitarre, Hochschule Regensburg, 2014

cards.question: Why did the Spanish maker Antonio de Torres build a guitar with papier-mâché back and sides?
cards.answer: To show where the voice comes from. In 1862 Torres built a guitar whose back and sides were pasted paper, around a spruce top braced with his fan of thin struts, and it played well. The top, not the showy rosewood around it, carried the tone. The guitar survives in Barcelona's Museu de la Música.
cards.move: To find which part matters, replace the others with something cheap.
cards.reference: Romanillos, Antonio de Torres, Guitar Maker: His Life and Work, Element Books, 1987

cards.question: Why is one gap in standard guitar tuning a major third when every other is a fourth?
cards.answer: So the hand can reach the chords and the outer strings agree. Tuning E, A, D, G, B, E breaks the fourths once, between G and B; all fourths would end on F, clashing with the low E. The habit is older than the guitar: lutes and vihuelas tuned in fourths with one third too.
cards.move: An exception inside a regular pattern usually pays for something elsewhere.
cards.reference: Tyler & Sparks, The Guitar and Its Music: From the Renaissance to the Classical Era, Oxford University Press, 2002

cards.question: Why does a spoken phrase, looped enough times, start to sound like singing?
cards.answer: Because repetition shifts attention from meaning to pitch. Diana Deutsch looped a phrase from her own spoken recording, "sometimes behave so strangely": after a few repeats listeners hear a melody, and repeat it as song. Nothing in the recording changes. Played once more inside the original sentence, the phrase still sounds sung.
cards.move: What is repeated stops being read for meaning and starts being heard as shape.
cards.reference: Deutsch, Henthorn & Lapidis, Illusory transformation from speech to song, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2011

cards.question: The average intro on US top-ten hits lasted over 20 seconds in the mid-1980s. How long by 2015?
cards.answer: About 5 seconds. Hubert Léveillé Gauvin timed the intros of US top-ten singles from 1986 to 2015: over 20 seconds in the mid-1980s, about 5 by 2015, a fall of about 78%. Titles were sung sooner too. A hit now opens with the singer, before a thumb can reach the skip button.
cards.move: When a starting figure is handed over, push the guess further than feels comfortable.
cards.trap: Halving the 1980s figure feels like a bold enough guess.

cards.question: True or false: on Spotify, about a quarter of all song plays are abandoned within the first five seconds?
cards.answer: True. Spotify researchers found that about a quarter of streams stop inside five seconds, and only about half play to the end. Skips crowd into the opening seconds, long before most choruses arrive. The opening bars of a song work like a shop window passed at walking pace.
cards.move: A person's own habits are a sample of one, and a flattering one.
cards.trap: Judging from one's own listening, where chosen songs mostly play through.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0239418

cards.question: Why did judges wipe out a $2.8 million verdict over the riff in Katy Perry's Dark Horse?
cards.answer: Because the riff was made of common parts. A 2019 jury found it copied the Christian rap track Joyful Noise; the judge voided the award in 2020; the Ninth Circuit agreed in 2022. A short run of evenly spaced notes from a minor scale is a building block, and building blocks belong to nobody.
cards.move: Before calling something copied, ask how many others already had it.
cards.reference: Gray v. Hudson, 28 F.4th 87, United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, 2022

cards.question: What makes one melody far likelier than another to get stuck in the head?
cards.answer: A familiar shape with an odd detail. Kelly Jakubowski's team compared tunes that 3,000 people reported as earworms with matched songs that were not. The sticky ones were faster, followed a common rise-and-fall contour, and had unusual intervals: unexpected leaps, or more repeated notes than usual. A well-worn path with one strange step in it.
cards.move: People remember the familiar best when one thing in it is slightly wrong.
cards.source: Jakubowski et al., Psychology of Aesthetics, 2017
cards.reference: Jakubowski, Finkel, Stewart & Müllensiefen, Dissecting an earworm: Melodic features and song popularity predict involuntary musical imagery, Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 2017

cards.question: Among Billboard Hot 100 singles from 1958 to 2012, what did more repetitive lyrics predict?
options: Better odds of reaching number one
A faster fall down the chart
Nothing, once a song had charted
cards.answer: Better odds of reaching number one. Joseph Nunes and colleagues scored Hot 100 lyrics across 54 years: the more repetitive ones were likelier to reach the top, and got there faster. Lab tests showed repeated words are processed more easily. A chorus heard twice is half-learned.
cards.move: What is easy to take in is often mistaken for what is good.
cards.trap: Expecting repetition to tire listeners and cut a song's run short.
cards.reference: Nunes, Ordanini & Valsesia, The power of repetition: Repetitive lyrics in a song increase processing fluency and drive market success, Journal of Consumer Psychology, 2015

cards.question: In a 2015 experiment, which activity cut how often a just-heard song replayed in people's heads?
cards.answer: Chewing gum. Philip Beaman's team at Reading played people catchy songs and counted how often each tune came back: gum cut both the wanted and the unwanted replays, while finger tapping, the control for plain busyness, did not. Inner singing seems to borrow the speech muscles. A busy jaw leaves the inner voice mouthless.
cards.move: To stop a habit of mind, occupy the machinery it runs on.
cards.trap: Choosing tapping, since any steady movement should crowd a tune out.

cards.question: What did the 2014 finding that Wannabe is the world's catchiest song actually measure?
cards.answer: How fast players of one online game named short clips. Over 12,000 played Hooked on Music, from the University of Amsterdam with Manchester's Museum of Science and Industry: Wannabe averaged 2.29 seconds, Mambo No. 5 2.48, Eye of the Tiger 2.62. It ranks which fragments those players had stored best.
cards.move: Before accepting a title like best ever, ask who was asked and from what list.
cards.reference: https://www.newstalk.com/news/wannabe-mambo-no-5-and-eye-of-the-tiger-named-as-catchiest-singles-684162

cards.question: True or false: most tunes that get stuck in people's heads are experienced as unpleasant?
cards.answer: False. Andrea Halpern and James Bartlett had people log each stuck tune in a diary as it happened: the large majority of episodes were not unpleasant, and many came from music the person liked and had heard recently. The maddening ones get reported. Mostly, the loop is a favourite song replaying itself.
cards.move: Complaints sample the bad days, not the ordinary ones.
cards.trap: The maddening episodes are the ones remembered and talked about.
cards.reference: https://digitalcommons.bucknell.edu/fac_journ/296/

cards.question: Why do so many recent pop hits credit five or more songwriters?
cards.answer: Because of track-and-hook writing. A producer builds the instrumental first; several topliners, writers of melody and words, then try hooks over it, and each hook that survives earns its writer a credit. John Seabrook describes Ester Dean improvising syllables over a beat until a phrase stuck. A chorus gets auditioned like an actor.
cards.move: Many names on a result can mean many tries, not many hands.
cards.reference: Seabrook, The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory, W. W. Norton, 2015

cards.question: How did New York keep Thelonious Monk out of its jazz clubs from 1951 to 1957?
cards.answer: Through the cabaret card. Anyone working in a New York venue that served alcohol needed an identity card issued by the police, and a drug conviction could cost it. Monk lost his after a 1951 narcotics arrest; Billie Holiday lost hers in 1947. The city abolished the cards in 1967.
cards.move: A permit to work is a quiet way to decide who gets heard.
cards.reference: Chevigny, Gigs: Jazz and the Cabaret Laws in New York City, Routledge, 1991

cards.question: Which songbook did nearly every jazz student own for three decades, although selling it was illegal?
cards.answer: The Real Book. In the 1970s two Berklee students copied the lead sheets, melody and chords, of hundreds of standards without licensing any of them, and copies spread through photocopy shops. Composers earned nothing from it until Hal Leonard cleared the rights and issued a legal edition in 2004, keeping the handwritten look.
cards.move: Standards are set by what gets copied, not by what gets approved.
cards.source: Kernfeld, The Story of Fake Books, 2006
cards.reference: Kernfeld, The Story of Fake Books: Bootlegging Songs to Musicians, Scarecrow Press, 2006

cards.question: Why did bebop take shape in the early 1940s with almost no commercial recordings of it?
cards.answer: Because the musicians' union had stopped its members making records. From August 1942 James Petrillo's American Federation of Musicians struck against the record companies, demanding payment for discs replacing live players on radio and jukeboxes. Decca settled in 1943, Victor and Columbia only in November 1944. Bebop grew meanwhile in late-night sessions at Minton's.
cards.move: A gap in the record can be a strike, not a silence.
cards.reference: DeVeaux, The Birth of Bebop: A Social and Musical History, University of California Press, 1997

cards.question: At very fast tempos, how uneven are the swung eighth notes jazz drummers play on the ride cymbal?
cards.answer: Close to even. Measuring drummers on recordings, Friberg and Sundström found the long-short ratio falls as tempo rises: as high as 3.5 to 1 at slow tempos, near 1 to 1 at fast ones. The short note stayed around 100 milliseconds, as if it could get no shorter.
cards.move: Notation is a shorthand; time what the players actually do.
cards.trap: The 2 to 1 triplet taught in lessons pulls the guess.
cards.reference: https://online.ucpress.edu/mp/article-abstract/19/3/333/61900/Swing-Ratios-and-Ensemble-Timing-in-Jazz

cards.question: True or false: for over 30 years, the first side of Kind of Blue sounded higher than the band played?
cards.answer: True. A tape machine at the 1959 session ran slow, so the master played back fast and a little sharp, well under a semitone, on So What, Freddie Freeloader and Blue in Green. An engineer caught the error only in 1992. Players transcribing those solos had found the band tuned somewhere between keys.
cards.move: The most copied version is not always the version that happened.
cards.trap: Assuming the best-selling jazz album was checked note for note.
cards.reference: Kahn, Kind of Blue: The Making of the Miles Davis Masterpiece, Da Capo Press, 2000

cards.question: Why is Buddy Bolden, named by New Orleans players as the first jazz bandleader, known only from their memories?
cards.answer: Because he stopped playing before jazz was recorded. Bolden was committed to the state asylum at Jackson, Louisiana, in 1907, a decade before the first jazz record, and died there in 1931. A cylinder he supposedly cut in the 1890s has never been found. His sound survives only in other players' descriptions.
cards.move: The first of anything is often the least documented.
cards.source: Marquis, In Search of Buddy Bolden, 1978
cards.reference: Marquis, In Search of Buddy Bolden: First Man of Jazz, Louisiana State University Press, 1978

cards.question: Why did bebop players like Charlie Parker write new melodies over the chords of existing songs such as Cherokee?
options: To show off their harmonic skill
Chords owed nothing; melodies earned royalties
cards.answer: Because a chord sequence cannot be copyrighted and a melody can. Recording Cherokee meant paying its publisher; Parker's Ko-Ko of 1945, a new line over the same changes, made Parker the composer, and saved the label a fee. Hundreds of bebop tunes sit on borrowed chords, those of I Got Rhythm above all.
cards.move: When something is copied, check which part the law lets through free.
cards.trap: Bebop's harmonic daring makes the showing-off story feel complete.
cards.source: Owens, Bebop: The Music and Its Players
cards.reference: Owens, Bebop: The Music and Its Players, Oxford University Press, 1995

cards.question: True or false: the word jazz first appeared in print describing music in New Orleans?
cards.answer: False. The earliest printed uses are Californian sports slang: in 1912 the Los Angeles Times described a pitcher's jazz ball, a pitch said to wobble, and San Francisco sportswriters used it for pep in 1913. Bands took the word up in the following years, in Chicago and beyond.
cards.move: The first written record of a word rarely shows where it was born.
cards.trap: The New Orleans birth story is told so often it claims the word too.
cards.reference: Los Angeles Times, Ben's Jazz Curve, 2 April 1912

cards.question: Should a jazz soloist earn a composer's royalty for an improvised solo on someone else's tune?
cards.answer: An improvised chorus is composition in real time: a new melody, often more memorable than the tune under it. Players transcribe and study famous solos as works in their own right. Yet the composer's credit, and the royalty with it, goes to whoever wrote the song, perhaps thirty-two bars written decades earlier.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether improvising counts as writing.
cards.counterpoint: The solo exists only because the tune's chords and form were there to improvise on, and the soloist is already paid as a performer, through session fees and recording royalties. Splitting composer credit among every soloist on every take would make licensing a standard unworkable and fence off the shared material jazz is built from.
cards.reference: Toynbee, Making Popular Music: Musicians, Creativity and Institutions, Arnold, 2000

cards.question: A 78 side held about three minutes. A band plays a 32-bar tune in 4/4 at 200 beats a minute. How many whole choruses fit?
cards.answer: So 4 whole choruses fit.
cards.move: A fixed container quietly writes the form of whatever goes into it.
cards.trap: Rounding 4.7 up to 5, though a chorus cannot stop halfway.
cards.hint: Count the beats in one chorus, then divide by the tempo.
steps: One chorus: 32 × 4 = 128 beats.
128 ÷ 200 = 0.64 minutes a chorus.
3 ÷ 0.64 = about 4.7 choruses.
So 4 whole choruses fit.
cards.source: Day, A Century of Recorded Music, 2000
cards.reference: Day, A Century of Recorded Music: Listening to Musical History, Yale University Press, 2000

cards.question: Why did Abbey Road engineers build a device in 1966 to fake a second vocal take?
cards.answer: Because John Lennon hated singing the same part twice. Double-tracking, recording a line again over the first take, thickened a voice but ate studio time. Ken Townsend fed the vocal to a second tape machine whose speed could be varied, so the copy trailed by a few wobbling milliseconds. Artificial double tracking arrived on Revolver.
cards.move: Automate the chore that someone talented refuses to repeat.
cards.reference: Lewisohn, The Beatles Recording Sessions, Harmony Books, 1988

cards.question: True or false: copying a vocal track onto a second track and playing both makes it sound double-tracked?
cards.answer: False. Identical copies add in perfect step: the voice gets about 6 decibels louder, same character. A real double works because two takes differ by a few milliseconds and a few cents of pitch, and the ear reads the smear as two singers. Stacking copies of one take just pushes up a fader.
cards.move: Copies of one source add volume, not evidence.
cards.trap: True, since two tracks of the same voice should sound like two.
cards.reference: Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques, Focal Press, 2010

cards.question: For I'm Not in Love, 10cc's three singers each sang every note of a chromatic scale, octave included, 16 times. How many voices?
cards.answer: 48 x 13 = 624 voices.
cards.move: Count the fence posts, not the gaps between them.
cards.trap: Using 12 notes and forgetting the octave at the top.
cards.hint: Build the choir for a single note first, then count the notes, both ends included.
steps: A chromatic scale up to its octave has 13 notes.
3 singers x 16 takes = 48 voices on each note.
48 x 13 = 624 voices.
cards.reference: https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-10cc-not-love

cards.question: A producer layers two punchy kick drum samples, and the combined kick sounds thinner and weaker. Why?
options: The ear tires of the attack
cards.answer: Their low waves partly cancel. A kick is mostly a low, nearly pure thump; where one sample's wave rises while the other's falls, they subtract. Sliding one by a few milliseconds, or flipping its polarity, brings the weight back. Two heavy blows, badly timed, land like one soft one.
cards.move: Two strengths can subtract when their timing is wrong.
cards.trap: The mix bus is clipping, since two loud sounds cause an overload.
cards.reference: Izhaki, Mixing Audio: Concepts, Practices and Tools, Focal Press, 2008

cards.question: Why did several early Queen albums carry a sleeve note saying no synthesisers were used?
cards.answer: Because listeners assumed the layered sounds were synthesised. Brian May built orchestral sections by recording his home-made guitar in many harmonised parts, one line at a time; the choirs were three band members overdubbed again and again. Their first album with a synthesiser was The Game, in 1980. The orchestra was one guitar, stacked.
cards.move: When a result looks machine-made, ask how many patient passes built it.
cards.source: Queen, A Night at the Opera, 1975
cards.reference: Queen, A Night at the Opera, EMI, 1975, sleeve notes

cards.question: How could Revolver be remixed in 2022 with instruments that four-track tape had merged in 1966?
cards.answer: By having software pull them apart. To fit Revolver onto four-track tape, engineers bounced several parts onto one track, merging them for good. Peter Jackson's team built a machine-learning tool for the Get Back film that separates instruments and voices in one recording; Giles Martin used it. The layers came back out of the mix.
cards.move: A merge once final can become reversible when a new tool arrives.
cards.reference: https://www.loudersound.com/features/breaking-down-the-beatles-giles-martin-and-the-miracle-of-the-revolver-de-mix

cards.question: How many singers, each as loud as a soloist and not in lockstep, does it take to sound twice as loud?
cards.answer: 10 times the power takes 10 singers.
cards.move: When perception runs on ratios, doubling the effect costs far more than doubling the effort.
cards.trap: Two singers, as if two voices made twice the sound.
cards.hint: Perceived loudness doubles for roughly every 10 decibels added.
steps: Perceived loudness doubles for about every 10 dB added.
Voices not in lockstep add their power.
+10 dB is 10 times the power.
10 times the power takes 10 singers.

diagram.caption: Ten singers give ten times the power of one, yet sound only twice as loud.

cards.reference: Stevens, The Measurement of Loudness, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1955

cards.question: Should a touring band use backing tracks to reproduce its layered studio sound on stage?
sides: No, play only what is played
cards.answer: A modern record is dozens of layers: stacked vocals, doubled guitars, synth pads. Four people cannot play forty parts, and an audience paid to hear the songs it knows. Tracks let a small band deliver the arrangement faithfully every night, while the players and the singer stay genuinely live on top of them.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a ticket buys songs or performance.
cards.counterpoint: A concert is worth attending because it can differ from the record. Tracks lock every song to a click, so the band cannot stretch a chorus or follow the crowd. When they fail, the illusion collapses, as when the wrong vocal track played for Ashlee Simpson on Saturday Night Live in 2004.
cards.reference: Saturday Night Live, NBC, broadcast 23 October 2004

cards.question: A vocal plays hard left and an exact copy, 10 milliseconds late, plays hard right. Where do listeners hear it?
options: As two voices, one each side
From the left, where it arrives first
cards.answer: From the left, where it arrives first. Within about 30 milliseconds the ear fuses a sound with its echo and places it at the first arrival. Helmut Haas found the late copy could be up to about 10 decibels louder before it pulled the image back. Wide doubles made by delay lean toward one speaker.
cards.move: Whatever reaches you first gets to say where it came from.
cards.trap: Equal levels in both speakers should put the voice in the middle.
cards.reference: Haas, Über den Einfluss eines Einfachechos auf die Hörsamkeit von Sprache, Acustica, 1951

cards.question: An engineer adds a quiet synth layer under a chorus, and the chorus now sounds better. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the chorus simply got louder
How the layer sounds in mono
cards.answer: Whether the chorus simply got louder. Side by side, the louder of two otherwise identical versions tends to sound fuller and clearer, even by a decibel, so any added layer starts with an unfair edge. Mastering engineers match levels before comparing. Turned down to the old level, many layers stop earning their place.
cards.move: Before crediting a change, check whether it also changed the amount.
cards.trap: Looking at what the layer plays, as if its content caused the lift.
cards.reference: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science, 2nd edn, Focal Press, 2007

cards.question: True or false: Mozart was buried in a pauper's grave because he died penniless?
cards.answer: False. He was buried in December 1791 in a shared grave at St Marx under Joseph II's burial rules, which sent most middle-class Viennese to common graves with no mourners at the graveside. His third-class funeral was the ordinary kind. He left debts, but in the 1780s he had been among Vienna's well-paid musicians.
cards.move: A vivid scene from a film is not a record of what happened.
cards.trap: The rain-soaked pauper's burial from films is the first picture.
cards.reference: Braunbehrens, Mozart in Vienna, 1781-1791, trans. Bell, Grove Weidenfeld, 1990

cards.question: What did a researcher find in a Prague music archive in 2015 bearing both Mozart's and Salieri's names?
cards.answer: A piece they wrote together. Per la ricuperata salute di Ophelia, a short cantata for the singer Nancy Storace's return to the stage in 1785, has music by Salieri, Mozart and a composer named Cornetti, to words by Lorenzo Da Ponte. The printed copy turned up in the Czech Museum of Music.
cards.move: A famous rivalry is usually a story told about colleagues.
cards.reference: Czech Museum of Music, presentation of Per la ricuperata salute di Ophelia, National Museum, Prague, 2016

cards.question: What do Vienna's death registers from the winter of 1791 suggest about how Mozart died?
cards.answer: An infection going round, not poison. Zegers and colleagues went through thousands of deaths in the city registers for the winters around 1791 and found a rise in deaths with oedema, swelling from fluid, among young men in the weeks around his. That fits a streptococcal infection damaging the kidneys, and his reported swelling.
cards.move: Before a special explanation, check what everyone else was dying of.
cards.source: Zegers et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2009
cards.reference: Zegers, Weigl and Steptoe, The death of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart: an epidemiologic perspective, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2009

cards.question: Where did the idea come from that Mozart composed whole works in his head and merely copied them out?
cards.answer: Largely from a letter forged in his name. Friedrich Rochlitz printed it in the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung in 1815, with Mozart describing whole pieces arriving at once. Hundreds of his sketches and unfinished fragments survive, including abandoned openings, and Ulrich Konrad catalogued them in 1992. Mozart crossed things out like anyone else.
cards.move: When a story flatters genius, check who wrote it and when.
cards.reference: Konrad, Mozarts Schaffensweise: Studien zu den Werkautographen, Skizzen und Entwürfen, Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1992

cards.question: Roughly what share of his 35 years did Mozart spend travelling away from home?
cards.answer: Over a quarter. Counted day by day, the journeys come to about ten years. The tour of 1763 to 1766 through Germany, Paris and London alone took nearly three and a half years, and three Italian trips followed. Much of his childhood was spent in a coach on bad roads.
cards.move: Count the days before you picture the life.
cards.trap: Picturing a composer at a desk in Salzburg or Vienna.
cards.reference: Halliwell, The Mozart Family: Four Lives in a Social Context, Oxford University Press, 1998

cards.question: Why is Mozart's Clarinet Concerto usually played today in a version he never wrote?
cards.answer: Because he wrote it in 1791 for Anton Stadler's basset clarinet, an instrument reaching a major third lower, and his manuscript is lost. The first printed editions, from 1801, rewrote the low passages to fit an ordinary clarinet. Scholars have reconstructed the original, and some players now perform it on rebuilt basset clarinets.
cards.move: When the original is lost, the copy quietly becomes the standard.
cards.reference: Lawson, Mozart: Clarinet Concerto, Cambridge Music Handbooks, Cambridge University Press, 1996

cards.question: Mozart died leaving his Requiem unfinished. Which part of it had he fully orchestrated?
cards.answer: Only the opening Requiem aeternam. For the Kyrie, the sequence and the offertory he left the voices and bass line, with some instrumental cues; helpers such as Joseph Eybler and Franz Xaver Süssmayr filled in the orchestra. The Lacrimosa stops after eight bars, and for the Sanctus onward no page in Mozart's hand survives.
cards.move: A sketch in a master's hand is not the finished thing.
cards.trap: The Lacrimosa, because the story says he died writing it.
cards.reference: Wolff, Mozart's Requiem: Historical and Analytical Studies, Documents, Score, University of California Press, 1994

cards.question: True or false: Mozart's Symphony No. 37 is mostly the work of another composer?
cards.answer: True. The symphony long catalogued as K. 444 is Michael Haydn's Symphony in G; Mozart copied it out in 1783, probably for a concert in Linz, and wrote only its short slow introduction. Because the manuscript was in his hand, 19th-century editors counted it among his works, and the numbering still carries the gap.
cards.move: Ask how a catalogue decided what belonged in it.
cards.trap: A symphony numbered among his works must be his work.
cards.reference: Zaslaw, Mozart's Symphonies: Context, Performance Practice, Reception, Clarendon Press, 1989

cards.question: How old was Mozart when he wrote his variations on the tune now sung as Twinkle, Twinkle?
cards.answer: About 25, not a child. The twelve variations K. 265, on the French song Ah, vous dirai-je, maman, were long dated to his Paris stay of 1778; study of the paper and handwriting puts them in Vienna around 1781 or 1782. The English words, Jane Taylor's poem of 1806, came to the tune later.
cards.move: A childish tune says nothing about the age of the person using it.
cards.source: Tyson, Mozart: Studies of the Autograph Scores
cards.reference: Tyson, Mozart: Studies of the Autograph Scores, Harvard University Press, 1987

cards.question: A dice game printed under Mozart's name in 1792 picks each of 16 bars by throwing two dice. Roughly how many possible throw sequences?
cards.answer: About 46 quadrillion. Two dice give 11 totals, 2 to 12, and each total points to a bar, so the choices multiply: 11 to the 16th power, about 4.6 × 10^16. Some tables repeat a bar, so distinct minuets are fewer, but played one a minute they would outlast the universe so far.
cards.move: When choices chain, multiply them; adding is how intuition fails.
cards.trap: Adding 11 choices for each of 16 bars gives 176.
cards.reference: Hedges, Dice Music in the Eighteenth Century, Music & Letters, 1978

cards.question: Why is a well-tuned piano deliberately out of tune with the textbook octave?
cards.answer: Because its strings are stiff. A stiff string's overtones run slightly sharp of whole-number multiples, so tuners widen each octave to match them. The stretch adds up: the top notes sit tens of cents sharp of strict equal temperament, a cent being a hundredth of a semitone. An exactly mathematical piano sounds sour up top.
cards.move: When the parts are imperfect, tune them to each other, not to the ideal.
cards.reference: Railsback, Scale temperament as applied to piano tuning, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1938

cards.question: What do the three strings on most piano notes give besides extra volume?
cards.answer: A long tail to the sound. Gabriel Weinreich showed in 1977 that a note's strings, never tuned perfectly alike, trade energy through the bridge. The loud first part dies fast; a quieter aftersound then lingers for seconds. A tuner's last nudge on a unison decides how long a chord hangs in the air.
cards.move: Two slightly different parts can outlast two identical ones.
cards.reference: Weinreich, Coupled piano strings, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1977

cards.question: While a pianist keeps a key held down after playing a note, where is its hammer?
cards.answer: Caught below the string. Bartolomeo Cristofori's escapement, built in Florence around 1700, releases the hammer so it flies the last stretch alone, strikes, and falls back onto a felt catch. A hammer left touching would choke the note at once. The finger never hits the string; it throws something that does.
cards.move: What starts an action is not always what finishes it.
cards.trap: Resting on the string, since the key is still held down.
cards.reference: Pollens, The Early Pianoforte, Cambridge University Press, 1995

cards.question: Estimate the combined pull of all the strings inside a concert grand piano, in tonnes.
cards.answer: About 18 tonnes.
cards.move: Add up many small pulls before calling anything delicate.
cards.trap: Picturing a guitar's gentle pull and guessing under a tonne.
cards.hint: Count strings rather than keys, then give each one a pull of tens of kilograms.
steps: 88 notes, most with two or three strings: roughly 230 strings.
Each string is pulled tight at about 80 kg of force.
About 18 tonnes.
cards.source: Fletcher & Rossing, Physics of Musical Instruments
cards.reference: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, Springer, 1998

cards.question: Can a pianist change a single note's tone by touch, beyond how loud it is?
cards.answer: The hammer is not all that reaches the ear. Werner Goebl and colleagues found that striking a key from above, rather than pressing it from its surface, adds a thump of finger and key that arrives just before the tone. Listeners hear that noise as part of the note, so two equal notes can differ.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether noise around a note counts as tone.
cards.counterpoint: Once the escapement releases it, the hammer flies free, and the string learns only one thing: how fast it arrived. Tests since Hart, Fuller and Lusby in 1934 find that matching hammer speed matches the tone. What pianists call colour is loudness, timing and pedalling across many notes: real artistry, but nothing hidden in a single key.
cards.reference: Goebl, Bresin & Galembo, Touch and temporal behavior of grand piano actions, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2005

cards.question: True or false: on a modern grand, the pedal marked una corda makes each hammer strike just one string?
cards.answer: False. On most notes it strikes two of three. The pedal slides the keyboard and action sideways, so each hammer misses one string and meets the others with less worn felt, changing colour as well as volume. The name dates from early pianos, whose shift could reach a single string.
cards.move: An old name can outlive the thing it once described exactly.
cards.trap: Una corda means one string, so one string it must be.
cards.reference: Palmieri (ed.), The Piano: An Encyclopedia, 2nd edn, Routledge, 2003

cards.question: What did Sébastien Érard's 1821 double escapement let a pianist do that the older action did not?
options: Sustain a note after letting go
Restrike a key before it fully rose
cards.answer: Restrike a key before it fully rose. In a single escapement the key must come nearly all the way up before the hammer can be thrown again. Érard added a lever that catches the hammer partway down and resets the action early. Fast repeated notes and trills became playable at the speed of Liszt.
cards.move: Speed is often limited by the reset, not by the stroke itself.
cards.trap: Assuming the great piano inventions were about loudness or sustain.
cards.source: Good, Giraffes, Black Dragons, and Other Pianos
cards.reference: Good, Giraffes, Black Dragons, and Other Pianos: A Technological History from Cristofori to the Modern Concert Grand, Stanford University Press, 2001

cards.question: What can the middle pedal of a concert grand hold that the right-hand pedal cannot?
cards.answer: Only the notes already down when it is pressed. The sostenuto pedal, patented by Steinway in 1874, keeps up the dampers of keys held at that moment, while every other damper works normally. A pianist can hold a deep bass note for bars and play crisp chords above it. One pedal, a selective memory.
cards.move: A tool that remembers only part of the moment can be the more useful one.
cards.reference: Lieberman, Steinway & Sons, Yale University Press, 1995

cards.question: A hammer strikes a 1,000 mm string 125 mm from its end. Which is the lowest harmonic it cannot excite? Give its number.
cards.answer: The lowest harmonic with a node at 1/8: the 8th.
cards.move: A push delivered exactly where something stands still cannot start it moving.
cards.trap: Answering 7, recalling the old lore that hammers silence the seventh.
cards.hint: Each harmonic has still points, nodes, at fixed fractions of the length.
steps: 125 / 1,000 = 1/8 of the length.
The nth harmonic has nodes at every 1/n of the string.
Striking at a node cannot set that harmonic going.
The lowest harmonic with a node at 1/8: the 8th.
cards.source: Helmholtz, On the Sensations of Tone
cards.reference: Helmholtz, On the Sensations of Tone, trans. Ellis, Dover, 1954

cards.question: Should pianists playing music written before about 1850 ask for an unequal temperament instead of equal tuning?
cards.answer: Many tunings of that era gave each key its own colour: near-pure thirds in C, edgier ones in keys with many sharps or flats. Composers chose keys knowing it. Equal temperament makes every key identical, so a key picked for its sweetness sounds like any other. It erases a colour the score assumed.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what is knowable about the tuning composers heard.
cards.counterpoint: The historical record is thinner than the argument. Broadwood had its tuners trained in equal temperament in 1846, and Alexander Ellis's 1885 measurements found working tuners already aiming at it. Which unequal tuning a composer heard is usually unknown, and choosing one imposes a guess. Equal tuning at least favours no key the composer never favoured.
cards.reference: Jorgensen, Tuning: Containing the Perfection of Eighteenth-Century Temperament, Michigan State University Press, 1991

cards.question: Where did the lush reverb on records cut in Capitol's Hollywood tower come from?
cards.answer: From concrete rooms about 9 metres underground. Les Paul helped design the first four, built with the Capitol Tower in 1956; four more were dug under its car park in 1969. A loudspeaker played the mix into a trapezoidal concrete room, and a microphone caught what came back, up to five seconds of it.
cards.move: Behind a famous sound, look for the room nobody photographs.
cards.reference: https://www.uaudio.com/products/capitol-chambers

cards.question: How did a hanging sheet of steel become the sound of countless 1960s and 1970s vocals?
cards.answer: By being shaken. The EMT 140, sold from 1957, hung a thin steel plate about 2 metres long in a frame; a driver shook it and pickups caught the shimmer. Moving a felt damper nearer or farther changed the decay time. A studio's cathedral fitted in a long wooden box against the wall.
cards.move: When space is scarce, imitate its behaviour rather than its size.
cards.reference: Välimäki, Parker, Savioja, Smith & Abel, Fifty Years of Artificial Reverberation, IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, 2012

cards.question: How can software make a vocal sound as if sung inside a cathedral it never visited?
cards.answer: By recording how the cathedral answers a single click. Engineers fire an impulse or a slow sine sweep there and record the reply; convolution then treats every instant of the vocal as a click and sums the echoes. Angelo Farina's 2000 sweep method made this clean. A building's acoustics now travel as a small file.
cards.move: Know how a system answers one knock, and its answer to anything follows.
cards.reference: Farina, Simultaneous measurement of impulse response and distortion with a swept-sine technique, Audio Engineering Society Convention 108, 2000

cards.question: The gated drum sound, a huge room roar chopped off abruptly, was discovered while recording which album?
options: Bruce Springsteen's Born in the USA
cards.answer: Peter Gabriel's third album, 1980. At London's Townhouse Studios, engineer Hugh Padgham heard Phil Collins's drums through a talkback microphone, heavily compressed and cut by a noise gate, which silences quiet signal: the room exploded, then went silent. Intruder was built on it; In the Air Tonight followed in 1981.
cards.move: The version everyone remembers is often the second one.
cards.trap: Face Value, because In the Air Tonight made the sound famous.
cards.reference: Peter Gabriel, Peter Gabriel (third album), Charisma Records, 1980, sleeve credits

cards.question: True or false: spring reverb was first invented for an electric organ, not a guitar amplifier?
cards.answer: True. Laurens Hammond filed a spring reverb patent in 1939, to make his electric organ sound as if it filled a church: coiled springs carried the signal as slow mechanical waves. Guitar amplifiers took up spring tanks built on his design in the early 1960s. Surf guitar's drip came from a church organ's problem.
cards.move: A tool's most famous user is often not the one it was made for.
cards.trap: False, since the sound is most famous from surf and twang guitar.
cards.reference: Hammond, Electrical musical instrument, US Patent 2,230,836, filed 1939, granted 1941

cards.question: Why did the first computer reverbs ring with a faint metallic pitch, and how was it tamed?
cards.answer: Because one repeating delay is a note. Manfred Schroeder built reverb from delays fed back into themselves; an echo returning every 30 milliseconds buzzes at about 33 hertz. He ran several in parallel, their lengths chosen to share no common rhythm, then smeared the result with further filters. Clashing repeats blur into a wash.
cards.move: Repeat one pattern and it becomes a signal; mix mismatched ones and it becomes texture.
cards.reference: Schroeder, 'Natural' Sounding Artificial Reverberation, Journal of the Audio Engineering Society, 1962

cards.question: How did London's Royal Festival Hall, judged too dry, get a longer bass reverberation in the 1960s?
cards.answer: With microphones and loudspeakers. P. H. Parkin and K. Morgan's assisted resonance used many channels, each tuned to prolong one narrow frequency: a microphone heard the hall, an amplifier fed it back. Empty, the 125-hertz band rose from about 1.4 to 2.5 seconds. A concert hall ran on a reverb unit.
cards.move: When the structure cannot change, check whether a signal can stand in for it.
cards.reference: Parkin & Morgan, 'Assisted Resonance' in The Royal Festival Hall, London: 1965–1969, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1970

cards.question: In a mix, which change to a vocal's reverb most makes the singer seem farther from the listener?
options: Less dry voice against the reverb
A longer gap before the reverb
cards.answer: Less dry voice against the reverb. As a source moves away, its direct sound fades while the room's reverberation holds steady, so their ratio tracks distance. Tail length describes the room. A longer gap before the reverb does the opposite: the voice arrives well ahead of the room, as a close voice does.
cards.move: When two cues usually arrive together, find out which one the judgement truly reads.
cards.trap: Big distant sounds are heard in big spaces, so length seems like distance.
cards.reference: Zahorik, Brungart & Bronkhorst, Auditory distance perception in humans: A summary of past and present research, Acta Acustica united with Acustica, 2005

cards.question: A vocal reverb has a 2-second decay, under a dense mix that hides anything 30 dB quieter. How long is the tail audible?
cards.answer: About 1 second. A reverb's decay time is how long its tail takes to fall 60 decibels, to a millionth of its energy. The tail loses a steady number of decibels each second, 30 here, so the mix swallows it halfway. Soloed, the same vocal would trail on for the full two seconds.
cards.move: Ask what threshold a quoted duration is measured to before planning around it.
cards.trap: Taking the 2 seconds on the dial as the time the tail is heard.

diagram.caption: The tail falls 30 dB a second, so a mix 30 dB down swallows it halfway.

cards.reference: Izhaki, Mixing Audio: Concepts, Practices and Tools, Focal Press, 2008

cards.question: Convolving audio directly with a 2-second hall recording takes roughly how many billion multiply-adds per second of sound?
cards.answer: 96,000 x 48,000 = about 4.6 billion.
cards.move: When every part meets every other part, the work grows as the square.
cards.trap: Counting the samples in the recording once, as if each were used once.
cards.hint: Count the samples in the hall recording, then how many output samples each one touches.
steps: Studio audio runs at about 48,000 samples a second.
A 2-second hall recording holds 2 x 48,000 = 96,000 samples.
Each output sample needs all 96,000 multiplied and summed.
96,000 x 48,000 = about 4.6 billion.
cards.reference: Gardner, Efficient Convolution without Input-Output Delay, Journal of the Audio Engineering Society, 1995

cards.question: What do the Cuban tresillo rhythm and a particle accelerator's timing system have in common?
cards.answer: The same algorithm. Spreading 3 beats as evenly as possible over 8 pulses gives 3+3+2, the tresillo under the habanera and countless pop grooves. Godfried Toussaint showed in 2005 that this rule, used by Eric Bjorklund to space pulses at a neutron source, generates dozens of traditional rhythms. Five over eight gives the Cuban cinquillo.
cards.move: When a pattern feels natural, look for the simple rule that makes it.
cards.reference: Toussaint, The Euclidean algorithm generates traditional musical rhythms, Proceedings of BRIDGES: Mathematical Connections in Art, Music and Science, 2005

cards.question: Do the tiny timing slips of a human drummer make a beat feel groovier?
cards.answer: Mostly not, in listening tests. Matthew Davies and colleagues added small timing deviations to short drum and bass patterns; listeners rated the strictly quantised versions as groovy or groovier, and larger deviations lowered the ratings. Other studies agree, though musicians still argue. Groove came from where notes fell in the bar, not from millisecond slips.
cards.move: A story about why something works needs testing with that thing removed.
cards.reference: Davies, Madison, Silva & Gouyon, The effect of microtiming deviations on the perception of groove in short rhythms, Music Perception, 2013

cards.question: In 2009, which animal was shown in a controlled test to keep dancing in time as a song's tempo changed?
cards.answer: A sulphur-crested cockatoo named Snowball. In 2009 Aniruddh Patel's team played him a Backstreet Boys song at a range of speeds, and his head-bobs locked onto the beat for stretches at many of them. A leading explanation: beat-keeping rides on vocal learning, which parrots have and apes lack. The zoo's best dancer is its mimic.
cards.move: A skill often follows a shared ability rather than the family tree.
cards.trap: A chimpanzee, since the closest relative should share the skill.
cards.reference: Patel, Iversen, Bregman & Schulz, Experimental evidence for synchronization to a musical beat in a nonhuman animal, Current Biology, 2009

cards.question: In an online study of funk drum breaks, which ones made listeners most want to move?
cards.answer: Moderately syncopated breaks. Syncopation means accents placed off the beat. Maria Witek's team found that both the urge to move and the pleasure rose with syncopation, then fell as it grew heavy: an inverted U. Too few off-beat accents leave the body nothing to fill; too many and it loses the pulse altogether.
cards.move: When some of a thing helps, test whether more of it keeps helping.
cards.trap: The most syncopated, if off-beat accents are what make funk groove.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0094446

cards.question: True or false: people tapping along to a steady metronome tend to hit slightly before each click?
cards.answer: True. The lead is usually tens of milliseconds, larger in non-musicians, and tappers do not notice it. Bruno Repp's review of the tapping literature calls it negative mean asynchrony; one explanation is that the fingertip's touch reaches awareness later than the click's sound. The hand leaves early so both arrive together.
cards.move: A body that seems to react may be predicting instead.
cards.trap: False, because reacting to a sound should make taps land late.
cards.reference: Repp, Sensorimotor synchronization: A review of the tapping literature, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2005

cards.question: Why does a beat stop feeling like a beat once it slows to one every three seconds?
cards.answer: Because prediction gives out. Beyond about two seconds between pulses, listeners stop anticipating the next sound and start reacting to it: their taps trail each click instead of meeting it. Justin London puts felt metre between roughly 100 milliseconds and 2 seconds per beat. A slow dirge is counted in the pulses inside each step.
cards.move: Past a certain gap, anticipation turns into reaction, and the pattern dissolves.
cards.reference: London, Hearing in Time: Psychological Aspects of Musical Meter, 2nd edn, Oxford University Press, 2012

cards.question: Listeners tapping along to music most readily settle on a beat near which rate per minute?
cards.answer: About 120, a beat every half second. Leon van Noorden and Dirk Moelants found tapping resonates around 2 beats a second, and Moelants found recorded music's tempos cluster near it. Walking cadence sits close by; the resting heart does not. Dance floors run at about the pace of a brisk walk.
cards.move: The rhythm nearest to mind is not always the one the body keeps.
cards.trap: The heartbeat is the body's most famous rhythm, so it sets the tempo.
cards.reference: van Noorden & Moelants, Resonance in the perception of musical pulse, Journal of New Music Research, 1999

cards.question: Two tones sound together on every beat; now and then one arrives early. Which one do tapping hands correct for more?
cards.answer: The lower tone. Michael Hove and colleagues found early low tones drew larger brain responses and larger tapping corrections than early high ones. A model of the inner ear traced the edge to the ear itself. It may be why bass and kick drum, not the melody, lay down the beat.
cards.move: Ask which channel carries the timing before trusting the one that carries the tune.
cards.trap: The higher tone, since melodies sit high and draw the attention.
cards.reference: Hove, Marie, Bruce & Trainor, Superior time perception for lower musical pitch explains why bass-ranged instruments lay down musical rhythms, PNAS, 2014

cards.question: At 125 beats per minute, a drum machine at 75% swing delays each second sixteenth note by how many milliseconds?
cards.move: Turn a percentage into time before judging how big a nudge is.
cards.trap: Taking 75% as a delay of three quarters of the whole beat.
cards.hint: Swing is a percentage of the time taken by a pair of sixteenths.
steps: A pair of sixteenths fills an eighth: 480 / 2 = 240 ms.
Straight, the second lands at 50% of 240 = 120 ms; at 75%, 180 ms.
cards.reference: https://www.attackmagazine.com/features/interview/roger-linn-swing-groove-magic-mpc-timing/

cards.question: True or false: in a train of identical, evenly spaced tones, the brain treats alternate tones as if accented?
cards.answer: True. Renaud Brochard and colleagues recorded brain waves during a steady train of identical tones, now and then making one quieter: the brain reacted more strongly to that change on odd-numbered tones, as if they were accented. The listener imposes the grouping. The tick-tock of a clock is written by the brain, not the clock.
cards.move: Before crediting a pattern to the source, check whether the observer supplies it.
cards.trap: Identical sounds should produce identical responses, so no accent can exist.
cards.reference: Brochard, Abecasis, Potter, Ragot & Drake, The ticktock of our internal clock: Direct brain evidence of subjective accents in isochronous sequences, Psychological Science, 2003

cards.question: What did John Cage hear inside Harvard's anechoic chamber, a room built to swallow every sound?
cards.answer: Two sounds, one high and one low. Cage later said an engineer told him they were his nervous system and his blood. Nerves make no audible tone, and the faint ringing that deep quiet exposes in many ears is a likelier source. Either way he concluded there was no such thing as silence.
cards.move: Remove every sound outside and the listener becomes the source.
cards.reference: Cage, Silence: Lectures and Writings, Wesleyan University Press, 1961

cards.question: What did the audience at the 1952 premiere of Cage's 4′33″ in Woodstock actually hear?
cards.answer: Wind, rain and themselves. David Tudor sat at the piano in a hall open to the woods, closed the lid to begin each of three movements and turned pages without playing. Cage recalled wind in the first movement, rain pattering on the roof in the second, and people talking or walking out in the third.
cards.move: Frame any stretch of time and whatever fills it becomes the content.
cards.source: Gann, No Such Thing as Silence, 2010
cards.reference: Gann, No Such Thing as Silence: John Cage's 4'33", Yale University Press, 2010

cards.question: Cage's 4′33″ lasts 273 seconds, and absolute zero is minus 273 °C. What best explains the match?
options: Coincidence, the lengths came by chance
A deliberate nod to absolute zero
The standard length of a radio slot
cards.answer: Coincidence. Cage fixed the lengths of the three movements by chance procedures, and the premiere's timings, 30 seconds, 2 minutes 23 and 1 minute 40, happen to add up to 273. The link to absolute zero rests on no statement of Cage's; it circulates because it sounds too neat to be an accident.
cards.move: With enough numbers around, some of them will match.
cards.trap: A match this exact feels too neat to be an accident.
cards.source: Pritchett, The Music of John Cage, 1993
cards.reference: Pritchett, The Music of John Cage, Cambridge University Press, 1993

cards.question: True or false: a completely silent score was published more than 50 years before Cage's 4′33″?
cards.answer: True. In 1897 the French comic writer Alphonse Allais printed a funeral march for a great deaf man: a page of empty bars, since great sorrows are mute. In 1919 Erwin Schulhoff wrote a movement made only of rests. Cage's piece was new in treating the room's sounds as the music, not in its silence.
cards.move: The famous case is often the survivor of several earlier tries.
cards.trap: The famous silent piece is the only one anyone still hears about.
cards.reference: Allais, Oeuvres anthumes, ed. Caradec, Robert Laffont, Bouquins, 1989

cards.question: Should concert audiences hold their applause in the silences between a symphony's movements?
cards.answer: The gap between movements belongs to the piece. A symphony is an arc, and the pause lets a last chord fade and the next begin from quiet. Mahler wrote into his Second Symphony a pause of at least five minutes after the first movement. A shared hush turns two thousand strangers into one audience.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether the pause belongs to the work.
cards.counterpoint: The hush is a recent rule. In 1778 Mozart wrote to his father that the Paris audience broke into applause in the middle of his new symphony's first movement, at a passage written to win it, and he was delighted. Many movements end in a blaze built to draw a response, and enforced silence makes newcomers feel like trespassers.
cards.source: Anderson, Letters of Mozart and His Family, 1985
cards.reference: Anderson (ed.), The Letters of Mozart and His Family, 3rd edition, Macmillan, 1985

cards.question: How did the performance of Cage's organ piece at Halberstadt, planned to last 639 years, begin in 2001?
cards.answer: With a silence of 17 months. ORGAN²/ASLSP, As Slow As Possible, opens with a rest; stretched to end in 2640, that rest lasted from 5 September 2001 to 5 February 2003, the bellows running and no pipe sounding. Now each chord change, months or years apart, draws a crowd.
cards.move: Stretch any plan far enough and its pauses become events.
cards.reference: John-Cage-Orgel-Stiftung Halberstadt, ORGAN²/ASLSP performance schedule, St Burchardi, 2001

cards.question: The quietest rooms ever measured reach about −20 decibels, below the 0 dB threshold of hearing. How many times less sound intensity?
cards.answer: So −20 dB is 100 times less than 0 dB.
cards.move: On a scale that multiplies, small numbers can hide very large ratios.
cards.trap: Reading 20 decibels as 20 times, as if the scale were linear.
cards.hint: Decibels count factors of ten, not equal steps.
steps: Every 10 decibels is a factor of 10 in intensity.
20 decibels is two such steps: 10 × 10.
So −20 dB is 100 times less than 0 dB.
cards.source: Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound
cards.reference: Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, 3rd edition, Addison Wesley, 2002

cards.question: True or false: Beethoven's Fifth Symphony begins with a rest, not with its famous notes?
cards.answer: True. The first bar opens with an eighth-note rest; three short Gs fill the remainder. The orchestra must enter together just after a beat that makes no sound, so conductors give a silent downbeat and the players come in off it. Misjudge the rest and the famous rhythm starts on the beat.
cards.move: A silent beat can be the part everyone has to agree on.
cards.trap: The four famous notes seem to be the very first thing written.
cards.source: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, ed. Del Mar
cards.reference: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, ed. Del Mar, Bärenreiter, 1999

cards.question: What does the brain do when a few seconds are cut out of a song the listener knows well?
cards.answer: It keeps hearing. Kraemer and colleagues scanned people listening to music with short gaps of silence inserted: during gaps in familiar songs, auditory cortex stayed more active than during gaps in unknown ones, and listeners reported the tune carrying on in their heads. Memory filled the silence with the missing bars.
cards.move: What the listener expects is part of what the listener hears.
