cards.reference: Kraemer, Macrae, Green and Kelley, Sound of Silence Activates Auditory Cortex, Nature, 2005

cards.question: In a 1953 study, 80 people with normal hearing sat alone in a soundproof room. How many reported hearing buzzing or ringing?
cards.answer: More than 9 in 10: Heller and Bergman reported 94%. Everyday noise masks the faint sounds a healthy hearing system makes; strip it away and most people notice them. Subjects were told to listen, which may have raised the figure; later studies found smaller shares. Clinics see only those who hear it through daily noise.
cards.move: Ask what the everyday noise was hiding before calling something rare.
cards.trap: Ringing in the ears sounds like a patient's complaint, so surely rare.
cards.reference: Heller and Bergman, Tinnitus Aurium in Normally Hearing Persons, Annals of Otology, Rhinology and Laryngology, 1953

cards.question: How does a theremin turn the distance of a hand into a musical pitch?
cards.answer: By beating two radio signals together. Two oscillators run far above hearing; the player's hand, acting as one plate of a capacitor with the antenna, detunes one. The circuit outputs only their difference: pull them 440 cycles a second apart and an A sounds. Léon Theremin's player is part of the circuit.
cards.move: A small difference between two large things can be the whole signal.
cards.source: Glinsky, Theremin: Ether Music and Espionage
cards.reference: Glinsky, Theremin: Ether Music and Espionage, University of Illinois Press, 2000

cards.question: What did Benjamin Franklin change about making music with rubbed glasses?
cards.answer: He set the glasses spinning. Franklin's 1761 armonica nested graded glass bowls on one rod turned by a treadle, so wet fingers could touch several at once and play chords. Rows of water-tuned wine glasses allowed a note or two at a time. His bowls were tuned by grinding, not by filling.
cards.move: Rearranging the same parts can open moves the old layout forbade.
cards.reference: Franklin, letter to Giambatista Beccaria, 13 July 1762, in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, vol. 10, Yale University Press, 1966

cards.question: Hitchcock's The Birds (1963) has no conventional score. What mainly produced its bird cries?
cards.answer: An electronic Mixtur-Trautonium. Oskar Sala played most cries and wingbeats on this German descendant of the 1930 trautonium, which adds subharmonics, tones at whole-number fractions of the note played; some real recordings were mixed in. The credits name Sala and Remi Gassmann. Hitchcock's most frightening flock was played by pressing a wire onto a rail.
cards.move: The most convincing version of a thing is often built, not captured.
cards.trap: Recorded gulls and crows, since real birds should sound most real.
cards.reference: Hitchcock (dir.), The Birds, Universal Pictures, 1963, opening credits

cards.question: The serpent is a snaking bass instrument of carved wood wrapped in leather. How is its sound made?
cards.answer: Lip-buzzed, like a tuba. It has a cup mouthpiece and finger holes; the player's lips do the vibrating, so it belongs with brass despite its wood. Said to have been devised in France around 1590 to support church chant, it later marched in military bands. The saxophone is the mirror case: brass body, cane reed.
cards.move: Classify a thing by how it works, not by what it is made of.
cards.trap: Reed-blown, because it is made of wood like a bassoon.
cards.reference: Baines, Brass Instruments: Their History and Development, Faber & Faber, 1976

cards.question: True or false: none of the original noise machines Luigi Russolo built for Futurist concerts survives today?
cards.answer: True. Russolo's intonarumori, wooden boxes with cranks, levers and horns that howled, crackled and gurgled, were all lost during the Second World War. What remains is drawings, photographs, a few recordings and his 1913 manifesto The Art of Noises. Every intonarumore heard today is a reconstruction, built from those drawings and photographs.
cards.move: Seeing a thing today does not mean the original lasted.
cards.trap: False, since exhibitions show them, the originals must be kept somewhere.

cards.question: Why were some ondes Martenot loudspeakers built with strings or a gong in place of a paper cone?
cards.answer: To give an electronic tone an acoustic halo. The ondes, an early electronic keyboard of 1928, fed its oscillator to a choice of speakers: the palme carried strings tuned to every semitone, which rang in sympathy, and the métallique drove a gong. The circuit made the note; the speaker lent it strings and metal.
cards.move: Where a sound comes out can matter as much as how it is made.
cards.reference: Holmes, Electronic and Experimental Music: Technology, Music, and Culture, 5th edn, Routledge, 2016

cards.question: How did a one-string bowed instrument with no frets come to be called the marine trumpet?
cards.answer: By playing only a trumpet's notes. The tromba marina's player touches its long string lightly at its still points, drawing out harmonics, the same series a valveless trumpet plays. A shoe-shaped bridge with one loose leg drums against the soundboard, adding a brassy rattle. Why marina, nobody knows; German convents called it the nuns' fiddle.
cards.move: Two instruments that share a limit can end up sharing a voice.
cards.reference: Adkins & Dickinson, A Trumpet by Any Other Name: A History of the Trumpet Marine, Frits Knuf, 1991

cards.question: True or false: electrically generated music was piped to paying subscribers over New York telephone lines before 1910?
cards.answer: True. From 1906 Thaddeus Cahill's Telharmonium, about 180 tonnes of spinning dynamos, played from Telharmonic Hall at 39th Street and Broadway to hotels, restaurants and homes; receivers wore paper horns. It folded, the machine was scrapped, and no recording of it is known. Electric music's first broadcast left nothing to play back.
cards.move: The history that gets told begins where the surviving evidence begins.
cards.trap: Electronic music seems to begin with the theremin, which left records.
cards.source: Weidenaar, Magic Music from the Telharmonium, 1995
cards.reference: Weidenaar, Magic Music from the Telharmonium, Scarecrow Press, 1995

cards.question: True or false: the wailing, sliding high line in the Beach Boys' Good Vibrations was played on a theremin?
cards.answer: False. Trombonist Paul Tanner played an Electro-Theremin, built with Bob Whitsell: a pure-tone oscillator whose pitch followed a handle slid along a marked scale, so exact notes were easy to find, unlike the air-played original. It only imitated a theremin. Pop's most famous theremin part was played with a hand on a slider.
cards.move: The famous name for a sound is not always the thing that made it.
cards.trap: The theremin is the one eerie electronic instrument everyone can name.
cards.reference: https://www.npr.org/sections/allsongs/2013/02/07/171385175/no-it-wasn-t-a-theremin-on-good-vibrations-remembering-paul-tanner

cards.question: A 0.5 mm wind-harp string is tuned to 160 Hz. In 4 m/s wind, eddies shed at 0.2 × speed ÷ thickness. Which harmonic sounds?
cards.answer: The string locks onto its 10th harmonic.
cards.move: When a push has its own rhythm, the thing pushed answers in that rhythm.
cards.trap: Expecting the string to sound its tuned 160 Hz note in any wind.
cards.hint: Work out how many eddies leave the string each second, then compare with its note.
steps: Eddies: 0.2 x 4 / 0.0005 = 1,600 a second.
The string locks onto its 10th harmonic.
cards.reference: Rayleigh, The Theory of Sound, vol. 2, Dover, 1945

cards.question: Where did Detroit techno get its name?
cards.answer: From a futurist's book and a British compilation. Juan Atkins took the idea of techno-rebels from Alvin Toffler's The Third Wave, published in 1980, which he met in a high-school class. The word stuck in 1988, when a British compilation titled Techno, The New Dance Sound of Detroit set it apart from Chicago house.
cards.move: Names often get fixed by whoever sells the thing abroad.
cards.reference: Sicko, Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk, Billboard Books, 1999

cards.question: Why did Berlin's first great techno clubs open in old strongrooms and empty basements after 1990?
cards.answer: Because reunification left East Berlin full of buildings nobody clearly owned. Tresor opened in March 1991 in the strongroom of the Wertheim department store, close to where the Wall had stood, and its label was soon releasing Detroit artists such as Jeff Mills. Ownership claims took years to settle, and the clubs moved in meanwhile.
cards.move: Watch what grows in the gap before ownership is settled.
cards.source: Denk & von Thülen, Klang der Familie, 2014
cards.reference: Denk and von Thülen, Der Klang der Familie: Berlin, Techno and the Fall of the Wall, Books on Demand, 2014

cards.question: Why was Berlin's Love Parade, a rave of hundreds of thousands, registered for years as a political demonstration?
cards.answer: Because a demonstration is a protected right, and the public covers its policing and street cleaning. The first parade, in July 1989, was about 150 people on the Kurfürstendamm under the slogan Peace, Joy, Pancakes. In 2001 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to restore that status, and the costs fell on the organisers.
cards.move: Ask who pays for the cleanup before calling an event free.
cards.reference: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/german-law-journal/article/cuttingin-on-the-dance-the-federal-constitutional-court-rejects-a-motion-for-a-temporary-injunction-from-berlins-love-parade/F64606DA9367958F183A7619C82704C8

cards.question: True or false: a German court ruled that a weekend of DJ sets at Berghain counts as a concert?
cards.answer: True. In 2016 the Berlin-Brandenburg fiscal court ruled that Berghain's club nights were concerts under the VAT law, so tickets are taxed at 7% rather than the 19% charged on entertainment. The tax office had treated the nights as parties; the court found the DJs' sets were what people came for.
cards.move: When a word sets the tax rate, expect a fight over the word.
cards.trap: Assuming records played by a DJ cannot count as a performance.
cards.reference: https://raue.com/en/news/industries/arts-and-cultural-institutions/raue-llp-secures-victory-for-berghain-before-fiscal-court/

cards.question: What was the Roland TB-303, the box behind acid's squelching basslines, originally built to do?
options: Make squelching effects for dance clubs
Stand in for a bassist at practice
cards.answer: To stand in for a bassist. Roland sold it from about 1981 as bass accompaniment for guitarists, and it flopped: about 10,000 were made before production stopped in 1984. Cheap second-hand units reached Chicago producers, who twisted its filter knobs while patterns played and found the squelch.
cards.move: A failed product may be waiting for users it was never designed for.
cards.trap: Judging the machine by the only use of it still remembered.
cards.reference: https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/hardware-focus/roland-tb-303/

cards.question: How did Detroit teenagers of the early 1980s come to hear Kraftwerk on a Black radio station?
cards.answer: Through one DJ, the Electrifying Mojo. From the late 1970s Charles Johnson ran long late-night shows on Detroit stations such as WGPR, mixing Prince and Parliament with Kraftwerk, the B-52's and European synth-pop, with no playlist imposed on him. The future techno producers of Belleville and Detroit have credited those nights with shaping their ears.
cards.move: One person with no playlist can reroute a city's taste.
cards.source: Brewster and Broughton, Last Night a DJ, 1999
cards.reference: Brewster and Broughton, Last Night a DJ Saved My Life: The History of the Disc Jockey, Headline, 1999

cards.question: A DJ pushes a vinyl turntable's pitch fader to +8% to match tempos. What happens to the music's key?
cards.answer: It rises by about 1.3 semitones. A turntable plays faster by spinning faster, so every frequency rises by 8%. A semitone is a ratio of about 1.06, so 1.08 is a semitone and a third. Two records matched in tempo this way can clash in key, so DJs learn to mix by key.
cards.move: When one dial moves several things, expect all of them to move.
cards.trap: Tempo and pitch feel like separate controls, as on digital decks.
cards.reference: Butler, Unlocking the Groove: Rhythm, Meter, and Musical Design in Electronic Dance Music, Indiana University Press, 2006

cards.question: What story did the anonymous Detroit duo Drexciya build around their electro records of the 1990s?
cards.answer: An undersea nation. Their sleeves told of the babies of pregnant African women thrown overboard from slave ships, born able to breathe water and grown into a people beneath the Atlantic. James Stinson and Gerald Donald kept their faces off the records, and their track titles read like dispatches from that ocean.
cards.move: A myth can carry a history too heavy for a plain statement.
cards.source: Eshun, More Brilliant than the Sun, 1998
cards.reference: Eshun, More Brilliant than the Sun: Adventures in Sonic Fiction, Quartet Books, 1998

cards.question: True or false: Berlin's techno club culture is on Germany's official register of intangible cultural heritage?
cards.answer: True. In March 2024 German authorities, advised by the German Commission for UNESCO, added techno culture in Berlin to the national inventory of intangible cultural heritage, the register that holds amateur choral singing and German bread culture. The application argued that the clubs are places where an art form is made, not just nightlife.
cards.move: Ask who applied before reading much into an official label.
cards.trap: News of clubs fighting closures makes the state look like techno's opponent.
cards.reference: German Commission for UNESCO, Nationwide Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage: Techno Culture in Berlin, 2024

cards.question: When new flats go up beside an established techno club, should the developer pay for the soundproofing?
cards.answer: The club was there first, and its noise was part of what the flat buyers knowingly took on. Without the rule, one complaint from a new neighbour can close a venue that ran legally for decades. England wrote this principle, that whoever brings the change pays for it, into national planning policy in 2018.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether arriving first creates a right.
cards.counterpoint: Residents' right to sleep does not lapse because a club came earlier, and cities need housing near transport, which is often where the clubs are. Loading every acoustic cost on new homes makes them dearer and fewer, and freezes land use around whatever happened to open first, however many people it now keeps awake.
cards.reference: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, National Planning Policy Framework, 2018

cards.question: What fertilises the Amazon?
cards.answer: Dust from Chad. Heavy rain strips phosphorus out of rainforest soil, and the shortfall is largely made up by dust blown across the Atlantic from the Bodele Depression — a dried lakebed that supplies a striking share of the phosphorus reaching the basin each year.
cards.move: The Amazon is fed by a dried-up lake three thousand miles away.
cards.source: Yu et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2015

cards.question: Why is the world running out of sand?
cards.answer: Because desert sand is useless for building. Wind rounds the grains smooth so they will not lock together in concrete; construction needs angular river and seabed sand. Demand has outrun supply enough to support organised theft and illegal dredging.
cards.move: A country can sit in a desert and still have to import sand.
cards.reference: UNEP, Sand and Sustainability: Finding new solutions for environmental governance of global sand resources, 2019

cards.question: How would you know if the ocean used to be fuller?
cards.answer: You probably would not. Each generation of scientists takes the sea they first studied as the natural baseline, so every generation measures decline from an already-depleted state. Daniel Pauly named this shifting baseline syndrome, and it makes long collapses look like normal variation.
cards.move: Everyone measures the decline from whatever they found when they arrived.
cards.reference: Pauly, Anecdotes and the shifting baseline syndrome of fisheries, Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 1995

cards.question: What was the largest mass extinction caused by?
cards.answer: Life inventing photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria began releasing oxygen roughly 2.4 billion years ago — lethal to almost everything then alive, and it stripped out the methane keeping the planet warm. The organisms that made the air we need caused one of the worst catastrophes in the record.
cards.move: The first great extinction was pollution, produced by life itself.

cards.question: Do trees really share food through a fungal network?
cards.answer: Less than the story suggests. Trees are certainly connected to fungi, but the claim that they deliberately send resources to their neighbours rests on a small number of studies, several of which do not support it on re-reading. Recent reviews find the popular version outran the evidence.
cards.move: The wood wide web is real. The generosity is not established.
cards.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023
cards.reference: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023

cards.question: What did counting rings in bristlecone pines do to the dates of European prehistory?
cards.answer: Pushed them back by centuries. Radiocarbon dating assumed the air's carbon-14 never varied; Hans Suess measured it in bristlecone rings of known age and found early dates came out too young. Corrected, Europe's megalithic tombs moved back before the eastern tombs they were supposed to copy.
cards.move: Check the instrument before arguing about what it measured.
cards.reference: Renfrew, Before Civilization: The Radiocarbon Revolution and Prehistoric Europe, Jonathan Cape, 1973

cards.question: True or false: in most tree species, the biggest trees add less wood each year than mid-sized ones?
cards.answer: False. Across 403 tropical and temperate species, Stephenson's team found yearly gain in mass kept rising with size in most. Rings get thinner as a tree ages, but each is laid round a far larger trunk. At the extreme, one big tree adds in a year as much carbon as a whole mid-sized tree holds.
cards.move: Slow growth on a big base can beat fast growth on a small one.
cards.trap: Reading thinner rings in old trees as slower growth.
cards.reference: Stephenson et al., Rate of tree carbon accumulation increases continuously with tree size, Nature, 2014

cards.question: On what kind of ground do the oldest bristlecone pines grow?
cards.answer: The worst. In the 1950s Edmund Schulman found that in California's White Mountains the oldest trees stood on dry, exposed dolomite slopes, where growth is slowest. Slow growth makes dense, resinous wood that resists rot and insects, and sparse cover starves fires. Many are mostly dead wood, kept alive by one living strip of bark.
cards.move: Fast growth and long life are often traded against each other.
cards.reference: Schulman, Longevity under adversity in conifers, Science, 1954

cards.question: What has happened to Africa's oldest baobabs since 2005?
cards.answer: Most have died or broken apart. While radiocarbon-dating the giants, Patrut's team recorded that 9 of the 13 oldest and 5 of the 6 largest died or lost their oldest stems within about 12 years. Climate change is suspected, not proven. Panke in Zimbabwe, about 2,500 years old, collapsed and died in 2010–11.
cards.move: A cluster of deaths is a question, not yet an answer.
cards.reference: Patrut et al., The demise of the largest and oldest African baobabs, Nature Plants, 2018

cards.question: An ancient oak has rotted hollow, leaving sound wood 30% of its radius thick. Treated as a tube, what percentage of its bending strength remains?
cards.answer: 1 − 0.24 = 0.76: about 76% of the strength remains.
cards.move: Material near the edge carries the load; the core mostly comes along.
cards.trap: Assuming strength falls with the wood lost, to about half.
cards.hint: The wood near the bark does most of the work when a trunk bends.
steps: The hollow's radius is 0.7 of the trunk's, so it removes 0.7² = 49% of the wood.
A tube's bending strength scales with R⁴ − r⁴ (outer and inner radius), not with its area of wood.
0.7⁴ = 0.24, so the hollow costs only 24% of the strength.
1 − 0.24 = 0.76: about 76% of the strength remains.
cards.source: Mattheck & Breloer, Body Language of Trees
cards.reference: Mattheck & Breloer, The Body Language of Trees: A Handbook for Failure Analysis, HMSO, 1994

cards.question: What did the rings of two old Japanese cedars reveal about the year 774?
cards.answer: A sudden burst of radiation from space. Miyake's team found carbon-14 in the ring for 774–775 rose about 1.2% in one year, roughly 20 times the usual yearly change; a huge solar storm is the likeliest cause. Such spikes pin dates: Norse timber in Newfoundland was dated to 1021 by a later one, from 993.
cards.move: A single odd year, recorded everywhere at once, can date all the rest.

cards.question: True or false: the trunk of a Swedish spruce whose roots date back about 9,500 years is itself under 1,000 years old?
cards.answer: True. Kullman radiocarbon-dated wood beneath Old Tjikko, on Fulufjället, at about 9,500 years, but the trunk standing today is a few centuries old. For millennia it survived as a low shrub, rooting new stems wherever branches touched the ground. What is ancient is the clone, assumed to be one plant, not any wood in sight.
cards.move: Before comparing ages, ask what exactly is being dated.
cards.trap: Taking a tree's age to be the age of its trunk.
cards.reference: Öberg & Kullman, Ancient subalpine clonal spruces (Picea abies): sources of postglacial vegetation history in the Swedish Scandes, Arctic, 2011

cards.question: Two churchyard yews: one solid, with 600 rings; one hollow, its remaining shell holding 500. Which is probably older?
cards.answer: The hollow one. Yew heartwood rots out after some centuries, so the rings missing from a hollow tree are exactly its oldest ones; 500 is a floor, not an age. Hollowing itself comes with great age. That is why Britain's oldest yews have no ring-counted age at all, only estimates that differ by centuries.
cards.move: The records that vanish first are often the oldest ones.
cards.trap: Comparing ring counts as if both trees had kept every ring.
cards.reference: Bevan-Jones, The Ancient Yew: A History of Taxus baccata, Windgather Press, 2002

cards.question: True or false: seeds from ginkgo trees about 600 years old germinate markedly worse than seeds from young ginkgos?
cards.answer: False. Comparing ginkgos aged 15 to 667 years, Wang and colleagues found trees up to about 600 had similar leaf area, photosynthetic efficiency and seed germination, and their growing layer under the bark showed no programmed decline. Old trees do die, but mostly from outside: drought, fungi, storms and wounds piled up over centuries.
cards.move: When something fails late, ask whether time wore it out or merely exposed it.
cards.trap: Reading death at great age as decline from within, not damage piling up.

cards.question: A living tree has 4,800 rings; a dead trunk, 3,000, its outer 400 matching the living tree's inner 400. How many years do they span?
cards.move: When two records overlap, count the overlap once.
cards.trap: Adding the two counts and forgetting the shared years.
cards.hint: Line the two trunks up on the rings they share before adding anything.
steps: Laid end to end, the two trees hold 4,800 + 3,000 = 7,800 rings.
The 400 matched rings are the same years, counted twice.
cards.reference: Ferguson, Bristlecone pine: science and esthetics, Science, 1968

cards.question: All the world's ants together weigh how much, compared with all the world's people?
cards.answer: About a fifth as much. Pooling hundreds of field counts from every continent but Antarctica, Schultheiss and colleagues estimated 20 quadrillion ants holding about 12 million tonnes of carbon, roughly a fifth of humanity's. The old claim of equal weight had never been measured. It still comes to some 2.5 million ants per person.
cards.move: A figure repeated often enough starts to sound measured; ask who measured it.
cards.trap: The famous claim that ants match humans by weight comes to mind.
cards.reference: Schultheiss et al., The abundance, biomass, and distribution of ants on Earth, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2022

cards.question: Why did Argentine ants stop fighting neighbouring nests once they spread beyond South America?
cards.answer: They lost the genetic variety that marks strangers. Few founders reached California, so nests there share nearly the same scent labels and treat each other as kin. Freed from border wars, they merge into supercolonies; one runs about 6,000 km along the coasts of southern Europe, its nests accepting one another throughout.
cards.move: A group that cannot tell outsiders apart may grow stronger, not weaker.
cards.reference: Tsutsui, Suarez, Holway & Case, Reduced genetic variation and the success of an invasive species, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2000

cards.question: Desert ants reached a feeder, then researchers glued stilts to their legs. On the walk home, what happened?
options: They walked straight to the nest
cards.answer: They overshot the nest. Saharan Cataglyphis ants gauge distance by counting steps: longer legs meant longer strides for the same count, so they walked past home. Ants with trimmed legs stopped short. Wittlinger, Wehner and Wolf showed in 2006 that the ant carries a pedometer, crossing sand where no scent trail would last.
cards.move: To learn what a system relies on, change one input and watch it err.
cards.trap: Ants follow scent, so the length of their legs should not matter.
cards.reference: Wittlinger, Wehner & Wolf, The ant odometer: stepping on stilts and stumps, Science, 2006

cards.question: When did ants first begin farming fungus, and what was happening to the planet then?
cards.answer: About 66 million years ago, around the time an asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs. Comparing the genomes of hundreds of ant and fungus species, Schultz and colleagues dated the start of farming to then, when fungi living on dead plants flourished in the aftermath. Leafcutters still feed their gardens fresh leaves.
cards.move: A catastrophe for most can be the opening for a few.
cards.reference: Schultz et al., The coevolution of fungus-ant agriculture, Science, 2024

cards.question: Roughly how many flowering plant species rely on ants to carry off and plant their seeds?
cards.answer: About 11,000. Such seeds carry an elaiosome, a fatty snack; ants haul the seed home, eat the snack and dump the seed on their refuse heap, a fertile, sheltered spot. The habit evolved independently over 100 times, by Lengyel's survey. Violets, trilliums and many Australian and South African shrubs are sown this way.
cards.move: Never having heard of something is weak evidence that it is rare.
cards.trap: Never having met the habit, it seems a botanical curiosity.
cards.source: Lengyel et al., Perspectives in Plant Ecology, 2010
cards.reference: Lengyel, Gove, Latimer, Majer & Dunn, Convergent evolution of seed dispersal by ants, and phylogeny and biogeography in flowering plants: a global survey, Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics, 2010

cards.question: Biologists paint-marked every worker in lab colonies of Temnothorax ants. Roughly what share turned out to be inactive most of the time?
cards.answer: About two in five. Charbonneau and Dornhaus followed individually marked ants and found a large, consistent group that rarely worked. Later removal experiments suggest they are partly a reserve: take away the busiest workers and some idle ones step in. The ants on a trail are the busy ones; the idle wait in the dark.
cards.move: The members seen working were chosen, in part, by being seen.
cards.trap: Judging a colony by its foragers, the only ants anyone watches.
cards.source: Charbonneau & Dornhaus, Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology, 2015
cards.reference: Charbonneau & Dornhaus, Workers 'specialized' on inactivity: behavioral consistency of inactive workers and their role in task allocation, Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology, 2015

cards.question: What do fungus-farming ants carry on their own bodies to keep a crop-killing mould out of their gardens?
cards.answer: Bacteria that make antibiotics. Currie and colleagues found leafcutter and other fungus-farming ants carrying filamentous bacteria in whitish crusts on their cuticle. The bacteria produce compounds that suppress Escovopsis, a parasitic mould that attacks only the ants' fungus gardens. The farmers carry their fungicide on their backs.
cards.move: Any farm run long enough ends up farming its own defences.
cards.reference: Currie, Scott, Summerbell & Malloch, Fungus-growing ants use antibiotic-producing bacteria to control garden parasites, Nature, 1999

cards.question: An ant lifts 20 times its own weight. Scaled up 100 times in every direction, how many times its own weight could it lift?
cards.answer: 20 × 10,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.2 times its own weight.
cards.move: Scale anything up and ask which parts grow as area and which as volume.
cards.trap: Assuming the ant keeps its twenty-to-one ratio at any size.
cards.hint: Strength grows with a muscle's cross-section; weight grows with its volume.
steps: Strength follows muscle cross-section: 100 × 100 = 10,000 times stronger.
Weight follows volume: 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 times heavier.
20 × 10,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.2 times its own weight.

diagram.caption: Scaled up 100 times, strength grows 10,000-fold but weight a millionfold: it lifts a fifth of itself.

cards.reference: Schmidt-Nielsen, Scaling: Why Is Animal Size So Important?, Cambridge University Press, 1984

cards.question: True or false: ant workers stolen as pupae and raised in a raiding species' nest never harm that colony's young?
cards.answer: False. Temnothorax workers taken by the raiding ant Protomognathus americanus tend their captors' brood, yet Achenbach and Foitzik found the captives killing many of the raiders' female pupae. The captives cannot escape or breed, but every pupa they kill is one fewer future raider attacking nearby nests, which are full of their relatives.
cards.move: Where open revolt is impossible, look for quiet sabotage.
cards.trap: Assuming ants raised in a nest cannot tell it is foreign.
cards.reference: Achenbach & Foitzik, First evidence for slave rebellion: enslaved ant workers systematically kill the brood of their social parasite Protomognathus americanus, Evolution, 2009

cards.question: What convinced biologists that ants leading a nestmate to food are genuinely teaching it?
cards.answer: The leader pays for it. In tandem running, a leader walks ahead while a follower taps her legs and body; when the taps stop, she waits. Franks and Richardson found leaders moving about four times slower than alone, while followers found the food faster than by searching. The lesson moves at the pupil's pace.
cards.move: Call it teaching only when the one who knows slows down for the learner.
cards.reference: Franks & Richardson, Teaching in tandem-running ants, Nature, 2006

cards.question: True or false: the world keeps more managed honeybee hives today than it did in 1961?
cards.answer: True. FAO counts show the global stock of managed hives growing by nearly half between 1961 and 2007, and still rising since. Colonies do die in large numbers each winter, but beekeepers split the survivors to replace them. The bees in real decline are mostly wild ones: bumblebees and solitary bees that nobody restocks.
cards.move: A loss that someone is paid to replace will not show in the count.
cards.trap: Headlines about dying honeybees make their numbers seem to be falling.
cards.reference: Aizen & Harder, The global stock of domesticated honey bees is growing slower than agricultural demand for pollination, Current Biology, 2009

cards.question: What did decoding thousands of honeybee dances reveal about the hardest season for English bees?
cards.answer: High summer, not spring or autumn. A waggle dance encodes how far a bee flew to food, so Couvillon, Schürch and Ratnieks read thousands of dances in Sussex over two years. Bees flew furthest in July and August, after spring blossom and before ivy. A green field in July can be a food desert.
cards.move: Green is not the same as useful; ask what is actually on offer.
cards.reference: Couvillon, Schürch & Ratnieks, Waggle dance distances as integrative indicators of seasonal foraging challenges, PLoS ONE, 2014

cards.question: Why do tomato growers buy boxed colonies of bumblebees rather than renting honeybee hives?
cards.answer: Tomato flowers keep their pollen locked in tubes that release it only when shaken. A bumblebee grips the flower and vibrates its flight muscles without flapping, and the pollen pours out; honeybees do not do this. Before bumblebees were reared commercially from the late 1980s, greenhouse workers shook each flower cluster with electric wands.
cards.move: Check that a helper can do the specific job before paying for it.
cards.reference: Velthuis & van Doorn, A century of advances in bumblebee domestication and the economic and environmental aspects of its commercialization for pollination, Apidologie, 2006

cards.question: True or false: varroa mites kill honeybee colonies mainly through the damage their feeding does?
cards.answer: False. Feeding weakens a bee, but the mite's worse harm is the viruses it injects, above all deformed wing virus. When varroa reached Hawaii, Martin and colleagues found that virus's prevalence in bees rose from about 10% to 100%, with a millionfold higher load. Workers emerge with crumpled wings that cannot fly.
cards.move: Look past the visible attacker to whatever it brings in with it.
cards.trap: The mite can be seen on the bee; the virus cannot.
cards.reference: Martin et al., Global honey bee viral landscape altered by a parasitic mite, Science 336, 2012, pp. 1304-1306, doi:10.1126/science.1220941

cards.question: Should cities encourage people and businesses to keep more honeybee hives to help pollinators?
cards.answer: Hives make people care. A beekeeper learns which flowers bloom when, pushes for planting, and notices poisoning and disease before anyone else. Honeybees still pollinate many crops, and city gardens and parks give them a varied diet with fewer pesticides than farmland. A hive on an office roof keeps pollinators in public view.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how many flowers each hive must share.
cards.counterpoint: Honeybees are one farmed species; the pollinators in trouble are wild bees, and hives compete with them for the same pollen and nectar and can pass diseases to bumblebees. Geldmann and González-Varo argued in Science that keeping honeybees is agriculture, not conservation. Where hives outgrow the flowers, wild bees lose.
cards.reference: Geldmann & González-Varo, Conserving honey bees does not help wildlife, Science, 2018

cards.question: A honeybee queen mates with about a dozen males. On average, how related is a worker to a sister chosen at random?
cards.answer: About three tenths. Sisters with the same father share three quarters of their genes, because a male passes on his whole genome; sisters with different fathers share a quarter. With a dozen fathers, most sisters are half-sisters, and the average falls to about 0.3, below the half a worker would share with her own young.
cards.move: The figure for the closest pair is not the average of the group.
cards.trap: Using the full-sister figure without asking how many fathers there were.
cards.source: Crozier & Pamilo, Evolution of Social Insect Colonies
cards.reference: Crozier & Pamilo, Evolution of Social Insect Colonies: Sex Allocation and Kin Selection, Oxford University Press, 1996

cards.question: If every pollinating animal vanished, by roughly how much would total world crop production fall?
cards.answer: Under a tenth. Three quarters of leading crop types benefit from animal pollination, but the staples that make most of the tonnage, wheat, rice and maize, are wind- or self-pollinated. Aizen and colleagues put the direct loss at 3 to 8% of output. Fruit, nuts and coffee would suffer; bread would not.
cards.move: Before crediting a helper with everything, ask what happens without it.
cards.trap: Treating every crop that bees help as a crop that needs them.
cards.source: Aizen et al., Annals of Botany, 2009
cards.reference: Aizen, Garibaldi, Cunningham & Klein, How much does agriculture depend on pollinators? Lessons from long-term trends in crop production, Annals of Botany, 2009

cards.question: How can a bumblebee sense, before landing, that another bee has recently visited a flower?
cards.answer: Partly through electricity. A flying bee builds up a positive charge, while a flower is usually slightly negative, and a visit shifts the flower's charge for a while afterwards. Clarke and colleagues found bumblebees learned to use electric fields to tell rewarding artificial flowers from empty ones. Each landing leaves a faint electrical footprint.
cards.move: When an animal seems to know too much, look for a sense you lack.
cards.reference: Clarke, Whitney, Sutton & Robert, Detection and learning of floral electric fields by bumblebees, Science, 2013

cards.question: True or false: in a colony with a healthy queen, honeybee workers seek out and eat eggs laid by other workers?
cards.answer: True. Workers can lay unfertilised eggs that would hatch as males, but in a colony with a queen almost none survive: other workers find and eat them, usually within a day. A worker is more closely related to the queen's sons than to a half-sister's. The hive polices its own nursery.
cards.move: Where interests differ even slightly, expect members to watch one another.
cards.trap: Assuming workers in one hive never act against each other.
cards.reference: Ratnieks & Visscher, Worker policing in the honeybee, Nature, 1989

cards.question: When a honeybee swarm chooses a new home, who makes the choice, and what stops the debate dragging on?
cards.answer: A few hundred scouts, not the queen; fading enthusiasm ends it. Scouts dance for the cavities they find, longer for better ones, but each scout dances less every time she returns. When enough scouts gather at one site at once, the swarm lifts off. On Seeley's island, swarms usually chose the best nest box offered.
cards.move: Let support for an option decay unless fresh evidence keeps renewing it.
cards.reference: Seeley, Honeybee Democracy, Princeton University Press, 2010

cards.question: What exactly were the dire wolf pups that Colossal Biosciences announced in 2025?
cards.answer: Grey wolves with 20 edits across 14 genes, chosen to give a bigger frame, a pale coat and other traits read from dire wolf DNA. The dire wolf's line split from the grey wolf's millions of years earlier, so the two differ across far more of the genome. What was revived was a look.
cards.move: Ask how much was changed before accepting what a thing is called.
cards.reference: Perri et al., Dire wolves were the last of an ancient New World canid lineage, Nature, 2021; Kluger, The Return of the Dire Wolf, Time, 2025, https://time.com/7274542/colossal-dire-wolf/

cards.question: True or false: a clone of an animal from an extinct subspecies has been born alive?
cards.answer: True. In 2003 a clone of Celia, the last bucardo, a Pyrenean wild goat that died in 2000, was born in Spain to a hybrid goat mother. The only one of 208 transferred embryos to reach birth, it died within minutes of a malformed lung. The subspecies was extinct, revived and extinct again.
cards.move: The first success can be brief; ask how long it lasted.
cards.trap: De-extinction is always reported as something coming, not something done.
cards.reference: Folch et al., First birth of an animal from an extinct subspecies (Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica) by cloning, Theriogenology, 2009

cards.question: Why did US wildlife officials clone a black-footed ferret from cells frozen in 1988?
cards.answer: To recover lost genes. Every black-footed ferret alive descends from seven animals bred after the species was found clinging on in Wyoming in the 1980s. Willa, a female whose cells were frozen, left no descendants; her clone Elizabeth Ann, born in 2020, carries variation missing from every living ferret. A freezer became a founder.
cards.move: Before a population shrinks further, save what its survivors have lost.
cards.reference: US Fish and Wildlife Service, announcement of the first cloned black-footed ferret, Elizabeth Ann, February 2021

cards.question: What went wrong when two German zoo directors tried to breed the extinct aurochs back?
cards.answer: They bred for a picture, not the animal. In the 1920s and 1930s, Heinz and Lutz Heck crossed Highland, Spanish fighting and other cattle until calves looked right. Heck cattle came out far smaller than aurochs bulls, which stood up to about 1.8 m at the shoulder. The last aurochs died in Poland in 1627.
cards.move: Matching the look of a thing is not recreating the thing.
cards.reference: van Vuure, Retracing the Aurochs: History, Morphology and Ecology of an Extinct Wild Ox, Pensoft, 2005

cards.question: In 1984 the quagga became the first extinct animal to have its DNA read. What did genetics eventually show it was?
options: A close cousin of the horse
cards.answer: A form of plains zebra. Fragments from a museum skin placed it among the zebras, and later work put it inside the plains zebra, differing mainly in coat. That is why a South African project has, since 1987, bred ordinary plains zebras for fewer stripes and browner backs, producing animals that look like quaggas.
cards.move: Looks can divide what ancestry joins; check the ancestry.
cards.trap: A half-striped brown coat looks too different to be the same zebra.
cards.reference: Higuchi, Bowman, Freiberger, Ryder & Wilson, DNA sequences from the quagga, an extinct member of the horse family, Nature, 1984

cards.question: Should public conservation money go towards bringing extinct species back to life?
cards.answer: Revival draws money that would never reach conservation otherwise: private investors have put hundreds of millions into de-extinction companies. The tools it builds, from frozen cell banks to gene edits for disease resistance, already help endangered living species. A revived grazer or seed-spreader can also restore ecological roles that have been empty for centuries.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether revival money would exist otherwise.
cards.counterpoint: Bennett and colleagues costed revival for New Zealand and New South Wales: keeping revived species alive in the wild would absorb money that could protect more living species, a net loss of biodiversity. A revived animal also needs the habitat and safety whose absence killed it the first time. Rescue is cheaper before the last one dies.
cards.source: Bennett et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017
cards.reference: Bennett et al., Spending limited resources on de-extinction could lead to net biodiversity loss, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017

cards.question: Comparing genomes, how many genetic variants are found in woolly mammoths but not in their closest living relative, the Asian elephant?
cards.answer: About 1.4 million. Lynch and colleagues found these variants changing the proteins made by about 1,600 genes, including genes for hair, fat and sensing heat. Revival projects edit only a small share; every other difference stays elephant. Any calf born of the work would be an elephant carrying a short list of mammoth traits.
cards.move: Before accepting a copy, compare the changes made with the differences that exist.
cards.trap: Anchoring on the handful of edits that revival projects announce.
cards.reference: Lynch et al., Elephantid Genomes Reveal the Molecular Bases of Woolly Mammoth Adaptations to the Arctic, Cell Reports, 2015

cards.question: True or false: new northern white rhino embryos are still being made, though only two females survive and neither can carry a calf?
cards.answer: True. Vets collect eggs from Fatu, the younger female, and fertilise them in the laboratory with sperm frozen from four dead males. By 2025 the BioRescue team had made about 29 pure northern white embryos. Southern white rhinos are meant to carry them to term. The species waits in a freezer for a surrogate.
cards.move: A population that cannot breed may still hold what breeding needs.
cards.trap: Assuming that with no breeding pair, no new offspring can exist.
cards.reference: https://www.biorescue.org/en/news/biorescue-scientists-produced-three-new-embryos-and-began-using-northern-white-rhino-embryos

cards.question: A revived population of effective size 10 loses 5% of its remaining genetic diversity each generation. About how many generations until half is gone?
cards.answer: So about 14 generations; worked exactly, about 13.5 generations.
cards.move: A loss taken as a share of what remains takes longer to halve it.
cards.trap: Dividing 50% by 5% and answering 10 generations.
cards.hint: Losses compound; the rule of 70 gives a halving time.
steps: Losses compound: each generation keeps 95% of what was left, not of the start.
Rule of 70 for halving times: 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
So about 14 generations; worked exactly, about 13.5 generations.
cards.source: Frankham et al., Introduction to Conservation Genetics
cards.reference: Frankham, Ballou & Briscoe, Introduction to Conservation Genetics, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2010

cards.question: Why were giant tortoises from Aldabra shipped to a small island off Mauritius, where they had never lived?
cards.answer: To do the job of Mauritius's own giant tortoises, eaten out by sailors centuries ago. On Île aux Aigrettes, Griffiths and colleagues found the newcomers eating the fruit of a rare native ebony and passing seeds that germinated well, spreading a tree that had lost its disperser. An ebony forest now relies on imports.
cards.move: When the original is gone, ask whether another can do its job.
cards.reference: Griffiths, Hansen, Jones, Zuël & Harris, Resurrecting extinct interactions with extant substitutes, Current Biology, 2011

cards.question: Why does a cloud holding hundreds of tonnes of water not fall out of the sky?
cards.answer: Its droplets do fall, too slowly to see. A droplet 0.02 mm across sinks about 1 cm a second, so the gentlest rising air holds it. The water is a tiny share: about half a gram per cubic metre, inside a kilogram of air. A cloud is air with a faint mist in it.
cards.move: Before asking why something stays up, check how fast it is coming down.
cards.reference: Wallace & Hobbs, Atmospheric Science: An Introductory Survey, 2nd edition, Academic Press, 2006

cards.question: Who gave clouds the Latin names still used today, and what did he do for a living?
cards.answer: Luke Howard, a Quaker chemist who made pharmaceuticals in London. In an 1802 lecture he sorted clouds into cirrus, cumulus and stratus, plus combinations, arguing that shapes follow the processes making them. Lamarck's French scheme of the same year faded; the Latin crossed borders. Goethe was taken enough to write poems in his honour.
cards.move: A name meant to travel should belong to no single language.
cards.reference: Hamblyn, The Invention of Clouds: How an Amateur Meteorologist Forged the Language of the Skies, Picador, 2001

cards.question: True or false: cloud droplets can stay liquid at −30°C?
cards.answer: True. Tiny pure droplets freeze only near −38°C unless a speck of the right dust, pollen or bacterium starts the ice, and such specks are scarce. Once some ice appears, it grows by stealing vapour from the droplets around it. That is why rain in cool climates usually begins high up as snow.
cards.move: A threshold measured in bulk can shift when the pieces get small.
cards.trap: Water freezes at 0°C, so anything colder in the sky is ice.
cards.reference: Rogers & Yau, A Short Course in Cloud Physics, 3rd edition, Pergamon Press, 1989

cards.question: A cloud droplet is 0.02 mm across; a small raindrop is 1 mm. How many droplets make one raindrop, in thousands?
cards.answer: 125,000 droplets, or 125 thousand.
cards.move: When size grows in every direction at once, multiply the growth three times.
cards.trap: Answering 50, as if droplets lined up end to end.
cards.hint: Droplets merge by volume; compare the widths first.
steps: 1 mm / 0.02 mm = 50 times wider.
Volume goes with the cube of width: 50 x 50 x 50.
125,000 droplets, or 125 thousand.
cards.reference: Pruppacher & Klett, Microphysics of Clouds and Precipitation, Kluwer, 1997

cards.question: By the best estimate for 2018, which of aviation's effects was warming the climate most?
cards.answer: Its contrail clouds. Lee and colleagues put contrail cirrus at about 57 milliwatts of warming per square metre, against about 34 for all aviation's carbon dioxide since 1940, though far less certain. Contrails vanish within hours; carbon dioxide stays for centuries. Some flights warm the planet mostly through a white line.
cards.move: Rank causes by their effect today and by their effect in a century.
cards.trap: Carbon dioxide is the famous greenhouse gas, so it must dominate.
cards.reference: Lee et al., The contribution of global aviation to anthropogenic climate forcing for 2000 to 2018, Atmospheric Environment, 2021

cards.question: Averaged over the whole globe and year, what do all of Earth's clouds together do to its energy balance?
cards.answer: Cool it. Satellite budgets since the 1980s find clouds reflect about 45 watts per square metre of sunlight and trap about 30 of the heat leaving below: a net cooling of roughly 15 to 20. That is several times the warming added by carbon dioxide so far. From space, clouds are Earth's brightest mirrors.
cards.move: The effect you feel at night is not the one that runs all day.
cards.trap: Remembering warm cloudy nights and forgetting the sunlight clouds turn away.
cards.reference: Ramanathan et al., Cloud-Radiative Forcing and Climate: Results from the Earth Radiation Budget Experiment, Science, 1989

cards.question: True or false: in tropical clouds, raindrops can form with no ice anywhere in the cloud?
cards.answer: True. Where cloud tops stay above freezing, bigger droplets fall faster than small ones, sweep them up and merge, growing into raindrops within tens of minutes. Satellite radar shows much of the rain over tropical oceans falling this way, from clouds whose tops never reach the freezing level.
cards.move: A rule learned in one climate may be only one of several routes.
cards.trap: Applying the rule that rain starts as snow to every cloud.
cards.reference: Lau & Wu, Warm rain processes over tropical oceans and climate implications, Geophysical Research Letters, 2003

cards.question: Surface air is 24°C, dew point 16°C. Rising, it cools 10°C per km and its dew point 2°C per km. Cloud base height, in metres?
cards.answer: 8 ÷ 8 = 1 km, so cloud base sits at 1,000 metres.
cards.move: When two things move at once, follow the gap between them.
cards.trap: Forgetting that the dew point falls too, and stopping at 800 metres.
cards.hint: Follow the gap between temperature and dew point as the air climbs.
steps: Starting gap: 24 − 16 = 8°C.
The gap closes by 10 − 2 = 8°C per km.
8 ÷ 8 = 1 km, so cloud base sits at 1,000 metres.
cards.reference: Ahrens, Meteorology Today: An Introduction to Weather, Climate, and the Environment, 9th edition, Brooks/Cole, 2009

cards.question: True or false: the WMO's International Cloud Atlas still refuses to name clouds made by aircraft, factories or fires?
cards.answer: False. The 2017 edition gave them Latin names in the same scheme as natural clouds: homogenitus for clouds made by human activity, such as a cooling-tower plume, flammagenitus for clouds raised by fire, and homomutatus for contrails that spread into ordinary-looking cirrus. A fresh contrail is now, formally, cirrus homogenitus.
cards.move: A classification survives by adding names, not by guarding the old ones.
cards.trap: Assuming a scheme from 1802 was never stretched to modern skies.
cards.reference: World Meteorological Organization, International Cloud Atlas: Manual on the Observation of Clouds and Other Meteors, WMO-No. 407, 2017

cards.question: How did researchers in Idaho in 2017 finally show that seeding clouds had made snow fall?
cards.answer: By making the snow carry a signature. An aircraft laid silver iodide across winter clouds in lines back and forth across the wind, and radar then showed matching lines of snow drifting downwind, a pattern no natural storm draws. Seven decades of seeding trials had failed to separate seeded snow from ordinary snow.
cards.move: When no control is possible, make the effect sign its own name.
cards.reference: French et al., Precipitation formation from orographic cloud seeding, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2018

cards.question: On average, how much of the energy of incoming waves does a coral reef remove before they reach shore?
cards.answer: About 97%, on average. Pooling measurements from reefs worldwide, Ferrario and colleagues found the reef crest alone, the shallow ridge where waves break, removes 86%; the flats behind it take most of the rest. A healthy crest is a breakwater that repairs itself; a dead one erodes and lets the sea through.
cards.move: Before removing a natural barrier, price the wall you would need instead.
cards.trap: About 30%, since a low, half-drowned reef looks too flimsy to matter.
cards.reference: Ferrario et al., The effectiveness of coral reefs for coastal hazard risk reduction and adaptation, Nature Communications, 2014

cards.question: True or false: bleaching caused most of the coral lost on the Great Barrier Reef between 1985 and 2012?
cards.answer: False. Analysing 27 years of surveys, De'ath and colleagues found coral cover fell from 28% to 14% and put 48% of the loss down to cyclones, 42% to coral-eating crown-of-thorns starfish and 10% to bleaching. The balance has shifted since: from 2016 onwards, repeated marine heatwaves have bleached the reef again and again.
cards.move: Split a loss by cause before choosing which cause to fight.
cards.trap: True, since bleaching is the cause that fills reef news.
cards.reference: De'ath, Fabricius, Sweatman & Puotinen, The 27-year decline of coral cover on the Great Barrier Reef and its causes, PNAS, 2012

cards.question: What happened when loudspeakers played healthy-reef sounds over dead coral?
cards.answer: Young fish moved in. Many reef fish spend their first weeks drifting as larvae in open water and find a reef partly by its noise: snapping shrimp, grunting and chattering fish. On degraded patches of the Great Barrier Reef, Gordon and colleagues' recordings doubled the number of young fish settling, with 50% more species.
cards.move: Silence can be the signal that keeps newcomers away.
cards.reference: Gordon et al., Acoustic enrichment can enhance fish community development on degraded coral reef habitat, Nature Communications, 2019

cards.question: How often is a typical coral reef now hit by severe bleaching?
cards.answer: About once every 6 years. At 100 reefs worldwide, Hughes's team found the median gap between severe bleaching events shrank from 25 to 30 years in the early 1980s to about 6 by 2016. The fastest-growing corals need at least 10 to 15 years to recover, so reefs are now struck again before they heal.
cards.move: Compare the time between blows with the time needed to heal.
cards.reference: Hughes et al., Spatial and temporal patterns of mass bleaching of corals in the Anthropocene, Science, 2018

cards.question: Should places ban sunscreens containing the UV filter oxybenzone to protect coral reefs?
cards.answer: In laboratory tests, Downs and colleagues found oxybenzone deformed and killed coral larvae at low concentrations, and crowded swimming bays can carry measurable amounts. Mineral sunscreens and swim shirts are cheap alternatives. When a small switch removes a plausible harm to reefs already weakened by heat, waiting for perfect proof lets damage pile up.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the dose actually found on reefs decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Field surveys mostly find oxybenzone far below the levels that harmed corals in the laboratory, and in 2022 the US National Academies judged the evidence too thin to characterise the risk. Heat is what is bleaching reefs worldwide. Bans let governments look busy, may put people off sunscreen, and pull attention from the emissions that matter.
cards.reference: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Review of Fate, Exposure, and Effects of Sunscreens in Aquatic Environments and Implications for Sunscreen Usage and Human Health, National Academies Press, 2022; Downs et al., Toxicopathological effects of the sunscreen UV filter, oxybenzone (benzophenone-3), on coral planulae and cultured primary cells and its environmental contamination in Hawaii and the U.S. Virgin Islands, Archives of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology, 2016

cards.question: NOAA sums °C × weeks above summer peak, skipping any under 1 °C. How many °C-weeks: 8 weeks at +0.9, then 4 at +1.5?
cards.move: A threshold can turn a long mild stretch into zero; apply it first.
cards.trap: Counting all twelve weeks and getting 13.2.
cards.hint: Check which weeks clear the threshold before multiplying anything.
steps: The 8 weeks at +0.9 °C fall below the 1 °C cut-off, so they add nothing.
The 4 weeks at +1.5 °C count in full: 4 × 1.5.
cards.reference: Liu et al., Reef-scale thermal stress monitoring of coral ecosystems: new 5-km global products from NOAA Coral Reef Watch, Remote Sensing, 2014

cards.question: What did drilling on Enewetak Atoll in 1951–52 hit beneath more than a kilometre of coral rock?
cards.answer: Volcanic basalt. Darwin had argued in 1842 that atolls are reefs on sinking volcanoes, the coral growing upward as the peak subsided. Drill holes went through more than 1,200 m of reef limestone, tens of millions of years old, to the volcano. Surface-dwelling corals had kept pace all the way down.
cards.move: A slow process sustained long enough builds what looks impossible.
cards.reference: Ladd, Ingerson, Towson, Russell & Stephenson, Drilling on Eniwetok Atoll, Marshall Islands, Bulletin of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists, 1953

cards.question: True or false: a coral colony collected alive has been radiocarbon-dated at more than 4,000 years old?
cards.answer: True. Roark and colleagues dated a black coral colony taken from hundreds of metres down off Hawaii at about 4,265 years, and deep-sea gold corals at about 2,700. They are among the oldest animals known. A trawl net dragged across such a bed can break in seconds what grew since the Bronze Age.
cards.move: Recovery time is set by the slowest grower, not the average one.
cards.trap: Picturing corals as fast-growing, short-lived reef builders like those in shallow water.
cards.reference: Roark et al., Extreme longevity in proteinaceous deep-sea corals, PNAS, 2009

cards.question: As seawater acidifies, which part of a coral reef is expected to switch first from building up to dissolving?
cards.answer: The sands and sediments. Eyre and colleagues found sediment dissolution about ten times as sensitive to acidification as coral growth, partly because microbes breathing in the sand already acidify the water between grains. Some reefs' sediments already dissolve on balance; most are projected to this century. The reef can wash away from below.
cards.move: The weakest link is often the part nobody photographs.
cards.trap: Picturing the living corals, the visible builders, as the first to fail.
cards.reference: Eyre et al., Coral reefs will transition to net dissolving before end of century, Science, 2018; Eyre, Andersson & Cyronak, Benthic coral reef calcium carbonate dissolution in an acidifying ocean, Nature Climate Change, 2014

cards.question: Should heat-tolerant corals be bred and planted out to help reefs survive warming seas?
cards.answer: Emissions cuts will come too late for many reefs: heatwaves already return too often. Some colonies survive heatwaves that kill their neighbours, and their offspring inherit part of that tolerance, so selective breeding and moving tolerant stock can buy decades. Waiting for the climate to settle means restoring reefs that no longer exist.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the question is whether planting can match the damage in scale.
cards.counterpoint: Scale defeats it. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park covers about 344,000 km², and restoration plants patches measured in hectares. Bred tolerance may cost growth or disease resistance, and the next heatwaves may exceed whatever breeding achieves. Money spent planting corals is money not spent cutting emissions, the one lever that works at the scale of whole reefs.
cards.reference: van Oppen, Oliver, Putnam & Gates, Building coral reef resilience through assisted evolution, PNAS, 2015

cards.question: How much of Western Europe's mild winter is the Gulf Stream's doing?
cards.answer: Less than the textbook says, though this is contested. Seager's team found winds do most of the work: westerlies off an ocean that stores summer heat, and a jet stream bent by the Rockies that chills eastern North America. Vancouver, beside a Pacific carrying less heat north, is nearly as mild in January as Paris.
cards.move: Before crediting the famous cause, check a case where it is absent.
cards.reference: Seager et al., Is the Gulf Stream responsible for Europe's mild winters?, Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, 2002

cards.question: In spring and summer, steady winds blow south along California's coast. What do they do to the coastal sea?
options: Warm it, piling surface water ashore
Cool it, drawing deep water up
cards.answer: Cool it, drawing deep water up. On a spinning planet, water pushed by the wind moves on average at right angles to it: to the right in the northern hemisphere, here out to sea. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it, feeding the coast's fisheries and chilling the air into San Francisco's summer fog.
cards.move: A push does not always move things the way it points.
cards.trap: Barely change it, as if the water simply moved with the wind.
cards.source: Talley et al., Descriptive Physical Oceanography, 2011
cards.reference: Talley, Pickard, Emery & Swift, Descriptive Physical Oceanography: An Introduction, 6th edition, Academic Press, 2011

cards.question: By weight, what makes up the largest share of the plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch?
cards.answer: Discarded fishing nets. From ships and aircraft, Lebreton's team estimated about 79,000 tonnes of plastic circling in the North Pacific gyre, with nets making up at least 46% of the mass. Tiny fragments were 94% of the 1.8 trillion pieces but only 8% of the weight. Less an island than a soup, with nets.
cards.move: Count by weight and by number before deciding what a pile is made of.
cards.trap: Bags and food packaging, the plastic in every news photograph.
cards.reference: Lebreton et al., Evidence that the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is rapidly accumulating plastic, Scientific Reports, 2018

cards.question: How has the Gulf Stream's flow past Florida been measured almost daily since 1982?
cards.answer: With a telephone cable. Seawater conducts electricity, so the current, pushed through the Earth's magnetic field, generates a voltage across the strait, like a dynamo. A cable between Florida and Grand Bahama reads that voltage, checked against ship surveys, and turns it into flow: on average about 32 million cubic metres a second.
cards.move: Old infrastructure can become a new instrument once you know what it senses.
cards.reference: Larsen & Sanford, Florida Current volume transports from voltage measurements, Science, 1985

cards.question: True or false: parts of the deep Pacific are still cooling from the Little Ice Age?
cards.answer: True. Water that sank from the surface centuries ago is only now reaching the deep Pacific. Comparing temperatures measured by HMS Challenger in the 1870s with modern ones, Gebbie and Huybers found cooling around 2 km down, a delayed echo of the cold centuries that ended around 1850, even as the surface warms.
cards.move: A slow system can still be answering a question asked centuries ago.
cards.trap: False, assuming the whole ocean warms in step with the air.
cards.reference: Gebbie & Huybers, The Little Ice Age and 20th-century deep Pacific cooling, Science, 2019

cards.question: What keeps the deep ocean's slow overturning going, beyond cold water sinking near the poles?
cards.answer: Mixing, powered by tides and winds. Cold water sinks easily; the hard part is bringing it back up, which takes turbulence mixing it with lighter water. Munk and Wunsch put the need at about 2 terawatts, roughly half from tides breaking over seafloor ridges and half from winds. The Moon helps pump the abyss.
cards.move: Ask what brings a thing back, not just what sends it away.
cards.reference: Munk & Wunsch, Abyssal recipes II: energetics of tidal and wind mixing, Deep-Sea Research I, 1998

cards.question: Why do the strongest ocean currents, such as the Gulf Stream and the Kuroshio, run along the western sides of ocean basins?
options: Winds blow harder over the west
Spin deflects more near the poles
cards.answer: Spin deflects more near the poles. Stommel showed in 1948 that if rotation's deflecting effect were the same everywhere, a wind-driven gyre would be symmetric. Because the effect grows poleward, the return flow is squeezed into a narrow, fast current on the western edge, while eastern sides get broad, slow drifts.
cards.move: When a pattern is lopsided, look for what changes across it.
cards.trap: Crediting the winds, which drive the gyre but not its lopsidedness.
cards.reference: Stommel, The westward intensification of wind-driven ocean currents, Transactions, American Geophysical Union, 1948

cards.question: True or false: most deep floats set adrift in the boundary current off Labrador rode it south along the North American coast?
cards.answer: False. Bower and colleagues tracked floats released in the deep current off Labrador, and few stayed in it: most peeled off into the open ocean, looping through eddies on their way south. The tidy picture of a deep conveyor belt hugging the coast had been drawn largely from instruments moored along that very coast.
cards.move: An instrument placed on the expected route will find the expected route.
cards.trap: Trusting the conveyor-belt picture, drawn from instruments on the coastal route.
cards.reference: Bower et al., Interior pathways of the North Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, Nature, 2009

cards.question: The world's rivers deliver about 37,000 km³ of fresh water to the sea each year. How many million cubic metres is that per second?
cards.answer: 37 million million / 31.5 million ≈ 1.2 million m³ per second.
cards.move: Put a river and a sea current in one unit before comparing them.
cards.trap: Losing a factor of a thousand when turning km³ into m³.
cards.hint: Turn cubic kilometres into cubic metres, and a year into seconds.
steps: 37,000 km³ is 37,000 × 1,000,000,000 m³, or 37 million million m³.
A year has about 31.5 million seconds.
37 million million / 31.5 million ≈ 1.2 million m³ per second.
cards.simply: Oceanographers call a million cubic metres a second one sverdrup. Every river on Earth together makes about one; the Antarctic Circumpolar Current alone carries well over a hundred.
cards.reference: Dai & Trenberth, Estimates of freshwater discharge from continents: latitudinal and seasonal variations, Journal of Hydrometeorology, 2002

cards.question: Is the Atlantic's overturning circulation already weakening because of global warming?
cards.answer: A patch of the North Atlantic south of Greenland has cooled while nearly everywhere else warmed, the fingerprint models predict for a slowing overturning. Caesar and colleagues read it as a weakening of about 15% since the mid-twentieth century, and sediment records suggest the circulation is at its weakest in over a thousand years.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the length of record needed to see a trend decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Direct measurement began only in 2004, with moorings strung across the Atlantic at 26°N, and twenty years of a noisy flow cannot separate a trend from natural swings. Worthington and colleagues' 30-year reconstruction from ocean data finds no significant decline. The cold patch has other plausible causes, including shifts in the atmosphere above it.
cards.reference: Caesar et al., Observed fingerprint of a weakening Atlantic Ocean overturning circulation, Nature, 2018; Worthington et al., A 30-year reconstruction of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation shows no decline, Ocean Science, 2021

cards.question: Ocean trenches reach almost 11 km down. How deep is the deepest fish ever filmed?
cards.answer: About 8.3 km: a snailfish filmed at 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench off Japan in 2022. Fish seem capped there because their cells need a molecule, TMAO, that shields proteins from pressure, and more of it the deeper they go. Near 8,200 m the dose would make their body fluids as concentrated as seawater.
cards.move: How far a space extends says little about how far its occupants go.
cards.trap: About 10.9 km, letting the trench's depth set the guess.
cards.reference: Yancey et al., Marine fish may be biochemically constrained from inhabiting the deepest ocean depths, PNAS, 2014; University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology, deepest fish filmed at 8,336 m, announced 2023

cards.question: What did wartime echo sounders mistake for a second seabed?
cards.answer: A layer of animals. In 1942 Navy-funded scientists off California found echoes from a false bottom a few hundred metres down in deep water. It rose towards the surface at dusk and sank at dawn, which Martin Johnson read in 1945 as life: fish, shrimp and jellies making the largest daily migration on Earth.
cards.move: When a fixed feature moves on a schedule, suspect something alive.
cards.reference: Eyring, Christensen & Raitt, Reverberation in the sea, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1948

cards.question: Which 1860 repair job undermined the belief that the deep sea was lifeless?
cards.answer: Raising a broken telegraph cable. Edward Forbes had argued in the 1840s that life petered out below about 550 m. The cable between Sardinia and Algeria came up from around 2,000 m crusted with corals and molluscs that had grown on it, so they could not have been snagged on the way up.
cards.move: Absence of evidence from places nobody sampled is only absence of sampling.
cards.reference: Rozwadowski, Fathoming the Ocean: The Discovery and Exploration of the Deep Sea, Harvard University Press, 2005

cards.question: Net hauls suggested fish and shrimp dominated the deep midwater. What did cameras on submersibles find there instead?
options: Even more fish than nets showed
Mostly squid, too quick for nets
cards.answer: Crowds of jelly-like animals. Jellyfish, comb jellies and their long colonial cousins turned out to be among the most abundant predators of the deep midwater. Nets had shredded their soft bodies into unrecognisable slime, so the catch held mostly sturdy fish and crustaceans. Only cameras could see who had been there.
cards.move: Ask what your sampling method destroys before counting what it keeps.
cards.trap: Even more fish, as if the nets had simply been too small.
cards.source: Robison, J. Exp. Mar. Biol. Ecol., 2004
cards.reference: Robison, Deep pelagic biology, Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology, 2004

cards.question: Should mining of metal-rich nodules from the deep Pacific seabed go ahead?
cards.answer: Batteries need nickel, cobalt and manganese. On land they come from cleared forest, tailings dams and, for most cobalt, troubled mines in DR Congo. Nodules lie loose on the deep ocean floor, several of those metals in one rock. Refusing them does not stop mining; it keeps it where the harm is already proven.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, weigh known harms on land against unknown harms at sea.
cards.counterpoint: The abyss recovers on geological time. Nodules take millions of years to grow a few centimetres, and plough tracks from a 1989 mining test off Peru were still stark, with fewer animals, 26 years later. Most species collected in the Pacific's main nodule field have no name yet. Mining first means destroying what has not been described.
cards.reference: Simon-Lledó et al., Biological effects 26 years after simulated deep-sea mining, Scientific Reports, 2019

cards.question: Why did oxygen rise inside sealed chambers on the Pacific seabed, 4 km down in total darkness?
cards.answer: Nobody agrees yet. Sweetman's team expected seabed life to use the oxygen up; instead it climbed. They proposed that metal-rich nodules carry small voltages which, added together, might split seawater. Critics, some funded by a mining company, blame air trapped in the instruments. Whether the abyss makes oxygen without light is unsettled.
cards.move: A reading that defies expectation is a discovery or a fault; find out which.
cards.reference: Sweetman et al., Evidence of dark oxygen production at the abyssal seafloor, Nature Geoscience, 2024

cards.question: Of the carbon fixed by plankton in sunlit water, roughly what share sinks all the way to an abyssal seafloor 4 km down?
cards.answer: About 1%. Only around a tenth of surface production sinks out of the top 100 m, as dead cells and droppings called marine snow, and animals and microbes eat it on the way down. Martin's traps showed the flux shrinking at every depth. Life on the abyssal plain feeds on the crumbs of crumbs.
cards.move: Small losses at every step leave almost nothing to arrive.
cards.trap: Counting the loss at the surface and forgetting every loss below it.

diagram.label: parts of carbon fixed
diagram.caption: Of every 1,000 parts fixed in sunlit water, roughly 100 sink out and 10 reach the abyss.

cards.reference: Martin, Knauer, Karl & Broenkow, VERTEX: carbon cycling in the northeast Pacific, Deep-Sea Research, 1987

cards.question: True or false: all the deep seafloor ever seen by cameras or human eyes would fit into a tenth of Belgium?
cards.answer: True. Tallying deep dives since the 1950s, Bell's team put the seafloor below 200 m ever seen at about 0.001% of the total, some 4,000 km². Most of it lies off just three countries: the United States, Japan and New Zealand. Sonar has mapped about a quarter of the seabed; eyes have seen a speck.
cards.move: Before trusting how much is known, ask what counted as seeing it.
cards.trap: Anchoring on the familiar mapping figures, which measure sonar, not sight.
cards.reference: Bell et al., How little we've seen: a visual coverage estimate of the deep seafloor, Science Advances, 2025

cards.question: Why can a small explosion about 1 km deep in the ocean be heard thousands of kilometres away?
cards.answer: It is trapped in a sound channel. Sound slows as water cools with depth, then speeds up again as pressure mounts, so it is slowest near 1,000 m. Waves straying up or down bend back towards that layer, as light does in a lens. Ewing and Worzel heard small charges across an ocean basin.
cards.move: A path that bends everything back towards itself becomes a channel.
cards.source: Ewing & Worzel, Geological Society of America, 1948
cards.reference: Ewing & Worzel, Long-range sound transmission, Geological Society of America Memoir 27, 1948

cards.question: In video surveys of Monterey Bay from the surface to 3,900 m, what share of the animals seen could make light?
cards.answer: About three-quarters. Classifying hundreds of thousands of animals filmed from remotely operated vehicles over many years, Martini and Haddock found 76% could produce light. In the open ocean below the sunlit layer, making light is the rule: it lures prey, startles attackers, and cancels a body's shadow against the faint light from above.
cards.move: The famous example of a trait can hide how ordinary the trait is.
cards.trap: Picturing glowing animals as rare curiosities like the anglerfish.
cards.reference: Martini & Haddock, Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea demonstrates its predominance as an ecological trait, Scientific Reports, 2017

cards.question: What were Luis and Walter Alvarez trying to measure when they found the iridium spike?
cards.answer: How long a thin clay layer at Gubbio, Italy, took to settle. Iridium is scarce in Earth's crust but arrives steadily in space dust, so they hoped to use it as a clock. The clay held about 30 times the usual level: one huge delivery, not a drizzle. The clock became the crime scene.
cards.move: An instrument built to answer one question can overturn a bigger one.
cards.reference: Alvarez, Alvarez, Asaro & Michel, Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction, Science, 1980

cards.question: Why were the bird lineages that survived the asteroid impact probably ground-dwellers?
cards.answer: Because the forests fell. Fossil pollen shows trees dying back across much of the world after the impact, and fern spores surging over bare ground. Field and colleagues reconstructed the ancestors of every living bird group as ground-living; treetop birds lost their habitat along with their perches.
cards.move: In a collapse, what survives is shaped by what it did not depend on.
cards.reference: Field et al., Early evolution of modern birds structured by global forest collapse at the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, Current Biology, 2018

cards.question: In one 2017 model, how likely was a mass extinction had the dinosaur-killing asteroid struck a random spot on Earth?
cards.answer: About one in eight, by one model. Kaiho and Oshima traced the killing darkness to soot from rocks rich in oil and organic matter, which underlie only about 13% of Earth's surface. The shelf off Yucatán was one. A strike almost anywhere else, open ocean included, would on their estimate have spared the dinosaurs' world.
cards.move: Ask how the same blow would have landed somewhere else.
cards.trap: A 10 km asteroid seems catastrophic wherever it happens to land.
cards.reference: Kaiho & Oshima, Site of asteroid impact changed the history of life on Earth: the low probability of mass extinction, Scientific Reports, 2017

cards.question: True or false: the lack of dinosaur fossils in the three metres of rock below the impact layer shows they were already dying out?
cards.answer: False. Fossils are rare, so the last one found almost always sits below the true last day; older rock has had more chances to yield one.
