In 2011 Lyson and colleagues found a horned dinosaur's fossil just 13 cm below the boundary in Montana. The gap was in the finds, not in the dinosaurs.
cards.move: Where nobody has found something is not where it stopped existing.
cards.trap: An empty stretch of rock looks like evidence that they had gone.
cards.reference: Lyson et al., Dinosaur extinction: closing the '3 m gap', Biology Letters, 2011

cards.question: Was the asteroid impact enough on its own to end the age of dinosaurs?
cards.answer: The extinction is abrupt and sits on the impact layer worldwide. Iridium, shocked quartz and a crater 180 km wide leave no doubt about the blow. Hull and colleagues found most gas from India's Deccan eruptions was released well before the boundary, without a matching extinction: the volcanoes had their chance.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on dating the eruptions to within millennia.
cards.counterpoint: The Deccan Traps poured out hundreds of thousands of cubic kilometres of lava around the boundary, with pulses of carbon dioxide and sulphur that swung the climate. Life already stressed may have been primed to collapse, and eruptions after the impact could have slowed recovery. Dating is contested: one team puts the biggest pulses just before the impact.
cards.reference: Hull et al., On impact and volcanism across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, Science, 2020

cards.question: How can fossil fish from North Dakota reveal the season in which the dinosaur-killing asteroid struck?
cards.answer: Through their bones. Paddlefish and sturgeon buried at Tanis laid down bone in yearly bands, like tree rings, and During and colleagues found each one's growth had just begun to quicken for the year: northern spring. Impact beads lodged in their gills show they died within about an hour of the strike.
cards.move: Anything that grows in layers keeps a calendar up to its last day.
cards.reference: During et al., The Mesozoic terminated in boreal spring, Nature, 2022

cards.question: Ruthenium isotopes in the impact layer reveal what kind of body struck Chicxulub. What was it?
options: A carbon-rich asteroid formed beyond Jupiter
An icy comet from the outer solar system
A stony asteroid from the inner belt
cards.answer: A carbon-rich asteroid formed beyond Jupiter. Fischer-Gödde and colleagues found ruthenium in the boundary clay matching carbonaceous meteorites, which formed in the outer solar system before settling into the asteroid belt, and not comets or the stony asteroids common near Earth. The killer was a dark rock from the belt's cold outer reaches.
cards.move: An origin far away does not settle what kind of thing arrived.
cards.trap: Linking an outer solar system origin with comets rather than asteroids.
cards.reference: Fischer-Gödde et al., Ruthenium isotopes show the Chicxulub impactor was a carbonaceous-type asteroid, Science, 2024

cards.question: Take the dinosaur-killing asteroid as 10 km across, 3,000 kg/m³, at 20 km/s. Energy, in billions of Hiroshima bombs (6 × 10¹³ J each)?
cards.answer: 3.2 × 10²³ ÷ (6 × 10¹³) ≈ 5 billion bombs.
cards.move: When speed is squared, a fast small thing can outweigh a slow huge one.
cards.trap: Reaching for millions, because no bomb scale feels big enough.
cards.hint: Kinetic energy is half the mass times the speed squared; start with the volume.
steps: Volume: a sphere fills about half its cube, so about 520 km³, or 5.2 × 10¹¹ m³.
3.2 × 10²³ ÷ (6 × 10¹³) ≈ 5 billion bombs.
cards.source: Collins et al., Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 2005
cards.reference: Collins, Melosh & Marcus, Earth Impact Effects Program: A Web-based computer program for calculating the regional environmental consequences of a meteoroid impact on Earth, Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 2005

cards.question: True or false: lizards and snakes came through the extinction that ended the dinosaurs with only light losses?
cards.answer: False. Longrich, Bhullar and Gauthier counted lizard and snake species in the last Cretaceous rocks of western North America and found about 83% vanish at the impact layer. Small size, often credited with saving mammals, was not enough. Today's thousands of species descend from the few lineages that came through.
cards.move: A crowded family today may descend from a handful of lucky survivors.
cards.trap: Seeing lizards everywhere today and assuming their ancestors sailed through.
cards.reference: Longrich, Bhullar & Gauthier, Mass extinction of lizards and snakes at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2012

cards.question: How quickly did mammals grow large after the asteroid, and what did plants have to do with it?
cards.answer: Within about a million years, in step with the plants. Fossils from Corral Bluffs, Colorado, show the largest mammals reaching about 6 kg within 100,000 years of the impact and about 50 kg by 700,000 years, roughly when the first legumes appear there. Protein-rich beans seem to have fed the first big mammals.
cards.move: A recovery at the top waits on what recovers at the bottom.
cards.reference: Lyson et al., Exceptional continental record of biotic recovery after the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction, Science, 2019

cards.question: Why do bats not deafen themselves with their own calls?
cards.answer: They brace their ears for each shout. Some bats call at up to 140 decibels at 10 cm, a level that would injure human ears if people could hear it. A muscle in the middle ear tightens just before each call, damping the bones that carry sound, then relaxes in time for the faint echo.
cards.move: To hear a whisper right after a shout, close the door while shouting.
cards.reference: Henson, The activity and function of the middle-ear muscles in echo-locating bats, Journal of Physiology, 1965; Surlykke & Kalko, Echolocating bats cry out loud to detect their prey, PLoS ONE, 2008

cards.question: Why can an oilbird find its way by echo in caves but not hunt insects that way?
cards.answer: Its clicks are too low-pitched. Oilbirds click at around 2 kHz, audible to people, and a sound wave at that pitch is about 17 cm long; much smaller objects barely echo. Most moth-hunting bats use 20 to 100 kHz: waves of 3 to 17 mm. The oilbird's sonar finds walls; it lives on fruit.
cards.move: No probe can make out anything much smaller than the waves it sends.
cards.reference: Konishi & Knudsen, The oilbird: hearing and echolocation, Science, 1979

cards.question: A bat hears a moth's echo. If the moth were twice as far away, how strong would the echo be?
cards.answer: A sixteenth, or weaker. The call spreads in all directions, so at twice the distance a quarter of the sound reaches the moth; the echo spreads again on the way back, another factor of four. Air also soaks up high pitches. Doubling a bat's range would take at least 16 times the power.
cards.move: When a loss applies twice, multiply it twice before judging the damage.
cards.trap: A quarter: applying the inverse-square law to the outward trip only.
cards.reference: Au, The Sonar of Dolphins, Springer-Verlag, 1993

cards.question: A bat's final buzz reaches about 200 calls a second. How close must prey be for each echo to beat the next call, in metres?
cards.answer: The sound must go out and back, so halve it: 1.7 / 2 ≈ 0.85 m.
cards.move: A signal that must return reaches only half as far as it travels.
cards.trap: Forgetting the round trip and answering 1.7 metres.
cards.hint: Find the time between two calls, then use the speed of sound, about 340 m/s.
steps: At 200 calls a second, calls are 1/200 s = 5 milliseconds apart.
Sound in air covers about 340 m/s × 0.005 s = 1.7 m in that time.
The sound must go out and back, so halve it: 1.7 / 2 ≈ 0.85 m.
cards.reference: Elemans, Mead, Jakobsen & Ratcliffe, Superfast muscles set maximum call rate in echolocating bats, Science, 2011

cards.question: True or false: at least one moth species defends itself by jamming bat sonar?
cards.answer: True. The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona answers an attacking bat with bursts of ultrasonic clicks from drum-like organs on its sides. In Corcoran and colleagues' flight-room trials, big brown bats easily caught silenced moths but mostly failed against clicking ones, whose sound scrambled the bats' reading of their echoes in the final approach.
cards.move: Every sense invites a countermeasure; an arms race runs both ways.
cards.trap: Sonar jamming sounds like military kit, not insect defence.
cards.reference: Corcoran, Barber & Conner, Tiger moth jams bat sonar, Science, 2009

cards.question: A 2013 genome scan linked nearly 200 genes to convergence between echolocating bats and dolphins. What did later control comparisons find?
options: As much convergence in non-echolocating pairs
cards.answer: As much convergence in non-echolocating pairs. Thomas and Hahn, and separately Zou and Zhang, ran the same test on mammals with no sonar in common and found as many shared changes or more; across thousands of genes, chance and shared constraints throw up matches. What survives is narrower, such as the hearing protein prestin.
cards.move: Search enough places and matches appear; ask how many chance alone would give.
cards.trap: Trusting hits from a scan of thousands of genes without a baseline.
cards.source: Thomas & Hahn, Molecular Biology and Evolution, 2015
cards.reference: Thomas & Hahn, Determining the null model for detecting adaptive convergence from genomic data: a case study using echolocating mammals, Molecular Biology and Evolution, 2015; Parker et al., Genome-wide signatures of convergent evolution in echolocating mammals, Nature, 2013

cards.question: A bat calling at 85 kHz flies at 5 m/s towards a wall; sound travels 340 m/s. How much higher is the echo, in kHz?
cards.move: Before reading a returning signal, subtract what your own motion did to it.
cards.trap: Counting the shift once, as if only the call moved: 1.25.
cards.hint: The bat is a moving source on the way out and a moving listener on the way back.
steps: Each leg shifts the pitch by the bat's speed over the speed of sound: 5 / 340.
The bat moves both as caller and as listener, so the shift doubles: 10 / 340.
cards.reference: Neuweiler, The Biology of Bats, Oxford University Press, 2000

cards.question: What call does a Mexican free-tailed bat make when a rival closes in on the same moth?
cards.answer: A jamming call. Corcoran and Conner recorded free-tailed bats giving a sweeping tone timed to overlap a competitor's final buzz of calls, the rapid burst that guides the strike. Played through speakers during real attacks, the tone made bats miss far more often. The moth-hunting arms race has a second front: hunters sabotaging each other.
cards.move: Rivals for one prize may gain more by spoiling each other's aim.
cards.reference: Corcoran & Conner, Bats jamming bats: food competition through sonar interference, Science, 2014

cards.question: True or false: a 230-decibel click underwater carries the same intensity as a 230-decibel sound in air?
cards.answer: False. Underwater decibels are measured against 1 micropascal, air decibels against 20, a 26 dB gap; and because water is so much denser and stiffer, equal intensity needs about 36 dB more pressure. Subtract roughly 62 dB to compare. A sperm whale's click, near 230 dB in water, is immensely loud, but on another scale.
cards.move: A decibel is a ratio; ask what it is a ratio to.
cards.trap: Reading a decibel figure as one absolute scale, whatever the medium.
cards.source: Au & Hastings, Principles of Marine Bioacoustics, 2008
cards.reference: Au & Hastings, Principles of Marine Bioacoustics, Springer, 2008; Møhl et al., The monopulsed nature of sperm whale clicks, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2003

cards.question: Why do big brown bats so often bite a luna moth's tail instead of its body?
cards.answer: The tails are sonar decoys. Each long hindwing tail twists as the moth flies, returning a strong, flickering echo. In Barber's flight-room trials, bats aimed about half their attacks at the tails, and moths with tails removed were caught far more often. The bat gets a scrap of wing; the moth flies on.
cards.move: The cheapest defence is a target you can afford to lose.
cards.reference: Barber et al., Moth tails divert bat attack: evolution of acoustic deflection, PNAS, 2015

cards.question: Why did the first weather forecast calculated from physics predict an impossible jump in pressure?
cards.answer: Its starting data were unbalanced; the physics was sound. Working by hand in wartime France, Lewis Fry Richardson spent about six weeks computing six hours of weather and got a pressure rise of 145 hectopascals, about a hundred times too big. Decades later Peter Lynch smoothed the same observations and got a realistic forecast.
cards.move: A sound method fed jittery measurements can still return nonsense.
cards.source: Lynch, The Emergence of Numerical Weather Prediction
cards.reference: Lynch, The Emergence of Numerical Weather Prediction: Richardson's Dream, Cambridge University Press, 2006

cards.question: What happened to Britain's first public weather forecasts after the man who began them died?
cards.answer: They were stopped. Robert FitzRoy, head of a small government weather office, began printing daily forecasts in The Times in 1861. After his death in 1865, a Royal Society review judged them to lack a scientific basis, and they ended in 1866. Protests from ports and shipping soon brought the storm warnings back.
cards.move: Judge a practice by what goes wrong when it stops.
cards.reference: Moore, The Weather Experiment: The Pioneers Who Sought to See the Future, Chatto & Windus, 2015

cards.question: A forecast for your town gives a 30% chance of rain tomorrow. What exactly is 30% likely?
options: Rain for about 30% of the day
Some rain at any given spot
cards.answer: Some rain at any given spot. The US National Weather Service defines it as the chance that at least 0.25 mm falls at a point in the area during the period. Surveying five cities from New York to Athens, Gigerenzer and colleagues found the same number read as hours, area or days.
cards.move: Before trusting a percentage, ask what it is a percentage of.
cards.trap: Reading the figure as a share of the day's hours.
cards.reference: Gigerenzer, Hertwig, van den Broek, Fasolo & Katsikopoulos, A 30% chance of rain tomorrow: How does the public understand probabilistic weather forecasts?, Risk Analysis, 2005

cards.question: Since the 1980s, how fast has the range of useful weather forecasts grown?
cards.answer: About one day per decade. Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet found skill 3 to 10 days ahead improving at that pace: a six-day forecast is about as good as a five-day one was ten years earlier. Satellites and computing did it. Chaos sets a ceiling near two weeks, and forecasts are still climbing towards it.
cards.move: Memorable failures hide slow, steady progress; check the long record.
cards.trap: Busted forecasts stick in the mind, so progress seems to have stalled.
cards.reference: Bauer, Thorpe & Brunet, The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction, Nature, 2015

cards.question: Should national weather services replace physics-based forecast models with machine-learning ones?
sides: No, keep physics at the core
cards.answer: The results are already in. Google DeepMind's GraphCast beat Europe's flagship physics model on 90% of 1,380 test measures, producing a ten-day forecast in under a minute on one chip instead of hours on a supercomputer. That speed buys bigger ensembles, more runs a day, and good forecasts for countries that cannot afford supercomputers.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on weather nobody has seen before.
cards.counterpoint: The learned models were trained on decades of reanalysis, the past weather reconstructed by physics models, and they still start each forecast from an analysis those models produce. They lean on what they would replace. They are also weakest at unprecedented extremes, outside anything in their training, where they tend to smooth the peaks that matter most.
cards.reference: Lam et al., Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting, Science, 2023

cards.question: Who put a butterfly into the title of Edward Lorenz's 1972 talk on chaos, and what creature had he used before?
cards.answer: The session's convener, Philip Merilees, when Lorenz sent no title: Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas? In a 1963 paper Lorenz had cited a single flap of a seagull's wings. The point was the same, that tiny errors grow until forecasts fail. The butterfly stuck.
cards.move: The wording that spreads an idea is often not its author's.
cards.reference: Lorenz, The Essence of Chaos, University of Washington Press, 1993

cards.question: US tornado warnings are in force for about 60% of tornadoes when they strike. Roughly what share of those warnings are false alarms?
cards.answer: About 7 in 10. Tornadoes are rare at any one spot, while radar shows many rotating storms that never put one down. To cover six tornadoes in ten, forecasters must warn on far more storms than will produce one. Brooks and Correia tracked it over three decades: most warned towns see only rain and hail.
cards.move: A net wide enough to catch a rare thing catches plenty besides.
cards.trap: Assuming a warning that catches most tornadoes must rarely be wrong.
cards.reference: Brooks & Correia, Long-Term Performance Metrics for National Weather Service Tornado Warnings, Weather and Forecasting, 2018

cards.question: Europe's main forecast model splits the atmosphere into columns about 9 km wide, each cut into 137 layers. Roughly how many grid points, in millions?
cards.answer: 6.3 million × 137 layers ≈ 860 million grid points.
cards.move: Size a problem in every dimension before calling it big.
cards.trap: Counting the columns and forgetting the layers stacked above each.
cards.hint: Divide Earth's surface by the area of one column, then stack the layers.
steps: Earth's surface: about 510 million km².
One column covers 9 × 9 = 81 km², so about 6.3 million columns.
6.3 million × 137 layers ≈ 860 million grid points.
cards.reference: ECMWF, IFS Documentation, Part III: Dynamics and Numerical Procedures, European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, 2023

cards.question: Covering an orchard against frost costs €1,000; an uncovered frost destroys €5,000 of fruit. Above what forecast chance of frost should the grower cover?
cards.answer: Above 20%. Covering costs €1,000 every time; not covering costs €5,000 times the chance of frost. The two break even when that chance is 1,000 ÷ 5,000, one in five. By this cost–loss ratio, a 30% forecast is decisive for this grower. The covers go on under a sky that will probably stay clear.
cards.move: Whether to act depends on the odds and on what each mistake costs.
cards.trap: Waiting until frost is more likely than not before acting.

diagram.caption: Covers cost €1,000; frost costs €5,000 times its chance. Above 20%, covering is cheaper.

cards.source: Katz & Murphy, Economic Value of Weather Forecasts
cards.reference: Katz & Murphy (eds.), Economic Value of Weather and Climate Forecasts, Cambridge University Press, 1997

cards.question: True or false: week-ahead forecasts for the Southern Hemisphere remain clearly worse than for the Northern, which has far more weather stations?
cards.answer: False. In the 1980s southern forecasts lagged well behind. From the 1990s, models learned to take in satellite measurements directly, and satellites see both hemispheres alike. By the early 2000s the gap had nearly closed, as Simmons and Hollingsworth showed. Over the empty Southern Ocean, most of the observing network is now in orbit.
cards.move: Check that an old handicap still binds before explaining anything with it.
cards.trap: Reasoning from the station map, which still favours the north.
cards.reference: Simmons & Hollingsworth, Some aspects of the improvement in skill of numerical weather prediction, Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, 2002

cards.question: True or false: swapping the magnetic field's north and south sends a migrating robin the wrong way?
cards.answer: False. Robins read the tilt of the field lines, not their polarity. In 1972 the Wiltschkos showed caged robins kept their heading when the whole field was reversed, yet turned round when only its vertical part was flipped. At the magnetic equator, where the lines lie flat, such a compass cannot tell poleward from equatorward.
cards.move: Two instruments can agree every day and still measure different things.
cards.trap: Picturing the bird's compass as a needle that points north.
cards.reference: Wiltschko & Wiltschko, Magnetic compass of European robins, Science, 1972

cards.question: Robins kept in huts on a German city campus lost their magnetic compass. Which test could isolate the cause?
options: Testing them at a rural site
Screening their huts with earthed metal
cards.answer: Screening their huts with earthed metal. Grounded aluminium sheets blocked the broadband radio-frequency noise of the city, and the robins oriented; unearthed, or with noise fed back in, they lost their way again. Engels and colleagues ran the tests double-blind over several years. The disruptive noise was far below human safety limits.
cards.move: Change one thing at a time, then change it back.
cards.trap: Testing them at a rural site, which changes everything at once.
cards.reference: Engels et al., Anthropogenic electromagnetic noise disrupts magnetic compass orientation in a migratory bird, Nature, 2014

cards.question: True or false: the iron-rich cells found in pigeons' upper beaks turned out to be immune cells?
cards.answer: True. Iron-rich nerve endings in the beak had been published as the pigeon's magnetic sensor. In 2012 Treiber and colleagues mapped iron-rich cells across whole beaks and found they were macrophages, immune cells that recycle iron, and that their numbers varied hugely from bird to bird: nothing like the fixed layout of a sense organ.
cards.move: Finding what you expected where you expected it is not yet proof.
cards.trap: False: they were widely reported as the pigeon's magnetic compass.
cards.reference: Treiber et al., Clusters of iron-rich cells in the upper beak of pigeons are macrophages not magnetosensitive neurons, Nature, 2012

cards.question: Why do magnetic bacteria in northern ponds swim towards magnetic north?
cards.answer: To go down. A chain of magnetite crystals inside each cell works as a compass needle, and in the northern hemisphere field lines dip into the ground, so swimming north along them leads into the low-oxygen mud they need. Southern strains swim south; at the magnetic equator, where lines lie flat, both kinds turn up.
cards.move: Ask what a navigator is trying to reach, not just which way it points.
cards.reference: Blakemore, Frankel & Kalmijn, South-seeking magnetotactic bacteria in the Southern Hemisphere, Nature, 1980

cards.question: What did 56 years of salmon catch records reveal about how the fish find home?
cards.answer: That they carry a magnetic address. Sockeye returning to British Columbia's Fraser River must pass Vancouver Island by its north or south end. As the Earth's field slowly drifted, the share taking each route shifted towards the entrance whose magnetic signature best matched the river mouth's when the fish had left it as juveniles.
cards.move: A slow drift in the background can expose a hidden mechanism.
cards.reference: Putman et al., Evidence for geomagnetic imprinting as a homing mechanism in Pacific salmon, Current Biology, 2013

cards.question: What did bonnethead sharks do when placed in the magnetic field of a site 600 km south of home?
cards.answer: They headed north, towards home. Keller and colleagues put bonnetheads caught off Florida in a tank ringed with electric coils that reproduced the field's strength and tilt at a distant spot. Under the southern field the sharks oriented northward, as if they knew they had been moved. They return to the same estuaries every year.
cards.move: A compass tells direction; a map also tells you where you are.
cards.reference: Keller et al., Map-like use of Earth's magnetic field in sharks, Current Biology, 2021

cards.question: Earth's field strength rises about 30,000 nT over the 10,000 km from equator to pole. Across how many km does it change 30 nT?
cards.move: A reading is only as sharp as the noise around it allows.
cards.trap: Imagining a magnetic map precise to metres, like satellite navigation.
cards.hint: Find how much the field changes in one kilometre first; 30 nT is a typical daily wobble.
steps: 30,000 nT over 10,000 km is about 3 nT per km.
A 30 nT change therefore spans 30 / 3 km.
cards.source: Lohmann et al., Journal of Experimental Biology, 2007
cards.reference: Lohmann, Lohmann & Putman, Magnetic maps in animals: nature's GPS, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2007

cards.question: Google Earth images suggested grazing cattle face north–south. When a Czech team checked other images, what did it find?
cards.answer: No detectable alignment. Hert and colleagues analysed a fresh set of herds and found cattle facing every way. The original authors replied that many of those images were unusable, with slopes, power lines or unclear animals, and that proper filtering restores the pattern. The dispute is over which pictures belong in the sample.
cards.move: When two teams disagree, first compare which cases each one let in.
cards.trap: Assuming a striking pattern across thousands of images must be robust.
cards.source: Hert et al., Journal of Comparative Physiology, 2011
cards.reference: Hert et al., No alignment of cattle along geomagnetic field lines found, Journal of Comparative Physiology A, 2011; Begall et al., Magnetic alignment in grazing and resting cattle and deer, PNAS, 2008

cards.question: True or false: under red light, migratory birds orient by their magnetic compass as well as under green light?
cards.answer: False. Wiltschko and colleagues found caged silvereyes oriented normally under blue or green light but lost their way under red. That fits the leading idea: the compass runs on a light-triggered reaction in the eye, probably in a protein called cryptochrome that absorbs blue-green light. The bird's magnetic sense seems to be something it sees.
cards.move: Test a sense under changed conditions to learn what it is built from.
cards.trap: Assuming a magnetic sense would work whatever the light.
cards.reference: Wiltschko, Munro, Ford & Wiltschko, Red light disrupts magnetic orientation of migratory birds, Nature, 1993

cards.question: Decades of studies reported fruit flies sensing magnetic fields. What did a large, blinded 2023 replication find?
options: A response only in blue light
cards.answer: No detectable magnetic effect. Bassetto, Mouritsen and colleagues repeated classic fly experiments with large numbers of flies, blinded scoring and careful control of heat and stray fields, and found nothing. Other labs still report effects, so the question is open. For years, positive results had piled up without anyone testing them this hard.
cards.move: A pile of agreeing results is not a test until someone tries to break one.
cards.trap: Expecting the often-reported blue-light effect to survive blinded testing.
cards.reference: Bassetto et al., No evidence for magnetic field effects on the behaviour of Drosophila, Nature, 2023

cards.question: Where does a migrating monarch butterfly keep the clock its sun compass needs?
cards.answer: In its antennae. Steering by the sun means knowing the hour, since the sun crosses the sky. Reppert's group found monarchs with antennae removed, or painted black to block light, lost their south-westward bearing; clear paint left them on course. The clock steering a flight of up to 4,000 km sits in two thin feelers.
cards.move: A compass that uses a moving reference needs a clock beside it.
cards.reference: Merlin, Gegear & Reppert, Antennal circadian clocks coordinate sun compass orientation in migratory monarch butterflies, Science, 2009

cards.question: About 3.5 trillion insects migrate high over southern Britain each year. Roughly how many tonnes is that?
cards.answer: 3.5 trillion mg / 1 billion mg per tonne = ~3,500 tonnes.
cards.move: The biggest migrations are often the ones nobody can see.
cards.trap: Picturing butterflies and moths rather than tiny flies and aphids.
cards.hint: Most are small flies, aphids and beetles; guess what a typical one weighs.
steps: Most migrants are small; take an average of about 1 mg each.
3.5 trillion insects x 1 mg = 3.5 trillion mg.
3.5 trillion mg / 1 billion mg per tonne = ~3,500 tonnes.
cards.reference: Hu et al., Mass seasonal bioflows of high-flying insect migrants, Science, 2016

cards.question: True or false: an insect has been shown to hold its migration course by the stars?
cards.answer: True. Bogong moths fly up to 1,000 km each spring to cool caves in the Australian Alps. Tethered in a flight simulator under a projected night sky, with the magnetic field cancelled, they held their seasonal heading; rotate the stars and the heading turned with them, scramble the stars and it was lost.
cards.move: Before ruling out an ability, test the animal under the conditions it uses.
cards.trap: Insect navigation is known for the sun and landmarks, not stars.
cards.reference: Dreyer et al., Bogong moths use a stellar compass for long-distance navigation at night, Nature, 2025

cards.question: How did scientists show that painted lady butterflies found in South America had flown across the Atlantic?
cards.answer: From their pollen and the chemistry of their wings. Painted ladies found on a beach in French Guiana carried DNA from West African pollen, and isotopes in their wings pointed to birthplaces in Europe or Africa. Winds that week blew west off Africa: a crossing of at least 4,200 km with nowhere to land.
cards.move: A traveller's baggage can tell you where it has been.
cards.reference: Suchan et al., A trans-oceanic flight of over 4,200 km by painted lady butterflies, Nature Communications, 2024

cards.question: What flips a solitary desert locust into the swarming kind?
cards.answer: Being jostled on its hind legs. When drying plants force locusts to crowd together, repeated touching of the back legs raises serotonin in their nervous system, and within hours shy, solitary insects become restless and seek each other out. Blocking serotonin stopped the change; adding it caused it without crowding. A swarm starts as bumping.
cards.move: Large collective shifts can start from a small, local trigger.
cards.reference: Anstey, Rogers, Ott, Burrows & Simpson, Serotonin mediates behavioral gregarization underlying swarm formation in desert locusts, Science, 2009

cards.question: Volunteers counted just 1,914 western monarchs at California's winter sites in 2020. What did the same count find in 2021?
cards.answer: Over 100 times more: 247,237. A record low owes something to one bad year of weather and breeding, and the next count tends to drift back. The rebound was not a recovery: estimates for the 1980s ran into the millions, and by 2024 the tally had sunk to about 9,000.
cards.move: After a record low, expect a bounce, and do not call it recovery.
cards.trap: Extending a collapse in a straight line from its lowest year.
cards.reference: https://westernmonarchcount.org/data/

cards.question: Is the loss of milkweed from farmland the main cause of the eastern monarch butterfly's decline?
cards.answer: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, and herbicide-tolerant crops let farmers clear it from maize and soya fields across the Midwest, where most monarchs once bred. Pleasants and Oberhauser estimated Midwest milkweed fell by about 58% from 1999 to 2010, tracking the shrinking winter colonies in Mexico. Replant milkweed and the butterflies should follow.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on where in the year the butterflies go missing.
cards.counterpoint: Counts of breeding adults across the north show no matching decline, Inamine and colleagues found; the losses seem to happen between the breeding grounds and Mexico. Nectar shortages along the autumn route, drought and damage to the wintering forests fit that pattern. Milkweed in every garden helps little if the butterflies die on the way south.
cards.reference: Pleasants & Oberhauser, Milkweed loss in agricultural fields because of herbicide use, Insect Conservation and Diversity, 2013; Inamine, Ellner, Springer & Agrawal, Linking the continental migratory cycle of the monarch butterfly to understand its population decline, Oikos, 2016

cards.question: How do moths migrating high above Britain at night keep the wind that carries them from blowing them off course?
cards.answer: They choose their night, height and heading. Radar studies by Chapman and colleagues found silver Y moths leaving in autumn mostly on northerly winds, climbing to where those winds blew fastest, and angling their bodies against any crosswind. They covered several hundred kilometres a night, far more than their own flight allows.
cards.move: To ride a current well, choose when to board, where, and which way to face.
cards.reference: Chapman et al., Flight orientation behaviors promote optimal migration trajectories in high-flying insects, Science, 2010

cards.question: A desert locust swarm packs about 40 million locusts into each km², each eating roughly its own weight daily. Tonnes eaten per km² daily?
cards.answer: 80 million g = 80 tonnes a day, as much as some 35,000 people eat.
cards.move: A tiny amount multiplied by an enormous count stops being tiny.
cards.trap: Picturing insects as nearly weightless and guessing a few kilograms.
cards.hint: Start from the weight of one locust, about that of two paper clips.
steps: An adult desert locust weighs about 2 g, so it eats about 2 g a day.
40 million × 2 g = 80 million g.
80 million g = 80 tonnes a day, as much as some 35,000 people eat.
cards.reference: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Locust Watch: Desert Locust frequently asked questions, FAO, 2020

cards.question: True or false: a dragonfly that breeds in rain-filled pools crosses the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa each year?
cards.answer: True. The globe skimmer reaches the Maldives in huge numbers each October, though the islands have almost no fresh water to breed in. Anderson inferred that it rides the monsoon winds from India to East Africa and back over several generations, a circuit of some 14,000 to 18,000 km.
cards.move: How small a traveller is says little about how far the wind can take it.
cards.trap: Assuming an insect of puddles and ponds could never cross an ocean.
cards.reference: Anderson, Do dragonflies migrate across the western Indian Ocean?, Journal of Tropical Ecology, 2009

cards.question: True or false: an elephant hawkmoth can tell blue from yellow by starlight alone?
cards.answer: True. Kelber, Balkenius and Warrant trained elephant hawkmoths to find sugar at blue or yellow targets, then dimmed the light: the moths still picked the right colour at starlight levels, where human eyes see only grey. Their eyes pool light from many facets onto each receptor, buying the sensitivity that colour vision needs.
cards.move: Your own limits are a sample of one, not a law.
cards.trap: False, assuming every eye goes grey in the dark, as ours do.
cards.reference: Kelber, Balkenius & Warrant, Scotopic colour vision in nocturnal hawkmoths, Nature, 2002

cards.question: Why is the DNA in a mouse's rod cells packed inside out?
cards.answer: To make each nucleus a lens. In nocturnal mammals, the densest DNA sits at the centre of each rod's nucleus instead of its rim, so it acts like a tiny lens. Stacked in columns, these nuclei channel light down through the retina with less scattering. Day-active mammals, humans included, keep the usual layout.
cards.move: Look for a second job in structures that seem to be mere housekeeping.
cards.reference: Solovei et al., Nuclear architecture of rod photoreceptor cells adapts to vision in mammalian evolution, Cell, 2009

cards.question: Why do the eyes of Arctic reindeer change colour between summer and winter?
cards.answer: To gather more light in the polar night. The mirror behind the retina shines gold in summer and deep blue in winter: pupils held wide for months probably raise pressure in the eye, squeezing the mirror's collagen fibres closer, so it reflects bluer light and scatters more through the retina. Sensitivity rises; sharpness falls.
cards.move: A trade-off can be reset by season rather than fixed for life.
cards.source: Stokkan et al., Proc. R. Soc. B, 2013
cards.reference: Stokkan et al., Shifting mirrors: adaptive changes in retinal reflections to winter darkness in Arctic reindeer, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2013

cards.question: How does one deep-sea dragonfish see its prey without being seen?
cards.answer: With a red searchlight. Most deep-sea animals see only blue, the colour that travels furthest through seawater. Malacosteus shines far-red light from organs beneath its eyes and detects it with a pigment built from chlorophyll, probably taken from its food. To its prey, the beam is darkness.
cards.move: The safest signal is one only you can read.
cards.reference: Douglas et al., Dragon fish see using chlorophyll, Nature, 1998

cards.question: Roughly how many times dimmer than direct sunlight is the light of a full moon?
cards.answer: About 400,000 times. The Sun shines at magnitude −26.7 and the full Moon at about −12.7, and those 14 steps, each a factor of about 2.5, multiply to roughly 400,000. The eye hides the gulf by widening the pupil and handing over from cones to rods, so moonlight feels merely dim.
cards.move: Senses report big ratios as small steps; measure before trusting brightness or loudness.
cards.trap: About 400 times, because moonlight feels only somewhat dimmer.
cards.reference: Cox (ed.), Allen's Astrophysical Quantities, 4th edition, Springer, 2000

cards.question: A single rod cell in the eye can respond to one photon. How many must rods absorb before a person reports a dim flash?
cards.answer: About five to ten. Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne found a reliably seen flash sent 54 to 148 photons into the eye, and only about 5 to 14 reached rods, each rod catching at most one. Rod pigment also fires by itself from heat, so a single event among millions of rods reads as noise.
cards.move: Among many sensitive detectors, one alarm alone is more likely noise than signal.
cards.trap: Forgetting how often rods fire on their own, with no light at all.
cards.reference: Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne, Energy, quanta, and vision, Journal of General Physiology, 1942; Barlow, Retinal noise and absolute threshold, Journal of the Optical Society of America, 1956

cards.question: House cats have vertical slit pupils; lions and tigers have round ones. What best predicts which kind a hunter gets?
options: The size of its usual prey
cards.answer: How high its eyes sit. Across 214 land species, Banks's team found vertical slits mostly in ambush predators with eyes near the ground, such as house cats and many snakes. A vertical slit sharpens the blur cues that judge distance, which pays most low down. Lions, eyes higher up, gain little.
cards.move: When a trait tracks two things, find cases where they come apart.
cards.trap: Crediting night hunting, though lions hunt by night as well.
cards.reference: Banks, Sprague, Schmoll, Parnell & Love, Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?, Science Advances, 2015

cards.question: Why did night-fighter crews in the Second World War wear red goggles indoors before flying?
cards.answer: To start their night vision early. Rods, the cells that see in dim light, barely respond to deep red, so red light let cones read maps and faces while rods rebuilt their light-sensitive pigment, which takes about half an hour of darkness. Crews could walk from a bright briefing room straight into the night.
cards.move: Protect the slow resource while the fast one does the work.
cards.reference: Hecht & Hsia, Dark adaptation following light adaptation to red and white lights, Journal of the Optical Society of America, 1945

cards.question: In the dark, a human pupil widens from about 2 mm across to 8 mm. By how many times does the light it admits rise?
cards.answer: 4 × 4 = 16 times.
cards.move: A gain that looks large can be small beside the range it must cover.
cards.trap: Answering 4, as if the light scaled with the width.
cards.hint: Think about the area of the opening, not its width.
steps: The light admitted scales with the pupil's area, which grows with the square of its width.
8 / 2 = 4 times wider.
4 × 4 = 16 times.

diagram.caption: Four times the width lets in sixteen times the light.

cards.reference: Wyszecki & Stiles, Color Science: Concepts and Methods, Quantitative Data and Formulae, 2nd edition, Wiley, 1982

cards.question: Why is each of a tarsier's eyeballs about as large as its whole brain?
cards.answer: Its ancestors probably lost the mirror. Most night-active mammals have a tapetum, a reflective layer behind the retina that gives light a second pass; the tarsier's lineage seems to have dropped it during a day-active phase. Back in the night without it, tarsiers could gather more light only with bigger eyes, too big to turn.
cards.move: A lost part is rarely regained; evolution builds a workaround instead.
cards.reference: Fleagle, Primate Adaptation and Evolution, 3rd edition, Academic Press, 2013

cards.question: The Amazon has about 16,000 tree species. How many of them make up half of all its trees?
cards.answer: About 230. From plots across the basin, ter Steege's team found that 227 species, dubbed hyperdominant, account for half of an estimated 390 billion trees, while thousands of the rarest species together make up a sliver of a per cent. A forest of 16,000 species is mostly a few common trees, sprinkled with rarities.
cards.move: In most big collections, a handful of members make up the bulk.
cards.trap: Halving the 16,000 to match half the trees.
cards.reference: ter Steege et al., Hyperdominance in the Amazonian tree flora, Science, 2013

cards.question: Terry Erwin's famous 1982 estimate of 30 million insect species was scaled up from beetles in how many trees?
cards.answer: 19, all of one species. In Panama, Erwin fogged the crowns of 19 Luehea seemannii trees with insecticide, counted about 1,200 beetle species, then multiplied through guesses: the share tied to that tree, 50,000 tropical tree species, beetles as 40% of arthropods. Later estimates put insects nearer 5.5 million species.
cards.move: Ask how big the sample was before believing how big the claim is.
cards.trap: About 2,000 trees, because a global figure seems to need one.
cards.reference: Erwin, Tropical forests: their richness in Coleoptera and other arthropod species, The Coleopterists Bulletin, 1982; Stork, How many species of insects and other terrestrial arthropods are there on Earth?, Annual Review of Entomology, 2018

cards.question: What sets off the rainy season over the southern Amazon?
cards.answer: The forest itself. Late in the dry season, trees still pull water from deep soil and breathe it out; satellites tracking a heavy form of water vapour show this moisture feeding shallow clouds that prime the air for storms. The rains start two to three months before winds bring in moisture from the ocean.
cards.move: Some systems start the conditions they need instead of waiting for them.
cards.reference: Wright et al., Rainforest-initiated wet season onset over the southern Amazon, PNAS, 2017

cards.question: What does hunting large monkeys do to a rainforest's carbon store?
cards.answer: It shrinks it, slowly. Spider monkeys, tapirs and big fruit-eating birds are the main carriers of the largest seeds, which mostly belong to dense-wooded trees. Hunt them out and those trees stop replacing themselves; lighter-wooded ones fill the gaps. In heavily hunted forests, Peres's team estimated a loss of a few per cent of biomass.
cards.move: When a carrier disappears, look for what stops arriving decades later.
cards.reference: Peres et al., Dispersal limitation induces long-term biomass collapse in overhunted Amazonian forests, PNAS, 2016

cards.question: Should companies be allowed to offset their emissions by paying to protect tropical forests?
cards.answer: Forests fall because cleared land earns money and standing trees earn little. Offsets are one of the few private flows that pay people to keep forest standing. Brazil cut Amazon clearing by about four-fifths between 2004 and 2012 when enforcement and money lined up. Weak projects need stricter baselines, not the end of the market.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on measuring what would have happened anyway.
cards.counterpoint: An offset only counts if the forest would otherwise have been cut, and that cannot be observed. When West's team compared project areas with similar unprotected forest, most projects showed little or no extra protection, yet sold credits as if they had. Each empty credit licenses a real tonne of emissions, so a bad offset is worse than none.
cards.reference: West et al., Action needed to make carbon offsets from forest conservation work for climate change mitigation, Science, 2023

cards.question: What lay unrecognised beneath the swamp forests of the central Congo Basin until 2017?
cards.answer: The largest tropical peatland known. Coring the swamps by hand, Dargie and colleagues mapped about 145,000 km² of peat, larger than England, holding roughly 30 billion tonnes of carbon: about three years of the world's fossil-fuel emissions. Permanent waterlogging stops dead leaves rotting, so they pile up for millennia under the trees.
cards.move: The biggest store in a system can be the one nobody thought to dig for.
cards.reference: Dargie et al., Age, extent and carbon storage of the central Congo Basin peatland complex, Nature, 2017

cards.question: Across the Amazon, how do tree species that people domesticated before 1492 compare in abundance with other species?
options: About as common as the rest
cards.answer: Far likelier to be dominant. Levis and colleagues found species domesticated by pre-Columbian peoples, such as Brazil nut and cacao, about five times as likely as others to rank among the hyperdominant trees, and commonest near archaeological sites. Groves tended for millennia outlived their tenders. Parts of the wild Amazon are abandoned orchards.
cards.move: Before crediting nature with a pattern, ask who lived there first.
cards.trap: Assuming the forest's make-up reflects soil and climate alone.
cards.reference: Levis et al., Persistent effects of pre-Columbian plant domestication on Amazonian forest composition, Science, 2017

cards.question: True or false: aircraft sampling found that south-eastern Amazonia gives off more carbon than it absorbs, even leaving out fires?
cards.answer: True. From 2010 to 2018, Gatti's team flew small planes up through the air at four Amazon sites. The south-east, heavily cleared and with hotter, drier dry seasons, was a net source even after fire emissions were subtracted: stressed trees grew less and died more. The standing forest there had stopped banking carbon.
cards.move: A label earned in one era needs checking against this era's measurements.
cards.trap: Assuming any standing rainforest must be soaking up carbon.
cards.reference: Gatti et al., Amazonia as a carbon source linked to deforestation and climate change, Nature, 2021

cards.question: Is the Amazon close to a tipping point beyond which much of it turns to savanna?
cards.answer: The forest makes much of its own rain, so clearing weakens the rain the rest depends on. Lovejoy and Nobre put the threshold at 20 to 25% deforestation, and about 17% was already gone. Boulton and colleagues found satellite signs of falling resilience across more than three-quarters of the forest since the early 2000s.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether the rain feedback works locally or basin-wide.
cards.counterpoint: The threshold is an argument from models, and the models disagree: many show dieback only under severe warming, and extra CO2 helps trees save water. Flores and colleagues project 10 to 47% of the forest exposed to compounding stresses by 2050, grave but patchy, region by region. A single basin-wide flip is not what the evidence shows.
cards.reference: Lovejoy & Nobre, Amazon tipping point, Science Advances, 2018; Boulton, Lenton & Boers, Pronounced loss of Amazon rainforest resilience since the early 2000s, Nature Climate Change, 2022; Flores et al., Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system, Nature, 2024

cards.question: What sets off the mass flowering of Borneo's dipterocarp forests, after years of near silence?
cards.answer: A signal from the Pacific. Every few years hundreds of species bloom within weeks of one another, and these general flowerings follow El Niño; the exact cue is debated, a run of cooler nights or a dry spell. Fruiting all at once swamps the pigs, birds and insects that eat seeds, so some escape.
cards.move: Scarcity punctuated by glut can beat a steady supply that feeds your enemies.
cards.reference: Ashton, Givnish & Appanah, Staggered flowering in the Dipterocarpaceae: new insights into floral induction and the evolution of mast fruiting in the aseasonal tropics, American Naturalist, 1988

cards.question: True or false: the Amazon supplies about a fifth of the oxygen people breathe?
cards.answer: False. The forest makes plenty of oxygen and uses almost all of it again: trees respire about half, and microbes rotting its leaves and wood take most of the rest. Its net contribution is close to zero. The oxygen in the air is a stock laid down over hundreds of millions of years.
cards.move: Before crediting a producer, subtract what it uses up itself.
cards.trap: Counting the oxygen a forest makes and forgetting what it burns.
cards.reference: https://nature.ox.ac.uk/research_stories/rainforests-are-not-the-lungs-of-our-planet/

cards.question: What was the first mammal extinction blamed on climate change, and what exactly finished it?
cards.answer: The Bramble Cay melomys, a small rodent found only on a coral cay of a few hectares in the Torres Strait, about 3 m high. Storm surges on higher seas washed over the island again and again, stripping the plants it ate. It was last seen in 2009; Australia declared it extinct in 2019.
cards.move: The smallest range goes first when the edge moves.
cards.reference: Gynther, Waller & Leung, Confirmation of the extinction of the Bramble Cay melomys Melomys rubicola on Bramble Cay, Torres Strait, Queensland Government, 2016

cards.question: True or false: one lighthouse keeper's pet cat wiped out New Zealand's Stephens Island wren?
cards.answer: False. Cats reached the island with the lighthouse settlement in 1894 and soon went feral. Galbreath and Brown traced a breeding population, not one pet, that wiped out a flightless wren science had only just described from birds the cats carried in to the keeper, David Lyall. The single named cat is a later embellishment.
cards.move: Every vivid detail added to a story is one more thing that must be true.
cards.trap: One named cat makes the tale feel precise, and so more credible.
cards.reference: Galbreath & Brown, The tale of the lighthouse-keeper's cat: Discovery and extinction of the Stephens Island wren (Traversia lyalli), Notornis, 2004

cards.question: Since 1900, 477 vertebrate species have gone or probably gone. How many would a normal 2 per 10,000 per century predict among 40,000?
cards.move: A count means little until you know what normal would produce.
cards.trap: Assuming a few hundred losses is roughly what nature always does.
cards.hint: Turn the background rate into a fraction lost per century first.
steps: 2 per 10,000 species per century = 0.0002 of species per century.

diagram.caption: Since 1900, 477 vertebrate species gone where 8 were expected: about 60 times the normal rate.

cards.reference: Ceballos et al., Accelerated modern human-induced species losses: Entering the sixth mass extinction, Science Advances, 2015

cards.question: Invasive predators such as cats, rats and stoats helped cause what share of modern bird, mammal and reptile extinctions?
cards.answer: About three in five. Doherty and colleagues found invasive mammal predators implicated in 142 recorded extinctions of birds, mammals and reptiles, 58% of the total. Cats alone featured in 63. Most were on islands, where animals evolved without such hunters and often nested on the ground. A few ship rats can undo a species.
cards.move: On an island, the newcomer that eats eggs outweighs almost any other threat.
cards.trap: Bulldozers and guns come to mind first, so predators seem a sideshow.
cards.reference: Doherty, Glen, Nimmo, Ritchie & Dickman, Invasive predators and global biodiversity loss, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2016

cards.question: How long before the last known thylacine died did Tasmania make the species legally protected?
cards.answer: 59 days. Protection came on 10 July 1936; the last known thylacine died in a Hobart zoo on 7 September. Until 1909 a government bounty had paid for 2,184 dead ones, and farmers and hunters killed many more. The law arrived when there was almost nothing left for it to protect.
cards.move: Protection that waits for certainty often arrives after the last case.
cards.reference: Paddle, The Last Tasmanian Tiger: The History and Extinction of the Thylacine, Cambridge University Press, 2000

cards.question: Of all the animal extinctions recorded since 1500, which group accounts for the largest number?
cards.answer: Molluscs, mostly land snails. The IUCN Red List counts about 300 extinct mollusc species, far more than birds, and Régnier and colleagues argued that many more went unlisted because nobody checked. Over 70% of the known losses were on oceanic islands. The typical recorded extinction is a small shell in a museum drawer.
cards.move: The best-told losses are rarely the most numerous ones.
cards.trap: Picking birds, because the dodo and its kind fill the stories.
cards.reference: Régnier, Fontaine & Bouchet, Not knowing, not recording, not listing: numerous unnoticed mollusk extinctions, Conservation Biology, 2009

cards.question: What wiped out most of the native tree snails of Tahiti and Moorea within a few decades?
cards.answer: Another snail, released on purpose. On Tahiti in 1974 and Moorea in 1977, the predatory rosy wolf snail was let loose to control the giant African land snail. It preferred native Partula tree snails and spread across the Society Islands: about 55 of their 61 species vanished from the wild. Several survived only in zoos.
cards.move: A remedy free to choose its targets may not choose yours.
cards.reference: Haponski et al., Deconstructing an infamous extinction crisis: Survival of Partula species on Moorea and Tahiti, Evolutionary Applications, 2019

cards.question: True or false: one fungal disease has been linked to declines in over 500 amphibian species, including about 90 presumed extinctions?
cards.answer: True. Chytrid fungus, carried round the world by the trade in frogs, infects the thin skin through which amphibians take in water and salts. Scheele and colleagues tallied 501 declining species in 2019, the largest recorded loss of biodiversity to one disease, though the count is disputed. Whole streams in Central America fell silent.
cards.move: A threat that travels with trade reaches every place the trade does.
cards.trap: Assuming one disease rarely wipes out a species, let alone dozens.
cards.reference: Scheele et al., Amphibian fungal panzootic causes catastrophic and ongoing loss of biodiversity, Science, 2019

cards.question: Of mammal species once listed as extinct or missing since 1500, what share had been found alive again by 2011?
cards.answer: More than a third. Fisher and Blomberg found that species written off after their habitat was cleared often reappeared in unsurveyed fragments, while those hit by introduced predators or disease rarely did. Few had been properly searched for. Many turned up once someone looked in the right patch of remaining forest.
cards.move: No sightings means little until you know how hard anyone looked.
cards.trap: Treating years without a sighting as proof that a species has gone.
cards.source: Fisher & Blomberg, Proc. R. Soc. B, 2011
cards.reference: Fisher & Blomberg, Correlates of rediscovery and the detectability of extinction in mammals, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2011

cards.question: How did scientists conclude in 2006 that the Yangtze river dolphin was probably gone, and what had killed it?
cards.answer: By searching its whole range, twice. A six-week survey in 2006 sent two boats about 3,400 km up and down the Yangtze, with observers and underwater microphones, and found no baiji. Turvey and colleagues blamed mainly accidental deaths in fishing gear, such as electrofishing, not hunting. Nobody had set out to kill it.
cards.move: Harm that nobody intends can still add up to an ending.
cards.reference: Turvey et al., First human-caused extinction of a cetacean species?, Biology Letters, 2007

cards.question: Where does a sugar maple send water at night during a drought?
cards.answer: Into the dry topsoil. After dark, with its leaves idle, water taken in by deep roots from moist soil leaks out of shallow ones into the parched upper layer: about 100 litres a night from a mature tree. Small plants beside the trunk drew up to 60% of their water from this night shift.
cards.move: Connections run both ways once the pressure behind them flips.
cards.reference: Dawson, Hydraulic lift and water use by plants: implications for water balance, performance and plant-plant interactions, Oecologia, 1993; Emerman & Dawson, Hydraulic lift and its influence on the water content of the rhizosphere: an example from sugar maple, Acer saccharum, Oecologia, 1996

cards.question: On forested islands in northern Sweden, where did most of the carbon stored in the soil come from?
options: Needles and leaves dropped on top
Roots and the fungi around them
cards.answer: Roots and the fungi around them. Using carbon-14 from 1960s bomb tests as a clock, Clemmensen and colleagues found that 50 to 70% of the stored carbon came from roots and their fungi, not from litter falling on the surface. The humus was built from below, out of dead fungal threads and roots.
cards.move: What you can see arriving is not always what stays.
cards.trap: Needles and leaves, because litter is what visibly piles up.

cards.question: True or false: a tree's roots rarely spread beyond the edge of its crown?
cards.answer: False. Gilman found roots reaching 1.7 to 3.8 times as far from the trunk as the edge of the crown, depending on species. They also stay shallow, nearly all in the top metre of soil. The real shape is a wide plate: a trench dug well outside the shade can still cut its supply.
cards.move: What is hidden rarely copies the shape of what shows.
cards.trap: Picturing the roots as a mirror image of the crown.
cards.reference: Gilman, Predicting root spread from trunk diameter and branch spread, Journal of Arboriculture, 1988; Perry, The ecology of tree roots and the practical significance thereof, Journal of Arboriculture, 1982

cards.question: Why did the first pines planted in Western Australia sicken and stop growing?
cards.answer: The soil lacked their fungi. Pines depend on ectomycorrhizal fungi, which sheathe their roots and gather phosphorus and nitrogen in exchange for sugar, and no pine had grown there before. In the 1920s foresters found the cure: soil carried in from an established pine plantation, worked into the nursery beds, set seedlings growing.
cards.move: Transplant anything alone and you may leave behind the partner that made it work.
cards.reference: Kessell, Soil organisms: the dependence of certain pine species on a biological soil factor, Empire Forestry Journal, 1927

cards.question: How does oak wilt spread from a dying oak to its healthy neighbours?
cards.answer: Mostly underground, through fused roots. Neighbouring oaks often graft root to root, joining their plumbing, and the wilt fungus travels through the joins, so dead trees appear in widening rings around the first. Crews stop it by ploughing a trench more than a metre deep between sick and healthy trees, cutting the grafts.
cards.move: The link that lets help through lets harm through too.
cards.reference: Juzwik, Appel, MacDonald & Burks, Challenges and successes in managing oak wilt in the United States, Plant Disease, 2011

cards.question: How does a leafless kauri stump in a New Zealand forest stay alive?
cards.answer: On its neighbours' water. Its roots are grafted to nearby kauri, and Bader and Leuzinger found its sap runs in reverse: water seeps in at night, when the intact trees rest, and stalls by day, when they pull hard. With no leaves of its own, it lives as an outgrowth of theirs.
cards.move: A part that looks dead may be running on someone else's supply.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31398586/

cards.question: Stripping a ring of bark from pines stops sugar reaching their roots. Within two months, how far did the soil's CO2 output fall?
cards.answer: By about half. In Högberg's boreal pine plots, soil respiration, the CO2 the ground gives off, fell about 54% against untouched plots within one to two months, and by up to 37% within five days. Half the soil's breath was sugar made in the needles days earlier, burned by roots and their fungi.
cards.move: To find what feeds a process, cut one supply and watch the output.
cards.trap: Assuming the soil's CO2 comes mainly from old leaves rotting.

cards.question: Pines, oaks, beeches and birches wrap their roots in a fungal sheath. What share of plant species do this?
cards.answer: About 2%. Brundrett and Tedersoo's census puts sheathing, or ectomycorrhizal, partnerships at 2% of vascular plant species; 72% host another kind, whose fungi grow inside root cells. Yet the 2% includes the trees that dominate northern and temperate forests, so counted by trunks rather than by species, the rare partnership is everywhere.
cards.move: What dominates the landscape can still be a rarity on the list of kinds.
cards.trap: Seeing it on every familiar forest tree and assuming it is typical.

cards.question: A fine root is 0.5 mm across; a fungal thread, 0.005 mm. Per unit of tissue volume, how many times more surface has the thread?
cards.move: When surface is what pays, split one thick thing into many thin ones.
cards.trap: Squaring the width ratio and getting 10,000, as if comparing cross-sections.
cards.hint: Work out surface divided by volume for a long cylinder before comparing the two.
steps: A long cylinder's surface divided by its volume is 2 divided by its radius.
So the ratio is the root's radius over the thread's: 0.25 mm over 0.0025 mm.
cards.reference: Smith & Read, Mycorrhizal Symbiosis, 3rd edition, Academic Press, 2008

cards.question: True or false: tree roots have been recorded more than 60 metres below the ground surface?
cards.answer: True. Canadell and colleagues' survey of 290 rooting records found roots of the shepherd's tree, Boscia albitrunca, at 68 m in the central Kalahari. That is the extreme: the average maximum depth across all records was 4.6 m. In dry country a few roots chase groundwater down while the rest spread near the surface.
cards.move: A rule about the bulk says nothing about how far the extremes reach.
cards.trap: Picturing roots as a shallow plate, never more than a few metres deep.

cards.question: In US hurricanes and tropical storms from 1963 to 2012, what killed the most people?
cards.answer: Storm surge from the sea. Counting every death over 50 years, Rappaport found water behind nearly nine in ten: surge 49%, rain floods 27%, surf and drownings offshore another 12%. Wind, the part a storm's category describes, killed 8%. The deadliest moment is a street filling quietly from the sea.
cards.move: The part of a danger you can see is rarely the part that kills.
cards.trap: Wind is what the category measures and what the cameras film.

cards.question: Project Stormfury seeded hurricanes from aircraft, and some weakened afterwards. Why was it wound down in 1983?
options: Unseeded storms weakened the same way
It worked, but cost too much
Seeded storms veered towards the coast
cards.answer: Unseeded storms weakened the same way. Silver iodide was meant to freeze supercooled water around the eyewall and widen the eye. Flights showed hurricanes hold little supercooled water, and that eyewalls collapse and re-form on their own, easing the wind for a while. Debbie's 31% drop in 1969 looked like ordinary weather.
cards.move: Before crediting the treatment, watch what the untreated cases do on their own.
cards.trap: Seeded storms did weaken, so the method seemed to have worked.
cards.source: Willoughby et al., Bulletin of the AMS, 1985
cards.reference: Willoughby, Jorgensen, Black & Rosenthal, Project STORMFURY: A Scientific Chronicle 1962–1983, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 1985

cards.question: True or false: no tropical cyclone can form within 200 km of the equator?
cards.answer: False. Typhoon Vamei formed in December 2001 at about 1.5° north, some 165 km from the equator, and came ashore beside Singapore. Cyclones need spin from Earth's rotation, which fades to nothing at the equator. There, a cold wind surge squeezed through the narrow southern South China Sea supplied the spin instead.
cards.move: A cause that fades to zero can be stood in for by another.
cards.trap: Earth's rotation gives no spin at the equator, so nothing can form.
cards.source: Chang, Liu & Kuo, Geophysical Research Letters, 2003
cards.reference: Chang, Liu & Kuo, Typhoon Vamei: An equatorial tropical cyclone formation, Geophysical Research Letters, 2003

cards.question: How much of the heat a hurricane releases ends up driving its winds?
cards.answer: About a quarter of one percent. NOAA's hurricane researchers put the heat released by condensing rain at around 600 terawatts, some 200 times the world's electricity-generating capacity. Keeping the winds going takes about 1.5 terawatts. Most of the heat is carried aloft and radiated to space: a vast furnace turning a modest fan.
cards.move: Judge an engine by what reaches the wheels, not by what it burns.

diagram.caption: Of 600 terawatts of heat, 1.5 drive the winds: a quarter of one percent.

cards.reference: https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd-faq/

cards.question: What did US forecasters strip out of the five hurricane categories in 2010?
cards.answer: Storm surge and pressure. The old scale promised surge heights for each category, but surge depends on a storm's size and how the seabed shelves. Katrina, a Category 3 at landfall, drove about 8 m of surge into Mississippi; Ike, a Category 2, flooded Texas like a stronger storm. It now rates wind alone.
cards.move: One number can rank only one of the ways a thing does harm.
cards.reference: Schott et al., The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, National Hurricane Center, NOAA, 2012

cards.question: Mobile radar clocked winds above 450 km/h inside the 2013 El Reno tornado, the widest on record. What was its official rating?
options: EF5, the top of the scale
EF3, the middle of the scale
cards.answer: EF3. The Enhanced Fujita scale rates a tornado by the damage surveyors find, matched against a list of buildings and trees, not by any measured wind. El Reno, up to 4.2 km wide, spent its fiercest minutes over open farmland. Where it blew hardest, almost nothing stood to be wrecked.
cards.move: A scale read from damage can only see what was there to be damaged.
cards.trap: Taking the scale as a measure of wind, when it grades wreckage.
cards.source: Wakimoto et al., Monthly Weather Review, 2016
cards.reference: Wakimoto et al., Aerial Damage Survey of the 2013 El Reno Tornado Combined with Mobile Radar Data, Monthly Weather Review, 2016

cards.question: A cyclone killed about 138,000 people in Bangladesh in 1991. Cyclone Sidr, of similar strength, struck in 2007. How many died?
cards.answer: About 3,400. Between the two storms Bangladesh built a warning network, with volunteers carrying alerts village to village, and some 2,000 raised concrete shelters. About 2 million people were moved out of Sidr's path before it landed. The sea rose much as before; this time families watched it from the upper floors of shelters.
cards.move: When the hazard stays the same, look at what changed on the ground.
cards.trap: Anchoring on the 1991 toll because the two storms were alike.
cards.source: Haque et al., Bulletin of the WHO, 2012
cards.reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3302549/

cards.question: Atlantic storms lasting two days or less rose from under one a year around 1900 to about five. What best explains it?
options: Warmer seas spawn more weak storms
Satellites and aircraft now spot them
Stronger El Niños cut storms short
cards.answer: Satellites and aircraft now spot them. A storm that lived a day over open ocean in 1900 entered the record only if a ship happened to cross it. Landsea and colleagues found that storms lasting longer than two days show little rise over the same century. The brief ones blew and died unwatched.
cards.move: Before trusting a rising count, ask whether the counting got better.
cards.trap: Reading a longer list as a warmer ocean rather than sharper eyes.
cards.source: Landsea et al., Journal of Climate, 2010
cards.reference: https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/clim/23/10/2009jcli3034.1.xml

cards.question: How did a dying tropical storm strengthen and form an eye over Oklahoma, three days after leaving the sea?
cards.answer: Wet ground stood in for the ocean. After an unusually rainy summer, central Oklahoma's soaked soils fed Erin's remnants heat and moisture, much as warm water feeds a hurricane. On 19 August 2007 an eye appeared on radar and sustained winds reached about 95 km/h. Farmland had become a shallow, muddy sea.
cards.move: When a supply is cut, check whether something nearby can pass for it.
cards.reference: Arndt et al., Observations of the Overland Reintensification of Tropical Storm Erin (2007), Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 2009

cards.question: Sea level rises about 1 cm per hectopascal of pressure drop. An eye reads 910 hPa, the air outside 1,010. Pressure-driven surge, in metres?
cards.answer: 100 cm = 1 metre.
cards.move: Before blaming one force, work out how much of the effect it can carry.
cards.trap: Crediting the low pressure with most of a surge several metres high.
cards.hint: Work out how far the eye sits below the surrounding pressure.
steps: Pressure deficit: 1,010 − 910 = 100 hPa.
Rise: 100 hPa × 1 cm = 100 cm.
100 cm = 1 metre.
cards.source: Pugh, Tides, Surges and Mean Sea-Level
cards.reference: Pugh, Tides, Surges and Mean Sea-Level, John Wiley & Sons, 1987

cards.question: Did cleaning up shipping fuel warm the planet?
cards.answer: Yes, measurably. Ships burned high-sulphur fuel that seeded brighter clouds over the oceans, reflecting sunlight. A 2020 rule cut that sulphur by around 80% almost overnight, the clouds dimmed, and one climate model puts the extra warming at up to three years' worth.
cards.move: One pollution rule ran the planet's most accidental experiment.

cards.question: Two drunk drivers, one hits a child. Are they equally guilty?
cards.answer: Both made the same decision and took the same risk; only one had a child step out. We punish them very differently, and most people feel that is right. But the difference was luck, and if luck can change how blameworthy you are, control is not what blame rests on.
cards.move: The only difference between the two drivers was who walked into the road.
cards.reference: Williams & Nagel, Moral Luck, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume 50, 1976

cards.question: Two boxes. Do you take one or both?
cards.answer: A reliable predictor has already put a million in box B if it foresaw you taking B alone, and nothing if it foresaw you taking both. Box A holds a thousand either way. Taking both dominates. Taking B alone has a far better track record. Decision theorists still split on it.
cards.move: Two solid arguments, opposite answers, fifty years and no resolution.
cards.source: Nozick, Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice, 1969
cards.reference: Nozick, Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice, in Essays in Honor of Carl G. Hempel, Reidel, 1969

cards.question: When does a heap stop being a heap?
cards.answer: Remove one grain from a heap and it is still a heap. Repeat. Somewhere it stops, but no single grain did it. This is not wordplay: the same structure decides who counts as poor enough for support, or ill enough for treatment. A line gets drawn where nature has none.
cards.move: Every threshold in every policy is one grain of sand away from arbitrary.
cards.source: The sorites paradox, attributed to Eubulides
cards.reference: Williamson, Vagueness, Routledge, 1994

cards.question: Is survival what you actually care about?
cards.answer: Parfit argued not. If you were replaced by someone psychologically continuous with you, what matters to you would carry on — so the question "but would it be me?" may be empty rather than hard. He wrote that seeing this made his own death seem less bad.
cards.move: Parfit's claim: identity is not what matters. Continuity is.
cards.reference: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, Oxford University Press, 1984, p. 281

cards.question: Is a bigger world a better one?
cards.answer: Take a happy population. Adding people whose lives are worth living seems no worse. Repeat, trading a little quality for more numbers each time, and you arrive at an enormous population whose lives are barely worth living — rated better than the first. Forty years on, nobody has an agreed way out.
cards.move: Every reasonable-looking rule about population leads somewhere nobody accepts.
cards.source: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, 1984; the repugnant conclusion
cards.reference: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, Oxford University Press, 1984, part four

cards.question: Molecules drift randomly between a box's two halves. At how many molecules does 'all on the left' first become rarer than one in a million?
cards.answer: So 20 molecules: 2 to the power 20 is the first to pass a million.
cards.move: Irreversible is mostly a matter of how many pieces are involved.
cards.trap: Guessing thousands, because a million sounds like it needs a crowd.
cards.hint: Each extra molecule halves the chance; count the halvings it takes to pass a million.
steps: Each molecule sits on the left with chance 1/2, independently of the rest.
All n on the left at once: a chance of 1 in 2 × 2 × … × 2, n times.
2 to the power 19 is 524,288; 2 to the power 20 is 1,048,576.
So 20 molecules: 2 to the power 20 is the first to pass a million.
cards.source: Feynman, The Character of Physical Law, 1965
cards.reference: Feynman, The Character of Physical Law, BBC, 1965, chapter 5

cards.question: True or false: every fundamental law of physics works the same whether time runs forwards or backwards?
cards.answer: False. Some weak-force processes tell past from future: the BaBar experiment reported in 2012 that B mesons change one way at a different rate than in reverse, and kaons had shown it before. Yet this plays no known part in why eggs break but never unbreak, which is about disorder, not these particles.
cards.move: A rule can have exceptions that explain nothing about the pattern you care about.
cards.trap: Repeating the textbook line that the basic laws ignore time's direction.
cards.reference: Lees et al. (BaBar Collaboration), Observation of Time-Reversal Violation in the B0 Meson System, Physical Review Letters 109, 211801, 2012

cards.question: In a universe at eternal equilibrium, which random fluctuation is far likelier: a whole ordered galaxy, or one brain with false memories?
cards.answer: One brain with false memories. Order that must appear at once gets exponentially rarer with every extra piece, so a lone mind dreaming a past vastly outnumbers real galaxies. Boltzmann floated the fluctuation idea in 1895; today the lonely brain is the standard objection to it, since any observer's memories would almost surely be false.
cards.move: Demand more order from chance and chance delivers it far less often.
cards.trap: Picking the galaxy, because it is the world observers find around them.
cards.source: Albrecht and Sorbo, Physical Review D, 2004
cards.reference: Boltzmann, On Certain Questions of the Theory of Gases, Nature 51, 1895; Albrecht & Sorbo, Can the universe afford inflation?, Physical Review D 70, 2004

cards.question: What finally stopped Maxwell's demon from breaking the second law of thermodynamics?
cards.answer: Its need to forget. The demon sorts fast molecules from slow by watching them; Charles Bennett showed in 1982 that watching can in principle be free, but wiping its memory to make room must release heat, as Rolf Landauer had argued in 1961. A 2012 experiment in Lyon measured that heat for one erased bit.
cards.move: Knowing can be free; it is forgetting that costs.
cards.reference: Bérut et al., Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics, Nature 483, 2012, pp. 187-189

cards.question: What did Karl Popper say a stone dropped into a pond shows about the direction of time?
cards.answer: An arrow that owes nothing to entropy, he claimed. Rings spread out from the splash; run the film backwards and rings would have to converge from the whole shore at once, fed by countless distant sources in perfect step. Popper argued so in Nature in 1956. Whether this arrow is truly separate is still debated.
cards.move: Ask what coordination the reverse of a process would require.
cards.reference: Popper, The Arrow of Time, Nature 177, 1956, p. 538

cards.question: What flaw did Josef Loschmidt find in Boltzmann's proof that a gas's disorder must grow?
cards.answer: That the laws it used run just as well backwards. Reverse every molecule's velocity in a spread-out gas and it gathers itself up again, obeying the same mechanics. So growing disorder cannot come from the laws alone; it needs a special start, what David Albert called the past hypothesis: a past of very low entropy.
cards.move: If a rule works both ways, the direction must come from where things started.
cards.reference: Albert, Time and Chance, Harvard University Press, 2000, chapter 4

cards.question: Earth sheds the energy it absorbs. Sunlight comes from a 5,800 K surface; Earth glows at 255 K. How many photons leave per photon arriving?
cards.answer: Energy out equals energy in, so about 23 photons leave for each one that arrives.
cards.move: A living system runs on the quality of its energy, not just the quantity.
cards.trap: Assuming energy in equals energy out means photons in equal photons out.
cards.hint: The energy balances; ask how much each photon carries at each temperature.
steps: A photon's typical energy is proportional to the temperature of its source.
Sun's surface about 5,800 K, Earth about 255 K: 5,800 / 255 = about 23.
Energy out equals energy in, so about 23 photons leave for each one that arrives.
