cards.reference: Penrose, Cycles of Time: An Extraordinary New View of the Universe, Bodley Head, 2010

cards.question: Which prediction about a shrinking universe did Stephen Hawking make in 1985 and then withdraw?
cards.answer: That time's arrow would turn round. Hawking argued that under his no-boundary proposal disorder would fall if the universe recollapsed. His student Raymond Laflamme and Don Page showed the proposal implied no such thing, and Hawking conceded in A Brief History of Time. On the way to a crunch, cups still break.
cards.move: A symmetry in the equations need not show up in the world they describe.
cards.source: Hawking, A Brief History of Time
cards.reference: Hawking, A Brief History of Time, Bantam, 1988, chapter 9

cards.question: Where does most of the observable universe's entropy, its measure of disorder, reside?
cards.answer: Black holes at galaxy centres. Egan and Lineweaver estimated in 2010 that supermassive black holes hold about 3 x 10^104 units of entropy, against roughly 10^89 in the background radiation: some thousand trillion times more. Black hole entropy grows with horizon area: the one at the Milky Way's centre outweighs all its stars together.
cards.move: Tally the biggest items first; they often outweigh everything else put together.
cards.trap: The background radiation, the famous afterglow that comes first to mind.
cards.reference: Egan & Lineweaver, A Larger Estimate of the Entropy of the Universe, Astrophysical Journal 710 (2), 2010, pp. 1825-1834

cards.question: True or false: the second law of thermodynamics forbids the total entropy of a system and its surroundings from falling, even briefly?
cards.answer: False. The law is a statement about large numbers. In 2002, Wang and colleagues dragged a single latex bead through water with a laser trap and saw it take heat from its surroundings, running against the law, over stretches of up to about two seconds. The fewer the molecules, the more often the arrow wobbles.
cards.move: A law about crowds can fail for a handful and still be a law.
cards.trap: Treating a rule that holds for trillions of molecules as absolute for a few.
cards.source: Wang et al., Physical Review Letters, 2002
cards.reference: Wang, Sevick, Mittag, Searles & Evans, Experimental Demonstration of Violations of the Second Law of Thermodynamics for Small Systems and Short Time Scales, Physical Review Letters 89, 050601, 2002

cards.question: A forecaster is 100% sure. Evidence arrives that is 1,000 times likelier if she is wrong. By Bayes' rule, her new probability?
cards.answer: Still 100%. Bayes' rule multiplies the odds held beforehand by the strength of the evidence, and certainty means infinite odds: a thousand to one against still leaves infinity. The statistician Dennis Lindley named the lesson Cromwell's rule, after Oliver Cromwell's 1650 plea to the Church of Scotland: think it possible you may be mistaken.
cards.move: Keep a sliver of doubt, or no evidence will ever reach you.
cards.trap: Letting the strength of the evidence stand in for the answer.
cards.reference: Lindley, Making Decisions, 2nd edition, Wiley, 1985

cards.question: After four years of checking, how sure were the referees of Thomas Hales's proof of the Kepler conjecture?
options: Certain, as with any accepted proof
cards.answer: 99% certain. Hales's 1998 proof of the densest way to stack spheres ran to hundreds of pages plus long computer calculations, and the twelve referees could not check every step. A chain of thousands of links is only as sure as all of them together. A machine-checked version was finished only in 2014.
cards.move: When a proof outgrows any single reader, certainty becomes a matter of trust.
cards.trap: Treating a proof too long to check as certain by definition.
cards.source: Hales et al., Forum of Mathematics, Pi, 2017
cards.reference: Hales et al., A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture, Forum of Mathematics, Pi 5, e2, 2017

cards.question: True or false: Augustine answered the sceptics with 'if I am deceived, I am' twelve centuries before Descartes?
cards.answer: True. In The City of God, answering the sceptics, Augustine wrote: 'If I am deceived, I am.' Shown the passage in 1640, Descartes went to his town's library to read it, then replied that Augustine used the thought to find the Trinity in the mind, and he to prove the mind immaterial.
cards.move: Before crediting a first, look for the older version nobody quotes.
cards.trap: Crediting the famous version with being the first one.
cards.source: Augustine, The City of God, XI.26
cards.reference: Augustine, The City of God XI.26, trans. Dods, Modern Library, 1950; Descartes to Colvius, 14 November 1640, in The Philosophical Writings of Descartes III, Cambridge University Press, 1991

cards.question: What puzzle did Descartes use to show that certainty good enough to live by can fall short of proof?
cards.answer: A coded letter. If shifting every letter one place along the alphabet turns a scramble into Latin words, nobody doubts the reading, though another key could hide another message. Descartes called this moral certainty, enough for the conduct of life, and claimed at least this for his physics: too much fitted to be chance.
cards.move: The more one reading explains, the less room is left for a rival.
cards.reference: Descartes, Principles of Philosophy IV.205, in The Philosophical Writings of Descartes I, trans. Cottingham, Stoothoff & Murdoch, Cambridge University Press, 1985

cards.question: What was Wittgenstein writing about in the last days before he died?
cards.answer: Certainty. The notes published as On Certainty answer G. E. Moore, who in 1939 held up his hands as proof of an external world. Wittgenstein replied that such things are not known but stand fast, hinges on which doubts turn. The last entry is dated two days before his death.
cards.move: Some beliefs are not conclusions at all; they are the ground doubt stands on.
cards.reference: Wittgenstein, On Certainty, ed. Anscombe and von Wright, Blackwell, 1969

cards.question: What circle did Antoine Arnauld find in the road Descartes took to certainty?
cards.answer: God propped up by clear ideas, and clear ideas by God. Descartes trusted clear and distinct perception because a good God would not deceive him, yet proved God from clearly perceived premises, as Arnauld objected in 1641. Descartes replied that an insight held in view needs no guarantee; only the memory of one does.
cards.move: Check whether the proof of a guarantee already relies on the guarantee.
cards.reference: Descartes, Fourth Set of Objections and Replies, in The Philosophical Writings of Descartes II, trans. Cottingham, Stoothoff & Murdoch, Cambridge University Press, 1984

cards.question: Asked general-knowledge questions, people sometimes gave odds of a million to one that they were right. How often were they?
options: All but once in a thousand
cards.answer: About nine times in ten. In Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein's 1977 experiments, answers backed at odds between 10,000 and a million to one were right only 85 to 90% of the time. The feeling had come loose from the record: wrong about once in eight, where the odds promised once in a million.
cards.move: Score how often your surest answers turn out right, then believe that score.
cards.trap: Letting the stated million-to-one odds set the expected hit rate.
cards.reference: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein, Knowing with certainty: The appropriateness of extreme confidence, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 3 (4), 1977, pp. 552-564

cards.question: Laplace counted 5,000 years of unbroken daily sunrises. By his rule of succession, what odds did he give tomorrow's, in millions to one?
cards.answer: 1,826,200 + 1 = about 1.83 million to one.
cards.move: However long the record, a count of successes never adds up to certainty.
cards.trap: Answering certainty, because the sun has never once failed.
cards.hint: Count the sunrises first; the rule's odds are one more than that count, to one.
steps: 5,000 years x 365.24 days = about 1,826,200 sunrises.
After n successes in n tries the rule gives odds of n + 1 to 1.
1,826,200 + 1 = about 1.83 million to one.
cards.reference: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, trans. Truscott & Emory, Wiley, 1902

cards.question: If someone truly knows a fact, why may they not simply ignore all later evidence against it?
cards.answer: Because the evidence can take the knowledge away. Saul Kripke's puzzle: if I know it, all counter-evidence is misleading, so I may disregard it. Gilbert Harman replied in 1973 that meeting the counter-evidence can leave you no longer knowing, and the argument's first premise is gone. A verdict stands only until the appeal.
cards.move: Being right today is no licence to stop listening tomorrow.
cards.reference: Harman, Thought, Princeton University Press, 1973, chapter 9

cards.question: True or false: the very first proof in Euclid's Elements relies on a step none of its axioms justifies?
cards.answer: True. To build an equilateral triangle, Euclid draws two circles and takes the point where they cross, but nothing in his postulates says they must cross. Every drawing showed them meeting, so the gap drew little notice until the nineteenth century; axiom systems such as David Hilbert's of 1899 closed it.
cards.move: A picture that always agrees with you cannot check your reasoning.
cards.trap: Trusting a proof that every diagram has confirmed for centuries.
cards.reference: Heath, The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements, vol. 1, Cambridge University Press, 1908, notes on Proposition I.1

cards.question: Brain activity creeps upward for about half a second before a freely timed movement. What did a 2012 model propose that creep is?
options: Random noise averaged back from movements
Muscles bracing ahead of the movement
cards.answer: Random noise averaged back from movements. Aaron Schurger's team modelled the brain as drifting activity that triggers a movement whenever it crosses a threshold. Align recordings on each movement and average them: only drifts that reached the threshold are counted, so a smooth ramp appears. The ramp is drawn by the averaging.
cards.move: Line up only the cases where something happened, and a build-up will appear.
cards.trap: Reading the early ramp as the brain deciding before the person knows.
cards.reference: Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene, An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109 (42), 2012

cards.question: What room for free will did Benjamin Libet keep after his own experiments seemed to rule it out?
cards.answer: A veto. In Libet's 1983 study the brain's build-up began about 550 milliseconds before a flick of the wrist; people reported deciding only about 200 milliseconds before it. Libet argued that the conscious mind, too late to start the act, was still in time to cancel it in the final tenth of a second.
cards.move: Where you cannot start something, look for the point where you can still stop it.

diagram.caption: The brain starts 350 ms before the felt decision, leaving the mind only a late veto.

cards.reference: Libet, Do We Have Free Will?, Journal of Consciousness Studies 6 (8-9), 1999

cards.question: True or false: the donkey starving between two equal haystacks is an example Jean Buridan used in his writings?
cards.answer: False. No such donkey appears in Buridan's surviving works; critics probably pinned it on him to mock his view that the will must wait until reason judges one option better. The puzzle is older: Aristotle describes a man equally hungry and thirsty, as far from food as from drink, stuck where he stands.
cards.move: A name attached to an idea may record who was mocked, not who wrote it.
cards.trap: Assuming a puzzle named after a philosopher comes from his books.
cards.reference: Rescher, Choice Without Preference: A Study of the History and of the Logic of the Problem of Buridan's Ass, Kant-Studien 51, 1959-1960

cards.question: A man is carried asleep into a locked room and, on waking, gladly stays. Did Locke think he stayed freely?
cards.answer: Willingly, but not freely. Locke's sleeper wakes beside someone he longs to talk to and is glad to stay, never knowing the door is locked. His staying is voluntary, because he prefers it; it is not free, because leaving was never in his power. He is choosing against a bolt he cannot see.
cards.move: Wanting what you got does not show you could have had anything else.
cards.reference: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding II.21.10, ed. Nidditch, Clarendon Press, 1975

cards.question: Can a choice be free if, given exactly the same past, it could not have gone otherwise?
cards.answer: Freedom means acting on your own reasons, without coercion or manipulation. A choice that flows from your character is yours even if a full history predicted it; one that could go either way from the same past would be luck, not control. About three in five philosophers surveyed in 2009 held this compatibilist view.
cards.move: It turns on whether freedom means acting from yourself or having real alternatives.
cards.counterpoint: If the laws of nature and the past fix every act, and neither the laws nor the world before your birth are up to you, then nothing you do is up to you. That is Peter van Inwagen's consequence argument. Calling a determined act free changes the word, not the fact: a thermostat also acts on its own readings.
cards.reference: Bourget & Chalmers, What do philosophers believe?, Philosophical Studies 170, 2014; van Inwagen, An Essay on Free Will, Clarendon Press, 1983

cards.question: What did Sartre tell a pupil torn between joining the Free French and staying with his mother?
cards.answer: You are free, so choose: invent. In his 1945 lecture, Sartre says no ethical doctrine could settle the case. The twist: whoever seeks advice has already chosen an adviser, and by coming to Sartre rather than a priest, the young man knew what he would hear. Picking the adviser was the decision.
cards.move: Choosing whom to ask is often choosing the answer.
cards.reference: Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism, trans. Macomber, Yale University Press, 2007

cards.question: Brain scans in a 2008 study foretold which of two buttons people would freely press, seconds early. How often were they right?
cards.answer: About six times in ten. Chun Siong Soon and John-Dylan Haynes decoded frontal and parietal activity up to 7 seconds before people felt they had decided. But left or right is a two-way choice: guessing blind scores 50%. The scan beat a tossed coin by roughly one call in ten.
cards.move: Before admiring a forecaster, ask how often a coin would have been right.
cards.trap: Hearing predicted seconds ahead and picturing a near-certain prediction.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18408715/

cards.question: True or false: Descartes held that the will is at its freest when nothing pulls it either way?
cards.answer: False. In the fourth Meditation, Descartes calls that indifference the lowest grade of freedom, a mark of ignorance rather than of power. The more clearly he sees that one option is true or good, the more freely he embraces it. His freest will is not balanced on a pin but carried along by the light.
cards.move: Being drawn by a good reason is not the same as being pushed.
cards.trap: Picturing freedom as a will poised evenly between equal options.
cards.reference: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, trans. Cottingham, Cambridge University Press, 1996

cards.question: Two addicts cannot resist the drug. One hates his craving; one welcomes it. On Frankfurt's view, who can be responsible for taking it?
cards.answer: The one who welcomes it. In his 1971 paper Frankfurt calls the unwilling addict a helpless bystander to a desire he rejects. The willing addict could not resist either, but he endorses the craving and makes it his own, so he may be morally responsible. Same craving, same drug: only one is on its side.
cards.move: Ask not only what someone wants, but whether they want to want it.
cards.trap: Assuming nobody answers for an act they could not have resisted.
cards.reference: Frankfurt, Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person, Journal of Philosophy 68 (1), 1971

cards.question: God replays Alice's choice 1,000 times from exactly the same past; she lies about half the time. What did van Inwagen conclude?
options: That her lies were fixed in advance
That she chose freely every time
That the outcome was mere chance
cards.answer: That the outcome was mere chance. Peter van Inwagen, himself no determinist, aimed this replay at views that ground freedom in undetermined choices. Watching results settle near half and half, anyone would treat her next choice like a coin toss. Nothing in her reasons picks this lie over that truth.
cards.move: Removing a cause does not put anyone in charge of the result.
cards.trap: Assuming that an undetermined choice must be a free one.
cards.reference: van Inwagen, Free Will Remains a Mystery, Philosophical Perspectives 14, 2000

cards.question: In what kind of book did Laplace set out an intellect able to calculate the whole future?
cards.answer: A book about probability. The all-knowing intellect, later called Laplace's demon, is best known from his Philosophical Essay on Probabilities of 1814: knowing every force and every position, it would see past and future alike. For Laplace chance lived in us, not in nature. Probability was the arithmetic of a mind that knows too little.
cards.move: When something looks random, ask whether the randomness is in the thing or in you.
cards.reference: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, trans. Truscott & Emory, Dover, 1951

cards.question: True or false: for a ball resting on one specially shaped dome, Newton's equations let it start rolling at an arbitrary moment, unpushed?
cards.answer: True. John Norton described a dome shaped so that Newton's second law admits many solutions: the ball stays on the peak forever, or rolls off at any moment, with no force to trigger it. Critics call the dome an unphysical idealisation; the mathematics stands. One ball, one past, endlessly many futures.
cards.move: Before calling a system predictable, check that its rules allow only one future.
cards.trap: Treating classical mechanics as the textbook model of perfect determinism.
cards.reference: Norton, The Dome: An Unexpectedly Simple Failure of Determinism, Philosophy of Science 75 (5), 2008

cards.question: Weather obeys deterministic physical laws. With near-perfect observations and models, how far ahead could daily weather ever be forecast?
cards.answer: About two weeks. The atmosphere is chaotic: errors in the starting state far too small to measure grow exponentially, spreading from small scales to large until they swamp the forecast. Simulations by Fuqing Zhang's team in 2019 put the ceiling for mid-latitude weather near two weeks. Today's forecasts reach about ten days.
cards.move: Exact rules give no forecast when small errors grow faster than knowledge.
cards.trap: Assuming exact laws mean better data buys an endless forecast.
cards.source: Zhang et al., J. Atmospheric Sciences, 2019

cards.question: What did Epicurus add to Democritus's atoms so that fate would not govern everything?
cards.answer: A swerve. Democritus's atoms moved only as earlier collisions drove them, so every future was fixed. Epicurus let atoms veer by the smallest amount, at no set time or place, and Lucretius says this breaks the bonds of fate. Cicero mocked it as an effect with no cause: a tremor in the rain of atoms.
cards.move: An event with no cause is not yet an event anyone chose.
cards.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, book 2
cards.reference: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II.216-293, trans. Rouse, rev. Smith, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1992

cards.question: Did Isaac Newton think his law of gravity would keep the planets in stable orbits forever?
cards.answer: No. In the Opticks, Newton wrote that the planets' small pulls on one another would build up until the system needed a reformation, which he left to God. Leibniz mocked in 1715 at a God who must wind up his watch from time to time. The self-running clockwork universe came later, with Laplace.
cards.move: A gap in a theory is not proof that someone must keep stepping in.
cards.reference: Alexander (ed.), The Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence, Manchester University Press, 1956; Newton, Opticks, Query 31, Dover, 1952

cards.question: In 1986, what did a leading British mathematician apologise for on behalf of his whole field?
cards.answer: For a false promise. Sir James Lighthill told the Royal Society that experts in mechanics had misled the educated public into equating Newton's determinism with predictability. Work on chaos after 1960 showed that many Newtonian systems are fully determined yet impossible to forecast. A whole discipline said sorry for its most famous boast.
cards.move: An expert's confident promise can outlive the evidence that once supported it.
cards.source: Lighthill, Proceedings of the Royal Society, 1986
cards.reference: Lighthill, The recently recognized failure of predictability in Newtonian dynamics, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A 407, 1986

cards.question: True or false: the experiments that won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics proved the world cannot be deterministic?
cards.answer: False. The tests by Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger ruled out local hidden variables: preset answers carried along by each particle. They left standing David Bohm's 1952 theory, fully deterministic, which predicts the same results by letting distant particles influence each other at once. Many-worlds is deterministic too. Dice are in the interpretation, not the data.
cards.move: Evidence that fits your theory proves little until the rivals fail to fit.
cards.trap: Reading no local hidden variables as no hidden causes at all.
cards.reference: Bell, Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics, Cambridge University Press, 1987

cards.question: A 15-metre error in Earth's position grows tenfold every 10 million years. How large after 100 million years, in millions of km?
cards.answer: 150 million km: about the distance from Earth to the Sun.
cards.move: An error that multiplies will outrun any error that merely adds.
cards.trap: Guessing a few kilometres, as if the error grew by steady additions.
cards.hint: Count how many tenfold steps fit into the time, then multiply.
steps: 100 million years is 10 periods of 10 million years.
Ten tenfold growths multiply the error by 10,000,000,000.
150 million km: about the distance from Earth to the Sun.

diagram.caption: Tenfold every 10 million years turns 15 metres into the distance to the Sun.

cards.source: Laskar, Is the Solar System Stable?, 2013
cards.reference: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1209.5996

cards.question: If it is fated that a sick man recovers, calling a doctor seems pointless. How did Chrysippus answer?
options: Effort is idle once the outcome is fixed
Fate stops where human choices begin
The doctor's visit is fated with the cure
cards.answer: The doctor's visit is fated with the cure. Cicero reports Chrysippus's reply to the lazy argument: some events are co-fated, so one comes only by way of the other. If recovery is fated, it is fated to come through the doctor. A wrestler fated to fight at Olympia is fated to have an opponent.
cards.move: An outcome being settled does not make the steps towards it optional.
cards.trap: Treating a fixed outcome as if it no longer needed its causes.
cards.reference: Cicero, De Fato 28-30, in De Oratore III, De Fato, Paradoxa Stoicorum, De Partitione Oratoria, trans. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1942

cards.question: What did Spinoza say a stone in flight would believe, if it could think?
cards.answer: That it moves freely, of its own will. In a 1674 letter Spinoza argued that a thrown stone, aware of its effort to keep moving but not of the hand behind it, would call itself free. People are alike: conscious of desires, blind to their causes. A drunkard, he adds, thinks he talks freely.
cards.move: Feeling that nothing pushed you is not evidence that nothing did.
cards.reference: Spinoza, The Letters, trans. Shirley, Hackett, 1995

cards.question: When his own sceptical arguments left David Hume in despair, what cured him?
cards.answer: Dinner and a game of backgammon. Reason could not dispel the doubts, Hume wrote in 1739, but nature could: he dined, played, talked and was merry with friends, and after three or four hours the arguments seemed so cold, strained and ridiculous that he could not bring himself to return to them.
cards.move: A doubt you cannot live by is a puzzle, not a plan.
cards.source: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, 1739
cards.reference: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 1.4.7, ed. Norton & Norton, Oxford University Press, 2000

cards.question: How did Sextus Empiricus say sceptics stumbled on peace of mind?
cards.answer: By giving up, like Apelles with his sponge. The painter could not render a horse's foam, gave up and flung at the picture the sponge he wiped his brushes with, and its mark made the foam. Sceptics sought calm by settling what is true, failed, suspended judgement — and calm followed, as if by chance.
cards.move: Some things arrive only once you stop grabbing for them.
cards.source: Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism, I.28
cards.reference: Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism I.28-29, trans. Bury, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1933

cards.question: How did Descartes defend doubting all his beliefs at once instead of one at a time?
cards.answer: With a basket of apples. If some are rotten and the rot might spread, tip the whole basket out, then inspect each apple and put back only the sound ones. Replying to the Jesuit Bourdin in 1642, Descartes said beliefs taken in since childhood need the same treatment, since the bad ones spoil the rest.
cards.move: When errors can spread, check everything once rather than patch one by one.
cards.reference: Descartes, Seventh Set of Objections and Replies, in The Philosophical Writings of Descartes II, trans. Cottingham, Stoothoff & Murdoch, Cambridge University Press, 1984

cards.question: Pyrrho, founder of Pyrrhonian scepticism, wrote nothing. Whose surviving books are the main record of what Pyrrhonists argued?
options: A doctor's, some five centuries later
His pupils', written in his lifetime
cards.answer: A doctor's, some five centuries later. Sextus Empiricus, a physician writing around 200 AD, is the only Pyrrhonist whose books survive whole; Pyrrho's pupil Timon survives in fragments. So ancient scepticism survives as one late author systematised it — the version printed in Latin in 1562 that fed Montaigne and provoked Descartes.
cards.move: Ask who wrote the only surviving account before trusting it as the whole story.
cards.trap: Assuming the records closest to the founder are the ones that survived.
cards.reference: Popkin, The History of Scepticism: From Savonarola to Bayle, Oxford University Press, 2003

cards.question: Blackstone's ratio: jailing an innocent is ten times worse than freeing a guilty person. Above what chance of guilt should juries convict, in per cent?
cards.move: Put a price on each kind of mistake before choosing how sure to be.
cards.trap: Turning ten to one into 90% instead of ten in eleven.
cards.hint: Weigh each mistake by its cost: at the tipping point, the two expected costs are equal.
steps: Acquitting risks freeing the guilty: chance p, cost 1.
Convicting risks jailing an innocent: chance 1 − p, cost 10.
Convict once p is greater than 10 × (1 − p), that is once 11p > 10.
cards.reference: Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book IV, chapter 27, 1769; Volokh, n Guilty Men, University of Pennsylvania Law Review 146, 1997

cards.question: Why did Hans Albert name an ancient argument for doubting every justification after Baron Münchhausen?
cards.answer: Because escaping it means pulling yourself out of a swamp by your own hair, as the baron claimed to have done. Every reason needs a reason: the chain runs on forever, circles back, or stops at a claim simply laid down. Albert named it in 1968; Sextus had listed the same exits.
cards.move: Every chain of reasons ends somewhere; know where yours stops and why.
cards.reference: Albert, Treatise on Critical Reason, trans. Rorty, Princeton University Press, 1985 (German original 1968)

cards.question: Why did Fred Dretske say you can know an animal in a zoo pen is a zebra, yet not know it is no painted mule?
cards.answer: Because evidence that settles one question need not settle another it implies. Stripes in a zoo pen rule out horses and antelopes, the live alternatives, but look the same on a painted mule. Dretske argued in 1970 that knowledge need not pass along every known implication. The sceptic wins the mule and loses the zebra.
cards.move: Ask which alternatives your evidence actually rules out before claiming all of them.
cards.reference: Dretske, Epistemic Operators, Journal of Philosophy 67 (24), 1970, pp. 1007-1023

cards.question: A witness is right 99 times in 100. By Hume's test, should you believe his report that a dead man rose again?
options: No, the event's rarity outweighs him
Only if a second witness agrees
cards.answer: No, the event's rarity outweighs him. Hume's 1748 rule: accept testimony only if its falsehood would be more miraculous than what it reports. A witness wrong once in a hundred is an everyday thing; a return from death has never been seen against countless deaths. Every grave that stayed shut testifies on the other side.
cards.move: Weigh how often a witness errs against how often such things happen.
cards.trap: Trusting the witness's 99% record and ignoring how rare the event is.
cards.reference: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section 10, ed. Beauchamp, Oxford University Press, 1999

cards.question: True or false: Hilary Putnam argued that a brain always kept in a vat cannot rightly think 'I am a brain in a vat'?
cards.answer: True. Putnam argued in 1981 that words refer through causal contact with their objects. A brain always in a vat means by vat the images its computer feeds it, so its thought is false; outside a vat, the thought is false anyway. The argument fails for a brain envatted last night.
cards.move: Before doubting everything, ask what your words could refer to if you were right.
cards.trap: Assuming words mean the same whatever the speaker has ever touched.
cards.reference: Putnam, Reason, Truth and History, Cambridge University Press, 1981, chapter 1

cards.question: When an equally careful friend reaches the opposite conclusion from the same evidence, should you move halfway?
cards.answer: Two friends split a restaurant bill and get different shares. Neither should keep trusting their own sum: nothing in the situation says which of two equally good calculators slipped. David Christensen and Adam Elga argued in 2007 that disagreement from a true equal is evidence of your own error, and should be weighed as such.
cards.move: It turns on whether your own reasoning counts as evidence about itself.
cards.counterpoint: If you reasoned correctly, the evidence supports you, and a friend's mistake does not change what the evidence says. Thomas Kelly argued in 2005 that splitting the difference rewards whoever reasoned badly. And applied to philosophy, politics or science, the halfway rule would dissolve almost every considered view, since some careful person always disagrees.
cards.reference: Christensen, Epistemology of Disagreement: The Good News, Philosophical Review 116 (2), 2007; Elga, Reflection and Disagreement, Noûs 41 (3), 2007; Kelly, The Epistemic Significance of Disagreement, Oxford Studies in Epistemology 1, 2005

cards.question: What did Kant say could happen if you lie to a murderer about where your friend is?
cards.answer: The lie could get him killed. You say your friend is out; unknown to you, he has slipped away, and the murderer, leaving, meets him in the street. Kant argued in 1797 that the death is then yours to answer for, while the truth might have kept the killer searching until neighbours seized him.
cards.move: When one option's dangers are spelt out, ask about the other option's dangers.
cards.source: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie, 1797
cards.reference: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy, in Practical Philosophy, trans. Gregor, Cambridge University Press, 1996

cards.question: True or false: the word deontology, now the name for duty-based ethics, was coined by a founder of utilitarianism?
cards.answer: True. Jeremy Bentham built the word from the Greek deon, what is binding, to name a utilitarian science of duty: conduct judged by the pleasure and pain it causes. His Deontology was published in 1834, two years after his death. Duty set against consequences is a later sense, fixed by C. D. Broad in 1930.
cards.move: Words outlive the meanings their inventors gave them.
cards.trap: Assuming a theory's name was coined by its own champions.
cards.reference: Bentham, Deontology, ed. Goldworth, Clarendon Press, 1983; Broad, Five Types of Ethical Theory, Kegan Paul, 1930

cards.question: True or false: Kant held that a person must never be used as a means to someone else's ends?
cards.answer: False. The formula says never merely as a means. A lying promise to repay a loan uses the lender in a way he could not possibly agree to, since he would refuse if he knew. Buying bread uses the baker too, but on terms he accepts: he is a means to breakfast, and rightly so.
cards.move: Before quoting a rule, find the word that limits it.
cards.trap: Remembering the slogan without its one qualifying word.
cards.source: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785
cards.reference: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, trans. Gregor, Cambridge University Press, 1998, 4:429-430

cards.question: When a stronger duty overrides a promise, what did W. D. Ross think remains of the promise?
cards.answer: Something still owed. In The Right and the Good (1930), Ross judged it right to break an appointment with a friend to help at an accident. Yet the promise does not vanish: compunction is fitting, and there remains a duty to make it up somehow to the friend left waiting.
cards.move: A duty that loses the argument still leaves a bill to pay.
cards.source: Ross, The Right and the Good, 1930
cards.reference: Ross, The Right and the Good, Clarendon Press, 1930, chapter 2

cards.question: Should it be a crime not to help a stranger in danger when helping carries no risk?
cards.answer: France punishes a bystander who could safely help, or call for help, and does neither: up to five years in prison and a €75,000 fine. The law asks only what any decent person would do anyway, and a floor matters most on the day when everyone present assumes someone else will act.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the question is whether a law can draw the line.
cards.counterpoint: Thomas Macaulay, drafting India's penal code in 1837, asked where such a law stops: is the rich man who lets a beggar starve a criminal, or the only surgeon able to operate who will not make the journey? Law can forbid harm cleanly. Commanding help makes every bystander a suspect, and punishes the frightened along with the callous.
cards.reference: Code pénal (France), article 223-6, in force since 1994; Macaulay, Notes on the Indian Penal Code, Note M, 1837

cards.question: What did J. O. Urmson's soldier who throws himself on a grenade show that moral theories lacked?
cards.answer: A place for acts beyond duty. In Saints and Heroes (1958), Urmson noted that nobody thinks the soldier who smothers the blast was obliged to, or blames the comrades who dived clear. A scheme that ranks acts only as required, allowed or forbidden files him beside someone buying a sandwich.
cards.move: A scale with three marks cannot record everything worth measuring.
cards.reference: Urmson, Saints and Heroes, in Melden (ed.), Essays in Moral Philosophy, University of Washington Press, 1958

cards.question: Kant grants that a world where nobody ever helps anybody could exist. Why, then, does refusing all help fail his test?
options: As a law, it contradicts itself
No one could will it, needing help someday
It would lower everyone's total happiness
cards.answer: No one could will it. Kant's universal-law test has two steps. A lying promise fails the first: made universal, promising collapses, so the maxim cannot even be conceived. Refusing help passes that step and fails the second, since anyone may one day need others' kindness and would have willed away all hope of it.
cards.move: When a rule fails a test, find out which part of the test it failed.
cards.trap: Treating every failed maxim as a contradiction, like the lying promise.
cards.reference: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, trans. Gregor & Timmermann, Cambridge University Press, 2012, 4:421-424

cards.question: True or false: if a man chose to set off too late to keep a promise, most say he no longer ought to keep it?
cards.answer: False. In Chituc and colleagues' 2016 experiments, most people said he still ought to meet his friend, though he no longer could. When a breakdown he was not to blame for stopped him, fewer said so. Their verdicts tracked blame, not ability: the old maxim that ought implies can fitted only the blameless.
cards.move: Before naming the cause, check what else always comes with it.
cards.trap: Crediting inability, which in everyday cases arrives together with blamelessness.
cards.reference: Chituc, Henne, Sinnott-Armstrong & De Brigard, Blame, not ability, impacts moral 'ought' judgments for impossible actions, Cognition 150, 2016, pp. 20-25

cards.question: If an island people agreed to dissolve their state, what did Kant say they must first do with the last murderer in prison?
options: Release him, as the state is gone
Exile him, since nobody is at risk
cards.answer: Execute him before they disperse. In The Metaphysics of Morals (1797), Kant made punishment a duty owed to desert, not a tool for protection. With no society left to shield, the sentence still stands, so that each receives what his deeds are worth and the blood guilt does not cling to the people.
cards.move: Ask whether a rule is justified by what it achieves or by what it answers.
cards.trap: Assuming punishment loses its point once nobody needs protecting.
cards.reference: Kant, The Metaphysics of Morals, trans. Gregor, Cambridge University Press, 1996, 6:333

cards.question: Does a promise made to someone on their deathbed still bind once they are dead?
cards.answer: A promise hands the promisee a claim on part of the promiser's future, and death does not cancel what was handed over. The law of wills rests on this. George Pitcher argued in 1984 that the dead can be harmed as the people they were before dying: breaking faith wrongs the man who asked.
cards.move: It turns on whether someone who no longer exists can still be wronged.
cards.counterpoint: An obligation is owed to someone, and after death there is nobody left to be let down or to release the promiser. Ernest Partridge argued in 1981 that the dead have no interests to set back. What remains are the living, relatives and a practice of trust; when keeping the promise hurts them, its reason is gone.
cards.reference: Pitcher, The Misfortunes of the Dead, American Philosophical Quarterly 21 (2), 1984, pp. 183-188; Partridge, Posthumous Interests and Posthumous Respect, Ethics 91 (2), 1981, pp. 243-264

cards.question: What was missing from the oldest known copy of the Daodejing, found in a Chinese tomb in 1993?
cards.answer: Most of the text, and its attack on Confucian virtue. The bamboo slips from Guodian, buried around 300 BC, hold only about two-fifths of the received chapters. Where later versions say discard humaneness and righteousness, the slips condemn artifice and scheming instead. The quarrel with Confucius may have been written in afterwards.
cards.move: Before reading a quarrel into a text, check the oldest copy.
cards.source: Henricks, Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching, 2000
cards.reference: Henricks, Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching: A Translation of the Startling New Documents Found at Guodian, Columbia University Press, 2000

cards.question: Which ancient Chinese school condemned wars of conquest and trained experts to defend besieged cities?
cards.answer: The Mohists. Mozi preached impartial care for all and called aggression theft on the largest scale; his followers wrote manuals on walls, ladders and siege tunnels. The Mozi tells how he walked ten days and nights to Chu, then beat its engineer's every attack in a war game, his belt laid out as the wall.
cards.move: Before choosing the best-known answer, ask who else was in the room.
cards.trap: Daoism, remembered for gentleness, feels like the natural home of pacifists.
cards.reference: Johnston, The Mozi: A Complete Translation, Columbia University Press, 2010

cards.question: How did the Buddhist monk Nagasena teach a Greek king that there is no enduring self?
cards.answer: With the king's chariot. In the Questions of King Milinda, Nagasena asks Menander, a Greek ruling in north-west India around 150 BC, whether the chariot is its pole, axle, wheels or frame. None of them, the king admits, nor anything apart from them. Chariot names the parts in order, says the monk; so does Nagasena.
cards.move: When nothing on the list is the thing, perhaps the thing is the list.
cards.reference: Horner, Milinda's Questions, vol. 1, Luzac, 1963

cards.question: True or false: the parable of blind men each describing an elephant by one part appears in early Buddhist scripture?
cards.answer: True. In the Udana, part of the Pali canon, the Buddha tells of a king who has blind men touch an elephant: the one at the head says a pot, the ear a winnowing basket, the tusk a ploughshare, until they come to blows. It is his picture of rival teachers clinging to partial views.
cards.move: Each person holding a different part can be right and still wrong.
cards.trap: Knowing it only from Jain, Sufi or nineteenth-century retellings.
cards.reference: Ireland, The Udana: Inspired Utterances of the Buddha, Buddhist Publication Society, 1990

cards.question: Is goodness born in people, as Mencius held, or made by training, as Xunzi held?
cards.answer: Anyone who sees a toddler about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, Mencius argued, before any thought of reward or reputation: goodness has sprouts that need only tending. Modern studies partly agree. In 2006, 18-month-olds picked up objects an adult had dropped and could not reach, unasked and unrewarded, again and again.
cards.move: It turns on whether early kindness or early violence better reveals human nature.
cards.counterpoint: Human nature is bad, Xunzi wrote; goodness comes from deliberate effort, as warped wood is straightened by steaming and pressing. Children bear him out too: Richard Tremblay's teams, following Canadian children, found hitting, biting and kicking common by 17 months, then fading for most as they grow. Nobody has to teach a toddler to hit.
cards.reference: Hutton (trans.), Xunzi: The Complete Text, Princeton University Press, 2014; Warneken & Tomasello, Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees, Science 311, 2006; Côté et al., The development of physical aggression from toddlerhood to pre-adolescence, Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology 34, 2006, doi:10.1007/s10802-005-9001-z

cards.question: How did Zhuangzi answer Huizi's challenge that, not being a fish, he could not know fish are happy?
cards.answer: By turning the question round. Huizi had asked how Zhuangzi knew; so, says Zhuangzi, Huizi already granted that he knew and was asking only how. The answer: from here, above the river Hao. Whether a quibble or a point about knowing by being there, the exchange ends with two men on a bridge, watching fish.
cards.move: Before demanding how someone knows, notice what the demand already concedes.
cards.reference: Zhuangzi, The Complete Works of Zhuangzi, trans. Watson, Columbia University Press, 2013

cards.question: What was Gongsun Long's point in claiming that a white horse is not a horse?
cards.answer: That the two terms pick out different things. Ask for a horse, and a yellow or black one will do; ask for a white horse, and they will not. So white horse is not identical with horse, though every white horse is one. The whole argument hangs on two senses of the word is.
cards.move: Ask whether is means the same as or belongs among.
cards.reference: Graham, Disputers of the Tao: Philosophical Argument in Ancient China, Open Court, 1989

cards.question: Sri Lankan tradition dates the Buddha's death to 544 BC. Where has most scholarship moved it since the late 1980s?
cards.answer: About 400 BC. Western scholars long used about 480, a correction of the Sri Lankan chronicles; after a 1988 symposium in Göttingen led by Heinz Bechert, many moved to a shorter chronology near 400. The field is still split. On the late date, the Buddha and Socrates died within a few years of each other.
cards.move: Correcting a traditional number once does not make the corrected number right.
cards.trap: Settling on 480 BC, the long-standing scholarly correction of tradition.
cards.source: Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha
cards.reference: Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha, Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1991-1992

cards.question: India's ancient materialists denied rebirth and any world beyond this one. Where does most of what is known about them come from?
options: Greek envoys' reports of Indian sages
Rival schools quoting them to refute them
cards.answer: Rival schools quoting them to refute them. The Carvaka or Lokayata texts, including a sutra ascribed to Brihaspati, are lost; scholars rebuild them from fragments in Buddhist, Jain and Hindu works written to defeat them. One sceptical treatise from the eighth century AD survives. The school stands trial with only the prosecution's papers.
cards.move: When only opponents kept the record, read it as a case for the prosecution.
cards.trap: Assuming a school's own founding text survived, as scriptures of rival schools did.
cards.reference: Bhattacharya, Studies on the Carvaka/Lokayata, Anthem Press, 2011

cards.question: True or false: Confucius said an upright son covers for a father who has stolen a sheep?
cards.answer: True. In Analects 13.18 the Duke of She boasts that in his land an upright man testifies against his father for stealing a sheep. Confucius replies that where he comes from, fathers cover for sons and sons for fathers, and uprightness lies in that. Chinese debates on family and law still argue over the passage.
cards.move: Loyalty and honesty sound like allies until they point at the same person.
cards.trap: Picturing Confucius as a law-and-order moralist who puts the state first.
cards.reference: Confucius, The Analects, trans. Lau, Penguin, 1979

cards.question: What did Boethius, awaiting execution, say separates the eternal from the merely endless?
cards.answer: Having it all at once. Eternity, he wrote in The Consolation of Philosophy around 524, is the whole of an endless life possessed together and complete. A world with no beginning or end would still live one moment at a time, losing yesterday and not yet holding tomorrow: everlasting, not eternal.
cards.move: More of the same is not a different kind of thing.
cards.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, V.6
cards.reference: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy V.6, trans. Walsh, Oxford University Press, 1999

cards.question: How did al-Ghazali use Saturn and the Sun to argue that the world cannot be eternal?
cards.answer: By counting circuits. If the world had no beginning, Saturn, once in thirty years, and the Sun, yearly, have each made infinitely many; yet the Sun's total should be thirty times Saturn's, and each must be odd or even. Around 1095 he judged it absurd. Cantor's mathematics now calls both totals the same size.
cards.move: When every answer to a question is absurd, suspect the question's assumption.
cards.source: al-Ghazali, The Incoherence of the Philosophers
cards.reference: al-Ghazali, The Incoherence of the Philosophers, trans. Marmura, Brigham Young University Press, 2000, First Discussion

cards.question: True or false: Thomas Aquinas held that reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning?
cards.answer: True. That the world did not always exist, he wrote in the Summa, is held by faith alone and cannot be demonstrated. In a short treatise of about 1271 he went further: a world created by God yet with no first moment involves no contradiction. Creation, for Aquinas, meant dependence, not a date.
cards.move: Know which of your beliefs you could prove and which you simply hold.
cards.trap: Assuming a medieval theologian would claim to have proved creation.
cards.source: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, I, q.46, a.2
cards.reference: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.46, a.2, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province, Benziger, 1947

cards.question: In 1979 Freeman Dyson argued life could think forever on finite energy by slowing down. What finding now stands most against it?
options: The heat death of the universe
cards.answer: Evidence that expansion is accelerating. Dyson's thinkers would cool, slow and hibernate, spending ever less energy per thought, so the cold end was already allowed for. But since 1998 the expansion has been found to speed up, and Lawrence Krauss and Glenn Starkman argued in 2000 that this caps what any thinker can ever gather.
cards.move: Check whether the famous objection was already answered before repeating it.
cards.trap: Blaming the famous heat death, which his plan already allowed for.
cards.reference: Dyson, Time without end, Reviews of Modern Physics 51, 1979; Krauss & Starkman, Life, the Universe, and Nothing, Astrophysical Journal 531, 2000

cards.question: Would a life that never ended eventually become unbearable?
cards.answer: Bernard Williams took Elina Makropulos, held at 42 by an elixir for three centuries, who refuses more: everything has happened to her before. A self that keeps its character runs out of new desires; a self that keeps changing is not really you surviving. Either way, endless life loses what made you want it.
cards.move: It turns on whether the best goods wear out with repetition.
cards.counterpoint: Boredom is a fact about some pleasures, not about life. Many goods renew themselves: a favourite piece of music, a meal with friends, a walk by the sea are wanted again and again, as John Martin Fischer argued in 1994. An endless life could be a rhythm of such returns, not a queue of used-up novelties.
cards.reference: Williams, The Makropulos Case: Reflections on the Tedium of Immortality, in Problems of the Self, Cambridge University Press, 1973; Fischer, Why Immortality Is Not So Bad, International Journal of Philosophical Studies 2, 1994

cards.question: In Plato's Timaeus, what were the Sun, Moon and planets made for?
cards.answer: To make time. The maker could not give the created world full eternity, so he made a moving image of it, time, proceeding by number, and set the Sun, Moon and five planets in their courses to mark it. Before the heavens there were no days or years. The sky was built as a clock.
cards.move: Ask whether a thing is measured by its instrument or made by it.
cards.reference: Plato, Timaeus, trans. Zeyl, Hackett, 2000, 37c-39e

cards.question: What did Augustine answer to the question: what was God doing before he made heaven and earth?
options: There was no before: time began with it
Preparing hell for people who pry
Contemplating the world he would make
cards.answer: There was no before: time began with it. In the Confessions, around 400, Augustine quotes the joke reply, preparing hell for those who pry, and refuses it as a dodge. God made time with the world, so there was no then in which to sit idle. The question asks for a date before dates.
cards.move: A witty answer that everyone repeats may be the one its author rejected.
cards.trap: The hell quip, the line everyone remembers from the passage.
cards.reference: Augustine, Confessions XI.12-13, trans. Chadwick, Oxford University Press, 1991

cards.question: Recurrence in miniature: a deterministic world has 1,000 possible states and changes once a second. At most how many seconds before it repeats?
cards.answer: Once a state recurs, determinism repeats all that follows: at most 1,000 seconds.
cards.move: Finite options and endless time make repetition a certainty, not a coincidence.
cards.trap: Assuming it could wander forever without coming back.
cards.hint: Count how many readings you can take before a new state runs out.
steps: Readings at seconds 0, 1, ... 1,000 make 1,001 readings.
Only 1,000 distinct states exist, so two readings must match.
Once a state recurs, determinism repeats all that follows: at most 1,000 seconds.
cards.source: Nietzsche, The Will to Power, section 1066
cards.reference: Nietzsche, The Will to Power, trans. Kaufmann & Hollingdale, Random House, 1967, section 1066

cards.question: Norman Kretzmann argued in 1966 that an unchanging God must be ignorant of something. Of what?
options: The future choices of free people
cards.answer: What time it is now. Knowing it is noon means knowing different things at different times: at noon that it is noon, later that it was. An unchanging being knows every dated fact, but never that a date is today. Timelessness answered the old puzzle of foreknowledge and left the clock without hands.
cards.move: A vantage point that sees everything can still miss where you are standing.
cards.trap: The free future, the very puzzle timelessness was meant to solve.
cards.reference: Kretzmann, Omniscience and Immutability, Journal of Philosophy 63 (14), 1966, pp. 409-421

cards.question: How did Wittgenstein's Tractatus say that a mortal could have eternal life?
cards.answer: By living in the present. If eternity means not endless duration but timelessness, he wrote in 1921, eternal life belongs to those who live in the present. Death, on the same page, is not an event in life: it is not lived through. Life has no end the way the visual field has no edge.
cards.move: Some limits cannot be seen from inside what they limit.
cards.reference: Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, trans. Pears & McGuinness, Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1961, 6.4311

cards.question: True or false: a Cretan who says all Cretans always lie has produced a genuine paradox, true if false and false if true?
cards.answer: False. If the sentence were true, the Cretan saying it would be lying, so it cannot be true. But it can simply be false: one Cretan who sometimes tells the truth suffices. The line is credited to the poet Epimenides; the New Testament letter to Titus quotes it and adds: this testimony is true.
cards.move: The opposite of all is not none; it is merely not all.
cards.trap: Treating it as false means every Cretan always tells the truth.
cards.reference: Prior, Epimenides the Cretan, Journal of Symbolic Logic 23 (3), 1958

cards.question: Which ancient poet's epitaph claimed he had been worn to death by the liar paradox?
cards.answer: Philitas of Cos, poet and tutor to the future Ptolemy II. The epitaph quoted by Athenaeus has him say that the Liar argument, and nights spent pondering it, killed him. It may be a joke, but logicians took the puzzle seriously: Chrysippus wrote several books on it. The sentence has outlived them all.
cards.move: Some questions deserve a name and a shelf before they deserve your nights.
cards.source: Sorensen, A Brief History of the Paradox, 2003
cards.reference: Sorensen, A Brief History of the Paradox, Oxford University Press, 2003

cards.question: Kurt Gödel built his 1931 incompleteness proof on a sentence modelled on the liar's. What does his sentence say about itself?
options: That it is both true and false
cards.answer: That it cannot be proved. Swap true for provable and the contradiction goes: if the sentence were provable, the system would prove a falsehood; so in a sound system it is unprovable, and therefore true. Every consistent, rule-based system rich enough for arithmetic has such truths. The paradox became a theorem.
cards.move: When an argument collapses into contradiction, change one word and see what survives.
cards.trap: Assuming Gödel used the liar itself, a sentence calling itself false.
cards.reference: Nagel & Newman, Gödel's Proof, New York University Press, 1958

cards.question: Can two ordinary sentences, each harmless on its own, become a liar paradox by accident?
cards.answer: Yes. In Saul Kripke's 1975 example, Jones says most of Nixon's statements about Watergate are false; Nixon says everything Jones says about Watergate is true. If Nixon's other Watergate statements split evenly between true and false, the pair has no consistent truth values. Whether a sentence is a trap can depend on the news.
cards.move: A statement can be safe or treacherous depending on facts nobody has checked.
cards.reference: Kripke, Outline of a Theory of Truth, Journal of Philosophy 72 (19), 1975

cards.question: Does a liar-style paradox need a sentence that talks about itself?
cards.answer: Perhaps not, argued Stephen Yablo in 1993. Take an endless list where each sentence says all later sentences are false. If any is true, all later ones are false, which makes the next true: contradiction. So all are false, which makes the first true. No sentence mentions itself; Graham Priest replied the circle is hidden.
cards.move: When blaming a single loop, check that no longer chain does the same thing.
cards.reference: Yablo, Paradox without Self-Reference, Analysis 53 (4), 1993; Priest, Yablo's Paradox, Analysis 57 (4), 1997

cards.question: What did Alfred Tarski conclude a language cannot contain, if the liar is to be kept out?
cards.answer: Its own word for truth. In 1933 Tarski proved that no consistent language able to describe its own sentences can define true for all of them. Truth for one language must be defined in a richer metalanguage, whose truth needs a richer one still. English, which applies true to itself freely, he judged inconsistent.
cards.move: A system that judges itself may need a second system to judge it.
cards.reference: Tarski, The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages, in Logic, Semantics, Metamathematics, trans. Woodger, Clarendon Press, 1956

cards.question: A theory rules liar sentences neither true nor false. Then what of the sentence 'This sentence is not true'?
options: It comes out true, and the paradox returns
It is neither, and the paradox is solved
cards.answer: It comes out true, and the paradox returns. If the sentence is neither true nor false, then it is not true, which is exactly what it says, so it is true. This strengthened liar, or revenge paradox, dogs every theory with truth-value gaps, Kripke's included. Each patch hands the liar a new word to use.
cards.move: Test a fix against the problem restated in the fix's own terms.
cards.trap: Checking the gap theory only against the sentence it was built for.
cards.source: Beall, Glanzberg & Ripley, Formal Theories of Truth
cards.reference: Beall, Glanzberg & Ripley, Formal Theories of Truth, Oxford University Press, 2018

cards.question: True or false: a liar-style paradox needs a word of negation, such as not or false?
cards.answer: False. In 1942 Haskell Curry showed that a sentence saying if this sentence is true, then the Moon is cheese proves anything. Assume it true: then its if-clause holds, so the Moon is cheese; that reasoning itself shows the sentence true. No negation anywhere, and logics built to tolerate the liar still struggle with it.
cards.move: A feature shared by every known case may not be the cause.
cards.trap: Generalising from the familiar liars, all of which contain a not.
cards.reference: Curry, The Inconsistency of Certain Formal Logics, Journal of Symbolic Logic 7 (3), 1942

cards.question: How many syllables are in the phrase: the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen syllables?
cards.answer: 5 + 4 + 9 = 18 syllables: it names in 18 what cannot be named under 19.
cards.move: A description can defeat itself by being shorter than it forbids.
cards.hint: Group the words by how many syllables each one has.
steps: the, least, not, in, than: 5 words of one syllable, so 5.
fewer, nineteen: 2 syllables each, so 4.
integer, nameable, syllables: 3 syllables each, so 9.
5 + 4 + 9 = 18 syllables: it names in 18 what cannot be named under 19.
cards.reference: Russell, Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types, American Journal of Mathematics 30 (3), 1908

cards.question: Should logicians accept that the liar sentence is both true and false?
cards.answer: Every consistent theory of truth so far has had to ban some sentence, restrict some word, or face a revenge version of the liar. Graham Priest argues the simpler answer is that some contradictions are true. Paraconsistent logics, in which a contradiction no longer proves everything, show this need not make every claim true.
cards.move: It turns on whether consistency is a fact about reality or a rule of reasoning.
cards.counterpoint: If contradictions can be true, disagreement loses its bite: an opponent may accept both a claim and its denial. Priest's logic also gives up familiar rules, such as inferring B from A or B together with not-A, which everyday reasoning uses constantly. Paying for one sentence with ordinary reasoning is a poor trade.
cards.reference: Priest, In Contradiction: A Study of the Transconsistent, Martinus Nijhoff, 1987

cards.question: Walking at 5 km/h towards Andromeda, 2.5 million light years away, shifts your 'now' there by how many days, compared with someone standing still?
cards.move: Before asking what is happening now far away, ask: now for whom?
cards.trap: Assuming a walking pace cannot move a distant now by anything measurable.
cards.hint: The disagreement equals your speed as a fraction of light's, times the distance measured in light-time.
steps: 5 km/h is about 1.39 m/s, 1 part in 216 million of light's 300,000,000 m/s.
The shift is that fraction of Andromeda's distance in light-time: 2,500,000 years ÷ 216,000,000.
cards.reference: Penrose, The Emperor's New Mind, Oxford University Press, 1989

cards.question: What did Arthur Prior think the words 'thank goodness that's over' show about time?
cards.answer: That the present is real. When a headache ends, Prior wrote in 1959, the relief cannot be about a date: nobody thanks goodness that the headache's end is dated Friday, 15 June 1954. Nor is it relief at a timeless ordering of events. What you are glad of is that it is over now.
cards.move: Some facts only show up in the present tense.
cards.reference: Prior, Thank Goodness That's Over, Philosophy 34 (128), 1959, pp. 12-17

cards.question: How wide is the present moment, as people experience it?
cards.answer: A few seconds, not an instant. William James wrote in 1890 that the present as lived is 'no knife-edge, but a saddle-back, with a certain breadth of its own on which we sit perched'. A tune is heard as a tune because its last notes linger as the next arrive.
cards.move: Ask how wide a now your question really needs.
cards.reference: James, The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, chapter 15, Henry Holt, 1890; Dover reprint, 1950

cards.question: What did J. M. E. McTaggart's 1908 paper, source of the A-series and B-series, set out to prove?
options: That time flows at one rate
cards.answer: That time is unreal. McTaggart held that change needs the A-series, events being past, present or future, but that every event would then have to be all three, a contradiction; the B-series of earlier and later alone gives no change. His conclusion won few converts, yet his two labels still organise the debate.
cards.move: An argument's vocabulary can outlive its conclusion by a century.
cards.trap: Linking his past-present-future series with the view that only now exists.
cards.reference: McTaggart, The Unreality of Time, Mind 17 (68), 1908, pp. 457-474

cards.question: If time really flows, at what rate does it flow?
cards.answer: One second per second, which critics say is not a rate. A rate measures change against time, so time's flow would need a second time to measure it, and that a third. J. J. C. Smart turned this on the moving now in 1949. Defenders reply that a rate of one is still a rate.
cards.move: Ask what a rate would be measured against before quoting it.
cards.source: Smart, The River of Time, Mind, 1949
cards.reference: Smart, The River of Time, Mind 58 (232), 1949, pp. 483-494

cards.question: If only the present exists, what makes it true today that Caesar crossed the Rubicon?
cards.answer: A property the present world has now, some presentists answer: having once contained Caesar crossing. John Bigelow called these Lucretian properties in 1996, after Lucretius, for whom the Trojan War exists now only as something that happened to lands and peoples still here. The river is still there; the crossing lives in its history.
cards.move: When a claim seems to need something missing, ask what present fact could carry it.
cards.reference: Bigelow, Presentism and Properties, Philosophical Perspectives 10, 1996, pp. 35-52

cards.question: Why did David Lewis dismiss the presentist's way of explaining how one person can be both bent and straight?
cards.answer: It discards the person's past and future along with the puzzle. Seated you are bent, standing straight; let only the present shape exist and the contradiction goes, but so does every other time to have a shape at. Nobody believes he has no future, Lewis wrote in 1986, unless at the moment of his execution.
cards.move: A solution that deletes what the problem was about has not solved it.
cards.source: Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds, 1986
cards.reference: Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds, Blackwell, 1986, section 4.2

cards.question: If the past stays real, and past people, still conscious, each feel they live at the newest moment, what follows?
options: You cannot know you are at the edge
Past people must lack all experience
The newest moment must feel different
cards.answer: You cannot know you are at the edge. On C. D. Broad's growing block, the past stays real; only the future is missing. Every past thinker is real, conscious and sure it is now, and they vastly outnumber those at the edge. Braddon-Mitchell pressed this in 2004. Odds are, your now is an old one.
cards.move: Before assuming you are in the special spot, count everyone who feels they are.
cards.trap: Hoping the newest moment feels different from the inside.
cards.reference: Braddon-Mitchell, How do we know it is now now?, Analysis 64 (3), 2004, pp. 199-203

cards.question: Einstein's line that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubborn illusion first appeared where?
options: In a condolence letter to a friend's family
In a Paris debate with Henri Bergson
cards.answer: In a condolence letter to a friend's family. Michele Besso, Einstein's friend since student days, died in March 1955; Einstein wrote to Besso's son and sister that Besso had left this strange world a little before him, which meant nothing to believing physicists. Einstein died four weeks later. The line was consolation first, physics second.
cards.move: Before quoting a famous line as doctrine, find the occasion it was written for.
cards.trap: The 1905 paper, because it is the most famous thing he wrote.
cards.reference: Einstein to the Besso family, 21 March 1955, in Speziali (ed.), Albert Einstein - Michele Besso: Correspondance 1903-1955, Hermann, 1972

cards.question: Relativity lets observers disagree about what is happening now. Which 'now' have leading presentists proposed as the real one?
options: The frame at rest with the cosmic glow
cards.answer: The frame at rest with the cosmic glow. A presentist cannot let existence depend on who is looking, so Dean Zimmerman and others pick one slicing of space-time: the one where the Big Bang's leftover radiation looks the same in every direction. Cosmologists use it for convenience; no experiment shows it to be privileged.
cards.move: If what exists depends on who is asking, you have given up on what exists.
cards.trap: Letting each observer's now count, which makes existence relative.
cards.source: Zimmerman, Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Time
cards.reference: Zimmerman, Presentism and the Space-Time Manifold, in Callender (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Time, Oxford University Press, 2011

cards.question: Black will secretly force Jones's decision only if Jones wavers. Jones decides alone, never wavering. Is Jones responsible, on Harry Frankfurt's argument?
options: No, he could not have chosen otherwise
Yes, the decision was his own
Only partly, since the outcome was fixed
cards.answer: Yes, the decision was his own. Frankfurt's 1969 case targets the old rule that blame requires being able to do otherwise. Jones could not, because Black stood ready, but Black never acted, so the unused safeguard played no part in what Jones did. What would have happened is not what did happen.
cards.move: Ask what actually did the work, not what else could have happened.
cards.trap: Assuming blame needs a real alternative, which Black silently removed.
cards.reference: Frankfurt, Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility, Journal of Philosophy 66 (23), 1969

cards.question: Told the universe is fully determined, people judged Bill, who kills his family to be with his lover. What share called him fully responsible?
cards.answer: About seven in ten. In Shaun Nichols and Joshua Knobe's 2007 study, 72% held Bill fully morally responsible. Another group, asked only whether anyone in such a universe could be fully responsible, answered no: 86% of them. In theory nobody is to blame; faced with a burning house and a named man, Bill is.
cards.move: What people endorse in the abstract can vanish when a concrete case arrives.
cards.trap: Expecting people to apply the determinism they have just accepted.

cards.question: What did P. F. Strawson think would survive even a proof that determinism is true?
cards.answer: Resentment, gratitude and indignation. In his 1962 lecture Freedom and Resentment, Strawson called these reactive attitudes part of having relationships with people at all, not conclusions drawn from a theory of causes. No proof could talk people out of them, any more than out of friendship. A betrayal is resented whatever physics says.
cards.move: Before arguing someone out of a feeling, ask whether reasoning ever put it there.
cards.reference: Strawson, Freedom and Resentment, Proceedings of the British Academy 48, 1962

cards.question: True or false: a large study of American felony cases found the insanity defence raised in more than one in twenty?
cards.answer: False. An eight-state study published in 1991 found it raised in under 1% of felony cases, and it succeeded in only about a quarter of those. The public knows it from a few trials, such as John Hinckley's acquittal in 1982 for shooting President Reagan. Of a hundred felony defendants, fewer than one pleads insanity.
cards.move: The cases you have heard of were picked by the news, not by chance.
cards.trap: Judging its frequency by the famous trials that made the news.
cards.source: Callahan et al., Bulletin of AAPL, 1991
cards.reference: https://jaapl.org/content/19/4/331.short

cards.question: Why did an ancient Greek lawgiver punish crimes committed drunk more harshly, not less?
cards.answer: Because getting drunk was the first step. Aristotle reports that Pittacus of Mytilene doubled the penalty for offences done in drink: the drunk man acts in ignorance, but had the power not to get drunk. Whoever causes his own ignorance, Aristotle argued, answers for what follows from it. The blame begins at the first cup.
cards.move: When someone could not help it, ask whether they could have helped getting there.
cards.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.5; Politics II.12
cards.reference: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.5, 1113b30-33, trans. Crisp, Cambridge University Press, 2000; Aristotle, Politics II.12, 1274b18-23, trans. Reeve, Hackett, 1998

cards.question: Who was Daniel M'Naghten trying to kill when his 1843 shooting gave the law its insanity test?
cards.answer: The Prime Minister, Robert Peel, by most accounts. M'Naghten shot Peel's secretary, Edward Drummond, instead and was acquitted as insane. Amid outcry, the Lords put abstract questions to the judges, and their answers became the rules: did he know what he was doing, or that it was wrong? The test was drafted in no courtroom.
cards.move: A rule born of public outrage can outlast the outrage by centuries.
cards.reference: Moran, Knowing Right from Wrong: The Insanity Defense of Daniel McNaughtan, Free Press, 1981

cards.question: A chairman knowingly harms the environment for profit; 82% say he did it intentionally. If the side effect helps instead, what share?
cards.answer: About a quarter: 23%. Joshua Knobe's 2003 stories differed only in harm or help, and in both the chairman said he did not care about the environment. Yet people judged the harm intended and the help not. Later replications, in several languages, found the same lopsided verdict. Blame reached back and rewrote the intention.
cards.move: Check whether your verdict on the outcome is writing your verdict on the mind.
cards.trap: Expecting the same share, since his foresight and indifference are identical.
cards.reference: Knobe, Intentional action and side effects in ordinary language, Analysis 63 (3), 2003

cards.question: True or false: in Hong Kong, India and Colombia too, most people said nobody in a deterministic universe is fully responsible?
cards.answer: True. In 2010 Hagop Sarkissian and colleagues ran the same scenarios in the United States, Hong Kong, India and Colombia. In every sample most people said our own universe is not deterministic, and that in a deterministic one nobody could be fully morally responsible. The intuition travelled like a human habit, not a Western one.
cards.move: Before calling a belief local, go and ask somewhere else.
cards.trap: Assuming a finding from American students reflects American culture.
cards.reference: Sarkissian, Chatterjee, De Brigard, Knobe, Nichols & Sirker, Is Belief in Free Will a Cultural Universal?, Mind & Language 25 (3), 2010

cards.question: Should evidence that a brain disorder shaped a violent crime reduce the sentence?
cards.answer: Responsibility tracks control, and a brain that damps fear and empathy leaves less control to blame. The law already lowers sentences for diminished capacity; neuroscience only shows where it applies. In a 2012 study, 181 American trial judges given such evidence about a psychopathic offender cut his sentence by about a year, from nearly 14.
cards.move: It turns on whether a sentence measures blame or manages danger.
cards.counterpoint: Every act has causes in the brain, so a cause cannot by itself be an excuse. The same evidence says this offender is more likely to strike again, and a sentence protects the public as well as measuring blame. Cutting it for a condition that raises the risk shifts the cost onto his next victim.
cards.reference: Aspinwall, Brown & Tabery, The Double-Edged Sword: Does Biomechanism Increase or Decrease Judges' Sentencing of Psychopaths?, Science 337, 2012

cards.question: P. F. Strawson defended blame. Why did his son Galen argue that nobody can be truly responsible?
cards.answer: Because nobody makes themselves. People act from how they are; to answer ultimately for that, they must have chosen how they are, which needs an earlier self fit to choose, and so on forever. Galen Strawson's 1994 Basic Argument adds that chance helps no one. Every chain of blame runs back to a cradle.
cards.move: Ask who shaped the chooser before blaming the choice.
cards.reference: Galen Strawson, The Impossibility of Moral Responsibility, Philosophical Studies 75, 1994

cards.question: In 1919 Karl Popper watched Alfred Adler's theory handle a case. What made him distrust it?
options: It fitted a child Adler never saw
Its prediction about the child failed
cards.answer: It fitted a child Adler never saw. Popper described a case that seemed a poor fit; Adler analysed it at once in terms of inferiority feelings, without meeting the child. Asked how he could be so sure, he cited his thousandfold experience. Popper replied that it had now become thousand-and-one-fold.
cards.move: Ask what would count against a theory before counting what fits it.
cards.trap: Assuming a bad theory is one whose predictions failed.
cards.reference: Popper, Conjectures and Refutations, Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1963, chapter 1

cards.question: Calculus, oxygen, natural selection, the telephone: each was found independently by several people. What did the sociologist Robert K. Merton conclude?
options: Such doubles are the normal pattern
cards.answer: Such doubles are the normal pattern. Studying hundreds of cases in 1961, Merton argued that discoveries come when a field's tools and questions are ready, so many people reach them at once; apparent one-offs are often races someone else lost by publishing late. Newton and Leibniz were a symptom, not a fluke.
cards.move: Ask how many people were trying before calling a match uncanny.
cards.trap: Treating each famous double as an uncanny coincidence.
cards.source: Merton, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 1961
cards.reference: Merton, Singletons and Multiples in Scientific Discovery, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 105 (5), 1961

cards.question: True or false: astrology has been put to a double-blind scientific test, and failed it?
cards.answer: True. In Shawn Carlson's study, published in Nature in 1985, astrologers matched each volunteer's birth chart to one of three personality profiles, one of them genuine. They chose correctly about a third of the time, the rate of pure guessing, after predicting they would manage at least half. Astrology is testable; it fails.
cards.move: A claim that can fail a test is a claim; check whether it did.
cards.trap: Filing astrology as untestable, the textbook case of pseudoscience.
cards.reference: Carlson, A double-blind test of astrology, Nature 318, 1985, pp. 419-425

cards.question: When two planets strayed from Newton's predictions, how did the same explanation end so differently?
cards.answer: One found a planet, the other invented one. Blaming an unseen world for Uranus's wanderings led Le Verrier to Neptune in 1846. Blaming another for an unexplained turn of Mercury's orbit gave Vulcan, which does not exist; relativity explained the turn, about a hundredth of a degree a century, in 1915.
cards.move: When a prediction fails, the evidence rarely says which assumption broke.
cards.source: Baum & Sheehan, In Search of Planet Vulcan
cards.reference: Baum & Sheehan, In Search of Planet Vulcan: The Ghost in Newton's Clockwork Universe, Plenum Press, 1997

cards.question: What did a theory of light built on a substance that does not exist correctly predict, to its own judges' disbelief?
cards.answer: A bright spot in the middle of a round shadow.
