Judging Augustin Fresnel's wave theory for a Paris prize, Siméon Poisson showed it implied this absurd-seeming spot; François Arago looked and found it. Fresnel's waves rippled through an elastic ether that was later abandoned. The spot is still there; the ether is gone.
cards.move: A theory can pass a bold test and still be wrong about what exists.
cards.reference: Worrall, Fresnel, Poisson and the white spot, in Gooding, Pinch & Schaffer (eds), The Uses of Experiment, Cambridge University Press, 1989

cards.question: When economists tested Max Planck's claim that science advances as its old guard dies, what did they find?
cards.answer: That it does. Azoulay, Fons-Rosen and Graff Zivin followed life-science fields after a star scientist died suddenly, in a 2019 study. The star's collaborators published less there afterwards, while outsiders moved in and wrote more of its papers, often citing different work. A single grave could reopen a door the living had held shut.
cards.move: Ask who guards the entrance to a field, not only who is right in it.
cards.source: Azoulay et al., American Economic Review, 2019
cards.reference: Azoulay, Fons-Rosen & Graff Zivin, Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?, American Economic Review 109 (8), 2019, pp. 2889-2920

cards.question: Logic says a white shoe supports 'all ravens are black'. How much, on the standard probabilistic answer?
options: Not at all, it is irrelevant
As much as a black raven does
cards.answer: A real but minute amount. 'All ravens are black' is logically equivalent to 'all non-black things are non-ravens', which a white shoe fits, as Hempel noted in 1945. But non-black things vastly outnumber ravens, so checking one of them risks almost nothing. A black raven could have come out white; the shoe never could.
cards.move: Evidence counts for as much as the chance it had of going the other way.
cards.trap: Weighing a shoe like a raven, forgetting how many non-black things exist.
cards.reference: Hempel, Studies in the Logic of Confirmation, Mind 54 (213), 1945, pp. 1-26; Hosiasson-Lindenbaum, On Confirmation, Journal of Symbolic Logic 5 (4), 1940

cards.question: Every emerald yet seen is green, and also 'grue': green if seen before 2030, blue after. What did Nelson Goodman say licenses predicting green?
options: Green's long record of use in predictions
Green, unlike grue, mentions no date
cards.answer: Green's long record of use in predictions. The date is no difference: to a speaker of grue and its twin bleen, green is the word defined by a date, and grue fits every emerald seen as well. Green has entrenchment, generations of successful forecasts: a habit of language, not a law of logic.
cards.move: The same evidence can back two futures; ask what made you pick one.
cards.trap: Thinking green is timeless, when timelessness depends on the starting vocabulary.
cards.reference: Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, Harvard University Press, 1955, chapters 3 and 4

cards.question: One hypothesis in 10 is true; studies catch 80% of true effects and flag 5% of false ones. What percentage of positive findings are true?
cards.move: Finding what is there is not the same as what is found being there.
cards.trap: Reading the 80% detection rate as a finding's chance of being true.
cards.hint: Imagine 1,000 hypotheses and count the true and the false among the positives.
steps: Take 1,000 hypotheses: 100 true, 900 false.
True ones detected: 100 x 0.8 = 80.
False alarms: 900 x 0.05 = 45.

diagram.label: hypotheses tested
diagram.caption: Of 125 positive findings, 45 are false alarms: only 64% are true.

cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124

cards.question: True or false: Karl Popper, champion of falsifiability, once called Darwinism not a testable scientific theory?
cards.answer: True. In his 1976 autobiography Unended Quest, Popper called Darwinism a metaphysical research programme: useful for guiding research, but not testable. Two years later, in a lecture printed in Dialectica, he publicly recanted, saying he had changed his mind about the testability of natural selection. The strictest gatekeeper had first shut out biology's central theory.
cards.move: A test for real science should be tried on the science everyone accepts.
cards.trap: Assuming the great falsifier never doubted biology's best-supported theory.
cards.reference: Popper, Unended Quest, Fontana, 1976, section 37; Popper, Natural Selection and the Emergence of Mind, Dialectica 32 (3-4), 1978

cards.question: Why did Socrates' execution have to wait about a month after his trial?
cards.answer: A ship was away. Each year Athens sent the ship said to have carried Theseus home from Crete on a sacred voyage to Delos, and no one could be executed until it returned. Plato's Phaedo says it was garlanded the day before the trial. Plutarch says Athenians kept it for centuries, replacing rotten timbers.
cards.move: Behind a famous thought experiment there is often a real object someone maintained.
cards.reference: Plato, Phaedo 58a-c, trans. Gallop, Clarendon Press, 1975; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 23, trans. Perrin, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1914

cards.question: What twist did Thomas Hobbes add to the old puzzle of a ship repaired plank by plank?
cards.answer: A second ship. Suppose someone keeps each old plank as it comes out, then reassembles them in the same order. Two ships now claim to be the original: the repaired one that never stopped sailing, and the rebuilt one of the first wood. Two ships numerically the same, Hobbes wrote in 1655, is absurd.
cards.move: When two things claim one identity, ask what the name was tracking.
cards.reference: Hobbes, De Corpore II.11.7, in Calkins (ed.), The Metaphysical System of Hobbes, Open Court, 1905

cards.question: Over a whole human lifetime, roughly what share of the heart's muscle cells ever gets replaced?
cards.answer: Under half. Carbon-14 from Cold War bomb tests, locked into a cell's DNA when it forms, let Olaf Bergmann's team date human heart cells in 2009. About 1% were renewed each year at age 25, under 0.5% at 75. Most muscle cells beating in an old person's chest are as old as the person.
cards.move: Renewal is rarely uniform; ask which parts are replaced and which never are.
cards.trap: The body renews itself every seven years, so the heart must too.
cards.reference: Bergmann et al., Evidence for cardiomyocyte renewal in humans, Science 324 (5923), 2009

cards.question: Was a Roman court whose judges had all been replaced still the same court, according to the jurist Alfenus?
cards.answer: Yes. In a ruling kept in Justinian's Digest, Alfenus Varus compared it to a legion whose fallen soldiers are replaced, a people whose members die and are born, and a ship repaired until no original plank remains: each stays the same while its form continues. A lawsuit could reach its verdict under entirely new judges.
cards.move: Ask whether a thing is its parts or the arrangement its parts keep.
cards.reference: The Digest of Justinian 5.1.76, ed. Mommsen, Krueger & Watson, University of Pennsylvania Press, 1985

cards.question: Should a band be allowed to keep its name once none of its founding members remain?
cards.answer: A band name is a brand built by writers, producers, managers and fans as much as by the first faces; whoever keeps the work going has earned it. Orchestras and football clubs outlive every founder. By late 2009 the Sugababes had no founding member left, and released an album under the name the next year.
cards.move: It turns on whether a name promises particular people or a continuing enterprise.
cards.counterpoint: Fans buy a band's name as a promise about who is on stage. When the three founding Sugababes re-formed in the early 2010s, they had to perform as Mutya Keisha Siobhan while a line-up with none of them had sold the old hits; only in 2019 did they get the name back. A label that no longer describes anything misleads.
cards.reference: https://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/showbiz/2019/10/18/sugababes-are-back-with-original-line-up-and-new-music/

cards.question: How has Japan's Ise shrine kept its ancient form when none of its wood is more than 20 years old?
cards.answer: By being rebuilt every 20 years on the empty plot beside it, identical to the joint, before the old one comes down. The rite goes back about 1,300 years, though it lapsed for over a century during the civil wars of the 1400s and 1500s. What endures is the carpenters' knowledge, not the timber.
cards.move: Some things last by being remade, not by being kept.
cards.reference: Tange & Kawazoe, Ise: Prototype of Japanese Architecture, MIT Press, 1965

cards.question: Did Heraclitus really say that nobody can step into the same river twice?
cards.answer: Perhaps not. The fragment most scholars trust reads: on those stepping into the same rivers, other and other waters flow. That keeps the river the same through changing water, nearly the reverse of the famous version, known through Plato and Plutarch. Which is his is disputed. The river stays; its water moves on.
cards.move: Check the original wording before building on a famous paraphrase.
cards.source: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers
cards.reference: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 1983

cards.question: Dion is a whole man; Theon is Dion minus one foot. Dion's foot is cut off. Which survives, according to Chrysippus?
options: Both survive, now in one body
cards.answer: Dion survives; Theon has perished. Philo reports the reasoning: two individuals cannot fill one and the same body, so one must go. Dion can survive losing a foot, as anyone can; Theon, though he lost nothing, is squeezed out. Many modern metaphysicians prefer the answer Chrysippus ruled out: two things sharing one body.
cards.move: Surviving a loss and surviving a merger are different questions.
cards.trap: Theon lost nothing, so surely it is Theon who survives.
cards.reference: Sedley, The Stoic Criterion of Identity, Phronesis 27 (3), 1982

cards.question: Each year a random 5% of a ship's planks are replaced, old or new alike. After how many years are under half the originals left?
cards.answer: Check: 0.95 multiplied 14 times is 0.49, just under half: 14 years.
cards.move: A steady percentage loss halves things slowly and never quite finishes.
cards.trap: Answering 10 years, as if 5% a year removed half in ten.
cards.hint: The originals shrink by a fixed share each year, not a fixed number.
steps: Each year 5% of the remaining originals go, so 95% stay.
A steady loss rate halves a stock in about 70 / rate years.
Check: 0.95 multiplied 14 times is 0.49, just under half: 14 years.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics 46, 1978

cards.question: Is a historic building rebuilt from new materials after its destruction still authentic?
cards.answer: Warsaw's Old Town was blown up by German forces in 1944 and rebuilt from paintings, drawings and surveys; UNESCO listed it in 1980 as a reconstruction. The 1994 Nara Document accepted that authenticity can lie in form, craft, use and spirit, not only in original fabric. Otherwise a city loses its past twice.
cards.move: It turns on whether authenticity lives in the material or in the continuing practice.
cards.counterpoint: A rebuilt facade tells visitors something that did not happen: continuity. Original fabric carries evidence, tool marks, repairs and damage no drawing records, and once lost it can only be imitated. The Venice Charter of 1964 told restorers to stop where conjecture begins. A copy, however loving, is testimony written after the fact.
cards.reference: ICOMOS, The Nara Document on Authenticity, 1994; ICOMOS, International Charter for the Conservation and Restoration of Monuments and Sites (Venice Charter), 1964

cards.question: What is the only complete surviving work about Socrates written while he was still alive?
cards.answer: A comedy. In Aristophanes' Clouds, staged in 423 BC, Socrates runs a thinking-shop, teaches students to make the weaker argument beat the stronger, and first appears hanging in a basket to study the sky. Plato and Xenophon wrote after his death in 399. In Plato's Apology, Socrates blames the play for the jury's prejudice.
cards.move: Check when a portrait was drawn, and by whom, before trusting it.
cards.reference: Aristophanes, Clouds, ed. K. J. Dover, Clarendon Press, 1968

cards.question: Socrates' jury is usually put at 500; he said 30 votes going the other way would have acquitted him. How many voted guilty?
cards.move: A vote that changes sides counts twice: once lost, once gained.
cards.trap: Reading 30 switched votes as a 30-vote margin, not a 60-vote one.
cards.hint: A switched vote leaves one pile and joins the other; in Athens a tie meant acquittal.
steps: Switching 30 votes takes 30 from guilty and adds 30 to not guilty.
A tie acquitted, so after the switch guilty would stand at exactly 250 of 500.
cards.reference: Plato, Apology 36a, trans. Grube, in Plato: Complete Works, ed. Cooper, Hackett, 1997

cards.question: The Delphic oracle declared that nobody was wiser than Socrates. According to Plato's Apology, what did he do next?
options: Began teaching as the god's chosen sage
Dismissed it as a riddle not worth solving
Looked for someone wiser to prove it wrong
cards.answer: Looked for someone wiser to prove it wrong. Socrates questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen, expecting to carry a counterexample back to the god. Each believed he knew things he did not. Socrates concluded he was wiser only in not thinking he knew what he did not. He tested a compliment by hunting for its refutation.
cards.move: To test a flattering claim, go looking for the case that breaks it.
cards.trap: Assuming a man told he is wisest takes it as a mission.
cards.reference: Plato, Apology 21a-23b, in The Last Days of Socrates, trans. Tredennick & Tarrant, Penguin, 2003

cards.question: What did Socrates say his inner divine sign had never once told him to do?
cards.answer: To do anything. The sign, his daimonion, only ever held him back, often over small matters, he says in Plato's Apology. On the day of his trial it stayed silent, when he left home and while he addressed the jury. Socrates took that silence as evidence that what lay ahead, even death, was no evil.
cards.move: A signal that only ever says stop makes its silence mean something.
cards.reference: Plato, Apology 31c-d and 40a-c, trans. Fowler, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1914

cards.question: Did Athens have a genuine case against Socrates, beyond religious prejudice?
cards.answer: His circle had nearly wrecked the city. Alcibiades, his favourite, defected to Sparta; Critias, another associate, led the Thirty Tyrants, who put more than a thousand citizens to death. Socrates mocked choosing officials by lot. An amnesty in 403 BC barred prosecution for political acts, so impiety and corrupting the young were the charges left.
cards.move: It turns on whether the company someone kept can ever be enough to convict.
cards.counterpoint: Socrates refused the Thirty's order to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution, and in 406 BC he alone of the presiding councillors opposed an illegal mass trial of generals under the democracy. He wrote nothing and led no faction. Condemning a man for his friends and his questions is what Athenian free speech was meant to prevent.
cards.reference: Stone, The Trial of Socrates, Little, Brown, 1988

cards.question: According to Xenophon, why did Socrates make so little effort to win his acquittal?
cards.answer: He thought it a good time to die. In Xenophon's Apology, Socrates tells his friend Hermogenes that death now would spare him old age: failing sight and hearing, slower learning, faster forgetting. Plato's Socrates argues for his life as a public duty; Xenophon's treats the verdict almost as a mercy. Two pupils, two different deaths.
cards.move: When two witnesses explain the same act, ask what each needed it to mean.
cards.reference: Xenophon, Conversations of Socrates, trans. Tredennick & Waterfield, Penguin, 1990

cards.question: Of Socrates' 500 jurors, 280 voted guilty; Diogenes Laertius says 80 more then voted for death. How many voted against death?
cards.answer: Against death: 500 - 360 = 140.
cards.move: A second vote is a new count, not a rerun of the first.
cards.trap: Answering 220, as if every acquitting juror voted against death again.
cards.hint: Find the votes for death first, then take them from the whole jury.
steps: Votes for death: 280 + 80 = 360.
So at least 80 jurors who had voted to acquit now voted to kill.
Against death: 500 - 360 = 140.
cards.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.42, trans. Hicks, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1925

cards.question: Which illegal order did Socrates defy while Athens was still a democracy?
options: Trying the Arginusae generals as one group
Arresting Leon of Salamis for execution
cards.answer: Trying the Arginusae generals as one group. In 406 BC, serving on the Council's presiding committee, Socrates alone opposed a single vote on the commanders blamed for abandoning sailors after a naval victory; the law required separate trials. The Leon arrest came later, under the Thirty. He defied a crowd first, then tyrants.
cards.move: The example that springs to mind first may belong to a different chapter.
cards.trap: The Leon story is better known, so it comes to mind first.
cards.reference: Plato, Apology 32a-e, trans. Grube, rev. Cooper, in Five Dialogues, Hackett, 2002

cards.question: Plato and Xenophon each wrote a defence speech for Socrates. Which of them was in court to hear the real one?
cards.answer: Plato only. Plato names himself twice among those present, once as a guarantor of the fine Socrates offered. Xenophon was away in Asia with Greek mercenaries and credits his account to Hermogenes. Yet Plato's Phaedo says Plato was ill on the day Socrates died: the most famous death scene in philosophy is secondhand.
cards.move: Before trusting a vivid account, ask where its author was standing.
cards.trap: Both, since each wrote the speech as if from the courtroom.
cards.reference: Plato, Complete Works, ed. Cooper, Hackett, 1997

cards.question: Does poison hemlock kill the way Plato's Phaedo describes the death of Socrates?
cards.answer: Probably, though it was long doubted. Critics said the plant brings vomiting and convulsions, so Plato must have prettified the scene. Enid Bloch showed that Conium maculatum can cause a creeping paralysis rising up the legs, as the Phaedo tells it, with the mind clear. The cold reached his waist before his last words.
cards.move: Before calling a witness a liar, check what the event could look like.
cards.reference: Bloch, Hemlock Poisoning and the Death of Socrates: Did Plato Tell the Truth?, in Brickhouse & Smith (eds), The Trial and Execution of Socrates, Oxford University Press, 2002

cards.question: According to his ancient biographer, what turned the merchant Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, to philosophy?
cards.answer: A shipwreck. Diogenes Laertius says Zeno lost a cargo of purple dye near Piraeus, walked up to Athens and sat reading Xenophon's memoir of Socrates in a bookshop. He asked where such men could be found; the bookseller pointed to the Cynic Crates, passing by. Zeno later said his voyage prospered when he was wrecked.
cards.move: Judge a disaster only after you have seen which door it opened.
cards.reference: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII.2-5, trans. Hicks, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1925

cards.question: True or false: Stoic teaching held that a true sage would not turn pale in a storm at sea?
cards.answer: False. Aulus Gellius watched a Stoic go white in a storm on a crossing to Brundisium and asked why. The philosopher produced a book of Epictetus: sudden terrors jolt even the wise before reason acts; the sage differs only in refusing to assent to them. The pallor was allowed; believing disaster had come was not.
cards.move: Judge people by what they do after the first jolt, not by the jolt.
cards.trap: Picturing the Stoic ideal as a man who feels nothing at all.
cards.reference: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 19.1, trans. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1927

cards.question: How, according to the historian Cassius Dio, did Seneca help provoke Boudica's revolt in Britain?
cards.answer: By calling in his loans. Dio writes that Seneca had lent the Britons 40 million sesterces they did not want, hoping for good interest, then demanded it all back at once, harshly. Dio disliked Seneca, so the charge may be hostile. The philosopher who called wealth no true good held one of Rome's great fortunes.
cards.move: When a source dislikes its subject, check the charge against a friendlier witness.
cards.reference: Cassius Dio, Roman History 62.2, trans. Cary, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1925

cards.question: True or false: the ancient logic of whole statements joined by if, and, or was worked out by Stoics, not Aristotle?
cards.answer: True. Aristotle's syllogisms link terms, such as men and mortal. Chrysippus and the Stoics built a logic of whole propositions on five basic forms, one being: if the first, then the second; the first; therefore the second. Long dismissed as trivial, it was recognised in the 1930s as an ancestor of modern propositional logic.
cards.move: The famous name in a field is rarely the only one who built it.
cards.trap: Crediting all ancient logic to Aristotle, the name everyone knows.
cards.reference: Mates, Stoic Logic, University of California Press, 1953

cards.question: In which language did the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius write the private notebook now called the Meditations?
cards.answer: Greek. Educated Romans did philosophy in the language of Zeno and Chrysippus, and Marcus wrote his notes to himself in it, some on campaign along the Danube. The title Meditations is a later label; the manuscripts call the work To Himself. The ruler of the Latin-speaking empire addressed himself in Greek.
cards.move: Ask what language a field thought in, not only where its thinkers lived.
cards.trap: A Roman emperor, so Latin, the language of Roman law and army.
cards.reference: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, trans. Hard, ed. Gill, Oxford World's Classics, Oxford University Press, 2011

cards.question: What small condition did Stoics attach to every plan, so that failure could not wound them?
cards.answer: If nothing prevents it. Seneca says the wise man undertakes everything with a reservation: I will sail, unless something stops me; I will become praetor, unless something stands in the way. What he staked was the effort, never the result. A storm that cancels the voyage cancels nothing the Stoic had promised himself.
cards.move: Promise the effort in full and the outcome only on conditions.
cards.reference: Seneca, On Benefits 4.34, trans. Griffin & Inwood, University of Chicago Press, 2011; On Tranquillity of Mind 13, in Dialogues and Essays, trans. Davie, Oxford University Press, 2007

cards.question: What did the early Stoics say would happen to the whole world, again and again?
cards.answer: It would burn up and be remade exactly as before. In the conflagration everything turns to fire; the same order then rebuilds the same cosmos, people included. Later reports say Socrates would again face the same accusers and drink the same poison. Stoics debated whether that Socrates is the same man or an exact twin.
cards.move: Ask whether a perfect copy is the same thing or only its twin.
cards.reference: Long & Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers, vol. 1, section 52, Cambridge University Press, 1987

cards.question: What rank did the Stoics give to health among the things worth having?
options: Preferred, but not good at all
cards.answer: Preferred, but not good at all. For Zeno and Chrysippus only virtue is good; health, wealth and reputation are preferred indifferents, naturally worth choosing but irrelevant to happiness. Aristotle's heirs called them lesser goods; the Cynics scorned them. One word apart, and it decides whether a sage on a sickbed can be perfectly happy.
cards.move: Worth choosing and worth being unhappy without are different measures.
cards.trap: Ranking health as a smaller good, the common-sense Aristotelian view.
cards.reference: Cicero, On Moral Ends, trans. Woolf, ed. Annas, Cambridge University Press, 2001

cards.question: Diogenes Laertius credits Chrysippus with 705 books. How many of them survive complete today?
cards.answer: None of them. Chrysippus built early Stoicism, but his books are known only from quotations, many by hostile critics such as Plutarch and Galen, plus charred scraps of Herculaneum papyri. The Stoicism most readers meet comes from Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius, centuries later. The founding library is a heap of fragments.
cards.move: The voice that survives is not always the voice that founded it.
cards.trap: Assuming a founder's main works survive, as Plato's and Aristotle's did.
cards.reference: Gould, The Philosophy of Chrysippus, State University of New York Press, 1970

cards.question: Does the Stoic focus on what one can control breed passivity towards injustice?
cards.answer: Teach people that only their own judgements matter, and injustice becomes weather. Seneca urged kindness to slaves in his forty-seventh letter but never called for abolition. Epictetus, himself once a slave, taught that chains touch only the body. A creed that makes suffering bearable also makes it easier to leave in place.
cards.move: It turns on whether accepting the unchangeable shrinks or steadies the fight for the rest.
cards.counterpoint: Under Nero and Vespasian the boldest senators were Stoics. Thrasea Paetus walked out rather than applaud Nero's murder of his mother, and was later forced to kill himself; Helvidius Priscus defied Vespasian and was executed. Believing death no evil made them hard to frighten. Indifference to outcomes let them act without hope of winning.
cards.reference: Tacitus, The Annals, trans. Woodman, Hackett, 2004

cards.question: Which debate was the runaway tram dilemma invented for, before anyone called it a trolley problem?
cards.answer: Abortion. Philippa Foot's 1967 paper tested the doctrine of double effect, a Catholic moral rule separating harm intended from harm merely foreseen, long applied to abortion. Her tram had a driver, not a bystander. Judith Jarvis Thomson named it the trolley problem in 1976, and the bystander at the switch arrived only in 1985.
cards.move: Ask what a famous example was built to test before arguing with it.
cards.reference: Foot, The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect, Oxford Review 5, 1967; Thomson, Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem, The Monist 59, 1976; Thomson, The Trolley Problem, Yale Law Journal 94, 1985

cards.question: Judith Jarvis Thomson, who named the trolley problem, finally concluded what about the bystander at the switch?
options: He may turn it, but need not
cards.answer: He may not turn it. In 2008 Thomson reversed her verdict. Suppose he could also send the trolley onto himself: if he would not pay that price to save the five, he cannot make the lone worker pay it. So the old puzzle, why he may turn it when a surgeon may not kill, vanished.
cards.move: Before making a stranger pay a price, ask whether you would pay it.
cards.trap: Assuming the case's champion kept the verdict almost everyone gives.
cards.reference: Thomson, Turning the Trolley, Philosophy & Public Affairs 36 (4), 2008

cards.question: True or false: professional philosophers' trolley verdicts shift less than non-philosophers' when the cases come in a different order?
cards.answer: False. Eric Schwitzgebel and Fiery Cushman gave philosophers and other academics the footbridge and switch cases in varying orders. Which came first moved philosophers' verdicts no less than the others', including those claiming expertise on the very question. A forced pause to consider other versions of the case did not shrink the effect.
cards.move: Knowing a bias by name does not switch it off.
cards.trap: Trusting training to shield a verdict from the case seen just before.
cards.reference: Schwitzgebel & Cushman, Philosophers' biased judgments persist despite training, expertise and reflection, Cognition 141, 2015

cards.question: When shipwrecked sailors killed one of their crew so three could live, what did an English court rule?
cards.answer: Murder: necessity is no defence. In 1884 Dudley and Stephens killed Richard Parker, the 17-year-old cabin boy, to feed themselves and a third man. Lord Coleridge asked who is to judge such necessity, and by what measure lives are compared — here the weakest had been chosen. The death sentences were commuted to six months.
cards.move: Never let the person who profits from an exception decide it applies.
cards.reference: R v Dudley and Stephens (1884) 14 QBD 273; Simpson, Cannibalism and the Common Law, University of Chicago Press, 1984

cards.question: Should a state be allowed to shoot down a hijacked airliner to stop it being flown into a crowd?
cards.answer: Passengers on an airliner aimed at a packed stadium die either way; shooting it down changes only how many die with them. A government that could stop the attack and refuses is choosing thousands of deaths to keep its own hands clean, and the people in the stands have a right to life too.
cards.move: Both sides turn on whether a life that is ending anyway still counts in full.
cards.counterpoint: Germany's constitutional court struck down exactly such a law in 2006: killing innocent passengers treats them as mere objects in a rescue of others, and a life with minutes left is still protected. And the crash is never certain in time — on United 93 in 2001, passengers fought the hijackers and the plane came down in an empty field.
cards.reference: Bundesverfassungsgericht, Judgment of the First Senate of 15 February 2006, 1 BvR 357/05, BVerfGE 115, 118

cards.question: What did Thomson's looping track do to the idea that the switch is allowed because nobody is used?
cards.answer: It took the idea's support away. In Thomson's 1985 loop, the side track curves back to the five, and only the lone worker's bulk will stop the trolley. His death is now the means of rescue, yet turning seems no less permissible. One short piece of rail changed the reason, not the verdict.
cards.move: Change one detail of a case and see whether the verdict follows the rule.
cards.reference: Thomson, The Trolley Problem, Yale Law Journal 94 (6), 1985, pp. 1395-1415

cards.question: About a third of people approve pushing the man off the footbridge by hand. What share approve shoving him with a long pole?
options: About a third, much the same
About two thirds, like a switch
cards.answer: About a third, much the same. In Greene and colleagues' 2009 study, the pole won no more approval than bare hands. What moved verdicts was muscle: dropping him through a trapdoor by a switch raised approval to about 60%. Touch and personal force had always come together; the pole pulled them apart.
cards.move: When two causes always travel together, find a case that separates them.
cards.trap: Crediting bodily contact, which always came packaged with muscular force.
cards.reference: Greene, Cushman, Stewart, Lowenberg, Nystrom & Cohen, Pushing moral buttons: The interaction between personal force and intention in moral judgment, Cognition 111 (3), 2009, pp. 364-371

cards.question: True or false: people facing real shocks to live mice diverted the shock onto one more often than people judging on paper?
cards.answer: True. In a 2018 Ghent study, 84% of people who believed the shocks were real pressed the button to spare five mice by shocking one; only 66% of those given the same dilemma on paper said they would. The shocks were secretly harmless. The hand on the button was bolder than the pen.
cards.move: What people say they would do is a separate measurement from what they do.
cards.trap: Expecting real stakes to make people shrink from causing harm.

cards.question: True or false: the people readiest to push one man to save five also show more concern for distant strangers?
cards.answer: False. Kahane and colleagues found in 2015 that approving the sacrifice went with higher scores on psychopathy and no greater readiness to give to people far away or to weigh everyone's welfare equally. Critics dispute how far this generalises. A shrug at harm and a love of the greater number can produce the same answer.
cards.move: Two people can give the same answer for opposite reasons; ask for the reason.
cards.trap: Reading willingness to sacrifice one as care for the many.
cards.reference: Kahane, Everett, Earp, Farias & Savulescu, 'Utilitarian' judgments in sacrificial moral dilemmas do not reflect impartial concern for the greater good, Cognition 134, 2015, pp. 193-209

cards.question: In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, 63% of philosophers would pull the switch. What share would push the man off the footbridge?
cards.answer: About a fifth. Bourget and Chalmers's survey of some 1,800 philosophers found roughly half against pushing and the rest undecided or elsewhere, while only 13% refused to switch. The people who argue about these cases for a living mostly hold the same split verdict the puzzle was invented to explain.
cards.move: A figure given in the question is not evidence about the answer.
cards.trap: Guessing near the 63% who switch, the figure just given.
cards.reference: Bourget & Chalmers, Philosophers on Philosophy: The 2020 PhilPapers Survey, Philosophers' Imprint 23, 2023

cards.question: Ten measures of food are too much for an athlete and two too little. What does Aristotle's trainer order?
options: Six, the midpoint of the two
An amount fitted to that athlete
The ration an average athlete needs
cards.answer: An amount fitted to that athlete. Aristotle's mean is relative to the person, not the midpoint of two numbers, and it holds for courage or generosity as much as for food. His own example: six measures would be too little for Milo, the legendary wrestler, and too much for a beginner.
cards.move: Before splitting the difference, ask whose difference it is.
cards.trap: Taking the two numbers given and splitting the difference.
cards.reference: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. Ross, rev. Brown, Oxford University Press, 2009, 1106a36-b7

cards.question: True or false: the saying 'We are what we repeatedly do' comes from Aristotle's own writings?
cards.answer: False. The sentence is Will Durant's, from The Story of Philosophy (1926), summing up Aristotle in modern words and then quoted as his ever since. Aristotle's point was that habit shapes only what nature leaves open: a stone thrown upwards ten thousand times never learns to rise.
cards.move: A thousand copies of one mistake are still one source.
cards.trap: Trusting a line because it is attributed to him everywhere.
cards.reference: Durant, The Story of Philosophy, Simon & Schuster, 1926, chapter 2; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, trans. D. P. Chase, Everyman's Library, 1911

cards.question: How, according to Aristotle, does the great-souled man walk and speak?
cards.answer: Slowly, in a deep voice, with level speech: someone earnest about few things is in no hurry. Greatness of soul meant claiming great honour and deserving it. Its owner is ashamed to receive kindnesses and repays them with interest, and remembers the favours he has done, not those done for him.
cards.move: Every list of virtues is also a portrait of the people who wrote it.
cards.reference: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. D. P. Chase, Everyman's Library, 1911, IV.3, 1124b-1125a

cards.question: For Aristotle, who is more virtuous: the person who resists a craving, or the one who never feels it?
cards.answer: The one who does not feel it. Aristotle's test of virtue is pleasure or pain: whoever abstains gladly is temperate, whoever abstains and minds it is not. Resisting a bad desire is self-control, which he called not a virtue but a mixed state. The virtuous person does not want the third drink.
cards.move: Judge character by what someone wants, not only by what they resist.
cards.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, II.3, IV.9, VII.9
cards.reference: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. Crisp, Cambridge University Press, 2000, 1104b3-8, 1128b33-35 and 1151b34-1152a3

cards.question: What did the 1958 paper that revived virtue ethics tell philosophers to stop doing?
cards.answer: Moral philosophy. Elizabeth Anscombe's Modern Moral Philosophy argued that the moral ought was a leftover from belief in a divine lawgiver, and that ethics should wait for an adequate account of intention, action and wanting. The same paper coined the word consequentialism, as a label for the views she was attacking.
cards.move: When the basic words are confused, stop arguing and fix the words.
cards.reference: Anscombe, Modern Moral Philosophy, Philosophy 33 (124), 1958, pp. 1-19

cards.question: Why do some virtue ethicists shrug at experiments meant to prove character traits do not exist?
cards.answer: Because their theory expected the results. Gilbert Harman argued in 1999 that studies like the hurried seminarians who walked past a slumped man show there are no robust traits of character. Defenders reply that Aristotle thought full virtue rare and slow to grow. A test most people fail shows most people lack it.
cards.move: Before calling a result a refutation, check what the theory predicted.
cards.source: Harman, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, 1999
cards.reference: Harman, Moral Philosophy Meets Social Psychology: Virtue Ethics and the Fundamental Attribution Error, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 99, 1999, pp. 315-331

cards.question: True or false: Aristotle held that a person could be fully brave while lacking the other virtues?
cards.answer: False. He allowed natural boldness without wisdom, but held that virtue in the full sense needs practical wisdom, and practical wisdom, once present, brings every virtue with it. Natural courage without it, he says, is like a strong body moving without sight: all the heavier its stumbles.
cards.move: Before counting qualities one by one, ask whether they share a root.
cards.trap: Treating the virtues as separate skills, learnt one at a time.
cards.reference: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. Irwin, 2nd edition, Hackett, 1999, 1144b1-1145a2

cards.question: True or false: David Hume placed humility in the catalogue of vices rather than virtues?
cards.answer: True. In his 1751 Enquiry, Hume rejected celibacy, fasting, penance, self-denial, humility, silence and solitude, the monkish virtues, because they serve nobody's use or pleasure. Men of sense, he wrote, count them as vices. The gloomy enthusiast, he added, may get a place in the calendar after death, but scarcely in company while alive.
cards.move: Ask of any praised trait whom it has ever helped.
cards.trap: Assuming a Christian virtue kept its place in every moral catalogue.
cards.source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
cards.reference: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals 9.1, ed. Beauchamp, Clarendon Press, 1998

cards.question: A habitual liar asks what he should do. Why does 'whatever a virtuous person would do' fail him?
options: Virtuous people would never need his remedies
Virtue cannot be defined without rules
cards.answer: Virtuous people would never need his remedies. Robert Johnson argued in 2003 that the liar ought to watch himself and practise honesty in small things, which a virtuous person, having nothing to cure, would never do. Right action for someone depends on who they are now: a crutch is right only for a broken leg.
cards.move: Advice for the finished version of you may be wrong for you now.
cards.trap: Reaching for the standard worry that good people disagree.
cards.reference: Johnson, Virtue and Right, Ethics 113 (4), 2003, pp. 810-834

cards.question: Is a bank robber who stays calm under fire to finish the job showing real courage?
cards.answer: Courage is mastery of fear in the face of danger, and the robber has exactly that: the same steadiness would earn a medal in a fireman. Philippa Foot granted in 1978 that a murderer can be courageous; the courage is simply not working as a virtue in him. Denying the word blurs a real trait.
cards.move: It turns on whether a virtue can be named apart from the end it serves.
cards.counterpoint: Aristotle says the brave face danger for the sake of what is noble, and Plato's Laches ties courage to knowing what is worth fearing. Risking death to take money is misjudging what matters, so it is recklessness, not courage. Calling it brave hands a thief the praise owed to someone who stays in a burning house.
cards.reference: Foot, Virtues and Vices, in Virtues and Vices and Other Essays in Moral Philosophy, Blackwell, 1978

cards.question: What were Zeno of Elea's paradoxes of motion originally meant to defend?
cards.answer: His teacher Parmenides, who held that change and plurality are illusions. In Plato's Parmenides, Zeno says his book repays Parmenides' mockers with interest: assume many things and motion, and worse absurdities follow. Proclus credits him with 40 such arguments. Only a handful survive, mostly in summaries by Aristotle, who set out to refute them.
cards.move: Before judging an argument, ask what position it was built to protect.
cards.reference: Plato, Parmenides 127d-128e, trans. Gill & Ryan, in Plato: Complete Works, ed. Cooper, Hackett, 1997

cards.question: Halve a 100-metre gap again and again. After how many halvings is what remains smaller than an atom, about 0.1 nanometres?
cards.answer: 39 halvings leave about 0.18 nm, so the answer is 40.
cards.move: Repeated halving reaches the tiny in far fewer steps than it feels.
cards.trap: Expecting an endless-feeling process to need millions of steps.
cards.hint: Count how many factors of a thousand separate metres from tenths of a nanometre.
steps: 100 m divided by 0.1 nm is 10 to the power 12.
Ten halvings divide by 1,024, roughly a thousand.
Four sets of ten, 40 halvings, divide by just over 10 to the power 12.
39 halvings leave about 0.18 nm, so the answer is 40.
cards.reference: Salmon (ed.), Zeno's Paradoxes, Bobbs-Merrill, 1970

cards.question: How did Aristotle answer Zeno's claim that nobody can cross infinitely many half-distances in a finite time?
cards.answer: First by dividing the time too: if the track splits endlessly, so do the seconds, so endless shrinking stretches fit into a finite run. Later he called that reply fine for the questioner but not for the truth: the halfway points are only potential. A runner who never stops at them never makes them real.
cards.move: When a problem seems impossible, check you divided both sides, not just one.
cards.reference: Aristotle, Physics VI.2 and VIII.8, trans. Waterfield, Oxford World's Classics, Oxford University Press, 1996

cards.question: True or false: checking often enough on an atom that is poised to change state can stop it from changing?
cards.answer: True. It is the quantum Zeno effect, predicted by Misra and Sudarshan in 1977. In 1990 Wayne Itano's team pushed beryllium ions from one energy level towards another while probing them with laser pulses: the more often they looked, the fewer ions made the jump. A watched pot, at this scale, does not boil.
cards.move: Check whether the act of checking is part of what you are measuring.
cards.trap: Assuming a measurement only records a change and cannot prevent it.
cards.source: Itano et al., Physical Review A, 1990
cards.reference: Itano, Heinzen, Bollinger & Wineland, Quantum Zeno effect, Physical Review A 41, 1990

cards.question: Achilles runs ten times as fast as a tortoise that starts 100 metres ahead. How far does Achilles run before drawing level?
cards.answer: About 111 metres. Zeno's stages are 100 metres, then 10, then 1, then 0.1, and so on; they add up to 111.1 recurring, or 1,000/9. Quicker: Achilles gains 9 metres on every 10 he runs, so the 100-metre gap closes after 1,000/9 metres. By then the tortoise has crawled just over 11 metres.
cards.move: Endless stages can sum to a finite total; add them before despairing.
cards.trap: Infinitely many stages feel as if they must take forever.
cards.source: Russell, Our Knowledge of the External World
cards.reference: Russell, Our Knowledge of the External World, lecture 6, Open Court, 1914

cards.question: What did Bertrand Russell say a flying arrow is doing at any single instant?
cards.answer: Nothing but being where it is. Russell granted Zeno that at each instant the arrow is at rest in one place, and denied that motion needs more: to move is to be at different places at different times. No state of moving hides inside an instant. Flight is a list of positions and times.
cards.move: Ask whether a change needs anything beyond different states at different times.
cards.reference: Russell, The Principles of Mathematics, chapter 54, Cambridge University Press, 1903

cards.question: True or false: if time came in indivisible instants, two blocks moving in opposite directions could pass without ever being side by side?
cards.answer: True. This is Zeno's moving rows. Let each row shift one place per smallest instant, in opposite directions. Their relative shift is two places per instant, so a block goes from just before its opposite number to just past it, with no instant between. Atoms of time leave the passing nowhere to happen.
cards.move: A model built from smallest steps can skip what seemed unskippable.
cards.trap: Assuming that passing always has a moment when the two line up.
cards.source: Huggett, Space from Zeno to Einstein, 1999
cards.reference: Huggett (ed.), Space from Zeno to Einstein: Classic Readings with a Contemporary Commentary, MIT Press, 1999

cards.question: A lamp, off at first, is flicked after 1 minute, then half a minute, a quarter, and so on. On or off at two minutes?
options: On, since the final flick turns it on
Nothing in the story settles it
cards.answer: Nothing in the story settles it. James Thomson's 1954 lamp has no last switch to fix its state. Paul Benacerraf replied in 1962 that the description covers only the times before two minutes; the lamp could be on or off at two without contradiction. An endless list of instructions need not say how things end.
cards.move: A sequence with no last step says nothing about what comes after.
cards.trap: Picturing a last switch, though the sequence of switches has none.
cards.reference: Thomson, Tasks and Super-Tasks, Analysis 15, 1954; Benacerraf, Tasks, Super-Tasks, and the Modern Eleatics, Journal of Philosophy 59, 1962

cards.question: A ball falls for 1 s. Its bounces last 1.6 s, then 0.8 times as long each time. Total time before it stops, in seconds?
cards.answer: 1 + 8 = 9 seconds, after infinitely many bounces.
cards.move: Count the steps and the time separately; endless steps can fit in seconds.
cards.trap: Assuming infinitely many bounces must take an infinite time.
cards.hint: Add the endless bounces as one shrinking series, then add the fall.
steps: Bounce times: 1.6 + 1.28 + 1.024 + ... without end.
A shrinking series sums to first term / (1 - ratio).
1.6 / (1 - 0.8) = 8 seconds of bouncing.
1 + 8 = 9 seconds, after infinitely many bounces.
cards.source: Lee & Seshia, Introduction to Embedded Systems
cards.reference: Lee & Seshia, Introduction to Embedded Systems: A Cyber-Physical Systems Approach, 2nd ed., MIT Press, 2017

cards.question: A 1 cm line is made of points, each of length zero. How can the zeros add up to 1 cm?
options: Each point has a tiny non-zero length
The line's true length is zero
Length adds only over countable collections
cards.answer: Length adds only over countable collections. Measure theory adds lengths over sets that can be listed one by one; a line's points cannot. Adolf Grünbaum used this in 1967 against Zeno's claim that a line of sizeless parts has no size. All the fractions between 0 and 1, taken together, have length zero.
cards.move: When parts cannot add to the whole, question the adding, not the parts.
cards.trap: Rescuing the sum by giving each point a sliver of length.
cards.source: Grünbaum, Modern Science and Zeno's Paradoxes, 1967
cards.reference: Grünbaum, Modern Science and Zeno's Paradoxes, Wesleyan University Press, 1967

cards.question: Should peer review be signed rather than anonymous?
cards.answer: Anonymity protects the reviewer who kills a rival's paper, sits on it for eight months, or demands their own work be cited. A name attached to a judgement makes the judgement more careful, and readers can finally see who vouched for what.
cards.move: Whichever you picked, the question is who carries the cost of an honest opinion.
cards.counterpoint: The junior reviewer who signs a hard review of a powerful lab is the one who pays for it, at their next grant or job application. Remove anonymity and criticism does not become fairer, it becomes quieter — and the people it goes quiet for are exactly those with the most power already.
cards.reference: Ross-Hellauer, What is open peer review? A systematic review, F1000Research, 2017

cards.question: What is the most reused six seconds in music?
cards.answer: A drum break from The Winstons' 1969 B-side "Amen, Brother". Sampled into hip-hop, then sped up into jungle and drum and bass, it underpins thousands of records across decades. The drummer, Gregory Coleman, received nothing for it and died without a home.
cards.move: Six seconds of drums from 1969 built two entire genres.
cards.reference: The Winstons, Color Him Father / Amen, Brother, Metromedia Records, 1969

cards.question: Why did records get louder for thirty years?
cards.answer: Because louder sounds better in a first comparison, so each release pushed the level up — flattening the quiet parts until the dynamics were gone. Streaming ended the incentive by normalising loudness on playback, so a squashed master now just sounds squashed.
cards.move: The loudness war ended when the platforms turned everything down equally.
cards.reference: Vickers, The Loudness War: Background, Speculation and Recommendations, Audio Engineering Society Convention Paper 8175, 2010

cards.question: Whose laughter is on old sitcoms?
cards.answer: Often people who died decades before the show aired. Most canned laughter came from a single machine, the Laff Box, built and jealously guarded by one engineer who recorded audiences in the 1950s. The same chuckles recur across hundreds of programmes.
cards.move: That laugh track is a recording of an audience from the 1950s.
cards.source: Charles Douglass and the Laff Box

cards.question: How were television ratings actually measured?
cards.answer: By a few thousand households standing in for a nation. Nielsen fitted meters to a small sample and extrapolated; shows lived or died on the result. Whole genres disappeared because the sample did not happen to contain many of the people who watched them.
cards.move: A few thousand homes decided what a hundred million people could watch.

cards.question: Who first described the celebrity as someone famous simply for being famous, and in what decade?
cards.answer: The historian Daniel Boorstin, in 1961. In The Image he called the celebrity "a person who is known for his well-knownness", a human version of the pseudo-event: something staged in order to be reported. He was writing about press agents and early television, decades before reality shows or influencers.
cards.move: Much of what gets reported happened only so that it would be reported.
cards.reference: Daniel J. Boorstin, The Image: A Guide to Pseudo-Events in America, Atheneum, 1961

cards.question: Which performers were sociologists studying when they coined the term for a one-sided bond with a famous stranger?
cards.answer: Television hosts, in 1956. Donald Horton and Richard Wohl named para-social interaction after watching announcers and quizmasters look into the lens and chat as if to one friend. They saw it as a performance style the medium built on purpose, not as a disorder of lonely viewers.
cards.move: When a stranger feels like a friend, look for who built the feeling.
cards.reference: Horton and Wohl, Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance, Psychiatry, 1956

cards.question: True or false: the rule Kim Kardashian broke with a paid crypto post in 2021 dates from 1933?
cards.answer: True. It was Section 17(b) of the Securities Act of 1933, aimed at paid touting of shares in newspapers and newsletters. She was paid $250,000 to post about EthereumMax tokens without saying so, and in 2022 settled with the SEC for $1.26 million. An Instagram story answered to a Depression-era law.
cards.move: Before asking for a new law, check whether an old one already fits.
cards.trap: New media seem to need new laws, so the rule must be recent.
cards.reference: https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2022-183

cards.question: A 2001 study found Oscar-winning actors outlived other nominees by almost four years. What did a 2006 reanalysis find?
options: Mostly an artefact of the counting
Mostly explained by wealth and status
cards.answer: Mostly an artefact of the counting. The first study credited winners with the years they lived before winning, and nobody wins an Oscar after dying. Counting each actor as a winner only from the night of the win shrank the advantage to about 1 year, too small to tell from chance.
cards.move: Ask what someone had to survive before they could be counted.
cards.trap: Crediting fame's perks, and missing that winners had to live to win.

cards.question: Why did one of America's best-known film actresses of 1909 appear on no poster by name?
cards.answer: Her studio did not name its players. Florence Lawrence was billed as the Biograph Girl until Carl Laemmle's IMP company hired her; in March 1910 it advertised, under the headline We Nail a Lie, that rumours of her death were false. Whether Laemmle began the rumour is disputed. The denial made her a name.
cards.move: A denial can spread a story further than the story ever went.
cards.reference: Richard deCordova, Picture Personalities: The Emergence of the Star System in America, University of Illinois Press, 1990

cards.question: How did a 1944 lawsuit by a film actress end the studios' power to keep stars under contract indefinitely?
cards.answer: By counting calendar years. Warner Bros. added every suspension, imposed when Olivia de Havilland refused a part, to the end of her seven-year contract. A California appeals court ruled that seven years meant seven calendar years. Record labels won a partial carve-out in 1987 and can still sue artists for undelivered albums.
cards.move: Read a contract's clock: who can stop it, and who can restart it.
cards.source: De Havilland v. Warner Bros. Pictures, 1944
cards.reference: De Havilland v. Warner Bros. Pictures, 67 Cal. App. 2d 225, California Court of Appeal, 1944

cards.question: Star A is known by 90% of people, star B by 20%. Each is named a favourite by 10%. Whose Q Score is higher?
cards.answer: Star B. The US research firm Marketing Evaluations computes a Q Score as the share naming someone a favourite divided by the share who know them. Star A scores 10 / 90, about 11; star B scores 10 / 20, or 50. It measures how well recognition turns into affection, not how famous someone is.
cards.move: Ask what a rate is divided by before comparing two of them.
cards.trap: Counting only the fans and ignoring who had heard of each.
cards.source: Kidscreen, on how Q Scores work, 1996

cards.question: Why did a US appeals court rule in 2012 that Marilyn Monroe's heirs could not control commercial use of her image?
options: Copyright in her photographs had expired
California gives the dead no such right
Her estate had called her a New Yorker
cards.answer: Her estate had called her a New Yorker. After her death in 1962 its executors told tax authorities she lived in New York, which gave no rights over a dead person's image. Decades later the heirs claimed California domicile to use its law. The court held them to their earlier word.
cards.move: What you claimed once to save money can bind you later.
cards.trap: Mixing up a photographer's copyright with control over the face pictured.
cards.source: Ninth Circuit, Milton H. Greene Archives, 2012
cards.reference: Milton H. Greene Archives, Inc. v. Marilyn Monroe LLC, 692 F.3d 983, 9th Circuit, 2012

cards.question: When Tiger Woods's scandal broke in 2009, roughly how much shareholder value did his sponsors lose, by one estimate?
cards.answer: About $5 to 12 billion. The economists Christopher Knittel and Victor Stango compared the share prices of his listed sponsors, among them Nike, PepsiCo, Electronic Arts and Accenture, with similar companies in the weeks after his car crash. The fall dwarfed his endorsement income of roughly $100 million a year.
cards.move: The cost of a scandal lands on everyone tied to the name.
cards.trap: Anchoring on his endorsement fees, which ran to tens of millions.
cards.reference: Knittel and Stango, Celebrity Endorsements, Firm Value, and Reputation Risk: Evidence from the Tiger Woods Scandal, Management Science, 2014

cards.question: Should a famous person's face and voice become free for anyone to use soon after they die?
cards.answer: Yes. Fame is built from public attention, films, broadcasts and news, and should return to the public like an expired copyright. Long monopolies let heirs veto biographies, satire and art they dislike. New York recognised no such right over the dead until 2021, and its culture of biography and parody thrived regardless.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a likeness is property or identity.
cards.counterpoint: No. A likeness is not an idea but a person's identity, and software can now make a dead star say or sell anything. California protects it for 70 years after death, so heirs can refuse a digital replica in an advert the star would have turned down. Without that, the most famous faces become the cheapest actors.
cards.source: California and New York publicity statutes
cards.reference: California Civil Code section 3344.1, as amended 1999; New York Civil Rights Law section 50-f, enacted 2020, in force 2021

cards.question: Which product won the first US appeals ruling that a single colour could be registered as a trademark?
cards.answer: Owens Corning's pink insulation. In 1985 the Federal Circuit held that pink, dyed into its glass-fibre insulation since 1956, did no technical job and had come to identify the maker, so it could be registered. The product sits hidden in lofts; buyers learned the colour from advertising, fronted by the Pink Panther.
cards.move: The most famous example is rarely the first one.
cards.trap: Tiffany's boxes: the best-known brand colour must have come first.
cards.reference: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/774/1116/10307/

cards.question: True or false: in 2013 a UK appeal court upheld Cadbury's trademark on its shade of purple?
cards.answer: False. The Court of Appeal struck out the application for Pantone 2685C because it claimed purple either as the whole surface of the wrapper or as its predominant colour. That left rivals unable to tell what was banned: a registration covering many possible signs is not one sign. Cadbury wrappers stayed purple, without the monopoly.
cards.move: A right nobody can locate precisely is a right nobody can respect.
cards.trap: True: a colour this familiar feels as if it must be owned.
cards.reference: https://www.designweek.co.uk/issues/october-2013/cadbury-loses-legal-fight-over-rights-to-pantone-2685c-purple/

cards.question: After a 2012 US appeals ruling, which shoes does Louboutin's red-sole trademark cover?
options: Only shoes sold under Louboutin labels
Any shoe with a red sole
Red soles contrasting with the upper
cards.answer: Red soles contrasting with the upper. The Second Circuit found buyers read the lacquered red sole as Louboutin's only when it stood out from the rest of the shoe, and ordered the registration narrowed. Yves Saint Laurent kept selling its all-red shoes, red soles included.
cards.move: Ask under which conditions a claim holds before assuming it always does.
cards.trap: Any red sole: the trademark sounds absolute once it is granted.
cards.reference: Christian Louboutin S.A. v. Yves Saint Laurent America Holding, Inc., 696 F.3d 206 (2d Cir. 2012)

cards.question: Why can't a printer find Tiffany's blue in a Pantone swatch book?
cards.answer: Because it was mixed for Tiffany alone. In 2001 Pantone standardised the shade as a private custom colour, numbered 1837 after the firm's founding year, and left it out of the public books. The colour is far older than the number: it had covered Tiffany's Blue Book catalogue since the nineteenth century.
cards.move: A standard can be built to keep others out, not only let them in.
cards.reference: https://press.tiffany.com/our-story/tiffany-blue/

cards.question: Why did UPS choose brown for its vans and uniforms in 1916?
cards.answer: For class and for dirt. Charlie Soderstrom, an early partner, picked the brown of Pullman railway carriages, then a byword for first-class travel, and it hid road grime on vans and uniforms. The shade stayed for over 80 years before UPS registered it as a trademark in 1998.
cards.move: A choice made for maintenance can end up carrying the whole identity.
cards.reference: https://thehill.com/homenews/nexstar_media_wire/3591855-brown-wasnt-always-upss-color-heres-why-it-is-now/

cards.question: Why won't EU trademark law accept a painted colour swatch alone to define a colour mark?
cards.answer: Because the swatch fades. In Libertel, a 2003 case over a Dutch telecom firm's orange, the EU's top court held that a paper sample may deteriorate with time, so it cannot fix the sign for good; a recognised code such as a Pantone number can. The mark can be renewed forever; the paper cannot.
cards.move: A record that changes with age cannot settle a dispute years later.
cards.reference: https://ipcuria.eu/details.php?t=1&reference=C-104%2F01

cards.question: Why are Hermès boxes orange rather than the cream they used to be?
cards.answer: Because of a wartime shortage, by the house's own account. In occupied Paris, Hermès's supplier ran out of the cream card it used, and orange paperboard was all that remained. The firm took it rather than go without boxes, and kept it after the war. A colour nobody had picked became the house's own.
cards.move: Many signatures began as whatever happened to be left in stock.
cards.source: The Fashion Law, on Hermès orange
cards.reference: https://www.thefashionlaw.com/a-shortage-of-product-packaging-during-wwii-led-hermes-to-adopt-a-new-hue-the-result-was-the-birth-of-a-color-mark/

cards.question: True or false: John Deere once lost a court case trying to stop a rival selling farm loaders in its green?
cards.answer: True. In Deere v. Farmhand, decided in Iowa in 1982 and upheld on appeal, a court found farmers wanted loaders that matched their tractors, so the green did a job beyond naming the maker. Deere has won other colour cases since. On a farm, matching paint counted as a feature, not a signature.
cards.move: If buyers want a feature for its own sake, nobody may own it.
cards.trap: A famous brand colour seems protected against everyone, everywhere.
cards.reference: https://www.leagle.com/decision/1982645560fsupp851621

cards.question: In 2014 a US court sided with T-Mobile's magenta against AT&T's Aio Wireless. What was Aio barred from using?
options: Any shade of pink or purple
Large blocks of one plum shade
cards.answer: Large blocks of one plum shade. A Texas federal judge found Aio's Pantone 676C, spread across shop walls and adverts, confusingly close to T-Mobile's magenta, and enjoined large swaths of it or similar shades. A colour mark reaches past its exact number, but only as far as confusion does.
cards.move: A right drawn around one number usually reaches its neighbours too.
cards.trap: Treating the registered Pantone number as the mark's exact boundary.
cards.source: T-Mobile US v. Aio Wireless, S.D. Tex., 2014
cards.reference: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/8730752/t-mobile-us-inc-v-aio-wireless-llc/

cards.question: Starbucks' first logo, in 1971, was brown. Where did the green that replaced it come from?
options: A coffee chain Starbucks merged with
cards.answer: A coffee chain Starbucks merged with. Howard Schultz had left Starbucks to found Il Giornale, whose logo was green; in 1987 he bought Starbucks and merged the two. The 1987 logo set the siren inside Il Giornale's green circle. The buyer's colour swallowed the seller's.
cards.move: Before reading meaning into a colour, ask who owned it first.
cards.trap: Green brings to mind eco-branding, so that story comes first.
cards.source: Starbucks, The Evolution of Our Logo
cards.reference: https://about.starbucks.com/history/the-evolution-of-our-logo/

cards.question: Why does Levi Strauss's name sit on the riveted trousers a Reno tailor invented?
cards.answer: Because the tailor needed a backer. Jacob Davis, in Reno, Nevada, was riveting the pocket corners of work trousers so they would not tear, but could not afford the patent fee, so he wrote to his cloth supplier in San Francisco, Levi Strauss. The patent was granted to both men on 20 May 1873.
cards.move: Ask who paid for an invention before asking whose name it carries.
cards.reference: Lynn Downey, Levi Strauss: The Man Who Gave Blue Jeans to the World, University of Massachusetts Press, 2016

cards.question: Why do worn jeans fade towards white instead of a paler, even blue?
cards.answer: Because the dye never reached the middle of the thread. Indigo is built up in repeated dips and clings to the outside of the cotton yarn, leaving a white core, and only the lengthwise warp threads are dyed; the crosswise weft stays undyed. Rubbing at knees and pockets strips the blue skin off each thread.
cards.move: How a thing wears out tells you how it was built.
cards.reference: James Sullivan, Jeans: A Cultural History of an American Icon, Gotham Books, 2006

cards.question: Across the whole life of a pair of jeans, which stage uses the most water?
options: Dyeing and finishing at the mill
cards.answer: Growing the cotton. Levi Strauss & Co.'s 2015 life-cycle study of its 501 jeans put the total at about 3,781 litres per pair, with cotton farming around two-thirds of it and home washing most of the rest. Mills pollute visibly, with blue effluent, but their share of the water drunk is small.
cards.move: The most visible damage is not always the largest.
cards.trap: Dyeing: pictures of blue rivers near denim mills are what sticks.
cards.reference: Levi Strauss & Co., The Life Cycle of a Jean: Understanding the Environmental Impact of a Pair of Levi's 501 Jeans, 2015

cards.question: Why did Turkey ban sandblasting of denim in 2009?
cards.answer: Workers were dying of silicosis. Blasting jeans with sand for a worn look filled small workshops with fine crystalline silica, which scars the lungs; young Turkish workers fell ill within a few years of starting, and some died. Big brands announced their own bans afterwards, and the work drifted to countries with weaker enforcement.
cards.move: When a product looks worn for free, someone paid for the wear.
cards.trap: EU rules: trade pressure seems the usual reason an industry changes method.
cards.source: Akgun et al., European Respiratory Journal, 2008
cards.reference: Akgun et al., An epidemic of silicosis among former denim sandblasters, European Respiratory Journal, 2008

cards.question: True or false: selvedge denim comes off narrower looms than most modern denim does?
cards.answer: True. Selvedge cloth is woven on old shuttle looms, whose shuttle carries one continuous weft thread back and forth, giving a fabric roughly 75 cm wide with self-finished edges. Modern projectile and air-jet looms weave cloth about twice as wide and cut the edges. The coloured line along the outer seam marks the narrower machine.
cards.move: A premium label often marks an older method, not a bigger one.
cards.trap: False: premium cloth sounds as if it needs the larger machine.
cards.reference: Graham Marsh & Paul Trynka, Denim: From Cowboys to Catwalks, Aurum Press, 2002

cards.question: What colour is denim yarn at the moment it comes out of the indigo dye bath?
cards.answer: Yellowish green. Indigo will not dissolve in water, so dyers chemically reduce it to leuco-indigo, a soluble pale yellow-green form that soaks into cotton. Lifted into the air, the yarn oxidises to blue within a minute or two, locking the dye in. Mills send it up over rollers between dips for air.
cards.move: Some finished colours exist only after the air has had its turn.
cards.reference: Jenny Balfour-Paul, Indigo: Egyptian Mummies to Blue Jeans, British Museum Press, 2011

cards.question: What has largely replaced the stones in the stonewashing of jeans?
cards.answer: Enzymes. Cellulases, proteins that break down cellulose, nibble the surface of the cotton in the washing drum and loosen indigo much as pumice did, without stones that battered machines, clogged drains and left grit in pockets. Lasers now draw many of the worn patterns too. The word on the label has outlived the rock.
cards.move: A process can keep its name long after it has dropped its method.
cards.reference: Roshan Paul (ed.), Denim: Manufacture, Finishing and Applications, Woodhead Publishing, 2015

cards.question: True or false: Levi Strauss & Co. called its riveted trousers overalls, not jeans, until about 1960?
cards.answer: True. For almost nine decades it sold them as waist overalls: work trousers held at the waist, without a bib. Jeans was the buyers' word, spread by students and teenagers after the war, and Levi's adopted it in its own marketing around 1960. The world's name for them came from customers.
cards.move: Check who first used a name before crediting whoever owns it now.
cards.trap: Assuming a firm always called its product by today's name.
cards.reference: Emma McClendon, Denim: Fashion's Frontier, Yale University Press, 2016

cards.question: Taking 28 g an ounce and 0.84 square metres a square yard, what is 14-ounce-per-square-yard denim in grams per square metre?
cards.answer: 392 / 0.84 = about 467 g per square metre.
cards.move: Convert every unit in a rate, the bottom as well as the top.
cards.trap: Converting the ounces and stopping at about 392 grams.
cards.hint: Convert the weight first, then spread it over a square metre instead of a square yard.
steps: 14 ounces x 28 g = 392 g per square yard.
A square yard is only 0.84 of a square metre, so divide by 0.84.
392 / 0.84 = about 467 g per square metre.
cards.source: NIST, Guide for the Use of SI Units
cards.reference: Thompson & Taylor, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI), NIST Special Publication 811, 2008

cards.question: Where have many of the oldest surviving Levi's jeans been found?
cards.answer: In abandoned mines. Work trousers were worn until they fell apart, then thrown out; pairs left in dry, dark mine tunnels escaped rot and light. The company's early records burned in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire, and in 2001 it paid $46,532 at auction for an 1880s pair from a Nevada mining town.
cards.move: Ask what conditions let the old examples survive before reading history from them.
cards.trap: A maker seems the obvious keeper of its own past.
cards.reference: Lynn Downey, Levi Strauss & Co., Images of America, Arcadia Publishing, 2007

cards.question: Who was turned away at the door of the very first World Science Fiction Convention in 1939?
cards.answer: Fans who would become the genre's professionals. The New York organisers, feuding with a rival club called the Futurians, barred several of its members, among them Frederik Pohl and Donald Wollheim. Pohl became a leading editor and novelist; Wollheim founded DAW Books. About 200 people attended the convention they were kept out of.
cards.move: Today's gatekeepers often lock out tomorrow's owners of the gate.
cards.reference: Harry Warner Jr., All Our Yesterdays: An Informal History of Science Fiction Fandom in the Forties, Advent Publishers, 1969

cards.question: How did Frank Sinatra's press agent make sure the first screaming crowds turned up in 1942?
cards.answer: He reportedly paid for them. George Evans is said to have hired teenage girls at the Paramount Theatre in New York, at $5 each, to scream and swoon on cue, with an ambulance waiting outside. Other girls in the audience copied them. By 1944 crowds of fans filled Times Square unpaid.
cards.move: A crowd is the best advertisement for a crowd.
cards.reference: James Kaplan, Frank: The Voice, Doubleday, 2010

cards.question: In 2015 organised voting slates filled several Hugo Award shortlists. What did the full electorate do in the final vote?
options: Voted No Award in five categories
Had the awards cancelled that year
cards.answer: Voted No Award in five categories. Nominations came from a small, coordinated bloc who each listed the same few works, while the wider membership nominated scattered favourites. When everyone voted, the slate lost almost everywhere. The rules were then changed so a bloc could no longer fill a whole shortlist.
cards.move: The people who choose the options are rarely the people who choose between them.
cards.trap: A bloc that filled the shortlist looks like the majority of voters.
cards.source: World Science Fiction Society, Hugo statistics, 2015
cards.reference: World Science Fiction Society, 2015 Hugo Award Voting Statistics, Sasquan, Spokane, 2015

cards.question: True or false: the Grateful Dead set aside a section at their concerts for fans to record the show?
cards.answer: True. From 1984 the band set aside a zone behind the mixing desk where fans could raise microphones on stands. The tapes were copied and traded free and spread the band to people who then bought tickets. Touring, not records, paid the Dead.
cards.move: Before blocking a free copy, ask what it would have sold for you.
cards.trap: Bands guard recordings, because every free copy looks like a lost sale.
cards.reference: Dennis McNally, A Long Strange Trip: The Inside History of the Grateful Dead, Broadway Books, 2002

cards.question: How did two fans keep Star Trek on the air for a third season in 1968?
cards.answer: With a mailing list. Bjo and John Trimble wrote to people whose addresses they had from science-fiction conventions, asking each to write to NBC and to recruit others. The network received a flood of letters, counts disputed, and renewed the show, then moved it to a late Friday slot, where it was cancelled.
cards.move: An organised few with addresses beat a scattered many with opinions.
cards.source: Trimble, On the Good Ship Enterprise, 1983
cards.reference: Bjo Trimble, On the Good Ship Enterprise: My 15 Years with Star Trek, Donning, 1983

cards.question: What did members of the Beatles' official fan club receive every December from 1963 to 1969 that no shop sold?
cards.answer: A Christmas record. Each year the band recorded a few minutes of jokes, carols and greetings for members only, pressed on a thin, bendable flexi-disc and posted out. The last ones were assembled from pieces each Beatle recorded separately, as the four drifted apart. The club was a mailing list with its own private release.
cards.move: A thing nobody else can buy turns customers into members.
cards.reference: Mark Lewisohn, The Complete Beatles Chronicle, Pyramid Books, 1992

cards.question: Teenagers and K-pop fans claimed to have booked vast numbers of free tickets to a 2020 Trump rally in Tulsa. Did that keep supporters out?
options: Yes: fans held most of the seats
No: sign-ups did not reserve seats
Partly: fans took about half the seats
cards.answer: No. Entry was first come, first served, and registering reserved no seat, so a fake sign-up could not block a real supporter. What the pranks inflated was the campaign's forecast: it boasted of over a million requests, yet the fire department counted about 6,200 people inside a 19,000-seat arena. The empty seats had other causes.
cards.move: Before crediting a cause, check it could have produced the effect.
cards.trap: Crediting the prank because it came just before the empty seats.

diagram.caption: The campaign boasted over a million requests; about 6,200 people came, to 19,000 seats.

cards.reference: Taylor Lorenz, Kellen Browning and Sheera Frenkel, TikTok Teens and K-Pop Stans Say They Sank Trump Rally, The New York Times, 21 June 2020

cards.question: What drove the Japanese idol group AKB48's repeated million-selling first weeks for singles in the 2010s?
options: Ballots and handshake tickets inside the CDs
A national habit of buying physical CDs
Heavy buying by fans across Asia
cards.answer: Ballots and handshake tickets inside the CDs. Each copy of the single before the group's annual election held one vote on which members would front the next record, and other editions held tickets to shake a member's hand. Devoted fans bought dozens of copies, some hundreds. A million copies did not mean a million buyers.
cards.move: Count the people behind a number, not just the units.
cards.trap: Crediting Japan's CD habit, real but far too weak for such totals.
cards.source: Galbraith and Karlin, Idols and Celebrity, 2012
cards.reference: Patrick W. Galbraith and Jason G. Karlin (eds.), Idols and Celebrity in Japanese Media Culture, Palgrave Macmillan, 2012

cards.question: Whom did the original Kiss Army of 1975 lay siege to, and how?
cards.answer: A radio station in Terre Haute, Indiana. Two teenagers, Bill Starkey and Jay Evans, pestered WVTS with letters and calls, signed as the Kiss Army, until it played Kiss; the band then booked a concert in the town. Kiss soon took over the name for its official fan club.
cards.move: A pressure group can become a brand if the brand adopts it quickly.
cards.reference: Ken Sharp with Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons, Nothin' to Lose: The Making of KISS 1972-1975, It Books, 2013

cards.question: After Holmes was killed off in 1893, about 20,000 readers reportedly cancelled The Strand, which sold roughly 500,000 copies. What percentage quit?
cards.answer: 4 / 100 = 4 per cent.
cards.move: A big count of complaints means little until you know the crowd.
cards.trap: Treating 20,000 as a revolt without asking out of how many.
cards.hint: Divide the cancellations by the magazine's sales, then read it as a percentage.
steps: That leaves 4 / 100.
4 / 100 = 4 per cent.
cards.reference: Daniel Stashower, Teller of Tales: The Life of Arthur Conan Doyle, Henry Holt, 1999

cards.question: Why does Zara make much of its clothing near Spain when Asia is cheaper per garment?
cards.answer: Because speed cuts the cost of guessing wrong. Making a large share of its fashion lines in Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Turkey lets Inditex produce small first runs, watch what sells, and restock within weeks. Paying more per piece is offset by fewer unsold clothes marked down at the end of a season.
cards.move: The cheapest unit is not cheap if too many units go unsold.
cards.reference: Ghemawat & Nueno, ZARA: Fast Fashion, Harvard Business School case 9-703-497, 2003
