cards.question: Why were thousands of garment workers inside Rana Plaza on the morning it collapsed?
cards.answer: Because they had been ordered back in. Cracks appeared in the eight-storey building near Dhaka on 23 April 2013, and a bank on a lower floor closed, but factory managers told workers to return. The next morning it collapsed, killing 1,134 people. Floors had been added without permits and carried heavy machines and generators.
cards.move: A warning ignored under deadline pressure is still a warning received.
cards.reference: International Labour Organization, The Rana Plaza Accident and its Aftermath, 2017

cards.question: Of all the material used to make clothes, how much ends up recycled into new clothing?
cards.answer: Less than 1%. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation estimated in 2017 that about 73% of clothing fibre ends up burned or landfilled, around 12% is downcycled into insulation, cleaning cloths and mattress stuffing, and under 1% returns as new garments. The equivalent of a rubbish lorry of textiles is burned or buried every second.
cards.move: A bin marked recycling tells you where things go in, not where they end.
cards.trap: About 15%: donation bins make recycling look routine.
cards.reference: Ellen MacArthur Foundation, A New Textiles Economy: Redesigning Fashion's Future, 2017

cards.question: True or false: world clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2014?
cards.answer: True. McKinsey estimated that production doubled over those years, passing 100 billion garments in 2014, while each item was kept about half as long. Doubling needs less than it sounds: growth of about 5% a year compounds to twice as much in 14 years, since 1.05 multiplied by itself 14 times is about 2.
cards.move: Steady modest growth doubles faster than anyone expects.
cards.trap: False: a doubling in 14 years sounds too steep for a mature industry.
cards.reference: Remy, Speelman & Swartz, Style that's sustainable: A new fast-fashion formula, McKinsey & Company, 2016

cards.question: Should governments add a per-item levy to ultra-cheap fast fashion?
cards.answer: Clothes this cheap push their costs onto others: landfill, burned stock, polluted rivers and bales of waste exported to poorer countries. A levy on each item folds some of that cost into the price, slows the flood of throwaway pieces and funds collection. French lawmakers have already voted for a penalty of this kind.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether price or use drives the waste.
cards.counterpoint: A flat charge per item falls hardest on the poorest buyers, for whom cheap clothes are the budget, not a luxury. It targets price rather than harm: an expensive garment can be worn as rarely as a cheap one. Online orders cross borders easily, so durability rules, takeback duties and honest labels would reach the waste more directly.
cards.reference: Assemblée nationale, proposition de loi visant à réduire l'impact environnemental de l'industrie textile, adopted at first reading, March 2024

cards.question: How did clothes from Shein and Temu reach American buyers without paying import duty?
cards.answer: Through the de minimis rule. From 2016 goods worth under $800 per person per day entered the US duty-free, so clothes posted parcel by parcel from Chinese warehouses skipped tariffs a container of them would pay. Customs handled over a billion such parcels a year before the exemption ended for China in 2025.
cards.move: Check where the rule's threshold sits before crediting a low price to efficiency.
cards.source: US Customs and Border Protection, e-commerce statistics
cards.reference: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, E-Commerce and de minimis shipment statistics, fiscal year 2024

cards.question: Of the used clothes arriving at Accra's Kantamanto market from richer countries, roughly how much leaves as waste?
cards.answer: About 40%, by the OR Foundation's estimate. Traders buy sealed bales unseen, and roughly four in ten garments are unsellable, ending in dumps, drains and beaches. The racks in a charity shop show the clothes kept at home; the bales hold what was sorted out. About 15 million garments arrive each week.
cards.move: What you see on sale is the part that was picked to be seen.
cards.trap: Donated clothes on shop racks look wearable, so most exports seem so.
cards.reference: The OR Foundation, Dead White Man's Clothes: Kantamanto research, 2022

cards.question: Roughly what share of the world's new textile fibre production in 2023 was polyester?
cards.answer: More than half: about 57%, by Textile Exchange's count, against roughly a fifth for cotton. Polyester is cheap, strong and made from oil at any scale, and its share has climbed for decades. Most fleece, sportswear and stretch blends depend on it. A wardrobe that looks like cotton is often mostly plastic.
cards.move: Check the label before trusting the fibre your hand expects.
cards.trap: Cotton is the fibre everyone pictures, so it seems to dominate.

diagram.caption: In 2023 the world made nearly three times as much new polyester as cotton.

cards.reference: Textile Exchange, Materials Market Report, 2024

cards.question: Where does almost all recycled polyester in clothing come from?
cards.answer: Plastic drinks bottles, about 98% of it by Textile Exchange's figures. Bottles are clean, single-material and easy to collect; old clothes mix fibres, dyes and zips. The catch is that bottles could have become bottles again; spun into fleece, the plastic leaves that loop. A recycled jacket is usually a bottle's last stop.
cards.move: Ask what a recycled product was before, and what it can become after.
cards.trap: Recycled clothing sounds like clothing made from old clothes.
cards.reference: Textile Exchange, Materials Market Report, 2023

cards.question: True or false: since July 2026, large companies may not destroy unsold clothes and shoes in the EU?
cards.answer: True. The EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation of 2024 bans large enterprises from destroying unsold apparel and footwear from 19 July 2026, with narrow exceptions; medium-sized firms follow later. France had banned destroying unsold goods from 2022. Unsold stock must now be sold, donated or recycled.
cards.move: Before assuming a practice is legal, check the date on the newest rule.
cards.trap: Stories of burned stock make the practice seem still permitted.
cards.reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1781/oj

cards.question: What gave two Chicago hobbyists the time to build the first dial-up bulletin board?
cards.answer: A snowstorm. Snowed in during a heavy Chicago storm in January 1978, Ward Christensen wrote the software and Randy Suess assembled the hardware; CBBS went online on 16 February. It ran on a single phone line, so callers dialled in one at a time and read what the last caller had left.
cards.move: Count the idle weeks behind a breakthrough, not only the talent.
cards.reference: https://www.edn.com/blizzard-brings-about-bulletin-board-systems-january-16-1978/

cards.question: Why does the anonymous forum 4chan trace its design back to Japan?
cards.answer: Because it copied a Japanese board. Hiroyuki Nishimura's 2channel, opened in 1999, made anonymous posting a mass habit in Japan, and its offshoot Futaba Channel inspired a 15-year-old, Christopher Poole, to launch an English copy in 2003. In 2015 the circle closed: Poole sold 4chan to Nishimura.
cards.move: Many things that seem homegrown are translations of somewhere else.
cards.reference: https://phys.org/news/2015-09-4chan-sold-founder-japanese-message.html

cards.question: True or false: most of Reddit's earliest posts came from its two founders under invented usernames?
cards.answer: True. In 2005 Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian gave their own submission page a hidden field that registered any new username they typed, so an empty site looked busy. Huffman has said nearly all submissions in the first weeks were theirs. The links they chose set the tone that the first real users copied.
cards.move: A crowd you can count by name is not yet a crowd of people.
cards.trap: False: a front page full of different names reads as independent agreement.
cards.source: Adweek, Reddit co-founder on fake users
cards.reference: https://www.adweek.com/performance-marketing/reddit-fake-users/

cards.question: In a typical large online community, roughly what share of users never post anything?
cards.answer: About 90%. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 summary of participation inequality found that in most communities about 90% only read, 9% contribute now and then, and 1% write most of what appears. A thread with a thousand replies may come from a few dozen regulars, watched by thousands who never type.
cards.move: The loudest voices in a room are a sample, not a census.
cards.trap: About 50%: the visible thread looks like everyone talking.
cards.reference: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/

cards.question: Usenet veterans date everything since AOL's 1993 influx as days of September 1993. Taking 1 September as day 1, which day was 1 January 2000?
cards.answer: So 1 January 2000 is day 2,314.
cards.move: Counting days across years, write down each leap day before adding.
cards.trap: Forgetting 1996's leap day, or starting the count at zero.
cards.hint: Count the rest of 1993 month by month, then whole years, minding leap years.
steps: September to December 1993: 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 122 days.
122 + 2,191 = 2,313 days, ending on 31 December 1999.
So 1 January 2000 is day 2,314.
cards.reference: Dave Fischer, post to the Usenet group alt.folklore.computers, 26 January 1994

cards.question: Why did three Usenet administrators set up the alt. hierarchy of discussion groups in 1987?
options: To route round a veto on new groups
cards.answer: To route round a veto. New groups in Usenet's main hierarchies needed the nod of the backbone cabal, the operators of its biggest relay sites, who refused ones such as rec.drugs. John Gilmore, Brian Reid and Gordon Moffett built alt.*, where groups needed no vote. Among the first were alt.drugs and alt.gourmand, for recipes.
cards.move: A gatekeeper who says no often creates the door around them.
cards.trap: Its later fame for adult groups makes that seem the reason.
cards.reference: Michael Hauben & Ronda Hauben, Netizens: On the History and Impact of Usenet and the Internet, IEEE Computer Society Press, 1997

cards.question: In 1995 a New York court treated Prodigy as publisher of a user's defamatory post; CompuServe had escaped in 1991. Why the difference?
cards.answer: Prodigy screened its boards. In Cubby v. CompuServe, a service that did not review posts was treated like a bookshop, unaware of what it stocked; in Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy, a service that policed content was treated as a publisher. Moderating raised the risk. Congress removed that penalty in 1996, in Section 230.
cards.move: Check whether a rule punishes the people who try hardest to comply.
cards.trap: Assuming the careful host must be the safer one in law.
cards.source: Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy, N.Y. Sup. Ct., 1995
cards.reference: Stratton Oakmont, Inc. v. Prodigy Services Co., 1995 WL 323710 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 24 May 1995)

cards.question: Reddit's 2023 API price was $0.24 per 1,000 calls. Apollo made about 7 billion calls monthly. Its yearly bill, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: $1.68 million x 12 = $20.16 million a year.
cards.move: Multiply a tiny unit price by the real volume before calling it cheap.
cards.trap: Skipping the per-thousand step and landing a thousand times too high.
cards.hint: Count the blocks of a thousand calls first, then price a month, then a year.
steps: 7 billion calls / 1,000 = 7 million blocks of 1,000.
7 million x $0.24 = $1.68 million a month.
$1.68 million x 12 = $20.16 million a year.
cards.reference: Christian Selig, post to r/apolloapp on Reddit's API pricing, 31 May 2023

cards.question: What did The WELL's founding rule, You own your own words, let members do to old threads?
cards.answer: Erase themselves from them. The WELL, a conferencing system founded near San Francisco in 1985 by Stewart Brand and Larry Brilliant, made members answerable for their own posts and gave them a command, scribble, to delete them later. When someone scribbled years of posts, replies stayed, answering nothing. Ownership meant the right to leave holes.
cards.move: Giving people control of their words also lets them unmake the record.
cards.reference: Katie Hafner, The Well: A Story of Love, Death and Real Life in the Seminal Online Community, Carroll & Graf, 2001

cards.question: Should large online forums be required to verify that users register under their real names?
cards.answer: Anonymity makes abuse cheap: harassment, defamation and coordinated lying cost nothing when nobody can be traced. A verified identity behind each account, even under a nickname, lets victims and courts reach offenders and makes people weigh a post before sending it. Signing what you publish is the ordinary price of speaking to thousands.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is who holds the identity records, and how safely.
cards.counterpoint: South Korea tried it. From 2007 big sites had to verify identities; studies found abusive comments fell only modestly while posting fell, and in 2011 hackers stole the stored details of about 35 million users of one portal. The Constitutional Court struck the rule down in 2012. Pseudonyms protect whistle-blowers, abuse survivors and dissidents.
cards.reference: Constitutional Court of Korea, 2010Hun-Ma47, decision on the internet real-name system, 23 August 2012

cards.question: How did a handheld with a greenish, unlit screen beat colour rivals through the early 1990s?
cards.answer: It ran for longer. Nintendo's Game Boy played for well over 10 hours on four AA batteries, while Sega's backlit colour Game Gear emptied six in roughly 3 to 5. Its designer, Gunpei Yokoi, preferred cheap, proven parts to new ones. On a long car journey, the colour machine went dark first.
cards.move: Judge a portable thing by how long it lasts away from the socket.
cards.reference: David Sheff, Game Over: How Nintendo Zapped an American Industry, Captured Your Dollars, and Enslaved Your Children, Random House, 1993

cards.question: How did the inventor of the PalmPilot test his design months before any circuit existed?
cards.answer: He carried a block of wood. Jeff Hawkins cut it to the size he wanted, kept it in his shirt pocket, and pulled it out in meetings to tap at imaginary screens with a stick. What he learned about size and daily habits shaped the first Pilot of 1996, which fitted that same pocket.
cards.move: Carry a fake version of the thing before building the real one.
cards.reference: Andrea Butter and David Pogue, Piloting Palm: The Inside Story of Palm, Handspring, and the Birth of the Billion-Dollar Handheld Industry, Wiley, 2002

cards.question: A text message carries 140 bytes, and each basic character uses 7 bits. How many characters fit?
cards.answer: 1,120 / 7 = 160 characters.
cards.move: A strange limit is often a round size divided by an odd unit.
cards.hint: Turn the bytes into bits before dividing.
steps: 140 bytes x 8 bits = 1,120 bits.
Each character in the basic alphabet takes 7 bits.
1,120 / 7 = 160 characters.
cards.reference: Friedhelm Hillebrand (ed.), GSM and UMTS: The Creation of Global Mobile Communication, Wiley, 2002

cards.question: True or false: the 1998 Furby could record words it heard and learn to say them back?
cards.answer: False. Furby had no recording chip. Its vocabulary was fixed at the factory; as it was played with, it gradually swapped its own babble, Furbish, for English words it already stored. Children heard new words soon after saying them. The US National Security Agency still banned it from its offices that winter.
cards.move: Something that says many things will sometimes say what you just said.
cards.trap: It said new words after people spoke nearby, so it must listen.
cards.reference: https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1999/01/13/a-toy-story-of-hairy-espionage/edb69b8a-1b41-47f8-8166-b8839cd637f3/

cards.question: True or false: Snake was an arcade game more than twenty years before it reached Nokia phones?
cards.answer: True. The idea came from arcades: Gremlin's Blockade of 1976 had players steering a growing line and trying not to hit it. Nokia engineer Taneli Armanto adapted it for the Nokia 6110 in 1997, where the phone's small grid and keypad suited it. A phone put a 1970s arcade idea into millions of pockets.
cards.move: Ask where a thing was before it reached the place you met it.
cards.trap: The phone version is the one millions played, so it feels original.
cards.source: Kent, Ultimate History of Video Games, 2001
cards.reference: Steven L. Kent, The Ultimate History of Video Games, Three Rivers Press, 2001

cards.question: What most likely grew inside the satellite whose failure silenced most American pagers in May 1998?
cards.answer: Tin whiskers: hair-thin crystals that sprout from tin-plated parts over years and can bridge two contacts. Engineers judged them the most likely cause of the short in PanAmSat's Galaxy IV main processor; the backup had already failed unnoticed. About 90% of US pagers, some 45 million, went quiet together.
cards.move: A backup nobody tests is a single point of failure in disguise.
cards.reference: https://nepp.nasa.gov/whisker/reference/tech_papers/2006-Leidecker-Tin-Whisker-Failures.pdf

cards.question: Motorola's Iridium satellite phone network cost over $5 billion and went bankrupt in 1999. What did buyers pay for it?
cards.answer: About $25 million, roughly half a cent per dollar spent. Brick-sized handsets cost about $3,000 and calls several dollars a minute, so far fewer customers signed up than planned. Buyers paid for what the 66 satellites could earn from then on. Motorola had been preparing to steer them into the atmosphere to burn.
cards.move: What something cost says nothing about what it is worth now.
cards.trap: Expecting a price near what was spent, as if cost set value.

diagram.caption: Iridium cost over $5 billion and sold for $25 million: half a cent on the dollar.

cards.reference: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/the-rise-and-fall-and-rise-of-iridium-5615034/

cards.question: A 1.44 MB floppy disk holds 2,880 sectors of 512 bytes. How many bytes does its MB stand for, in thousands?
cards.move: When a unit looks round, check which base it was rounded in.
cards.trap: Assuming a megabyte is either a million bytes or 1,048,576.
cards.hint: Write 512 as half of 1,024 and see what 2,880 becomes when halved.
steps: 2,880 sectors x 512 bytes = 1,440 x 1,024 bytes.
The label calls that 1.44 MB, so 1 MB = 1,000 x 1,024 bytes.
cards.reference: Scott Mueller, Upgrading and Repairing PCs, 11th edition, Que, 1999

cards.question: Over a 56k dial-up modem around 1999, roughly how many minutes did a 4 MB MP3 song take to download?
cards.answer: 640 / 60 = about 11 minutes.
cards.move: Check whether a speed is quoted in bits or in bytes.
cards.trap: Reading 56k as kilobytes a second, eight times too fast.
cards.hint: Turn bytes into bits first; the 56 counts bits per second.
steps: 4 MB x 8 bits = 32 megabits, or 32,000 kilobits.
Good lines gave about 50 kilobits a second, below the 56 on the box.
640 / 60 = about 11 minutes.
cards.reference: International Telecommunication Union, ITU-T Recommendation V.90, Geneva, 1998

cards.question: Why did 1990s DVDs carry region codes that stopped a disc bought in America playing in Europe?
options: To protect staggered cinema release dates
Because of PAL and NTSC television
To stop pirates copying studio masters
cards.answer: To protect staggered release dates. Films then opened in cinemas months apart around the world, and a disc sold in America could undercut a European premiere. The television explanation fails a test: Japan, which used NTSC like America, was put in region 2 with Europe. The codes followed the release calendar, not the wiring.
cards.move: Find the case the popular explanation cannot fit, then look again.
cards.trap: Blaming PAL and NTSC, a real split the region map ignores.
cards.reference: Jim Taylor, DVD Demystified, McGraw-Hill, 1998

cards.question: True or false: the man who drew the Trollface grin has earned money from licensing it?
cards.answer: True. Carlos Ramirez drew the face in Microsoft Paint in 2008 and later registered its copyright. By 2015 he said licences and settlements had brought in more than $100,000, and a video game using the face had been pulled from Nintendo's online store. Every reposting was free; every printed shirt was not.
cards.move: Free to share and free to sell are different permissions.
cards.trap: False: a face copied millions of times seems to belong to everyone.
cards.reference: https://kotaku.com/the-maker-of-the-trollface-meme-is-counting-his-money-1696228810

cards.question: Why did Mike Godwin first spread his rule about Nazi comparisons across Usenet groups?
cards.answer: As a deliberate experiment in spreading an idea. From 1990 Godwin, a lawyer, posted his rule, that a long online argument will sooner or later compare someone to Hitler, to make careless comparisons look foolish. He called it a counter-meme and described the test in Wired in October 1994. Others soon cited it unprompted.
cards.move: An idea spreads furthest when it is short enough to quote.
cards.reference: Mike Godwin, Meme, Counter-meme, Wired, issue 2.10, October 1994

cards.question: Where did the distracted boyfriend photograph come from before it became a meme?
cards.answer: A stock-photo catalogue. Antonio Guillem shot it in Girona in 2015 as part of a staged series, captioned for buyers as a disloyal man looking at another woman. It sold as an ordinary licence for about two years before spreading in 2017, and the same two models appear across the rest of the series.
cards.move: Images built to be generic travel furthest, because anyone can fill them.
cards.reference: Antonio Guillem interviewed on the distracted boyfriend meme, The Guardian, 30 August 2017

cards.question: What did the buyer of the Charlie Bit My Finger NFT actually get for $760,999?
cards.answer: A token, not control of the video. In May 2021 the Davies-Carr family auctioned an NFT of their 2007 clip and said the original would leave YouTube, but the sale transferred no copyright and copies stayed online. The buyer owned a blockchain entry pointing at a scene anyone could still watch.
cards.move: Before paying for ownership, ask exactly what it lets you stop.
cards.reference: https://www.nbcnews.com/pop-culture/viral/charlie-bit-my-finger-youtube-video-sells-nft-760-999-n1268322

cards.question: Should images that become memes be free for anyone to reuse, adverts included?
cards.answer: A meme is made by the crowd that remixes it, not by whoever held the camera; its value comes from millions of reuses. Billing for it would chill parody and reward luck. Copyright exists to reward creation, and going viral is something that happens to an image, not something its owner did.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the line between a joke and a sale decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The image is still someone's work, often someone's face, and brands profit from it. Grumpy Cat's owners licensed their cat for a coffee drink; when the maker sold products beyond the deal, a US jury in 2018 awarded them $710,001. Free use for jokes is one thing; free use to sell goods is another.
cards.reference: https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2018/01/25/580588088/grumpy-cat-awarded-710-000-in-copyright-infringement-suit

cards.question: What was the 1996 Dancing Baby animation made for, before it spread by email?
cards.answer: To sell software. Michael Girard and Robert Lurye built it as a sample file for Character Studio, a plug-in for animating figures in 3D Studio Max. Passed on as a looping GIF, it was dancing on Ally McBeal by 1998. An early mass-shared animation was an advert for the tool that drew it.
cards.move: Ask who made the first copy, and what they wanted it to show.
cards.reference: Limor Shifman, Memes in Digital Culture, MIT Press, 2014

cards.question: Why do heavily reshared meme images turn blotchy even when nobody edits them?
cards.answer: Because every save throws a little more away. JPEG compression splits a picture into 8-by-8 pixel blocks and discards detail the eye tends to miss; each screenshot or re-upload repeats the cut, and errors pile up as blocky edges and smeared colour. The grain on an old reaction image is its travel record.
cards.move: A copy of a copy keeps the losses of every copy before it.
cards.reference: ITU-T Recommendation T.81, Digital compression and coding of continuous-tone still images, International Telecommunication Union, 1992

cards.question: In 2013 Baauer's Harlem Shake entered the Billboard Hot 100 at number one. What mainly put it there?
options: Radio play after the dance craze
Download sales from a TV advert
A new rule counting YouTube plays
cards.answer: A new rule counting YouTube plays. Billboard began adding YouTube data to the Hot 100 that very week, and plays of thousands of fan-made clips using the track's audio counted towards it. The dance videos did not merely advertise the song; they were its numbers.
cards.move: When a record falls, check first whether the measuring changed.
cards.trap: Assuming the chart counted the same things as the week before.
cards.reference: Billboard, Hot 100 chart news on adding YouTube data and the Harlem Shake debut, 20 February 2013

cards.question: True or false: the EU copyright directive of 2019 banned memes built on copyrighted images?
cards.answer: False. Campaigners warned that Article 17, which makes large platforms liable for uploads, would kill memes, but the final text requires every member state to let users upload quotation, criticism, review, caricature, parody and pastiche. Before, those exceptions were optional. The directive written to police uploads made the joke a legal right across the EU.
cards.move: Read the final text before repeating what the campaign said it contained.
cards.trap: The meme ban headlines were vivid and repeated, so they stick.
cards.reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj

cards.question: How many Britons saw the 1939 Keep Calm and Carry On poster on a wall during the war?
options: Hardly any: it was held back
cards.answer: Hardly any. The Ministry of Information printed about 2.45 million copies in 1939 to post after heavy bombing or invasion, never issued them, and most were pulped. A bookseller in Alnwick found one among old books in 2000 and framed it; reprints did the rest. The wartime poster is mostly a twenty-first-century one.
cards.move: The one copy that survived can stand in for a past that never happened.
cards.trap: It is everywhere now, so it seems it was everywhere then.
cards.source: Lewis, Keep Calm and Carry On, IWM, 2017
cards.reference: Bex Lewis, Keep Calm and Carry On: The Truth Behind the Poster, Imperial War Museum, 2017

cards.question: In 1991 Billboard's album chart switched from shop reports to counting barcode scans at tills. What happened?
cards.answer: Country and rap rose. The old chart relied on staff at selected shops reporting what sold best, which record labels could lobby and big-city stores dominated. Once SoundScan counted real sales, Garth Brooks and N.W.A reached No. 1 within months. The audience had been there all along, uncounted.
cards.move: Before trusting a ranking, ask who was doing the reporting.
cards.trap: Assuming a chart built from shop reports already measured real sales.
cards.reference: Billboard, first Billboard 200 chart compiled from Nielsen SoundScan data, issue of 25 May 1991

cards.question: Why did the engineer who shaped the MP3 format test it again and again on one a cappella song?
cards.answer: Because a lone voice has nowhere to hide. Karlheinz Brandenburg found that compression flaws, masked by drums and guitars in fuller music, sounded plainly in Suzanne Vega's unaccompanied Tom's Diner. He tuned the codec against it through hundreds of listenings. Her quiet 1987 track became the format's benchmark.
cards.move: Test a method on the case where its flaws would show first.
cards.reference: Stephen Witt, How Music Got Free: The End of an Industry, the Turn of the Century, and the Patient Zero of Piracy, Viking, 2015

cards.question: True or false: the grunge slang glossary The New York Times printed in 1992 came from Seattle musicians' real speech?
cards.answer: False. A reporter asked Megan Jasper, who had worked at the Sub Pop label, for the scene's slang, and she made it up on the spot: lamestain for an uncool person, harsh realm for bummer. The paper printed the list. A small magazine, The Baffler, exposed the hoax the following year.
cards.move: If you arrive wanting an answer, someone will happily supply one.
cards.trap: A source inside the scene seemed to confirm exactly what was sought.
cards.reference: Rick Marin, Grunge: A Success Story, The New York Times, 15 November 1992

cards.question: Did file-sharing cause the collapse in recorded music sales that began around 1999?
cards.answer: The timing is hard to ignore. US recorded-music revenue peaked in 1999, the year Napster launched, and more than halved over the next fifteen years. Tens of millions of people were suddenly getting for nothing what they had bought on CD. Most studies of the period found downloads displaced at least some sales.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what would have sold anyway.
cards.counterpoint: The best-known study, by Oberholzer-Gee and Strumpf, matched actual downloads to album sales and found an effect indistinguishable from zero. Other forces were at work: fans could now buy single tracks rather than whole albums, DVDs and games competed for the same money, and the CD replacement boom was ending.
cards.reference: Oberholzer-Gee and Strumpf, The Effect of File Sharing on Record Sales: An Empirical Analysis, Journal of Political Economy, 2007

cards.question: Why did Richard Ashcroft receive no songwriting royalties from Bitter Sweet Symphony for over twenty years?
cards.answer: Because of borrowed strings. The 1997 hit looped a sample from an orchestral cover of the Rolling Stones' The Last Time. The rights holder argued the band used more than licensed, and the songwriting credit and royalties went to Mick Jagger and Keith Richards. They handed them back to Richard Ashcroft in 2019.
cards.move: Read the licence before building a house on borrowed ground.
cards.reference: https://variety.com/2019/music/news/bittersweet-symphony-royalties-rolling-stones-verve-richard-ashcrof-1203224722/

cards.question: Why were CDs sold in America until 1993 inside cardboard boxes twice their height?
cards.answer: To fit shops built for vinyl. The longbox, about 30 cm tall, let a CD stand in racks made for LPs and was harder to slip into a pocket. Artists and campaigners attacked the waste, and the labels dropped it in 1993. R.E.M. printed a voter-registration petition on theirs in 1991.
cards.move: Packaging often fits the old shelf rather than the new product.
cards.reference: Steve Knopper, Appetite for Self-Destruction: The Spectacular Crash of the Record Industry in the Digital Age, Free Press, 2009

cards.question: How did the big record labels keep US CD prices high in the late 1990s, by the regulators' account?
options: They withheld ad money from discounters
They set a legal minimum retail price
cards.answer: They withheld advertising money from discounters. Under minimum advertised price rules, a shop that advertised a CD below the label's floor lost its share of promotional funds. In 2000 the Federal Trade Commission estimated buyers had overpaid about $480 million since 1997, and the five major labels agreed to drop the policies.
cards.move: A price can be fixed without anyone ever naming the price.
cards.trap: Assuming a price floor must be written openly, which the law forbade.
cards.source: Federal Trade Commission, CD pricing settlement, 2000
cards.reference: Federal Trade Commission, Record Companies Settle FTC Charges of Restraining Competition in CD Music Market, 10 May 2000

cards.question: True or false: Don't Speak, top of Billboard's US radio airplay chart for 16 weeks, never appeared on the Hot 100?
cards.answer: True. Until December 1998 a song had to be on sale as a single to enter the Hot 100, and No Doubt's label kept Don't Speak on the album only, to sell albums. Radio hits such as Iris and Torn were missing for the same reason. The chart archive under-records the decade's radio.
cards.move: An archive keeps only what its rules let in.
cards.trap: Treating the Hot 100 archive as a full record of the decade's hits.
cards.reference: https://billboard.com/articles/columns/chart-beat/8458527/hot-100-rule-change-1998-airplay-singles

cards.question: Hootie & the Blowfish's 1994 debut sold over 20 million copies in the US. How many did its 1996 follow-up sell there?
cards.answer: About 3 million, certified triple platinum by 1998. Cracked Rear View had needed everything to go right: the radio format of the moment, four hit singles, years of touring. Fairweather Johnson entered the chart at No. 1 and still sold about a seventh as much. A freak success is a poor forecast.
cards.move: After an outlier, expect the next result to be closer to ordinary.
cards.trap: Expecting a sequel to keep half a record-breaking debut's sales.
cards.reference: Recording Industry Association of America, Gold & Platinum certifications for Cracked Rear View and Fairweather Johnson, 1998

cards.question: True or false: Oasis's Wonderwall never reached No. 1 on the UK singles chart?
cards.answer: True. It peaked at No. 2 in November 1995, held off by Robson & Jerome's cover of I Believe, sung by two actors from the television drama Soldier Soldier. Oasis's next single, Don't Look Back in Anger, did reach No. 1. The song still sung in every pub lost its week to a soldier-show duo.
cards.move: What lasts and what won at the time are measured differently.
cards.trap: Assuming the song everyone still knows must have topped the chart.
cards.source: Official Charts Company, Oasis chart history
cards.reference: Official Charts Company, Official Singles Chart archive, Oasis and Robson & Jerome, November 1995

cards.question: What happened on camera in American television's first fly-on-the-wall family series, broadcast in 1973?
cards.answer: A marriage ended. PBS crews followed the Loud family of Santa Barbara for seven months in 1971, and in the 12 broadcast episodes Pat Loud tells her husband Bill she wants a divorce. Their son Lance was seen living openly as a gay man in New York. The family later disputed the edit in public.
cards.move: Filming ordinary life for long enough stops it being ordinary.
cards.reference: Jeffrey Ruoff, An American Family: A Televised Life, University of Minnesota Press, 2002

cards.question: True or false: Survivor was first devised and broadcast as an American programme?
cards.answer: False. The format was devised by the British producer Charlie Parsons and first made in Sweden, as Expedition Robinson, in 1997. CBS licensed it for 2000. Reality hits are usually sold as formats: a rulebook, a set design and a production manual, rebuilt country by country with local contestants.
cards.move: The famous version of a thing is rarely the first one.
cards.trap: The American series is the one everyone saw, so it seems original.
cards.reference: Jean K. Chalaby, The Format Age: Television's Entertainment Revolution, Polity, 2016

cards.question: In the BBC's televised prison study of 2002, what did the volunteers cast as guards do?
options: Grew harsher as the role demanded
Never cohered into a united authority
Walked out on the first day
cards.answer: They never cohered. The psychologists Stephen Reicher and Alex Haslam found the guards did not identify with their role, while the prisoners bonded as a group and overturned the regime. The volunteers set up an equal commune; when it faltered, some pushed for a harsh new order. Roles alone made nobody cruel.
cards.move: A uniform does little until people feel they belong to it.
cards.trap: The famous 1971 prison story says a role turns people cruel.
cards.reference: Reicher and Haslam, Rethinking the Psychology of Tyranny: The BBC Prison Study, British Journal of Social Psychology, 2006

cards.question: How can a reality contestant be shown saying a sentence they never said?
cards.answer: By a frankenbite: editors join words recorded at different moments, even in answer to different questions, into one line. A cutaway shot covers the join so the mouth is not seen. Story editors, who shape unscripted shows much as writers shape scripted ones, use it to build arguments a season needs.
cards.move: Treat any quote you cannot hear in full as an assembly.
cards.reference: Jennifer L. Pozner, Reality Bites Back: The Troubling Truth About Guilty Pleasure TV, Seal Press, 2010

cards.question: When did British broadcasting rules first protect the wellbeing of adults taking part in reality shows?
cards.answer: Only in 2021. After two former Love Island contestants and a Jeremy Kyle Show guest died by suicide in 2018 and 2019, Ofcom added rules for programmes entering production from 5 April 2021. Broadcasters must warn contributors of risks and take due care of anyone at risk of significant harm.
cards.move: Rules usually arrive after the harm they were written to prevent.
cards.reference: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/tv-radio-and-on-demand/broadcast-standards/new-protections-for-people-taking-part-in-tv-and-radio-shows

cards.question: How did a 1988 strike by Hollywood screenwriters help put Cops on American television?
cards.answer: It made a show without writers attractive. Networks had passed on John Langley and Malcolm Barbour's unscripted police ride-alongs for years; with the Writers Guild on strike, the young Fox network took them up as cheap programming no union writer could withhold. Cops premiered in March 1989 with no host, script or narrator.
cards.move: A shortage of one thing is a market for whatever needs none of it.
cards.source: LAist, The Frame, on making Cops
cards.reference: https://laist.com/shows/the-frame/cops-on-tv-inside-the-making-of-cops-the-longest-running-reality-show-in-tv-history

cards.question: Six years after The Biggest Loser, contestants had regained most of their weight. How did their resting metabolism compare?
options: Back to normal for their size
About 500 kcal a day below expected
Faster than before, from extra muscle
cards.answer: About 500 kcal a day below expected. A team at the US National Institutes of Health followed 14 contestants: they had lost 58 kg on average and regained 41 kg, yet burned about 500 kcal a day less at rest than people of their size and build. The slowdown outlasted the weight loss.
cards.move: The damage from an extreme can outlast the extreme itself.
cards.trap: Assuming metabolism recovers once the weight has come back.

cards.question: True or false: France's highest appeal court ruled that contestants on a reality dating show were employees?
cards.answer: True. In June 2009 the Cour de cassation upheld that people filmed on L'Île de la tentation, a Temptation Island format, worked under employment contracts. They took part in imposed activities, at set times, away from their ordinary lives, and were expected to produce reactions. Flirting on camera was ruled to be work.
cards.move: Whether something is work depends on who sets the hours and tasks.
cards.trap: Treating contestants as volunteers because they applied to be on screen.
cards.source: Cour de cassation, chambre sociale, 3 June 2009
cards.reference: https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/juri/id/JURITEXT000020708141/

cards.question: An American Family's crew shot about 300 hours of film for 12 one-hour episodes. What percentage of the footage aired?
cards.answer: 0.04 x 100 = 4 per cent.
cards.move: What you are shown is a choice from what was recorded.
cards.trap: Assuming a documentary shows most of what the camera saw.
cards.hint: Put the hours that aired over the hours that were shot.
steps: Broadcast time: 12 episodes x 1 hour = 12 hours.
12 / 300 = 0.04 of the footage.
0.04 x 100 = 4 per cent.
cards.reference: Jeffrey Ruoff, An American Family: A Televised Life, University of Minnesota Press, 2002

cards.question: Which film gave its name to a delusion psychiatrists began meeting in the 2000s: living inside a hidden reality show?
cards.answer: The Truman Show. The psychiatrist Joel Gold and his brother, the philosopher Ian Gold, described patients who believed concealed cameras were filming them for a secret programme. Persecutory delusions are ancient, but their content follows the age: earlier patients feared radio waves or spies, these feared an unseen television audience.
cards.move: Fears take the shape of whatever technology feels most watchful at the time.
cards.reference: Joel Gold and Ian Gold, Suspicious Minds: How Culture Shapes Madness, Free Press, 2014

cards.question: PepsiCo had spent heavily on Tropicana's 2009 carton redesign. What did it do when sales slumped?
options: Brought back the old carton within weeks
Kept the new carton for a year
Cut prices to support the new look
cards.answer: Brought back the old carton within weeks. The minimalist design reached shelves in January 2009; by late February unit sales were down about 20%, as regular buyers failed to spot their juice, and PepsiCo announced the orange pierced by a straw would return. The design budget was gone whichever carton sat on the shelf.
cards.move: Money already spent is the same whichever way you now decide.
cards.trap: Keeping it a year so the redesign budget is not wasted.
cards.reference: Zmuda, Tropicana Line's Sales Plunge 20% Post-Rebranding, Advertising Age, 2 April 2009

cards.question: When Dunkin' Donuts dropped the word Donuts from its name, roughly what share of its sales were drinks?
cards.answer: About 60%. Coffee and other drinks already brought in most of the money when the chain announced in September 2018 that it would trade simply as Dunkin' from January 2019. The name described the shop of 1950; the till described a coffee seller that happened to sell doughnuts.
cards.move: A name records what a business was, not what it now sells.
cards.trap: About 20%: the word on the sign pulls the guess toward doughnuts.
cards.reference: https://www.npr.org/2018/09/26/651905960/dunkin-deletes-donuts-from-its-name

cards.question: True or false: Andersen Consulting renamed itself Accenture to escape the Enron scandal?
cards.answer: False. The name changed on 1 January 2001, months before Enron collapsed. An arbitrator had let the consultants split from Arthur Andersen in 2000 but barred them from keeping the Andersen name, at a cost of about $1 billion paid to the firm. When the auditor fell in 2002, the consultants were already Accenture.
cards.move: Check the dates before letting the famous event explain the change.
cards.trap: True: Enron is the Andersen story everyone remembers, so it explains everything.
cards.reference: https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU0010/S00185/andersen-consulting-announces-new-name-accenture.htm

cards.question: How did ValuJet get a new name after its 1996 crash?
cards.answer: It bought one. After Flight 592 burned and crashed in the Everglades in May 1996, killing all 110 aboard, and regulators grounded the airline for months, ValuJet bought the much smaller AirTran Airways in 1997 and took its name for the combined company. The larger partner disappeared inside the smaller one's livery.
cards.move: When a name becomes a liability, buying a smaller one can be cheaper than repair.
cards.reference: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/valujet-flight-592-crash

cards.question: What was painted on British post vans during the Consignia years?
cards.answer: Royal Mail, as before. Consignia, adopted in 2001 when the Post Office became a public limited company, was the name of the holding group; letters still went out in Royal Mail and Parcelforce vans. The ridicule fell on a word most customers never saw, and in 2002 the group became Royal Mail Group.
cards.move: Before mocking a rename, check which name the public actually meets.
cards.reference: https://postandparcel.info/6311/news/change-of-consignia-name-to-royal-mail-could-cost-gbp-1m/

cards.question: Jaguar's European registrations fell 97.5% in April 2025, months after its much-mocked rebrand. What mainly explains the fall?
options: It had almost no cars to sell
cards.answer: It had almost no cars to sell. Jaguar had wound down its petrol and diesel models through 2024 to relaunch as electric-only, with no new car due until 2026. That one decision caused both the new identity and the empty showrooms. Europe registered 49 that April, against 1,961 a year earlier.
cards.move: Before blaming the loudest change, check what else stopped at the same time.
cards.trap: A mocked rebrand followed by collapse reads as cause and effect.
cards.source: Autoblog, Jaguar's April sales in Europe, 2025
cards.reference: https://www.autoblog.com/news/jaguar-europe-sales-decline

cards.question: In 1998 and 1999, US firms renamed themselves with dotcom names. How did their shares react, with or without internet business?
options: Both jumped, by about the same
cards.answer: Both jumped, by about the same. Cooper, Dimitrov and Rau found gains beyond the market's of about 74% over the ten days around the announcement, and the jump was similar whatever a firm's actual internet involvement. Firms with no online business made the comparison: they changed nothing but the name. Investors were buying three letters.
cards.move: To credit the substance, find a case that had only the label.
cards.trap: Assuming investors paid for real internet business, not the label.
cards.source: Cooper, Dimitrov & Rau, Journal of Finance, 2001

cards.question: What did Nissan do with the Datsun name almost three decades after dropping it?
cards.answer: Revived it for buyers who had never owned one. Nissan phased Datsun out in the early 1980s, then relaunched it in 2013 as a budget badge for India, Indonesia, Russia and South Africa. Sales stayed weak, and by 2022 the badge was gone again. The name's goodwill had been earned elsewhere.
cards.move: Old goodwill lives with the people who remember it, not with the name.
cards.reference: https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2022/04/datsun-is-dead-again/

cards.question: How many times did Blackwater change its name in the four years after the Nisour Square shooting?
cards.answer: Twice. After its guards killed 17 Iraqi civilians in Baghdad's Nisour Square in September 2007, Blackwater became Xe Services in 2009 and, under new owners, Academi in 2011; in 2014 Academi was merged into a group called Constellis. Government security contracts kept coming under each new sign.
cards.move: Follow the contracts and the people, not the letterhead.
cards.reference: https://foreignpolicy.com/2014/07/01/blackwaters-descendants-are-doing-just-fine/

cards.question: True or false: Pearl Milling Company, which replaced the Aunt Jemima brand in 2021, was a name newly invented by marketers?
cards.answer: False. It was the name of the mill in St. Joseph, Missouri, behind the self-rising pancake mix of 1889. Retiring the Aunt Jemima image, a racial caricature, PepsiCo's Quaker Oats reached into its own history. The newest name on the box was the oldest one.
cards.move: Before calling a new name invented, look in the company's own past.
cards.trap: New corporate names sound focus-grouped, so this one seems invented too.
cards.reference: PepsiCo, Aunt Jemima Brand to Change Name to Pearl Milling Company, press release, 9 February 2021

cards.question: How did NBC find the money for Seinfeld's first season after its own research panned the pilot?
cards.answer: It came out of the specials budget. After the 1989 pilot tested weakly, programming executive Rick Ludwin gave up some of his own department's money for specials to fund four more episodes, one of the smallest season orders a US network has placed. The show that followed ran nine seasons.
cards.move: When the official budget says no, look for a budget someone else controls.
cards.reference: Jennifer Keishin Armstrong, Seinfeldia: How a Show About Nothing Changed Everything, Simon & Schuster, 2016

cards.question: Where is most of the drawing and painting of The Simpsons' animation done?
cards.answer: South Korea. Scripts, voices and storyboards are made in the United States; studios such as AKOM in Seoul turn them into finished animation. A 2005 report found Korean artists doing the work for a fraction of American rates. Springfield is drawn in Seoul.
cards.move: Ask where the labour is done, not where the credits are written.
cards.trap: Japan comes first because its animation industry is the famous one.
cards.reference: https://www.today.com/popculture/simpsons-rides-seoul-train-wbna7069645

cards.question: True or false: I Love Lucy was shot on film mainly so that its stars could stay in Hollywood?
cards.answer: True. In 1951 network comedy went out live from New York, and the West Coast saw a blurry kinescope, a film shot off a monitor. Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz refused to move, so the show was filmed in Los Angeles before an audience. Desilu took less money and kept the negatives.
cards.move: A technical innovation often starts as someone refusing to relocate.
cards.trap: Assuming film was chosen for picture quality or for later reruns.
cards.reference: Coyne Steven Sanders and Tom Gilbert, Desilu: The Story of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, William Morrow, 1993

cards.question: Why do British sitcoms often end after a dozen episodes while American ones run past a hundred?
cards.answer: Different machines make them. A British series is often six episodes by one or two writers; The Young Ones is 12 episodes across 1982 and 1984. A US network season is around 22, written by a staff room, because about 100 episodes are needed to sell daily reruns to local stations.
cards.move: The length of a thing often tells you how it is paid for.
cards.reference: Brett Mills, The Sitcom, Edinburgh University Press, 2009

cards.question: Should streaming services cut or pull old sitcom episodes whose jokes now read as slurs?
cards.answer: A library is a publisher, and publishers choose what they sell. A slur played for laughs lands on viewers who never agreed to hear it, including children browsing at random. Nothing is destroyed: the episode survives on disc and in archives. Streaming simply stops pushing it into living rooms by autoplay.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the question is who the joke laughs at.
cards.counterpoint: Cutting a scene removes its context too. In the 1975 Fawlty Towers episode pulled by UKTV in 2020, the slurs belong to a senile major the show mocks, and the episode came back within days with a warning. An edited stream quietly becomes the only version most people ever see.
cards.reference: https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-06-12/fawlty-towers-episode-removed-by-uktv-overracial-slur/12348070

cards.question: Why did the BBC's broadcasts of M*A*S*H sound quieter than the American ones?
cards.answer: The BBC dropped the laugh track. The show's makers, Larry Gelbart and Gene Reynolds, never wanted canned laughter; CBS insisted, and the compromise kept it out of the operating-room scenes. British broadcasts ran without it altogether. The same episodes played as comedy in Ohio and nearer to drama in Leeds.
cards.move: The same material changes genre when you change what surrounds it.
cards.reference: Larry Gelbart, Laughing Matters: On Writing M*A*S*H, Tootsie, Oh, God!, and a Few Other Funny Things, Random House, 1998

cards.question: True or false: The Simpsons clip of Donald Trump riding an escalator aired before he launched his 2016 campaign?
cards.answer: False. Trump rode down the Trump Tower escalator to announce his run on 16 June 2015; the animated short Trumptastic Voyage, showing a similar descent, came out in July 2015. A 2000 episode did joke about a President Trump, but the famous clip followed the event it seemed to foresee.
cards.move: Check the date on a prophecy before admiring its accuracy.
cards.trap: Trusting a clip because it matches the later event so exactly.
cards.reference: The Simpsons, Trumptastic Voyage, animated short, Fox, July 2015; and Bart to the Future, season 11, Fox, 2000

cards.question: True or false: in a 2019 experiment, adding recorded laughter made listeners rate feeble jokes as funnier?
cards.answer: True. Qing Cai, Sophie Scott and colleagues in London played 40 groan-worthy jokes with and without laughter added. Posed laughter lifted the ratings by about 5%, spontaneous laughter by about 13%. Autistic and non-autistic adults were swayed alike. The audience on the soundtrack votes before the viewer does.
cards.move: Other people's reaction is part of what you think you are judging.
cards.trap: Assuming people discount laughter they can tell is recorded.
cards.reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982219306876

cards.question: After Seinfeld, three of its stars each led a new sitcom cancelled within two seasons. How good is the evidence for a curse?
options: Strong: three flops in a row is rare
Weak: most new series flop anyway
Strong, but only for the two men
cards.answer: Weak. Most new network series fail: US networks cancel roughly half in their first year, and fewer still survive a second. If two in three fail, three flops from three tries happens nearly one time in three. Julia Louis-Dreyfus then won a 2006 Emmy for The New Adventures of Old Christine.
cards.move: Before explaining a run of failures, ask how often things fail anyway.
cards.trap: Judging three failures rare without knowing how often new shows fail.
cards.source: The Hollywood Reporter, TV Long View, 2020
cards.reference: https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/networks-first-year-cancellation-rate-stays-low-2019-20-1302859/

cards.question: Why did all six Friends leads earn exactly the same fee per episode from 1996 onwards?
cards.answer: Because they bargained as one. From the third season the cast negotiated together, reportedly at the urging of David Schwimmer, then the best-paid of them, so none could be played off against another. By the last two seasons each earned about $1 million an episode. A walkout by one meant a walkout by six.
cards.move: A group that cannot be split can ask for what none could alone.
cards.reference: Saul Austerlitz, Generation Friends: An Inside Look at the Show That Defined a Television Era, Dutton, 2019

cards.question: True or false: the shoe the NBA barred Michael Jordan from wearing in 1984 was the Air Jordan 1?
cards.answer: False. The league's February 1985 letter objected to a black-and-red Nike Air Ship, worn in October 1984 before his own shoe was ready, under its uniform rules. Nike's 1985 television advert for the Air Jordan 1 told the story as if the new shoe were the one banned, and that version stuck.
cards.move: The version of a story that sells is the version that gets retold.
cards.trap: True: the Air Jordan 1 is the shoe the famous advert showed.
cards.reference: National Basketball Association, letter to Nike on the black-and-red Air Ship, 25 February 1985

cards.question: Why do some imported canvas trainers have a thin layer of fabric glued to the sole?
cards.answer: To be taxed as a lower-duty kind of shoe. US tariffs classify footwear by the material of the outer sole that touches the ground, and rubber-soled canvas shoes pay far more than ones soled in textile. A felt skin over most of the tread wears off within days, but it counts at the border.
cards.move: When a product has a strange detail, check the rulebook it was designed around.
cards.reference: US International Trade Commission, Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, Chapter 64: Footwear, 2024

cards.question: What building gave Nike the idea of showing the air cushion inside a shoe?
cards.answer: The Centre Pompidou in Paris. Tinker Hatfield, trained as an architect, was struck by a building that shows its pipes and structure on the outside, and cut a window into the midsole so buyers could see the air unit. The Air Max 1 went on sale in 1987 with its cushioning on display.
cards.move: Showing how something works can be the whole selling point.
cards.source: Abstract: The Art of Design, Netflix, 2017
cards.reference: Abstract: The Art of Design, season 1, episode Tinker Hatfield: Footwear Design, Netflix, 2017

cards.question: In lab tests, how much less energy did runners use in Nike's Vaporfly prototype than in top racing flats?
cards.answer: About 4%. Hoogkamer and colleagues measured 18 high-calibre runners on a treadmill; the thick foam and carbon plate cut the oxygen cost of running by about 4% on average against established racing shoes. Records fell soon after, and in 2020 World Athletics capped road-racing soles at 40 mm.
cards.move: Small percentages decide contests that are won by small margins.
cards.trap: About 0.4%: a shoe seems too small a thing to change elite physiology.
cards.reference: Hoogkamer et al., A Comparison of the Energetic Cost of Running in Marathon Racing Shoes, Sports Medicine, 2018

cards.question: What persuaded Adidas to give a rap group a shoe deal in 1986?
cards.answer: A concert crowd holding its trainers in the air. In 1986 Run-DMC asked a Madison Square Garden audience to raise their shoes while an Adidas executive watched thousands go up. A deal reported at $1 million or more followed, among the first for musicians rather than athletes. The group wore Superstars without laces.
cards.move: Before paying for demand, find a way to see it with your own eyes.
cards.reference: Barbara Smit, Pitch Invasion: Adidas, Puma and the Making of Modern Sport, Allen Lane, 2006

cards.question: Why can trainers kept unworn in their box since the 1990s crumble the first time they are worn?
cards.answer: Because the midsole decays on the shelf. Many midsoles are polyurethane foam; moisture in the air slowly splits its polymer chains, a reaction called hydrolysis, worn or not. After a decade or two the foam turns brittle and gives way under a step. Collectors pay dearly for pairs that may not survive a walk.
cards.move: Unused is not the same as unaged; ask what decays just sitting still.
cards.reference: Yvonne Shashoua, Conservation of Plastics: Materials Science, Degradation and Preservation, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2008

cards.question: Who kept the Nike Air Force 1 alive after the company planned to drop it in 1984?
cards.answer: Three Baltimore shoe shops. Their customers kept asking for the 1982 basketball shoe, so the retailers persuaded Nike to keep making it in colours sold only through them, a new one each month. Buyers travelled from New York to get them, and Nike reissued the shoe nationally in 1986. Demand was proved at three counters.
cards.move: Before a product is cancelled, ask the people who sell it every day.
cards.reference: Bobbito Garcia, Where'd You Get Those? New York City's Sneaker Culture: 1960-1987, Testify Books, 2003

cards.question: Adidas bought Reebok in 2006 for about €3.1 billion. Roughly what did it sell Reebok for in 2021?
cards.answer: About €2 billion. Adidas agreed in 2021 to sell Reebok to Authentic Brands Group for up to €2.1 billion, after years of shrinking sales. Fifteen years of inflation make the loss larger than the headline gap. The 2006 price set no floor for the 2021 buyer.
cards.move: What you paid tells a buyer nothing about what the thing is worth.
cards.trap: The purchase price feels like a baseline the sale should match.
cards.reference: Adidas, adidas to divest Reebok to Authentic Brands Group, press release, 12 August 2021

cards.question: Jordan Brand made about $5.1 billion in fiscal 2022. A reported 5% royalty is how many times Jordan's $94 million career NBA salaries?
cards.answer: 255 / 94 = about 2.7 times his NBA career salaries.
cards.move: A small cut of a large, recurring sum can beat a large one-off.
cards.trap: Assuming the playing salaries must dwarf a small percentage.
cards.hint: Find one year's royalty first, then divide by the salaries.
steps: 5% of $5,100 million is 0.05 x 5,100.
0.05 x 5,100 = $255 million in one year.
255 / 94 = about 2.7 times his NBA career salaries.
cards.reference: Forbes, estimate of Michael Jordan's earnings from Nike, 2022

cards.question: True or false: Nike's first shoe with an air cushion was a basketball shoe?
cards.answer: False. It was a running shoe: the Tailwind of 1978 carried a gas-filled bag devised by Frank Rudy, a former aerospace engineer, and was launched at the Honolulu Marathon. The Air Force 1, the first basketball shoe with the cushion, came four years later. For years Air was sold as a feeling, not a look.
cards.move: The version everyone remembers is rarely the first version made.
cards.trap: Air's most famous early shoes are basketball ones, so they come to mind.
cards.reference: Phil Knight, Shoe Dog: A Memoir by the Creator of Nike, Scribner, 2016

cards.question: Why did Netflix never put the $1 million prize-winning recommendation algorithm into service?
cards.answer: It was not worth the plumbing. The 2009 winner blended over a hundred models to predict DVD star ratings about 10% better. Netflix engineers judged the extra accuracy too small for the work of running it, and by then most members were streaming, where what people play says more than what they rate.
cards.move: A contest fixes the question just before the question changes.
cards.reference: Amatriain and Basilico, Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 Stars (Part 1), Netflix Technology Blog, 2012

cards.question: True or false: America's most-streamed television show of 2020 was a streaming service's own original series?
cards.answer: False. Nielsen measured 57 billion minutes of The Office, an NBC sitcom that ended in 2013, well ahead of any original. Second was Grey's Anatomy, another network show. Originals win the publicity; old network series, with hundreds of episodes to leave running, win the hours.
cards.move: Count the hours people spend, not the launches people discuss.
cards.trap: Originals get the headlines and the awards, so they seem most watched.
cards.reference: https://www.nielsen.com/insights/2021/tops-of-2020-nielsen-streaming-unwrapped/

cards.question: In 2020, how much of a title did a Netflix account need to watch for Netflix to count it?
cards.answer: Two minutes. From late 2019 Netflix counted any account that watched two minutes as having chosen a title, replacing a rule of 70% of a film or of a single episode. The company said the new count ran about 35% higher on average. A pressed play button became a viewer.
cards.move: Before comparing two counts, check that both count the same thing.
cards.trap: Assuming a view means someone watched most of what they started.
cards.reference: Netflix, Fourth Quarter 2019 Letter to Shareholders, 21 January 2020

cards.question: Squid Game's first season logged 1.65 billion viewing hours in 28 days. Roughly how many complete viewings is that, in millions?
cards.answer: 1,650 / 8 = about 200 million complete viewings.
cards.move: Convert a total into units of the thing itself before being impressed.
cards.hint: Find how long one full run of the season takes.
steps: The season has 9 episodes of roughly 55 minutes each.
9 x 55 = about 495 minutes, roughly 8 hours per full viewing.
1,650 / 8 = about 200 million complete viewings.
cards.reference: https://variety.com/2021/digital/news/squid-game-all-time-most-popular-show-netflix-1235113196/

cards.question: Why did HBO's owner take its own finished series Westworld off its streaming service?
cards.answer: To stop it costing money. In late 2022 Warner Bros. Discovery pulled Westworld and other shows from HBO Max, a cut widely reported as a way to shed residuals, the fees owed to cast and crew for continued use. It then licensed them to free, advert-funded channels on Roku and Tubi.
cards.move: A shelf that charges rent will be emptied, whatever sits on it.
cards.reference: https://deadline.com/2023/01/westworld-gets-new-home-as-warner-bros-discovery-strikes-roku-tubi-fast-channel-deals-1235245347/

cards.question: In Netflix's first full viewing report, for January to June 2023, what share of hours went to titles it licensed from others?
cards.answer: About 45%. Netflix's own films and series took 55% of nearly 100 billion hours spread across more than 18,000 titles. Originals fill the home page and the awards lists; licensed shows, many made for broadcast networks years earlier, quietly filled almost half the evenings. The shop window is not the stockroom.
cards.move: What is advertised most is rarely where most of the time goes.
cards.trap: Judging viewing by the originals Netflix promotes most loudly.
cards.reference: http://about.netflix.com/en/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report

cards.question: True or false: Netflix's subscriber numbers fell after it began charging for shared passwords in 2023?
cards.answer: False. Paid sharing reached the United States in May 2023, amid loud anger online. Netflix then added 5.9 million members in the second quarter, 8.8 million in the third and 13.1 million in the fourth. Many borrowers opened accounts of their own. The people posting about cancelling were a small, noisy slice.
cards.move: The loudest reaction is a sample of the loud, not of everyone.
cards.trap: Taking the anger online as a sample of all subscribers.
cards.reference: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528023000272/ex991_q323.htm

cards.question: What did Hollywood writers win in 2023 that finally tied their streaming pay to how many people watched?
cards.answer: A success bonus. Under the deal that ended the 2023 strike, a streaming series or film seen by at least 20% of a service's domestic subscribers in its first 90 days earns its writers a bonus of 50% of the fixed residual, the fee for reuse. Before, a flop and a global hit paid alike.
cards.move: Ask whether the people who make a hit share in its size.
cards.source: Writers Guild of America, 2023 contract summary
cards.reference: Writers Guild of America, Summary of the 2023 WGA Memorandum of Agreement, September 2023

cards.question: HBO Max reportedly paid $425 million for five years of Friends, 236 episodes. Roughly what is that per episode per year, in thousands of dollars?
cards.answer: $85 million / 240 = about $350 thousand.
cards.move: A big total shrinks fast once you divide it by what it buys.
cards.trap: Stopping at $425 million and judging it a reckless sum.
cards.hint: Spread the price over the years first, then over the episodes.
steps: $425 million / 5 years = $85 million a year.
Round 236 episodes to about 240.
$85 million / 240 = about $350 thousand.
cards.reference: WarnerMedia's five-year Friends streaming deal for HBO Max, reported by The Wall Street Journal, July 2019

cards.question: Should governments require streaming services to fill part of their catalogues with locally made programmes?
cards.answer: Yes. Without rules, global services fill catalogues with whatever is cheapest to buy at scale, mostly American libraries. The European Union already requires at least 30% European works in on-demand catalogues, given prominence, and several countries add investment duties. A quota keeps local writers, crews and languages on the screens their own viewers pay for.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a quota counts titles or viewing.
cards.counterpoint: No. A catalogue quota counts titles, not viewing: a service can reach 30% with cheap filler buried deep in the menus. Money spent hitting a quota is money not spent on what subscribers want. Local shows that audiences love, such as Spain's Money Heist or South Korea's Squid Game, travelled the world because people chose them.
cards.reference: Directive (EU) 2018/1808 amending the Audiovisual Media Services Directive, Official Journal of the European Union, 2018

cards.question: What did bringing grunge to the catwalk in 1992 cost the designer Marc Jacobs?
cards.answer: His job. His spring 1993 collection for Perry Ellis, shown in late 1992, remade thrift-shop flannel shirts and floral dresses in costly fabrics. Buyers and critics balked, and the company dismissed him. Years later the show was treated as prophetic; in 2018 he reissued the collection under his own name.
cards.move: Being early looks exactly like being wrong until the calendar catches up.
cards.reference: Valerie Steele, Fifty Years of Fashion: New Look to Now, Yale University Press, 1997

cards.question: When and where was the Wonderbra's plunging push-up design first created?
cards.answer: Canada in the 1960s. Louise Poirier designed the plunge push-up model for the Montreal maker Canadelle in 1964. The 1990s craze came when the licence changed hands and Britain relaunched it in 1994, with billboards of Eva Herzigova. A thirty-year-old design was sold as the news of the season.
cards.move: The year a thing became famous is rarely the year it was made.
cards.trap: Britain in the 1990s, when the billboard campaign made it famous.
cards.reference: Jane Farrell-Beck and Colleen Gau, Uplift: The Bra in America, University of Pennsylvania Press, 2002

cards.question: Who publicly condemned fashion photography's heroin chic look in 1997, and what prompted it?
cards.answer: The President of the United States. In May 1997 Bill Clinton accused the fashion industry of glamorising addiction, months after the death of Davide Sorrenti, a 20-year-old fashion photographer who had used heroin. The gaunt, hollow-eyed look had sold clothes and scent for years before it was named in the White House.
cards.move: A style is judged by its effects only once someone is harmed.
cards.reference: Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: William J. Clinton, 1997, Book I, US Government Printing Office, 1998

cards.question: True or false: George Michael did not appear in the video for his 1990 single Freedom '90?
cards.answer: True. Tired of selling himself as a pin-up, he cast five models from Peter Lindbergh's January 1990 British Vogue cover to lip-sync his words instead: Naomi Campbell, Linda Evangelista, Cindy Crawford, Christy Turlington and Tatjana Patitz. The video, by David Fincher, made them household names. The supermodel era began in a pop star's absence.
cards.move: Removing the obvious centre can make the edges famous.
cards.trap: A pop star's video is where the pop star is shown.
cards.reference: British Vogue, January 1990 issue, cover photographed by Peter Lindbergh

cards.question: How did a preppy American label become part of hip-hop's uniform in the early 1990s?
cards.answer: Mostly without paying for it. Tommy Hilfiger's brother Andy gave clothes to rappers, and when Snoop Doggy Dogg wore an oversized Tommy shirt on Saturday Night Live in 1994, shops reportedly sold out of it within days. The brand then cut its clothes looser and made its logo bigger.
cards.move: The customers who adopt a brand can redesign it more than its designers.
cards.reference: Tommy Hilfiger with Peter Knobler, American Dreamer: My Life in Fashion and Business, Ballantine Books, 2016

cards.question: Who mailed American personnel managers a guide to dressing down for work in 1992, and why?
cards.answer: Levi Strauss, maker of Dockers khakis. Its Guide to Casual Businesswear went to about 25,000 human-resources managers, with photographs and rules for looking relaxed but not sloppy. The trousers in the pictures did the selling. Casual Friday reached many offices as a trouser maker's dress code.
cards.move: When a rule arrives looking neutral, ask who wrote the first draft.
cards.reference: https://www.levistrauss.com/2014/07/07/dockers-and-the-birth-of-casual-fridays/

cards.question: Generra sold $50 million of colour-changing Hypercolor clothes between February and May 1991. Where was the company by mid-1992?
options: Bought out by a sportswear giant
cards.answer: In bankruptcy protection, filed in July 1992. Demand overshot anything Generra had planned for, and it chased dye supplies and factory capacity just as the fad peaked. The heat-sensitive colour faded with washing. Shirts that changed colour with body heat went cold within a year.
cards.move: Build for the ordinary year, not the best one.
cards.trap: Extrapolating a peak season as if the fad would hold its height.
cards.reference: https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19930330/1693271/generra-slashes-its-operations

cards.question: True or false: tattooing was illegal in New York City until 1997?
cards.answer: True. The city banned it in 1961, blaming a hepatitis outbreak, and for 36 years tattooists worked in back rooms and flats or across the river in New Jersey. The City Council lifted the ban in 1997, just as tattoos went mainstream. Oklahoma kept its ban until 2006.
cards.move: The law and the street can disagree for decades.
cards.trap: Assuming a city full of tattoos must have allowed tattooing.
cards.source: New York City Council, tattoo law, 1997
cards.reference: New York City Council, local law amending the Health Code to license tattooing, 1997

cards.question: By James Laver's 1937 timeline of taste, how should a 1990s look strike people about 30 years later?
cards.answer: Amusing. The costume historian set out a timetable: a style looks indecent ten years before its time, smart in it, hideous ten years after, ridiculous at twenty, amusing at thirty, quaint at fifty and, many steps later, beautiful at 150. Grunge flannel and slip dresses were back in shops around 2020.
cards.move: Taste runs on a clock; judge old styles by their age.
cards.trap: Stopping at hideous, which is Laver's verdict only ten years on.
cards.reference: James Laver, Taste and Fashion: From the French Revolution to the Present Day, Harrap, 1937

cards.question: Should governments require fashion models to prove they are healthy before they can work?
sides: No, leave it to the trade
cards.answer: Yes. The 1990s waif look showed that the industry rewards extreme thinness and cannot police itself: agencies profit from whichever body sells. France has required models to hold a medical certificate since 2017, and digitally slimmed photographs must be labelled as retouched. A model's health should not depend on the season's fashion.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a certificate can measure harm.
cards.counterpoint: No. Thinness is a poor proxy for health: a body-mass cut-off catches naturally slender people and misses illness in others, and a doctor's letter is easy to obtain. Such laws police young women's bodies while leaving alone the photographers and buyers who create the demand. Better contracts, fair pay and unions protect models more directly.
cards.reference: Loi n° 2016-41 du 26 janvier 2016 de modernisation de notre système de santé, with implementing decrees of May 2017

cards.question: Why does a running shoe carry a large mark on its side at all?
cards.answer: Because the side mark began as structure. Early spikes had leather strips stitched across the midfoot to steady the upper, and Adi Dassler's shoes wore them as stripes. The trade kept calling any side logo a stripe: in 1971 Phil Knight asked a design student for a stripe that suggested motion.
cards.move: Before reading a symbol as decoration, ask what job it once did.
cards.reference: Phil Knight, Shoe Dog: A Memoir by the Creator of Nike, Scribner, 2016

cards.question: How long did Nike keep its own name printed inside its main logo?
cards.answer: About 24 years. From 1971 the curve travelled with the word Nike beside or across it; in 1995 the company judged the mark recognisable alone and dropped the wordmark from its primary logo. The shape was only lightly refined over the years: the stroke a student sketched in 1971 now carries the name by itself.
cards.move: A name can be dropped only after years of paying to attach it.
cards.source: Nike, company history of the Swoosh
cards.reference: https://about.nike.com/en/magazine/nike-swoosh-logo-history

cards.question: True or false: Adidas bought the rights to its three stripes from another shoemaker?
cards.answer: True. In the early 1950s Adidas bought the three-stripe mark from the Finnish firm Karhu, reportedly for the equivalent of about €1,600 and two bottles of whisky; the whisky rests on Karhu's own telling. Karhu, Finnish for bear, carried on under its own name while its stripes went to Germany.
cards.move: The name that made a sign famous is not always the name that made it.
cards.trap: False: a brand's signature mark feels like its founder's own invention.
cards.reference: https://www.thedrinksbusiness.com/2021/09/two-bottles-of-whisky-helped-in-purchase-of-adidas-logo/

cards.question: Why did an EU court in 2019 uphold cancelling one of Adidas's three-stripe trademarks?
options: Plain stripes can never be trademarks
Its recognition was proven in too few countries
Karhu had registered the stripes first
cards.answer: Its recognition was proven in too few countries. A sign that is not distinctive on its face must show it became known through use across the whole EU, and the evidence Adidas filed covered only five member states. The judgment, case T-307/17, concerned one registration; the brand's other stripe marks were not before the court.
cards.move: Evidence from a few places proves little about everywhere else.
cards.trap: Assuming a shape this simple is plainly beyond the reach of law.
cards.reference: General Court of the European Union, Case T-307/17, adidas AG v EUIPO, judgment of 19 June 2019

cards.question: Should a sportswear brand be able to own simple parallel stripes on clothing?
cards.answer: Decades of spending taught buyers that three stripes mean one maker. When a rival copies them, shoppers are misled and the owner loses sales it earned. Trademark law already demands proof that the public links the sign to one firm; where that proof exists, protecting the mark protects buyers, not just the firm.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is what buyers actually believe a shape means.
cards.counterpoint: Stripes are among the most basic marks in design, used on tracksuits, uniforms and trim long before any brand claimed them. Letting one firm own them taxes every competitor's collection. In 2023 a New York jury found Thom Browne's four stripes did not infringe Adidas's marks, and an EU court had already voided one stripe registration.
cards.reference: adidas America, Inc. v. Thom Browne, Inc., US District Court for the Southern District of New York, jury verdict, January 2023

cards.question: In 1983 Nike gave the swoosh's designer 500 shares. Six two-for-one stock splits followed. How many shares, in thousands, did they become?
cards.answer: 500 x 64 = 32,000 shares, or 32 thousand.
cards.move: Count repeated doublings as powers of two, never as additions.
cards.trap: Adding 500 shares per split, as if each split repeated the gift.
cards.hint: Work out what one split does to the count, then do it again six times.
steps: Each two-for-one split doubles the number of shares held.
Six splits multiply it by 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64.
500 x 64 = 32,000 shares, or 32 thousand.
cards.source: CNBC, on the swoosh designer's shares, 2018
