cards.reference: https://www.cnbc.com/2018/09/05/heres-how-much-nikes-billionaire-founder-paid-for-its-swoosh-logo.html

cards.question: Why do some football shirts carry the maker's logo woven faintly into the fabric itself?
cards.answer: To get round a size cap. UEFA's kit rules limit a manufacturer's mark to 20 square centimetres, about a matchbox face. They allow a tone-on-tone weave repeating a small maker's mark across the cloth, which FIFA bans at its own tournaments. The chest logo stays small; the shirt wears it dozens of times.
cards.move: When a rule caps the size of something, look for where the copies went.
cards.source: Footy Headlines, UEFA and FIFA kit rules
cards.reference: https://www.footyheadlines.com/9825058572/jacquard-brand-patterns-are-allowed-by-uefa-but-banned-by-fifa.html

cards.question: Why did the photographer of the leaping Jordan picture lose his case over Nike's Jumpman logo?
cards.answer: Nobody owns a pose. Jacobus Rentmeester photographed Michael Jordan leaping for Life magazine in 1984; Nike restaged the leap with its own photographer, and its silhouette became the Jumpman. In 2018 the Ninth Circuit found Nike had not copied his choices of light, angle and setting. His Jordan leapt over grass, Nike's over a skyline.
cards.move: Copyright guards how a thing was shown, not the thing shown.
cards.reference: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/15-35509/15-35509-2018-02-27.html

cards.question: Roughly what share of Nike's revenue went on advertising, athlete deals and other marketing in fiscal 2024?
cards.answer: About 8%. Nike reported demand creation expense, its name for adverts, endorsement contracts, free kit and brand events, of $4.3 billion against revenue of $51.4 billion. Making and delivering the goods cost far more: about $28.5 billion. The swoosh is everywhere because the shoes are, not because the budget is vast.
cards.move: How often a name is seen says little about what it spends.
cards.trap: A brand seen everywhere seems to spend a third of its takings on it.
cards.reference: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320187/000032018724000044/nke-20240531.htm

cards.question: True or false: the swoosh was on shoes before the company that sold them was called Nike?
cards.answer: True. The mark was drawn in 1971 and first sold on shoes in 1972, when the firm was Blue Ribbon Sports, an importer of Japanese running shoes; Nike was only its new shoe line. The company took Nike as its legal name in 1978. For six years the swoosh named a brand, not a firm.
cards.move: A product can outgrow the company, and then the company takes its name.
cards.trap: Assuming the logo was drawn for a company already named Nike.
cards.reference: J. B. Strasser & Laurie Becklund, Swoosh: The Unauthorized Story of Nike and the Men Who Played There, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1991

cards.question: How did tabloid investigators get into famous people's voicemail in the early 2000s without any hacking skill?
cards.answer: With the factory PIN. Mobile voicemail could be dialled from any phone, and many owners never changed the default four-digit code their network set. A private investigator working for the News of the World needed only a number and that code. The Leveson Inquiry laid out the method in 2012.
cards.move: Most locks are opened by the key that came in the box.
cards.reference: Lord Justice Leveson, An Inquiry into the Culture, Practices and Ethics of the Press, The Stationery Office, 2012

cards.question: After Merseyside boycotted The Sun over its 1989 Hillsborough coverage, how did local Euroscepticism move compared with similar areas?
cards.answer: It fell. The political scientists Florian Foos and Daniel Bischof compared Merseyside with similar areas where the paper kept selling; where far fewer people read The Sun's anti-EU campaigning, attitudes to the EU turned more favourable. A boycott gave what a survey cannot: readers who stopped for reasons unrelated to politics.
cards.move: To see what a message does, find people who stopped hearing it by accident.
cards.trap: Readers choose papers that agree with them, so papers change nobody.
cards.reference: Foos and Bischof, Tabloid Media Campaigns and Public Opinion: Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Euroscepticism in England, American Political Science Review, 2022

cards.question: Why would a tabloid pay a fortune for a celebrity story it never intends to print?
cards.answer: To bury it. In catch and kill, a publisher buys exclusive rights so nobody else can run the story. In December 2018 the National Enquirer's owner, American Media, admitted to federal prosecutors that it paid a model $150,000 in 2016 for her account of an affair with Donald Trump, to keep it from voters.
cards.move: Paying for silence can look exactly like paying for news.
cards.reference: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release on American Media Inc. non-prosecution agreement, 12 December 2018

cards.question: Should newspapers have to warn people before publishing stories about their private lives?
cards.answer: Damages come too late: once intimate details are printed, no court can unpublish them. A warning gives a judge the chance to weigh the public interest before the harm, not after. Max Mosley won his 2008 privacy case against the News of the World, yet the story had already been read by millions.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who can afford an injunction.
cards.counterpoint: In Mosley's own case, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2011 that the law did not require prior notice. A warning invites an injunction, and the rich and powerful are best placed to obtain one, so the stories most worth telling about them would be the easiest to stop.
cards.reference: European Court of Human Rights, Mosley v. the United Kingdom, application no. 48009/08, judgment of 10 May 2011

cards.question: Before it described newspapers, what was the word tabloid registered as a trademark for?
cards.answer: Compressed medicine tablets. Burroughs Wellcome registered Tabloid in 1884 for its pills, and the word came to mean anything condensed. Around 1900 it was applied to small-format papers that squeezed the news into short, punchy stories. The news came in pill form.
cards.move: A word's first owner rarely keeps control of what it comes to mean.
cards.trap: The printing press, because the word now names a paper size.
cards.reference: Roy Church and E. M. Tansey, Burroughs Wellcome & Co.: Knowledge, Trust, Profit and the Transformation of the British Pharmaceutical Industry 1880-1940, Crucible Books, 2007

cards.question: Why did the 2014 drugs trial of the singer Tulisa Contostavlos collapse before the jury could decide?
cards.answer: Because the reporter behind the sting was found to have probably lied. Mazher Mahmood of The Sun on Sunday, known as the Fake Sheikh, had posed as a film producer and drawn her into a cocaine deal. His driver's statement had been altered at his urging; in 2016 Mahmood was jailed for 15 months.
cards.move: Whoever builds the trap has reasons to describe the catch generously.
cards.reference: The Guardian, report of Mazher Mahmood's sentencing at the Old Bailey for conspiracy to pervert the course of justice, October 2016

cards.question: Before 2013, why did American celebrities sometimes sue American tabloids in London rather than at home?
cards.answer: English libel law favoured them. In London a published claim was presumed false and the paper had to prove it true; in the United States a public figure must prove the paper knew it was false or recklessly ignored the truth. Kate Hudson won damages from the National Enquirer's British edition in 2006.
cards.move: Where a case is heard can decide it before anyone speaks.
cards.reference: Defamation Act 2013, c. 26, United Kingdom; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 1964

cards.question: True or false: News of the World hackers were shown to have deleted Milly Dowler's voicemails, giving her family false hope?
cards.answer: False. Her phone was hacked in 2002, and her family later received £2 million in settlement. But in December 2011 police told the Leveson Inquiry the deletions that raised her parents' hopes were probably automatic, not the hackers' doing, and The Guardian corrected its report. The plain charge was true; the vivid detail was not.
cards.move: Each vivid detail added to a charge is one more thing to prove.
cards.trap: Believing the detailed version because it was the one most repeated.
cards.reference: Nick Davies, Hack Attack: How the Truth Caught Up with Rupert Murdoch, Chatto & Windus, 2014

cards.question: In 2016 a celebrity's name was all over foreign websites. Did Britain's Supreme Court still bar The Sun on Sunday from printing it?
options: Yes: printing would add fresh intrusion
No: the secret was already out
No, but it awarded him damages
cards.answer: Yes. In PJS v News Group Newspapers the court kept the injunction by four to one. Privacy guards against intrusion, not only disclosure, and British front pages would add a flood of fresh intrusion that scattered websites had not. The couple's young children weighed too. Lord Toulson dissented: the story was out.
cards.move: Judge a step by what it adds, not by what already happened.
cards.trap: Treating privacy as a secret that is lost once anyone knows.
cards.source: UK Supreme Court, PJS v News Group, 2016
cards.reference: PJS v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2016] UKSC 26, judgment of 19 May 2016

cards.question: The Sun backed the winning party at every UK general election from 1979 to 2024. What does that record best show?
options: That its endorsement decides close elections
That its readers vote as one bloc
That it backed whoever was already ahead
cards.answer: That it backed whoever was already ahead. It switched to Labour in March 1997, with Labour far ahead in the polls, and back to the Conservatives in 2009, before their return. Studies disagree on how far its readers moved in 1997; none finds enough to explain a landslide. A weathervane points where the wind blows.
cards.move: When a predictor always matches the outcome, check which one moved first.
cards.trap: Reading a perfect record of backing winners as a record of making them.
cards.reference: John Curtice, Was It The Sun Wot Won It Again? The Influence of Newspapers in the 1997 Election Campaign, CREST Working Paper 75, 1999

cards.question: In a study of New York Times articles, which emotion made readers less likely to email a story on?
cards.answer: Sadness. Berger and Milkman tracked thousands of articles over three months and found that stories stirring high-arousal feelings, such as awe, anger and anxiety, were shared more, while sadness, a low-arousal state, cut sharing. What counted was how stirred up the reader felt, not whether the feeling was pleasant.
cards.move: Sort feelings by how much they make people move, not how nice they are.
cards.trap: Anger: an unpleasant feeling seems likely to stop people passing a story on.
cards.source: Berger & Milkman, Journal of Marketing Research, 2012
cards.reference: Berger & Milkman, What Makes Online Content Viral?, Journal of Marketing Research, 2012

cards.question: True or false: bots were the main reason false news outran true news on Twitter?
cards.answer: False. Vosoughi, Roy and Aral traced about 126,000 rumour cascades from 2006 to 2017; falsehoods were about 70% more likely to be retweeted than the truth. Bots spread true and false stories at similar rates, so removing them left the gap intact. People, drawn to what seemed new, did the spreading.
cards.move: Before blaming the villain in the headline, check what remains once it is removed.
cards.trap: True: bots are the vivid, much-reported culprit in every misinformation story.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aap9559

cards.question: What did the money from the 2014 ice bucket challenge help find?
cards.answer: A gene linked to motor neurone disease. The ALS Association reported about $115 million raised that summer, and part went to Project MinE, an international effort to sequence patients' genomes. In 2016 it helped tie variants of a gene called NEK1 to the disease. Critics had dismissed the craze as buckets of water.
cards.move: Judge a fad by where its money went, not by how silly it looked.
cards.reference: Kenna et al., NEK1 variants confer susceptibility to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Nature Genetics, 2016

cards.question: In 2014 Gangnam Style neared the ceiling of YouTube's view counter, a signed 32-bit integer. What was that ceiling, in billions?
cards.answer: That is about 2.1 billion views.
cards.move: Every counter has a ceiling set by whoever built it, long before anyone hits it.
cards.trap: Using all 32 bits and answering about 4.3 billion.
cards.hint: A signed integer spends one of its 32 bits on the sign.
steps: 31 bits are left for the count itself.
The largest count is one less: 2,147,483,647.
That is about 2.1 billion views.
cards.reference: YouTube, Google+ post on the Gangnam Style view counter, December 2014

cards.question: How do most posts that reach huge audiences online actually get there?
cards.answer: Mostly through one big broadcast, not long chains of friends. Goel, Anderson, Hofman and Watts studied about a billion diffusion events on Twitter and found popularity depended chiefly on the size of the largest single broadcast, and was only weakly tied to how chain-like the spread was. Most huge audiences trace back to one account.
cards.move: When something spreads, look for the one big megaphone before the chain.
cards.reference: Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts, The Structural Virality of Online Diffusion, Management Science, 2016

cards.question: Researchers released the same 48 unknown songs into eight separate online worlds where listeners saw download counts. What happened?
options: The same songs led every world
cards.answer: The leaders differed between worlds. Salganik, Dodds and Watts had 14,341 people choose among the songs; a ninth world, with counts hidden, served as the control. Visible counts made success more unequal and less predictable. The best songs rarely flopped and the worst rarely won, but in between, an early lead often decided the order.
cards.move: To judge whether the winner deserved it, rerun history and see who wins again.
cards.trap: Assuming quality alone decides a hit, so every world agrees.
cards.reference: Salganik, Dodds & Watts, Experimental Study of Inequality and Unpredictability in an Artificial Cultural Market, Science, 2006

cards.question: What came of the goal behind the Kony 2012 film, one of that year's most-shared videos?
cards.answer: It was never met. Invisible Children's film drew about 100 million views in six days in March 2012, urging the capture of Joseph Kony, the Lord's Resistance Army leader, within the year. The US and Uganda ended their hunt in 2017 with him still free. The most watched arrest warrant of 2012 remained unserved.
cards.move: Count what changed on the ground, not how many people watched.
cards.source: Pew Research Center, The Viral Kony 2012 Video
cards.reference: Rainie, Hitlin, Jurkowitz, Dimock & Neidorf, The Viral Kony 2012 Video, Pew Research Center, 2012

cards.question: True or false: UK police confirmed cases of children harmed by the 2019 Momo challenge?
cards.answer: False. Warnings that a staring face was urging children to hurt themselves swept Britain in February 2019, but the NSPCC, the Samaritans and internet-safety groups said they had seen no evidence of harm, and warned the publicity itself was the risk. The face was a Japanese artist's 2016 sculpture. The warnings did the spreading.
cards.move: A warning shared a million times is evidence of the warning, not the danger.
cards.trap: So many urgent warnings made the harm seem proven.
cards.reference: Jim Waterson, report on charities calling the Momo challenge a hoax, The Guardian, 28 February 2019

cards.question: True or false: the first YouTube video to pass a million views was an advert?
cards.answer: True. In late 2005 Nike's Touch of Gold, a clip of Ronaldinho hitting the crossbar again and again, became the first on the site reported to reach a million views. It looked like shaky amateur footage, which helped it travel. Brands learned early that an advert spreads best when it does not look like one.
cards.move: The homemade look is itself something that can be manufactured.
cards.trap: Early viral hits seem homemade, so an amateur clip comes first to mind.
cards.reference: Kevin Allocca, Videocracy: How YouTube Is Changing the World, Bloomsbury, 2018

cards.question: Should messaging apps cap how many chats a single message can be forwarded to?
cards.answer: Falsehoods travel by forwarding, and a cap slows them without anyone reading messages. After WhatsApp limited frequently forwarded messages to one chat at a time in April 2020, it reported a 70% drop in them. In India in 2018, forwarded rumours of child kidnappers preceded mob killings. A little friction can save lives.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether friction slows lies more than truths.
cards.counterpoint: A cap is blunt: it slows a flood warning or a missing-child alert exactly as much as a lie, and people just copy and paste. Researchers modelling public WhatsApp groups in India, Brazil and Indonesia found forwarding limits delayed viral spread but did not stop it. Labelling and debunking target the lie; a cap taxes everyone.
cards.source: Melo et al., WhatsApp forwarding limits, 2019
cards.reference: de Freitas Melo, Coimbra Vieira, Garimella, Vaz de Melo & Benevenuto, Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?, Complex Networks, 2019

cards.question: Why do IQ tests keep being rescored?
cards.answer: Because raw scores kept rising — roughly three points a decade through the 20th century, across many countries. Tests are re-normed to keep the average at 100, which hides the drift. Score as an average adult today and you would have sat near the top of the distribution a century ago.
cards.move: The average is held at 100 by moving the goalposts every few years.

cards.question: Who were the experiments actually run on?
cards.answer: Overwhelmingly, undergraduates in rich Western universities — a group later shown to be among the least typical humans on measures from fairness to visual illusions. A field describing "human nature" had been sampling the most unusual population available, because it was the one down the corridor.
cards.move: The default human in psychology was a Western undergraduate.
cards.source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2010
cards.reference: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, The weirdest people in the world?, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2010

cards.question: Does a confident witness mean a reliable one?
cards.answer: Only weakly — and confidence moves after the fact. Witnesses told they picked the right person become markedly more certain, and also recall a better view and a clearer memory. The confidence a jury hears in court has already been shaped by what happened after the identification.
cards.move: Confidence in the witness box is partly manufactured after the event.
cards.source: Wells & Bradfield, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1998
cards.reference: Wells & Bradfield, Good, you identified the suspect: feedback to eyewitnesses distorts their reports of the witnessing experience, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Do you know how a zip works?
cards.answer: Ask someone to rate their understanding of a zip, a toilet or a bicycle and they rate it high. Ask them to write the step-by-step mechanism and the rating collapses. We routinely mistake familiarity for understanding, and only notice when forced to produce the explanation.
cards.move: Try explaining how a zip works. Out loud. Right now.
cards.reference: Rozenblit & Keil, The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth, Cognitive Science, 2002

cards.question: Would you notice if your own choice were swapped?
cards.answer: Often not. Shown two faces, asked to pick the more attractive, then handed back the other one and asked why — most people explain the choice they did not make, in detail, without noticing the swap. The reasons arrive after the decision and fit whatever is in front of us.
cards.move: People will argue confidently for a choice they never made.
cards.reference: Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in a simple decision task, Science, 2005

cards.question: When is an attempt to change a household's everyday habits most likely to work?
cards.answer: Soon after they move house. Verplanken and Roy offered households an intervention to live more sustainably, and it changed behaviour more among people who had moved in the previous three months. A move scrambles the cues that ran old routines, opening a short window before new ones set: the habit discontinuity hypothesis.
cards.move: Launch a change when life has already shuffled the old routines.
cards.reference: Verplanken & Roy, Empowering interventions to promote sustainable lifestyles: testing the habit discontinuity hypothesis in a field experiment, Journal of Environmental Psychology, 2016

cards.question: Six months on, 22% of smokers told to quit abruptly and 15.5% told to taper were abstinent. How many smokers per extra success?
cards.answer: About 15 smokers.
cards.move: Turn two rates into extra successes per hundred before judging a difference.
cards.trap: Comparing the two rates as a ratio instead of a difference.
cards.hint: Work out how many extra quitters per 100 smokers the abrupt route gives.
steps: 22 − 15.5 = 6.5 extra abstainers per 100 smokers.
About 15 smokers.
cards.source: Lindson-Hawley et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016
cards.reference: Lindson-Hawley, Banting, West, Michie, Shinkins & Aveyard, Gradual versus abrupt smoking cessation: a randomized, controlled noninferiority trial, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016

cards.question: When Schachter surveyed two ordinary communities, what share of those who had ever tried to quit smoking had succeeded?
cards.answer: More than half, most with no treatment at all. Clinic studies had painted relapse as the norm, but clinics see people who failed on their own, the hardest cases. Asking around a university psychology department and a seaside town, Schachter found about six in ten who had tried had stopped, on average for years.
cards.move: Those who come for help are the ones who could not manage alone.
cards.trap: Applying clinic relapse rates, drawn from the hardest cases, to everyone.
cards.reference: Schachter, Recidivism and self-cure of smoking and obesity, American Psychologist, 1982

cards.question: What does the best-tested behavioural treatment for nail-biting and hair-pulling ask people to do?
cards.answer: Catch the urge early and do something incompatible with it. Habit reversal, devised by Azrin and Nunn in 1973, first trains awareness of the earliest movements of the habit, then a competing response, such as clenching the fists or gripping an object, held until the urge passes. A hand busy gripping cannot also bite.
cards.move: Rather than resist an urge, give the same hands a different job.
cards.source: Azrin & Nunn, Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1973
cards.reference: Azrin & Nunn, Habit-reversal: a method of eliminating nervous habits and tics, Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1973

cards.question: True or false: in daily life, people high in self-control fight off temptations more often than other people do?
cards.answer: False. When Hofmann and colleagues beeped 205 adults at random for a week, those high in self-control reported weaker desires, less conflict and fewer bouts of resisting. Their edge seemed to lie upstream, in lives arranged so the fight came up less often: no biscuits in the cupboard, the gym bag packed by the door.
cards.move: The easiest temptation to beat is the one arranged out of reach.
cards.trap: Crediting their good record to winning more fights with temptation.
cards.reference: Hofmann, Baumeister, Förster & Vohs, Everyday temptations: an experience sampling study of desire, conflict, and self-control, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2012

cards.question: If each unaided quit attempt independently has a 4% chance of lasting, what is the percentage chance that at least one of 15 succeeds?
cards.answer: At least one success: 1 − 0.54 = 0.46, about 46%.
cards.move: A method that rarely works each time can still work eventually.
cards.trap: About 4%, as if one try's odds were a lifetime's odds.
cards.hint: Work out the chance that every single attempt fails.
steps: Each attempt fails with probability 0.96.
0.96 is about e to the −0.041, so fifteen failures ≈ e to the −0.61 ≈ 0.54.
At least one success: 1 − 0.54 = 0.46, about 46%.
cards.reference: Hughes, Keely & Naud, Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers, Addiction, 2004

cards.question: What did a two-day strike on the London Underground in 2014 reveal about commuters' daily routes?
cards.answer: That many were not the best available. Larcom, Rauch and Willems tracked travel-card data: forced off their usual lines, about one commuter in twenty kept the new route after the strike ended. The minutes those switchers saved over the following months outweighed the time the strike cost everyone. A habit had stopped them looking.
cards.move: A routine never compared with another has been repeated, not chosen.
cards.reference: Larcom, Rauch & Willems, The benefits of forced experimentation: striking evidence from the London Underground network, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2017

cards.question: Why can an if-then plan built around 'I will not eat crisps' backfire on a snacking habit?
cards.answer: It rehearses the very link it means to cut. Adriaanse and colleagues found that plans negating a habit, such as 'if I watch television, I will not eat crisps', worked worse than plans naming a replacement, and could tie the cue more tightly to the snack. The crisps stay in the plan.
cards.move: Name what to do instead, not only what to stop.
cards.reference: Adriaanse, van Oosten, de Ridder, de Wit & Evers, Planning what not to eat: ironic effects of implementation intentions negating unhealthy habits, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2011

cards.question: Among people quitting smoking, how many of those who slip and smoke once go on to return to regular smoking?
cards.answer: The large majority. Brandon and colleagues followed quitters after treatment and found about nine in ten who lapsed returned to regular smoking. Whether the first cigarette causes the fall or marks someone already struggling is still argued. Either way, a slip is rarely an isolated event: it is usually the first of many.
cards.move: Treat the first exception as the start of a pattern, not a one-off.
cards.trap: A small minority, since one cigarette seems a separate event from the rest.
cards.reference: Brandon, Tiffany, Obremski & Baker, Postcessation cigarette use: the process of relapse, Addictive Behaviors, 1990

cards.question: Should health services pay smokers cash rewards for staying off cigarettes?
cards.answer: Money works where exhortation fails. In Volpp and colleagues' trial, employees offered up to $750 were about three times as likely to have quit 9 to 12 months on, 14.7% against 5.0%, and the gap held after payments ended. Each quitter saves a health system far more than the reward costs.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is what happens after the last payment.
cards.counterpoint: The effect shrinks once the money stops: 15 to 18 months on, the same trial showed 9.4% against 3.6%. Payments reward some who would have quit anyway, strike many as unfair to those who never smoked, and may teach that health is a job done for wages. Free medication and counselling have firmer long-term records.
cards.reference: Volpp et al., A randomized, controlled trial of financial incentives for smoking cessation, New England Journal of Medicine, 2009

cards.question: Long before psychologists named confirmation bias, who described it in detail, and with what example?
cards.answer: Francis Bacon, in 1620. Once the mind adopts an opinion, he wrote, it draws all things to support it and neglects the rest. His example: a man shown temple paintings of sailors who prayed and survived shipwreck asked where those who prayed and drowned were painted. The negative instance, Bacon added, is the more forcible.
cards.move: Before counting the hits, ask where the misses are kept.
cards.reference: Bacon, The New Organon, ed. Jardine & Silverthorne, Cambridge University Press, 2000

cards.question: Are more intelligent people better at judging evidence that goes against their own side?
cards.answer: No better, on average. Myside bias, judging evidence by whether it favours one's own side, barely tracks intelligence. Asked whether a dangerous German car should be banned from American roads, or a dangerous American car from German ones, American students favoured banning the German car, and higher SAT scores made no difference.
cards.move: A sharp mind argues its side better, not more fairly.

cards.question: Told that 2-4-6 fits a hidden rule, people propose their own triples to test guesses. Why do most announce a wrong rule?
options: They test only triples their guess allows
The hidden rule is too complex to guess
They are allowed too few test triples
cards.answer: They test only triples their guess allows. The rule was simply any three rising numbers, so a guess like even numbers going up by two keeps earning yeses. Only a triple the guess forbids, such as 1-2-3, could expose it. Seeking yeses often works; it fails when the truth is broader than the guess.
cards.move: When every test says yes, ask whether a broader rule would say yes too.
cards.trap: Assuming people fail because the hidden rule must be complicated.
cards.source: Wason, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1960
cards.reference: Wason, On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1960

cards.question: True or false: correcting a false belief usually makes people cling to it harder?
cards.answer: False. Across five experiments with more than 10,100 people and 52 politically charged claims, corrections moved beliefs towards the facts, even among partisans who disliked them; none produced a backfire. The famous digging-in effect came from far smaller studies. The relative who never concedes at dinner is memorable, not typical.
cards.move: Judge persuasion by the average listener, not the loudest holdout.
cards.trap: Remembering arguments where someone dug in, and taking them as the rule.

cards.question: In standard psychology papers, 96% confirm their first hypothesis. In Registered Reports, accepted before any data exist, what share do?
cards.answer: Fewer than half: 31 of 71, or 44%, against 146 of 152 standard papers. When a journal commits to publishing before results exist, a yes is no longer the ticket to print, and nothing is gained by reporting only the analyses that give one. The 96% measures the road to publication.
cards.move: Ask whether the result was allowed to come out either way.
cards.trap: Reading the 96% as how often psychologists' hypotheses are simply correct.

cards.question: In the classic 1979 study where mixed evidence drove death-penalty views apart, how was the widening measured?
cards.answer: By asking people how far their views had shifted. Supporters and opponents read the same two studies, rated the one agreeing with them as better, and reported moving further apart. Later studies that measured attitudes directly, before and after, mostly found no widening. The biased rating held up; the polarisation lived largely in the self-report.
cards.move: When people say they changed, check whether anyone measured the before.
cards.source: Miller et al., J Personality Social Psychology, 1993
cards.reference: Miller, McHoskey, Bane & Dowd, The attitude polarization phenomenon: role of response measure, attitude extremity, and behavioral consequences of reported attitude change, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1993

cards.question: Cards show A, K, 2 and 3. To test the rule that an A never has a 2 behind it, which do most people turn?
options: A and 3, which fit the rule
cards.answer: A and 2, the ones named, which here is correct. Jonathan Evans showed in 1973 that people mostly turn the cards a rule mentions, whatever the logic. With the plain rule that habit looks like seeking confirmation; with the negated rule it looks like flawless falsification. The famous error was largely attention to named things.
cards.move: Change the question slightly and see whether the mistake follows the logic or the wording.
cards.trap: Expecting people to seek the cards that would confirm the rule.
cards.source: Evans & Lynch, British Journal of Psychology, 1973
cards.reference: Evans & Lynch, Matching bias in the selection task, British Journal of Psychology, 1973

cards.question: Five fingerprint experts saw a match each had made years before, told it was a notorious misidentification. How many still called it a match?
cards.answer: One. Itiel Dror and colleagues gave the experts prints they had themselves identified, with the story that these were a famous wrongful match by the FBI. Three now declared the prints did not match and one could not decide. Same ridges, same examiners, different verdicts, steered by what they expected to find.
cards.move: Hide the story from whoever checks the evidence until the checking is done.
cards.trap: Trusting experts to read their own verified work the same way twice.
cards.source: Dror, Charlton & Péron, Forensic Science International, 2006
cards.reference: Dror, Charlton & Péron, Contextual information renders experts vulnerable to making erroneous identifications, Forensic Science International, 2006

cards.question: True or false: in the 2-4-6 rule task, calling the feedback two named rules instead of yes and no roughly triples success?
cards.answer: True. In the standard task about one person in five names the rule at the first attempt. When Tweney and colleagues said each triple fitted either a rule called DAX or one called MED, about 60% did. Hunting for MED examples sent people outside their own guess, so disconfirming felt like confirming.
cards.move: To test a belief, go looking for evidence of its rival.
cards.trap: Assuming a mere change of labels cannot change how people reason.
cards.source: Tweney et al., Quarterly J Experimental Psychology, 1980
cards.reference: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1080/00335558008248237

cards.question: Is favouring one's own side a defect of reasoning, or a feature that works in groups?
cards.answer: A defect. Doctors, analysts and investors mostly reason alone or among colleagues who already agree, and there myside bias does its damage unchecked. No opponent is guaranteed to turn up. A faculty that works well only when someone else happens to challenge it is a faculty with a flaw, and training should aim at it.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether anyone is there to argue back.
cards.counterpoint: A feature. Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber argue reasoning evolved to make and judge arguments among others: people are lazy critics of their own reasons and sharp critics of other people's. Groups that argue solve logic problems, such as Wason's card task, that most individuals fail. Spread across a debate, the bias becomes a division of labour.
cards.source: Mercier & Sperber, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2011
cards.reference: Mercier & Sperber, Why do humans reason? Arguments for an argumentative theory, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2011

cards.question: In diaries of everyday life, how much of what people did was repeated almost daily in the same place?
cards.answer: About 43%. Wood, Quinn and Kashy had students record what they were doing, thinking and feeling at intervals through the day. Acts done nearly every day in a stable setting made up roughly two-fifths of the entries, and during them thoughts were usually elsewhere. The setting ran the routine while the mind wandered.
cards.move: Change the setting and a routine loses the thing that was running it.
cards.reference: Wood, Quinn & Kashy, Habits in everyday life: thought, emotion, and action, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002

cards.question: At a cinema, people who habitually eat popcorn there were handed week-old stale popcorn. How much did they eat?
cards.answer: About as much as fresh. Neal and colleagues found habitual cinema snackers ate stale popcorn as readily as fresh during a film, though they disliked it. In a meeting room, the same people ate less of it, and eating with the non-dominant hand broke the pattern. The cinema, not the taste, was steering the hand.
cards.move: When behaviour ignores the reason given for it, look at the setting.
cards.trap: Assuming people eat a snack mainly because of how it tastes.
cards.source: Neal et al., Pers Soc Psychol Bulletin, 2011
cards.reference: Neal, Wood, Wu & Kurlander, The pull of the past: when do habits persist despite conflict with motives?, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2011

cards.question: How can an experimenter tell whether a rat pressing a lever is acting from habit or for a goal?
cards.answer: Spoil the reward and watch. In Adams's experiments, rats learned to press a lever for sugar, which was then made sickening by pairing it with nausea. Briefly trained rats stopped pressing; heavily trained ones went on pressing for a reward they no longer wanted. A habit is the act that outlives its reason.
cards.move: To learn why something is done, remove the reason and see what continues.
cards.reference: Adams, Variations in the sensitivity of instrumental responding to reinforcer devaluation, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1982

cards.question: Employees were mailed a flu-clinic reminder; some were also asked to write the date and time they would go. By how much did vaccination rise?
cards.answer: About 4 percentage points. In Milkman and colleagues' study, about 33% of employees who got only the reminder were vaccinated, against about 37% of those prompted to note a date and time. Tying the act to a moment on the calendar helped, but most of those 37% would have gone anyway.
cards.move: Most of what follows a nudge would have happened without it.
cards.trap: Crediting the plan with everyone who got the jab afterwards.

diagram.caption: Of 37 in 100 vaccinated, 33 would have gone anyway; writing a date added 4.

cards.reference: Milkman, Beshears, Choi, Laibson & Madrian, Using implementation intentions prompts to enhance influenza vaccination rates, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2011

cards.question: True or false: for acts done often in a stable setting, past behaviour predicts what people do next better than their intentions?
cards.answer: True. Ouellette and Wood's meta-analysis found that for frequent acts in stable settings, like buckling a seatbelt, past behaviour predicted future behaviour directly and intentions added little. For rare or shifting acts, like giving blood, intentions did most of the predicting. What someone did last Tuesday outranks what they meant to do.
cards.move: To predict a routine, ask what was done yesterday, not what is planned.
cards.trap: Assuming people do what they intend, since that is how choosing feels.
cards.reference: Ouellette & Wood, Habit and intention in everyday life: the multiple processes by which past behavior predicts future behavior, Psychological Bulletin, 1998

cards.question: True or false: extended training in the lab reliably makes people keep working for a snack they no longer want?
cards.answer: False. Rats do it, and a 2009 human study reported it after three days of training. De Wit and colleagues then tried five times to induce it in people, with longer training and varied designs; none worked. Failures like these rarely reach print, so a lone success can stand for years.
cards.move: Ask how many attempts failed quietly before trusting the one that worked.
cards.trap: True, since the rat result and one human study seem to settle it.
cards.source: de Wit et al., JEP: General, 2018
cards.reference: de Wit et al., Shifting the balance between goals and habits: five failures in experimental habit induction, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2018

cards.question: When students moved to a new university, what decided whether an old exercise habit carried on?
cards.answer: Whether the setting still looked like the old one. Wood, Tam and Witt followed transfer students. Where cues stayed similar, such as the same kind of place, the habit continued whatever the students now intended. Where cues changed, behaviour followed intentions again. A new gym put the choice back in their hands.
cards.move: A change of scenery hands the decision back to the person.
cards.reference: Wood, Tam & Witt, Changing circumstances, disrupting habits, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2005

cards.question: Should shops be barred from placing sweets and crisps at the checkout?
cards.answer: The till is a cue placed where a queue, a bored child and an empty hand meet. Ejlerskov and colleagues found British households bought about 15% fewer small packs of sweets and crisps a year after their supermarkets cleared checkouts. England restricted such placement from 2022. Few measures reach so many shoppers so cheaply.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether removed cues cut intake or relocate it.
cards.counterpoint: Moving the sweets may only move the purchase. That study counted small packs, not total sugar eaten, and a family can buy a larger bag in the next aisle. A rule on placement burdens small shops, invites loopholes, and targets a cue that a shopping list or a snack from home already removes.
cards.reference: Ejlerskov, Sharp, Stead, Adamson, White & Adams, Supermarket policies on less-healthy food at checkouts: natural experimental evaluation using interrupted time series analyses of purchases, PLoS Medicine, 2018

cards.question: Shown pictures of cigarettes or drugs, which response in people with addictions moves the most?
cards.answer: Their reported craving. Carter and Tiffany pooled cue-reactivity studies: drug cues raised self-reported craving strongly, while heart rate and sweat responses rose only a little. The cue speaks loudest to the want itself. A glimpse of a lighter can bring on the urge while the pulse barely changes.
cards.move: The body's signals are not always the truest measure of a pull.
cards.trap: Their heart rate, since the body seems to react before the mind admits it.
cards.reference: Carter & Tiffany, Meta-analysis of cue-reactivity in addiction research, Addiction, 1999

cards.question: Does being persuaded to vote once make a person likelier to vote in the next election, unprompted?
cards.answer: Yes. Gerber, Green and Shachar used a randomised canvassing campaign before the 1998 elections in New Haven. The people it nudged to the polls were also likelier to vote in the 1999 local election, though nobody contacted them again. Voting once seems to build a habit, with election day as the cue.
cards.move: Getting someone to do a thing once can outlast the reason they did it.
cards.reference: Gerber, Green & Shachar, Voting may be habit-forming: evidence from a randomized field experiment, American Journal of Political Science, 2003

cards.question: Where does the popular claim that refocusing after an interruption takes about 23 minutes come from?
cards.answer: From timing something else. Gloria Mark's team shadowed office workers and found that an interrupted project was picked up again, on average, roughly 25 minutes later, after about two other tasks in between. That is how long the work sat waiting, not how long a mind takes to settle after a ping.
cards.move: A duration means little until you know when the clock started and stopped.
cards.reference: Mark, González & Harris, No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work, Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 2005

cards.question: What kind of background sound most disrupts memorising a string of digits, even when it is ignored?
cards.answer: Sound that keeps changing, speech above all. In serial recall, unattended speech hurts even in a language the listener does not know, while steady noise does little, and loudness matters less than change. Shifting syllables break into the silent rehearsal that holds the order: an overheard phone call costs more than a louder, steady fan.
cards.move: Steady noise can be tuned out; variation keeps claiming the ear.
cards.reference: Salamé & Baddeley, Disruption of short-term memory by unattended speech: implications for the structure of working memory, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 1982

cards.question: In a 16-hour waking day, roughly how many hours is the mind on something other than the task at hand?
cards.move: What happens a few seconds at a time can add up to a working day.
cards.trap: Picturing mind-wandering as rare lapses rather than a default state.
cards.hint: Imagine a phone pinging at random: how often would it catch you elsewhere?
steps: Phone check-ins with 2,250 adults found minds wandering in 46.9% of samples.
A waking day is about 16 hours.
cards.reference: Killingsworth & Gilbert, A wandering mind is an unhappy mind, Science, 2010

cards.question: True or false: repeated tests confirm that a silent phone lying face-down on the desk lowers working-memory scores?
cards.answer: False. In 2017 Ward and colleagues reported that a phone on the desk, even silent and face-down, lowered working-memory scores compared with one left in another room. When Ruiz Pardo and Minda repeated the design in 2022, they found no reliable effect. The phone on the desk turned out to weigh less than the headline.
cards.move: Expect the first dramatic result on any question to shrink when repeated.
cards.trap: Taking a striking first result as the true size of the effect.
cards.reference: Ruiz Pardo & Minda, Reexamining the brain drain effect: a replication of Ward et al. (2017), Acta Psychologica, 2022

cards.question: Should secondary schools ban pupils' phones for the whole school day?
cards.answer: A phone within reach competes with every lesson, and the pupils least able to afford distraction pay most. After English schools banned phones, Beland and Murphy found test scores rose about 6% of a standard deviation, over twice that for the lowest achievers. A whole-day rule is also easier to enforce.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether the harm happens in school hours.
cards.counterpoint: The English gains come from schools that chose to ban, often alongside other changes, so the cause is uncertain. A 2025 comparison of 30 English secondary schools found pupils under restrictive rules no better on wellbeing, sleep or grades than those under permissive ones; what tracked worse outcomes was more total phone and social media time.
cards.reference: Beland & Murphy, Ill communication: technology, distraction and student performance, Labour Economics, 2016

cards.question: True or false: people who multitask the most, such as phoning while driving, are the ones best able to do it?
cards.answer: False. Sanbonmatsu and colleagues found that those who multitasked most scored lower on a test of juggling tasks in mind, while rating their own ability higher. Frequent multitaskers also scored higher on impulsivity and sensation seeking. The habit tracks a temperament that finds single tasks dull, not a talent that makes several easy.
cards.move: Ask what kind of person chooses a behaviour before crediting the behaviour with a skill.
cards.trap: True, because practice at anything should make people better at it.
cards.reference: Sanbonmatsu, Strayer, Medeiros-Ward & Watson, Who multi-tasks and why? Multi-tasking ability, perceived multi-tasking ability, impulsivity, and sensation seeking, PLoS ONE, 2013

cards.question: In a driving simulator, which conversation hurt driving more: one with a passenger, or one on a hands-free phone?
cards.answer: The hands-free phone call. Drews, Pasupathi and Strayer asked talking drivers to leave the motorway at a rest stop. Those on the phone missed the exit far more often. A passenger sees the road too, pausing the talk when traffic thickens and sometimes pointing out the exit. The caller talks on, blind to the lorry.
cards.move: A helper who shares the view is worth more than one who shares the words.
cards.trap: Neither, since a conversation seems equally demanding wherever the other person sits.
cards.reference: Drews, Pasupathi & Strayer, Passenger and cell phone conversations in simulated driving, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 2008

cards.question: True or false: an interruption lasting under three seconds can double the errors people make in a step-by-step task?
cards.answer: True. Altmann, Trafton and Hambrick broke into a sequence of steps with a brief typing task: interruptions averaging 2.8 seconds roughly doubled errors on resuming, and about 4.4 seconds tripled them. The place in the sequence was lost, not time. A nurse glancing at a monitor mid-dose can lose the step.
cards.move: Judge an interruption by what it knocks loose, not by how long it lasts.
cards.trap: False, because a pause that short leaves almost no time to forget.
cards.reference: Altmann, Trafton & Hambrick, Momentary interruptions can derail the train of thought, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

cards.question: In seven hours at a computer, roughly how many times does an office worker's attention switch to a different screen?
cards.move: A small number repeated all day is a large number by evening.
cards.trap: Assuming people stay on one screen for several minutes at a time.
cards.hint: Work out the seconds in the day, then guess how long one screen holds attention.
steps: Seven hours is 7 × 3,600 = 25,200 seconds.
Measured attention on one screen averages about 47 seconds.
cards.reference: Mark, Attention Span: A Groundbreaking Way to Restore Balance, Happiness and Productivity, Hanover Square Press, 2023

cards.question: Why is overhearing one side of a phone call more distracting than overhearing both sides of a conversation?
cards.answer: Because the missing half cannot be predicted. Emberson and colleagues found that a half-conversation, or halfalogue, hurt performance on attention tasks more than the full dialogue did, though it held fewer words. Filtered to the same sounds but unintelligible, it did no extra harm. The mind keeps trying to fill the silences it cannot foresee.
cards.move: What cannot be predicted keeps pulling at the ear.
cards.reference: Emberson, Lupyan, Goldstein & Spivey, Overheard cell-phone conversations: when less speech is more distracting, Psychological Science, 2010

cards.question: Pooling eight studies that planted invented childhood events, how often did people come to remember the event?
cards.answer: About three times in ten. Scoboria and colleagues recoded 423 cases from eight studies with one scheme: 30.4% counted as false memories, and another 23% accepted the event without recalling it. Where the suggestion carried personal details and an instruction to imagine, with no photograph, the rate reached 46%.
cards.move: Ask whether a memory could have been assembled from what others told you.
cards.reference: Scoboria, Wade, Lindsay, Azad, Strange, Ost & Hyman, A mega-analysis of memory reports from eight peer-reviewed false memory implantation studies, Memory, 2017

cards.question: Did a 2015 study really lead 70% of students to remember committing a crime?
cards.answer: Not by a stricter test. Shaw and Porter counted 70% after three suggestive interviews. Recoding the same transcripts, Wade, Garry and Pezdek separated believing the story from recalling it, and only 26 to 30% met the bar for a false memory. The larger figure included people who believed but pictured little.
cards.move: Before quoting a rate, ask exactly what was counted as a case.

cards.question: A week after a crash film without broken glass, 32% asked about cars smashing recalled glass. What share of those asked nothing about speed did?
cards.answer: About one in eight. In Loftus and Palmer's 1974 study, 16 of 50 people in the smashed group reported glass, against 7 of 50 asked about cars hitting and 6 of 50 asked nothing. The loaded verb doubled false reports, but the crash alone already led some viewers to supply the glass.
cards.move: Before crediting the push, count what happens with no push at all.
cards.trap: Assuming false details appear only when someone plants them.
cards.reference: Loftus & Palmer, Reconstruction of automobile destruction: an example of the interaction between language and memory, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 1974

cards.question: True or false: after hearing a list of related words, people recall an unheard theme word nearly as often as heard ones?
cards.answer: True. Hear bed, rest, awake, tired, dream and ten more, and sleep, never spoken, comes back. In Roediger and McDermott's second experiment it was recalled 55% of the time, against 62% for words actually on the lists, and people often said they remembered hearing it.
cards.move: The more neatly a detail fits the story, the less its presence proves.
cards.trap: Trusting memory to keep what was heard apart from what was inferred.
cards.reference: Roediger & McDermott, Creating false memories: remembering words not presented in lists, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 1995

cards.question: True or false: memories of hearing the 9/11 news stayed more accurate than everyday memories from the same days?
cards.answer: False. On 12 September 2001, 54 Duke students wrote down how they heard the news and an ordinary recent event. Retested up to 32 weeks later, both accounts drifted by the same amount. What differed was confidence: vividness and belief in accuracy fell only for the ordinary memory.
cards.move: How clear a memory feels says little about whether it is right.
cards.trap: Taking a vivid, emotional memory for a well-recorded one.

cards.question: True or false: at a fair first lineup, most witnesses who declare high confidence have picked the right person?
cards.answer: True. Wixted and Wells's 2017 review found that at a first, fair, double-blind lineup, high-confidence picks were highly accurate, often above 90% correct in laboratory studies, while low-confidence picks were often wrong. The weak link between confidence and accuracy comes from certainty measured later, after feedback and rehearsal, by the time of the trial.
cards.move: Ask when a certainty was first measured, not how strong it sounds now.
cards.trap: False, because witness confidence is known to predict accuracy only weakly.
cards.reference: Wixted & Wells, The relationship between eyewitness confidence and identification accuracy: a new synthesis, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2017

cards.question: After hearing nurse, hospital, sick, medicine and similar words, which group most often recalls the unheard word doctor?
cards.answer: Adults. Brainerd, Reyna and Ceci reviewed studies in which false recall of the unheard theme word rose with age, from early childhood into adulthood. The error comes from grasping the meaning that links the list, and five-year-olds extract that gist less readily. The same children remain more suggestible when an interviewer leads them.
cards.move: A weakness in one skill can be armour against a particular error.
cards.trap: Children of about five, since young children are the most suggestible.
cards.reference: Brainerd, Reyna & Ceci, Developmental reversals in false memory: a review of data and theory, Psychological Bulletin, 2008

cards.question: How common is it to keep a vivid memory of an event one no longer believes happened?
cards.answer: Common enough: about a fifth of the people Mazzoni, Scoboria and Harvey surveyed reported at least one. These nonbelieved memories kept most of the sensory detail of believed ones. Belief was usually withdrawn because someone, often family, said the event never happened. The picture of the day stayed; the conviction behind it left.
cards.move: Seeing a scene clearly and believing it happened are separate verdicts.

cards.question: Should a criminal conviction ever rest on a single eyewitness identification alone?
cards.answer: Many crimes have one witness and no forensic trace; a corroboration rule would leave them unprosecutable, often assaults on the most vulnerable. A quick, confident first identification from a fair double-blind lineup is strong evidence. Courts should judge how the identification was obtained, not throw out a whole class of testimony.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is how the identification was first collected.
cards.counterpoint: Mistaken identification played a part in about 69% of the more than 375 DNA exonerations the Innocence Project counted in the United States from 1989 to 2020, more than any other factor. Those witnesses were sincere and jurors believed them. Evidence the defence cannot test after the fact should not convict on its own.
cards.reference: https://innocenceproject.org/dna-exonerations-in-the-united-states/

cards.question: Abuse memories recovered in suggestive therapy were compared with ones that returned spontaneously. Which could independent evidence corroborate?
cards.answer: Only those that returned spontaneously. Geraerts and colleagues sought independent corroboration: 37% of memories that came back unexpectedly outside therapy were confirmed, close to the 45% for memories never forgotten, against none of those recovered in suggestive therapy. How a memory comes back says more than whether it was ever lost.
cards.move: Sort cases by how they arose before judging them all together.
cards.trap: Neither kind, since recovered memories are known from discredited court cases.

cards.question: What could still terrify a patient who, with both amygdalae damaged, felt no fear of snakes or spiders?
cards.answer: Air laced with carbon dioxide. Asked to breathe 35% CO2, she and two other patients with the same damage all had panic attacks; only 3 of 12 healthy volunteers did. The amygdala seems to handle threats from outside the body. A threat sensed inside, like suffocation, reaches terror by another road.
cards.move: The part that handles most cases is not always the part that handles all.

cards.question: What switches on a baby's fear of heights?
cards.answer: Getting about on their own, not age. Lowered towards the deep side of a visual cliff, a glass sheet over a drop, infants of the same age reacted according to how long they had been crawling. Babies given practice in walkers grew wary early; one boy who could not move himself showed no wariness.
cards.move: Before calling something instinct, ask what experience arrived just before it.
cards.reference: Campos, Bertenthal & Kermoian, Early experience and emotional development: the emergence of wariness of heights, Psychological Science, 1992

cards.question: How short can successful therapy for a lifelong phobia of spiders or dogs be?
cards.answer: A single sitting of a few hours. In Öst's one-session treatment the patient approaches the feared animal step by step, for up to three hours. In his 1989 series of 20 patients, sessions averaged 2.1 hours, and about four years later 90% were much improved or recovered. Decades of fear, undone in a long afternoon.
cards.move: How long a problem has lasted says little about how long it takes to fix.
cards.reference: Öst, One-session treatment for specific phobias, Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1989

cards.question: Lab-raised monkeys watched videos of monkeys recoiling in fear, edited to show either toy snakes or flowers. What did they learn?
options: To fear whichever object was on screen
To fear the snakes, but not the flowers
Nothing: fear needs a real encounter
cards.answer: To fear the snakes, but not the flowers. The fearful behaviour on screen was identical; only the object had been spliced in. Observers came to fear toy snakes and a toy crocodile, and did not come to fear flowers or a toy rabbit. The same lesson stuck to one object and slid off the other.
cards.move: Some lessons stick at the first telling because the learner was built for them.
cards.trap: Assuming a watching monkey copies any fear, whatever its object.
cards.source: Cook & Mineka, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 1989
cards.reference: Cook & Mineka, Observational conditioning of fear to fear-relevant versus fear-irrelevant stimuli in rhesus monkeys, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 1989

cards.question: True or false: exposure therapy cures a phobia by erasing the fear memory behind it?
cards.answer: False. Exposure lays down a second memory, that the feared thing is now safe, which competes with the first instead of deleting it. The new memory is tied to where it was learned: in rats and in people, extinguished fear returns when tested elsewhere. A phobia beaten in the clinic can be waiting at home.
cards.move: Suppressed is not deleted, so test the fix where it will be used.
cards.trap: The fear has gone, so the memory behind it must be gone.
cards.reference: https://learnmem.cshlp.org/content/11/5/485.full.pdf

cards.question: Does the amygdala produce the conscious feeling of being afraid?
cards.answer: Probably not, argues Joseph LeDoux, who mapped its threat circuits. Shown snakes or angry faces too briefly to be seen, people still sweat and the amygdala responds, yet they report no fear. On his view it runs the defence; cortical circuits build the feeling. The palms can brace for a snake the eyes never saw.
cards.move: A body reacting and a person feeling are two measurements, not one.
cards.source: LeDoux & Pine, American Journal of Psychiatry, 2016
cards.reference: LeDoux & Pine, Using neuroscience to help understand fear and anxiety: a two-system framework, American Journal of Psychiatry, 2016

cards.question: Of 298 women seen at a Stockholm clinic within a month of a sexual assault, how many said they could not move during it?
cards.answer: About 7 in 10. 70% reported significant tonic immobility, an involuntary paralysis under extreme fear, and 48% an extreme degree of it. Those who froze were more likely to have post-traumatic stress disorder and severe depression months later. The body had chosen stillness before the mind could choose anything.
cards.move: Before judging how someone reacted to danger, ask whether their body let them choose.
cards.trap: Picturing fear as fight or flight, the version films show.

cards.question: True or false: in a New Zealand birth cohort, children who had serious falls before age 9 feared heights more at 18?
cards.answer: False. The Dunedin study, following about a thousand people from birth, found no link between early falls and fear of heights at 11 or 18. The falls happened mostly to children without the fear, and those who feared heights at 18 had climbed least as children. The fear was there before any lesson.
cards.move: Before tracing a fear to a bad experience, check the people who never had one.
cards.trap: Assuming a painful fall is how a fear of heights is learned.
cards.source: Poulton et al., Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1998
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9648329/

cards.question: True or false: exposure therapy for a phobia only works if the fear subsides before each session ends?
cards.answer: False. How far fear falls within a session predicts the outcome months later poorly; patients still frightened at the end can improve as much. Michelle Craske's team argues that what counts is learning that the feared outcome did not come. The lesson is that the dog did not bite, not that the heart slowed.
cards.move: Judge a treatment by what lasts, not by how the session felt.
cards.trap: Taking calm at the end of a session as the sign of cure.
cards.source: Craske et al., Behaviour Research and Therapy, 2008
cards.reference: Craske, Kircanski, Zelikowsky, Mystkowski, Chowdhury & Baker, Optimizing inhibitory learning during exposure therapy, Behaviour Research and Therapy, 2008

cards.question: In 1934 Bregman tried Watson's loud-noise method on 15 infants, with wooden blocks and curtains instead of a rat. How many learned fear?
cards.answer: None of them. Bregman failed to condition fear of a single object in any infant. Watson's success rested on one child and a furry animal; later work on preparedness found fear attaches readily to snakes, spiders and heights, barely to furniture. The textbooks kept the rat and lost the curtains.
cards.move: A classic is one success; ask how many attempts were never retold.
cards.trap: Treating the one famous success as what the method usually does.
cards.reference: Bregman, An attempt to modify the emotional attitudes of infants by the conditioned response technique, Journal of Genetic Psychology, 1934

cards.question: True or false: when working adults were paged at random, flow turned up more often at work than in free time?
cards.answer: True. Csikszentmihalyi and LeFevre paged workers at random moments for a week. Flow, high challenge met by high skill, appeared in 54% of reports from work and 18% of those from leisure, much of which went on television. Yet at work people more often said they wished to be doing something else.
cards.move: Where a feeling was first studied is not where it mostly happens.
cards.trap: Picturing flow as climbers and chess players, the cases first studied.
cards.reference: Csikszentmihalyi & LeFevre, Optimal experience in work and leisure, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1989

cards.question: What habit of painters at work first pointed Csikszentmihalyi towards the idea of flow?
cards.answer: They lost interest in the finished canvas. Watching art students in the 1960s, he saw them work for hours, ignoring hunger and fatigue, then set the completed picture aside and begin another. If the finished work were the reward, it should have held their attention most. The reward seemed to lie in the painting itself.
cards.move: When people ignore the prize they worked for, look at the work itself.
cards.reference: Csikszentmihalyi, Beyond Boredom and Anxiety, Jossey-Bass, 1975

cards.question: Is an easy task matched to modest skill enough to produce flow?
cards.answer: No. The first model placed flow wherever challenge matched skill. When Massimini and Carli in Milan sampled people's daily lives, easy tasks met with low skill felt apathetic, not absorbing. Flow appeared only when both challenge and skill ran above the person's own average. Folding laundry is perfectly matched to ability, and dull.
cards.move: Balance is not enough; both the demand and the ability have to be high.
cards.reference: Massimini & Carli, The systematic assessment of flow in daily experience, in Csikszentmihalyi & Csikszentmihalyi (eds), Optimal Experience, Cambridge University Press, 1988

cards.question: In a lab study that stressed people before a task, at what level of bodily arousal was flow highest?
cards.answer: At moderate arousal. Peifer and colleagues put people through a stress test, then tracked cortisol and heart activity during a demanding task. Flow rose with arousal up to a point, then fell away, tracing an inverted U. The mind may feel effortless in flow while the body is working hard.
cards.move: How easy something feels says little about how hard the body is working.
cards.trap: Reading flow's calm, effortless feel as a body at rest.
cards.source: Peifer et al., J Experimental Social Psychology, 2014
cards.reference: Peifer, Schulz, Schächinger, Baumann & Antoni, The relation of flow-experience and physiological arousal under stress: can u shape it?, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2014

cards.question: Should apps and games be deliberately designed to keep their users in a state of flow?
cards.answer: Flow is among the most satisfying states people report, and it comes from clear goals, quick feedback and a challenge matched to skill. Software can supply all three better than most jobs or classrooms, adjusting difficulty moment by moment. Designing for absorption is simply designing things people find worth doing.
cards.move: The hinge is whether absorption is judged by itself or by what it serves.
cards.counterpoint: The same recipe powers slot machines. Natasha Dow Schüll's interviews with Las Vegas gamblers describe players seeking the zone, where time, money and self fall away, and machines tuned to keep play continuous. Flow does not check whether the activity is good for the person in it; a design that maximises it maximises time spent, whatever the cost.
cards.reference: Schüll, Addiction by Design: Machine Gambling in Las Vegas, Princeton University Press, 2012

cards.question: Do people in flow report feeling happy while it is happening?
cards.answer: Not at the time. Csikszentmihalyi noted that someone deep in a task has no attention spare for checking their feelings; to notice happiness they would have to step out of the absorption. The glow is reported afterwards, looking back. A climber on a hard pitch is thinking about the next hold, not about joy.
cards.move: Some good states can only be recognised once they have ended.
cards.reference: Csikszentmihalyi, Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience, Harper & Row, 1990

cards.question: How much of the difference between people in how readily they fall into flow is down to their genes?
cards.answer: Roughly a third, by one large twin study. Mosing and colleagues asked thousands of Swedish twins how often they felt flow at work, at home and at leisure. Identical twins resembled each other more than non-identical ones, putting the heritable share at roughly 30%. The rest lay in experiences not shared.
cards.move: A trait can run in families without being settled at birth.
cards.source: Mosing et al., Twin Res Hum Genet, 2012
cards.reference: Mosing, Magnusson, Pedersen, Nakamura, Madison & Ullén, Heritability of proneness for psychological flow experiences, Twin Research and Human Genetics, 2012

cards.question: Should practice aimed at mastery be designed to feel like flow?
cards.answer: Mastery takes thousands of hours, and nobody sustains that without wanting to come back. Flow arises from clear goals, instant feedback and a stretch just beyond skill, which are also the conditions good practice needs. A learner absorbed in the task keeps going through the long middle years in which most people quit.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether improvement needs failure to feel bad.
cards.counterpoint: Ericsson's work on expert violinists holds that improvement comes from solitary practice at the edge of failure, fixing specific weaknesses: effortful work he described as not inherently enjoyable. Flow thrives when skill already meets the challenge, so seeking it steers practice back towards what one can already do: the favourite piece, played well again.
cards.reference: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer, The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance, Psychological Review, 1993

cards.question: Students rated flow reached alone and flow reached with other people. Which kind did they rate as more enjoyable?
cards.answer: Flow reached with others. Walker compared flow in solitary activities, in ones done alongside others, and in ones needing interaction, like a team game. Social flow was rated more enjoyable than solitary flow, and interactive flow most of all. Picture a band locked into a groove.
cards.move: The picture that comes to mind first is not a survey of the cases.
cards.trap: Flow reached alone, because absorption calls up the lone painter or coder.
cards.reference: Walker, Experiencing flow: is doing it together better than doing it alone?, Journal of Positive Psychology, 2010

cards.question: True or false: Chinese students, like American ones, felt most intrinsically motivated when a task's challenge matched their skill?
cards.answer: False. In Moneta's 2004 study of students in Hong Kong, intrinsic motivation peaked when skill exceeded challenge, a comfortable state the flow model calls relaxation, not in the matched high zone that American samples favoured. A model built on one population had been read as a law of minds.
cards.move: Before calling a finding universal, ask who was in the room.
cards.trap: True, because a model of optimal experience sounds like a human universal.
cards.reference: Moneta, The flow model of intrinsic motivation in Chinese: cultural and personal moderators, Journal of Happiness Studies, 2004

cards.question: True or false: most radiologists searching lung scans for nodules missed a gorilla drawn into the images?
cards.answer: True. Drew, Võ and Wolfe inserted a gorilla 48 times the size of a typical nodule into a chest CT, and 20 of 24 radiologists missed it. Eye tracking showed that most of those who missed it had looked straight at it. Hunting for small round nodules, they did not register an ape.
cards.move: Expertise sharpens what you look for and blinds you to the rest.
cards.trap: Expecting trained experts, looking carefully, to see anything that large.
cards.reference: Drew, Võ & Wolfe, The invisible gorilla strikes again: sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers, Psychological Science, 2013

cards.question: Listeners with high or low working memory repeated one voice aloud while their name was played in the ignored ear. Which group noticed it more?
cards.answer: The low group. Working memory here means holding information in mind while shutting out distraction. Conway, Cowan and Bunting found that 65% of low scorers heard their own name in the channel they had been told to ignore, against 20% of high scorers. Hearing it meant attention had leaked away from the task.
cards.move: Noticing everything can be a sign of weak control, not keen awareness.
cards.trap: Assuming a better memory catches more of what goes past.
cards.reference: Conway, Cowan & Bunting, The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: the importance of working memory capacity, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2001

cards.question: In a rapid stream of letters, why is a second target often missed when it follows the first closely?
cards.answer: Attention is still busy with the first. At about ten items a second, a second target arriving 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first is often missed, while one arriving immediately after is usually caught. Raymond, Shapiro and Arnell named this gap the attentional blink: the eyes stay open while the mind looks away.
cards.move: Right after catching one thing is the worst moment to catch another.
cards.reference: Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell, Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: an attentional blink?, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 1992

cards.question: How soon does attention start to fail during a long watch for rare signals?
cards.answer: Within the first half hour. At the RAF's request, Norman Mackworth had people watch a clock hand that jumped every second and report its rare double jumps. Misses rose within 30 minutes and kept rising over a two-hour watch. Nothing on the dial had changed except the time spent staring at it.
cards.move: Schedule the relief before the watcher feels tired, not after.
cards.reference: Mackworth, The breakdown of vigilance during prolonged visual search, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1948

cards.question: Volunteers searched bag images for tools. How did their misses change when tools appeared in 1% of bags rather than half?
cards.answer: They rose about fourfold. Wolfe, Horowitz and Kenner found observers missed about 7% of targets when half the bags held one, and about 30% when targets were rare. Searchers learned to answer no quickly and quit each bag sooner, so the rare knife was the one most likely to slip through.
cards.move: The rarer the thing you search for, the sooner you stop looking.
cards.trap: Expecting a rare target to stand out, so vigilance sharpens.
cards.reference: Wolfe, Horowitz & Kenner, Rare items often missed in visual searches, Nature, 2005

cards.question: How many identical dots, drifting among identical decoys, can a person keep track of at once?
cards.answer: Anywhere from one to eight. Alvarez and Franconeri found observers tracked about eight dots when they moved slowly, and only one when they moved fast. Franconeri later argued that speed matters mainly by bringing targets close to decoys. The limit belongs to the display as much as to the mind.
cards.move: Before quoting a capacity, ask under what conditions it was measured.
cards.trap: About four, the capacity figure textbooks give for tracking.
cards.reference: Alvarez & Franconeri, How many objects can you track? Evidence for a resource-limited attentive tracking mechanism, Journal of Vision, 2007

cards.question: Why does a flash at one spot first speed up, then slow down, responses to a target there?
cards.answer: Attention jumps to the flash, then is steered away from it. Posner and Cohen found targets at a flashed spot were detected faster for roughly the first 150 milliseconds, but more slowly after about 300, when nothing had appeared there. This inhibition of return keeps a searching eye from rechecking where it just looked.
cards.move: A quick second look at the same place is usually wasted.
cards.source: Posner & Cohen, Attention and Performance X, 1984
cards.reference: Posner & Cohen, Components of visual orienting, in Bouma & Bouwhuis (eds), Attention and Performance X, Erlbaum, 1984

cards.question: A visual search task is made harder by adding more items to scan. What happens to interference from an irrelevant flanking letter?
options: It grows, as focus gets stretched
It shrinks, as spare capacity runs out
cards.answer: It shrinks. In Lavie's load theory, a crowded display uses up perception, leaving none to process the distractor. Loading working memory does the reverse: holding digits in mind increased flanker interference in Lavie and colleagues' 2004 study, because control of what gets in weakened. Busy eyes filter well; a busy mind filters badly.
cards.move: Ask which part of the system is busy before predicting what leaks through.
cards.trap: It grows, since a harder task seems to make focus more fragile.
cards.reference: Lavie, Hirst, de Fockert & Viding, Load theory of selective attention and cognitive control, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2004

cards.question: Scanning 30 items at 40 ms each and stopping at a randomly placed target, how many ms longer is 'absent' than an average 'present'?
cards.move: Proving something is absent takes far longer than finding it.
cards.trap: 600, taking an average 'present' to need exactly 15 checks.
cards.hint: Ask at which position, on average, a randomly placed target turns up.
steps: 'Absent' needs every item checked: 30 × 40 = 1,200 ms.
'Present': the target is equally likely at positions 1 to 30, so on average (1 + 30) / 2 = 15.5 checks.
cards.reference: Treisman & Gelade, A feature-integration theory of attention, Cognitive Psychology, 1980
