cards.question: People tracking white shapes miss an unexpected cross. What property of the cross decides whether they see it?
cards.answer: How closely it resembles what they are tracking. Most and colleagues had people follow white shapes and ignore black ones. An unexpected white cross was usually noticed; a black one, matching the ignored set, was mostly missed, and grey fell between. Attention filters by feature, and the filter hides whatever matches the rejected pile.
cards.move: What gets missed is whatever looks like the things being ignored.
cards.reference: Most, Simons, Scholl, Jimenez, Clifford & Chabris, How not to be seen: the contribution of similarity and selective ignoring to sustained inattentional blindness, Psychological Science, 2001

cards.question: How did Ebbinghaus measure a memory he could no longer recall at all?
cards.answer: By timing how fast he relearned it. Lists of nonsense syllables that he could no longer recite a day later took about a third less effort to learn again; a month later, about a fifth less. Material that felt entirely gone still left a trace a stopwatch could find.
cards.move: Being unable to recall something is not the same as having lost it.
cards.reference: Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology, trans. Ruger & Bussenius, Teachers College, Columbia University, 1913

cards.question: When Ebbinghaus's forgetting experiment was repeated in 2015, what bump appeared in the curve, and at what delay?
cards.answer: A rise at 24 hours. One of the authors spent 70 hours learning and relearning syllable lists, and retention after a day was higher than the smooth curve from shorter delays predicted. The authors point to sleep. The 1880s data flatten at the same spot: 36% saved after nine hours, 34% after a day.
cards.move: Before smoothing a curve, check whether its lumps sit where something happens.

diagram.caption: Ebbinghaus's curve flattens overnight: 36% saved after nine hours, still 34% after a day.

cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0120644

cards.question: True or false: of two memories equally strong today, the more recent one will fade more slowly?
cards.answer: False. The older one fades more slowly. Forgetting is fastest just after learning and slows with time, so a memory that has already lasted sits on the flat part of its curve. Adolf Jost stated this in 1897. A fact from years ago that is as clear as last week's is the safer bet.
cards.move: What has lasted a long time has already passed the tests that remove most things.
cards.trap: Assuming fresh means firm, because new memories feel vivid.
cards.reference: Wixted, The psychology and neuroscience of forgetting, Annual Review of Psychology, 2004

cards.question: What happens over the next fifty years to Spanish learned at school and never used again?
cards.answer: It falls for three to six years, then stops falling. Harry Bahrick tested 733 former students: what survived the first years stayed roughly level for up to 30 years before a last decline in old age. How much survived depended on how well it was first learned, since most had barely practised since.
cards.move: The first years of loss say little about what the next thirty hold.
cards.reference: Bahrick, Semantic memory content in permastore: fifty years of memory for Spanish learned in school, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 1984

cards.question: To remember a set of facts for a year, when should one single review session follow the first study?
cards.answer: About a month later. In a study of more than 1,350 people, the best gap between study and review grew with the wait until the test: 20 to 40% of a one-week wait, but only 5 to 10% of a year. For a test a year away, that is three to five weeks.
cards.move: Space the practice to match how long the result has to last.
cards.trap: Reviewing the next day, while the material still feels fresh.

cards.question: True or false: averaging many people's forgetting curves can produce a shape that none of the individual curves has?
cards.answer: True. Suppose each person forgets exponentially, losing a fixed share per hour, but people differ in their rate. The group average then sags into a power curve: steep at first, then a long flat tail. Murre and Chessa proved it mathematically in 2011. A law found in the average may describe nobody in the room.
cards.move: Check a pattern in the individuals before crediting the average with it.
cards.trap: False: an average of similar curves should look like each of them.

cards.question: Once students could recall a Swahili word, which extra practice raised their recall of it a week later?
cards.answer: Retesting it. In Karpicke and Roediger's study, words that kept being tested were recalled about 80% of the time a week later; words dropped from testing, about 35%, however often they were restudied. Restudying added nothing over dropping the word altogether. The students' own predictions barely differed between the conditions.
cards.move: Practise pulling the answer out, not putting it back in.
cards.trap: Restudying it, because seeing the answer again feels like learning.
cards.reference: Karpicke & Roediger, The critical importance of retrieval for learning, Science, 2008

cards.question: Ebbinghaus's savings were 44% an hour after learning, 25% after six days. What percentage of the six-day loss came within the first hour?
cards.move: Ask when the loss happened, not only how large it grew.
cards.trap: Comparing 44 with 25 and concluding most of the loss came later.
cards.hint: Savings start near 100% at the moment the list is mastered.
steps: Just after learning, savings are close to 100%.
Lost in the first hour: 100 − 44 = 56 points.
Lost over six days: 100 − 25 = 75 points.
cards.reference: Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology, trans. Ruger & Bussenius, Teachers College, Columbia University, 1913

cards.question: In a nine-year study of foreign vocabulary, what let half the review sessions do the work of twice as many?
cards.answer: Wider gaps between them. Harry Bahrick and three family members relearned 300 word pairs over years. Five years after training ended, 13 sessions held 56 days apart had kept about as many words as 26 sessions held 14 days apart. Words had partly faded before each session, and relearning them then counted for more.
cards.move: Let some of it fade before going over it again.

cards.question: Can repeated attempts to recall a list, with no restudy in between, make the total recalled rise?
cards.answer: Yes. Each attempt loses some items and recovers others missed before; when recoveries outnumber losses, net recall climbs, an effect called hypermnesia. Payne's 1987 review found it most reliably with pictures and vivid images, less with plain word lists. A curve built from one test per delay never sees the items that come back.
cards.move: Before recording a loss, try again later from another angle.
cards.reference: Payne, Hypermnesia and reminiscence in recall: a historical and empirical review, Psychological Bulletin, 1987

cards.question: Where was the halo effect first measured, and what gave it away?
cards.answer: In army officers' ratings of their own soldiers, published in 1920. Edward Thorndike found that marks for physique, intellect, leadership and character moved together far more than such different traits could; the correlations, he wrote, were too high and too even. A soldier who stood well also got judged clever.
cards.move: When every score on a sheet agrees, suspect one impression wrote them all.
cards.reference: Thorndike, A constant error in psychological ratings, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1920

cards.question: Can people tell when a halo is shaping their own judgement?
cards.answer: Rarely. Students watched one of two videos of a lecturer with a European accent, acting warm or cold. Those who saw him warm found his looks, mannerisms and accent appealing; those who saw him cold found them irritating. Both groups denied that liking him coloured those ratings; some insisted it ran the other way.
cards.move: Ask whether the reasons came before the liking or after it.

cards.question: Which qualities do people credit to good-looking strangers, and which do they not?
cards.answer: Social ease far more than virtue. Pooling studies of the beautiful-is-good stereotype, Alice Eagly's team found the boost from attractiveness was largest for social competence, middling for adjustment and intellect, and near zero for integrity and concern for others. Beauty buys the assumption of charm, not of honesty.
cards.move: An impression spreads to neighbouring traits first; check how far it has travelled.
cards.reference: Eagly, Ashmore, Makhijani & Longo, What is beautiful is good, but...: a meta-analytic review of research on the physical attractiveness stereotype, Psychological Bulletin, 1991

cards.question: The business press calls a thriving firm's culture strong and its boss decisive. After profits fall, how are those same traits described?
cards.answer: As rigid and reckless. Phil Rosenzweig showed business writers re-describing firms whose cultures and leaders had not changed, only their results: a strong culture became rigid, decisiveness became recklessness. Studies that rate culture once the results are known inherit the same tint. The results paint the traits said to explain them.
cards.move: Rate the process before learning the result, or the result will rate it.
cards.trap: Culture changes slowly, so the praise should survive a bad year.
cards.reference: Rosenzweig, The Halo Effect... and the Eight Other Business Delusions That Deceive Managers, Free Press, 2007

cards.question: True or false: a careful replication of Asch's 1946 warm-cold studies found warmth outweighing competence in first impressions?
cards.answer: False. Rerunning the Asch studies most cited as proof that warmth dominates impressions, researchers in 2014 found no primacy of warmth: how much it weighed depended on which other traits it came with. The textbook lesson does not readily follow even from Asch's own word lists.
cards.move: Reread the original before repeating what everyone says it showed.
cards.trap: Recalling the textbook lesson that warm or cold colours everything else.

cards.question: What happened when performance raters were trained to stop giving people matching scores across different traits?
cards.answer: Their ratings became less accurate. John Bernardin and Elaine Pence found that training raters to avoid halo, scoring each trait separately, spread the numbers out but moved them further from the truth. Real strengths often do cluster: a diligent worker is frequently an accurate one too. Some of what looked like error was signal.
cards.move: Before removing a pattern as bias, check whether the world contains it too.
cards.source: Bernardin & Pence, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1980
cards.reference: Bernardin & Pence, Effects of rater training: creating new response sets and decreasing accuracy, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1980

cards.question: In real small-claims courts, did a baby-faced defendant always do better than a mature-faced one?
cards.answer: No: it depended on the charge. Leslie Zebrowitz and Susan McDonald found baby-faced defendants more likely to win cases alleging intentional harm, and less likely to win cases alleging negligence. A face that looks innocent also looks naive and careless. The same round cheeks helped against one accusation and hurt against the other.
cards.move: A good impression is specific; ask which quality it is vouching for.
cards.source: Zebrowitz & McDonald, Law and Human Behavior, 1991
cards.reference: Zebrowitz & McDonald, The impact of litigants' baby-facedness and attractiveness on adjudications in small claims courts, Law and Human Behavior, 1991

cards.question: Given six-second clips of the top three finalists in music competitions, which version let people pick the real winner most often?
cards.answer: Silent video only. In Chia-Jung Tsay's experiments, novices and trained musicians picked winners above chance from silent clips, and at or below chance, one in three, with sound. Juries who believe they reward sound seem to reward visible passion. A 2018 replication confirmed it, but found it depends on which clips are chosen.
cards.move: Take away the channel you think you are judging, and see if verdicts change.
cards.trap: Assuming music is judged by ear, so sound must carry the verdict.
cards.reference: Tsay, Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2013

cards.question: Thousands of managers were each rated by bosses, peers and subordinates. How much of the variation in scores came from the raters themselves?
cards.answer: More than half. Steven Scullen, Michael Mount and Maynard Goff found each rater's own tendencies, general impression and leniency included, outweighed the managers' actual performance, which explained only about a fifth. Bosses, peers and subordinates each had their quirks. A rating is largely a portrait of the person holding the pen.
cards.move: Before reading a score as a measure of someone, ask who wrote it.
cards.trap: Assuming a rating mostly measures the person being rated.
cards.source: Scullen et al., Journal of Applied Psychology, 2000
cards.reference: Scullen, Mount & Goff, Understanding the latent structure of job performance ratings, Journal of Applied Psychology, 2000

cards.question: Plain-looking workers earn roughly 5 to 10% less. Taking 7.5% of a £30,000 salary over 40 years, what is the gap in thousands of pounds?
cards.answer: £90,000 = 90 thousand pounds.
cards.move: A small percentage that follows someone every year becomes a large sum.
cards.hint: Find one year's gap first, then stretch it across a career.
steps: Over 40 working years: 2,250 x 40 = £90,000.
£90,000 = 90 thousand pounds.
cards.reference: Hamermesh & Biddle, Beauty and the labor market, American Economic Review, 1994

cards.question: People with chronic insomnia say they are exhausted all day. Do they fall asleep faster in daytime nap tests?
cards.answer: No: as fast as good sleepers, or slower. Offered a series of daytime chances to nap under recording, people with insomnia typically take as long or longer to drop off, despite feeling drained. Their metabolic rate runs high around the clock too. They are tired but wired, aroused day and night.
cards.move: Feeling tired and being sleepy are different states; test which one it is.
cards.reference: Fernandez-Mendoza & Vgontzas, Insomnia and its impact on physical and mental health, Current Psychiatry Reports, 2013

cards.question: Can treating insomnia in older adults prevent depression?
cards.answer: In one trial it roughly halved new cases. Of 291 adults over 60 with insomnia but no depression, those given two months of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia developed major depression over three years at 12.2%, against 25.9% with sleep education alone. Those whose insomnia stayed in remission fared best.
cards.move: A symptom can also be a cause; treat it and watch what follows.
cards.reference: Irwin, Carrillo, Sadeghi et al., Prevention of incident and recurrent major depression in older adults with insomnia: a randomized clinical trial, JAMA Psychiatry, 2022

cards.question: When people with insomnia sleep in a laboratory, how does the recording compare with their own account?
cards.answer: It usually shows more sleep than they report. Many people with insomnia overestimate how long they took to fall asleep and how long they lay awake, and underestimate their total sleep, compared with brain recordings. The gap is part of the disorder: a night that felt sleepless can show hours of recorded sleep.
cards.move: Measure before trusting a feeling about how much of something happened.
cards.reference: Buysse, Insomnia, JAMA, 2013

cards.question: Which instruction is a core part of the leading non-drug treatment for chronic insomnia?
options: Go to bed earlier to catch up
cards.answer: Spend less time in bed. Sleep restriction, introduced by Arthur Spielman in 1987, first limits time in bed to roughly the time spent asleep, then extends it as sleep becomes efficient. Hours lying awake teach the brain that bed is a place for waking; a shorter window builds sleep pressure and knits sleep together.
cards.move: Sometimes the cure is less of what seems to be missing.
cards.trap: Going to bed earlier seems the obvious way to recover lost sleep.
cards.reference: Spielman, Saskin & Thorpy, Treatment of chronic insomnia by restriction of time in bed, Sleep, 1987

cards.question: Treating 13 older adults with sedatives yields one extra good sleeper; treating 6 yields one extra side effect. How many side effects per good sleeper?
cards.answer: 13 / 6 ≈ 2.2 side effects per good sleeper.
cards.move: Put benefits and harms over the same number of people before choosing.
cards.trap: Counting the people helped and never setting the harmed beside them.
cards.hint: Picture a group whose size divides by both 13 and 6, and count each outcome.
steps: Take 78 treated people, since 78 = 13 x 6.
78 / 13 = 6 extra good sleepers.
78 / 6 = 13 extra side effects.
13 / 6 ≈ 2.2 side effects per good sleeper.

cards.question: Why can telling a person with insomnia to try to stay awake help them fall asleep?
cards.answer: Because the effort to sleep is part of what keeps them awake. Sleep comes when arousal drops, and straining for it raises arousal: clock-watching, counting hours left, willing the body off. Told to lie in the dark and keep their eyes open, many relax the effort and drift off. Chasing sleep scares it away.
cards.move: Some states arrive only when you stop trying to produce them.
cards.reference: Morgenthaler, Kramer, Alessi et al., Practice parameters for the psychological and behavioral treatment of insomnia: an update, Sleep, 2006

cards.question: Do all people with chronic insomnia face the same raised health risks?
cards.answer: No: the risk gathers in those who sleep short when measured. In Pennsylvania cohorts, people with insomnia who slept under six hours in the laboratory had more hypertension and diabetes, and the men higher mortality; those sleeping six hours or more looked much like good sleepers. Two people can complain identically and carry different risks.
cards.move: Split a diagnosis by what can be measured before assuming one risk fits all.
cards.source: Vgontzas et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2013
cards.reference: Vgontzas, Fernandez-Mendoza, Liao & Bixler, Insomnia with objective short sleep duration: the most biologically severe phenotype of the disorder, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2013

cards.question: About a third of adults report insomnia symptoms; about 6% meet full diagnostic criteria. What percentage of the symptomatic meet them?
cards.answer: 18 / 100 = 18 percent.
cards.move: Before a rate reassures or alarms you, ask what it is a share of.
cards.trap: Answering 6, the disorder's share of all adults, not of the symptomatic.
cards.hint: Picture 300 adults and count who falls in each group.
steps: Of 300 adults, a third, 100, report symptoms.
6% of 300 = 18 meet the criteria, all among those 100.
18 / 100 = 18 percent.

diagram.label: adults
diagram.caption: The 18 with the disorder are 6% of all adults but 18% of the symptomatic.

cards.reference: Ohayon, Epidemiology of insomnia: what we know and what we still need to learn, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2002

cards.question: Should an app, rather than a therapist, be the first treatment offered for chronic insomnia?
cards.answer: Yes. Trained therapists in cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia are scarce, so most patients get pills or nothing. Digital versions have worked in large trials: in one with 3,755 university students, an online course reduced insomnia, and paranoia and hallucinations with it. Scale matters: a good treatment nobody can reach helps nobody.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who drops out and who is missed.
cards.counterpoint: No. The trials enrol motivated people who log on; in ordinary care many drop out after a session or two. Sleep restriction, the strongest ingredient, makes people sleepier for weeks, and without someone to adjust the schedule and catch warning signs, such as untreated apnoea or bipolar disorder, the difficult cases are the ones an app fails.
cards.reference: Freeman, Sheaves, Goodwin et al., The effects of improving sleep on mental health (OASIS): a randomised controlled trial with mediation analysis, Lancet Psychiatry, 2017

cards.question: True or false: in trials of modern sleeping pills, people given dummy pills also fell asleep noticeably faster?
cards.answer: True. Pooling trial data submitted to the US drug regulator, Huedo-Medina and colleagues found that placebo groups improved by a substantial share of what the drug groups gained. People join trials after a run of bad nights, which tend to ease anyway; expectation helps too. The pill gets credit for much of the recovery.
cards.move: Ask how people who got nothing fared before crediting the treatment.
cards.trap: Forgetting that people enrol at their worst, and bad runs ease anyway.
cards.reference: Huedo-Medina, Kirsch, Middlemass, Klonizakis & Siriwardena, Effectiveness of non-benzodiazepine hypnotics in treatment of adult insomnia: meta-analysis of data submitted to the Food and Drug Administration, BMJ, 2012

cards.question: In a conversation, who laughs more: the person talking or the person listening?
cards.answer: The one talking. Recording 1,200 bouts of everyday laughter, Robert Provine found speakers laughed 46% more than their listeners, and most laughs followed remarks that were not jokes. Laughs landed at pauses between phrases, almost never mid-phrase. Laughter works less like applause for wit than like a comma between two people.
cards.move: A laugh says more about the relationship than about the joke.
cards.reference: Provine, Laughter punctuates speech: linguistic, social and gender contexts of laughter, Ethology, 1993

cards.question: Is dopamine the brain's pleasure chemical?
cards.answer: Not quite: it drives wanting more than liking. Rats stripped of nearly all their dopamine will not seek out or eat food on their own, yet sugar on the tongue still brings the lip-licking face of pleasure, and bitter still brings the face of disgust. Craving a thing and enjoying it run on different wiring.
cards.move: Wanting something and enjoying it are separate dials; check which one moved.

cards.question: Swedish lottery winners were surveyed 5 to 22 years after a big win. What had the money changed?
cards.answer: Life satisfaction, more than happiness. Against matched players who won little or nothing, big winners rated their lives higher for over a decade, with no sign of fading; the effect on happiness and mental health was clearly smaller. The belief that winners soon adapt traces to a 1978 study of 22 winners.
cards.move: A small study that became famous deserves a second, larger look.
cards.trap: Trusting the famous finding that lottery winners quickly adapt back.
cards.source: Lindqvist et al., Review of Economic Studies, 2020
cards.reference: doi:10.1093/restud/rdaa006

cards.question: True or false: the statistics that found happiness spreading between friends also find height spreading between them?
cards.answer: True. Applied to American teenagers, the standard method detected acne, headaches and even height passing between friends, though none of them can spread that way. Once shared surroundings were allowed for, all three effects became small and insignificant. Friends share schools, towns and incomes, and those move moods too.
cards.move: When friends change together, check what they share before crediting influence.
cards.trap: Height cannot spread, so a sound method would find nothing.

cards.question: True or false: a smile that crinkles the eyes is a reliable sign of real enjoyment?
cards.answer: False. The crinkle, made by the muscle ringing the eye, grows with how broad a smile is, whatever the feeling. Filming over 100 people while amused, embarrassed, frightened or in pain, researchers found that once smile size was allowed for, the crinkle's link to amusement shrank sharply. The eyes track a smile's size.
cards.move: A sign that grows with intensity may say nothing about sincerity.
cards.trap: Relying on the famous rule that eye crinkles mark a genuine smile.
cards.reference: Girard, Shandar, Liu, Cohn, Yin & Morency, Reconsidering the Duchenne smile: indicator of positive emotion or artifact of smile intensity?, IEEE ACII proceedings, 2019

cards.question: What became of the claim that flourishing needs positive emotions to outnumber negative ones by 2.9013 to 1?
cards.answer: It was withdrawn. The ratio, published in American Psychologist in 2005, came from equations for fluid turbulence applied to business teams without justification. In 2013 Nicholas Brown, a part-time graduate student, with Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman, showed the maths was baseless, and the journal withdrew the model. The four decimal places were the warning.
cards.move: Distrust precision that the measurement beneath it could never have delivered.
cards.reference: Brown, Sokal & Friedman, The complex dynamics of wishful thinking: the critical positivity ratio, American Psychologist, 2013

cards.question: In 2010, emotional well-being seemed to stop rising above about $75,000 a year. What did a 2023 joint reanalysis find?
options: It holds only for an unhappy minority
The plateau holds for nearly everyone
Well-being falls again at high incomes
cards.answer: It holds only for an unhappy minority. Kahneman and Killingsworth, whose studies disagreed, reanalysed jointly with Barbara Mellers as arbiter. For most people well-being kept rising with income; only in the least happy fifth or so did it level off, near $100,000. The 2010 measures had mostly registered unhappiness, and saw where misery stops shrinking.
cards.move: An average curve can describe the unhappiest few and almost nobody else.
cards.trap: Reading a famous threshold as a ceiling that applies to everyone.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36857342/

cards.question: True or false: in German panel data, life satisfaction fully recovered once people who had lost their jobs found work again?
cards.answer: False. Following thousands of Germans for 15 years, Lucas and colleagues found life satisfaction fell sharply with unemployment and, on average, did not climb back to its earlier level even after re-employment. The set point, the level people supposedly drift back to, had itself moved. The job came back; the old satisfaction did not.
cards.move: Recovery from a blow is a claim to check, not a law to assume.
cards.trap: Assuming everyone drifts back to a fixed personal level of happiness.
cards.reference: Lucas, Clark, Georgellis & Diener, Unemployment alters the set point for life satisfaction, Psychological Science, 2004

cards.question: Does happiness really dip in middle age before rising again in later life?
cards.answer: Yes. David Blanchflower found the U-shape in data from 145 countries, with its low point in the late forties. Antidepressant use peaks in midlife too, and keepers' ratings of captive chimpanzees and orangutans trace a similar curve. A pattern that survives so many countries, measures and species is unlikely to be a statistical accident.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on comparing different people or following the same ones.
cards.counterpoint: No. Most U-shapes come from comparing different people at different ages in one survey, often only after adjusting for income, health and marriage, which themselves change with age. Reviewing studies that follow the same people over years, Nancy Galambos and colleagues found the midlife dip inconsistent: in many, well-being holds steady or rises through middle age.
cards.reference: Blanchflower, Is happiness U-shaped everywhere? Age and subjective well-being in 145 countries, Journal of Population Economics, 2021

cards.question: Students in California and the Midwest rated their own life satisfaction, then guessed the other group's. Who was more satisfied?
cards.answer: Neither: they were about equal. Both groups predicted Californians would be happier, citing climate, and Californians were indeed far more pleased with their weather. But weather barely moved overall satisfaction. Imagining a life elsewhere, people focused on what differed between the places and forgot the jobs, friends and worries that did not.
cards.move: Nothing weighs as much in a life as it does while being compared.
cards.trap: Letting sunshine, the obvious difference, stand in for a whole life.
cards.reference: Schkade & Kahneman, Does living in California make people happy? A focusing illusion in judgments of life satisfaction, Psychological Science, 1998

cards.question: What did a Roman rhetoric handbook from the 80s BC advise about the images used to memorise a speech?
cards.answer: Make them outrageous. The anonymous Rhetorica ad Herennium says ordinary sights slip away while the strange, shameful or ridiculous stick. So images should be very beautiful or very ugly, crowned, stained with blood, or comic. The fifth place along the route holds a golden hand, the tenth a friend called Decimus.
cards.move: Make the thing to be kept impossible to overlook, and it will stay.
cards.reference: [Cicero], Rhetorica ad Herennium, trans. Caplan, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1954

cards.question: What happened when people with ordinary memories practised the memory-palace technique for six weeks?
cards.answer: Their recall more than doubled, and their brains began to resemble the champions'. After 30 minutes a day of placing items along imagined routes, they recalled more than twice as many words from 72-word lists, and resting brain scans shifted towards the connectivity of top memory athletes. Most of the gain held four months later.
cards.move: A rare ability may be an ordinary one trained for longer.
cards.reference: Dresler, Shirer, Konrad, Müller, Wagner, Fernández, Czisch & Greicius, Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory, Neuron, 2017

cards.question: A student trained his digit span from seven to about eighty. What happened when he was tested on letters?
cards.answer: His span fell back to about six. SF, a keen runner, had learned to recode digits as race times, so 3492 became 3 minutes 49.2 seconds for a mile, and to group those chunks into larger blocks. The skill lived in that code, not in any general capacity to hold things in mind.
cards.move: Before calling a skill general, test it where its tricks do not apply.

diagram.caption: Eighty digits, but only six letters: the skill lived in his code for digits.

cards.reference: Ericsson, Chase & Faloon, Acquisition of a memory skill, Science, 1980

cards.question: Brain scans of ten world-class memory competitors were compared with those of controls. What set the competitors apart?
options: Larger memory structures in the brain
More activity in spatial brain regions
cards.answer: More activity in spatial brain regions. Maguire and colleagues found no difference in brain structure or in general cognitive ability. While memorising, the champions used areas involved in navigation, and nine of the ten said they placed items along an imagined route. The method, not the organ, made them exceptional.
cards.move: Look for the technique before crediting the hardware.
cards.trap: Recalling the enlarged hippocampi of London taxi drivers and expecting the same.
cards.reference: Maguire, Valentine, Wilding & Kapur, Routes to remembering: the brains behind superior memory, Nature Neuroscience, 2003

cards.question: True or false: a major 2013 review of ten study techniques rated keyword mnemonics among the most useful?
cards.answer: False. Dunlosky and colleagues rated the keyword mnemonic, tying a foreign word to a vivid image of a similar-sounding one, low utility. It suits word pairs, takes effort to build, and in some studies its edge faded after a delay. Only practice testing and spaced practice were rated high.
cards.move: Judge a method by what is left a week later, not by how it feels.
cards.trap: Trusting a technique because its images are so easy to picture.
cards.source: Dunlosky et al., Psychological Science, Public Interest, 2013
cards.reference: Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan & Willingham, Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013

cards.question: After twelve 10-word lists, students who had woven each list into a story recalled 93% of all words. Controls given equal study time?
cards.answer: About 13%. In Bower and Clark's 1969 study, each control got a story-maker's study time, and straight after each list both groups recalled nearly everything. The gap opened on the final test of all twelve, when plain lists had blurred together. The stories kept each list in its own room.
cards.move: Test a method at the end of the week, not the end of the lesson.
cards.trap: About 80%, because a strong group's score sets where the other feels plausible.
cards.reference: Bower & Clark, Narrative stories as mediators for serial learning, Psychonomic Science, 1969

cards.question: True or false: long training in the memory palace narrowed the recall gap between adults in their twenties and in their seventies?
cards.answer: False. It widened. Kliegl, Baltes and colleagues trained both age groups in the method of loci over dozens of sessions. Everyone improved, but the young improved more, until the two groups' scores barely overlapped. Training did not level the field; it revealed a limit in the older group that ordinary testing had hidden.
cards.move: Practice can widen a gap as easily as close it.
cards.trap: True, since the weaker group seems to have more room to improve.
cards.reference: Baltes & Kliegl, Further testing of limits of cognitive plasticity: negative age differences in a mnemonic skill are robust, Developmental Psychology, 1992

cards.question: What did medieval scholars mainly train their memories for, if not to store texts word for word?
cards.answer: To compose. Mary Carruthers argues that monastic and scholastic memory training built an ordered stock of material a mind could search. The Latin inventio meant both finding and inventing: a preacher walked the places of his memory to gather what to say. A sermon was assembled from the shelves, not recited from a page.
cards.move: A store that can be searched beats one that is merely full.
cards.reference: Carruthers, The Book of Memory: A Study of Memory in Medieval Culture, Cambridge University Press, 1990

cards.question: Under which condition do bizarre mental images reliably beat ordinary ones for later recall?
options: When every image in the list is bizarre
When recall is delayed by a week
When bizarre images are mixed with ordinary ones
cards.answer: When mixed with ordinary ones. McDaniel and Einstein found bizarre sentences recalled better than plain ones only when both kinds sat in the same list. In lists made entirely of bizarre images the advantage vanished. Strangeness works by standing out, and nothing stands out in a room where everything is strange.
cards.move: What makes a thing memorable is how it differs from its neighbours.
cards.trap: When every image is bizarre, since more strangeness should mean more memory.
cards.source: McDaniel & Einstein, JEP: Learning, Memory, Cognition, 1986
cards.reference: McDaniel & Einstein, Bizarre imagery as an effective memory aid: the importance of distinctiveness, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 1986

cards.question: A memoriser folds every three playing cards into one person-action-object image. How many places must a route hold for one shuffled deck?
cards.answer: The lone card needs a place of its own: 17 + 1 = 18 places.
cards.move: Count what is left over before deciding how much room is needed.
cards.trap: Seventeen, by rounding 52 divided by 3 down and losing a card.
cards.hint: Divide the deck into threes and see what is left over.
steps: A deck has 52 cards.
52 / 3 = 17 full images, with 1 card left over.
The lone card needs a place of its own: 17 + 1 = 18 places.
cards.reference: Foer, Moonwalking with Einstein: The Art and Science of Remembering Everything, Penguin Press, 2011

cards.question: Every sleeper cycles into rapid eye movement sleep. Why did science notice it only in 1953?
cards.answer: Because sleep was thought a steady shutdown, and all-night recordings rarely tracked the eyes. Eugene Aserinsky, a graduate student in Nathaniel Kleitman's Chicago laboratory, did, recording sleepers including his 8-year-old son, Armond. Bursts of darting eye movements came at regular intervals, and sleepers woken during them usually reported dreams.
cards.move: What nobody measures, nobody discovers, however often it happens.
cards.reference: Aserinsky & Kleitman, Regularly occurring periods of eye motility, and concomitant phenomena, during sleep, Science, 1953

cards.question: Does the sleeping brain still tell its own name from other names?
cards.answer: Yes. Played a string of recorded names while asleep, people produced more K-complexes, a large brainwave of light sleep, to their own name than to others, and reacted more to names they had been told to listen for. The ears stay open all night; the brain decides what counts as news.
cards.move: Attention does not switch off; it switches to a shorter list.

cards.question: A 2011 review of 35 studies estimated how many people have had sleep paralysis, waking unable to move, at least once?
cards.answer: About 1 in 13: 7.6% of the general population, and 28% of students. The mind wakes while the body is still held in the paralysis of REM, the dreaming stage. Dream imagery can then spill into the waking room, often as an intruder or a weight on the chest.
cards.move: Silence about an experience is not evidence that it is rare.
cards.trap: Never having heard it discussed, assuming it must be very rare.
cards.reference: Sharpless & Barber, Lifetime prevalence rates of sleep paralysis: a systematic review, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2011

cards.question: Adults spend about a fifth of their sleep in REM, the dreaming stage. What share does a newborn baby spend?
cards.answer: About half. Charting sleep across the lifespan, Roffwarg's team found REM, called active sleep in infants, filling roughly half of a newborn's 16 or so hours, then falling to a fifth to a quarter in adults. One proposal is that it helps wire the growing brain. A newborn spends about eight hours a day there.
cards.move: Before reusing a familiar figure, check it was measured on the same kind of case.
cards.trap: Staying near the adult fifth, as if sleep were the same at every age.
cards.reference: Roffwarg, Muzio & Dement, Ontogenetic development of the human sleep-dream cycle, Science, 1966

cards.question: Roughly how many years of an 80-year life are spent in REM sleep?
cards.answer: 6% of 80 years ≈ 5 years.
cards.move: What happens every night, unnoticed, can still fill years.
cards.trap: Picturing dreams as brief flashes before waking, not hours each night.
cards.hint: Start from the hours of REM in one night and the share of a day they make.
steps: An adult sleeps about 7.5 hours, roughly a fifth of it in REM.
7.5 / 5 = 1.5 hours of REM a day.
1.5 / 24 = about 6% of every day.
6% of 80 years ≈ 5 years.
cards.reference: Carskadon & Dement, Normal human sleep: an overview, in Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine, 5th edition, Elsevier, 2011

cards.question: When thousands of trained scorers staged the same sleep recordings, how often did they agree?
cards.answer: About 83% of the time overall, and only about 63% for N1, the lightest stage. In the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's own agreement programme, REM was scored most consistently, N1 and deep N3 least. Sleep stages are rules applied by eye to 30-second pages of brainwaves. One scorer's light sleep is another's wakefulness.
cards.move: When a category needs a judge, ask how often two judges agree.
cards.reference: Rosenberg & Van Hout, The American Academy of Sleep Medicine inter-scorer reliability program: sleep stage scoring, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2013

cards.question: In which stage of sleep does sleepwalking begin, and why does that matter?
cards.answer: Deep non-REM sleep, mostly early in the night, not the dreaming stage. In REM the muscles are held slack; in slow-wave sleep they are not, so a brain whose motor regions stir while the rest stays asleep can walk, talk or eat. The walking comes from a brain partly awake, not a dream escaping paralysis.
cards.move: Ask what state allows a behaviour before asking what story explains it.
cards.reference: Zadra, Desautels, Petit & Montplaisir, Somnambulism: clinical aspects and pathophysiological hypotheses, Lancet Neurology, 2013

cards.question: Men spent 18.9% of the night in deep sleep aged 16 to 25, and 3.4% aged 36 to 50. By what percentage did it fall?
cards.answer: 0.82 = about 82 percent.
cards.move: A fall in percentage points and a fall in percent are different numbers.
cards.trap: Answering 15.5, the change in points rather than the relative fall.
cards.hint: Subtract first, then divide by where it started, not where it ended.
steps: Drop in share: 18.9 - 3.4 = 15.5 percentage points.
Relative to the start: 15.5 / 18.9 ≈ 0.82.
0.82 = about 82 percent.
cards.reference: Van Cauter, Leproult & Plat, Age-related changes in slow wave sleep and REM sleep and relationship with growth hormone and cortisol levels in healthy men, JAMA, 2000

cards.question: True or false: most of a healthy adult's night is spent in deep sleep or REM sleep combined?
cards.answer: False. Stage N2, a light but stable sleep marked by bursts of brainwaves called spindles, fills roughly half the night on its own. Deep sleep takes perhaps 15 to 20% in young adults and less later, and REM about a fifth to a quarter. The unglamorous middle stage is where most sleeping happens.
cards.move: The stage everyone talks about is rarely the one taking up the time.
cards.trap: Picturing sleep through its two famous stages, REM and deep sleep.
cards.reference: Ohayon, Carskadon, Guilleminault & Vitiello, Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters from childhood to old age in healthy individuals, Sleep, 2004

cards.question: From which stage of sleep is a person usually hardest to wake with a sound?
cards.answer: Deep slow-wave sleep. Sounds must be loudest to wake people from it, and those woken are groggiest. In REM, despite the vivid dreams, waking thresholds are closer to those of light N2 sleep. Dreaming vividly is not sleeping deeply.
cards.move: How absorbing an experience is says little about how hard it is to interrupt.
cards.trap: Assuming the stage with the most vivid dreams must be the deepest.
cards.source: Rechtschaffen et al., Perceptual and Motor Skills, 1966
cards.reference: Rechtschaffen, Hauri & Zeitlin, Auditory awakening thresholds in REM and NREM sleep stages, Perceptual and Motor Skills, 1966

cards.question: Volunteers repeated one new daily habit in the same setting. What was the longest estimated time for it to become automatic?
cards.answer: About 8 months: 254 days. Lally and colleagues followed 96 volunteers repeating an eating, drinking or exercise habit daily. The median, 66 days, is the figure now quoted everywhere, but estimates ran from 18 to 254 days, and the slowest were projected well past the 84 days the study lasted.
cards.move: Ask how far the slowest cases sit from the quoted average.
cards.trap: Recalling the widely quoted 66 days, which was only the middle case.

diagram.caption: The quoted 66 days is only the median; the slowest habit needed an estimated 254.

cards.source: Lally et al., European J Social Psychology, 2010
cards.reference: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle, How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world, European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010

cards.question: True or false: while a daily habit is forming, skipping a single day barely dents progress towards automaticity?
cards.answer: True. In Lally and colleagues' 12-week study, a single missed opportunity had no measurable effect on the rise in automaticity: the curve picked up where it left off. What undid habits was drifting away over many days, not one gap. An app that resets the counter to zero is stricter than the brain.
cards.move: Judge a routine by its run over weeks, not by its worst day.
cards.trap: Believing one missed day resets a habit, as a streak counter does.
cards.reference: Lally & Gardner, Promoting habit formation, Health Psychology Review, 2013

cards.question: Besides New Year, which dates send more people to the gym and to searching for diets?
cards.answer: Any date that feels like a new chapter. Dai, Milkman and Riis found gym visits rising at the start of each week and month, after holidays and after birthdays, and searches for diet peaking on Mondays. A landmark walls off a past self who failed. Every Monday is a small New Year.
cards.move: Borrow any date that feels like a beginning to start something hard.
cards.reference: Dai, Milkman & Riis, The fresh start effect: temporal landmarks motivate aspirational behavior, Management Science, 2014

cards.question: Across years of gym check-ins, what best predicted whether a member would turn up on a given day?
cards.answer: How recently they had last been. Buyalskaya and colleagues fed check-in records from tens of thousands of gym members into machine-learning models: days since the previous visit outweighed other predictors, and habitual members kept to the same weekdays. The gym habit took months to settle, far longer than hand-washing among hospital staff.
cards.move: The best forecast of tomorrow's routine is how long since it last ran.
cards.reference: Buyalskaya, Ho, Milkman, Li, Duckworth & Camerer, What can machine learning teach us about habit formation? Evidence from exercise and hygiene, PNAS, 2023

cards.question: Do streak counters in habit apps help people build lasting habits?
sides: No, they get in the way
cards.answer: A visible streak turns a vague goal into a daily fact, and reluctance to lose a run gets people practising on bad days. Daily repetition in a stable setting is what builds automaticity, and a streak rewards exactly that repetition. The counter is scaffolding for the weeks before the habit can stand on its own.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the test is what happens the day after a break.
cards.counterpoint: A counter rewards the count, not the practice, so people do the minimum that keeps it alive. It also makes one miss look like failure, though a single missed day barely affects how a habit forms, and a broken run can feel like a reason to stop. The habit leans on the app, and goes when the app goes.
cards.source: Wood & Rünger, Annual Review of Psychology, 2016
cards.reference: Wood & Rünger, Psychology of habit, Annual Review of Psychology, 2016

cards.question: Someone keeps a daily habit with 95% probability each day, independently. What is the chance, in percent, of an unbroken 30-day streak?
cards.move: Nearly reliable, repeated many times, is nearly certain to slip once.
cards.trap: Around 80 or 90%, since 95% a day sounds almost perfect.
cards.hint: Find how many days it takes for the survival odds to halve.
steps: Each day the run survives with probability 0.95.
0.95 multiplied 14 times is about 0.488: the odds halve roughly every two weeks.
Thirty days is two such halvings plus two days: 0.488 × 0.488 × 0.9025 ≈ 0.215.

diagram.caption: Each day is 95% safe, yet fewer than one streak in four survives a month.

cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, 3rd ed., Wiley, 1968

cards.question: Students were paid to visit the gym eight times in one month. Once payment ended, what did former non-regulars do?
options: Kept going about twice as often
Went less than before the pay
cards.answer: Kept going about twice as often. Charness and Gneezy found that paying for a month of visits raised attendance for weeks after the money stopped, almost entirely among students who had not been regulars. Those already going had no habit to build. The paid month bought a run that kept itself going.
cards.move: Pay for the first stretch of a habit, not for every step.
cards.trap: Returned to their old rate, because the reason for going had disappeared.
cards.reference: Charness & Gneezy, Incentives to exercise, Econometrica, 2009

cards.question: Among people keeping New Year's resolutions, what predicted who was still at it months later?
cards.answer: How much they enjoyed it, not how much it mattered to them. Woolley and Fishbach surveyed people about their resolutions early in the year and again weeks later: the pleasure they took in the activity predicted persistence, while its rated importance did not. A run that feels good today keeps going; a worthy one breaks.
cards.move: Choose the version of a good habit that feels good while doing it.
cards.reference: Woolley & Fishbach, Immediate rewards predict adherence to long-term goals, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2017

cards.question: When paid gym visits had built a habit in students, what largely erased it?
cards.answer: The winter holiday. Acland and Levy found that paying students to attend left a real rise in visits after the money stopped, but much of it was gone after the break. The students had also predicted they would go far more than they did. A month away cut the run the cash had started.
cards.move: Plan the restart before a break, not after it.
cards.reference: Acland & Levy, Naiveté, projection bias, and habit formation in gym attendance, Management Science, 2015

cards.question: A car wash gave loyalty cards needing eight stamps, or ten stamps with two already filled. Which card was completed more often?
cards.answer: The card with two filled: 34% of those customers earned the free wash, against 19% with the plain eight-stamp card. Nunes and Drèze called it the endowed progress effect. Both cards needed eight more washes; only one looked a fifth done. A run that seems already under way is harder to abandon.
cards.move: Show people how far they have come, not only how far remains.
cards.trap: Both about equally, since each card needs exactly eight more washes.
cards.source: Nunes & Drèze, Journal of Consumer Research, 2006
cards.reference: Nunes & Drèze, The endowed progress effect: how artificial advancement increases effort, Journal of Consumer Research, 2006

cards.question: Who first called honouring sunk costs the Concorde fallacy, and about what?
cards.answer: Two biologists, writing about animal parents deserting a mate. In 1976 Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle argued that a parent does not stay with a brood because of what it has already put in; only future costs and benefits should count. They named the opposite error after the jet Britain and France kept funding.
cards.move: Behind a choice that seems to honour the past, look for a future reason.

cards.question: Did NBA teams give high draft picks more playing time than their performance justified?
cards.answer: Apparently yes, but less than first claimed. Staw and Hoang found that, performance held equal, earlier picks got more minutes and lasted longer in the league, as if teams were honouring the price of the pick. Camerer and Weber's reanalysis found a weaker effect. Coaches may also know things about talent that statistics miss.
cards.move: Before blaming bias, rule out that the insiders simply know more.
cards.reference: Staw & Hoang, Sunk costs in the NBA: why draft order affects playing time and survival in professional basketball, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1995

cards.question: A health club bills its members twice a year. In which month does attendance peak?
cards.answer: The month dues are paid. At a club billing twice a year, attendance was highest in the month dues were paid, declined over the next five, then rose again with the next bill. A payment feels like a debt to be used up, and the feeling fades as the payment recedes.
cards.move: Spread payments out if the point is to keep people coming.
cards.trap: Expecting visits to follow motivation, since the money is gone either way.
cards.source: Gourville & Soman, Journal of Consumer Research, 1998
cards.reference: Gourville & Soman, Payment depreciation: the behavioral effects of temporally separating payments from consumption, Journal of Consumer Research, 1998

cards.question: True or false: mice and rats, like people, get less likely to quit a wait the longer they have already waited?
cards.answer: True. In matched foraging tasks, mice and rats queued for flavoured food and people for short videos; in all three species, the more time already sunk into a wait, the less likely they were to abandon it. The pull built up only after the decision to wait, not during the deliberation before it.
cards.move: Decide how long to wait before starting, when the past cannot argue yet.
cards.trap: Honouring sunk costs seems a human quirk of pride or money.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aar8644

cards.question: Should money already spent and unrecoverable ever count in deciding whether to carry on?
cards.answer: Past spending often carries information: heavy funding suggests people who knew more judged the project promising. Quitting can wreck a reputation for finishing things, which has future value, and on a tight budget abandoning may leave nothing to show. Economists have shown that, in such cases, letting sunk costs weigh can be the rational choice.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether the past carries news about the future.
cards.counterpoint: Every one of those reasons is about the future: information, reputation and budgets can be counted as future costs and benefits. The spent money itself adds nothing. Treating it as a reason is the reflex that kept Concorde flying; in one classic survey, 33 of 61 people picked a ski weekend they expected to enjoy less because it cost more.
cards.reference: McAfee, Mialon & Mialon, Do sunk costs matter?, Economic Inquiry, 2010

cards.question: Do people honour sunk time as strongly as they honour sunk money?
cards.answer: Much less. Dilip Soman found that people who had invested hours in an option were far less swayed by it than people who had paid money; time is not booked like cash. Once people were taught to price their time, the sunk-time effect appeared. The wasted afternoon never shows up on a statement.
cards.move: A cost nobody records is a cost nobody feels obliged to recover.
cards.source: Soman, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2001
cards.reference: Soman, The mental accounting of sunk time costs: why time is not like money, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2001

cards.question: Students told their own earlier funding choice had failed, and others told a predecessor made it, split new money. Who gave the failing division more?
options: Those who had made the choice
cards.answer: Those who had made the choice. In Barry Staw's 1976 study, students who had personally picked a division that then failed put more of the new money into it than students handed the same failure. Later reviews count personal responsibility among the steadiest drivers of escalation. The money was the same; only the signature differed.
cards.move: Hand a failing project to someone who did not start it.
cards.trap: Expecting the people who chose to learn fastest from their own failure.
cards.source: Staw, Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 1976
cards.reference: Staw, Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action, Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 1976

cards.question: Once spending on a project passes the budget its owner set, what happens to their appetite for further worthwhile spending?
options: They escalate, to rescue the money
They refuse, even when it would pay
They judge only the future returns
cards.answer: They refuse, even when it would pay. Chip Heath found people track spending against a mental budget: below it, sunk costs pull them onward; once it is exceeded, they turn down investments with good prospects. Both errors look backwards at money already gone. A house left one roof short is the same mistake, inverted.
cards.move: Past spending is a bad reason to stop as well as to continue.
cards.trap: Assuming sunk costs can only ever push people to keep going.
cards.source: Heath, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1995
cards.reference: Heath, Escalation and de-escalation of commitment in response to sunk costs: the role of budgeting in mental accounting, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1995

cards.question: True or false: in a US study, older adults were less prone than young adults to throwing good money after bad?
cards.answer: True. JoNell Strough and colleagues gave younger and older adults scenarios pitting money already spent against a better option, such as a dull film already paid for. Older adults more often chose the better future. One proposed reason is that older people dwell less on past losses. Here experience outran the quicker minds.
cards.move: Do not assume every mental skill declines on the same schedule.
cards.trap: Assuming decision-making simply gets worse as people age.
cards.reference: Strough, Mehta, McFall & Schuller, Are older adults less subject to the sunk-cost fallacy than younger adults?, Psychological Science, 2008

cards.question: With $9 million of $10 million spent on a plane a rival outclasses, 85% would finish. With nothing spent yet, what share would invest?
cards.answer: About one in six. In Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer's scenario, the last $1 million bought the same inferior plane either way. With the $9 million behind them, most people chose to complete it, while those starting from nothing mostly declined. The rival's better plane was on the market in both versions.
cards.move: Ask whether you would start this today, knowing what you now know.
cards.trap: Expecting the same choice, since the future on offer is identical.
cards.reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0749597885900494

cards.question: What happens to a crying face in a photograph when the tears are digitally removed?
cards.answer: It stops reading as sad. With the tears erased, viewers rated the same faces as less sad, and many saw puzzlement, concern or even awe in them instead. Without tears the face is ambiguous; with them the sadness is plain. A few drops of salt water carry much of the message.
cards.move: Before calling a reaction useless, ask who it is aimed at.

cards.question: Does a good cry at a sad film leave people feeling better, and when?
cards.answer: Yes, but not at first. Of 60 viewers of two sad films, the 28 who cried felt worse straight after, were back to their starting mood 20 minutes later, and felt better than before after 90 minutes. The 32 who stayed dry felt no change. The relief comes late, after a dip.
cards.move: Judge a remedy by its whole curve, not the moment after.
cards.source: Gračanin et al., Motivation and Emotion, 2015
cards.reference: Gračanin, Vingerhoets, Kardum et al., Why crying does and sometimes does not seem to alleviate mood: a quasi-experimental study, Motivation and Emotion, 2015

cards.question: In a Dutch survey, what share of parents of six-month-olds admitted shaking, slapping or smothering their crying baby?
cards.answer: About one in twenty. That share said they had smothered, slapped or shaken their baby at least once because of its crying, and it was higher where the crying seemed excessive to the parents. A cry is built to summon care and usually does; past a limit, it can summon harm.
cards.move: Any alarm loud enough to compel help can also wear out the helper.
cards.reference: Reijneveld, van der Wal, Brugman, Hira Sing & Verloove-Vanhorick, Infant crying and abuse, The Lancet, 2004

cards.question: True or false: the gap between how often women and men cry is larger in richer, more democratic countries?
cards.answer: True. Surveys of students across dozens of countries found women crying more than men almost everywhere, but the gap was larger in wealthier, more democratic countries. One reading: where feelings may be shown freely, differences between the sexes have room to appear, and in stricter places they stay hidden.
cards.move: Freedom to express a difference can make the difference look bigger.
cards.trap: Strict gender roles in poorer countries should silence men's tears most.
cards.source: van Hemert et al., Cross-Cultural Research, 2011

cards.question: True or false: a long cry sheds far too little fluid to lower stress hormones by flushing them out?
cards.answer: True. The flushing idea comes from biochemist William Frey, who found stress-linked hormones such as prolactin in tears and proposed that crying excretes them. But a long cry yields a few millilitres at most, against about five litres of blood. Whatever relief crying brings, it is not a drain on the bloodstream.
cards.move: Before accepting a mechanism, check whether the quantities involved could possibly do it.
cards.trap: Relief after crying feels like something harmful has left the body.
cards.reference: Vingerhoets, Why Only Humans Weep: Unravelling the Mysteries of Tears, Oxford University Press, 2013

cards.question: Can a person sob uncontrollably while feeling no sadness at all?
cards.answer: Yes. After strokes, multiple sclerosis or motor neurone disease, some people burst into crying or laughter at trivial triggers with no matching feeling, a condition called pseudobulbar affect. Damage to pathways that normally gate the brainstem's crying programme is thought to release it. The face weeps while its owner waits for it to stop.
cards.move: An expression and the feeling it usually signals can come apart.
cards.reference: Parvizi, Anderson, Martin, Damasio & Damasio, Pathological laughter and crying: a link to the cerebellum, Brain, 2001

cards.question: Kung San babies in Botswana are carried all day and nursed several times an hour. How did their crying compare with Dutch babies'?
cards.answer: As many bouts, but shorter. Barr and Konner found Kung infants cried as often as Dutch infants, with the same peak in the first three months, but their total crying time was about half. Constant carrying and feeding shortened each cry without preventing it. The early crying peak looks human, not Western.
cards.move: Before blaming a custom for a problem, find people who live without the custom.
cards.trap: Assuming Western childcare creates crying that constant carrying would prevent.
cards.source: Barr et al., Dev Med Child Neurol, 1991
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1879624/

cards.question: Ninety-seven women logged about 1,000 crying episodes in daily diaries. After what share did they report feeling better?
cards.answer: About a third. Most episodes brought no change in mood, and some left the crier feeling worse. Relief came more often when someone offered comfort, and less often for people who struggle to name their feelings. Asked about crying in general, people say it helps: the good cries are the ones memory keeps.
cards.move: Ask whether the evidence was logged at the time or recalled later.
cards.trap: Going by memory, where the relieving cries are the ones that stand out.
cards.source: Bylsma et al., J Research in Personality, 2011

cards.question: True or false: across 41 countries, faces with tears added were generally judged less competent than the same faces without?
cards.answer: False. In a large experiment run in 41 countries, adding tears made the same face look warmer and more helpless, and raised people's willingness to offer support. Competence ratings did not drop in general, only under particular conditions. Tears asked for help without, in most settings, making their owner look less capable.
cards.move: A signal that brings help need not cost the sender standing.
cards.trap: Assuming crying reads everywhere as weakness, as the stereotype says.
cards.reference: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/352005575_Tears_do_not_influence_competence_in_general_but_only_under_specific_circumstances_A_systematic_investigation_across_41_countries

cards.question: Roughly how many hours, in total, does a typical baby spend fussing or crying in its first twelve weeks?
cards.move: A small daily amount, multiplied by weeks, becomes a burden nobody pictured.
cards.trap: Counting only the loud episodes and forgetting the long stretches of fussing.
cards.hint: Take a daily figure for the early weeks and a lower one for the later weeks.
steps: For the first 6 weeks, about 2 hours a day: 42 x 2 = 84 hours.
By week 12 it is near 70 minutes a day, so take weeks 7 to 12 at about 1.25 hours.
cards.source: Wolke, Bilgin & Samara, Journal of Pediatrics, 2017
cards.reference: https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(17)30218-4/fulltext

cards.question: What did people who could not remember playing Tetris see as they fell asleep that night?
cards.answer: Falling Tetris pieces. Three patients with dense amnesia from brain damage played the game and, at sleep onset, reported the same drifting blocks as healthy players, while unable to recall ever playing. Some experienced players even saw older versions of the game they had played before. The images come from memory the dreamer cannot consult.
cards.move: Forgetting an experience is no proof it has stopped shaping the mind.

cards.question: What happens when a sleeper is woken every time REM sleep begins, night after night?
cards.answer: The brain pushes back. In William Dement's 1960 experiments, sleepers woken at each onset of REM, the stage richest in dreams, tried to re-enter it more and more often, and on free nights afterwards spent extra time there, a rebound. He called it dream deprivation; the psychological harms he reported remain disputed.
cards.move: Something the body fights to get back is probably doing a job.
cards.reference: Dement, The effect of dream deprivation, Science, 1960

cards.question: Matched against diaries of the dreamers' days, how often did a dream replay an event just as it happened?
cards.answer: Almost never. People logged their days and reported their dreams, and the two were matched. Fragments of waking life, a person, a place, a worry, turned up often, but a waking episode replayed as it happened was vanishingly rare. Dreams borrow the day's props, not its script.
cards.move: A story built from real fragments can still be a story nobody lived.
cards.trap: Recalling a few vivid dreams that seemed to replay the day.
cards.source: Fosse et al., Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 2003
cards.reference: Fosse, Fosse, Hobson & Stickgold, Dreaming and episodic memory: a functional dissociation?, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 2003

cards.question: True or false: dreams happen only during REM sleep?
cards.answer: False. Since David Foulkes's studies in 1962, sleepers woken from non-REM sleep have regularly reported dreams, usually shorter, vaguer and more thought-like than REM dreams, but dreams all the same. Any theory that explains dreaming purely as REM machinery at work has to account for the dreams REM leaves out.
cards.move: Where something happens most is not the only place it happens.
cards.trap: Learning that REM is the dreaming stage, and reading it as the only one.
cards.source: Foulkes, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 1962
cards.reference: Foulkes, Dream reports from different states of sleep, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 1962

cards.question: Do dreams themselves do a job, or are they a by-product of what the sleeping brain does?
cards.answer: People who dream about a maze they have just learned get better at it than those who sleep without such dreams, a finding repeated overnight in 2019. One theory holds that nightmares rehearse threats, and dream content tracks waking worries. An experience so organised around what matters is unlikely to be mere exhaust.
cards.move: Everything turns on whether the experience does the work, or only the brain beneath it.
cards.counterpoint: Most dreams are forgotten within minutes, so any job they do cannot depend on the dreamer knowing it. The maze findings rest on the few people who happen to dream of the task, and may only show which memories the brain was already busy with. The work may be sleep's; dreams may be its sparks.
cards.source: Wamsley & Stickgold, Journal of Sleep Research, 2019
cards.reference: Wamsley & Stickgold, Dreaming of a learning task is associated with enhanced memory consolidation: replication in an overnight sleep study, Journal of Sleep Research, 2019

cards.question: Can brain damage abolish dreaming while REM sleep carries on normally?
cards.answer: Yes. The neuropsychologist Mark Solms found patients who stopped dreaming entirely after damage to forebrain regions, including white matter deep in the frontal lobes, while their REM cycles continued. Damage to the brainstem that disrupts REM rarely ended dreaming. The dream machine and the REM switch turned out to be separate parts.
cards.move: Two things that usually happen together may still run on different machinery.
cards.reference: Solms, Dreaming and REM sleep are controlled by different brain mechanisms, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2000

cards.question: After an experience, on which nights is it most likely to turn up in a dream?
cards.answer: The next night or two, and again about five to seven days later. Tore Nielsen's team found this dream-lag effect in REM dreams, and other labs have repeated it. One reading is that memories are still being reworked days after the event. Tuesday's argument may return the following Monday.
cards.move: If an effect fades, check whether it comes back before calling it over.
cards.source: Nielsen et al., Journal of Sleep Research, 2004
cards.reference: Nielsen, Kuiken, Alain, Stenstrom & Powell, Immediate and delayed incorporations of events into dreams: further replication and implications for dream function, Journal of Sleep Research, 2004

cards.question: People who said they never dreamt were woken in a laboratory during REM sleep. How often did they report a dream?
cards.answer: About half the time. In a 1959 study, self-described non-dreamers woken from REM reported dreams on roughly half the awakenings, against over nine in ten for people who said they dreamt often. Everyone dreams; what differs is how much survives the trip to morning. A dreamless night is usually a forgotten one.
cards.move: A report of never is often a report of not remembering.
cards.trap: Taking people's word that nothing happened because they recall nothing.
cards.source: Goodenough et al., J Abnormal Social Psychology, 1959
cards.reference: Goodenough, Shapiro, Holden & Steinschriber, A comparison of dreamers and nondreamers: eye movements, electroencephalograms, and the recall of dreams, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 1959

cards.question: Roughly what percentage of their REM dream periods does a typical adult remember in a year?
cards.move: What memory keeps is a thin sample of what happened.
cards.trap: Assuming the dreams recalled are most of the dreams had.
cards.hint: Count the chances to dream in a year, then the dreams people report.
steps: A night holds about 4 to 5 REM periods: take 4.5.
4.5 x 365 ≈ 1,640 REM periods a year.
Most adults recall about 1 or 2 dreams a week: take 1.5 x 52 ≈ 78 a year.
cards.reference: Schredl, Researching Dreams: The Fundamentals, Palgrave Macmillan, 2018

cards.question: True or false: rehearsing a rewritten version of a recurring nightmare while awake makes it return less often?
cards.answer: True. In imagery rehearsal therapy, patients write a changed version of the nightmare and rehearse it for minutes a day. In a 2001 trial with 168 sexual assault survivors, nightmares fell markedly against a waiting-list group given nothing yet. The waking mind edited the script, and the sleeping mind often used the new version.
cards.move: Rehearse the version you want, and the old one gets less airtime.
cards.trap: Assuming nothing done by day can reach what happens in dreams.
cards.reference: Krakow, Hollifield, Johnston et al., Imagery rehearsal therapy for chronic nightmares in sexual assault survivors with posttraumatic stress disorder: a randomized controlled trial, JAMA, 2001

cards.question: Should schools sort pupils into classes by ability?
cards.answer: A single class spanning four years of attainment fails at both ends: the strongest coast, the weakest drown, and the teacher aims at a middle that nobody occupies. Grouping lets the material meet the pupil where they are, which is the one thing that reliably moves attainment.
cards.move: Ask what happens to the child placed in the bottom set by mistake, and how they would ever get out.
cards.counterpoint: The gains concentrate almost entirely in the top set, and the bottom set loses more than the top gains. Placement tracks family income as much as ability, gets made early, and rarely gets revisited — so a decision about a nine-year-old quietly becomes a decision about their adult life.
cards.reference: Education Endowment Foundation, Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Setting and streaming, 2021

cards.question: Should city centres have a default speed limit of 30 km/h?
cards.answer: The survival curve is not gradual: being struck at 50 kills a pedestrian far more often than being struck at 30, and city journeys are so dominated by junctions and lights that the lower limit costs almost no real time.
cards.move: Notice that one side is arguing about physics and the other about behaviour. Both can be right.
cards.counterpoint: Compliance is what actually determines speed, and a limit drivers regard as absurd gets ignored, which erodes the limits that matter. The same money spent on separating pedestrians from traffic saves more lives than a number on a sign.
cards.reference: Rosén & Sander, Pedestrian fatality risk as a function of car impact speed, Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2009

cards.question: How did we know what a kilogram was?
cards.answer: Until 2019, a kilogram was a metal cylinder in a vault near Paris. Its official copies drifted apart by around 50 micrograms over a century — and nobody could say which had changed, because the cylinder was the definition. It is now fixed to a constant of nature instead.
cards.move: For 130 years the kilogram could not be wrong, only different.
cards.reference: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, 2019

cards.question: When did peer review become normal?
cards.answer: Later than you would guess. Nature only made external refereeing compulsory in 1973. Einstein's 1905 papers were not refereed, and neither was Watson and Crick's DNA structure. "Peer reviewed" describes a process younger than the polio vaccine, not a timeless standard.
cards.move: Peer review is younger than the polio vaccine.
cards.source: Baldwin, Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 2015
cards.reference: Baldwin, Credibility, peer review, and Nature, 1945-1990, Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 2015

cards.question: Where did the nitrogen in your body come from?
cards.answer: Roughly half of it passed through a factory. Air is 78% nitrogen that living things cannot use; the Haber-Bosch process forces it into fertiliser. That reaction now underwrites the food supply of about half the people alive, which makes it hard to name a more consequential chemistry.
cards.move: About half the nitrogen atoms in you came out of a chemical plant.

cards.question: Does ordinary ice lose all its disorder as it is cooled towards absolute zero?
cards.answer: No. The oxygen atoms line up in a neat lattice, but each hydrogen can sit nearer either end of its bond, and those choices freeze in at random. In 1935 Linus Pauling counted the arrangements and predicted the leftover disorder, or entropy: 3.4 joules per kelvin per mole, close to what heat measurements showed.
cards.move: A neat frame can still hold choices that were never settled.
cards.source: Pauling, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1935
cards.reference: Pauling, The Structure and Entropy of Ice and of Other Crystals with Some Randomness of Atomic Arrangement, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1935

cards.question: Where does the helium-3 that the coldest refrigerators depend on come from?
cards.answer: Mostly from nuclear weapons. Tritium, the radioactive hydrogen in warheads, decays into helium-3 with a half-life of about 12 years, and the gas is skimmed off when the tritium is purified. Dilution refrigerators, which hold quantum-computer chips near a hundredth of a kelvin, need it. After 2001, radiation detectors at ports ran the stockpile down.
cards.move: Trace a scarce material back to whatever it is a by-product of.
cards.source: Congressional Research Service, The Helium-3 Shortage, 2010
cards.reference: Shea & Morgan, The Helium-3 Shortage: Supply, Demand, and Options for Congress, Congressional Research Service, 2010

cards.question: What stops even the best refrigerator from ever reaching absolute zero?
cards.answer: Every cooling step is smaller than the last. Magnetic cooling, for example, exploits the gap in disorder between a salt in a strong field and in a weak one. The third law says that gap closes near absolute zero, so each round only divides the temperature: 1 kelvin, then 0.1, then 0.01, never zero.
cards.move: Halving what remains, again and again, never gets you to nothing.
cards.source: Blundell & Blundell, Concepts in Thermal Physics, 2010
cards.reference: Blundell & Blundell, Concepts in Thermal Physics, 2nd edition, Oxford University Press, 2010

cards.question: True or false: a gas measured at a negative temperature on the kelvin scale is colder than absolute zero?
cards.answer: False. It is hotter than any positive temperature. Temperature measures how disorder changes with added energy; when energy has a ceiling and most particles crowd near it, adding more makes the system tidier, and the temperature comes out negative. Such a potassium gas, made in Munich in 2013, would give heat to anything it touched.
cards.move: Before trusting a minus sign, ask what the scale is built from.
cards.trap: Reading the minus sign as below zero, as on a thermometer.
cards.reference: Braun, Ronzheimer, Schreiber, Hodgman, Rom, Bloch & Schneider, Negative Absolute Temperature for Motional Degrees of Freedom, Science, 2013

cards.question: Near absolute zero, how much pressure does it take to freeze ordinary helium solid?
cards.answer: About 25 times air pressure. Helium atoms are so light, and attract each other so weakly, that their quantum jiggle, a motion that persists even at absolute zero, shakes any crystal apart. At ordinary pressure helium would stay liquid at absolute zero itself: the one element that cold alone cannot freeze.
cards.move: Rules learned from ordinary cases can fail at the extremes.
cards.trap: Assuming cold alone freezes everything, as it does every familiar liquid.
cards.source: Wilks & Betts, Introduction to Liquid Helium, 1987
cards.reference: Wilks & Betts, An Introduction to Liquid Helium, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1987
