cards.question: How do physicists take the temperature of a gas cooled to a millionth of a kelvin?
cards.answer: They switch off the trap and photograph the cloud as it spreads. Any thermometer would be far hotter than the gas and would warm it, so the atoms' own speeds are measured instead: how fast the cloud swells gives the temperature. At a millionth of a kelvin, sodium atoms drift about 2 centimetres a second.
cards.move: When any probe would disturb a thing, let it go and watch.
cards.reference: Ketterle, Durfee & Stamper-Kurn, Making, probing and understanding Bose-Einstein condensates, Proceedings of the International School of Physics Enrico Fermi, Course CXL, IOS Press, 1999

cards.question: True or false: near absolute zero, a crystal gets easier to warm by a given step the colder it already is?
cards.answer: True. The heat needed to raise its temperature one degree falls with the cube of temperature in an insulating crystal, as Peter Debye showed in 1912: ten times colder, a thousand times easier to warm. Particle detectors use this: held at a hundredth of a kelvin, a crystal warms measurably from one particle's energy.
cards.move: A small input looks large wherever there is little to absorb it.
cards.trap: False, picturing the heat per degree as fixed for each material.
cards.source: Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics
cards.reference: Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th edition, Wiley, 2005

cards.question: What is the exact temperature of water's triple point, now that the kelvin has been redefined?
cards.answer: Nothing exact any more. From 1954 the scale was defined by that point, so it was 273.16 K by decree. Since May 2019 the kelvin rests on a fixed Boltzmann constant, which links energy to temperature, and the triple point became a measurement: 273.16 K, give or take a ten-thousandth of a kelvin.
cards.move: Redefine a standard and its old anchor becomes just another measurement.
cards.source: BIPM, The International System of Units, 2019
cards.reference: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, 2019

cards.question: A perfect fridge in a 300 K room removes 1 joule from something at 3 K. Minimum work needed, in joules?
cards.answer: Only 1 joule came from the cold side, so work = 100 − 1 = 99 joules.
cards.move: The colder the target, the dearer each last step of progress becomes.
cards.trap: Expecting about 1 joule, as if cooling merely moved heat along.
cards.hint: Heat divided by temperature is entropy, and a perfect machine never creates or destroys any.
steps: 1 joule leaving at 3 K carries 1/3 joule per kelvin of entropy.
Releasing that entropy into the 300 K room takes 300 × 1/3 = 100 joules of heat.
Only 1 joule came from the cold side, so work = 100 − 1 = 99 joules.
cards.source: Pobell, Matter and Methods at Low Temperatures
cards.reference: Pobell, Matter and Methods at Low Temperatures, 3rd edition, Springer, 2007

cards.question: In a sealed, insulated cell below about 0.3 K, liquid helium-3 is squeezed until part of it freezes. What happens to its temperature?
options: It rises, as freezing releases heat
It falls, as freezing absorbs heat
cards.answer: It falls. Freezing usually releases heat because the solid is tidier than the liquid. In cold helium-3 it is reversed: quantum rules hold the liquid in near-order, while in the solid each nucleus's spin points any which way. So freezing draws heat in. Cornell physicists squeezed their way to about 2 thousandths of a kelvin.
cards.move: When a rule rests on which side is tidier, check which side is.
cards.trap: Expecting heat to be released, as when water turns to ice.
cards.reference: Richardson, The Pomeranchuk effect, Reviews of Modern Physics, 1997

cards.question: True or false: US regulators found that antibacterial hand soaps prevent more illness than plain soap and water?
cards.answer: False. In 2016 the US Food and Drug Administration asked makers for proof, got none it accepted, and ruled 19 antibacterial ingredients, triclosan among them, out of consumer hand washes. Plain soap works mostly by lifting germs off the skin so that water can carry them away.
cards.move: Before praising the new version, ask how the plain one did.
cards.trap: Assuming a product that kills more germs must prevent more illness.
cards.source: US FDA, consumer antiseptic wash rule, 2016
cards.reference: https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/consumer-antiseptic-wash-final-rule-questions-and-answers

cards.question: True or false: alcohol diluted to about 70% with water kills bacteria better than pure alcohol does?
cards.answer: True. Alcohol kills by unravelling a microbe's proteins, and that happens faster with water present; pure alcohol mainly dries things out. US federal guidance for hospitals puts the best range at 60–90% alcohol in water, with strength falling off sharply below 50%. A bottle of absolute ethanol is the weaker disinfectant.
cards.move: More of the active ingredient is not the same as more effect.
cards.trap: Assuming the purer the alcohol, the stronger the disinfectant.
cards.source: CDC Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization, 2008
cards.reference: Rutala, Weber and HICPAC, Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities, US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2008

cards.question: A disinfectant kills 99.999% of bacteria; a cheaper spray kills 99.9%. How many times more bacteria survive the cheaper spray?
cards.answer: About 100 times as many. What matters is what is left: 0.1% against 0.001%. The European test for a bactericidal product, EN 1276, demands the 99.999%, within five minutes. On a chopping board carrying a million bacteria, that is 10 survivors against 1,000.
cards.move: Near 100%, compare what is left over, not what was removed.
cards.trap: Reading 99.9% and 99.999% as practically the same number.

diagram.caption: From a million bacteria: 10 survive a 99.999% kill, 1,000 survive a 99.9% kill.

cards.reference: European Committee for Standardization, EN 1276:2019, Chemical disinfectants and antiseptics, quantitative suspension test for bactericidal activity, 2019

cards.question: What did the first enzyme washing powders do to the people who made them?
cards.answer: Gave many of them asthma. In the 1960s, stain-digesting enzymes from bacteria went into detergents as a fine powder; factory workers breathed the dust and became allergic, and the first cases were reported in 1969. The fix was mainly physical: each enzyme dose sealed inside a dust-free granule, like a seed in a husk.
cards.move: When a product is safe to use, ask about the people who make it.
cards.source: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene, 2015

cards.question: What were phosphates doing in washing powder before Europe capped them?
cards.answer: Softening the water. Phosphates grab the calcium and magnesium in hard water, which would otherwise tie up the detergent. The EU capped laundry doses at 0.5 g of phosphorus from 2013 and dishwasher doses at 0.3 g from 2017, because rinsed into rivers they fed the algae that choke lakes.
cards.move: Before banning an ingredient, ask what job it was doing.
cards.reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/259/oj/eng

cards.question: Household bleach is sold at about pH 12. Brought down to pH 7 at the same strength, does it kill germs faster or slower?
options: About the same, being equally strong
cards.answer: Much faster. Bleach kills mainly as hypochlorous acid, which dominates below about pH 7.5; at pH 12 nearly all of it sits as hypochlorite ion, some 80 to 100 times less potent. Makers keep it alkaline for shelf life, because the acid form breaks down quickly, and acidified further it gives off chlorine gas.
cards.move: The form that keeps on the shelf is not always the form that works.
cards.trap: Much slower, since a milder, less caustic liquid seems weaker.
cards.reference: Black & Veatch Corporation, White's Handbook of Chlorination and Alternative Disinfectants, 5th edition, Wiley, 2010

cards.question: What lets the oxygen bleach in European washing powder whiten clothes at 40 °C?
cards.answer: A booster called TAED. Oxygen bleach, sodium percarbonate, releases hydrogen peroxide, which bleaches well only from about 60 °C. TAED reacts with that peroxide to make peracetic acid, a stronger oxidiser that works at 40 °C and below. It spread across Europe as wash temperatures fell: an ingredient whose job is to spare the boiler.
cards.move: When a process needs heat, look for a helper that lowers the bar.
cards.reference: Smulders, Laundry Detergents, Wiley-VCH, 2002

cards.question: Kitchen sponges their owners regularly boiled or microwaved were compared with uncleaned ones. How did their bacteria compare?
cards.answer: About as many. In a 2017 German study of 14 used sponges, those regularly heated held no significantly fewer bacteria, and more of the kinds linked to bad smells. Heat kills most cells, but survivors regrow within days in warm, wet, food-fed foam. The authors advised replacing sponges weekly instead.
cards.move: Judge a fix by the state a week later, not the moment after.
cards.trap: Far fewer, because boiling and microwaving kill bacteria.
cards.reference: Cardinale, Kaiser, Lueders, Schnell & Egert, Microbiome analysis and confocal microscopy of used kitchen sponges reveal massive colonization by Acinetobacter, Moraxella and Chryseobacterium species, Scientific Reports 7, 5791, 2017

cards.question: True or false: mixing bicarbonate of soda with vinegar makes a stronger cleaner than vinegar alone?
cards.answer: False. The fizz is the two cancelling out: acid meets base and leaves carbon dioxide, water and sodium acetate, a mild salt. Whichever is in excess is all that still cleans. Vinegar alone dissolves limescale; bicarbonate alone scours and lifts grease. Poured together, they send bubbling salty water down the drain.
cards.move: Before crediting the dramatic step, compare it with the plain one alone.
cards.trap: True, because the vigorous fizzing looks like cleaning at work.
cards.reference: Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles: The Quest for Insight, 5th edition, W. H. Freeman, 2010

cards.question: Should families clean their homes less to lower their children's risk of allergies?
cards.answer: Yes. Children raised on traditional farms, among animals and dust, have far less allergy and asthma: Amish children in Indiana had about a quarter of the asthma of Hutterite children with similar genes but industrial farms. The immune system seems to need early microbial training, and a scrubbed, disinfected home withholds it.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether household cleaning is the exposure that matters.
cards.counterpoint: No. The protective exposures in those studies are farms, livestock, siblings and pets, not dirty kitchens, and no trial shows that cleaning less prevents allergy. Kitchen and hand hygiene still stop real infections such as salmonella and norovirus. The better rule is targeted hygiene: clean where and when germs spread, and get children outdoors.
cards.reference: Stein et al., Innate Immunity and Asthma Risk in Amish and Hutterite Farm Children, New England Journal of Medicine 375, 411, 2016

cards.question: A 5 g spoonful of bicarbonate of soda, 84 g per mole, fizzes with enough vinegar. How many litres of carbon dioxide come off?
cards.answer: A mole of gas fills about 24 litres at room temperature: 0.06 x 24 = 1.4 litres.
cards.move: A solid that turns to gas swells hundreds of times over.
cards.trap: Picturing the gas as roughly the size of the spoonful.
cards.hint: Each unit of bicarbonate gives one unit of gas, and a mole of any gas fills about 24 litres.
steps: 5 g / 84 g per mole = 0.06 moles of bicarbonate.
Each mole of bicarbonate releases one mole of carbon dioxide: 0.06 moles.
A mole of gas fills about 24 litres at room temperature: 0.06 x 24 = 1.4 litres.
cards.reference: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights, Standard atomic weights of the elements, 2021

cards.question: True or false: the temperature at which table sugar turns liquid depends on how fast it is heated?
cards.answer: True. Sugar crystals do not melt at a fixed point as ice does: they break down chemically, and the crystal falls apart as they do. Illinois food chemists showed in 2011 that the faster sucrose is heated, the hotter it gets before it liquefies. Runny sugar in a pan is already decomposing.
cards.move: A number printed in a table may depend on how it was measured.
cards.trap: Assuming every solid has one fixed melting point, like ice.
cards.source: Lee et al., J. Agric. Food Chem., 2011
cards.reference: Lee, Thomas and Schmidt, Investigation of the heating rate dependency associated with the loss of crystalline structure in sucrose, glucose, and fructose using a thermal analysis approach (Part I), Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry 59, 684, 2011

cards.question: What turns a cut onion's chemistry into tear gas?
cards.answer: A second enzyme, found only in 2002. Cutting lets the enzyme alliinase break down sulphur compounds, and the tear gas was assumed to be a by-product. Japanese researchers found lachrymatory-factor synthase, which builds it on purpose. Suppress that gene, they suggested, and an onion could keep its flavour without the tears.
cards.move: When a harmful result looks accidental, check whether something is built to make it.

cards.question: Why do green beans turn khaki when dressed in lemon juice or vinegar?
cards.answer: Acid evicts a metal. Chlorophyll holds a magnesium atom at its centre; hydrogen ions from the acid knock it out, leaving olive-brown pheophytin. Heat speeds the swap, which is why cooks dress greens at the last moment. A pinch of bicarbonate keeps them bright, but alkali also dissolves their cell walls into mush.
cards.move: Every fix has a side effect; ask what the improvement costs.
cards.source: Belitz, Grosch and Schieberle, Food Chemistry, 2009
cards.reference: Belitz, Grosch and Schieberle, Food Chemistry, 4th edition, Springer, 2009

cards.question: What draws the grey-green ring round the yolk of an overcooked hard-boiled egg?
cards.answer: Iron sulphide. Long heating frees sulphur from the proteins of the white as hydrogen sulphide, which drifts inward to the cooler yolk and meets the iron there. Older eggs, which are more alkaline, make more of it. Plunging eggs into cold water pulls the gas outwards instead and keeps the yolk yellow.
cards.move: Moisture and gas drift towards the cold, so choose where the cold is.
cards.reference: McGee, On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen, Scribner, 2004, ISBN 978-0-684-80001-1

cards.question: Where does the cream of tartar in a baker's cupboard come from?
cards.answer: From wine. As grape juice ferments and alcohol builds up, potassium bitartrate, a salt of tartaric acid, grows less soluble and crystallises on the insides of vats and barrels and in the sediment. Scraped off and purified, it becomes the acid half of many baking powders and the pinch that steadies whisked egg whites.
cards.move: Before asking how an ingredient is made, ask whose leftover it might be.
cards.source: Ribéreau-Gayon et al., Handbook of Enology, 2006
cards.reference: Ribéreau-Gayon, Glories, Maujean & Dubourdieu, Handbook of Enology, Volume 2: The Chemistry of Wine, Stabilization and Treatments, 2nd edition, Wiley, 2006

cards.question: A pressure cooker lifts boiling water from 100 °C to about 120 °C. If cooking reactions double every 10 °C, how many times faster?
cards.answer: 2 x 2 = 4 times faster.
cards.move: When a rate compounds, count the steps, not the size of the numbers.
cards.trap: About 20% faster, comparing 120 with 100.
cards.hint: Count the ten-degree steps, then double once for each.
steps: 120 - 100 = 20 °C, which is two steps of 10 °C.
Each step doubles the rate.
2 x 2 = 4 times faster.
cards.reference: Damodaran, Parkin & Fennema (eds), Fennema's Food Chemistry, 4th edition, CRC Press, 2008

cards.question: Why does vitamin C on a cut apple delay browning rather than simply slow it?
cards.answer: Because it undoes the damage instead of stopping it. The apple's enzyme keeps turning phenols into quinones, which link up into brown pigment; vitamin C converts each quinone back and is used up doing so. While any remains the flesh stays pale; once it runs out, browning starts at full speed.
cards.move: A shield that is used up by its work buys time, not safety.
cards.source: Nicolas et al., Crit. Rev. Food Sci., 1994
cards.reference: Nicolas, Richard-Forget, Goupy, Amiot & Aubert, Enzymatic browning reactions in apple and apple products, Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition 34, 109, 1994

cards.question: Should foods high in acrylamide, such as coffee and crisps, carry cancer warnings?
cards.answer: Yes. Acrylamide forms when starchy foods are fried, roasted or baked hot, and it causes cancer in rodents; the WHO's cancer agency rates it probably carcinogenic to humans. Buyers can cut their intake easily, by toasting lighter or choosing other products. A warning costs little and lets people decide.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is how much animal evidence counts without human confirmation.
cards.counterpoint: No. Large studies of people's diets have found no consistent link between dietary acrylamide and cancer, and the rodent doses were far above anything eaten. In 2019 California exempted coffee from its warning law on that basis. A label on every roasted food teaches shoppers to ignore labels.
cards.reference: International Agency for Research on Cancer, IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Volume 60: Some Industrial Chemicals, 1994

cards.question: A tomato sauce holding 0.6 mg of iron per 100 g simmers in an unenamelled cast-iron pot. Roughly how much iron afterwards?
cards.answer: About 6 mg, roughly ten times as much. Acid in the tomatoes dissolves iron from the pot wall during a long simmer. In a 1986 US test, spaghetti sauce rose from about 0.6 to nearly 6 mg per 100 g. One serving then carries a good share of an adult's daily iron.
cards.move: A container can be an ingredient; ask what it gives up.
cards.trap: About 0.7 mg, as a seasoned pot seems to add almost nothing.
cards.source: Brittin & Nossaman, J. Am. Diet. Assoc., 1986
cards.reference: Brittin & Nossaman, Iron content of food cooked in iron utensils, Journal of the American Dietetic Association 86, 897, 1986

cards.question: When did fire first appear on Earth?
cards.answer: About 420 million years ago, in the last tenth of Earth's history. Fire needs fuel, oxygen and a spark. Lightning was always there, but fuel arrived only with land plants, and oxygen had to rise high enough. The oldest charcoal is that old: for four billion years, lightning struck ground with nothing to burn.
cards.move: A thing needs all its ingredients; the last one to arrive sets the date.
cards.reference: Glasspool, Edwards & Axe, Charcoal in the Silurian as evidence for the earliest wildfire, Geology, 2004

cards.question: How does a halon extinguisher stop a fire without removing its oxygen?
cards.answer: By breaking the chain reaction. A flame runs on short-lived fragments of molecules, hydrogen atoms and hydroxyl radicals, that carry the reaction from one fuel molecule to the next. Bromine from the halon captures them and is freed to capture more, so a few per cent of halon suffices. The oxygen stays; the messengers go.
cards.move: To stop a chain reaction, go after what carries it, not what feeds it.
cards.source: Drysdale, An Introduction to Fire Dynamics, 2011
cards.reference: Drysdale, An Introduction to Fire Dynamics, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2011

cards.question: Why can a heap of rags used to apply linseed oil catch fire on its own?
cards.answer: Because the oil dries by reacting with oxygen, not by evaporating, and the reaction gives off heat. On a thin coat the heat escapes; in a heap of rags it builds up, and warmth speeds the reaction, which makes more warmth, until the pile ignites, often hours after the work is finished.
cards.move: Heat that cannot escape becomes the fuel for more heat.
cards.source: Bowes, Self-Heating: Evaluating and Controlling the Hazards, 1984
cards.reference: Bowes, Self-Heating: Evaluating and Controlling the Hazards, HMSO, 1984

cards.question: In a fire test, a room with older furniture took nearly half an hour to reach flashover. How long did a modern room take?
cards.answer: Under 4 minutes. Flashover is when a burning room gets hot enough for everything in it to ignite at once. Foam and synthetic fabrics release heat far faster than natural fibres and solid wood; in Underwriters Laboratories' side-by-side test, that cut the time to flashover from about half an hour to minutes.
cards.move: A rule of thumb is only as current as the world it measured.
cards.trap: About 25 minutes: adjusting down from the older room's time.
cards.reference: Kerber, Analysis of Changing Residential Fire Dynamics and Its Implications on Firefighter Operational Timeframes, Fire Technology, 2012

cards.question: Should forest managers deliberately burn far more land to prevent bigger wildfires?
cards.answer: A century of putting out every fire, by 10 a.m. the next day under a US Forest Service rule of 1935, has packed dry forests with fuel that frequent low fires once cleared. Burning in chosen weather is the only way to remove it at scale; otherwise it burns anyway, in the worst weather.
cards.move: The fuel must go either way; the fight is over which risk to run.
cards.counterpoint: Planned burns escape. New Mexico's largest recorded wildfire, in 2022, began as two Forest Service burns that got away and destroyed hundreds of homes. Smoke harms health whoever lights the fire, warming is shrinking the windows of safe weather, and thinning by machine around towns removes fuel where it matters with far less risk.
cards.reference: North et al., Reform forest fire management, Science, 2015

cards.question: How do fire laboratories measure how much heat a burning sofa gives off?
cards.answer: By the oxygen it uses up. Wood, foam, plastics and petrol all release about 13.1 megajoules per kilogram of oxygen consumed, give or take 5%, as Clayton Huggett showed in 1980. So labs burn the sofa under a hood, measure the oxygen missing from the exhaust, and multiply: the heat is read from the air.
cards.move: When an output scatters everywhere, measure the input it cannot avoid using.
cards.reference: Huggett, Estimation of rate of heat release by means of oxygen consumption measurements, Fire and Materials, 1980

cards.question: Indonesia's 1997 fires burned largely in peat, smouldering underground. Their carbon equalled what share of that year's global fossil-fuel emissions?
cards.answer: Roughly a quarter: between 13% and 40%, by the estimate of Susan Page's team, or 0.81 to 2.57 billion tonnes of carbon. Most came from peat, waterlogged plant matter metres deep, drained for plantations and then set smouldering for months. A smoulder shows little flame and can burn on underground through the rain.
cards.move: Judge a fire by what it consumes, not by how bright it looks.
cards.trap: About 1%, since a low smoulder looks too feeble to matter.
cards.reference: Page, Siegert, Rieley, Boehm, Jaya & Limin, The amount of carbon released from peat and forest fires in Indonesia during 1997, Nature, 2002

cards.question: A 1 mm layer of dust weighing 500 kg per cubic metre is blown up through a 4 m high room. Grams per cubic metre?
cards.answer: Spread through 4 m of height: 500 / 4 = 125 grams per cubic metre.
cards.move: Before calling a layer harmless, ask what it becomes once airborne.
cards.trap: Judging a film thin enough to write a name in too slight to matter.
cards.hint: Work per square metre of floor: weigh the dust, then find the air it spreads into.
steps: Each square metre of floor holds 1 mm × 1 m² = 1 litre of dust.
1 litre at 500 kg per cubic metre weighs 500 g.
Spread through 4 m of height: 500 / 4 = 125 grams per cubic metre.
cards.source: Eckhoff, Dust Explosions in the Process Industries
cards.reference: Eckhoff, Dust Explosions in the Process Industries, 3rd edition, Gulf Professional Publishing, 2003

cards.question: What did droplets of heptane fuel do aboard the space station after their flames went out?
cards.answer: Many kept burning, unseen. In NASA's FLEX experiment, one large droplet's bright flame died, yet the droplet went on shrinking steadily: a cool flame, a slower reaction hundreds of degrees cooler and too dim for the eye, had taken over. On Earth such flames are fleeting; in weightlessness they held.
cards.move: When the visible sign stops, check whether the process has stopped too.
cards.source: Nayagam et al., Combustion and Flame, 2012
cards.reference: Nayagam, Dietrich, Ferkul, Hicks & Williams, Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?, Combustion and Flame, 2012

cards.question: Should furniture foam be required to resist a small open flame, even if that means adding flame retardants?
cards.answer: Many deadly house fires grow from upholstered furniture, and modern foam burns fast and hot. Britain's strict 1988 furniture rules were followed by a long fall in fire deaths, and government reviews credited them with lives saved. Chemicals can be swapped for safer ones; a sofa that shrugs off a match buys escape time.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how much escape time the chemicals buy.
cards.counterpoint: California's 1975 rule made foam pass a small-flame test, so makers loaded it with retardants, since found in household dust and in people's blood. Reviews found little sign it saved lives: deadly furniture fires mostly start from a smouldering cigarette on the fabric, not a flame reaching the foam. In 2013 California switched to a smoulder test.
cards.source: Shaw et al., Reviews on Environmental Health, 2010
cards.reference: Shaw et al., Halogenated flame retardants: do the fire safety benefits justify the risks?, Reviews on Environmental Health, 2010

cards.question: What stood in the way of sending telephone calls down glass fibres in the 1960s?
cards.answer: Impurities, mostly. In 1966 Charles Kao argued that glass itself was not the problem: traces of iron and other metals absorbed the light. Purified glass, he said, could lose under 20 decibels per kilometre, leaving 1% of the light after a kilometre. Corning managed it in 1970. Today's fibre still keeps 1% after 100 km.
cards.move: Before blaming the material, check what else is in it.
cards.source: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Nobel background, 2009
cards.reference: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Scientific Background on the Nobel Prize in Physics 2009: Two Revolutionary Optical Technologies, 2009

cards.question: How is window glass made so flat without being ground or polished?
cards.answer: By floating it on molten tin. Most flat glass is now poured as a ribbon onto a bath of liquid tin, which is perfectly level, a method Alastair Pilkington brought into production in 1959. Left alone, the glass spreads until gravity and surface tension balance at about 6 mm thick; rollers stretch it thinner.
cards.move: The cheapest precision is the kind physics supplies for free.
cards.source: Pilkington, Proceedings of the Royal Society, 1969
cards.reference: Pilkington, Review Lecture: The Float Glass Process, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A, 1969

cards.question: Do physicists have an agreed theory of how a cooling liquid turns into glass?
cards.answer: No. In 1995 the Nobel laureate Philip Anderson called it probably the deepest unsolved problem in solid-state theory, and it is still argued over. As molten glass cools, it stiffens more than a billionfold, yet its atoms stay as jumbled as in the liquid: a solid that looks like a snapshot of a liquid.
cards.move: A thing can be useful for millennia before anyone can explain it.
cards.reference: Anderson, Through the Glass Lightly, Science, 1995

cards.question: True or false: a toughened glass panel can shatter by itself, years after fitting, with nothing touching it?
cards.answer: True. The best-known culprit is a speck of nickel sulphide trapped when the glass was made. Toughening freezes it in a high-temperature crystal form; over months or years it reverts and swells by a few per cent, enough to release the stress stored in the pane. Baking panes at about 290 °C weeds most out.
cards.move: A flaw can wait years for the conditions that set it off.
cards.trap: Glass only breaks when something hits it or bends it.
cards.source: EN 14179, heat soaked toughened safety glass
cards.reference: EN 14179-1:2005, Glass in building — Heat soaked thermally toughened soda lime silicate safety glass — Part 1: Definition and description

cards.question: White sand and window glass are both mostly silica. Why is sand opaque?
options: Light scatters off countless grain surfaces
Its atoms are arranged in crystals
cards.answer: Light scatters off countless grain surfaces. Each boundary between silica and air bends and reflects a little light, and after thousands of them nothing passes straight through. Crystals are not the reason: a single quartz crystal is clear. Crush a clear pane and the heap turns white too, as clear ice turns into white snow.
cards.move: When two things differ in several ways, test each difference separately.
cards.trap: Crystal versus glass is the famous difference, so it must be the cause.
cards.reference: Bohren & Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles, Wiley, 1983

cards.question: How is phone cover glass made several times stronger without being quenched like toughened glass?
cards.answer: By swapping atoms. The glass soaks in molten potassium nitrate at around 400 °C, and potassium ions replace the smaller sodium ions near its surface. Crammed into sites built for smaller ions, the surface layer is squeezed tight, and a scratch must beat that squeeze to open. The glass is stuffed, not chilled.
cards.move: Build in the opposite of the stress you expect to face.
cards.source: Varshneya, Int. J. Applied Glass Science, 2010
cards.reference: Varshneya, Chemical Strengthening of Glass: Lessons Learned and Yet To Be Learned, International Journal of Applied Glass Science, 2010

cards.question: True or false: a thin glass fibre can bear far more load per square millimetre than a thick glass rod?
cards.answer: True. Glass breaks at its worst flaw, a microscopic scratch where stress gathers, and a thick rod has far more surface for a bad one to lurk in. Alan Griffith showed it around 1920 with fibres he drew himself: thinner and fresher meant stronger. Pristine fibre can be a hundred times stronger than window glass.
cards.move: The more places something can fail, the likelier one of them will.
cards.trap: False, since strength per square millimetre belongs to the material.
cards.reference: Griffith, The Phenomena of Rupture and Flow in Solids, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A, 1921

cards.question: What does it take to turn a molten metal into a glass instead of a crystal?
cards.answer: Speed. Metal atoms find their crystal places almost at once, so the melt must be cooled faster than they can line up. In 1960 Pol Duwez's group at Caltech made the first metallic glass, gold with silicon, by splatting drops onto cold copper at about a million degrees a second: flakes micrometres thick.
cards.move: Order takes time; deny it the time and disorder is what stays.
cards.reference: Klement, Willens & Duwez, Non-crystalline Structure in Solidified Gold–Silicon Alloys, Nature, 1960

cards.question: A glassworks switches from sand and soda to 100% crushed recycled glass. Roughly how much furnace energy does it save?
cards.answer: About a quarter. Each 10% of recycled glass, called cullet, cuts furnace energy by about 2.5 to 3%. Cullet skips breaking down soda ash and limestone, but must still be melted again at around 1,500 °C. Aluminium saves about 95% because it skips freeing metal from ore; glass has no such step.
cards.move: A saving is only as large as the step it lets you skip.
cards.trap: About 90%, by analogy with the famous saving on recycled aluminium.
cards.source: Worrell et al., Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2008
cards.reference: https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/glass_guidebook_en.pdf

cards.question: Each glass surface reflects about 4% of light striking it head-on. What share passes straight through a double-glazed window?
cards.answer: About 85%, before any absorption. A double-glazed window has four glass surfaces, and light must pass them all: 0.96 × 0.96 × 0.96 × 0.96 is about 0.85. The 4% comes from glass's refractive index of 1.5: (0.5 ÷ 2.5)² = 0.04. At night, with the room lit, the pane shows faint doubled reflections.
cards.move: When every stage takes a small cut, multiply the stages.
cards.trap: About 96%, counting one reflection for the window as a whole.
cards.reference: Hecht, Optics, 5th edition, Pearson, 2017

cards.question: Satellite orbits measure Earth's pull, Newton's constant G times its mass, to about nine significant figures. To how many is its mass known?
cards.answer: About five. An orbit reveals only the product; separating the mass needs G itself, measured in laboratories with masses small enough to lift, where gravity is feeble and hard to isolate. G is pinned to barely five figures, so Earth's mass stops at 5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg.
cards.move: A result is only as sharp as the bluntest number it depends on.
cards.trap: Assuming the mass is known as precisely as its pull.
cards.reference: Petit and Luzum (eds.), IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, 2010

cards.question: Descend 2,900 km from the surface to the top of Earth's core. What does gravity do on the way down?
options: It rises by about a tenth
It falls by about a tenth
cards.answer: It rises by about a tenth, to roughly 10.7 m/s². The rock above cancels itself out, and so much of Earth's mass is packed into its iron core that nearing it outweighs the rock left behind. George Airy found the pull already stronger at the bottom of a 383 m coal pit in 1854.
cards.move: Ask where the weight is concentrated before assuming things thin out evenly.
cards.trap: Picturing a uniform Earth, where gravity falls steadily with depth.

cards.question: A bathroom scale shows 70 kg at the equator, where gravity is 9.780 m/s². How many grams more at a pole, where it is 9.832?
cards.move: A scale measures a pull, and the pull depends on where you stand.
cards.trap: Assuming a scale weighs mass, so the reading cannot change.
cards.hint: Work out how much stronger the pull is at the pole, as a percentage.
steps: 9.832 / 9.780 = 1.00532: the pull at a pole is 0.532% stronger.
A scale measures that pull, so it reads 0.532% more.
cards.reference: NIMA, Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984, Technical Report TR8350.2, third edition, 2000

cards.question: How can two satellites weigh the water under northern India?
cards.answer: By its pull. The GRACE twins flew 220 km apart, and extra mass below tugged the leading one ahead, stretching the gap by microns that their microwave link could measure. Between 2002 and 2008 the pull over Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana weakened: 109 km³ of groundwater gone, twice India's largest reservoir.
cards.move: What you cannot see, you can sometimes still weigh.

cards.question: What did Henry Cavendish's famous 1798 experiment with lead balls set out to measure?
cards.answer: The density of the Earth. He reported 5.48 times that of water; an arithmetic slip, spotted decades later, hid the 5.45 his data gave, against 5.51 today. Physicists began quoting a value of G only in the 1870s, and textbooks later recast his experiment as its measurement.
cards.move: Ask what the original author thought they were measuring.
cards.reference: Clotfelter, The Cavendish experiment as Cavendish knew it, American Journal of Physics 55, 210, 1987

cards.question: Why is Earth's gravity in metres per second squared, 9.81, so close to π squared, 9.87?
cards.answer: Because the metre nearly was a pendulum. A pendulum whose single swing takes one second is g/π² metres long, and in 1791 the French Academy weighed it as the new unit. It chose instead a ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator arc, since gravity varies with latitude; that arc landed within 0.6% of the pendulum.
cards.move: When two numbers match too well, look for a shared history before calling it luck.
cards.source: Alder, The Measure of All Things, 2002
cards.reference: Alder, The Measure of All Things: The Seven-Year Odyssey and Hidden Error That Transformed the World, Free Press, 2002

cards.question: The Sun has 333,000 times Earth's mass and sits about 390 times farther from the Moon. Which pulls the Moon harder?
options: The Sun, about twice as hard
cards.answer: The Sun, about twice as hard. Divide 333,000 by 390 squared, about 152,000, and the Sun wins by 2.2 to 1. The Moon stays with Earth because the Sun pulls both almost equally, so only the small difference counts. Traced from above, the Moon's path round the Sun never loops; it always bends sunward.
cards.move: Before naming the strongest influence, ask what acts equally on everything nearby.
cards.trap: Earth, by far, because the Moon is visibly circling Earth.
cards.reference: Roy, Orbital Motion, 4th edition, Institute of Physics Publishing, 2005

cards.question: True or false: the open ocean's surface, tides and waves aside, never strays more than a few metres from a perfect ellipsoid?
cards.answer: False. Still water settles along the geoid, the surface that gravity makes level, and gravity is uneven. South of India, over a deficit of mass deep below, the sea sits about 106 m under the ellipsoid; near New Guinea it stands about 85 m above. A ship crossing the dip feels perfectly level throughout.
cards.move: Level is defined by gravity, and gravity differs from place to place.
cards.trap: True, because sea level is the zero every height starts from.
cards.reference: Pavlis, Holmes, Kenyon & Factor, The development and evaluation of the Earth Gravitational Model 2008 (EGM2008), Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 2012

cards.question: Air pressure is the weight of the air overhead. Roughly how many trillion tonnes does Earth's whole atmosphere weigh?
cards.answer: 10 x 510 = about 5,100 trillion tonnes.
cards.move: Multiply a small load by the area it covers before calling it light.
cards.trap: Guessing small, because air feels as if it weighs nothing.
cards.hint: Start from how many tonnes of air press on one square metre.
steps: Sea-level pressure, about 101,000 pascals, is the weight of about 10 tonnes of air on each square metre.
Earth's surface is about 510 trillion square metres.
10 x 510 = about 5,100 trillion tonnes.
cards.reference: Trenberth & Smith, The Mass of the Atmosphere: A Constraint on Global Analyses, Journal of Climate 18, 864, 2005

cards.question: Why did the official uncertainty on Newton's constant G grow about twelvefold in 1998?
cards.answer: Because one careful laboratory disagreed. In 1995 PTB, Germany's national standards institute, reported a G about 0.6% above the accepted value, far outside everyone's error bars. With no fault found in it, CODATA, which sets the recommended constants, widened its uncertainty from about 0.013% to 0.15%. Later measurements did not repeat the German value.
cards.move: An honest error bar can grow even as the evidence improves.
cards.source: Mohr & Taylor, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2000
cards.reference: Mohr & Taylor, CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 1998, Reviews of Modern Physics 72, 351, 2000

cards.question: Is there a size of infinity between the whole numbers and the real numbers?
cards.answer: The standard axioms, the starting rules of mathematics, cannot say. Cantor guessed there is none, and the question headed Hilbert's list of great problems in 1900. Kurt Gödel showed in 1940 that the axioms cannot refute the guess; Paul Cohen showed in 1963 that they cannot prove it. Mathematicians may assume either answer without contradiction.
cards.move: Before hunting for an answer, check the rules can deliver one.
cards.reference: Cohen, The Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 1963

cards.question: How common are numbers that, like π, solve no polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients?
cards.answer: Almost every number is one. In 1874 Cantor showed that the numbers which do solve such equations can be listed one by one, while the real numbers cannot, so a number picked at random solves none. Yet proofs are hard: e was settled in 1873, π in 1882, and π + e remains open.
cards.move: What is almost everywhere can still be almost impossible to point at.
cards.reference: Dauben, Georg Cantor: His Mathematics and Philosophy of the Infinite, Harvard University Press, 1979

cards.question: Can adding up the same endless list of numbers in a different order change the total?
cards.answer: Yes, if its positive and negative terms each add up to infinity alone. Bernhard Riemann showed in the 1850s that such a series can be reordered to reach any total. 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 … comes to about 0.693; take one positive then two negatives, and the same terms make half that.
cards.move: When huge amounts nearly cancel, small choices decide what is left.

diagram.caption: The same terms, reordered: the usual order settles near 0.693, one plus then two minus on half that.

cards.reference: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1976

cards.question: True or false: every fraction between 0 and 1 can be covered by intervals whose lengths add up to a millionth?
cards.answer: True. The fractions can be put in a single list. Cover the first with an interval half a millionth long, the second with a quarter of a millionth, and so on, halving each time: the lengths add up to a millionth, yet every fraction is covered, although there is a fraction between any two numbers.
cards.move: Something can be everywhere and still take up no room.
cards.trap: Fractions are everywhere on the line, so covering them covers everything.
cards.reference: Royden & Fitzpatrick, Real Analysis, 4th edition, Pearson, 2010

cards.question: The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … grows without limit. How many terms does it take to pass 100?
cards.answer: A 44-digit number: roughly 15 followed by 42 zeros. The total grows like a logarithm: each extra 1 needs about 2.7 times as many terms as the one before. A billion terms reach only about 21; a computer adding a billion terms a second since the Big Bang would be near 62.
cards.move: Growing forever is not the same as growing large.
cards.trap: About a trillion: a number that big feels like it must be enough.

x.label: terms, as a power of ten

diagram.caption: A billion terms reach only 21; passing 100 takes a number 44 digits long.

cards.reference: Havil, Gamma: Exploring Euler's Constant, Princeton University Press, 2003

cards.question: What did Galileo conclude in 1638 on noticing that the square numbers pair off with all whole numbers?
cards.answer: That equal, greater and less do not apply to infinite quantities. Squares thin out, 10 up to 100 and only 100 up to 10,000, yet every number n pairs with its square n². Galileo therefore stopped comparing. Cantor, some 240 years later, took the pairing itself as the meaning of equal size.
cards.move: When a word stops working, choose between dropping it and redefining it.
cards.reference: Galileo, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, trans. Crew & de Salvio, Macmillan, 1914

cards.question: Write 4 as 2², change each 2 to 3, subtract 1; rewrite in base 3, exponents too, and repeat upwards. Where does it end?
options: It falls into a repeating loop
cards.answer: It reaches zero. The values climb for an absurdly long time, but every such sequence ends at zero, as Reuben Goodstein proved in 1944; from 4 it takes about 3 × 2^402,653,211 steps. In 1982 Kirby and Paris showed ordinary arithmetic cannot prove it: the proof must count past every whole number.
cards.move: However long a trend has run, ask what could force it to turn.
cards.trap: It grows forever, since every term checked is bigger than the last.
cards.source: Kirby & Paris, Bull. London Math. Soc., 1982
cards.reference: Kirby & Paris, Accessible independence results for Peano arithmetic, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society, 1982

cards.question: A solid ball can, in theory, be cut up and reassembled into two balls of the same size. How few pieces suffice?
cards.answer: Five. Raphael Robinson proved in 1947 that five suffice and no fewer will do; one can be a single point. The pieces are so scattered that no volume can be assigned to them, and building them needs the axiom of choice, which picks from infinitely many sets without saying how. No knife could cut them.
cards.move: Find the one ingredient a strange result rests on before doubting the rest.
cards.trap: Infinitely many, since a finite set of cuts seems unable to create volume.
cards.reference: Robinson, On the decomposition of spheres, Fundamenta Mathematicae, 1947

cards.question: True or false: a square contains exactly as many points as one of its sides?
cards.answer: True. Cantor proved it in 1877, in letters to Dedekind. Interleaving the digits of a point's two coordinates gives one number on the side; Dedekind spotted a snag with decimals like 0.1999…, which equals 0.2, and Cantor repaired the pairing so it matched exactly. A solid cube holds no more points than a line segment.
cards.move: Bigger in size and more in number are different questions.
cards.trap: Thinking a square must hold more, since it holds whole lines of points.
cards.reference: Gouvêa, Was Cantor Surprised?, American Mathematical Monthly, 2011

cards.question: Start with a triangle of area 1. Each round, every edge sprouts a triangle one ninth the size of the previous round's. Final area?
cards.answer: Final area: 1 + 3/5 = 1.6.
cards.move: A boundary can grow forever around something that stays finite.
cards.trap: Expecting an endless area, because the outline grows without limit.
cards.hint: Each edge turns into four edges, so count the new triangles as well as their size.
steps: Round 1: 3 triangles of 1/9 each add 1/3.
Each round has 4 times as many triangles at 1/9 the size, so it adds 4/9 of the last round.
Final area: 1 + 3/5 = 1.6.
cards.source: Mandelbrot, The Fractal Geometry of Nature
cards.reference: Mandelbrot, The Fractal Geometry of Nature, W. H. Freeman, 1982

cards.question: How can a solid insulate better than the still air it is mostly made of?
cards.answer: By making its pores smaller than the distance an air molecule travels before hitting another, about 70 nanometres. Inside silica aerogel, molecules mostly strike pore walls instead of passing energy to each other, so the gas carries less heat. The best aerogels, over 90% air, conduct about half as much heat as still air.
cards.move: Make a space small enough and different rules take over inside it.
cards.reference: Hüsing & Schubert, Aerogels—Airy Materials: Chemistry, Structure, and Properties, Angewandte Chemie International Edition, 1998

cards.question: What was the vacuum flask invented to hold?
cards.answer: Liquefied gases. James Dewar built it at the Royal Institution in 1892 to stop liquid air and oxygen boiling away: two glass walls with a vacuum between them block conduction and convection, and silvering the walls reflects radiant heat. From 1904 a Berlin firm, Thermos, turned the laboratory vessel into a picnic flask.
cards.move: Ask what problem an everyday object was first built to solve.
cards.source: Mendelssohn, The Quest for Absolute Zero, 1966
cards.reference: Mendelssohn, The Quest for Absolute Zero: The Meaning of Low Temperature Physics, Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1966

cards.question: What share of a single-glazed window's resistance to heat loss comes from its 4 mm of glass?
cards.answer: About 2%. Glass conducts heat well. What slows the heat is the thin layer of still air clinging to each face: by the standard glazing calculation, the two films resist heat flow about 40 times more than 4 mm of glass does. Double the glass and the window loses barely less heat.
cards.move: Before crediting the visible barrier, look for the invisible one.
cards.trap: About 90%: the glass is the only solid thing in the way.
cards.reference: EN 673:2011, Glass in building — Determination of thermal transmittance (U value) — Calculation method

cards.question: True or false: a metre-thick sandstone wall keeps heat in better than 10 cm of mineral wool?
cards.answer: False. Sandstone conducts heat about 60 times more readily than mineral wool, so a metre of it resists heat flow roughly six times less than 10 cm of wool. What thick walls do well is store heat, evening out day and night, which is why a stone church feels cool on a summer afternoon.
cards.move: Slowing a swing is not the same as stopping a flow.
cards.trap: Cool stone churches in summer make thick walls seem good insulators.
cards.source: ISO 10456, tabulated thermal values of materials
cards.reference: ISO 10456:2007, Building materials and products — Hygrothermal properties — Tabulated design values and procedures for determining declared and design thermal values

cards.question: True or false: under a clear Antarctic winter sky, most of an emperor penguin's outer plumage is colder than the surrounding air?
cards.answer: True. The feathers insulate so well that little body heat reaches their outer surface, while that surface keeps radiating heat to the sky. Thermal cameras at an Antarctic colony found most of the plumage below air temperature, so the birds were gaining a little heat from the air around them, not losing it.
cards.move: A cold surface can mean the insulation is working, not failing.
cards.trap: A warm-blooded body should warm the surface that wraps it.
cards.reference: McCafferty, Gilbert, Thierry, Currie, Le Maho & Ancel, Emperor penguin body surfaces cool below air temperature, Biology Letters, 2013

cards.question: Why do spacecraft insulation blankets stack many thin metal-coated layers that must not touch each other?
cards.answer: In a vacuum heat crosses only as radiation, and each shiny layer reflects most of it back, so more layers mean proportionally less flow. Layers that touch conduct heat, so fine netting keeps them apart. Stitched, pinned and pressed at the edges, a fitted blanket often does several times worse than a flat sample.
cards.move: Extra layers help only while each one stays apart from the next.
cards.reference: Gilmore (ed.), Spacecraft Thermal Control Handbook, Volume 1: Fundamental Technologies, 2nd edition, The Aerospace Press, 2002

cards.question: In an ordinary double-glazed window, how does most of the heat cross the gap between the panes?
options: By conduction through the trapped air
By infrared radiation from pane to pane
By convection currents circling the gap
cards.answer: By infrared radiation. Plain glass absorbs and re-emits infrared almost like a black surface, so in a typical gap about two thirds of the heat crosses as radiation. A metal coating thinner than a wavelength of light reflects that infrared back, cutting the heat crossing the gap by more than half.
cards.move: Block the path that carries the most, not the one easiest to picture.
cards.trap: Picturing the trapped air as the barrier the heat must conduct through.
cards.reference: ISO 15099:2003, Thermal performance of windows, doors and shading devices — Detailed calculations

cards.question: True or false: people in homes with the worst energy ratings tend to burn more heating fuel than the ratings predict?
cards.answer: False. Across 3,400 German homes, occupants used on average 30% less heating energy than their calculated rating, and the gap widened as ratings worsened. Ratings assume every room kept warm; people in draughty houses heat fewer rooms, less. So insulation priced against the rating saves less than forecast: part of the waste was never burned.
cards.move: Measure a saving against what was really used, not what was modelled.
cards.trap: Assuming a leaky house wastes even more in practice than on paper.

cards.question: Metal fixings cover 1% of an insulated wall and pass 25 times more heat per square metre. By what percentage does total heat loss rise?
cards.answer: 0.99 + 0.25 = 1.24, so heat loss rises by 24%.
cards.move: A sliver of the area can carry a large share of the flow.
cards.trap: Expecting about 1% more, since the metal covers 1% of the area.
cards.hint: Weight each part of the wall by its area and by the heat it lets through.
steps: Call the insulated wall's loss 1 unit per square metre.
99% of the area at 1 unit gives 0.99; 1% at 25 units gives 0.25.
0.99 + 0.25 = 1.24, so heat loss rises by 24%.

diagram.caption: Metal fixings cover 1% of the wall but carry a fifth of its heat loss.

cards.reference: ISO 6946:2017, Building components and building elements — Thermal resistance and thermal transmittance — Calculation methods

cards.question: In water of the same temperature, why does a neoprene wetsuit keep a diver less warm at 20 metres than at the surface?
options: The water inside is flushed out faster
Pressure crushes the gas bubbles in the foam
Denser deep water draws heat away faster
cards.answer: Pressure crushes the gas bubbles in the foam. Neoprene insulates because it is mostly trapped gas; the water film inside does little. Total pressure doubles by 10 metres and triples by 20, so bubbles shrink, the suit thins and conducts more. Drysuit divers add gas as they descend to stop that squeeze.
cards.move: Find what a material's virtue is made of, then ask what squeezes it.
cards.trap: Blaming the water inside the suit, the part divers are told warms them.
cards.source: Bardy et al., Journal of Physics D, 2005

cards.question: Laser goggles are rated by optical density. What fraction of the beam do goggles rated OD 5 let through?
cards.answer: About one in 100,000. Optical density counts powers of ten: OD 1 passes a tenth, OD 2 a hundredth, OD 5 a hundred-thousandth. A 1-watt beam leaves 10 microwatts. The rating holds only at the colours printed on the frame; goggles dense for green laser light can be nearly clear to infrared.
cards.move: On any scale that counts powers of ten, each step multiplies.
cards.trap: Reading OD 5 as five times weaker, like a simple scale.
cards.source: ANSI Z136.1, Safe Use of Lasers
cards.reference: American National Standards Institute, ANSI Z136.1, American National Standard for Safe Use of Lasers, Laser Institute of America, 2014

cards.question: True or false: a green laser pointer can shine invisible infrared light strong enough to harm the eye?
cards.answer: True. Most green pointers make their colour in steps: a diode's infrared pumps a crystal that emits longer infrared, and a second crystal halves its wavelength to green. A filter should stop leftovers. In 2010 US government testers found some cheap pointers leaking infrared past safe limits: invisible light that triggers no blink.
cards.move: Check what a process leaves behind, not only what it was built to make.
cards.trap: Assuming a green beam contains nothing but the green you see.
cards.reference: Galang, Restelli, Hagley and Clark, A Green Laser Pointer Hazard, NIST Technical Note 1668, 2010

cards.question: What was the first biological tissue IBM researchers carved with the ultraviolet laser now used to reshape eyes?
cards.answer: Leftover Thanksgiving turkey. In November 1981 Rangaswamy Srinivasan took turkey cartilage into the lab and found a 193 nm ultraviolet laser carved it cleanly. Its photons break molecular bonds outright, so tissue vanishes in thin layers without scorching what is next to it. Eye surgeons adapted the method to sculpt the cornea.
cards.move: A tool's best use often turns up far from the job it was built for.
cards.reference: https://www.optica.org/about/newsroom/news_releases/2013/how_a_leftover_thanksgiving_dinner_gave_us_lasik_surgery/

cards.question: Why did the man who coined the word laser wait decades for his patents?
cards.answer: Because rivals patented first and he had filed late. In 1957 Gordon Gould sketched the device in a notebook headed laser and had it notarised at a Bronx sweet shop, but a patent went to Charles Townes and Arthur Schawlow. Gould's claims were granted from 1977 onward, after a legal war lasting three decades.
cards.move: Priority is proved by paperwork, and paperwork has its own timetable.
cards.reference: Taylor, Laser: The Inventor, the Nobel Laureate, and the Thirty-Year Patent War, Simon & Schuster, 2000

cards.question: Should selling handheld laser pointers stronger than 1 milliwatt to the public be banned?
cards.answer: Below about 1 milliwatt, the blink reflex protects the eye; stronger pointers can burn a retina faster than anyone looks away, and a beam across a cockpit window can dazzle a pilot on landing. Nobody needs that power to point at a slide. A sales ban stops the hazard at the one point anyone controls.
cards.move: Both sides want fewer injuries; they differ on whether sales or aim can be policed.
cards.counterpoint: Bans on sale are easily dodged: powerful lasers are bought online, often mislabelled, so a ban mainly burdens astronomers, surveyors and teachers who use brighter beams responsibly. The harm comes from pointing lasers at people and aircraft, which can be targeted directly, as Britain did in 2018 with prison terms for shining lasers at vehicles.
cards.reference: International Electrotechnical Commission, IEC 60825-1:2014, Safety of laser products, Part 1: Equipment classification and requirements, 2014

cards.question: True or false: photons in a steady laser beam reach a detector at random moments, like raindrops, not evenly spaced?
cards.answer: True. A laser's wave is steady and orderly, yet its photons arrive independently of one another: counts per time slice scatter like raindrops on a roof. Light from a bulb or star is lumpier still: its photons bunch. Evenly spaced photons need special sources, such as a single atom emitting one by one.
cards.move: An orderly whole can be built from parts that arrive at random.
cards.trap: False, because perfectly ordered light should deliver photons in step.
cards.source: Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light, 2000
cards.reference: Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light, 3rd edition, Oxford University Press, 2000

cards.question: Blu-ray reads with a 405 nm laser against DVD's 650 nm, and its lens focuses more steeply. How much more does one layer hold?
cards.answer: About 5 times: 25 GB against 4.7. Data is read by a focused laser spot whose width scales with wavelength, so its area shrinks with the square: 1.6 squared is 2.6. The steeper lens, numerical aperture 0.85 against 0.60, narrows the spot again, and the two together shrink its area about fivefold.
cards.move: When a length shrinks, ask how many dimensions feel the saving.
cards.trap: About 1.6 times, scaling capacity with wavelength alone.
cards.source: Blu-ray Disc Association, BD-ROM white paper
cards.reference: Blu-ray Disc Association, White Paper Blu-ray Disc Format: 1.C Physical Format Specifications for BD-ROM, 2010

cards.question: True or false: shining bright enough light on a collection of two-level atoms can put most of them in the upper level?
cards.answer: False. Light that lifts atoms up also stimulates excited ones to drop back, equally likely per atom. However bright the light, the populations only approach half and half, where the material turns transparent. That is why every laser uses three or four energy levels, pumping by one route and lasing on another.
cards.move: If a push also undoes itself, more push buys only a stalemate.
cards.trap: True, since more light should keep pushing more atoms up.
cards.reference: Siegman, Lasers, University Science Books, 1986

cards.question: In 2022 America's National Ignition Facility got 3.15 MJ of fusion from 2.05 MJ of laser light. What did the lasers draw from the grid?
cards.answer: About 300 MJ. The shot beat the light delivered to the target, the milestone called ignition, but the flash lamps powering NIF's lasers turn under 1% of their electricity into ultraviolet light on target. Counted from the wall socket, the shot returned about one joule for every hundred spent.
cards.move: Ask where the boundary was drawn before accepting a claimed gain.
cards.trap: About 2 MJ, taking the laser energy as the whole bill.
cards.reference: Abu-Shawareb et al. (Indirect Drive ICF Collaboration), Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment, Physical Review Letters 132, 065102, 2024

cards.question: Why does a laser spot on a matt wall look grainy and shimmer as you move your head?
cards.answer: Because the grain is made inside your eye. A matt wall scatters the laser's single, orderly wave along paths of slightly different lengths, and on the retina they interfere, bright where they add and dark where they cancel. Formed in the eye, this speckle stays sharp with glasses off, and drifts as the head moves.
cards.move: Some patterns belong to the observer, not to the thing observed.
cards.reference: Goodman, Speckle Phenomena in Optics: Theory and Applications, Roberts and Company, 2007

cards.question: Chromium atoms make rubies red. What colour is the chromium oxide that painters buy as a pigment?
cards.answer: Dull green. It is the same chromium, but its surroundings decide which light it absorbs. Squeezed tightly by oxygen in a ruby's crystal, it absorbs yellow-green and looks red; held more loosely in its own oxide, it absorbs orange-red and looks green. Emeralds owe their green to the same looser grip.
cards.move: The same ingredient can do opposite things in a different setting.
cards.trap: Assuming an element carries its colour wherever it goes.
cards.source: Nassau, The Physics and Chemistry of Color, 2001
cards.reference: Nassau, The Physics and Chemistry of Color: The Fifteen Causes of Color, 2nd edition, Wiley, 2001

cards.question: Why do the trees in many 17th-century Dutch landscape paintings look blue?
options: Old varnish has turned them blue
cards.answer: Their yellow has faded. Painters often mixed greens from a stable blue and a yellow lake, a dye fixed onto a chalky base, and those yellows fade in light. The blue survived and the yellow did not, so leaves painted green now read as blue-grey.
cards.move: What looks like the original taste may be only what lasted.
cards.trap: Taking the colours that survived for the colours that were painted.
cards.source: Saunders and Kirby, National Gallery Technical Bulletin, 1994
cards.reference: Saunders and Kirby, Light-induced colour changes in red and yellow lake pigments, National Gallery Technical Bulletin 15, 1994

cards.question: Why does a splash of water make a T-shirt or a patch of sand look darker?
cards.answer: Water hides the surfaces that scatter light. In dry cloth or sand, every boundary between air and solid bounces light back. Water bends light nearly as much as the solids, so when it fills the gaps those boundaries barely reflect, and light travels deeper and is absorbed. Pigment ground in oil darkens the same way.
cards.move: What happens at the edges can matter more than what things are made of.
cards.reference: Lekner and Dorf, Why some things are darker when wet, Applied Optics 27, 1278, 1988

cards.question: What finally made ultramarine, the blue once ground from Afghan lapis lazuli, cheap enough for everyone?
cards.answer: A prize. In 1824 a French industrial society offered 6,000 francs for an artificial ultramarine costing under 300 francs a kilo; Jean-Baptiste Guimet claimed it in 1828 by roasting clay, soda, charcoal and sulphur. His blue matched the stone's chemically, and a colour once kept for the Virgin's robe ended up in laundry blue.
cards.move: A standing reward can buy what no single inventor sets out to find.
cards.reference: Plesters, Ultramarine blue, natural and artificial, in Roy (ed.), Artists' Pigments: A Handbook of Their History and Characteristics, vol. 2, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1993

cards.question: Should titanium dioxide, the white pigment in sweets and icing, be banned from food, as the EU has done?
cards.answer: Its only job in food is cosmetic, making sweets and icing brighter white, so it must clear a high bar. In 2021 Europe's food-safety agency said it could no longer rule out damage to DNA from the nanoparticles it contains, and set no safe daily intake. A colour nobody needs does not earn that doubt.
cards.move: The disagreement is not about the evidence but about what an unexcluded risk should cost.
cards.counterpoint: The same data did not show harm, only an inability to exclude it, and regulators in Britain, Canada and Australia reviewed it and kept it. It passes through the gut largely unabsorbed. Banning on an unexcluded risk invites banning almost anything, and the substitutes, from rice starch to calcium carbonate, give duller, less stable whites.
cards.reference: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings, Safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171) as a food additive, EFSA Journal 19(5), 2021

cards.question: White paint hides what lies beneath with grains of titanium dioxide. What grain size scatters light best?
options: About a quarter of a micrometre
cards.answer: About a quarter of a micrometre, roughly half the wavelength of visible light. Much bigger grains offer fewer scattering surfaces per gram; much smaller ones are too small for light waves to notice, and let them pass. Nanoscale titanium dioxide, the same compound, scatters so weakly that sunscreens made with it rub in clear.
cards.move: More of a good thing works only until the scale changes the rules.
cards.trap: A few nanometres, since finer grinding always means more surfaces.
cards.source: Braun et al., Progress in Organic Coatings, 1992
cards.reference: Braun, Baidins & Marganski, TiO2 pigment technology: a review, Progress in Organic Coatings 20, 105, 1992

cards.question: Why do cadmium yellows and reds have such clean, sharp colours?
cards.answer: Because they are semiconductors. Cadmium sulphide absorbs every photon energetic enough to lift an electron across its band gap and reflects the rest, so its colour stops at a sharp edge: blue and violet go, longer waves return. Swapping some sulphur for selenium narrows the gap, sliding the edge through orange to deep red.
cards.move: A clean boundary in what comes out often means a threshold inside.
cards.reference: Fiedler & Bayard, Cadmium Yellows, Oranges and Reds, in Feller (ed.), Artists' Pigments: A Handbook of Their History and Characteristics, vol. 1, National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1986

cards.question: True or false: a fluorescent orange paint can send back more orange light than the orange light falling on it?
cards.answer: True. An ordinary pigment can only return part of each colour it receives. A fluorescent one also absorbs blue and ultraviolet and re-emits that energy as orange, so at orange wavelengths its measured reflectance can pass 100%. That extra glow, made from light the eye barely registers, is why safety vests seem lit from within.
cards.move: Check whether the output was converted from something you were not counting.
cards.trap: False, because no surface returns more light than it receives.
cards.reference: Christie, Colour Chemistry, 2nd edition, Royal Society of Chemistry, 2015

cards.question: Why has Maya blue outlasted centuries of tropical rain when indigo, the dye that colours it, fades on its own?
cards.answer: Because the dye is caged in clay. Maya painters heated indigo with palygorskite, a clay whose crystals are threaded with channels under a nanometre wide; the molecules lodge in or over them, shielded from light and chemicals. The pigment resists acids that strip plain indigo, and still colours the Bonampak murals.
cards.move: A fragile thing can last if it is given a hard place to live.
cards.reference: Van Olphen, Maya Blue: A Clay-Organic Pigment?, Science 154, 645, 1966

cards.question: Each transparent glaze passes 70% of light per crossing, and light crosses down and back. What share returns through three glazes, in per cent?
cards.answer: 0.49 x 0.49 x 0.49 ≈ 0.12, about 12 per cent.
cards.move: Losses that stack multiply, so a few thin layers can swallow most light.
cards.trap: Subtracting 30% per glaze, as if losses simply added up.
cards.hint: Count the crossings first, then multiply by 0.7 once for each.
steps: Three glazes, down and back, make 6 crossings.
0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49, so each glaze passes about half, both ways.
0.49 x 0.49 x 0.49 ≈ 0.12, about 12 per cent.
cards.reference: Kubelka & Munk, Ein Beitrag zur Optik der Farbanstriche, Zeitschrift für technische Physik 12, 593, 1931

cards.question: What did the makers of one of the first plastics claim it would save?
cards.answer: Elephants and tortoises. Celluloid, patented by John Wesley Hyatt in 1870, stood in for ivory and tortoiseshell in combs, knife handles and piano keys, and its makers advertised it as relief for animals hunted for those scarce materials. Early plastic was sold as a conservationist's answer: a comb that did not cost a tortoise.
cards.move: A fix for one scarcity can become the next glut.
cards.source: Meikle, American Plastic: A Cultural History, 1995
cards.reference: Meikle, American Plastic: A Cultural History, Rutgers University Press, 1995

cards.question: What happened to 'biodegradable' shopping bags left in the sea and in soil for three years?
cards.answer: Many survived intact. In a Plymouth study, bags sold as biodegradable, along with oxo-degradable and ordinary ones, spent three years buried in soil or sunk in seawater and could still hold a load of shopping. Only open air broke them up, into fragments. A compostable bag was gone from the sea within three months.
cards.move: A label that says it breaks down should say where, and how fast.
cards.reference: Napper & Thompson, Environmental Deterioration of Biodegradable, Oxo-biodegradable, Compostable, and Conventional Plastic Carrier Bags in the Sea, Soil, and Open-Air Over a 3-Year Period, Environmental Science & Technology, 2019

cards.question: Of all the plastic made from 1950 to 2015, what share was made in the last 13 of those 65 years?
cards.answer: About half. Production grew from 2 million tonnes in 1950 to about 380 million in 2015, and growth that fast piles much of the total into the latest years. Of 8,300 million tonnes made by 2015, about half dates from 2002 on: younger than euro coins.
cards.move: When something keeps growing, most of it is recent.
cards.trap: About a fifth: 13 of 65 years is a fifth of the time.
cards.reference: Geyer, Jambeck & Law, Production, use, and fate of all plastics ever made, Science Advances, 2017

cards.question: Roughly what share of the world's oil goes into making plastics?
cards.answer: About 6%, by a 2016 estimate: roughly what all the world's aircraft use. Most oil is burned as fuel in engines and boilers and vanishes as it is used, while plastic stays in view all day, in every room and every bin.
cards.move: What you see all day is not necessarily what uses the most.
cards.trap: About 30%: plastic is everywhere, so it must take much of the oil.
cards.source: Ellen MacArthur Foundation, The New Plastics Economy, 2016
cards.reference: World Economic Forum, Ellen MacArthur Foundation & McKinsey & Company, The New Plastics Economy: Rethinking the future of plastics, 2016

cards.question: Should shops be pushed to replace plastic packaging with glass, paper or metal?
cards.answer: Plastic's harm is not its carbon but its persistence. Between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes reached the oceans in 2010 alone, breaking into fragments that never leave. Glass, paper and metal are inert, degradable or collected far more reliably. Emissions can be cut with clean energy; plastic in the sea cannot be recalled.
cards.move: Both sides want less harm; they disagree on which harm to count first.
cards.counterpoint: Swapping usually makes climate harm worse. A 2024 study found plastic had lower greenhouse emissions than its alternatives in 15 of 16 uses, because glass and metal are heavy and energy-hungry to make and move. Most ocean plastic leaks from places without waste collection; building collection there beats changing materials everywhere.
cards.source: Meng et al., Environmental Science & Technology, 2024
cards.reference: Meng, Brandão & Cullen, Replacing Plastics with Alternatives Is Worse for Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Most Cases, Environmental Science & Technology, 2024

cards.question: Where does the widely quoted figure of 450 years for a plastic bottle to break down come from?
cards.answer: From no experiment anyone can find. Collin Ward and Christopher Reddy traced it in 2020: about three quarters of the lifetimes quoted for a bottle were 450 years, repeated from infographics by NOAA and others, with no study behind them. Real rates depend on sunlight, heat and shape; no bottle has been watched that long.
cards.move: Ask where a round number was measured before repeating it.
cards.reference: https://www.pnas.org/content/117/26/14618

cards.question: What did most chemists of the early 1920s believe rubber and plastics were made of?
cards.answer: Loose clusters of small molecules held by weak forces, like particles in a glue. From 1920 Hermann Staudinger argued they were giant molecules, chains of thousands of atoms joined by ordinary chemical bonds; many colleagues insisted no molecule could be so large. Measurements bore him out, and a Nobel Prize followed in 1953.
cards.move: When a claim sounds too big to be true, check it against measurements.
cards.reference: Staudinger, Über Polymerisation, Berichte der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft, 1920

cards.question: Microbeads in cosmetics were banned in several countries. By a 2017 estimate, what share of the tiny plastic shed straight into oceans were they?
cards.answer: About 2%. The IUCN's estimate put synthetic textiles, shedding fibres in the wash, at about 35% and tyres wearing down on roads at 28%, with city dust next. Microbeads were easy to picture and easy to ban, so the law came first. The bigger sources are the laundry and the road.
cards.move: Before cheering a ban, ask what share of the problem it touched.
cards.trap: About 30%, because microbeads were the source that made the headlines.
cards.reference: Boucher & Friot, Primary Microplastics in the Oceans: A Global Evaluation of Sources, IUCN, 2017

cards.question: True or false: more than half the weight of PVC plastic comes from common salt rather than oil or gas?
cards.answer: True. PVC's repeating unit, C₂H₃Cl, is 57% chlorine by weight, and that chlorine comes from brine split by electricity, which also yields caustic soda. Only the rest comes from ethylene made from oil or gas. Hence PVC burns reluctantly, and burning it releases hydrogen chloride, which turns to hydrochloric acid in water.
cards.move: Ask what a thing is made of by weight, not by reputation.
cards.trap: False, since every plastic is assumed to be made from oil.
cards.reference: Allsopp & Vianello, Poly(Vinyl Chloride), Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry, Wiley-VCH, 2000

cards.question: Should plastic turned back into oil by chemical recycling count towards official recycling targets?
cards.answer: Mechanical recycling, melting and remoulding, suits only clean, sorted waste of one polymer; films, layered packets and dirty mixtures get burned or buried. Chemical recycling breaks them into oil or building blocks that make plastic as good as new, food-grade included. Excluding it removes any reason to build plants for waste nothing else handles.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how much output truly becomes plastic again.
cards.counterpoint: Pyrolysis, the commonest method, turns much of its input into fuel that is simply burned, and plants need steady clean feedstock, heat and money. Counting their output as recycled rests on accounting that spreads recycled content on paper across a refinery's products. Targets exist to keep material in use; counting fuel lets companies claim circularity while burning plastic.
cards.reference: Vollmer et al., Beyond Mechanical Recycling: Giving New Life to Plastic Waste, Angewandte Chemie International Edition, 2020

cards.question: How close together have primes been proved to keep turning up, forever?
cards.answer: Within 246 of each other. The twin prime conjecture says pairs 2 apart, like 11 and 13, never run out, but until 2013 nobody could prove any bound. Then Yitang Zhang, a little-known lecturer, proved one: 70 million. Within a year, an online collaboration using James Maynard's new method had cut it to 246.
cards.move: A first finite bound, however huge, is often the hard part.
cards.source: Polymath, Research in the Mathematical Sciences, 2014
cards.reference: D. H. J. Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals with many primes, Research in the Mathematical Sciences, 2014

cards.question: Has the number 1 always been excluded from the primes?
cards.answer: No. Many mathematicians counted it as prime into the twentieth century; D. N. Lehmer's 1914 table of primes up to ten million starts with 1. It was dropped for convenience: with 1 as a prime, factorising stops being unique, since 6 = 2 × 3 = 1 × 2 × 3.
cards.move: A definition is a tool; ask what would break if it changed.
cards.source: Caldwell & Xiong, Journal of Integer Sequences, 2012
cards.reference: Caldwell & Xiong, What is the Smallest Prime?, Journal of Integer Sequences, 2012

cards.question: Nearly every record-holding prime is a power of two minus one. Why?
options: Most numbers of that form are prime
That form has an especially fast test
Such primes are proved never to run out
cards.answer: That form has an especially fast test. The Lucas–Lehmer test settles whether 2^p − 1 is prime in about p squarings. For an ordinary number with millions of digits, no proof anywhere near that fast exists. The record list maps where primes can be proved, not where they lie.
cards.move: A list of discoveries maps where people could look, not what exists.
cards.trap: Most numbers of that form are prime: the record list seems to say so.
cards.reference: Crandall & Pomerance, Prime Numbers: A Computational Perspective, 2nd edition, Springer, 2005

cards.question: Roughly one in how many 100-digit numbers is prime?
cards.move: Thinning out slowly is not the same as running out.
cards.trap: Assuming primes that large must be vanishingly rare, one in billions.
cards.hint: The prime number theorem links how far apart primes are to the natural logarithm.
steps: Near a large number N, roughly one number in every ln N is prime, ln being the natural logarithm.
For 100-digit numbers, N is about 10^100, and ln(10^100) = 100 × ln 10.
cards.reference: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, 6th edition, Oxford University Press, 2008

cards.question: True or false: in the first 100 million primes, a prime's last digit tells you nothing about the next prime's last digit?
