cards.answer: False. After a prime ending in 1, the next ends in 1 only 18.5% of the time, against 25% if the digits were independent; it ends in 3 or 7 about 30% of the time. Every final digit shows the same reluctance to repeat, a pattern explained in 2016 by a conjecture still unproved.
cards.move: Random-looking is not the same as independent; check what follows what.
cards.trap: Primes look random, so one's final digit should say nothing about the next.
cards.reference: Lemke Oliver & Soundararajan, Unexpected biases in the distribution of consecutive primes, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 2016

cards.question: 3, 5 and 7 are evenly spaced primes. How long can a run of evenly spaced primes get?
cards.answer: Any length, Ben Green and Terence Tao proved in 2004. Unless a run starts at a small prime, as 3, 5, 7 does, its step must be a multiple of every prime up to its length, or some term would divide by it. A run of 26, found in 2010, steps by multiples of 223,092,870.
cards.move: Before hunting for a pattern, ask what shape it is forced to take.
cards.reference: Green & Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics, 2008

cards.question: True or false: Gauss's formula, which overestimates the count of primes at every point ever computed, overestimates it forever?
cards.answer: False. Littlewood proved in 1914 that the true count overtakes the estimate, called li(x), and falls back again infinitely often. Nobody has seen it happen: the first crossing lies somewhere between 10^19 and about 10^316, beyond any computer. Stanley Skewes's first bound on it, in 1933, was a tower of three powers of ten.
cards.move: Where the numbers grow too big to check, only a proof can speak.
cards.trap: True, since every one of trillions of checks agrees.
cards.reference: Littlewood, Sur la distribution des nombres premiers, Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 1914

cards.question: In 2012, researchers recovered the private keys of tens of thousands of web servers, keys built from pairs of huge primes. How?
options: Devices had too little randomness to pick primes
By chance, many keys shared a prime
cards.answer: Devices had too little randomness to pick primes. Routers made keys just after booting, before gathering unpredictable data, so separate machines chose the same prime. Two keys sharing a prime are split instantly by Euclid's method for common factors. By chance a match is hopeless: there are about 10^151 primes of the size used.
cards.move: When independent choices keep matching, look for what they share.
cards.trap: Blaming chance, as millions of keys make some matches inevitable.
cards.source: Heninger et al., USENIX Security Symposium, 2012
cards.reference: Heninger, Durumeric, Wustrow & Halderman, Mining Your Ps and Qs: Detection of Widespread Weak Keys in Network Devices, USENIX Security Symposium, 2012

cards.question: Pick two whole numbers at random. What is the chance they share no prime factor at all?
cards.answer: About 61%: exactly 6/π². Both numbers are even a quarter of the time, both divisible by 3 a ninth, by 5 a twenty-fifth. Each prime spoils a sliver of pairs, but the survivals multiply: 3/4 × 8/9 × 24/25 and on. Euler's sum of 1/n² supplies the π. Two pairs in five share a factor.
cards.move: Count every small way to fail before trusting the total.
cards.trap: About 95%, since a shared factor seems rare between random numbers.
cards.source: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory
cards.reference: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Springer, 1976

cards.question: Does Euclid's proof that primes never run out show that 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 is prime?
cards.answer: No, and it is not: 30,031 = 59 × 509. Euclid's argument, in Book IX of the Elements, says only that such a number leaves remainder 1 when divided by each listed prime, so its prime factors lie outside the list. Those can be new primes smaller than it: 59 and 509 were missing.
cards.move: Read what a proof shows, not what its recipe seems to promise.
cards.reference: Euclid, The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements, trans. Heath, Cambridge University Press, 1908

cards.question: In 1901 a mathematician estimated π by dropping a needle on ruled lines 3,408 times. What was wrong with his result?
cards.answer: It was too good. Mario Lazzarini's 1,808 crossings gave 355/113, π to six places, when honest runs that long miss by about 0.05. And with his needle length, 355/113 can only come out if the drops number a multiple of 213. He made 3,408: exactly 16 × 213, as if he stopped when it matched.
cards.move: When a result is better than the method allows, ask how it stopped.
cards.reference: Badger, Lazzarini's Lucky Approximation of π, Mathematics Magazine, 1994

cards.question: Two players bet on a fair coin tossed every second for a year. How long is the luckier one usually ahead?
cards.answer: Most of the year. In half of games the leader is ahead for more than 311 days; in one game in 20, for all but about 14 hours. Erasing a lead takes an equal run the other way, and such runs are slow, so one player often stays in front for months on end.
cards.move: A long lead in a fair game is evidence of nothing but time.
cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1, 3rd edition, Wiley, 1968

cards.question: Two players stake 32 coins each on first to three wins. Play stops at 2–1. What is the leader's fair share, in coins?
cards.answer: 3/4 of 64 = 48 coins.
cards.move: Divide by what could still happen, not by what already has.
cards.trap: Splitting 2 to 1 by rounds won, as a 1494 textbook did.
cards.hint: Ask how the unfinished game could end, not how it stood.
steps: The trailing player takes the pot only by winning the next two rounds.
Chance of that: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, so the leader's chance is 3/4.
3/4 of 64 = 48 coins.
cards.reference: Devlin, The Unfinished Game: Pascal, Fermat, and the Seventeenth-Century Letter That Made the World Modern, Basic Books, 2008

cards.question: Flip a coin four times and note the share of heads among flips right after a head. Averaged over many runs, what is it?
cards.answer: About 40%: 17/42. Each flip is fair, but picking flips that follow a head selects within a short run: once a head is picked, the flips left in that run hold one head fewer. The 1985 study that called basketball's hot hand a fallacy measured shooting this way; corrected, its data point the other way.
cards.move: How you pick the cases can bias a count even when each case is fair.
cards.trap: About 50%: coins have no memory, so every flip is even.
cards.reference: Miller & Sanjurjo, Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers, Econometrica, 2018

cards.question: True or false: four riffle shuffles can leave a 52-card deck in any of its possible orders?
cards.answer: False. A riffle cuts the deck and interleaves the halves, so four of them leave at most 16 strands of the original order woven together. Orders needing more strands are impossible, and they are almost all orders: under one in two million is reachable. It takes about seven to get close to random.
cards.move: A pattern you cannot see is not a pattern that is gone.
cards.trap: Four shuffles look thoroughly mixed, so any order seems possible.
cards.source: Bayer & Diaconis, Annals of Applied Probability, 1992
cards.reference: Bayer & Diaconis, Trailing the Dovetail Shuffle to Its Lair, Annals of Applied Probability, 1992

cards.question: A chord is drawn at random across a circle. What is the chance it is longer than a side of the inscribed equilateral triangle?
cards.answer: That depends on what random means, as Joseph Bertrand showed in 1889. Join two random points on the rim and the chance is 1/3. Cut a random radius at a random distance and it is 1/2. Drop the chord's midpoint anywhere inside the circle and it is 1/4. Three sensible methods, three answers.
cards.move: Before computing a chance, say exactly how the thing was chosen.
cards.reference: Jaynes, The Well-Posed Problem, Foundations of Physics, 1973

cards.question: A gambler bets £1 at a time on red at a single-zero wheel, until £100 becomes £200 or nothing. Chance of reaching £200?
cards.answer: Under 1%: about 0.45%. The house's small edge compounds bet after bet: the odds against doubling come to 19/18, losing chances over winning ones, to the 100th power, about 223 to 1. One £100 bet on red wins 18 times in 37. That bold bet is over a hundred times likelier to double the money.
cards.move: When the odds lean slightly against you, play as few rounds as possible.
cards.trap: About 49%, since each bet is nearly a coin toss.

diagram.caption: Betting £1 at a time reaches £200 just 0.45% of the time; one £100 bet, 48.6%.

cards.reference: Dubins & Savage, How to Gamble If You Must: Inequalities for Stochastic Processes, McGraw-Hill, 1965

cards.question: Early in 2020, Italy's overall COVID-19 case fatality rate was higher than China's. What did a comparison by age group show?
options: Italy lower in every age group
Italy higher in every age group
Italy higher in most age groups
cards.answer: Italy lower in every age group. Its confirmed cases were far older than China's, and older patients die far more often, so the mix of who was infected pushed Italy's total up while each age band fared better. Two totals built from different mixes of people compared the mixes, not the care.
cards.move: Before comparing two totals, check that they are made of the same mix.
cards.trap: Italy higher in every group, as a total usually reflects its parts.
cards.reference: von Kügelgen, Gresele & Schölkopf, Simpson's Paradox in COVID-19 Case Fatality Rates: A Mediation Analysis of Age-Related Causal Effects, IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, 2021

cards.question: True or false: precinct vote counts whose first digits break Benford's law are a reliable sign of electoral fraud?
cards.answer: False. Benford's law, where about 30% of numbers start with 1, holds for figures spread over many orders of magnitude. Precincts are drawn to similar sizes, so their counts cluster, say between 200 and 800, and cannot follow it. Tested on real elections, even a subtler second-digit version flagged honest counts and missed known fraud.
cards.move: A test works only on data shaped like the data it was built for.
cards.trap: True, because invented numbers do tend to break the law.
cards.reference: Deckert, Myagkov & Ordeshook, Benford's Law and the Detection of Election Fraud, Political Analysis, 2011

cards.question: Beauty is woken once if a coin lands heads, twice with memory wiped if tails. On waking, should she rate heads at one third?
cards.answer: Of all the wakings the experiment produces, two in three follow tails. Betting at every waking, even odds on heads would lose money over many runs, while odds of one in three would break even. Each waking is one of three moments she cannot tell apart, and only one comes after heads.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether waking up counts as evidence.
cards.counterpoint: She knew the coin was fair, and waking tells her nothing new: she was certain to wake either way. Belief should move only with new information, so it stays at one half. Counting wakings changes the payoff of a bet, not the chance of the coin. Philosophers remain split: Adam Elga argued a third, David Lewis a half.
cards.reference: Elga, Self-locating belief and the Sleeping Beauty problem, Analysis, 2000

cards.question: True or false: a radon atom that has already lasted a month is more likely to decay this week than a newly formed one?
cards.answer: False. A nucleus does not wear out: a radon-222 atom a month old has the same 50% chance of decaying in the next 3.8 days as one just formed. A sample shrinks because atoms leave it, not because survivors age. Uranium atoms older than the Earth decay at the rate they did when forged.
cards.move: Ask whether a thing can wear out before calling it overdue.
cards.trap: Treating an old atom like an old machine, near the end.
cards.source: Institute of Physics, IOPSpark, decay constant
cards.reference: https://spark.iop.org/decay-constant-radioactive

cards.question: In 2015 the ATLAS detector saw an excess of photon pairs at 750 GeV, a one-in-20,000 fluke at that mass. What became of it?
options: It was traced to a faulty cable
cards.answer: It vanished. One in 20,000 was the chance of a fluke at 750 GeV alone; the search had scanned many masses and widths, and a bump that size somewhere was about a 1-in-50 event. Data from 2016, nearly four times as much, showed nothing there, after months of theorists racing to explain it.
cards.move: A fluke somewhere is far likelier than a fluke right here.
cards.trap: Treating one-in-20,000 odds as too rare to be chance.
cards.reference: https://atlas.cern/updates/briefing/high-mass-di-photon-resonances-first-2016-atlas-results

cards.question: True or false: most of the mass of the atoms in your body is given to them by the Higgs field?
cards.answer: False. The Higgs gives quarks their own masses, but in a 2018 supercomputer calculation those masses made up about 9% of a proton. The rest is the energy of quarks and gluons held by the strong force, weighed through E = mc². In a 70 kg body, that is over 60 kg.
cards.move: When one cause gets all the credit, ask what share it carries.
cards.trap: Hearing that the Higgs gives particles mass, and assuming it gives most.
cards.source: Yang et al., Physical Review Letters, 2018
cards.reference: doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.212001

cards.question: What was Schrödinger's cat originally meant to prove?
cards.answer: That something had gone wrong. In 1935 Schrödinger set a cat beside poison triggered by one radioactive atom to show the absurdity of letting quantum indecision spread to everyday objects; he called it a quite ridiculous case. Einstein had written to him of a charge of gunpowder, both exploded and not.
cards.move: Check whether a famous example was meant as a model or a mockery.
cards.reference: Trimmer (trans.), The present situation in quantum mechanics: a translation of Schrödinger's cat paradox paper, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 124, 323, 1980

cards.question: What is the heaviest object yet shown to spread across two paths at once, like a wave?
cards.answer: A cluster of over 7,000 sodium atoms. In 2026 a Vienna team sent such clusters, 8 nm wide and heavier than most proteins, through gratings and saw them interfere like waves, each one spread over 133 nm. It took ultra-high vacuum, since one stray gas molecule would betray a cluster's path.
cards.move: What looks like a limit of size may be a limit of isolation.

cards.question: Why doesn't a lump of ordinary matter collapse under the electric attractions inside it?
cards.answer: Because electrons refuse to share a state. In 1967 Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that Pauli's rule, barring two electrons from one quantum state, keeps bulk matter stable; Dyson also showed that electric forces alone would not. Binding energy would then outgrow the amount of matter, and merging two lumps would release an explosion.
cards.move: A rule about what cannot happen can hold up more than any force.
cards.reference: Dyson & Lenard, Stability of Matter. I, Journal of Mathematical Physics 8, 423, 1967

cards.question: The 2015 Delft Bell test, the first to close its main loopholes at once, rested on how many entangled pairs?
cards.answer: About 245. Electron spins in two diamonds 1.3 km apart became entangled only when photons from both happened to meet, about once an hour, so 18 days yielded 245. That beat the classical limit with about a 4% chance of a fluke. Two photon experiments later that year, with far larger samples, confirmed it.
cards.move: Ask how many cases a landmark result stands on, not only its verdict.
cards.trap: About 245 million, since physics results rest on huge datasets.
cards.reference: Hensen et al., Loophole-free Bell inequality violation using electron spins separated by 1.3 kilometres, Nature 526, 682, 2015

cards.question: A tunnelling microscope's current falls about tenfold per 0.1 nm of gap. Widen the gap by 0.3 nm: by what factor?
cards.answer: 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 times smaller.
cards.move: When each step multiplies, the nearest point does nearly all the work.
cards.trap: Three times smaller, reading the gap change as proportional.
cards.hint: Count the tenfold steps first, then multiply them.
steps: 0.3 nm is three steps of 0.1 nm.
Each step divides the current by 10.
10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 times smaller.
cards.simply: The tip is a blunt mountain, but the one atom at its summit sits about 0.3 nm closer to the surface than its neighbours, so it carries roughly a thousand times their current. That is why a rough tip can still see single atoms.
cards.source: Binnig & Rohrer, Reviews of Modern Physics, 1987
cards.reference: Binnig & Rohrer, Scanning tunneling microscopy: from birth to adolescence, Reviews of Modern Physics 59, 615, 1987

cards.question: In 1922 Stern and Gerlach split a beam of silver atoms in two, as the old quantum theory predicted. What had they really seen?
cards.answer: Electron spin, not yet proposed. The orbit theory forecast two beams for the wrong reason: silver's outer electron has no orbital motion to split. The split came from spin, first proposed in 1925. The silver traces were so faint that Stern's cigar breath, rich in sulphur, blackened them into view.
cards.move: Matching the forecast does not prove the forecaster understood why.
cards.trap: Proof of the orbits, since the result matched the prediction.
cards.reference: Friedrich & Herschbach, Stern and Gerlach: How a Bad Cigar Helped Reorient Atomic Physics, Physics Today 56(12), 53, 2003

cards.question: Did Google's 2019 Sycamore chip do something no classical computer could practically match?
cards.answer: Yes. Sycamore sampled a random 53-qubit circuit in about 200 seconds, a job Google put at 10,000 years on the best supercomputer. Later classical tricks cut that estimate, but each needed enormous resources to catch one 2019 chip, and larger quantum chips have since moved the target out of reach again.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether an advantage must outlast better classical methods.
cards.counterpoint: No. The claim was a moving target from the start: within days IBM argued that using disk storage would bring the classical time down to about 2.5 days, and in 2022 a Chinese team reproduced the sampling in about 15 hours on 512 graphics chips. A task chosen only for being hard, and matched anyway, shows no lasting advantage.

cards.question: The first rainbow sits 42° from the point opposite the Sun, the second at 51°. Where does a third rainbow appear?
cards.answer: Around the Sun itself, roughly 40° from it. Light that bounces three times inside a raindrop is thrown forward, not back, so the third bow circles the Sun, where glare swamps it. It was predicted centuries ago, but the first convincing photographs of a natural one were only published in 2011.
cards.move: Do not assume the next step in a series continues the pattern.
cards.trap: Extending the pattern outward, one bow stacked beyond the last.
cards.reference: Grossmann, Schmidt and Haussmann, Photographic evidence for the third-order rainbow, Applied Optics 50, F134, 2011

cards.question: Midsummer noon, London: the Sun is 62° high. A rainbow rings the opposite point at 42°. How many degrees below the horizon is its top?
cards.answer: The top is 20° below the horizon.
cards.move: Know the geometry and you know when to stop looking.
cards.trap: Measuring the 42° up from the horizon instead of the shadow point.
cards.hint: Start by finding how far below the horizon the point opposite the Sun lies.
steps: The point opposite the Sun lies as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it: 62°.
The bow's top is 42° above that point: 62 − 42 = 20.
The top is 20° below the horizon.
cards.source: Minnaert, Light and Colour in the Outdoors, 1993
cards.reference: Minnaert, Light and Colour in the Outdoors, trans. Seymour, Springer, 1993

cards.question: Why is the sky between the two arcs of a double rainbow darker than the sky around it?
cards.answer: Hardly any raindrop sends light there. Drops bouncing light once inside return it within 42° of the point opposite the Sun, brightening the sky inside the first bow; drops bouncing it twice send it only beyond 51°. Between the two, the sky is dim: Alexander's band, named after a Greek writer of about AD 200.
cards.move: A dark gap can be evidence as good as a bright line.
cards.source: Lee and Fraser, The Rainbow Bridge, 2001
cards.reference: Lee and Fraser, The Rainbow Bridge: Rainbows in Art, Myth, and Science, Penn State University Press, 2001

cards.question: What do the faint pastel stripes just inside some rainbows reveal about light?
cards.answer: That it travels as a wave. Rays taking different paths through a drop leave at the same angle and interfere, adding up in some directions and cancelling in others. Straight-line ray optics cannot make these bands; Thomas Young cited them in 1804 as evidence for waves. They need small drops of even size.
cards.move: The faintest detail is often the one the old theory cannot explain.
cards.reference: Boyer, The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics, Princeton University Press, 1987

cards.question: Why does a rainbow in fog come out almost white?
cards.answer: Because fog droplets are tiny, under about 0.05 mm across. Light passing drops that small spreads out, an effect called diffraction, which smears each colour's bow so wide that the bands overlap and mix back to white. What remains is a broad, pale arc, sometimes with a faint red outer edge.
cards.move: Shrink anything far enough and the rules that sorted it stop working.
cards.reference: Greenler, Rainbows, Halos, and Glories, Cambridge University Press, 1980

cards.question: True or false: tilting polarised sunglasses can make parts of a rainbow almost vanish?
cards.answer: True. Reflected inside each drop near the angle that polarises light most, rainbow light leaves about 96% polarised, vibrating along the arc. A polarising lens passes it one way and blocks it turned a quarter circle. Ordinary sunglasses, built to cut glare from the ground, erase the top of the arch and leave its ends.
cards.move: A filter that seems neutral can quietly choose what you get to see.
cards.trap: False, because sunglasses dim all light evenly.
cards.reference: Können, Polarized Light in Nature, Cambridge University Press, 1985

cards.question: Water drops make a rainbow 42° from your head's shadow. Tiny glass beads bend light more strongly. Where does their bow sit?
cards.answer: Closer in, near 23°. Stronger bending turns each ray further round inside the bead, sending it back closer to the way it came, so the bright ring tightens around your shadow. For glass, with a refractive index near 1.5 against water's 1.33, the arithmetic gives about 23°. The same rainbow, drawn tighter.
cards.move: A famous number belongs to its material; change the material and recheck it.
cards.trap: Also at 42°, as if the angle were a rule of geometry.
cards.reference: Adam, The mathematical physics of rainbows and glories, Physics Reports 356, 229, 2002

cards.question: What splits a single rainbow into two arcs that branch from the same base?
cards.answer: Raindrops of two different sizes. Large drops fall fast enough for the air to squash them into flattened buns, and each size of flattened drop bends light to a slightly different angle. A shower mixing two populations draws two overlapping primary bows. Computer simulations published in 2012 were the first to reproduce such twinned rainbows.
cards.move: When one pattern splits in two, look for two populations mixed together.
cards.source: Sadeghi et al., ACM Trans. Graphics, 2012
cards.reference: Sadeghi et al., Physically-based simulation of rainbows, ACM Transactions on Graphics 31(1), 2012

cards.question: In Britain's prevailing westerly weather, which rainbow is the better sign that rain is heading your way?
cards.answer: A morning rainbow. A rainbow always lies opposite the Sun, so in the morning it hangs in the west: the shower is upwind, and weather there drifts east towards you. An evening rainbow sits in the east, where the rain has already passed. The old sailors' rhyme about morning warnings has geometry behind it.
cards.move: Where a sign appears can tell you more than the sign itself.
cards.trap: Neither, since weather rhymes sound like folklore.
cards.source: Lynch & Livingston, Color and Light in Nature
cards.reference: Lynch & Livingston, Color and Light in Nature, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2001

cards.question: When the Sun is low, what shape does a dewbow, the rainbow in dew on a lawn, draw on the grass?
cards.answer: A hyperbola, its arms sweeping away from you. Every rainbow is a cone of light opening 42° around the line from the Sun through your eye. Distant rain shows that cone as a circle. Flat ground slices it at a slant, and with the Sun lower than 42° the slice is a hyperbola.
cards.move: The same shape looks different depending on the surface that catches it.
cards.source: Walker, The Flying Circus of Physics, 2007
cards.reference: Walker, The Flying Circus of Physics, 2nd edition, Wiley, 2007

cards.question: Heating a mug of water from 20 °C to boiling adds energy, and energy has mass. How many nanograms heavier does it get?
cards.answer: 9 × 10⁻¹³ kg ≈ 0.9 nanograms.
cards.move: Every change in energy is a change in weight, however small.
cards.trap: Assuming E = mc² only matters inside reactors and bombs.
cards.hint: Work out the heat in joules first, then divide by the speed of light squared.
steps: A mug holds about 250 g of water, heated by 80 °C.
Water takes 4.2 J per gram per degree: 250 x 4.2 x 80 = 84,000 J.
Mass = energy / c² = 84,000 / (9 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 9 × 10⁻¹³ kg.
9 × 10⁻¹³ kg ≈ 0.9 nanograms.
cards.reference: Einstein, Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhängig?, Annalen der Physik 18, 639, 1905

cards.question: In 1919, one of three sets of eclipse photographs measured starlight bending by Newton's amount, not Einstein's. What was done with it?
cards.answer: It was set aside. Heat had blurred that telescope's images, the team judged, and the other two sets gave 1.98 and 1.61 seconds of arc, against Einstein's 1.75 and Newton's 0.87. Critics later called that bias, but the rejected plates, remeasured in 1979, gave 1.55: Einstein's side.
cards.move: Before trusting a verdict, ask what happened to the data that disagreed.
cards.trap: Assuming a famous confirmation must have counted every plate.
cards.reference: https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/testing-relativity-from-the-1919-eclipse-a-question-of-bias

cards.question: Why is mercury liquid at room temperature when its neighbours in the periodic table are solid?
cards.answer: Largely because of relativity. Mercury's 80 protons pull its innermost electrons to over half the speed of light, which makes them heavier and draws the outer electrons in tight, so the atoms bond only weakly. Switching relativity off in a 2013 simulation raised the melting point by 105 °C, to about 82 °C.
cards.move: The ordinary behaviour of a thing can rest on extreme conditions inside it.

cards.question: How small a difference in height has been shown to make two clocks tick at different rates?
cards.answer: About a millimetre. In 2022 JILA physicists compared the top and bottom of a single millimetre-tall cloud of about 100,000 strontium atoms and found the upper part ticking faster, as general relativity predicts: time runs slower deeper in gravity. The gap was about one part in 10¹⁹, across the width of a sharp pencil tip.
cards.move: An effect called negligible is often just below the current ruler.
cards.reference: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/02/jila-atomic-clocks-measure-einsteins-general-relativity-millimeter-scale

cards.question: What would a snapshot of a ball flying past at nearly light speed show?
cards.answer: A round ball, apparently rotated. Its length really does shrink, but light from its far parts must set off earlier to reach the camera with the rest, and the two effects add up to a turn. Predicted in 1959, it was first shown in 2025, with laser pulses mimicking a light speed under 2 m/s.
cards.move: What is true and what a camera records can be two different things.

cards.question: In 1971 atomic clocks flew round the world, eastward and westward. Compared with clocks left on the ground, which came back behind?
cards.answer: Only the eastbound clocks, by about 59 nanoseconds; the westbound ones gained about 273. The ground spins eastward too, so judged from Earth's centre an eastbound plane moves faster than the airport and a westbound one slower. Weaker gravity aloft sped up both sets, and only the westbound clocks kept that gain.
cards.move: Ask what the reference itself is doing before calling anything moving.
cards.trap: Both, because moving clocks always run slow.
cards.reference: Hafele & Keating, Around-the-World Atomic Clocks: Observed Relativistic Time Gains, Science 177, 168, 1972

cards.question: The LHC was built to raise protons from 450 GeV to 7,000 GeV, about a fifteenfold jump in energy. How much faster do they go?
cards.answer: About 0.0002% faster. At 450 GeV a proton already moves within about two millionths of light speed, and near that limit extra energy goes into momentum, not speed. At 7,000 GeV the gap shrinks to about one hundred-millionth. A lap of the 27 km ring takes about 89 microseconds before the ramp and after it.
cards.move: Near a hard limit, more effort buys almost nothing of what you measure.
cards.trap: About fifteen times, taking more energy to mean proportionally more speed.
cards.reference: Brüning et al. (eds), LHC Design Report, Volume 1: The LHC Main Ring, CERN-2004-003, CERN, 2004

cards.question: How can relativity matter in a wire whose electrons drift at well under a millimetre a second?
cards.answer: Because magnetism is relativity's correction to electricity. To a charge moving alongside, the wire's electrons and nuclei shrink by different amounts, so it stops looking neutral. The imbalance has twenty-odd zeros after the decimal point, but electric forces are so huge and so exactly cancelled that this sliver is the whole magnetic pull.
cards.move: A small effect can be large when it is all that survives a cancellation.
cards.reference: Purcell, Electricity and Magnetism, Berkeley Physics Course vol. 2, McGraw-Hill, 1965

cards.question: What did LIGO's first convincing gravitational-wave signal, seen in September 2010, turn out to be?
cards.answer: A planted fake. A few insiders could secretly inject simulated signals into the detectors to test the analysis. The 2010 event, nicknamed the Big Dog, passed every check; the collaboration wrote a paper and voted to submit it. In March 2011 a sealed envelope revealed the injection. The real first detection came in 2015.
cards.move: A checking process is proven only once it has been fed a convincing fake.
cards.source: Collins, Gravity's Ghost and Big Dog, 2013
cards.reference: Collins, Gravity's Ghost and Big Dog: Scientific Discovery and Social Analysis in the Twenty-First Century, University of Chicago Press, 2013

cards.question: Mercury's orbit swivels about 5,600 arcseconds a century as seen from Earth. How much of that is general relativity's doing?
cards.answer: About 43 arcseconds, under 1%. Some 5,026 come from Earth's own slowly wobbling axis, which shifts the sky's reference grid, and about 532 from the pulls of other planets; Newton's physics explained all that. Relativity's triumph is the small residue, first flagged by Le Verrier in 1859, that nothing else could account for.
cards.move: Subtract what would have happened anyway before crediting the famous cause.
cards.trap: Nearly all of it, since the orbit is relativity's famous proof.
cards.reference: Clemence, The Relativity Effect in Planetary Motions, Reviews of Modern Physics 19, 361, 1947

cards.question: Without relativity corrections, how far would a GPS satellite's clock drift from ground clocks each day?
cards.answer: About 38 microseconds. Weaker gravity 20,200 km up makes the satellite clock gain about 46 microseconds a day, and its orbital speed makes it lose about 7. Because positions come from light-travel times, 38 microseconds of error is roughly 11 km of drift in a single day.
cards.move: Multiply a small timing error by the speed of light before calling it small.
cards.trap: Assuming relativity only matters close to the speed of light.

cards.question: True or false: iron rusts faster in seawater than in a brine several times saltier?
cards.answer: True. Salt speeds rust by letting electric current flow through the water between patches of metal, but rust also needs dissolved oxygen, and the saltier the water, the less oxygen it holds. The rate peaks at a few per cent salt, about seawater's strength, and falls in a saturated brine of 26%.
cards.move: When more of a cause stops working, something else has run short.
cards.trap: Assuming that the saltier the water, the faster the rust.
cards.source: Revie and Uhlig, Corrosion and Corrosion Control, 2008
cards.reference: Revie and Uhlig, Corrosion and Corrosion Control, 4th edition, Wiley, 2008

cards.question: A 2016 study priced the world's corrosion damage. About what share of global GDP did it come to?
cards.answer: About 3%. NACE International, the corrosion engineers' body, put it at US$2.5 trillion a year, 3.4% of world output, across every sector of the economy. Corrosion rarely makes news because it works slowly and fails piecemeal. The study reckoned 15–35% could be saved with methods already known.
cards.move: Slow, scattered losses often outweigh the dramatic ones.
cards.trap: Rust feels like a nuisance, because it never makes headlines.
cards.reference: Koch et al., International Measures of Prevention, Application, and Economics of Corrosion Technologies Study, NACE International, 2016

cards.question: Aluminium reacts with air more readily than iron does. Why doesn't a can crumble away the way a nail rusts?
cards.answer: Its oxide stays put. The film on aluminium takes up only a little more room than the metal it replaced, so it clings, a few nanometres thick, and seals the surface. Rust needs about twice the space of its iron, so it cracks and flakes, and each flake bares fresh metal to the air.
cards.move: How readily something reacts matters less than whether its first damage protects it.
cards.source: Pilling and Bedworth, J. Inst. Metals, 1923
cards.reference: Pilling and Bedworth, The oxidation of metals at high temperatures, Journal of the Institute of Metals 29, 529, 1923

cards.question: Why has Delhi's iron pillar, set up about 1,600 years ago, barely rusted?
cards.answer: Chemistry, not a lost secret. The wrought iron is unusually rich in phosphorus, and as Delhi's weather wets and dries it, a thin, tight film rich in iron phosphate builds up instead of flaking rust. Metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam set out the explanation in 2000; the pillar is armoured by its own first corrosion.
cards.move: Before crediting a lost secret, check the ingredients and the weather.
cards.reference: Balasubramaniam, On the corrosion resistance of the Delhi iron pillar, Corrosion Science 42, 2103, 2000

cards.question: Why does a scratch rust faster on a tinned steel can than on a galvanised steel bucket?
cards.answer: Zinc corrodes in the steel's place; tin makes the steel corrode instead. Where zinc and iron touch in wet air, zinc gives up electrons first, protecting even a bare scratch. Tin corrodes less readily than iron, so at a scratch the exposed iron dissolves, faster than on an uncoated can.
cards.move: A protective layer can make the damage worse wherever it breaks.
cards.source: Jones, Principles and Prevention of Corrosion, 1996
cards.reference: Jones, Principles and Prevention of Corrosion, 2nd edition, Prentice Hall, 1996

cards.question: Steel and copper touching in seawater: which fails faster, steel rivets holding copper plates, or copper rivets holding steel plates?
options: Both at about the same rate
cards.answer: Steel rivets in copper plates. Steel corrodes either way, at a rate set by how much copper surface draws electrons from it. A small steel rivet in a broad copper plate takes the whole attack on a tiny area and is eaten quickly; a broad steel plate spreads it thin, barely pitted round copper rivets.
cards.move: Judge a harm by how concentrated it is, not only by its size.
cards.trap: Both at the same rate, since the same two metals touch.
cards.reference: Fontana, Corrosion Engineering, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1986

cards.question: Why were the nails at the heart of a Roman hoard buried in Scotland almost free of rust?
cards.answer: Because the outer nails used up the oxygen. Leaving its fortress at Inchtuthil around AD 87, the Roman army buried some 875,000 iron nails, weighing several tonnes, rather than leave them. Dug up in 1960, the outer layer had rusted into a solid crust that sealed out air; inside, nails lay almost as forged.
cards.move: The first part to fail can end up protecting the rest.
cards.source: Angus et al., J. Iron Steel Inst., 1962
cards.reference: Angus, Brown & Cleere, The iron nails from the Roman legionary fortress at Inchtuthil, Perthshire, Journal of the Iron and Steel Institute 200, 956, 1962

cards.question: How did the Parthenon's early 20th-century restoration end up cracking the marble it was meant to save?
cards.answer: Its iron rusted. Nikolaos Balanos joined blocks with unprotected iron clamps and dowels; as they corroded they swelled and split the stone from inside. The ancient builders had sealed their iron in molten lead, which kept water out, and many of their clamps survived. Today's restorers have swapped his iron for titanium.
cards.move: When copying an old technique, copy the precautions that made it last.
cards.reference: Economakis (ed.), Acropolis Restoration: The CCAM Interventions, Academy Editions, London, 1994

cards.question: A hand warmer holds 20 g of iron powder; rusting frees about 7 kJ per gram. At 3 watts, how many hours of heat?
cards.move: Slow release can make a vigorous reaction look like nothing at all.
cards.trap: A few minutes, picturing heat on the scale of a struck match.
cards.hint: Find the total energy first, then divide by the rate it is spent.
steps: 20 g x 7 kJ = 140 kJ, or 140,000 joules.
At 3 joules a second: 140,000 / 3 ≈ 46,700 seconds.
cards.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 2016
cards.reference: Haynes (ed.), CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th edition, CRC Press, 2016

cards.question: Carbonation creeps into concrete as the square root of time: 10 mm after 16 years. When does it reach steel 30 mm deep?
cards.answer: 9 x 16 = 144 years.
cards.move: When progress slows as it goes, extra distance costs far more time.
cards.trap: 48 years, tripling the time to triple the depth.
cards.hint: Ask how much the time must grow for the depth to triple.
steps: 30 mm is three times 10 mm.
Tripling the depth takes three squared, 9 times the time.
9 x 16 = 144 years.
cards.simply: Concrete keeps steel from rusting because it is strongly alkaline. Carbon dioxide from the air slowly neutralises it from the surface inward; when that front reaches the reinforcing bars, they start to rust, swell and push the concrete off.

series.label: depth grows as root of time

diagram.caption: Three times the depth takes nine times as long: 16 years for 10 mm, 144 for 30 mm.

cards.reference: Neville, Properties of Concrete, 5th edition, Pearson, 2011

cards.question: Why did some welded wartime ships break in two while sitting in calm water?
cards.answer: Cold made their steel brittle. Constance Tipper showed that the plate, tough when warm, cracked like glass below a transition temperature that cold seas reached. Welding made each hull one continuous piece, so a crack from a square hatch corner could run round it. The tanker Schenectady split in two at its dock in 1943.
cards.move: Test materials at the worst conditions they will meet, not the average.
cards.reference: Tipper, The Brittle Fracture Story, Cambridge University Press, 1962

cards.question: What stops old steel from being recycled into the best new steel?
cards.answer: Copper. Shredded cars bring wiring and motors into the scrap, and steelmaking cannot remove copper: being less reactive than iron, it stays in the melt instead of passing into the slag. A fraction of a per cent makes steel crack when rolled hot, so contaminated scrap ends up in reinforcing bar, not in car doors.
cards.move: A material recycles only as well as its worst passenger can be removed.
cards.source: Daehn et al., Environmental Science & Technology, 2017
cards.reference: Daehn, Cabrera Serrenho & Allwood, How Will Copper Contamination Constrain Future Global Steel Recycling?, Environmental Science & Technology, 2017

cards.question: Why was Bessemer's cheap steel useless with much of Europe's iron ore?
cards.answer: Phosphorus: much of that ore carries it, Bessemer's converter could not remove it, and it makes steel brittle in the cold. In 1879 Sidney Gilchrist Thomas, a police-court clerk and night-school chemist, and his cousin Percy Gilchrist lined the converter with dolomite, a limestone-like rock, pulling the phosphorus into a slag later sold as fertiliser.
cards.move: A cheap process is only cheap for the inputs it was built around.
cards.reference: Carr & Taplin, History of the British Steel Industry, Harvard University Press, 1962

cards.question: True or false: in a fire, structural steel has lost about half its strength by the time it reaches 600 °C?
cards.answer: True. Steel melts near 1,500 °C but only has to soften to fail. By the European design code it keeps full strength to 400 °C, 47% at 600 °C and 23% at 700 °C; a standard test fire passes 840 °C in half an hour. Hence the fireproofing sprayed on steel beams.
cards.move: Ask when a thing stops doing its job, not when it disappears.
cards.trap: Steel stays strong until it melts, far above any room fire.
cards.reference: EN 1993-1-2:2005, Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures — Part 1-2: General rules — Structural fire design

cards.question: A free 1 km steel rail warms 40 °C. Steel grows by 12 millionths of its length per degree. How many cm longer?
cards.move: Anything that cannot grow will push; plan for where the push goes.
cards.trap: Assuming stiff steel could only grow by a few millimetres.
cards.hint: Work out the growth for one degree first, then scale up.
steps: 1 km is 100,000 cm.
cards.reference: Esveld, Modern Railway Track, 2nd edition, MRT-Productions, 2001

cards.question: Why did new high-strength steel rods on San Francisco's Bay Bridge crack soon after being tightened in 2013?
cards.answer: Hydrogen embrittlement. Hydrogen atoms, small enough to slip between iron atoms, had got into the steel and, under high tension, gathered at the seams between its microscopic crystals until cracks opened. The stronger the steel, the likelier this is. Of 96 rods, 32 broke, and a $25 million steel saddle took over their job.
cards.move: The strongest version of a material can carry the most delicate weakness.
cards.reference: Toll Bridge Program Oversight Committee, Report on the A354 Grade BD High-Strength Steel Rods on the New East Span of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, 2013

cards.question: Where does a stainless steel fitting in seawater usually corrode first?
options: In tight gaps starved of oxygen
Where waves splash it with air
cards.answer: In tight gaps starved of oxygen. Stainless steel is guarded by a chromium oxide film nanometres thick that repairs itself with oxygen. Under a gasket or a barnacle the oxygen runs out, the film cannot heal, and chloride from the salt turns the trapped water acidic. The splashed surface stays bright while the joint rots.
cards.move: If protection needs feeding, look where the supply is cut off.
cards.trap: Where waves splash it, since ordinary iron rusts fastest with air.
cards.reference: Sedriks, Corrosion of Stainless Steels, 2nd edition, Wiley, 1996

cards.question: Carbon strips the oxygen from iron ore, Fe₂O₃, and leaves as CO₂. At minimum, how many tonnes of CO₂ per tonne of iron?
cards.answer: 13.4 thousand moles × 44 g ≈ 590 kg, about 0.59 tonnes of CO₂.
cards.move: When emissions come from the chemistry itself, cleaner energy cannot remove them.
cards.trap: Guessing near zero, as if the carbon were only fuel for heat.
cards.hint: Count atoms: iron weighs 56 per atom, CO₂ 44 per molecule, and Fe₂O₃ sets the oxygen per iron.
steps: 1 tonne of iron is 1,000,000 g ÷ 56 g ≈ 17.9 thousand moles of iron atoms.
Fe₂O₃ holds 1.5 oxygen atoms per iron atom: 17.9 × 1.5 ≈ 26.8 thousand moles of oxygen.
Each CO₂ carries off 2 oxygens: 26.8 ÷ 2 = 13.4 thousand moles of CO₂.
13.4 thousand moles × 44 g ≈ 590 kg, about 0.59 tonnes of CO₂.
cards.reference: Allwood & Cullen, Sustainable Materials: With Both Eyes Open, UIT Cambridge, 2012

cards.question: How many tonnes of steel are in use per person in a rich industrial country, counting buildings, vehicles and machines?
cards.answer: 10 + 1.5 + 1.3 + 0.6 ≈ 13 tonnes per person.
cards.move: The largest stocks are built into ground and walls, not carried around.
cards.trap: Picturing the family car, about a tonne, and stopping there.
cards.hint: Split it into construction, vehicles, machinery and appliances; construction dwarfs the rest.
steps: Buildings and infrastructure: reinforcing bar, beams, pipes and rails, about 10 tonnes a head.
Vehicles: cars, buses, trains and ships, about 1.5 tonnes.
Machinery: factory tools, cranes and turbines, about 1.3 tonnes.
Appliances and containers: about 0.6 tonnes.
10 + 1.5 + 1.3 + 0.6 ≈ 13 tonnes per person.
cards.source: Pauliuk et al., Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 2013
cards.reference: Pauliuk, Wang & Müller, Steel all over the world: Estimating in-use stocks of iron for 200 countries, Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 2013

cards.question: True or false: the Eiffel Tower, finished in 1889 as cheap steel spread across Europe, is built of steel?
cards.answer: False. It is puddled iron, a wrought iron made by stirring molten pig iron to burn out its carbon, then hammering out the slag. Bessemer steel existed, but its quality still varied, and Eiffel's firm had built its viaducts in wrought iron. Some 2.5 million rivets hold its 7,300 tonnes together.
cards.move: Builders reach for the material they know, not the newest one on offer.
cards.trap: True, since a landmark of 1889 sounds like a steel-age showpiece.
cards.reference: Loyrette, Gustave Eiffel, Rizzoli, 1985

cards.question: Should some research grants be handed out by lottery among the proposals that clear a quality bar?
cards.answer: Panels agree on which proposals are excellent and then cannot reliably separate the top slice from each other — re-scoring the same applications gives different winners. A lottery admits that honestly, costs a fraction of the reviewing effort, and stops rewarding whoever writes grants best rather than whoever does science best.
cards.move: Both sides accept the scoring is noisy. They disagree on whether noise is worse than no judgement at all.
cards.counterpoint: A draw removes the one moment where a field decides what matters most right now. Ranking is noisy, but it is not random, and the top of a good panel's list does outperform the middle. A lottery also strips accountability: nobody has to defend a bad allocation, because nobody made it.
cards.source: Trialled by the Health Research Council of New Zealand and the Volkswagen Foundation
cards.reference: Fang & Casadevall, Research Funding: the Case for a Modified Lottery, mBio, 2016

cards.question: Should we fund research into cooling the planet by putting particles in the stratosphere?
cards.answer: Not studying something does not stop it happening; it just guarantees that whoever tries it first will do so without knowing what follows. Research is not deployment, and the option value of understanding a lever we may be desperate for in forty years is very high.
cards.move: Research and deployment are separable in principle. The disagreement is whether they have ever been separated in practice.
cards.counterpoint: Every serious programme of this kind has ended in deployment, and the moral hazard is not hypothetical: the credible promise of a thermostat weakens the argument for cutting emissions today. It also hands one country a lever over everyone else's rainfall, with no mechanism to say no.
cards.reference: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Reflecting Sunlight: Recommendations for Solar Geoengineering Research and Research Governance, 2021

cards.question: Why does the catalogue of known planets look so strange?
cards.answer: Almost every exoplanet was found either by the star wobbling or by the star dimming as the planet crosses it. Both work best on big planets orbiting close in. So the catalogue is not a census of planets — it is a census of the planets those two methods can see.
cards.move: The list of known planets is a list of what the instruments can detect.
cards.reference: Akeson et al., The NASA Exoplanet Archive: Data and Tools for Exoplanet Research, Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 2013

cards.question: What actually limits how far a probe can go?
cards.answer: Not physics — plutonium-238. Deep-space probes run on its heat because sunlight is too weak out there. The United States stopped making it in 1988, ran down its stock, and only restarted production in 2015. Missions were planned around the size of a shelf.
cards.move: The edge of the solar system is a supply-chain problem.
cards.source: US Department of Energy, Pu-238 supply programme
cards.reference: National Research Council, Radioisotope Power Systems: An Imperative for Maintaining U.S. Leadership in Space Exploration, National Academies Press, 2009

cards.question: Where does the atmosphere end?
cards.answer: Nowhere in particular. The Karman line at 100 km is a round number chosen for convenience, not a boundary in nature. There is still enough air well above it to drag satellites down, which is why the space station has to be pushed back up several times a year.
cards.move: The edge of space is an agreed convention, not a discovery.
cards.source: Federation Aeronautique Internationale; ISS reboost logs
cards.reference: McDowell, The edge of space: Revisiting the Karman Line, Acta Astronautica, 2018

cards.question: Where did most of the tracked space junk come from?
cards.answer: Two events. A 2007 anti-satellite test and a 2009 collision between a working satellite and a dead one together produced a large share of everything now catalogued in low orbit. The problem is not gradual litter; it is a handful of very bad days.
cards.move: Most of the debris up there came from two afternoons.
cards.reference: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, Orbital Debris Quarterly News 13(2), 2009

cards.question: Is space really silent?
cards.answer: Sound needs a medium, and space has a thin one. Ripples through the gas of the Perseus galaxy cluster have been measured as pressure waves — a note about 57 octaves below middle C. Space is not silent so much as impossibly deep and impossibly quiet.
cards.move: There is a note in the Perseus cluster. Nobody could ever hear it.

cards.question: Among the stars within 32 light-years of the Sun, what share are small, dim red dwarfs?
cards.answer: Well over half. In the Gaia-era census within 32 light-years, 61% of all stars and brown dwarfs are red dwarfs. Yet not one is easy to see without a telescope: the brightest, AX Microscopii, sits at the very limit of perfect skies. The night sky is a catalogue of the rare, bright few.
cards.move: The easiest members to see are rarely the typical ones.
cards.trap: The naked-eye sky has almost no red dwarfs, so they seem rare.

cards.question: Why do most stars look white to the eye, though photographs show them orange, yellow and blue?
cards.answer: Because their light is too faint for colour vision. The eye's colour sensors, the cones, need much more light than the rods, which see in grey. Most stars are too dim to stir the cones enough to judge colour, so they look white; only the brightest, like orange Arcturus or red Antares, show a tint.
cards.move: A sensor below its threshold reports the default, not the truth.
cards.source: Clark, Visual Astronomy of the Deep Sky, 1990
cards.reference: Clark, Visual Astronomy of the Deep Sky, Cambridge University Press and Sky Publishing, 1990

cards.question: Where in the rainbow is sunlight at its brightest?
cards.answer: It depends on how the spectrum is sliced. Measured per nanometre of wavelength, the Sun's output peaks near 500 nm, blue-green. Measured per unit of frequency, the same light peaks near 880 nm, in the infrared. Neither is the true peak; the claim that eyes evolved to match it assumes one.
cards.move: Before trusting where a curve peaks, ask how its axis was cut.
cards.source: Soffer & Lynch, American Journal of Physics, 1999
cards.reference: Soffer & Lynch, Some paradoxes, errors, and resolutions concerning the spectral optimization of human vision, American Journal of Physics 67, 946, 1999

cards.question: What makes a blue star's spectrum look so different from a red star's?
cards.answer: Mostly temperature, not ingredients. In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that heat decides which atoms keep their electrons, and so which dark lines appear; beneath the differences, stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium. After Henry Norris Russell objected, her thesis called the hydrogen figure almost certainly not real. Four years later Russell confirmed it.
cards.move: Before blaming what things are made of, check the conditions they are in.
cards.reference: Payne, Stellar Atmospheres: A Contribution to the Observational Study of High Temperature in the Reversing Layers of Stars, Harvard Observatory Monographs No. 1, 1925

cards.question: Old star clusters should have lost all their blue stars billions of years ago, yet a few remain. What are they?
options: Pairs of old stars merged into one
Young stars formed from leftover gas
Foreground stars in front of the cluster
cards.answer: Pairs of old stars merged into one, or one fed by its partner. The extra mass makes a star hotter and bluer, and stirs in fresh hydrogen. Allan Sandage found these blue stragglers in the cluster M3 in 1953. Globular clusters hold almost no gas for new stars, so blue there never means young.
cards.move: When something outlives its expected lifespan, ask what has been feeding it.
cards.trap: Blue stars are young stars, so new ones must have formed.
cards.reference: Sandage, The color-magnitude diagram for the globular cluster M 3, The Astronomical Journal 58, 61, 1953

cards.question: Why can colour tell a 5,000 K star from a 10,000 K one, but not a 40,000 K star from a 100,000 K one?
cards.answer: Because the eye sees only the tail of a very hot star's glow. Such stars pour most of their light out in the ultraviolet, and the visible slice keeps almost the same blend of colours whatever the temperature. All of them look the same pale blue; their spectral lines, not their colour, give the temperature.
cards.move: A gauge near the end of its scale stops telling cases apart.
cards.reference: Wyszecki & Stiles, Color Science: Concepts and Methods, Quantitative Data and Formulae, 2nd ed., Wiley, 1982

cards.question: True or false: the hottest stars show the strongest hydrogen lines in their spectra?
cards.answer: False. Hydrogen lines peak in white A-type stars near 10,000 K, like Vega. The visible lines need hydrogen atoms whose electron already sits one step up; hotter stars strip the electron off entirely, cooler ones leave it at the bottom. That is why the old alphabetical classes were reshuffled into O, B, A.
cards.move: A signal that rises with its cause can fall when the cause goes further.
cards.trap: Assuming more heat always means a stronger hydrogen signal.
cards.reference: Gray & Corbally, Stellar Spectral Classification, Princeton University Press, 2009

cards.question: A blue-white dwarf star is 1/100 of the Sun's width and twice as hot. How many would shine as brightly as the Sun?
cards.answer: Each gives 16/10,000 of the Sun's light, so 10,000 ÷ 16 = 625 white dwarfs.
cards.move: Check the power in a rule before guessing how far a change carries.
cards.trap: Expecting twice the temperature to give twice the light, not 16 times.
cards.hint: Radiated light depends on the glowing area and on the temperature raised to the fourth power.
steps: Light output scales with surface area times temperature to the fourth power.
Area: (1/100)² = 1/10,000 of the Sun's; heat: 2⁴ = 16 times.
Each gives 16/10,000 of the Sun's light, so 10,000 ÷ 16 = 625 white dwarfs.
cards.reference: Carroll & Ostlie, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, 2nd ed., Pearson Addison-Wesley, 2007

cards.question: A cool brown dwarf's sodium vapour swallows most of its yellow and green light. What colour would it look up close?
cards.answer: Magenta, according to model spectra. Broad sodium absorption removes the middle of the visible spectrum, and what escapes is mostly deep red with a little blue: a purple-red. The name brown dwarf, coined by Jill Tarter in 1975, was chosen before any had been seen, not from a measurement.
cards.move: A name records what someone expected, not what was later seen.
cards.trap: Picturing any cooling hot body glowing dull red, like an ember.
cards.source: Burrows et al., Reviews of Modern Physics, 2001
cards.reference: Burrows, Hubbard, Lunine & Liebert, The theory of brown dwarfs and extrasolar giant planets, Reviews of Modern Physics 73, 719, 2001

cards.question: Dust between the stars makes a distant star look redder. What does that dust do to its dark spectral lines?
options: Erases the ones in the blue
cards.answer: Leaves them where they were. Dust scatters blue light more than red, dimming colours unevenly, but it moves no wavelength. That is the lever astronomers use: the line pattern gives the star's type and so its true colour, and the gap between that and the colour seen measures the dust in the way.
cards.move: A filter changes the mix of notes, never the notes themselves.
cards.trap: Treating dust reddening as a redshift, the stretch that motion causes.
cards.reference: Draine, Physics of the Interstellar and Intergalactic Medium, Princeton University Press, 2011

cards.question: How was the temperature of the cosmic background measured in 1941, 24 years before its discovery?
cards.answer: Through a molecule in space. In 1941 Andrew McKellar in Canada found cyanogen, a carbon-nitrogen molecule seen in starlight, slightly more excited than empty space should allow, as if bathed in radiation about 2 degrees above absolute zero. Nobody knew what was warming it until the cosmic background was found in 1965.
cards.move: An unexplained number in an old paper may be tomorrow's discovery.
cards.source: McKellar, Publications of the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory, 1941
cards.reference: McKellar, Molecular Lines from the Lowest States of Diatomic Molecules Composed of Atoms Probably Present in Interstellar Space, Publications of the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory 7, 251, 1941

cards.question: True or false: astronomers can measure how fast Earth is moving relative to the universe as a whole?
cards.answer: True. The cosmic background looks about 0.1% warmer in the direction the Sun is heading and cooler behind. The Planck satellite measured the Sun's speed through it at about 370 km/s, towards the stars of Leo and Crater. Relativity forbids a preferred frame for physics' laws, not a cosmic one for measuring motion.
cards.move: Every speed is relative to something; the question is to what.
cards.trap: Motion is relative, so there seems to be nothing to measure against.
cards.reference: Planck Collaboration, Planck 2018 results. I. Overview and the cosmological legacy of Planck, Astronomy & Astrophysics 641, A1, 2020

cards.question: In 2014 BICEP2 announced a swirl pattern in the cosmic background, hailed as gravitational waves from the universe's first instant. What mostly caused it?
options: Gravitational waves from the first instant
cards.answer: Dust in the Milky Way. Grains aligned by the galaxy's magnetic field glow with polarised light that makes the same swirls. BICEP2 had leaned on early, uncertain estimates of the dust; in 2015 a joint analysis with Planck's dust maps found the signal consistent with dust alone. The primordial waves are still undetected.
cards.move: When the result is exactly what you hoped for, check the dust first.
cards.trap: The pattern matched what the team had built the telescope to find.
cards.reference: doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.101301

cards.question: Why did NASA's WMAP team point out Stephen Hawking's initials in their map of the cosmic background?
cards.answer: As a warning. The letters S and H stand out clearly in the map; the odds of those exact shapes arising by chance are tiny, but so are the odds of any particular pattern. The team's 2011 review of claimed anomalies argued that oddities spotted after looking cannot be scored as if predicted.
cards.move: Decide what counts as strange before you look, not after.
cards.reference: Bennett et al., Seven-Year Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) Observations: Are There Cosmic Microwave Background Anomalies?, The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series 192, 17, 2011

cards.question: What colour was the cosmic background radiation when it was released, 380,000 years after the Big Bang?
cards.answer: Orange-white, like a lamp filament: the gas was about 2,700 °C when it turned transparent. Expansion has since stretched that light about 1,100 times, into microwaves. For a few million years the sky kept glowing, dimming through red into infrared; then the universe went dark until the first stars lit.
cards.move: Ask what a signal looked like before the journey changed it.
cards.reference: Loeb, How Did the First Stars and Galaxies Form?, Princeton University Press, 2010

cards.question: Which instrument did two Soviet physicists name in 1964 as the one able to detect the Big Bang's afterglow?
cards.answer: Bell Labs' horn antenna in New Jersey. Doroshkevich and Novikov calculated that the afterglow should dominate the radio sky at short wavelengths and cited measurements made with that antenna. A year later Penzias and Wilson, on that horn and unaware of the paper, found a hiss of about 3.5 K they could not remove.
cards.move: A prediction nobody reads is as good as one never made.
cards.reference: Doroshkevich & Novikov, Mean Density of Radiation in the Metagalaxy and Certain Problems in Relativistic Cosmology, Soviet Physics Doklady 9, 111, 1964

cards.question: How has the cosmic background's temperature been measured as it was more than 10 billion years ago?
cards.answer: With McKellar's 1941 trick, taken far away. Atoms in a gas cloud seen against a distant quasar are stirred by the background radiation of their own era. Srianand's team found carbon atoms in a cloud at redshift 2.34 excited as if by 6 to 14 K, bracketing the 9.1 K predicted: an older, hotter sky.
cards.move: A method that works nearby can be carried where nobody can go.
cards.reference: Srianand, Petitjean & Ledoux, The cosmic microwave background radiation temperature at a redshift of 2.34, Nature 408, 931, 2000

cards.question: A galaxy cluster's hot gas scatters the cosmic background, leaving a faint shadow on it. How does that shadow fade with distance?
options: Faster than the cluster's own light
cards.answer: Barely at all. The shadow is a fixed fraction of the background's brightness, and the background lies behind every cluster, however far. A cluster's own light fades with distance, but its dent in the microwave sky does not. Surveys use it to find clusters from when the universe was under a third of its age.
cards.move: Measured against the backdrop behind it, distance stops mattering.
cards.trap: Assuming everything seen across space dims with the square of distance.
cards.reference: Birkinshaw, The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, Physics Reports 310, 97, 1999

cards.question: True or false: the cosmic background holds more energy today than all the starlight and dust glow filling intergalactic space?
cards.answer: True. Summed over the sky, the afterglow of the Big Bang outshines the combined glow of every galaxy, from ultraviolet to far infrared, by ten to one or more. Stars have shone for over 13 billion years, yet the leftover heat of one early moment still carries most of the light in the universe.
cards.move: The brightest thing in view is not always the largest stock.
cards.trap: Picturing starlight, visible everywhere, as the universe's main light.
cards.reference: Hauser & Dwek, The Cosmic Infrared Background: Measurements and Implications, Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics 39, 249, 2001

cards.question: Why can the largest patterns on the cosmic background never be measured much more precisely than they are now?
options: Only one sky exists to sample
Galactic dust hides them for good
cards.answer: Only one sky exists to sample. The largest patterns span a quarter of the sky or more, so there are only a handful: five at the very largest scale. Measured perfectly, they are still five draws from chance. Planck has reached that limit; an odd pattern there can never be retested on a fresh sky.
cards.move: When the sample is everything there is, no instrument adds certainty.
cards.trap: Blaming foreground dust, which better maps could in principle remove.
cards.reference: Dodelson & Schmidt, Modern Cosmology, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2020

cards.question: Near the Sun, dark matter averages about one proton's mass per 3 cm³. How many grams of it fill a volume the size of Earth?
cards.move: Dominant overall and negligible in any one place can both be true.
cards.trap: Expecting tonnes, since dark matter outweighs ordinary matter about five to one.
cards.hint: Work out Earth's volume in cubic centimetres first.
steps: Earth's radius is about 6,400 km, so its volume is 4/3 × 3.14 × (6.4 × 10^8 cm)³ ≈ 1.1 × 10^27 cm³.
At one proton's mass per 3 cm³, that holds about 3.7 × 10^26 proton masses.
cards.reference: Read, The local dark matter density, Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 41, 063101, 2014

cards.question: How can a galaxy with almost no dark matter count as evidence that dark matter exists?
cards.answer: Because the main rival struggles to explain it. If the extra pull seen in galaxies came from modified gravity, it should follow ordinary matter everywhere. In 2018 van Dokkum's team found star clusters in NGC 1052-DF2 moving as if its stars were nearly all its mass. A substance can go missing; a law cannot.
cards.move: The strongest evidence can be an absence where an idea says none is possible.

cards.question: True or false: experiments copying the crystals of DAMA, the detector behind the best-known yearly dark matter signal, have confirmed it?
cards.answer: False. DAMA, under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy, has reported since the late 1990s a yearly rise and fall in its sodium iodide crystals, as Earth's orbit should vary its speed through dark matter. ANAIS-112 in Spain and COSINE-100 in South Korea used the same kind of crystal and found no such swing.
cards.move: Repeating a result is not the same as having it repeated.
cards.trap: A signal that repeats every year for decades feels too steady to be wrong.
cards.source: Amaré et al., Physical Review D, 2021
cards.reference: Amaré et al., Annual modulation results from three-year exposure of ANAIS-112, Physical Review D 103, 102005, 2021

cards.question: In a big cluster of galaxies, where is most of the ordinary matter, the kind made of atoms?
options: In the stars of its galaxies
In hot gas between its galaxies
In cold dust inside its galaxies
cards.answer: In hot gas between the galaxies. At tens of millions of degrees it shines mainly in X-rays, so ordinary photographs miss it, yet in the richest clusters it outweighs the stars several times over. Even so, gas and stars together are a small fraction of a cluster's total mass; most is dark matter.
cards.move: What shows up in the picture depends on the camera, not the world.
cards.trap: Pictures of clusters show galaxies, so the stars seem to be the mass.
cards.reference: Gonzalez, Sivanandam, Zabludoff & Zaritsky, Galaxy Cluster Baryon Fractions Revisited, The Astrophysical Journal 778, 14, 2013

cards.question: What did the world's most sensitive dark matter detectors finally catch in 2024?
cards.answer: Neutrinos from the Sun, near-massless particles that pass through almost anything. XENONnT in Italy and PandaX-4T in China each saw first hints of them bumping xenon nuclei, the same tiny recoil a dark matter particle would leave. It marks the start of the neutrino fog, a background no shielding can block.
cards.move: A detector sensitive enough to find something also finds everything like it.
cards.reference: XENON Collaboration, First Indication of Solar 8B Neutrinos via Coherent Elastic Neutrino-Nucleus Scattering, Physical Review Letters, 2024

cards.question: Why did two theorists conclude in 1973 that spiral galaxies need heavy unseen halos, before rotation measurements settled it?
cards.answer: Because in their simulations a flat, spinning disc of stars on its own was unstable. Ostriker and Peebles found that it quickly twisted itself into a bar. Only a massive, roughly spherical halo, heavier than the disc, kept it calm. Real spirals are mostly calm discs, so something heavy and unseen held them.
cards.move: When a thing should fall apart and does not, look for a hidden support.
cards.reference: Ostriker & Peebles, A Numerical Study of the Stability of Flattened Galaxies: or, can Cold Galaxies Survive?, The Astrophysical Journal 186, 467, 1973

cards.question: Cosmic dark matter outweighs ordinary matter about five to one. In the dwarf galaxy Segue 1, by how much does it outweigh the stars?
options: More than a thousand to one
cards.answer: More than a thousand to one. Simon and colleagues measured the motions of Segue 1's faint stars and found roughly 3,400 Suns' worth of mass for every Sun's worth of light, where stars alone give about 2. Tiny galaxies lose their gas easily and make few stars, leaving their dark matter almost bare.
cards.move: An average ratio says little about the extremes it averages over.
cards.trap: Letting the cosmic five-to-one set the scale for every galaxy.
cards.reference: Simon et al., A Complete Spectroscopic Survey of the Milky Way Satellite Segue 1: The Darkest Galaxy, The Astrophysical Journal 733, 46, 2011

cards.question: Galaxies' extra pull appears where acceleration falls below 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m/s². At that rate, how many years to reach 1 m/s from rest?
cards.move: Tests in strong conditions say nothing about how things behave when faint.
cards.trap: Expecting a flaw in the law of gravity to show up in a laboratory.
cards.hint: Divide the speed by the acceleration, then turn the seconds into years.
steps: Time = speed ÷ acceleration = 1 ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 8.3 × 10⁹ seconds.
A year is about 3.15 × 10⁷ seconds.
cards.source: McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert, Physical Review Letters, 2016
cards.reference: McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert, Radial Acceleration Relation in Rotationally Supported Galaxies, Physical Review Letters 117, 201101, 2016

cards.question: Halo dark bodies would magnify only about one background star in a million at a time, Paczyński calculated. How could that be tested?
options: Watch millions of stars every night
Watch one bright star for decades
cards.answer: Watch millions of stars every night. With enough targets, a one-in-a-million alignment happens all the time. From the early 1990s the MACHO and EROS teams monitored millions of stars in the Magellanic Clouds. They caught some brightenings, but far too few: such dark bodies make up at most a small share of the halo.
cards.move: To catch a rare event, multiply the chances instead of waiting longer.
cards.trap: Waiting patiently on one target instead of multiplying the targets.
cards.reference: Paczyński, Gravitational microlensing by the galactic halo, The Astrophysical Journal 304, 1, 1986

cards.question: After decades of null results, should physicists build a xenon dark matter detector ten times larger?
cards.answer: A larger detector would cover most of the remaining range where particles of the long-favoured kind could hide, down to the neutrino fog where the method runs out. The cost is modest next to a collider, the technology is proven, and a clean null result would close off a whole class of theories.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the worth of a clean null result decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Forty years of ever-larger detectors have found nothing, and the Large Hadron Collider found none of the new particles that made this kind of dark matter attractive. Lighter candidates such as axions remain far less explored and far cheaper to test. The next detector would buy a thinner slice of possibilities for more money.
cards.source: Aalbers et al., Journal of Physics G, 2023
cards.reference: Aalbers et al., A next-generation liquid xenon observatory for dark matter and neutrino physics, Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 50, 013001, 2023

cards.question: An astronaut falls straight into a black hole. Which one lets her cross the event horizon in one piece?
options: Neither would let her through intact
cards.answer: The one of 4 million solar masses. The stretch from head to toe at the horizon falls with the square of the mass. At 10 solar masses it passes 100 g some 1,700 km outside the horizon and reaches 20 million g at it; at 4 million, it is about a ten-thousandth of a g.
cards.move: Find where a danger peaks before assuming it peaks at the famous line.
cards.trap: Picturing the famous stretching into spaghetti as the fate at every horizon.

diagram.caption: The small hole stretches her by 20 million g; the giant, by a ten-thousandth of one.

cards.reference: Thorne, The Science of Interstellar, W. W. Norton, 2014

cards.question: In the Event Horizon Telescope's black hole images, how wide is the dark centre compared with the horizon itself?
cards.answer: About 2.5 times as wide. Light skimming the hole is bent so hard that rays aimed well outside the horizon are still swallowed: for a non-spinning hole, the dark patch has 2.6 times the horizon's radius. The picture shows the horizon's silhouette, magnified by the hole's own gravity acting as a lens.
cards.move: Ask how much of what you see is the lens rather than the object.
cards.trap: Taking the black disc in the picture for the horizon itself.
cards.source: Falcke, Melia & Agol, Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2000
cards.reference: Falcke, Melia & Agol, Viewing the Shadow of the Black Hole at the Galactic Center, Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2000

cards.question: True or false: when two black holes merge and radiate away energy, their total horizon area can shrink?
cards.answer: False. The first merger ever detected, in 2015, turned holes of 36 and 29 solar masses into one of 62, shedding 3 as gravitational waves. But horizon area grows with the square of the mass, so the single hole has far more surface than the pair. Hawking's 1971 theorem forbids any fall, quantum effects aside.
cards.move: Squares of the parts never add up to the square of the whole.
cards.trap: Assuming a hole that loses mass must lose surface too.

diagram.caption: Horizon area goes with mass squared: three suns lost, yet four fifths more area.

cards.source: Isi et al., Physical Review Letters, 2021
cards.reference: Isi, Farr, Giesler, Scheel & Teukolsky, Testing the Black-Hole Area Law with GW150914, Physical Review Letters, 2021

cards.question: Can you already be inside a black hole's event horizon while the space around you is still perfectly flat?
cards.answer: Yes. An event horizon is defined by the future: it bounds the region from which light will never escape. If a heavy shell of matter is falling towards you, the horizon is born at the centre, in empty flat space, and swells outwards to meet the shell. No instrument could feel it pass.
cards.move: Some boundaries are drawn by what will happen, not by what is.
cards.source: Ashtekar & Krishnan, Living Reviews in Relativity, 2004
cards.reference: Ashtekar & Krishnan, Isolated and Dynamical Horizons and Their Applications, Living Reviews in Relativity, 2004

cards.question: Would a distant observer really see someone falling into a black hole hang frozen at its edge forever?
cards.answer: Only in principle. Her light is stretched and dimmed faster and faster as she nears the horizon: at a black hole of 10 solar masses, its wavelength more than doubles every fifth of a millisecond. Light arrives in photons, so one of them is the last. The frozen figure goes black in a blink.
cards.move: A process that never quite ends can still be over in practice.
cards.reference: Misner, Thorne & Wheeler, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman, 1973

cards.question: Averaged over the space inside its event horizon, how dense is a black hole of a billion suns?
cards.answer: Far less dense than water: about 18 kg per cubic metre, about 15 times air. The horizon's radius grows in step with the mass, so the volume inside grows with its cube, and the average density falls with the mass squared. A hole of one sun averages 80 times denser than a nucleus.
cards.move: When the container grows faster than its contents, the average thins out.
cards.trap: Picturing every black hole as matter crushed beyond nuclear density.
cards.reference: Carroll, Spacetime and Geometry: An Introduction to General Relativity, Addison-Wesley, 2004

cards.question: An astronaut falls into a large black hole from far away. Looking straight up as she crosses the horizon, what does she see?
options: The sky above, redder and dimmer
The universe's whole future flashing past
Nothing, as all light is cut off
cards.answer: The sky above, redder and dimmer. Outside clocks do not race for her: she is falling away from the light that chases her in. For a fall that starts at rest far away, light from straight overhead reaches her at half its original frequency. The stars behind her redden; no future flashes by.
cards.move: What one side sees of the other need not mirror what the other sees.
cards.trap: Reasoning that if outsiders see her frozen, she must see them race.
cards.source: Hamilton & Lisle, American Journal of Physics, 2008
cards.reference: Hamilton & Lisle, The river model of black holes, American Journal of Physics, 2008

cards.question: M87's black hole weighs 6.5 billion suns; horizon radius is 3 km per sun. How many Earth–Sun distances (150 million km) is that?
cards.answer: 19.5 billion km / 150 million km = 130.
cards.move: Compact describes how tightly packed something is, never how big it is.
cards.trap: Picturing a black hole as small because it is compact.
cards.hint: Multiply the mass by the radius per sun, then divide by the Earth–Sun distance.
steps: 6.5 billion suns x 3 km = 19.5 billion km of radius.
19.5 billion km / 150 million km = 130.
