diagram.caption: M87's horizon alone reaches over four times as far out as Neptune's orbit.

cards.reference: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole, Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2019

cards.question: How can astronomers measure the spin of a black hole whose horizon they cannot see?
cards.answer: By finding where its gas disc ends. Around a non-spinning hole no orbit is stable inside three horizon radii, so the disc stops there; around a fast spinner the edge closes in almost to the horizon. X-rays from iron in the innermost gas, smeared by gravity and speed, show how close it gets.
cards.move: When the thing itself hides, measure where its surroundings stop behaving.
cards.reference: Tanaka et al., Gravitationally redshifted emission implying an accretion disk and massive black hole in the active galaxy MCG-6-30-15, Nature, 1995

cards.question: How much of a fast-spinning black hole's mass could, in principle, be taken out again as energy?
cards.answer: Up to about 29%. The spin's energy sits outside the horizon, where space itself is dragged round; a particle split there can send one half out with more energy than it brought. What stays is the irreducible mass, fixed by the horizon's area. For a maximal spinner it is 1/√2 of the whole.
cards.move: Separate what a system stores from what it can give back.
cards.reference: Christodoulou, Reversible and irreversible transformations in black-hole physics, Physical Review Letters, 1970

cards.question: True or false: telescopes can see galaxies that are receding from Earth faster than light?
cards.answer: True. Relativity's speed limit governs motion through space, not the stretching of space. In the standard model, any galaxy whose light arrives stretched past two and a half times its original wavelength is receding faster than light today. Many already were when that light set out; it was dragged backwards before it gained ground.
cards.move: Check which rule a limit belongs to before applying it everywhere.
cards.trap: Nothing moves faster than light, so no galaxy can recede faster.

cards.question: Why did the 1931 English translation of Lemaître's paper on cosmic expansion leave out his expansion rate?
cards.answer: Because Lemaître cut it himself. His 1927 paper, in a Belgian journal, had derived the expansion and estimated its rate two years before Hubble. The missing paragraphs later fuelled talk of censorship, until Mario Livio found Lemaître's letter in 2011: he had judged his old estimate superseded and saw no point in reprinting it.
cards.move: Before suspecting a cover-up, check whether the author made the cut.

cards.question: Edwin Hubble's 1929 measurement of the expansion rate implied a universe of what age?
cards.answer: About 2 billion years. Hubble's rate was about seven times today's value, because his distances were far too small. Run backwards, that made the universe younger than the Earth's rocks as geologists were dating them. The clash eased only in the 1950s, when Walter Baade recalibrated the distance scale.
cards.move: A measurement is only as good as the ruler behind it.
cards.trap: The well-known modern age of 13.8 billion years comes to mind first.
cards.reference: Kragh, Cosmology and Controversy: The Historical Development of Two Theories of the Universe, Princeton University Press, 1996

cards.question: Could astronomers living 100 billion years from now discover that the universe is expanding?
cards.answer: Probably not. Accelerating expansion will have carried every galaxy beyond our merged home group out of sight, so there will be nothing receding to measure. The cosmic background will be stretched too thin to detect. Krauss and Scherrer argued that such astronomers would conclude, as people did before 1920, that the universe is static.
cards.move: Some evidence exists only for a while, so gather it while it lasts.
cards.source: Krauss & Scherrer, General Relativity and Gravitation, 2007

cards.question: Does the clash between two measurements of the universe's expansion rate point to new physics?
cards.answer: The early universe, read from the cosmic background, predicts an expansion rate about 8% slower than nearby stars used as distance markers measure. Independent teams, instruments and methods keep landing on either side, and the gap exceeds five standard deviations. Errors that large would have surfaced by now; something in the standard model is missing.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether the distance ladder's errors are really understood.
cards.counterpoint: The biggest gap rests on one distance ladder, built on pulsating stars in crowded images. When Wendy Freedman's team rebuilt it with the James Webb telescope using other kinds of stars, they landed about halfway, within reach of the early-universe value. And every new physics proposed to fix this number breaks some other measurement.
cards.source: Di Valentino et al., Class. Quantum Grav., 2021
cards.reference: Di Valentino et al., In the realm of the Hubble tension: a review of solutions, Classical and Quantum Gravity 38, 153001, 2021

cards.question: How was cosmic time dilation finally seen in quasars, after a 2010 study had found none?
cards.answer: By treating their flicker as random and fitting it across 190 quasars watched for two decades. Expansion should make events at redshift 4 look five times slower, as it already does for distant supernovae. Lewis and Brewer found exactly that stretch in 2023: seen from here, the young universe runs in slow motion.
cards.move: Finding nothing may only mean the clock was too noisy to read.
cards.reference: Lewis & Brewer, Detection of the cosmological time dilation of high-redshift quasars, Nature Astronomy 7, 1265, 2023

cards.question: Expansion has stretched every wavelength of a distant galaxy's light 4 times. How many times dimmer does each patch of its surface look?
cards.answer: 16 × 16 = 256 times dimmer per patch.
cards.move: When several effects each multiply, the total runs away from intuition.
cards.trap: Stopping at 4, as though stretched wavelengths were the only effect.
cards.hint: Count every way expansion thins the light: energy per photon, arrival rate, and apparent size.
steps: Each photon arrives with a quarter of its energy, and photons arrive a quarter as often: 4 × 4 = 16.
The image covers 4 × 4 = 16 times more sky than a static universe would give, thinning the light again.
16 × 16 = 256 times dimmer per patch.
cards.reference: Lubin & Sandage, The Tolman Surface Brightness Test for the Reality of the Expansion. IV., The Astronomical Journal 122, 1084, 2001

cards.question: True or false: since cosmic expansion is accelerating, the Hubble rate, recession speed per unit of distance, is rising?
cards.answer: False. The Hubble rate has fallen throughout cosmic history and still falls, from about 67 km/s per megaparsec, or 3.26 million light-years, today towards about 56. Acceleration means each galaxy's recession speed grows, but its distance grows faster, so speed divided by distance shrinks. Then it settles, and distances double every 12 billion years.
cards.move: A growing quantity can have a shrinking rate of growth.
cards.trap: Reading faster expansion as a larger expansion rate.
cards.reference: Ryden, Introduction to Cosmology, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 2017

cards.question: Do DESI's 2025 results show that dark energy, the cause of accelerating expansion, is weakening over time?
cards.answer: Three independent kinds of data point the same way. DESI's map of millions of galaxies, combined with the cosmic background and supernova distances, prefers a dark energy that fades with time, by 2.8 to 4.2 standard deviations depending on the supernova set. A constant dark energy, fixed forever, fits worse as the data grow.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the supernova calibration is what decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The signal's strength depends heavily on which supernova catalogue is used, and supernova calibrations have shifted before. Below five standard deviations, physics has watched many three-sigma hints fade. The best fit also has dark energy behaving in a physically awkward way in the past, a hint that a simple formula may be fitting noise.
cards.reference: DESI Collaboration, DESI DR2 Results II: Measurements of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and Cosmological Constraints, 2025

cards.question: Light sent today can reach galaxies now within 16 billion light-years; the observable universe spans 46 billion. What percentage of its volume is reachable?
cards.answer: About 4.3% of the observable volume.
cards.move: Cube a ratio of distances before judging how much space it holds.
cards.trap: Stopping at the ratio of distances, about a third.
cards.hint: The share of a radius is not the share of a volume.
steps: 16 ÷ 46 ≈ 0.35 of the radius.
Volume goes with the cube: 0.35 × 0.35 × 0.35 ≈ 0.043.
About 4.3% of the observable volume.
cards.reference: Davis & Lineweaver, Expanding Confusion: Common Misconceptions of Cosmological Horizons and the Superluminal Expansion of the Universe, Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia 21, 97, 2004

cards.question: True or false: in a kerosene-burning rocket, most of the propellant by mass is kerosene?
cards.answer: False. About 70% of it is liquid oxygen. A car or a jet takes its oxygen from the air; a rocket must carry all of it, and kerosene engines burn about 2.3 to 2.7 kg of oxygen for every kilogram of fuel. The tank of kerosene is the smaller one.
cards.move: Count what a machine must carry that others get for free.
cards.trap: A car carries only fuel, so a rocket's tanks seem mostly fuel too.
cards.reference: Huzel & Huang, Modern Engineering for Design of Liquid-Propellant Rocket Engines, AIAA, 1992

cards.question: Why do hydrogen rocket engines deliberately burn with too little oxygen?
cards.answer: Because light exhaust is fast exhaust. Burning hydrogen completely takes about 8 kg of oxygen per kilogram; the Shuttle's main engines used 6. The spare hydrogen leaves unburnt, and its tiny molecules lower the average weight of the exhaust, so the same heat drives it out faster. The engine wastes fuel to gain speed.
cards.move: The efficient setting is not always the complete one.
cards.reference: Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed., Wiley, 2017

cards.question: A kerosene engine's exhaust leaves at 3 km/s, and reaching orbit takes 9 km/s. What percentage of a single-stage rocket must be propellant?
cards.answer: 19 ÷ 20 = 95% propellant.
cards.move: Anything that must carry its own fuel pays compound interest on it.
cards.trap: Guessing about 75%, as if three times the speed needed three times the fuel.
cards.hint: Each 3 km/s of speed multiplies the starting mass by e, about 2.7.
steps: The rocket equation: liftoff mass ÷ burnout mass = e^(9 ÷ 3) = e^3.
e^3 ≈ 20, so 20 kg at liftoff leaves 1 kg at burnout.
19 ÷ 20 = 95% propellant.
cards.reference: Tsiolkovsky, Exploration of Outer Space by Means of Reaction Devices, Nauchnoye Obozreniye, 1903

cards.question: Why did the engine that lifted Apollo astronauts off the Moon have no igniter?
cards.answer: Because its propellants ignite on contact. A hydrazine blend and nitrogen tetroxide burst into flame the moment they meet, so the engine needed only valves to open; pressurised helium pushed them in, so it had no pumps either. With no backup, every part left out was one that could not fail.
cards.move: The most reliable part is the one that is not there.
cards.reference: Kelly, Moon Lander: How We Developed the Apollo Lunar Module, Smithsonian Institution Press, 2001

cards.question: What kept every Space Shuttle on the ground for months in 1990?
cards.answer: Hydrogen leaks. Liquid hydrogen is kept at −253 °C and is the smallest molecule; fittings that seal at room temperature shrink in that cold and let it seep out. Columbia's countdown was halted in May, Atlantis leaked in June, and no shuttle flew until October. Artemis I scrubbed for the same reason in 2022.
cards.move: The smallest thing in a system is usually the one that escapes.
cards.reference: Jenkins, Space Shuttle: The History of the National Space Transportation System, the First 100 Missions, 3rd ed., Cape Canaveral: Dennis R. Jenkins, 2001, ISBN 0-9633974-5-1

cards.question: How do many satellites fire their thrusters using a single propellant and no oxidiser at all?
cards.answer: By tearing hydrazine apart rather than burning it. Passed over a bed of iridium-coated pellets, hydrazine decomposes into hot nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia, with no spark and no oxygen, even starting at room temperature. It fires reliably for years. The cost is the fuel itself: toxic enough that technicians load it in sealed suits.
cards.move: Energy can come from taking one thing apart, not only from joining two.
cards.reference: Brown, Spacecraft Propulsion, AIAA Education Series, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, 1996

cards.question: What was the main fuel burned in the Space Shuttle's solid rocket boosters?
cards.answer: Aluminium powder. By mass the propellant was about 70% ammonium perchlorate, which supplies the oxygen, 16% aluminium and 12% rubbery binder, which also burns. The metal raises the flame temperature and so the thrust. Each launch left aluminium oxide and hydrochloric acid in the white column that hung over Florida.
cards.move: The ingredient named on the label is not always the one doing the work.
cards.reference: NASA, National Space Transportation System Reference, NSTS 1988 News Reference Manual, 1988

cards.question: Kilogram for kilogram, how does kerosene mixed with its oxygen compare with TNT in the energy it releases?
options: TNT releases about ten times more
The propellant, two to three times more
cards.answer: The propellant, two to three times more. Burned kerosene releases about 43 MJ per kilogram; spread over the oxygen it needs too, that is about 10 MJ per kilogram of mixture. TNT gives about 4.2 to 4.6. An explosive is fast, not rich: its oxygen sits inside the molecule, released all at once.
cards.move: Violence is about speed; energy is a separate question.
cards.trap: Picturing explosives as the most energetic stuff by weight.
cards.reference: Cooper, Explosives Engineering, Wiley-VCH, 1996

cards.question: Shuttle engines burned 6 kg of oxygen (1,141 kg/m³) per kg of hydrogen (71 kg/m³). How many times more tank volume did hydrogen need?
cards.answer: 14.1 ÷ 5.3 ≈ 2.7 times the volume.
cards.move: Weigh and measure separately; the lightest ingredient can fill the room.
cards.trap: Assuming the ingredient used in the smaller amount needs the smaller tank.
cards.hint: Find how many times denser the oxygen is, then allow for its six-fold mass.
steps: 1 kg of hydrogen fills 1 ÷ 71 ≈ 0.0141 m³, about 14.1 litres.
6 kg of oxygen fill 6 ÷ 1,141 ≈ 0.0053 m³, about 5.3 litres.
14.1 ÷ 5.3 ≈ 2.7 times the volume.
cards.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 2004
cards.reference: Lide (ed.), CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 85th ed., CRC Press, 2004

cards.question: True or false: nitrous oxide, the laughing gas used by dentists, can explode with no fuel present?
cards.answer: True. Nitrous oxide breaks down into nitrogen and oxygen, giving off heat, so a hot spot can set off a runaway decomposition inside the tank itself. In 2007 a nitrous flow test at Scaled Composites in Mojave, with no fuel present, exploded and killed three workers.
cards.move: Check whether a harmless ingredient can react with itself.
cards.trap: Treating an oxidiser as inert until a fuel is added.
cards.reference: Karabeyoglu, Dyer, Stevens & Cantwell, Modeling of N2O Decomposition Events, AIAA 2008-4933, 44th Joint Propulsion Conference, 2008

cards.question: True or false: a lone black hole of one solar mass, with no gas falling in, is growing rather than shrinking?
cards.answer: True. It glows at about 60 billionths of a kelvin, while the cosmic background it bathes in is 2.7 K, so it absorbs more than it radiates. Only a hole under about 60% of the Moon's mass is hotter than the sky around it. Known black holes will grow until the universe cools below them.
cards.move: Ask what the surroundings give back before declaring something in decline.
cards.trap: Assuming Hawking radiation means every black hole is shrinking now.
cards.reference: Hawking, Particle Creation by Black Holes, Communications in Mathematical Physics, 1975

cards.question: In 2020 Penrose's team reported cosmic-background spots said to come from black holes of a previous universe. What did re-analysis find?
options: Similar spots in ordinary simulated skies
A fault in the satellite's detectors
cards.answer: Similar spots in ordinary simulated skies. Scan a whole sky at many sizes and positions and some patches will look special by chance. When independent researchers ran the test on simulated skies with no earlier universe in them, the real sky did not stand out. The spots are real; the signal was not.
cards.move: Search enough places and something will look like a signal.
cards.trap: Reading one striking pattern, found by searching a whole sky, as a discovery.
cards.reference: Jow & Scott, Re-evaluating evidence for Hawking points in the CMB, Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics, 2020

cards.question: What would a black hole finishing its evaporation today have weighed when it formed in the early universe?
cards.answer: About as much as a mountain: some 500 billion kilograms, packed into less than the width of a proton. Evaporation time grows with the cube of the mass, so anything much heavier is still here and anything lighter is long gone. Gamma-ray telescopes have watched for their final bursts. None has been seen.
cards.move: Where lifetime climbs steeply with size, the ones ending today share one size.
cards.source: Carr et al., Physical Review D, 2010
cards.reference: Carr, Kohri, Sendouda & Yokoyama, New cosmological constraints on primordial black holes, Physical Review D, 2010

cards.question: Does Hawking radiation really come from particle pairs splitting right at the edge of a black hole?
cards.answer: Not in any literal sense. Its typical wavelength is roughly 16 times the horizon's radius, so it cannot be pinned to the horizon, still less to a pair split on it; Hawking himself called that picture heuristic. For a hole of one solar mass, its photons are radio waves some 50 km long.
cards.move: A picture that helps you remember a result may not be how it happens.
cards.reference: Giddings, Hawking radiation, the Stefan-Boltzmann law, and unitarization, Physics Letters B, 2016

cards.question: Do laboratory black holes made of sound confirm that real black holes emit Hawking radiation?
sides: No, they test only the analogy
cards.answer: Hawking's derivation barely uses gravity: any horizon, for light or for sound, in any flowing medium, should give off a thermal glow at a temperature set by how sharply the flow changes. In 2019 a sound horizon in an ultracold gas did exactly that, at the predicted temperature. Same mathematics, same result, now measured.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether matching equations mean matching nature.
cards.counterpoint: An analogy confirms only what two systems share, and whether they share the physics that matters is the very question. A sound horizon in cold gas says nothing about the quantum gravity near a real horizon, where the derivation leans on wavelengths shorter than any known physics reaches. Only a real black hole could settle it.
cards.reference: Dardashti, Thébault & Winsberg, Confirmation via Analogue Simulation: What Dumb Holes Could Tell Us about Gravity, British Journal for the Philosophy of Science, 2017

cards.question: Why did Hawking at first reject the idea that a black hole has a temperature?
cards.answer: Because anything with a temperature must glow, and nothing escapes a black hole. A graduate student, Jacob Bekenstein, argued that a horizon's area measures entropy; Hawking and colleagues replied in 1973 that the likeness was only formal. His own quantum calculation, in 1974, found that black holes do glow, and fixed Bekenstein's rule exactly.
cards.move: A calculation meant to refute an idea is also the best test of it.
cards.reference: Bardeen, Carter & Hawking, The four laws of black hole mechanics, Communications in Mathematical Physics, 1973

cards.question: A 500-billion-kg black hole lasts about 14 billion years. Lifetime goes with mass cubed. What mass lasts 14 years, in thousand tonnes?
cards.answer: 500 billion kg / 1,000 = 500 million kg = 500 thousand tonnes.
cards.move: When an effect goes with a cube, a vast change needs only a modest step.
cards.trap: Dividing the mass by a billion, as if lifetime followed mass.
cards.hint: Ask which number, cubed, gives the factor by which the lifetime shrinks.
steps: 14 billion years / 14 years = a lifetime 1 billion times shorter.
The cube root of 1 billion is 1,000, so the mass is 1,000 times smaller.
500 billion kg / 1,000 = 500 million kg = 500 thousand tonnes.
cards.reference: Page, Particle emission rates from a black hole: Massless particles from an uncharged, nonrotating hole, Physical Review D, 1976

cards.question: Why can't dark matter be primordial black holes weighing between 1 and 100 billion tonnes?
options: They would have evaporated long ago
They would have merged into heavier ones
Their Hawking glow would show in gamma rays
cards.answer: Their Hawking glow would show in gamma rays. Holes this heavy have not had time to evaporate, yet are still hot enough to shine. If they made up the dark matter, their combined gamma rays would outshine the background actually measured. Holes from there up to asteroid mass remain allowed.
cards.move: Near a cut-off, look at what is still alive, not only at what died.
cards.trap: Assuming the limit comes from holes that died, not ones still shining.
cards.reference: Carr & Kühnel, Primordial Black Holes as Dark Matter: Recent Developments, Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, 2020

cards.question: Does the information in whatever falls into a black hole come back out in its Hawking radiation?
cards.answer: Quantum theory has never lost information anywhere else, and the best-tested models from string theory describe black holes as ordinary quantum systems that cannot lose it. Since 2019, calculations have reproduced the curve Don Page predicted in 1993: radiation ever more scrambled until mid-life, then giving the information back. Hawking himself conceded in 2004.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how far model universes speak for ours.
cards.counterpoint: Those calculations work in simplified model universes, or lean on assumptions about quantum gravity nobody can test. Hawking's original result follows from well-established physics, and a hole that ends in truly random radiation contradicts no observation. Unruh and Wald argue that information loss is a genuine prediction, which physics should accept rather than explain away.
cards.reference: Unruh & Wald, Information loss, Reports on Progress in Physics, 2017

cards.question: True or false: a spinning black hole evaporating by Hawking radiation loses its spin faster than it loses its mass?
cards.answer: True. Angular momentum leaves several times faster than energy, because spin boosts the emission of particles that themselves spin, such as photons and gravitons, sent out along the rotation. A fast spinner slows almost to a halt before it has given up most of its mass: old evaporating holes should be nearly still.
cards.move: When a thing drains through several outlets, they need not empty at one pace.
cards.trap: Assuming mass and spin drain away together, in proportion.

cards.question: Why was every Apollo landing timed for early morning, by the Moon's own clock?
cards.answer: For shadows. With the Sun roughly 5° to 15° above the horizon, every boulder and crater cast a long shadow; under a high Sun the grey ground looks flat and slopes cannot be judged. A lunar day lasts about 29.5 Earth days, so each site offered one good morning a month.
cards.move: The best time to look at rough ground is when the light is low.
cards.reference: Wilhelms, To a Rocky Moon: A Geologist's History of Lunar Exploration, University of Arizona Press, 1993

cards.question: Why is the Moon's south pole both the most prized and the most awkward place to land?
cards.answer: Because the Moon's axis is tilted only about 1.5°, so at the pole the Sun never climbs higher than that. Some crater floors nearby have not been sunlit for perhaps billions of years and sit below −230 °C, cold enough to trap water ice, while the Sun skims the rims and throws shadows kilometres long.
cards.move: A place's prize and its hazard often have the same cause.
cards.reference: Paige et al., Diviner Lunar Radiometer Observations of Cold Traps in the Moon's South Polar Region, Science, 2010

cards.question: What set the farthest the Apollo astronauts could drive their lunar rover from the lander?
options: The charge in the rover's batteries
The radio range to the lander
The distance the crew could walk
cards.answer: The distance the crew could walk. Planners assumed the rover might break down at the worst moment, so each drive stayed within the distance two astronauts could cover walking back, on the oxygen and cooling water left in their backpacks. Apollo 17's longest trip reached about 7.6 km from the lander.
cards.move: Plan the trip around the breakdown, not around the working machine.
cards.trap: Assuming the machine's own range, its battery, was the limit.
cards.reference: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center, Apollo 17 Mission Report, 1973

cards.question: True or false: the rocks the Apollo crews brought home are a fair sample of the Moon's surface as a whole?
cards.answer: False. All six Apollo sites lie on the near side, and several sit in or beside one odd region rich in thorium, which orbiters later showed covers a small part of the surface. Lunar meteorites, knocked off at random, are mostly thorium-poor highland rock. The first far-side sample came back only in 2024.
cards.move: Before trusting a big haul, ask how many places it came from.
cards.trap: Assuming 382 kg of rock from six sites speaks for the whole Moon.
cards.source: Jolliff et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2000
cards.reference: Jolliff, Gillis, Haskin, Korotev & Wieczorek, Major lunar crustal terranes: Surface expressions and crust-mantle origins, Journal of Geophysical Research, 2000

cards.question: Should the six Apollo landing sites be protected by international law as heritage that no one may disturb?
cards.answer: They hold the first footprints on another world, and hardware that shows how materials age in space. One careless landing nearby could sandblast it all. NASA already asks its partners to stay 75 m from the Apollo 11 descent stage; a treaty would bind everyone, not just NASA's contractors.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether protecting a place means owning it.
cards.counterpoint: A protected zone on the Moon is territory in all but name, and the 1967 Outer Space Treaty forbids any nation to claim territory there. If America may fence its sites, others may fence theirs, and heritage becomes a way to stake the best ground. Map and photograph the sites in detail, and keep access open.
cards.reference: NASA, NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities: How to Protect and Preserve the Historic and Scientific Value of U.S. Government Lunar Artifacts, 2011

cards.question: India's Chandrayaan-3, hailed in 2023 as the first landing near the Moon's south pole, set down at 69° south. Roughly how far from the pole?
cards.answer: About 600 km. The Moon's circumference is some 10,900 km, so each degree of latitude spans about 30 km, and the 21° between 69° south and the pole make roughly 630 km: farther than London to Edinburgh. The regions studied for crewed landings lie within 6° of the pole itself.
cards.move: Before trusting near or far, turn the angle into a distance.
cards.trap: Taking near the pole, in the headlines, to mean a few dozen kilometres.
cards.reference: Indian Space Research Organisation, Chandrayaan-3 mission: Vikram lander touchdown at 69.37° S, 32.32° E, 23 August 2023

cards.question: Orbital photos suggested Apollo 16's highland landing site was covered in volcanic lava. What did the crew's rocks show?
options: Rock shattered and welded by impacts
Lava flows, as the photos suggested
Sediment laid down by ancient water
cards.answer: Rock shattered and welded by impacts. The smooth Cayley plains looked like lava, and the site was chosen partly to sample volcanism in the highlands. Nearly every rock the crew brought back was breccia: older rock broken and fused by impacts. The plains are now read as debris thrown from distant basins.
cards.move: A resemblance seen from far away is a hypothesis, not a finding.
cards.trap: Trusting that ground which looked like lava from orbit was lava.
cards.reference: NASA, Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report, NASA SP-315, 1972

cards.question: Why did no spacecraft land on the Moon's far side until 2019?
cards.answer: Because nothing there can talk to Earth directly. The far side always faces away, so a lander needs a relay. China first sent a satellite, Queqiao, to loop beyond the Moon near a balance point of Earth's and the Moon's gravity, in 2018; only then did Chang'e-4 set down in Von Kármán crater.
cards.move: Where a signal cannot reach, the first thing to build is the messenger.
cards.source: Jia et al., Planetary and Space Science, 2018
cards.reference: Jia et al., The scientific objectives and payloads of Chang'E-4 mission, Planetary and Space Science, 2018

cards.question: True or false: Japan's SLIM probe came down within 100 m of its target in 2024, even though it ended up upside down?
cards.answer: True. SLIM landed about 55 m from its aim point, far closer than earlier robotic landers, by matching craters below against a map on board. But one of its two main engines lost a nozzle some 50 m up, and the lander tipped onto its nose, its solar cells facing west.
cards.move: Hitting the target and landing well are two separate tests.
cards.trap: Assuming a lander that tipped over must have missed its mark.
cards.reference: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM): landing results briefing, January 2024

cards.question: Is there anywhere near the Moon's south pole where the Sun never sets?
cards.answer: No. Nineteenth-century astronomers imagined peaks of eternal light, but laser height maps show that even the best spots, on ridges near Shackleton crater, go dark each year. The best are lit for over 80% of the time, yet still face spells of darkness lasting a day or more. Planners weigh such rims hour by hour.
cards.move: Almost always is a different engineering problem from always.
cards.reference: Mazarico, Neumann, Smith, Zuber & Torrence, Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, 2011

cards.question: Launch windows open when Earth and a target planet line up right. For which planet do they come round least often?
cards.answer: Mars. A window returns each time one planet laps the other, and Earth gains on Mars slowest of all: every 780 days, 26 months. Neptune barely moves, so Earth realigns with it every 367 days; Venus returns every 19 months. Mars, the neighbour, is the one that makes missions wait longest.
cards.move: How often two things meet depends on their difference, not their distance.
cards.trap: Neptune, the farthest planet, seems the hardest to line up with.
cards.source: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 2020
cards.reference: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2020

cards.question: NASA's Psyche probe missed its 2022 launch window and left 14 months later. How much later did its arrival at the asteroid become?
cards.answer: About 3.5 years. The route relies on a Mars flyby, and planets do not wait: the 2022 plan would have reached the asteroid in January 2026, while the 2023 launch had to loop the Sun until Mars came round again in 2026, and arrives in August 2029.
cards.move: A small delay in a fixed schedule can cost a whole cycle.
cards.trap: Assuming a 14-month launch slip simply shifts arrival by 14 months.
cards.reference: NASA, Psyche Independent Review Board Final Report, 2022

cards.question: True or false: tilting a satellite's orbit by 10 degrees takes more fuel than raising it by 1,000 km?
cards.answer: True, by more than double. From a 400 km orbit, a 10-degree turn costs about 1.3 km/s of speed change, because the whole orbital velocity must be redirected; a 1,000 km climb costs about 0.5 km/s. That is why station launches must leave the moment Earth's spin carries the pad under the orbit.
cards.move: Changing direction can cost more than going further.
cards.trap: Climbing 1,000 km sounds like a journey; tilting sounds like steering.
cards.source: Vallado, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications, 2013
cards.reference: Vallado, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013

cards.question: Why may a rocket not launch through a cloud that has produced no lightning at all?
cards.answer: Because the rocket can make the lightning. A tall conductor trailing a long, ionised exhaust plume distorts the electric field in a charged cloud enough to trigger a strike. Apollo 12 was hit twice within its first minute in 1969, with no storm reported; in 1987 triggered lightning destroyed an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
cards.move: Check whether your own action creates the danger you are watching for.
cards.reference: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center, Apollo 12 Mission Report, MSC-01855, 1970

cards.question: Why do Mars probes leave Earth months before Mars makes its closest approach?
cards.answer: Because they aim where Mars will be. The cheapest route is half an orbit around the Sun, seven to nine months, so probes leave with Mars some 44 degrees ahead and meet it after the close pass. The trip runs to about half a billion km, to a planet that can pass within 56 million.
cards.move: Aim at where the target will be, not where it is.
cards.source: Bate, Mueller & White, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics, 1971
cards.reference: Bate, Mueller & White, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics, Dover, 1971

cards.question: Why do the cheapest Mars launch windows come round only about every 15 years, not every 26 months?
cards.answer: Because Mars's orbit is lopsided. Its distance from the Sun swings between about 207 and 249 million km, so some windows aim at a nearer Mars than others. Seven windows of about 26 months add up to 15 years, almost exactly eight Martian years, so only then does the same geometry come back.
cards.move: When two cycles nearly share a multiple, expect a slow rhythm on top.
cards.reference: Sergeyevsky, Snyder & Cunniff, Interplanetary Mission Design Handbook, Volume I, Part 2: Earth to Mars Ballistic Mission Opportunities, 1990–2005, JPL Publication 82-43, 1983

cards.question: Why did ESA's Rosetta spacecraft end up studying a different comet from the one it was built for?
cards.answer: Because it missed its launch window. Rosetta was due to leave in January 2003 for comet Wirtanen, but a new version of its Ariane 5 rocket failed in December 2002 and the fleet was grounded. No later departure could reach Wirtanen, so ESA chose comet 67P, launched in March 2004 and arrived in 2014.
cards.move: When the deadline cannot move, be ready to change the destination.
cards.source: Glassmeier et al., Space Science Reviews, 2007
cards.reference: Glassmeier, Boehnhardt, Koschny, Kührt & Richter, The Rosetta Mission: Flying Towards the Origin of the Solar System, Space Science Reviews 128, 1, 2007

cards.question: Forecasters give each of three consecutive launch days a 30% chance of a weather scrub. How likely is losing all three?
cards.answer: More than 2.7%. Multiplying assumes each day's weather is separate, but weather comes in systems that sit over a coast for days: the stalled front that scrubs Monday is often still there on Tuesday. One scrub raises the odds of the next, so a run of three is likelier than the product.
cards.move: Before multiplying chances, ask whether one outcome makes the next likelier.
cards.trap: Multiplying the three chances as if each day's weather were separate.
cards.reference: Wilks, Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences, 3rd ed., Academic Press, 2011

cards.question: True or false: sending a probe from Earth into the Sun takes more change of speed than sending it out of the solar system?
cards.answer: True. Earth carries everything round the Sun at about 30 km/s; to fall in, a probe must cancel nearly all of that, while leaving the solar system takes only about 12 km/s more. Parker Solar Probe, which merely grazes the Sun, left in a window timed for Venus, whose seven flybys shed its speed.
cards.move: Moving sideways fast makes the centre the hardest place to reach.
cards.trap: Picturing the Sun as downhill, so falling in must be easy.
cards.source: Fox et al., Space Science Reviews, 2016
cards.reference: Fox et al., The Solar Probe Plus Mission: Humanity's First Visit to Our Star, Space Science Reviews 204, 7, 2016

cards.question: A minimum-energy path to Neptune, 30 times Earth's distance from the Sun, is half an orbit. Roughly how many years does it take?
cards.answer: The trip is half that orbit: 61 ÷ 2 ≈ 31 years.
cards.move: When the direct route takes a lifetime, find something to borrow speed from.
cards.trap: Scaling up from the eight-month Mars trip by distance alone.
cards.hint: Kepler: period in years is the orbit's average distance, in Earth–Sun units, to the power 1.5.
steps: The path's orbit spans 1 to 30 Earth–Sun distances: average (1 + 30) ÷ 2 ≈ 15.5.
Kepler: period ≈ 15.5 to the power 1.5 ≈ 15.5 × 4 ≈ 61 years.
The trip is half that orbit: 61 ÷ 2 ≈ 31 years.
cards.reference: Murray & Dermott, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press, 1999

cards.question: True or false: a good share of the stars seen with the naked eye have already died?
cards.answer: False. Most naked-eye stars lie within about 1,000 light-years, so the light arriving tonight left them within the last millennium. Stars live millions to billions of years. Only a rare giant near its end, such as Betelgeuse, has even a small chance of being gone.
cards.move: A line repeated often enough starts to sound like a measurement.
cards.trap: The dead-stars line is repeated so often it sounds like a fact.
cards.reference: ESA, The Hipparcos and Tycho Catalogues, ESA SP-1200, 1997

cards.question: How did astronomers take a spectrum of Tycho Brahe's 1572 supernova in 2008?
cards.answer: By catching light that took a detour. Some of the 1572 flash struck dust clouds and bounced towards Earth by a longer route, arriving more than four centuries after the direct light. Spread into its colours, that echo showed a normal white dwarf explosion. Tycho saw the first copy; the second was still travelling.
cards.move: Look for the echo when the original is gone.

cards.question: Voyager 1 travels at about 17 km/s. How long would it take to cover the 4.2 light-years to the nearest star, in thousands of years?
cards.answer: 40 trillion ÷ 540 million ≈ 74,000 years.
cards.move: Put the distance in the traveller's units before calling it near.
cards.trap: Assuming the fastest craft leaving the Solar System would get there in centuries.
cards.hint: Turn light-years into km, and the speed into km per year.
steps: A light-year is about 9.5 trillion km, so 4.2 light-years is about 40 trillion km.
A year has about 31.6 million seconds, so 17 km/s is about 540 million km a year.
40 trillion ÷ 540 million ≈ 74,000 years.
cards.reference: Bell, The Interstellar Age: Inside the Forty-Year Voyager Mission, Dutton, 2015

cards.question: When a galaxy is reported as 13.4 billion light-years away, what does that number measure?
cards.answer: How long its light travelled, not where the galaxy is. Space stretched while the light was in transit. GN-z11's light set out about 13.4 billion years ago, when the galaxy was some 2.7 billion light-years from here; today it is about 32 billion. The headline number is neither.
cards.move: Ask what a number measures before asking how big it is.
cards.reference: Bunker et al., JADES NIRSpec Spectroscopy of GN-z11, Astronomy & Astrophysics 677, A88, 2023

cards.question: In 2022 James Webb images suggested a galaxy, CEERS-93316, was the most distant ever seen. What did its spectrum show in 2023?
options: It was an ordinary nearer galaxy
It was a star in our galaxy
cards.answer: An ordinary, nearer galaxy. Its spectrum showed it as it was 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang, not the 240 million claimed. Dust and bright oxygen emission had mimicked the colours of a far younger, more distant galaxy. It had been picked out of thousands of candidates precisely for looking extreme.
cards.move: The most extreme result in a big pile is the one to recheck first.
cards.trap: Expecting a record-breaking first measurement to hold up on a second look.
cards.reference: Arrabal Haro et al., Confirmation and refutation of very luminous galaxies in the early universe, Nature 622, 707, 2023

cards.question: How could Henrietta Leavitt compare the true brightness of stars in 1912 without knowing how far away any of them were?
cards.answer: Because they were all at the same distance. She studied pulsing stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, one remote cloud of stars, so differences in how bright they looked were real differences. The slower a star pulsed, the brighter it was. Once one such star's distance was measured, the rule became a ruler for galaxies.
cards.move: Put everything at one distance and the differences you see become real.
cards.reference: Leavitt & Pickering, Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, Harvard College Observatory Circular 173, 1912

cards.question: What did a burst of gamma rays arriving 1.7 seconds after a gravitational wave reveal about the speed of gravity?
cards.answer: That gravity travels at the speed of light, to within about one part in a thousand trillion. Both signals left two merging neutron stars some 130 million light-years away. A speed difference of one part in ten million would have opened a gap of about 13 years; the gap was under two seconds.
cards.move: A tiny difference, carried far enough, grows large enough to measure.

diagram.caption: Speeds one part in ten million apart would mean 13 years; the gap was 1.7 seconds.

cards.source: Abbott et al., Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2017
cards.reference: Abbott et al., Gravitational Waves and Gamma-Rays from a Binary Neutron Star Merger: GW170817 and GRB 170817A, The Astrophysical Journal Letters 848, L13, 2017

cards.question: In about 1.3 million years the star Gliese 710 will pass the Sun. How close will it come?
cards.answer: About 0.2 light-years, roughly 10,000 times the Earth–Sun distance. Gaia's measurements put its path through the Oort cloud, the far shell of icy bodies circling the Sun, where it may nudge some of them inwards. For a while, Alpha Centauri's 4.2 light-years will look like a long way.
cards.move: The present arrangement is one frame of a moving picture.
cards.trap: Letting today's nearest distance, 4.2 light-years, set the scale.
cards.reference: Bailer-Jones, Rybizki, Andrae & Fouesneau, New stellar encounters discovered in the second Gaia data release, Astronomy & Astrophysics 616, A37, 2018

cards.question: Andromeda's light left it 2.5 million years ago, and it approaches the Milky Way at 110 km/s. How many light-years closer is it now?
cards.move: An old picture is only stale if its subject moves fast.
cards.trap: Assuming a picture 2.5 million years old must be badly out of date.
cards.hint: Compare the galaxy's speed with the speed of light; the travel time is given.
steps: In 2.5 million years light covers 2.5 million light-years; Andromeda covers the share 110 ÷ 300,000 of that.
cards.source: van der Marel et al., Astrophysical Journal, 2012
cards.reference: van der Marel, Fardal, Besla et al., The M31 Velocity Vector. II. Radial Orbit toward the Milky Way and Implied Local Group Mass, The Astrophysical Journal 753, 8, 2012

cards.question: In a catalogue of every star bright enough to detect, the farther stars are, on average, intrinsically brighter. Why?
options: Bright stars gather far from the Sun
Only luminous stars are seen that far
Nearby stars are younger and fainter
cards.answer: Only luminous stars are seen that far. Close to the Sun a catalogue picks up faint and bright stars alike; far away, only the brightest clear the limit. Gunnar Malmquist described this bias in the 1920s. Assume a typical brightness for a distant star in such a catalogue and it lands too close.
cards.move: Far away only the loudest are heard, so average them with care.
cards.trap: Taking a pattern in the catalogue as a pattern in the sky.
cards.reference: Binney & Merrifield, Galactic Astronomy, Princeton University Press, 1998

cards.question: Why is the whole Martian atmosphere heavier in some months than in others?
cards.answer: Because part of it freezes out. Mars's air is mostly carbon dioxide, and in polar winter it settles on the ground as dry ice, returning as gas in spring. From 1976 the Viking landers watched surface pressure rise and fall by up to a quarter over a Martian year: a planet breathing in and out.
cards.move: When a quantity swings, ask where it goes while it is missing.
cards.source: Hess et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 1980
cards.reference: Hess, Ryan, Tillman et al., The annual cycle of pressure on Mars measured by Viking Landers 1 and 2, Geophysical Research Letters 7(3), 1980

cards.question: Why do the dust storms that wrap all of Mars start in the southern hemisphere's spring or summer?
cards.answer: Because Mars is then closest to the Sun. Its orbit is stretched enough that sunlight at the nearest point is about 45% stronger than at the farthest, and the nearest point falls in late southern spring. Extra heat drives stronger winds, which lift dust, which soaks up more sunlight: a storm that feeds itself.
cards.move: An uneven input can make one season far wilder than its mirror.
cards.source: Zurek and Martin, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1993
cards.reference: Zurek and Martin, Interannual variability of planet-encircling dust storms on Mars, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 98(E2), 1993

cards.question: How does a Martian dust storm help the planet lose what remains of its water?
cards.answer: By lifting water to where sunlight can break it. Dust absorbs sunlight and warms the middle atmosphere, so vapour that would normally freeze out low rises tens of kilometres higher. There ultraviolet light splits the molecules and the light hydrogen escapes. During the 2018 global storm, the water reaching those heights surged.
cards.move: Weather can carry a thing to the place where it gets destroyed.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aba5229

cards.question: True or false: snow falls from clouds on Mars?
cards.answer: True. In 2008 the Phoenix lander's laser, pointed up at night, saw water-ice crystals falling in streaks from clouds about 4 km high. In the polar night, orbiters detect clouds of carbon dioxide that drop dry-ice snow. Rovers have not caught it: they land near the equator, and mostly work by day.
cards.move: Where the cameras go decides what the pictures can show.
cards.trap: Rover photos show only dry red ground, so no snow.
cards.reference: Whiteway et al., Mars Water-Ice Clouds and Precipitation, Science 325, 2009

cards.question: A 100 km/h gust on Mars pushes like what wind speed on Earth, in km/h?
cards.move: When force goes with the square, compare square roots.
cards.trap: Dividing by the density ratio and getting a near-still 2 km/h.
cards.hint: The push of wind grows with air density and with the square of speed.
steps: Air at the Martian surface is about 0.020 kg per cubic metre; Earth's is about 1.2.
Density ratio: 1.2 / 0.020 = 60.
Push goes with density times speed squared, so divide speed by √60 ≈ 7.7.
cards.source: Haberle et al., Cambridge University Press, 2017
cards.reference: Haberle, Clancy, Forget, Smith and Zurek (eds), The Atmosphere and Climate of Mars, Cambridge University Press, 2017

cards.question: How can Martian air, holding almost no water, still leave the soil briefly wet at night?
cards.answer: Through salts. Curiosity's weather station found that on winter nights at Gale crater the air cools until its trace of vapour nears saturation, and perchlorate salts in the soil soak it up, dissolving into brine in the top few centimetres. By day it dries. Each night a film of liquid; each morning, dust.
cards.move: How much of a thing is present matters less than how near its limit.
cards.reference: Martín-Torres et al., Transient liquid water and water activity at Gale crater on Mars, Nature Geoscience, 2015

cards.question: When the 2018 global dust storm darkened the sky over Curiosity, what happened to the air temperature there?
options: Colder by day and by night
Warmer by day and by night
cards.answer: Cooler days and warmer nights. Dust high in the air absorbed sunlight, so less reached the ground by day, then gave off heat downwards after dark. The daily swing, normally around 60 °C, shrank by about 30 °C. The storm did not freeze the surface; it flattened the day.
cards.move: A layer that blocks the light can also hold in the heat.
cards.trap: Picturing a nuclear winter, where blotted-out sunlight means cold round the clock.
cards.source: Guzewich et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2019
cards.reference: Guzewich et al., Mars Science Laboratory Observations of the 2018/Mars Year 34 Global Dust Storm, Geophysical Research Letters, 2019

cards.question: Mars's surface pressure is about 600 pascals and its gravity 3.7 m/s². How many kg of air sit above each square metre?
cards.move: Pressure tells you weight; divide by the local pull to find the mass.
cards.trap: Scaling Earth's 10 tonnes by the pressure ratio alone, ignoring weaker gravity.
cards.hint: A pascal is one newton of weight on each square metre.
steps: Pressure is the weight of the air above: 600 newtons on each square metre.
Mass = weight / gravity.
cards.source: Read & Lewis, The Martian Climate Revisited, 2004
cards.reference: Read & Lewis, The Martian Climate Revisited: Atmosphere and Environment of a Desert Planet, Springer-Praxis, 2004

cards.question: True or false: on Mars, spring in the northern hemisphere lasts about as long as spring in the southern?
cards.answer: False. Northern spring runs 194 Martian days, southern spring only 142. Mars's orbit is stretched, and a planet moves slowest when farthest from the Sun, which Mars is in late northern spring. So the mild northern seasons drag on, while the hotter southern summer passes quickly.
cards.move: Before assuming equal shares, check whether the thing moves at a steady pace.
cards.trap: Assuming seasons split the year evenly, as they nearly do on Earth.
cards.source: Allison & McEwen, Planetary and Space Science, 2000
cards.reference: Allison & McEwen, A post-Pathfinder evaluation of areocentric solar coordinates with improved timing recipes for Mars seasonal/diurnal climate studies, Planetary and Space Science, 2000

cards.question: Why does the sky around the setting Sun on Mars turn blue, when the daytime sky is butterscotch?
cards.answer: It is the size of the dust. Grains a few thousandths of a millimetre across absorb blue and scatter red widely, tinting the day sky, but they throw blue light forward, close to its original path. At sunset, looking towards the Sun through a long path of dust, the forward glow forms a blue halo.
cards.move: The same particles can colour a scene differently from every angle of view.
cards.reference: Lemmon et al., Atmospheric imaging results from the Mars Exploration Rovers: Spirit and Opportunity, Science, 2004

cards.question: What did some scientists fear, before 1966, would happen to a spacecraft landing on the Moon's dark plains?
cards.answer: That it would sink. In 1955 the astronomer Thomas Gold argued that the dark plains were deep drifts of fine dust, and nobody could yet rule it out. In 1966 the Soviet Luna 9 and then America's Surveyor 1 came down and stayed on top; Surveyor's footpads pressed in only a few centimetres.
cards.move: One landing can settle what a decade of argument could not.
cards.reference: Gold, The Lunar Surface, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 1955

cards.question: Apollo 12 landed less than 200 m from the old Surveyor 3 probe. What did its landing do to the probe?
cards.answer: Sandblasted it. The descent engine's exhaust drove fine grit low and fast across the surface. When the crew walked over and cut off parts to bring home, the side that had faced their lander was pitted and scoured, with sharp outlines where struts had shielded it. Every lunar landing is also a small dust storm.
cards.move: Every arrival changes the place it arrives at.
cards.reference: Immer, Metzger, Hintze, Nick & Horan, Apollo 12 Lunar Module exhaust plume impingement on Lunar Surveyor III, Icarus, 2011

cards.question: Why is a full moon far more than twice as bright as a half moon?
cards.answer: Because of the dust. At full moon the Sun is directly behind the observer, so every grain hides its own shadow, and light scattered back along its path reinforces itself. From first quarter to full, the lit area only doubles but the brightness rises about tenfold: a field of dust with every shadow switched off.
cards.move: When an effect far outruns its obvious cause, look for a second mechanism.
cards.reference: Hapke, Nelson & Smythe, The Opposition Effect of the Moon: The Contribution of Coherent Backscatter, Science, 1993

cards.question: With no wind or rain, how often is the top 2 cm of the Moon's soil churned over by impacts?
cards.answer: About every 80,000 years. Before-and-after images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter caught over 200 new craters and thousands of faint splotches from their spray, churning the surface about 100 times faster than older models said. The Apollo bootprints, a centimetre or two deep, should be scrambled within about 100,000 years, not millions.
cards.move: Many small unseen events can outwork one large visible one.
cards.trap: No wind or rain, so the soil must lie still for millions of years.
cards.reference: Speyerer, Povilaitis, Robinson, Thomas & Wagner, Quantifying crater production and regolith overturn on the Moon with temporal imaging, Nature, 2016

cards.question: True or false: the Moon's soil grows darker, not paler, the longer it lies exposed at the surface?
cards.answer: True. Micrometeorite strikes and the solar wind coat each grain in glass studded with iron particles a few millionths of a millimetre across, and these absorb light. Rock freshly dug out by an impact is bright, which is why young craters such as Tycho wear pale rays, while older rays fade into the grey.
cards.move: Exposure does not always fade a thing; sometimes it coats it.
cards.trap: Expecting sunlight to bleach the soil, as it bleaches things on Earth.
cards.reference: Pieters & Noble, Space weathering on airless bodies, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 2016

cards.question: What made a thin line of light glow along the Moon's horizon after sunset, as three Surveyor landers saw?
cards.answer: Dust hovering just above the ground. Sunlight and the solar wind charge the surface, and along the sharp edge between sunlit and shadowed ground the electric field grows strong enough to lift grains about a hundredth of a millimetre across. Floating 3 to 30 cm up, they scattered the last sunlight into a bright thread.
cards.move: When nothing seems able to move a thing, look for a quieter force.
cards.reference: Rennilson & Criswell, Surveyor observations of lunar horizon-glow, The Moon, 1974

cards.question: Soil temperatures at the Apollo 15 and 17 sites kept rising for years after the crews left. What warmed them?
options: Heat leaking from the probes themselves
A slow rise in the Sun's output
Soil darkened by boots and rover wheels
cards.answer: Soil darkened by boots and rover wheels. Trampling disturbed the pale top layer and exposed darker grains, which absorb more sunlight. Orbital images show the dark paths, and models fit a surface warming of a few degrees once the probes went in, seeping downwards for years. The experiment was recording its own footprints.
cards.move: Before reading a trend, ask what the act of measuring changed.
cards.trap: Suspecting the instruments, the usual culprit when a probe reads warm.

cards.question: True or false: Apollo lunar soil in a kitchen microwave starts to melt before a cup of water would boil?
cards.answer: True. Nearly every grain carries specks of pure metallic iron, the same ones that darken old soil, and microwaves couple strongly with them. The specks also let a magnet lift much of the finest dust. Paving for a lunar base could be made this way: dust baked into solid slabs by microwave, with no binder.
cards.move: A trace ingredient can decide how the whole material behaves.
cards.trap: Assuming rock powder, like sand, ignores microwaves.
cards.reference: Taylor, Schmitt, Carrier & Nakagawa, The Lunar Dust Problem: From Liability to Asset, AIAA 1st Space Exploration Conference, 2005

cards.question: A fenderless rover wheel flings Moon dust at 3 m/s and 45°. Gravity is 1.6 m/s², no air. How many metres does it fly?
cards.move: Remove the air and the smallest things fly as far as the largest.
cards.trap: Picturing Earth's dust, which air stops within centimetres.
cards.hint: At 45°, with no air, range is the speed squared divided by gravity.
steps: At 45° with no air, range = speed squared / gravity.

diagram.caption: The same flick of dust: under a metre on Earth, 5.6 m on the Moon.

cards.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics
cards.reference: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, Wiley, 2013

cards.question: Why are grains of Moon dust jagged like broken glass, when desert sand is rounded?
cards.answer: Because nothing on the Moon has ever tumbled them. Sand is rounded by wind and water grinding grains together for ages. Lunar dust is made by impacts that shatter rock and splash melt, which freezes into glass shards and clumps with hooked edges. The grains snagged in suit fabric and scratched the Apollo crews' visors.
cards.move: The shape of a grain records what it has been through.
cards.reference: Heiken, Vaniman & French (eds), Lunar Sourcebook: A User's Guide to the Moon, Cambridge University Press, 1991

cards.question: Five of Perseverance's 43 sample tubes were never meant to hold Martian rock or soil. What are they for?
cards.answer: Blanks that record Earthly contamination. They are opened to the rover's surroundings on Mars but never take in Martian material, so labs can later tell which organic traces rode along from Earth. Without them, a hint of life in a real sample could not be told apart from the builders' fingerprints.
cards.move: Before trusting a detection, ask what an empty test would have shown.
cards.trap: Missions always carry spares, so the extras must be spares.
cards.source: Moeller et al., Space Science Reviews, 2021
cards.reference: Moeller et al., The Sampling and Caching Subsystem (SCS) for the Scientific Exploration of Jezero Crater by the Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover, Space Science Reviews, 2021

cards.question: True or false: Perseverance has found a Martian rock whose chemistry only living things could have produced?
cards.answer: False. In 2024 it sampled a mudstone nicknamed Cheyava Falls, with millimetre-wide leopard spots rimmed by iron minerals that on Earth often form where microbes feed on organic matter. Published in 2025 as a potential biosignature, it still has non-living explanations nobody has ruled out. Only the sample, in a lab on Earth, could decide.
cards.move: Evidence that fits your idea is not yet evidence against the rival idea.
cards.trap: Taking features that fit life as features only life can make.
cards.reference: Hurowitz et al., Redox-driven mineral and organic associations in Jezero Crater, Mars, Nature, 2025

cards.question: MOXIE, Perseverance's oxygen maker, managed 12 g an hour at best. How many years to make the 25 tonnes a four-person launch needs?
cards.answer: 2,083,000 / 8,760 hours a year ≈ 237.8 years.
cards.move: Proof that something works says nothing yet about making enough of it.
cards.trap: Taking a successful demonstration as nearly a working supply.
cards.hint: Turn the tonnes into grams, the grams into hours, and the hours into years.
steps: 25 tonnes is 25,000,000 g.
2,083,000 / 8,760 hours a year ≈ 237.8 years.
cards.reference: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, NASA's Oxygen-Generating Experiment MOXIE Completes Mars Mission, 2023

cards.question: On Mars, why would the high notes of a distant tune arrive before the low ones?
cards.answer: Because Martian air carries sound at two speeds. Perseverance's microphone, timing the cracks of its laser on rocks, found sounds above about 240 Hz travel near 250 m/s and lower ones about 10 m/s slower: thin carbon dioxide lags behind quick pressure swings. Over 100 m, a chord splits by a sixtieth of a second.
cards.move: Check whether the medium treats every part of a message alike.
cards.reference: Maurice et al., In situ recording of Mars soundscape, Nature, 2022

cards.question: How did Perseverance land in a crater that earlier Mars missions would have ruled too dangerous?
cards.answer: It picked its own spot. Hanging under its parachute, the lander photographed the ground, matched the pictures to a map on board, worked out where it was to within tens of metres, then steered for the safest patch in reach. Cliffs, boulder fields and dunes were scattered across the landing zone; it missed them all.
cards.move: Knowing exactly where you are turns a hazard map into a route.
cards.source: Farley et al., Space Science Reviews, 2020
cards.reference: Farley et al., Mars 2020 Mission Overview, Space Science Reviews, 2020

cards.question: Is bringing Perseverance's sealed samples back to Earth worth the billions it would cost?
cards.answer: The samples were chosen with care from an ancient lake bed and its delta, and some hold textures that on Earth would hint at life. Only laboratories on Earth, with instruments too large to fly, can settle what they contain, and those labs will keep improving for decades. The tubes are already filled and sealed.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what the same money would buy instead.
cards.counterpoint: In 2023 an independent review put the plan at 8 to 11 billion dollars, with no samples home before the late 2030s, and in 2025 the White House proposed cancelling it. That money could fly several missions to other worlds, while instruments landed on Mars keep getting better. A sealed tube can wait; budgets cannot.
cards.reference: NASA, Mars Sample Return Independent Review Board-2 Final Report, 2023

cards.question: In January 2024 Ingenuity, the helicopter carried to Mars by Perseverance, flew for the last time. What ended its flights?
options: Dust settling on its solar panel
Bland sand its camera could not track
Its batteries failing in winter cold
cards.answer: Bland sand its camera could not track. Ingenuity judged its speed by following features on the ground; over smooth ripples it found too few, came down too fast and tilted, and all four rotor blades snapped. It had flown 72 times, against a plan of five, until the ground gave it nothing to hold.
cards.move: A system that steers by what it sees fails where there is nothing to see.
cards.trap: Blaming dust on the panels, the famous end of other Mars craft.
cards.reference: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-performs-first-aircraft-accident-investigation-on-another-world/

cards.question: In 2021 Perseverance's first attempt to core a rock sealed a tube with no rock inside. Why was it empty?
options: The drill jammed before reaching rock
The core slipped out as the tube rose
cards.answer: The rock crumbled to powder. It was so weathered that the percussive drill broke it up, and nothing held together in the tube. The team kept the sealed tube anyway: it holds a sample of thin Martian air, taken in by accident, and became the mission's only atmospheric sample.
cards.move: When a tool comes back empty, question the material before the tool.
cards.trap: Blaming the machine, when the failure lay in the material.
cards.reference: Simon et al., Samples collected from the floor of Jezero crater with the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 2023

cards.question: True or false: the first rocks Perseverance cored on the floor of Jezero crater, a former lake, were lake sediments?
cards.answer: False. Jezero was chosen for its lake and river delta, and its floor was widely expected to be lake mud. Instead the first cores, in 2021, were igneous rock, one built from olivine crystals that settled in a thick body of melt. Water had later altered them and left salts in their pores.
cards.move: What a place is famous for may not be what its ground is made of.
cards.trap: Assuming a former lake's floor must be made of lake sediment.
cards.reference: Farley et al., Aqueously altered igneous rocks sampled on the floor of Jezero crater, Mars, Science, 2022

cards.question: Why does Perseverance carry a slice of a Martian meteorite that was found in Oman?
cards.answer: To check its own eyes. The slice, of Sayh al Uhaymir 008, sits on the calibration target of SHERLOC, an instrument that reads minerals and organic traces with an ultraviolet laser. A known Martian rock lets the team tell a drifting instrument from a real novelty. Beside it, spacesuit fabric and visor samples weather.
cards.move: To trust a measurement of the unknown, carry something already known.
cards.source: Fries et al., Space Science Reviews, 2022
cards.reference: Fries et al., The SHERLOC Calibration Target on the Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover: Design, Operations, Outreach, and Future Human Exploration Functions, Space Science Reviews, 2022

cards.question: Why can a Falcon 9 booster not simply hover while it lines up its landing?
cards.answer: Because even one engine at its lowest setting pushes harder than the nearly empty booster weighs. A Merlin engine can only be throttled part of the way down, and at landing the stage is mostly empty tank. So the final burn is timed to reach zero speed exactly at the pad, with no second try.
cards.move: A system that cannot pause must get its timing right the first time.
cards.reference: Blackmore, Autonomous Precision Landing of Space Rockets, The Bridge 46(4), National Academy of Engineering, 2016

cards.question: What becomes of the Space Shuttle's main engines when they fly on NASA's SLS rocket?
cards.answer: They are dropped in the ocean. Built to be reused, and flown on Shuttle missions, the engines now ride the SLS core stage four at a time and sink with it after one flight. When the stock runs out, their replacements fly once too: in 2020 NASA ordered 18 for about $1.79 billion.
cards.move: Reusable is a property of the plan, not of the hardware.
cards.reference: NASA, NASA Commits to Future Artemis Missions With More SLS Rocket Engines, press release, 1 May 2020

cards.question: NASA quoted about $450 million as the cost of launching a Space Shuttle mission. What did a flight cost averaged over the whole programme?
cards.answer: About $1.5 billion. The $450 million was roughly the running cost of one more flight; it left out design, building the orbiters, the pads and a standing army of staff. Pielke and Byerly divided the programme's lifetime cost, in 2010 dollars, by its 135 flights.
cards.move: Ask whether a price is for one more, or for the whole thing.
cards.trap: Taking the quoted per-flight figure as the whole cost of a flight.

cards.question: True or false: the first rocket booster to reach space and land upright again was a SpaceX Falcon 9?
cards.answer: False. Blue Origin's New Shepard crossed 100 km and landed on 23 November 2015; a Falcon 9 first stage landed on 21 December. The gap in difficulty was larger than the gap in dates: New Shepard went straight up and down, while the Falcon stage had to shed thousands of km/h of sideways speed.
cards.move: The version everyone saw is not always the one that came first.
cards.trap: Falcon 9 landings are the famous footage, so they seem to be first.
cards.reference: Davenport, The Space Barons: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and the Quest to Colonize the Cosmos, PublicAffairs, 2018

cards.question: Is booster reuse the main reason the cost of reaching orbit has fallen?
cards.answer: A rocket's first stage is most of its cost, and a Falcon 9 booster flies again and again, so that cost is spread across many flights. Reuse also makes a launch every few days possible: building a fresh booster each time would cap the pace and keep prices where the old expendable rockets left them.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, ask who kept the money that reuse saved.
cards.counterpoint: Falcon 9 undercut its rivals before any booster flew twice: in 2016, with every stage still new, its list price was about $62 million, far below other American rockets. Since reuse became routine, that price has risen, to about $67 million by 2022. In-house manufacturing, simpler design and fixed-price contracts did the cutting; reuse fattened the margins.
cards.source: Jones, International Conference on Environmental Systems, 2018
cards.reference: Jones, The Recent Large Reduction in Space Launch Cost, 48th International Conference on Environmental Systems, 2018

cards.question: How did engineers hold physical evidence of damaged booster seals years before Challenger was lost in 1986?
cards.answer: Because the boosters were fished out of the sea for reuse. Recovered casings showed the rubber O-rings in their joints scorched and eroded on flight after flight, from the second Shuttle mission in 1981, with the worst soot after a cold launch in January 1985. Each safe return was read as proof the margin held.
cards.move: A near miss that keeps happening is a warning, not a record.
cards.reference: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Report to the President, Washington DC, 1986

cards.question: Why did SpaceX design its Super Heavy booster to be caught by arms on the launch tower instead of landing on legs?
cards.answer: To save weight and time. Legs strong enough for a booster that size would ride to the edge of space and back on every flight, costing payload. Caught by the tower's arms, the booster also ends up where it can be refuelled and stacked again. The first catch came on 13 October 2024.
cards.move: The cheapest part to carry is the one left on the ground.
cards.reference: Chang, SpaceX Catches Returning Rocket in Mechanical Arms, The New York Times, 13 October 2024

cards.question: True or false: a rocket took off, hovered and landed upright on its own engines as early as 1993?
cards.answer: True. McDonnell Douglas's DC-X, a 12-metre test vehicle, first flew at White Sands, New Mexico, in August 1993, and made a dozen flights in all, none higher than a few kilometres. In 1996 a landing leg failed to extend; it toppled and burned. Funding ended, and the idea waited two decades for a sponsor.
cards.move: Inventions that died leave no fleet to remind anyone of them.
cards.trap: Dating vertical landing from the programmes that survived to fly today.
cards.reference: Launius & Jenkins, Coming Home: Reentry and Recovery from Space, NASA SP-2011-593, 2012

cards.question: Which extra kilogram of hardware costs a two-stage rocket the most payload to orbit?
cards.answer: One on the upper stage. It rides all the way to orbital speed, so each added kilogram costs about a kilogram of payload. A first-stage kilogram is dropped a few minutes in, far short of orbital speed, and costs only a fraction of that. That is why upper stages are thrown away.
cards.move: Weight matters most on whatever goes the whole distance.
cards.trap: Treating a kilogram as a kilogram wherever it rides.
cards.reference: Humble, Henry & Larson, Space Propulsion Analysis and Design, McGraw-Hill, 1995

cards.question: True or false: landing a Falcon 9 booster for reuse costs less than a tenth of the payload it could otherwise lift?
cards.answer: False. The booster must hold back fuel to turn or brake, re-enter and land, and carry legs and grid fins, so it lets the upper stage go at a lower speed. SpaceX has listed 8.3 tonnes to a high transfer orbit expended against 5.5 tonnes landed: a third of the payload left behind.
cards.move: Every way back has to be paid for on the way out.
cards.trap: Picturing the landing as a last small puff of spare fuel.
cards.reference: SpaceX, Falcon 9 vehicle page, payload to geosynchronous transfer orbit, expendable and reusable, spacex.com/vehicles/falcon-9, 2023

cards.question: The largest share of the iron in human blood was made in which kind of stellar death?
options: A white dwarf blowing itself apart
A red giant shedding its layers
cards.answer: A white dwarf blowing itself apart. A collapsing giant keeps its iron core, crushed into a neutron star or black hole, and throws out only a little new iron. Each exploding white dwarf forges about half a Sun's mass of it; most estimates credit them with more than half of the Solar System's supply.
cards.move: Where something is made matters less than whether it gets out.
cards.trap: Giants end their lives with iron cores, so they seem the obvious source.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aau9540

cards.question: The last supernova clearly seen in the Milky Way was Kepler's, in 1604. Roughly how often does one go off?
cards.answer: About once every 50 years. Estimates put collapsing-star explosions alone at about 1.6 a century, with white dwarf explosions on top. Most go unseen because dust in the galaxy's disc hides them from the eye. The youngest known remnant, G1.9+0.3, exploded around 1900 near the galactic centre, and nobody noticed.
cards.move: Before judging how rare something is, ask how much of it you could see.
cards.trap: Four centuries without a sighting make them seem that rare.
cards.reference: Rozwadowska, Vissani & Cappellaro, On the rate of core collapse supernovae in the Milky Way, New Astronomy 83, 101498, 2021

cards.question: Why did underground detectors register supernova 1987A hours before any telescope saw it?
cards.answer: Because its light was trapped inside the star. The collapsing core released neutrinos, particles that cross matter almost unhindered; light had to wait for the shock wave to reach the surface. On 23 February 1987 three detectors caught about two dozen neutrinos in 13 seconds, two to three hours before the light.
cards.move: The signal that arrives first is often the one nobody is watching for.
cards.source: Hirata et al., Physical Review Letters, 1987
cards.reference: doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.1490

cards.question: Why have some white dwarfs, the cooling cores left by dead stars, stopped cooling?
cards.answer: Their cores are freezing, and the crystals float. In some white dwarfs the solid that forms is lighter than the surrounding liquid, so it rises and pushes heavier liquid down, releasing gravitational energy. Bédard and colleagues showed in 2024 that this holds some steady for billions of years, so they look younger than they are.
cards.move: When something refuses to cool, look for a hidden source of heat.

cards.question: True or false: no red dwarf, the smallest kind of hydrogen-burning star, has yet died of old age?
cards.answer: True. A red dwarf burns its hydrogen so slowly that it lasts from tens of billions of years to trillions, the smallest longest. The universe is 13.8 billion years old, and only stars above about 80% of the Sun's mass have had time to run out. Almost every red dwarf ever formed is still shining.
cards.move: Judge a lifetime against its own clock, not against ours.
cards.trap: Assuming 13.8 billion years is long enough for any star to burn out.
cards.source: Adams & Laughlin, Five Ages of the Universe
cards.reference: Adams & Laughlin, The Five Ages of the Universe: Inside the Physics of Eternity, Free Press, 1999

cards.question: What put radioactive iron-60 into seabed crusts across the world's oceans about two million years ago?
cards.answer: Supernovae a few hundred light-years away. Iron-60 has a half-life of 2.6 million years, so none survives from Earth's formation; any found must be recent. Wallner's team found it in crusts and sediments from three oceans, mostly laid down 3 to 1.5 million years ago: stardust settling while early humans walked in Africa.
cards.move: A clock that runs out tells you the thing is recent.
cards.reference: Wallner et al., Recent near-Earth supernovae probed by global deposition of interstellar radioactive 60Fe, Nature 532, 69, 2016

cards.question: When a massive star's core collapses and the star explodes, what share of the energy released leaves as light?
cards.answer: Under 0.01%. About 99% escapes as neutrinos, carrying off the energy of a core falling in to a ball some 20 km across. About 1% drives the blast outwards, and the light is a hundredth of that or less. That sliver is still enough to outshine a galaxy of billions of stars for weeks.
cards.move: What can be seen of an event may be its smallest part.
cards.trap: Taking the flash that outshines a galaxy as most of the output.
cards.reference: Janka, Explosion Mechanisms of Core-Collapse Supernovae, Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science 62, 407, 2012

cards.question: A star born with about 200 times the Sun's mass and few heavy elements comes to the end of its life. What remains?
options: A black hole of about 100 Suns
cards.answer: Nothing at all. Its core grows so hot that light turns into pairs of electrons and positrons, robbing the core of pressure. It falls in, burns its oxygen at once and blows itself apart. This is why single stars should leave no black holes between roughly 50 and 130 Suns: the biggest cores erase themselves.
cards.move: A trend that holds through the middle can break at the ends.
cards.trap: Assuming a bigger star always leaves a bigger remnant.
cards.reference: Heger & Woosley, The Nucleosynthetic Signature of Population III, The Astrophysical Journal 567, 532, 2002

cards.question: True or false: Betelgeuse's sudden dimming in 2019 and 2020 was a sign that it was close to exploding?
cards.answer: False. A cooler patch on its surface let gas the star had puffed out condense into dust, which hid part of its face. Most models give Betelgeuse something like 100,000 years before it explodes, so the chance of that in any one year is around 1 in 100,000. Dust was always the likelier story.
cards.move: Before reading an omen, ask how often the rare thing happens at all.
cards.trap: Reading a dramatic change as the long-predicted explosion arriving.
cards.reference: Montargès et al., A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming, Nature 594, 365, 2021

cards.question: True or false: as the dying Sun swells into a red giant, the orbits of Mars and Jupiter will grow wider?
