cards.answer: True. The swelling Sun blows away about a third of its mass as wind, so its grip weakens and every planet drifts outwards, by about half again. Earth may not escape this way. Schröder and Smith calculated that tides raised on the bloated Sun would still drag Earth inwards to be swallowed.
cards.move: When the centre loses weight, whatever circles it drifts away.
cards.trap: Picturing the Sun that swallows Earth as pulling planets closer.
cards.reference: Schröder & Smith, Distant future of the Sun and Earth revisited, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 386, 155, 2008

cards.question: At its top feeding rate, a black hole doubles in mass every 35 million years. How long from 100 suns to a billion?
cards.answer: About 800 million years. The limit is set by the glare of infalling gas pushing the rest away. From 100 suns to a billion is a factor of 10 million, only 23 doublings: 23 × 35 million years. Yet a quasar seen 690 million years after the Big Bang already held 800 million suns.
cards.move: Count the doublings before judging how long a huge multiple takes.
cards.trap: A ten-millionfold gain sounds as if it needs most of cosmic history.

diagram.caption: Doubling every 35 My, little shows for 700 My; the last three doublings add seven eighths.

cards.reference: Bañados et al., An 800-million-solar-mass black hole in a significantly neutral Universe at a redshift of 7.5, Nature, 2018

cards.question: True or false: the Milky Way's central black hole shines more brightly than the stars crowded around it?
cards.answer: False. It is one of the dimmest things there: its total output is under a ten-millionth of the most a hole of 4 million suns could give. Little gas reaches it, and that hot, thin gas radiates poorly. S2, a star that swings past it every 16 years, outshines the hole it orbits.
cards.move: Capacity says nothing about output until you know the supply.
cards.trap: Picturing every giant black hole as a blazing quasar.
cards.source: Genzel et al., Reviews of Modern Physics, 2010
cards.reference: Genzel, Eisenhauer & Gillessen, The Galactic Center Massive Black Hole and Nuclear Star Cluster, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2010

cards.question: What can happen when two stars orbiting each other wander too close to the Milky Way's central black hole?
cards.answer: The pair is split: one star is captured into a tight orbit around the hole, and the other is flung out carrying the energy its partner lost. In 2019 astronomers found a star leaving the galaxy at about 1,700 km/s, traced back to the centre some 5 million years ago.
cards.move: Break a partnership, and the energy that bound it goes somewhere.
cards.reference: Koposov et al., Discovery of a nearby 1700 km/s star ejected from the Milky Way by Sgr A*, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2020

cards.question: How do astronomers know that giant black holes put on most of their weight while shining, not silently?
cards.answer: By adding up old light. Count the energy all quasars have ever radiated, assume about a tenth of the mass falling in became light, and the mass implied matches what now sits, dark, in the centres of nearby galaxies. Andrzej Sołtan set out the sum in 1982. The quiet giants are the receipts.
cards.move: Total the output, and it tells you what the input must have been.
cards.reference: Sołtan, Masses of quasars, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 1982

cards.question: Why does a galaxy's central black hole grow in step with stars far beyond the reach of its gravity?
cards.answer: Nobody is sure. The hole weighs a few tenths of a percent of the galaxy's central bulge and its pull dominates only a small core, yet its mass tracks how fast stars move across the whole bulge, thousands of light years wide. The favoured idea: a feeding hole's winds blow away the gas both need.
cards.move: When two things keep pace across a distance, look for the go-between.
cards.reference: Kormendy & Ho, Coevolution (Or Not) of Supermassive Black Holes and Host Galaxies, Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2013

cards.question: Gas spiralling into a non-spinning black hole radiates about 6% of its mass as light. Around a hole spinning near its limit?
cards.answer: About 30%. The light leaves before the gas reaches the horizon, radiated as it spirals down to the last stable orbit. Around a fast spinner that orbit lies several times closer in, so the gas sinks deeper before it is lost. The yield rises fivefold, to some 40 times what fusion gets from hydrogen.
cards.move: Ask what a thing gives off on the way, not only where it ends.
cards.trap: Letting the given 6% hold, as if spin could not matter.
cards.reference: Thorne, Disk-accretion onto a black hole. II. Evolution of the hole, Astrophysical Journal, 1974

cards.question: After two galaxies merge, why can their central black holes stall for ages a few light years apart?
cards.answer: Because they run out of stars to throw. The pair sinks by flinging passing stars away, each carrying off some orbital energy, and soon the nearby stars are gone. Gravitational waves only take over much closer in. In 2023, pulsar-timing arrays reported a background hum of such waves: a sign that pairs do get through.
cards.move: A process that feeds on its surroundings stalls when it has used them up.
cards.reference: Begelman, Blandford & Rees, Massive black hole binaries in active galactic nuclei, Nature, 1980

cards.question: At its limit, a black hole shines 30,000 suns per solar mass. How many million solar masses match a galaxy shining like 30 billion suns?
cards.answer: 30 billion / 30,000 = 1 million suns.
cards.move: Judge a source by what each kilogram gives, not by its size.
cards.trap: Expecting a hole to need a galaxy's mass to match its light.
cards.hint: Divide the light you need by the light each solar mass of hole can give.
steps: Light to match: 30 billion suns.
Light per solar mass of hole: 30,000 suns.
30 billion / 30,000 = 1 million suns.
cards.reference: Frank, King & Raine, Accretion Power in Astrophysics, 3rd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2002

cards.question: Why did X-rays from a galaxy seen 470 million years after the Big Bang upset ideas of how giant black holes begin?
cards.answer: Its black hole already weighed tens of millions of suns, about as much as all the galaxy's stars together. A hole grown from a dead star of 100 suns could hardly have got there in time. It fits a seed born big: a gas cloud collapsing straight into a hole of 10,000 suns or more.
cards.move: When something is already huge at birth, ask whether it started big.
cards.reference: Bogdán et al., Evidence for heavy-seed origin of early supermassive black holes from a z≈10 X-ray quasar, Nature Astronomy, 2024

cards.question: True or false: the more massive a galaxy's central black hole, the more violently it tears apart a star that strays too close?
cards.answer: False. Above about 100 million suns, a star like the Sun is swallowed whole, without a flare. The stretching force near the horizon weakens as the hole grows, while the horizon itself widens, so the star is inside before it can be torn. Only lighter holes, or fast spinners, shred Sun-like stars in view.
cards.move: A bigger version of a thing can lose the very effect it is known for.
cards.trap: Assuming a bigger hole must have a stronger grip on everything nearby.
cards.reference: Hills, Possible power source of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs, Nature, 1975

cards.question: The Sun pulls on Earth about 180 times harder than the Moon does. How big is the Sun's tide next to the Moon's?
cards.answer: About half as big. A tide is the difference in pull between Earth's near and far sides, and that difference falls with the cube of distance. The Sun is 390 times farther off than the Moon, so its tide is only 46% of the Moon's: enough to swell the tides at new and full moon.
cards.move: Ask whether an effect follows the force or the difference across it.
cards.trap: Letting the 180-times figure set the size of the tide.
cards.reference: Cartwright, Tides: A Scientific History, Cambridge University Press, 1999

cards.question: True or false: the Moon drives the tides mainly by pulling water sideways, not by lifting it upwards?
cards.answer: True. Straight up, the Moon's tidal pull is about a ten-millionth of Earth's gravity: it lightens the water by a hair and lifts almost nothing. The sideways part of that pull is just as small, but nothing resists it. Over thousands of kilometres it herds water towards the points under and opposite the Moon.
cards.move: A tiny force nobody resists can do more than a large one resisted.
cards.trap: Picturing the Moon hoisting the sea straight up beneath it.
cards.reference: Pugh & Woodworth, Sea-Level Science: Understanding Tides, Surges, Tsunamis and Mean Sea-Level Changes, Cambridge University Press, 2014

cards.question: Earth is 81 times the Moon's mass and 3.7 times its radius. How many times stronger is Earth's tide on the Moon than the reverse?
cards.answer: 81 / 3.7 ≈ 21.9, so about 22 times.
cards.move: Equal forces between two bodies can still do very unequal things.
cards.trap: Action equals reaction, so the two tides must be equal.
cards.hint: A tide grows with the mass doing the pulling and with the width of the body being stretched.
steps: The heavier puller multiplies the stretch by 81.
The Moon's smaller width divides it by 3.7.
81 / 3.7 ≈ 21.9, so about 22 times.
cards.reference: Murray & Dermott, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press, 1999

cards.question: Why did the energy of the particle beams in CERN's 27 km LEP collider rise and fall with the Moon?
cards.answer: Because the Moon raises tides in rock as well as in water. The ground swells and settles twice a day, and the stretching changed the ring's 27 km circumference by about a millimetre, enough to shift the beam energy measurably. The biggest collider of its day had to correct for where the Moon was.
cards.move: Even the ruler moves; ask what your reference is standing on.
cards.source: Arnaudon et al., Nuclear Instruments and Methods, 1995
cards.reference: Arnaudon et al., Effects of terrestrial tides on the LEP beam energy, Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research A, 1995

cards.question: Earth's tidal bulge tugs the Moon forward along its orbit. Why does the Moon end up moving more slowly?
cards.answer: Because a push along an orbit raises it, and a higher orbit is a slower one. The energy taken from Earth's spin lifts the Moon about 3.8 cm farther away each year, a rate measured by timing laser pulses bounced off mirrors the Apollo crews left. The month lengthens as the day does.
cards.move: A push can slow a thing down if it also makes it climb.
cards.reference: Dickey et al., Lunar Laser Ranging: A Continuing Legacy of the Apollo Program, Science, 1994

cards.question: Why do some coasts, such as parts of the Gulf of Mexico, get only one high tide a day?
cards.answer: Because the Moon is rarely over the equator. Its orbit carries it up to about 28° north and south, so the two tidal bulges sit off-centre and a coast passes through one squarely and the other barely. Where a basin also responds best to a daily rhythm, the second tide all but vanishes.
cards.move: Tilt a regular pattern slightly and its two halves stop matching.
cards.reference: Hicks, Understanding Tides, NOAA National Ocean Service, 2006

cards.question: What mainly gives the Bay of Fundy tides of up to 16 m?
options: Its funnel shape squeezing the water
Its position facing the open Atlantic
Its water sloshing at the tide's rhythm
cards.answer: Its water sloshing at the tide's rhythm. The bay and the Gulf of Maine together have a natural period of about 13 hours, close to the 12.4-hour lunar tide, so each Atlantic tide pushes just as the water swings back, like a hand on a swing. The funnel adds height; resonance does most of it.
cards.move: Small pushes, timed to a thing's own rhythm, build enormous motion.
cards.trap: Crediting the funnel shape, which anyone can see on a map.
cards.reference: Garrett, Tidal Resonance in the Bay of Fundy and Gulf of Maine, Nature, 1972

cards.question: True or false: in parts of the open North Sea, the Moon raises almost no tide at all?
cards.answer: True. The tide there does not rise and fall as one bulge; it wheels round points called amphidromes, like water swirling in a tilted bowl. At each centre the level barely changes, while coasts around it see metres. The North Sea has three such points, and the crest takes about 12 hours to circle each.
cards.move: A turning pattern can have a still centre that everything moves around.
cards.trap: Picturing the tide as one bulge lifting every sea alike.
cards.reference: Proudman & Doodson, The principal constituent of the tides of the North Sea, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 1924

cards.question: Devonian corals, about 400 million years old, laid down some 400 daily growth lines a year. How many hours long was a day?
cards.answer: 8,766 hours / 400 days ≈ 21.9 hours.
cards.move: When a ratio changes, check which side of it moved.
cards.trap: Assuming the year, not the day, must have changed.
cards.hint: The year's length in hours has barely changed; only the number of days that fill it.
steps: A year lasts about 365.25 x 24 = 8,766 hours, then as now.
8,766 hours / 400 days ≈ 21.9 hours.
cards.reference: Wells, Coral growth and geochronometry, Nature, 1963

cards.question: Ancient eclipse records show the day lengthening 1.8 ms a century; the Moon's tides alone should add 2.3. What makes up the gap?
options: Land still rising since the ice age
Errors in the ancient eclipse records
The Moon's pull weakening as it recedes
cards.answer: Land still rising since the ice age. Freed of their ice sheets, Canada and Scandinavia are rebounding, so Earth grows less flattened; like a skater drawing in her arms, it spins faster, trimming about 0.5 ms a century. Babylonian and Chinese eclipse timings, checked against lunar laser ranging, record both effects at once.
cards.move: When a measurement falls short of theory, look for a second cause pulling back.
cards.trap: Blaming old records, when two real causes pull against each other.
cards.reference: Stephenson, Morrison & Hohenkerk, Measurement of the Earth's rotation: 720 BC to AD 2015, Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 2016

cards.question: Why can't a cup of pure water stay liquid on most of the Martian surface, even on a warm afternoon?
cards.answer: The air is too thin to hold it. Average surface pressure is about 6 millibars, close to the 6.1 below which water cannot be liquid at all. Ice turns straight to vapour; liquid boils barely above 0 °C. Only deep basins such as Hellas, at twice the pressure, open a window of about ten degrees.
cards.move: Warmth alone does not make a liquid; the pressure has to allow it.
cards.source: Haberle et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2001
cards.reference: Haberle, McKay, Schaeffer et al., On the possibility of liquid water on present-day Mars, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 106(E10), 2001

cards.question: How can telescopes on Earth gauge how much water Mars once had, from the thin vapour left today?
cards.answer: By weighing its hydrogen. Light hydrogen escapes to space more easily than the heavy kind, deuterium, so leftover water grows richer in it. Martian water carries about seven times Earth's share. Working back, a 2015 study found at least a 137 m global layer: an ocean on almost a fifth of the planet.
cards.move: What leaks out first leaves its mark on what stays behind.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aaa3630

cards.question: True or false: Mars's dark seasonal slope streaks, announced in 2015 as salty water, are still thought to be wet?
cards.answer: False. In 2017 Dundas and colleagues showed that the streaks, called recurring slope lineae, stop at the same angle at which dry sand stops sliding on Martian dunes, and appear only on slopes steep enough for dry grains to flow. Most researchers now read them as dry sand flows, with little or no water.
cards.move: The claim you heard loudest is not always the claim still standing.
cards.trap: Remembering the 2015 headlines, not the quieter 2017 correction.

cards.question: In 2008, bright crumbs the Phoenix lander had dug up vanished from its trench within four days. What were they?
cards.answer: Water ice. Salt cannot vanish, and dry ice could not survive in summer soil tens of degrees too warm for it. Water ice, once exposed to the dry air, turns straight to vapour over days. The team took the disappearance as the proof: a vanishing act served as the chemistry test.
cards.move: How a thing disappears can tell you what it was.
cards.trap: Bright white crumbs in dry soil look like desert salt.
cards.reference: Smith et al., H2O at the Phoenix Landing Site, Science 325, 2009

cards.question: Does the bright radar echo beneath Mars's south polar ice come from a lake of liquid water?
cards.answer: In 2018 the MARSIS radar on Mars Express found a patch about 20 km wide, 1.5 km under the ice, echoing more strongly than the ice surface itself. On Earth, echoes that bright under ice sheets come from subglacial lakes. Salts such as perchlorates can keep brine liquid far below 0 °C.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the heat under the ice decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Keeping even salty water liquid there needs more heat than the region is known to have. Frozen smectite clays, common on Mars, give equally bright echoes, as Smith and colleagues showed in 2021, and similar bright spots turn up where the ice base is far too cold for brine. A solid explanation fits without special pleading.
cards.reference: doi:10.1126/science.aar7268

cards.question: What did Curiosity find in 2023 that points to seasons of wet and dry on ancient Mars?
cards.answer: Hexagonal cracks. Mud dried once splits in T-shaped cracks; only when it is wetted and dried again and again do the junctions relax into Y-shapes and the pattern into hexagons, as on dry lake beds on Earth. Ancient rocks in Gale crater show just that: a climate that cycled, not one flood.
cards.move: The shape of a crack can count how often something happened.
cards.reference: Rapin et al., Sustained wet–dry cycling on early Mars, Nature, 2023

cards.question: A 2021 model found escape to space too slow to have dried out early Mars. Where does it put the rest of the water?
options: Bound into minerals in the crust
cards.answer: Bound into minerals in the crust. Reacting with rock, water was locked into clays and other minerals, taking up, by the model's range, 30% to 99% of the early water. Escape alone cannot match both the amount lost and the heavy hydrogen left behind. Much of the ocean may sit in the rocks.
cards.move: Before saying something escaped, check whether it was absorbed where it stood.
cards.trap: Pointing to the polar ice, the water everyone has seen in pictures.
cards.reference: Scheller, Ehlmann, Hu, Adams & Yung, Long-term drying of Mars by sequestration of ocean-scale volumes of water in the crust, Science, 2021

cards.question: Mars's south polar ice deposits hold about 1.6 million km³. Spread over the planet's 145 million km², how many metres deep?
cards.move: A huge volume spread over a whole planet becomes a thin coat.
cards.trap: Losing three zeros when turning kilometres into metres.
cards.hint: Divide the volume by the area, and keep kilometres until the end.
steps: 1.6 million km³ / 145 million km² ≈ 0.011 km.
cards.reference: Plaut et al., Subsurface Radar Sounding of the South Polar Layered Deposits of Mars, Science, 2007

cards.question: True or false: the 2024 case for liquid water 11 to 20 km under Mars rested on seismometers at several sites?
cards.answer: False. It rested on one seismometer, on NASA's InSight lander in Elysium Planitia. Marsquake waves travelled beneath it at speeds that fit rock with water-filled cracks; extrapolated planet-wide, that would be enough for an ocean 1 to 2 km deep. The reading is contested. One instrument, one spot, a claim about a planet.
cards.move: Ask how many places were measured before accepting a claim about everywhere.
cards.trap: Assuming a planet-wide claim must stand on planet-wide measurements.
cards.reference: Wright, Manga & Panning, Liquid water in the Martian mid-crust, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2024

cards.question: Was early Mars warm enough for rain and flowing rivers over long stretches, rather than mostly frozen?
cards.answer: Valley networks branch like river systems fed by rain, and deltas such as Jezero's and lake beds such as Gale's record water standing for long periods. Clays formed in water are widespread in the oldest rock. A frozen planet with brief melts struggles to carve so much; some greenhouse mix must have kept it warm.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on how long the water had to flow.
cards.counterpoint: The young Sun was about a quarter fainter, and no climate model keeps Mars above freezing for long with plausible gases. An icy highland climate, melted now and then by volcanic outbursts or impacts, can carve valleys and fill lakes in bursts. The rivers are real; a long warm climate is not required to explain them.
cards.reference: Wordsworth, The Climate of Early Mars, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences, 2016

cards.question: In the best-known altitude-training trial, which arrangement made runners faster over 5,000 m?
cards.answer: Living high and training low. In Levine and Stray-Gundersen's 1997 study, runners who slept at 2,500 m but did hard sessions at 1,250 m improved by about 13 seconds. Those who also trained high made more red blood cells too, but thin air forced slower sessions, and their race times did not improve.
cards.move: A gain in one place can be spent in another; measure the finished result.
cards.source: Levine & Stray-Gundersen, Journal of Applied Physiology, 1997
cards.reference: Levine & Stray-Gundersen, Living high-training low: effect of moderate-altitude acclimatization with low-altitude training on performance, Journal of Applied Physiology, 1997

cards.question: How quickly does living at altitude add to the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity?
cards.answer: Slowly: about 1% more haemoglobin for every 100 hours spent high. The kidneys raise their output of the hormone erythropoietin within hours, but new red cells take weeks to mature. That is why camps last three to four weeks at around 2,000 to 2,500 m, and a short trip up the mountain does almost nothing.
cards.move: Ask how long the body needs to build what the signal asks for.
cards.source: Gore et al., Br J Sports Med, 2013
cards.reference: Gore et al., Altitude training and haemoglobin mass from the optimised carbon monoxide rebreathing method determined by a meta-analysis, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2013

cards.question: At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, 2,240 m up, which track and field events produced world records?
options: Distance races, won by highland runners
None, since thin air slowed everyone
cards.answer: Sprints and jumps. Thinner air means less drag, and short events barely depend on oxygen: records fell in the 100 m, 200 m, 400 m, long jump and triple jump, where Bob Beamon reached 8.90 m. Distance times were slow. Runners raised at altitude won most of them by coping better, not by running faster.
cards.move: Who won and how fast they went are two different questions.
cards.trap: Recalling highland-born champions and assuming altitude speeded their races.
cards.reference: Ward-Smith, Air resistance and its influence on the biomechanics and energetics of sprinting at sea level and at altitude, Journal of Biomechanics, 1984

cards.question: True or false: air at a 2,500 m training camp contains a smaller percentage of oxygen than air at sea level?
cards.answer: False. Oxygen makes up about 20.9% of dry air at any height athletes train at. What falls is the pressure: at 2,500 m it is about three quarters of sea level, so each breath carries fewer molecules of everything. Altitude tents work the other way, removing oxygen to mimic the same shortage.
cards.move: Separate how much of the mixture is there from how much mixture there is.
cards.trap: Assuming thin air means air with less oxygen in the mix.
cards.source: West, Schoene & Milledge, High Altitude Medicine, 2007
cards.reference: West, Schoene & Milledge, High Altitude Medicine and Physiology, Hodder Arnold, 2007

cards.question: Air pressure falls to half its sea-level value near 5,500 m. How much remains at Everest's summit, 8,849 m?
cards.answer: About a third. Pressure halves over each similar climb, so it falls by a fixed fraction, not a fixed amount: 8,849 m is about 1.6 halvings, which leaves roughly a third. Measured on the summit in 1981, it was 253 mm of mercury against 760 at sea level. Most climbers there breathe from bottles.
cards.move: When something shrinks by halves, never extend it with a ruler.
cards.trap: Extending the fall in a straight line, which gives about a fifth.
cards.source: West et al., Journal of Applied Physiology, 1983
cards.reference: West et al., Barometric pressures at extreme altitudes on Mt. Everest: physiological significance, Journal of Applied Physiology, 1983

cards.question: Cyclists slept four weeks in rooms thinned to match 3,000 m or in normal air, with nobody told which. The result?
options: Neither group improved more than the other
Only the thin-air group got faster
Both improved, thin air twice as much
cards.answer: Neither group improved more than the other. In Siebenmann and colleagues' double-blind trial, 16 hours a day in air matching 3,000 m, for four weeks, did not improve endurance performance beyond placebo. Earlier open trials had reported gains, but there the athletes knew they were sleeping high and expected to benefit.
cards.move: Hide the treatment from the people who hope it works.
cards.trap: Crediting thin air with gains that expectation and training could explain.
cards.source: Siebenmann et al., J Appl Physiol, 2012
cards.reference: Siebenmann et al., Live high-train low using normobaric hypoxia: a double-blinded, placebo-controlled study, Journal of Applied Physiology, 2012

cards.question: Why do altitude camps often begin with a blood test for iron rather than for red cells?
cards.answer: Because thin air cannot build blood without iron. In 1992 Stray-Gundersen's group reported that runners who arrived at altitude with low iron stores, measured as serum ferritin, did not increase their red cell volume at all, while runners with adequate stores did. Camps now commonly screen ferritin weeks ahead and supplement anyone low.
cards.move: Before pressing the accelerator, check there is fuel in the tank.
cards.source: Stray-Gundersen et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1992
cards.reference: Stray-Gundersen et al., Failure of red cell volume to increase to altitude exposure in iron deficient runners, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 1992

cards.question: Why does an athlete's haematocrit climb within days of arriving at altitude, long before new red cells are ready?
cards.answer: Because the blood loses water. In the first days high up, plasma volume falls, partly through extra urine and moisture lost in faster breathing, so the same red cells sit in less fluid and the haematocrit, the share of blood made of cells, rises. New cells take weeks: the early climb is a shrinking denominator.
cards.move: When a percentage rises, check whether the part grew or the whole shrank.
cards.source: Sawka et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2000
cards.reference: Sawka, Convertino, Eichner, Schnieder & Young, Blood volume: importance and adaptations to exercise training, environmental stresses, and trauma/sickness, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2000

cards.question: Should altitude tents be banned, since they raise red cell mass without the athlete leaving home?
cards.answer: Anti-doping rules target methods that enhance performance against the spirit of sport, and a tent manufacturing thin air in a bedroom aims at the same result as an EPO injection: more red cells. It favours athletes who can afford the equipment, and in 2006 the World Anti-Doping Agency seriously considered prohibiting it.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether the means or the result defines cheating decides it.
cards.counterpoint: The body does only what it would do in any mountain town: no drug enters the blood, and the gain is capped by physiology rather than by dose. A ban could not be enforced in private homes, and athletes born at altitude carry the same advantage all their lives. The agency left the tents legal.
cards.source: Levine, Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2006
cards.reference: Levine, Should artificial high altitude environments be considered doping?, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2006

cards.question: Top oxygen uptake, VO2max, falls about 6.3% per 1,000 m above 300 m. How much lower is it at 2,300 m, in percent?
cards.move: Before multiplying a rate, check where its counting starts.
cards.trap: Counting from sea level and answering about 14.5%.
cards.hint: Check the height the 1,000 m steps are counted from.
steps: Height above the starting point: 2,300 - 300 = 2,000 m.
cards.source: Wehrlin & Hallén, Eur J Appl Physiol, 2006

cards.question: Olympia's shortest footrace ran one stade: 600 local feet of about 32 cm each. How long was it, in metres?
cards.move: A unit that sounds fixed can mean different lengths in different towns.
cards.trap: Assuming the ancient sprint matched a modern 200 m.
cards.hint: Convert one foot to metres first, then multiply by the number of feet.
steps: One Olympic foot is about 0.32 m.
cards.reference: Miller, Ancient Greek Athletics, Yale University Press, 2004

cards.question: Why did ancient Olympic long jumpers take off holding stone or lead weights in their hands?
cards.answer: To jump farther. Swung forward at take-off, hand weights of 2 to 9 kg add distance to a standing jump. Minetti and Ardigò's simulations and tests put the gain at no less than 17 cm on a 3 m jump, and the best mass they found matched weights excavated from ancient sites.
cards.move: Before calling an old practice a ritual, test whether it simply worked.

cards.question: What paid for the row of bronze Zeus statues lining the entrance to Olympia's stadium?
cards.answer: Fines imposed on cheats. Pausanias records that the first six were paid for in 388 BC, after the boxer Eupolus of Thessaly bribed three opponents. Each base named the offender, and the statues stood where every competitor walked into the stadium. Sixteen of their stone bases still stand in a line there.
cards.move: A penalty seen by everyone who comes next works twice.
cards.trap: Olympia is famous for victors' statues, so these seem like more of them.
cards.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Book 5, trans. W. H. S. Jones, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard, 1926

cards.question: True or false: a surviving decree of Emperor Theodosius I banned the Olympic Games in AD 393?
cards.answer: False. No law in the Theodosian Code names the Games. The year 393 rests on a Byzantine chronicle written some seven centuries later. Evidence from Olympia suggests the festival went on into the fifth century, fading with its funding and cult; Remijsen places the last Games under Theodosius II, who reigned from 408.
cards.move: Ask what document a neat date rests on before repeating it.
cards.trap: One late chronicle survived, so its tidy date became the story.
cards.source: Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics, 2015
cards.reference: Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics in Late Antiquity, Cambridge University Press, 2015

cards.question: What did an Athenian who won at Olympia receive back home, beyond the olive wreath?
cards.answer: Cash, and later free meals for life. Plutarch reports that Solon's laws paid an Olympic victor 500 drachmas and an Isthmian victor 100, when a sheep was valued at one drachma. By the fifth century BC, Olympic victors could also dine at public expense in the city's town hall, the prytaneion.
cards.move: A prize that looks symbolic may sit on top of one that is not.
cards.reference: Plutarch, Lives, Volume I: Solon, trans. Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard, 1914

cards.question: What happened to a runner who left the start too early in an ancient Greek footrace?
cards.answer: He was beaten. In Herodotus, a Corinthian commander reminds Themistocles that at the games those who start too soon are struck with rods, and officials holding rods stand beside runners on painted vases. Later, stadiums at Nemea and Isthmia had a starting gate, the hysplex, that dropped cords in front of every runner at once.
cards.move: When fairness hangs on one instant, build a machine for that instant.
cards.reference: Herodotus, The Persian Wars, Volume IV: Books 8–9, trans. A. D. Godley, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard, 1925

cards.question: What did Egyptian wise men tell envoys from Elis about the fairness of the Olympic Games?
cards.answer: That the Games could not be fair while Eleans competed. Herodotus says the Eleans boasted of their rules to King Psammis; his sages asked whether men of Elis took part, and hearing yes, warned that judges from the host city would favour their own. Elis kept both roles: its citizens judged and competed.
cards.move: Before trusting a verdict, ask whether the judge has a stake in it.
cards.reference: Herodotus, The Persian Wars, Volume I: Books 1–2, trans. A. D. Godley, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard, 1920

cards.question: Kyniska of Sparta, the first woman recorded as an Olympic victor, won in the 390s BC. In which event?
cards.answer: The four-horse chariot race. At Olympia the crown for equestrian events went to the owner of the horses, not the driver, so a rich Spartan woman who never took the reins could win it, twice. Her monument at Olympia boasted that she was the only woman in Greece to have won that crown.
cards.move: Ask who a prize is awarded to, not who did the work.
cards.trap: Assuming women could win only at Hera's separate races for girls.
cards.source: Kyle, Sport and Spectacle in the Ancient World
cards.reference: Kyle, Sport and Spectacle in the Ancient World, Blackwell, 2007

cards.question: True or false: the Olympic truce obliged Greek states to halt all their wars while the Games were held?
cards.answer: False. The truce protected Elis, the festival and people travelling to and from it; wars elsewhere went on. Where it applied, it had teeth: Thucydides records that in 420 BC Elis fined Sparta 2,000 minae, two for each of 1,000 soldiers sent in during the truce, and barred Spartans from the Games.
cards.move: Check the scope of a famous promise before crediting it with more.
cards.trap: Reading the modern peace-for-all ideal back into the ancient rule.
cards.reference: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Volume III: Books 5–6, trans. C. F. Smith, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard, 1921

cards.question: Counting 776 BC as the first Olympiad and one every four years, which Olympiad fell in AD 393, given no year zero?
cards.answer: 292 + 1 = the 293rd Olympiad.
cards.move: When counting events across a span, check both ends of the fence.
cards.trap: Dividing the span by four and forgetting the first Games themselves.
cards.hint: Count the years between, then the four-year gaps, then the Games.
steps: With no year zero, 776 BC to AD 393 spans 776 + 393 − 1 = 1,168 years.
1,168 ÷ 4 = 292 four-year gaps after the first Games.
292 + 1 = the 293rd Olympiad.
cards.source: Bickerman, Chronology of the Ancient World
cards.reference: Bickerman, Chronology of the Ancient World, Thames and Hudson, 1968

cards.question: The 2014 World Cup ball had six panels, two fewer than the 2010 ball. How did its total seam length compare?
cards.answer: About 60% longer: 327 cm of seam against 203 cm. Its panels were shaped like pinwheel arms, so fewer pieces still meant more edge. Seams roughen a ball and shift the speed at which its drag suddenly drops; the smoother 2010 ball met that change near free-kick speeds and was notorious for wobbling.
cards.move: When shapes change, count the edges, not the number of pieces.
cards.trap: Fewer panels sounds like fewer seams, so a shorter total.
cards.reference: Goff, Asai & Hong, A comparison of Jabulani and Brazuca non-spin aerodynamics, Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part P, 2014

cards.question: How can an old, scuffed cricket ball bowled fast swing the opposite way to a new one?
cards.answer: Because at high speed the air turns turbulent on both halves. A new ball swings towards where its seam points: there the seam trips the air into turbulence, which clings longer. With both halves turbulent, the seam-side layer thickens and lets go first, and the ball veers towards its shiny half.
cards.move: An effect that works one way can flip once the conditions behind it change.
cards.reference: Mehta, An overview of cricket ball swing, Sports Engineering, 2005

cards.question: True or false: MLB's scientists traced the 2015–17 home run surge mainly to hitters changing their swings?
cards.answer: False. Scientists reporting to Major League Baseball in 2018 found that balls hit the same way were carrying farther, because the balls had less air drag. They could not tie the lower drag to any property they measured, and drag varied more from one ball to the next than from year to year.
cards.move: When two things change at once, measure each before crediting the famous one.
cards.trap: The swing-angle fashion was the visible change, so it gets the credit.
cards.reference: https://www.mlb.com/press-release/major-league-baseball-receives-report-on-increased-home-run-rate-278136100

cards.question: How do golf's rule-makers plan to shorten the longest drives from 2028 without changing a single club?
cards.answer: By testing balls with a faster robot swing. Under the new test, a ball struck at a clubhead speed of about 201 km/h may not travel beyond about 290 m; the old test swung at about 193 km/h. Balls passing the harder test fly shorter; the longest hitters should lose around 12 to 14 m.
cards.move: To change a limit without rewriting it, change the test that enforces it.
cards.reference: https://www.cbssports.com/golf/news/usga-r-a-announce-universal-golf-ball-rollback-to-limit-distance-with-implementation-set-for-2028

cards.question: Why are tennis balls sold in sealed, pressurised tins rather than in open boxes?
cards.answer: Because a pressurised ball starts losing its inner gas the moment it meets ordinary air. The rules require a ball dropped from 254 cm onto concrete to rebound between 135 and 147 cm, and a leaking ball soon falls short. Sealed at matching pressure, the air in the tin keeps the air in the ball.
cards.move: A product that decays on contact is sold inside its own protective conditions.
cards.source: ITF, Rules of Tennis, Appendix I
cards.reference: International Tennis Federation, Rules of Tennis, Appendix I: The Ball, 2024

cards.question: Why must a legal golf ball fly the same way however it is placed on the tee?
cards.answer: Because of a ball that tamed slices. The Polara, designed by two scientists in the 1970s, had normal dimples in a band round its middle and shallow ones elsewhere; teed correctly, it spun steadily and curved far less. The USGA answered with a symmetry rule in 1981, and later settled Polara's lawsuit for $1.375 million.
cards.move: A rule written against one product often reads like a portrait of it.
cards.reference: USGA and The R&A, Equipment Rules, 2019

cards.question: Compared with a smooth sphere of the same size and speed, what does a tennis ball's felt do to air drag?
cards.answer: Raises it. Dimples cut a golf ball's drag by making the airflow cling longer, but a tennis ball's fibres stick out into the stream, each a tiny obstacle with drag of its own. Mehta and Pallis measured drag coefficients well above a smooth sphere's. Part of what slows a tennis ball is its own coat.
cards.move: An analogy borrowed from a neighbouring case needs its own evidence.
cards.trap: Borrowing the golf-ball lesson that a rough surface always cuts drag.
cards.reference: Mehta & Pallis, The aerodynamics of a tennis ball, Sports Engineering, 2001

cards.question: Batters swear a hard, backspinning fastball rises as it reaches them. What does the ball do?
cards.answer: It drops less than gravity alone would make it. Backspin creates lift, but at any spin a pitcher can give it the lift stays below the ball's weight, so the pitch still falls, only less than the batter expects. The batter swings under a ball that never climbed.
cards.move: Something falling less than expected is easily mistaken for something rising.
cards.trap: Taking the batter's sense of a rise as a real upward climb.
cards.reference: Adair, The Physics of Baseball, 3rd edition, HarperCollins, 2002

cards.question: True or false: a dry leather football from the 1950s weighed about the same as the ball used in today's game?
cards.answer: True. The laws have set nearly the same dry weight for most of a century; today it is 410 to 450 g. The old ball earned its reputation in the rain: untreated leather soaked up water and grew markedly heavier as a wet match went on. That is the ball players remember heading.
cards.move: The worst days of anything are the ones that get remembered.
cards.trap: Remembering the heavy ball of wet days as the ball of every day.
cards.source: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 2
cards.reference: The International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 2024/25, Law 2: The Ball, 2024

cards.question: A ball reads 86 kPa above the 101 kPa outside air at 21 °C. Cooled to 10 °C, how many kPa does its reading lose?
cards.move: Scale from true zero, not from the zero a gauge shows.
cards.trap: Scaling only the 86 kPa gauge reading and getting about 3.
cards.hint: Gas pressure follows absolute temperature and total pressure, not the gauge's reading.
steps: The gas law needs total pressure: 86 + 101 = 187 kPa.
In kelvin, 21 °C is 294 K and 10 °C is 283 K.
cards.reference: Wells, Karp & Reisner, Investigative Report Concerning Footballs Used During the AFC Championship Game on January 18, 2015, NFL, 2015

cards.question: Dutch clubs that sacked their manager during a slump then improved. How did clubs with a similar slump that kept theirs do?
cards.answer: They recovered about as much. Studying the Dutch top flight from 1986 to 2004, ter Weel compared clubs that sacked their manager with clubs that hit a similar run of results and kept him. Both bounced back. A slump is partly bad luck, and luck evens out whoever sits on the bench.
cards.move: Judge a fix made at the lowest point against what would have happened anyway.
cards.trap: The new manager arrived just before the recovery, so he gets the credit.
cards.reference: ter Weel, Does Manager Turnover Improve Firm Performance? Evidence from Dutch Soccer, 1986–2004, De Economist, 2011

cards.question: True or false: an economist's analysis of NFL games found coaches go for it on fourth down too often?
cards.answer: False: too rarely. David Romer valued each option using thousands of plays and found teams punted or kicked in many situations where going for it would, on average, have won more games. A failed gamble is replayed and blamed; a timid punt is soon forgotten. Teams have grown bolder since.
cards.move: Count the cost of playing safe as carefully as the cost of risk.
cards.trap: Failed fourth-down gambles are vivid, so coaches seem reckless.
cards.reference: Romer, Do Firms Maximize? Evidence from Professional Football, Journal of Political Economy, 2006

cards.question: Who picked the England football team during Walter Winterbottom's sixteen years as its manager?
cards.answer: A committee of Football Association officials. Winterbottom, manager from 1946 to 1962, coached and advised, but a selection committee chose the players. Alf Ramsey took the job only on condition that he alone would pick the side, and four years later England won the World Cup.
cards.move: Before blaming the person in charge, check who actually made the decisions.
cards.reference: Wilson, The Anatomy of England: A History in Ten Matches, Orion, 2010

cards.question: Why can practice that makes athletes look worse in training leave them better when it counts?
cards.answer: Because mixing skills makes each one harder to settle into, and that effort sticks. In Shea and Morgan's 1979 study, people practising three movement tasks in random order were slower in practice than those drilling one at a time, yet faster when tested later. The effect is clearest in laboratory tasks.
cards.move: Practice that feels smooth is not always practice that lasts.
cards.reference: Shea & Morgan, Contextual interference effects on the acquisition, retention, and transfer of a motor skill, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 1979

cards.question: Should football clubs judge their managers on expected goals rather than on results?
cards.answer: Yes. Goals are rare, so a season's results carry a large share of luck; expected goals, which rate every shot by its chance of scoring, settle far sooner. A side that creates good chances and concedes poor ones is being coached well, and sacking its manager after bad luck only resets the work.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is how much of one season is luck.
cards.counterpoint: No. Expected-goals models rate shots as if taken by average finishers against average keepers, so they miss much of what coaching may add: sharper finishing, rehearsed set pieces, game management. Clubs are paid in points, not probabilities, and a side that keeps losing while playing well may have a flaw the model cannot see.
cards.reference: Anderson & Sally, The Numbers Game: Why Everything You Know About Football Is Wrong, Viking, 2013

cards.question: Why did the 2018 Tampa Bay Rays start some games with a relief pitcher who threw only an inning or two?
cards.answer: To blunt the cost of facing hitters repeatedly. Batters do better each time they meet the same pitcher in a game, as they read his pitches and he tires. An opener faced the dangerous top of the order once; the usual starter came in later and met those hitters fewer times. Rivals soon copied it.
cards.move: Spend a resource that weakens with use where it counts most.
cards.reference: Tango, Lichtman & Dolphin, The Book: Playing the Percentages in Baseball, Potomac Books, 2007

cards.question: Runner on first, nobody out: a sacrifice bunt moves him to second at the cost of an out. What happens to expected runs?
cards.answer: They fall, by roughly a quarter in run-expectancy tables since Lindsey's in 1963: an out is worth more than a base. Yet the chance of scoring at least one run barely moves, so late in a close game, when one run decides it, the bunt is near break-even.
cards.move: Before judging a move, ask whether the goal is many points or one.
cards.trap: Assuming a runner in scoring position must be worth the out.
cards.reference: Lindsey, An Investigation of Strategies in Baseball, Operations Research, 1963

cards.question: An ice hockey team trails by one goal. By one analysis of NHL data, when should it pull its goalie for an extra skater?
cards.answer: With about 6 minutes left. Asness and Brown weighed the extra skater's scoring chance against the risk of an empty-net goal: one down, pulling around six minutes out gave the best chance of tying. Coaches usually waited for the last minute or two. Losing by two counts the same as losing by one.
cards.move: When losing is already likely, a bigger loss costs almost nothing.
cards.trap: Treating the familiar final-minute pull as the careful, proven choice.
cards.reference: Asness & Brown, Pulling the Goalie: Hockey and Investment Implications, AQR Capital Management working paper, 2018

cards.question: True or false: among German professional footballers, those born late in the youth selection year tended to earn more than early-born ones?
cards.answer: True. Ashworth and Heyndels found that players born just before the cut-off date, the youngest in their youth age groups, later earned more. Youth coaches favour the physically older children, so the late-born who still reach the top have cleared a harder filter. Fewer of them make it; those who do are, on average, better.
cards.move: Those who got through a harder gate are often the stronger group.
cards.trap: Assuming the early-born head start must carry into adult pay.
cards.reference: Ashworth & Heyndels, Selection bias and peer effects in team sports: the effect of age grouping on earnings of German soccer players, Journal of Sports Economics, 2007

cards.question: Should a basketball coach call plays to feed the player who has just hit several shots in a row?
cards.answer: Yes. The famous finding that the hot hand is an illusion rested on a subtle error in how streaks in short sequences were counted. Miller and Sanjurjo corrected it and found a real, modest effect in the same data. A shooter in rhythm deserves the ball.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is what the effect survives once defences react.
cards.counterpoint: No. Even the corrected effect is a few percentage points. Tracking data from the NBA show that players on a streak take harder shots and draw tighter defence, which roughly cancels their improvement. Plays built for one man become predictable. The better bet is the best available shot, whoever takes it.
cards.reference: Miller & Sanjurjo, Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers, Econometrica, 2018

cards.question: What did needle biopsies of Swedish volunteers in the 1960s show about diet and endurance?
cards.answer: That stored muscle glycogen sets how long hard exercise lasts. After days on a high-carbohydrate diet, subjects cycled roughly three times as long before exhaustion as after a fat-and-protein diet, and their thigh muscles held several times more glycogen. Carbohydrate loading before endurance races grew from these experiments.
cards.move: Measure what is stored inside before arguing about willpower.
cards.source: Bergström et al., Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 1967
cards.reference: Bergström, Hermansen, Hultman & Saltin, Diet, muscle glycogen and physical performance, Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 1967

cards.question: Up to what dose does caffeine keep improving endurance performance?
cards.answer: About 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight, taken roughly an hour before: for a 70 kg athlete, 210 to 420 mg, two to four strong coffees. Higher doses add side effects, such as jitters and poor sleep, rather than speed. Caffeine has not been a banned substance since 2004.
cards.move: Find the dose where the benefit stops before buying the bigger one.
cards.reference: Guest et al., International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance, Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2021

cards.question: Earlier studies suggested muscle could use only about 20 g of protein per meal. A 2023 trial gave 100 g. What happened?
options: The extra was burnt as fuel
The excess was stored as fat
cards.answer: Muscle built more, for longer. After whole-body resistance exercise, 100 g of milk protein raised muscle protein building more than 25 g did, and kept it raised through all 12 hours measured. Earlier trials had used smaller doses and watched for only a few hours, so a slower, longer response looked like a ceiling.
cards.move: A limit found by looking briefly may only be a limit of the looking.
cards.trap: Holding to the familiar 20 g ceiling and expecting the rest wasted.
cards.source: Trommelen et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023
cards.reference: Trommelen et al., The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans, Cell Reports Medicine, 2023

cards.question: True or false: nitrate-rich beetroot juice boosts elite endurance athletes more than it boosts recreational ones?
cards.answer: False. The benefit is clearest in moderately fit people, and it shrinks or disappears in the highly trained, whose muscles already use oxygen efficiently. Many of the trials behind the headlines tested recreationally active volunteers. A shot of juice that trims a club runner's time may do nothing on an Olympic start line.
cards.move: Ask who was tested before assuming a result applies to you.
cards.trap: Assuming whatever elite athletes drink must work best for elite athletes.
cards.source: Porcelli et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2015
cards.reference: Porcelli et al., Aerobic fitness affects the exercise performance responses to nitrate supplementation, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2015

cards.question: Should sports scrap lightweight categories because of what athletes do to their diets to make weight?
cards.answer: Weight limits reward starving and dehydrating the body before each weigh-in, and years of low energy intake bring hormone disruption and weak bones. Sports medicine now names this relative energy deficiency. Lightweight rowing has been dropped from the Olympic programme after Paris 2024, and rapid weight cutting persists wherever categories remain.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether weigh-in rules can stop the dieting decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Without categories, sports like rowing and boxing belong to the tall and heavy, and smaller athletes lose their place. The harm comes from how weight is policed, not from the categories themselves: weigh-ins closer to competition, hydration tests and minimum body-fat checks can curb crash dieting while keeping the sport open.
cards.source: Mountjoy et al., IOC consensus on RED-S, 2018
cards.reference: Mountjoy et al., IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): 2018 update, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

cards.question: Elite race walkers on a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet burned fat far faster than before. How did their race times change?
options: Improved about as much as others
Did not improve, unlike the others
cards.answer: Did not improve, unlike the others. In Burke's three-week study, fat adaptation raised fat burning to exceptionally high rates, but walking at race pace then cost more oxygen. Walkers eating plenty of carbohydrate cut roughly 5 to 7% from their 10 km times; the fat-adapted group gained nothing.
cards.move: A better number inside the machine is not a faster machine.
cards.trap: Taking record fat burning as proof of better endurance.
cards.source: Burke et al., Journal of Physiology, 2017
cards.reference: Burke et al., Low carbohydrate, high fat diet impairs exercise economy and negates the performance benefit from intensified training in elite race walkers, Journal of Physiology, 2017

cards.question: Why can rinsing a sports drink round the mouth and spitting it out improve a one-hour time trial?
cards.answer: Because the mouth reports carbohydrate to the brain. Carter, Jeukendrup and Jones found cyclists rode a one-hour time trial almost 3% faster after rinsing with a carbohydrate solution than with a placebo, though none was swallowed. Brain scans later showed such rinses light up reward areas: the legs work harder when the brain expects fuel.
cards.move: Some signals change behaviour before the thing they announce arrives.
cards.source: Carter et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2004
cards.reference: Carter, Jeukendrup & Jones, The effect of carbohydrate mouth rinse on 1-h cycle time trial performance, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2004

cards.question: True or false: cyclists given only dummy capsules produced more power the higher the caffeine dose they were told they had taken?
cards.answer: True. Beedie and colleagues gave trained cyclists placebo capsules before 10 km time trials. Told they had taken none, they produced 1.4% less power than baseline; told 4.5 mg per kg, 1.3% more; told 9 mg per kg, 3.1% more. Belief alone traced a dose-response curve, from an empty capsule.
cards.move: Without a dummy version to compare against, a result also measures hope.
cards.trap: Assuming a capsule with nothing in it can do nothing.
cards.source: Beedie et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2006
cards.reference: Beedie, Stuart, Coleman & Foad, Placebo effects of caffeine on cycling performance, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2006

cards.question: In thousands of kilocalories, about how much energy does a Tour de France rider use on an average racing day?
cards.answer: 4,500 + 1,500 = about 6 thousand kcal.
cards.move: Turn effort into watts and hours, and the calories follow.
cards.trap: Starting from a normal 2,500 kcal day and merely doubling it.
cards.hint: Start from the power a rider holds and the hours in the saddle.
steps: Riding: 250 watts x 5 hours x 3,600 s = 4,500 kJ of work.
Muscles turn about a quarter of food energy into work, so 1 kJ of work costs about 1 kcal: 4,500 kcal.
The other 19 hours, resting and digesting: about 1,500 kcal.
4,500 + 1,500 = about 6 thousand kcal.
cards.source: Saris et al., Int J Sports Med, 1989
cards.reference: Saris et al., Study on food intake and energy expenditure during extreme sustained exercise: the Tour de France, International Journal of Sports Medicine, 1989

cards.question: Why do endurance sports drinks mix glucose with fructose instead of simply adding more glucose?
cards.answer: Because the gut absorbs them through different doors. The transporter that carries glucose across the intestine saturates at about 60 g an hour; fructose uses a separate one. Mixing the two lets athletes absorb and burn roughly 90 g of carbohydrate an hour, where extra glucose alone would sit in the gut and cause distress.
cards.move: When one route is full, look for a second route, not a bigger load.
cards.source: Jeukendrup, Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care, 2010
cards.reference: Jeukendrup, Carbohydrate and exercise performance: the role of multiple transportable carbohydrates, Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care, 2010

cards.question: How did England line up for the first official international football match, against Scotland in 1872?
cards.answer: With seven or eight forwards. England played roughly one back, one or two half-backs and the rest in attack, dribbling in packs; Scotland used two backs, two half-backs and six forwards, and passed more. The match, at Partick in Glasgow, ended 0–0. Defending was a job for a few stragglers.
cards.move: Before judging an old method, ask what problem its users thought they had.
cards.reference: Goldblatt, The Ball Is Round: A Global History of Football, Viking, 2006

cards.question: Why did English teams in the late 1920s start playing three defenders at the back instead of two?
cards.answer: Because a new offside law flooded the game with goals. From 1925 an attacker needed only two opponents, not three, between himself and the goal line. Herbert Chapman at Arsenal pulled his centre-half back between the full-backs, turning the old 2-3-5 into the W-M shape that ruled English football for decades.
cards.move: Change one rule and watch every shape built around it rearrange.
cards.reference: Studd, Herbert Chapman, Football Emperor: A Study in the Origins of Modern Soccer, Peter Owen, 1981

cards.question: In Hungary's 6–3 win at Wembley in 1953, how did centre-forward Nándor Hidegkuti confuse England's defence?
cards.answer: By not staying up front. Wearing the number 9, he dropped into midfield, and England's centre-half, Harry Johnston, drilled to mark the centre-forward, could neither follow him nor leave him free. Hidegkuti scored a hat-trick. It was England's first home defeat by a side from outside the British Isles.
cards.move: A system built to mark a position fails when the player leaves it.
cards.reference: Wilson, Inverting the Pyramid: The History of Football Tactics, Orion, 2008

cards.question: Where was the sweeper-based defensive system later called catenaccio first developed?
cards.answer: In Switzerland. In the 1930s the Austrian coach Karl Rappan, working with Swiss clubs and the national team, built the verrou, the bolt: an extra defender behind the back line. Italian clubs such as Nereo Rocco's Triestina and Helenio Herrera's Inter later made it famous and gave it an Italian name meaning door-bolt.
cards.move: A method is usually named after whoever made it famous, not whoever made it.
cards.trap: The name is Italian, and Italy's famous defences come to mind first.
cards.reference: Wilson, Inverting the Pyramid: The History of Football Tactics, Orion, 2008

cards.question: True or false: England won the 1966 World Cup final without fielding a single out-and-out winger?
cards.answer: True. Alf Ramsey tried three different wingers in the group games, then dropped them all for a narrow midfield of four, with Alan Ball covering the right flank. The side was nicknamed the Wingless Wonders. Its shape, four defenders, four midfielders and two strikers, became the 4-4-2 English football leaned on for decades.
cards.move: Judge a formation by the players available, not by the fashion of the day.
cards.trap: Picturing 1960s football with wingers hugging both touchlines.
cards.reference: McKinstry, Sir Alf: A Major Reappraisal of the Life and Times of England's Greatest Football Manager, HarperSport, 2006

cards.question: What did the Chicago Bears' 73–0 win in the 1940 NFL Championship game do to American football formations?
cards.answer: It made the T-formation standard. The Bears set their quarterback directly behind the centre and sent a back running sideways before the snap, a man in motion, hiding where the play would go. Washington had beaten them weeks earlier. Within about a decade almost every professional and college team ran some version of the T.
cards.move: One lopsided result can convert a field faster than years of argument.
cards.reference: Peterson, Pigskin: The Early Years of Pro Football, Oxford University Press, 1997

cards.question: Bodyline relied on a packed leg-side field. How many fielders, besides the wicket-keeper, may now stand behind the batter's crease on that side?
cards.answer: No more than two. Bodyline ringed the leg side with catchers while fast bowlers aimed at the batter's body, so any fend-off lobbed to a fielder. A law of 1957 allows at most two fielders, besides the wicket-keeper, behind the batter's crease on that side. Short bowling survived; the net waiting for it did not.
cards.move: To stop a tactic, remove the piece that makes it pay.
cards.trap: Guessing none at all, as if the whole leg-side ring were banned.
cards.reference: Marylebone Cricket Club, The Laws of Cricket, 2017 Code, Law 28.4, 2017

cards.question: True or false: until 2001, the NBA's rules forbade teams from playing a zone defence?
cards.answer: True. For most of the league's history, illegal-defence rules made each defender guard a man rather than an area, which left stars free to beat one opponent at a time. In 2001 the NBA allowed zones but added defensive three seconds: no defender may wait in the lane that long without closely guarding someone.
cards.move: Look for the rule behind a style that everyone calls natural.
cards.trap: Assuming the pro game always allowed what schools and colleges played.
cards.reference: National Basketball Association, Official Rules of the National Basketball Association 2001–02, 2001

cards.question: Leicester City won the 2015–16 Premier League with a counter-attacking 4-4-2. Roughly what was its average share of possession?
cards.answer: About 42%, among the lowest in the league. Leicester conceded the ball, defended in two compact banks of four and broke fast into the space behind. Possession follows quality, and teams that are losing tend to hold more of it, so it says little about who wins. The champions spent the season watching others pass.
cards.move: Ask what else raises a number before treating it as the goal.
cards.trap: Treating possession as the cause of winning rather than its companion.
cards.reference: Cox, The Mixer: The Story of Premier League Tactics, from Route One to False Nines, HarperCollins, 2017

cards.question: Is a team's listed formation, such as 4-3-3, still a useful description of how it plays?
cards.answer: Yes. The starting shape decides who covers which space when the ball is lost, and that is when most goals are conceded. Coaches still pick players for the slots, and switching from four at the back to three changes every duel on the pitch. A line of numbers compresses a lot of real structure.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is which phase of play you describe.
cards.counterpoint: No. Modern teams change shape with the ball: a side listed as 4-3-3 may attack as 3-2-5 and defend as 4-4-2, with full-backs stepping into midfield. Tracking data shows players drifting constantly. A single line of numbers describes the kick-off picture and little of the ninety minutes after it.
cards.reference: Cox, Zonal Marking: The Making of Modern European Football, HarperCollins, 2019

cards.question: Why did football stop sending off every defender who fouls to deny a goal inside his own box?
cards.answer: Because the team was punished three times: a foul that denied an obvious goal-scoring chance in the box brought a penalty, a red card and a suspension. Since 2016, a defender who genuinely tries to play the ball gets a yellow instead; holding or pushing with no attempt at the ball is still a red.
cards.move: When one act draws several penalties, check whether they punish the same harm twice.
cards.reference: https://www.skysports.com/football/news/12010/10308834/euro-2016-triple-punishment-kick-offs-penalties-new-ifab-football-laws-on-show-in-france

cards.question: What happened when experienced referees judged the same recorded tackles with and without crowd noise?
cards.answer: With the crowd audible, they gave 15.5% fewer fouls against the home side. Qualified referees watched the same video of Premier League challenges; the only difference between the two groups was the soundtrack. The home fans' roar at a tackle was being heard as evidence of how hard it was.
cards.move: Ask what the judge heard, not only what the judge saw.
cards.reference: Nevill, Balmer & Williams, The influence of crowd noise and experience upon refereeing decisions in football, Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2002

cards.question: When German league matches were played without fans in 2020, what happened to visitors' disadvantage in yellow cards?
cards.answer: It shrank. With crowds, referees in the top two divisions had booked visitors more often than hosts for similar play. In empty stadiums that gap narrowed, most of all where away fans had been scarce. Analyses differ on whether hosts were booked more or visitors less, but the tilt had come from the stands.
cards.move: Take the audience away and watch which decisions change.
cards.trap: Assuming referees book only what they see, so nothing would change.
cards.reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165176520303815

cards.question: True or false: in rugby union, foul play that stops a probable try now earns seven points without a kick?
cards.answer: True. Since 2017 a penalty try counts seven points automatically, with no conversion taken. Before, it was five points plus a kick from in front of the posts that was almost never missed. Making it automatic saved the time and removed any hope that the kick might fail.
cards.move: A rule is only as strong as the cheapest way round it.
cards.trap: Picturing the usual five-plus-two sequence and expecting a conversion to follow.
cards.reference: https://rugby365.com/laws-referees/news/laws-on-trial-become-law/

cards.question: Should elite football send players to a sin bin for ten minutes for tactical fouls?
sides: No, keep cards as they are
cards.answer: A yellow card for a cynical foul that kills a counter-attack costs almost nothing, so the foul pays. Ten minutes a player down costs something now, in the match where the foul was committed. The FA's grassroots trials reported dissent falling by about 38%, and rugby union has used sin bins for over twenty years.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how reliably referees can tell a tactical foul decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Football is low-scoring, so ten minutes a player down can decide a match, and whether a foul was tactical is a judgement referees already find hard. More discretion means more controversy and more delay. Grassroots dissent is not elite tactical fouling, and the planned professional trial was postponed in 2024 amid opposition.
cards.source: NBC News, IFAB sin bin trial, 2023
cards.reference: https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/soccer-sin-bin-trial-okd-opening-door-major-rule-change-rcna127051

cards.question: An NBA possession averages about 1.1 points. Fouling a 45% free-throw shooter sends him to the line twice. How many points does each foul save?
cards.answer: Saving: 1.1 - 0.9 = 0.2 points per trip.
cards.move: Price a deliberate sacrifice against the ordinary outcome it replaces.
cards.trap: Reading 45% as nearly nothing and expecting a huge saving.
cards.hint: Work out what two free throws are worth on average first.
steps: One free throw is worth 1 x 0.45 = 0.45 points on average.
Two free throws: 2 x 0.45 = 0.9 points.
Saving: 1.1 - 0.9 = 0.2 points per trip.
cards.reference: Oliver, Basketball on Paper: Rules and Tools for Performance Analysis, Potomac Books, 2004

cards.question: Why did football's lawmakers retreat, after two seasons, from disallowing every goal that followed an accidental attacking handball?
cards.answer: Because it punished bad luck. From 2019 any accidental touch on an attacker's arm just before a goal wiped the goal out, even when the ball had struck a team-mate's arm in the build-up. From 2021 only the scorer's own accidental handling, immediately before scoring, cancels the goal; a team-mate's no longer does.
cards.move: A rule written to remove all doubt often removes the innocent too.
cards.reference: International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 2021/22, Law 12 Fouls and Misconduct, Handling the ball

cards.question: True or false: a defender who drags back a striker through on goal escapes every card if the referee plays on and the striker scores?
cards.answer: True. Denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity normally costs a red card. But if the referee plays advantage and the goal is scored anyway, the Law imposes no disciplinary sanction: the foul ended up denying nothing. If advantage is played and no goal follows, the defender is booked when the ball next goes out.
cards.move: Ask whether a penalty punishes the act or the harm it did.
cards.trap: Assuming the punishment is fixed the moment the foul is committed.
cards.source: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 12
cards.reference: https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/fouls-and-misconduct/

cards.question: Since 2022, what does the NBA award when a defender fouls on purpose to stop a fast break?
options: Two free throws and the ball
One free throw and the ball
Only the ball, as for most fouls
cards.answer: One free throw and the ball. A foul that killed a fast break used to cost only an inbound pass, cheap against a likely dunk. Since the 2022–23 season the attacking side also shoots one free throw, taken by any player on the court, so its best shooter steps up and it keeps possession.
cards.move: Make the price of a shortcut exceed what the shortcut buys.
cards.trap: Assuming the league still prices a tactical foul like any other.
cards.reference: National Basketball Association, Official Playing Rules 2022-23 season, transition take foul

cards.question: In NHL games, once one team has been called for a penalty, which team is more likely to be called for the next?
cards.answer: The other team. Studying several NHL seasons, Abrevaya and McCulloch found the next penalty went to the opposite side far more often than chance would give, even after allowing for score, time and home ice. The side with fewer penalties so far tends to receive the next: the referees are keeping a running tally.
cards.move: Judges who keep count of their own calls are not judging each call alone.
cards.trap: Treating each call as judged on its merits, apart from the last.
cards.reference: Abrevaya & McCulloch, Reversal of fortune: a statistical analysis of penalty calls in the National Hockey League, Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports, 2014

cards.question: Measured against the budget promised when they won the bid, by how much have Olympic Games overrun on average?
cards.answer: About 170%, in real terms. Flyvbjerg, Budzier and Lunn found that every Games since 1960 with usable data overran, by 172% on average, the worst record of any kind of megaproject they studied. A fixed opening date and no way to shrink the event leave cost as the only thing that can give.
cards.move: A deadline that cannot move turns every problem into a cost.
cards.trap: Starting from the bid budget, a fifth over already sounds like a scandal.
cards.reference: Flyvbjerg, Budzier & Lunn, Regression to the Tail: Why the Olympics Blow Up, Environment and Planning A: Economy and Space, 2021

cards.question: How long did it take Quebec to pay off the debt from Montreal's 1976 Olympics?
cards.answer: About thirty years: the last of it was cleared in November 2006. The stadium, nicknamed the Big Owe, got its retractable roof only in 1987, and it never worked well. A special tobacco tax helped pay. A Games lasting about two weeks was still being paid for by smokers born after it.
cards.move: Ask who pays for a party after the guests have gone home.
cards.reference: https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-s-big-owe-stadium-debt-is-over-1.602530

cards.question: True or false: by the time the IOC voted on the 2022 Winter Games, only two cities were left in the race?
cards.answer: True. Stockholm, Kraków, Lviv and Oslo withdrew, some after public votes or lost government backing, leaving Beijing and Almaty; Beijing won by 44 votes to 40 in 2015. The IOC later changed method, picking hosts through private talks rather than open races, as it did with Brisbane for 2032.
cards.move: When the bidders thin out, the seller has to change its terms.
cards.trap: The Games look like a prize that cities queue up to win.
cards.reference: International Olympic Committee, Report of the 2022 Evaluation Commission, 2015

cards.question: Why could Los Angeles dictate its own terms for hosting the 1984 Summer Olympics?
cards.answer: Because it was the only city bidding. After Montreal's debts, Tehran had pulled out, and the IOC had to accept a privately run Games with no city money at risk. Organisers reused the 1932 Coliseum, sold sponsorships and made a surplus of over $200 million, part of which still funds youth sport in Los Angeles.
cards.move: The side with no competitors writes the contract.
cards.reference: Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee, Official Report of the Games of the XXIIIrd Olympiad Los Angeles 1984, 1985

cards.question: Should the Summer Olympics move to one permanent host site instead of rotating between cities?
cards.answer: Yes. Venues built once would be used every four years instead of left to decay, as many from Athens 2004 were. The overruns that come with each new host would end, and so would bidding contests that invited bribery. A site under long-term international management could run the Games as routine rather than emergency.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is who would govern a permanent site.
cards.counterpoint: No. Rotation spreads the Games' attention and benefits across continents; a single host would hand one government a permanent political prize and a say over who may come. Its climate, time zone and travel costs would favour some nations forever. Paris and Los Angeles show rotating Games can lean on venues that already exist.
cards.reference: Zimbalist, Circus Maximus: The Economic Gamble Behind Hosting the Olympics and the World Cup, Brookings Institution Press, 2015

cards.question: Why were the 1976 Winter Olympics, awarded to Denver, held in Innsbruck instead?
cards.answer: Because Colorado's voters refused to pay. Denver won the Games in 1970, but costs climbed and venues drifted far from the city; in November 1972 a statewide ballot barred public money for them, with about 60% voting yes. Denver handed the Games back, and Innsbruck, host in 1964, stepped in with venues already built.
cards.move: A promise made by officials is only as firm as the voters behind it.
cards.reference: Guttmann, The Olympics: A History of the Modern Games, University of Illinois Press, 2002

cards.question: Which ordinary words could land a London business in legal trouble if paired in its adverts around 2012?
cards.answer: Words like Games, 2012, gold and summer. The London Olympic Games and Paralympic Games Act 2006 gave organisers a right against any advert suggesting a link with the Games, and listed pairings a court could take as evidence, such as Games with 2012, or 2012 with gold or summer. Sponsors had paid for the silence.
cards.move: What a sponsor buys is often the right to stop others speaking.
cards.reference: London Olympic Games and Paralympic Games Act 2006, Schedule 4, UK Parliament, 2006

cards.question: In August 2012, the month of the London Olympics, how did overseas visits to the UK compare with August 2011?
cards.answer: About 5% lower, by the Office for National Statistics' count. Olympic visitors came, but ordinary tourists and business travellers stayed away from the expected crowds, closures and prices. Those who did come spent more per head. The Games filled London's hotels partly with people who had replaced someone else.
cards.move: An event's crowd is net of the crowd it scares away.
cards.trap: Counting the Olympic visitors without asking who stayed away because of them.
cards.reference: Office for National Statistics, Overseas Travel and Tourism, Monthly Release, October 2012

cards.question: Several cities submit honest but uncertain cost forecasts, and the cheapest-looking bid wins. How will the winner's forecast compare with its real cost?
cards.answer: Too low, on average. Each honest forecast errs both ways, but picking the lowest selects the one whose errors ran furthest in its favour. This is the winner's curse, first described in auctions for oil leases; Andreff applied it to sporting mega-events. Selection alone builds an overrun into the winning bid before anyone lies.
cards.move: The pick of many noisy guesses is usually the luckiest error.
cards.trap: Assuming honest errors cancel out, so the winning bid is unbiased.
cards.source: Andreff, Handbook on Mega Sporting Events, 2012
cards.reference: Andreff, The winner's curse: why is the cost of sports mega-events so often underestimated?, in Maennig & Zimbalist (eds), International Handbook on the Economics of Mega Sporting Events, Edward Elgar, 2012

cards.question: True or false: Great Britain won more Olympic medals at Rio in 2016 than at its home Games in London?
cards.answer: True: 67 in Rio against 65 in London, a rare rise for a nation just after hosting. Much of the London haul came from National Lottery money aimed at sports likely to win medals, and that funding kept rising after 2012. The home crowd went away; the money stayed.
cards.move: Before crediting the obvious cause, watch what happens when it leaves.
