cards.trap: Crediting home crowds for the London haul and expecting a fall.
cards.reference: International Olympic Committee, Official Results Book, Rio 2016 Olympic Games, 2016

cards.question: True or false: the fastest marathon ever run as of April 2011, at Boston, could not count as a world record?
cards.answer: True. Geoffrey Mutai ran 2:03:02, under the record, but the course was ineligible. Record courses may drop no more than 1 m per km overall, and start and finish may be no further apart than half the distance. Boston runs point to point and loses about 140 m, and that day the wind was behind.
cards.move: Before crediting the performer, check what the setting added.
cards.trap: Assuming the fastest time ever run must be the record.
cards.source: World Athletics, Competition and Technical Rules
cards.reference: World Athletics, Competition and Technical Rules, Book C, 2023 edition

cards.question: Kelvin Kiptum ran the 2023 Chicago Marathon in 2:00:35. On average, how many seconds did each 100 m take?
cards.answer: 7,235 / 421.95 = about 17.1 seconds.
cards.move: Shrink a long effort to one small unit before judging how hard it is.
cards.trap: Picturing a jog because the event lasts two hours.
cards.hint: Turn the time into seconds and the distance into 100 m stretches.
steps: 42.195 km is 421.95 stretches of 100 m.
7,235 / 421.95 = about 17.1 seconds.
cards.reference: World Athletics, official world records list, men's marathon, Kiptum 2:00:35, ratified 2024

cards.question: What physically runs out when a marathon runner hits the wall around 30 km?
cards.answer: Stored carbohydrate. Muscles and liver hold glycogen worth roughly 2,000 kcal, while running costs about 1 kcal per kg per km: close to 3,000 kcal over the distance for a 70 kg runner. Fat can cover the gap, but it releases energy more slowly, so the pace sags when glycogen is spent.
cards.move: Find which store empties first; that sets the limit, not the average.

diagram.caption: At about 70 kcal a km, the 2,000 kcal of glycogen runs out near 29 km.

cards.reference: Rapoport, Metabolic factors limiting performance in marathon runners, PLoS Computational Biology, 2010

cards.question: Why did athletics have no official marathon world record until 2004?
cards.answer: Because no two courses are alike. Hills, bends and weather differ from city to city, so fast times were listed only as world bests. From 1 January 2004 records were ratified, but only on courses measured with a calibrated bicycle, plus one extra metre per kilometre so that no approved course can turn out short.
cards.move: A ranking means little until everyone has faced the same test.
cards.source: IAAF/AIMS, The Measurement of Road Race Courses
cards.reference: IAAF & AIMS, The Measurement of Road Race Courses, 2nd edition, 2004

cards.question: Should a women's marathon record set behind male pacemakers count as the women's world record?
cards.answer: Pacemakers are legal in every big-city marathon, and men pacing women are simply the pacers available at that speed. The runner still covers every metre on her own legs. Paula Radcliffe's 2:15:25 of 2003 was run within the rules of its day, and splitting records by who ran alongside invites endless reclassification.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how much pace-setters really help is what decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Running in a pack saves energy by cutting air resistance; a woman surrounded by faster men gets more shelter and pacing than any woman in a women-only race can. Drafting studies put the energy saved at a few per cent, and at this level a few per cent is minutes. Hence a separate women-only record.
cards.reference: Hoogkamer, Kram & Arellano, How biomechanical improvements in running economy could break the 2-hour marathon barrier, Sports Medicine, 2017

cards.question: Of the nine men's marathon world records set between 2003 and 2023, how many were run in Berlin?
cards.answer: Eight. Every record from Paul Tergat's 2:04:55 in 2003 to Eliud Kipchoge's 2:01:09 in 2022 was set in Berlin; only a Chicago run in 2023 broke the sequence. The course is flat with few sharp turns, late September is usually cool, and the organisers build the elite field and pacing around record attempts.
cards.move: When results cluster in one place, ask what that place selects for.
cards.trap: Three: picturing records shared among London, Chicago and New York.
cards.source: World Athletics, men's marathon record progression
cards.reference: World Athletics, Records by event: men's marathon world record progression, 2024

cards.question: In 1991, with the record at 2:06:50, a physiologist put the best measured aerobic capacity, endurance and economy into one runner. His limit?
cards.answer: About 1:58, far under it. Michael Joyner combined the highest oxygen uptake, the largest share of it sustainable for hours and the thriftiest stride then measured, and got 1:57:58. Each trait existed in someone; no one runner had all three. In 2019 Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna, with rotating pacers, unratified.
cards.move: A limit built from everyone's best parts describes nobody yet.
cards.trap: Anchoring on 2:06:50 and allowing the limit only a small margin.
cards.reference: Joyner, Modeling: optimal marathon performance on the basis of physiological factors, Journal of Applied Physiology, 1991

cards.question: True or false: among 643 finishers of a French marathon, those who had lost the most body weight tended to finish fastest?
cards.answer: True. Zouhal and colleagues weighed runners before and after the race: the more weight a runner had lost, the faster they had tended to finish, though the link was loose. Faster runners sweat more and spend less time drinking. The weight loss was a mark of the effort, and it did not cause the speed.
cards.move: A cost that rises with effort will look like a cause of success.
cards.trap: Knowing dehydration slows runners and assuming the thirstiest finish last.
cards.source: Zouhal et al., Br J Sports Med, 2011
cards.reference: Zouhal et al., Inverse relationship between percentage body weight change and finishing time in 643 forty-two-kilometre marathon runners, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2011

cards.question: Why does a warm day slow the back of a marathon field more than the runners at the front?
cards.answer: Partly because slower runners are out in the heat longer. Analysing years of results from several big-city marathons, Ely and colleagues found times rose steadily as heat stress increased, and the slowdown grew down the field: smallest for the leaders, largest for the slowest. Two hours of warm air is a smaller dose than five.
cards.move: Measure exposure in hours, not just in degrees.
cards.source: Ely et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2007
cards.reference: Ely, Cheuvront, Roberts & Montain, Impact of weather on marathon-running performance, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2007

cards.question: Across millions of marathon results, how does the number of finishers change just either side of four hours?
options: A spike just over four hours
A spike just under four hours
cards.answer: A spike just under four hours. Allen, Dechow, Pope and Wu studied nearly 10 million finishing times and found runners bunched just below round numbers, most sharply at 4:00: far more finish at 3:59 than at 4:01. The target is arbitrary, yet runners find extra speed in the final kilometres to beat it.
cards.move: Expect people to bend their effort towards round numbers.
cards.trap: Expecting millions of runners to smooth away any single number.
cards.reference: Allen, Dechow, Pope & Wu, Reference-dependent preferences: evidence from marathon runners, Management Science, 2017

cards.question: Jim Thorpe's 1912 Olympic titles were restored in 1982. Why did the IOC rule on his case again in 2022?
cards.answer: Because 1982 made him only a co-champion. Stripped in 1913 for having been paid to play minor-league baseball, he was reinstated alongside the athletes promoted into his places. In July 2022 the IOC listed him as the sole winner of the pentathlon and decathlon, 69 years after his death.
cards.move: A correction can leave half the original wrong standing beside it.
cards.reference: International Olympic Committee, Jim Thorpe to be displayed as sole Olympic champion of 1912 pentathlon and decathlon, press release, 15 July 2022

cards.question: After a horse-riding scandal at Tokyo 2021, what replaces riding in modern pentathlon from Los Angeles 2028?
cards.answer: An obstacle course. Pentathletes rode horses they had never met, drawn by lot, and at Tokyo a horse refused to jump for the leader, Annika Schleu, while her coach was filmed punching it. The event, built in 1912 on a cavalry officer's skills, dropped the horse for walls, rings and ropes.
cards.move: When a tradition's defining piece becomes indefensible, the name survives the piece.
cards.trap: Cycling fits a multi-sport event, so it seems the natural swap.
cards.reference: Union Internationale de Pentathlon Moderne, Obstacle discipline confirmed for the Olympic Games Los Angeles 2028, 2023

cards.question: True or false: the US-led boycott of Moscow in 1980 was the first time several nations boycotted an Olympics?
cards.answer: False. In 1956 several nations stayed away from Melbourne over the Suez crisis and the Soviet invasion of Hungary. In 1976 more than 20 countries, most of them African, left Montreal because the IOC would not ban New Zealand, whose rugby team had just toured apartheid South Africa.
cards.move: The best-remembered case of something is rarely the first one.
cards.trap: Moscow 1980 is the boycott everyone remembers, so it feels like the first.
cards.reference: Guttmann, The Olympics: A History of the Modern Games, University of Illinois Press, 2002

cards.question: A Paris 2024 gold medal's 6 g of gold, about 0.3 cm³, covers roughly 120 cm². How thick is it, in micrometres?
cards.answer: 0.025 mm = 25 micrometres.
cards.move: Check whether a name describes the surface or the substance.
cards.trap: Picturing gilding as a film far too thin to measure.
cards.hint: Divide the volume of gold by the area it covers, then convert the units.
steps: 0.025 mm = 25 micrometres.
cards.reference: https://www.oxfordeconomics.com/resource/economists-notebook-how-much-is-a-paris-olympic-gold-medal-worth/

cards.question: What medal did a winner at the first modern Olympics, Athens in 1896, receive?
cards.answer: A silver one. Winners at Athens took a silver medal and an olive branch; runners-up received a copper medal and a laurel branch, and third places got nothing at the time. The order of gold, silver and bronze first appeared at St Louis in 1904.
cards.move: Customs that feel ancient are often younger than the institution they decorate.
cards.reference: Mallon & Widlund, The 1896 Olympic Games: Results for All Competitors in All Events, McFarland, 1998

cards.question: How did Wyndham Halswelle come to win the 1908 Olympic 400 m final running entirely alone?
cards.answer: By walkover, after a row over whose rules applied. British judges ruled that the American John Carpenter had blocked Halswelle, which American rules allowed and British ones did not, and ordered a rerun without him. The other two finalists, both American, refused to start. Halswelle ran the rerun alone, and gave up racing soon after.
cards.move: Agree whose rules apply before the contest, not after it.
cards.reference: Cook, The Fourth Olympiad: Being the Official Report of the Olympic Games of 1908, British Olympic Association, 1908

cards.question: Why did the Olympics stop awarding medals for painting, music and literature after 1948?
cards.answer: Because the artists were professionals. Art contests ran from 1912 to 1948, but Olympic rules then barred anyone who earned a living from their event, and painters, composers and writers lived by selling their work. The IOC swapped the contests for exhibitions without medals. The art medals no longer appear in national medal totals.
cards.move: A rule written for one kind of competitor can shut out another by accident.
cards.source: Stanton, The Forgotten Olympic Art Competitions
cards.reference: Stanton, The Forgotten Olympic Art Competitions, Trafford, 2000

cards.question: The first athlete disqualified from an Olympics for doping, at Mexico City in 1968, was caught with what?
cards.answer: Alcohol. Hans-Gunnar Liljenwall, a Swedish modern pentathlete, reportedly drank beer to steady his hand before the shooting; his test was over the limit and Sweden lost its team bronze. 1968 brought the first Olympic drug tests, and steroids were not screened for until Montreal in 1976.
cards.move: What a test can detect decides what gets caught first.
cards.trap: Picturing the steroid scandals that later came to define doping.
cards.source: Wallechinsky & Loucky, Complete Book of the Olympics
cards.reference: Wallechinsky & Loucky, The Complete Book of the Olympics, Aurum Press, 2012

cards.question: The United States topped the medal table at St Louis in 1904. Roughly what share of all competitors were American?
cards.answer: About four in five. Few Europeans made the long, costly trip to Missouri, so most events were contests among Americans, and several were national championships in all but name. The host's huge medal haul measured the entry list more than the athletes. A table ranks only those who turned up.
cards.move: Before praising a winner, ask who else was able to enter.
cards.trap: Assuming an Olympic field was international, as today's fields are.
cards.reference: Mallon, The 1904 Olympic Games: Results for All Competitors in All Events, McFarland, 1999

cards.question: True or false: Paris 2024, officially the Games of the XXXIII Olympiad, was only the 30th officially recognised Summer Games held?
cards.answer: True. An Olympiad is a four-year period, and it keeps its number whether or not Games take place. The Games of 1916, 1940 and 1944 were cancelled by war, yet the VI, XII and XIII Olympiads still count. Take those three away from 33 and Paris was the 30th Summer Games held.
cards.move: Check whether a number counts the events or the slots they could fill.
cards.trap: Taking the Roman numeral as a count of Games actually held.
cards.reference: International Olympic Committee, Olympic Charter, 2023

cards.question: Under the Football Association's first laws of 1863, when was a player offside?
cards.answer: Whenever he was ahead of the ball. As in rugby, a player in front of the ball could not take part in play, so passing forward to a team-mate was impossible and teams advanced by dribbling in packs. In 1866 the rule was relaxed: three opponents between attacker and goal made him onside.
cards.move: Look at what a rule forbids to see which game its makers had in mind.
cards.source: Harvey, Football: The First Hundred Years, 2005
cards.reference: Harvey, Football: The First Hundred Years: The Untold Story, Routledge, 2005

cards.question: True or false: a striker's outstretched arm beyond the last defender can make him offside?
cards.answer: False. For offside the hands and arms of every player, goalkeepers included, are ignored, and the law puts the top of the arm at the bottom of the armpit. A shoulder, a knee or a toe can be offside; a fingertip cannot, since a player may not legally score with it.
cards.move: Before judging whether a line was crossed, ask which parts are allowed to count.
cards.trap: Assuming any part of the body past the line counts.
cards.source: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 11
cards.reference: https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/offside/

cards.question: When assistant referees got offside wrong at the 2002 World Cup, which mistake was most common?
cards.answer: Flagging attackers who were onside. About 26% of offside situations were judged wrongly, and most errors were raised flags. A forward in motion is seen slightly ahead of where he really is when the pass is struck, so level looks beyond. The attack that was wrongly stopped leaves nothing to replay.
cards.move: The mistakes that end the story are the ones nobody sees on the replay.
cards.trap: Recalling goals given from offside, which are replayed endlessly.
cards.source: Helsen et al., Journal of Sports Sciences, 2006
cards.reference: Helsen, Gilis & Weston, Errors in judging offside in association football: test of the optical error versus the perceptual flash-lag hypothesis, Journal of Sports Sciences, 2006

cards.question: Why can an assistant referee with perfect eyesight still misjudge offside from where he stands?
cards.answer: Geometry. Unless the assistant is exactly level with the second-last defender, the offside line is seen at a slant, so players on the far side of the pitch appear shifted towards or away from goal. A study of 200 real decisions found 40 wrong, in the directions the viewing angle predicted.
cards.move: Before trusting a judgement of level, check where the judge was standing.

cards.question: Offside cameras locate players 50 times a second. At 10 m/s of relative speed, how many centimetres can the gap change between two samples?
cards.move: A measurement is only as fine as the gap between its samples.
cards.trap: Treating a line drawn on one frame as the exact moment.
cards.hint: Work out how far the players move in one fiftieth of a second.
steps: 10 m/s is 1,000 cm every second.
One sample lasts 1/50 of a second.
cards.reference: https://inside.fifa.com/innovation/world-cup-2022/semi-automated-offside-technology

cards.question: An attacker in an offside position collects the rebound from a defender's goal-line block. What does the referee give?
options: Offside: the block counts as a save
Play on: a deliberate touch resets it
Play on: offside is judged at the rebound
cards.answer: Offside. A deliberate play by a defender normally frees an attacker who was in an offside position, but the Law makes one exception: a save, meaning any attempt to stop a ball going into or very close to the goal. A block on the line is a save, so the attacker is still penalised.
cards.move: Learn the exception before leaning on the rule it breaks.
cards.trap: Knowing that a defender's deliberate touch normally wipes out offside.
cards.source: The FA, Laws of the Game, Law 11
cards.reference: https://www.thefa.com/football-rules-governance/lawsandrules/laws/football-11-11/law-11---offside

cards.question: Until 1990, what happened to an attacker standing exactly level with the second-last defender?
cards.answer: He was offside. The Law treated level as ahead until 1990, when the International Football Association Board, which writes the Laws, made level onside. The change moved the benefit of the doubt: an equal position now favours the attacker, so a line drawn through two matching heels lets the goal stand.
cards.move: When a rule decides ties, look at which side it hands them to.
cards.reference: International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 1990, Law XI Off-side

cards.question: A forward pass reaches an attacker while the goalkeeper is stranded upfield behind him and one defender guards the line. Offside?
options: Onside: a defender is still goal-side
Offside: one opponent is not enough
Onside: the keeper is out of play
cards.answer: Offside. The Law counts opponents, not a defender plus a goalkeeper: at the moment of the pass an attacker needs at least two of them level with him or nearer their goal line. With the keeper caught upfield, a lone defender on the line leaves him offside, however empty the goal looks.
cards.move: Check what a rule actually counts, not the usual picture of it.
cards.trap: Picturing the goalkeeper as always the last man back.
cards.reference: https://www.tff.org/Resources/TFF/Documents/MHK/2024-2025/laws-of-the-game.pdf

cards.question: Should an attacker be offside only when there is clear daylight between him and the defender?
cards.answer: Offside exists to stop goal-hanging, not to cancel goals over a toenail. Camera frames, and a kick point that can be misjudged by one frame, cannot honestly separate bodies a few centimetres apart. A daylight rule would restore the benefit of the doubt, keep celebrations spontaneous and make attackers gamble on early runs again.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether any margin just creates a new borderline decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Daylight only moves the line: there will still be a sliver between some daylight and none, and defenders would lose the offside trap, since holding a line would no longer catch a runner half a body ahead. With video review, one study found key refereeing decisions rose from about 92% to about 98% correct.
cards.source: Spitz et al., Journal of Sports Sciences, 2021
cards.reference: Spitz, Wagemans, Memmert, Williams & Helsen, Video assistant referees (VAR): the impact of technology on decision making in association football referees, Journal of Sports Sciences, 2021

cards.question: True or false: a defender who steps off the pitch no longer counts when judging offside?
cards.answer: False. A defender who leaves the field without the referee's permission is treated as standing on his own goal line or touchline, until play stops or his side clears the ball towards halfway and out of its penalty area. Stepping behind the goal to strand a forward keeps that forward onside.
cards.move: A rule that could be dodged by walking away usually has a clause for it.
cards.trap: Assuming a player off the field has left the game's geometry.
cards.source: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 11
cards.reference: International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 2025/26, Law 11 Offside

cards.question: If lactic acid is not to blame, what makes muscles ache a day or two after unusual exercise?
cards.answer: Small-scale damage from lengthening contractions, and the inflammation that repairs it. Lactate returns to resting levels within about an hour of stopping, long before the ache begins. The worst soreness follows work where muscles brake under load, such as running downhill, which produces little lactate at all.
cards.move: If the pain arrives after the suspect has left, look for another cause.
cards.reference: Cheung, Hume & Maxwell, Delayed onset muscle soreness: treatment strategies and performance factors, Sports Medicine, 2003

cards.question: Why does the same punishing downhill run leave far less soreness when repeated a few weeks later?
cards.answer: The first bout protects against the next. Known as the repeated-bout effect, it appears after a single session and lasts for weeks. Nerves recruit the muscle differently, connective tissue stiffens and the inflammatory response is damped. The second descent does less damage, not merely hurts less.
cards.move: The first hard dose of anything teaches the body what to expect.
cards.source: McHugh, Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2003
cards.reference: McHugh, Recent advances in the understanding of the repeated bout effect, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2003

cards.question: True or false: regular ice baths after weight training help muscles grow bigger and stronger?
cards.answer: False. In a 12-week trial, men who sat in cold water after each strength session gained less muscle and strength than men who did an active cool-down instead. Cold damps the inflammation and blood flow that signal muscles to adapt. It can help an athlete feel fresher for tomorrow's match.
cards.move: Feeling better and getting better are different results; check which one was measured.
cards.trap: Taking less soreness the next day as proof of better recovery.
cards.source: Roberts et al., Journal of Physiology, 2015
cards.reference: Roberts et al., Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training, Journal of Physiology, 2015

cards.question: Eleven university basketball players spent ten hours a night in bed for weeks and shot about 9% better. What follows?
options: Promising, but practice could explain it
Nothing, since eleven is too few
cards.answer: Promising, but practice could explain it. The Stanford study had no comparison group: the same players were training through their season, so some gain would have come anyway. Sleep was tracked with wrist monitors, and the result fits wider sleep research. It is a lead, not a measured effect.
cards.move: Ask what would have happened to the same people doing nothing different.
cards.trap: Crediting all of the improvement to the one change that was announced.
cards.reference: Mah, Mah, Kezirian & Dement, The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players, Sleep, 2011

cards.question: A runner starts a new recovery remedy at the height of post-race soreness. Three days later the pain has gone. Why?
options: The remedy only masked the pain
cards.answer: It would have faded anyway. Delayed soreness peaks one to three days after hard exercise and clears within about a week, whatever is done. People reach for remedies at the peak, so almost anything tried then is followed by improvement. Trials against untreated controls find most remedies make small differences at best.
cards.move: Anything started at the worst moment will seem to work.
cards.trap: Crediting the remedy because relief followed it.
cards.reference: Connolly, Sayers & McHugh, Treatment and prevention of delayed onset muscle soreness, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2003

cards.question: How do sports doctors tell overtraining syndrome apart from ordinary heavy fatigue?
cards.answer: Mostly in hindsight. No blood test or marker settles it, so the diagnosis is made by ruling out other causes, and the clearest difference is how long recovery takes: days to weeks after functional overreaching, weeks to months after the non-functional kind, and months or longer in the full syndrome. The calendar gives the label.
cards.move: When no test separates two states, watch how long each one lasts.
cards.source: Meeusen et al., ECSS and ACSM consensus, 2013
cards.reference: Meeusen et al., Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the ECSS and the ACSM, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2013

cards.question: In the fortnight before a big race, what should an athlete cut to taper well: training volume or intensity?
cards.answer: Volume. Pooling taper studies, Bosquet and colleagues found the best results came from tapers of about two weeks that cut weekly training volume by roughly 41 to 60%, while keeping intensity and the number of sessions the same. Easy, gentle weeks lose the sharpness that hard sessions keep: fewer kilometres, still run at speed.
cards.move: To rest without going stale, cut the amount and keep the edge.
cards.source: Bosquet et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2007
cards.reference: Bosquet, Montpetit, Arvisais & Mujika, Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2007

cards.question: After long exercise, cyclists ate carbohydrate either at once or two hours later. How did their muscle glycogen compare after 24 hours?
options: Much higher if eaten at once
Higher if eaten two hours later
cards.answer: About the same either way. Ivy's 1988 study had shown glycogen refills fastest right after exercise, and that a two-hour delay slows the early rate. But Parkin and colleagues found no difference at 8 or 24 hours once enough carbohydrate was eaten. The rush matters when the next session is hours away, not a day.
cards.move: Ask over what stretch of time a head start still counts.
cards.trap: Stretching the fast early refilling into an advantage for the whole day.
cards.source: Parkin et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1997
cards.reference: Parkin, Carey, Martin, Stojanovska & Febbraio, Muscle glycogen storage following prolonged exercise: effect of timing of ingestion of high glycemic index food, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 1997

cards.question: Compared with simply resting, what does massage do to the clearance of lactate from a hard-worked muscle?
cards.answer: Slows it down. Measuring forearm blood flow after hard handgrip exercise, Wiltshire and colleagues found massage mechanically impeded flow into the muscle, and lactate cleared more slowly than with passive rest; gentle active exercise cleared it fastest. The flushing story lasted because massage feels good, and feeling good was taken as the proof.
cards.move: A treatment that feels good has passed one test, not every test.
cards.trap: Speeds it up: the familiar picture of massage flushing out waste.
cards.source: Wiltshire et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2010
cards.reference: Wiltshire, Poitras, Pak, Hong, Rayner & Tschakovsky, Massage impairs postexercise muscle blood flow and lactic acid removal, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2010

cards.question: Should athletes take anti-inflammatory painkillers to get through soreness during heavy training?
cards.answer: Soreness that stops an athlete training costs more fitness than a few pills. In adults over 60, Trappe's group found that ibuprofen taken through twelve weeks of resistance training increased muscle growth rather than blunting it. Refusing relief on principle can mean skipped sessions and altered technique, which carry their own risks of injury.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the dose and who takes it decide the answer.
cards.counterpoint: Inflammation is part of the signal to adapt. In young adults, Lilja and colleagues found that high daily ibuprofen doses over eight weeks of training blunted gains in muscle size and strength, and endurance athletes who dose up for long events risk kidney injury. Masking pain also hides the warning that separates useful soreness from damage.
cards.reference: Lilja et al., High doses of anti-inflammatory drugs compromise muscle strength and hypertrophic adaptations to resistance training in young adults, Acta Physiologica, 2018

cards.question: True or false: in the 2019 Wimbledon men's final, the loser won more points and more games than the champion?
cards.answer: True. Roger Federer won 218 points to Novak Djokovic's 204, and 36 games to 32, yet lost in five sets. Tennis counts points only inside games, games only inside sets, and Djokovic won all three tie-breaks. Federer's surplus sat in sets he had already won, including one taken 6-1.
cards.move: A total can favour one side while every decisive count favours the other.
cards.trap: Assuming whoever wins more points must win the match.
cards.reference: https://www.tennis.com/news/articles/2019-top-matches-no-1-djokovic-d-federer-wimbledon-final

cards.question: Why did international volleyball stop letting only the serving team score?
cards.answer: To make matches fit a schedule. Under side-out scoring a long run of rallies could pass with no point at all, so nobody could say how long a match would last. In 1999 the international federation switched to rally scoring, a point on every rally, and match lengths became predictable enough to sell to television.
cards.move: When something must fit a schedule, expect its rules to bend to the clock.
cards.source: LSU Athletics, a point on every play
cards.reference: https://lsusports.net/news/2006/08/21/549142/

cards.question: A basketball team makes half its two-point shots. What three-point percentage scores the same per shot, in percent?
cards.answer: p x 3 = 1, so p = 1/3, about 33.3%.
cards.move: Compare options by what each attempt is worth, not by how often it succeeds.
cards.trap: Expecting a harder shot to need a similar success rate to pay.
cards.hint: Work out how many points one two-point attempt is worth on average.
steps: A 50% two is worth 0.5 x 2 = 1 point per shot.
A three is worth p x 3 points per shot.
p x 3 = 1, so p = 1/3, about 33.3%.

diagram.caption: A three made one time in three scores as much per shot as a 50% two.

cards.reference: Goldsberry, SprawlBall: A Visual Tour of the New Era of the NBA, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019

cards.question: Why did gymnastics give up the perfect 10 in 2006?
cards.answer: A ceiling on the score was a ceiling on the sport. Under a maximum of 10, a harder routine performed slightly less cleanly could lose to a safe one done perfectly. The new code split marks into an open-ended difficulty score, built up from zero, and an execution score that starts at 10 and falls.
cards.move: Cap the reward and people stop attempting the hard thing.
cards.reference: https://www.nbcolympics.com/news/gymnastics-101-olympic-scoring-rules-and-regulations

cards.question: A tennis server wins 55% of points, each independently. About what share of service games does he win?
cards.answer: About 62%. A game needs four points and a two-point margin, so a small edge on each point compounds: all the paths through 40-15 and deuce are tilted the same way. At 60% of points the figure is about 74%. Sets and matches magnify it again, which is how small edges become lopsided scorelines.
cards.move: A small edge repeated through a winner-takes-all format becomes a large one.
cards.trap: Expecting the share of games to mirror the share of points.

series.label: if a game were one point

diagram.caption: Winning 55% of points holds 62% of service games; 60% of points holds about 74%.

cards.source: Newton & Keller, Studies in Applied Mathematics, 2005
cards.reference: Newton & Keller, Probability of winning at tennis I. Theory and data, Studies in Applied Mathematics, 2005

cards.question: Why did a rugby try once count for less than the kick at goal that followed it?
cards.answer: Because it was only a licence to kick. Grounding the ball earned a try at goal, and goals decided matches. Once points came in, a try scored 1 and a conversion 2 until 1891. The try rose to 3 in 1893, 4 in 1971 and 5 in 1992, tilting value from boot to hands.
cards.move: A name often preserves what a thing was worth before the rules changed.
cards.reference: https://rugby365.com/laws-referees/news/scoring-down-the-years/

cards.question: In the decathlon, is cutting 0.1 seconds from a 100 m worth more points to a 10.2-second sprinter or an 11.2-second one?
cards.answer: To the 10.2-second sprinter. The table awards 25.4347 × (18 − time)^1.81 points; an exponent above 1 makes the curve steepen as times fall, so 0.1 seconds is worth about 24 points at 10.2 but about 22 at 11.2. Every event's table bends this way: strong events pay more than weak ones repaired.
cards.move: Before fixing a weakness, check whether the scoring pays more for strengths.
cards.trap: Assuming diminishing returns, as if the faster man sits near a ceiling.
cards.source: IAAF Scoring Tables for Combined Events
cards.reference: International Association of Athletics Federations, Scoring Tables for Combined Events, 2001

cards.question: Diving drops the top two and bottom two of seven marks: 8, 8, 8.5, 8.5, 9, 9, 9.5. Points lost if one 8 becomes 3?
cards.answer: Same marks counted, so the dive loses 0 points.
cards.move: A trimmed average shrugs off one wild judge; that is what it is for.
cards.trap: Averaging all seven marks, as if every judge's number counted.
cards.hint: Sort both sets of marks and see which three survive each time.
steps: Before: drop 8, 8, 9 and 9.5; the middle three are 8.5, 8.5, 9.
After: drop 3, 8, 9 and 9.5; the middle three are still 8.5, 8.5, 9.
Same marks counted, so the dive loses 0 points.
cards.reference: World Aquatics, Competition Regulations: Diving Rules, 2023

cards.question: True or false: after rain, cricket's Duckworth–Lewis–Stern method can set the chasing side a target above the first side's total plus one?
cards.answer: True. The method treats overs and wickets as resources. If rain cuts the first innings short, the side batting first paced itself for 50 overs and lost its final surge with wickets in hand, so the chasers, who know their allowance from the start, are set more than was actually scored.
cards.move: When a contest is cut short, ask what each side still had left.
cards.trap: Assuming rain can only ever lower a target, never raise it.
cards.reference: Duckworth & Lewis, A fair method for resetting the target in interrupted one-day cricket matches, Journal of the Operational Research Society, 1998

cards.question: Why does a tennis tie-break change server after the first point and then after every two?
cards.answer: To share the server's edge evenly. Top players win most points on serve, so the order runs A, BB, AA, BB: after every even number of points both have served the same number, and at any moment the gap is at most one. Neither player can take the tie-break by holding serve alone.
cards.move: To judge whether a sequence is fair, check who leads at every step.
cards.reference: International Tennis Federation, Rules of Tennis 2024, Rule 5 Score in a game, tie-break game

cards.question: In one study of top-league penalties, goalkeepers dived to a side 94% of the time. Which choice saved most often?
cards.answer: Staying in the centre. Bar-Eli and colleagues found that keepers who stayed put stopped about a third of the kicks they faced, against about 13% for those who dived. Kickers aimed at the middle nearly a third of the time. A goal conceded while standing still looks like doing nothing, so keepers dive.
cards.move: When doing nothing is the best option, it still has to be chosen.
cards.trap: Diving looks like effort, and effort feels like the best chance.

diagram.caption: Keepers dived 94% of the time, yet staying put saved over twice as often.

cards.source: Bar-Eli et al., J Economic Psychology, 2007
cards.reference: Bar-Eli, Azar, Ritov, Keidar-Levin & Schein, Action bias among elite soccer goalkeepers: The case of penalty kicks, Journal of Economic Psychology, 2007

cards.question: Does the team that shoots first in a penalty shoot-out really win more often?
cards.answer: Perhaps slightly; the evidence is contested. Apesteguia and Palacios-Huerta found first-shooting teams won 60% of 269 shoot-outs and blamed the pressure of chasing. Kocher, Lenz and Sutter, with twice as many shoot-outs, found no significant edge. Football's lawmakers trialled a tennis-style A-B-B-A order, then dropped it in 2018.
cards.move: A striking result from one dataset is a question for the next.
cards.reference: Apesteguia & Palacios-Huerta, Psychological Pressure in Competitive Environments: Evidence from a Randomized Natural Experiment, American Economic Review, 2010

cards.question: NFL kickers made 99.3% of extra points before a 2015 rule pushed the kick back, then 94.2%. How many times more often did they miss?
cards.move: When success is close to certain, compare the failures instead.
cards.trap: Reading a five-point drop in success as a small change.
cards.hint: Work out the share of kicks missed in each season first.
steps: Missed before: 100 − 99.3 = 0.7%.
Missed after: 100 − 94.2 = 5.8%.

items.label: Missed after the kick moved back

diagram.caption: Success slipped from 99.3% to 94.2%, but misses rose from 0.7% to 5.8%: over eightfold.

cards.reference: Pro-Football-Reference, NFL Kicking statistics, 2014 and 2015 seasons, 2015

cards.question: Since 2019, how close may attackers stand to a defensive wall of three or more at a free kick?
cards.answer: No closer than 1 m. Attackers used to squeeze into the wall and peel away as the ball was struck, opening a gap or blocking the goalkeeper's view. The lawmakers called it time-wasting with no legitimate tactical purpose. An attacker within 1 m when the kick is taken now concedes an indirect free kick.
cards.move: A tactic that lives in a rule's silence lasts until the rule speaks.
cards.reference: The International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 2019/20, 2019

cards.question: True or false: when football introduced the penalty kick in 1891, the kicker could shoot from anywhere along a line?
cards.answer: True. The 1891 law let the kick be taken from any point about 11 m out from the goal line, and the goalkeeper could advance about 5.5 m to meet it. The penalty spot arrived in 1902, with the penalty area still marked today. The idea came from William McCrum, an Irish goalkeeper.
cards.move: Details that look timeless were usually added one fix at a time.
cards.trap: The spot looks so basic it must have come with the kick.
cards.source: Harvey, Football: The First Hundred Years, 2005
cards.reference: Harvey, Football: The First Hundred Years, The Untold Story, Routledge, 2005

cards.question: Why is a goal scored straight from a corner kick called an olympic goal in Latin American football?
cards.answer: Because the first famous one beat Olympic champions. Scoring direct from a corner became legal in 1924, and that October Cesáreo Onzari of Argentina curled one in against Uruguay, who had just won football gold in Paris. The name honours the victims. Such goals stay rare: the ball must beat a keeper already in place.
cards.move: Names often record who was beaten, not who did the beating.
cards.source: Galeano, Football in Sun and Shadow
cards.reference: Galeano, Football in Sun and Shadow, trans. Mark Fried, Fourth Estate, 1997

cards.question: In top-level football, roughly what share of direct free kicks shot at goal end up in the net?
cards.answer: About 1 in 15; most analyses put it around 5 to 7%. A wall covers much of the goal, the kick is usually 20 m or more out, and the keeper sets himself first. The replays show the ones that curl in, not the dozens that hit the wall or clear the bar.
cards.move: A highlight reel is a list of exceptions.
cards.trap: Judging the rate from replays, which show mostly the ones that score.
cards.reference: Anderson & Sally, The Numbers Game: Why Everything You Know About Football Is Wrong, Viking, 2013

cards.question: In major-tournament shoot-outs, how did kicks that would win the match compare with kicks that had to score to avoid defeat?
options: Kicks to win scored far more
cards.answer: Kicks to win scored far more often: about 92% against 62%, in Jordet and Hartman's study of World Cup, European Championship and Copa América shoot-outs. Same spot, same goal, same kind of kicker; only what a miss would mean had changed. The goal was the same width; the stakes were not.
cards.move: The same task changes odds when failure, not success, is on the line.
cards.trap: Assuming a penalty is a penalty, whatever hangs on it.
cards.reference: Jordet & Hartman, Avoidance motivation and choking under pressure in soccer penalty shootouts, Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology, 2008

cards.question: True or false: in Palacios-Huerta's study of 1,417 professional penalties, kickers chose sides in patterns a goalkeeper could exploit?
cards.answer: False. Kickers' choices looked like fair coin tosses: where they aimed last time did not predict where they aimed next. Scoring rates were also statistically equal whichever way they went, as game theory predicts when both sides mix their choices well. A keeper studying a kicker's recent penalties learns nothing he can use.
cards.move: Against a sharp opponent, the best plan may be to be unpredictable.
cards.trap: Expecting humans to fall into habits that a sharp keeper can read.
cards.reference: Palacios-Huerta, Professionals Play Minimax, Review of Economic Studies, 2003

cards.question: A penalty is struck at 100 km/h from 11 m. How many seconds does the ball take to reach the goal line?
cards.answer: Rounded, about 0.4 seconds.
cards.move: When reacting takes longer than the event, decide before it starts.
cards.hint: Turn km/h into metres per second by dividing by 3.6.
steps: Rounded, about 0.4 seconds.
cards.source: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 1
cards.reference: The International Football Association Board, Laws of the Game 2024/25, Law 1: The Field of Play, 2024

cards.question: Why do people raised running barefoot mostly land on the front of the foot?
cards.answer: Because landing on a bare heel hurts. Filming Kenyan and American runners, Lieberman's team found habitual barefoot runners mostly touch down forefoot first, which avoids the sharp force spike a heel strike sends up the leg. Most runners in cushioned shoes land heel first and let the foam absorb that spike.
cards.move: Padding a problem can remove the signal that taught people to avoid it.

cards.question: True or false: sawing through the carbon plate of a Nike Vaporfly wipes out most of its energy saving?
cards.answer: False. Healey and Hoogkamer made six cuts across the forefoot plate. Energy cost rose by only about 0.5%, not a significant change, against the roughly 4% the shoe saves. The benefit seems to come from the thick, springy foam and the shoe's shape working together. A shoe with a sawn plate ran almost as well.
cards.move: Take the famous part out and see whether anything stops working.
cards.trap: The rigid plate is the visible novelty, so it gets the credit.
cards.source: Healey & Hoogkamer, J Sport Health Sci, 2022
cards.reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2095254621000739

cards.question: A shoe cuts an elite marathoner's energy cost at race pace by 4%. Roughly how much faster can they run?
cards.answer: About 2.5% faster. The energy needed rises faster than speed, partly because air resistance climbs steeply as a runner speeds up, so a 4% saving buys only about two-thirds as much pace. Kipp, Kram and Hoogkamer put it at 2 to 3%. For a 2:04 marathoner, that is still about three minutes.
cards.move: Before turning a saving into a result, ask whether costs rise in a straight line.
cards.trap: Assuming a saving in effort converts one for one into speed.
cards.source: Kipp, Kram & Hoogkamer, Frontiers in Physiology, 2019

cards.question: What does World Athletics actually measure to decide whether an elite racing shoe is legal?
cards.answer: Mainly the thickness of the sole and the number of plates. A road shoe may be at most 40 mm thick under the foot and hold one rigid plate; sprint spikes are capped at 20 mm. The foam's chemistry is not limited. Thickness stands in for spring because a measurement can check it.
cards.move: When the real cause is hard to police, rules cap something easy to measure.
cards.reference: https://worldathletics.org/download/download?filename=b723c6b6-7d1f-40ad-8b27-1d3f956c6c99.pdf&urlslug=C2.1A+%E2%80%93+Athletic+Shoe+Regulations+(effective+from+01+January+2022)

cards.question: Should road-running records set in carbon-plated super shoes be listed apart from older ones?
cards.answer: Yes. These shoes change the event itself: lab tests found the first model cut running's energy cost by about 4%, worth minutes over a marathon. Marathon records that had stood for years fell within a few seasons of their arrival. A 2023 time beside a 1998 one compares equipment, not athletes.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether this change differs in kind.
cards.counterpoint: No. Running has always changed with its kit: cinder tracks gave way to synthetic ones, spikes improved, pacing lights arrived, and nobody split the lists. World Athletics already caps sole thickness and approves every racing model, so rivals race on the same terms. A separate list needs an arbitrary line, and the next invention would need another.
cards.reference: Hoogkamer, Kipp, Frank, Farina, Luo & Kram, A Comparison of the Energetic Cost of Running in Marathon Racing Shoes, Sports Medicine, 2018

cards.question: Why was John Carlos's 19.92 in the 200 m at the 1968 US Olympic trials never ratified as a world record?
cards.answer: Because of his shoes. Carlos ran in Puma's new brush spikes, whose soles carried dozens of short pins instead of the few spikes the rules allowed. The Echo Summit run beat the world record of the day but stands in no record book. Vince Matthews's 400 m in the same shoes went too.
cards.move: A result can be real and still be ruled out by what produced it.
cards.reference: https://www.olympedia.org/athletes/78197

cards.question: Which one lab measurement set the foam of Nike's Vaporfly prototype apart from older midsoles?
cards.answer: Energy return: how much of each squash the foam gives back. In Hoogkamer's 2018 tests, the prototype's PEBA foam, a light elastic plastic, returned 87% of the energy stored when compressed; an adidas Boost midsole returned 76% and Nike's older EVA racing flat 66%. The rest leaks away as heat, some 20,000 times a marathon.
cards.move: Judge a spring by what it gives back, not by how soft it feels.

cards.question: At 14.5 km/h, how did impact forces in thick maximalist running shoes compare with those in conventional running shoes?
cards.answer: About 10% higher. Kulmala's team measured the impact peak 10.7% higher and the loading rate 12.3% higher in the highly cushioned shoe. Runners met the softer sole by stiffening their legs, so the body came down harder on top of the foam. A mattress under the foot changed the leg above it.
cards.move: Expect people to adjust when a device takes over part of their job.
cards.trap: Assuming a softer sole must mean a softer landing for the body.
cards.reference: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-35980-6

cards.question: True or false: once shoe weight was matched, habitual barefoot runners spent less energy barefoot than in light cushioned shoes?
cards.answer: False. Franz, Wierzbinski and Kram taped weights to bare feet to match shoes of about 150 g. Mass for mass, shod running cost about 3 to 4% less energy than running barefoot. Studies favouring bare feet had let the shoes' weight count against them. Mass aside, foam spares the legs some cushioning work.
cards.move: Before comparing two options, make them equal in everything but one.
cards.trap: Crediting bare feet with a saving that came from carrying less weight.
cards.reference: https://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/fulltext/2012/08000/metabolic_cost_of_running_barefoot_versus_shod__is.14.aspx

cards.question: Each 100 g added to a running shoe raises energy cost by about 1%. How many extra grams per shoe would cancel a 4% saving?
cards.answer: 4 × 100 g = 400 g per shoe.
cards.move: Put a percentage into a unit you can hold in your hand.
cards.hint: Count how many of the 1% penalties fit inside the saving.
steps: Each 100 g on each shoe costs about 1% more energy.
A 4% saving is four of those 1% steps.
4 × 100 g = 400 g per shoe.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22367745/

cards.question: What was unremarkable about Usain Bolt's 9.58-second 100 m world record in Berlin in 2009?
cards.answer: His start. His reaction to the gun, 0.146 seconds, was slower than that of some of the men he beat. The record was built later: laser measurements put his top speed at 12.34 m/s, about 44 km/h, reached between 60 and 80 m, well past halfway.
cards.move: Find where a winner gained the time before praising the obvious part.
cards.source: Graubner & Nixdorf, New Studies in Athletics, 2011
cards.reference: Graubner & Nixdorf, Biomechanical analysis of the sprint and hurdles events at the 2009 IAAF World Championships in Athletics, New Studies in Athletics, 2011

cards.question: True or false: a sprinter who leaves the blocks after the gun has fired can still be disqualified for a false start?
cards.answer: True. Sensors in the blocks disqualify anyone who pushes within 0.100 seconds of the gun, on the view that nobody reacts that fast. Devon Allen was thrown out of the 2022 world championship hurdles final for a reaction of 0.099. Laboratory studies of trained sprinters have recorded genuine reactions quicker than the limit.
cards.move: A fixed threshold catches the cheats and the unusually fast alike.
cards.trap: Assuming a false start means moving before the gun fires.
cards.source: World Athletics, sprint start research project
cards.reference: https://worldathletics.org/news/news/iaaf-sprint-start-research-project-is-the-100

cards.question: A 100 m is run with a 2 m/s tailwind, the legal limit for records. How much faster than in still air?
cards.answer: About 0.1 seconds. Linthorne's analysis of championship races put the gain from a legal-limit tailwind at 0.10 seconds for men and 0.12 for women. That is roughly a metre at the line, more than the margin in many finals. A headwind of the same strength costs more than the tailwind gives.
cards.move: Measure a small push against the margins that decide the contest.
cards.trap: Hearing 2 m/s as a gentle breeze and pricing it near nothing.
cards.reference: https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/jab/10/2/article-p110.xml

cards.question: Why are sprint records from before 1977 not comparable with later ones, even to a tenth of a second?
cards.answer: Because they were timed by hand. Timekeepers started their watches on seeing the gun's smoke, after a human reaction delay, and tended to stop them early as runners neared the line. Statisticians add 0.24 seconds to a hand-timed 100 m to compare it with electronic times. From 1977, records needed fully automatic timing.
cards.move: Before comparing two figures, ask whether the same instrument produced both.
cards.source: Hymans, Progression of IAAF World Records, 2015
cards.reference: Hymans & Matrahazi, Progression of IAAF World Records, 2015 Edition, IAAF, 2015

cards.question: What is odd about the wind reading for the women's 100 m world record, 10.49 seconds, set in 1988?
cards.answer: It read exactly zero. The race was a quarter-final at the US Olympic trials in Indianapolis, and the anemometer on the triple jump runway nearby logged a tailwind of 4.3 m/s, more than twice the legal limit. The track gauge is widely thought to have failed, yet the record was ratified and stands.
cards.move: A reading of exactly zero is worth checking before it is believed.
cards.source: Daily Relay, oral history of the 10.49
cards.reference: http://dailyrelay.com/the-wind-read-zero-an-oral-history-of-florence-griffith-joyners-100-meter-world-record/

cards.question: Jamaica's 4 × 100 m relay record is 36.84 seconds. By how many seconds does it beat four times Bolt's 9.58?
cards.answer: Difference: 38.32 - 36.84 = 1.48 seconds.
cards.move: Count how many times a job pays its start-up cost.
cards.trap: Expecting four runners to be slower than the fastest man four times.
cards.hint: Only the first of the four runners starts from blocks.
steps: Four solo records back to back: 4 x 9.58 = 38.32 seconds.
Difference: 38.32 - 36.84 = 1.48 seconds.
cards.reference: World Athletics, official world records list, men's 4 x 100 m relay, Jamaica 36.84, London 2012

cards.question: True or false: Bolt's 200 m world record, 19.19 seconds, is faster than twice his 100 m record?
cards.answer: False. Twice 9.58 is 19.16, so the 200 m record is 0.03 seconds slower, although its second half begins at full speed. The bend and the fatigue of the last 50 m cost almost exactly what the flying start gives back: both records average about 10.4 metres per second.
cards.move: List what a longer version adds and what it costs before comparing.
cards.trap: Crediting the flying second half and forgetting the bend and the fade.
cards.reference: IAAF, 12th World Championships in Athletics, Berlin 2009, official results, men's 100 m and 200 m finals

cards.question: How does a sprint time measured to the thousandth of a second become the hundredths in the record book?
cards.answer: Always upwards. Under World Athletics rules, a fully automatic time not ending in zero goes to the next longer hundredth: 10.041 becomes 10.05, while 10.040 stays 10.04. No runner is credited with time they did not run, and places come from the photo, so two runners can share a time yet not a place.
cards.move: When rounding, ask which direction protects the claim being made.
cards.reference: World Athletics, Competition and Technical Rules, 2024 edition, TR 19 Timing and Photo Finish

cards.question: What do the winning times of the Kentucky Derby suggest about how far the 100 m record can fall?
cards.answer: That records have a ceiling. Derby times stopped improving decades ago despite intense breeding, and greyhound times levelled off too. Fitting the same kind of levelling curve to men's 100 m records, the biologist Mark Denny estimated a limit of about 9.48 seconds in 2008, a year before the record fell to 9.58.
cards.move: Look at a race that stopped improving to see where yours is heading.
cards.reference: Denny, Limits to running speed in dogs, horses and humans, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2008

cards.question: What mainly lets the fastest sprinters reach higher top speeds than slower runners?
options: Hitting the ground with more force
Swinging their legs through the air faster
Having longer legs than their rivals
cards.answer: Hitting the ground with more force. Weyand's team found that runners with very different top speeds swung their legs through the air in about the same time. The faster ones pushed harder during briefer ground contacts, travelling farther with each step. Speed is made in the instant a shoe is on the track.
cards.move: Look for the cause in the part that is hardest to see.
cards.trap: Seeing a blur of legs and crediting how fast they swing.
cards.source: Weyand et al., Journal of Applied Physiology, 2000
cards.reference: Weyand, Sternlight, Bellizzi & Wright, Faster top running speeds are achieved with greater ground forces not more rapid leg movements, Journal of Applied Physiology, 2000

cards.question: A major swimming championship usually brings a handful of world records. How many fell at Rome in 2009?
cards.answer: About 40: 43 world records fell in eight days of racing. Rome was the last world championships before polyurethane bodysuits were banned in January 2010. The Beijing Olympics a year earlier, already called a record glut, had produced 25. Some Rome marks stood for over a decade, set in suits nobody may now wear.
cards.move: When the rules of a game change, old baselines stop applying.
cards.trap: Scaling up from ordinary meets, a record-rich one sounds like ten.
cards.reference: https://www.swimmingworldmagazine.com/news/eight-years-later-the-super-suit-era-still-plagues-the-record-books/

cards.question: True or false: world records set in the banned polyurethane bodysuits were left standing after the 2010 ban?
cards.answer: True. The swimming federation, then called FINA, banned the suits from January 2010 but never erased what they produced. Some marks outlived the suits by years: Paul Biedermann's 1:42.00 in the 200 m freestyle, set at Rome in 2009, still stood as the world record in 2025, the oldest individual long-course mark.
cards.move: Banning a tool does not undo what it already produced.
cards.trap: A ban on the equipment sounds like a ban on its results.
cards.reference: https://swimswam.com/with-biedermanns-400-free-mark-broken-what-are-the-oldest-remaining-lcm-world-records/

cards.question: Why would a ski-jumping team secretly restitch the crotch seam of its athletes' suits?
cards.answer: Because a jumping suit is partly a wing. Rules tie its cut closely to the athlete's body, since spare or shaped fabric catches air and adds lift. At the 2025 world championships in Trondheim, Norwegian staff were filmed adding an extra stitch there; two jumpers were disqualified and three staff later banned for 18 months.
cards.move: Where a rule measures size, look for gains hidden in shape.
cards.reference: https://theconversation.com/the-ski-jumping-cheating-scandal-how-suits-were-illegally-altered-for-unfair-advantage-254854

cards.question: Midway through Sochi 2014, US long-track speed skaters swapped their new high-tech suits for older ones. What followed?
cards.answer: Still no medals. A team that had won four long-track medals in 2010 left Sochi with none, its first shut-out since 1984, in either suit. A review months later cleared the suit and blamed preparation, above all a final camp at altitude on an outdoor rink in Italy before an indoor, sea-level Games.
cards.move: When removing the suspect changes nothing, it probably was not the cause.
cards.trap: If the suits were to blame, dropping them should have fixed it.
cards.reference: https://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/olympics/bs-bz-under-armour-speedskating-20180130-story.html

cards.question: What made the 2008–09 polyurethane swimsuits fast, beyond feeling slippery in the water?
cards.answer: They trapped air and squeezed the body. Air held in the polyurethane added buoyancy, so swimmers rode higher with less drag, and tight compression smoothed the body's outline. That is why the 2010 rules allow only permeable textile, reaching from navel to knee for men and no further than shoulders and knees for women.
cards.move: To find what a rule really targets, read what it forbids.
cards.reference: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/winning-skin/

cards.question: Why do judo officials measure the sleeves of each fighter's jacket before a contest begins?
cards.answer: Because a jacket that is hard to grip is hard to throw. Fighters learned to wear tight, stiff, short-sleeved jackets that left opponents little cloth to hold. Judo's federation now requires sleeves reaching the wrist, loose around the arm, checked with a gauge. A fighter in a narrow jacket is sent to change.
cards.move: Anything an opponent must hold can be made harder to hold.
cards.reference: International Judo Federation, IJF Judogi Rules, 2022

cards.question: Foil and sabre fencers wear a metallic jacket over their whites, but épée fencers do not. Why?
options: The whole body is a valid target
Épée touches are scored without electricity
cards.answer: The whole body is a valid target. The scoring box only learns that a tip pressed on something; the conductive jacket, called a lamé, tells it whether that was valid target. It covers the torso in foil and everything above the waist in sabre. In épée every touch counts, so nothing needs sorting.
cards.move: Equipment that sorts right from wrong is needed only where wrong exists.
cards.trap: Assuming épée alone kept the old scoring by judges' eyes.
cards.reference: Fédération Internationale d'Escrime, Material Rules, 2023

cards.question: In a cycling time trial, roughly what share of the air drag comes from the rider rather than the bike?
cards.answer: About three quarters. A bike is thin and edge-on to the wind; the rider is a broad, blunt shape on top, and reviews put the body's share at roughly 70 to 80%. So teams lavish care on skinsuits and helmets. The fabric wraps the largest drag source in the race.
cards.move: Look for the cost where the mass is, not where the engineering shows.
cards.trap: Seeing sculpted carbon frames and guessing the bike makes half the drag.
cards.reference: Crouch, Burton, LaBry & Blair, Riding against the wind: a review of competition cycling aerodynamics, Sports Engineering, 2017

cards.question: True or false: lab tests found that the shark-skin texture of Speedo's Fastskin swimsuit fabric cut drag as real shark skin does?
cards.answer: False. Oeffner and Lauder flapped shark skin and the swimsuit fabric on flexible foils in flowing water. Shark skin, with its tiny toothlike scales, helped the foil swim faster; the fabric's surface gave no measurable gain. Whatever such suits did for swimmers, the texture was not it. The likeness was skin deep.
cards.move: A resemblance to nature is a hypothesis, not a result.
cards.trap: Trusting the likeness to shark skin instead of a test against plain fabric.
cards.reference: Oeffner & Lauder, The hydrodynamic function of shark skin and two biomimetic applications, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2012

cards.question: Should elite swimming require every racer at a championship to wear one identical, officially issued suit?
cards.answer: Yes. The 2008–09 bodysuits proved that fabric can move times more than a year of training, and approval lists always trail the latest cut. One issued suit, like a regulation ball, would make every record a record of swimmers. It would also close the gap between sponsored athletes and the rest.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether one suit fits every body equally.
cards.counterpoint: No. Bodies differ, and one cut would fit some swimmers far better than others, handing out advantage by lottery instead of by research. Makers' competition also pays for much of the sport. The 2010 textile rules already capped the gains: within those limits, suits now differ by fractions, not by the seconds of the bodysuit years.
cards.reference: World Aquatics, Requirements for Swimwear Approval (FRSA), 2023

cards.question: What happens when two Olympic swimmers touch the wall in exactly the same hundredth of a second?
cards.answer: They share the medal. Swimming stopped separating racers by thousandths after 1972, when Gunnar Larsson won the Olympic 400 m medley by 0.002 seconds. So ties stand: at Sydney in 2000, Anthony Ervin and Gary Hall Jr both clocked 21.98 in the 50 m freestyle, and two gold medals were awarded.
cards.move: When the measurement cannot separate two results, do not invent a winner.
cards.reference: Organising Committee for the Games of the XXth Olympiad, Official Report, Munich, 1974

cards.question: A 50 m pool lane may be built up to 3 cm long. At 2 m/s, how many hundredths of a second is that?
cards.answer: 0.015 seconds = 1.5 hundredths of a second.
cards.move: Before trusting a tiny margin, ask how precisely the course was built.
cards.trap: Treating a few centimetres of concrete as too small to matter.
cards.hint: Divide the extra distance by the swimmer's speed.
steps: 3 cm is 0.03 m.
0.03 m / 2 m/s = 0.015 seconds.
0.015 seconds = 1.5 hundredths of a second.
cards.reference: FINA, Facilities Rules 2017-2021, FR 2.2 pool dimensions and tolerances, 2017

cards.question: Why must swimmers in most strokes surface within 15 m of the start and each turn?
cards.answer: Because underwater is faster. A body submerged by about a metre escapes the surface waves that make up much of a swimmer's drag. At the 1988 Olympics David Berkoff and others kicked most of a backstroke length underwater; the sport capped it at 10 m that year, and settled on 15 m in 1991.
cards.move: If the loophole is faster than the sport, the sport will close it.
cards.reference: Maglischo, Swimming Fastest, Human Kinetics, 2003

cards.question: Over 200 m freestyle, which pool produces the faster world record, and why?
cards.answer: The 25 m pool: more push-offs. Seven turns instead of three means seven more pushes off a wall, each faster than swimming, followed by a stretch underwater. That is why short-course and long-course records are kept separately, and short-course times run two to three seconds quicker over 200 m.
cards.move: Count how often the rules let someone push off something solid.
cards.trap: Picturing turns as pauses that break the swimmer's rhythm.
cards.reference: Counsilman, The Science of Swimming, Prentice-Hall, 1968

cards.question: Why was one dolphin kick made legal at the start of each breaststroke length in 2005?
cards.answer: Because the officials could not stop it. At the 2004 Olympics Kosuke Kitajima was accused of a hidden kick in his winning 100 m breaststroke; underwater footage suggested it, but judges on deck could not see it. The governing body legalised a single downward butterfly kick on each pull-out the following year.
cards.move: A rule nobody can see being broken will soon be rewritten.
cards.reference: FINA, Swimming Rules 2005-2009, SW 7.1 Breaststroke, 2005

cards.question: True or false: a relay swimmer whose take-off pad reads 0.02 seconds before the team-mate's touch is disqualified?
cards.answer: False. The block and wall sensors do not fire at the exact instant of the events they record, so the rules allow a reading of up to 0.03 seconds before the touch. A swimmer shown leaving 0.02 early may still have been on the block when the hand hit the wall.
cards.move: Before judging by an instrument, learn which way it errs.
cards.trap: Taking the sensor reading as the exact moment the swimmer left.
cards.reference: https://swimswam.com/why-was-australias-0-03-relay-start-not-a-dq-a-rules-deep-dive/

cards.question: In elite freestyle races, what separates faster swimmers: more strokes per minute or more distance per stroke?
cards.answer: Distance per stroke. Filming swimmers at the US Olympic trials, Craig and colleagues found the faster ones travelled farther with each stroke, and that swimmers slowed late in a race mainly because each stroke carried them less far, not because their arms turned over more slowly. Long strokes, not busy arms, marked the fastest swimmers.
cards.move: Count how much each repetition achieves before counting the repetitions.
cards.source: Craig et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1985
cards.reference: Craig, Skehan, Pawelczyk & Boomer, Velocity, stroke rate, and distance per stroke during elite swimming competition, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 1985

cards.question: At the 2013 world championships, 50 m swimmers moving from lanes 1–4 to lanes 5–8 improved about 1%. Those moving the other way?
cards.answer: Got about 0.6% slower. Cornett, Brammer and Stager also found 1,500 m splits differing by direction of travel, the signature of a slow current along the Barcelona pool. Seeding is symmetrical across the two halves, so the lanes, not the swimmers' form, were shifting results by more than the gaps between medals.
cards.move: When everyone who moves one way gains, suspect the ground they moved to.
cards.trap: Crediting later-round improvement to the swimmers rather than their lanes.
cards.source: Cornett et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2015
cards.reference: Cornett, Brammer & Stager, Current controversy: analysis of the 2013 FINA World Swimming Championships, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2015

cards.question: World Aquatics points are 1,000 × (base time ÷ swim time) cubed. A swim 10% slower than base time scores how many points?
cards.move: When a score is raised to a power, small gaps become large ones.
cards.trap: Taking 10% off 1,000 and answering 900.
cards.hint: Work out the ratio of the two times before cubing it.

diagram.caption: Cubing turns a 10% gap in time into a 25% gap in points.

cards.reference: World Aquatics, Points Table: calculation of World Aquatics points, 2024

cards.question: Why did swimming approve sloped ledges on pool walls for backstroke starts in 2014?
cards.answer: Because toes slipped. Backstrokers start in the water, pushing off a wet vertical wall, and toes sliding at the signal could lose a race before it began. The ledge is a narrow anti-slip step angled at 10 degrees for the toes to push against; the swimming federation approved Omega's version in December 2014.
cards.move: When the start decides too much, fix the footing before the athletes.
cards.source: Swiss Timing, OBL2 Pro backstroke ledge
cards.reference: https://www.swisstiming.com/fileadmin/Resources/Data/Datasheets/DOCM_AQ_OBL2_Pro_1015_EN.pdf

cards.question: Where does the internet physically go?
cards.answer: Under the sea. Around 99% of intercontinental data travels through a few hundred fibre-optic cables lying on the seabed, not through satellites. "The cloud" is mostly glass on a seafloor, and its main hazards are ships' anchors and fishing trawlers.
cards.move: The cloud is a few hundred cables on the bottom of the ocean.

cards.question: Was QWERTY designed to slow you down?
cards.answer: Almost certainly not. The jamming story is folklore attached after the fact. The arrangement grew from how early machines were built and used — including telegraph operators transcribing Morse, who needed certain letters close together. It stuck because everyone had already learned it, which is the real lesson.
cards.move: The layout on your phone was settled by 1870s telegraph habits.
cards.reference: Yasuoka & Yasuoka, On the Prehistory of QWERTY, ZINBUN 42, Kyoto University, 2011

cards.question: Why can a helium shortage close a hospital?
cards.answer: MRI scanners need liquid helium to keep their magnets superconducting. Helium cannot be manufactured — it is collected as a by-product of certain natural gas wells, and it escapes Earth's gravity once released. Shortages have delayed scans and shut machines down.
cards.move: Helium is not made. It is found, used once, and lost to space.
cards.source: US Geological Survey, helium commodity summaries
cards.reference: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries: Helium, 2024

cards.question: What is the most software-heavy thing you own?
cards.answer: Probably your car. A modern vehicle runs on the order of a hundred million lines of code across dozens of processors — considerably more than a passenger aircraft. Most of it is not the engine; it is entertainment, comfort and the screens.
cards.move: Your car carries more code than the plane you flew in.

cards.question: Why did laying the first undersea telegraph cables strip forests in Southeast Asia?
cards.answer: For gutta-percha, the one insulation that held up under the sea. This latex from Palaquium trees of the Malay peninsula and Borneo stayed stable in cold salt water, and collectors usually felled a whole tree to drain it. As cable routes multiplied after 1850, the best-yielding species all but vanished from the wild.
cards.move: Ask what a new technology eats before counting what it connects.
cards.reference: Tully, A Victorian Ecological Disaster: Imperialism, the Telegraph, and Gutta-Percha, Journal of World History 20(4), 2009

cards.question: How do the amplifiers strung along a cable on the ocean floor get their electricity?
cards.answer: Down the cable itself. Stations on shore push a steady direct current of around one amp through a copper layer around the fibres, at thousands of volts, to amplifiers spaced tens of kilometres apart. There is no return wire: the current goes back through the seawater, and the ocean completes the circuit.
cards.move: Ask how a remote machine is powered; that is usually its real limit.
cards.reference: Chesnoy (ed.), Undersea Fiber Communication Systems, 2nd edition, Academic Press, 2016

cards.question: In 1929 an earthquake off Newfoundland was followed by 12 transatlantic cables snapping one after another over 13 hours. What broke them?
cards.answer: A mud avalanche racing downslope. The quake shook loose sediment on the continental slope, which poured down as a dense underwater current. Cables nearest the epicentre broke at once; those farther downslope failed hours later. The timed breaks let geologists clock the flow at tens of kilometres an hour, strong early proof such flows exist.
cards.move: When failures arrive in sequence, the timing is a clue to the cause.
cards.trap: The earthquake's shaking, because the breaks followed the quake.
cards.source: Heezen & Ewing, American Journal of Science, 1952
cards.reference: Heezen & Ewing, Turbidity currents and submarine slumps, and the 1929 Grand Banks earthquake, American Journal of Science 250, 1952

cards.question: Light in optical fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond. What is the fastest possible round trip, in milliseconds, over a 5,600 km transatlantic cable?
cards.answer: Round trip: 28 x 2 = 56 ms.
cards.move: Distance sets a floor on delay that no upgrade can remove.
cards.trap: Using light's speed in a vacuum and forgetting glass slows it.
cards.hint: Work out the one-way time first, then add the time for the reply to come back.
steps: Glass slows light to about two-thirds of its vacuum speed: about 200 km per millisecond.
Round trip: 28 x 2 = 56 ms.
cards.reference: Agrawal, Fiber-Optic Communication Systems, 4th edition, Wiley, 2010

cards.question: True or false: a fishing boat that cuts away its own net to spare a submarine cable can claim compensation from the cable's owner?
cards.answer: True. Article 115 of the Law of the Sea convention has states make cable owners repay a ship that sacrifices an anchor, net or other gear to avoid damaging a cable, provided it took reasonable care beforehand. The rule dates from an 1884 treaty: a net costs less than a cable repair.
cards.move: If you want people to protect something, pay them for what it costs.
cards.trap: False, because the law surely punishes whoever threatens the cable.
cards.source: UN Law of the Sea Convention, 1982
cards.reference: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Article 115, 1982

cards.question: How did the Soviet Union find the American tap on its undersea military cable in 1981?
cards.answer: It was told. From the early 1970s US submarines kept a pod on a Soviet cable in the Sea of Okhotsk that read its signals by induction, without cutting in. In 1980 Ronald Pelton, a former NSA employee, sold the secret to the Soviets for about $35,000. In 1981 Soviet ships retrieved it.
cards.move: The weak point of a secret is usually a person, not the hardware.
cards.reference: Sontag & Drew, Blind Man's Bluff: The Untold Story of American Submarine Espionage, PublicAffairs, 1998

cards.question: Why does mending a cable five kilometres down take at least three passes with a grapnel?
cards.answer: Because a loop hauled up whole from that depth would likely snap. The ship drags a grapnel that cuts the cable, then hooks one end and buoys it, then raises the other. A spare length is spliced in on deck, and the last joint goes down as a loop kilometres long.
cards.move: When lifting something whole is impossible, cut it and fetch the halves.
cards.source: Burnett, Beckman & Davenport, Submarine Cables handbook
cards.reference: Burnett, Beckman & Davenport (eds.), Submarine Cables: The Handbook of Law and Policy, Martinus Nijhoff, 2014

cards.question: Roughly how often is a submarine cable damaged somewhere in the world?
cards.answer: Nearly four times a week. TeleGeography counted an average of about 199 faults a year from 2010 to 2023, a rate that has barely moved. About two-thirds come from fishing gear and dragged anchors. The odd break in a tense sea makes the news; the rest are quietly mended by specialist repair ships.
cards.move: Before calling an event suspicious, find out how often it happens anyway.
cards.trap: Only the breaks that make the news come to mind.
cards.reference: https://resources.telegeography.com/submarine-cable-maintenance-data

cards.question: On a new transatlantic cable, what caps how much data it can carry?
options: How much light glass fibre can carry
The electrical power sent from shore
How many fibres fit inside the cable
cards.answer: The electrical power sent from shore. Seabed amplifiers run on current fed down the cable at up to about 15 kilovolts, and turn only a small share of it into light. So designers spread the power thinly: Google's Dunant cable of 2021 runs 12 fibre pairs, each below its own limit, sharing pump lasers.
cards.move: Find the scarcest input; everything else gets rationed around it.
cards.trap: Glass seems the bottleneck, since light is what carries the data.
cards.reference: https://www.subcom.com/documents/2021/Dunant_RFS_Final_3FEBRUARY2021.pdf

cards.question: True or false: traders' fastest links between Chicago and New York dropped optical fibre for microwave radio?
cards.answer: True. Light in glass travels about a third slower than radio through air. In 2010 Spread Networks laid a near-straight fibre route for about $300 million, cutting the round trip to roughly 13 milliseconds; microwave tower chains soon did it in under 9. Heavy rain fades radio, so firms keep fibre as backup.
cards.move: Check what a signal travels through, not just what carries it.
cards.trap: Fibre sounds like the fastest medium, since it carries light.
