cards.reference: Harper et al., Recycling lithium-ion batteries from electric vehicles, Nature, 2019

cards.question: If every electric car sold in 2014 were recycled in 2024, what share of 2024's new car batteries could they supply?
cards.answer: Under 2%. Roughly 300,000 electric cars were sold worldwide in 2014 and more than 17 million in 2024, over fifty times as many, and 2014's battery packs were smaller. Batteries return only after a decade or more on the road. Recycling feeds on the market of ten years ago.
cards.move: In a fast-growing market, the past is always smaller than it feels.
cards.trap: About half, as if the market were steady and scrap matched sales.
cards.reference: International Energy Agency, Global EV Outlook 2025, 2025

cards.question: Why is the cheapest kind of electric-car battery the least rewarding to recycle?
cards.answer: Because its positive electrode holds nothing valuable but the lithium. Lithium iron phosphate cells, now in a large share of new electric cars, swap the nickel and cobalt whose resale paid for most recycling for iron and phosphate. Once the lithium is out, what remains of that electrode is the stuff of rust and fertiliser.
cards.move: Follow the resale value to predict what actually gets saved.
cards.reference: Gaines, Lithium-ion battery recycling processes: Research towards a sustainable course, Sustainable Materials and Technologies, 2018

cards.question: Should lithium-ion batteries carry a refundable deposit, like the one many US states put on car batteries?
cards.answer: Deposits make waste worth collecting. Car batteries come back at about 99% in the US, where retailers add a charge refunded when the old one is returned. Lithium cells have no such pull: thrown into household bins, they are crushed in lorries and start fires. A deposit makes each one worth picking up.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, ask whether deposits or scrap value drive returns.
cards.counterpoint: Car batteries come back because the lead is worth money: scrap dealers pay for old ones, deposit or not. Most lithium cells are small and sealed inside phones, earbuds and vapes, so a deposit on each is hard to charge and harder to refund. Drop-off points, shop take-back and bans like the UK's on disposable vapes do more for less.
cards.source: Battery Council International, recycling rate study, 2019
cards.reference: Battery Council International, National Recycling Rate Study, 2019

cards.question: What would a recycler gain by keeping a worn cathode's crystal intact instead of dissolving it?
cards.answer: The cost of making it again. Smelting and acid leaching reduce a cathode to metal salts, from which a factory must rebuild the precise layered crystal, baking it for hours above 600 °C. Direct recycling instead tops up the lithium the worn crystal lost and reuses it. The long bake is skipped.
cards.move: Sometimes the value lies in the arrangement, not in the ingredients.
cards.reference: Gaines et al., Direct Recycling R&D at the ReCell Center, Recycling, 2021

cards.question: In the early 2020s, what supplied most of the material entering lithium-ion battery recyclers?
cards.answer: Scrap from battery factories. New plants reject much of their output while they learn, and cutting coated foil leaves offcuts; all of it arrives fresh, sorted and in bulk. Electric cars sold in large numbers only from about 2018, and most are still driving. Recyclers were fed by the gigafactories' mistakes.
cards.move: Before picturing where supply comes from, ask what has actually reached its end.
cards.trap: Picturing the retired electric cars that recycling is always said to await.
cards.source: International Energy Agency, Global EV Outlook 2023
cards.reference: International Energy Agency, Global EV Outlook 2023: Catching up with climate ambitions, 2023

cards.question: True or false: from 2031, EU law requires new electric-car batteries to contain at least a quarter recycled lithium?
cards.answer: False. The EU Batteries Regulation sets 6% for lithium from 2031, rising to 12% from 2036; nickel starts at 6%, cobalt at 16%. Higher shares would outrun supply, because few batteries have yet come back. Lead, whose recycling loop has run for a century, gets 85% from the same year.
cards.move: A target reveals what supply the rule-makers believe exists.
cards.trap: Assuming a green law would demand a large recycled share at once.
cards.reference: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning batteries and waste batteries, Article 8, 2023

cards.question: Should carmakers be barred from gluing battery cells into packs that cannot be taken apart?
sides: Yes, require packs that come apart
cards.answer: A pack foamed or glued solid turns one failed cell into a scrapped battery, and denies repairers and second-life users the good cells beside it. Recyclers must shred everything together and sort it afterwards. Designing for disassembly costs little when drawn up at the start and a fortune when attempted at the end.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, how often packs fail before the car decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Dropping modules, brackets and fasteners lets the same cells carry the car further for less money, and that is what gets people out of petrol cars. Shredding works whatever holds the cells together, and packs now mostly outlast the cars around them. A rule fixed today would freeze pack design while it is still improving fast.
cards.reference: Thompson et al., The importance of design in lithium ion battery recycling: a critical review, Green Chemistry, 2020

cards.question: Hard-rock lithium ore often holds about 0.5% lithium. How many times richer is LiFePO4 cathode powder (Li 7, Fe 56, P 31, O 16)?
cards.answer: 4.4% / 0.5% = 8.8 times richer.
cards.move: Judge a waste stream as an ore: its grade matters more than its origin.
cards.trap: Assuming a battery's waste must be poorer in metal than a mine.
cards.hint: Work out lithium's share of the powder's mass first.
steps: Lithium's share: 7 / 158 = about 4.4%.
4.4% / 0.5% = 8.8 times richer.
cards.source: Kesler et al., Ore Geology Reviews, 2012
cards.reference: Kesler, Gruber, Medina, Keoleian, Everson & Wallington, Global lithium resources: Relative importance of pegmatite, brine and other deposits, Ore Geology Reviews, 2012

cards.question: Why does American television run at 59.94 fields a second instead of a round 60?
cards.answer: Because of colour, in 1953. The colour signal rode on a second wave near 3.58 MHz, which clashed with the 4.5 MHz sound carrier to make visible patterns. Retuning the sound would have broken existing black-and-white sets, so engineers slowed the picture by 0.1%. Editing software still offers 29.97 frames a second.
cards.move: Compatibility with what people already own usually beats elegance.
cards.reference: Poynton, Digital Video and HD: Algorithms and Interfaces, 2nd edition, Morgan Kaufmann, 2012

cards.question: Why could a 60 Hz tube television show motion more sharply than a 60 Hz flat screen?
cards.answer: Because the tube flashed and the flat screen holds. A tube's phosphor glowed for a millisecond or two, then went dark; an LCD or OLED keeps each frame lit for the full 16.7 ms. Eyes tracking a moving object slide across that held image, smearing it. Makers now insert black frames to imitate the flash.
cards.move: What stays still while you move smears; brief glimpses stay sharp.
cards.reference: Kurita, Moving picture quality improvement for hold-type AM-LCDs, SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers 32, 2001

cards.question: True or false: people can see flicker artefacts on a display refreshing 500 times a second?
cards.answer: True. In a 2015 study, viewers spotted artefacts at 500 Hz when their eyes swept across a high-contrast edge: each flash landed on a different spot of the retina, leaving a trail of copies. With a steady gaze, flicker fuses near 50 to 90 Hz. A sweeping eye turns flashes into a dotted line.
cards.move: A threshold found in one condition is not a threshold in all of them.
cards.trap: False, anchored on the idea that eyes top out near 60 Hz.

cards.question: European television showed 24-frame-per-second films at 25 frames per second. How many minutes did a 120-minute film last?
cards.move: A small change of rate, applied to everything, adds up to minutes.
cards.trap: Assuming the length stays the same because every frame is shown.
cards.hint: Count the frames first: they do not change, only how fast they go by.
steps: The film holds 120 x 60 x 24 = 172,800 frames.
At 25 frames a second: 172,800 / 25 = 6,912 seconds.
cards.reference: Ascher & Pincus, The Filmmaker's Handbook, 4th edition, Plume, 2012

cards.question: In NVIDIA's 2019 aiming experiments, which helped players hit targets more?
cards.answer: Cutting 30 ms of delay. The researchers varied delay and refresh rate separately, which ordinary hardware rarely does, since faster screens usually also cut delay. Removing 30 ms improved aiming more than raising the refresh rate above 60 Hz. Much of the edge players credit to smoother motion may come from the screen answering sooner.
cards.move: When two improvements always arrive together, test them apart before crediting either.
cards.trap: Refresh rate, because smoother motion is what players can see.
cards.reference: Spjut et al., Latency of 30 ms Benefits First Person Targeting Tasks More Than Refresh Rate Above 60 Hz, SIGGRAPH Asia Technical Briefs, 2019

cards.question: How does a phone or watch screen manage to refresh just once a second when idle?
cards.answer: By holding each pixel's charge with transistors that barely leak. Ordinary polysilicon transistors leak, so the image must be redrawn many times a second or it fades. LTPO panels mix in oxide transistors, whose leakage is tiny, so a frame can sit for a full second. Apple's first always-on watch, in 2019, relied on it.
cards.move: To save effort, first make each result last longer between efforts.
cards.reference: https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2019/09/apple-unveils-apple-watch-series-5/

cards.question: Where did the open standard for variable refresh on gaming monitors come from?
cards.answer: From laptop power saving. Embedded DisplayPort, the link inside laptops, let a panel stretch the pause between frames to save energy. In 2014 AMD showed the trick could make a monitor wait for the graphics card rather than tick on a fixed clock; VESA made it Adaptive-Sync. Nvidia's G-Sync module had arrived months earlier.
cards.move: Look for tomorrow's feature in yesterday's efficiency trick.
cards.reference: VESA, VESA Adds Adaptive-Sync to Popular DisplayPort Video Standard, press release, 12 May 2014

cards.question: Which upgrade cuts the time between frames more: 30 to 60 Hz, or 60 to 360 Hz?
cards.answer: 30 to 60 Hz. Frame time is one second divided by the rate: 30 Hz gives 33.3 ms and 60 Hz gives 16.7, a saving of 16.7 ms. Going from 60 to 360 Hz takes 16.7 ms down to 2.8, saving 13.9. Each doubling saves half what the last one did.
cards.move: When a rate rises, compare the time it saves, not the rates.
cards.trap: A sixfold jump in rate looks bigger than a mere doubling.
cards.reference: Larrick & Soll, The MPG Illusion, Science 320, 2008

cards.question: In 2013 reviewers captured what two linked AMD graphics cards really showed on screen. How did that compare with software frame counters?
options: It fell well short of them
cards.answer: It fell well short of them. Counters such as FRAPS logged frames as the game handed them over, but with two cards taking turns many frames reached the screen as runts, slivers a few pixel rows tall, or not at all. PC Perspective's capture method discarded those, and AMD shipped a frame-pacing fix that summer.
cards.move: Measure where the result is used, not where it is produced.
cards.trap: Trusting the counter, since it counts every frame the game made.
cards.reference: https://pcper.com/2013/03/frame-rating-dissected-full-details-on-capture-based-graphics-performance-testing/6/

cards.question: True or false: a film projector running at 24 frames a second flashes light onto the screen 24 times a second?
cards.answer: False. A spinning shutter blanks the light while each frame is pulled into place, and extra blades interrupt each frame again while it stands still, so the screen flashes 48 or 72 times a second. Twenty-four images a second is enough for motion but not for flicker: at 24 flashes the picture would visibly throb.
cards.move: Two thresholds that sound alike can sit far apart.
cards.trap: Assuming one frame on film means one flash of light.
cards.reference: Happé, Basic Motion Picture Technology, Focal Press, 1971

cards.question: Why does each key on a touch-tone phone sound two notes at once?
cards.answer: So a voice cannot dial by accident. Single tones turn up in speech and music, so Bell Labs gave each key one note from a low group and one from a high group, none a harmonic of another: the 1 key is 697 plus 1,209 hertz. Speech rarely produces that exact pair.
cards.move: Make a signal something the noise around it cannot imitate.
cards.reference: Schenker, Pushbutton Calling with a Two-Group Voice-Frequency Code, Bell System Technical Journal, 1960

cards.question: How does a landline keep a man's voice deep when it cuts every sound below 300 hertz?
cards.answer: The listener's brain puts it back. A man's voice has its lowest note, the fundamental, near 120 hertz, plus harmonics at whole multiples: 240, 360, 480 and up. The brain reads their spacing and hears the missing note. The deepest sound in the call never travels down the wire.
cards.move: Sometimes the most important part of a signal is inferred, not sent.
cards.reference: Plack, The Sense of Hearing, 3rd edition, Routledge, 2018

cards.question: Why did an old landline phone keep working when a power cut blacked out the house?
cards.answer: Its power came down the line. Exchanges fed every line from their own battery rooms at about 48 volts, kept negative to slow corrosion of the copper. Digital lines run on household electricity, so as Britain retires its copper network, providers must offer vulnerable customers at least an hour of backup for emergency calls.
cards.move: When a service moves to new wiring, check what the old wiring quietly supplied.
cards.source: Ofcom, emergency calls during power cuts, 2018
cards.reference: Ofcom, Protecting access to emergency organisations when there is a power cut at the customer's premises, 2018

cards.question: True or false: in 2002 the US Congress declared Antonio Meucci the inventor of the telephone?
cards.answer: False. Only the House of Representatives acted, with a resolution that has no force of law: it honoured Meucci and said his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged. It noted that had he paid $10 to keep his 1871 notice of invention alive, Bell's patent could not have been issued.
cards.move: Before repeating what a body declared, read what the document says.
cards.trap: Mistaking a one-chamber resolution, retold in headlines, for a legal ruling.
cards.reference: US House of Representatives, H.Res. 269, 107th Congress, 2002

cards.question: When US towns switched telephone exchanges to automatic dialling, cutting operator jobs, what happened to employment among the next generation of young women?
options: It held, as they found other work
It fell with the lost operator jobs
cards.answer: It held. Economists comparing cities switched at different times between 1920 and 1940 found cutovers cut young women's operator jobs by 50 to 80%, yet later cohorts were no less likely to work: they moved into clerical and service jobs. The cost fell on operators already in post, more of whom ended in worse-paid work.
cards.move: Count what people did next, not only the jobs that vanished.
cards.trap: It fell, since every lost operator job looks like a lost worker.
cards.source: Feigenbaum & Gross, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024
cards.reference: Feigenbaum & Gross, Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024

cards.question: A phone channel carries sound up to 4,000 hertz, sampled at twice that rate in 8-bit samples. How many kbit/s for 24 calls?
cards.answer: 24 calls × 64 kbit/s = 1,536 kbit/s.
cards.move: Find the rate for one, then multiply by how many share the line.
cards.trap: Multiplying 4,000 by 8 bits and forgetting to double the sampling rate.
cards.hint: A signal must be sampled at least twice as often as its highest pitch.
steps: Sampling at twice 4,000 hertz: 8,000 samples a second.
8,000 samples × 8 bits = 64 kbit/s for one call.
24 calls × 64 kbit/s = 1,536 kbit/s.
cards.reference: ITU-T Recommendation G.711, Pulse code modulation (PCM) of voice frequencies, 1988

cards.question: True or false: on the classic digital phone network, calls between North America and Europe must be converted between two voice encodings?
cards.answer: True. Both squeeze loudness onto a curve, with fine steps for whispers and coarse ones for shouts, but on different curves: North America and Japan use mu-law, Europe and most of the world A-law. Every sample crossing between the two regions is translated at a gateway, millions a second on a busy route.
cards.move: Something that works seamlessly may be hiding a translator in the middle.
cards.trap: Assuming a network that connects everyone must share one format.
cards.reference: Bellamy, Digital Telephony, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2000

cards.question: With every mast powered and undamaged, why do phone networks still jam in the hour after a disaster?
options: They are sized for callers acting independently
Emergency calls are given most of the lines
Crowded signals interfere with one another
cards.answer: They are sized for independent callers. Since A. K. Erlang's work in 1917, engineers have provided lines for the chance that unrelated calls overlap: a small share of subscribers at once. A disaster makes everyone call in the same minutes. On 7 July 2005, London's mobile networks were swamped within minutes of the bombs.
cards.move: Capacity built for separate chances fails when one event moves everyone together.
cards.trap: Blaming priority for emergency calls rather than everyone calling at once.
cards.reference: London Assembly, Report of the 7 July Review Committee, Greater London Authority, 2006

cards.question: Why were Bell System telephones built to survive decades of drops and daily use?
options: Makers simply built things better then
Bell owned the phones and paid repairs
cards.answer: Because Bell owned them. For most of the 20th century Americans rented their phones from the Bell System, which made them through Western Electric and paid for every repair. A phone that lasted thirty years was profit; one that broke was cost. Once customers could buy their own, throwaway phones arrived.
cards.move: To predict how long a thing lasts, ask who pays when it breaks.
cards.trap: Crediting the era's craftsmanship when the repair bill decided it.
cards.reference: Wu, The Master Switch: The Rise and Fall of Information Empires, Knopf, 2010

cards.question: Why did New York City get the area code 212 in 1947, rather than, say, 909?
cards.answer: Because 212 was among the quickest to dial. A rotary dial sends one pulse per unit, ten for 0, so 2-1-2 took five pulses against 28 for 9-0-9. The 1947 plan gave big cities the fastest: Los Angeles 213, Chicago 312. Each had 0 or 1 in the middle, unlike any local exchange code.
cards.move: Where every user pays a small cost, give the cheapest option to the most users.
cards.reference: Nunn, Nationwide Numbering Plan, Bell System Technical Journal, 1952

cards.question: Where, and for what job, was the first finger-operated capacitive touchscreen built?
cards.answer: At the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, England, for air traffic control. In 1965 E. A. Johnson described a screen that sensed the electrical effect of a fingertip, letting controllers pick flights by touching them instead of typing. Versions of it served British air traffic control into the 1990s, decades before smartphones.
cards.move: Ask who needed a technology first; it is rarely who uses it now.
cards.reference: Johnson, Touch display: a novel input/output device for computers, Electronics Letters 1(8), 1965

cards.question: Where did the multi-finger gestures on the first iPhone come from?
cards.answer: Largely from a PhD born of hand pain. Wayne Westerman, whose repetitive strain injury made typing hard, wrote his 1999 University of Delaware thesis on tracking many fingers on a touch surface. With his adviser John Elias he founded FingerWorks to sell gesture keyboards. Apple bought the company in 2005, two years before the iPhone.
cards.move: Tools built for people with a limitation often end up serving everyone.
cards.source: Westerman, PhD thesis, University of Delaware, 1999
cards.reference: Westerman, Hand Tracking, Finger Identification, and Chordic Manipulation on a Multi-Touch Surface, PhD thesis, University of Delaware, 1999

cards.question: Why did folding phones have to abandon the invisible conductor used in ordinary touchscreens?
cards.answer: Because that conductor, indium tin oxide, is brittle. It is a ceramic that carries current yet lets light through, laid in patterned films a fraction of a micrometre thick, and bent over and over it cracks. Folding screens moved to meshes of metal lines too fine to see, or to silver nanowires.
cards.move: A material chosen for one virtue brings its weaknesses along.
cards.reference: Hecht, Hu & Irvin, Emerging Transparent Electrodes Based on Thin Films of Carbon Nanotubes, Graphene, and Metallic Nanostructures, Advanced Materials 23, 2011

cards.question: True or false: people can notice a 10-millisecond lag when dragging an object across a touchscreen?
cards.answer: True. In Microsoft Research tests, people dragging on a 1 ms prototype noticed added lag of about 6 ms on average, and as little as 2 ms, while typical devices of 2012 lagged 50 to 200 ms. Under a moving finger, lag shows up as distance: the object trails behind the fingertip like a leash.
cards.move: Delay is invisible in a reply and obvious in anything that follows you.
cards.trap: False, anchored on the tenth of a second usually called instant.
cards.reference: Ng, Lepinski, Wigdor, Sanders & Dietz, Designing for Low-Latency Direct-Touch Input, ACM UIST, 2012

cards.question: True or false: most of the error when tapping small targets comes from fingertips simply being too wide?
cards.answer: False. Holz and Baudisch found most of the error is systematic: each person, at each finger angle, lands a consistent distance off target, because the screen reads the centre of the contact patch, not the point being aimed at. Correcting for finger posture roughly doubled accuracy. The finger was steady; the screen's guess was off.
cards.move: Errors that repeat the same way are a bias you can correct.
cards.trap: True, blaming fat fingers, the explanation everyone repeats.
cards.reference: Holz & Baudisch, The Generalized Perceived Input Point Model and How to Double Touch Accuracy by Extracting Fingerprints, ACM CHI, 2010

cards.question: Where is the touch sensor in most recent phone screens, if not in a layer on top?
cards.answer: Inside the display itself. Since the iPhone 5 in 2012, many LCD phones use in-cell touch: electrodes that set the pixels' voltage double as touch sensors, and the chip alternates drawing and sensing within every frame. OLED phones build the sensor straight onto the thin seal over the pixels, saving a sheet of glass.
cards.move: When two jobs need the same part, take turns rather than duplicate it.
cards.reference: Apple, Apple Introduces iPhone 5, press release, 12 September 2012

cards.question: A touch sensor reads each row and each column on its own. Two fingers land at once. How many possible touch points can it compute?
cards.answer: Four, two of them ghosts. Two rows and two columns register, and they cross at four places; the sensor cannot tell which diagonal pair is real. Such grids manage one reliable touch. Phones instead measure every crossing of a row and a column, a mutual-capacitance scan, so each finger appears where it is.
cards.move: Totals for the rows and the columns do not fix what sits inside.
cards.trap: Two fingers seem to make two readings, one each.
cards.reference: Walker, A review of technologies for sensing contact location on the surface of a display, Journal of the Society for Information Display 20(8), 2012

cards.question: How did the PLATO IV teaching terminals of 1972 tell where a student's finger touched the screen?
options: The finger's effect on an electric field
Beams of infrared light it interrupted
Pressure pushing two conductive sheets together
cards.answer: Beams of infrared light it interrupted. A frame round the plasma screen shone a 16 by 16 grid of infrared beams across its face; a fingertip broke one beam each way, fixing its square. Illinois students answered lessons by pointing, decades before phones. Many large kiosks and whiteboards still work this way.
cards.move: The method that won is rarely the first one that worked.
cards.trap: Today's phones sense a finger's charge, so that method comes to mind.
cards.reference: Dear, The Friendly Orange Glow: The Untold Story of the PLATO System and the Dawn of Cyberculture, Pantheon Books, 2017

cards.question: A Wacom-type stylus reports its position and how hard it presses, with no battery inside. What powers it?
options: Nothing; the screen just senses the nib
Energy stored while it sits docked
A magnetic field from behind the screen
cards.answer: A magnetic field from behind the screen. A grid of coils under the display pulses a field; a coil and capacitor in the pen resonate with it and send back a faint signal the grid locates. Pressing the nib alters that reply. Samsung's first Galaxy Note pen, in 2011, worked this way.
cards.move: Before assuming a gadget carries its own power, look for what feeds it.
cards.trap: A pen that clips into its slot seems to charge there.
cards.reference: https://support.wacom.com/hc/en-us/articles/1500006270401-What-is-the-EMR-Electro-Magnetic-Resonance-method-incorporated-in-a-pen-tablet

cards.question: Should car safety ratings require physical buttons for key controls instead of touchscreens?
cards.answer: A button can be found by feel; a touchscreen needs eyes off the road. In a 2022 Swedish magazine test at 110 km/h, a set of tasks took 10 seconds in a 2005 Volvo and 44.6 seconds, about 1.4 km, in an MG Marvel R. Euro NCAP's ratings began rewarding buttons in 2026.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on measured glances away, not on hardware.
cards.counterpoint: One magazine's small test is thin evidence. Owners learn their layouts, and voice control and steering-wheel switches already cover the common tasks. Screens let makers fix and add functions by software update, where buttons for everything cost money and dashboard space. Ratings should score measured distraction, whatever the hardware, not freeze one design.
cards.source: Vi Bilägare, buttons versus touchscreens test, 2022
cards.reference: https://www.vibilagare.se/english/physical-buttons-outperform-touchscreens-new-cars-test-finds

cards.question: Why did Meta train its small Llama 3 model on far more text than the 'optimal' recipe says?
cards.answer: Because that recipe minimises the wrong bill. The Chinchilla rule, about 20 word-pieces per adjustable number, buys the best model for a fixed training budget. A model is trained once and used billions of times, and small ones cost less to run. Meta fed its 8-billion-number model over 15 trillion word-pieces, nearly 1,900 per number.
cards.move: Optimise for the cost you pay most often, not the one you pay first.
cards.reference: Meta, Introducing Meta Llama 3: The most capable openly available LLM to date, 2024

cards.question: What happens when AI models learn only from text written by earlier AI models, generation after generation?
cards.answer: They collapse. Each generation slightly over-represents what is common and drops what is rare, so unusual cases vanish first, then variety itself. In a 2024 Nature study, text that began on medieval architecture had turned, nine generations later, into a list of jackrabbits with different-coloured tails.
cards.move: A copy of a copy keeps the average and loses the edges.

cards.question: Who taught ChatGPT's safety filter what violent and abusive text looks like?
cards.answer: Workers in Nairobi. To teach a filter to catch harmful text, OpenAI needed tens of thousands of examples labelled by hand; through an outsourcing firm, Sama, Kenyan staff read and tagged passages describing sexual abuse, torture and suicide. In 2023 TIME reported their take-home pay at about $1.32 to $2 an hour.
cards.move: Ask who did the unpleasant work that makes a product feel clean.
cards.reference: Perrigo, Exclusive: OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour to Make ChatGPT Less Toxic, TIME, 2023

cards.question: True or false: more than nine in ten of the words GPT-3 was trained on were English?
cards.answer: True: about 93% by word count, as OpenAI's GPT-3 paper reports; every other language together made up the remaining 7%. The model's picture of the world was drawn mostly from English pages, which is part of why early chatbots handled other languages, and the places where they are spoken, less well.
cards.move: Ask what the sample was made of before trusting its picture of the world.
cards.trap: False, picturing a multilingual web rather than the text actually chosen.
cards.reference: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2020

cards.question: Should AI companies need permission, and pay, to train on copyrighted books and articles?
cards.answer: A model that has absorbed a million books competes with their authors for the same readers, and its makers pay for chips, power and staff but not for the text that gives it value. Licensing markets already exist, with news agencies and publishers selling training data, so asking permission is possible; it is only dearer.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether the model's output replaces the books decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Reading to learn has never needed permission, and a model mostly keeps patterns, not copies. In 2025 a US judge ruled that training on lawfully bought books was fair use, while pirated copies led to a $1.5 billion settlement. Require a licence for every text ever written and only the richest firms could afford to train at all.
cards.source: US Copyright Office, AI report part 3, 2025
cards.reference: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training, pre-publication version, 2025

cards.question: How many days would 1,000 chips at 100 trillion operations a second take to train 70 billion adjustable numbers on 1.4 trillion word-pieces?
cards.answer: 5.9 million / 86,400 = about 68 days.
cards.move: Price a big job by its unit cost times its count before guessing.
cards.trap: Counting one operation per number per word-piece instead of about six.
cards.hint: Each word-piece read in training costs about six operations for every adjustable number.
steps: About 6 operations per number per word-piece: 6 × 70 billion × 1.4 trillion ≈ 5.9 × 10^23.
1,000 chips × 10^14 = 10^17 operations a second.
5.9 × 10^23 / 10^17 = 5.9 million seconds.
5.9 million / 86,400 = about 68 days.
cards.reference: Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, arXiv:2203.15556, 2022

cards.question: Why does the same message cost more, and fit less, when written to a chatbot in some languages?
cards.answer: Because its word-pieces were learned mostly from English. The tokeniser, which chops text into the chunks a model reads, gives common English words one piece but splits rarer scripts into many. A 2023 study found the same text could take up to 15 times as many pieces. They pay more per sentence.
cards.move: A tool shaped by its commonest users charges everyone else a hidden tax.
cards.reference: Petrov, La Malfa, Torr & Bibi, Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages, NeurIPS, 2023

cards.question: The computing power used to train leading AI models has grown about 4 to 5 times a year. What is that over five years?
cards.answer: About 2,000 times. Growth of 4.5 times a year compounds: 4.5 multiplied by itself five times is about 1,850. Epoch AI's range of 4 to 5 a year gives 1,000 to 3,000 times over five years. Five doublings would give 32; five quadruplings already give 1,024.
cards.move: Multiply growth rates together; never multiply them by the years.
cards.trap: Multiplying the yearly rate by the number of years: five times five.
cards.reference: https://epoch.ai/publications/training-compute-of-frontier-ai-models-grows-by-4-5x-per-year

cards.question: As language models grew, some skills seemed to appear suddenly at a certain size. What did a 2023 study mainly blame?
options: A size at which reasoning switches on
Test answers leaking into training text
cards.answer: All-or-nothing scoring. If a model must get all 5 digits of an answer right, and its accuracy per digit climbs steadily from 50% to 90%, its score leaps from 3% to 59%. Given partial credit, the same models improved smoothly. The jump was in the ruler, not in the model.
cards.move: A score that needs every step right turns steady progress into a sudden leap.
cards.trap: Reading a sharp jump in scores as a sharp change in ability.

diagram.caption: The same steady gains per digit look like a sudden leap when all five must be right.

cards.reference: Schaeffer, Miranda & Koyejo, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?, NeurIPS, 2023

cards.question: Why do AI labs delete near-identical passages from the text they train models on?
cards.answer: Because repeated text gets memorised and recited. Lee and colleagues found one 61-word English sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4, a widely used web dataset. Models trained after duplicates were removed emitted memorised text about ten times less often. The web's boilerplate is what a model learns by heart.
cards.move: Whatever is repeated most is learned by rote, not understood.
cards.reference: Lee et al., Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better, ACL, 2022

cards.question: How did a Chinese typewriter cope with a script of thousands of characters?
cards.answer: By choosing rather than pressing. A tray held a couple of thousand metal characters; the typist slid a selector over the grid and pressed a lever to strike the chosen one onto the page. From the 1950s typists arranged trays so characters used together sat side by side: predictive text in metal.
cards.move: When choices outnumber buttons, put the likely ones closest.
cards.source: Mullaney, The Chinese Typewriter, MIT Press, 2017
cards.reference: Mullaney, The Chinese Typewriter: A History, MIT Press, 2017

cards.question: In 1984, NSA engineers found Soviet bugs inside 16 IBM typewriters used by US diplomats in the USSR. What did they capture?
cards.answer: Every keystroke. Hidden in a metal bar running across each machine, sensors read the movements that selected each character and radioed the text out in short bursts. Some had been in place since 1976, capturing words before they could be encrypted. It was the first known electronic keylogger.
cards.move: Guard the place where a secret is written, not only where it travels.
cards.trap: Room conversations, the job of a classic hidden microphone.
cards.source: Maneki, NSA Center for Cryptologic History, 2007
cards.reference: Maneki, Learning from the Enemy: The GUNMAN Project, NSA Center for Cryptologic History, 2007

cards.question: True or false: on the first commercially successful typewriter, the typist could not see the words being typed?
cards.answer: True. The 1874 Sholes and Glidden, sold by Remington, struck upwards against the underside of the paper roll, so each line stayed hidden until the typist lifted the carriage. It typed only capitals, too. Machines that showed the text as it was typed took over only in the early 1900s, led by the Underwood.
cards.move: What seems essential in a tool was often added a generation later.
cards.trap: Assuming a writing machine would, of course, show its writing.
cards.reference: Current, The Typewriter and the Men Who Made It, University of Illinois Press, 1954

cards.question: On many typewriters, which key typed the number 1?
cards.answer: The lowercase l. Many machines had no key for 1, because every key needed its own metal arm and a small l looked close enough. An exclamation mark was an apostrophe, a backspace and a full stop. The same thrift left one straight quotation mark for opening and closing, and computer keyboards kept it.
cards.move: Where users can improvise a missing part, makers will leave it out.
cards.reference: Houston, Shady Characters: The Secret Life of Punctuation, Symbols, and Other Typographical Marks, W. W. Norton, 2013

cards.question: In the 1880s, what could it mean to hire a typewriter?
cards.answer: To hire a person, often a young woman: the word meant the machine and its operator into the 1890s. Typing was a new job that no male trade had claimed, and women cost less than male clerks, so offices filled with them. By 1930 over nine in ten US typists and stenographers were women.
cards.move: New jobs with no tradition are where outsiders get in first.
cards.source: Davies, Woman's Place Is at the Typewriter, 1982
cards.reference: Davies, Woman's Place Is at the Typewriter: Office Work and Office Workers, 1870–1930, Temple University Press, 1982

cards.question: How did IBM's 1961 Selectric print any of 88 characters without a single typebar?
cards.answer: By tilting and turning a ball. Its golf-ball element carried four rows of 22 characters; each key set a few latches, and linkages called whiffletrees summed them into one of four tilts and one of 22 turns, much as weighted digits sum to a number. No bars could clash, and fonts swapped in seconds.
cards.move: A choice among many can be built from a few small yes-or-no steps.
cards.reference: Beeching, Century of the Typewriter, Heinemann, 1974

cards.question: Why did 1980s Romania make typewriter owners register their machines with the police and hand over typed samples?
cards.answer: Because every typewriter signs its work. Worn, bent or slightly misaligned letters make each machine's print unique, so a sample on file could tie an anonymous leaflet to one machine. A 1983 decree required registration, a permit and fresh samples each year. In a police archive, a typeface became a fingerprint.
cards.move: Anything that wears in its own way leaves a signature behind.
cards.reference: Deletant, Ceaușescu and the Securitate: Coercion and Dissent in Romania, 1965–1989, Hurst, 1995

cards.question: True or false: leaving a wider gap after a full stop than between words began with the typewriter?
cards.answer: False. Hand-set printing, above all in the 19th century, often put a wider space after a full stop than between words. Typing manuals copied that habit with the only unit a typewriter had, one fixed character width, so the wide gap became two keystrokes. The typewriter did not invent the gap; it made it countable.
cards.move: Before accepting a tidy origin story, look at what came before it.
cards.trap: Crediting fixed-width letters, a neat reason that nobody checks against print.
cards.source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style
cards.reference: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style, 3rd edition, Hartley & Marks, 2004

cards.question: Did QWERTY survive because typists and employers locked themselves into a worse keyboard?
cards.answer: Once typists trained on QWERTY and offices bought QWERTY machines, each side's choice bound the other and nobody could switch alone, as the economist Paul David argued. US Navy trials in the 1940s reported that retraining typists on August Dvorak's layout quickly repaid its cost. A better design lost because it arrived second.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether any fair test showed the rival faster decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Liebowitz and Margolis traced those Navy trials to Dvorak himself, the layout's patent holder. A 1956 US government study under Earl Strong found retrained Dvorak typists no faster than QWERTY typists given the same extra training. Later tests show small gains at most. The layout that lost was never shown to be clearly better.
cards.source: Liebowitz & Margolis, Fable of the Keys, 1990
cards.reference: Liebowitz & Margolis, The Fable of the Keys, Journal of Law and Economics, 1990

cards.question: On a typical manual typewriter, what did pressing the shift key physically do?
options: It swapped in a second set of typebars
It raised the carriage or lowered the typebars
It turned each typebar's head halfway round
cards.answer: It moved the carriage or the typebars. Each bar carried two letters on one slug, capital above small, and shift lifted the carriage or dropped the basket of bars so the other half struck. One bar per key halved the moving parts. Lifting a whole carriage was heavy work for a little finger.
cards.move: When one part does two jobs, look for what moves to switch between them.
cards.trap: Picturing capitals as a separate set of letters needing their own parts.
cards.reference: Adler, The Writing Machine: A History of the Typewriter, Allen & Unwin, 1973

cards.question: Should courts use algorithmic risk scores when deciding bail?
cards.answer: The alternative to the algorithm is not neutrality, it is a tired judge before lunch. A score is at least consistent, auditable and testable — you can measure whether it is biased, which is more than anyone has ever been able to do to a bench.
cards.move: Auditable and fair are different properties. A model can be perfectly consistent about the wrong thing.
cards.counterpoint: A model trained on past arrests learns where police went, not where crime was, and then hands that pattern back wearing the authority of arithmetic. And the judge who follows it is answerable to nobody: the defendant cannot cross-examine a score, and the vendor will not release the weights.
cards.reference: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig & Mullainathan, Human Decisions and Machine Predictions, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2018

cards.question: Should an AI system be allowed to make a diagnosis without a doctor signing it off?
sides: No, keep a doctor in the loop
cards.answer: In several narrow tasks these systems already match specialists, and they do it at three in the morning in places with no specialist at all. Requiring a signature from someone who is not available is not a safety measure, it is a shortage dressed as one.
cards.move: The real question is not accuracy on average. It is what happens on the case that falls outside the training data.
cards.counterpoint: A doctor who signs off catches the case the model has never seen, and the model does not know which case that is. Add a rubber-stamping human and you get the worst of both: nobody actually checking, and nobody clearly responsible when it is wrong.
cards.reference: Topol, High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence, Nature Medicine, 2019

cards.question: Should political advertising be banned from targeting narrow groups?
cards.answer: A promise made to eight thousand people that nobody else ever sees cannot be checked, contradicted or held against you. Broadcast advertising was accountable precisely because everyone saw the same claim — remove that and a campaign can tell every group a different story.
cards.move: Both sides are describing the same feature: reaching a few people cheaply.
cards.counterpoint: Targeting is also what lets a small campaign reach the people it is actually for, without buying national airtime. Ban it and the advantage returns to whoever can already afford to talk to everyone, which is the incumbent.
cards.reference: Information Commissioner's Office, Democracy disrupted? Personal information and political influence, 2018

cards.question: A school of 2,000 screens every pupil for a condition that affects 1 in 500. The screen catches 90% of cases and wrongly flags 5%. A child is flagged. Odds they have it?
cards.answer: Four children in 2,000 have it and the screen finds three or four of them. But 5% of the other 1,996 — about 100 children — are flagged too. Roughly 3 real cases against 100 false ones: under one flagged child in twenty actually has it.
cards.move: How rare the thing is matters more than how good the test is.
cards.trap: Reading 90% as the chance the flag is right.
cards.simply: Picture a village of 2,000. Four people are ill. The machine points at those four — and at about a hundred healthy people as well. When it points at you, look around: you are standing in a crowd of roughly a hundred, and four of you are ill.

diagram.label: pupils screened
diagram.caption: Of 517 pupils flagged, 18 have it: about one in thirty.

cards.source: Base rate neglect in universal screening
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: Marco is 45, cycles to work and reads a lot about climate. Which is more likely?
options: He owns a car and has solar panels
cards.answer: Every person with a car and panels also has a car, so the second group sits entirely inside the first and cannot be larger. Adding a detail that fits the story makes a claim feel likelier while making it strictly less likely.
cards.move: Adding detail makes a claim more convincing and less probable at the same time.
cards.trap: The second one fits the picture better, so it feels more probable.
cards.simply: Every dog wearing a hat is a dog. So there can never be more dogs-in-hats than there are dogs. However well the hat fits the story.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: You are one of three finalists. A panel member privately tells you that one of the other two has been rejected. Have your chances improved?
cards.answer: They were always going to be able to name a rejected candidate among the other two, whoever wins — so hearing one name tells you nothing about you. Your one-in-three stands, and the remaining finalist now carries two-thirds.
cards.move: Information only moves the odds if it could have come out differently.
cards.trap: Two candidates left, so it feels like a coin flip.
cards.reference: Gardner, Mathematical Games, Scientific American, October 1959

cards.question: Order codes are generated at random from a million possibilities. After how many orders is a repeat more likely than not?
cards.answer: With n orders there are about n squared over two pairs that could clash, and a clash beats even odds once that count nears a million — around 1,200 orders. Collisions come from pairs, and pairs grow far faster than the list does.
cards.move: Coincidence needs far fewer people than anyone expects.
cards.trap: Thinking about your code, rather than every pair of codes.

diagram.caption: Out of a million possible codes, a repeat is more likely than not by 1,200 orders.

cards.source: The birthday bound, applied to identifiers
cards.reference: Diaconis & Mosteller, Methods for Studying Coincidences, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989

cards.question: "Vintage tools were better made — every one I own still works." What is wrong?
options: The broken ones were thrown away decades ago
cards.answer: You are looking at what survived fifty years of use and disposal. The badly made ones broke and went in the bin long ago, so the tools left to buy are the durable tail of their generation — not a fair picture of what was on sale.
cards.move: Anything you can still buy from 1960 is, by definition, what did not break.
cards.trap: The surviving objects are treated as a sample of what was made.
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: You took a new remedy on the very worst day of a cold, and felt clearly better the next morning. What is the safest reading?
options: The worst day is usually followed by a better one
It works but only when you are very ill
cards.answer: You reach for a remedy when you feel worst, and the worst point of anything that fluctuates is usually followed by improvement whatever you do. That is why almost every treatment tried at the bottom appears to work.
cards.move: Anything you try at your worst moment will seem to help.
cards.trap: The improvement is real, so it feels like it needs a cause.
cards.source: Regression to the mean in self-treatment
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: Rule: anyone hired without a degree must have five years' experience. Four files: no degree / has degree / six years' experience / two years' experience. Which two must you open?
cards.answer: The no-degree file could break it, so open that. The two-years file could break it if that person has no degree, so open that. The degree file is not covered by the rule, and six years' experience can never break it — checking those two can only confirm what you already believe.
cards.move: Look for the file that could prove you wrong, not the one that agrees.
cards.trap: Checking the case that would confirm the rule rather than break it.
cards.source: The Wason selection task, in a hiring file
cards.reference: Wason, Reasoning about a rule, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1968

cards.question: A delivery firm's on-time rate fell this year, although it improved in every single city it serves. Possible?
options: No, one of the numbers is wrong
Yes, if the mix of cities changed
cards.answer: If the firm grew fastest in its hardest cities, those now carry more weight in the total. Every city can improve while the overall average falls, because the average is over a different mix of deliveries than last year.
cards.move: A total and its parts can honestly point opposite ways.
cards.trap: Assuming the total has to move with its parts.
cards.simply: Two classes both got better at spelling this year. But the big struggling class grew and the small strong class shrank. The school's average went down. Everybody improved and the school looks worse.
cards.reference: Simpson, The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 1951

cards.question: Buy three, get the cheapest free. The items cost €10, €20 and €30. What is the discount?
cards.answer: You pay €50 instead of €60, so you save a sixth. One item in three is free, which sounds like 33% — but it is the cheapest item, and it was never a third of the money.
cards.move: One item in three free is nothing like a third off.
cards.trap: The word "free" attaches to an item, not to the bill.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A landfill fills in 40 years at current waste growth of 7% a year. At 10% growth, roughly how much sooner?
cards.answer: About eight years. What fills a landfill is the running total. At 7% growth, forty years add up to about 200 years of today's waste; at 10% the same total piles up in about 32 years. Three points on the growth rate take a fifth off the landfill's life.
cards.move: Small changes in a growth rate are large changes in the total.
cards.trap: Treating a few extra percent as a small change.
cards.simply: A pile that doubles every ten years is nothing for ages and then swallows the room. Make it double every seven instead and you do not add a little — you lose a decade.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A random quality check has passed 40 units in a row. Is the next more likely to fail?
options: Yes, the machine is warming up
cards.answer: If the checks really are independent, the line has no memory of the last 40. The run should make you ask a different question instead: whether the failure rate is lower than you assumed, or whether the check is actually testing anything.
cards.move: A run of luck does not owe you anything, but it might be telling you something else.
cards.trap: Feeling that a run has to even out.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Belief in the law of small numbers, Psychological Bulletin, 1971

cards.question: A city has spent €400m of a planned €1bn tunnel. New figures show it will never repay its cost. What should decide whether to continue?
options: Only the remaining €600m against the benefit
cards.answer: The €400m is gone whichever way you choose, so it cannot favour either. The only live question is whether the remaining €600m buys more than €600m of anything else. Counting the spent money is how projects that everyone knows are failing get finished.
cards.move: The money already spent has no vote.
cards.trap: The spent money feels like it would be wasted by stopping.
cards.reference: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985

cards.question: An estate agent shows you the most expensive house on the street first. Why?
options: Every later price is judged against it
cards.answer: The first number becomes the reference the rest are measured from, even when you know it was chosen to impress. The effect persists when people are warned about it, and when the anchor is plainly arbitrary.
cards.move: Whoever names the first number has already moved yours.
cards.trap: Believing your sense of a fair price is your own.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: After a widely reported plane crash, bookings fall and more people drive instead. What happens to total deaths?
options: They fall, flying is riskier for a while
They rise, because driving is more dangerous per kilometre
cards.answer: Road travel kills far more people per kilometre than flying. Measured after the 2001 attacks, the shift from planes to cars in the following months was estimated to have cost more American lives than were lost aboard the aircraft.
cards.move: The safest place after a plane crash is on a plane.
cards.trap: Fear tracks how vivid a risk is, not how large.
cards.reference: Gigerenzer, Out of the Frying Pan into the Fire: Behavioral Reactions to Terrorist Attacks, Risk Analysis, 2006

cards.question: A recruiter believes graduates of one university do better, so only interviews those. How could they ever discover they were wrong?
options: From the performance of who they hire
They could not — the test never runs
cards.answer: Everyone hired comes from that university, so every good hire confirms the rule and no rejected candidate ever gets to disprove it. The belief is not surviving tests; it is preventing them.
cards.move: Ask what result would have changed your mind. If none could, nothing is being tested.
cards.trap: A belief that keeps being confirmed feels like a belief that keeps being tested.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Judges were shown a sentencing demand rolled on dice before deciding a case. What happened?
options: Nothing — they are trained to ignore it
cards.answer: Experienced judges gave longer sentences after a high roll than a low one, knowing the number came from dice. Expertise does not remove the anchor; it makes people more certain they were not anchored.
cards.move: Whoever names a figure first has already moved the room, expert or not.
cards.trap: Assuming expertise protects against an irrelevant number.
cards.reference: Englich, Mussweiler & Strack, Playing Dice With Criminal Sentences, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2006

cards.question: A shop marks an item "was €200, now €80". Why does the crossed-out price work even when it was never charged?
options: People assume it is a real discount
It sets the number you judge €80 against
cards.answer: The first figure becomes the reference point, and €80 is then read as a saving rather than as a price. It works on people who doubt the original price was ever real — which is why the practice is regulated rather than merely mocked.
cards.move: The crossed-out number is not information. It is the ruler.
cards.trap: Thinking the effect depends on believing the old price.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: A camera that identifies faces with 99% accuracy scans 100,000 travellers to find one wanted person. Roughly how many alarms will be wrong?
cards.answer: One per cent of 100,000 innocent people is about 1,000 false alarms, against the single real match. Almost every alarm is wrong — not because the camera is bad, but because there is only one of them and a hundred thousand of us.
cards.move: A very accurate test looking for something very rare is mostly wrong.
cards.trap: Hearing 99% and picturing a system that is almost always right.
cards.source: Base rate neglect applied to screening
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: A hiring tool spots the 5% of applicants who become top performers, with 80% accuracy. You are flagged. What are your odds?
cards.answer: Of 1,000 applicants, 50 are top performers and 40 get flagged. But 20% of the other 950 get flagged too: 190 more. So about 40 of 230 flags are real — under one in five.
cards.move: Ask how rare the thing is before you ask how good the test is.
cards.trap: Reading the tool's accuracy as the chance it is right about you.
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: You think a colleague dislikes you, and start noticing the evidence. Why does the evidence keep arriving?
options: Because you are only counting what fits
Because they can tell you suspect it
cards.answer: The neutral moments are not stored, so the pile can only grow one way. The test that would tell you something is looking for the times they went out of their way for you — and noticing whether you had been discounting them.
cards.move: A theory that only ever gains evidence is not being tested.
cards.trap: Treating a growing pile of confirming moments as proof.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Should social media have a legal minimum age of 16?
cards.answer: A minimum age treats a designed-to-be-addictive product the way we treat alcohol and gambling. Parents cannot realistically opt one child out of where every classmate lives, so the choice is not free in practice — a floor removes that trap for everyone at once.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the enforcement question is the one that decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Bans push teenagers to lie about their age rather than stay off, which makes them less visible and less protected. Enforcement means verifying identity for everyone, handing platforms more personal data than they hold now. And the evidence on harm is contested — much of it is correlational, and the effect sizes found are often small.
cards.reference: Orben & Przybylski, The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019

cards.question: A self-driving car must choose: swerve and kill one, or continue and kill five. What should it be built to do?
cards.answer: A machine should do what a clear-headed person would want in advance, and almost nobody, asked in the abstract, prefers five deaths to one. Building anything else means writing a rule that some lives count less because of where they are standing.
cards.move: The gap between what people say they want and what they would buy is the whole problem.
cards.counterpoint: People say they want the car to minimise deaths, and then say they would not buy that car. A vehicle that might sacrifice its passenger will not sell, so the ethical version never reaches the road and the far larger benefit — fewer crashes overall — never arrives.
cards.reference: Bonnefon, Shariff & Rahwan, The social dilemma of autonomous vehicles, Science, 2016

cards.question: Should people be paid for donating a kidney?
cards.answer: People die on waiting lists while healthy kidneys go undonated. Iran, the one country with a regulated payment system, reported its kidney waiting list cleared by 1999. We already pay surgeons, nurses and hospitals — the only person forbidden to benefit is the one taking the risk.
cards.move: Both sides agree people are dying. They disagree about what counts as a free choice.
cards.counterpoint: A price makes the poor the supply. If the offer is life-changing money, refusing stops being a free choice, and the burden of organ removal lands almost entirely on people with no other options. Consent given under financial pressure is the thing the rule exists to protect.
cards.reference: Ghods & Savaj, Iranian Model of Paid and Regulated Living-Unrelated Kidney Donation, Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2006

cards.question: Should we bring back extinct species we have the technology to revive?
cards.answer: We caused most of these extinctions, and restoring a lost species can repair an ecosystem that lost its engineer. The techniques developed also help species that are still alive but failing.
cards.move: The strongest objection is not scientific. It is what the promise does to the incentive.
cards.counterpoint: The money is finite, and it competes directly with protecting species that still exist. A revived animal returns to a habitat that has moved on without it, and the promise of reversal weakens the argument for not causing extinctions in the first place.
cards.reference: Bennett et al., Spending limited resources on de-extinction could lead to net biodiversity loss, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017

cards.question: How many tonnes of coffee does Italy drink in a year, in thousands of tonnes?
cards.answer: x 365 = ~300,000 tonnes. The reported figure is around 370,000.
cards.move: Two espressos a day, times a country, is a third of a million tonnes.
cards.hint: Start from cups per person per day and the grams in a cup.
steps: About 59 million people, and roughly 2 servings a day on average across everyone.
An espresso uses about 7 g, so ~14 g per person per day.
14 g x 59 million = ~830 tonnes a day.
x 365 = ~300,000 tonnes. The reported figure is around 370,000.
cards.reference: International Coffee Organization, domestic consumption statistics, 2019

cards.question: How many bricks are in a typical four-storey apartment building, in thousands?
cards.answer: 2,500 x 60 = ~150,000. With party walls and returns, a few hundred thousand.
cards.move: The building you live in is a quarter of a million bricks somebody laid by hand.
cards.hint: Work out the wall area, then bricks per square metre.
steps: A brick face is about 21 x 6 cm with mortar, so ~60 bricks per square metre per leaf.
A 20 m x 12 m building, 12 m tall: perimeter 64 m x 12 m = ~770 square metres of wall.
Two leaves and internal walls, call it ~2,500 square metres of brickwork.
2,500 x 60 = ~150,000. With party walls and returns, a few hundred thousand.
cards.reference: BS 3921:1985, Specification for clay bricks

cards.question: How many words does a person speak in a day?
cards.move: Men and women came out within a few hundred words of each other when it was measured.
cards.hint: Speaking runs at roughly 130 words a minute; the question is how many minutes.
steps: Recorded speech runs about 130 words per minute.
People actually speak for perhaps 2 hours of a waking day.
cards.reference: Mehl, Vazire, Ramírez-Esparza, Slatcher & Pennebaker, Are Women Really More Talkative Than Men?, Science, 2007

cards.question: How many passenger journeys does one city bus make in its working life, in millions?
cards.answer: A bus serves 12 to 15 years: ~1.7 million boardings.
cards.move: One bus moves more people in its life than live in Milan.
cards.hint: Journeys per day, times days per year, times years of service.
steps: A busy city bus carries roughly 400 boardings a day.
It runs around 320 days a year: ~128,000 a year.
A bus serves 12 to 15 years: ~1.7 million boardings.
cards.reference: Department for Transport, Annual bus statistics: England, 2019

cards.question: How many hours of video are uploaded to the world's video platforms every minute, in thousands?
cards.answer: That is more than a month of footage produced every minute.
cards.move: More video is uploaded each minute than one person could watch in a month.
cards.hint: You only need the order of magnitude, not the exact platform figures.
steps: Reported uploads to the largest platform alone run to several hundred hours a minute.
Adding the rest brings it to the order of a thousand hours per minute.
That is more than a month of footage produced every minute.
cards.reference: YouTube, press statistics: 500 hours of video uploaded every minute, 2019

cards.question: "Every successful founder I interviewed woke at 5am. So waking early makes you successful." Where does this break?
options: Waking early is not that helpful
Nobody asked the founders who failed
Five is too early to be realistic
cards.answer: The sample was chosen by its outcome. If half of all failed founders also woke at 5am, the habit tells you nothing. You cannot learn what causes success by studying only successes.
cards.move: Ask who is missing from the sample before you argue about the finding.
cards.trap: Arguing about whether waking early works, instead of about the sample.
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: "Hospitals are dangerous: far more people die in them than at home." What is wrong?
options: The figures are probably made up
People go to hospital because they are already dying
cards.answer: The comparison assumes the two groups are alike, and they are not: hospitals concentrate the sickest people. Judging a treatment needs comparable groups, which is what a control group is for.
cards.move: Any statistic comparing two groups invites one question: who ended up in each?
cards.trap: Treating a place where sick people are sent as a cause of their outcome.
cards.reference: Kyriacou & Lewis, Confounding by Indication in Clinical Research, JAMA, 2016

cards.question: "After the new mayor, crime fell 8%. The policy worked." What is missing?
options: Eight percent is too small to matter
What crime did everywhere else over the same period
cards.answer: If crime fell 12% nationally, this mayor did worse than doing nothing. A number with no comparison group cannot support a claim about cause — that is what a counterfactual is for.
cards.move: "Compared to what?" is the most useful question in any argument.
cards.trap: Judging a change without anything to compare it against.
cards.reference: Holland, Statistics and Causal Inference, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1986

cards.question: A study tests 20 foods against cancer risk and finds one significant at p < 0.05. What should you think?
options: Convincing — that is the standard threshold
Expected by chance: 20 tests, 1 in 20 odds
They should have tested more foods
cards.answer: A 5% threshold means one false positive in twenty tests on average. Run twenty tests and finding one "result" is what should happen if nothing is going on. The fix is to say up front what you are testing.
cards.move: Ask how many things they measured before you believe the one they report.
cards.trap: Reading a single p-value without asking how many tests were run.
cards.reference: Ioannidis, Why Most Published Research Findings Are False, PLOS Medicine, 2005

cards.question: "Nobody I know voted for it, so the result must be rigged." Where is the error?
options: They probably did not check carefully
The people you know are not a random sample
One election is too small a sample
cards.answer: People cluster with people like themselves, so your circle is one of the least random samples available. Pauline Kael is often misquoted saying this about Nixon; the underlying error is real regardless.
cards.move: Your social circle is evidence about your social circle.
cards.trap: Treating the people around you as if they were drawn at random.
cards.reference: Squire, Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed, Public Opinion Quarterly, 1988

cards.question: A survey is emailed to customers and 4% reply, overwhelmingly positive. What has it measured?
options: The views of people who still open your email
cards.answer: A small random sample would be fine. This one is not random: it excludes everyone who has stopped opening your email, which is exactly the unhappy. The size is not the problem — who is missing is.
cards.move: The people who did not answer are the finding.
cards.trap: Reading a low response rate as merely a small sample.
cards.reference: Groves, Nonresponse Rates and Nonresponse Bias in Household Surveys, Public Opinion Quarterly, 2006

cards.question: Online ratings for most products cluster at five stars and one star, with little between. Why?
options: Products really are either great or terrible
Only the delighted and the furious bother to write
cards.answer: Writing a review costs effort, and only strong feeling pays for it. The many people who found it fine never appear, so the distribution is about who writes, not about what the product is like.
cards.move: The middle of any rating scale is missing, not empty.
cards.trap: Reading the shape of the ratings as the shape of the experience.
cards.reference: Hu, Pavlou & Zhang, Overcoming the J-shaped distribution of product reviews, Communications of the ACM, 2009

cards.question: A cyclist rides 6 km uphill at 10 km/h and straight back down at 30 km/h. What is the average speed, in km/h?
cards.answer: 12 km in 0.8 hours is 15 km/h.
cards.move: Average the times, not the speeds, when the distance is fixed.
cards.trap: Averaging 10 and 30, because both legs cover the same distance.
cards.hint: Work out how long each half takes, not how fast it is.
steps: Uphill: 6 / 10 = 0.6 hours.
Downhill: 6 / 30 = 0.2 hours.
12 km in 0.8 hours is 15 km/h.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A magnitude 8 earthquake against a magnitude 6: how much more energy does the bigger one release?
cards.answer: About 1,000 times. Each whole step on the magnitude scale is ten times the shaking recorded and about 32 times the energy, so two steps are roughly 32 × 32. A magnitude 8 releases in one event what a thousand magnitude 6 quakes would.
cards.move: On a scale that counts powers, one step is never one step.
cards.trap: Knowing each step is ten times, and stopping at the shaking.

diagram.caption: Two steps up the scale, and the energy grows about a thousandfold: 32 × 32.

cards.reference: Kanamori, The energy release in great earthquakes, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1977

cards.question: Driving 10,000 km a year, which upgrade saves more fuel: 5 to 10 km per litre, or 20 to 40?
cards.answer: 5 to 10. At 5 km per litre the year takes 2,000 litres and at 10 it takes 1,000: a saving of 1,000. Going from 20 to 40 cuts 500 litres to 250: a saving of 250. Both double, but one doubling starts from a far thirstier engine.
cards.move: Judge an improvement by what it saves, not by its ratio.
cards.trap: Both are doublings, and the bigger numbers look like the bigger gain.
cards.reference: Larrick & Soll, The MPG Illusion, Science, 2008

cards.question: A pill cuts a disease's yearly risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. How many must take it to spare one person?
cards.answer: About 1,000. The pill halves the risk, but the risk was 2 in 1,000 to begin with, so it removes one case per 1,000 people a year. Doctors call this the number needed to treat. The same halving on a 1-in-2 risk would spare one person in four.
cards.move: Ask what a halving is a halving of before you are impressed.
cards.trap: Hearing that the pill halves the risk and picturing half the patients saved.
cards.reference: Laupacis, Sackett & Roberts, An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment, New England Journal of Medicine, 1988

cards.question: True or false: a shop that prices goods at cost plus 50% keeps half of each sale as margin?
cards.answer: False. Buy at €100 and sell at €150, and the €50 kept is a third of the price, not half. Markup is measured on the cost and margin on the sale, so the same €50 is 50% one way and 33% the other.
cards.move: Name the base of every percentage before you compare two of them.
cards.trap: Reading fifty per cent on the cost as fifty per cent of the price.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A rope hugs the equator. Add 1 m to its length and raise it evenly all round. Can a cat crawl under?
options: Yes, the gap is about 16 cm
Barely, the gap is about 1 mm
cards.answer: Yes, easily. A circle's circumference is 2π times its radius, so adding 1 m to the rope lifts it by 1 ÷ 2π, about 16 cm, all the way round — whatever the size of the circle. The same extra metre around a football would lift it by the same 16 cm.
cards.move: When the intuition comes from size, check whether size appears in the formula.
cards.trap: One metre spread over 40,000 km feels like nothing at all.
cards.source: Circumference and radius of a circle
cards.reference: Courant & Robbins, What Is Mathematics?, revised by Stewart, Oxford University Press, 1996

cards.question: A launch needs five independent steps done on time, each 90% likely. How likely is an on-time launch?
cards.answer: About 60%. Every step must succeed, so the chances multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 is 0.59. Each step looks safe on its own, and the plan still fails two times in five. Ten such steps would fail more often than they succeed.
cards.move: Multiply the odds of every step a plan needs before trusting it.
cards.trap: Each step is safe, so the whole plan feels safe.

diagram.caption: Every step is safe, and five of them still fail two times in five.

cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: A new café opens on your street, with a gifted barista. Which is more likely?
options: It wins an award and survives three years
cards.answer: Surviving three years. Every café that wins an award and survives is also a café that survives, so the second can never be the likelier. The award supplies a reason, and a reason makes a story feel probable while cutting down the number of ways it can come true.
cards.move: Each added reason is one more thing that has to be true.
cards.trap: The award explains the survival, so the story feels more likely.
cards.source: Conjunction rule, applied to a forecast
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: True or false: a team with a 70% chance of winning each of its last four matches will probably win all four?
cards.answer: False. Each win has to happen, so the chances multiply: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 is about 0.24. A team that is favourite in every single match still has only about one chance in four of winning the lot.
cards.move: Being favourite at every step is not being favourite for the journey.
cards.trap: Favourite in every match feels like favourite for the whole run.
cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1, Wiley, 1968

cards.question: A €1,000 card debt grows at 2% a month, unpaid, for three years. Roughly what is owed?
cards.answer: About €2,040. Each month's 2% is charged on the interest already added, so the debt multiplies by 1.02 thirty-six times, which is a little over 2. Simple interest would give €1,720: the gap is interest on interest, and it widens every month.
cards.move: Turn a monthly rate into a yearly one before deciding it is small.
cards.trap: Adding 2% thirty-six times instead of multiplying by it.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A drug's level in the blood halves every 6 hours. After a 400 mg dose, how many mg remain a day later?
cards.answer: 25 mg remain after a day.
cards.move: What halves never reaches zero; count the halvings, not the amount lost.
cards.trap: Taking off a fixed 100 mg every six hours, as if steady.
cards.hint: Count how many six-hour halvings fit in a day.
steps: A day is 24 / 6 = 4 half-lives.
400 halved four times: 200, 100, 50, 25.
25 mg remain after a day.
cards.reference: Rowland & Tozer, Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2011

cards.question: True or false: most crashes happen within a few kilometres of home, so driving near home is riskier?
cards.answer: False. Most crashes happen near home because most driving happens near home. The share of crashes in a place says where people drive, not how dangerous each kilometre there is. To compare risk, divide the crashes by the kilometres driven in each place.
cards.move: Where most accidents happen is mostly where most people are.
cards.trap: Reading the share of crashes as the danger of the place.
cards.reference: Evans, Traffic Safety, Science Serving Society, 2004

cards.question: Two friends each roll a die in secret. You ask whether either rolled a six; they say yes. Chance both did?
cards.answer: 1 in 11. Of the 36 equally likely pairs, 11 contain at least one six, and only one of those is a double six. The yes ruled out the 25 pairs without a six, but it did not tell you which die showed it, so the other die is not a fresh roll.
cards.move: Ask exactly what you were told, and which cases it rules out.
cards.trap: One die shows a six, so the other feels like a fresh roll.

diagram.label: equally likely pairs
diagram.caption: The yes leaves 11 pairs with a six, and only one of them is a double six.

cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1, Wiley, 1968

cards.question: Ana outshoots Bea from close range and from long range, yet Bea has the better overall percentage. Possible?
options: No, the figures must be wrong
Yes, if Bea takes more close shots
Only if they played different games
cards.answer: Yes. Close shots go in far more often than long ones. If most of Bea's attempts are close and most of Ana's are long, Bea's total is weighted towards easy shots and beats Ana's, although Ana is better at each kind. The total measures the shot mix as much as the shooter.
cards.move: A total is a weighted average; ask who chose the weights.
cards.trap: Assuming someone better at every part must be better overall.
