Government moved to buildings at Brades, in the north, but Plymouth was never replaced in law. A British territory's capital is a town half-sunk in grey ash.
cards.move: What the law says and where life happens can drift far apart.
cards.trap: Assuming a capital must be where the government actually sits.
cards.reference: Central Intelligence Agency, The World Factbook: Montserrat, 2024

cards.question: Besides raising hairs in the cold, what does the tiny muscle behind gooseflesh do for hair growth?
cards.answer: It anchors a nerve that wakes hair stem cells. In mice, Ya-Chieh Hsu's team at Harvard found that the sympathetic nerve which makes the muscle contract also wraps the follicle's stem cells, and in prolonged cold its noradrenaline spurs them to grow new hair. A quick bristle and a slowly thickening coat share one wiring.
cards.move: A part that looks useless may be holding something else in place.
cards.reference: Shwartz et al., Cell types promoting goosebumps form a niche to regulate hair follicle stem cells, Cell, 2020

cards.question: True or false: some people can raise gooseflesh on their skin at will, with no cold or emotion?
cards.answer: True. Heathers and colleagues studied 32 people who could do it; most described a kind of inner tensing, often starting at the back of the head, and some could raise it on one side of the body only. As a group they scored higher than usual on openness to experience.
cards.move: A reflex called involuntary is sometimes just one nobody has tried to steer.
cards.trap: Assuming a nerve response outside conscious control can never be steered.
cards.reference: Heathers et al., The voluntary control of piloerection, PeerJ, 2018

cards.question: When can a wave of gooseflesh be the sign of a seizure?
cards.answer: When it arrives in brief waves with no cold or emotion behind it, often on one side. These pilomotor seizures usually start in the temporal lobe, and many have been tied to limbic encephalitis, in which the immune system attacks the brain. A patient may notice nothing but a creeping shiver lasting seconds.
cards.move: A familiar sensation in the wrong context is a symptom, not a mood.
cards.reference: Rocamora et al., Pilomotor seizures: an autonomic semiology of limbic encephalitis?, Seizure, 2014

cards.question: When music gives a listener chills, when does the brain start releasing dopamine?
options: Only at the moment of the chill
Only once the music has stopped
Already in the seconds before it
cards.answer: Already in the seconds before it. Scanning listeners with PET, Salimpoor and colleagues found dopamine released in the caudate while they anticipated a favourite passage, and in the nucleus accumbens at the peak itself. Two regions, two moments: the wanting and the having. A familiar crescendo pays out before it arrives.
cards.move: Much of a pleasure is paid out in waiting for it.
cards.trap: Assuming the reward lands with the thrill itself.
cards.reference: Salimpoor et al., Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music, Nature Neuroscience, 2011

cards.question: What did Darwin think bristling hair was for in frightened or angry animals?
cards.answer: Looking bigger. In The Expression of the Emotions, 1872, Darwin argued that raised hair, feathers and spines make an animal seem larger and more fearsome to a rival or predator, and he gathered observations from keepers at London Zoo. Humans kept the reflex after losing the fur: a display with almost nothing left to display.
cards.move: A reflex can outlive the body it was built for.
cards.source: Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions
cards.reference: Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, 3rd edition, ed. Ekman, Oxford University Press, 1998

cards.question: Why does gooseflesh come with the start of a fever rather than with its end?
cards.answer: Because the brain raises its thermostat first. Immune signals push the hypothalamus's set point up, so a body at 37°C now registers as too cold: skin vessels close, hairs rise, muscles shiver. When the fever breaks, the set point falls and sweating starts. The chill is the heating coming on.
cards.move: A body fighting a change may be obeying a new target.
cards.reference: Hall and Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition, Elsevier, 2021

cards.question: How can human skin that looks almost hairless still bristle visibly with gooseflesh?
cards.answer: Because the follicles never left. Comparing primates, Kamberov and colleagues found human skin has a chimpanzee-like density of hair follicles; the hairs shrank into fine, pale down rather than disappearing. Each follicle kept its small muscle, which still pulls the hair upright and puckers the skin. Human fur was turned down, not removed.
cards.move: Something that looks absent may only have been made smaller.
cards.source: Kamberov et al., J Hum Evol, 2018
cards.reference: Kamberov et al., Comparative evidence for the independent evolution of hair and sweat gland traits in primates, Journal of Human Evolution, 2018

cards.question: True or false: gooseflesh on a body recovered from water is good evidence that the person drowned?
cards.answer: False. After death, the tiny muscles that raise hairs stiffen in rigor mortis like any other, and cold water adds its effect, so puckered skin follows many kinds of death. Pathologists read it as cold or rigor, useless for proving drowning. It shows where the body lay, not how death came.
cards.move: A sign that turns up in every case proves none of them.
cards.trap: Taking a sign often seen in drownings as a sign of drowning.
cards.reference: Saukko and Knight, Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, CRC Press, 2016

cards.question: A man paralysed from the neck down gets gooseflesh on his legs and a pounding headache. What is the likeliest trigger?
options: A cold draught on his legs
cards.answer: A full bladder. Below a high spinal injury, a stretched bladder sets off an unchecked nerve surge that raises hairs, clamps blood vessels and sends blood pressure soaring, beyond the brain's reach. This is autonomic dysreflexia, an emergency, and emptying the bladder comes first. The gooseflesh is an alarm from below the break.
cards.move: Read a familiar symptom together with everything else you know about the person.
cards.trap: Blaming cold, the usual cause, and ignoring the headache and the injury.
cards.reference: Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine, Acute Management of Autonomic Dysreflexia, 2nd edition, Paralyzed Veterans of America, 2001

cards.question: Clinicians score gooseflesh as one item on a standard bedside scale. Which condition does that scale measure?
cards.answer: Opioid withdrawal. The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale grades gooseflesh alongside sweating, yawning, a running nose and wide pupils, because the sympathetic nervous system rebounds as opioids wear off and raises the skin's hairs. It is one proposed origin of the phrase cold turkey. A nurse can grade withdrawal partly by looking at a forearm.
cards.move: Ask what else can pull the same lever as the obvious cause.
cards.trap: Picking hypothermia, because cold is what gooseflesh always suggests.
cards.source: Wesson and Ling, J Psychoactive Drugs, 2003
cards.reference: Wesson and Ling, The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS), Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, 2003

cards.question: What does a human hiccup have in common with the breathing of a tadpole?
cards.answer: Possibly its wiring. A tadpole pumps water over its gills while its glottis shuts to keep water out of its lungs; a hiccup is a sudden intake cut off by the glottis slamming shut. Straus and colleagues noted that carbon dioxide damps both. The hic may be a gill-breathing circuit the brainstem never deleted.
cards.move: An odd habit of the body can be a leftover from an older job.
cards.reference: Straus et al., A phylogenetic hypothesis for the origin of hiccough, BioEssays, 2003

cards.question: Which remedy for stubborn hiccups earned its discoverers an Ig Nobel Prize in medicine?
cards.answer: Digital rectal massage. Francis Fesmire reported in 1988 that it ended a patient's intractable hiccups, and Majed Odeh's team in Israel reported another in 1990; both shared the 2006 prize. The logic runs through the vagus nerve, part of the hiccup reflex, which the rectum can stimulate strongly. The evidence remains a few case reports.
cards.move: A remedy that works once in a case report has been tried once.
cards.reference: Fesmire, Termination of intractable hiccups with digital rectal massage, Annals of Emergency Medicine, 1988

cards.question: In a 2021 survey of people who bought a hiccup-stopping straw, over 90% said it worked. What does that show?
options: That it works for most people
That it works only as a placebo
cards.answer: Little, without a comparison group. Most bouts of hiccups stop within minutes on their own, so almost any remedy tried during one is followed by silence. Respondents had bought the device and answered an online questionnaire; nobody got a dummy straw. Sips of water, sugar and sudden frights earned their reputations the same way.
cards.move: Anything tried just before a problem ends on its own gets the credit.
cards.trap: Reading a 90% success rate as proof the straw works.
cards.source: Alvarez et al., JAMA Network Open, 2021
cards.reference: Alvarez et al., Evaluation of the forced inspiratory suction and swallow tool to stop hiccups, JAMA Network Open, 2021

cards.question: True or false: the one drug the US regulator has approved for hiccups is an antipsychotic?
cards.answer: True. Chlorpromazine, the first antipsychotic, from the 1950s, still carries a US licence for intractable hiccups. Doctors often try other drugs first, off licence, such as baclofen or metoclopramide, because chlorpromazine sedates and can drop blood pressure. Nothing newer is approved: a hiccup that lasts for months still meets a drug designed for psychosis.
cards.move: Where a problem is small, old approvals linger because nobody pays for new ones.
cards.trap: Expecting a minor complaint to have a mild, purpose-made remedy.
cards.source: Steger, Schneemann and Fox, Aliment Pharmacol Ther, 2015
cards.reference: Steger, Schneemann and Fox, Systemic review: the pathogenesis and pharmacological treatment of hiccups, Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics, 2015

cards.question: How did the man with the longest recorded bout of hiccups finally get rid of them?
cards.answer: Nobody knows. Charles Osborne of Iowa started hiccupping in 1922 while lifting a hog for slaughter and went on for 68 years, at first about 40 times a minute: an estimated 430 million hiccups. No treatment worked. They stopped on their own in 1990, about a year before he died.
cards.move: A problem that ends by itself leaves no lesson about the cure.
cards.reference: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/67619-longest-attack-of-hiccups

cards.question: Why might premature babies spend around 15 minutes a day hiccupping?
cards.answer: Possibly to map their own breathing muscles. Recording 13 newborns, Whitehead and colleagues at UCL found that each hiccup's sharp contraction of the diaphragm set off a large wave of brain activity, which may teach the cortex where those muscles are. Preterm infants hiccup about 1% of the time. The jolt may be a lesson.
cards.move: A glitch in a young system may be how it calibrates itself.
cards.reference: Whitehead et al., Event-related potentials following contraction of respiratory muscles in pre-term and full-term infants, Clinical Neurophysiology, 2019

cards.question: Watching a developing foetus by ultrasound, which of these movements appears first?
cards.answer: Hiccups. Filming early pregnancies by ultrasound, de Vries, Visser and Prechtl first saw hiccups at about 9 weeks, breathing movements at about 10, and sucking and swallowing weeks later. So the hiccup is no glitch of mature breathing: its circuit runs before breathing has started. The first rhythm on the screen is the jerk.
cards.move: An apparent malfunction may be older than the system it disrupts.
cards.trap: Choosing breathing, since a hiccup looks like a breath gone wrong.
cards.source: de Vries et al., Early Hum Dev, 1982
cards.reference: de Vries, Visser and Prechtl, The emergence of fetal behaviour. I. Qualitative aspects, Early Human Development, 1982

cards.question: True or false: days of hiccups with nausea can be the first sign of an autoimmune disease of the optic nerves?
cards.answer: True. In neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, antibodies attack the area postrema, a brainstem patch that senses toxins and triggers vomiting. The 2015 diagnostic criteria list unexplained hiccups or vomiting as a core symptom, which can come before any attack on vision or the spinal cord. A stomach complaint can be a brain lesion's first sign.
cards.move: A common symptom in an uncommon pairing deserves a second look.
cards.trap: Filing lasting hiccups under stomach trouble, where they usually belong.
cards.reference: Wingerchuk et al., International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, Neurology, 2015

cards.question: About 8 in 10 people with hiccups lasting over two days are men. A man starts hiccupping. What is most likely?
options: The bout stops soon, like most bouts
An 8 in 10 chance it lasts days
A 1 in 2 chance it lasts days
cards.answer: The bout stops soon, like most bouts. The 8 in 10 says who the rare persistent cases are, not how often a man's hiccups persist; nearly every bout, in anyone, ends within hours. Reviews put the male share of persistent cases at 80% to 90%. Being a man raises tiny odds, which stay tiny.
cards.move: Who the cases are says little about how likely a case is.
cards.trap: Reading the share of men among the cases as a man's own risk.
cards.source: Lee et al., J Pain Symptom Manage, 2016
cards.reference: Lee et al., Gender differences in hiccup patients: analysis of published case reports and case-control studies, Journal of Pain and Symptom Management, 2016

cards.question: A patient's hiccups return with every chemotherapy cycle. Swapping which drug most often stops them?
options: The painkiller given with each cycle
cards.answer: The steroid given against nausea. Dexamethasone rides along with many chemotherapy regimens, so its hiccups get blamed on the cancer drugs. In a 2017 crossover trial, switching to another steroid, methylprednisolone, cut hiccup intensity without worsening nausea, and hiccups returned in cycles given dexamethasone. The culprit was the passenger, not the driver.
cards.move: When two things always arrive together, test them separately before blaming one.
cards.trap: Blaming the chemotherapy, the drug that is always there when hiccups start.
cards.reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5679820/

cards.question: Why have mayors of some French villages issued decrees forbidding residents to die?
cards.answer: To force a decision on a full cemetery. Le Lavandou's mayor did it in 2000 and Sarpourenx's in 2008, when there was no room left to bury people and plans for new ground had been blocked in court. The decrees could never be enforced; they were protests dressed as bylaws.
cards.move: When a rule is absurd on purpose, look for the audience it addresses.
cards.reference: https://www.npr.org/2008/03/07/87974995/mayor-bans-death-in-french-town

cards.question: What did a federal appeals court decide in 2018 about sharing meals in Fort Lauderdale's parks?
cards.answer: That a public meal can be protected speech. In 2014 the city restricted outdoor food sharing, and Arnold Abbott, a 90-year-old volunteer, was charged for feeding homeless people. The court held that a group's weekly meal in a park was expressive conduct under the First Amendment. A shared plate can carry a message.
cards.move: Ask what an act says before judging a rule that bans it.
cards.reference: Fort Lauderdale Food Not Bombs v. City of Fort Lauderdale, US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, 2018

cards.question: Carmel-by-the-Sea in California requires a permit to wear very high heels. Why?
options: Noise on the boardwalks at night
cards.answer: Uneven pavements and lawsuits. Tree roots buckle the town's footpaths, and the 1963 rule covers heels over about 5 cm with a tip smaller than about 6.5 cm². A wearer who takes the free permit from city hall accepts the risk of falling. The ordinance is a liability waiver disguised as a fashion rule.
cards.move: Behind an odd rule, look for who would otherwise pay.
cards.trap: A ban on heels looks like a quirky rule about style.
cards.reference: Carmel-by-the-Sea Municipal Code, high-heeled shoes permit ordinance, 1963

cards.question: How did London cut the pigeon flocks in Trafalgar Square in the 2000s?
options: Ending seed sales and flying hawks
cards.answer: Ending seed sales and flying hawks. The licensed seed stall closed in 2001, feeding the birds was banned, and trained Harris hawks were flown to scare them off. Flock size follows food: kill birds where food is plentiful and newcomers fill the gap. Take away the food and the flock leaves on its own.
cards.move: To shrink a crowd, remove what drew it rather than its members.
cards.trap: Removing birds directly seems the quickest way to have fewer of them.
cards.reference: Greater London Authority, Trafalgar Square and Parliament Square Garden Byelaws, 2012

cards.question: True or false: a Paris police order requiring women to seek permission to wear trousers was formally set aside only in 2013?
cards.answer: True. The prefecture's order of November 1800 required women to get police permission to dress as men. It was eased in 1892 and 1909 for women holding a bicycle's handlebars or a horse's reins. In January 2013 the minister for women's rights declared it implicitly repealed, after generations of being ignored.
cards.move: An unenforced rule still stands until someone formally takes it down.
cards.trap: Assuming a rule from 1800 must have lapsed a century or more ago.
cards.reference: Journal officiel de la République française, Sénat, réponse ministérielle sur l'ordonnance du 7 novembre 1800, 31 janvier 2013

cards.question: From 1989 Mexico City banned each car from driving one weekday a week, by number plate. What happened to air quality?
options: It improved markedly within a year
It improved, then slowly slipped back
cards.answer: No measurable improvement was found. Davis compared pollution just before and after the rule began, across pollutants, and saw no drop. Vehicle numbers rose instead, as households bought second cars, often older and dirtier, for the banned day. A rule meant to take a fifth of cars off the road each weekday added cars.
cards.move: Before counting what a ban removes, ask what people buy to escape it.
cards.trap: Assuming a fifth fewer cars each day means a fifth less smog.

cards.question: After Californian towns banned thin carry-out bags, how much of the plastic saved was cancelled by extra bin-bag purchases?
cards.answer: About 30%. Using shop scanner data, Taylor found the bans cut carry-out bag plastic by about 18,000 tonnes a year, while bin-bag purchases rose by about 5,400 tonnes, offsetting about 29%. Sales of the smallest bin bags jumped 120%. The free shopping bag had been doing a second job under the kitchen sink.
cards.move: Ask what second job the banned thing was quietly doing.
cards.trap: Treating the old bags as used once, then thrown straight away.
cards.source: Taylor, J. Environmental Economics and Management, 2019
cards.reference: Taylor, Bag leakage: The effect of disposable carryout bag regulations on unregulated bags, Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 2019

cards.question: True or false: Longyearbyen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, has a law forbidding residents to die there?
cards.answer: False. The town's small cemetery stopped taking new burials decades ago because bodies barely decay in permafrost; in 1998 scientists exhumed miners killed by the 1918 flu to search for the virus. The seriously ill are usually sent to mainland Norway for care. The famous ban is a headline about a cemetery.
cards.move: A strange rule reported everywhere may be a practice nobody wrote down.
cards.trap: Remembering the widely shared story of a town that outlawed death.
cards.reference: Duncan, Hunting the 1918 Flu: One Scientist's Search for a Killer Virus, University of Toronto Press, 2003

cards.question: What exactly does Singapore's 1992 chewing gum law forbid, and what did a trade deal later change?
cards.answer: Importing and selling gum, not chewing it. The ban followed gum jamming door sensors on the new metro trains. From 2004, under a free trade agreement with the United States, therapeutic gum such as nicotine gum became legal, sold only by pharmacists and dentists, who record each buyer's name. Chewing was never the offence.
cards.move: Read which step of a chain a ban targets before judging it.
cards.reference: United States Senate, Report 108-117, United States–Singapore Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act, 2003

cards.question: Why did Flagstaff, Arizona, ban advertising searchlights in 1958?
cards.answer: To protect the telescopes. Lowell Observatory and the US Naval Observatory's new station on the edge of town needed a dark sky, and one searchlight could wash it out. The 1958 ordinance is generally counted the first lighting law written to keep skies dark. In 2001 Flagstaff became the first International Dark Sky City.
cards.move: Protect a quiet resource before the noise that would drown it arrives.
cards.source: City of Flagstaff, Dark Sky History
cards.reference: https://flagstaff.az.gov/3855/Dark-Sky-History-in-Flagstaff

cards.question: Which two surnames on a 1977 urology paper helped give nominative determinism its name?
cards.answer: Splatt and Weedon. Their article on incontinence in the British Journal of Urology was among the examples readers sent to New Scientist's Feedback column, which in 1994 named the idea of people drifting into work that suits their names. Another exhibit was a book on the polar regions by Daniel Snowman.
cards.move: A name that fits the job is remembered; the thousands that do not vanish.
cards.reference: https://improbable.com/2013/09/22/nominative-determinism/

cards.question: Why might an economist named Abbott reach tenure more easily than an equally able one named Young?
cards.answer: Because economists list co-authors alphabetically. Einav and Yariv found surnames early in the alphabet linked to tenure in top US departments and to fellowship of the Econometric Society. Psychology, which orders authors by contribution, showed no such link. In a crowded reference list, Abbott is the name before the et al.
cards.move: Where credit follows an arbitrary order, the order itself becomes an advantage.
cards.source: Einav and Yariv, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2006

cards.question: Why did hurricanes with women's names look deadlier in a much-publicised 2014 study?
cards.answer: Critics pointed to its sample. From 1953 to 1978 every Atlantic hurricane got a woman's name, and storms of that era killed more people on average, before modern forecasts and evacuation plans. The authors defended their result, but here a name's gender and a storm's decade moved together.
cards.move: When two things changed in the same years, either could be doing the work.

cards.question: US couples share a surname initial more often than chance predicts. What did a 2011 reanalysis find behind it?
options: Surnames clustering by ethnicity and region
An unconscious liking for one's own letters
Clerks filing couples under one initial
cards.answer: Surnames clustering by ethnicity and region. People tend to marry within their own community, and initials are not spread evenly across communities: Dutch-American surnames, for instance, often start with V. Simonsohn replicated the original pattern, then showed that such confounds could produce it without any pull of the name.
cards.move: Before crediting attraction, ask what else the matching pairs already share.
cards.trap: Taking the textbook story of an unconscious pull towards one's own name.
cards.reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21299311/

cards.question: True or false: Abraham Lincoln had a secretary named Kennedy, just as John F. Kennedy had one named Lincoln?
cards.answer: False. Kennedy's personal secretary really was Evelyn Lincoln, from his Senate years to his death. Lincoln's secretaries were John Nicolay and John Hay, with William Stoddard as an assistant; there was no Kennedy. The mirror comes from a coincidence list that circulated in the 1960s, where one true detail carries an invented twin.
cards.move: When a story is perfectly symmetrical, check the half nobody bothered to source.
cards.trap: Letting the true half vouch for the tidy mirrored half.
cards.reference: Burlingame (ed.), With Lincoln in the White House: Letters, Memoranda, and Other Writings of John G. Nicolay, 1860–1865, Southern Illinois University Press, 2000

cards.question: Did Dutch families pick absurd surnames in 1811 to mock Napoleon's order to register one?
cards.answer: Mostly not. The 1811 decree required fixed surnames, but many Dutch families already had one, and the famous examples predate the decree: Naaktgeboren, born naked, was in use long before Napoleon was born. Leendert Brouwer of the Meertens Institute traced them. The prank story fits the names, not the registers.
cards.move: When a story explains an oddity too neatly, check the dates first.
cards.reference: Brouwer, De naammythe van Napoleon, Respons: Mededelingen van het Meertens Instituut 8, 2006

cards.question: Which effect of a person's own name has held up across a dozen languages?
cards.answer: A liking for its letters. Speakers of 12 European languages, asked for their favourite letters, picked those in their own names more often than other people did, Jozef Nuttin reported in 1987; later studies keep finding it. Bolder claims, that names steer careers or spouses, have mostly dissolved. The bias stays inside the alphabet.
cards.move: Keep the small effect that replicates; drop the big story built on it.
cards.reference: Nuttin, Affective consequences of mere ownership: the name letter effect in twelve European languages, European Journal of Social Psychology, 1987

cards.question: The bell-shaped curve of errors is called Gaussian. Who published it first?
cards.answer: Abraham de Moivre, in 1733. He derived it to approximate coin-toss odds, 76 years before Gauss used it for errors in astronomy. The statistician Stephen Stigler later stated the rule that no discovery is named after its first discoverer, and credited it to the sociologist Robert Merton. The law obeys itself.
cards.move: A name on an idea records who made it famous, not who made it.
cards.trap: Trusting that a discovery carries the name of whoever found it.
cards.reference: Stigler, Stigler's law of eponymy, Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1980

cards.question: South Korea's 2015 census: Kim 21.5%, Lee 14.7%, Park 8.4%. What % chance do two random strangers share one of these three surnames?
cards.move: For two things to match, multiply the chances first, then add the ways.
cards.trap: Adding the three shares to 44.6%, which describes one stranger, not two.
cards.hint: A surname counts only if both strangers carry it.
cards.reference: Statistics Korea, 2015 Population and Housing Census: surnames and family origins, 2016

cards.question: Should the state be able to refuse the name parents choose for a child?
cards.answer: A name is imposed on someone who cannot object and follows them into every classroom. In 2008 a New Zealand court made a nine-year-old girl a ward of court so she could shed the name Talula Does The Hula From Hawaii. Registrars refusing a handful of names a year protect children at almost no cost.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who judges harm, and how often.
cards.counterpoint: Naming is among the most personal choices a family makes, and officials are poor judges of what will embarrass. Iceland's naming committee rejected Blær as a boy's name; in 2013 the girl given it won a court case to keep her name, after years registered simply as Stúlka, girl. Rules made for oddities end up policing ordinary families.
cards.reference: Personal Names Act No. 45/1996 (Lög um mannanöfn), Althingi, Iceland, 1996

cards.question: A deep-sea octopus in Monterey Canyon guarded one clutch of eggs. For how long?
cards.answer: About 4.5 years. Researchers recognised the same Graneledone boreopacifica female by her scars on 18 dives between May 2007 and September 2011, about 1,400 m down; she was never seen eating. Cold water slows development, so her roughly 160 eggs took 53 months to hatch, the longest brooding known for any animal.
cards.move: A figure learned in one setting can mislead badly in a colder one.
cards.trap: Shallow-water octopuses brood for weeks or months, so months sounds right.
cards.reference: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/727610

cards.question: What happens to a brooding mother octopus if her optic glands are removed?
cards.answer: She abandons her eggs, starts eating again and lives for months longer. Jerome Wodinsky showed this in 1977 with two-spot octopuses. In 2022 a team found the gland shifts its cholesterol chemistry in mothers, producing steroids that drive the fatal decline. The mother's death is switched on by a gland, not by exhaustion.
cards.move: When an ending looks like wear, look for a switch that triggers it.
cards.reference: https://biologicalsciences.uchicago.edu/news/octopus-cholesterol-death-spiral

cards.question: True or false: a patch of octopus skin, cut away from the body, still reacts to light?
cards.answer: True. In excised skin of the California two-spot octopus, light made the pigment sacs called chromatophores expand, fastest under blue light. The skin makes opsin, the light-detecting protein of eyes, in its own sensory cells. With no eye and no brain attached, a cut patch of skin still flushed dark under a lamp.
cards.move: Before assuming a signal comes from the centre, test the edge alone.
cards.trap: Colour change seems to need the eyes and brain to direct it.
cards.reference: Ramirez & Oakley, Eye-independent, light-activated chromatophore expansion (LACE) and expression of phototransduction genes in the skin of Octopus bimaculoides, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2015

cards.question: How does an octopus retune its nerve proteins when its water turns cold?
cards.answer: By editing its RNA, the working copies of genes, while the DNA stays unchanged. California two-spot octopuses kept at 13 °C instead of 22 °C raised protein-altering edits at more than 13,000 sites in the nervous system within days. The same gene then yields slightly different proteins: a winter wardrobe from the same pattern.
cards.move: A fixed blueprint can still yield different products if the copies change.
cards.source: Birk et al., Cell, 2023; Marine Biological Laboratory
cards.reference: https://www.mbl.edu/news/masters-acclimation-octopuses-adjust-cold-editing-their-rna

cards.question: Wild gloomy octopuses in Jervis Bay were filmed throwing silt and shells. How do they throw?
cards.answer: A jet from the siphon. The octopus gathers debris in its arms, then blasts water from its siphon to fire the load out from under its body. In 24 hours of footage, about 10 octopuses threw 102 times; one female repeatedly hit a male who was trying to mate with her.
cards.move: Ask what the body is built to push before guessing how it throws.
cards.trap: Throwing means an arm swing, so eight arms seem the obvious launcher.
cards.reference: https://www.sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2022/11/10/octopuses-witnessed-hurling-silt-shells-and-algae.html

cards.question: True or false: the common octopus, a master of colour camouflage, has only one kind of light-sensitive pigment in its eyes?
cards.answer: True. Its retina carries a single visual pigment, most sensitive to blue-green light, so it cannot compare wavelengths the way eyes with two or more pigments do. Behavioural tests by Messenger in 1977 found no sign that octopuses tell colours apart. Yet the same animal vanishes against red weed and green algae.
cards.move: A result that looks like skill may run on a different sense entirely.
cards.trap: Assuming an animal that matches colours so well must see them.
cards.reference: Messenger, Evidence that Octopus is colour blind, Journal of Experimental Biology, 1977

cards.question: What is the heaviest giant Pacific octopus ever reliably weighed?
cards.answer: About 70 kg. The best-documented giant, weighed alive, came in at 71 kg. The 272 kg figure that circulates rests on an anecdotal report nobody checked on a scale. Typical adults weigh nearer 15 kg. Even the record animal was the weight of a large dog, not a small car.
cards.move: A record figure with no scale behind it should be weighed as a rumour.
cards.trap: Reaching for the famous 272 kg figure because it circulates widely.
cards.reference: Cosgrove & McDaniel, Super Suckers: The Giant Pacific Octopus and Other Cephalopods of the Pacific Coast, Harbour Publishing, 2009

cards.question: An octopus has about 500 million neurons, two-thirds of them in its eight arms. How many million per arm?
cards.answer: 333 million / 8 arms ≈ 41.7 million per arm.
cards.move: Where the neurons sit tells you where the decisions get made.
cards.trap: Dividing all 500 million by eight and forgetting the brain's share.
cards.hint: Take the arms' share of the total first, then split it eight ways.
steps: Two-thirds of 500 million is about 333 million neurons in the arms.
333 million / 8 arms ≈ 41.7 million per arm.
cards.reference: Hochner, An embodied view of octopus neurobiology, Current Biology, 2012

cards.question: Should octopus farming be banned outright, as Washington and California did in 2024?
cards.answer: Octopuses are solitary, curious animals that explore, learn and escape, and a crowded tank denies them all of it. A 2021 review for the UK government found strong evidence that cephalopods can suffer, and no humane way of killing them at scale has been established. Banning an industry before it exists costs almost no jobs.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether humane farming is possible at all decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Octopus is already eaten in large quantities, and nearly all of it comes from wild catches that deplete populations and kill with no welfare rules at all. Farms could be licensed, inspected and held to written standards that a fishing boat never meets. A ban does not end demand; it hands supply to fisheries and to countries with weaker rules.
cards.source: Birch et al., LSE sentience review, 2021
cards.reference: Birch, Burn, Schnell, Browning & Crump, Review of the Evidence of Sentience in Cephalopod Molluscs and Decapod Crustaceans, LSE Consulting, 2021

cards.question: What lets an octopus taste whatever its suckers touch?
cards.answer: Receptors found only in cephalopods. Van Giesen and colleagues showed that sensory cells in the suckers carry chemotactile receptors, kin to the brain's receptors for acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter. They respond to terpenoids, oily compounds that barely dissolve and so must be touched rather than smelled. A sucker pressed on prey samples it like a tongue.
cards.move: Some signals can only be read by contact, never at a distance.
cards.reference: van Giesen, Kilian, Allard & Bellono, Molecular Basis of Chemotactile Sensation in Octopus, Cell, 2020

cards.question: What are the earliest surviving laws written in English mostly made of?
cards.answer: A price list for injuries. The laws of King Æthelberht of Kent, from around 600, set payments for harms down to a front tooth, a fingernail or a toe, and scaled many by the victim's rank. Paying compensation replaced the feud: a broken tooth was settled in shillings rather than blood.
cards.move: Putting a price on harm can be a way of stopping revenge.
cards.reference: Oliver, The Beginnings of English Law, University of Toronto Press, 2002

cards.question: Under an 1847 Act still in force, what is the maximum fine for beating a carpet in an English street?
cards.answer: £1,000. Section 28 of the Town Police Clauses Act 1847 covers carpets, rugs and mats beaten or shaken to the annoyance of residents or passers-by, doormats before 8 am excepted. Its penalty is now level 3 on the standard scale, so the old shillings became modern pounds. The rule stayed Victorian; the fine did not.
cards.move: An old rule's penalty may have been quietly updated even if the rule was not.
cards.trap: An 1847 penalty sounds like a few shillings, so a token sum.
cards.reference: Town Police Clauses Act 1847, section 28, penalty as amended by the Criminal Justice Act 1982

cards.question: When Chicago's public libraries scrapped overdue fines in 2019, what happened to book returns?
options: They fell as borrowers stopped caring
cards.answer: They rose, including long-lost books. Chicago also wiped existing debts, and returns of overdue items jumped in the following months. Fines had kept many borrowers, often poorer ones, away from the library altogether, the book still on a shelf at home. The penalty meant to bring books back had been keeping them out.
cards.move: Before crediting a penalty, ask what people would do without it.
cards.trap: Fines seem to be what makes borrowers bring books back at all.
cards.reference: https://www.chipublib.org/news/mayor-lightfoot-and-chicago-public-library-announce-elimination-of-late-fees-outstanding-debt-to-increase-access-to-libraries-citywide/

cards.question: Why did CBS never pay the fine for the 2004 Super Bowl half-time show?
cards.answer: Because the courts threw it out. The FCC fined CBS $550,000, the maximum $27,500 for each of 20 stations it owned. In 2011 an appeals court ruled that punishing a fleeting image of nudity broke the regulator's own earlier policy without fair notice. In 2012 the Supreme Court declined to revive it.
cards.move: A penalty is only as strong as the notice given before it.
cards.source: CBS Corp. v. FCC, Third Circuit, 2011
cards.reference: CBS Corporation v. Federal Communications Commission, US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, 2011

cards.question: A Finnish day-fine is a sixtieth of monthly net income after a €255 allowance. In euros, what do 10 cost on €6,255 a month?
cards.move: A fine scaled to income stings the rich and the poor alike.
cards.trap: Taking a day-fine as a whole day's pay doubles the answer.
cards.hint: Take off the allowance before dividing by 60.
steps: €6,255 − €255 = €6,000 counted income.
€6,000 / 60 = €100 for each day-fine.
cards.reference: Criminal Code of Finland (39/1889), chapter 2a, section 2, as amended 1999

cards.question: How did a rich Roman turn the Twelve Tables' fixed fine for assault into a game?
cards.answer: He slapped strangers and paid on the spot. The Tables fixed the penalty for such an injury at 25 asses, a sum inflation had made trivial. Aulus Gellius tells of Lucius Veratius, who struck free men in the face while a slave counted out the coins. The praetors switched to damages assessed case by case.
cards.move: A penalty fixed in coins shrinks every year that prices rise.
cards.reference: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, trans. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1927

cards.question: Before 2002, which UN diplomats in New York ran up the most unpaid parking tickets per diplomat?
cards.answer: Those from high-corruption countries. Diplomatic immunity meant no fine could be enforced, so only habit restrained them. Fisman and Miguel found unpaid tickets tracked corruption at home, even allowing for national income. When New York began removing diplomatic plates for unpaid fines in 2002, violations fell by about 98%. Norms mattered; enforcement mattered more.
cards.move: When nobody can be punished, behaviour shows the habits people brought.
cards.trap: Assuming rich countries' diplomats simply shrug off fines they can afford.
cards.reference: Fisman & Miguel, Corruption, Norms, and Legal Enforcement: Evidence from Diplomatic Parking Tickets, Journal of Political Economy, 2007

cards.question: Haifa day-care centres fined parents for late pick-ups, then scrapped the fine. What did lateness do after the fine went?
options: Fell back to its old level
cards.answer: Stayed at the higher level. Introduced in six of ten centres, the fine had sharply raised late arrivals: parents read it as the price of extra childcare, not a sign of wrongdoing. When it was withdrawn after 12 weeks, lateness did not come back down. A guilt, once priced, stayed a purchase.
cards.move: Once a duty has a price, removing the price may not restore the duty.
cards.trap: Expecting that removing the fine would simply undo its effect.
cards.reference: Gneezy & Rustichini, A Fine Is a Price, Journal of Legal Studies, 2000

cards.question: What share of Ferguson, Missouri's general fund did its 2015 budget expect to raise from fines and fees?
cards.answer: About 23%. The Justice Department's 2015 investigation found the share had nearly doubled from 12% in 2010, as city officials pressed police and the court to raise more. Missed payments brought arrest warrants and fresh fees. In a town of about 21,000 people, the municipal court had become a revenue office.
cards.move: When a punishment funds its enforcer, expect more of it.
cards.trap: Assuming fines are a small side income for any town.
cards.source: US Department of Justice, Ferguson report, 2015
cards.reference: https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/opa/press-releases/attachments/2015/03/04/ferguson_police_department_report.pdf

cards.question: Should fines for minor offences be scaled to the offender's income?
cards.answer: A flat fine is a price the rich can ignore and a sentence the poor cannot pay. Scaling to income, as Germany and Switzerland do with day-fines, makes one offence cost the same share of every income. It keeps deterrence real at the top and stops unpaid fines becoming debt at the bottom.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether incomes can be measured fairly decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Income-based fines need courts to know what people earn, which is intrusive and easy to dodge for anyone paid in assets, dividends or cash. The offence, not the bank balance, should set the penalty: two drivers over the same limit did the same wrong. Six-figure headline fines also breed resentment and appeals rather than respect for the rule.
cards.reference: Swiss Criminal Code, Article 34, day-penalty system, as revised in force from 2007

cards.question: How did researchers learn that a clam dredged off Iceland was the oldest individual animal ever precisely aged?
cards.answer: By sectioning its shell and counting growth lines, which only works on a dead clam. The ocean quahog, dredged in 2006, had been frozen on board as routine. A first count of the hinge said about 405 years; a recount in 2013 said 507. It hatched before Henry VIII took the throne.
cards.move: Some measurements can only be taken once, so decide what is worth it.
cards.reference: Butler et al., Variability of marine climate on the North Icelandic Shelf in a 1357-year proxy archive based on growth increments in the bivalve Arctica islandica, Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology, 2013

cards.question: How old is the oldest seed ever to sprout into a living plant?
cards.answer: About 2,000 years. A date palm seed from the excavations at Masada, radiocarbon-dated to between about 155 BC and 64 AD, was planted in 2005 and grew into a tree nicknamed Methuselah. Older plants have been regrown from frozen tissue in laboratories, but none sprouted from a seed on its own.
cards.move: Read how a record was defined before comparing it with another.
cards.reference: Sallon et al., Germination, genetics, and growth of an ancient date seed, Science, 2008

cards.question: What has yielded the oldest DNA sequenced so far?
cards.answer: Frozen sediment in Greenland. Soil from Kap København, about 2 million years old, held DNA fragments from mastodons, reindeer, hares and forest plants. Mammoth teeth from Siberia gave DNA over a million years old. Dinosaur bones, 66 million years and older, have given none: DNA breaks down long before that.
cards.move: Judge what survives by its chemistry, not by the size of the creature.
cards.trap: Bones last for millions of years, so their DNA seems to last too.
cards.reference: Kjær et al., A 2-million-year-old ecosystem in Greenland uncovered by environmental DNA, Nature, 2022

cards.question: True or false: female Greenland sharks are estimated to reach breeding age at around 150 years?
cards.answer: True. Dating the eye lens cores of 28 sharks, whose proteins form before birth and never renew, gave an estimated maturity age of about 150 years and lifespans of at least 272. Carbon from 1950s bomb tests marked the youngest. A shark born in the Napoleonic wars would have bred first in the 1950s.
cards.move: Scale every life stage to the lifespan before judging it slow.
cards.trap: Most sharks mature within a few decades, so 150 sounds absurd.
cards.reference: Nielsen et al., Eye lens radiocarbon reveals centuries of longevity in the Greenland shark, Science, 2016

cards.question: Why could the man who recorded a voice singing a French folk song in 1860 never hear his recording?
cards.answer: His machine only drew sound. Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph traced vibrations as wavy lines on soot-blackened paper, to be read by eye. His 1860 tracing of Au clair de la lune, the oldest recognisable recording of a human voice, was first played back in 2008, from scans of the lines.
cards.move: An old record may hold more than its makers could read.
cards.reference: Rosen, Researchers Play Tune Recorded Before Edison, The New York Times, 27 March 2008

cards.question: Carbon-14 halves every 5,730 years. In a 57,300-year-old bone, what percentage of the original carbon-14 remains?
cards.move: Ten halvings leave a thousandth; twenty leave a millionth.
cards.trap: Taking away a fixed share each interval instead of halving what is left.
cards.hint: Count the half-lives first, then halve that many times.
steps: Ten halvings leave 1 / 2^10 = 1 / 1,024 of the original.
cards.reference: Godwin, Half-life of Radiocarbon, Nature, 1962

cards.question: What is the oldest dated fragment of Earth's own crust?
options: A zircon crystal from Western Australia
A grey rock outcrop in northern Canada
cards.answer: A zircon crystal from Western Australia. A grain from the Jack Hills, a fraction of a millimetre across, was confirmed in 2014 at about 4.37 billion years old. The oldest whole rocks with undisputed ages, in Canada, are around 4 billion. The early crust was melted and recycled; zircon, hard and chemically stubborn, came through.
cards.move: Where everything gets recycled, the oldest survivor is the hardest crumb.
cards.trap: Assuming the oldest piece of Earth must be a whole rock.
cards.reference: Valley et al., Hadean age for a post-magma-ocean zircon confirmed by atom-probe tomography, Nature Geoscience, 2014

cards.question: What finally ended Kongō Gumi, the temple builder run by one family's descendants since 578?
cards.answer: Debt from property speculation. In Japan's 1980s bubble the firm borrowed heavily to invest in land; when prices collapsed, the assets behind its loans shrank, while commissions for temples dwindled. In 2006 it was absorbed into the Takamatsu construction group. Fourteen centuries of carpentry were undone by two decades of borrowing.
cards.move: Old institutions rarely die of age; they die of a new bet.
cards.reference: Hutcheson, The End of a 1,400-Year-Old Business, BusinessWeek, April 2007

cards.question: Some solid grains found on Earth are older than the Earth itself. How old are the oldest dated?
cards.answer: About 7 billion years. Heck and colleagues dated silicon carbide grains from the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, by neon that cosmic rays made in them in space. Most had drifted under 300 million years; a few, about 3 billion. They are dust from stars that died before the Sun formed.
cards.move: The age of a container says little about the age of its contents.
cards.trap: Taking the Solar System's age as a ceiling on anything we can hold.

cards.question: Why were the ancient human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated a second time?
cards.answer: Because the first dates came from water plants. Ditch-grass seeds in the layers gave 21,000 to 23,000 years, and critics argued that aquatic plants absorb old carbon from dissolved rock, making them look older. In 2023 pollen from land plants and quartz grains gave consistent ages. The oldest footprints in the Americas passed the retest.
cards.move: When a date rests on one material, ask what that material absorbs.
cards.reference: Pigati et al., Independent age estimates resolve the controversy of ancient human footprints at White Sands, Science, 2023

cards.question: What simple test did Francis Bacon use to find out why sunlight makes some people sneeze?
cards.answer: He faced the sun with his eyes shut. The Aristotelian answer had been the sun's heat on the nose; Bacon found that without light entering the eyes the sneeze did not come, so the eyes were the route. The photic sneeze reflex is estimated to affect about 18 to 35% of people.
cards.move: To find which route a cause takes, block one route and watch.
cards.reference: Provine, Curious Behavior: Yawning, Laughing, Hiccupping, and Beyond, Harvard University Press, 2012

cards.question: What unusual trigger for sneezing did doctors describe running through one family in 1989?
cards.answer: A full stomach. Teebi and al-Saleh described relatives who sneezed repeatedly and uncontrollably after a large meal, whatever the food, and the trait passed from parent to child as a dominant one. They named it snatiation, from sneeze and satiation. The sneeze reflex, it seems, can be wired to more than the nose.
cards.move: A reflex fires on whatever signal its wiring reaches, not only the obvious one.
cards.source: Teebi and al-Saleh, J Med Genet, 1989
cards.reference: Teebi and al-Saleh, Autosomal dominant sneezing disorder provoked by fullness of stomach, Journal of Medical Genetics, 1989

cards.question: What happened to a man who pinched his nose and shut his mouth to stifle a sneeze?
cards.answer: He tore his throat. The trapped pressure burst through the back of his pharynx, and air leaked into the tissues of his neck and chest, which crackled when pressed. Doctors in Leicester fed him through a tube and kept him in hospital for a week, then reported the case in 2018.
cards.move: Blocking an outlet does not remove the force; it chooses where it goes.
cards.reference: Snap, crackle and pop: when sneezing leads to crackling in the neck, BMJ Case Reports, 2018

cards.question: True or false: African wild dogs use sneezes to settle whether the pack sets off to hunt?
cards.answer: True. Watching packs in Botswana, Walker and colleagues found that a rally ended in departure once enough dogs had sneezed. The number needed depended on who started it: when a dominant dog began, a few sneezes could do; a junior one needed many more. A sound usually filed as a reflex works as a ballot.
cards.move: Before dismissing a signal as noise, check whether anyone acts on it.
cards.trap: Assuming a sneeze is a reflex that cannot carry information.
cards.source: Walker et al., Proc R Soc B, 2017
cards.reference: Walker et al., Sneeze to leave: African wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) use variable quorum thresholds facilitated by sneezes in collective decisions, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2017

cards.question: Which part of the brain coordinates the sequence of a sneeze?
cards.answer: The brainstem. A sneezing centre in the lateral medulla runs the sequence: a deep breath, a closed throat, then a blast through nose and mouth. A patient whose stroke damaged that area still felt the tickle in the nose but could no longer sneeze. The nose only raises the alarm.
cards.move: Feeling an urge and carrying it out can live in different places.
cards.trap: Assuming a blast this forceful needs the thinking brain in charge.
cards.reference: Seijo-Martínez et al., Sneeze related area in the medulla: localisation of the human sneezing centre?, Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 2006

cards.question: Which single chemical signal did researchers find mice need in order to sneeze?
cards.answer: A peptide called neuromedin B. Li and colleagues found that nerve cells in the nose carrying it pass irritant signals to a small cluster of brainstem neurons; mice lacking the peptide, or with those neurons removed, no longer sneezed at irritants. A reflex that looks like plumbing turns out to need one molecular key.
cards.move: A reflex that looks mechanical may hinge on a single messenger molecule.
cards.reference: Li et al., Sneezing reflex is mediated by a peptidergic pathway from nose to brainstem, Cell, 2021

cards.question: How far can the droplets of an uncovered sneeze travel indoors, and why so far?
cards.answer: Up to 7 or 8 metres. Filming with high-speed cameras, Lydia Bourouiba's laboratory at MIT showed that a sneeze is a turbulent puff of warm, moist gas carrying droplets of every size inside it, keeping them aloft long after their weight alone would have dropped them. The two-metre rule assumed each droplet flew alone.
cards.move: Check whether a thing travels alone or rides inside something larger.
cards.reference: Bourouiba, Turbulent gas clouds and respiratory pathogen emissions: potential implications for reducing transmission of COVID-19, JAMA, 2020

cards.question: Galápagos marine iguanas sneeze constantly, leaving white crusts on their heads. What are they getting rid of?
cards.answer: Salt pulled from their blood. Grazing seaweed underwater, they swallow far more salt than their kidneys can clear, because reptile kidneys cannot make urine saltier than blood. Glands beside the nostrils concentrate it into brine, which a sharp snort sprays out. Schmidt-Nielsen and Fänge described the glands in 1958; the white crust is dried salt.
cards.move: When a body throws something out, ask where it was made.
cards.trap: Picking trapped seawater, the obvious nuisance for an animal that dives.
cards.reference: Schmidt-Nielsen and Fänge, Salt glands in marine reptiles, Nature, 1958

cards.question: True or false: blessing a sneeze began with Pope Gregory the Great during the Roman plague of 590?
cards.answer: False. More than five centuries earlier, Pliny the Elder asked in his Natural History why people wish good health to someone who sneezes, and noted that even the gloomy emperor Tiberius insisted on the greeting, in his carriage too. The plague story may explain one prayer, not the custom. Pliny already found its origin lost.
cards.move: Every extra detail in an origin story is one more thing to check.
cards.trap: A story with a pope, a plague and a year sounds documented.
cards.source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 28
cards.reference: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 28, trans. W. H. S. Jones, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1963

cards.question: In the first year of a sneezing fit lasting nearly three years, Donna Griffiths sneezed about a million times. One sneeze every how many seconds?
cards.move: Turn a huge total into a rate before judging whether it is plausible.
cards.trap: Guessing every few seconds, because a million sounds like nonstop sneezing.
cards.hint: Count the seconds in a whole year, nights included.
steps: A year has 365 × 24 = 8,760 hours.
cards.reference: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/67595-longest-sneezing-fit

cards.question: Whom is the English offence of handling salmon in suspicious circumstances aimed at?
cards.answer: Buyers of poached fish. Section 32 of the Salmon Act 1986 makes it an offence to receive or dispose of salmon believed to be caught illegally. Like handling stolen goods, it follows the money: poaching pays only if someone buys. It targets the back door of a restaurant kitchen, not the riverbank.
cards.move: To stop a theft, make the buyer as liable as the thief.
cards.reference: Salmon Act 1986, c. 62, section 32, United Kingdom Parliament, 1986

cards.question: What does the oldest statute still in force in England deal with?
cards.answer: Seizing goods for debt, and tenants spoiling land. The Statute of Marlborough, passed in 1267 after a civil war, still has a few chapters in force. Most curb distress, taking a debtor's goods without a court's order; one forbids tenants to waste the land they farm. Its clauses have outlived the barons by 750 years.
cards.move: Rules written to end a crisis tend to outlast the crisis by centuries.
cards.source: Baker, An Introduction to English Legal History
cards.reference: Baker, An Introduction to English Legal History, 5th edition, Oxford University Press, 2019

cards.question: What do seven US state constitutions still say about atheists holding public office?
cards.answer: That they may not. Arkansas, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas keep clauses barring those who deny a Supreme Being. None can be enforced: in 1961 the Supreme Court struck down Maryland's religious test in Torcaso v. Watkins. Deleting them needs a constitutional amendment, so they stay in print.
cards.move: A dead rule stays on paper when removing it costs more than ignoring it.
cards.source: Torcaso v. Watkins, US Supreme Court, 1961
cards.reference: Torcaso v. Watkins, 367 U.S. 488, Supreme Court of the United States, 1961

cards.question: True or false: Kentucky officials taking office still swear they have never fought a duel?
cards.answer: True. Section 228 of Kentucky's constitution requires officers, and lawyers admitted to the bar, to swear that as citizens of the state they have not fought a duel with deadly weapons, sent or accepted a challenge, or acted as a second. New governors still recite the clause at their swearing-in.
cards.move: A claim that sounds invented deserves a check, not a shrug.
cards.trap: An oath about duels sounds like an invented item from a weird-law list.
cards.reference: Constitution of Kentucky, Section 228, oath of officers and attorneys, as in force 2026

cards.question: Should every law expire after a fixed period unless lawmakers vote to renew it?
cards.answer: Laws outlive their reasons: duelling oaths and medieval debt rules still stand because nobody is obliged to look. In 2013 Britain needed a single Act to repeal hundreds of dead statutes at once. An expiry date forces a review, a vote and a record of who wanted the rule kept.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, whether lawmakers have time to renew decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Expiry creates cliff edges: taxes, contracts and criminal offences lapse if a busy or deadlocked parliament misses a deadline. Renewals then become rubber stamps, as long-running security powers show. People and businesses plan on stable law, and obsolete statutes do little harm because courts and prosecutors simply leave them unused.
cards.reference: Statute Law (Repeals) Act 2013, c. 2, United Kingdom Parliament, 2013

cards.question: True or false: a Chester law still lets a person shoot a Welshman with a longbow inside the city walls after midnight?
cards.answer: False. The Law Commission's repeal team traced the story to a supposed 1403 city order imposing a curfew on Welsh people after Glyndŵr's rising, and could not confirm even that order existed. No law has ever permitted such a killing; it would be murder at any hour. The bow and the midnight are decoration.
cards.move: Each added detail should make a story harder to believe, not easier.
cards.trap: The precise weapon, place and hour make the rule sound documented.
cards.reference: Law Commission, Legal Curiosities: Fact or Fable?, Statute Law Repeals team, March 2013

cards.question: True or false: publishing a call to replace the British monarchy with a republic is still, on paper, punishable by life imprisonment?
cards.answer: True. Section 3 of the Treason Felony Act 1848 punishes publishing an intent to depose the monarch with up to life, and nobody had been prosecuted under it since 1883. In 2003 the House of Lords, asked by The Guardian's editor, called it a relic no peaceful republican need fear, and left the section standing.
cards.move: A promise not to enforce a law is not the same as repealing it.
cards.trap: Assuming Parliament must have repealed such an obviously dead offence.
cards.reference: https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld200203/ldjudgmt/jd030626/rus-1.htm

cards.question: Which legal system in Britain lets an old statute lapse through long disuse, with no formal repeal?
cards.answer: Scotland. Scots law, drawing on Roman civil law, holds that an old Act can fall into desuetude: long neglect plus a settled contrary practice ends its force. English law has none, which is why in 1818 an English court had to grant a defendant's demand for trial by combat; Parliament abolished it in 1819.
cards.move: Whether silence can kill a rule depends on whose rulebook it is.
cards.trap: Believing every law stands until formally repealed, as English law holds.
cards.reference: Brown v Magistrates of Edinburgh, 1931 SLT 456, Court of Session, 1931

cards.question: Under a statute from the 1320s, who owns a whale or sturgeon taken off the English coast?
cards.answer: The Crown. De Prerogativa Regis, a statute usually dated to about 1324, makes whales and sturgeon royal fish, and it has never been repealed. Strandings and catches are reported to the Receiver of Wreck, the official who handles wreck and royal claims. A carcass on the sand belongs, in law, to the King.
cards.move: Old rules survive when keeping them costs nobody anything.
cards.reference: Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book 1, ed. Lemmings, Oxford University Press, 2016

cards.question: Why does an 1873 US law against mailing obscene material matter to abortion pills today?
cards.answer: Because it still bans mailing any article designed or intended for producing abortion. The Comstock Act went unenforced on this for decades. In December 2022 the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel advised that mailing abortion drugs breaks it only when the sender intends unlawful use. Another administration could read the same words differently.
cards.move: A dormant law is a tool waiting for a new reader.
cards.source: US Office of Legal Counsel, December 2022
cards.reference: https://www.justice.gov/olc/opinion/application-comstock-act-mailing-prescription-drugs-can-be-used-abortions

cards.question: What sets the ceiling on how tall any tree can grow?
cards.answer: Water. A tree pulls water up through thin tubes against gravity and friction, and near the top of the tallest redwoods the leaves are water-starved, smaller and thicker. Measuring that stress up the trunk, Koch's team projected a maximum of about 122 to 130 m. The crown of a giant is always thirsty.
cards.move: Find what gets scarcer with every step, and the limit is there.
cards.reference: Koch, Sillett, Jennings & Davis, The limits to tree height, Nature, 2004

cards.question: What happens now to a hiker caught visiting Hyperion, the tallest known living tree?
cards.answer: They risk up to six months in jail and a $5,000 fine. In 2022 Redwood National Park closed the area around the tree, about 116 m tall, after visitors trampled its base and left rubbish and human waste. Its fame, from a location posted online, had become the threat.
cards.move: Publishing where a rare thing is can be the thing that harms it.
cards.source: National Park Service, Redwood National Park, 2022
cards.reference: National Park Service, Redwood National and State Parks, Hyperion area closure notice, July 2022

cards.question: About how much of the Burj Khalifa's 828 m is spire above its highest usable floor?
cards.answer: About 30%. A 2013 study by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat put the unusable top at 244 m, about 29% of the height. That stretch alone would be one of the taller skyscrapers in many European cities. The spire is there to win the height record.
cards.move: Ask how much of a headline figure does any work.
cards.trap: A spire looks like a slim tip, so a few per cent seems right.
cards.reference: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, Vanity Height: The Empty Space in Today's Tallest, 2013

cards.question: True or false: an antenna fixed on a skyscraper's roof counts towards its official height?
cards.answer: False. The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat counts spires, built as part of the design, but not antennas, flagpoles or signs. The line is a judgement: in 2013 it ruled One World Trade Center's 124 m mast a spire, which made the tower 541 m, a height chosen to echo 1776.
cards.move: When a ranking settles a contest, read the rule before the result.
cards.trap: Height seems to be simply the highest point anything reaches.
cards.reference: The New York Times, One World Trade Center height ruling, 12 November 2013

cards.question: Ignoring friction, what suction in megapascals must hold water up to the top of a 116 m redwood?
cards.answer: About 1.1 MPa, roughly 11 atmospheres of pull.
cards.move: Water can be pulled far harder than air pressure can ever push it.
cards.trap: Assuming suction tops out at one atmosphere, about 10 m of water.
cards.hint: Start from the weight of one metre of water column over one square metre.
steps: A water column's pressure is density × gravity × height.
1,000 kg/m³ × 9.8 m/s² = 9,800 Pa for each metre of height.
About 1.1 MPa, roughly 11 atmospheres of pull.
cards.reference: Tyree & Zimmermann, Xylem Structure and the Ascent of Sap, Springer, 2002

cards.question: True or false: before the Burj Khalifa, the tallest structure ever built was a radio mast in Poland?
cards.answer: True. The Warsaw radio mast, finished in 1974, stood about 646 m on steel guy wires. It fell in August 1991 during work on those wires, and nothing as tall stood again until the Burj Khalifa rose past it in the late 2000s. For some 17 years the record belonged to a ruin.
cards.move: The tallest of the past may be the one no longer standing.
cards.trap: Judging past records by the towers that are still standing today.
cards.source: TVP World, Warsaw radio mast collapse
cards.reference: https://tvpworld.com/79715989/remembering-the-collapse-of-the-warsaw-radio-mast-the-worlds-tallest-manmade-structure

cards.question: The 1958 Lituya Bay wave in Alaska is recorded at 524 m. What does that figure measure?
options: The wave's crest height in the bay
How high water surged up a hillside
How high the spray was thrown
cards.answer: How high water surged up a hillside. A rockslide plunged into the fjord, and the displaced water ran up the opposite slope, stripping trees to 524 m. That is run-up, not wave height; a scale model put the crest in the bay near 150 m. Still colossal, but under a third of the famous number.
cards.move: Ask exactly what a record height was measured from and to.
cards.trap: Reading the headline height as the size of the wave itself.
cards.reference: Fritz, Hager & Minor, Lituya Bay case: rockslide impact and wave run-up, Science of Tsunami Hazards, 2001

cards.question: What finally stopped the tallest living man from growing?
cards.answer: Targeted radiation to his pituitary gland. Sultan Kösen, about 251 cm tall, had a tumour there pouring out growth hormone. In 2010 surgeons at the University of Virginia treated it with focused beams of gamma rays, alongside drugs. By 2012 his growth had stopped.
cards.move: To halt a runaway process, find what keeps feeding it.
cards.reference: https://www.uvahealth.com/news/worlds-tallest-man-stops-growing

cards.question: China's 2005 survey put Everest at 8,844 m while Nepal used 8,848 m. What explained most of the gap?
cards.answer: China measured rock, not snow. Its 2005 survey used ice-penetrating radar to find the rock summit, about 3.5 m beneath the snow, and published that. In 2020 the two countries announced a joint figure of 8,848.86 m, taken to the top of the snow. The world's highest point wears a cap several metres thick.
cards.move: Before comparing two measurements, check they measured the same surface.
cards.trap: Knowing that heights depend on where sea level is taken to be.
cards.reference: https://kathmandupost.com/national/2020/12/08/it-s-official-mount-everest-is-8-848-86-metres-tall

cards.question: A giraffe's brain sits 2 m above its heart; mercury is 13 times as dense as blood. How many mmHg lift blood there?
cards.move: Height costs pressure, and the pump pays it before any work begins.
cards.trap: Treating 2 m as trivial next to a heart's ordinary push.
cards.hint: Ask how tall a column of mercury would press as hard as the blood.
steps: A 2 m column is 2,000 mm of blood.
Mercury is 13 times as dense, so the same pressure needs a column 13 times shorter.
cards.source: Mitchell et al., J. Exp. Biology, 2006
cards.reference: Mitchell et al., The origin of mean arterial and jugular venous blood pressures in giraffes, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2006

cards.question: Why can Vatican citizenship not be passed down through a family for generations?
cards.answer: Because it comes with a job, not a birth. It goes to cardinals resident in Rome, the Holy See's diplomats and certain staff, and lapses when the post ends. Children of citizens keep it only until 18. The state's citizens are replaced by appointment, one office at a time.
cards.move: Ask what a membership is attached to, and it tells you how it ends.
cards.reference: Law No. CXXXI on Citizenship, Residence and Access, Vatican City State, 2011

cards.question: What became of the fortune Nauru earned by mining away most of its own island?
cards.answer: Most of it was lost. Phosphate made Nauruans briefly among the richest people per head on Earth, and royalties went into a trust meant to outlast the mines. Poor investments drained it, from property abroad to a failed London musical about Leonardo da Vinci. The mined interior remains a field of bare coral pinnacles.
cards.move: A fund that outlives its source needs better judgment than the source did.
cards.source: McDaniel and Gowdy, Paradise for Sale, 2000
cards.reference: McDaniel and Gowdy, Paradise for Sale: A Parable of Nature, University of California Press, 2000

cards.question: True or false: Tuvalu's total land area grew between 1971 and 2014, while the sea around it rose?
cards.answer: True. Comparing aerial photographs and satellite images of all 101 islands, Kench and colleagues found net land area up 2.9%, about 73 hectares, although local sea level rose at about twice the global rate. Waves and storms keep piling up coral sand and gravel: some islets shrank, others grew and shifted.
cards.move: A rising threat can reshape a thing before it drowns it.
cards.trap: Picturing low islands simply going under as the water rises.

cards.question: Who chooses one of the two heads of state of Andorra?
cards.answer: French voters. Andorra's co-princes are the Bishop of Urgell, in Catalonia, and whoever is President of France, a role inherited from the Counts of Foix through the French kings. Andorrans elect their own parliament, but under the 1993 constitution the co-princes still sign its laws, and Andorrans choose neither of them.
cards.move: Check who actually picks an office before assuming whom it answers to.
cards.trap: Assuming a modern parliamentary democracy elects its own head of state.
cards.reference: Constitution of the Principality of Andorra, 1993

cards.question: Monaco covered about 2.02 km². Its new Mareterra district, built on the sea, adds about 6 hectares. By what percentage does that enlarge the country?
cards.answer: About 2.97%.
cards.move: For a tiny whole, even a small addition is a large share.
cards.hint: Put both areas in square kilometres before dividing.
steps: 6 hectares = 0.06 km², since 100 hectares make 1 km².
About 2.97%.
cards.reference: IMSEE (Monaco Statistics), Monaco en Chiffres, 2024

cards.question: What did Tuvalu write into its constitution in 2023 in case its islands disappear under the sea?
cards.answer: That the state lasts for ever. The amended constitution, in force from 1 October 2023, declares that Tuvalu shall remain in perpetuity despite any loss of territory, and keeps its maritime baselines unchanged whatever happens to the coast. Statehood has long rested on land; Tuvalu is betting its legal existence can outlast its ground.
cards.move: Where the facts may vanish, fix the rules before they do.
cards.source: Library of Congress, Global Legal Monitor, 2023
cards.reference: https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2023-09-28/tuvalu-constitutional-amendment-enshrines-statehood-in-perpetuity-in-response-to-climate-change/

cards.question: Tuvalu had about 10,600 residents in 2022. Australia's Falepili treaty offers 280 migration places a year. What % could move in 10 years?
cards.move: Multiply a small yearly rate by the years before calling it small.
cards.trap: Hearing 280 a year as a trickle rather than a quarter per decade.
cards.hint: Total the places first, then divide by the population.
steps: 280 places × 10 years = 2,800 places.
cards.reference: https://devpolicy.org/the-first-falepili-union-visa-ballot-a-preliminary-assessment-20250826/

cards.question: Should small states be allowed to sell citizenship to wealthy investors?
cards.answer: For a small island with few industries, citizenship is a rare export. St Kitts and Nevis has run such a scheme since 1984, and Dominica used investor money to rebuild after Hurricane Maria in 2017. Buyers get mobility and a refuge; the state gets roads and hospitals without new debt.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who carries the risk of a bad buyer.
cards.counterpoint: A passport is not a local product: it carries visa-free entry to other countries, which bear the risk. Weak checks have sold papers to people escaping investigations. In 2025 the EU Court of Justice ruled Malta's scheme contrary to EU law, holding that citizenship cannot be granted as a mere transaction. What is sold is partly other people's trust.
cards.source: Court of Justice of the EU, 2025
cards.reference: Court of Justice of the European Union, Commission v Malta, Case C-181/23, judgment of 29 April 2025

cards.question: Which statistical quirk does most to make Liechtenstein's economic output per resident look so high?
options: Over half its workers live abroad
The prince's fortune counts as output
Its banks' foreign assets count as output
cards.answer: Over half its workers live abroad. Liechtenstein has more jobs than its roughly 40,000 residents; more than half of employees commute in from Switzerland and Austria. Their work counts in output, but not in the population it is divided by. Every morning, output arrives by bus from people the statistic never counts.
cards.move: Before comparing per-head figures, check who the heads are.
cards.trap: Crediting the prince's wealth, the most famous fortune in the country.
cards.reference: https://finance.li/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/PDF-Economic-and-Financial-Data-Liechtenstein-2024.pdf

cards.question: True or false: Sealand, the wartime sea fort declared a principality in 1967, lies outside British territorial waters?
cards.answer: False. In 1968 an English court ruled the fort beyond its jurisdiction, because Britain then claimed only about 5.5 km of sea. The Territorial Sea Act 1987 extended the limit to about 22 km, and the fort, some 12 km off Suffolk, has been inside ever since. The famous ruling expired with the old map.
cards.move: A ruling rests on the law of its day; check what changed since.
cards.trap: Relying on the 1968 ruling that every account of Sealand repeats.
cards.reference: Territorial Sea Act 1987, Parliament of the United Kingdom, 1987

cards.question: How did the twin brothers who gave Twinsburg, Ohio, its name end their lives?
cards.answer: On the same day, of the same illness. Moses and Aaron Wilcox married two sisters, farmed as partners and held their property in common. They offered land for a town square if the settlement took the name Twinsburg. Both died in 1827, within hours of each other, and were buried in one grave.
cards.move: Ask how many ordinary pairs lived and died unremarked beside the famous one.
cards.source: Twins Days Festival, Community of Twinsburg
cards.reference: https://twinsdays.org/about/community-of-twinsburg/

cards.question: How did doctors in Brisbane realise a pair of twins was neither identical nor fraternal?
cards.answer: The scans contradicted each other. At six weeks the twins shared one placenta, the mark of identical twins; at 14 weeks they were a boy and a girl. One egg had been fertilised by two sperm before splitting, so they match fully on the mother's side, partly on the father's. One earlier pair was known.
cards.move: When two tests disagree, the contradiction is often the discovery.
cards.reference: https://www.abc.net.au/news/2019-02-28/semi-identical-twins-brisbane-world-first-in-utero-discovery/10857398

cards.question: True or false: twin births in Brazil's 'town of twins' surged after Josef Mengele's alleged visits in the 1960s?
cards.answer: False. Church baptism records for Cândido Godói from 1959 to 2008, 6,262 births in all, show no spurt in twins in 1964–1968, when the Nazi doctor was said to be at work. Twins were already common before then. The likelier cause is a founder effect: a town settled by a few related families.
cards.move: Before blaming a newcomer, check whether things were already so before he came.
cards.trap: Accepting the vivid Nazi story without looking at the earlier years.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0020328

cards.question: Two separated identical twins each married a Linda, then a Betty. What best explains matches like these in a twin study?
options: Chance across many pairs and questions
cards.answer: Chance across many pairs and questions. The Minnesota study compared about 137 reared-apart pairs on tests and questionnaires with hundreds of items each, so a few uncanny matches were bound to turn up. Its claims about genes rest on correlations measured across all the pairs, not on the one pair whose wives shared names.
cards.move: Count the chances a match had to happen before calling it uncanny.
cards.trap: Reading a spectacular match as a genetic signal, not a lottery win.
cards.reference: Segal, Born Together—Reared Apart: The Landmark Minnesota Twin Study, Harvard University Press, 2012

cards.question: About 12 in every 1,000 deliveries worldwide are twin deliveries. Roughly what share of babies born is a twin?
cards.answer: About 1 in 42. Each twin delivery produces two babies, so 1,000 deliveries give 988 single babies and 24 twins: 24 out of 1,012. The global rate has risen by a third since the 1980s, with fertility treatment and later motherhood, to about 1.6 million twin pairs a year.
cards.move: Check whether the count is of events or of the people in them.
cards.trap: Dividing 1,000 by 12 and forgetting each delivery brings two babies.
cards.source: Monden, Pison and Smits, Human Reproduction, 2021
