cards.reference: https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2021-03-12-twin-peaks-record-international-number-twin-births

cards.question: Can a DNA test tell apart identical twins, whose genomes are supposed to match letter for letter?
cards.answer: Sometimes. Sequencing 381 identical pairs, Jonsson and colleagues found they differ on average by 5.2 mutations that arose in the early embryo, and in about 15% of pairs one twin carries many that the other lacks. Sequenced deeply enough, a crime-scene sample need not point equally at both twins.
cards.move: Identical describes where two things started, not everything that happened since.

cards.question: Of 1,000 twin pairs, 340 are boy–girl. Fraternal pairs come out mixed-sex about half the time. How many pairs are identical?
cards.answer: Identical: 1,000 − 680 = 320 pairs.
cards.move: Use the cases you can identify to count the ones that look alike.
cards.trap: Counting all 660 same-sex pairs as identical, as if fraternal twins were always mixed.
cards.hint: Mixed-sex pairs can only be fraternal; ask how many fraternal pairs hide among the same-sex ones.
steps: Fraternal pairs split evenly between mixed-sex and same-sex.
So same-sex fraternal pairs also number about 340.
Fraternal total: 340 + 340 = 680 pairs.
Identical: 1,000 − 680 = 320 pairs.

diagram.label: twin pairs
diagram.caption: Of 660 same-sex pairs, 340 are fraternal, as many as the mixed pairs; only 320 are identical.

cards.reference: Fellman and Eriksson, Weinberg's differential rule reconsidered, Human Biology, 2006

cards.question: Across countries, twin birth rates differ more than twofold. Which kind of twinning accounts for nearly all of that difference?
cards.answer: Fraternal twins, from two eggs. Identical twinning, one embryo splitting, runs at about 4 per 1,000 births almost everywhere. Releasing two eggs at once varies with a mother's genes, age and fertility treatment, and is most common in Central Africa. The world map of twins is a map of double ovulation.
cards.move: When a total varies, find the part of it that stays constant.
cards.trap: Picking identical twins, the kind people assume runs in families.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0025239

cards.question: True or false: a fraternal twin can carry the other twin's blood cells for life?
cards.answer: True. Fraternal twins whose circulations join in the womb can swap blood stem cells, which settle in each other's marrow. With a sensitive test, van Dijk and colleagues found mixed blood groups in 8% of twin pairs and 21% of triplet sets. One sample from such a twin can show two blood groups.
cards.move: A boundary drawn at birth may have been crossed long before it.
cards.trap: Picturing each fraternal twin with its own sealed-off circulation from the start.
cards.reference: van Dijk, Boomsma and de Man, Blood group chimerism in human multiple births is not rare, American Journal of Medical Genetics, 1996

cards.question: Do twin studies overstate how much of a trait comes from genes?
cards.answer: Twin studies assume identical twins share their surroundings no more than fraternal twins do. They do not: identical twins are dressed alike and treated alike, and any extra likeness from that is booked as genetic. Studies using DNA from unrelated people often find far lower heritability, a shortfall known as missing heritability.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether similar treatment follows similar genes.
cards.counterpoint: The assumption has been tested and mostly survives. Twins whose parents were wrong about whether they were identical resemble each other according to their real genes, not the label. Adoption studies, which need no such assumption, also find substantial heritability. For height, DNA-based estimates from millions of people have closed most of the gap with twin figures.
cards.reference: Polderman et al., Meta-analysis of the heritability of human traits based on fifty years of twin studies, Nature Genetics, 2015

cards.question: Where along a wombat's gut do its droppings get their flat faces and corners?
cards.answer: Inside the intestine, well before the exit. Dissections showed the cubes form in the last 17% of the gut, where the wall has bands about twice as thick and four times as stiff as the tissue between them. Stiff bands squeeze faster and flatten faces; soft ones lag and leave edges.
cards.move: Uneven stiffness can shape a thing as surely as a mould.
cards.source: Yang, Hu et al., Georgia Tech, 2021
cards.reference: https://hu.gatech.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Hu21-wombat.pdf

cards.question: Camera traps watched 34 southern hairy-nosed wombat burrows on an island for six months. What was recorded using them most?
cards.answer: Black-footed rock-wallabies. On Wedge Island in 2015 they were logged using burrows 1,795 times, against 1,674 for the wombats that dug them. Bettongs, skinks, dragons and little penguins came too. A warren is a public building: the owner is only one of many tenants coming in from the heat.
cards.move: Ask who else uses a thing before crediting it to its builder.
cards.trap: People only see wombats at burrows, so wombats seem the main users.
cards.reference: https://www.publish.csiro.au/am/am15052

cards.question: Why did treating wild wombats for mange need a drug that stays in the body for weeks?
cards.answer: Because a wild wombat can rarely be dosed twice. Ivermectin and moxidectin are short-acting, so one dose often fails to kill every mite and weekly repeats are needed. Fluralaner, sold as a dog flea treatment, lingers for weeks; in a small trial one dose cleared mange in wild wombats within three to four weeks.
cards.move: Choose the remedy that works on the only chance you will get.

cards.question: True or false: the northern hairy-nosed wombat recovered from about 35 animals mainly through captive breeding?
cards.answer: False. Recovery happened in the wild, at Epping Forest in Queensland. The site became a national park, cattle competing for grass were removed, and a predator-proof fence went up against wild dogs in 2002. From about 35 animals in the early 1980s, numbers passed 400 by 2024.
cards.move: Before crediting the rescue, ask what stopped the losses in the first place.
cards.trap: Species rescues are pictured as zoo nurseries, so captivity seems likely.
cards.reference: https://www.stateoftheenvironment.detsi.qld.gov.au/biodiversity/case-studies/northern-hairy-nosed-wombat

cards.question: How much does the temperature swing in a day deep inside a wombat warren?
cards.answer: Less than 1 °C. On the surface above, the same day can swing by about 24 °C. Deep, interconnected tunnels in packed earth buffer both heat and cold, which is why many other animals shelter in them during fires and heatwaves. A hole in the ground works as a thermostat.
cards.move: Depth in soil buys stability that no wall above ground can match.
cards.reference: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/news/2020/01/the-truth-behind-heroic-wombats/

cards.question: True or false: the wombat's widely quoted top speed of 40 km/h comes from a timed field study?
cards.answer: False. It surfaced in a 1984 guide to Australian mammals, credited to a zoologist who later said he did not recall anyone timing a wombat with a stopwatch. Only decades later did a biologist report his car's speedometer touching 40 km/h beside fleeing southern hairy-nosed wombats: the number first, a rough check afterwards.
cards.move: A figure repeated in every book can still have no measurement underneath it.
cards.trap: Assuming a number printed everywhere must have been measured once.
cards.reference: https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2024-04-13/how-fast-can-a-womat-actually-run-faster-than-usain-bolt/103648118

cards.question: Where do wild wombats get most of their water, even in the dry season?
options: Water held in the plants they eat
Dew licked from grass at night
cards.answer: From the plants they eat. Measuring water turnover in all three species, Evans and colleagues found water already inside their food was the main source in wet and dry seasons alike. Wombats also ran lower field metabolic rates than any other Australian marsupial measured: a slow engine needs little cooling and little drink.
cards.move: Before asking how a system refills, ask how little it spends.
cards.trap: Picturing a large grazer that must walk to water every night.
cards.reference: Evans, Green & Newgrain, The field energetics and water fluxes of free-living wombats (Marsupialia: Vombatidae), Oecologia, 2003

cards.question: True or false: a wombat's teeth have no roots and keep growing throughout its life?
cards.answer: True. Wombats are the only living marsupials whose teeth are all rootless and ever-growing, a trait better known from rodents and rabbits. Tough, gritty grasses grind the crowns down, and steady growth replaces what wears away. When upper and lower teeth stop meeting squarely, nothing grinds them and they overgrow.
cards.move: Whatever wears away every day has to be rebuilt every day.
cards.trap: Linking ever-growing teeth only with rodents, the familiar example.
cards.reference: Triggs, Wombats, Australian Natural History Series, CSIRO Publishing, 2009

cards.question: What was the largest marsupial that ever lived, and how is it related to wombats?
cards.answer: Diprotodon, a member of the vombatiforms, the group that holds wombats and koalas. It weighed up to about 2,700 kg, the size of a rhinoceros, and roamed Australia until roughly 40,000 years ago. The burrowing wombat is the small survivor of a lineage that once included the heaviest marsupials known.
cards.move: A small survivor may be the last branch of a family of giants.
cards.source: Wroe et al., Proc. Royal Society B, 2004
cards.reference: Wroe, Crowther, Dortch & Chong, The size of the largest marsupial and why it matters, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2004

cards.question: Why were some of the rarest wombats moved to a second refuge in southern Queensland from 2009?
cards.answer: So that one disaster could not end the species. Every northern hairy-nosed wombat lived at Epping Forest, where a single fire, flood or outbreak could wipe them out. From July 2009, 15 were moved in several transfers to Richard Underwood Nature Refuge near St George; the first joey there was confirmed in 2011.
cards.move: Keep a second copy of anything a single accident could destroy.
cards.reference: https://www.australianwildlife.org/sanctuaries/richard-underwood-nature-refuge
